_childDocuments_.review: Resolutiion, no the name’s not a typo, it’s clever wordplay, I think!Resolutiion is an action-adventure videogame with enough neon pinks and 90s synth music to satisfy any indie gamer. The 16-bit style graphics and color saturation remind me of Hyper Light Drifter, but you'll hear that a lot. Monolith of Minds has borrowed some aesthetics from their competitors but there's enough here to make it unique.Unfortunately, the story is a bit cliche. A robot named Valor has lost its memory and has to retrace its steps with the help of a sympathetic AI named Alibii who is trying to patch into the Cradle Network. Yes, plenty of techno-babble to keep any sci-fi fan happy. The only hint you get to Valor’s past is a cut scene at the beginning of the game where Valor is transformed into, well Valor! The story doesn’t give much away. Snippets of narrative are delivered to you by Alibii and various NPCs which are sprinkled throughout the game.Resolutiion: Look & FeelYou wander past monolithic skyscrapers, lofty walkways, and pixel-scapes of neon pinks and blues as you descend from Cloud City where the color scheme is slightly more orangey-beige. In the desert of Giants, there’s a burrowing sand cat a la Dune that chases you but there's no way to kill it. Like many things in Resolutiion, it's just there as a perfunctory obstruction to pad out the game. There's plenty of chaotic combat in the form of a simple slice-and-dice combo but that's it. No melee attack upgrades, just simple mechanics.The combat and environmental puzzles open new areas, but the one-button combo does become boring very quickly. If you're looking for a game with more combat options then you will find Resolutiion severely lacking. This wouldn't be such a problem if the game relied on dialogue choices like an RPG to guide you, but Resolutiion's mechanics are more combat-centric.As you ooo and ahhh at the profound, yet strangely cliche world, your audio senses are tickled with a Daft Punk-esque score. The techno sync punctuates the gameplay like a good conductor guiding an orchestra. It enhances the game in ways that the gameplay, sadly doesn't. However, in other areas, the music is profoundly melodic and haunting.Once you reach the Light/Dark Forest you can speak to the animals like Doctor Dolittle, but yet again they yield very little info so go ahead and slash them into bits with your claw-like hands. The music is particularly haunting with a melody that reminded me of the piano concerto in World War Z. I found it quite depressing after a while. There are some strange, if not damn right bizarre things in the forest like an abandoned Mad Hatters tea party table, a desperate head-thumping bear, and a huge beating heart. None, of them seem to have any consequence or purpose.You can pick up weapon upgrades such as the Stardust bomb, the Chromatic aberration that changes the way you see things, and the Martyr's Boot which turns you into yellow goop. There's a lot to like here, and the upgrades are quite original in concept. If you find a flashing NPC you might get a helpful hint, but you have to search for them at the beginning.Resolutiion: Mechanics and gameplaySave points are quite frequent which is handy for whenever you're obliterated into tiny cyborg bits. You just respawn with a full health bar and carry on. enemies don't respawn in the same session which makes it easy to focus on those more challenging boss battles. Speaking of boss battles, there are a few difficulty spikes that push you to your limit. So be prepared!Each biome makes excellent use of color and shade and it is one of the best things about Resolutiion. It's nice to look at, and it sustains you while you wrestle with the confusing map which looks like a badly wired circuit board. It offers no use except to give you a vague direction of where you're going.You will spend the majority of your gameplay retracing your environment. The more you progress, the more defined are your objectives and goals, but the environments are designed to be confusing, to mix the foreground with the background so you miss those exits, or overlook an important piece of info. Standard game design stuff that prolongs the gameplay.Levels are designed like a Metroidvania game. Some obstacles prevent you from progressing to the next area and unlocking upgrades, however, the upgrades sadly don't change your combo attack. As the game progresses more NPCs vomit exposition. These are normally profound and deliberately obtuse like a Yogi who's just fasted for two weeks and has reached total enlightenment.When you find the AI Shinto shrine things get trippy! You can use the Chromatic aberration upgrade to extend walkways and access other areas. Be careful of the Conspirator who says he can make you invisible for the dead cheap price of 33iec. What are iecs? Don't know! He then sends you down a pitch-black well only to find the words "Voila" graffitied on the walls.As the game progresses you're tasked with more mini quests, like using the stardust bomb to access the phantom pit and activating the pumps in the mechanical mine. Here you combat monks whiplashing you with the rubber-like goop from the mines, and why not? Spiritual enlightenment doesn't mean you can't thwack someone and knock their teeth out!Resolutiion: Graphics and soundMany of the bosses feel like they've escaped from a Mario game or some kind of Cuphead spin-off. The style is very eclectic and doesn't always feel like it fits with the overall tone of the game. One boss looks like a giant yellow wiener with legs. But the overall tone is philosophical and thought-provoking with strong anti-imperialistic undertones.Resolutiion suffers from too much form and not enough substance. In the early stages, it takes a little too long to get going and feels like it meanders. It also suffers from a lack of identity with too many different concepts and styles thrown into the gameplay.The Sprites are minimalistic which seems to be the vogue style at the moment. But the aesthetic clarity and artistic direction are bright and colorful with neon colors to promote a 70s retro style. However, the visual style is a little too similar to HyperLight Drifter.

_childDocuments_.review: I liked a lot of things about this game…For example, music is really good. I could listen to it outside the game and still enjoy it quite a lot. Pixel graphics are suitable for this game too. Visual style is very good. And by that I mean that I like it. You may like it too. Or you may not.Of course there are things I didn’t like and you could find them unpleasant or even annoying. For example the game world is quite good and beautiful in its own way but it may be somewhat confusing to navigate. I often found myself not knowing where to go because there would be too many paths. Surely I would like to explore but I also don’t want to go down the wrong path and have to start all the way at the start to try and find the place I wanted to explore but couldn’t because I couldn’t go back. And then I would forget about it, which is a shame.But you definitely should go back and explore when you get new abilities because you want those upgrades. You see, there aren’t a lot of enemies in the game but they can be really annoying and kill you before you figure out how to kill them. You will start at the checkpoint with progress save but you would still be annoyed. The enemies don’t respawn until you reload the game and that is a very good decision made by the developers.You get almost all the abilities by just playing the game but you will also get a few useful ones that will make navigation and fighting easier.Remember those upgrades I talked about earlier. Go out there and find them when you unlock the necessary abilities. Because there are bosses that will suck out the fun out of the game. You will later realize that they are not as hard when you figure out how to kill them. But it made me furious about it and I wanted to give this game a negative review. Take all your stamina at a whim and that makes them even less fun.Eventually you will kill them and get your dopamine dose and think that the game is not that bad. Or you may not and you will give up and give it a negative review. Which seems to be the case if you look at the review score for this game.A word of advice for Steam Deck users: some bosses are a lot easier on a big screen. I killed one of the bosses almost right away once I plugged in the monitor.And a word of advice to the developers: make the game scale with the pixel density of the screen.In conclusion: despite its flaws I enjoyed the game.

Nice graphics never been a friend of terror carricatures which is the main thing inside the game.

_childDocuments_.review: Could be such a fun game and for a niche audience probably is.The good: - pixel art is great overall, some varying quality, sometimes paths/enemies hard to see- music superb with adaptive elements when fighting or low on health- music and graphics create a good atmosphere- combat is simple but good enemy variety, some enemies seem a bit weak and some overpowered thoughThe bad:- punching boxes gets old quickly- inconsistent difficulty, enemies like to start attacks from off screen- upgrades too hard too find which makes later bosses too tough- worst metroidvania sin: behind item gates obstacles there's often another obstacle the player cannot overcome yet, backtracking results in time waste- no markers on map! have fun taking notes- no teleport from the start, according to patch notes made obtainable earlier but still too lateThere seems to be a lack of polish to make the game more accessible. Contrary to other reviews I had no big trouble finding the main quest path but stopped at a trio of bosses I couldn't defeat without upgrades. According to patch notes these were made more difficult as well...Maybe the game tries to compensate its small scale with crypticness. Some may surely like it but to repeat the initial statement: if you have this niche taste you might enjoy.

_childDocuments_.review: Picked this game up on the day that it came out, and have been loving it so far. Only problem I've run into an area in the game where it crashes every time I try to enter it, which I think is a bug. For people looking to buy the game on Windows, don't let the idea of a game bug scare you off as I'm pretty sure this issue is exclusive to Linux, the OS that I'm running it on. I'm pretty sure I can still complete the game while avoiding the one area which induces the crash, as I've had no problems running through any of the other rooms in the game so far. if the dev sees this, I can give more details on where exactly the crash occurs and my system specs for them to hopefully fix the issue.For anyone else looking to purchase the game, it truly is a great coeval to Hyper Light Drifter, so if you're looking for an atmospheric exploration pixel fighting game, Resolutiion really is the tits.

name: Dwarf Fortress
detailed_description: Prepare for the deepest, most intricate simulation of a world that has ever been created. Not just generated geometry -- a whole simulated world. Generated rise and fall of civilizations, personalities, creatures, cultures, etc. Infinite hours of gameplay. Now with beautiful pixel graphics! Learn the basics with in-game tutorials A lifetime “living” project - created/updated since 2003, with no end in sight Generate your unique world and manage a bustling colony of dwarves, even as they probably mine towards their eventual demise. A new endless hobby, just for you! The legendary Dwarf Fortress is now on Steam! Build a fortress and try to help your dwarves survive, despite threats of starvation, dragons, and madness. In this complex construction/management/roguelike simulation, every generated world brings a unique challenge, whether it’s dwarves with their own simulated personalities or aquifers. Observe what makes your civilization fall into eventual decline, and learn for next time… until something else inevitably goes wrong. The combat model includes skills, body parts, material properties, aimed attacks, wrestling, pain, nausea, various poison effects, and much more. It’s difficult to convey the depth of the generation. Hundreds of animals and monsters, many of which are randomly created for each world, as well as generated poetry, musical forms, instruments, and dances for your dwarves to practice and perform. A dynamic weather model tracks wind, humidity, and air masses to create fronts, clouds, storms, and blizzards. Over two hundred rock and mineral types can appear, in their proper geological environments. Remember: Losing is fun! Nothing substantial is new or changed, under the hood. It’s still good old Dwarf Fortress, but with graphics support and music by default. A few bells and whistles won’t change that. You may already be familiar with the tile set mod packs from Michał “Mayday” Madej and Jacob 'Ironhand' Bowman. Together, their efforts are creating an all-new tileset featuring brand new pixel art by artists Carolyn Jong and Neoriceisgood. Dwarf Fortress Steam edition will have a 15 track soundtrack by Dabu, Simon Swerwer and Águeda Macias including tracks in the Dwarvish language! It's never been easier to start playing! We've improved the new player experience with the addition of tutorials to guide you through building your first fort and keeping your dwarves happy. Command your dwarves as they search for wealth in their generated mountain. Your dwarves will need a steady supply of food and beer, but they’ll also need your guidance in surviving attacks from hostile civilizations, the wilderness, or even the dead. Craft treasures and furnitures from various materials Establish a barony and support the increasingly demanding nobility Read your dwarves’ thoughts to keep them happy Build floodgates to divert water for farming, and/or prevent magma mishaps Build structures and watch your dwarves discover and build their culture, like taverns, libraries, temples, honey, wax, pottery, animal training, bookbinding, and more. The original inspiration for RimWorld, Prison Architect, Minecraft and more. One of the first video games acquired by the Museum of Modern Art in New York Updated for over 16 years by two brothers, Tarn “Toady One” and Zach “Threetoe” Adams With the goal of simulating all of existence, Bay 12 estimates they’re only about 44% done.

_childDocuments_.review: (Long time DF player here, the premium version that is available here on Steam is a great upgrade to the original and makes it much more accessible. Even if you're content with the ASCII graphics I still would consider purchasing this edition as a show of gratitude to the amazing development process that has made this game thrive)I love all kinds of games. If you take a peek at my profile you'll see a whole lot of racing titles for example. But there's no greater game in the history of mankind than Dwarf Fortress. It simply is one of the greatest achievements we'll ever witness in the gaming industry, for no matter how far graphical fidelity will stretch beyond our imaginations, the pixelated dwarves will forever stay victorious. It is an experience you will never ever forget, and once you've opened pandora's box, your view of the world will never ever be the same again. Don't hesitate. Buy it. This is one of the few games I'd consider a no brainer almost no matter the price. It really is that good.

_childDocuments_.review: Dwarf Fortress is a complex game with unparalleled depth. As one of the earliest games in the survival management genre, it offers a unique and engaging experience. The ASCII graphics can be intimidating, but mods can help alleviate this issue.However, the game's biggest flaw is the building and task menu. While the depth is impressive, the lack of filters and fine controls can be frustrating. This can make it difficult to keep track of your dwarves' needs and assign tasks efficiently. Overall, Dwarf Fortress is a game that rewards perseverance and patience, but it is not for everyone.

_childDocuments_.review: "The King said I was daft to build a Fortress in the Swamp, but I built it all the same just to show em.  The dwarves starved and It sank into the swamp, so I built a second one.  That one was overrun by Goblins and then sank into the swamp.  So I built a third one, the dwarves dug too deep and let loose the scourges of hell and that one burned down tipped over and sank into the swamp, but the fourth one stayed standing and that is what you are going to get lad." *Most games are a refinement on established norms of the industry,  Only a few games actually expand the bounds of what gaming can be and inspire a new generation of game developers to go into entire new direction.  Dwarf Fortress is one of those boundary expanding games, one the most influential games of the last 20 years, and its legacy will be felt for decades to come.*

_childDocuments_.review: This is without a doubt the most detailed colony / kingdom management game you will ever play, probably in your whole life (unless my review and steam is somehow accessible after 100 years or something, which if that's the case please ignore the above statement). However, with great details come great complications, and boy you better prepare for some insane complications.A lot of reviews stated that the game was incredibly complex and difficult because of the archaic interface, and is much easier now. That statement is true, but that doesn't mean it is easy now. It's still significantly more complex. Expect 10x the headaches you get from learning Rimworld, because the detail and complexity in Rimworld is nothing compared to this. And if you ever think Rimworld is hard to understand, please just ignore this game entirely. This is the game that will require you to spend hours just to properly play and have a prosperous colony.The game doesn't care at all about you and your colony. Unlike Rimworld that would actually generate raids or depending on the storyteller will make things easier or harder based on your progress, in Dwarf Fortress you are quite literally just a single colony in a living world. Think of it this way: In Rimworld sometimes you will see notification like "a machine somewhere activated and start spewing smoke". In Dwarf Fortress, that means there are actual simulated NPCs going somewhere and activate said machine. The simulation that runs behind the game is so insanely detailed, that each time you start a new world the game will generate civilizations, complete with their own cultural artifacts. They simulate other dwarven colonies mining, prospering, being attacked, raiding, or digging too deep. The world runs alongside you, and your allied village next door just might get obliterated the next time you open the world map, or even conquered by evil goblins.

_childDocuments_.review: if you thought a simplified interface would solve your Dwarf Fortress problems you are sadly mistaken!!! _childDocuments_.review: Dwarf Fortress is a world simulator that creates a long and in depth history and many unique civilizations and people that the player can interact with. The game is a top down city builder and resource management type of deal, where the player controls a fortress of dwarves and tries to meet their needs and develop their settlement. This is the first game that I have been excited for in the last decade. Despite being a re-release of the ASCII Dwarf Fortress, Tarn has managed to release a product that:- is a fun and accessible game that anyone could pick up and enjoy- works from launch as intended and was not delayed-  has no paid DLC or microtransactionsIf every developer was like the Adams brothers and Kitfox, and every game was like Dwarf Fortress, the world would be a be a better place. Thank you for making my year and releasing the only game I picked up at launch without a second thought and with no regrets.

_childDocuments_.review: Dwarf Fortress is the OG. It's Rimworld's enormous, gangly, monstrous, genius brother that was always referred to, but never seen. More of a myth than a game. Pick a game system you love from Rimworld or a 'rimworld-like'. Dwarf Fortress made it. And they did it better.It is a roguelike in the truest sense of the word. It is NOT a rogue-light. You will die. Civilizational collapse is par for the course - be it tapping away the wrong rock, releasing a biblical flood into your subterraneon home and drowning everything, or breaking through into a Balrog nest and losing your colony Durin-style.Similar to the Dark Souls games - You'll find the game gets easier and makes more sense every few days of playing. There's so much to learn that you will realize the RNG isn't nearly as deadly as your own ignorance. You will want another monitor up with the wiki on it.I've had this game for far longer than a decade, free, and even donated once, but here I am dropping 30 bucks to write a review. More than anything I just want to say publically - Thank you tarn and Zach.
_childDocuments_.name: Dwarf Fortress

_childDocuments_.review: I have been playing this game since the first release nearly 20 years ago, I'm so glad this is finally on Steam since it's more accessible for newer folks. If you can think/dream it you can likely do it in this game. You wanna make a giant pyramid, you can do it. You want to make a medievil torture room you can. The game will take a bit to learn if you're new but the tutorial helps you at least start and understand the basics. You can play with just the knowledge learned in it if you really want to. Or you can use that and build on top of such knowledge. You're going to lose forts, but don't worry losing is fun! You can resettle in your forts with a new group if you really like the site and don't want to find a new one (there are likely to be some new spider inhabitants though so careful). I don't say these things just to hype the game or to repeat known memes within the community. Losing is fun is the point of the game, think of roguelites which are part of what inspired this complex game to exist. You can learn from your failures and start a new save using this new knowledge to have a fort go for longer, or you can willingly destroy it to see how long they last or whatever other reason you choose. The systems are well fleshed out and not half baked vs other games, memories and such work like a proper memory unlike say Skyrim or whatever other game you can think of. It's fun to even jsut mess around and try things to learn different systems. Deepnding on you're likely going to have someone die or get a bit frustrated but that's part of the whole, losing is fun statement for this game. If you like Rimworld and haven't played this yet, do it. Rimworld was inspired by this game for a reason, and if you especially want more to do with the group well this doesn't need mods for such it just already has more.

_childDocuments_.review: Dwarf Fortress is an important game in gaming history, influencing the likes of Minecraft and Rimworld. The sick will lie in the hospital with their intestines hanging out waiting for surgery, but the doctor is wasted in the tavern for a week straight. _childDocuments_.review: I started playing Dwarf Fortress in 2006, eighteen years before this Steam release.  Some things to bear in mind:The game has changed a lot, and will continue to evolve over the next 20 years.  It does not look or play like it did in 2006 or even like it did in 2014.  In a few years, it wont be like it is now.  It is constantly growing and changing.  It isn't flagged as EA here on Steam but it is a "continuous development" game.This is a huge living world "fantasy novel simulator" that is amazingly deep, and happens to have a couple of games on the surface that you can play.  You can mine the deeper world details and discover these stories through Legends Mode and uncover the famous stories like that of Cacame Awemedinade.  While you play Fortress or Adventure mode, pieces of these stories surface in your game.Dwarf Fortress is the direct inspiration for hundreds of games including Minecraft and Rimworld, and indirectly help to drive the explosion of "roguelike" games and rich use of procedural generation that we have seen over the past decade.  There are reasons that it is so influential, and you can sample that by diving in.As of this review (on release day) the new UI is still very fresh and raw.  The developers are not professional UI designers, and lots of things still need to be ironed out and cleaned up.  The original ASCII support will be coming in a patch, as well as Adventure mode and a host of other long-time features that need to be re-enabled to work with the updated UX.  I probably won't update this so, if you are reading this review some weeks or months or years after release, expect that to be different.But, whatever changes, this game is not for the faint of heart!

_childDocuments_.review: Dwarf Fortress is a game that demands a lot from its players. It's a complex and challenging game that offers an incredibly deep and rewarding experience. If you're willing to put in the effort to learn its intricate systems, you'll find an experience unlike anything else.Gameplay-wise, Dwarf Fortress is all about managing a colony of dwarves in a harsh and unforgiving world. You'll need to keep your dwarves fed, happy, and safe from various threats, including hostile creatures and other civilizations. The game's systems are incredibly detailed, and there are a huge number of different things to manage, from individual dwarves' needs and personalities to resource production and trade with other civilizations.Graphically, Dwarf Fortress is not the most impressive game out there. While this may be off-putting to some, it does allow the game to be incredibly detailed and complex, and the lack of fancy graphics can be part of the game's charm.One downside of Dwarf Fortress is its notoriously steep learning curve. The game can be incredibly daunting for new players, and it can take many hours to get a handle on all of the game's systems. However, if you're willing to put in the time and effort to learn the game, it can be an incredibly rewarding experience.Overall, Dwarf Fortress is an incredibly deep and rewarding game that offers a unique experience that is unmatched by any other game out there. It's not for everyone, but if you're willing to put in the effort to learn its systems, you'll find a game that offers endless hours of challenge and entertainment.Gameplay: ★★★★★★★★★★ 10/10Market: ★★★★★★★★★☆ 9/10Social: ★★★★★★★★★☆ 9/10Narrative: ★★★★★★★★☆☆ 8/10Graphics: ★★★★★☆☆☆☆☆ 5/10Technical: ★★★★★★★★☆☆ 8/10Value: ★★★★★★★★★☆ 9/10Audio: ★★★★★☆☆☆☆☆ 5/10

_childDocuments_.review: I can see why Dwarf Fortress is not for everyone. You have to be patient, willing and through trial and error force yourself to read beyond what is shown to you from the game. Honestly I feel that this is its weakest point and what will lose the majority of players. While the steam version certainly starts to bridge the gap on bringing more players into the DF world it is still a bridge pitted with holes. Hopefully something future patches and/or mods will start to fill.As for myself, I initially found it an incredibly difficult game to get into. The tutorial barely scratched the surface and you are left to learn the majority of the game yourself by researching the answers online. I dropped the game so many times before I discovered the gem hidden beneath.So many hours I would put in and feel I hadn’t accomplished or understood a thing. It was both a long learning process and honestly a tough hurdle you simply have to be willing to climb.I often questioned what the objective or purpose was but I would time and time again dive into the game and simply learn the mechanics, controls, GUI etc. But something kept bringing me back, my stubbornness perhaps to understand?Thankfully, after a year of on and off playing, I can say it was well worth the steep learning curve. I have learnt to absolutely adore this game. Rimworld was the only game I could compare and had just as many hours in and yet it differs so much.While there are many similarities it’s the comparisons that will have you finding ‘flaws’ if you can call them that. It cannot be compared as this game is nothing like anything I’ve played. The surface level looks like a colony sim but the world that is built is absolutely dripping in history. So much so that it feels lived in, it’s your world and yet you have very little control on how it is shaped. Politics, economy, war. It all plays a huge part in how the land came to be and what it will be. As your colony grows, you become a part of its history and what happens next, well, you’ll just have to play and see. The term losing is fun plays a big part here as it shapes the whole dynamic of what comes next. This is your story even if it doesn’t always go your way.I find Dwarf Fortress a true piece of gaming history, while it may not be for everyone it will shape how we play games in the future and how we can role play and find enjoyment in the most bizarre situations.

_childDocuments_.review: I spent a lot of time playing the original ASCII graphics version since it was free and I was a kid with no money. This new version instantly takes me back to the same enjoyment I've gotten from this game over the years, and the new improvements make it that much easier to pick back up. The expanded soundtrack is great, and the graphics are much easier to read than the text based visuals (and they are also much better than any previously possible graphics mod for the previous versions of the game). If you are new to the game there is an excellent tutorial now included, as well as an in game explanation of important concepts/mechanics/strategies. _childDocuments_.name: Dwarf Fortress

_childDocuments_.review: Maybe an hour ago as of writing this, a little baby dwarf was just born in a new fortress. I've never felt such genuine joy at the birth of a cluster of pixels. When the first child, a baby girl named Odol Udosdatan, was born to my fledgeling band of dwarves, I felt a brief moment of genuine happiness. Not for myself, but for her adoring mother as I read her thoughts on the matter. There's a real magic to Dwarf Fortress, and I'm not even ankle-deep in the game. The many wacky, zany, and even heartfelt stories you'll come across are unique to you. Every book, item, poem, character, monster, civilization, landmass, and historical event was generated by the game for you and you alone. I can't recommend Dwarf Fortress enough to anyone looking for a deep, complex, addictive game which is endlessly replayable, completely unpredictable, and occasionally less-than-serious in temperament. Don't be afraid to fail, because that's just part of the fun.Oh, and one more thing. Tell your stories. Post tales of your misadventures to forums, make videos, or even just tell your friends. No one else knows your dwarves like you do. Don't let those magnificent alcohol-fueled stubby bastards be fotgotten. These guys and gals are dynamic, complex, and unique. Once a dwarf is lost, there will never be another like him or her. So take care of them, rage at them, cheer them on in their triumphs, laugh at their antics, raise a mug to them when they fall, and cherish them while you have them, will ya?

_childDocuments_.review: It's a fun game but overhyped, and I do not recommend paying for it while it's in this state, especially since there is an analogous free version. Play that instead if you haven't already bought it. The development priorities are misplaced to say the least; there are countless game-breaking bugs that have been widely known and documented, yet remain unfixed for years or even for over a decade. Some of the bugs are coming close to 15 years in age. These bugs will evidently never be fixed. And unfortunately they are not rare by any means, many of these are bugs that most (or even all) players will run into at some point. Some of the bugs and broken features will cause problems in every single fortress, to the point that the community has to find convoluted hacks to work around them and make the game playable in the way it was intended. These workarounds then become embedded in the core of the gameplay, a necessary yet deeply unintuitive part of being able to experience Dwarf Fortress. The importance of knowing these workarounds and quirks are part of the reason why the learning curve is so steep compared to other games, and why newbie forts tend to be fleeting. They are also the source of most of the tedious micromanagement that is inevitably required in any fort which lasts more than a year or two in-game.Hunting bugs and reworking decades old mechanics is probably boring and frustrating compared to giving the game graphics or a proper UI, but playing a broken game is frustrating too, and the players are the ones in the exchange who are paying for this experience. Not to mention that it's difficult to experience new features in the first place when gameplay necessitates navigating a labyrinth of tech debt, or spending hours editing raw game files to make something work. That's why my suggestion for prospective buyers is to stick with the free version until that changes, because this level of brokenness and lack of attention to quality and the end-user experience isn't good enough for your money. The premium version has been out for almost two years now, it has sold at least 800,000 copies (at this point I'm guessing that number is even higher), and yet the dedication towards addressing bugs hasn't changed. Using a fraction of that money to hire even one programmer would go a long way, and the obstinate refusal to do so now that people are being charged and so many resources are available is unacceptable from a customer's perspective. You can guarantee your money won't be spent on development as you would expect from other indie games.Last point: I have always disliked this attempt at gaslighting where players are told that "losing is fun." Fun is subjective and its meaning will be different in the eyes of each player. I understand the sentiment, that crazy and wacky events happening which end a fortress in flames can be entertaining to behold, but this phrase is too often used to excuse and dismiss criticism about bugs, or broken and notably unfun mechanics. The worse of which will prematurely end players' games, whether outright by corrupting their save file, or by certain mechanics becoming glitched and rendering whole features of the game as permanently unavailable until you start over from the beginning. You can't pass off broken and clunky mechanics as intended features and expect people to like them. And when you tell people what things they should and shouldn't find fun you are insulting the intelligence of your community.

_childDocuments_.review: I have a few hundred hours previous to the steam version, the game is lacking adventure mode for now which is my only complaint despite that, this game is a real 10/10 even without adventure mode. Everything that can be proc genned is for example dwarfs have physical differences, memories, moods, likes and dislikes. It's the original colony sim, with legends mode and logs you can see everything involving all of the 1-10000 years of history. It's worth the price of purchase on steam for the fact that the controls are streamlined alone, I was very much against the fact that they changed everything and introduced mouse controls, but that was silly, it's become perfection enabling more players to find it accessible as well as making it easier on veterans.  Worlds:Every world has it's own procedurally generated history, and landscape. Viewable with a legends mode before you embark on your adventure. You can choose where to place your fort, making it upto you how hard or easy you want the game to be, despite this you will eventually lose.Dwarfs:Dwarfs have their own feelings, memories, history, likes and dislikes, physical traits, and ailments. You can direct dwarfs but you don't have control over them directly. For example, the amount of fingers and toes each dwarf has is taken note of and tracked in this game. Fortress mode:The current release only has fortress mode, you chose where to embark after you create a world with it's very own original landscape and history, you take 7 dwarfs who are all randomly generated with their own things going on, as described above, and you point them in a direction on what to do, but you don't directly control them in the end. As you build up your fort you'll meet other races, monster slayers, traders, etc, bringing their own personalities and traits to you. You will get migrants (I recommend capping total migrants at 180, cause after 200 even the best cpu to date will chug) that will arrive adding to the number of dwarfs and people in your fort(monster slayers can reside if you have an inn and tavern; and will not necessarily but can be dwarfs). You will lose, that is part of the fun, you get to start a new world with a new history and new dwarfs on the next run. The updated from original game:Tileset, very nice, with workshop you can customize as you please. Ease of access, the game is extremely easy to get into now in my opinion, with the ease of controls and mouse support you'll be at home after reading the wiki some.The game feels like it runs better than it did back in the day. What to look forward to:Adventure mode: You can make a new world or enter the one you built and retired your fort in, and run around the world doing quests, making trouble, whatever you so choose, as virtually whatever you choose. For example: Back in the day I played a Spider-man grappler, well as a spider man you walk with two legs, and have six free ones, and i proceeded to grab some civilian in a human village by the jaw and rip out their teeth one by one and throw them at passerbys. You can even visit your fort!This game even without adventure mode as it is, is the only game I think I could play for the rest of my life. It's a 10/10 even without adventure mode, with adventure mode(coming out in 2024), it can even surpass it. It's absolutely worth the full price cost, it never tires. Don't forget, STRIKE THE EARTH! and that losing is fun!

_childDocuments_.review: As a caves of qud player of over 2,000 hours, yet someone who didn't find rimworld as enticing, I think I'll enjoy Adventure mode more than most when it comes to this version of the game. The game's been in development for over two decades, and I think $30 is a fine price for all who already enjoy open-world, replay value, and continued development games as I've learned for a while now that the AAA gaming market has undergone a huge shift towards visual-heavy games that they can then put an arbitrarily high price tags on which are not proportional to the quality of the actual content within them. _childDocuments_.review: This is mostly UI improvements to a dated game, but it fell out of the actually-improve-the-interface tree and missed every low hanging fruit branch on the way down.  Badly executed all over.  Want to build the best bed in your stockpile?  ♥♥♥♥ you, the build menu is grouped by type of wood not quality, and you have to expand every category individually.  Farms don't even show a visual difference between "things are growing" and "it's empty", that's how lazy this is.I could recommend DF for nostalgia purposes, but this update whiffed every chance it had to make the game more accessible.  It's a tossup whether these controls or the originals are better, but I'd lean towards the original - there's a lot of micro in this game, and when you learn the keyboard shortcuts, you can go real fast.  But on some of the menus where you used to just hit 'enter' to pick the first option, you're now forced to click, and it just feels slow and grating.The new music is good, but the new random sound effects are obnoxious.  You will learn to hate that hawk within the first hour or two.Honestly, it's hard to disrecommend Dwarf Fortress since I had such great adoration for (and was a donator to) the ASCII original.  But DF gives a striking look at just how much Rimworld and other modern genre games revolutionized the genre's core design fundamentals.  Dwarf Fortress was a pioneer, and it revealed a lot of annoying busywork in its gameplay that its successors removed.  The Steam version has stayed true to its original design and now it's dated as hell.The crashes don't help, when the game takes forever to autosave and doesn't do it very often.  If you pick this up, give it some time for the crashes to get fixed or you're going to lose a lot of progress and be very unhappy.

_childDocuments_.review: Is this my most anticipated game release ever?  Maybe!  But let's face it: Rimworld kinda already stole DF's thunder.  But will Rimworld remain in development until its devs are dead?  Unlikely.  Dwarf Fortress is for life.  I haven't played a game of DF since I bought into the RW early access direct from Ludeon in 2012.  I am reviewing it positively despite having barely played it because I already know what it is: the most complex entertainment simulation of a society ever made.  If you like management and colony sims, this is pretty much the apex of the genre that is unlikely to ever be surpassed in our lifetimes.  Maybe there will be AI-written games later that will eclipse DF in complexity.  Maybe.Not for casuals.  Even with the GUI this is a monster of a game.  Remember: Losing is fun.

_childDocuments_.review: Many would think this is a colony survival game.  Oh.. how wrong they would be.  This is a life simulator. Dwarf Fortress is a masterpiece of the highest caliber.  The original had a steep learning curve and even now this version has that same learning curve.  However, the UI is absolutely gorgeous to behold.  It's easy to maneuver, clear what you're doing.  The graphics overhaul is amazing and everything is just beautiful.Even with a wonderfully built UI, the game still has a massive learning curve.  You will lose.  You will lose often.  But always remember: Losing is !!FUN!!

_childDocuments_.review: I have been playing this game for more than a decade, and it has never failed to interest, infuriate, and excite me every time I load it up. No other game has its staying power or replayability, and only Minecraft comes close in ability to reshape the world around you. Dwarf Fortress has taught me about (or forced me to learn about) about leadership, bravery, creativity, geology, biology, economy, environmentalism, diplomacy, tradecraft, psychology, and more in my time playing, and I am still discovering new interactions and testing new ideas each playthrough.If you are a fan of base-building, colony simulation, resource management, production management, pure open-world gaming, old-school text adventures, classic fantasy, or even if you were just that kid who loaded up SimCity to ruin his save file with every disaster available, Dwarf Fortress has something for you, and in my personal opinion there is no better game you could buy.

_childDocuments_.review: One of the most interesting and rich games I've ever played, and Kitfox has done so much work with the interface to bring it to where it is now. I really want to like this game, but there is SO MUCH work left to be done, mainly on the interface. It is, without exaggeration, the worst and most aggravating UX I have ever seen in a game. When it comes to equipping military squads, organizing work orders, assigning labor, and a hundred other things big and small, I just constantly feel like I'm fighting with an interface that was built by someone who wants me to suffer. I really hope that future updates make major changes so that, as a player, I can focus on all the interesting choices possible in this game rather than spend my time scrolling through a list of 200 dwarfs over and over and over.
_childDocuments_.name: Dwarf Fortress

_childDocuments_.review: There are incredibly few games that are actually masterpieces, and Dwarf Fortress is one of them. Its very hard to describe the kind of thing this game does, but to put it bluntly, some games will spend years and they will find themselves getting maybe a fraction of the mechanical, story, character, role-playing and world-building depth that this game has.Everything is dynamic or player directed, you can have Dwarfs who's backstories are informed by real things that occurred in the past for real in the game world, and those backstories inform their personalities, and how they react to situations. And then that can inform events in your current game, history, culture, war, religion is all decided by real events. Those dwarfs can read real books written by real characters in your world about real events that happened in the past, or listen to music or watch plays about actual heroes from ages past and the adventures they really had. You can find ancient caverns and ruins from real ancient civilisations and recover artefacts and relics that were made again, by real characters in your world and your seed. Those relics can be cornerstones for culture and religion. Your heroes can slay real ancient mythical monsters and demons that all of course have their own personalities and backstories informed by real events in the setting. Sometimes your characters can even have their backstories informed by those monsters and you can witness truly epic moments of heroics or tragedy as a mother stands off against a monster that killed its family in the past. (Though its not in this version yet), you don't even have to be restricted to building a city, you can even embark on ARPG adventures in your world and explore if you feel the itch.There is a very good reason why this game has maintained the feverish and loyal cult following its had for over 15 years. Dwarf Fortress might be one of the best games ever made, and I mean that with absolutely no hyperbole. it was made by like two primary devs and looked like a graphing calculator for most of its life, and I won't lie to you it is a struggle to learn still (though this version makes it much much easier to pick up) but the game will reward you in mountains what you put into it.Get into it early, you won't be disappointed, as the mods grow and stuff like the legends viewers and graphical mods are added into this version. You're in for quite the treat.
_childDocuments_.name: Dwarf Fortress

_childDocuments_.review: I used to play Dwarf Fortress filled with mods, but I've never had enough grasp (or effort to learn)of the game in its entirety, making most of my time the equivalent of reading hieroglyphs reports of a badly maintained ant farm killing itself through hilariously chaotic ways.Now? I can fully interact with the world, and understand at a glance that the giant weretapir that fell through a single unprotected hole on the ceiling is going to be my downfall.My colony is still going to die as miserably as it did in classic, but I won't have to spend an hour translating ASCI to understand what happened, and the experience is much better for it. And you can use your mouse now.

_childDocuments_.review: The granddaddy of modern survival crafting and simulation management games. If you've heard of Minecraft, Rimworld, or any of the hundreds of games inspired by these, they all owe respect to this, the original. In development for most of my entire life, the deepest most TTRPG-like experience in a game, brought into the modern age with mouse controls, a legible gui and cutie little pixel art graphics, the absolute wealth of storytelling and worldbuilding is actually accessible to folks who dont have the time or inclination to bash together their own game client.STRIKE THE EARTH!
_childDocuments_.name: Dwarf Fortress

_childDocuments_.review: I heard some interesting and funny stories about this game so after a long time of just being passively curious I finally bought it and gave it a shot.This thing is not remotely user friendly, even with the massive modernisation overhaul to the graphics and interface, it's painful to get anything done other than simply digging a tunnel.And the level of agency you have is completely arbitrary along with what you can and can not automate. Take the work orders for example, you can automate crafting wooden chairs when the number of chairs is low, neat, but you cant automate collecting wood when wood resource is low. No, you have to manually order wood cutting. Foraging is so similar, but handled differently for some reason, you manually designate a foraging zone which is then automatically foraged.Nothing is intuitive, outside of the new introduction tutorial, you have to look up every little thing online or else you will never figure it out because of how detailed or specific the steps are to getting anything done.This is CLEARLY a passion project, that much is undeniable, and i wish it lots of success purely on that basis.But as a product for the public to play with, especially in this relatively modern age compared to the ASCII days, its a bit rough. I can't really recommend this to anyone who is not ready to dedicate a hell of a lot of time to just working out how to get setup. I put ~6 hours in and I'm pretty sure the only reason my dwarfs aren't all dead yet is because half the game time was spent paused.If they put some significant work into quality-of-life updates to make most interactions more streamlined, with a more focused overall design around what level of control the player is meant to have, then it would be much better and more accessible in general.

_childDocuments_.review: Finally Dwarf Fortress is on steam and damn does it look good. Firstly, as someone who has played many hours of DF and only really knows how to make basic forts, this game is one of the most enduring, complex and interesting story builder out there. The Steam release offers two major benefits, firstly a way to give Zach and Tarn who have worked on this game for 20 years and want to continue on it, the money that they deserve for their work. Secondly, it opens this game up to a whole new audience. Many people I have spoke with in the past have talked about how complex DF is to play and too look at, and while the complexity is still there, the first barrier has been removed. It is very easy to understand what is going on, why Dwarves are happy, upset. What equipment they have, what they are doing and what group of dwarves they belong to. As mentioned the complexity of the game is still there, but the new UI and menus make it far far far easier to get a hang of and understand. Cool little tricks like 'Grab nearest item' and 'continue building after placing' for things like beds removes much of the tedious keyboard shortcuts that often ended in one bed in a room actually ending up as an armour stand. There is so much joy to be had in discovering resources, dealing with threats and building a great fortress. I would recommend highly that you make some notes of things that happened as you go and you'll see your own story emerge. Now there are some issues in the game, mostly for those who played the old games which can make it a bit odd. I for example have really struggled with the labours screen and often go to make a separate job for each type of labour. In the old game Dwarves entered the fort with their best skills already enabled, and things like building enabled too, this meant that if you had a Gem Cutter, and you built jewellers, this workshop would be built. However, now you have to set this for the dwarves. They enter the fort initally willing to do every labour, even if they are grand master jewellers. Meaning that sometimes jobs that are constant, like weaving or farming get done by dwarves that have no skill, and this is both a pain to deal get stuff done and unproductive. As mentioned I end up creating many many different jobs, (pretty much one for each workshop) and then set dwarves to that. It works, but it is clunky and annoying. However, this is something from an old player, and its not game breaking, it allows for greater control and interaction in your fort allowing you to make sure that you know exactly who is doing what. Finally one bit of advice. SEND NEW SOLDIER DWARF MOTHERS ON MATERNITY FOR A YEAR.

_childDocuments_.review: Dwarf Fortress is a complex simulation game with incredible emergent storytelling. You'll see dwarves standing tall in the face of danger, dwarves throwing tantrums over the smallest things, and everything in between. Dwarf Fortress could be described as similar to RimWorld, but with much more depth (z-levels baby!) and less gamification. This gives the game a slower pace than many other similar games, and those who are easily bored might find waiting on Dwarves a bit tedious. However, if you like planning, scheming, learning, and dealing with the horrific aftermath of a tavern brawl caused by someone throwing a glove at someone's pet turkey, then this is the game for you! Prepare to wall off your play area for hours at a time as you learn the ins and outs of this game, and remember, losing is FUN!

_childDocuments_.review: I'm not sure if Dwarf Fortress is a game you should play, but it's definitely a game you should own... And if you do want to play it, this version is worth paying for.I've heard a claim that Dwarf Fortress is unlabelled "Early Access" but... not really? I mean, it's been available for  at this point, nothing about what we have today is "early". Plus, Early Access implies some theoretically future game which is "done", and that the version available now is just a stepping stone to that. That isn't really what Dwarf Fortress is about. The game is a vast, deep, endless simulation game like nothing else out there, that will be in constant development to add more detail for as long as the devs care to. I'd call it a bizarre mix of Minecraft and The Sims, except it vastly predates the latter, and doesn't really feel anything like the former.Let's try and get this review back on track, shall we?The first things that happens when you start the game is that you make a world. Again, I'm reluctant to mention Minecraft here, but I feel I have to as a point of contrast. In Minecraft, world generation is a purely physical process; you're going to spawn in , so the game will figure out where to put dirt, stone, water, caves, rivers and trees around that area. Dwarf Fortress does do that too, but mostly as as an incidental thing. What it's  doing is generating a . A hundreds years, by default, generating thousands of people and monsters and gods and cultures, and what they spent that time doing, how their fates criss-crossed and led to the world you're going to be playing in. What is the point of this, from a gameplay perspective? I don't know yet, but I do know I spent an hour poring through the legends of my world, learning of the first Dwarven king who had a long reign and died, only to be resurrected years later by a necromancer from another culture. That necromancer was taught these secrets by a master necromancer who, purely by coincidence, was the first lover of the king in his younger days. That's some good procedural storytelling, right there.(The master necromancer learnt how to raise the dead from an artifact, a stone slab on which a god had inscribed "the secrets of life and death". That wasn't a typo; the slab literally contained just the words "the secrets of life and death" on it, and apparently reading those words is enough to, in fact, actually give a dwarf the secrets of life and death. Bit weird, but, sure!)For a lot of people, Dwarf Fortress has always been more compelling to read about than to actually play. You've heard of "Boatmurdered", right?  OK, you might want to make a hot drink, get in a comfy chair, and go read about it, it's great. Dwarf Fortress is an amazing story generation system, but as a game, it's depth, combined with it's ASCII graphics and keyboard-only controls, have always been a big barrier for entry. It's all just so *much*, and so hard to play. This, then, is the genius of the Steam version. I can't overstate how much of a benefit it is to just be able to see what's going on in a way that makes intuitive sense, rather than trying to parse what various ASCII symbols mean, or being able to just click on buttons that tell you what they do instead of having to memorise multiple layers of keypresses to do anything. Combined with a basic tutorial to get you up and running, and we have a version of this game that's actually playable, all by itself.Dwarf Fortress is never going to be a simple game to play, but this version puts the game's complexity into it's interconnected systems where it belongs, rather than in trying to understand what's happening and how to do things. It still may not be the game for you... But if you can afford it, you should buy it anyway. They've been giving this game away *for free* for over 2 decades, and adding to the world of gaming simply by dint of existing, and it's time to give them their dues. And then you can go read about some Dwarf Fortress stories. You've heard about the alcoholic cats, rights?If you're really on the fence, you could go try the free version, I guess. Mechanically, it's essentially the same as this one (perhaps even a bit more mature?). But do keep in mind that, in terms of onboarding, that version is dramatically behind this one. If it seems too intimidating... well, this version does a  to fix that.

_childDocuments_.review: I was really looking forward to playing this game and bought it day one. I was ultimately pretty disappointed though. The game is missing a lot of features that have been pretty standard in any game I've played in this genre. Ultimately, I asked for a refund.Task management in this title requires quite a bit more micro managing than I would really deem as acceptable and I was getting frustrated trying to maintain my colony just in the first season. There is no way to assign a repeatable task and mark the task as "do this when able" and so the second an actor can't do the task they cancel it and you have to re-add it to the queue. You can't place furniture or objects before it's already built, so you can't plan out a room and have it generate the required tasks like you can in Gnomoria or Ingnomia either. Planning the resources so that you COULD build the furniture or objects is made even more difficult by the fact the UI doesn't even tell you what resources are required to build said object...For a game that is played almost entirely via UI interaction, the UI lacked too many basic features to warrant the price tag and frustration. The game has been around for a long time, unfortunately it hasn't picked up many of the modern improvements the genre has seen since it was initially released and the title really is showing it's age.

_childDocuments_.review: In short, it’s complex, it’s absurd, and it’s totally addictive. If you’re ready to turn frustration into laughs, Dwarf Fortress is the game you never knew you needed.Mods for Dwarf Fortress on Steam bring tons of variety and fun to the game, enhancing everything from visuals to gameplay mechanics. With Steam Workshop integration, players can easily add custom tilesets, quality-of-life improvements, new creatures, magic, and even additional civilizations. Some mods streamline the user interface for easier navigation, while others introduce entirely new challenges and features, like multiplayer or advanced weaponry. Whether you’re after a prettier fortress, a smoother experience, or just more chaos, mods let you tailor Dwarf Fortress into whatever kind of madness you want.

_childDocuments_.review: This version of Dwarf Fortress replaces the ASCII user interface with a more modern UI containing buttons and sprite artwork. I found this made Dwarf Fortress far more approachable to pick up and learn. This game is the grandfather of the sandbox city builder survival genre. It draws you in with its deep interconnected systems and infamous difficulty curve. Then you'll keep coming back for the interesting stories that arise as you play. If you start reading through the flavor text and really dig into the lore the game provides, the story begins to feel like Fantasy Survival Mad Libs. Dwarf Fortress is truly something special and I look forward to see the game continue to evolve in the future.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm going to open this review by saying if you're coming into this expecting Rimworld-levels of QoL, don't. This update gives the game mouse control and an actual UI, but it's not polishing things up to the level that Rimworld does. The UI makes things more intuitive, but you aren't going to get a menu telling you exactly why your Dwarves are unhappy, or even a numerical value as to what their skills are. That's all flavor text, and if that, understandably,  sounds frustrating or outdated, then you'll probably not enjoy your time with Dwarf Fortress.  People have been excusing a lot of this by saying the game's been in development for twenty years, but I think that gives new players the wrong impression. Instead, I'll say that this game is twenty years old and directly inspired Rimworld, which came LONG after this game's basic features were set in stone. (Pun intended.)  I really hope that future updates to this version add extra ways of providing information to the player. You're left in the dark with a lot of stuff, and it can be a real struggle to figure out *why* something is happening, let alone how to actually fix it.I could ramble about this port for a while, because I really am mixed on it, but I'll cut to the chase and  just the answer the question; Should you buy this game? If you're a fan of Dwarf Fortress, Yes. Full stop. After twenty years, we can finally pay for our dwarf spreadsheet simulator.If you're a new player to DF, or someone who tried and couldn't get into the free version, I'd still cautiously recommend this release. See the above paragraph for why, but the TL;DR of it is that the QoL changes that are here might not be enough to make this game appeal to new players. Alright, time for the rambling.The new music is fantastic and helps achieve the main goal of immersing the player in the daily lives of their little digital Dwarfs. My complaints on how the mouse controls handle aren't met to detract from the fact that this makes the game SO much more enjoyable to play. As someone who tried to play the original but just couldn't get past the learning curve, this version helps immensely. The art's also beautifully done as well. The paid version of DF is a brilliant glow-up of a twenty-year old game and is absolutely more than worth the thirty dollar price point...but only to some people. If any new players are willing to take a chance on this version, I wish you the best of luck, and I heavily advise against going into it expecting something like Rimworld. Understand that there's still a learning curve, it's just been made a bit less steep. DF expects you to learn a lot of the game's features and mechanics by experimentation, which often means a lot of failing. It took me three fortresses to understand how to dig a deep hole that didn't cave it. Stick with it though, and you'll find a ton to love with this passion project.A lot positive reviews are from people who already play Dwarf Fortress. What negative reviews exist are all from people who either play Rimworld and want to check out the game that inspired it, or are from people who've only heard the stories and hype about the game. Both groups of reviews are totally fair, and they each make great points. This isn't a game for everyone, and I don't think it'll ever be. However, it's also clear that's there still work that could be done to make the Steam version feel deserving of the game's legacy.

_childDocuments_.review: Tried so hard to like it but just naw... every time I try to have fun, the game tries its damnedest to find a way to make it not fun. This game is absolutely NOT for anyone just started colony sims too, and anyone coming from Rimworld will be met with a HUGE downgrade in mechanics that make colony sims and builders, like Rimworld, some of my favorite games of all time. Anyone who isn't familiar with the genre, or even dwarf fortress itself, will be met with absolute sloppy nonsense when they play this.Let's be completely honest with ourselves for a second here, if this was the first installation of Dwarf Fortress and the old DF never existed all those years ago, never collecting an absolute cult following over the decades, this game would have MIXED reviews at best, but I bet it'd be dipping more into negative.One example out of the MANY negatives in this game is your dwarves' needs. An interesting mechanic made . Oh, your dwarf feeling chronically sad because he hasn't touched something shiny in a while despite working near the storage area WITH shiny things 24/7? Micromanage and force him to stand near boxes of nice ♥♥♥♥ until he stops being pissy. Is he now suicidal because he hasn't been able to ARGUE with a fellow dwarf in a while despite being next to other dwarves literally 24/7? Micromanage and lock him in a room with another dwarf and hope for the best that something happens. Now manage those 2 needs plus 40-50 other ridiculous needs like them with 100-200 dwarves. Sounds exhilarating doesn't it?Idk, I'm just ranting at this point, but my favorite part about all of this is that these awful needs are in place but with no actual programmed automatic processes for the dwarves AI to go out fulfill these needs himself. They are usually solved by (back to the need for shiny things) if the dwarf just so HAPPENS to pathfind near a box with shiny things. He will NOT take a second out of his day to drag his dumb little sprite over to a box himself.If this game DOES have automated ways to deal with needs like these, it is so poorly implemented that I personally never saw it happen and the game might as well not have them.Honestly I'm surprised they made eating and drinking automated where don't have to lock them in a room with food and alcohol in hopes they consume it, like you have to do with 60% of the other needs.

_childDocuments_.review: DF has always been an unintuitive mess of menus, and features.The Steam version goes a long way to fixing a lot of these issues. The menus make more sense, and concepts are grouped together in intuitive ways. The graphics are better than any tileset I've used, and the soundtrack is astounding. That said, some smoothing as units move between tiles would be a welcome change.The tutorial goes a long way to getting you started, but still could be much better. It could guide you all the way to a "functional" fortress, instead of abandoning you 3/4 of the way there. It won't be so bad for players who like a complex game, but more casual players will feel frustrated and upset.There is always room for improvement with DF, but that's why they've been working on it for 20 years. Zach and Tarn are wonderful guys, who have done a lot to build a community over that time, and have shown real dedication to this game and the fanbase. Every dollar that goes to them is a dollar well spent. It's also a dollar that will undoubtedly go back into DF. Adding features, squashing bugs, and building on the titan of a legend this game is. Minecraft, Terraria, Factorio, and all those crafting systems in your favorite FPS, can all be ultimately blamed on DF. It's a bit of a mess, but it's a legendary gem for a reason.Check out a vid, and buy it if you like a challenge! Just don't dig too deep...

_childDocuments_.review: First and foremost: This is not the Dwarf Fortress that the greybeards are used to. The change in UI and graphics makes it an entirely different experience to play. The controls have been massively reworked, and not only is mouse support natively supported now, it is heavily leveraged to control the new interface, plus the old system of hotkeys and shortcuts has been completely overhauled, such that hitting the keys one is used to hitting does not produce the same results. Notifications are completely different, and certain milestones - like strange moods, or migrant arrivals - pass with only minimal alert to the player by icon popups. The change to a new tileset makes familiar features such as soil, gemstones, and ore deposits difficult to recognize on first glance, not unlike using a tileset for the first time in prior versions of DF.All that being said, this is still ultimately the game that has been in development for twenty years, given a glorious new layer of polish, with the barriers to entry heavily lowered, and the same soul of idiosyncratic dwarves surviving dangers both trivial and terrifying, avoidable and inevitable. They still love cheeses, and cows for their haunting moos, and despise getting caught in the rain, and need a drink to get through the working day. You will get attached to heroes and losers, cheer their triumphs and mourn their losses, and ultimately everything goes to hell and everybody dies - and you'll either be laughing or cursing the whole way.It's Dwarf Fortress, but not like anything that has come before. If it's new to you, then now is the time to hop in: the water is fine, and the carp are no longer an existential threat to your dwarves. If you're a Dwarf Fortress veteran, then you owe it to yourself (and Toady and Threetoe) to get this: take some time to learn the new interface, but everything that lies beneath is the same game you have come to know and love. With stout labor comes sustenance. A new chapter of dwarven history begins at this game. Strike the earth!

_childDocuments_.review: I tried to poke at Dwarf Fortress a few times before the Steam release, but always bounced off the labyrinthine UI, so after years of hearing people's fun stories and seeing their cool-looking fortresses, I was eager to give it a try once it released on Steam with an actual UI and graphics parsable by a normal human eyeball.What it mostly makes me feel is that the stories I've been hearing have been more fanfiction than something with grounding in the game, because Dwarf Fortress during its current release is one of those games where I can never tell if something not working is because: It simply isn't working, there's a reason it isn't working and its obscured to the player, there's a reason it isn't working that's technically visible to the player but buried under five submenus.In declaring that "losing is fun," Dwarf Fortress proudly states that it's a story simulator more than a game. Which is a fair enough statement: There is no end victory state, so this is reasonable.The problem is that for something to not just be an RNG roll, but a story, and to be that to the player, it needs a sense that things are happening for reasons. Things do happen, but I'll be damned if I could tell you the reasons, and fortresses are such fragile things that a story rarely gets an ebb or a flow, it just gets a start... and then a sudden annihilation, not assisted by the aforementioned bugs and obscurity. As a few examples...On the low end of meaningless chaos: Dwarves seem to often hold meetings atop tall trees, which they then can't get out of(how did they even get up there in the first place? It's like seven Z-levels up), and if you don't catch it and hack down the tree(which will probably just kill or cripple half of them), they starve to death and you get a message about it a month later when someone spots the bones.On the high end of meaningless chaos: Your map may attract giant birds. There is no warning when they arrive, dwarves ignore burrow orders so they won't stay underground, if they catch an unaware and unarmed dwarf said dwarf is dead in seconds and they can apparently open doors. So what happens is that all of a sudden you get an "X is fighting! X has been found dead!"-message and you discover that a giant parrot has dismembered a quarter of your fort population before you even had a chance to center on the action.Giving orders is also stuck in that really awful limbo where the dwarves aren't intelligent enough to do things on their own, but you also can't give them direct orders for a lot of things AND the game obscures why they sometimes don't do things. Why haven't they built this workshop I have the materials for in six months? Why haven't they placed this door or this bed in a literal year? I'm quite convinced I've tried literally every combination of orders and priorities possible. And then I'll get up and grab a drink and when I get back, randomly, they've decided to build half the outstanding things, but not the other half.I've had merchant caravans declare that they're leaving, but instead get lost in my fortress or in the swamp outside, while also leaving half their stuff in the trade depot, bugging it out, even after they died in the swamp thanks to the giant parrots and ravens. My dwarves have dozens of personality traits, but as far as I can tell they all result in the same thing: Small alcoholics that seem completely incompetent at any task except for digging holes, about the only thing you can reliably tell them to do and which will get done. Aside from that there's also just a mess of tiny quality of life issues. For instance you can't order a wall be replaced with another material, you have to remove the original, THEN order the new wall built... and then wait a decade for it to happen. You can't smoothe or replace floors when something else is built on top of them, which might be "realistic" but is a fiddly annoyance in practice.Dwarves will say "oh hang on buddy, I'm not hacking into this aquifer!" and thanks for the warning, but they'll happily hack down trees and get buried under falling branches and trunks, instantly killing them, which means you have to carefully select the trees they actually cut down. Hunters will pepper animals with bolts until right before they're dead... and then walk away, letting them recover fully before returning to repeat the performance, and unlike dwarves, the giant animals recover perfectly from these fun times. I'm not sure whether some exciting new bugs got introduced for the Steam release, or some features pared back(because when I read about the pre-Steam releases there do actually seem to be "build these ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ things"-order priority that functions), but this is just a mess. It's a funny, absurd mess for the first ten hours or so, but then once you feel like advancing beyond seeing what damage a giant beak can do to a dwarf or how the idiots can get themselves killed in the woods, it just starts being an exercise in frustration.The tileset is nice, though.

_childDocuments_.review: Great work. But. After long years of waiting Dwarf Fortress has hit Steam. The graphics and mouse interactions made this game so much more accessible to a new player, otherwise, I highly doubt that I could find my wife sitting in front of this game for hours, sharing the fun I experienced in the classical version of the game. Thank you Kitfox for bringing a fantastic game to a broader audience.The graphics and music are superb. The original dwarf vibe was well-preserved with a modernized arcade art style. I can see that the UI/UX has been completely reworked. The mouse interaction, once you get the hang of it, is pretty straightforward. It adds more interactiveness to the keyboard experience of the classic version. I especially like the uniform rectangular swipe for all the region-related operations. Much less confusing than the original where two kinds of modes exist.Now, the drawback. I have to say that this game really should have been labeled early access.There are bugs. The game sometimes hangs when one wants to name a save file. Sometimes there is quite some lag after the game autosaves during season change (on my Linux machine).Some quality-of-life functionalities are still missing.Someone mentioned adventure mode in other reviews. It will come, one day. Right?Overall, nice work from Kitfox. I would recommend it to anyone who is interested in similar sim games and tell them to be careful because this game is in fact in early access. I would also look forward to UI/UX updates in the future.

_childDocuments_.review: As a RimWorld fan I wanted to finally give Dwarf Fortress a try, considering it basically established the colony sim genre. I highly respect the devs for giving Dwarf Fortress more "accessible" graphics for the average gamer (like me), but the UI needs a serious revamp to boost Dwarf Fortress to new accessibility heights. As a complete beginner, having the wiki open as a reference while you play is a requirement, because there is no other way to know what certain workshops are for, and what certain items are for, and why you should bother making them. The game provides little to no information in tooltips, and I get that the devs expect you to figure it out somehow as you play, and lose and die a lot as you bumble around, it sort of diminishes the fun factor for me when I feel like the UI itself is providing the conflict, and not the game mechanics. (If there ARE UI tooltips explaining what certain things do, then I must be blind because I've never found it.)For example, it took me diving into the wiki just to figure out how to set up and equip a military squad. And even then, I'm still confused as to why my squad is refusing to equip certain pieces of armor that I crafted for them. It's a bit of a nightmare, and the game fails to explain any of it to you in a way that is obvious to the player. This is ultimately my only complaint- and it's a big one- because the game itself should be the challenge and not the navigation thereof. That said, if you don't mind alt-tabbing into Wikipedia whenever you encounter something confusing, you will get a lot out of Dwarf Fortress and you will be able to appreciate its vast scope and depth. If you don't like doing that in your games, then Dwarf Fortress probably isn't for you.
