_childDocuments_.review: Played Dwarf Fortress about 10 years ago. I couldn't get into it not because it was a hard game but because it was difficult for me to memorize what every letter meant and all the key binds. When the Steam version released, with an overhaul on the graphics, I gave it another shot. This time around, due to not having to memorize symbols, I had a new experience and have loved it. What has happened to me so far?Fort 1: A spy tried sneaking into my base so I sent my squad out to kill the spy. Well  I was occupied I didn't notice a surprise attack on the inside of my Fort which started in the Tavern and eventually made it around my entire Fort. I lost almost every Dwarf but won the fight. Fort 2: I didn't know much about how the water pressure worked in this game. I ended up releasing a full strength river into my Fort and drowned all my Dwarfs well attempting to make an underground fishing pound.Fort 3: I had a pretty good fort going when a Titan attacked. My commander got in a lucky blow and killed the Titan in a few quick chops. Then came the deer.... Hunter went out looking for meat and found the deer. To make a long story short I either had the worst luck or that Deer was the real titan. It killed my hunter, head stomped two of my children to death and took out one of my soldiers when i sent my army to kill it. I decided to remain in the fort until I made a mistake building a moat. I didn't know if you cut a tree down after digging out the layer below the tree would collapse through each layer until it came to the bottom. Long story short, cut the tree, it crashed onto a dwarf farming, and two dwarfs walking the halls. One died and the 2 others were out cold with broken legs. Every mistake I have made or battle I have fought I have learned from and made each fort better and better. Losing may feel like a loss at first but in my opinion that is where the fun really is.

_childDocuments_.review: It's Dwarf Fortress. For those who aren't aware, this is Rimworld's inspiration and (probably) the more ambitious, expansive game. Before this release, the game's primitive UI and graphics were completely arcane and a massive barrier to entry. That's not an issue anymore if you're willing to pay, and the old ASCII version is still available for free. Highly recommended. You can basically do whatever the hell you want and it will probably work. There's still a significant learning curve, even with the new bells and whistles, but it's worth it.Also to note, there's some slightly annoying bugs floating around in this version. Nothing gamebreaking, though - but definitely noticeable.

They've done well to update the game to a more palatable format for the masses but it's missing years of QOL fixes that this new experience needs.

_childDocuments_.review: Foreword: I bought this game having never played DF classic, and only having a passing knowledge that DF classic even existed. Thus my review is not tainted by 20 years of nostalgia. If you played DF classic, this recommendation isn't for you. To everyone else:I do recommend this game, but it comes with caveats. Starting out is incredibly frustrating. This game REQUIRES you to use the wiki. Of course the big downside here is that the wiki is based on DF classic. Instead of explaining how to do things, many of the wiki pages simply say to do p-r-q-x-z to do something. Well that doesn't work here. It's going to be difficult to do even the most basic things if you've never played DF before.But enough about the wiki, how is the GAME? Well, it's addicting once you get past that frustration hurdle. The core gameplay is very compelling for the most part. I found myself thinking about resource flows and base designs quite a bit even when not playing. The interface is... well it's there. I'm sure it represents a massive improvement over the classic system (basing this entirely on screenshots, again I've never played classic). But the camera controls are jarring to say the least. A grid-locked view makes sense in a keyboard only case. Less so when the game has mouse support. Don't expect any kind of sensible sorting in menus either. As an example, I decided to make a bunch of stone mugs to sell to traders. These mugs were stored in iron bins for easy transport and condensed storage. But when I search for "mug" in the trading menu, I see the contents of EVERY iron bin in my fort, regardless of whether it has mugs in it or not. Why? Because there is at least 1 iron bin with a mug in it. Maddening.There's also a lot of complexity where there seems to be no need for it. For example, every living animal has a different type of tallow item (horse tallow, pig tallow, goblin tallow, etc) Despite this, there is NO difference between them AFAICT. Tallow is tallow is tallow. And yet if I want tallow from the trader, I have to select every type of tallow there is. Why?It's going to take you several hours to figure anything out, but if you can stick with it then you can have a lot of fun (and not the meme kind everyone talks about, I mean actual fun). On that note, the community is both helpful and not newbie friendly which is odd. When asked a direct "how do you do <thing>" you'll usually get a quick response, but it usually has to go through about 7 levels of translation before the gibberish makes sense to a newbie. And don't even think about sharing something you designed unless you want to hear about how stupid and not META it is.The soundtrack is incredible. Nuff said.I know it sounds like I have a lot of complaints; and I do. But I don't regret my purchase for an instant, and if you're not easily dissuaded then I think you will like it also. The complexity of everything makes the industry much more interesting than most games because you can't just dig up some iron and make a sword. There's granularity which is very fun to play with (except when that granularity doesn't add anything RE: tallow).I have not yet experienced any fun story telling that DF players like to talk about, but that's probably because I haven't gotten very far. The sheer mass of things being simulated is bound to result in something interesting sooner or later.

_childDocuments_.review: Newcomer here, and my oh my what a damn game... At first it is a HUGE uphill climb to overcome the vastness of this game. There is absolutely no hand holding and the tutorial is bare bones. What has me hooked is the sheer randomness of EVERYTHING. It is truly comical. Simply put, whatever you build or do, your dwarfs react. I built a floor in the tavern, assigned a performer/musician, and within the hour a full on concert developed. The dwarfs danced and got drunk, fights broke out, etc. Wild times lol Then moments later I get raided by an army of the dead with giant spiders and a high elf as their leader. Take it easy, newcomers, laugh and enjoy.

_childDocuments_.review: I love Dwarf Fortress and played the original for way too many hours, when I've heard they made a version for steam with neat graphics I got excited but wanted to wait a bit longer until this version was more fleshed out.Well, it isn't any better than the original version. In fact in some ways it is even WORSE.-- Labor system --They slapped a weird system on top of the skills where you can assign your dwarfs to certain labor categories, sounds cool at first because you think "neat, I can group all hunting skills together", but as your fort progresses and you try to make certain categories for niche skills you constantly have to create new labor categories, and the worst part is the icons for these skills are very limited, it's honestly baffling. Basically only the starting categories have proper icons and you cannot add new ones, if you add another category after the basic ones you get a "I" icon, then "II", "III", "IV", "V", "VI", "VII", "VIII", and that's it. 8 more icons and the completely insane part about this is how they wrap around, so if you create your 9th category it starts back at a yellow "I". Would it have been too much to ask for extra icons or atleast different colors on the roman numbers? It feels like whoever designed this system hasn't played more than 2 hours of dwarf fortress, because it provides no benefits if you play for a bit longer while causing you extra work. You also cannot save presets of these should you intend to start a new fortress essentially adding a massive extra overhead every time you create  a new fort.-- No Quality of Life --I hoped that the steam version would be more player friendly since it tries to appeal to a large audience, this is absolutely not the case, the standard game with DFhack has a LOT more QoL and you really notice it missing in this version. It starts with how some menus dont allow for selecting everything at once. Need some leather? Okay, enjoy receiving carpal tunnel from the caravan during negotiatons as you click through "Elk leather", "Elk bird leather", "Elk man leather" and the 1239847 other categories of leather this game has. Oh and you have to do this EVERY. SINGLE. TIME. for all caravans. What in the good christian ♥♥♥♥? I mean it's awesome this game has so much variety but why in gods name does everything need to be this click intensive? you also cannot use shift click to select multiple items, you essentially need macros to play this game or else you will quickly become unhappy with it. Oh and the best part if you only right click a SINGLE TIME your negotiation window will get canceled (WITHOUT CONFIRMATION) and you will have to click on every single ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ item again. What is this madness??!?A lot of the menus are also really bad as they don't let you click on Dwarfs. For example you see a Dwarf who has Labor categories "Woodcutting", "I, "II", "II", "IV" and you want to know what these categories are (they have no text on mouseover because ♥♥♥♥ convenience). So you want to click on the dwarf but oh that does nothing. I have to manually read the name of the dwarf and find it in the list of all dwarfs (which at some point will be 200+ names), click on him, then click on his labor skills and now I can see which labor categories he has enabled. WHY?-- No upwards staircase --This was the thing which made me question the existance of a god in our reality. You cannot build a simple up stair case in this version. You have to make a selection for the staircase which spans multiple Z-levels, however if there is already a down staircase above which your miners dug out you CAN NOT connect the constructed upward staircase, the game simply refuses to build it forcing you to build a different staircase next to your actual staircase and also forcing you to mine out and replace the staircase you dug initially if you want a staircase that goes all the way down and spans the whole region. sure, this can be avoided by planning ahead and building the staircase correctly but it's absolutely crazy that you cannot connect the built staircase in this way to a mined-out staircase and honestly made me wonder a second time if whoever ported this crap has played the game for longer than 20 minutes because they didn't understand how stairs work in the original DF at all.-- No adventure mode --The saddest part was that I initially got the steam version because I wanted to play some adventure mode but they just didn't add it to steam yet for whatever reason, I wouldn't even be mad if most of the graphics were missing, just let me have the experience of dying 10 times on the way to my old fortress ffs.This game has been on steam for 1.5 years and the state it is in is honestly pathetic. Don't get me wrong I am not salty about buying this game as I wanted to support the developer either way (and I hope most of the profits go to the original creator and not whoever ported this mess to steam), but some of these QoL things such as "select all" for menus can be done in a single work day and copy pasted to all other menus. So why has it not been done? I suspect that incompetence and a lack of feel for this game is the issue as what has been done for the steam version of this game is the bare minimum.tl,dr: Thank you for listening to my Ted Talk. Just get the free DF version with DF hack or preferably a "lazy noob pack" for the convenience and if you want to support the original developer then consider donating to him via patreon, which is linked on his website on bay12games. Don't support this steam version because it sucks a metric ton of rear.edit: I did NOT receive this game for free and I honestly dont know why it doesnt count my review, but I guess that's a neat way of courating your review score

_childDocuments_.review: It's really hard for me to put into words how to review this game. I recommend it because it's one of the greatest computer projects to simulate a Lord of the Rings style fantasy world. It has depth that goes beyond any game out there as it builds it's own history to be used in game. All your actions in the game are remembered forever in your save. However Dwarf Fortress is not for everyone. I caution anyone who wants to play this game to be prepared to spend many hours learn how the game works and flows.Those who played Rimworld will find many similar features in Dwarf Fortress. I think DF is much more interesting and flexible because you run a city of 100+ dwarves vs the 15 folks in Rimworld.Originally my review didn't include the updates to the free dwarf fortress. As of now, you can enjoy many of the quality of life features that the steam version has. The downside is you don't get the visuals or the music the steam version includes. The graphical additions are impressive because all in game descriptions are reflected in the sprite work. Let me repeat that, all in game descriptions of their looks, skin, hair, items they hold and everything else is reflected in game. I like seeing the game in the new sprite work so I still highly recommend the steam version.Try the free version yourself.  I promise it's the same game even if it looks like moonrunes.

_childDocuments_.review: If you aren't sure if this game is for you, you can play it for free. Go to Bay12 games, look for the LNB, or Lazy Newb Pack. It has sprite graphics but lacks mouse support. There is some unexpected wonk and the learning curve for new player is flattened a bit but it's still a steep ride. You'll want wiki's and guides handy. Reddit's got some good players, and the Bay12 community is stellar. Do not expect "modern" polish. The engine is still 20 years old and is still developed organically. . _childDocuments_.review: First, let me give a disclaimer...my play time shows 12.9 hours, but I've got thousands of hours in Dwarf Fortress, with my first playthroughs happening around the time that the game started featuring multiple z-levels. There might not even be another game I have played as much as this one.So, why haven't I played the Steam version. This comes down to a change in the way the UI was handled that means that the Steam version requires the mouse for play, while the older 0.47 version allows me to play with keyboard only. I'm currently hoping that they are working towards making the game playable without ANY mouse inputs at all, and should they do so, I'll likely install this again.So...why am I suggesting it? Well, in the case that you're a new player who has no experience with the game, none of the problems I have with the Steam version will be problematic for you, except perhaps the odd poorly laid out UI elements or clunky interface elements (the irony here being that being mouse-based makes poor UI choices even more evidence since hotkeys memorization essentially nullified the clunky UI for veteran users).In the case that you're a veteran of the game, you might have issues with the way the UI has been adapted in a similar vein as I do. Still, Toady deserves your support. This work of digital artistry and passion deserves financial recompense for the time you've already played it before the Steam release.This game is absolutely not for everyone. A great number of people will never be able to connect with it, either because of the pacing, the complexity, the propensity for losing (its FUN!!), or even the graphics. A part of me still thinks that everyone should play it, in the same way that I feel on some level that, even if you don't like Classical music, every person should give Bach or Beethoven a listen. This game is a piece of modern history...and one of the fundamental inspirations behind Minecraft, and the various games that then were inspired by Minecraft like Terraria. Playing this game is like listening to the Beatles...you don't realise how much of its ideas are spread throughout the gaming world until you play it.This game is an influential work of art, and thus, you should experience it, even if you won't like or play it in the long run. For my own part, I've still got 0.47 on my computer.

_childDocuments_.review: I am a long time Dwarf Fortress player and v0.50 is the same amazing experience with an easier to understand interface. I suspect many people complaining about it have not really spent the time to understand it (tip you'll definitely be creating lots of custom work details).If you are new to Dwarf Fortress, this is the easiest it has ever been to get started.  If you are on the fence, I'll say this:  Dwarf Fortress requires that you be okay with abandoning a fortress because you made a mistake and there is no way to recover (more experienced players will be better at saving a fortress, new players should just restart).  Each fortress is a chance to learn something, even when it inevitably ends in disaster. If that sounds interesting, a challenge, then give Dwarf Fortress a try.  If that sounds unpleasant, then Dwarf Fortress may not be for you.

_childDocuments_.review: Figured when they released it as a paid product I should finally give them some money for the 10's of thousands of hours I have put into this game in one form or another :P.You remember dwarf fortress for the stories: A carpenter engraves an image of him beheading his wife, foreshadowing the future, then goes and does it, then throws himself in the drinking well from grief, dooming the entire fortress.And there is always the "your engraver has engraved a picture of himself engraving this very engraving of an engraving of himself, engraving this engraving". Self centred or uber meta? you decide...But some of my favourite lasting memories, are the 'features'...Not the "I can't load/save my game without crashing" style features (glares at GTA), more the "They just introduced temperature affects into the game and my cats have gone thermonuclear, setting my fortress and entire forest on fire"Some aren't even bugs par-se`...One of my forts, the Dwarf King married a (half?)goblin leader from a conquered site.... kinky, but makes sense.Decided to make my fort his home... fort was huge, so makes sense.Everyone in the fort tolerated the queen, because she was married to the king... true to life, so makes sense.Fort had a dumping pit I would throw my enemies to make them explode, for, uh, reasons... questionable, but makes senseThe queen would like to visit the bodies for some reason... disturbing, but makes senseThe Dragon they worshipped at the conquered site escaped, so payed me a visit, because, uh, reasons.... sucks, but makes sense.My dwarfs managed to capture said dragon and tame it... not very realistic, buts makes sense.Tied up the dragon in my dumping pit to burn the enemies I threw in said pit... Smart!With the Dragon installed every time my queen would visit, the dragon would then see the queen, and because of the mess of faction relationships, the dragon would attack its former most loyal follower... friend of my enemy is my enemy, makes sense?The queen was smart enough to know the dragon was hostile to her, so would run away, but not the other dwarfs... SMART QUEEN GO FAST!So the Dragon would breathe fire at the retreating queen, would always miss, but would usually incinerate an unfortunate dwarf bystander... unfortunately awesomeTrying to move the dragon to prevent further incidents, the dwarf handler and dragon ran into the queen going for a drink... bad timingthe dragon having incinerated the handler, was now free to roam, and determined to get his revenge, ran after the queen ... troublingThe dragon, running through the halls of his now 'allies' barbecuing dwarfs oblivious to the threat, as the queen ran away... hilariousLong story short, the Dragon burned half the fortress because he hated the queen for being captured... pricelessThe game:It is difficult to learn, and sometimes quite obscure, but once you get over that, you can spend a lifetime here.This is not an easy game, some level of masochism is required to play, and you can die to the stupidest things.No, not can, WILL, and you will die a lot. but once you get past that, you can have a hell of a time.This new version is a bit of a change to the old versions of barely functional, no frills GUI, so will take some time for the old guard to get used to.Recommended, only because there is company in misery :P but it is the good kind of misery...

_childDocuments_.review: A great rendition of the evergreen Dwarf Fortress with simpler controls and much better graphics. Definitely has a much less intensive player learning curve, while still allowing for the same gameplay as the original. Definitely a recommended version of the game, and is worth the price if you're interested in this genre of game.BUTThere's one thing that prevents me from calling this the definitive version of Dwarf Fortress. This version of the game does not have the logs, which are used to keep track of the story of your fortress. You can't go back and look at events from (in-game) months or years ago if you've already dismissed the alerts. My suggestion is to buy this version to learn the game and play a bit more casually, when you want a simple experience. Buy this game and then go download the OG Dwarf Fortress, which I consider to be the definitive addition.Tarn, Zach, I speak to you now: When you have the time, the addition of the logs would certainly be appreciated and would truly make this version of Dwarf Fortress the definitive edition.

_childDocuments_.review: This game had its origins as a story generator and it shows.  The world itself is generated, then the creatures in it, with their own histories and interactions.  Every object has known material strengths, melting points, hardness, weight.  Every creature has wants, needs, preferences, relations, and histories.Eventually you get stories that you tell everyone.  Here's mine:I lost a good 20 dwarves to a weredeer.  I looked into the legends viewer to see where it came from.  The weredeer was a dwarf before it changed.  She was bit by a human, who was bit by a dwarf, who was bit by another dwarf, who was bit by a human, who was bit by a goblin.  That goblin one day walked up to a god's temple and knocked something over.  The god got angry and cursed it to become a weredeer.  Decades later, twenty of my dudes die, dozens traumatized and mourning, because one goblin couldn't keep from being a jerk for five dang seconds in a temple.  So it goes.My current fort has a volcano.  I use the magma to power my industry.  I build a garbage pit to chuck things--prisoners, mostly--into the lava.I love this game.

_childDocuments_.review: If you're on the fence about Dwarf Fortress, there's really only one question you're asking, and it's this:"Is this game too complicated for me?"Everyone not asking that question should buy it immediately. But if you're still concerned, that's appropriate; even with all the updates to the visuals, sound, music, and (vitally) the interface, the game itself is still EXTREMELY deep and broad. There's tons to keep track of, loads to learn through wikis and frantic Google searches, lots of edge cases and weird interactions that aren't intuitive. This learning process is going to involve a lot of failure, dead dwarves, and burned-out forts. It's totally possible that you won't have a good time investing this much effort in a game, and that's okay. The game probably isn't for you! And if you want to enjoy or support it, buy a copy for someone who has the time and energy, and read their stories instead, which are going to be fantastic... commensurate with the amount of effort put into them.If the game had come with Adventure mode at launch, it might've been recommendable to the fence-sitters, as a fantasy world generator that you could romp through as a snail-man or any of a million other things. At this very moment, though, it's still a huge time and energy sink, although a much more compelling one than previously.It's still an incredible game and an amazing achievement, so I can't NOT recommend it, just know that if you need convincing, you might want to at least wait a bit for it to fill out.
_childDocuments_.name: Dwarf Fortress

_childDocuments_.review: A friend of mine got me into Dwarf Fortress over 10 years ago, but it never really stuck. When Rimworld came out, I found it to be much more rewarding, if dramatically less complex. With 100 to 200 mods or so, it could be decent enough. But Dwarf Fortress always called to me. Many times I tried to get back into it. The Steam release seems to finally have done the trick. It has its annoyances and imperfections, but I think that the work on sound and graphics makes up for it. I've finally been able to see some of the insanity this game has to offer. The depth of its simulation is unrivaled and continues to amaze me.
_childDocuments_.name: Dwarf Fortress

_childDocuments_.review: The famous 20-year project finally comes to Steam.From its inception it was widely known to be complicated with its convoluted UI, hard-to-understand game mechanics and ASCII 'graphics'.This version of the game improves on all of that (plus Steam Workshop support!). A definitive way to play Dwarf Fortress if you ever wanted to try it, but were too intimidated by its complexity.The developers of this game deserve all your support, with a price point being relatively reasonable for what you get. It is sure to give you many interesting and weird stories to tell your friends, and keep you playing for a long time to come.Strike the Earth!
_childDocuments_.name: Dwarf Fortress

_childDocuments_.review: The UI is trash. The music is repetitive. The steam version is much more tedious than the free version. Many features like mine carts and scholars are black magic that requires reading multiple huge Wikipedia pages to learn the best approximations  and hypothesis community research has found on the systems. Unironically, modding in DF is than parsing the menus and stuff in game .Not only that the game is super easy and poses no challenge. I liken it to Hardcore Minecraft, a game DF inspired, all you have to do is dig a hole and seal the top and you can never die. Of course, no one actually plays hardcore Minecraft like that and you should not play DF like that. DF is best played when you put your Dwarves at risk, when you try new stuff, give yourself lofty goals. I like learning and there is no end to what you can learn in DF. If you want to do something, with enough research and black magic you can probably do it. Dwarf Fortress is one of my all time favorite games. It has such a smooth pace of play. Start a fort with a goal (Such as making a fort all about farming) either succeed in the face of great adversity or fail spectacularly. Start a new fort with a new goal (such as raising a grizzly bear army but now you can set up some quality farms as you mastered that in the last fort. succeed in the face of great adversity or fail spectacularly. Start a new fort with a new goal. Build a glass base on the bottom of the ocean but now you can set up quality farms and train animals for defense with minimal effort. And so on.There is no in game progression in DF. No tech tree to push through, no new features to unlock, permanent upgrades. An yet, for me at least, Dwarf Fortress has the most satisfying progression out of any game I have every played as every fort gives you a new skill that you the player have mastered. A new tool in you the players proverbial tool box. Every fort gives a new understanding of game mechanics. Ever fort increases you the players mastery. Dwarf fortress is a sandbox. It is a sandbox that emulates so many stupid little things there is no end to what you can learn. No end the journey of mastery. Like an asymptote that gets infinitely closer to the point but never reaches complete personally master in DF is impossible. But that is okay, even with just a moderate understanding you can do so much cool stuff. Dwarf Fortress is a game that is easy to survive in, damn near hard to thrive in, and gets more fun the more you play and the more you understand. Thus, we have a game that gets more fun the better you are and a game that it is impossible to have perfect knowledge of. That is why Dwarf Fortress has the loyal following it has who put up with years of no content and the bugs and the interface and the graphics and all that. Because, there is no limit to the amount of fun you can have, no end were you have learned everything. Infinite fun so to say. I like having fun.

_childDocuments_.review: I am new to the world of Dwarf Fortress, having only downloaded the game since its release on Steam. _childDocuments_.review: An in depth if labyrinthine civ management game, you indirectly wrangle your dwarves into crafting and combat through an imperfect UI, setting tasks and goals and awaiting their execution by your stout mountain denizens. Like some sort of cross between Oregon Trail and Terreria, your dwarves mine out resources block by block, layer by 2D layer, and you must provide them food and shelter from the elements.The game randomly generates a playable world complete with randomly generated events and lore. In my opinion this is one of the more overhyped elements of the game, as lots of the random text such as place and government names feels like gibberish. "The Vestibule of Pleats" is my current state for instance, not very inspiring sounding. This is utilized in crafting, as arts made by dwarves will recognize other things in game, sometimes resulting in items engraved with images of engravings of items, so on so forth. Diplomacy plays a role here as well, as you can attempt to manage your relations with other species, such as the Elves, Goblins, and Humans, and such numerous beast men as the dingo and opossum men. Numerous environments make for very different play throughs, as you can start anywhere from an enchanted fairy forest to a haunted sun blasted desert, affecting the available resources and nearby societies and wildlife.Worth a play if: You enjoy management, civ sim, sort of dad games, and a fantasy aesthetic.Not worth it if: you are expecting tightly controlled combat, easy action or rts style play.
_childDocuments_.name: Dwarf Fortress

_childDocuments_.review: The UI and overall interface is terrible. This game has inspired so many colony-sim games but I can't recommend the dated interface. It's basically an MS-DOS prompt the way the construction and game logic works. Many things cannot be placed on their own. Furniture and such need to be built first then placed.Acquire material> Order item at specific workshop > place itemIt's a bit of a chore, it's not intuitive. It can become a second job just learning things that should have been straightforward to begin with. If you're used to Factorio, Oxyen Not Included or Rimworld's intuitive and easier to navigate UI then this game will offer a lot of initial challenges just learning to place simple structures or furniture. The game feels dated and the controls tedious.If you're unwilling to endure and learn dated 90's eras style of controls, it's not worth your time.  The game offers a great deal of complexity but take caution if you're used to modern games.05/2023: The UI is still horrible. It's awful. Underneath the trash UI is a great game. I still can't recommend it. You need several hours of gameplay just to get used to the Interface and understand the backwards obtuse logic the game follows when placing the simplest of items. WHY CAN'T YOU JUST DIRECTLY PLACE A FREAKING CHAIR???? Good luck to you when you have to reorganize dozens of furniture. There's no mass orders for that. Take flooring. Rimworld, you click on the flooring icon and set the material then drag-click to place the order. Rimworld will take into account any door, furniture and items then tailor the order to that. It even gets better with mods when replacing stuff.Dwarf Fortress, you click on Build menu>constructions>Flooring. Drag click then choose the materials needed. Now the problem is that when there's obstacles in the way you have drag and click again avoiding said obstacles. If you multiple rooms like say 10 bedrooms, you have to do this ten times then again clicking on what material to use each time. It's bonkers. It's carpal tunnel syndrome territory. Zeus Master of Olympus was released in 2000. That game has 10x better interface, clear and informative!This game still doesn't have that. Prepare to watch Youtube tutorials and Google everything. 20 year difference and the "modern" game DF has just the most unintuitive interface and build/construct logic.

_childDocuments_.review: Cancels Sleep: Interrupted by Dwarf FortressSame tagline I used when I supported this game aeons ago, but now shiny enough for humans to use and not end up dreaming in ASCII, with a tutorial (Short, but it's an entry point, this game doesn't hold your hand, ever) and a UI that involves the mouse (SHOCK!!)Played it for countless hundreds of hours previously, but in the past few hours alone the following has happened in my forts 3 years:- Forgot water pressure existed, so nearly flooded my first Steam fort when digging out my well and irrigation- Didn't have the right type of cloth, so one dwarf ended up going insane and running naked through the halls until she died of dehydration- Next artifact looked promising, Urist McUseless spent a whole season crafting....an animal trap decorated with the same wood it was made of....-Out of my 28 population, 9 were children. In a shocking turn of events, 5 of the remaining useful adults were related to some Noble stunted alcoholic maniac and inherited their positions within a bloody year- Giantess decided to come curb stomp me, called everyone to the burrows, the 5 nobles stood in the above ground fields having a chat. Cue said Nobles knee-capping the Giantess, gutting her and then sticking a pickaxe in her and then gather round the corpse to continue chatting.- Second person went insane because I didn't have the right type of cloth, cue nude streaking while muttering something about pencils, noses and "Wibble"And this is only the beginning... It's not for everyone, it's hard as balls, and if you're after graphics move on (Although a nice touch how the dwarf sprites actually follow their IG descriptions), but you'll never hear better stories than from DF

_childDocuments_.review: Dwarf Fortress is an incredible experience. If you give it a chance and don't treat it like just another game, you are likely to experience absolutely absurd and hilarious sessions unlike anything else you've seen. Well, if you're a fan of Rimworld, you've scratched a surface. I've sunk hundreds of hours in the original game, very happy to see this more user friendly version of the game on Steam. You start in a unique generated world with its events, heroes and villains. All of this acts as a rich backstory to your game, and you see references to these events as you play further. As a player you establish a dwarven colony in your preferred location. This can go right, or usually wrong sooner than later. Dwarves have their own minds, quirks and vices. Fill a colony with 100 of them and things start to unfold: relationship drama, barfights, cats walking on spilt beer and becoming drunk, travelling merchants with incredible stories, goblin poets, suspicious visitors with their agendas, bloody sieges, undead scholars, fortresses sunk in magna, crafted and soon stolen artifact thongs, mythic beasts beaten by dwarf kiddos. Things just get more absurd. Just grab some popcorn and enjoy.  Give it a change - it's worth it!

_childDocuments_.review: REVIEW UPDATEI bought this game on the hype last year. It's a great concept and I played it hard for a month or three until the bugs and poor implementation made more frustration than joy. My previous 7/10 review was predicated on the Devs making the hard course corrections they were started on, but now a year after purchase, it's still the exact same buggy mess it was a year ago. If you have money to burn and are curious about what one mediocre programmer can do with 20 years, and want to see what would have been cool in 1985 buy the game. But if you are looking for a fun game that works correctly, anywhere near modern standards, this is definitely not it.I'll give it another 20 years, and if I'm still alive by then I'll update my review- if there are any changes. I'm a tough reviewer. Let's start there. It's 2023 and I expect a certain level of quality in modern games. I also try lots of Early Access games, so I'm kind of jaded to small studios presenting their EA game, then poofing without finishing the project.     So it was with great trepidation that I dropped the $30 on Dwarf Fortress. But this tiny dev team has been quietly beavering away under a bridge somewhere for 20 years for close to free. And the reviews were all positive, and resource management/ mine stuff to dig with, dig stuff to mine with' games are my jam. I LOVE Factorio, it's my Gold Standard for EA games that kept polishing until they hit greatness. So I dropped the coin just before the Holidays.     Since then I have lost 6 inches on my height, I can't shave my beard fast enough and I've taken on a mysterious predilection for short, hairy women- and honey mead.    Seriously, this is a terrific game. If you like this kind of game, you'll like this. Totally playable. Very complete. Extremely addicting. It's a simple, 2D isometric map- with more going on under the hood than the Millenium Falcon for depth and complexity that will keep your interest.     You have my two thumbs up.     That said, now the tough part of my review....    It's a terrific game, with the potential for greatness, buuuut... that tiny dev team just doesn't have the manpower- yet.     This is already changing. All that sweet Steam money, including my $30 helps. They've brought on two more folks, and their road map is interesting and ambitious.     Changes are coming, but they are not here yet. Some really fundamental QoL features are missing (one obvious example- no hyperlinks to your Dwarfs (Dorfs) character sheets, and no scrolling between them, makes assigning tasks or military units tougher than it should be), along with some features that seem pretty necessary but are not even on the radar, like a side/ elevation view. It's a game about digging deep, with no way to see how deep you've dug. And no blueprints, so you are manually drawing everything, every time. And no, the macros don't count. This isn't 1986. Cut and paste is a thing now. But not in Dwarf Fortress.    Part of this is the origin of the game. It was pretty esoteric before the pretty tileset came along with the premium version. That kept the fanbase pretty small, tight, and loyal. But opening the game up to the larger gaming community took away that immunity.  Now they are a fish in a pool full of photo realistic, 3D games, and gamers who have come to expect what they have already seen 100 times - even from tiny dev teams.  Seeing a sideview of the old text based graphics wouldn't have looked cool. But seeing my fortress from the side is what I would consider a basic and fundamental feature.    So in it's current format, I give the game a strong 7/10, with the likelihood of that going up into the 9's if they can pivot their focus to appeal to a wider gaming audience. The deep geekery is what made this game so interesting in the first place. Credit where due. This game has layers of layers built into it's layers. Its a remarkable achievement, unlike any other game I've played, but also just the sort of game I love. But I believe they need to continue the course correction they started when they decided to make a pretty tileset. To appeal to the widest audience they need a bit more QoL and a bit more bling. The depth is already there.   I look forward to upgrading to an 8 or 9 as the game progresses. No game has ever scored a ten, though Factorio is a 9.9. Dwarf Fortress has the same potential.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm not entirely convinced that this is a video game so much as it is work of high art with video game programming as a medium. This is absolutely incredible, I am unfamiliar with anything else like it, and I am very glad that I got to experience it in a way that was accessible to me. However, much like other forms of high art, I question if it is intended to be functional. For instance, from what I have read, my i9-12900H is getting slowed to a crawl by constant temperature calculations which almost never serve a game-play function. That each dwarf tooth which got knocked out in a bar fight adjusts towards ambient temperature in real time is art. That it slowly renders the game unplayable is not functional, which makes it high art.

_childDocuments_.review: Trying to review something like Dwarf Fortress is incredibly hard. Not only is the game for a specific kind of player, but even those specific types of players might have a hard time grasping the game even if they come from other colony simulators. The depth in simulation in the game is insanely detailed. You have empires and civilizations rise and fall all in the matter of seconds (or minutes depending on how much you want to simulate) and you can go back to read everything that has happened in that world. From civilizations, artifacts, notable beings, to even notable events. There's a mode called Legends Mode you can use to read up on the history of your world. There's colored text indicating important things (like items or people) that you can click to further expand on what you're reading. The amount of world building you get from that alone is incredible because you can use it to fuel your imagination to fit all the pieces together. Or you can use it as a world and story builder for maybe a D&D campaign you've had in mind. I myself use it just to pass the time and see what the people have lived through. Then you have what's called Fortress Mode. Fortress Mode has you building out a fortress in the side of a mountain or underground. Your objective is just to survive as long as you possibly can. The tutorial is a great place to start, but I would probably recommend going through it once to get down the controls and then starting a new world with a Youtube tutorial series. There's notable Dwarf Fortress content creators like Blind or Nookium who have their own starter tutorial playthroughs to get you going. If they're not up to your standard there's so many more people who have dedicated their time to helping others. When building your fortress you want to take care of carving out a place for your dwarves to eat, sleep, cook, hang out, farm, or create things like crafts to trade with traders who come in to visit. When you get far along and your fortress grows in to something worth visiting, you'll have people try and move in. Or you'll have performers asking to come to your taverns to entertain your guests and citizens. Then if you get too popular you might attract the attention of other people or beasts that want you dead. Anything and everything can happen in Dwarf Fortress. What you have to figure out is how you want to have fun. You can build all types of specific fortresses you desire and make a mark on the world as you go along. That's Dwarf Fortress, a story creator and you're there to watch the chaos slowly unfold and you'll cry and laugh along the way from the ridiculousness of it all.

_childDocuments_.review: Breaking the 11 years of review silence on my Steam account to tell you to get this game, and to just spend some time with it.I have often seen Dwarf Fortress described as a difficult, complex, even obtuse experience, especially for newcomers, for a number of reasons. And there is truth in that: the game is very complex. Making a dyed piece of clothing for your manager to wear is a lengthy combination of growing crops, processing them (in separate workshops) into dye and thread, weaving the thread into cloth, dying the cloth, and then finally making clothing with it; the material of the floor actually matters when determining how hard your dwarves will collide with it, as does the thickness of their body fat when determining how much of the hit they can absorb; and, to be honest, Dwarf Fortress has caused me to learn far more about geology than I care to admit. But, at the same time, Dwarf Fortress allows the player to access that complexity when and how they wish, while fading it into the background at all other times. You do not have to set up industry chains like the one above or scour the minutiae of the wiki to survive in DF. You don't have to make soap or clothing, outfit a military, or even change your dwarves' labors to have a successful, prosperous fort filled with the events and stories that make Dwarf Fortress the endless experience that it is. At the end of the day, your fort can survive off a minimal amount of farmland growing plump helmets (mushrooms) all year, with 1 dwarf dedicated to growing and harvesting. Brew the mushrooms into wine after, and you now have a near-infinite source of food and drink that is only dependent on your storage capacity. You can feed like 100 dwarves with 1 guy just planting mushrooms. If you're worried about safety, put a door at the start of your fort and lock it when enemies come. The vast majority of them cannot do anything about this. Items that are difficult to acquire can just be traded for — you can request pretty much any item you could possibly want, and the game will bring it to you, meaning you can just ask for clothes, soap, instruments, armor, etc. With a crafting workshop and some stone you can produce any good for trading that you want and, with enough of it, buy out the whole trading cart. Most importantly, you don't need to do any of that to have FUN!Most most importantly, you don't have to learn it on ASCII glyphs and keyboard controls! I tried to pick up classic DF a few times and I honestly just couldn't. The Steam version is an absolute treasure with a beautiful, atmospheric soundtrack and ambience that could not be more fitting, not to mention the lovingly hand-crafted pixel art that somehow depicts DF's endless detail and brings it to life in all its glory. The game looks really good, honestly, and YOU CAN TELL WHAT'S GOING ON! Being able to see what's happening on screen through immediately-recognizable sprites and textures made learning the game a task I actually wanted to undertake. You could play it all with your mouse if you wanted to, which is really nice. As with its systems, Dwarf Fortress lets you familiarize yourself with the UI and keyboard shortcuts at your own pace. I now find myself playing in ASCII mode sometimes and enjoying it, and even wishing I could do more with the keyboard.Dwarf Fortress has quickly become my favorite game BECAUSE of its complexity. And I think the more that you play, the more you will appreciate that complexity, too. The infinite, procedural, unique, and entirely customizable worlds Dwarf Fortress creates are somehow consistent and coherent at the same time. Everything that happens in your Dwarf Fortress world happened for a reason. The people who come to reside in your halls are there because they heard about how well the place was doing from the outpost liaison who spread the news (same reason for the goblins). You can see that the dwarf chained up by your necromancer Queen for illegally selling copper goblets (adorned with dog bone and encrusted with turquoise cabochons) to the last caravan is coated in his own tears; you can see the remorse he feels for this in his thought page, as well as his admiration for the handiwork of the craftsdwarf who forged his chain. One of my favorite things is just having a library in the fort. Your dwarves will read, write, ponder, postulate, and produce actual pieces of work of varying length and quality. You can read about all the stories told, songs sung, and dances danced in your tavern as they're happening. All the descriptions, all the detail, and all the complexity create this endless array of possibilities, of distinct characters, circumstances, and playthroughs that you will undoubtedly remember.Somehow, Dwarf Fortress will have you anywhere from belly-laughing to teary-eyed over the fates and feelings of the handful of pixels — or even just the smiley faces — that represent your dwarves. And it got me to write this needlessly long review singing its praises when there are already thousands doing exactly the same. So, if for whatever reason you’ve read all this and haven’t done so already, just pick up the game and try it out. It could not be more worth the price.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't recommend this game yet. What I mean is the game is an absolute gem but it has some pretty glaring rough edges and until those are fixed I at least wont touch it. DF has a pretty steep learning curve and I have had to spend some time searching for answers that could have been included as tooltips or in-game accessable info. The multilayering z system is a genious idea but as of now its pretty hard to use for example if you want to make minecart haul routes or sometimes even basic stairs cause trouble. Raiding and military is pretty clunky since you can only order a squad to do something and not individual dwarves. Furthermore ordering anyone in particular to do anything is not possible which means that even most important tasks like raising drawbridges to protect from invaders will be done at an extremely leisurely pace. Furthermore if you order a squad to kill something or station them they wont immediately rush to do it. They will slowly trickle there as if It wasn't raining goblins.The game in some aspects is incredibly micromanage intensive but some aspects you cant control at all for example allowed spaces are possible to create as in the form of burrows but then again you cant order inhabitant to stay inside them at all which means when you get attacked half your civilians will run straight into enemies.The complete lack of any magic in an otherwise magical world where magical races like dwarves, elves, goblins and trolls live is also questionable, why cant I use/make/buy healing potions? Spells? Healing potions or some sort of cure would be pretty handy considering that werebeasts are everywhere and they will wreck your fortress by infecting everyone especially since quarantining is impossible because movement cant be restricted and because you don't have a good interface to keep tabs on your pops and quickly sort them.DF has many good aspects and features on which I wont elaborate because this isn't about praising the game I have already said that it has limitless potential. My "rant" is about the issues of the game which if addressed would surely make the game better.

_childDocuments_.review: It's like it casts a strange spell. At some points I felt aimless and what's even the point, but I realize that was my fault for not setting a personal goal and generating a very young world so no major external events really happened to force me to act. And thinking back on the things that did happen is somehow fascinating and makes me want to have another go.First and only fort (so far) - everyone's a strict vegan because I have not figure out how to make them butcher any animals in the pen (there were dozens grazing and birthing more), and the fisherdorf only brought back pond turtle shells (So.Many.Shells.Everywhere! One craftsdorf became REALLY good at making expensive shell crafts though).I wanted to dig as deep as I could, then find a path around the magma to reach the lowest layer.ALERT - all miners are MIA. I go to the layer - every bit they dug out is filled with magma, no corpses to be found, only some fire snakes swimming around ominously.And of course the usual someone goes crazy and murders a baby, every year at least one manages to not drink their water and dies, mayor mandates we do not export ballista bolts (even though we've never made any and no one's asked for them before), and someone got into a fey mood and created a magnificent artifact (coffin).There was an epic after action battle report between a stray dog and a bird (the dog charges and knocks it down, four times in a row, but the bird just kept getting back up, what a legend, but then it was no longer enraged and just flew off).Oh, and there's an elephant just roaming around the fort from day 1, never caused any issues, the most reliable constant in my life.

_childDocuments_.review: So here's my crazy Dwarf Fortress story, this is from DF2014 so I'm not sure it can be replicated anymore:So one of my megaproject forts was draining a volcano, and I had gated off all of the drains with floodgates so I could remotely turn on and off the flow. Was making last minute tweaks to the exit drain off the map (this was about 25z levels down). An elven caravan came by selling giant tigers, and I scrambled to buy a mating pair so I could create a massive army of trained giant war tigers because of course I did.Now giant tigers are carnivores so I couldn't leave them cooped up in their poor cages so I just let them roam free because literally NOTHING in that biome could even come close to harming them.As I continued smoothing the floor for the drain (not necessary just an aesthetic choice) I accidentally broke into the cavern below me and quicker than I could seal it up a cave troll broke through!Now I had no prepared militia that could even stand up to such a threat, so I retreated hoping to escape with my stoneworker's lives. The terrifying troll crushed one's skull in a single blow and began chasing after the others. After a few ticks it broke a floodgate holding the lava back, and as it ran down the wall it just kept breaking floodgate after floodgate. My two remaining stoneworker were running towards the stairs but I knew that no door in the fort could stop the howling regenerating menace bent on splattering my poor remaining workers.Suddenly out of the staircase, the female tiger sprang through the door and confronted the cave troll. I was hoping with all prayers to Armok that she would be strong enough to take out the menace. They traded blow after blow, knocking out teeth and crunching limbs. The poor tigress was getting the worst of it but she did not give up and kept the troll busy long enough for the lava to catch up with him. He died sizzling and she tried crawling away but was soon also lost to the hungry wall of liquid death. But she bought us time to close the door, and later crews would come in to obsidian cast and clear out the mess. That fort survived only due to the brave sacrifice of that beautiful giant tiger. I built a statue of solid bear fat soap in her honor (oldbeards know how sincere that is).I have played Dwarf Fortress in nearly every form since 2009 and it remains my most played game by hours by a LONG shot.There is so much richness and detail lovingly given to nearly every facet of this game, it is truly a work of passion by a very small group of incredibly talented and mad-in-the-most-beautiful-way individuals. To be honest, I prefer the non-steam version and am a lot faster in designing and designating that it's all muscle memory for me and most any feature can be used with three keystrokes. That said I bought this immediately when it became available because the Tarn and Zach deserve every penny for their life's dedication to such an amazing, deep, and constantly surprising title.11/10 would Embark again

_childDocuments_.review: I've been playing Dwarf Fortress on and off for over 10 years at this point and I have to say this release has been a dream come true for me.Pros:It's Dwarf Fortress!: It's the same amazing colony/city simulation that made the classic game great but with a fresh coat of paint in the form of actual graphics. The game play is deep and interesting and you can easily lose track of time playing it.Mouse support: While this sounds funny to those who haven't played classic, the addition of actual baked in mouse support has really opened up the game. With classic you were basically required to learn keyboard shortcuts to actually play the game.Cons:Mouse support: While it is great to be able to use a mouse to control the game, this has come at the cost of ripping out the shortcuts that you used to be able to use to navigate menus. If you are at risk of RSI you should keep this in mind.Map scrolling: it’s not smooth and that can be an issue for people that suffer from motion sickness.

_childDocuments_.review: Years ago I tried the classic version and it was just too much to learn all the ascii symbols and frustration level was too much, so I tried various graphical mods which definitely helped but all the mods that I tried were super clunky and I couldn't really get into the game with or without the mods.  I am a huge fan even though I never played the game very much previously, and an equally huge fan of Rimworld with over 1000 hours in it.  I wishlisted Dwarf Fortress the day Tarn announced it was coming to steam with actual graphics and was crazy excited to get into the game on a deeper level than I ever got to before.  The day it came out  of coursed I purchased it and started playing.  With my work schedule during the week I haven't been able to play that much but this weekend will be hunkered down and tethered to my PC.   So having only played about 16 hours at the time of this review I can say that I am absolutely blown away at the ease of play, and of course the graphics are awesome compared to ascii.  If you love base building, story generating, and management games then this is the literal granddaddy of them all and you really should give it a go.  Definitely do the tutorial which is pretty thorough on the basics of the game, but understand there will still be a lot to learn though trial and error because the depth of this game is unmatched by any game ever released.  While I love Rimworld enough to have put in over 1000 hours, Dwarf Fortress makes Rimworld seem like a shallow version of Dwarf Fortress in space.  That's not to criticize Rimworld as the devs state themselves it was heavily inspired by Dwarf Fortress.  Whats amazing is Rimworld has so many different events and things that can happen to your colony so when you are new to Rimworld it can feel overwhelming and you will lose your colony, but that is the fun of the game its a how long can you survive type game where you will absolutely lose no matter what its just a matter of how and when.  Dwarf Fortress is the same you will lose, just a matter of how and when.  Whats different between the 2 is Rimworld has 100 different ways you can lose your colony and Dwarf Fortress has by comparison about 10,000 ways you can lose your dwarfs/colony.  One thing I can say definitively Dwarf Fortress will be one of those games in my library that will join the 1000+ hours club.

_childDocuments_.review: A small introductory story: In my second fortress there was a dwarf that collected turtles in his room. He managed somehow to get elected as the fort mayor and as his first act as mayor, he cut off the leg of one of the fort's dogs. He then proceeded to start a collection of bones and animal corpses in his office. One day he decided to haul a whole barrel of beer and another barrel full of food into his office which enraged both the tavern and the inn keepers. He used the chopped off dog's leg to fend them off, took all of his clothes off and then stormed off into the distance, never to be seen again.This is by far the best game I have ever played.As a colony builder, Dwarf Fortress is one if not the most in depth colony (fortress) builder that has ever come into existence. You have to take into consideration every little detail to get your fort to sustain itself without the need to buy stuff from the seasonal visiting merchants. The game is amazing at generating stories and simulating history to a degree that is almost daunting to get into. It randomly generates everything when you are creating a new world. Literally everything. History, deities, religions, demons, artefacts, whole civilisations and relations between them. I really cannot put into words how in depth this game can get.On the other hand if you don't want to get neck deep into history and relations you can just create a colony and go from that, not caring about news from the world or anything. Just keep your dwarfs happy and intoxicated. The most important thing is that the game allows you to create your own fun. If you find it fun creating new fortresses all the time, get them to a point where the colony is easily self sustaining and move on to the next fort. You want to create a sprawling dwarven citadel and stay with it for years upon years, you can do that if your PC can handle hundreds of dwarfs with their own routines.There are many ways you can lose a fortress either by conquest or inner strife but it is always fun and part of the game, as advertised, losing is fun. Losing creates it's own stories and your world keeps on living, waiting for you to start the next fort. This game is simply amazing. Don't even think about it and just get it, it is 100% worth it.

_childDocuments_.review: In many ways, Dwarf Fortress is the Ur-example of an entire genre of games that may not have existed without its creation.  We have this game to thank for excellent titles like Rimworld, Oxygen Not Included, and I suppose more average but not necessarily terrible titles like Gnomoria, Clanfolk and Caves of Qud (though I haven't really played either of those last two, so your own mileage may vary).However, it must be said that being the primeval version of an entire genre of gaming does not necessarily mean it is the  version in all ways.  Older is not always better, and in many ways, Dwarf Fortress has been left behind by modern iterations of its genre.  The graphical edition on steam has made great strides to improving the UI of the game and make things more readable, but the underlying jank of the game is inescapable.  Playing this game after playing Rimworld unavoidably brings to mind minor frustrations that the Dwarf Fortress game engine has baked in - why is it impossible to build flooring unless there is nothing currently in that space?  Even a chair or door in the way will result in the game refusing to let you lay down flooring, and sometimes even dwarves (or kobolds, if you are using the mod) standing in the way can make construction plans suspend themselves.  Construction is also impossible in diagonals, so many times your fortress will build around a corner and then be unable to finish the wall because the corner piece of blocked off, requiring you to disassemble a wall, finish the corner, then rebuild a new wall.These are just small examples of QoL improvements that were added into newer iterations of the genre, but still haven't quite made it into Dwarf Fortress.  Selecting building materials is another such hassle, as there are DOZENS of types of wood and stone in the game, and each one appears on a list of material options.  Or you can just select 'pick nearest material' and watch a patchwork ugly floor and wall be constructed of 6+ different colored materials.  I don't necessarily blame the dev for this - as I understand, Tarn was a solo dev for over a decade on this game. And it was the first of it's kind, so props to that. However, I suspect that trying to comprehend and fix all the spaghetti contained within the code of this game would be enough to drive another poor soul mad.    What Tarn did wrong people were able to see and build better in later games, though.That being said, if you can work around the jank of the clumsy systems in the game, in many ways it has more complexity and depth than anything else the newer games manage.  What it lacks in polished systems and UI it more than makes up with in the scope of what is possible.  Where else can I build a fortress on the side of a volcano, dig deep underground and create a machine that, with the flip of a switch, floods the overworld with lava, melting those  into slag?  And should a forgotten monstrosity try to crawl from the depths into  fortress, they'll have to slither over half dozen fully armed traps stuffed with steel giant serrated blades.  More like forgotten , am I right?And there are many other delightful things you can discover hidden within the mechanics of the game.  Do you want your fortress to become a bastion of learning, where scholars and sages come from afar to peruse your vast library and pen their own tomes within it?  You can do that! Do you want to capture a dragon in a cage and use it to burn anyone who tries to enter your fortress?  I wouldn't recommend it, it will very likely go horribly, but technically it's possible!And that's really the core of the fun of Dwarf Fortress.  There are so many creative ways to manipulate this vastly complex game engine to see and do things you wouldn't have expected.  But the learning curve is very steep!  You will fail very often, and in ways that are more esoteric and frustrating that anything you would see in Rimworld.  Just wait until you have to deal with a werecreature plague that gets worse every full moon, an attacking bronze titan, or a loyalty cascade. Or you're going to discover what lies in store if you dig too deep!You're going to ♥♥♥♥ up and everyone is going to die, multiple times!  Over and over!  But every time you will learn from the experience, and the next time, you'll do better.  Unlike modern games, there is no difficulty settings.  The only gameplay setting is Dwarf Fortress (I mean, you can edit the world settings during generation I guess, but that's not going to do a lot to change the overall gameplay).That's why the mantra of this game has long been: Losing is Fun!Buy it now and experience it for yourself.  Do it.  And get the kobold mod, it's really cute.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm sure a lot of this can be chalked up to inexperience, but I was disappointed by Dwarf Fortress. With all the incredible reviews out there I expected more.  There were just so many frustrating things where I felt like something was missing or simply was too hard to find.  The biggest thing I felt was missing is that there was no way to prioritize construction projects. Especially in urgent situations (like an enemy attack) I couldn't put up emergency walls or anything.  I had thought the "Burrow" system was meant to be an emergency "get to a safe spot!" concept, but apparently not.  One of my first fortresses got attacked by a titan (some black elephant that breathed fire), and all of the dwarves just ran around dying like the world wasn't on fire.  I used the burrow system immediately when the titan was spotted, but 90% of the dwarves just ignored it. I don't see the point in the burrow system if you can assign dwarves to a safe burrow, but they ignore it and carry on with their day.  Also, the game performance was attrocious during the attack.  I bought my latest gaming PC a month ago with near top-of-the-line specs, and yet once the titan attacked the game turned into a slide show. How can it be so badly optimized that one titan attack can drop the FPS to <10?Yes, I know I can turn off Titans, but I feel like this type of thing could happen with any attacks. The dwarves with weapons don't go into defense mode or anything when the fortress is under attack.  They ignore it and go on with their farming, building, etc.  By the time the titan was dead, half the base was wiped out. I did not look forward to creating tombs and such for 60+ dead dwarves. I ended up just retiring the fortress.  The thought of starting over again is daunting, so I might take a break and come back to this game later.  I'm sure there are a lot of things I would do differently on the next time through.TLDR After spending 9+ hours in my first "successful" fortress, it got wiped out by a randomly generated Titan. The lack of direct control or any good "combat" mechanics meant I lost most of my dwarves and stored materials. I'm hoping at some point I can give this game another shot. Maybe next time I'll be able to flip this to a positive review.

_childDocuments_.review: Dwarf Fortress is unmatched in the realm of emergent storytelling. Because the dwarves have detailed descriptions, relationships, and forms of artistic expression, you can really get attached to them. The wildness of the game gives you enough ammunition to craft a satisfying narrative in your own head.     My one warning to people considering this game--which I highly recommend despite this caveat--is that Dwarf Fortress can be a bit janky. Some of the micromanagement elements can be fiddly. Ex: Early in my fort's life I have to disable cooking with alcohol so that my dwarves don't cook up all of our precious booze. However, the various booze types don't get added to the Kitchen tab of the Labor menu until you actually have booze of that variety in stock. This means you have to wait for a dwarf to make that kind of booze and then update the assignment before someone cooks with it or drinks it.I consider the level of jank to be completely manageable. There is a learning curve, but once you run a couple of fortresses into the ground, you get accustomed to the game, and build the next one stronger. Losing is FUN. Genuinely, some of the best stories will come from the fall of your fort. This is definitely a game where you don't want to savescum. Embrace the direction the game takes you, even if it leads to ruin.TL;DR I would highly recommend this game to anyone, despite it's flaws. If you can get over the learning curve and some of the more fiddly fortress management elements, you will unlock stories so compelling that you may never forget them. When it comes to emergent storytelling, few games generate tales as compelling as the ones you will create in Dwarf Fortress.

It feels as if there's potential here for something really cool and fun, but I'm really tired of feeling lost and clueless. The age of this game definitely shows in how unintuitive some of the mechanics seem to me, but that's the nature of the beast.

_childDocuments_.review: I heard about Dwarf Fortress maybe three years ago, therefore I had a lot of catching up to do. I then installed the Lazy Newb Pack and dived into the world of Dwarfs.After a friend of mine (who brought DF to my attention) told me that it is made by two guys and is ongoing since 2002, I started to read into the history of it and listened to the DF-Udpate-Podcasts that where made some time back. The more I read into the bug reports, ideas and functions the more I was in awe. I found a game that I never thought existed and it pulled me into a comfortable rabbit hole that I never wanted to leave.I then stopped playing it because I had no time for it, but I came back now and then just to see what was new and what the road map is. When I heard that it came to Steam, I immediately followed it on Steam and started to play again, and of course chuckled at the release date “Time is subjective”.I had to abandon it again because of time and had to focus on other things, then I got a notification that it released.I not even had to think about it, I bought it immediately and hoped to have time to play it a bit, I was just happy that the two brothers now can get the money they deserve. I know that a lot donated (me included) but a release on Steam hopefully gives them an even more stable income.So, there I was sitting Infront of my PC, downloaded it and thought: “Just take a quick look, see what’s new”. _childDocuments_.review: Dwarf Fortress is a captivating settlement-management game that immerses players in a world of procedural generation and rich storytelling. Here’s why it’s worth your attention:Procedural Depth: Dwarf Fortress drapes every piece of gameplay in layers of procedural simulation. From the moment you start, it builds an entire world for you1. The complexity lies not only in managing your dwarven colony but also in the intricate systems governing everything from mining to livestock management.Emergent Storytelling: As you guide your dwarves, you’ll witness bizarre and memorable events. Picture one-armed dwarven generals strangling ancient dragons or artisans crafting puzzleboxes of obsidian and bone after months trapped in caves. These emergent stories make each playthrough unique.Challenging Complexity: Dwarf Fortress isn’t for the faint-hearted. It demands research, planning, and a willingness to learn. The Steam release makes it more approachable, but it’s still a game that rewards dedication and curiosityIn summary, Dwarf Fortress is a masterwork of procedural mythmaking—a game that grows on you the longer you play. Dive into its depths, and you’ll discover a world unlike any other 🌟

_childDocuments_.review: Don't be fooled by the simple graphics. This is, by far, one of the deepest, most complex, most rewarding games you will ever play. The stuff going on underneath the hood of this game is ridiculous. So many times I've had to stop and say "Haha, what? That can happen?" Everything seems to have some sort of use and function that influences your world and how your dwarves behave in it. Bottom line: if you enjoy sims, city builders, rpgs, rts games then you should consider trying this one out. The original is free and has graphics mods but the learning curve is higher due to keyboard controls. But, it's a good place to try the game out. Personally, I think these guys made such a killer game, and gave it away for free, that I had no problem forking over $30 to support them. It is well-earned. Plus, this new version has made the game a lot less intimidating so it's a great place to start. Best part: WORKSHOP SUPPORT! Give it some time and I guarantee you are going to start seeing some awesome mods / content pop up in there.
