_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: 100x improvement in accessibility over the original. I have my gripes, but that doesn't mean I'm not having fun.I will now proceed to ramble about some of those gripes, with the disclaimer that I could just be wrong about some of these details or simply having a skill issue. I originally wrote these around the original release, and am in the process of going back to edit this review more positively now that I'm getting back into the game and finding that several of my old complaints have been addressed! So, keep up the good work devs!Random gripe 1: (Need to test a bit more next time I get in a fight, but I think this is still accurate)Combat goes by fast. The game includes a button for advancing a single frame. That button does NOT work while the combat log is open. If you want to advance combat frame-by-frame, something that appears commonly desired from my skimming, you currently have to:Close the combat log, Advance a frame, Reclick the notification that combat has started, Reclick the button to show the right creature's combat log, Then scroll back to the bottom to see maybe something new has happened.Also you can't unpause in certain menus and this is one of them, so afaik yeah this is kinda awkward.Gripe 2: (Definitely skill issue, but I still think this could be better)I understand that there appears to be a system where manager dwarves are required for exact count stock of items, that's pretty neat. But why is the only way to find out which furniture buildings you even have available to place, to try placing them and then get an error? Experienced players will set up production for these at some personally comfortable levels and take it in stride that large construction projects need to be arranged far ahead of time with manual work orders, and after playing for a bit I can understand it. But for new players having some options grayed out with a "0", with others having a "~10" or whatever, would explain this whole mechanic INSTANTLY without any text required. Also just much more usable for trying to see how your current stock of those items is without looking for them individually in the massive stocks list.Gripe 3(Rainbows are cool but I wanna know what they mean!):The game uses color coding in basically every screen to indicate various things, sometimes obvious and sometimes not. Job titles are colored to group similar together(Blue - Fishing, Lime - Animal Care, etc), which makes sense. Most players looking at the menu listing all jobs will immedialy understand that classification and its wonderful. But then for example you open the trade menu, and some items are colored gold, while others are white. Apparently the distinction is for which items were produced at your settlement vs. imported? Most things in the game being color coded is nice, but only when there's some way to understand which colors indicate important distinctions, which are mostly cosmetic, and what the alternative colors might indicate. Same goes for all the symbols that item names can acquire to indicate their quality/forbidden/dead/whatever history. Cool as hell in theory tho. This is a pretty minor criticism, just something I thought of early on while playing and struggling to understand the UI. The color jumped out as "Oh this might indicate something important", but didn't actually, and made learning the interface harder rather than easier.Gripe 4(Workers go brrr):Work labor setup is also somewhat clunky compared to Rimworld. You start with a set of presets that cover some absolute basics and have custom icons. But then for the overwhelming majority of EVERY OTHER task in the game, you have at most 8 repeating non-descriptive icons to play with. Want to know what task Urist McSucksAtFarming is doing? Well he has a III, a VI, and an I beside his name. I sure hope you like frantically scrolling up and down and clicking around to try figuring out what this single dwarf is actually even doing with his life. When you have <20 this isn't too bad, but this is a game with a default pop cap of 200 so I'm kinda dreading getting to the level of having to organize that many workers.Compare this to rimworld, where at a glance you can not only look at a single worker and immediately look across their row to see what they do, you can also pick a column and look down through the entire column to see if they currently have workers that do them.DF only has the equivalent of looking at individual columns, you have to MAKE the column yourself by grouping together tasks, and then that column is indicated by an entirely random roman numeral outside of the interface. There are already community made icon packs, but to my knowledge all you can do is replace the existing 8? If this system was combined with the equivalent icon-generator/picker used for burrows it could actually be really cool tho, ngl.In summary:This is a game that has been largely playable over the past many years on the back of a dozen different quality of life mods to enable easier management of the base systems. And despite these gripes the game really has(after a rockier start) done a decent step towards rectifying that.Just please make it so the interface for something as crucial as "Make dwarfs do tasks" doesn't feel like the equivalent of developer placeholder art.Original ending:I'm not going to give up on the game yet of course, and I am glad that the game is finding massive success. But hopefully feedback like this can be used to make the game reach an even greater level of quality!Edit a year later:I didn't give up on the game, and it didn't give up on me <3Honestly I'm still kinda confused with some of the smaller elements that are missing, but a lot of those are more weird design quirks/bugs rather than the gamechanging problems I was originally concerned about. For example, there seem to finally be in-game options for customizing the alert system! I originally said that exclusion was the one main reason I had wrote the review so negatively, so with that out of the way I can take out half the review and it's suddenly a positive review! YippeeeeeeeeeAlso just for posterity thanks to the 44 helpfuls/2 funny on the scathingly negative(but still hopefully constructive) older version of this review. You will now be banished.

Murhpy's Laws are the unshakeable cornerstone of the reality.3. It is absolutely viable to place whole fortress with 200 dwarves on one (1) ☼Elf Tallow Soap Pillar☼4. Lava is the ultimate answer to any problem, challenge or question.5. Casually dropping prisoners down  a 100m shaft into the busy tavern is the best way to harden the fragile dwarven psyche.6. Dwarves are obedient. If a bag with a snatched, yet rescued kid inside is by default set to {Forbidden} then after few weeks the dwarves will notice a kid is missing and fortress will be haunted.7. Occasionaly, if you ask your manager to issue working orders, he might decide to climb a tree and die of dehydration there. Only solution: lumberjack (or lava).8. Flying creatures might give birth mid-air, leading to randomly splattered organs across the map. 9. Never produce lead or gold bins, barrels or any carriable containers.10. If your fortress gets flooded with way too many visitors, then grapeshotting the tavern with a minecart loaded with axe blades is perfect solution. (Lava works too).11. Dwarven skulls are made out of crêpe paper which might get shattered by web falling on top of their head, or a child throwing a blueberry (if the child is proficient in throwing of course).12. Turning into a werewagon kills your adventurer when you move, with a very ominous closing caption: you have been scuttled.13. It is possible for dwarves to get so fat, that the very act of eating in their case slows down time-continuum.14. If 12 legendary dwarves fought a dragon, but the last, killing blow has been dealt by a frightend, cornered cow, then the cow in question will not only earn a Nom de Guerre but majority of your artworks for the next 20 years will have cattle striking menacing poses in them.15. There is a 50% chance that your freshly elected mayor is, in fact, a vampire.16. There are no sieges, but Goblin Christmas! Given proper, creative treatment of merchants, one can also organize Human or Elf Christmas.17. What is worse than a dwarf on fire? A thirsty dwarf on fire, that just beelines toward the tavern with an alcohol stockpile.18. It is not possible to place multiple items on the same pile, unless you tell the dwarves to dump them.19. Best door is a raised drawbridge. Best catapult is a drawbridge getting raised. Best atom smasher is the drawbridge getting lowered.20. Goku trained and fought for ages to obtain the Dragon Balls. _childDocuments_.review: It's Dwarf Fortress.If you haven't heard of it, search youtube, search old lets plays. This game is old as hell but keeps iterating on itself. The 'simulator' aspect of it is insanely detailed to the point where weird emergent properties have happened. Here's an example for the unfamiliar:Cat Colony collapse///After an update (before steam version), suddenly cats started dying left right and center in people's colonies. When dwarves adopt a cat, they don't like their cats dying, many tantrums and colony collapses followed.When troubleshooting the bug, players isolated it to the point at which they had built their first Tavern.Turns out: when dwarves got a higher priority assignment mid-drink, they'd just toss their cup to the floor, spill beer all over, and run off to the job. Cats are programmed to lick themselves to clean themselves. Cats were cleaning so much booze off their fur that they were dying of alcohol poisoning. Adding in the ability for cats to pass out when they take in near-lethal amounts of booze and sleep it off was the bug fix.This game is ridiculous.

_childDocuments_.review: I usually don't write reviews but here goes. I've played many hours on the classic version and have recently put a bit of time into this steam version.To put it frankly, this game is very buggy and in a lot of ways a step back from the original version. It frustrates me that despite it's price this game lacks basic functionality you would simply expect, and very critical game features are seemingly broken and have been for years with no fix in sight. To list a few: - You can't rebind hotkeys. Many of the things which had hotkeys in the old version are now mouse only (meaning I can't play this in bed anymore).- Many menus are missing a search feature meaning you'll be doing things like scrolling through a list of 100+ dwarfs trying to find the right one to add to your squad. Oh, and after you add a dwarf it resets you back to the top of the list so you'll have to scroll all the way back to where you where.- There is no way to sort you dwarfs by anything but name, occupation or stress. Hope you like checking all your dwarfs individually to try to find one with a certain skill, or traits, or looking for injured dwarfs, or dwarfs who are hungry / thirsty, or dwarfs who don't have required equipment, etc. - For some reason, your military just won't pick up their gear. I lost a Legendary + 5 hammer dwarf to a beast because despite being in a squad with a required steel hammer, and having a steel hammer allocated to him, he just never picked up his weapon. Archers don't pick up ammo.- You now must have time paused to see the combat logs, meaning to read about a fight as it's happening you have to open the alert, scroll down, read the bottom, exit the menu, press play for a few seconds, pause again, open the alert, scroll all the way down, repeat.Now despite all these problems which are, in my opinion, pretty ridiculous given the price, I would still recommend this game to the right type of person. Dwarf Fortress is a game which heavily relies on players to make their own fun by coming up with stories about their dwarfs, getting invested and watching the simulation unfold. Because the game relies so much on the player getting themselves invested, rather than attempting to hook them with interesting gameplay or a page-turning story, it doesn't really matter that it's broken and tedious. I didn't buy this game, my friend gifted it to me. He did that because he isn't a masochist and didn't want to actually suffer through playing it like me, but he did want to hear the story of my fortress, and watch the crazy things that happen in it unfold. There is truly no other game I have ever experienced that can offer what Dwarf Fortress does, so for that it gets my recommendation.

If you can even call something an improvement when it wasn't really there in the first place. Playing with mouse, properly? fantastic.  The sound design is great but a little repetitive and gnawing.  My only gripes are the removal of a few skills that some people argue the game is better without. (it probably is) Is it worth the price tag? _childDocuments_.review: This review hurts to write. I have been playing this game on an off since the 2d era. Each time I would get overwhelmed by the number of bugs get frustrated and quit. This was fine for a passion project released for free by a single developer. But this is now a commercial game. Some of the bugs are 14+ years old at this point. Traders get stuck on the map, the broker refuses to trade, dwarves will get stuck in a socialization/drinking loop, buckets get stuck in wells. The game is filled with complex subsystems that are all about 80% compete. Meanwhile the developer is off working on adventure mode. The bugs will never get fixed stop asking. The UI is terrible, you can't click on dwarves names to bring up information about them, it's just a random list of names most times. Dwarves all have two names, in the justice menu it uses one name, in the alert and labor menu it is a totally different name. The game actively hides information you need and requires external tools like DF hack to play. Fans of the game will point to the wiki and the pages of convoluted workarounds developed over the years to get around the bugs, but it gets to the point where you are mostly bug fixing a collapsing fortress and not really playing the game. This game is amazing in it’s scope, but it may end up being known for the games in inspired.

_childDocuments_.review: Borag the fruit gatherer was good at his job and loved it.  One day, he climbed into a tree and was savagely attacked by a giant grey squirrel.  He fought the squirrel off, but fell to the ground, shattering his left leg.  Alone and unable to walk, he slowly bled to death and died.His corpse remained where he fell, untouched for some time.  It rotted away, leaving behind only bones and the clothing he once proudly wore.   For years, nobody claimed his remains for burial.  And it pissed him off.Borag rose from the dead a vengeful ghost.  He would strike at his former guild-mates when they least expected it, always going for and often severing their left legs.  With each grievous wound inflected, he grew stronger and stronger.  His taste for blood reached a fever pitch when he killed the baron's 3rd child.Finally realizing what had to be done, a memorial was carved in remembrance of Borag the fruit gatherer.  After maiming a dozen dwarfs and killing the baron's heir, he was finally put to eternal rest.Losing has never been so fun.
_childDocuments_.name: Dwarf Fortress

_childDocuments_.review: This is exactly what I was looking for in an enhanced Dwarf Fortress release.   The new UI and mouse support are game changers, and make the game way more intuitive and enjoyable to play for the average player.  The soundtrack is fantastic, and I really like the new sprites.  If you're curious about Dwarf Fortress, now is the perfect time to dive in and try it.
_childDocuments_.name: Dwarf Fortress

_childDocuments_.review: 4/14 After 300 hours of gameplay I can still say I'm addicted as hell. There are some bugs random crashes and laggy save processes but after 300 hours I still can't stop playing the game. I made sure to circle back and edit my review as I see it's fit. I'll be changing my thumbs down to a thumbs up because like I stated below the game is great, but losing hours of gameplay due to unexpected crashes really killed my soul. There's a few things I've done to semi stop crashes and make saving a bit faster leaving less room for crashes and or the game getting hung up. Work still needs to be done, but this game is great.3/21Stay away till they fix this game. Buried under all the positive comments are people who have the game crash for NO reason. You could run this game on a phone with the spec needed and my computer is a high end rig, but this game crashes for ZERO reason, and when it crashes you lose your progress. Start up again, play for a little and the game shuts again. I tried all the work arounds "Verify your files, go in the exe and change the compatibles, change the resolution, and so on and so forth" nothing works. The sad part about all this is I played 28 hours, I'm addicted but I can't play longer than 30 minutes before I lose progress and it kills me. I hope they fix this because this game is addicting as hell and I love it, but in the same breath, I want to toss my computer off the wall when I spend like 40 mins making something, the game crashes and I need to build things over again. For the price this game is asking, I would wait off on it till they fix this problem. Is the game good? Yes! Is THE STATE OF THE GAME worth 25 bucks? Not unless you're sadistic and love to be miserable. Feel free to send me fixes that let me play longer than 1 hour or so, and I'll change my review. Till then. Hard nope!New Bug Found : If for some reason you're playing in window mode, hit F11 and make it full screen, you can no longer tab back into the game, the game will just be running in the back with zero way to resume, initially forcing you to hard exit the game, and lose progress.
_childDocuments_.name: Dwarf Fortress

_childDocuments_.review: Undeniably charming and deeply addicting. I first heard about the game on the Noita discussions page and decided to check it out, saw that this version was coming to Steam and wishlisted immediately.I haven't even started producing metal yet but had to abandon a few forts as I came to grips with farming and appointing nobles. My current fort doesn't want for food, but I need to find a way to generate or find some mud underground before the drink supply dries up.The worlds you generate all being unique adds a ton to the replay value and I can see myself losing thousands of hours just creating storied forts. The level of detail is honestly borderline insane. Recent updates have mostly been QoL upgrades and that's a super exciting prospect given the nature of the game.If you like life sim games this is probably the best I've played to date since it actually managed to hook me. Just be ready to lose before you get a fortress going good and proper. Make sure to read the tutorial on your first run or two and there's zero shame using the wiki or looking up a playthrough just to come to grips with the core features.Leave no dwarf behind!
_childDocuments_.name: Dwarf Fortress

_childDocuments_.review: There are games where the fun is handed to you on a platter and a helpful waiter places it in your mouth spoonful by spoonful.Dwarf Fortress is a game where you must go into the woods, at night, in a snowstorm, and extract the fun from the bark and the dirt as wolves nip at your heels. For some, this is perfection.10/10, would dig too deep again.
_childDocuments_.name: Dwarf Fortress

_childDocuments_.review: It definitely has its flaws in terms of quality of life, additionally it has a fairly steep learning curve. But after failing a bunch of times and getting the hang of it, this is a very fun, sometimes crushing and yet rewarding game with rich lore. I'm very keen to see what the modding community does with this game now that it has come to the workshop, with bringing QOL improvements!
_childDocuments_.name: Dwarf Fortress

_childDocuments_.review: This review is to discuss the main differences to the interface between this version and the old. Firstly, with the new scheme and graphical improvements, it is much easier to learn the game than previously. Besides the graphical improvements, the changes to the labor interface have made assigning tasks easier to manage, as generally dwarfs can do any job now unless restricted, when previously it was the inverse. This does mean that it is more difficult to micro-manage them, however. At the present time, there do not seem to be readable combat logs, which aren't strictly necessary, but do add in the process of learning the game and in storytelling.Finally, most of the hotkeys have been changed, which means I have to re-learn that part of my muscle-memory or rebind everything.That said, these are more of minor annoyances for me rather than flaws and will probably only be relevant to you if you're a returning player. It is still one of the best and highest-detailed games I have ever seen and I recommend trying it if you're interested.
_childDocuments_.name: Dwarf Fortress

_childDocuments_.review: After knowing about this game for 5+ years but never being able to get over the hurdle of the interface in the original, I'm so incredibly stoked to finally actually be able to play Dwarf Fortress and experience the kinds of ridiculous and amazing stories that this game is capable of generating. I imagine this must be what it's like when someone with very poor eyesight finally puts on glasses for the first time.This is one of the most remarkable video games (if you wanna call it that) of all time and this release finally lets so many more people see that.
_childDocuments_.name: Dwarf Fortress

_childDocuments_.review: I've been playing this since about 2007 and still find it incredible. This is the most important computer game of the last two decades. It has influenced and shaped a huge amount of other games, and has even redefined what games are. It is, quite literally, a work of art. It was displayed in the Museum of Modern Art as a piece of art. I have had the "are computer games art?" debate with some of my more refined artistic friends and it was great to always have this as an example of what computer games can be, and just how furious it can make someone who is more at home with oil paints and sculpture to have to admit that it is. You know you've done something right when it hits a nerve in that way. Thank you Tarn and Zach for bringing so much joy and wonder to the world!

_childDocuments_.review: So a gigantic roc bird as large as a dragon landed near my fortress and I called on the militia, bravest sons of LulledBlockades, to defend the fort. Two of the less experienced ones turned up, the others never did for some reason. The roc killed them both, but the second to die was a necromancer.Before the necromancer died he resurrected the largest remaining part of the first dwarf, his left arm. The medical screen on the bio of his arm described it as unable to breath, ability to stand lost, ability to grasp somewhat impaired.At this point a gigantic mob of dwarf children boiled out of the fort entrance and slowly collectively beat the monstrous bird to death with their bare child hands while a guineahen grasped it by the head and shook it around in defiance of all physics.Strike the earth!

_childDocuments_.review: Less of a game, and more of a fantasy world simulation.  There is no win condition, so the game goes on until you inevitably fail in some spectacular and memorable way.  Every playthrough, even on the same world, is different from the last.  There is a really high replay value here.  You could spend years playing Dwarf Fortress, and still not come across everything possible in it.  The game is somewhat hard to get into at first, but there is plenty of tutorial information online, as well as built into the game iteslf.

_childDocuments_.review: I never played the original, so this is a review from a casual new player.Pros:1. It is an innovative simulation game with more depth that its competitors (Rimword, Honey I Joined a Cult, Prison Architect and many others)2. It has a series of Hotkey binds that allow you to quickly and seamlessly traverse their UI3.  2 Very heartfelt developers who truly care about a product that they produced and continuously have been updating it over many years.4.  Interesting storytelling moments VIA generated events and history (which has fueled many reviews).5.  Multi-depth universe built into a 2D plane in a polished manor.6. The game incentives mods which help refine and add more content to the game7. I have not noticed any bugs in my 30+ hrs of playing.Cons:1. No real attachments to the individual dwarfs when your population hits 100+ its hard to keep track and micromanage everyone.2.  Hard to learn.  Many times I found myself on the wiki for dumb things like, "How to destroy a rode" or, "How do I add members to a squad"3.  The individual sprites could use some additions. For example, squads should have more banners, custom work details you should be able to make a logo for, and more variety in different dwarf looks.Overall, It is a solid game I highly recommend if you enjoy simulation building games.

_childDocuments_.review: I love dwarf fortress, I used to play the ASCII version a long time ago and decided that I would try this version out because I've just kind of been a slump for games to play.  The presentation for the game is definitely improved over the original version, and the interface is much less clunky compared to the game I played 6-10 years ago.  However there are little issues with this version that make it impossible for me to recommend this version, the biggest one being that I can't assign ammunition to my crossbow dwarfs unless I use the built in archer uniform,  there is more search "Steam Dwarf Fortress Issues" on Reddit to get a more complete list.  The issue with the ammunition has been around for at least 2 months now it seems, and it feels like being able to make your dwarfs use crossbows would be a fairly high profile issue to fix quickly.  I put 60 hours into this version of the game over the last few weeks and I think I'm just going to download Masterwork Dwarf Fortress and play this game how I used to. _childDocuments_.review: It's the same massive and enthralling game of dwarves and their tales of triumph and treachery, but with a vastly improved and more accessible UI, a beautiful soundtrack, and a really wonderful graphics overhaul. _childDocuments_.name: Dwarf Fortress

_childDocuments_.review: Dwarf fortress is something truly special. When I was in high school I remember learning about dimensions and wormholes in a way that was always described a species of 2 dimensional being called flatlanders. These flatlanders existed in an entirely 2 dimensional existence and could only see infinitely small slices of a 3 dimensional reality surrounding them. The complexity and level of depth this game has can only be properly described as utterly absurd. I finally understand what it is like to BE that flatlander, only seeing a small slice of the massive existence this game is played within.I recommend this game in absolutes. Of all the colony sim games I have played this one absolutely shines at the very top. The game is now easy enough to get into, with a level of complexity that you will never feel limited by the mechanics of the game. There is always something new to try, and the only limiting factor is your own imagination. It can be intimidating at first, but if you have the patience to go through the tutorials and experiment, you will master the game's basics in no time.
_childDocuments_.name: Dwarf Fortress

_childDocuments_.review: This game has acquired mythological status but if you take a sober look at it and not like the inebriated drunk dwarves who cannot get through the day without booze you will see it leaves a lot to be desired. I’ve seen fans of this game reason that the infuriatingly obtuse ui is part of its charm and that losing wouldn’t be as fun with a clear, accessible interface - you know, one that does not look like it was made by 2 amateurs in a basement in the nineties.  I hope the devs will spend part of their millionaire proceeds to hire a competent ui crew that can actually bring this game up to par with modern standards. By, for instance, using clear fonts and colors and all the ui tricks there are to present information in an accessible way. Because every piece of information in this game right now has the same weight.If this is done intentionally to sort of gatekeep this game for… masochistic reasons? then I know for sure this “game” is made for a certain type of (inebriated) masochist.Also, the fabled storytelling in this game could use a bit fo a reality check. X does Y in Z does not equal magnificent storytelling. 1000 lines of X does Y in Z does not create a story by itself. Story is about motives, obstacles and characters wanting things but being thwarted in their desires. “The chicken laid an egg on Tuesday” is not much of a story. “The cat scared the chicken and then it didn’t lay an egg on Tuesday” is the beginning of a story. Every time I start a fortress I have 7 dwarves with a wagon. Why do they start their fortress? What is their motivation? I don't know, it's the same every time. You know, a game like Stardew Valley, made by one person btw in 4 years (!), has a better grasp of what storytelling is. A boy inherits a piece of farmland from his grandfather, moves into his dilapidated house and then starts on a adventure by getting to know the village community. Yes the comparison is not fair, these games are wildly different, I know that. But at least there's an arc here. Every time I hear a fan about their “fun” DF story it is some dwarf got mad/vampire/werebeast or some giant bird/xxx/xxx/ attacked and killed their fortress. Wooptido. Well, violence does not equal a great story in my book. Having fight logs that go on and on and on about tendons that tear and spines that break and organs that gush - is that actual storytelling or obsessively detailed pathology? I’m not sure. Yes the world building is impressive, it tracks the alcohol dwarfs spill on paws of cats and the specific teeth that get knocked out during a brawl - sure, I can recognize it as some sort of maniacal form of art in itself. But as for my experience (I played only two hours but watched dozens and dozens of hours with different streamers to understand the “magic” of this game) with this actual 2022 steam game, there is little enjoyment to be had. I could go on about many other things, like the jarring blinking sprites that represent movement, the workshops all being 3x3 tiles that look the samish, no torches, lighting or braziers (apparently dwarves can see in the pitch dark but I could not find that piece of info anywhere in this gem of “realism”), and a general lack of making something impressively dwarfish (some random statues that look complete unepic), but I just leave it here. Please don’t take this review too seriously. If you are having fun, bless you. I exaggerate because I have a feeling everyone is exaggerating in their insanely hyped up reviews of this game. It’s mostly for balance, and genuine bewilderment why people are liking this game so much. I am willing to grant Dwarf Fortress a 10 for its legendary status, but no way this actual steam version of a game deserves a 10 - or a 96% approval rate imo. If I give the world building & ambiance a 9, the storytelling a 7 and the UI a 3, it’s somewhere around a 6. Fair enough from my perspective.

_childDocuments_.review: I found out what happened to the Dwemer.My fortress gets raided, I call everyone inside behind the drawbridges. _childDocuments_.review: Dwarf Fortress has always been a great game. Now it has graphics and an GUI. While that GUI is still as convoluted as the game logic always has been and may not seem as straight forward as one would at first glance expect, that is just how dwarf fortress has always been. But now you can click on stuff and its just way easier on new people. And under those sometimes unintuitive but endearing systems is one of the best games of all time.
_childDocuments_.name: Dwarf Fortress

_childDocuments_.review: A simulator of a dwarvish civilization, I guess it's a game, but it's a weird hodgepodge of simulator, narrative generator, city builder, and adventure game. The version on Steam is in some ways a step forward and others a step back.The interface is overall improved from the older versions. There are some regressions though. The game does seem to run better than previous versions, but it still becomes a slog on large maps with large histories.If you decide to pick this up, make sure to pick up the free mod DFHack from the Steam Workshop. It creates workarounds for many of the annoyances.I have 500 hours in it as I write this, it's easily paid for itself in entertainment.
_childDocuments_.name: Dwarf Fortress

_childDocuments_.review: I've played this game since I was a child and have likely put in a few thousand hours in my lifetime. I haven't touched the game in years, but seeing all of the QOL changes and the tileset brought me back in. I'd likely have paid the money without getting a fancy version of the game, so this edition is just gravy on top. Thank you for all of the memories, and one of the greatest games of all time Toady and Threetoe
_childDocuments_.name: Dwarf Fortress

_childDocuments_.review: Buys brand new $1500 gaming rig. Plays Dwarf Fortress.  Imagine if developers were still this good.  I wouldn't have to pretend to like Gotham Knights.Alright here are my real thoughts.  Tbh, I find this game to be quite intuitive. I've tried to play Rimworld like 3 times and Rune Factory a few.  Gave Stardew Valley a fair chance.  Nothing ever clicked with those games.  They said they were open world.  Said I could do whatever I wanted.  Said my play through would be special. But in the end, they were all on rails.  Get this, go there, do that, find some ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ so you can continue some throw away story that's just filler making you grind so can do the things you really wanted to do in the first place.  I hated them for it.  Because I always knew there was a way that I could love a game like that.  A game that actually lived up to its promises by a thousand miles.  Dwarf Fortress is that game.  Failure is going to be my only tutorial for a long long time.  Everyone that suggests watching videos and reading Wiki before even starting is doing you a disservice.  Just start playing.  Start failing.  Like the game says Losing is Fun.   When things do seem overwhelming, just do one thing.  Think of one thing.  Figure out how to do it.   I guarantee you'll have a more rewarding introduction.  There are in-game help sections you can reference as well.  Just figure out what you're trying to do.  Not what the game is telling you to do.  Kudos to the developers for a wonderful life long passion project.  I'm in awe and can't wait to put my first thousand hours in.
_childDocuments_.name: Dwarf Fortress

_childDocuments_.review: It is painful to write the negative review for the game I once loved and spent hundreds of hours playing when all put together over the years.  Any time I started to play original DF again I had to go through daunting process of relearning how to play so I appreciate changes  just an hour of play I have encountered bugs that make me really disappointed.That game was always buggy and I remember browsing internet looking for solutions but that was the past.There are different standards now and more expectations. So that overwhelmingly positive reviews might soon go through reality check with enticed newcomers that will not be as forgiving.
_childDocuments_.name: Dwarf Fortress

_childDocuments_.review: I recommend this game with a large caveat. The game takes more than a bit of time to learn and the best way to learn how to play the game are tutorial videos. They help you learn the basics and then you have to rely upon the old adage "losing is fun" as something usually goes wrong or you reach a point where you're done with the fort.The fact the world continues and evolves as you play is one of the more amazing things. One of the things I've wanted to do a lot is just play 1 continuous world over a long period of time but the thing that keeps me away from doing that is just available time. You can generate a lot of worlds with interesting lore without much work.One other bad part is you kind of need to apply your own story to the game. Stories happen but you somewhat have to investigate and tie things together in that very human way. The game does a lot of simulation and you need to be the one to connect the dots and understand the larger picture as the different puzzle pieces interlock and come together.Overall, I recommend the game because of the infinite joy I've had as well as the joy they keep bringing with updates over many many years. The only problem is that it is complicated and takes more than a bit to start understanding the game and that understanding is almost always done better with outside materials like the wiki or youtube videos.
_childDocuments_.name: Dwarf Fortress

_childDocuments_.review: I've found that my own incompetence when it comes to managing a fortress has ended runs faster than any raid or giant monster ever could. _childDocuments_.review: Been playing Dwarf Fortress for over 10 years since I was in highschool, even when the graphics were just ASCII. Just by the details of each world, the amount of ways you can play this game makes it worth thousands upon thousands of hours of content. If you've played Adventure Mode you know what I mean.
_childDocuments_.name: Dwarf Fortress

_childDocuments_.review: Absolute downgrade.  The interface is horrid, the keybindings are obtuse,  The menus have ZERO design to them, so you can't tell what layer you're on or navigate backwards.  You have to cancel and redo.  You have to click through these menus half a dozen times to do one thing, then over again as you can not place or make work orders in multiples.  You can't tell when the game is paused, please change the music or add more visible indications.  The keybind menu is so smashed and cluttered you can't tell what keys are for what.  Mouse scroll is reversed.  Autosaves are not working.  Resolution scale does not change unless you restart, unplayable at 4k.  Scaling options are ridiculously complicated.Basically everything you would expect from a quality of life standpoint just doesn't exist.  There are no animations in the menus, the scaling is ugly.  Creatures still snap with no animation so movement is impossible to follow.  Menus cover menus.  The tutorial is broken because you can not get behind the menu to see the lesson.  It's also wrong, asking you to click an accept button that does not exist.This is ridiculously bad.  The original game WITH the keyboard controls is easier to use and has a less obtrusive UI.  Dude, why didn't you hire a designer?  Not worth 30$ for a skin that makes the game more difficult to play.  Why on Earth does it not just play like any RTS that's been released for 20+ years?  If Rimworld had the complexity of DF, I'd never play DF again.  JUST to avoid the migraine of these ridiculous controls and UI issues.Why would I play this?  Why did I spend $30 on this garbage when FREE DF + Stonesense not only looks better, but plays better?
_childDocuments_.name: Dwarf Fortress

_childDocuments_.review: Idk if it's just me but with how "unpolished" every game coming out is I expected this to work rather flawlessly and with little frustration with boasting about "decades" of development but i cant even connect stairs to each other so instead I'm left with this nagging suspicion that these indie devs just don't know wtf they are doing and want steam workshop modders to make all the new and original content for their games for them while they sit back and absorb other people's ideas into the base game and not do much and it's just kind of a sickening feeling really...because I see more hype than hope I'm rating negative. Also i was refused a refund even though i had about 2 hours playtime and 18 hours of letting the game run while googling simple things like how to plant a seed so many lessons learned here for me...all anyone involved in product sales wants is your money it isn't about anything else.

_childDocuments_.review: Dwarf Fortress is, and I don't usually like to throw this label around, a masterpiece, and a true marvel of software engineering. At its core, it's a game that procedurally generates and simulates a full fantasy world, from facets as broad as whole civilizations down to the unique personalities of individual peasants. You take the role of a modest group of dwarves which seek to strike out and forge a community in this generated world. The game was once too niche to recommend to the average gamer. It used to be broadly impenetrable, with a confusing UI controlled by a mind-numbing amount of arguably nonsensical keybinds. But now, with this Steam release, the game has been brought closer to modernity. It can still be rough around the edges when compared to its new peers in the colony sim genre, but easy to wrap your head around. Any friction remaining is a symptom of the game's mind-boggling complexity under the hood. For a piece of software as intricate as Dwarf Fortress, it's nothing short of a miracle that the game could have improved as much as it did while keeping so much of it intact.There were casualties over the jump to Steam, however. Adventurer mode, one of the most memorable gaming experiences I've ever had is woefully missing from this release. I completely understand why this is the case. It wasn't even close to finished, or up to the standard of similar wide-scale roguelike games. Its presence would be confusing to new players. But I seriously miss the crazy in-depth wrestling system.Fortress mode itself has a few idiosyncrasies, itself also being "unfinished". Dwarf Fortress might have been called "Early Access" were it from an era where the term was popular. The game has been moulded slowly over the course over the last twenty years by just two guys. Many pieces of the game had to be left behind, promised to be returned to, and whose day has yet to come again. So, there are a lot of vestigial, unfinished, and/or useless features that remain in the game to this day. Absolutely none of them get in the way, however. All of the odd little bits fade invisibly into the background, and only make the game more interesting when you notice them or look for them.As I briefly mentioned, even Dwarf Fortress has the occasional spot of friction. Out of fairness, otherwise this review would be sickeningly positive, I'll only talk about the one that bothers me the most (which isn't much, really). When you set out into the world, or 'embark' with your Dwarves, it's hard to know what kind of place you're getting into. This is a really good thing if you're a new player, and don't know what to expect, but if you're looking for somewhere really precise, like an evil biome that has the very specific random trait of passively reanimating corpses into zombies (so cool), you have to spend far too long generating worlds and embarking over and over, just hoping to get lucky. The randomness of the world, while it can create incredible emergent moments, and makes no two fortresses the same, also makes it pretty much impossible to get something a little more controlled and specific short of getting a seed from another player.Dwarf Fortress is probably the single most technologically impressive game ever made. How fun and addictive it is on top of being such a marvel almost brings a tear to my eye. This is one of those really important games, and it brings me nothing but joy that it's become accessible so I can recommend it to anyone who's interested. It's my personal game of the year for 2022. What an achievement.

_childDocuments_.review: Interesting game with a lot of details. The user interface has a lot of potential for improvement though and it is quite cumbersome to use at times. I understand this might be a sensitive topic since this game has so many hardcore fans that are used to things being exactly as they are. But I think even the hardcore fans would appreciate a more powerful, better looking and easier to use UI once they try it. As a C++ programmer / UI designer I see so many things in the UI that could easily be improved with just a few hours of work.Some examples of things that can be improved in the UI:1) Better search when adding tasks : Many workstations have their tasks sorted into groups, but the search only searches in the list of groups, not inside the group. So if you don't know which category an item is located in, you have to manually go into every category and have a look since you cannot search for it, and often the categories and sub categories. I spent like 5-10 minutes just to find where the pipe was located.2) Same for search when adding items in work order conditions, I couldn't for the life of me find some items in that list, searched in every category and didn't find it. But it must exist somewhere since the item I wanted to find was suggested as conditions for work orders of other items.3) Better mouse input handling. I noticed that many times when I click to place a furniture nothing happens and it doesnt even register the click. But if I click, hold the mouse button down for a while before releasing it, then it registers as a click. Pausing the game makes the input handling faster and it misses clicks less often. It would be easy to make a change to trigger on a mouse click event, instead of checking for mouse down in the render loop. In general the UI should have highest priority and not be sluggish when the game rendering is slow. I don't mind rendering the game at a slower frame rate, but the UI should always be responsive.4) If you are in a submenu and want to go back, right clicking will close all the menus and not just take you back one step, and you have to start all over. Add a way to make it possible to go back only one level.5) Just general overhaul of the whole user interface to look over each feature to see if its placed logically, and if the icon could be improved. High res icons that are clearer to see. Tooltip on icons to explain the what it does. Furniture buttons could show if items are in stock for example. Reduce the number of clicks needed for common tasks. Borrow some ideas from Rimworld UI. 6) Make room quality visible somewhere.7) Make dwarf names clickable and take me to the dwarf information screen. For example if you are in the nobels menu and want to check the information of one of the dwarfs, you gotta remember it's name, then go to the citizen menu, sort by name, scroll the list until you find it, then click the information button. There is no search function so you gotta search the list manually. Everywhere in the UI where a dwarf name is shown, it should always be clickable and take me to that dwarf. 8) Allowed pawn zones, like Rimworld, that makes it impossible for pawns to walk outside them. I know you can set a priority so they have general path finding preference, but it still doesn't stop 100 dwarfs from all jumping into the river and drowning even if you cover the whole river with lowest priority zone. I built a bridge over a body of water, set the bridge to highest priority, set all the water and surrounding tiles to lowest priority, made sure to forbid every item in the water. Still one managed to fall in,  and then they all followed like lemmings and drowned. Fun times though :-)I could keep writing, like I said, there is a lot of potential for UI improvements :-)Anyway, thanks for making this awesome game and for bringing it to Steam with improved graphics.

_childDocuments_.review: The game attracts the player with the big depth it offers, both in terms of the procedurally generated storylines, world generation, relationships between civilizations, settlements, as well as the depth and variety of activities and ways to develop Your settlement it offers.But unfortunately it's got several fundamental issues:- First of all is it's bad UX. Many oversights in terms of "quality of life" features. Unintuitive, fractured, complicated UI. Crusader Kings II UI is wonderfully clear in comparison. Game requires tedious micromanagement, which often ends up ultimately insufficient anyway, in order to overcome inexplicable dwarf AI behaviour. You can read a wiki article or steam discussiong about how some mechanic is supposed to work 10 times and still not be able to understand why a dwarf refuses to do the work You want him to. Incredibly frustrating.- A problem which most "grand strategy" games struggle with, is that You, the player, end up waiting for the game, instead of it being the other way around. The game is very computationally complex, which will slow down the flow of game time and make the game lag noticeably, once Your fortress is complex enough. In other words You will end up wasting Your time, even without the lag. This game DOES NOT respect Your time, and You will not be able to get much done in short sessions.- In a way there is TOO MUCH depth. The amount of macro and micro level game mechanics will take an incredibly large amount of time to even find out they exist, let alone learn them. This is one of those games that have poorly designed in-game progression and instead force the player to rely on 3rd party guides, wikis, and advice to progress through the game "properly" (there is no proper progression because it was never designed). Personally I consider this type of design fundamentally flawed in any game and I hate game design where the player cannot be reasonably expected to progress, learn and enjoy the game without 3rd party guidance.- A smaller concern is that if You pay attention, the procedurally generated history is underwhelming and You can feel it's synthetic. Very impressive for procedurally generated lore, but ultimately insufficient.Having followed the devlogs I conclude that the developer is focusing on adding new content and new functionality/mechanics, increasing the scope of the game, instead of focusing improving the user experience of the content that's here. Therefore I don't recommend buying the game, unless You are ready to invest more time into it than it's actually worth.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is the definition of made with passion and care. This game is a masterpiece, and I don't say that lightly.I was one of those people who tried the original Dwarf Fortress and loved the idea of the game but just couldn't get into it. With the Steam version of the game I can say I love it and I'm hooked. I also wanted to support the Devs Tarn and Zach Adams because they seem like such cool guys and really love this game and pour everything into it. They supported this game for 15+ years for FREE. This game has incredible storytelling, this game is pure lore - sometimes it's hilarious, sometimes it's sad, sometimes it's just flat out crazy but there are endless things that can and will happen in your world and it never gets old. The game tells you everything that you need and want to know about the world that you generated with the Legends menu. You can learn about ancient artifacts that were created and where it was made, who made it, where it is now, how many things were killed by it etc. It's insane, I couldn't stop reading the Legends menu and learning about bad asses, crazy creatures, rise and falls of civilizations, and items from the past and present, 100's and 100's of years of lore that never gets old.Don't let the 2d sprites fool you, the depth of this game is so deep and rich that you barely even really notice it, but you still become attached to your dwarves. Hell, I needed a hunter so I gave a crossbow and some bolts to a dwarf who had zero experience hunting, he went out and kept trying to kill a boar, every day he would shoot at it, hit it and retreat and finally he killed after numerous attempts... I then got a notification that he fancies his crossbow now and he eventually became an legendary hunter. I follow him on his trips sometimes. Do the 2d sprites bother me? hell no. There are so many little things that this game accounts for, every body part, even the nervous system is covered. I've seen a dwarf get their spine damaged and they couldn't walk and needed to get carried around. Somebodies left 4th toe got ripped off... the list goes on. I can't really stop gushing about this game, it's the colony sim/storyteller that gave inspiration to other similar, brilliant games like Rimworld, Terraria, etc. There are some minor flaws like the UI not being perfectly intuitive but you get used to it, it's not that bad. I can't recommend this game enough and I highly recommend supporting these two geniuses and wonderful guys Tarn and Zach, thank you for making this game, thank you for updating it to steam and thanks Kitfox games.Dr. Crane approves.

_childDocuments_.review: First of all, ignore the nearly sixty hours I've put into this game on Steam. I've put hundreds more into it before it came to Steam. Secondly, I whole-hardheartedly endorse this game, but with one big caveat: It has an extremely steep learning curve.Dwarf Fortress is a game where you will fail many times before you succeed. It does not hold your hand and does not do tutorials. You will be thrown in the deep end and it can seem overwhelming. However, with persistence, the Dwarf Fortress wiki, and some guidance from the wider Dwarf Fortress community (see r/DwarfFortress or the Bay 12 forums) a player will find themselves slowly mastering the many layers of interlocking systems that make up this game.Once you do start to have a handle on it though, you'll find that Dwarf Fortress is one of the most complex and rewarding colony-simulation games out there. You have to make your own fun, but it's such a wide sandbox with so many things to explore and exploit that you'll never run out of options. If you can tolerate pushing past the learning curve, you're going to love this game.And hey, if you're not sure if it'll be worth the price to try out, the non-Steam version is always free. :)

_childDocuments_.review: God, what do I say about this game. Well, first of all, it's great. Despite the simple pixel graphics, there's a truly mind-boggling level of depth built into it. Creatures have preferences, hopes and dreams, short- and long-term memories, can experience mental trauma, can become depressed, can form all manner of relationships, etc. Combat can involve fighters knocking out each others' teeth, hacking off limbs, pulping various body parts, removing fingers and toes, and various other gruesome and potentially permanently-disfiguring actions. Never in any other game have I seen a demon go up against a kitten and be instantly killed because the kitten got lucky and managed to break its spine.Beyond the complexity (and I'm only scratching the surface of it here, believe me) the game is just such a relaxing joy to play. It's unforgiving, yes, anyone will tell you that, but you can get a great amount of enjoyment from just watching your dwarves go about their daily lives, eating, drinking, conversing with each other, and working on projects you've given them. Additionally, there's simply so much to do, and you'll never run out of things to try. Want to dig as deep as possible and see what riches (and terrors) lie below? Go for it. Want to build a gargantuan fortress-complex that puts Erebor to shame? Awesome. Howabout making a railgun to simultaneously impale a dozen different attacking goblins? Fully possible. Conquer the world? Also doable. You'll really never get tired of this game, and if you get tired of your current fortress (assuming it doesn't collapse from your mismanagement), you can always just retire it and start a new one, with the old one still existing in the same world and you being able to interact with it.Now, with all of that said, there are a few negative things you'll have to deal with playing Dwarf Fortress. For one, there are a considerable amount of bugs. None of them are entirely game-breaking mind you, just irritating. It's coded entirely by a team of two people, so these bugs can take a while to solve and updates come out... sparingly. Not for lack of trying of course, Zach and Tarn Adams are incredibly dedicated devs, there's just only so much two people can do in a timely fashion. Additionally, the game is very difficult to get into without the help of a myriad of tutorials. This can be a good thing if you're a fan of vertical learning curves and figuring things out through trial and error, but if you aren't, please do make use of the multitude of helpful youtube tutorials out there. They'll stop you from making rookie mistakes like getting children to haul corpses and permanently traumatizing them.10/10 game, wonderful work Tarn and Zach, only game where I can feed my dwarves roasts made out of the brains of their own dogs and they'll like it.

_childDocuments_.review: As someone that played the 'classic' dwarf fortress, this is a much MUCH better way to get into Dwarf Fortress than the original as someone that enjoys the survival/building/base management sorta games. While there is a charm to the old 'graphics' of the OG Dwarf Fortress, for the uninitiated it can be almost impossible to approach it without some major learning. The Steam DF (AKA 'Premium') has beautiful spritework, designs, and is visually easy to figure out what exactly is going on compared to the ASCII style. However, if you're an old player uncertain about this - There's always the ability to turn on the OG look!For the setting, Dwarf Fortress is a pretty classical 'low fantasy' setting but with some darker elements. There's really only 'evil' magic users such as necromancers. Your dwarfs do not and cannot use magic (unless they themselves become necromancers). But, your Dwarfs have a great boon under their beards: The riddle of steel and high quality armor - as well as your own noggin to make devious traps, pit falls, or weaponizing draw bridges to smash unsuspecting nay-do-wells. Normally the only civilizations you will mostly come across are: Elves, Humans, and other Dwarfs. Though there are 'animal men' beings that occasionally come by and are either a problem or soon-to-be problem.The combat in Dwarf Fortress can be visceral, brutal, horrifying, and even depressing - if you read the combat logs at least. Otherwise visually the sprites just kind of stand next to each other while blood forms around them and they eventually kill over dead. Trust me, a big part of this game is using your imagination paired with the detailed combat logs and the thoughts of both your dwarfs, and your opponents!Dwarf Fortress is, from what I have heard, the inspiration for games such as Rimworld. All with the complexity and wildness that is managing moods of your citizens, their food, health, drinks, etc. Your dwarfs have their own needs, wants, desires, moods, personalities, thoughts, and so much more. You will have to overcome so many issues and rise from worrying about if you have enough crops for the first few years, to battling horrific monsters that will come and try to make your fort into their new home.Last, but certainly not least is the crazy modding scene that exists within Dwarf Fortress. Don't like playing Dwarfs? There's countless mods that let you play as anything and (almost) everything to your heart's desires. Game not hard enough? There's a mod for that! The modding scene can only go up from here and it gets better almost every week.Dwarf Fortress is a game that holds no punches. There IS thankfully a tutorial, but once you learn the ropes - it's up to you if you can dig deeper and see what the world has to offer. It can be a huge hill to climb the steep learning curve of Dwarf Fortress, it can be extremely unforgiving, but as it goes: Losing is fun!

_childDocuments_.review: Dwarf fortress is, and always has been, an advanced game with a high barrier of entry for the unengaged. The current steam build feels like it was made with accessibility to new players at the forefront of design. Id like to preface this by saying that I have been around DF since the days of Armok (I know, I'm getting old)A part of what made dwarf fortress, dwarf fortress, was the seemingly insurmountable difficulty. Being faced with a myriad of issues and misconceptions, the first obstacle the player encounters against them is the UI itself. It was like staring into the matrix, seeing those 7 smiley faces blinking in a sea of semicolons. My primary complaint with the new UI is that it has sacrificed elegance and high end maneuverability in favor of a more typical interface. The steam build has never been easier to use, and understand. But as a veteran who has ran the game analog for all these years it feels like the soul has been sapped out of the experience.A lot of veterans, my self included, preferred the OG tileset because it added that additional layer of inaccessibility. Having people look over your shoulder and audibly go "WTF am I looking at" was a point of pride. The new tile set looks great, and it is easy to discern what is what, but gone are the days of speculation. Picturing what an enemy looked like based off its body parts, or instantly telling the difference between animals at a glance, all meaningless frills that gave DF more soul than it's competitors. Most of my complaints about this build of DF are periphery. The game runs great, and has never been more accessible. My complaints of UI, the tileset, the event system, etc feel like the setting pains of this games future. I hope no one forgets that world of dots and letters, that world of insurmountable odds and nigh divine might, that world we all loved and hated through thick and thin. To all the old players, and especially the new, just remember,Losing is Fun!

_childDocuments_.review: I've played the text based version of DF for years. I like the keyboard driven interface, and the obtuse graphics. The lack of direction and bizarre, inconsistent menu systems didn't scare me off. Nor did the frequent WTF moments when dwarves were going bezerk and the colony would collapse spectacularly. So I was supportive, but skeptical, about this release.The hardcore DF fans are going to love this game if it was a turd in a box; the fan base can be rabid, to say the least. But I don't think this release was aimed at them. This release is aimed at new players who couldn't stomach all the annoying, frustrating, not so fun elements of a very flawed but oh so amazing game. Because of this, I don't think it's fair to jump in and leave a shining, 11/10 review without considering that context.So, how does it stack up? In all honesty, it's pretty great. Seeing these things I had been imagining in my head all these years come to life and actually look like what I had envisioned is no small feat. It's still the same "losing is fun" game that I know and love, but with just enough visual feedback and a built in help system that takes much of the frustration out of navigating menus and finding that one option buried 6 layers deep in some labyrinth of screens and dialogs that you didn't even know existed. It was a relief to just be able to play without devoting so much mental energy into keeping track of these unseen interactions and events that, without careful inspection, would escape all but the most seasoned players.And, returning to the text based game today, I was pleasantly surprised to find that I had developed new intuition about the game from the Steam release. Having been so much more accessible, the Steam version has improved my understanding of the original game, which not only exceeded my expectations, but also seems to prove that they have accomplished their goal.It's not going to suit your average player. It's not a casual gaming experience. The graphics are infinitely better than before, but still rudimentary. The tutorial is beyond basic, but that's OK as long as you are the kind of player who accepts their fate with grace and learns what not to do next time. It's far from smooth or polished, and it probably never will be. But it is objectively a one of a kind, and very special game that I know will capture the imagination of a new generation of DF players.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm not ashamed to say my eyes could not handle the classic DF look, so I have been loving the deluxe version.I've survived on a fortress that has ~108 resident dwarves, I'm beginning to establish a justice system, I have a militia and a steady supply of platinum to fund trades with visiting traders, and I have a famous visitors tavern on the first floor that is now getting way overcrowded with tourists.A historical figure had been visiting here for quite a while, a Legendary weaponsmith dwarf who wielded an Artifact warhammer that is worth a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ fortune that they made, and they apparently were seeking out rumors on the location of another artifact they were tracking down and spent a lot of time in our tavern talking to people and listening to the bards.But then he decided he wanted to move on and he left the fortress, but out in the wilds before he left the map a squad of soldiers from a hell-fortress appeared, ambushed and assassinated him. _childDocuments_.review: Dwarf Fortress is a complex settlement simulator that creates epic storylines. The player builds and manages a subterranean (typically) fortress located in a unique procedurally generated world. The rich multidimensional simulation creates unpredictable individual geographies, historical contexts, personalities and needs. Threats like starvation, dangerous creatures, flooding and even mental illness can befall your dwarves and visitors. Prepare yourself to optimize resources, development choices, and defence against enemies!I have played DF only in 'Fortress Mode', the main mode where you build and manage your fortress, and only in the Steam version, which makes DF more accessible and visually appealing. DF has a famously steep learning curve, but for some of us that is also what makes it a very rewarding gameplay.Dwarves in Dwarf Fortress have unique needs, desires, and mental states that can affect their behaviour and you will struggle to satisfy. There is no endpoint, just an emergent story from multiple layers and layer of complexity you won't find in any other game.

As an old head DF player none of this stuff has felt essential to me and I do miss some of the things lost in the name of streamlining (mostly that there's a bunch of menus that had their most important parts shoved somewhere else. combat reports and petitions are just a type of alert, all military management happens through the squad sidebar, menus seem pretty rigid in what can be accessed from where etc) but it's still the same game underneath and just as enjoyable. Dwarf fortress is a game unrivaled in its complexity and detail.This is a colony simulator. You begin your fortress with seven dwarves and no Snow White. Your job is to provide direction and advice to your dwarves. Order constructions, designate mining shafts, order the gathering of plants. Your dwarves are tired, hungry, and not all that bright but they will attempt to follow your guidance to the best of their abilities.It is not for the faint of heart, and you will spend lots of time reading wiki pages on how various concepts and gameplay mechanics work in this game before you even begin to understand what is really going on.There is no “winning” in this game, but only !!FUN!!. Your goals are whatever you decide they are. At any time, you may retire your fortress and place its management in the hands of your capable dwarven leaders and begin a new fortress or adventure anywhere else in the world.Worlds? Every world is randomly generated and carefully infused with years of history and civilizations. Tales of war and peace, men and beasts, and civilizations of ages long ago will fill your taverns, all a part of each world’s generated history. Your fortress is no exception, and as you play your fortress and civilization will be remembered in the history books for future adventures in your world.If you are decently literate and don’t mind using your noggin a bit, go ahead and buy this game. Just remember to take breaks and go outside from time to time. Your dwarves will be just fine…

For example, 2 entities stacked on top of each other are not immediately obvious. The tile version had a rotating "/" to indicate that there are other things on the same tile but now it instantly switches to the other entity on the tile. It doesn't offer the same kind of instant overview of where everything could be at a glance.

_childDocuments_.review: I'd tried to get into Dwarf Fortress for the last 12 years, on and off. The triple threat of its old, byzantine UI, its lack of tutorials for even the most basic things, and its indecipherable ASCII graphics scared me off every time.With the Steam release and its shiny new tileset, its clean, common-sense UI, and its inviting tutorials, I was able to wrap my head around Dwarf Fortress in a way that I never could before; what I discovered was a game that I'm sorely regretting not getting into sooner.The depth of mechanics in Dwarf Fortress is unparalleled. After creating a mighty fortress, sprawling miles wide and miles deep, only to have it plunged into a civil war after the noxious stench of a corpse pit sent a powerful axe-dwarf into a murdering frenzy? I'm not sure I could ever go back to Rimworld, which now seems quaint in comparison.If you loved the stories you've heard of Dwarf Fortress but were scared off by its complexity, buy this. The game will teach you just enough to stand a chance, then throw you to the wolves. You'll have the time of your life fighting them off.

_childDocuments_.review: I will preface this by saying I have been an avid Dwarf Fortress player for quite some time and know the (original) game well. Dwarf Fortress is, at first glance, a deceptively simple looking game, but it is anything but. Having to understand and master multiple systems all at once to maintain a healthy fortress (do not underestimate tantrum spirals from your dwarves suddenly running around naked, plant that pig tail!), the scope of Dwarf Fortress is limited, really, only by the player's imagination. Do you want to create a coliseum, where you pit your captured foes against wild beasts? You can do that. Do you want to create a sprawling labyrinth beneath your fortress and populate it with a minotaur? You can do that, too. The new Steam version has nice art, lovely music, some very nice QoL features (thank you very much, Blueprint mode) and is, in my opinion, worth the money if you're planning on sticking around and learning the, at times, obtuse systems. Here's a protip: always embark with green glass, lobster and spider silk. Never know when you're going to get that strange mood...If nothing else, it is a charming little game. Do it for Scamps.
_childDocuments_.name: Dwarf Fortress

_childDocuments_.review: If I had to pick one game to play for the rest of my life, I would pick dwarf fortress. It's beauty is impossible to describe unless you play it. The emergent things that happen in this game set it apart from anything else you've ever played. It is hard. Incredibly hard. The UI is still cumbersome, but now usable. Give yourself the gift of powering through the UI. You'll come out the other side with stories to tell your friends.

_childDocuments_.review: Played on and off for several years now, it's rather intimidating at first but with the in game tutorials and multitude of guides and videos online you will ease into it in no time, and you'll be so glad you did.It's really hard to get across what makes this so excellent without getting immersed yourself in your own world with its own history and lore, and then you can (try) guide your little cherubs to their ultimate doom with the best intentions at heartsolid 10/10 go ahead and flood an entire cave system because you forgot that water does indeed flow, and rather quickly in enclosed spaces.

_childDocuments_.review: A weregiraffe came out of nowhere and started killing my dwarves so I gave my militia a kill order. Just as they arrived, the weregiraffe transformed back into the little dwarf girl she was and began running away in terror. I felt awful, but maintained the kill order. When she finally died, I discovered her clothes were drenched in her own tears.My dwarves laid her to rest with the highest honors they could bestow with their meager wealth. Whoops.

_childDocuments_.review: I've been playing Dwarf Fortress for years. I even had a YouTube channel where I would post lets plays of the game. Suffice it to say, I enjoy the game. In fact, the game is my favorite game of all time, bar none. As for the Steam version? I won't try and claim it is perfect. However, it does have an interface that is massively more user friendly and it has actual graphics. Besides that, Toady has been working on this game for around two decades and he doesn't plan to stop so I trust him to keep making the game better.As for what the game is? You've likely played similar games before as in the time it has been out, Dwarf Fortress has spawned its own genre. Games like Rimworld, Oxygen Not Included, and many others all follow in its footsteps. Yet Dwarf Fortress is still unique and an experience like no other. If you like those games but want something more, it wouldn't hurt to give Dwarf Fortress a try.You start the game similarly to many in the genre, by generating a new world. Except in Dwarf Fortress, that has a deeper meaning. The game generates hundreds of years of history that not only has an effect on your game, but that you can dive into and follow people through history. Notice that for some reason a human is the queen of an elven civilization? You can discover how that happened as it is all recorded. Note, the built in Legends Viewer, which is how you natively look through it all isn't the easiest to parse, the community has developed tools that massively improve the experience. Besides that though, even if you don't want to follow the life story of a goblin that after living five years, gets squished by a dragon, you at least know it is there.Then there is the main game, Fortress mode. Those who have played Rimworld will be familiar with this, except it has so much more depth. <- That's a pun by the way. One of the things Dwarf Fortress has and none of the other major titles in the genre does is multiple z-levels/layers. Anyway, your place in the game is similar to Rimworld or any number of other games where you aren't exactly a person in the game, but rather some otherwordly force guiding it all. You set out tasks to complete and work to be done so as to build a thriving home for the dwarves in your settlement. Not that the outside world is going to let you get away with that too easily.Whether it is a nearby necromancer who during world generation happened to find the secrets to eternal life and raising the undead, or the nearby human civilization you didn't pay too much attention too when choosing your location, but oops, at some point your dwarven civilization got into a bit of a tiff with and now they're at war. Never mind the fact that some of the natural wildlife will be happy to make trouble for you and even the weather can lead to disaster. There is a reason the classic motto for the game is that "Losing is Fun". Some people might feel that losing all you've done a bit of a demerit. Except you haven't lost everything. If you start a new game on the same world, you can choose to reclaim what was lost. Oh, and if a dragon happened to be the cause of your downfall, it might not have left yet either.Overall, there is a reason me and many others have been playing this game, even when everything was done with obscure nested menus navigable using only key commands and purely in ASCII.

Pros: - So much depth after the decades of development.- finally graphics that actually lets new users see what's happening.Cons: - UI Is clunky to put it nicely. _childDocuments_.review: I've been playing the free version for over 10 years.. This game is a masterpiece. I want to preface and say that its not for everyone, there is a wild amount of info you need to learn just to play the basics, but the attention to detail to the mechanics is unbelievable. The steam version fixes a lot of the hurdles it takes to run the game (RIP Lazy Newb Pack).
_childDocuments_.name: Dwarf Fortress

_childDocuments_.review: A classic beyond the reach of many for years. I tried it a handful of times but I was raised in the Sims era, not the Dos era, so I needed some basic graphics to truly enjoy it. You could've always just used Lazy Newb Pack, but the premium edition is far and away a better graphic experience than the mods provided. Plus its supporting devs who care. It has its bugs and quirks but no game can match DF's level of complexity. If you get good at this game, you'll be fighting it for fps at the endstages looking for more optimal ways to organize your dwarves and layout. When you're just starting out, you're trying to figure out why you're suddenly out of plump helmets and your dwarves are all angry. What is this unmet need prayer? Why does this dwarf worship three deities that no other dwarf has heard of? Why do waves of immigrants keep coming? I can't clothe or feed this many they are all starving to death and even worse, the dwarves are sobering up. The dwarven child had a tantrum and beat your best gem cutter to death? Tough, the justice system doesn't deal with minors. Figure out a suitable punishment and enact it yourself, as the God you are. A fickle one with limited control over the world but blessed with the foresight your dwarves will lack. Dwarf Fortress is a good, complex game that isn't for everyone but it might be for you. You will need incredible patience or the outdated wiki and video walkthroughs because this game is not going to tell you a lot of very vital information.
_childDocuments_.name: Dwarf Fortress

_childDocuments_.review: My first fortress was overrun by Werecapybaras, lycanthropes who every full moon turn into huge vicious capybaras. They transformed in the middle of the tavern and slaughtered everyone, it was a bloodbath.This game is amazing in ways words fail to capture. Less a game than a tool for procedural story generation, truly an infinite amount of content sits in wait. The developers, Zach and Tarn Adams, are wonderful human beings who have blessed us with this masterpiece of programming. I'm very glad that with the steam release this gem has become more accessible for everyone who hasn't yet experienced it.If you're not sure you want to purchase just yet, the game is available for free at  albeit without the graphics pack. The ascii text graphics are difficult to understand, but it is possible with some practice.While the game is fully playable, there are community made mods, like DFHack, available for free that can help with the more tedious aspects of gameplay and are wonderful tools for all players.
