_childDocuments_.review: This game saved my life.I am 22.My ex-wife and I have a daughter together, and adopted our son together. They are now both 4 years old.When we were going through our separation, I found myself lost and miserable. I was self destructive. I got so mad one day from everything spiraling out of my control that I punched some concrete in a moment of overwhelming emotion. That caused me to break my 5th metacarpal in my right hand... my working hand... my games hand.. the hand that I held and carried my children to bed with.. The hand I desperately needed to make sure I could continue to provide.After learning of the severity of my self-inflicted damage, I was borderline suicidal. Keep in mind that just a few months before this, I was the happiest man with no history of depression or anxiety. I have never had fits of rage, or been one to break down and cry, but I was in a low spot that just really buried me from being able to see the light on the other side.Having nothing better to do, I searched for a game I could play, ONE HANDED while I recovered. I somehow stumbled upon this game and read some of the reviews. I decided that it had to be worth a shot... I must admit, I didn't beat the game, or play nearly as long as some of you. In fact, I may have only played this game a day or two.. With that being said, after doing so, I had a new found joy and hope for life. I was able to put behind me the pain and suffering that had been cast over me. I was able to experience other peoples joy and happiness. I was able to see the fruits of my "labor". I relaxed for 5 ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ minutes to this music long enough to realize that I was going to be okay.After coming to that realization, I turned the game off, and I went back to work. It hurt my hand like hell but I was motivated. I stopped feeling so damn sorry for myself, and I became the father I needed to be in that moment, not the weak boy I was behaving as.Today, I am close friend with my kids mother. We don't fight, or argue, or say hurtful things to each other. We are parents, and friends.I now have 3 kids. My third child is, wait for it, ALSO 4 YEARS OLD. The woman I am with was going through a very similar situation at the time of my own separation, and we just stumbled in to each others life unexpectedly. We have been in a relationship for a year now, and are very happy together.Moral of the story, you never know what life holds in store for you, and if I would have given up when all the odds were stacked against me, I wouldn't be where I am today. This silly little game helped me realise that.Thank you

_childDocuments_.review: This game is beautiful, the pixel graphics are truly a work of art, and I enjoyed playing through half of the game, after deciding to stop.The Reason I stopped playing, is the only gripe I have with the game, which is 3 things:1. The Repetitive Level Designs reminiscent of platformers2. The Linear Storyline3. The Overall Difficulty1. In every section of the game, there will be places where you're in a town, able to talk to residents, and all that, and there was a fair bit of worldbuilding and excitement for the idea of being in an underground village in an abandoned subway. But when you get to the levels inbetween these places, the story is replaced with fast placed hack and slashing, as well as the occasional puzzle and platorming obstacle course. This aspect of the game was a real chore, and detracted from my enjoyment of the game, and upon viewing how much harder the game gets as you pass the level I was on, it just gets even harder, and I was playing on the supposed casual mode, so I was very frustrated. And The Save bot was always preaching to me, and that got very tedious too, like shut up, I'm trying to save here, I don't need to be hear it. All in All, there could've been better deigned transitional levels, it felt less like an open world exploration of a big new world, to being a survival game, mixed with a platformer in 2d, which I wasn't a big fan of.2. The Linear Storyline locked your path in place, you followed one path, no room to move around and explore. When watching ads and seeing the early artwork on the web places, It looked absolutely excellent, I wanted to see more of the world, and not just slash more enemies, but the path of the game, guided me in only one direction, when I wanted to go in ten. The Developers really missed the boat on this aspect of the game, and they ought to make up for it, buliding an open world rpg in 2d, because with these graphics and mechanics, it would totally work, and I would enjoy playing such a game, in a casual easy mode throughout the game. Multiple Endings, depending on your choices, the story felt more like a generic rpg with sci-fi elements, which could've worked, but all of the game's focus was on the girl, which was very disappointing, because it felt like the whole game was about her, not the cool rugged dude with the beard going on a quest, leaving the safety of the abandoned subways. The game probably would've been way more fun to play if this was about the guy, who's character was far more intriguing and developed, as opposed to the rude little girl that the game insists you're supposed to love and feel bad for, and that's sad to me. I don't care if she's a mutant science experiment who's bratty and stupid, or she has an evil twin part of her conscious, I was not engaged.3. The Difficulty of the game, as I mentioned, was too hard. While I could've sat down and played the game as intended, and tried to, but by the time i reached chapter 3, I was disengaged. I was going through the motions, and wasn't enjoying the game at all.Like many games, it looks beautiful, but has too many small problems to be worth playing all the way through.Though, I could see movies being made in pixel art this way.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a good game that is just on the very cusp of being an all time great game- if not a classic.It's rare to see games coming out that manage to evoke the feelings of older experimental and rare properties like Earthbound, but Pixpil have managed to touch on that vein and strike it very hard with the world of Eastward. Gameplay was fun and offered a decent amount of challenge- Evoking the control schemes of Top-Down Zelda titles mixed with a bit of Secret Of Mana's combat as well. Involving the use of weapons and abilities to dispatch the variety of enemies and puzzles that are littered throughout. Weapons always felt good, even if some were more useful than others. I found myself defaulting to the Frying Pan and Bang-Bang Gun when I played- As those two covered most of what I needed when playing. I never felt particularly overwhelmed by the combat challenges. Bosses were fun and cleverly designed- And you are never long without options to fight whatever comes at you. With John's Arsenal and Sam's psionic abilities. While Sam did get reduced to being more of a stun option and puzzle solver- Her abilities did come into play when they were needed.The story has strong beats. It starts off like RPGs of old, with the discovery of something of the wider world and the exile from the home village- Eastward starts off strong with a intoduction to the world that John and Sam live in. You see a myriad of beautiful spritework and music- Despite how dreary and down Potcrock Isle is meant to be. As the story picks up, the game's tone becomes apparent. A funny adventure that is willing to make some dire turns. And it's a strong start that continues until the half-way point.The story begins to wane after this. Becoming a series of distractions that, while fun and do engage the player, aren't going to feel as connected or as important. Some parts left me rather frustrated, especially when the story does pick right back up, only to hit a very hard wall. And this repeats from the half-way point on. Sadly leaving the story with a number of loose ends and potential that was not quite reached. Despite all of this- I could not help but to see the good of this game. It's flawed. It's repetative- Very obviously padding itself out by making the player re-visit places they've been again and again and reusing resources a lot. But it's a game with heart. It's got that spark that you have to stop and appreciate. I want to see more from this world. The ending left me in a place similar to Mother 3's ending. But nowhere near as satisfied. And if I can't see more from the world of Eastward, then I'd love to see more from Pixpil. If this is just them getting their feet wet in the world of games- Then experiencing them at their full stride will be something remarkable.

_childDocuments_.review: Finally having beaten the game nearly 100% (minus Earthborn), although missed some things due to mistakes, I do think this was a really good game with some issues here and there.For the good, the game's strong suit was the music, sound design, characters, and general story writing. Particularly Sam, she was obviously my favorite of the bunch. I do think they could have focused more on the general twists, but at the same time the storytelling was very obviously leaning in that direction due to the mysterious nature of Sam. It just feels like a whiplash sometimes when you go from Greenberg to New Dam and then everything suddenly becomes a family style slice of life, which I loved, then snaps right back but still keeping a general cheery nature. Which I still liked the darker tone to the story as well, but I understand how that can be jarring for some people and it can make it easy to forget about what's actually happening in the world.Although some were unhappy with it, I'm glad this game took the time to develop all the side characters. A lot of games tend to just gloss over them and call it a day, but everyone is developed in some way making the game feel a bit more alive. End result is that there is obviously a lot of text, but this is meant to be a story heavy game to begin with. For instance at start I actually disliked William but he grew on me over time due to how his character writing went.Puzzles were also fun for what they were. Albeit pretty simplistic.For what I felt was weak, I would say it was the gameplay. It's very clear that the story was the focus and sadly that was put behind. It's not bad in the least bit, in fact for the most part it feels good. At the same token though since there wasn't much combat, it's hard to tell but it feels like that was compensated by just giving enemies a crap ton of health thus making them pretty much bullet sponges. Some more than others. So some parts end up feeling like they drag on as a result as I mashed that X button like my life depended on it. On the plus side, I do like how Sam's abilities interacted with enemies. Freezing enemies in place is always dope if they're being annoying. ...Unless they break out in life half a second, or they get pushed too far away. Otherwise it was fine. At the same time, it was annoying how sometimes enemies can get into my hitbox and suddenly I was just dead, although that happened to me more often in the early game.. sometimes late game.Give it a go. You may enjoy the story. I personally liked it, it's not the best I've experienced there are other games reserved for that, but it definitely has its cute moments and likable characters. Just don't expect anything phenomenal from the combat or anything. And as always, I enjoyed the references these indie games like to pull out of nowhere.

_childDocuments_.review: how would i describe this game.. i'm so happy yet so sad.bare in mind there may be spoilers ahead but that will be more below the bottom, if you want a brief summery here you go, it is a very happy and cheerful game yet it can also flip on a dime very quickly and suddenly turn very dark, if i had to give a example it is a lot like undertale, in the aspect that it can be gleefully cheerful yet sad at the same time, it even has game mechanic's that surprised me as well with each chapter, everytime i thought i'd seen everything it has to offer me it surprises me, not to mention how expressive the characters are in the dialog- i'd say that's the best selling point besides the beautiful graphic's, it's gotta be the expressive dialog! it doesn't feel wasted and all well put together! also the soundtrack is really good as well!and i believe that wraps up the non-spoiler section, i think my first steam review for a game i sunk 28 hours in, hopefully this convinces you to play, should you beat it though and want to come back to see if you shared your thoughts about this game with me, feel free to let me know if you agree or not, i do not mind ether which way, i hope you have a lovely time.now for the actual spoilers, primarily the ending and how i feel about it.your all set? all ready? ok lets do this, i don't really like the ending, but that's perfectly ok, i just don't like those kinds of ending's where it ends like- *that* to say the least, but it's still so good yet so sad at the same time, while most did get a happy ending, i won't lie when i was strung along by isabel's feeble attempts to save alva's life, between sam and alva it was like a little sister and big sister combo that was a delight to see, john's a complete mute which is fine but having someone like that be so cheery and happy and letting sam be a kid, and not some goddess of life and death, it was truly a wonderful sight, but then i see the happiness fade, alva's gone, isabel's delusional, we left the only home she was really happy in, and sam had to sacrifice herself just to stop what i can only assume is some automated program with a vague amount of understanding when it comes to emotions, attempting to emotionally break her will just so it can take over and do it's job to wipe the slate clean, only to end up reincarnated in who knows where and bump into john again, with no memory of him whatsoever. i have yet to play the DLC btw, i understand it's a alternate universe where some of these events are ether different or- just didn't happen entirely, but that's a whole different universe, and not the ending where we saved alva, got the friends back, let sam continue being a kid again, maybe in the DLC she could but unfortunately that's not the case in the main one, and it is saddening, if i didn't had a problem crying irl i probably would've shed a tear or so, but as i said, the ending itself is perfect and fine the way it is for this game, this is merely stating my unbridled sadness that i couldn't see the character's i got so invested into couldn't get the happy ending they deserve.mind you- the only reason i could remotely get so interested is just because of how exprESSIVE the characters are, and just how thorough they are with the line of dialog, it's not just some random dialog, you can feel it, if you had any inner dialog within your mind and a library of voices of dozens if not hundreds of voices you could easily construct voices yourself for each character just because of how expressive and well written they are, each one has there own purpose and each one you can tell how'd they sound should you meet them.

_childDocuments_.review: After beating this game, I give this a 7.5/10. Why not an 8, 9 or 10? Think of this game like a slightly under cooked cake. It looks great, smells great and tastes great, but when you bite into it, you can still feel the clumps of batter in your mouth. That's Eastward. The pacing of the story was okay, not bad by any means but it could've been better. I felt one of the early chapters was kind of pointless, where another early chapter that felt too short could've been more fleshed out to give the player sentimental value to some of the characters and environment. Characters didn't get the arcs they deserved. This game has many interesting and charming characters that make you smile whenever they're on screen yet they barely get any backstory to really make you feel attached.Combat is basic, but that's not really a problem as this is a very classic-zelda inspired game.Finally the ending of this game just left me with unanswered questions and even more questions which kind of pissed me off.I feel like Eastward needed a bit more time in the oven to fix its writing, as the overall story is okay but it had so much potential which is really frustrating.Despite all that, for what it is, it's price and the quality you're getting, this game definitely didn't feel like a waste of my time. The art is astounding, the humor is charming, the soundtrack has some bangers and the overall story is pretty good. Eastward isn't perfect but for it's price I definitely recommend this game.

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like this game but it never really grabbed me. The actual gameplay is incredibly simple Zelda-esque puzzle dungeons with a neat 2-person switch mechanic. A lot of narrative driven games have weaker gameplay, but the narrative is not up to the task of carrying the game. It shares a lot of themes with Mother 3, which is completely fine, but it's not really delivered well. It's hard to explain something so subjective but the dialogue felt very stiff and unnatural. The characters themselves from what I've played are very one-note, and it doesn't help that the main duo might be the worst part. Having both a gruff silent protagonist and an energetic kid sounds fun, but the former ends up standing there doing nothing most of the time outside of gameplay, and the latter is really overplayed and just has way too much text dedicated to shouting about whatever is currently happening in the story. I get they wanted to show that she's energetic and excitable but there could have seriously been half the amount of text boxes conveying this, or at least balanced it out with dialogue about anything else. From what the other reviews have said it doesn't seem to get much better. I really wanted to like this and I think the dev team could do something great in the future, but 5 hours in I have to call it for this one.

_childDocuments_.review: I fell in love with Eastward from the minute I saw the trailer, that beautifully animated story accompanied with an amazing track, it's heavily influenced by Studio Ghibli, yet has it's own charm and personality. The pixel art is gorgeous, full of details and Easter eggs. The gameplay is easy to master with diverse weapons that make the journey even more fun as you progress the story.The only thing I feel it needs are animated cut-scenes, I was expecting Eastward to be like Ni No Kuni or Professor Layton that have several animated cut-scenes that give a bit more life to the story, yet the beautifully crafted environments and diverse characters found in this game kept me interested. What definitely fulfilled my expectations was the soundtrack, the main theme is great but there a lot of ambient tracks that help me relax and enhance the exploring experience.The combat and different weapons were fun to use, and exploring to find resources to upgrade them felt rewarding. It is a very linear game without much backtracking except for one big chapter. The pace might be a bit slow and the final city felt like it needed something more. Be aware that the ending leaves a few things up to your imagination, yet I think that's a good thing, not every game has to explain absolutely everything for it to have a good conclusion. There's also a whole JRPG mini-game on this thing. To finish this review I want to say that you'll definitely love the soundtrack, the story will keep you going and the combat will keep things fresh, a Must Play.
_childDocuments_.name: Eastward

_childDocuments_.review: I thought the art, writing (English), music and gameplay were all very good. No complaints in these departments.However I felt that the story was not fully developed in the end, so that was a bit disappointing. The title took the approach of slowly unveiling the underlying mystery through the course of present events, and I think with this narrative style you do expect that after the climax a reasonably coherent explanation for everything that happened should be in place. Instead I felt that I left with more questions than answers. Perhaps a follow up title could get to the bottom of it all.That said during the game per se the narrative was enough to keep me engaged, and I never felt that it was too slow. Overall I'd still highly recommend it.

The characters are also designed really well and interesting.The main characters are very well built. John, as the silent type portrays his emotions via actions or gaining hearts.The last levels are also done well as I have never seen such a design and it feels really alien and suits the atmosphere.The music supports the story so well that I'm happy to have a pack of tissues lying next to me.If you're thinking about buying this game and hesitating, thus reading the reviews: get it, this is your cue!Negative aspects:My first try had a corrupt gamefile and crashed my old PC. _childDocuments_.review: An incredibly charming game held back by its focus on its storyEastwards is set in a post-apocalyptic world where humanity is currently rebuilding after some unknown events caused a large scale collapse of society despite being incredibly technologically advanced. The various towns, cities and settlements explored throughout the story have a variety of cultural and historical influences from their former selves which make a unique setting to explore. The devs even put a full scale 1980's RPG in the game (in the form of a arcade machine you occasionally find) for the player to explore and try which adds probably one of my favourite bit of side content that I've ever played in a game, it even has a New Game+ which adds a bunch more content to the already optional side-game.It has a gorgeous art style that is fun to look at, fun and unique characters that make you want to explore and talk to every NPC in town and an interesting story that stretches over a well made and expansive world.My biggest problem though with Eastwards is that despite having all that, it just decided not to do anything with it. There are no little lore dumps that explains the world that they developers have created (which it could certainly use). There are only a handful of side quests to do across 8 chapters and all of them are either hidden or not pointed out to the player making them difficult to find or complete and the combat remains to the very end of the story to be incredibly basic offering little challenge to the player despite the fact that the mechanics to do so are there.I have these criticisms as someone who went out of their way to get all the achievements in this game, which was by and large a very painful experience. Everything in this game is missable, and I mean everything. From chests to food recipes, shop sold consumables, to ingredients. There is no way to go back and find any of these things past a certain point and that point is frequently the end of the chapter. With the exception of the recipes/ingredients they won't even tell which of those you are missing, just that you are in fact missing them. They later added a chapter selection (after the 1.0 release) after you beat the game for the first time but they don't tell you that until you get there, for those who care that was a great thing to addDespite those things I think Eastwards is an incredible game, especially for the first game made from this studio as far as I can tell at least. I'd recommend giving it a shot
_childDocuments_.name: Eastward

_childDocuments_.review: +This game has a TON of charm, +beautiful art, +well imagined locations, +entertaining characters, +well-executed plot and +plenty to do.+The main characters are character you really grow to like, and you really feel for them as you go through this quirky sci-fi adventure. [] It is somewhere along an action RPG in gameplay, but it has distinct stealth sections and other digressions of style.[] The gameplay on a first run seems like it'd take no less than 24 hours, possibly more, to complete. If a dollar an hour of gameplay is worth it to you then this is a plus, if that seems lacking then you may find this disappointing, but I feel it is worth it on my end, and I tend to shop cheap.[] While there is a lot of experience to be had, that time does blaze by. This is good in the sense that it is gripping, but bad in that it really felt like it went by quickly. The number of locations feels small (even though those locations, themselves, feel enormous, at times.) I feel like you also could do well to explore some of the things that are showcased in more depth at times. There's several places that look like you should be able to enter and explore, but they are just set dressing. This is not a full negative, rather neutral, to me, because, really, if it took me (exploring a lot) almost 40 hours to complete, there clearly _is_ substance. - The minigames are a mixed bag. The side-minigames really don't feel worth delving too much into, though I did enjoy the gatcha since it doesn't really intrude on the gameplay, and doesn't affect the main story, I will also give the gatcha mechanic, conceptually a pass. (If the gatcha were in some way required to beat the game, this would be a second minus.)- The story has a couple pitfalls that kind of disappoint me, personally, but not every note is going to hit everyone just right.- There can be a BIT of busywork to the gameplay.- The way this game gets dark when it does has some level of sour taste in its actions that don't fully feel like they always push the plot forward, or they push it forward in ways that feel a bit mean-spirited to the player in a narrative sense.- Some of the things that happen also make it feel like it wouldn't be fun to replay if you get connected heavily to characters (not in the Undertale sense of that experience, in a different sense.) Replayability isn't mandatory to a good game, but it is worth noting, here.
_childDocuments_.name: Eastward

_childDocuments_.review: This is a special one. At first it didn't really grab me, but by the 2nd chapter or so I was sucked completely into the mysteries of the story, the artwork that speaks for itself and the love lettering to lighthearted day-to-day-life fun juxtaposed with an overarching narrative that gets... heavy. The bleakness presented here is the kind that underlies everything to the smallest details when you get to know it. It's no matter that the story and the world of this game has made me think and feel some kind of closure about the human condition (seriously) after finishing it that I think I really needed personally. I'm not sure everyone will get the same experience as mine from the game. But I'd say, even if the plot can make it a bit confusing what is up and down at times at least on paper, the raw way the game hits instinctively at when it does should offer some good starting points for further soul searching. Huh, I guess this must be like how religious people feel at times.Gameplay is good too but not on the level of the Zelda classics it takes inspiration from, which is fine. One thing though; I never could care for cooking in Breath of the Wild or its sequel, but it won me over here with the vibes and simplicity of it. So it also has that going for it I guess.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall great game. The visuals are outstanding if that's not obvious from the trailers. But you should only actually play this if you're a stupid nerd who doesn't mind reading, cause you're gonna be doing that for a good 60% of your playtime.Gameplay-wise, it's literally Zelda but you play as two characters. The combat's incredibly basic, which isn't a bad thing except that it takes until halfway through the game for the more interesting enemies to show up. Puzzles are pretty straight forward, but satisfying (you won't spend hours stuck in a dungeon confused).When it comes to the story, it's a plot that I feel like I've seen before, but done pretty well. The main duo is very charming, and the towns you run across each have great purpose in the plot, and are just fun to explore. The only main gripe I have with the story is that I'm not super interested in the main antagonists.The music's incredible, although I have one pet peeve with it. You'll be listening to a lot of the same upbeat cutscene themes over and over during dialogue. HOWEVER, the town, dungeon, boss, and overall rest of the soundtrack is amazing and really sets the mood they want for the game.Last thing I want to mention is that this game does a good job with its moments. There're a decent amount of good moments in the game that I'll remember long after having completed it when I think back to it. Although I have some pet peeves with it, Eastward is a beautiful and bittersweet story that I'm not gonna forget.

_childDocuments_.review: Full disclaimer: I haven’t actually beaten the game yet, but I have gotten further than… 82% of players at time of posting. I intended to write this up as I played, up to the game’s conclusion, and I do kind of want to see how it ends to see if any of the narrative payoff is worth it. But I have to force myself to launch the game, there are days or even weeks in between sessions. So I offer this to you now, to perhaps save someone from buying it.Ahem.Prior to its release, I was hoping Eastward would come out swinging in the leagues of Undertale, LISA, and Omori. An Earthbound-like game with lots of color and weird people and enemies to encounter. It is technically that, but it doesn’t hit nearly as hard as the big players. The biggest reason for this is the game’s writing.The game stars John, a bedraggled man who does not speak (except for when he inexplicably does), acting as caretaker to the ever precocious young girl, Sam. John can cook and can hit things real hard, Sam is adorable and is.. magic? The game actively strives to not explain this, or have other characters even acknowledge it, for quite a long time despite it being the central plot.The original version of this review recounted the problems with the story bit by bit as I played it, but there were so many minor and side events that don’t matter at all to the story that I eventually had to just cut all the fat. So here is the condensed version- Most characters are just there until they aren’t, and are victims of a weak, poorly-paced overarching narrative. The writers decided certain things need to happen and so the characters are there to enact those things or see (and rarely appropriately react) to them happening. There’s a strange rollercoaster of moods that doesn’t snap hard enough to really register as tonal whiplash, and the pacing and sense of stakes suffer for it.There’s.. a lot of things I could go on about. John’s complete lack of agency, the utter fumbling of Sam’s backstory, Jasper’s character in its entirety (seriously I hate Jasper for so many reasons, and I'm not alone because I know someone who might have straight up stopped playing because of how much they dislike him). Threatening or enacting pointless deaths for no reason because the narrative demands a weightless tragedy that it’ll forget about in five minutes. A few bits of random anime horniness. The pacing of the dialogue (and by extension cutscenes) is on the slower side and the writing isn’t good enough to warrant it, and across a game this long it adds up to a lot of frustration. There’s multiple very obvious plot points and the characters absolutely refuse to engage in them for the sake of a “twist” later. There’s a game within a game that is constantly brought up in the first Chapter, and is kinda mentioned as a background element in later ones, but doesn’t really have any weight or meaning to its inclusion until Chapter 7. Save points are fridges with talking screens, each with its own Deep Message that means nothing at all. Minimal to no backtracking means the various new tools you get carry less weight and if you miss any resources they’re gone forever.I originally thought the game was going to focus on the journey, being named after a cardinal direction. (This is NOT why it’s called Eastward, by the way.) I pictured going on a long trek as John while he escorts little Sam to a vague destination. A cuter version of Last of Us. Then I learned about Earth Born, the ingame media giant, and thought it was going to focus on that, considering how much the kids talked about it in the beginning and gaining the ability to play it is one of the first things you do. The eventual payoff takes so long to come to fruition and ultimately it’s just.. there. They made a mediocre game inside their mediocre game. It’s another symptom of the team having a lot of ideas and little direction. For a game named.. Yeah.

_childDocuments_.review: I'll cut to the final question here. Should you buy this game? Absolutely! While the gameplay takes a bit of a backseat It's one of my favorite RPG*s I've played recently. While there were moments that made me a TEENSY bit uncomfortable (probably specific to my life though), This story was fun! while not really pushing any boundaries story-telling wise, it was very effective at getting you to feel emotions such as:• Wonder• Anxiety• Monkeys!!!• Anxiety• Anxiety• "NO NO NO NO NO"• Despair• Hope?This game will most likely leave you wanting for more! Which I always say is a really good position for any story to leave you in. Though, this game  be pusing that motto a little.Not to say it's an incomplete story — It's absolutely not! But you don't really get anything AFTER the moment the big bad thing™ is defeated (Maybe a couple minutes of cutscene?) And you don't even really get to see what the state of the world or most of the characters you've met along the way is. _childDocuments_.review: Eastward is probably one of the best narrative-driven ARPGs I’ve played in a very long time. It carries with it an emotional weight and whimsical charm no doubt inspired by works like Earthbound, as well as a fun snappy gameplay similarly inspired from Zelda, but takes those inspirations and combines them with its own unique ideas. Its characters are lovable and endearing, but also human and by no means invincible. When a person dies, they aren’t meant to come back, after all. It’s a story that left me wishing there was more—so many loose ends left with only meager answer, if any at all. And yet, I’m satisfied with it. Eastward understands the power of emotional investment in its world, its story, and its characters, coupled with the engagement that comes out of fun gameplay backed by an amazing soundtrack, so if any of that sounds appealing to you, I'd highly recommend you give it a go.

_childDocuments_.review: EDIT: Completed the game (sorry for bad english, not native, might not review the game with a lot of details)I'm okay with the difficulty, but the puzzles are the reason why I almost uninstalled it but in the end I tried not to do it. The more you explore, the more tricky the puzzle. At least for me who is not fan of puzzle games or game with a lot of puzzles btw. Some pixel based games rely too much on puzzle things, at least for some games that I've played. CrossCode is one of example that have a lot of difficult puzzles. Eastward is no exception. It also rely on puzzle that makes my broken controller give me tough time to solve it. I'm not saying the whole puzzle is difficult, its ez to solve but my broken controller makes it more difficult lol.In some cases I just, "please no more puzzle, I just want to enjoy the story, I have a lot of unfinished backlogs" and that makes me not really enjoy the game.But at the other side, I want to know how the story goes, so... yeah, love it or hate it I must finish it.The story is sadly not explain a lot, it has strong story at first about 2-3 hours, then, meh and boring. It become little bit exciting when we arrived at some climax of its story. There are a lot of unexplained things such as how this become that (no spoiler sorry). Surely in the end, it ends cute but, still, I want to know about what exactly happened in its world.To put it simply, the story is all about daily life of John and Sam in mining town, but things become bad after they try to leave the town. Mayor seems has some explanation about why they cant leave the town and it seems he also have some 'contract', but it leaves us as mystery until the end.They should've explain the ending about how mayor etc conditions and not leave us questioning about it. The character writing is so strong, you will enticed to love or hate them. You will feel devs have gone a lot of hardships writing the characters, it has their own charms. Sadly the plot is not. It has a lot of potential but the linear story not exploring things that should've been exciting to explore.For example, what happened to the world by explaining this and that (again, no spoiler). Why they're become like this. What is Miasma, why it exist. Some are quite exciting if it explained properly, but no.The music is very good, reminds me to my own childhood playing old Nintendo or arcade games, but it has not much variations. In some cases, they just using the same music again and again for some scenes. Need strong memorable music to represent city or battle or sad scene tbh.Eastward's visual is beautifully crafted for a pixel game. I like how dev set the lighting and choose the color for the game. Some colors explain how the dark and gritty the world is. It may be the best pixel game ever made in terms of visual.The world is so much detailed and crafted with love. I loved it. Buy it.You like story? Wait until it gets discounted.

_childDocuments_.review: 10/10 One of my Favorite Games of all time.This title will haunt me until the day I die.Eastward is better described as an Odyssey. You are John, and you take care of Sam.By the time you get to the end, you will feel like an age has passed, and you're a different person than you were when you went in.The beginning is a slow-burn, but it picks up speed and then keeps gaining speed through the entire journey, until you get to the end and suddenly you're left there, empty, probably crying, desperate for more. But you know deep down that to add more would probably ruin the beautiful thing you just witnessed.There's some flaws, mostly things that become a bit apparent when you realize this was started by 3 guys in China - a fact quickly forgotten - who managed to get a small studio going. And their studio was in a Shopping Mall when the Pandemic hit. It's a bit of a miracle that they finished.You can tell they intended for the journey to be longer, there's places where they could have easily lengthened the game and it would have been welcome. As a result, the flaw is more that the story jumps in a few places where it seems like there was *going* to be things and they had to be cut.The only other flaw would be that if you speed up the text in the options, sometimes the text isn't under your control and it speeds by way to fast, but the slow speed is agonizingly slow.Also. If you don't like talking to everyone, you might have an issue with that part. You don't have to talk to *everybody*, but the more thorough you are the more you will see and the more things will make sense. It's totally possible to run right past something pretty important if you're not doing it at all. There are posts on Reddit complaining about the story and it's abundantly clear that these people missed a lot.

_childDocuments_.review: This game touched me on an entirely different plane than most. Eastward is addictive and mysterious, you find yourself desperate to understand the surroundings and meanings behind one of our main characters, Sam. The game's art/graphics are beautiful. The worlds are all so unique, quirky, and memorable. Every time you progress, there's an empty feeling leaving the last area behind. The soundtrack has to be one of my all time favorites of any game.... especially the cooking theme. What really makes this game though are the characters. John is our classic silent protag, who takes in a mysterious girl named Sam and raises her as his own. Despite not being the main plot, I found this game's story to be about the radiating love that these two characters have for one another. Any well-done game with a strong father/daughter plot like TWD, Lisa, or Eastward gets me crying like a baby back ♥♥♥♥♥.Long story short: Buy the game. I wish John were my dad.

However, the sequencing of this game completely squanders its potential.Too many redundant events and extraneous dialogue that disrupt the progress of the story. Not enough "informative" conversations, just dumb, forgettable ♥♥♥♥. Due to the overabundance of unnecessary events, I got lost in what the story was meant to actually be. _childDocuments_.review: [Updated 09/19/2021]Current place in the game: Chapter 1 Total playtime at update time: 3.1 hours———————————————————————————< Artistic aesthetics: 8/10 >After another 2 hours of gameplay, I have to admit that the resolution of Eastward is one of the things that's holding it back, hence reducing the point from 10 to 8. Yes, the pixel art in this game is still very delightful to see - the vintage hue is just the right fit for a game like Eastward. Notably, the animations of the characters move very smoothly. Eastward requires less movement accuracy from players compared to Stardew Valley and To The Moon (just pulling up 2 other pixel-style games I've played before): John could walk through a tunnel without having to adjust his position on the map to fit the entrance. [bold] However [/bold], after a long period of playing the game, the blurriness of the graphics starts to become a huge problem. Because of the vintage color scheme, there is little contrast between the background and character, and everything gradually blurs as consistent playtime increases. The rulebook of Earthbound is easily more visible compared to Eastward itself *sigh*. I played Eastward on PC, but I assume that this aspect should be less of a problem on game consoles. Cooking animation is great!< Character design: 8/10 >Every character I've interacted with so far seems to have their unique personalities - they're all highly identifiable in both appearance and dialogues (*camera zooms onto Carota*). What prevented me from rating the game a 10/10 is the lack of "freshness" in the dialogues. There is an achievement that requires lots of talking from John to other characters, and the fact that there is little useful information from most characters just greatly reduces my motivation in trying to chat with everyone.< Level/Puzzle Design: 6/10 >So far my only weapon is still just the  pan.  The variety of enemies did increase after a few more hours of exploration, yet there isn't really a lot of strategies that I could apply to the enemies. In order to solve the puzzles, John has to sometimes walk long distances, and sometimes that could bore the player real quick. Camera transitions after placing bombs are smooth though!< User Interface: 7/10 >Thank you user @Gegar for pointing out the shortcut for opening the map (press F); knowing about the shortcut does help with the player navigating with a backpack and other tools in the menu. However, I still hope that there'd be more instructions on how to use the shortcuts. So far, a lot of things that could increase the player experience of the game are left for the players themselves to explore. Albeit the shortcut, the map itself is still very confusing; I still can't tell where I am on the map based solely on the map - yes, I could locate myself, but I have no idea where is this exact room I am in at the moment. There could be more features on each room when viewing the map than just the mere shapes of every room. < Story: 8/10 >The post-apocalyptic/cyberpunk theme continues to develop in Eastward (the RVs are still very awesome). The opening animation showed great promises to what's yet to come, and I am very intrigued about what will happen to John and Sam .< Music/SFX: 9/10 >Eastward's music continues to impress me :) The music at different stores is designed to fit in very naturally. The background music in each room provides a comfortable ambiance as well.  I'm not an expert in the music field, but the 8-bit music style fits just right for a pixel game like Eastward!———————————————————————————Thank you for all the upvotes and awards as well as rare support and kindness in the comment section - I will continue to update as I play. For the comments not so kind, I honestly don't care what you're saying about  review. If you find it unhelpful, just filter out reviews by play hours or simply click unhelpful and move on. Peace.

_childDocuments_.review: Very pretty and enticing pixel artwork, but the gameplay just isn't there, at least not for me.I played this as a sort of calming palette-cleanser, hoping for just an easy-going pixel-told tale with easy-enough combat and intriguing enough characters.Instead you have a silent protagonist who people fawn over, a story with nothing but side characters who are only interesting in appearance, and have nothing really useful or funny or lore-building to say, music that's fine until you realize they repeat tracks throughout the game vs. unique tracks per city/area, and a lot of jack-of-all-trades business, master of none.This game is HEAVILY inspired by EarthBound, which is a great game to be inspired by, sure, and I'm all for that-- but what you have is akin to Las Vegas; homages to great things, but empty husks on the inside. Like everyone else has said-- and you can see for yourself-- the pixel artist did their work in spades. The artwork is magnificent and is the reason I put as much time into this as I did....but the story is just arduous, so much dialogue to X your way through, and the small bits of gameplay ranges from easy-as-hell puzzles to frustratingly out-of-place-hard combat, with enemies respawning whenever you backtrack and a timed rhythm game at the end out of nowhere. And there's no difficulty setting, so you're just kinda stuck here. And there's an optional-but-is-everywhere minigame that is nothing but a grindfest akin to Dragon Warrior 1 where you can play an arcade game in the game and progress through that. Another homage, sure, but not a very rewarding one.Pass on this, sadly. So much great artwork and settings without the writing or game design to back it up.

_childDocuments_.review: The main plot of this game was not as interesting as I'd hoped, but the stories of the individual characters and the strange environments you journey through made up for it. That, combined with the awesome pixel art and catchy soundtrack, made Eastward a solid experience for me.If you are a completionist, a chapter select mode is added to the main menu after beating the game. You can use your existing save data and hop around the game's chapters to knock out any achievements you might have missed.

_childDocuments_.review: An action adventure game with great pixel art, music, combat, puzzles, and characters. As described by many people, it is something of a mix between Earthbound in regards to its colorful characters and Zelda in regards to combat and puzzles.However, it is rather on rails, so don't expect something like Link to the Past with a large open world to explore freely. Dialogue and story is also a large part of the game. For people who don't like reading a lot of dialogue, this may not be for you.If you are okay with story-centric games, this one will give you a good mix of story, combat, and puzzles.

_childDocuments_.review: I initially bought and played this game (along with the DLC) on Switch. I loved it so much that I put in the effort to 100% it. My love for the game made me want to buy it all on Steam and go through it all again just so I could show off all the achievements here.If you're a fan of old-school Zelda games, it has a very similar combat style. The fact that you can explore and hunt down treasure chests gives you a reason to look at every inch of the pretty pixel art. There are a few parts where the story could seem confusing but putting it all together at the end is fun. While the DLC isn't necessary, it does have some interesting implication for the world as a whole. That's all I'll say as I don't want to spoil the story.I'd say give it a try. I personally enjoyed it and found it worth the money. If you don't enjoy the first hour, then you probably won't like the rest of the game.

_childDocuments_.name: Eastward

_childDocuments_.review: Tbh I loved the game a lot. It took me the 33.2 hours to beat the game, but I enjoyed it from the game play to the story. I read some of the reviews and understand why people were not happy although I think I went into the game without any expectations and thus did not feel any disappointment. While it is true the story can be lacking in areas and end up leaving certain plot points behind for others, I still enjoyed it the whole time. I do wish they filled in those points, but I accepted it for what it is. Some characters may have been annoying (like Jasper), but you don't see them the whole time. At least, according to their page so for that I think it turned out really good!My one con is: they don't fully explain some mechanics. _childDocuments_.review: It's pretty rare that a replay or rewatch makes me cry a second time, but Eastward did just that. 10/10If you're expecting the best top down action gameplay ever, you might be disappointed. It's good enough though, and the real treat is the beautiful and unique story. It pays homage to the greats while in the same stroke, taking jabs at them. It's weird, clever, funny, somber, and hopeful. It will take you on a wild ride that you won't soon forget.My only real complaint is that the game is extremely easy until the difficulty ramps leagues higher very abruptly at the end. Without warning, it becomes Rhythm Heaven on Steroids. Otherwise, solid.

_childDocuments_.review: This game has an interesting story and some fun gameplay. _childDocuments_.review: The coziest post-apocalyptic setting ever. Amazing gameplay, story, art, music. Heartbreaking at times, hilarious at others. _childDocuments_.review: I have genuinely struggled with whether I'd pick recommend or not for this game - the game is beautiful and the soundtrack amazing, the world is super captivating as are the characters. Ultimately, I chose to recommend it because I don't regret the time I invested in playing, even though the ending was disappointing. Spoilers belowI have to say, towards the middle-end of the game, the story takes a turn that seemingly derails entirely from the narrative built up until that point. At first, you're trying to understand, mostly, Sam's backstory - that supposedly relates to a lot of things going on in the world:   Once you leave New Dam City, though, nothing of that is a priority anymore. At first it seems the NDC chapter just ends on a cliff hanger that would drive the player to other places, to fully understand the questions the game sets up so far, but no. The game fully spirals into some David-Lynch grade abstraction, not answering any of the questions that were the premise for interest in the story in the first place, and leaves it at that. The last chapters feel either like fillers or super rushed, the other locations aren't as well developed or immersive. I genuinely think Eastward could have been launched a year or two in the future, and gotten more love from, especially, the writers to tie the ending better.A lot of the times the last chapters contradicts the story so far, or seems to entirely discard it  To address some of the things other people have commented negatively on: I, personally, did not dislike how much reading was involved in playing Eastward. In fact, I absolutely loved it, I felt like exploring the world made sense - everyone has something to say, some characters adapt their dialogue to whats currently going on in the world (as in, influenced by John and Sam's actions) and they were all clearly very lovingly designed. What I disliked is that, for a game seemingly so focused on story-telling and world interaction, it does not truly reach a satisfactory narrative point. It just... ends. All in all, you should go into it not expecting any of the narrative hooks to actually be addressed, otherwise it'll just be incredibly frustrating.Beyond that, there's a major change in playability in the end as well, where combat is suddenly a lot harder and puzzles aren't... really puzzles anymore. All things considered, it's a fun game, for the most part it's immersive, wholesome and absolutely beautiful. It's easy to connect with the characters and the aesthetics, animation, art and soundtrack are genuinely incredible. You could spend hours just appreciating the setting the artists worked so hard to develop. My only recommendation is to keep an open mind as to where the narrative will take you, whitout getting too attatched to the path it initially seems it'll follow.

_childDocuments_.review: Eastward is a great roleplaying game that offers a good story and decent gameplay. _childDocuments_.review: I enjoyed this game. It is very visually pleasing, has a nice soundtrack, and a variety of different game components like combat, puzzles, dungeons, cooking, and quests. The characters are really adorable and it has a fantastic mini arcade game built in called Earth Born. After I tried it a few times, I liked Earth Born almost better than the main game.There are a couple cons that need to be weighed before you spend 20-25 hours playing the game. The storyline is super vague all the way through. You think they are going to eventually give you answers, but it never happens which is a bummer because a lot of the characters could have had rich backstories. _childDocuments_.review: every bit of this game oozes passion and love, admittedly these days games with that kind of property aren't seen so much, but this game is def an exception.  Everything from the art to the music to the writing just oozes creativity and love, you could really tell when the creators were just having fun with what they were making in this.  The fact this game isn't talked about as much as it should be honestly is a bit of a crime, because it's genuinely a work of art, art in a very weird sense I'll admit but art nonetheless. That being said there are a few issues I did find with the game, albeit small.  The most glaring of issues is the odd pacing of the story, the story of this game is very dramatic and a lot of its most heart breaking moments don't get enough time to shine before the next goofy, upbeat moment comes to ruin it.  In other words, this game has an odd sense of timing when it comes to playing with the emotions of the player, because one moment you'll be hit with tension immediately to be broken by very very very inappropriately timed music.  There also lies an issue with the controls during combat, the combat in this game is admittedly rather  clunky, depth perception is often an issue and switching weapons is not nearly as smooth as it should be during fast combat.  I used a lot more healing items than was really necessary most of the time because I kept getting stuck between weapons when switching.  It's such an odd issue with the game that after a while is something I just slowly got used to but even so it's a bit frustrating.beyond that, it's in short a good game worth it's price tag

_childDocuments_.review: Did you know this is a 3D game rendered to look like it's 2D? That's why - if you squint - you can see sprites clipping into each other at certain points. I assume that's how they make the lighting so utterly gorgeous and the effects so pretty.Overall, this game is a pretty solid one. Awesome looking visuals and fun gameplay lends itself to an enjoyable experience, and although a lot of the characters are Mary Sues in their own respective departments, I still find them enjoyable. Sure, the writing can be pretty "tell instead of show" at times, but I ultimately didn't mind.But the game has its problems.The soundtrack gets old fast when it's the same 5 songs repeating again and again. The story is jumbled and hard to understand at times, and although I beat the game, there are still some aspects I'm confused about. And the difficulty... it's a pretty slow creep for most of the game, allowing the player to get stronger at a reasonable pace as the game gets steadily harder. But then, for the last few hours of the game, everything just becomes ridiculously difficult. PARTICULARLY one fight against a particular sword-wielding blondie.BUT.The game is still a trek I'd say is worth taking, because despite all of that, it is still a fantastic experience. You may need to look up a guide for a few puzzles, but most are straight-forward and rewarding. I'd say give it a go :)

_childDocuments_.review: This game is best played blind. This was the cherry on top of my experience whilst playing eastward as everything was unexpected, left the player surprised at certain instants and really lets you discover the mysteries of this world whilst also being in the dark of the truth. The dialogues are well thought out as the interactions are often oriented towards Sam, a little girl,  which makes the words used either more simple or hides their true intention.  At least, that's what I felt whilst playing  the game. The NPCs are a mix of simple and complicated, but they're all very likeable and funny. Especially Sam and John, the main characters that you play as whilst playing the game. The areas you explore are drop dead gorgeous and also bare an amazing OST to go along with it. Every songs fits the atmosphere they try to display and really makes the experience immersive. Other then that, the fighting mechanics  are pretty simple and fights aren't that difficult, but do demand a certain amount of strategies and some boss fights later on in the game do raise how challenging it is. But in my honest opinion, Eastward isn't just about it's combat, it's about the story line. A story that is so deep and truly impacts the world the game is set in.  There's also extra content in the game that makes the game and it's world further more complete. It may not be for everyone, just like any other games, but this game is truly worth trying out ! You may not like it or on the contrary, love it, but that's for you to discover and for you to give this game a chance to capture your heart like it did for me.

_childDocuments_.review: I’m overwhelmingly glad that I stuck with this game through to the end, because I very nearly didn’t. True to what other people have said - Eastward is glacial; largely disinterested with stringing the player along with explosive story beats, overarching goals and villains. While the game shares many similarities to Zelda: Minish Cap and Mother 3 in its aesthetics, dungeon schema and quirky ensemble cast, it feels closer in spirit to Moon: Remix RPG. Eastward is primarily a story of a journey, a potpourri of emotions and vignettes, and it expects you to inhabit the communities of the microworlds you visit on your journey. I wish I had known this going in, and I’d like to start my review by stating as such as a primer for anyone reading because when I clocked what Eastward’s intentions were and met it halfway, I finally found myself sinking in.Eastward is an adventure RPG revolving around the story of John, a stoic, taciturn miner and his mysterious wide-eyed adoptive daughter named Sam - each born into an isolated town deep beneath the surface. The narrative is ostensibly a one-way ticket on a train powered by Sam’s positive energy and curiosity as she yearns to see the sun for the first time with a thoroughly convincing and endearing childlike wonderment. Upon reaching the surface, I was right there with her.The world is presented through the dichotomy of John and Sam’s polar opposite personalities. Sam is contagiously cheerful and childishly chatty, but she often fails to perceive the more adult dramas and contradictions. Despite John being ghoulishly silent throughout the game, he exhibits warmth and intelligence at points that the player can fill in themselves. This is particularly noticeable in moments like when Sam and John encounter incubators for artificial human beings hidden deep within ruins for the first time. For Sam, those seem almost like hyper-technological playgrounds, while for John, and consequently also for the player, their mysterious and threatening nature is very evident. It’s all surprisingly effective as far as Game Dad character interactions go.Eastward is a post-apocalyptic setting fraught with danger, but dotted along the tracks are pockets of humanity small and large, towns and cities with cultures cultivated over time in isolation. Each is inhabited by characters that are of course quirky, but surprisingly fleshed out and genuinely memorable. It’s been a very long time since a game world has felt so alive and well-told down to its minute details, helped in no small part to the stellar pixel work in the meticulously realised characters and environments. Some of the best pixel art I have ever seen. Honestly, it left me genuinely inspired - to take in every inch of the world, but also to create for myself.I often found myself thinking back to the steps on the path I had already walked, about the characters I could no longer return to, and wondering what they were doing while I was not there to watch. Personally speaking, I can ask nothing more of a game. Eastward acted as a beacon of positive vibrations and inspiration to me. As someone who has never grown out of pinning himself to a train window and imagining the lives of the people in the towns I zoom by, the experience of this game was incisive to something I hold dear. Favourite game of 2021 by far.

_childDocuments_.review: I really liked Eastward but there were some things that made me really frustrated about the game and wishing for more. To start off, Eastward is beautiful, I absolutely adored the art style and environments. Eastward is the best looking pixel art game I've seen personally. I also really liked the puzzles. In my opinion, the devs did a pretty great job with the puzzles and I really enjoyed myself solving them. However, the core gameplay was really frustrating at times. John doesn't have the ability to dodge which makes it really frustrating fighting enemies at times. To add on, even if I managed to dodge an attack with John, Sam often gets hit instead as shes right behind him. It doesn't make sense to me why I'm getting penalised for a character I'm not even controlling. Furthermore, boss fights are generally good and fun but there were a few boss fights that were extremely hard for no reason whatsoever or that they suddenly had brand new mechanics that were never introduced beforehand. For example, the final two fights involve parrying as others have mentioned when the game has never involved parrying at any point.  It can be incredibly frustrating figuring out these mechanics on your own. I really appreciate the ability to fast forward dialogues and fast travelling (added very recently) and can definitely understand the frustration of others not being able to do so previously. The maps are incredibly huge and quests often involve a lot of backtracking. Do note that fast travelling is allowed only within large cities and you still have to run to and fro around the outskirts. The dialogues in this game can be incredibly tedious and off-putting so it helps being able to fast forward them. Certain segments of this game were extremely unnecessary and tedious for no reason whatsoever. They do not help to advance the story and feels like they were added in to drag out the game. Overall, I still really enjoyed this game and can definitely tell that a lot of love and effort went into its making. However, this is not a game for everyone and it requires a lot of patience to complete. Anyways, I'm really looking forward to the DLC and hope it won't suffer from the same issues as Eastward :)
_childDocuments_.name: Eastward

_childDocuments_.review: I really wish I could give this game a positive review. It has some of the best pixel art I've ever seen- absolutely beautiful. It also has enjoyable if not particularly interesting gameplay, and a lot of unique and interesting characters. I played it all the way through, and it just does not manage to stay strong in the last stretch of the game. The later areas never match the unique feel and openness of the first three stops, the plot frays out into a completely incoherent, confusing soup, and the gameplay becomes somewhat more challenging but mostly just more tedious with a special mention for an extremely annoying 'swordfight' minigame that you have to go through in the finale.Seriously, keep the amazing art and characters and get some new writers.

_childDocuments_.review: Eastward is a real tricky game to talk about. Right off the bat, mood and pacing and flavor and theme are all over the place!The biggest hurdle for me is that the game's method of storytelling is at direct odds with its intentional SNES  gameplay model. The story itself is linear, literally from left to right, as you travel on a train going in one direction, stopping a few times to see what life is like, and then moving on. You're a tourist with a one-way ticket.The gameplay is Zelda-esque in that you gain new items and upgrades, opening new possibilities for combat and puzzles. But, because there is no backtracking, all of the air is taken out of that. In a -like you might see a cracked wall near the beginning section of the game and then return gleefully when you get bombs. Every new item or upgrade lets you think, "now how can I apply this to what I've already experienced?" But because Eastward is all about going forward, there's nothing to reflect on. There ARE no cracked walls before you get bombs, there ARE no flammable plants before you get the Flamethrower. Everything you can and will do with your new items are things you haven't encountered yet.This is made more glaringly obvious by enemy design. As you move forward, enemies also change completely. So when you upgrade your weapon, you never actually feel if its stronger because you're fighting new enemies instead of familiar ones. There's a satisfaction in going back to an enemy that used to give you grief and beating them casually with your upgrades. Eastward doesn't do that too often. In fact it kind of feels like you're powering down in some cases. The enemies in the previous chapter took 4 hits with your LV.1 weapon, and now enemies in this chapter take 6 hits with your LV.2 weapon. Maybe they would take 12 hits if your weapon were still LV.1, but how would you know? (To be fair, there's a gauntlet of previous enemies near the end of the game, but by that point it'd been so long that I couldn't remember what they were like to fight against.)As for the story, its best idea is super unrealized.  What a ride! Is this the game? Going from place to place like a vagabond—world-hopping, in a sense—and then moving on, no looking back, little tastes of culture as we head Eastward!?Mmmmm'kinda.In the end, you only visit, like, 3 places after you board the train (not counting another train you visit while on the tracks). So this really cool idea is dropped almost as soon as it's offered. There's a moment in the ending where you reflect back on all the places you've been and it's mostly a bunch of shots from New Dam City in Chapter 3 where you stayed at the longest. Part of me thinks the game is supposed to be all about New Dam City, and the other places are just floppy bookends.Oh and the reason you stay at New Dam City the longest is that suddenly it becomes a bunch of anime filler episodes where two entire dungeon sections are dedicated wholly to finding ingredients for a meal to appease some random guy for zero stakes, and then you go to a hot springs for five minutes just because Hot Spring Episode!It's at this moment that I realized the team wasn't sure what kind of story they wanted to tell.Is it a Father/Daughter survival thing like Telltale's  or ? Is it an  travel adventure? Is it a character study about a man who had lost all hope? Is it a slice of life anime? Is it a  style time loop narrative? Is it a post-apocalypse "let's rebuild the world" scenario? Or a generic Good-versus-Evil fantasy? Or is everything a science fiction -style simulation we're trying to break free from?Yes.To all of that. But not enough to feel intentional.There's a cooking minigame. You can throw in totally odd ingredients and make something completely unreasonable. Octopus, cherries, and chicken will somehow make a delicious-looking hamburger. And it does look like a good burger!Eastward is a lot like that cooking minigame. You have a pan with milk and crab and cheese and whole pumpkins and a pineapple—all these completely random ingredients!—just flopping around over a blue flame, and then POOF, it says "here's your Perfectly Normal Fruit Pie!" And you believe it. It looks like Fruit Pie. But when you take a bite you know the truth.

_childDocuments_.review: One of the most gorgeous pixel art, 16 bits inspired, graphics used in a modern game. The sprites are rich and detailed, the backgrounds makes you want to explore what you can just so you can see them in more detail. The gameplay is simple and reminiscent of classic The Legend of Zelda era: John can use his pan as Link used his sword while also having your trusty bombs for damaging both monsters and walls/obstacles. You can then control Sam, which starts with a power that stuns also similar to Link's boomerang, changing between characters adds a bit of depth with puzzles that separates our duo or just to overcome character-specific obstacles. That are power ups and upgrades. Some bosses can feel less challenging than some everyday monsters.You can cook food, for healing and buffs, collect ingredients and recipes. The slot-machine mini-game, which can result on bonus food quality, combined with the food animation does feel out of place and unnecessary long, especially since you can't skip the animation until after you learn the recipe.The writing reminds me of games from the SNES era like Chrono Trigger, Final Fantasy or EarthBound. That's to say that some jokes while amusing can be a hit or miss. There is a lot of long cutscenes/exposition that due to characters voices being done the old way, by sound tones, can feel a bit drag out. The story feels familiar but still interesting and mysterious enough to be engaging. There is also a full fledged 8-bit RPG game, completed with a gacha system and a manual, which is popular with the game's NPCs(adding dialog flavor) and that can also be played by Sam/the player.Game is meant to be played with a controller and i have had no problems with slowdowns, crashes nor bugs so far.Overall, its a must play for lovers of the NES/SNES era, an instant classic and a contender for, at very least, indie game of the year,

_childDocuments_.review: Beautiful art. Lovely soundtracks. Cool game design and ok gameplay. But the writing of Eastward is unfortunately not on par with how gorgeous its artwork is. The story is supposed to be Eastward's lifeblood given that the dialogue and story takes up about 60-70% of the entire playthrough. It really would've been more enjoyable if not for the writing.  You can see what it was trying to do but at the end it didn't really deliver. You're not really sure what it was about. Quite a lot of the dialogues just didn't advance the plot, some of it is fine to get you to feel the characters are lovable or relatable, but about 60% through the entire game, it started to feel as if all NPC dialogues were meaningless and you just couldn't wait for it to end. And after 20 or so hours of that constant factor, you just couldn't help but feel disappointed because you wanted to be fully invested in everything.TL;DR: Eastward would've been the perfect game if its storytelling was a bit more polished.

_childDocuments_.review: Eastward is a charming lil game. I think its easy to see the Mother influences in it, but it is quite a unique experience. Without spoiling anything, as the name implies, Eastward is a game that finds our two main characters traveling to the east. Along the way you'll visit some strange and interesting locations and meet the people who live there. The game is kinda post apocalyptic, but it doesn't feel so doom and gloom. The beautiful art and music help in that regard as well. It's a gorgeous game with a really lovely soundtrack. That's kinda how I look at Eastward, as almost a slice of life game that has our duo meeting new people and places. There is an overarching story, but unfortunately it is kinda vague and cryptic. There's a lot of questions left unanswered or left up to your own interpretation. The other major aspect of the game is its gameplay and I found it to be satisfying although it feels clunky sometimes. It's pretty basic button mashing with some different weapons thrown in. I had a few instances where I kinda got stunlocked by an enemy, but it's simple enough and mostly fun. I enjoy real time combat in games like these because it keeps the pace fast. Sometimes this game does feel like it suffers from bad pacing though. Some parts of the story kinda dragged a bit and it can sometimes feel like there's too much talking versus going out and fighting stuff. Eastward has some flaws, but I found it to be very enjoyable. There's also a fairly deep minigame I haven't mentioned which is kinda like a classic Dragon Quest game with some roguelike elements. It ended up being addicting and a lot of fun. To me, this was a pleasant surprise, I bought this game like a year ago and only got around to playing it recently and I regret not having tried it sooner. It really is charming and lovely. I think I would have just preferred the story be less open ended. That aside, I recommend giving Eastward a try. Thanks for reading.

_childDocuments_.review: It's an awful pity, but I feel like I'd just be giving the game a pass solely off the aesthetic if I gave this thing a thumbs up.I've got four major gripes with this game:Story Characters, Christ Almighty...CombatExplorationTo start off, this game's story and dialogue is just so ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ . I won't go into much detail because this game is primarily plot driven (which ultimately is why I chose to thumbs down this game) and fairly linear, but the plot is pretty generic which by itself isn't really an issue (the plot holes out the wazoo certainly are, but the story as a whole is such a mess you just sorta stop caring after the first 2 or 3). You'd be hard pressed to find a story, whether in game or book format, that didn't take SOME inspiration from something already done. However, what helps is to give it engaging aspects to make up for predictability or staleness of the story. Like say... Characters! Something this game claims to have a colorful assortment of! Buuuuut they're all generic as hell too, or just completely boring, underdeveloped and honestly? I blame the dialogue. The dialogue is pretty damn basic it's the type of dialogue you want a faster text speed for and for a story driven game, that's a problem. The most colorful thing about really any of the cast are their designs. The characters are either gone too quick to really get attached to them, boring as ever loving hell (which was the vast majority of them), or are just weird stereotypes hoping to come off as quirky.Beware, a spoiler teeming character rant ahead:Combat... sucks. I wish I was just whining, but I don't think aiming my weapons with a game-pad should be as irritating as it is. Hitboxes can be choppy, like a miss looking as if it should've connected. Enemies are something of a respawning free-for-all. I guess they're that way to try and force you to utilize Sam's stun (because outside plot devices and two-man puzzles she's fairly useless) instead of just giving us a damn dodge button. Bosses... are nothing to write home about. They had a good thing going with the first one where they had you utilizing bombs to make it vulnerable to attacks... and then they stopped that trend almost immediately and instead you steamroll till like the last 2 bosses. Speaking of those 2, they introduced timing your attacks to 'clash' at the very end of the game. It would've been a nice mechanic to do for mini-bosses instead of spawnwaves.Exploration was such a missed opportunity man. This one actually makes me sad because of how beautiful the environments look, but there isn't much point to them. There aren't any lore based secrets hiding around or new gear. The best you'll come across is some game currency (salt), heart orb piece (think LOZ's heart pieces), or 'gears' which are a required material to upgrade your weapons. The linear environment doesn't even have much to interact with.Okay, tangent over. I'm more than happy to answer any questions since it's the least I could do after such a long tangent.
