_childDocuments_.review: Alright.  is done and dusted. It was actually a fairly lengthy game with a really cool pixel art style and an interesting take on a post apocalyptic setting. You play as two characters, *John*, a mute warrior and *Sam*, a girl he found and has been raising. The story follows their travels as they are first exiled from their town and then fight to stay ahead of and possibly defeat the *Miasma*, a death fog that kills everything it touches. Basically.The artwork is particularly noteworthy in this game. There is a very real emphasis on hand crafted assets. The level of detail and attention to the use of color and shading makes for a fairly stunning visual experience. Considering how many unique set pieces there are in the game, this is highly impressive.I enjoyed this game, but it definitely has some misses depending on your preferences as a gamer. The combat is fairly representative of top down action RPGs, which works well. The RPG mechanics are centered around upgrading your pack and weapons which can be purchased from vendors with the requisite items/money in your possession; and collecting food and recipes to for buff items, which can be found, cooked, and purchased. Quest progression is mostly linear, and there were only a few quests that were search or map dependent. Fortunately, the map is pretty informative and the levels are pretty straightforward overall. I never got lost.The story is very, very dialogue heavy, and this is probably where people will make a determination as to whether they enjoy the game or not. The intro and first chapter also move pretty slowly. However, the pacing increases as you progress. The character development, both protagonists and NPCs, is quite well done. Similarly, the story is well thought out. It takes some cues from anime, which I guess is also the source material, but it never becomes too surreal and the ending makes sense.The final chapters rely heavily on a time loop mechanic, which was fine and contextually sound for the story, but also probably the weakest part of the game, and the time loop puzzles were definitely bordering on annoying.My total playtime was just under 26 hours. It's a game that is easy to recommend, but with caveats as mentioned above. Solid chance you'll enjoy it, but I could also understand if a person didn't find it to be their thing. It is perfectly Steam Deck compatible, which is always nice to see.
_childDocuments_.name: Eastward

_childDocuments_.review: This isn't to say Eastward is awful, but it definitely is not a game for my style of game (despite my yearn for more bizarre or creative games), and not a game I can suggest to others.It could be that I've played too many fun narrative focused/Earthbound-esque games, but I found most of the dialogue here tedious, the machismo culture tiring, and the pacing awful. While this game definitely has the budget to be huger than most similar games, it fails to capture me like the majority of other RPG's do in both story and gameplay. Additionally, while the art itself feels creative, the writing fails to be creative and feels so copy-paste of not only every sympathetic manly gamer trope, but also of itself for how much the same few conversations happen over and over (like an anime padding run time).Eastward will likely be studied by artists for a long time for how beautiful it is, and I think the animation is amazing and the sound design is solid.The parts where you actually fight feel good to me, even if simplistic, however in over two hours of playing, I've only had a few minutes of actual gameplay due to the length of all the cutscenes. Funnily enough, there is a live stream of Eastward playing in the corner while I write this review. I glance over every few seconds to see what is happening and I kid you not: it's been a cutscene the whole time. Just dialogue with no control and slowly panning cameras (and this is definitely of a part later in the game I haven't seen yet, so I know it's not just because the game has a weirdly long beginning).Most of the gameplay is just going through rather repetitive dialogue, then being forced to walk to an area often already visited and see another cutscene that half regurgitates what was already said, then return to the first section. There is minimal exploration to find useful/interesting stuff to pace it out, and the actual combat/puzzle areas where I thought I'd be playing the game for more than a couple minutes lasted... A couple minutes. Then it was right back to long, repetitive talking.On a more personal level, I also find it hard to like any game that uses manly women as a joke, feminine men as a joke, and fat people as a joke - of which this game has much of. The general treatment of women is uncomfortable to say the least, where the majority exist solely to talk about men, be a one-note mom with no other purpose (unlike the tons of different men that exist), or as pointless eye candy, sometimes put in uncomfortable situations for the fantasy of the straight men.So really, while I cannot say the game is bad or that people won't like it (I'm sure people will DESERVEDLY find this game quite good), I cannot personally suggest this game for anyone except artists who want to study some incredible animation.

_childDocuments_.review: I was really looking forward to this one after seeing some initial art and scenes. It was looking fantastic, and as long as delivered on story and gameplay, it would have been an instant classic. However, while the art is still great, the remaining bits get old really fast. The story is boring and it is hard to push through. The pacing is excruciatingly slow and not at all helped by the "quests" you are given. I am soooo sick to death of these mundane fetch quests. Fetch a ticket. Fetch a cooking item. Fetch some other dumb item that is boring and uneventful. I hate (HATE) it when a game makes you back-to-back walk the distance of an area over (and over) again. Don't even get me started on the dialogue. It never ends! I think 90% of this game might be pointless, boring dialogue. Most games balance out dialogue with some action, but this is the other way around. You will listen to some NPCs blather on for 15 minutes about nothing, then you may get about 2 minutes of actual combat. Don't expect much from the combat either. It is rudimentary at best. At worst, it is boring, tedious, and repetitive. I really doubt I am going to finish this game. If I do, it will be solely because of the art.

_childDocuments_.review: I absolutely adored the artwork, animation, and environmental design for this game! I couldn't comprehend how anyone could dislike a game with so much character and style. For the first two chapters I loved the storytelling, dialog, and the pacing. The in-game game, Earth Born, was a very charming additional activity.I really enjoyed talking to the NPCs initially! However... The third chapter is where the game switches pace and kind of loses focus. I would have explored all of the side-quests had they been optional, but to tack them on to the main storyline felt unnecessary and a bit meandering. Which shocked me, I didn't expect to lose interest in any aspect of this game.There are 8 chapters. I found it difficult to enjoy chapters 4-7, although chapter 6 has some interesting new characters. The puzzles throughout this game are cute, not terribly challenging, I found them very fun! That is until chapter 7 where they start to become repetitive. Always love seeing new enemies, but the combat is not very robust and it's usually over quickly. You do have options to make combat more interesting, though! Like switching between the two characters and combining their abilities.Of the 8 chapters I enjoyed 1, 2, and 8. The rest probably could have been a little more condensed. Great game if you're looking for something slow, easygoing, fun to look at, and full of dialog.

Without an in-depth review of the script and plot, there is not much I would change. The story is interesting and (most of) the characters are enjoyable. (It was refreshing to see a same-sex couple done tastefully for a change, one that doesn't detract/ distract from the story as a whole.)The art style really grew on me after a little while and I would like to see similar effort in pixelated games in the future.

_childDocuments_.review: This overpriced game is graphically sumptuous. Unfortunately, this is its only plus. The rest of the experience is a boring mess, a rambling chaos:         1) the plot makes little sense, for multiple reasons, e.g., the characters' motivations for adventuring (repeatedly risking their lives): the protagonist is a mute miner about whom the player knows nothing else nor will learn anything during the game; the co-protagonist/damsel in distress/little helper/daughter/... is a sort of magical creature/messiah/ghost/... with no other reasons apart from an instinctual curiosity for doing what she does and travelling the world; the world itself is as shallow as it can be, reduced to the basic terms both conceptually (nothing is told about it) and practically (your path is traced, rigid and limited); other characters are a mixture of freaks and stereotypes.        2) the game has no clear identity: it is inspired by classical Nintendo (FC, SFC, GB) RPGs but (as other reviewers also noted) consists mainly of clicking through dialogues, which are nauseatingly lengthy and terribly stupid; there is no need to play the Earth Bound mini-game, despite its being repeatedly mentioned throughout the game and often accessible during it (which is a pity, because merging the two experiences significantly would have given the experience some originality); vast parts of the plot and consequently the level design are incomprehensible/absurd, i.e., inconsistent or not justified enough in relation to the world building and (non-existent) lore, the sort of settings that could only be justified by asserting that the whole thing was just dream or something like that...        4) Many characters appear inserted wantonly, without finding any sensible justification. This does not impact the main characters for the sad fact that in most occasions they make even less sense. Relationships between characters are childish or utterly nonsensical throughout the game. As other reviewers noted, this is extremely serious a shortcoming for a game whose experience is dialogue-centric.        5) Dungeons do not make any sense, for the simple fact that they are not supported by any lore and therefore are as absurd as graphically pleasant, with enemies and puzzles as basic in their patterns as nice they are to look at. Gameplay in combat or otherwise hastly phases is not bad but could benefit form a different solution for controlling weapons, because with a mouse (I played with mouse and keyboard) it is too easy to turn towards a wrong direction, thus complicating otherwise pretty smooth encounters. The cooperation between the protagonists to solve part of the puzzles and an almost negligible part of the fights is a plus within this subset of the game experience but nothing so relevant to make me recommend it.        6) The music is unbearably repetitive and the grunts of the protagonist in combat unpleasant.As a whole, Eastward can be seen as a sketch of a real game, a demonstration of Pixpil's potential, which has not bloomed yet.

_childDocuments_.review: Man, I love this game. It turned me into a pixel art lover!I loved every aspect of this game except for some minor issues, the character's design, the sometimes goofy, sometimes serious dialogue, the pixel art, and the gameplay.You will be John who lives in a city called Potcrock isle, deep underground, built to escape the apocalypse. Our story starts many years after the apocalypse. He meets a strange girl named Sam on one of his trips to the mines and decides to adopt her, but strangely she has some mystery powers, so a mix of wanting to explore the outside world and to find out what is so special about Sam is the core of the first act of the story.The gameplay is extremely fun and they always throw a new Idea for you to play with, at first you play with a pan as your weapon, but as you progress more, they will introduce new weapons, new enemies, new puzzles and much more. As for me, I loved it and never felt bored except for the times they overdid it, For example, before you enter a boss room, for instance, they make you go three routes to power up some generator and it gets stile after the fourth or fifth time.The characters and the places you go to in the adventure are always cool, a village using old boats as houses, a city built on a dam, or the starting city, Potcrock Isle. all of them are unique and Man, they are beautiful!you will meet all sorts of people in your adventure and ALL of them have a unique look and personality, you have Jasper the silly clown, Sam the cheerful child, Captain Pam with his pirate lingo and bright nature, Alva the scientist/princess, Isabela, the adventurer and the knight of the princess, and many MANY more.Don't get me started on the art because they nailed every aspect of it, and dare I say the best pixel art game I've ever played! every city has an identity, every place is special. I can not praise it enough.Now the music is very well handled especially with the cooking mechanic, but I feel like they have been reused A LOT, they are wonderful don't get me wrong, great to hear but if I hear the same boss music ever again...Anyway, the music is good.I didn't understand the story much, but I just fully embraced the vibes of the story and that's it.it took me around 30 hours to beat it because I went everywhere twice and almost finished the game inside of the game, oh yeah, didn't I mention that? They made a full fledged game inside of the game It's crazy! but you could easily finish it in 15 hours or even less.Idc when it was published it's my game of the year for now, I can easily give it 9.5/10 loved it

_childDocuments_.review: This game was not what I had expected. I had so much fun with it and it didn't bore me at the ending, which is an accomplishment. Games I have played sometimes really drag out the ending, but this was just great!The controls were easy, so it was easy to switch between characters and weapons.The environment was in each city/place so different that it made me curious what the next stop would look like. The characters were fun and, even though pixelated, I had a good image what they looked and were like. So much that I was inspired to make some fan-art.The music accompanied the game so well and really set the mood.When exploring in places/cities it felt really slow (not in a bad way) and exploring in combat area's felt fast paced, so there was a nice consistant change in how fast or slow the game felt.I also liked that there was a fastforward button, because some scenes were stretched out with a long black out or walking.It's a pity that I only realised at the end of the game that you could fast travel, but I liked walking through the cities and talking to the npc's. That was a lot of fun. The game had many innuendo's and I really liked that. The game could be innocent at moments because of Sam and other children, but could be experienced as 'oh my... >:}'. The reality of some things said or done by npc's sometimes made me realise how grown-up this game is.But what I really really really liked were the satisfying sounds of walking, wind, rain, talking, fighting, etc. The sound was such a big influence.I honestly loved it.So I definitely recommend this game. It was so much fun!

_childDocuments_.review: I really want to love this game, but I can't honestly recommend it on PC. It's got some great pixel graphics, lovely character design, some excellent sprite work, and the setting has a ton of promise. However, it's got some glaring issues that made me request a refund:- Graphics options barely exist; on 1440p, it looks awful on fullscreen and far too small on windowed, so doesn't look great however you play it on PC.- It just takes forever for it to do anything. Dialogue text takes ages to get through, with no way of speeding it up. Cutscenes indulgently pan and hover with not much on show, to the point I found myself scrolling through things on my phone sometimes because I'd seen what the scene had to offer. Even getting to the main menu is a waiting game, with no way to skip the many logos and taking ages even when you skip the intro cinematic (which mercifully does have an Esc to Skip prompt).- Story is... promising? The setting is great, some of the characters are full of charm, but it's really let down by its writing. It's too wordy (which is compounded by the technical issues with dialogue text) and seems just slightly too proud of how clever it is, and ultimately just wasn't able to pull me in. - Much of it is just wandering around doing fetch quests. I actually quite enjoyed some of the gameplay elements (whacking enemies with your trusty frying pan, the added layer of party member skills, and the split-party sections were all very satisfying) but they're brief moments of fun before returning to more walking and more dialogue.Overall - so promising, but ultimately too tedious to be actually good.

_childDocuments_.review: Folks keep praising this game for it's story and I dunno what story they're seeing. It starts off pretty strong, really enjoyed the first chapter but from then on the pacing gets unbearable and characters just don't make any sense. The gameplay:narrative ratio in this game is probably around 1:4, so for every half hour of the zelda-style gameplay youre getting an hour and a half of cutscenes or walking back and forth around town. And yeah, its an RPG so you're supposed to spend a good deal of time going back and forth, but it just feels more tedious as time goes on as youre just bouncing between spots where some new cutscene plays out. It's all really linear and the actual exploration/combat gameplay always ends right when its starting to do something interesting with the mechanics. I've seen people say the full game is 20-22 hours. I'm at 14 hours of playtime and I really cant/do not want to justify 6-7 more hours on this. The overall production value is excellent. I love so much of the visual design, polished and clean and unique. Soundtrack is full of absolute bangers.

_childDocuments_.review: I've just got to say, that whoever did the pixel art for this game - they really earned their paycheck. Nearly every NPC looks unique and detailed, even ones that serve zero purpose other than just dialogue. It is seriously impressive - unique idle and walking animations that all play up to their designs. I loved it. The environments are also a treat, with so much life and care and personality put into every new area you visit. If there was any recycling of assets, they were hidden well enough to where I never noticed.The gameplay, however, is extremely simple... a lot of the time, it just boils down to spamming the X button while enemies are against a wall. Bosses, while visually stunning, don't get too interesting either (with a few exceptions, of course, but most of them have that standard "hit him when vulnerable to get to the next phase out of three" thing going on.) I think it was around Chapter 5 where I stopped going out of my way to find weapon upgrade parts in the world - why bother when the game is this simple and easy?The story, along with the game's visuals, kept me playing until the end. The characters especially are memorable and fun. The game takes the MOTHER 3 approach (one of the many, many things Eastward borrows from it) whereupon after major story beats, character dialogue changes all across the map - I found myself revisiting areas I was only required to visit once just so I could talk to the NPCs and find new dialogue. I love it when games do this, and there is even a fast travel option to facilitate it. The story does meander quite a lot, though, with tons of dialogue and cutscenes that... really don't matter? Most egregious in Chapter 3, but Chapter 6 also left a sour taste in my mouth. I think whether or not this kills the game for people depends on if you end up caring for the characters - I loved them all, but even I had to question the pointlessness of the many errands the protags were constantly going on when there were way bigger fish for them to fry, so to speak...The music is also pretty great, catchy, though not particularly memorable. Standout tracks for me probably include the New Dam City theme, and the boss fight music. At the very least, it stays consistent throughout, and never feels out of place.I'm glad I gave Eastward a chance, despite the negative things I've read about it from people who gave up on it. It's not perfect, but it kept me interested until the very end, and if a game does that, there's no way I can say it's a bad game.

_childDocuments_.review: Eastward is adorable in its presentation and a joy to have played, doing the majority of things well or better, but certain aspects of its presentation hold it back from being truly excellent. Having said that, what it does present is still worthy of the time investment. This is especially so if the considering player is unfamiliar with the genre or is on the younger side.The areas in which Eastward excels and has shortcomings tend to promote this. The visual and audio presentation is praiseworthy, featuring adorable sprite-work and a charming style that references certain classical Asian landscapes or culture. In some ways it's representative of the insidious Western influence upon it, most clearly noticeable from the recipe variety.Its overindulgence in these matters is demonstrative of the title's shortcomings, however. Eastward is ultimately the story of Sam, and as such is the primary focus, having many endearing sprites to outwardly and with childlike innocence represent her many different emotions. Her counterpart and silent protector, the guardian that is John conversely has relatively few sprites - appearing rather sparse in comparison.Likewise, it is charming at first to demonstrate this relationship visually, but in conjunction with the approach to storytelling can become a little tedious. In the small world of the prologue where the stakes are low it matters little should someone with custody of a young and spirited child allow them to make decisions and determine directions in order to learn consequences, but John's lack of intervention during legitimately dangerous scenarios and resolve to be utterly silent, following and being at the whims of a child in times of peril, ultimately go against his character and what he ostensibly stands for. What Eastward does best in my opinion; that representation of youthful innocence, curiosity, and sense of justice that is exemplified by the relationship between the two protagonists can terminate by becoming a flaw of presentation. Eastward makes frequent use of dramatic irony, which is suitable for a pantomime where the only recourse for the audience is to shout in hopes of altering the script, or to realise and gaze through their fingers - unable to look away from the mounting inevitability. But for the protagonists of a video game to do this, characters which the player controls to act out the story, can become tedious and a little annoying when used repeatedly. In an attempt to lower raised tension to provide the player with appropriate respite, the story can often be advanced by very convenient means that the player seemingly has little control over. To bring the aforementioned together, there is one instance where the simple intervention of John, made clear by dramatic irony - a scenario where an innocent child would happily part with something dear and important to aid another, but would not fool a sentient adult, would prevent the aimless setback of the player - all in the name of advancing the plot.The game-play itself, how the player can and is able to interact with the world is fun, simple, but nothing to write home about. The combat and the puzzles match the same description but exemplify the simple to the point of being a little easy and repetitive, hence why it would be a suitable and enjoyable introduction.Eastward wears its reference material on its sleeves, which is nostalgic and pleasant as a sign of appreciation for what game before, but can give merit to the argument that Eastward is a little too referential and derivative rather than original. When a work is too much so, it can become a lesser sum of its parts, attempting to replicate and copy from too many sources without excelling in one of its own. It is so in this case, as I may consider greater past titles that excel in Eastwards components. For instance, one may point to Mother 3 and Chrono Trigger for the world, storytelling, and graphical influence, Cross Code for puzzle and game-play elements, and so on.What makes Eastward captivating would almost be better suited to something akin to a slice of life - where it matters not if characters don't grow as a consequence of their actions, an almost static world where the current representation of characters and their interactions with others and the everyday comings and goings is able to shine more readily.

_childDocuments_.review: Eastward has amazing visuals and a great soundtrack, but it is unfortunately bogged down by mediocre gameplay and irritating characters. Its more positive aspects gave me enough motivation to finish the game, but that might not be the case for everyone.I don't need to sell you on how great this game looks, it's obvious from the get-go that a lot of time and effort has gone into making Eastward look as incredible as it does, and that care applies to every single location and character throughout the game. The OST also features some stand-out tracks like Sam's theme, and although some songs tend to repeat more than others, it never felt like a problem for me.It's... passable. It feels nice to whack the hell out of baddies, but there's little reason to engage them while exploring the overworld as they rarely drop anything useful*. You're better off ignoring them altogether to save up on ammo and health. Aside from a few bosses, obligatory encounters never feel too exciting as you have no options to reliably dodge attacks, making most combat scenarios feel formulaic. You either stun the enemy with Sam then attack, or just tank the damage and mash the action button to kill them as fast as possible. The puzzles aren't particularly hard, but it feels nice to solve them and continue on at a brisk pace. And Earth Born is a nice distraction from the main story. Speaking of...Starting with John. I thought he was the "gruff, but fun and reliable" type when I first looked at his official art and in-game portrait, but it turns out he's actually just an empty husk with no thoughts, backstory or motivations besides "care for Sam". Oh, but he IS reliable though, as the game will tell you a thousand times about how he's a "combat master" and a "master chef", never expanding his character further and continuously repeating the same head scratch animation everytime Sam asks him a question. There's plenty of ways to make a good silent protagonist and this is NOT of them. Any scene that focuses on John is a complete waste of time because it never goes anywhere. Thankfully Sam doesn't have these problems since she y'know... actually expresses herself, but that brings on another issue - the dialogue. It never clicked for me. The length of the cutscenes wasn't a problem personally, but a lot of conversations that tried being endearing or comical just fell flat, making most characters rely on their charming animations to make me care about them at all. This is noticeable from the very first chapter and my opinion didn't change throughout the game. If you start to feel bored by the third chapter, don't expect things to get much better.Anyway, back to Sam - I like her! She's adorable and has fun quirks like how she emphasizes "the" everytime she says "Mr. THE Sonic Punk" or how she gets sad when separated from John, not to mention her cute dances. Sadly, she's also integral to why I dislike the story. Like I said, John has no motivations other than protecting Sam, so the story primarily focuses on her whims as she constantly makes rash decisions that lead into unnecessary or annoying scenarios. Chapter 3 is the biggest example of this, and it demonstrates that the writers were more focused on presenting zany situations than elaborating and improving on the main cast and the mysteries of the world. Sam's psychic abilities aren't talked about AT ALL which brings its own set of annoyances, but this review is too long already, so let's just skip to the other characters.Which are, uh... Uva, a woman that somehow falls in love with John in a day... Jasper, a cowardly showman that is forgotten and tossed aside without any resolution to his character... Alva who I actually like, but could've had more screen time... And Isabel, who I guess is supposed to mirror John with the exception that she talks... and that she sliced a dog in half that one time. Oh, and Solomon exists and he's supposed to be a villain or something? Honestly, I didn't understand his part in the story at all.It hurts to not recommend Eastward, but the below average characters and subpar story coupled with some questionable game design* really hurt the experience for me. If you still decide to give it a try, I sincerely hope you have more fun than me! Regardless of its issues we can all agree that this game looks absolutely fantastic and that alone could be reason to buy it. It's just a shame that the rest of the game doesn't shine as bright as its visuals.*: Seems like they fixed enemy drops and added some nice quality of life changes. Nice!... Still can't recommend it wholeheartedly though lol.

_childDocuments_.review: Hey, I beat this game in almost 22 hours. I liked it, but I have several critiques, and some reasons why this may not really be everyone's cup of tea. I'm honestly a little bit disappointed.The story's fine at the beginning for what it is. It's slice-of-life but clearly focused on this girl, Sam, who follows the main character (John) around. Through the story you meet a deal of unique enough characters and the story as your party continues to travel has its ups and downs as far as being happy and sad, which is good and refreshing. I can stand the less urgent talk between things like combat and serious story moments, and actually found it kind of endearing a lot of the time. I enjoyed that much of it.My problem is far late in the game the story takes a turn for the really absurd and less relatable, and it only spirals out of control from there. It also just kind of ends up being shrouded less by mystery and more by an overly cryptic lack of sense. That's the most I can say without spoilers. Maybe there's more sense in there somewhere that I missed, I'm not sure, but I wasn't quite sure where to find that extra sense if there was, because even in only ~22 hours to complete this game, I actually kind of think that I probably spoke to most if not all of the characters that could shed some light on things if there were any. As a spoiler, aside from the ones the story makes you interact with, it doesn't really seem there are.That brings me to my next problem. This is an adventure game. I got the impression going into this from the trailers and such that there was going to be a bit more world to explore - and don't get me wrong - the game shows you quite a bit of world, but there is ALSO only one, singular, linear storyline to follow that guides you to those parts of the world. There isn't really much reason to go around talking to all the characters and looking everywhere you can like I did; they don't have a lot for you. There are no side-quests, no ways to change story outcomes in the single storyline you get and while there're some incentive to explore and find secrets, it's all just loot which is more often than not just health upgrades. None of it really helps make sense of the story, changes anything or introduces much new with the exception of some cooking recipes via getting new food items to cook with. This all just kind of leads to a serious lack of replayability, at least for me. I liked most of the main story, I just wanted more than the main story. I was really hoping there would be ways to explore these different characters that clearly have a lot of history and importance in this setting beyond that main story. It was disappointing to me. I feel like it's a lot of wasted potential.I hate to leave a negative review on a game I've been anticipating so much, and even liked a lot. I just really don't think many like-minded people would though, as I'm still disappointed even if I did enjoy a lot of it.

_childDocuments_.review: I had doubts before playing and upon finishing, I tried so hard to hold up tears but failed. For me, Eastward is a hidden gem. But it's not a perfect game, as of June, 17, 2023, only 16.2% player have finished the game. It has flaws but cannot obscure the splendor of the jade.The pixel art is utterly beautiful and elegant. Fascinating, I'll put it in this way. From all those places- future city, countryside, cropland field, underground places to grocery stores, pubs, apartment buildings, labs to single rooms, each look different and has its own glamour. The graphic is definitely a highlight, pixel art at its peak, looking fabulous in different times of the day and under various weathers, the light and shadow are executed extremely well.Playing this game is like watching a road film. Travel to places, sightseeing, new equipment, get to meet new people and know  places, chase your goal while helping them, develop friendship and eventually bid goodbyes. You know you won't stay at one place for too long because you don't belong. Many characters are loveable, the lines are short but straight to the point, be it humorous, sarcasm, and give facts - facts so right at some point it hits me, if I've played this game earlier I'll handle some sad moments better. You'll see ups and downs in this game like real life, witness the greatness of love and faith, then accept that even the best of the best can fail.This is life.Puzzle-solving and battle takes 50% of the game, they get a bit annoying in the last 2 chapters when you have to reach a certain point before time runs out, without a checkpoint. But the rest are pretty okay for me, as puzzles are easy and battles can be avoided except for the bosses, you can cook foods with various ingredients like in Zelda games. The rest 50% is walking sim and dialogues, the dungeons are fun to explore as well as the cities, usually containing multiple smaller maps with some treasures, collect them to get more hearts and part for upgrades.The story is not hard to follow, if you pay attention to dialogues you don't need to pay extra to understand. It's good the game does not keep throwing more questions, it gives many hints and explanations along the way, and tells everything at the end, the story unfolds with good path and speed. At the end even I could foresee the end I still cried, for the sadness and a new hope.Writing here, a quote pops "If you don't fear life, you should not fear death, as it is just one of them". But how to face one you love so much yet you still can't save them?

_childDocuments_.review: This is a game that shows how much care and dedication it took to be made. It excels in presentation, provides content for more than 20 hours and, even though the core mechanics may be too simplistic or unpolished for some, they do not stain the overall experience too much, and lets the game be enjoyed as its own thing.The art style is stunning. Aside from enemies and a few obstacles, I don't recall any sprite as being notoriously reused throughout the game. Also, as another commenter made me notice, every NPC has their own sprites. Moreover, some of the main tools, like the fridge and the stove, are so well-presented that made me wish I had a physical miniature of them.The soundtrack is arguably one of my top-three favorites ever in gaming. Even though it's all retro-styled, the quality that modern tools provide shines in it, merging the nostalgic feel that the retro synths evoke with the melancholy tone of a post-apocalyptic setting. It's surprising how some quite frequent tunes, like Home, Weather Talk and Cooking are such masterpieces despite their brevity, raising the annoyance threshold of having to listen to them over and over again quite a bit. Other longer themes like Eastward, Rust and Strange Quest are top tier bangers.Overall, the presentation manages to create that sensation of longing that most memorable pieces of entertainment achieve, where you crave for a bit of that weird beauty and fantasy in your real life. The art crew did a really good job in making this pixelated world come to life and be remembered.The story is a typical hero's journey, but the context where it takes place makes it quite enjoyable nevertheless. The world is interesting, the characters feel alive, and the underlying lore, although not entirely clear, combines a few ideas (time-travel, dystopian future, life and death) in a very interesting way. I presume that the writers had a very personal idea or something they wanted to say to the world and delivered it through this game. And despite the use of clear references, still came out as something original in the end, at least in my opinion.My only complaints would be the excess of sexist humor and the randomness of one of the chapters, which, as several other commenters have pointed out, appears more as a filler than as a continuation of the story.I feel that the criticism has been a bit unfair for what the game is worth. I had seen some trailers before buying it and, in my experience, offered just what it promised me, no more, no less: a beautiful pixel-art adventure, with an ambitious world-building. The only thing that I didn't consider was that the soundtrack was ridiculously good, so that came as an extra to me. Maybe it's not worth the full price, but if you catch it on sale and are a fan of retro-inspired adventure games and music, give this one a try.

_childDocuments_.review: I was so, so excited for this game. I watched the original trailer several times and the moment the game released I bought it. To be completely fair, I am aware of the very difficult development process the team went through, I respect them for sticking through to the end. That being said, I just wish they would have delayed the game's release. Between the awful progression system that is downright irritating at times, and the story that hops all over the place without reason or explanation, this game was a quick finish and uninstall for me. The amount of times I have gone to get a chest or something with my brand new ability, only for the game to say "No! You missed your chance and now you aren't allowed over there!" when the item is 1 screen away is infuriating. The progression is incredibly linear and forced. Speaking of the story, this game's story bounces all over the place, leaving so many question unanswered. Chapters 1 and 2 set up a decent amount of mystery and questions, the first 2 chapters are easily the best ones. But everything past there is a mess. Spoilers ahead: It is never explained how Alva died, which is kind of a big deal considering how important of a character she is, it is not explained how Isabel knew of Ester City (it is also not explained how she even got to Ester city due to the time fog bs), it is not explained why we fight 3 different Solomons (are they clones? That still wouldn't make sense since the oldest is the last one encountered despite also being the furthest back in time due to the Ester city loop), Ester city being in a time loop to begin with is not explained at all, the fact that John and Sam were magically inserted into said time loop. In all honesty, the villains were extremely boring because nothing about them was ever explained. The villains were simply there. The ending was such a cop-out as well because it was just another "Oh no! Child is dead! Boohoo so sad!" only for her to be reborn or something, which is just another thing that never gets explained. This game looks great but the story was just lazy and poorly written.

_childDocuments_.review: + Likeable characters+ Great atmosphere+ Charming graphics+ Good level design; decently designed puzzles+ Simple, but enjoyable combat- Dialogue cannot be sped up nor skipped, and there's way too much of it- Missable achievements/items, but with no option for new game+ or chapter selection- Some parts of the story are pure filler, tedious, and repetitive to play through- Too many characters are introduced as important only for them to be quickly forgotten+/- Much of the dialogue consists of mostly inane banter, but still has its charming moments+/- Overall story is good enough to keep you interested, but lacks real depthPixpil's primary goal is to convey a sense of nostalgia. The game is all about travelling, meeting new people, and then bidding farewall once you move on. Every time you close a chapter, the game gets you to miss the places you've been, and the characters you've met; and it is all done pretty well. This instillment of nostalgia, charming atmosphere, and good level design kept me playing the game.But while Eastward has its charms, it also has 2 major flaws: too much banter dialogue and no option for chapter selection. If you're the type who does not care at all about story or one who gets impatient quickly, you'd probably want to avoid this game. There are some parts of the game which can have 10 mins straight of continuous dialogue, and all you can really do is mindlessly tap the continue button while it goes on. Why the developers couldn't have at least allowed the option to speed up text bubbles is beyond me. I see this as a major factor in contributing to quick refunds.The second major flaw is that the game doesn't tell you that if you fail to acquire an item in a chapter before moving on, there is no way of going back and getting it. Once you've moved on, the only way of getting those missed items is to start a fresh save. This is a major turn off for completionists and kills the potential for replayability. I wouldn't foresee myself putting myself through all that unskippable dialogue again.If you like charming and happy games with an easy to medium amount of challenge, Eastward is well worth a buy. But if you're impatient and hate the thought of dealing with tons of dialogue, you'll probably wanna give this a pass.

_childDocuments_.review: I truly loved this game. I would be happy if this incredible story was turned into a major motion picture but knowing Hollywood they would probably destroy it. The dungeons are really cleverly designed. The puzzles never frustratingly hard. Overall the dungeons strike this balance between relaxing and engaging. And the music... OMG THE MUSIC. SO CATCHY. There are definitely a few tracks going on my favorites list.

_childDocuments_.review: As others have stated, there are many things to love about this game. The music, setting, characters, and pixel art are all fantastic. The problem is that the story starts to break down a little over half way through the game. It seems like there's going to be some big pay off at the very end, but then it ends and you're left with even more open questions that won't be answered unless there is a sequel. Those who care about storytelling will be disappointed. The fact that the game  draws you with all the previously mentioned positive elements and a strong start makes the ending even more painful by contrast. It feels like they fired their writers towards the end of development and had a different team wrap up the story. Perhaps they just couldn't write a good conclusion. We may never know.
_childDocuments_.name: Eastward

_childDocuments_.review: Eastward suffers from one of my biggest problems with indie developers nowdays: Make the game pretty, forget to make it fun.But it also goes an extra mile by trying to be something that truly didnt need to: EarthboundAnd also failing doing it.Ignoring the obvious praise of the art direction of this game (seriously is real good) the game is basically a slog to play. According to the devs its 30 hours long (it took me 24 hours with like 3 being on a mini game that is more fun than the game itself) which you would mostly spend talking with NPCs, putting bombs to solve easy puzzles and talking to more NPCs for the first 10 hours of the game.Then after it you would unlock the other mechanic of the game which would add another button to your current putting bomb button. Repeat this for another 10 hours.While doing this you also get to read the story which, on a basic level, it has a lot of potential with an interesting setting and lore behind but that it crashes by the awful pacing and obvious lack of direction cause at the end of the day, the devs didnt know what to do with their characters.There are, in my opinion, 6 prominent characters in this game, that you get to know during it just so at the end most of them end up doing nothing. It's a great disrepect for probably one of the 3 interesting aspects of the game.Speaking of characters, this game could theorically have a rock or a box as the main character and i dont think it would change anything. So much ♥♥♥♥ happening in this world and in front of his eyes and he doesn't react or act to almost anything. It also doesn't help that his sprite makes him look like the most boring and uninterested person ever.Then, after 20 hours of slog, you reach the final 2 chapters, which are filled with interesting concepts not only story wise but gameplay wise and you are wondering why wasn't the game cut 10 hours so you could just play this sections earlier.And at the end of the day, thats the real curprit i mentioned earlier: this game is too big. Too big of a story that wasn't developed well enough. Too big of a game that was basically empty from mechanics up to the last 2 hours.And too big of a disappointment, cause when you really think about the good parts, you can only think what this game could have been if it wasn't trying to be what it isnt.

I was knee deep invested in the storyline, the characters, the game play- but so much was never explained and I was waiting till the end to have everything wrapped up. The ending made me super disappointed at how anti-climatic it was and felt so thrown together instead of complex and thorough like everything else in the game was. I adored Sam and Johnʻs dynamic, I loved the world building, I loved all the side quests/storylines going on- but it all felt for naught at the end.Love the art, love the overall game, just felt really really disappointed with the ending.

_childDocuments_.review: The graphics are great, the story is great, the boss fights are great. the characters are great, the game within the game is great, but there's one thing that isn't great and it's basically what you do the major part of the game when you're trying to explore, which is the combat... The combat is SO BAD!It ruined the experience of this game for me. It's clunky, unrewarding and disappointing. You get materials for cooking, health, ammo or salt (the currency), that's it. You don't level up so there's no point in battling with such clunky mechanics, it's stressful.I started avoiding the battles very early. Still,I had to force myself to keep playing through so many areas due to the combat being so boring. The damage you take is also weird, some enemies deal more damage than bosses do for some reason, some simple silly enemies can deal 2 health points of damage, which doesn't sound like a lot, but with your limited health and backpack in the beginning, makes the game annoying. I wanted to finish it with all achievements, but remembering how awfully bad the combat experience was, it stops me from replaying it, I just can't.If you're in only for the story and the beautiful graphics, you should go for it.If you're looking for a nice dungeon crawler experience in combat, stay very very very away from this game.

_childDocuments_.review: Environments & details.Character designs.Music & atmosphere.Puzzles are interesting.Player hitbox: why does your partner count as a second hitbox while together?Difficulty pacing: miasma ch2, some enemies take forever to kill and some have no pre-animation for attacks making you rely on timing. Some parts I have no need to recover health, other parts I go through my entire backpack's worth of food.Invincibility frames: little to no time to recover from mistakes, your health can drop super quick.Hitboxes + invincibility frames: either frames are too short or your partner doesn't share invincibility frames, either way great game designTeam tagging gameplay: I get the idea behind this but why does the energy bubble have so little stun duration, in fights with multiple enemies you might as well just stick to John 100% of the time instead of switching back and forth.Story: not my cup of tea, but might appeal to some.Story pacing: dear god is it ever so slow and the filler is meaningless.Cutscenes: be prepared to go through hours of cutscenes followed by 15-30 minutes of gameplay.John: I get not making him talk but personally it just ruins the connection between him and Sam. So many cutscenes devoted to building the bond between the 2 just wasted on a relationship I don't care for imo.Upgrades: weapon upgrades are generic and not clear in how much of a damage upgrade they provide.Charged attacks: kinda useless in combat, afaik stun duration is not changed.Bosses: laughable boss design, some are good like the big pot crab which utilize an earlier presented mechanic, but many are damage sponges.Jasper: tldr; wallpaper generator

_childDocuments_.review: Overall a beautiful game.Beautiful art, lovable characters, nice music, and well built.The story is written really well, even thought Chapter 6 feels a bit out of place, like it was written to make the game just a tiny bit longer.However, I think that - if the game is played as it is structured (ie: taking a break before starting new chapters) - this won't be very much noticeable, if at all.Another thing is achievement tracking, especially for those that revolve around doing all of a certain thing, like discovering recipes, obtaining ingredients, and so on.Those may become unobtainable in game, and it can become frustrating when trying to find the last few chests you forgot (but you really didn't).This is the biggest issue I had.Other than that, I loved the game and I think you'll love it too.

_childDocuments_.review: So I love the artwork and it plays okay but storywise Im not a fan. (Very mild spoilers ahead) If I wanted to play a game that just introduced characters to kill them off, I'd play The Walking Dead. Having the kid is beyond annoying to me.  For "storys" sake she keeps undoing your work, you work hard to get something and someone feeds you a BS story WHO COULDNT BE MORE OBVIOUS THEY ARE LYING? She just gives it to them. _childDocuments_.review: I wish I had a good, detailed reason why I don't like Eastward, but I think the best I can do is say it gave me a general feeling of walking through molasses. Everything I did felt like it took longer than it had to, got interrupted by more dialogue that wasn't particularly funny or interesting, etc. which was a darn shame because it felt like there was a ton of love put into this game, and a lot of excellent visual and sound design.But it also felt like the developers didn't trust me to discover it on my own, and instead decided to yank me away from actually playing the game constantly. Of the little over a half hour I played, it felt like most of it was dedicated to getting yanked into extremely slow dialogues(it's all just text, but there's no option, like there would be in a damn SNES RPG or something, to just click once to have the entire text pop out, instead I had to wait for the sloooooooooooooooooooooooow text scroll to get it over with) that I really didn't find myself caring about.And getting forced into side activities I had no interest in.Maybe it's just me getting older, but these days I just have such a low tolerance for games that have super-intrusive tutorial sections. Delaying my freedom to actually *play* the game so much just chafes me and leaves me with no real interest in seeing the rest of the game.

_childDocuments_.review: There are some very minor spoilers ahead. You have been warned.Before I begin I want to make it clear: I actually finished the game even though I was tempted to actually just stop playing several times. This usually doesn't happen. I don't usually just stop playing games. Anyway...There's definitely a lot of work and love that went into environment design, pixel art and animations. There's no denying that. This is one of the prettiest pixel art games that I have played.The music is alright, but feels schizophrenic sometimes. At some points the game tries to be very retro-like with the audio and at other times it's full-on 80s synth (which is where the music shines the most IMO). I'm not sure why some tracks are using such a limited palette of samples.Combat? Eh, it's not really fun. It's more of a chore. The Zelda inspiration is clear (just like the heart container health bar, 4 heart orbs to get a new heart container, the Solomon keys of Wisdom, Strength and Courage, bombs, even the cooking reminds me of BOTW in both animation and utlitiy, etc.), but it's not even close to a Zelda game in finesse. While initially the combat feels ok, as more dynamic and powerful enemies start to show up, the combat starts to become more of a chore than fun. e.g. The mushroom head zombies in chapter 2 are pure damage sponges and just plain boring. It felt like killing one of them took 20 hits and all you really do is stand there and wail on the until they die. If you don't manage to kill it, it will start going after you. And this is one of the worst parts of the combat: the hit boxes. Some enemies are fairly fast and swinging the frying pan just a fraction of a second too early or too late means you'll get hit. And you can't even damage boost from that situation most of the time because the frying pan hit box doesn't extended to John's position. Yes, if an enemy hits you and stays in roughly the same spot as John (which happens easily 80% of the time as most enemies attack with their bodies), you can't hit the enemy back until you move away first. This just adds to the frustration of the combat. While it's possible to use some alternate weapons, those consume ammo and are barely stronger or have more range than the frying pan. Mini-bosses repeat way too often and oftentimes mini-bosses are just a bunch of normal enemies cramped into a smaller space in larger numbers. This becomes a chore yet again. The only thing in combat I can praise is boss design. All bosses are distinguishable, well thought-out and interesting to fight. My only gripes with bosses is that the difficulty curve is weird. The train boss (Solomon adult) was probably the hardest boss in the game and the sword-fight boss (I won't spoiler the name) right before the final boss was pure ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ because it was just a glorified button prompt and very annoying. I had to spend my entire stash of healing items on that boss. Then I went to the final boss and didn't use a single healing item because there was actual skill involved in fighting him rather than just being precise with timing button prompts.The story? Oh boy. At first it felt like the game would have a rich world with many different and distinct characters in a whimsical and goofy manner. I don't mind slower beginnings as it takes time to get accustomed to the world. But here? The game repeats this pattern over and over. I love story-rich games and I never skip dialog, but in this game I wish there was a way to skip dialog. Why? Because most dialog is just dribble and fluff. There was so little story-relevant dialog in the game that in the end I wasn't even sure what the actual story was or who the villain was (ie. why the villain existed or why there are 3 Solomons). Characterization is cool and all, but at the point where you meet the 50th character and you're supposed to care about his goals and dreams in life as well, it just becomes a slog. I don't even remember the names of most of the side-characters. I remember Jasper, William and Daniel because they were around long enough to actually start caring. I remember Mung because his characterization stood out from the crowd. I remember Thomas and Ivan because they were kinda relevant. And obviously Isabel, Alva and Lee. That's it. 90% of the plot is FILLER. 90% of the characters are FILLER. Take it all out, it doesn't affect the game's story in the slightest. There are 3, maybe 4 events in the game that have any impact on the game's actual story. And ironically enough a good deal of the story is really dark. And this becomes very jarring in contrast to the whimsical world-building that permeates the rest of the game.I really wanted to like the story. I was ready to put up with mediocre combat and annoying side characters. But in the end it was so exhausting that I didn't even care about what happened in the aftermath of the game's story.So if you don't mind doing stupid side-quests (which are actually the main quest!) for stupid characters that you barely care about, then this game is for you. If not, stay away from it.And I hope you like missable collectible because basically everything is missable.

_childDocuments_.review: Input registry is really bad. Whenever your character gets hit or there's a cutscene of monsters spawning or doors closing or whatever else, the game stops taking input of your character's actions, which gets super frustrating in combat as you'll occasionally not move when you need to get out of the way. Somehow, it feels at the last possible minute, the developers decided to delete the dodge-roll feature that was in the game all along and ship the game.Now in the current state of the game, with no dodge-roll, melee combat feels VERY stiff and unresponsive. And sadly, there's a LOT of combat in this game.Ranged combat isn't any better because you need to be within hugging distance of the enemy for ranged weapons to work.Franky, combat should have taken a major backseat in this game, but sadly it shares equal parts with dialogue and puzzles, which makes this game a chore to grind through when it comes to combat and boss battles.Do be sure to check out this game's DLC Octopia which a massive thumbs-up from me. If you get this game, get the DLC as well. 20 hours of pure farming fun. 'nuff said.

_childDocuments_.review: - Overview - Eastward is an incredibly charming little adventure-action game that has a lot going for it: a badass stoic-and-silent older-male protagonist adventuring alongside a younger, plucky, adorable, and sometimes downright-mischievous female sidekick whom he seems to be something of a father-figure for. Think Joel and Ellie, Leon and Mathilda, or Booker and Elizabeth.- Story/feel; 3.5/5The story is fine; a world-impacting mystery that sees you pulling you through various towns and cities that seems to heavily revolve around your faithful snow-haired companion Sam that all resolves itself quite satisfyingly in the end. I didn’t click with the protagonists as easily as I usually do for this kind of character pairing, and I’m not quite sure why, finding myself a little more interested in almost every other pair of characters than the protagonists, especially the story of William and  Daniel. - Main mechanics; 2/5With a lot of this game is focused around combat, and some of the encounters you have are amazing, it’s a shame that there seem to be an almost equal number of encounters that are equally frustrating, feeling long and drawn out. While I opted to use the frying pan weapon as much as I could (which may have impacted my combat-ability), even using other later-obtainable weapons would have felt a little hamstrung by having two characters. I couldn’t help but feel that the game may have been built around a co-op experience; two characters that have their own hitboxes and a shared health pool? While the default setup has the current character you aren’t controlling follow close by your controlled character, they can still be hit and damaged by enemy attacks, leading to many moments of frustration. Of course you can split the party up to control them 100% independently (though still only one at a time – and are required to do this for numerous puzzle areas throughout the game), it still requires you to keep an eye on both the characters at all times. Unfortunately, there were moments that I found myself getting actually irritated by the game because of this (especially when, during one combat encounter, the aim function just stopped working, requiring me to redo the fight entirely – I was still able to use the joystick to navigate menus, it just refused to work outside of it.)- Side mechanics; 3/5There aren’t a huge number of side mechanics in this game. There is an arcade game called Earth Bound, however due to certain audio issues (covered in the next section) I had to forgo playing this. There is a gatcha-style collectable-game featuring characters from the aforementioned game (that I believe affects the arcade game in some way). I realised that each place you visit has its own gatcha-toys a little late, so wasn’t able to collect them all. There is also a food-crafting gambling minigame. You buy ingredients, and cook them (i.e. combine them together) at various stoves throughout the game. How you combine the ingredients you’ve bought will create different recipes. Some recipes you’re told about, some are found through trial-and-error. Each of the foods cooked can be eaten for health & energy ,with each food helping in different ways, modified by adding spices, and a line-em-up roulette wheel. Like everything else about this game, this is an incredibly charming addition, though after awhile it can get a little grating. Thankfully you are given the option to skip the animations if you chose. - Music & noise; 4/5I don’t tend to pick up on music in games (to the point of being unable to recall any non-diagetic music after the fact if someone else mentions their appreciation of it) and while by and large Eastward is no different, the final-fight musical accompaniments are very much a (as the kids may or may no longer) say; a bop, to the point that I might consider buying the OST just to listen to them on my own time (the only other games I can recall doing that for are for a number of Supergiants’ games, as well as bioshock infinite). What I did notice however was a large absence of music (or really much ambient noise throughout large periods of the game (to the point I wasn’t sure if I had somehow muted some track. I had not). Like many games, Eastward is set to 100% volume at the start, and unfortunately, I found the volume mixing a little over the place. Even after dropping audio down, the Earth Born game (as previously mentioned in the Side Mechanics section)  was still ear-splittingly loud, and finding the settings to make it palatable meant other sounds in the game were barely audible. - Graphics; 4.5/5While subjective, I’d find it hard to believe that anyone would say the art in this game is ‘bad’. Obviously, people might not like pixel-art artstyles, but personally I would argue this the quality of this is second-to-none. Every place you visit has so much detail it would feel almost overwhelming if everything weren’t so charming, filled with what I like to dub ‘cozy clutter’ (Think of the houses in a ghibli films, and extrapolate that feeling to entire towns). Of course, unfortunately, there are times when the game isn’t entirely clear with what is where, with the artstyle making it a little hard to distinguish between foreground and background elements (both of which may be traversed at some point during the game).- Overall; 7.48/10Generated using a weighed scoring system based on my own preferences:Story & Feel: 3.18/4.5Mechanics: 2/3Music: 0.5/0.5Graphics: 1.8/2
_childDocuments_.name: Eastward

_childDocuments_.review: Eastward excels at presentation, while being dramatically held back by its story and game play. The sheer variety of pixel art and music on display is impressive, as well as environments in the world and areas the game takes you to. No two places within the game feel the same or cookie cutter. It is this sheer variety alone that kept me playing Eastward. I'd recommend Eastward to anyone who wants to experience some high quality pixel art and some stellar music. This games variety is both its greatest strength and weakness. There are a LOT of different characters, all feel uniquely designed, have their own unique animations and some only have one-liners in the background. However, this is severely let down by the games story, in many respects. None of these characters, even the main ones, get any sort of development. You meet them, learn a bit about them for an hour and then its onto the next chapter and you never see these characters ever again. It has a pacing problem. The game has a serious plot going on in the background, but the story mainly feels like "Sam dragging along ragdoll John on random adventures", John would happily watch Sam get robbed by a Nigerian prince, I'm not even kidding. He's the character you play and he has zero characterisation, other than randomly caring for Sam. He has no backstory, spoken words, nothing. This makes it extremely hard to care for him in moments where the plot really wants you to care about John and his connection with Sam. Sam is basically the only character in this game, she takes up most of the screen time and is generally characterised rather well, but misses the mark in having much depth portrayed other an "excited kid". I was waiting for the main plot of the story to have a pay off or explain ANYTHING it was driving at, it never does. Plot holes remain, character motivations remain unexplored, it feels half-baked. Which is a shame, given the effort that went into the characters, environments and visuals. Game play is a massive let down. It's basically Legend of Zelda, but instead of a sword, you have a frying pan and the combat feels very stiff and uninspired. To its credit, the game strength in variety comes in here. There's always new enemy designs, mechanics, environments, music etc. This kept me barely engaged enough to keep moving through the game. The mechanics however are the weakest part. The game play itself is a 2D puzzle game focused around dungeons. You gain items in dungeons to progress pass certain parts. however these items are swiftly forgotten, one dungeon to the next. There's no game play cohesion between areas. Puzzles are brain dead simple, and also repetitive. I don't see how the 55th puzzle of pushing block over button is meant to be engaging or using the dungeons item to do same thing 50 times, without variation. Combat is very dissatisfying. You have no movement abilities in the game, which makes dodging sometimes feel like an impossible task in some situations. The problem is, you have so much health, you an unga bunga your way through the game without much difficulty. You can get hit over and over and over, and eat food items to tank through anything. From this perspective the game does not offer any challenge in terms of puzzles or combat. The bosses however were very visually appealing and the music made the game play tolerable. It makes me wish there were a better "game" here. Overall, the variety in Eastward could keep you engaged until the end. It's story, combat and puzzles will not give you much to write home about. They're not "bad" by any means, simply very mediocre. It is worth a mention this game has a sub-game within it called "Earth Born", I did not play this since it is a generic RPG and did not interest me. But if the games hints are to be believed, in that sub-game it expands the world and builds on the overall plot. Though after my first playthrough, I'm not too motivated to play this again or much more deeply.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall this game has a really cool aesthetic, creative world-building, and insane attention to detail when it comes to the work put into various animations (some of which only happen once in the game!). My main qualms with this game come with the premise/story telling. The dialogue is somewhat poorly written, and I felt the writers gave little reason for the player to care about the characters and story other than "oh this character is cool and quirky".  There aren't many unpredictable aspects to the dialogue that could make it more exciting, and it seems like the writers sort of disregarded the idea of "show don't tell", which made for some stale cutscenes. Additionally, the game relies heavily on dialogue instead of gameplay to advance the story. This is mainly a dialogue based game interrupted by some action sequences rather than vice versa. If you enjoy dialogue-focused games and you can appreciate the aesthetic and the work put in, play this game! But if not, I can't say that I would recommend it. This is all just my own personal opinion, so please take it with a grain of salt! I will say I plan on finishing this game anyway just to see what happens. So let that be known. o_o

_childDocuments_.review: A wonderful sort of zelda-like RPG with team-splitting mechanics and an odd but well-merged blend of DNA from lots of other games. There's also a game-within-a-game; a small sort of roguelite take on classic JRPGs called Earth Born tucked away in many of the hub areas.So far, I think the best way I could sum up both the praises and criticisms of this game is just by saying that it's very Chucklefish. It comes with all of the hallmarks that you'd expect from a Chucklefish game: There's a big focus on gorgeous visual design and animations to the point where the pacing sometimes feels sluggish, similar to how Wargroove could feel frustratingly slow; a lot of the dialogue tries to be that corny sort of charming, and some of it falls flat and feels almost irritating instead; there's a lot of super clear DNA from other games here, but they've managed to merge it very effectively and it doesn't feel out of place.All things considered, if Eastward just rubs you the wrong way for some reason, you're in no short supply of gripes to bring up. There's definitely plenty of ammunition here if you're looking for reasons not to like it... But they're all kind of minor. It's just that kind of cheesey charm that will grate on you if you let it, but can just as well sweep you up if you want it to.The gameplay is honestly pretty tight. The main game loop is similar to a 2D Zelda, but it starts to pepper in more mechanics - you can cook ala Breath of the Wild to fill up your inventory with powerful healing and buffs, you get a second character with their own set of skills, and you really start to realize that there's something special here the first time they split the two up and you have to hot-swap between them through a series of puzzles and obstacles to. It feels fantastic to team them up and tackle the split-party puzzles.Overall, I encourage folks looking for a kind of leisurely paced adventure with a charming and vibrant visual style and setting to pick Eastward up. But if you want something that takes itself a little more seriously, you may want to look elsewhere, or at least hold off until you're in the mood for something that tries to be a bit lighthearted.UPDATE:After completing the game, a few more notes...Most of the original review is relevant for the whole game. Visually, Eastward is gorgeous from start to finish. The music is also excellent - and every time a new song pops up, it's absolutely a banger. Between some stunning graphics and incredible music, you get some truly breathtaking scenes. Where the game is strong, it stays strong! Likewise, where it's weak, it stays weak. The dialogue often feels grating, and it's made much worse by *some* characters getting different dialogue when you speak to them a second time, but you always risk getting the same long dialogue a second time instead. Without spoiling too much, there's a later part where this feels *especially* glaring. Honestly, the game needs a skip button for dialogue you've heard before, the same way you can skip the cooking scene if you've made that meal before. It would really help the most major shortcoming Eastward has.The cooking gets a little stale later on. There's not really much way to find recipes besides rubbing three foods (and a spice) together and seeing if something comes up with a question mark. There's a lot of combinations that are possible from this, and it's hard to justify spending the time to try them all. Further, there's no reminder of what food has what effects, so it feels like best practice to just remember a couple of good ones and stick to them.Finally, just to address it, a friend had told me that they'd heard Eastward makes fun of fat people, so I tried to keep an eye out for that - but I didn't really see it. It doesn't really make fun of anyone, persay... but many of the characters are absolute caricatures, and a couple veer close to unfortunate, with several fatter characters being probably the most obvious. To be fair, it doesn't feel mean-spirited as much as a choice to give the animations more lively with bigger expressions and interesting body shapes and designs. They don't stand out as visual outliers in a game this eye-catching, and it's never teased or mocked or otherwise treated as a negative thing in the game's dialogue.

_childDocuments_.review: Grate animation, the characters are lovable, the game play and puzzle are overall pretty fun, but the plot design is nothing but trash.The biggest problem is the ending, the game is linear and slow paced, in the early few chapters the dialogues are lengthy, at times long winded, but it overall did a great job in terms of holding your hand, guiding you through the story, telling you what is going on and making you invested.
