_childDocuments_.review: Short Version; Eastward is a modern attempt at a *very* linear Legend of Zelda style game that's a bit heavy on dialogue, perhaps excessively so to those that prefer to always be in control. If you look at it like a Young Adult Novel with Gameplay and go in expecting that and the number of times you'll have to sit through plot, it's a really good time.-----------------I haven't finished Eastward, but I can tell I'm going to. I absolutely love the game to bits. Despite this, this is a game I wish I could give a "hmmm" to, as far as recommendations go. Loving a game and recommending it to others are two very different things. Yet, I had to get my thoughts out now because it's both a blessing and a head-scratcher to be playing something like this.I didn't get the game when it first came out because it had a "mostly positive" review rating. I waited until it was on sale and when it had "very positive" for it's reviews of all time. I think the people that don't like the game have their right to not like it, but I also think it's harsh to not recommend it the way they do, like the design is flummoxed or lacks intention. This game is made with a lot of intention, love and care... for mostly better, sometimes worse.I'm reminded of the frustration people have been having with the latest Legend of Zelda, Tears of the Kingdom. A common complaint I see is the story is vapid, utterly nothing, that it sometimes doesn't even feel like a sequel to the last game because of how so much of the last game's events are just ignored entirely. Meanwhile, you're given no time to actually interact with characters. This is intentional, to give the player as much freedom as possible. A butchered quote I see applied to Miyamoto, master of Nintendo and a man known to stick his fingers in all the games, is he hates games that try to tell him what to feel and instead wants to leave the feeling to the player. To that end, it can sometimes seem the Zelda games don't feel much of anything if you aren't prepared to do a fair bit of legwork to get emotionally invested.Playing Eastward is like playing a bizzarro reality where the word "Freedom" was forgotten almost entirely when a legend of Zelda game was made, and making you feel a certain way was always the goal. Just as the freedom at the cost of plot isn't a bad thing, neither is plot at the cost freedom. The only issue, I think, is not being told one way or another that this is what you're getting into. It's a mistake a lot of games make, in their attempts to maintain the mystique of being a new world, reality or experience. In this game, you take on the role of John, at first, and I do believe you'll be playing him through most of the game. Later, you also play as his adoptive daughter as the two try to survive in this crazy world while said daughter, Sam, has magic powers she doesn't understand and there's people that believe the world above ground is a wasteland. It isn't... until you arrive and perhaps cause the second apocalypse.Although the writing is simple and quirky on the surface, it uses the minimum amount of words and visuals possible to express it's dense story. More than that, it works hard to make you feel like our two main characters. This is impressive, considering John is a silent protagonist who doesn't look anything like a legendary chosen here. In another game, his sprite could be any NPC's. Here, though, his silent demeanor is a real character trait; he's a man of few words and doesn't like small talk. But something you'll find out quick, if you pay attention, is he's a kind man who cares deeply for Sam. In this way, the game has its cake and eats it too with how its main character feels; you can project onto John a bit, but John will always be John.Sam is, on the other end, vibrant and loud. She's a kid, a real one. The writing here is spectacular, but if you're the kind of person who doesn't like to be told how you feel, Sam might be annoying. The game attempts to endear you to her through John, as John clearly loves her and wants to do what's best for her. Doesn't matter what you want, though, cause John's gonna take care of her. But hey, at least she takes care of John, too. In a way, it's another Dad simulator, but I'd call it a family simulator.The writing in the game is superb, and I don't just mean the spoken words. If you're attentive, there's a lot of details you can notice, such as how John's house at the start of the game only has one bed, and how he sleeps sitting up. Sam's a new addition to his life, and John had no question in what was best for her, giving his bed to her. Likewise, several seeds and questions are expertly planted that are answered later, when you might have forgotten you'd even asked. The artstyle is also phenomenal. It's as if Legend of Zelda and Earthbound had a baby, then uncle Fallout came to visit, said the baby was cute, and offered old clothes. The game is charming and quirky, with pixel art made with oodles of love and care. The fact John, who wield's a frying pan like a sword, isn't an ambidextrous sprite and turns like a person and doesn't just flip between two sprites says a lot too. They want John and Sam to feel like real people down to how they move, and I'd say they succeeded. The pixel work is like the days of the SNES, but we never stopped advancing it. In a word, gorgeous. In another word, schizophrenic, but never unintentionally so. Some bits of the UI and character design feels odd (like how the character portraits for John and Sam are anime as heck, with John having an epic smile and a seemingly out of character determination in his eyes), but it feels intentional. It doesn't clash, but sticks out, like it wants to tell you something. The second biggest flaw with the game is the pacing can sometimes be a bit... absurd. I was struck by a feeling of whiplash as John and Sam made it to the second town and after only being there a day, the town's prettiest lady falls for John. At the same time, we've gone from the slight octane of a boss fight and getting to a beautiful new world via what we first thought was a death hole to hazing a grand, slow, peaceful time at this new village. The romance plot feels like a way to get us more attached to this place so leaving will be all the more bitter. It can feel a bit like they were throwing out as many hooks to make sure you bit and became caught up in loving this place. Some things were slow, others fast, all at the same time. Give the game patience, take it with a bag of 50 salt (it'll make sense when you play) and it'll pass, but I can see this as a deal breaker for some and I wouldn't blame them.Perhaps the biggest flaw with this game was to even be a game in the first place. Maybe it would be better received as a book or a comic. But this wanted to be a game and it had good reasons to be, but not everyone is going to agree with that or buy into it. Control is regularly taken from the player for long cutscenes and characters talking to each other for minutes at a time. It's good dialogue, and if you come in expecting it, it's like playing a visual novel with Legend of Zelda (classic) gameplay. But the dialogue is programmed in a way where skipping it isn't fast. It expects you to be here. If you're here to "play", you may be here for the wrong reasons.If you come to Eastward, come to feel it and experience it. Don't come to play it like a free roaming game, come to play it like a story that has something to tell you. If you don't want that, play something else. Eastward isn't for everyone, and it's beautiful for being willing to do that.

_childDocuments_.review: BE WARNED: Although the narrative is great and the visual are stunning, a glitch might ruin your entire experience (like it did to me) :cABOUT THE GAME: I really like how they built an entire universe in the most magical way to keep you in love and intrigued to carry the story on and grasp for the next chapters. All characters are very interesting and captvitaing, accompanied by these amazing and very fun dialogues and all sorts of dinamic interactions. The world inside the mines it's very cool to explore and puzzles altough not that complicated are fun to solve and do not keep you stuck on how to proceed the levels.->For as much as I was in love with the game since the minute the intro started I have to warn you: I played for 11 HOURS and ended having to delete my save to start a new one.<NO spoilers ahead c:>THE PROBLEM: Theres a point of the story where you need to break from a certain place trough a certain Mansion and all you need to do is pull a leaver. Pretty simple right? It turns out the lever is supposed to reveal a allegedy "sliding" bookcase so you can get your way out. Well... if it only. After 11 HOURS playing a game and eager to keep playing for another 11 hours this "sliding" bookcase suffers a glitch and get stuck in the middle making it IMPOSSIBLE for you to advance (and there is no other way out). I tried EVERY SOLUTION you can imagine, even tried replaying all my autosaves, but I always ended hitting up aggainst this bookcase glitch.ITS SO FRUSTRATING that I had to erase a 11 HOURS SAVE over a glitch that was supposed to have been fixed in the previous patch (a lot of ppl reported crashing the game in the same area and even loosing their files). _childDocuments_.review: To me, this is the best looking game I’ve seen in a long time. The animation works in concert with the art style that works with the setting and is all complimented by the music. There’s a weirdness that permeates through everything and Eastward revels in it. It has faults, the game needs much tighter scene and dialogue editing and the beginning is quite slow. There are large parts of the game where it loses all momentum. However when everything is working together, it’s one of the best experiences of the year.Positives:-gorgeous pixel art and animation-creative and interesting world-revels in its weirdness-charming characters-outstanding lighting effects-good amount of combat options-fun puzzles-music sets the mood perfectlyNegatives:-starting combat is bland-saving takes far too long-I can read much faster than the game presents dialogue-some scenes needed to be edited down-can’t return to previous areas if something is missed

_childDocuments_.review: This game has beautiful sprite-work, wonderful music, and pretty decent gameplay. However, the story pacing, writing, and characters were all a letdown.I was hoping for an adventure where our characters had a reason/goal driving them Eastward, but that's not what this game is. Instead, for most of the game, you exist in a location and do some slice-of-life style questing until circumstances or events force you to leave. Things like helping out farmers, or gathering cooking ingredients. You might enjoy this game more if you keep your expectations in check.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a truly a gem in the space of RPGs on Steam. The production value and polish on Eastward makes the combat feel so satisfying, with boss fights and real-time combat that doesn't pull you from your immersion within the environments you explore. The dungeon puzzles remind me of a Mario&Luigi GBA game, and the visuals are so stunning I have to remind myself its all pixel work. If Zelda and Earthbound combined, you would get the aesthetic that this game brings to the table. The only thing I can think of to critique is the story and some of the pacing, where the plot itself seems a bit convoluted at times and there is an intense amount of exposition done through dialogue, but it isn't enough of a fault to take away from the unique experience that Eastward is.

_childDocuments_.review: First impressions are pretty fantastic! Firstly, the art style reminds me of Stardew Valley combined with Studio Ghibli - both of which are my absolute favourites (they even made a Hayao Miyazaki looking character in-game!). The game world looks astonishingly good for an indie title, with detailed characters & backgrounds. Talking about the gameplay, it's pretty straightforward with responsive controls. _childDocuments_.review: After 17 hours, I had to change my review, which was positive originally, afte only three hours. It's negative now.The game is not too bad, but it's utterly and overly stupid. It's juvenile, it's not even childish, it's puerile!The story doesn't have any pathos, you are supposed to save people you don't give a damn about simply because the game doesn't make these people feel real, alive. They're just sprites, some pretty and some ugly, with an annoying dancing animation that makes me wanna scream "stop it now!"For instance, the circus quest. You can't enter an area for no reason at all, the game simply says you can't go on until everything is ready, but no other explanation is offered. Later, you can enter the area and there's nothing there, just a bunch of clowns chilling. Why was not I allowed to enter bedore if nothing was happening? Even later, when I acually had osmething important to do: the stupid brat that clings along with her white hair made a bet with a mafia boss that I could cook him something amazing, and when i had the ingredients, she gave them away to an obvious liar who simply wanted my ingredients; she didn't ask, she just took my stuff and gave it away. next day, I had everything for an even better dish, but she asked me to go train the damn clowns so they could make a good show and not be kicked out. But, why? I'm a digger, I am not a clown, I can't teach clowns how to do their damn jobs! But I had not choice, the stupid brat promised I would, and my dish overcooked and only one day's left to make a good dish and not be killed or something.It's been three sessions since I had any fun. Fun, in this game, comes from combat. But combat is shallow and repetitive. Still fun, specially ehen everything else is so bad (except the graphics; the graphics are so good... not the NPCs constantly dancing for no reason). But it's been a few hours since I had some combat, and now I've been through story, but the story in this game is drivel. All that circus thing? That's not story, that's just drivel.In a walking simulator, when you go to another house and open a door, the story moves, goes on, there's progress, that's the game, the story is the game. Eastward wants to be story and gameplay, and it thinks gameplay is having an NPC asking you to go to some house, find three items, and bring them back. Yeah, simple fetch quest like any RPG. Except, the house is a few screens away, but 20 seconds tops, and inside there are three rooms, open, along a single hallway, each containing one item. You enter, grab the item, and leave. 20 seconds later, you go back and give the items... it's so asburds, it's so pointless, there's no challenge. Literally no challenge, not a single enemy, nothing, just walking, pontless walking, the story doesn't move, this quest is not story, and almost every single quest in this game, is drivel.I don't mind whether a game's writing is Shakespeare or Coelho (i.e. great or sh*t) as long as the game is fun to play. I don't care if a game's gameplay is simple and not too fun, as long as the story is worth to read and see through. This game has sub-par gameplay and bad writing. The graphis are excellent but the graphics can't save a game if the other factors are this flawed. Music... forgetable; not bad, only not interesting, just average.The first few hours were good, the story seemed to make sense, the NPCs had some charm, but after you leave the first location, every NPCs is shallow and empty and more than silly. I can't recommend this game, I feel cheated.***Original review, after three hours:Super good game.Only a couple minor flaws: Controlling the characters with the stick is imprecise, and the main character doesn't talk, aren't you tired of silent protagonists? And a nitpick: school bullying is so clichéd, we've been reading and watching stories about school bullying for four decades now.Other than that, the game is wonderful, at least the prologue and the first episode, and I can't wait to play the next episodes this next weekend! I'm afraid the game will be shorter than expected, but if it keeps this quality for another 10 hours, then no complains from me (but for a game like this, I would like 20-25 hours).The characters are fun and charismatic, the animation is excellent, the art-style is wonderful, the mechanics are fun.

_childDocuments_.review: A game that sounds, looks, plays and feels like a DS game. Even though the game is very detailed and the characters are very charming, it's rather slow and tedious at times. People that enjoy the slow pacing of retro JRPG games will most likely enjoy this game; if you're like me and utterly despise slow games, don't worry - the beautiful art direction, characters and overall story still make the experience worthwhile. Pro tip: if you're interested, try it out and see if you actually like it or refund it if you don't.
_childDocuments_.name: Eastward

_childDocuments_.review: The storytelling methods brings nostalgia. Nowadays, due to the "fast food" entertainment trends, the mainstream storytelling of games is to put players right into actions. Eastward, on the other hand, starts out and lays the background in a slow path, similar to RPG games I've played in my childhood era. It is nor good or bad, rather a choice of personal tastes, but in today's gaming culture, the progression pace at the beginning could cause players to lose interest. I only started to get hooked about 4 or 5 hours into the game, which is 1/5-1/6 of the total time I spent to reach the ending.Aside from some longer-than-necessary dialogues with no important purposes and the abrupt, out-of-place chapters of the monkey train, overall I exceedingly enjoyed Eastward. The art style is adorable, the characters are relatable, the puzzles are with adequate difficulties, and the ending is a nice mixture of melancholy and happiness. One thing that stands out to me is that one of the main characters "John" never spoke a word through out the entire game, no dialogue texts, no animation portraying him speaking, and even no narration describing him doing so. I wonder if this is an implicit tribute to the silent adventurer of Ys series, Adol, or to Half-Life's Gordon Freeman.

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoyed my time with Eastward but there are some very apparent flaws with the game that make it impossible for me to recommend. I want to give this warning to the people who are considering buying Eastward. If you are looking for a "life changing story" and a "Zelda-like gameplay experience" like some of the reviews are promising then you will probably be disappointed by Eastward.Spoilers ahead:Its easy to praise Eastward on some corners. You would be hard pressed to find a person that wouldn't call the visuals beautiful, Sam has a nice energy to her, and the music serves its purpose even though the game could benefit heavily from more tracks. I wont dwell too much on these positives because they have already been stressed more times than you could count in other reviews, just take note that those aspects are there.The main gameplay of Eastward would make you believe that the game is meant for young teens, I'm not a god gamer and I was almost never at any real risk of dying with the one exception being the epic anime samurai battle vs Isabel. Weirdly enough after this fight comes the final boss in which I only got hit once, The main reason why the game is so easy is it utilizes Breath of the Wild's food system which was one of that games biggest detriments. Since you can eat at any time during battle with no cooldown your healthbar isn't actually how many hearts you have its your number of hearts plus the amount of hearts you can get in total from all the food in your inventory which is an insane amount so getting hit is never really a threat. The puzzles are also very simple, I don't think there was a part in the game where i had to think for more than 10 seconds about what to do. None of this is inherently bad because Eastward is very much a narrative driven game, after all 75% of your time in Eastward will be spent reading dailogue so having easy access gameplay ensures everyone will get to experience the story. The problem with this is that the game depends entirely on the story, an area in which it falls flat.the first two chapters of the game is strong and a good setup, The people in the potcrock isle think that the outside world is a dark place plagued with maisma and believe in dark god Charon (which is just a train). We as a player and sam as a character who has seen the outside world know that this isn't true and it makes us excited to get out of potcrock isle. The great part is the twist in which the miasma is a real plague and Charon is a real threat. This was a great twist and a good way of getting the player invested in the story and mystery. Unfortunately this is as good as the narrative gets and if you are interested in the mysteries that the story poses you are going to have to wait till the very end..... in which your questions will still not be answered. This is a serious problem in Eastward, it eludes to so many big reveals and that "in time you will understand", makes you wait for the entire chapters 2-7 in which the main story isn't progressed at all and mysteries are just reiterated, and then either very loosely gives you an explanation or doesn't mention it ever again. After playing Eastward i'm still just so confused about what what actually happens that it makes the ending, which tries to be emotional, just feel empty. Sam is explained away as a perfect evolutionary being but lacks everything that that would entail, such as omnipotence and omniscience. Instead she can just use magic? Why does Sam have a second soul bipolar personality living inside her? I understand its suppose to be her from the past but it's very apparent it's an entirely different entity that thinks and acts purely independent of Sam. Why was Sam asleep in a chamber underground in the first place? did she lock herself down there to stop the factories from activating? if that were the case she could you know.... just stop activating the factories. Who even is Solomon? He is very involved with time science but that doesn't really explain why there are three of him at different ages running around and why the keys that they have open the final door in Charon. Isabel is Heavily alluded to being a robot/test tube baby like 3 times and then never mentioned again. what was the cure that Isabel and Alva were searching for to? Why does Sam merging with mother at the very end stop the harvest? Why can Alva just be a ghost???? All of these are questions that I didn't have answered to me playing the game. I can infer possible answers to a couple but they remain pure speculation without concrete evidence. The longer I sat through the ending of Eastward the more and more I feel like it was taking heavy inspiration from the End of Evangelion, there's a lot of similarities to be seen between the two. What made EoE work despite its janky convoluted plot was its interesting characters and themes. Eastward has neither of these things, John is a silent protagonist that just does whatever, Sam is cute but not interesting, Alva and Isabel are somewhat interesting and their conflict resolution is alright but not enough to carry the game. The game almost has no themes or philosophy besides the refrigerator you save at that talks like a 15 year old kid who just read some John Locke and then smoked weed. The game tries to be philosophical and hits towards some deeper meaning but never talks about it.Eastward wears a lot of its inspiration on its sleeves. Earthbound is the most obvious but I was initially surprised to see just how anime influenced it as well. The most obvious one is Hayao Miyazaki and Studio Ghibli as Miyazaki is a shop keeper in the game but given a different first name. I don't mind media showing off what inspired it and you are allowed to deviate from it but you should still be in the spirit of what is inspiring you. What I'm getting at is it's almost insulting to show off Miyazaki in a game where you add ample amounts of fanservice. The game goes overtly out of its way to add in a bunch of anime horniness whenever it can and It gets weird. At the very least the brothel in New Dam City makes sense, making us retrieve a dominatrix outfit from it is odd but it makes sense in the world. But for the love of god please explain to me why the monkeys have a virtual anime cat girl glory hole machine? like seriously? and out of the three girls that have some importance in the story and aren't 9 why do two of them have to have comically large chest? Ulva is a mature woman so i can see her character design reflecting that but its still out of proportion. And when you see the Alva replicas inside Charon my god they are just massive and for what? it doesn't add any personality to the story or characters and it doesn't serve any theme so why?Eastward is far from a bad game but i seriously don't know who I could recommend it too. If you wanna play for the gameplay the story takes up too much time. if you want to play for the story the gameplay will be a boring slodge to get through, the non main characters aren't really interesting at all, and nothing really happens till chapter 8. And if you wanna play for both then you will probably be disappointed by aspects of each. The easy gameplay and nature of the story wants you to think its for kids but the off the walls story and "adult" moments makes it seem like its aimed towards an older crowd. the most enjoyable time I had in Eastward was playing Earth born, in which I got both endings. I think Earth Born was a great addition to the game however whoever on the development team designed the gull knight fight can perfectly parry my ass.

_childDocuments_.review: Eastward is a top-down, pixel art, narrative-driven role-playing game published by Chucklefish and developed by Chinese developer Pixpil. I was drawn into the world of Eastward with its fantastic visuals and unique character design. It has undeniable charm and offers some innovative gameplay particularly in its minigames. However, a convoluted story, flat characters and frustrating gameplay mechanics mired this game to the point where, by the last chapters of my playthrough, I wasn’t having fun anymore.Eastward is a game with huge potential, it has so much going for it: a cool visual style that harkens back to great old Nintendo classics like EarthBound, Chrono Trigger and Final Fantasy. It wears those references proudly on its sleeve, it even features an entire playable game within the game called “EarthBorn,” that I’ll come back to later. Overall, it’s dripping with nostalgia but still has some amazing 21st century graphics. In particular, the water, foliage and “miasma” were just so cool and while the game felt like an homage to the old titles, it certainly lived up to a modern aesthetic in that regard.Unfortunately, the great graphics and style did not make up for frustrating gameplay particularly in regards to combat and story progression. Eastward really likes to take its time with its story. At times, the slow pace felt like a meditation that added to the feeling of making the best of a tough situation, but mostly it felt constipated. Fetch quests and mandatory side missions would make areas quickly feel stale. Every objective had character development which did help flesh out the world, but as I’ll talk about later in this review, despite the attempt I think it mostly failed in that regard.Combat in Eastward was frustrating and often felt unfair. You are armed with an arsenal of interesting weapons. For instance, your main weapon throughout the game was a frying pan. But the speed at which you unlock new weapons and abilities and the difficulty spike of enemies in the mid-game felt uneven. Enemies rarely give you time to charge your weapon or abilities, and unclear hitboxes or invulnerability frames would often lead to missed hits or accidental damage. With no dodge roll or evasive maneuvers, your best bet is to back up and wait for enemies to come to you or heal through the damage. Frequent healing also required opening a menu that would pause combat, throwing off the flow. Bosses were often easier to beat than regular mobs because they, at least usually, had consistent mechanics. By the end of the game, I dreaded going into the dungeon areas because the combat was so frustrating.Despite the issues with combat, Eastward’s many dungeons did have some really nice puzzles that made them a little more bearable. In general, they felt challenging but never so much as I had to look up how to solve them online. I particularly liked a brief section where you had to sneak past a bunch of guards, it was little asides like this that broke up the gameplay and were, in my opinion, some of the best parts of the game. However, because of the combat issues, I would often leave areas unexplored. It’s really too bad that a game that put so much work into creating beautiful landscapes and interesting puzzles would have areas skipped because of irritating gameplay issues. As I mentioned, the best sections of the game are where it strayed from its normal gameplay loop. Minigames like a quick aside to rally some floating pigs for a farmer by hitting them with your frying pan, or the Breath of the Wild style cooking minigame where a slot machine would determine the quality of your dish were really innovative and fun. The real gem was its game-within-a-game “EarthBorn,” an old-school turn-based RPG where you have 7 days to defeat the “Demon King,” who plagues the land, with a group of unlikely adventurers. The game is impossible to beat on your first try, but by using items you get in the outerworld from another clever coin-slot vending machine game gives you keys, revive items and power ups you can use permanently in subsequent playthroughs. I found that “EarthBorn” was honestly more fun than the larger game it was a part of.Eastward’s sound design was thoughtful and evocative of the best old-school adventure games and the music was delightful, but repetitive at times. Treasure chest opens and the cooking minigame had particularly memorable jingles. But, not to harp on combat yet again, but it would have been nice if more monsters had sound cues before their wind-ups. The music was really quite good, very bold and endearing, however I did feel like it got stale by the end of the game. It felt like certain characters or areas should have had different musical queues; instead it often relied on the same limited set of music throughout the game only opening up the repertoire near the end of the game.Unfortunately for a heavily story-driven game, the story in Eastward felt convoluted and while not completely predictable, ultimately unsatisfying. I think the most egregious aspect of the story was the complete lack of character development, particularly of the main characters and flat or confusing side characters. It is possible that there was some stuff lost in the English translation of the game, but for the most part I don’t think that excuses the often disjointed ambitions and attitudes of the characters. I’ll give some examples, but beware of spoilers below.We’ll start with John, the main character who you play throughout the game, who is silent. It is not uncommon to have a muted main character, however in order to give that character depth they either need to be very emotive or have very clear motives in the story. John has neither. It’s clear he cares about Sam, a child he’s decided to adopt and follow to the ends of the earth, but every time he’s asked about intentions or feelings, he gives the same character animation where he scratches the back of his neck. It’s fine to have a character that is stoic, but with John it mostly felt flat. Sam, the secondary character and intrigue of the game, is obnoxious and even apathetic at times. The narrative will reveal game-changing plot points or an NPC will evolve the story and Sam seemingly forgets everything every time, instead remaining clueless and childish until the very end of the game. The idea that she’s incapable of processing trauma and just shunts it into her subconscious feels like a lazy way of leaving questions unanswered and pushing the story forward with a faultless protagonist even though it’s clear she’s not. I kept asking myself, “isn’t John horrified by the atrocities Sam is committing?” She literally brings on the destruction of an entire town early in the game without repercussion.The overarching story for the game left me scratching my head, it felt like it was meant to be deep but it was just confusing. The game was also pretty conservative; it felt ripe for queer characters or any act of political subversion, a critique of capital or just something profound but ultimately felt like a lazy interpretation of stories long ago told in better forms like Evangelion or The Matrix. Side characters were so often disappointing with their interesting relationships but confusing motives. For instance you could try to read Alva and Isabel as a queer couple in the game, they are two women living together, obviously protective of each other and they even mention a love between them, but it turns out Isabel is just a robot guardian with a more maternal relationship with Alva and it felt like the game went out of its way to make sure the subtext doesn’t add up.

_childDocuments_.review: Oh, how amazing that game is! I'm not typically a huge fan of hack-and-slash games, nor was I particularly drawn to Zelda-like titles, despite many reviewers comparing it to such. However, I must admit that the design is one of the best I've experienced in its pixel art style, creating an incredible mood. I swiftly dove into the DLC because I adore farming sims, and while it does progress rather slowly, once you unlock some mechanics, the game becomes incredibly rich in content (and for that price, it's doubly impressive). It's innovative too; despite having played numerous fishing and crop harvesting games, this one offers something refreshingly different. I was pleasantly surprised by almost every aspect and wholeheartedly recommend both the main game and its DLC. Don't let the genre deceive you - it truly has something special and is worth trying, even if it's not your typical type of game at first.

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like this game. The art style is BEAUTIFUL. The music fits perfectly. The combat is dialed, the gamefeel is superb. Sadly, the story is very weak. Mostly it's the dialog; there's WAY TOO MUCH dialog. This game would benefit from a screenwriting class. Start a scene late, end early. Does this bit advance the story? GET ON WITH IT. There's an amount of meaningless cuteness that is delightful, but this is way too much. My eyes start rolling back in my head. It just goes on and on sometimes! I love when games give you the freedom to walk away from conversations, but here you're locked in. Worse, they occasionally FORCE you to walk, which makes me find myself hurting my thumb pressing the joystick so hard to move. Very frustrating. And weird because you can't choose to walk normally, only run. LAME! I feel like in the 7 hours I've played, only 30 minutes has been fun. I just want to explore and fight! The combat is FUN! The world is BEAUTIFUL! LET ME HAVE IT!!! I can't stand the monotony. All the characters feel the same, quirky outcast weirdos, and the dialog goes on and on and on. I keep thinking, ok this scene is over, and then it goes on like 6 times longer.  If they made a streamlined version, trimming the script WAY down, it would be a joy. But as it is, I can't even continue playing. A slog. I'm sad, I can tell a lot of love when into this game.

_childDocuments_.review: I was intrigued by the trailer and bought it on a whim. This is a cute little game with a host of funny and well written characters. The game gets progressively darker in tone as you play, taking breaks here and there to lighten things up with well-written humor. The locations you visit have a real sense of "place." I often found myself forgoing fast travel and walking through the towns and villages on foot just to soak up more of my surroundings. The combat is a bit simple, with melee and ranged options being fairly limited and only involving 1 button press to attack. Moving the cursor around to "aim" is a bit wonky on MKB hence why the game likely recommends a controller - but it was manageable. There are puzzles that get progressively more complex as you advance the story. Some puzzles will require you to switch between John and Sam to leverage their different strengths and abilities to solve them. In the final act of the game these puzzles can become a bit tedious in their frequency, but this doesn't bog the game down too much thankfully.The story of John and Sam is surprisingly heartfelt. I felt a deep connection to these characters, which probably has something to do with being a father to a little girl myself (though John is just John). Any time Sam was even slightly in danger I felt my pulse quicken a bit, and when bad things happen to other characters I felt genuine concern for them. I do feel that the final act, and especially the chapter or two leading up to it, overstayed its welcome a bit. However, the payoff was worth it for the ending and if anything the brutal puzzle segments leading up to the finale help contribute to the feeling of catharsis when you finish the game.Overall I'd rate this game an 8/10 and highly recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: Eastward

_childDocuments_.review: A very weird, undeveloped and slow moving story presented in the worst possible way by having to click through endless though bubbles of text, a majority of it not progressing the story at all.  There is no backstory or explanation for why the world is the way it is and the ending doesn't resolve any of it.  The gameplay itself is quite straightforward and repetitive consisting of mostly fetch quests with a small amount of exploration and simple combat.  There are a few timed puzzles which are ok.  Its always pretty clear what you need to do next and there is little else to do.  There is an unnecessarily complicated cooking minigame which you need to play to make food for healing yourself.  The graphics style and music are good and the game ran without any noticeable bugs.  I used an xbox controller without any issues.  I can't recommend it because of the way the story is presented which takes away any fun of playing the game.
_childDocuments_.name: Eastward

_childDocuments_.review: It took a minute for me to really appreciate what Eastward is doing -- or, what I'm getting from it, at least. It does a great job paying homage to the champions of yesteryear, but still builds upon the genre with deeper exploration of what a mini-game can do for the narrative, how to hide sleek and modern effects within a retro palette, or how to serve both escort-mission and tag-team-duo without feeling  . The whole deal is very dense, and if you can take some time and really let it wash over you without playing it with the same intentions as you might another game, the game feels brilliant. It took me a second to find that mindset and let it happen. This might be a unique experience for me, though I hope if someone else finds themselves feeling like you're starting to drudge through it, that they find something helpful in this review.
_childDocuments_.name: Eastward

_childDocuments_.review: Despite its beautiful art, Eastward falls short in several key areas. While the character animations are detailed, the pacing of cutscenes is awkward and the transitions between gameplay segments are jarring. The UI is also cumbersome, making the overall experience more tedious than it should be. The combat, although reminiscent of Zelda, lacks meaningful decisions and feels too simple as a result. Additionally, sound effects seem to be missing in several parts of the game. And finally, the post-processing effects intended to enhance the in-game lighting are a nice touch, but they unfortunately smear dialogue boxes and menus into a discolored mess. Playing Eastward has made me appreciate the little things that are normally done well in other games. As someone who is in love with Eastward's Mother 3-like style, I still hesitate to recommend buying it, even on sale. John and Sam’s story is buried under a lot of grime that might not be worth digging through.

_childDocuments_.review: I would describe Eastward as a beautiful 5 season animated series that unfortunately got roughly shoved into a single video game. Despite the egregious amount of cutscenes (and annoying fetch-quests for the purpose of showing even more cutscenes), Eastward still doesn't manage to tell a cohesive or entertaining story. The plot is confusing (and full of holes), the lore is not explained well, character motivations are unclear, there are TOO MANY characters, there's a tone shift problem, and much of the driving conflict hinges on the fact that the main character is unwilling to ever communicate relevant information to the appropriate characters. The story definitely felt like it could use breathing room and would have been much better if they were continuous scenes instead consecutive short cutscenes with conceited gameplay undercutting them constantly.Speaking of gameplay, it's not great. Combat is repetitive with only around 5 reskinned enemy types. It never feels worth it to stay and kill enemies. The reward for beating them is very low and it's much easier to tank damage and walk by them. They also are able to stun lock you because nothing prevents them from running into your hitbox during your recovery frames. Don't worry though, it's laughably easy to stay alive by using consumables from the underdeveloped cooking system. Also some weapons are absolutely useless and are just there to get you through 3 puzzles. The boss fights are alright, but always completely fail to communicate how to "solve" them. It takes a fair bit of trial and error to find the "solution" to the fight. This isn't necessarily a bad thing, it's just obvious that there's not thought to why the solutions would work on the particular boss. Why on this boss Sam's beam works and on the other doesn't? Who knows!As for the art. Yes, it's visually stunning. All the animations are gorgeous. Any screenshot from the game I would happily hang up on my wall. But is it good video game art? Eh......Let me explain. First and worst is the contrast issues in some areas. Alva's apartment comes to mind. Whatever filter or re-color they have over these areas makes everything really hard to see because it makes all the colors look the same value. Sometimes, I had to squint at my screen to even tell where my character was. Second is clear pathing. The artist is obviously talented, but DOES NOT indicate which doors and which roads are actually openable/walkable. There are some especially bad parts of the environment where a setpiece in the front COVERS UP the walkable road, making it difficult to tell if it's accessible. There's a lot of closed doors and paths leading nowhere where I felt like i wasted time trying to get to.Overall I didn't enjoy my experience with Eastward. I wouldn't recommend it to others. However, I see what other people see in it. The gorgeous art makes up for a lot of its mistakes, and there's good story in there -- it just needs 5 seasons as an animated show.

_childDocuments_.review: Eastward is a difficult game to review, on the one hand the game if full of charm and fantastic attention to detail both in its visual style and its wonderfully retro yet modern sounding soundtrack by Joel Corelitz. On the other sits some fairly bland gameplay with some bizarre design choices. It is a game that I feel some nostalgia for despite the fact that it is undeniably a modern video game. The games story starts out incredibly strong with a tightly knit set of core characters and connections as well as a decent dose of mystery and sinister overtones surrounding the Town. However, it is not too long before you begin to set out on a journey literally to the east. Unfortunately (no spoilers though) the quality of the story begins to dip and slows down considerably over the course of the game, only to begin to throw things at you in the last couple of chapters and then come to an abrupt stop. It is because of the strong start and well written characters that it makes the low points of this games story even more obvious. (and In some cases fairly nonsensical moments, fellow players of this game would be likely familiar with what I am talking about.) Gameplay wise it is a fairly straightforward action combat game with few weapon choices (which are a bit too clumsy to swap between) and the occasional fairly easy puzzle solving sections. Generally, it is nothing to really write home about and it usually didn’t get in the way of my enjoyment of the game, however as you near the end it becomes more and more apparent that instead of your power really increasing of the mechanics being built on top of in a logical progression, they instead change over time to be different rather than innovating on what was already there. Why new mechanics where being introduced as late as the last chapters is beyond me but they don’t build on existing ones and therefore are a little confusing at first and feel out of place. Another awkward moment is a forced stealth section that has very little margin for error and some frustratingly placed checkpoints.With all of this being said I still recommend Eastward, the games visual style and soundtrack alone deserve praise and it is still a thoroughly enjoyable experience despite its flaws. I will continue to watch this developer (Pixpil) with interest in their future projects

_childDocuments_.review: ---{Story}---You are John, a hobo-looking digger who dug up a capsule with a little girl named Sam, who has special powers.  You live in an underground city that is deathly afraid of the poisons on the surface trying to make due.Overall the characters are interesting and unique.  You're driven forward by events largely outside of your control and encouraged to explore a strange world.  The story seems to be entirely linear.---{Graphics}---This game is done in a pixel aesthetic.  The pixeling is very well done, and they manage to make the characters very expressive even with just three pixels for a mouth.  The palletes really set the right moods in each area and there are effects like lights, shadows and reflections.I don't have a 4K monitor but I heard some complaints about black bars and the dev addressed those with a hotfix, though it might be necessary in some cases to play with Microsoft Windows settings to avoid having it automatically upscale the game on you, so read the forums if this applies to you.---{Gameplay}---There are no levels, everything is item based and there are many secrets to discover, so the base gameplay is very much like the original Zelda in that sense.  The game itself is linear and many things are missable because you can't go back to past areas in some cases.  It's not always obvious when the cutoffs will happen, so if you take the wrong route you may lose your chance to find an item or explore a place.  That aside, objectives are marked on your map most of the time and you can use this to know where to avoid until you have finished your exploration.There's also Earth Born, an RPG minigame you can enjoy.  That's a roguelite with progression that plays a bit like the original Dragon Warrior.  You can gather party members (which are permanent) and in the main game you can collect tokens that are redeemed for capsules.  These capsuels monsters work sort of like an amiibo in that your character automatically scans them and they give a bonus when playing Earth Born, specifically they give you items or unlocks there, which can be used once per game.  The game itsef lasts for 7 days after which you are forced to fight the Demon Lord to win.  You will probably die the first several times unless you gather quite a few items.  This game appears to be purely optional, though collectors will want to get all of the capsules.---{Audio}---There are some nice tunes, especially in the bar.---{Audience}---There are a handful of PG-13 elements, like being able to replace the mayor's speech with the "Wild Love" magazine.  The mayor absolutely had it coming, though.---{PC Requirements}---It doesn't seem to take much in the way of resources, my older laptop is running just fine without being stressed in the slightest.---{Difficulity}---You will probably die a few times, but it has autosave and continues.  The game is rather linear and you will not be able to revisit past areas.  The memory fridge will attempt to give you an existensial crisis, though.---{Grind}---There's no grind, only a hunt for missable items & secrets.  Buy the treasure detector early!  You want to save often and you may have to revert to a prior save if you accidentally go to the next section before fully exploring everything for treasures.  There's also an achievement for talking to people, so you want to do that, too, because there's no going back.  The people generally have amusing things to say.---{Bugs}---I had one minor freeze, but recovered from my autosave one room away, so it was no big deal.

The combat is much more fun once you've unlocked all the weapons, and the puzzles at the end are just more fun.I can't recommend this game to most people though, unless you're willing to slog through 15-20 hours of boring gameplay and story. _childDocuments_.review: This review was not edited after writing so I apologize for any potential grammar or wording mistakes.TLDR: Good art style but boring, chaotic story.The full review:I've just finished the game - it took me 32 hours including winning the mini-RPG arcade game within the game (once).It's difficult for me to write this review. I believe people should try games on their own before reading too much about them but I feel like Eastward is being advertised (at least by some part of the community) as something that it is not. But let's start at the beginning.The game starts off strong and the plot seems interesting enough. The art direction if phenomenal, not enough good things can be said about it. Pixel-art games are plentiful these days, to the point where I slowly start losing fascination with this genre (?), but Eastward proves that if it’s done right, a pixel-art game can not only look fantastic but in many aspects will be superior to titles which are based more on detailed visual representation of events and less on a player’s imagination. Eastward’s animations are spot on, colors of each location reflect its mood and the whole package is simply wonderful to look at even if most items are static only.The music, too, works very well. Some of Eastward’s tracking are interesting enough for me to consider buying the soundtrack and listening to the on their own so that I can better understand their composition and written in ideas. It’s nostalgic, relaxing, something menacing but always at the right moment.However, the game suffers very much from low writing level and this is an unforgivable sin in my world in which I play video games for a story first and foremost.There are interesting elements all over the game but unfortunately, they just don’t stick together. Events are chaotic, or chaotically depicted, characters are well overwritten and simply talk way too much and about trivial things that pull attention away from main or even side story lines. The story itself is hard to follow and ultimately ends up incoherent. And mind the plot lasts about 25 hours and there’s lots of material to get through – I think about 10 hours in my first “wait, what?” came up and stayed with me for the most of the game afterwards. I think Eastward tries very hard to be philosophical but philosophy has its own rhythm of asking questions leading to others questions and the plot in the game doesn’t quite nail it. Sure, some smart line or two are thrown our way but they get lost in this weird way of telling the story. I have nothing against weird stories of course, there are many of them around the market and some are incredibly satisfying (Hollow Knight, What Remains of Edith Finch, etc.) but the ones that work well have a definitive plot line discovered by players one way or another. Eastward gets lost in its own story, making it difficult for players to follow it.This game is not Zelda-like, like some players try to suggest. It has a couple of dungeons (some of which are very good) but probably around 60% of Eastward is looking at speech bubbles (well animated speech bubbles, though) and reading what characters have to stay. There’s also no way to skip them so if you’re not into reading, you may have to rethink your purchase. Eastward is a story-based game with a lot of weird cutscenes and occasional dungeons. There’s also no real sense of character progress unless you count in extra hearts and some few weapons you get along the way.I played though the whole game because I can’t afford too many of them these days and once I purchase something I try to at least finish it but I’d be lying if I said I wasn’t tempted to quit a few times because ultimately the weak, or weakly told story made it way more boring than it should be.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a very pretty game, the pixel art is top notch and the music is good, but I can't really get into the story, and I found the characters I came across were mostly weird, dull or irritating.Also, the way the characters are constantly "wobbling" about is a bit distracting. _childDocuments_.review: This game seemed to have all of the makings of a classic, which is why I bought it at full price ($25) but there are just too many places where it falls short to give it a rave review. The art is gorgeous, and the music is pretty well done but the writing is lacking. The game clearly wears its Earthbound influence on its sleeve artistically...but it is lacking the personality and depth that made those games so memorable!  It just didn't wow me consistently, which is an issue when your game is text heavy.The combat was also disappointing. Your bread and butter is a Zelda style melee with a frying pan with a charge up move, but everything else that you unlock is almost pointless in combat. The gun is short range, which is a very strange choice considering your melee costs no ammo or energy. The bombs are okay, but take a long time to detonate. And then there's the . Some will hate it, some will tolerate it. I am on the tolerating side, as I feel that it  realistic if nothing else, but it absolutely cost me a few boss fights earlier than they would have otherwise. Definitely frustrating at the least. Nothing really dazzled me animation wise either. Eastward just could have been so much more. It  me that the writing couldn't match the incredible artwork! This could have been an absolute smash hit if they had tied up loose ends and given everything just a little more personality (Sam excluded, she carries a lot of it.) Also - and I seem to be in the minority here - but the music didn't really blow me away. Production wise, it is very well done, but not a single song stuck with me. I find myself humming songs from a lot of games but I don't even remember the music from this one. With all of that being said I do have a feeling that this studio is going to nail a release soon, since they came so close with this one. Can't wait to see the next release. I would still recommend the game, but not at $25. Wait for the inevitable sale. There is NO replay value, as there are no choices to make and you can't even backtrack.

_childDocuments_.review: ✔️ Very beautiful game with an very solid art direction - it is both very anchored in the traditional pixel art & chiptune aesthetics, and manages to have a very personal and unique style. The intro cinematic is crazy good too, and enjoyable to rewatch once you've played through the game.✔️ Intriguing and zany worldbuilding.✔️ The game is overall very complete, with an outstanding attention to detail and self-referencing. There's a lot of minor characters with their own little stories to meet, a few minigames, and it is all very fun to go through.✔️ Nice enough game feel overall.✔️ Enjoyable alternation of paces between exploration, narration, combat, and puzzles.✔️ The cooking minigame is surprisingly entertaining.💭 The game is pretty linear. Make sure to complete areas before venturing forth too, because it won't let you go back.❌ While a lot of things about the worldbulding are very enticing, I can't help but feel that the story itself lacks something. In the end it didn't make me feel much despite its clear intention to be pretty emotional. It's probably due to the general tone of the game being very gimmicky and lighthearted, which kinda prevented me from getting very attached to characters. Also got a somewhat "why did I do all this again?" feeling in the end.❌ While there's an enjoyable variety of gameplay, and the gameflow feels nice overall, the gameplay itself is pretty basic. You kinda just bash stuff with a pan, with not much more to it. I'm caricaturing a bit, but still, I would have enjoyed some more interesting enemy patterns that force you to think your actions through a bit more. There are a few, but they tend to be pretty limited. Part of the issue is that they put an ammo system for all the ranged weapons, which means they couldn't require you to use them in fights, because you could just get stuck if they did.❌ Aiming is somewhat difficult, especially in combat, and especially when you have to charge an attack. Not a big issue, but can be annoying on the long run.Overall I do recommend it as a fun little (not so little actually, took me 37 hours to finish) game, with quite a bit of worldbuilding depth, and light but entertaining gameplay. Just don't expect a particularly touching story and you won't be disappointed (and maybe you'll have a good surprise if it works better on you than it did on me).

_childDocuments_.review: Okay, so Eastward is generally very good. It does take a lot of inspiration from EarthBound, but mostly just its tone. Mother 3's slogan "strange, funny, heartrending" would probably apply here, somewhat. Mechanically, it's an action game that plays a bit like A Link to the Past. It has Breath of the Wild's cooking minigame, and also an entire game-within-a-game called Earth Born (get it?) that actually plays and looks very much like Dragon Quest.But enough about what it derives from, let's talk about what Eastward does by itself. Eastward follows the story of a man, John, and his adopted daughter, Sam, who get kicked out of their underground home and have to venture across the ruined surface world. Along the way they stumble on some ancient conspiracy that Sam has some unclear at first link to. And they'll get to meet a lot of people, some good, some bad, but most complicated, and eventually change the world.The art is gorgeous and the music really slaps. Actually I can't overstate how good the game looks. Finally, an EarthBound inspired game that doesn't look like a Mother 3 romhack, but has its own style. Every nook and cranny is incredibly well detailed, cities are full of life, dungeons are mysterious and foreboding. Gameplay involves controlling either John or Sam or both to solve puzzles and defeat enemies. John is your standard action protagonist, and Sam has supportive abilities, and you can switch between the two, and keep them together or even split them up to solve problems like it's Banjo-Tooie. I didn't end up using Sam's abilities too often, it was just more expedient to shotgun my way through most enemy encounters with John. That said, there's cool bosses and plenty of hidden secrets to find if you like exploration.So, let's talk about the thing most people might find problematic here: this game moves slowly, very slowly. At the time of writing, the any% speedrun world record is slightly over 7 hours long, which is half the time I actually spent finishing the game as a casual player. Granted, I barely touched Earth Born, but still. Most of your time will be spent watching cutscenes, and in a 2D top down game that means reading dialogue. A lot of the plot gets padded by what you could consider filler, which isn't helped by the fact that the "mysterious conspiracy you discover by accident" trope means you only discover the overarching goal when you're almost done with the story, so at many points in the game the narrative feels like it meanders around with no clear objective. Just like Mother 3, the story is chapter based, and most chapters involve moving to a new location, which has the side effect of making side quests impossible, since you might not be around later to turn them in (which is probably why they made Earth Born, which serves as basically the one side quest for the whole game).But of course this all has a point: to make you spend time with the world and its characters. And I felt like that was a worthwhile trade. The game is full of interesting people that you want to learn more about, and it is cool to learn about the communities you visit. But, of course, you might feel different. If you're not a fan of somewhat contemplative character studies, you might come out of this thinking that a quarter of the story could be excised without losing anything meaningful.One thing the game does not do very well is foreshadowing. By that I mean that the game will pretty much tell you in advance about things that will happen, and is not subtle about it. Whenever some catastrophe happened, I saw it coming. Either my brain is bigger than I thought, or Eastward is a bit too obvious about things. Or maybe that was the whole point. What this mean is that the bits that probably were meant to tug at my heartstrings just fell flat. Hence why I'm not sure "strange, funny, heartrending" fully applies here: it's strange, for sure, and really funny at times, but you can't really render a heart without the element of surprise.Anyway, I enjoyed it. No matter how fast I would mash through some of the dialogue, I still wanted to power through to see what would happen next to those characters I learned to care about. If that sounds like something you'd like, then give it a shot.

_childDocuments_.review: I am conflicted as I write this review, on one hand Eastward has one of the best art style I have ever seen in a pixel game and the overall graphic design is incredible. However the writing has pacing issues and gets especially messy towards the end. Many plot points are left unanswered and character development is unsatisfying. _childDocuments_.review: Yes, I wholeheartedly recommend this wonderful game to anyone who's thinking of buying it. It's a labor of love, and you can tell that from every detail they put into it.However I do want to point out a few things that have bothered me from day 1 and they don't seem to be keen on addressing any of it:1) There is an awful lot of unnecessary dialogue that the game forces you to go through. It doesn't add much to the story and basically just feels like it wants to slow you down. While it's fun to read at first it quickly becomes a reason I don't want to start the game. Especially when you realize that all most of said dialogue could have been reduced to a single sentence. So please just add options to skip or speed this up. 2) The interface of the game. Every time you start the game it has to go through many screens. No option to speed up or skip any of it? Why? I get that you want to tell everyone who was involved. But not every time surely?3) Dying. Thankfully I don't die a lot, but for the love of all that you can skip: Add an option to either disable or skip the dramatic death animation. You want to quickly go through that instead of having to wait for the screen to load, play the music and return you to the last save...So yes three points that considerably reduce the fun that I do have in this game. Perhaps these are things that don't bother others, but to me these elements are very important and are usually present in many of the games I enjoy playing. But I do love this game. The story and its characters are wonderful. John and Sam as a team really works. The artwork is beautiful and reall well done. All the little details they put in are a treat to the eyes. Same goes for the sound design. I hope they will address these issues at least.

The level of detailing everywhere that you go is absurd. Sound design is absurd as well, so damn good, everything feels real even though its not even a realistic-looking (graphics-wise) game. _childDocuments_.review: Waste of time.This game really. Really-really likes to waste your time. That includes long and pointless rambling dialogues from the characters that game does not make you care about. You might see someone for the first or second time and they already have a dialogue for like 5 minutes, telling you about their life or something similar. Some characters it *tries* to make you care about, but it's hard to do so. No one is anything interesting, really. I will admit I skipped almost the entirety of the game with fast forward button (wasn't in the game until recently), but even then, it took absurd amount of time. And after such a dialogues you need to backtrack over artificially big and long locations, thankfully majority of them have fast travel, but what's the point of just skipping all of the locations like that? They could've been smaller and shorter, but remain as beautiful. I should mention the train location. It's very long, and couple of times you need to navigate it manually from one end to the other to just accept or end the quest. Game really loves to do that with you. Go from A to B, get a minute of pointless dialogue, go from B to A again.Then the timeloop location, near the end of the game. Three times in a row you read the same lines and do the same quest over a big location. It's just there to waste your time and nothing else. Probably something else was intended by the developers, but it feels like a timewaste.Eastward also likes to waste your time with their Zelda inspired jingles and animations. Won a battle? Here's a 5 second unskippable scene of your characters cheering! Cooking a meal? Here is a 10 second unskippable scene of ingredients on the pan (5 seconds if you already have the recipe and can skip it). Solving a puzzle? We'll pan the camera to what you just unlocked for a couple of seconds. Repeatedly, if that's some kind of a switch. I wouldn't be surprised if out of 18 hours of gameplay, a couple or a few of them were taken by time where I couldn't skip or control the character.This game also has an identity crisis. It tries to be a very cozy and lighthearted experience, but then it mentions "smell of napalm in the morning" and "glory hole", implied BDSM room in the Casino and so on. So much inappropriately adult stuff in such a cute game, so what does it want to be? It is not cozy and clean enough to be a cheery story for kids, but it doesn't have the nerve to be adult and vulgar either, it overshoots and underperforms in both directions at the same time. It's in some limbo state inbetween, where it's just exactly not right for both audiences.Same identity crisis can be seen in the gameplay itself. If anything, it's more of a Zelda-like. The old Zeldas, of all. You kill enemies, you solve puzzles, you do some NPC quests. Oh, wait, there are almost no sidequests. It's just the main story. But alright, what's the problem? Game has a very-very poor pacing. It doesn't balance it's elements well enough. You can get stuck in an exclusively narrative and backtrack'ey section for an hour or so, and then you'll get some action. Or the other way around, you are stuck in a quite lengthy dungeon with enemies and nothing else to do (although this is paced better, dungeons are not as long as narrative segments). It's too casual and annoying if you want action, and it's too hard and combat focused if you're only here for the story.It has one of the best pixel art graphics I've seen. Style is not amazing though, all of the characters are rather unappealing, with the exception for a few of them. You could argue that "Well yes, this is post apocalypse. Everyone is ugly!" That'd make sense if Sam was THE only visually nice character of the entire game, it'd make a contrast, but there are other characters that are pretty nice and the rest is just abominations. More memorable character designs could've helped this game, albeit it wouldn't help much. I feel like there's just too much characters in general. The more the merrier, one could argue, but it's a quantity vs. quality problem here. If the intent was to create LISA-like unappealing characters, then they did a good job. I'm not going to remember a single one, except for some pretty girls.It's been a real chore to try and complete this game. After 3-4 hours in I made an almost year long break, because I couldn't stomach this game's ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. I decided to give it another shot and see if it improves and to see how it ends. And also the QoL update released recently, so it only amplified my desire. It wasn't worth it. It just wasted my time and became ridiculous. It was a pretty sight though. But that's pretty much it.I cannot recommend this game to anyone.

The first half of the game feels amazing: the cast of characters are charming and interesting and you go in feeling like there will be some type of exposition or lore drop. But there isn't barring  . _childDocuments_.name: Eastward

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a very mixed bag. I'm a big fan of SNES RPGs and pixel art games so that is what immediately drew me to this game and it is still the game's biggest strength. It's great to see what a well-made modern, 2D pixel art game can look like in the modern day. Characters all have interesting designs and are very well animated.Unfortunately, the gameplay and the story don't live up to the same standards and let the game down. Gameplay is very shallow and basic. Despite looking very much influenced by them, this game is not an RPG. There is no levelling up in the traditional sense and no weapons/armour to buy and equip. The game is entirely linear and things like weapon upgrades are mostly tied to the story. Instead, you just run from screen to screen fighting entirely optional enemies for no real purpose. Outside of a few mandatory fights tied to progression, you can skip combat entirely to no detriment. You might as well, because combat is extremely basic. There are no interesting combos to pull off, almost all enemies can be killed in exactly the same way, and there's no real reward for killing them anyway. Change screens and they all respawn anyway.The shallow gameplay might be OK if the story was any good, but it raises more questions than it answers. The game introduces plot threads and side characters that never go anywhere and just get forgotten about. I kept playing thinking the game would eventually fill these things in, but it never does. These are some very fundamental questions about major characters too. Questions like: . The most the game will do is hint at answers to some of these questions and you have to infer the rest. The problem is, this extends to major antagonists like Solomon and Charon too. Who are they and why do they do what they do?It's a pretty game but ultimately that's all. I would say it's worth a single playthrough if you enjoy games like Earthbound and other 'quirky' 2D games, but it's missing too much substance to be anything more than OK.
_childDocuments_.name: Eastward

_childDocuments_.review: Maybe i'm just impacient, but the small bit that i played of this game was just incredibly boring. Long drawn out conversations with little to no character developement at all, the most boring combat system i've seen in my life, a werid cooking system with way too many recepies (everytime i looked at all my missing dishes it felt so annoying knowing that i'd eventually have to find all of them), weird music changes as you pass through different areas, story line was very straight forward and it felt like everything was a side quest AND SO ON.The graphics and music were absolutley gorgeous, and everybody seems to agree on that. But for me that isn't enough to make a great game. I could look at the art and listen to the music for free!I haven't played a lot of these games in my life, but from my personal experience this game will be a waste of your time.
_childDocuments_.name: Eastward

_childDocuments_.review: Eastward is very much a story-first, gameplay second type of game, which personally I enjoy but it might not be to everyone's liking.The main selling point of Eastward is in its beautifully rendered artstyle, which allows for some quite stunning animations, and character/background designs. The story itself is interesting enough, albiet a bit predictable at times. The main duo in John and Sam are captivating and likable enough to keep you invested, as are most of the NPCs you encounter. If you're looking for a story-rich and easy going game with plenty of visual style, I recommend giving Eastward a try.That said the game does lack in a few places, primarily in the gameplay department. While by no means bad, the core gameplay loop of combat is a bit on the simplistic side, with little variation as the game goes on. And while the story is fine enough to keep you going, pacing does drag a bit at times, often with very long cutscenes and dialogue expositions between relative brief moments of actual gameplay.Overall Eastward was an enjoyable experience and worth a playthrough, the final act in particular made excellent use of the game's core strengths in visuals and story. My only issue is that as a video game it can be a bit simple and repetitive at times.7.5/10

_childDocuments_.review: Even though I really liked the visual aspect of the game, music, its mechanics & simple but interesting puzzles, I just couldn't bring myself to love it.The biggest plus in the game is the ability to watch cut-scenes & skip through dialogues on x2 speed, because those scenes are dragging so slowly it's just ridiculous. Often I was ready to scream "stop talking, let me finally kick monsters & solve some puzzles".

_childDocuments_.review: Just finished this gem a few days from writing this and wow what a great game! As much as I want to gush about what I liked about this game and its story I won't say anything about it as I think it's best to go in blind. And speaking of the story its best to know this: the story can be slow at times as I think pacing is this game's biggest "issue" as well as a lot of long cutscenes with gameplay interspersed between. The reason I say "issue" is that this wasn't a problem for me personally but can understandably be a turnoff to some people. If you can get passed that, then this game is an absolute treat with a beautiful art style, some really solid music and a good story.
