_childDocuments_.review: It's not a bad game, but it makes a few terrible design choices, so bad that I feel it deserves to be featured in a class on how NOT to design a game. Ultimately, I don't recommend it over other games in its genre, hence this negative review.And to the game designers, who probably read every review: I apologize. You have crafted something beautiful that I could not have made myself. And there are definitely many positive aspects to your game. But for me, the bad overshadows the good. My two biggest issues:There are systems upon systems, many with subsystems attached to them. All poorly explained. And many, I feel, contribute very little to the gameplay.Example 1: Card upgrades. In Slay the Spire, cards can either be upgraded or not. In Monster Train or Roguebook, cards can have 1 to 3 upgrades attached to them. But in Gordian Quest? Cards have FOUR power tiers, with more than one way to improve a card's tier. AND cards can have a "mastery", which is a choice of one of two upgrades specific to that card. AND cards can be attached to an item, with some items having attributes that modify cards attached to them. AND cards can be affected by upgrades attached to the same item that the card is attached to (just writing that sentence down shows how needlessly complex that is). AND this is all before flat bonuses to cards from items. And before bonuses from hero stats, which are in turn granted from skills and items.Example 2: The world map is composed of nodes of different types (combat encounter, story event, quest, rest node, etc.) that you can travel between on specific paths. Cool. But some nodes actually open up to a "dungeon", which is basically a mini-world with its own nodes of various types. Okay so far. And dungeons ALSO have different floors that you can travel between, which is something I just can't think of a good reason for. AND some of the nodes are actually exploration nodes, which open up to yet another map with various node types, except that THIS map actually introduces COMPLETELY different rules for travel and node interaction. It's just outright ridiculous. There are multiple other systems I could have made similar complaints about, such as character progression, action point system, ability targeting modes, and more - all needless complicated. And this is a genre that's supposed to be easy to learn and hard to master!Gordian Quest is clearly heavily inspired by Slay the Spire and other games of the genre: there's a deck with attacks and defends, you see the enemies' intents and have to respond to them, there's a set number of action points that reset every turn, etc. And yet it seems to fail at applying some core gameplay elements from that genre:1. You barely actually build a deck! Card drafting is incredibly infrequent compared with how many combat encounters you have. It means you're stuck in combat after combat with the same deck, and you have very little chance to customize your deck in response to other cards/items you encounter along your way. The game tries to compensate for that with many other ways of customizing each hero (class choice, items, overly-complex talent grid, etc.), but these don't fix the fundamental issue of not really letting you build your deck... in a deck builder!2. The pacing is bad, at least in regular difficulty. Even as a completely inexperienced player who doesn't understand half the systems, it's very rare for me to actually receive any damage at all during a combat encounter; and even when I do lose HP, it's really easy to heal in-between encounters. This includes supposedly "elite" battles. A hallmark of this genre is to make combat dangerous enough to force you to think deeply about your strategy, and to have attrition build up between battles; but this game is just all-around significantly easier, which takes away from the challenge of smart tactical gameplay.* One final note, about this entire review: I might have made mistakes about game mechanics. Maybe some veteran player will look and think "No, this is not how it works! You got it wrong!". But the fact is that if after more than 4 hours of gameplay I still got these basic wrong, it's another point emphasizing the needless complexity of this game.

_childDocuments_.review: Am I allowed to be offended by a game wasting its own potential?When it is so close to being a classic but clearly going in the wrong direction?Unfortunately the price tag did not equate the playtime. The game suffers from too many incredible ideas that are ultimately a bunch of sweet synergies an optimized deck will never play.Too many cards are overcosted.Too many of the classes explore ideas that a good deck at a high difficulty would never play.Game is just too easy and boring equating no reason to replay. If you are okay with this pricetag for a game you run one or two times then I would recommend it. Actually love the art style. Really like the idea of StS with a party. The battlefield itself is interesting but the enemies are easy to clear wave after wave of. Excellent game concepts, great mechanics, wonderful art design, but unfortunately not a game I can recommend to friends in its current state or where the roadmap says where it is going. At this point I've done one run on normal, one on nightmare, one on endless and am now bored and moving on.Edit after dev response: It's interesting that the developer responds here asking a player to "feel free to share what else can be improved for you" when before posting this review I did join their discord and post in suggestions. "Hey there, sorry to hear you didn't enjoy it!" -- I did enjoy the game, my negative review was from feeling as if the playtime didn't equate the price tag when comparing pricetags of simlarly priced games in my steam inventory and how long I played them. Since I tried out the game the devs pushed out another character who, like the previous characters, explore really cool ideas with cards that are overcosted and poorly stated. There are very few cards in an entire character pool worth drafting or upgrading if you are the type of player who enjoys high difficulty optimized gameplay. The devs perfect audience appears to be players who enjoy exploring cool ideas and not just trying to win. I shouldn't have to hamstring myself by deciding to play bad strategies.It is incredibly frustrating to get to the rare cards for a class and literally have NONE of them be playable additions to your deck. For example; in two of the three runs I did I played the paladin. Once on a Strength build and once on an int build -- none of the rares were remotely playable in my runs. Another example -- in one of my runs I played an elemental druid and none of her in class ways of gaining charge were remotely playable when I could instead splash efficient charge off items.Your game is so cool and really is close to being up there with games like StS and Monster Train. I do plan on checking back in maybe... a year? But why are you releasing new characters instead of making the ones you already have not have so many dead cards? On top of this there are some other core design issues. Runs of any kind are super tedious once you have an optimized deck. Drawing through my entire draw pile every turn to play 6 stabs and clear 6 enemies that are not interactive just isn't fun wave after wave. The game length itself (in both the story mode and endless) goes on far too long after I've finished building an optimized deck. Mechanics like them gaining thorns are a breath of fresh air because it forces me to think and not just click. There has to be more enemy interaction to keep a run interesting. Such as enemies that cap how many card I can play or enemies that always act first (forcing my defensive cards to matter).Or... how orange items make some build uninteresting. This isn't true for every build but for the most part once you find a strong orange weapon it is correct to build your deck to have multiple cards of the attack card that they buff (because the buff applies to all copies in your deck). This leads to me not having an interesting diversified deck but a boring deck when it comes to executing it in combat.

_childDocuments_.review: Gordian Quest is refreshingly unique. The combat system is fluid, there are tons of ways to customize your builds, and the characters are mostly really well balanced. After 40 hours, there have been moments where I've wished for more content (spells, classes, etc) but being honest,  I'm getting a little ahead of myself since I just think this game has crazy potential. There is plenty to keep you busy for a full playthrough, and I don't think you could ever go wrong buying this game if you like turn based strategy games.

_childDocuments_.review: The art direction is absolute Kino, whoever designed and/or drew these characters needs to be getting A LOT more work - for as basicas the character representations are, only a few drawings of each character, they are bursting with personality.  Seriously the thumbnails of these guys alone have more personality than most characters in AAA releases.  The amount of heart and passion that clearly went into this project is through the roof and it gushes out at every opportunity.   I'd love to see these characters in a more traditional, text and story heavy RPG that flushes out their personalities, backstories, and presents their narratives in a more focused way.  The plot is, at least at the point where I'm at, very standard fare.   Nothing mind blowing has happened but it doesn't really need to.   There's a town, there are undead attacking, there's some kind of evil ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ trying to level-up to God-Tier behind it all who needs a'thumpin - you know the drill.   I'm normally huge into games having rich and developed stories, but I recognize that for what this game is going for that's all I really need.   The gameplay is fun and breezy.  Not normally a huge Card based RPG fan, but this one won me over very quickly.  The Rogue-y elements sorta remind me a bit of Darkest Dungeon except fun instead of a miserable nightmare that makes you hate the game, the world, and yourself.

_childDocuments_.review: Welcome to my review of Slay the Spire: party of three. In Slay the Spire: party of three, you can select up to three heroes to fight Gordian and complete the ultimate Quest. I liked this game in this age of so many remasters and sequels. I am happy to say I enjoyed slaying the Gordian for about 25 straight hours! I give it a 7 out of 10, let's see the good side of the videogame and what can be done better for the already announced reboot called simply Slay the Spire: party of three (2023)The good:- In Slay the Spire: party of three, you make a party of three. Then you kill monsters for 4 acts, reach the Gordian and finish the game. Combat is fun! You have to position yourself and as the game progresses you will have so many cards on hand that you will need to customize your mouse DPI to select exactly what you want to select. Each class also has 3 specific trees, usually focusing on strenght, intelligence or dexterity, with unique spells. I had Ida, the druid, as a spellcaster showering the Gordianites with lightning bolts and it was fun.- Campaign is good lenght. Around 25h to finish on normal mode, which is about the entire Call of Duty campaigns since Modern Warfare back in 2007. Endgame is also cool and you can take your OP heroes to face some challenges to open new achievements.- Art, spell effects and all that is pretty well done. - Ida could have some cool fan art if explored more, but don't show her to DeviantArt.What can improve:- Exploration nodes could have been handled way better. Sometimes you will see your entire party moving at once and collecting resources in a single map, but these rewards are usually ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ ♥♥♥♥ and it just drags. - Resources *I think* also don't matter that much? And why is camping so complicated? It's similar to Darkest Dungeon but more obtuse. - Way too much useless loot. Less Nioh, more Dark Souls. Make loot more meaningful, guys.- Might need some UX/UI courses on Figma to make some screens easier to read. Some important stuff from vendors is way too hidden, like the gambling service and even how to spend your renown.- Quests could have been way better and more diverse. Most quests are about going to point A and killing something. Why not an objective where you just needed to survive X turns to complete? Or a quest in an arena where you needed to fight wave after wave of enemies? Or a quest to share the hot springs with Ida and Catherin? There are so many options, even character specific quests to open new skins could have been cool.Still, cool game, can't wait for the remastered sequel.

_childDocuments_.review: I played about five hours into the game when writing this review, so take it with a grain of salt.My opinion? So far so good, and I like it!The game is a simple, yet intricate RPG deck-building game with three characters in the party to your liking. I believe there are eight(?) characters in total that you can choose from the game as of February, 2021, but I believe the developers are still improving this game with more contents and new characters to come in the future.To summarize, it has fantasy components, random luck dungeon factors, and somewhat interesting story for the main game mode. It also incorporates in-depth and customizable components that any gamers can enjoy such as different map routes and unique skill paths for each character. You are also able to choose a game difficulty. Personally, I am not really a hardcore gamer, so games like Dark Soul puts me off in looking for and actually playing such games. This game, however, has three modes: story, rogue-lite, and rogue-like. Enabling these options somehow make more fun for casual gamers like me since I want to play a game where my characters can feel OP. Also, I can see where the developers were really trying to work on -- that is, convenience of character movement. The game has portal scrolls and portals for gamers to easily move around the map. This is a small detail, but this is what makes the game so much better.Honestly, the game is currently in Early Access, so it is not perfect. For example, the Acts are not finished; there are way too many mob fights that they make the game somewhat dull; and there are no tutorials on how to socket gems/use potions during battle/get materials for blacksmith-ing. (Let me know if you know how to.)But, I do believe that this game will set another prime example of how rogue deck-building game should be when the developers address what they currently lack in the game.Again, I recommend this game!4/5 stars.

_childDocuments_.review: I wanted to like this game. It sits in the intersection of genres that I love: roguelites, deckbuilding games, and turn-based tactics games. The visuals look great to me, and I don't know of any game quite like it. But Gordian Quest falls flat to me, even though I love Trials of Fire, which is one of the more similar games you can find on Steam and my second favorite roguelite deckbuilder after Slay the Spire. I checked in periodically throughout early access, but Gordian Quest never really felt like it fundamentally improved for me.Some of that is down to personal preferences for the genre. I don't see people talking about this much in reviews, but I prefer a roguelite deckbuilder that forces you to adapt your deckbuilding to the cards you are offered. Gordian Quest is almost as deterministic as it gets in terms of deckbuilding. You can use respec points to manipulate the already small card pool into giving you exactly the cards you want, and then freely remove cards from your deck (up to a limit) to only draw your desired cards. This also makes the late game combat much less interesting than it should be, since you can effectively draw your whole deck each turn. And finally, it undermines the challenge of the game, since as long as you can plan a half-decent build using your chosen characters, you can ensure that the plan will be executed eventually and then you will start to steamroll through all enemies. Even putting that aside, though, it says something that in a game designed for a party of three, you can beat its roguelite mode (called Realm Mode) on the highest difficulty with a party of one, with at least some of the available characters.So, we have a relatively easy game with relatively deterministic deckbuilding and combats that (late game) become bland. It's basically the opposite balance of Slay the Spire or Monster Train, both of which are more difficult games (at higher difficulties) that force you to be flexible in deckbuilding and have more interesting decisions in combat. However, if what you want out of the genre is a sandbox game where you can plan out and execute a build while becoming an untouchable god in the late game, then Gordian Quest may appeal more to you. There are tons of combinations of characters that you can try, each with multiple powerful ways to build. In that sense, the replay value is pretty high.There is also an RPG campaign, in addition to Realm Mode. The campaign is a decent introduction to the large number of systems in Gordian Quest, but I remember it becoming tedious to the point where I almost gave up. And that was when the campaign only had 2 acts, so it is even longer, now. It may make sense to play through some of the first two acts of the campaign before trying the Realm Mode, to get a feel for the game mechanics and to try out a bunch of the different characters a bit. Ultimately, though, I cannot recommend either way of playing.A lot of the rest of my complaints revolve around tedium and unnecessary complexity and are echoed across a lot of the other reviews I see here, but I'll list a few anyway, for completeness:* It feels like there are too many types of resources, mechanics, and systems. In campaign mode, they make the game more tedious if you try to interact with all of them, and especially if you try to utilize them optimally. In Realm Mode, the runs are short enough that you can barely interact with many of them in any given run.* Equipment is generally pretty unimpactful and I found the crafting system tedious, random, and generally unsatisfying. You're also not necessarily going to have the resources to be doing too much crafting in your Realm Mode runs, anyway, and you can't even craft anything except when visiting a specific type of map node that you may never encounter. Choosing what equipment to use is generally not much of a decision either, as I usually don't find enough equipment for all three characters to even get fully equipped in a Realm Mode run.* One particular thing that was added since I first played in early access is "Exploration". It's essentially a loot chest with more clicks and very minimal decision making. I'd rather just have the free stuff.* I don't really like metaprogression in general in this genre, but it's relatively extreme in Gordian Quest, requiring over 100,000 metaprogression points to unlock everything, while you only gain a couple thousand per run on the highest difficulty. You can't choose the order in which you unlock things, either, and some of the unlockables have a noticeable effect on your power level (but the game is very easy to beat without unlocking anything).* Runs are fairly long for the genre. A Realm Mode run has 5 realms of ~12 floors each, and each realm generally takes me around an hour, though your experience may vary.

_childDocuments_.review: It has potential.But it doesn't know what it wants to be, and it is incapable of taking shape.Let me start off by saying that the best part about this game is the combat. The combat is incredible and there are many classes and combinations for very different fighting styles and experiences, with good bit of strategy involved.The problem is everything else.If this was just a simple roguelite like Slay the Spire or Monster Train, then it would be great and everything would end there. But there are way too many low-quality features and garbage game modes. The campaign, which is the main game mode, is comprised of a single story, with randomly generated maps and dungeons, random events, and respawning enemies. The randomness doesn't even have a purpose, because the events are mundane and barely attribute to your growth or demise, and the overworld and dungeons are just node maps, so they all end up looking the same anyways. Add this with the fact random enemies respawn after a certain amount of arbitrarily added time, and you end up with a game that feels unrewarding of your time and progress. One of the game modes is similar to slay the spire, and plays slightly better, but it still has the same low quality features pulled from the main game. The "Low-quality" features:- 10 Armor slots for each character. Normally this could be a fun and interesting addition to a game, but this is a "roguelike"-esque game. And armor drops are pretty uncommon. Pair that with the broad array of randomly generated armor, and you have a low chance of obtaining the gear you need. By the time I was at the third act, I only had 4 or 5 decent gears equipped on my characters. The rest were level 1 junk because I either never found those armor types or they were useless to my character. In the roguelike gamemode, I only found 2 pieces of gear, neither of which useful, 40 minutes in.- The vendors. The vendors in this game sell a small collection of goods at relatively low rarity. You would be lucky to find something to buy at the vendors. There are many armor types and weapon types, all with their own bonuses and detriments. So many in fact, you will likely not find one that your party can even use in the tiny collection offered at shops. The vendors even have additional tabs for services they can provide the player. There are many of these tabs. And you will probably never use them except once or twice maybe in the late game.-The card management system and the skill tree. You need to go out of your way to get cards and spend skill points to do so. So when you get a bad hand, you not only lost skill points that could have been used to strengthen your character, but you could mess up your deck as well and gain nothing from it. You could ruin your 20 hour run by simply drawing a bad hand and being forced to add a bad card or remove a good one. -Equipment features. I'm not even going to start. You'd need a 4 page manual to explain all the potential each piece of gear has. It doesn't even matter if your equipment is strong enough. Otherwise its wasted investments.I hope to see this game make some major positive changes to its overarching gameplay. Remove the unnecessary randomness from the world maps and dungeons. Make vendors exciting to visit by increasing the quantities of goods they sell. Remove the unnecessary equipment features that no one uses, and with it, the corresponding services provided by vendors. And when given a poor set of options at card selection, provide an option to at least gain some tangible bonus out of it. Even if it is +2 HP  or +1 attribute, it is still detriment to the player, but it wont end their career.

_childDocuments_.review: Incredible ideas. Great art. Impenetrable and janky, but full of so much potential I can look past it. I haven't played the story mode yet, but I'm excited to take it for a spin. Did you know that each of the 9 characters has 4 different starting builds? Hot dog. Did I see dungeons in the Story Mode thumbnails? Oh my.I'm especially impressed when I think about how of the many mechanics that make me go "ooh" and "hmmmm", most of them were added in the most recent update (I bought the game during the Summer Sale). That says a lot about how the game is being developed, and to say I'm excited to see what happens next would be an understatement. I'm a sucker for Early Access games with aggressive update schedules, and Gordian Quest is currently occupying a rent-free living space in my brain. Since they read these reviews, here are some items of feedback I have:-Realm Mode needs better tutorialization. I haven't played the Story Mode, so things might be explained better there, but some of the elements were pretty tough to pick up on - respec points, adding pieces to the Skill Tree, deck editing, the Synergy System, Unstable Artifacts, and Cell Effects were confusing, to name a few.-Cell effects are still confusing. Sometimes, it feels like they don't work consistently/how I'd expect them to. It's pretty tricky to even read them without accidentally moving a character into an adjacent cell. Also, does the drain effect from Blood Pools scale? (it should.) How would I even find that information?-I'm not sure Unstable Artifacts are working as intended. Why can't I buy them and use them while I'm still in the shop menu? I need more favor to buy Legendaries!-This game seriously needs an "undo" button, even if it's just within the current character's turn. There is so much going on and so much complexity that mistakes and misclicks are inevitable, and currently it all feels way too punishing.-What's the point of the camp system exactly? I'm the kind of guy who's happy to play a 15-minute minigame with punishing stakes to get the equivalent of 50 gold worth of healing, but I'm probably in the minority. It feels a bit redundant at the moment.-I'm not a huge fan of how character death works, at least in roguelite Realm mode. Currently, it feels like losing a character = run end, but you still have to mess around for 20 more minutes trying to cheese out another encounter or two. I like the idea of losing a character costing you some of the XP you'd gain, but imo your dead characters should just come back to life at 1 hp. I think that would still keep losing a character costly, without immediately nuking your whole run.-You have effectively 36 characters to choose from, once you realize you can change out starting decks. This is tight as hell. It makes party composition and pregame theorycrafting feel like an entire game in itself. HOWEVER, it feels like Gordian Quest might be running into a similar problem that One Step From Eden, another excellent roguelite with many characters and multiple loadouts per character ran into, and that issue is scaling. If you can pick from 4 largely complete strategies per character before the game even starts, what does that do to card selection during the game? In OSFE, you generally start your run with 80% of the "good", synergistic pieces you need, and you spend the run not taking cards while you reroll and sift for the 1-3 rare and relics you need to finish your deck. While the immediate dopamine hit from realizing how many builds are available is enormous, it doesn't have much staying power once you realize that each loadout basically comes pre-packaged. Once you've played each loadout a handful of times, there's not much to come back for.For a game with in-run progression systems as broad, deep and complex as Gordian Quest, I'm concerned that the current loadout system could be a threat to the game's future, if not a crutch at the very least. I think the current system has the potential to work out, but it's on the developers to add enough versatile, impactful cards to the draw decks, especially at higher rarities, to keep players on their toes throughout a run. I think Legendary items help out in this regard - I just played a run where I had planned on running Kudo as a Blood Pool tank, but once I found the Bloodletter I ended up pivoting him into a Bleed-based bruiser because the synergy was too much to pass up.-The character designs are dope, both visually and mechanically. Golemancer = good. Sonneteer = good. Tactician = good. It's all good, and it all feels fresh. 10/10. I can't praise it enough.This game is not one I'd recommend to casual players at the moment, based on my limited experience in Realm Mode - calling it the Path of Exile of roguelite deckbuilders seems appropriate, if cliche - but the level of customization, strategy, freshness, and raw charm here is just plain off the charts. I'd recommend this game to anyone who will listen to me rant about it, and I can't wait to see what happens next.

_childDocuments_.review: I actually think nightskyy's review is spot on, but I gave the game a thumbs up on potential instead of a thumbs down. I will not speak to difficulty because I only completed normal, however the game feels like it needs some more time to bake, if you will. Everything nightskyy said about events and treasures in the random dungeons is true as of the date of this review. Itemization in general is really lackluster. Items in the game kinda feel like Diablo 3 prior to Reaper of Souls... loot 10000 items, maybe 5% have stats you actually care about for the character intended to use them, and getting that piece you want for the build you're pushing is like searching for a unicorn. Getting new items in a game with loot progression should be exciting. Instead getting items most of the time means the hassle of unloading your inventory in town. AND, the answer to that problem IS NOT to turn the game into a limited space "inventory simulator" game... I would be plenty happy with less loot that was more impactful when you get it. I don't really feel like the progression trees really mesh together well. Talents + skills + items + gems etc etc, it just doesn't come together into a product that makes progression fun. It doesn't really feel like you get enough card choices to put a build together unless you put points into getting cards, but that means you miss out on putting that point into something else. Overall it feels like cards should be obtained in a different manner, outside of the trees.All this aside, I gave the game a thumbs up because it is just oooozing with potential. Combat is enjoyable, although I wish you had more control over where your heroes start combat. Monster types are repetitive, although I have not yet started Act 2. Even though it feels like the cleric archetype is mandatory for your group, the classes I have tried so far all feel sufficiently unique. I do wish the party size was 4 and not 3. I quite enjoyed the "exhaust a card" mechanic, allowing you to boost certain rolls. It felt good to try to get the bonus I needed while also keeping in mind the fights ahead. I liked the take on pathing in dungeons, allowing you to explore. Giving the completionists the option to search everything while allowing the people who just want to move forward feels good, almost a sort of "curated sandbox" feel. In conclusion, I am excited to go in and play some more. I feel like this is a game I could get a lot of enjoyment from, especially considering the price point. I hope the devs keep working to address some of the concerns above and from nightskyy's review, I feel like he expressed things much better than I. I want to see what the future holds for this game.

_childDocuments_.review: Sadly, not that good. The major flaw is that the game gets easier and easier as you go on (and it's pointlessly easy in anything but the highest difficulty), while it should be the other way. The hardest battle in campaign act I is the one where you get your third party member, and once you are past that you'll roll all the way to the end. This is due to having little agency at the beginning (you play with the default decks), and once you start to customize, the game doesn't scale in a way that offers a meaningful challenge.-The developer response here is fair, and I'll be following with the updates. The focus on balancing does seem to be in the right direction. -As of Strategies and Synergies update, the state is the same. The problem is not that the difficulty is too low, it's that it doesn't scale right. It's always off-putting when a game becomes easier as you progress through it (that blocks entry when you are new, then offers little of interest later on); and that's still how it is with the campaign act 1. I can't find it in me to push through the tedium to see the later parts.

_childDocuments_.review: Basically 7/10 card game. VERY mediocre "rogue" game as of july 2020, like if this was just turned based strategy roguelite and not a card game it would be a poo poo/10. StS but you control 3 characters with more simplified card pools. More than half the time is spent tabbed out watching netflix. Sorely lacking in any special encounter or event. Imagine the StS map but just normal and elite enemy fights only. "Shrines" are supposed to spice things up but they literally (and I mean literally) just change enemies into elite enemies and that's it. Recommended because I don't mind a mediocre roguelite. EDIT: After finishing the game I almost changed it into a thumb down due to the massive disappointment that is the stat system. This will be a not recommended if things stay like this when it leaves Early Access.I will keep it simple: think Dead Cells, but somehow *more* simplified. Red cards scale with the red stat, blue cards scale with the blue stat and so on. Except every card only has ONE color, and there's no colorless card. Because of that, this card game has LESS flexibility than a fast paced action sidescroller. Not to mention that a stat system like dead cells is really bad for this kind of game. In normal RPG's strength may mean higher melee dmg and carrying capacity and so on, and you would select your equipment based on the archetype of your character. Here? Why must my mage have a lot of strength? Because I got unlucky and draw several strength cards in a row. You don't find equipment to suit your character but upgrade your character to suit the equipment (gears/cards). Oh and not all cards actually scale. Only damage and defense values will scale, which hurt the balance even more.The debuffs are frankly  boring. Everything is damage with no actual "debuff" effect. Maybe burning will cause enemies to panic? Bleeding will cause them to receive more damage from slash? Nope, just damage. The same for vulnerable, poison, might, critical, shock, etc. "cold" is the only example of a good debuff as it increases AP cost for enemy cards.

_childDocuments_.review: The first time I played this, I was immediately overwhelmed by the amount of stuff going on in this game, and the less than adequate tutorial didn't help, so I stopped playing. Then after a while, I set aside a big chunk of free time, determined to give it another try, and was pleasantly surprised by how good this game actually is. The number one complaint among the current comments is the content bloat, which is inevitable when you fuse so many genres into one, but I think the fusing is actually executed relatively well since all the mechanisms can significantly impact the gameplay if you know what you're doing. The combat can get a little still and more pronounced enemy specialties would be welcome. Fortunately, because it has so many systems, at least for me the combat is not the most important part of the game. I enjoy collecting and equipping my characters with the best items, increasing my characters' strength in all the different ways, and simply exploring the map and missions in Campaign Mode. Just like in many RPG games, almost everything you do has impact on your subsequent combats, but the reasons you do them aren't necessarily solely for that purpose.The tutorial leaves a lot to be desired, and the devs have said that this is one of their priorities, but honestly I don't think a better tutorial is gonna help flatten the learning curve that much. It's like you don't expect that after going through the tutorials in Europe Universalis or Football Manager you'll immediately know what you're doing in them. You have to spend hours to explore the game before you can start having fun and you'll still learn something new from time to time. I'm not saying this game is on the same level of complexity as the games I just mentioned, but it's certainly much more complicated than games like Slay the Spire where you only have some cards in one deck to manage. Be prepared to spend some effort learning the game, but after you do it's a lot of fun.
_childDocuments_.name: Gordian Quest

_childDocuments_.review: Gordian Quest is one of the first games with the Slay The Spire formula that I honestly think compares favorably. If you like the Deck Builder RPG genre, you will probably enjoy playing this game. The campaign is a fun way to learn the game, with a predictable plot that you will likely skip through. The game really shines in Realm Mode, particularly in the Nightmare difficulty (which the achievements of the game seem to point towards as the ideal difficulty).I won't go into to many details, but I think Gordian Quest does a great job of expanding on the Deck Building RPG genre with a battle system that feels tactical without being weighed down by it. The skill trees feel complex but also not overwhelming. Leveling up your character feels meaningful, but without overshadowing the importance of player skill. It's a game that you feel you get better at as you make mistakes and learn lessons.Overall, highly recommended to fans of the genre. If you are new to the genre, this would be a recommendation second only to Slay the Spire (which I think is a little more friendly for new players).

_childDocuments_.review: Although a pretty good game it can feel lackluster at some points. More traps would be recommended for a real existential threat. Also the spells should be balanced a bit more. Despite it's flaws I had a fun time playing it and I'm looking forward to the second act.

_childDocuments_.review: After you start getting characters and equipment, and building out your skill trees its absolutely awesome. Good steady sense of progression, and crazy amounts of depth and choices to make.I think ultimately the rouge-lite mode doesn't beat something like Slay the Spire as you have a lot of different stat based mechanics to juggle, making it feel a little overwhelming. Condensing all these mechanics into a 2-3 hour run is just a bit much.The campaign mode is worth it alone though, as it nails that sense of long term growth and progression in a similar way that Path of Exile or Diablo does. Getting those good legendaries and upgrading/augmenting you gear is tons of fun, and after the campaign you get adventure mode, which basically lets you run the realm mode without the rogue-lite death element as your end game. Keep in mind this is still a card game, so equipment still comes secondary to honing and playing your deck intelligently too.

_childDocuments_.review: I really like this game -- the atmosphere, the mechanics, equipment, etc. The basic card types and abilities remind me a lot of Slay the Spire, but there are some unique synergies and card styles. It's interesting to put together a team that compliments each other and modifying their equipment to maximize potential. Fun game play in my opinion and the story is interesting and gives a sense of purpose to what you're doing. As others have said, it is a bit on the easy side and I played on hard with permadeath. (I did have intent on.) I set up the wizard guy to shock the hell out of everyone and then dropped rain of arrows which often resulted in a first round win and finished off the last guy without any sense of being at risk... of losing a single hit point. I'm not sure if I even took any damage. Enemies don't coordinate well, if at all, and their actions often seem pointless. Enemy action points could probably be doubled. The vast majority of the time enemies only play one card and that seems insufficient to provide a challenge. So, hopefully this gets a bit of work.Two other (minor) issues: when using the portal, the screen zooms in awkwardly. It would be nice if it didn't or zoomed back out after reaching the destination. Second, map travel, in general, is kind of awkward. Certain actions would seem to be automatic, but are not. For example, if I click on a portal scroll, I would expect to automatically focus in on the group if viewing another part of the map. These are really very minor issues.Again, really like the game and I look forward to playing the complete version. I'll play it whatever happens, but I do hope that the difficulty is adjusted. I'd like to feel as if there is a decent risk of losing and I'm just not getting that from its current state.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a marriage of some of my favourite types of games; it is a Roguelike/ Deckbuilding/Tactical RPG hybrid that offers a ton of depth. Influenced by some of the finest - both popular (such as Darkest Dungeon, Path of Exile, and Slay the Spire) and less mainstream titles such as Card Hunter; Gordian Quest has you leading a group of heroes through procedurally generated areas. Each character has its own class and respective deck which the player can customised through leveling up or equipping items. Currently there are six classes (but between 10-16 are coming) and one act (of an eventual total of four). Already there is a ton of content here to play (well worth the price tag) and a ridiculous amount of replayability. -  is incredibly fun and rewarding. Combat feels like a combination of Slay the Spires deck based abilities and enemy intentions and Radiant Historia's (an incredible turnbased rpg from Atlus) grid based movement that utilizes movement and strategic placement.- The  is completely charming and suits this style of game perfectly. - The  is amazing, it does not feel as restrictive and luck-based as some of the other titles in the genre. Instead of having to add new cards to your deck, you can choose to replace a card in your deck with a new one. You can also use equipment which gives new cards (a lovely feature from Card Hunter) to circumvent some of your decks weaknesses. - The  each feel unique, but at the same time flexible in how you choose to build them. Oh and there is a ton more planned!- The  really tunes in to what makes RPGs great. Whist there is an overworld that you can freely travel around (from one node to the next), there are also little mini dungeons to explore, and a camping feature for those long journeys (Darkest Dungeon <3). Events, are traditional in the sense that they use a D20 dice and a character's stats to produce outcomes. BUT whats awesome is the player can exhaust one of the characters cards (effectively rendering the card useless until the next time you rest) to increase your odds of success.- The  fills me with confidence that this game is going to be a huge success. The devs behind the game are very communicative and receptive to player feedback. And the Roadmap! just look at the ROADMAP!!If your looking for a Slay the Spire Deck Builder on RPG steroids - look no further. This game is a gem with a ton of depth that I am thoroughly loving, that just keeps on surprising!

So theoretically you can just report all the issues and they will be fixed. This is fine, but there are limitations to this. If something in the design itself is flawed it would take a lot of work. I do appreciate how responsive the devs are so i was thinking about not posting the review for negative but this is just my honest feeling, i wouldn't reccomend it at this time. The two biggest problems with this game (they are related) is that:1. There is too much bloat complexity in the game in general. 2. The systems in the game individually don't feel impactful enough Essentially because there are so many different systems in the game, the developers can't allow any one of them to be too impactful (skills, stats, skills, items, sockets, enchantments, cards). However, in order to keep all the systems in place that the game currently has, the systems have to add 'Something'. The 'Something' is often useless (+9% cold resist, when almost no enemies do cold damage) but it is neccessary for the current state of the game, because the bloat allows more systems to exist. In general I think the design needs some retooling. I would1. Eliminate some of the systems currently in the game to allow the remaining systems to be more impactful2. Eliminate 'useless' stats. Just get rid of them.3. allow more player choice in the itemization without making them wade through a pool of useless trinkets or have a gigantic inventory that has hundreds of situational items that will never actually be used. I think the devs are moving in the right direction, they are reportedly going to eliminate a system in battles where the enemy has different cards in hand and can change them depending on your movements (this might sound good but in practice it messes up the intent system and means to check every enemies hand before you do anything, every turn) and making combat more puzzle based. But currently I don't reccomend it, it would have to have a few more design changes.

_childDocuments_.review: A very enjoyable tactical RPG which gives me the same amount of build diversity as a the likes of ARPGs like Diablo and PoE. If you enjoy making builds on individuals characters you will like this game. If you enjoy combining these characters with your squad to make fun synergies you will love this game. The crafting is quite basic but enjoyable and allows for a little extra power, while fulfilling that loot grind. If you don't enjoy playing the campaign over and over again, a new game mode has been added for shorter and randomly generated runs which can allow you to test and create fun builds, with a potential leaderboard coming(?). Combat is very rewarding especially once you get familiar with the battlefield and how to read enemies, it makes you feel very in control and powerful when you combo your characters.If I am to talk about a negative side of the game it would be the supply system, it seems more annoying that intuitive, where I just sink gold into it occasionally to top it up rather than make any meaningful decisions with it. Also the resistance is kind of annoying how you need an increment of 5 to increase the resistance at all, meaning if you get a bunch of items that have 2 of each resistance on them, they are useless. It would be much preferred say if you got 2% per point, and then gave you 15% when you reached 5 points of resistance, so you still get the same amount but still get the power increase for investing.Since it is Early Access if you're worried about patches, we do get constant bug fixes and balance changes, with big patches progressing the game further every couple of months. I would definitely say this is a game worth buying in it's current state, and can give many hours of enjoyment and experimentation.

_childDocuments_.review: Played the game for a bit, after getting it for christmas. Was pretty busy and bounced off it, going to give it a fresh shot, taking notes as I go. button to advance to act 1 looks cut off, light effect on said button doesn't re-center if switching from windowed to fullscreen.character sorting is a bit strange. the characters are sorted in in 2 columns, but top down and then left right. so almost how one would read, left to right and then down, but not quite.Each character having three schools, that are distinct but similar to the four specializations is not ideal. The first character has a swordsmanship school, but also a swordhand specialization. That naming convention is not helping a new player keep all these terms straight. What is the complexity representing? Should new players avoid the high complexity characters? I assume not if they're availabe for a first run, but then what is it attempting to communicate to me? Specializations affect your starting deck, but have no mouse over text describing how each differs. This is exactly where you'd want a brief blurb talking about how each starter deck works. The flavor text doesn't help, it says "Catherin is a cleric" even if I don't pick the Cleric starting deck! Clarity matters.Difficulty selector is sorta misusing how rogue lite and rogue like are usually used, but thats a nitpick. It defaulted to easy, is that what I should be starting with? Unclear, I would usually associate that with normal.First tutorial fight and my guard friend immediately used some attack. I see no place where I can see what he did, a discard pile, combat log, nothing. Great feature in card games. Small detail, but because I gave the second monster vulnerable at the end of the first round, I was able to kill it without triggering my guard friend's trigger attack of opportunity.Captain's voice matches appearance better than guard friend's does theirs. I click on the blacksmith, see equipment with sockets. I think, what does a socket do, let's try chatting with the blacksmith. Intro text choice, great I need that. Nope, the blacksmith just says she's the blacksmith. Why isn't there an option for her to explain how weapon mechanics work?When I talk to sister ophelia she has a quick introduction, why doesn't Jun?I get to pick a new character, would be cool if the game recommended combinations for me, or told me anything about party composition. I'll pick the monk, he has dexterity and my cleric doesn't.First fight with the monk man, why does my card/hand layout use so much wasted space. My dodge card has 3 words on it, and yet I can't see its effect in my hand without scrolling over to it because the bottom is chopped off. It's great that I can see the art, name, and cost, but why am I looking at a bunch of beige background in the rules text. Change the card layout so I can see my three words of rules text.There are so many mechanics, and so much of the art is great. It feels like real effort went in to making this, but a lot of these mishaps I've talked about are really fundamentals of good design. I think some designer(s) need to sit down with players new to the game and watch them play, see the questions they have, the elements left unclear or mechanics confusing.

_childDocuments_.review: The game clearly has a LOT of effort put into it from the technical and art side, however the gameplay suffers severely from spreading itself too thin and a lack of clear image of what it wants to be. Is it a card drafting game? Kind of. But the acquisition of cards is fairly slow, and you have to commit to a build quite early on, so it doesn't excel at it. You have a bunch of characters to choose from, but realistically will have to commit to 3 you will use in your run. On top of the main game, you have a bunch of minigames, crafting, consumables, equipment management and enchanting and a few more systems, but they have SUCH a minor impact on the main gameplay loop, I question why they're even there in the first place. It has these hints of a roguelite, too, but considering a single runs takes ~30 hours to complete, I don't think any sane person is going to genuinelly commit to that. Especially considering the worst offender in the game...The balance is a mess. 95% of the battles are a boring slog where nothing poses a threat, but then there's the occasional 'ALT F4 if you got a bad position or the enemy rolled high initiative at the start of battle or it's over'  out of absolutely nowhere. Ability balance is about the same. Would you rather spend multiple turns applying debuffs for a big payoff, or use two abilities and kill almost anything on the same turn in an AOE? How about a minor Heal over Time, or a masisve burst heal that also doubles your healthpool?Also, please, no company mandated developer responses. I appreciate giving the impression of caring, but c'mon guys...

_childDocuments_.review: is a mixture of many genres: strategy RPG with turn-based battles using cards with a roguelike option, all on a nodal map in a campaign that allows you to choose your own adventuring paths.The game is launched now into Early Access and currently there is only 1 act out of 4 that will eventually be available. The single available act is already a rather sizeable map, with many nodes of interest to explore. Currently available also are 6 heroes, 500 skill cards, and 200 unique items. The full game will feature many more heroes, the full 4 acts, and an ambitious goal of thousands of skill cards and items.With so many deckbuilding card games released in recent times it has become more difficult to make a game unique. I think these developers managed to put together a well-made game with the card-driven battles and the deck-building only a part of the game. The RPG aspect is great too, and you will find yourself easily immersed in this game.The game starts off with a simple interactive tutorial for the battle system, with progressive introduction of more game elements as you encounter them.You will choose among 6 heroes to start, with the others introduced as you play on. You will see 4 difficulty settings, with the hardest difficulty, Nightmare, locked in the beginning. You can also choose roguelike mode, manifesting in permadeath of the characters as they fall in battle. In normal mode if your entire party falls in battle, it will be a game over. Otherwise, you can heal up fallen party members after battles.As expected during the battle sequences, you will see a lot of action using the cards. You will draw cards, use available AP to play the cards or to move around on your side of the field. Each character has his/her own private deck of cards and AP. While mostly the cards affect the player playing the card, they also have some AOE cards that can offer for good strategic formations. After the battles, the characters earn experience, level up, gain money, etc. The RPG management system is pretty well developed with plenty of useful and interchangeable items, talents and abilities, skill-point based build-modifications that can be put together to complement other party members, etc.In addition, you will find plenty of quests and assignments when you return to the garrison/base. There will be plenty to do, such visiting a healer, buying equipment, talking to other townsfolk, etc. Some converstaions will lead you down certain possible adventure paths. You will have to make some important decisions as well during these.The full game will feature 4 full acts, with only the first available right now in the beginning of Early Access, as mentioned above.The graphics are very well-done with the hand-drawn art and plenty of detail to impress the players. The style and the colors used also make for a memorable experience. The animations are subtle but nice.The game can be fully played with a mouse.Even though it is starting off in Early Access,  already offers plenty of content to keep the players happy for some rather lengthy game sessions. It's become more and more difficult to create something unique in the aftermath of  and  due to their overwhelming popularity leading to a huge explosion in the genre. I think this game definitely offers some unique gameplay and experience--the card battles are just part of the encompassing well-made game with fleshed out RPG aspects.There is so much to do in this game and while a lot of people enjoy roguelikes, I do think it's great that the developers have made that as an optional setting. There are some incentives for the player to take on the roguelike mode, such as better drop rates for rarer items, but it is also nice to know that the developers want everyone to enjoy this game, including the casual players who may not want to see the characters that they painstakingly built up fall in battle permanently.With the promise of the full game featuring so much more content, we can look for this game shining even more among those indie gems.Definitely recommended.

_childDocuments_.review: Gordian Quest is sitting between the deckbuilding and RPG genres and I don't think it did a particularly good job combining the two.Deckbuilding is usually done to introduce some variability into combat, but in Gordian Quest after just a few levels you can easily draw the majority of your deck (and drawing the entirety of it is likely after some more levels) so combat quickly becomes samey. The majority of card upgrades and equipment just increase the numbers on your cards to compensate for enemies getting more HP. There are some neat ideas in the Legendary equipment that are actually interesting, or being able to socket your skills to modify them PoE-style, but the actually interesting bits are drowned out by all the management of boring +stat loot.There's a campaign mode which follows a story quest with the same set of characters, and a roguelite mode with shorter runs. For me, the campaign's progression was too slow and I was doing too many similar fights. The roguelite mode was held back by all the inventory management -- after each fight I'd have multiple level ups on each of my three characters so I'd need to manage their skill trees, possibly add and remove cards, handle any equipment that dropped... I'm okay with complex systems in games but these weren't really interesting decisions and just dragged the game out.

_childDocuments_.review: the reviewer is friends with one of the developers at Mixed Realms.Gordian Quest is a turn-based tactical RPG where you play cards from a deck to determine what skills your party uses during combat. When the game gets going and hits its stride, it becomes quite addictive, fulfilling that "one more battle" itch from turn-based games.However, it is also riddled with a lot of tiny niggling problems that nip away at your enjoyment. The chief issue is that GQ has a ridiculous amount of mechanics and features — many of them are quite obtuse and require deliberate trial and error for the player to grasp. For example, you can choose to earn Respec Points when leveling up. To most RPG gamers, "respec" means the ability to reset your skill points. But in GQ, it actually allows you to swap out a card from your current deck and replace it with another randomly drawn one. You  reset your skills, but it is done elsewhere from an artifact item.While there is a tutorial menu to teach you all these hidden mechanics, I feel like the developers should have cut down on the "feature creep" and focused more on the fewer stuff that matters. Rather than "telling" the player about these mechanics through text tutorials, why not "show" them organically through an actual battle or quest? It took me a very long while to understand how Armour works and how important it is to stack it with Guard — but only becuase I got lucky and picked a defensive card that came with Armour.I like the ability to customise your deck and level up your cards to give them new abilities and effects. I also like how you can reroll sockets and upgrade the rarity level of your items — it keeps them relevant and usable until the late game.I don't like the Avert mechanic and the Tier 3 talent that gives you invulnerability in exchange for Fate. Imagine this: the final boss has a lethal attack that deals 1,000+ damage. You can either move your party out of the targeted squares to evade it... or you can just drink the almighty Avert potion. It sounds quite silly on paper, but it's a necessary tactic on Torment difficulty because you might run into situations where you simply can't avoid incoming (lethal) damage.Overall, Gordian Quest is a fun, but slightly flawed tactical RPG from a Singapore indie studio. I am patiently waiting for the day where the studio decides to create a true, DnD-inspired CRPG. Don't waste all of that fantasy music and artwork on just a card game!

_childDocuments_.review: I’m not a CCG or Deckbuilder dude. Strategic depth and replayability are often a draw -pun intended- for fans of the genre. I’m a huge lore ♥♥♥♥♥ and like me some compelling characters and story, something CCGs don’t deliver that often.Despite some reservations, this one intrigued me, so why don’t I explain why this could be your lucky draw as well.Let’s break it down…This one has all the right bits in its Combat UI: Your card hand, your draggy-droppy indicators, status effects, health, the actions you have left etc. As a kicker it tells you which enemy wants  to ruin which character’s day. I found the Combat UI to be very intuitive and comprehensive.Unfortunately, the rest of the UI went shopping hungry and brought home a way too large bag of elements.There’s a lot of UI, since this game has to cater to a lot of mechanics, many of which you will have to access regularly. I always felt slightly inconvenienced by the process of navigating through the different elements as they’re right now. Examples would be showing equipped items by default in a situation where I can’t / shouldn’t do anything with them in the active menu, having to click on a Waystone to use my town portal (but only sometimes), and the sheer number of menus, be it shop owners you bounce between or the multitudes of decks and card-angles you can check and cross-reference.The card-art doesn't seem like much, very standard fantasy without much fanfare. It’s all very readable, though,  i.e. very memorable, and there are nice details and often depictions of the character they belong to in action.Gameplay visuals, especially the characters have a distinct anime look to them which I find appealing, as it reminds me hard of Record of Lodoss war and similar fantasy spins... and I’m a sucker for that kind of nostalgia. It’s this incredible charm of maturity and a bit of grit mixed with an over the top playfulness of impractical but undeniably cool gear and a townguard grunt who has the face of a supermodel.This blend pulls the right strings for a high fantasy atmosphere with detailed backgrounds, snappy animations, flashy effects, as well as  solid character and monster design. The latter despite the fact that all your enemies are pulled from the ranks of ‘Generic Fantasy Goons inc’: zombies, skellingtons, wolves, spiders, cultists and bandits. They are used to good effect and I cannot deny that a lot of love went into their creation to make them just distinct enough to be endearing.The sound is serviceable. I’m not blown away, but it does what it’s there to do: combat sounds are visceral, impactful and fit their respective triggers. I like the weight they add. The main screen theme is really nice, while combat music and exploration theme lack a clear identity. They’re just… there. They dispasionately inform me of the current mood, but none is as evocative as, let’s say the frantic tunes of desperate survival / heroism in Darkest Dungeon. There are no voice-overs, understandably. The only time someone speaks is during the intro cinematic which establishes the world for us. It is fine, but also deeply cliched in both narrator choice, tone and information given.Just as with the enemies, though, cliches are cliches for a reason. And that is not always a bad thing.There were ancient people. They ♥♥♥♥♥♥ up. The world isn’t well. You are a hero, please make the world well again.That’s our story. I wish I could say there’s more to it, but even with 3 chapters still to come, I think it is a safe bet to say, what we see here is exactly what we get. It’s a simple RPG story for a game that frankly had a right not to bother with one, but gave us a world, some lore, a story and characters nonetheless. I can appreciate that.While the lore is simple, I really can’t say it feels tacked on or lackluster. It’s just uncompromisingly straightforward. If story and lore are serviceable -and I’m sure you begin to notice a pattern- what about the characters?Gordian Quest’s heroes have all these cool little details, the style and markings of characters you could get attached to. Unfortunately, each of them not only gets a definitive name, but also gets a small blurb what their exact deal is and it couldn be more generic: Scoundrel wants money, Wizard wants knowledge, Paladin wants to protect people. It creates this weird disparity, where I know enough to find them boring and can’t find an angle to care, but I still find their concepts and presence cool.Or, to be blunt: The characters  have a lot of identity thanks to visuals and gameplay, but zero personality. Their barks don’t mitigate that at all, as they’re just as generic and don’t come near the variety of Darkest Dungeon or even Deep Sky Derelicts.I think if the devs go forward with this, I’d love to see more barks, fluff texts on the heroes’ cards and maybe even some more vignettes /personal stories to flesh them out more.Again, though:  we got a lot more than most other games in this bracket would give us, so let’s go where the real meat is.Gordian Quest is a wild grab-bag with plenty of familiar concepts. You form a party of 3 heroes out of  6 (at this time) which you unlock over the course of the first act. You play cards with flavors of attack, defense, buff, debuff, all separated in attribute categories. The respective attributes usually make cards stronger, as does upgrading them to a mastered version. You heard right, attributes! It’s also an RPG: Your heroes can level to get more cards, more stats and enhancing talents to complement your playstyle. There’s also gear, party buffs, camping, map events with d20 skill challenges, for which you can use cards as an amplifier. You can also (dis)enchant your gear, put sockets for runes into it for various bonuses, and of course, there’s gear galore. And if that’s not enough, there’s altars on the map which alter encounters for more risk/reward gameplay.All this may seem overwhelming, but after a while it becomes second nature, and if i can do it, anyone can.Combat takes place on a grid with rows (vertical) and lanes (horizontal) which influence your reach and who you can attack or be attacked by. The action economy is your typical flavor of action points and turn order is determined by initiative rolls. I have yet to find monsters that are consistently faster than I am, so I don’t know why it’s not just: your guys go, then bad guys. Technically, there are initiative debuffs, but your enemies rarely use them and you probably won’t either, because:This is also another game where more action points and bonus card-draw can very easily become your crutch. That’s sad, as there are many interesting cards I’ll never play since there are many faster ways to kill my enemies.Right now, I think it is too easy to snowball the game in your favor and some heroes are definitely easier to handle than others and dominate the battlefield. As happy as I am that there is a story at all, the quests we have right now are little more than glorified checkpoints and the reward is often pocket change and a resource you can only spend in your next run. The gameplay loop is still satisfying, and really scratches that treasure and card hunter itch. It’s incredibly enjoyable to build your deck based on the combos you like, create synergies between your party and wreck shop across the map.I’m confused. Judging by my own words what we have here is a game that’s nothing special. It works, it’s decent, it does just enough.This game practically begs you to realize it is nothing special.And yet it definitely is. There lies true beauty in its straightforwardness. It knows it’s a slightly cheesy fantasy Deckbuilder RPG and Gordian Quest proudly flies these colors. What you see is what you get. And what we get, will improve as time goes by. And as far as I’m concerned, that’s pretty special these days.Hard recommendation.

_childDocuments_.review: Gordian Quest is a turn-based strategy game with deckbuilder and rogue-like elements. The Review will mainly focus on the campaign mode. You can play the Campaign-, Realm- mode or skirmish.Campaign three acts, you can select one of five difficulties as well as standard mode, Rogue-lite, or rogue-like mode. In standard mode, heroes will be revived after battles. The rogue-lite mode will end, if your entire party dies within a battle, and in rogue-like mode, you can't revive heroes in town.You can change the difficulty within the campaign at any time. The Campaign consists of three acts, each with different missions. You move around a map, battle enemies, get into events that require you to do challenges. You pick a hero and try the challenge by picking a skill and rolling dice then. The map consists of different nodes. Once you've traveled to a node, you can travel there without doing a battle in the future. In the town are several buildings to get new heroes, artifacts, heal or revive heroes for gold, buy items or equipment, unlock new buildings, etc. This is like a safe place and you can regroup your party there as well as plan ahead. There is gold, supplies, fate, and renown. With gold, you can buy items and equipment, renown is used for buying artifacts, fates grants you a chance to reroll a dice when failing a challenge, and supplies are needed for traveling. Are turn-based. On the top, it shows you the turn-order. Every hero has three AP's and his own deck.There are three different lanes. This adds tactical depth to the game because this will determine who you and your enemies can attack. It depends on the character and his cards. Some cards can be played on all lanes, some just in the lane you're standing at, etc. Each lane also has three fields. If an enemy stands on the first field and another one on the third (all in the same lane) some cards can't be played on the enemy standing behind. Aside from AP, there is SP. You get SP after playing cards. Some cards require SP to be played. Your Heroes gain EXP for every battle. After every level up, you get a skip point. There is a skill tree with nodes to spend them on. It's pretty big and allows you to boost stats, HP, or even new talents.You will also get equipment during your run like shoes, helmets, etc. They will boost your starts or/and add new cards to the specific deck. Characters need to fulfill certain requirements for certain items to equip them (like 9 Dexterity, etc.).You can freely edit a hero's deck (remove or add cards to it) depending on the deck pool. The deck pool has cards from the equipment they wear, tactical cards which you get for building up synergy, or skills you get by leveling up. Heroes also have synergy depending on how they fight together. Building up synergy grants access to more tactical cards. This is a roguelike mode. You have a map with nodes and different ways to get to the boss. There is no town to regroup, heal, etc. You will have to do all of that on certain nodes. There are battles, events, safe passages (to heal and get supplies), explorations, shrines, merchants, etc. For every node you move, you use one supply, while you start with 20, you have several chances to get some back. Heroes still level up, you can get new skills, edit your deck and get equipment.  Renown earned in realm-mode can be used in the campaign mode and vice-versa.   Gordian Quest is a fun and addictive turn-based strategy game. There is a lot of content already, different modes and difficulty settings for casuals as well as core gamers, and battles are tactical demanding. The gameplay overall is very smooth and the campaign is engaging thanks to a very good level-up system for heroes, their skill-trees, types of equipment, and a story to complete (well, not as of now, there will be more acts later). The rogue-like mode sadly feels more like a grind to the campaign and a small, not fully-fleshed-out additional mode to pass time. You also should know that this isn't a deckbuilder first and foremost. I definitely recommend Gordian Quest to fans of turn-based strategy fans. If you want a roguelike deckbuilder like StS, Monster Train, etc. you probably won't be as satisfied because this isn't a deckbuilder first and foremost. Still, it's a fun game and very well worth full price.

_childDocuments_.review: Gordian Quest is a game of mixed genre made by Mixed Realms (huh, gotcha! :)) It combines two of nowadays popular gameplay mechanics: roguelike crawling and deckbuilding. But not in their full glory since it's just a start of Gordian Quest Early Access period. The roguelike element is limited to a linear first act (as far as I noticed in 1h play) with randomly generated loot and enemies, and the deckbuilding is limited to gaining access to new cards through leveling skills and equipping new gear. I haven't find out yet if there is a way to create my own deck of cards.But fear not :) the limitations will be covered by huge amount of skills, items and plenty of heroes. Every new game can be started with one of the following 6 heroes: a Straw-haired Knight, a Battle Nurse, a Steampunk Ranger (with no gun?), a Scoundrel with evil smirk, an old french Merlin, or a Rabid Teenage Bearkin elf girl. And there's more to come! 10 to 16 more heroes will be added (according to full release plans), so it will be 16-22 heroes in the end.The art style of this game reminds me of , but with lesser character animations (yet it looks pretty good). Somehow it shows worse performance on a min required spec than it shows in Battle Chasers, though. Also there is no voice acting in Gordian Quest (not quite sure if it's only for EA period), so prepare to read some text.Considering all above, I still recommend this game as a very promising and good looking title. Also the devs are pretty active and responsive in game discussions. And this is a very encouraging sign.

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of the best deckbuilder RPGs that I've played in the last several years.You choose 3 heroes (from many possible) and that is per se a very important choice, because of potential synergies between them. You also get to develop them and build their decks from 3 archetypes for every one of them; that gives the game a lot of replayability.I like the story, it's the "enemies have invaded the world" type, but it's not that important. The fights are. And the fights are beautiful, fast paced and give you that addictive feeling of One more fight before I go to bed.It's very satisfying to create combos. For example, I play with the assassin, and he has some equipment with 2 Surge cards (Surge gives him one more action per turn). He also has a small deck and 3 Stab cards, which damage the enemies depending of how many cards you play before them in a turn. So he gets to attack with a lot, and I mean huge damage at the end of his turn. You also can trade, explore sites, hoping you find some treasure, craft your magical equipment, chat with your teammates and, of course, tweak your decks.The game may be played as a rogue-like, but I only tried that in the beginning of early access, so I can't tell you a lot about that. I prefer the campaign now. It has four acts, a few dozens hours of playing and, of course you feel that you must replay it with different heroes.The difficulty has spikes mostly in the beginning of the acts and, of course, when you fight bosses. For example, the first time when I encountered several flamethrowers, my party got wiped out. You must find a strategy to beat them, the best is to kill everything in the first two turns. I like that you can make the game as hard as you like, because I really hate to loose a whole run because I had bad luck with a roll of dice or a missing card. I also get the feeling that you can win the game with any combination of heroes, so the game seems really well balanced in this regard.Pros:- very engaging and addictive game- beautiful and fast-paced fights- fair difficulty and you can tweak it as you like- you get attached to your heroes, so you feel that you must find the right decks for them; it's also a game that gradually reveals to you more complex cards and synergies, so it's a very good place to learn how to build a deck- huge replayability, because you must choose 3 from many heroes (15-20? I'm not sure) and every hero has 3 possible archetypes to build them. You can bring any hero in your team, but as I said, you get attached to the ones you already have- the game is very well optimized, no heated CPU or loud fansCons:- I hardly think of anything, maybe that you find too many junk pieces of equipment when exploring the special treasure maps.
