_childDocuments_.review: It's For The King meets Slay The Spire but with a Bethesda game's worth of bugs and almost zero clarity in the design sensibilities.Am I enjoying it? Sure. Could I play it on anything but a cheesy build at higher difficulties? Not in the current state. Everything is so muddled, unclear, and broken that you're blindly hoping/guessing most of the time instead of making meaningful choices or building a tactical deck.I'd like to recommend this one but it's not done. It needed to stay in Early Access until the internal systems were ironed out and made to work. It's desperately needs QA.A small example. You can build your own skill trees (cool!). You travel from node to node to get your power ups. But what's this? You literally can't apply certain nodes, so your path just... stops. This is the kind of 30 second to 10 minute QA you'd ~demand~ out of a finished product.Wait until it's done. Or it may never be done, in which case... don't play it.
_childDocuments_.name: Gordian Quest

_childDocuments_.review: In the scheme of things, it's not a bad game. There are a lot of things to love about it. Cards being tied to equipment makes it so your strategy can adapt based on what you find. This is a great idea. I love the rewards you gain for leveling and fighting. Unfortunately, this eventually becomes unimportant when you get a build going and you've pretty much found all the legendaries you need. This doesn't sound like too bad of a thing except this happens way too early in the run and the game goes on long after I develop my strategies so I just end up using the same cards for 70% of the game with too few changes to the overall gameplay as you progress.When you compare this game to games like it (Slay the Spire, Griftlands, Monster Train, etc.) there are a lot of things this game does right, but the things it does wrong are what make it stand out. The runs take way too long and the difficulty is nowhere near the level of it's competitors. Where I can play a game of any of the other three I mentioned quite quickly, a full game of Gordian Quest takes hours. The runs definitely overstay their welcome because by the time I've developed a good build, there's still hours left in a run. The difficulty of encounters never really made me feel like my decisions mattered. It became "play cards to clear enemies and heal damage" quite quickly and there was very little thought involved. Playing cards in other deck building rogueish games often requires some thought process. I would normally have to plan the entire turn out before playing, but Gordian Quest has very little depth to its strategy in terms of playing cards to kill enemies. The animations and effects of the cards do have some "oomph" to them so they can be fun to play, but overall the strategy is quite lacking. The story isn't very engaging. Which for a game with such a long rogueish run style is quite disappointing. Griftland's story was quite entertaining, and even then I'm not sure it's necessary for that game to even be fun. It's core gameplay loop was fun and challenging. About halfway through my run of Gordian Quest I stopped paying attention to the text because it's all very generic fantasy script. The characters were mostly bland, and overall it was just slowing down what is already too long of a game. My recommendation would be to let the characters interact with each other. The way it is now, it feels like the characters are speaking to a wall because there's no conversation, they just spew out information and you move on. Engaging dialogue happens when you see people react, not when you just read exposition.So what did I like the most? The early game. Progression ramps up quite fast in the early game. This made me enjoy that section of the game a lot more. I was constantly finding new things to use and experiment with. But that is what these games should focus on. The reason runs are so enjoyable is trying out all the different combination of items, cards, and other various modifiers. And once you find a "build," you beat the game and restart so you can try something totally different. The late game started feeling like a chore because progression slowed way down and my decks just stopped changing altogether. I kept thinking about all the cards I didn't try because it would clutter my deck with unsynergistic stuff. I didn't want to do another run though because I knew I'd be bored with the game again well before the run was over. I won't say Gordian Quest is a bad game, but currently its design lends itself to be fun for only a couple of hours before the boring repetition of what started to feel like endless encounters kicked in. I think they need to either shorten the game's runs, create a larger pool of evolving gear, or find a way to make progression feel significant the whole way through. Currently I give the game a 6/10. The only reason I won't recommend it is simply because there are better deck building rogue-lite games. I'll come back to it once the game has more content and hopefully they will make some important design changes by that point.

_childDocuments_.review: Ambitious, but mechanically jumbled, Gordian Quest dumps a lot of opaque gameplay on the player very quickly, but once you get a feel for it, there's a lot here to play with. An ambitious take on the deckbuilder that can get a little abstract - many abilities will seem useless and overly convoluted until you find the perfect card to pair them with that renders them incredibly potent. This game is at its most rewarding when the prep work of tinkering with all the little ways to tweak your build pays off by letting you play an absurd combo of interlocking abilities. It's at its most annoying when you're learning to navigate the dozens of discrete subsystems - skill trees, item socketing, item enhancement, camping, exploration, dungeoneering - most of which have very little overlap with each other.Sidenote; Normal difficulty is a bit too easy - most fights can be won without taking any damage with even a mediocre hand.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall I have been really enjoying Gordian Quest, it's like my favorite rpg adventure games mixed with my favorite roguelite games such as Slay the Spire. There are a lot of good things to say about the game, in that the core gameplay loop, the deckbuilding, and the art are all incredibly fun and well made.  You can really tell that the devs have put a lot of effort into making a very fun and polished game, but I definitely have some major gripes that I would really like to see get addressed in the future.  Right now, the game is a 8/10 for me but I feel like it could be a 9 for me if some basic issues get addressed.Currently, my single biggest gripe about the game is the fact that during random events, if you lose a skill check it is possible to lose legendary items.  I had this happen to me today, with a legendary that I had been investing stat points into specifically to be able to use it and it was incredibly upsetting to me.  It feels like a huge investment of time and resources that went completely down the drain, and that I was severely punished for choosing to explore.I am very used to the idea of losses in games because I play many roguelikes, but given the duration of the campaign and how much investment it takes to actually acquire legendary items (especially ones that are actually suited for your party) I find this kind of punishment to be completely contrary to the core gameplay and reward system.  I realize that this was probably just an extremely bad stroke of luck, but I this really ruined my experience of play for the last few hours, and I don't think players should feel like that all because of a single bad roll.  I would even be okay if this mechanic remained on the hardest difficulty but on normal mode for a first time casual playthrough it just feels like it completely ruins your fun. I really hope the devs are still considering major alterations in future patches, because this mechanic is extremely upsetting.Another complaint I have is about combat pacing. It feels like 50% of the encounters drag on with nothing interesting that happens (for instance there are easy encounters with 3 waves of enemies, none of which pose any challenge), and there are many encounters in a row that give me that impression. I think it would be more fun with fewer encounters that pose greater challenge and better reward. There are also some extremely basic UI elements that feel like they're lacking or unintuitive.  For a specific instance, if I highlight a consumable item in the shop there is no easy way to see how many (if any) I currently own - you have to totally back out of the menu into another one to see that info.

If I'm waiting for anything, it's more character relationship depth; the current synergy systems are nice, but I hope to see it more developed!So much love for this game, and I fully recommend it to anyone who enjoys turn-based RPGs and rogue-like card games. _childDocuments_.review: All the best parts of turn-based RPGs and cardbuilders in one game. The roguelike aspect is there, but it's more WIP, although there is permadeath for those that want to do new runs constantly. The world is handcrafted and there is no machine-text generator just to give the illusion of "infinite content" either, which is a huge plus.The game is simple, yet fun. The aesthetic is clean and unpretentious without being boring. The game basically does everything right in the genre, the only thing lacking is more content, enemy variation and some balance fine tuning.It's a great example of why having a good foundation that you can expand upon in an Early Access game is way more important than trying to do a bunch of different things at once on top of an innately flawed and unfixable foundation.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a mix of RPG-style for story + character equipment + party building, deckbuilder for actions (with multiple upgrade paths), open world exploration for strategy, and grid-based movement + turn-based combat for tactics. Unfortunately, I think it spreads itself too thin and doesn't do any of these particular well.First, the art and music are amazing. However, the story is so-so. While there is character equipment, and you'll see a lot of it, the vast majority doesn't really change anything in an interesting way (just +1 damage, +1 block, etc.). In fact, I'd go so far as to say that's the defining characteristic of the game: tons and tons of decisions, that I spent a lot of time agonizing over, but very few actually mattered.Party building seemed promising, except that you're faced with 32 options to choose from with zero information except a list of their cards. Not even a brief description of what the character/class/subclass does or a general idea of their playstyle. Just read through each of the 10-20 starting cards and figure it out. Times 32. In skirmish mode, you're stuck with the characters you start with. In campaign mode, you'll unlock new characters (which is neat), but it takes a LOT of effort to pivot the party to a different makeup. And while you're trying to switch things around or try something new, the enemies keep scaling up.The level-up system is neat enough, although I didn't really see a point in mixing archtypes with the grids. The variable placement mechanic was fine, though I wish it let me rotate grids before placing them. I wish there were more card-level-up nodes, given how weak a level-up is and how many cards you tend to have in the deck. It really felt like the game was pushing towards a super-thin deck with 1-2 leveled up and mastered cards, which made experimentation hard.I liked the deckbuilder in general, except that most cards reward you for picking a single stat to stick with. This means that most of the off-stat cards offered by equipment are just diluting an already large card pool. It's super easy to get new cards, but removing or modifying cards is not, which made experimentation hard.The combat grid is a neat idea, but just doesn't end up impacting much. There are good and plentiful options to move the PCs around, which is good. But there are very few ways to influence the enemy's positions, so sometimes you're just stuck with bad placement. I'm fine with being in a bad position because of a decision I made and can learn from, but that's not this game.Finally, the UI needs some work. It's very unclear which enemy is doing what without mousing over every one of them. Sometimes the estimated damage is wrong. There are way too many times I asked "why did that happen?" without any way of figuring it out. More information is needed.There's a ton of potential here and I'm excited for Gordian Quest 2 (or whatever the devs do next)!

_childDocuments_.review: I'm happy this got released. I thought I already left a review actually. I played it partway in EA and decided to hold off before completing it. _childDocuments_.review: 3rd Review update (1st is at the bottom.)I've removed this game from my list. There's an unkillable boss. You get her down to 1hp and then she's invulnerable, and then comes back with full hp! It doesn't matter how well you've done and equipped, you get her you're dead. Until that's changed, I'm done and I don't recommend the game. Frustrating AF!2nd Review updateThis game is still Early Access. The developers actually respond to issues, so that's good. Overall I like the game but it is incredibly frustrating at times. With the pandemic still ongoing, most people aren't up for a game that is pointlessly stressful. This needs to be addressed by allowing players to choose a Low Difficulty. It would be best to have multiple options for difficulty modes. From low-stress to the extreme high-stress that already is the standard.PROs:*Campaign mode is an easy way to learn the basics. You can use Renown to get Artifacts that help with future runs.*Pretty card graphics.*Well designed battle structure.*Amazing evolving Skill Trees.*Steady growth of characters in a run. From Skills to Equipment.*Multiple Starting Decks for every Character class. (Hit the little double-arrow on the character class to switch it.)CONs:*Unclear directions and lack of information hinders learning.*Damage doesn't scale well for players. Your powers only improve so much. But you can take lots more damage at start than you can soak or dish out.*All characters need some Healing cards.*Max level is 60. Seems like to keep playing a Run you'd need to continue leveling.*Realm mode is a very steep learning curve. *Realm mode usually ends quickly in pointless deaths.*I've only succeeded in Realm mode to max level 60 with Jendaya, because she has a Golem that can soak damage. The golem resets between battles.*Not all character classes have an X skill which allows you to do massive damage to elites and bosses.*Only the Evoker (wizard) Pierre can do the majority of damage. There's some 'damage all enemies' cards for some other classes but limited.*The female sorcerer Boss is a near impossible win. Better to just end the run if you get her. This makes for a pointless run. Other players have commented about ridiculous bosses but it has not been fixed.- - - - - -1st Review (200 hours)Campaign mode is boring after play through several times, and completing it is still bugged.  Realm mode is way too hard. You just die and die and die.  If it was easier to play, Realm would be ideal. Even with half the Artifacts, I hate Realm mode. If there was an EASY MODE where you could Heal and Res dead characters, then it would be a fun unlimited game. As it is though I see absolutely no fun in this game beyond playing the Campaign a few times.  If there's serious improvements to the Realm mode then I'll change this review.

_childDocuments_.review: I like Gordian Quest.I recorded some of my progress with Gordian Quest.Gordian Quest is an Indie, Turn Based Tactics RPG that combines a good campaign, with a Roguelite Procedural Generation mode, and tosses in a side PvP mode as well!Gordian Quest is like getting two games for the price of one, as you get a nice turn-based tactics RPG card game single player campaign, with fun deckbuilding that feels very influenced by Slay The Spire, plus with a 3 person party, plus with a dynamic movement and battle system, plus the Roguelike mode that offers Procedural Generation of the map, Permadeath, and Meta Progression to amass.Gordian Quest is so good! Gordian Quest allows you to pick which ever character you want at the start; no requirement to play with the starting character to unlock others, and no being forced to plays character you don’t want; good!After each battle you gain exp, you get rewards, and on lvl up, get to spend 1 skill point on the heroes’ skill grid, and you can unlock new skill grids as you lvl, selecting one of three and snapping them into place where you want it; it’s unique and interesting.There is a Slay the Spire influence, with the pick your path through the lvls to progress here, and the three AP system, but it also combines a bit of lane battling, with the heroes able to move and completely evade enemy attacks if they pay attention.There are also curses that can trigger off events, debuffing you for a time, lasting either a set number of turns, or the entire next battle, as well as blessing to find for the next battle as well.The campaign mode is good.There are five difficulty modes here, along with two optional versions of permadeath, with 1 that disallows raising fallen companions.When your party is killed in the campaign mode, by default you respawn back in town low on hp with all your loot and gear; so no lost progress.In The Realm Roguelite Mode, you pick your party of three heroes, and then pick from one of three zones at the start; if you make it to the boss, you get a boon, pick one of three, than pick one of the three next zones to fight through it: the Unlike in the Campaign mode above, you don’t have a safe city to return to if you need supplies or rest, In the PermaDeath Realm mode, you cannot go backwards, only forward brave heroes! In this Realm Roguelite Mode, the Meta Progression is Renown, which is used to buy powerful gear from found merchants in the runs, and unlock Artifacts, which grant powerful Meta Progression power! And these can be upgraded for even more renown!The within run currency is gold, used to purchase gear and supplies for located merchants, and fate you can find to reroll bad event; handy.So, if an Indie, Turn-Based Tactics RPG Deckbuilder with an optional awesome and engaging Perma Death Roguelite mode interests you, check out Gordian Quest, and enjoy the feeling of getting and playing two great games in one!Watch?

While many people are complaining how light the card-building aspect is, I for one am very happy with it.   A ten hour chapter run is not blown up at hour 9 because of card selection RGN.  While the character system LOOKS complicated it does not seem at this point you have to worry about min-maxing in order to play and things are documented reasonably well.   Especially at the sale price of $14 I have no complaints. at this point.There are some balance issues but overall the game is fun and the different combos of characters keeps it interesting for replays.Magic items and crafting could use some tuning but to be fair it is still Early Access.   Crafting is too random to be much use at this point but still there is an interesting foundation.I look forward to seeing the final product.   It would be nice if you could save more than one run at a time... I am not suggesting that they abandon their core concept of one save per run, but I would like to be able to experiment with multiple runs going at a time.  Keep up the great work.

_childDocuments_.review: This is genuinely one of the toughest reviews I had to make. Most definitely one that makes me wish for a "neutral" score.I obviously love this game,I have 65+ hours in it and I honestly expect to have even more.It's a party based rogue-like deckbuilder with 10 cool heroes with 3(ish) playstyles to each, to mix and match as you want. What's not to love, right? And I do. I love the visuals (boy do I, those character designs are what immediately sold this game to me) and the game's core gameplay mechanics.However. I think there is one big issue with this game in that... it is boring.Not so boring that it stops me from playing it, but all the excitement was drained from it over the years.One of the most fun things about deckbuilders is finding some broken build. Something that in a game with, say, 60 damage per hit, lets you do 60000. But pretty much every single find like that was nerfed to the ground by the devs.This game is not difficult, it does not NEED broken builds to play it. But what you have is a bunch of heroes who mostly feel the same, a bunch of upgrades that don't feel meaningful, a bunch of cards that just feel completely useless compared to the few good ones left.So instead of having 10 heroes with distinct playstyles, interesting variations between them, cool hero combinations that help each other, what you're left with is asking yourself "ok, so who still has good aoe that hasn't been destroyed by the nerf hammer". And when you still find cool combos, it just makes every other build and character that does similar things feel underwhelming, because they've been nerfed or require way too much effort to achieve inferior results.Same goes for upgrades. Oftentimes it's barely a choice of which you should get, and many of them are just uninspired number increases. The rare abilities that add stuff like "doesn't count towards draw count for the turn" or "adds channel" (which is a resource that makes certain spells cheaper) are the remnants of fun this game still has, compared to choices like "deal 5 more damage or apply 5 more bleed".Although props where it's due, if you fiddle with equipment, there is some potential to make certain abilities more fun. But the loot is random and you can't really rely on it.So, is this a good game? Yeah, I would say it's good. I never regretted buying it and I will keep playing it.But it could've been so much better, if only devs weren't so scared of strong builds that they made everything in this game... boring.

_childDocuments_.review: As others have mentioned, Gordian Quest is a game with a lot of features borrowed from many other games such as Slay the Spire (deck building, rogue-like obviously), Thronebreaker (RPG element, player choice), Darkest Dungeons (tactical movement, food supply, resting, equipment), D&D (dice roll, skill check), etc. Here are some of the cons and pros.Pros:- It is quite polished as an early access game. I have not had any bug or crash yet- The art style is quite pleasant. Reminds me of Battle Chasers- Music is quite soothing and sound is ok- A combination of many features, a little something for everyone as IGN will say- While not as good as Slay the Spire, there are some interesting strategies and card synergies in the gameCons:- Need better synergy for some heroes. I started as the Mage and I was very disappointed half way through. The hero heavily relies on channel to function properly but he himself has very few efficient ways to generate them, especially in comparison to the Cleric. On the other hand, the Rogue is quite fun to play, slaughtering everything by himself. There is certainly some balance issue here (hi dev, I am not asking you to nerf the Rogue but to make other heroes better)- Most equipment is quite meh. So far the only good perks imo on equipment are +attack damage, +spell damage, get a card after kill, +max channel. All the other perks are just underwhelming to be honest. There are some rare equipment that look interesting but they are also extremely expensive.- Some of the game designs feel weird. Why put a healing node in dungeon if I can simply get out of the dungeon and rest in town? In fact, it seems you can walk back to the town any time you want after a battle, so things like healing potions are less useful than they initially appear. In addition, unlike Darkest Dungeon, the layout of dungeon in this game seems to have very few effects on gameplay.- Leveling up is not as impactful as I expected. You either get a new card, upgrade a card, or discard a card. Granted you can choose a talent at some point but most talents feel meh as well.In the end, this is a decent game and is quite fun to play even now at its early stage. I am satisfied with the experience for the price I pay. I can imagine a lot of the things in this game can be improved throughout the EA process and if the dev do it right there is no doubt it can become much better in future.

_childDocuments_.review: Fun game, Slay the Spire meets Darkest Dungeon meets Diablo. Addicting.EDIT: Did a playthrough at full release. The game is solid. You have 8 different toons of the usual fantasy archetypes and get to lead 3 into battle. You can change the roster between fights. The toons gain perks from a skill tree like in Path of Exile and have card decks like in Slay the Spire. You have inventories, gems, sockets, all sorts of stuff for minimaxing. There is a campaign of 4 acts and also adventure mode and challenges. The one thing I didn't like was a minor - a weird exploration minigame that slowed down the pace of the game.Overall a solid addition into the genre. 9/10

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty good but some major flawsGameplay Loop:Campaign:1)	Pick a hero from a selection of 10.2)	Pick a starter deck from a selection of 3. Each deck usually represents one of the 3 attributes in the game (strength, dexterity, and intelligence).3)	Pick a difficulty from a list of 5 and pick a game mode (normal, rogue-lite, rogue-like).4)	Explore a node-based map system.5)	Head back to a hub to do your RPG thing like hiring more party members (3 max), heal, revive, shop, advance the story, etc. Everything is node-based so you won't see your characters walking around.6)	Repeat 4 & 5 until you get to the end of the chapter. Then you fight the boss and advance to the next chapter. There are 4 in total. Then you get a Path of Exile/Diablo map/rift system to continually playing (presumably) forever.Realm loop (Rogue-lite mode aka Slay the Spire)1)	Create a party of 3 people from a list of 10.2)	Select a difficulty from a list of 5. 3)	At the same time, pick from a selection of artifacts to start with using (possibly) the worst interface ever design by human hands. The artifacts are the meta progression for this game.4)	Start the game. Pick a modifier for your current realm. Example includes, more gold, hidden paths, less resistance, etc. 5)	Pick a node on your path and traverse to the node.6)	Do whatever is needed in that node. Fight, camp, shop, etc.7)	Get to the end of the map and fight the boss8)	Repeat 5-7 five times.  Battle loop1)	Initiative is determined2)	When it’s your characters turn you get a selection of cards3)	Then move, attack, use items. You get AP to use per turn and a persistent SP that gets filled up as you do things. Different cards use different resources points.4)	Did you win? If not, get repeat 1-3 until you do or loseWhy I would recommend the game•	 Lots of characters and all of them are interesting to use with different synergies between each•	The character customization is varied. The leveling process is always a dopamine hit.•	The combat system is engaging with enough enemy variety and modifiers to separate each engagement for most of the game. Somethings to consider if you’re on the fence•	The interface is one of the worst in seen in this type of game. There are times where I skip parts of the gameplay design just so I don’t have to use the interface. Fortunately, the battle interface is not bad. It’s serviceable and average at best but at least it doesn’t hate you like your Ex. •	There are much too many systems in this game. Camp is its own system; exploration is its own system. Then there’s the upgrade/enchant/augmentation system. I don’t think they really add to the game.  This is especially true in the Realm mode. The biggest issue is that these systems combined with the annoying interface although really test your patience. •	A good part of the loot is useless. Once again, combined with the interface makes looting tedious. •	The progression system makes the game easier. This is not something I enjoy. I like my progression system to open new opportunities for character development. Plus the selection of the artifacts is amazing painful due to the… interface.Full achievement takes ~100 hours depending on how fast you grind for the renown points.  I give this game 75 bleeding stacks out of 100. It’s not bad and there are good ideas with great potential but it’s really crippled by the interface that permeate the game.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: The game has very few extremely minor issues. The gameplay is solid with incredible depth and variety, the enemy designs are interesting, the story is solid, the character and environmental design rocks, etc. Solid 9.5/10 for me. Would highly recommend.----Yes, this is an Early Access game and, naturally, the label probably makes you wary. Rest assured, the developers have already put out a product that I am happy paying the entry fee for, especially during the 2021 Winter Sale here. There seems to be more than enough to do, especially if you do multiple runs to experiment with your character selection, build options, and more. Act 1 took me nearly 8 hours to complete on the "Hard" difficulty. The game definitely became slightly challenging during that first boss fight against the Rift Lord... until my Spirit Bear summon clawed it to pieces! You can definitely feel some really intense moments here during battle, as some mobs can randomly draw a particularly potent hand. I had a death suuuuper early on where a mob drew two cards that each did 32 to damage to a full row, which then full-wiped my party in the blink of an eye! There should be plenty of unexpected moments just like that left to come. I really love the variety in the enemy design, especially with the individual mob variants. You can see a good mix of creatures, supernatural terrors, opportunistic humans, and more when it comes to the types/species of enemy. The art is all pretty well-done in this regard and I have no complaints to speak of. Same goes for the designs of the main party and the environmental work. There is some really lovely depth to the equipment system. You can enchant items, you can reroll their perks, you can reset items to a blank slate, you can slot jewels into items for new effects, you can attach skills onto items, etc. You can create a very powerful combination of items for the character that YOU want to build, which is a unique amount of freedom that you don't typically see in games nowadays. For example, I found a common two-handed sword that came with an Attached Skill, Cleave, which I then added 3 slots onto and upgraded into the "Rare" rarity; I had created a god-tier weapon that I used to demolish all in my path in Act 1. This all goes hand-in-hand with the skill tree and some other stuff too!You get to dump points into three attributes -- Strength, Dexterity, and Intelligence. There is a way, via the Talent selection of the Skill Tree, to add in some free stat points without leveling; If one has 14 in Strength, but 6 in Intelligence/Dexterity, they can take half of their Strength value (7) and add it to either Intelligence or Dexterity (or whatever set up you wanna go for in terms of stat distribution). Not only do you get the side benefits that each stat provides (HP, Initiative, etc.), you also get to hit the required Stat total to be able to equip certain weapons or armor in the game. This way of handling stats gives you a huge degree of freedom, I love this. The Skill Tree is pretty neat and you can choose between a lot of different things for your upgrades. You can rank skills up and also increase their effectiveness via skill mastery to make them pack an even harder punch! Some of the characters have unique choices, like the casting class can reduce their overall deck size, making for a much tighter and precise selection of spells for battles. You get basic stat increases and can also learn specific skills/spells for the branch of your choosing. You also get to add the specific branches and BUILD your own skill tree!! How cool is that? The Talent Tree is suuuuper comprehensive and I haven't even seen a fraction of what all those different choices can do. Rest assured, there's a TON going on there. It gets pretty wild.There's an exploration minigame that honestly doesn't have much going on, but can net you some pretty good rewards. Glad I came across this game, can't wait to see what comes next!

_childDocuments_.review: Gordian Quest is like going to a restaurant where the menu offers everything from Hamburgers, to Ethiopian, to Thai food. The food will fill you up and you'll likely enjoy your meal, but none of the dishes will stand out in a way a specialty restaurant with a smaller menu does.There's a lot to like here, but Gordian Quest biggest drawback is that it's too ambitious for its own good. It tries to combine deck building and card based combat with an RPG style loot system & progression, DND dice rolls to succeed/fail skill checks, and Roguelite mechanics. The main problem is that not all these systems feel as complete and flushed out as they should. For example while there are lots of classes, the card pool for each class feels disappointingly limited in the ways you can play them. One of my favorite characters, a sorcerer with an animated golem companion, playstyle is essentially 'Be in the same row behind your golem for additional DMG/Status effects on your cards'. I wish there were more ways to build and engage your characters so you could have the party you want.Despite all those flaws however, it's a very enjoyable and fun game and worth the current asking price. If you're on the fence, it's absolutely worth adding to your list and picking up during a sale. I feel like with a bit of polish and flushing out of systems this game could be one of the greats.

_childDocuments_.review: I'll keep this short : This game has an absolutely absurd number of mechanics and none of them have any real depth or balance.  It feels like developers tried to combine the mechanics of Slay the Spire, Diablo, D&D5E and Final Fantasy X without removing anything nonfitting.To give a small example, you run a party of three characters, each with a two-slot consumable inventory, 8 slots of gear, a combat deck, levels, and a sphere-grid style skilltree. The gear has rarity and gem slots of different colors as well as per-class attributes to govern their skills.  That's just the character management alone. This level of complexity extends to every facet of the game and at any given time there's so much going on it's nearly impossible to figure out how effective your builds or choices are. You probably won't care though because the game gives you several broken characters in the first hour who are able to absolutely flatten encounters up to the next-to-highest difficulty with ease due to how broken their mechanics are. High difficulty scores you more EXP, which gets you more stat points, which means more time spent shuffling between the 5 character management screens.This is the very definition of too many cooks spoiling the broth.
_childDocuments_.name: Gordian Quest

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like this game. I'm a fan of roguelike deckbuilders, and having enjoyed Across the Obelisk (which I would recommend), I was eager to try this one out, especially since it seemed more ambitious than AtO (which is mostly just Slay the Spire, but using Darkest Dungeon's simple positioning to handle multiple characters).Gordian Quest has skill trees, complex in-battle positioning with rows & lanes, equipment with socket-able gems that give generic buffs or add specific riders to cards, and more characters & cards than a lot of other similar games. How could that not be great?Well, because it had all of those things but not the  to do them all right. Gordian Quest contains good ideas. A  of good ideas.  to properly refine them all. The complex positioning system can be largely ignored by simply doing what roguelike deckbuilders generally reward you for anyway: killing enemies as quickly as possible. A third of the socket-able gems are... well, they're not useless, but you would almost never to choose to socket them over other options, and in the long run you're going to have as many of each gem type as you need. There are strange gaps in the equipment selection (what if I want a shield that boosts Int-based block abilities?).In particular, the balance between characters, and the balance between some of the builds available to individual characters, feels rough. The game has a story mode and a randomized roguelike mode (which feels a little tacked on), and there is definitely a sweet spot in the story for balance. In act 1 your characters aren't really developed yet; they're largely defined by which of the 4 starter decks you chose (some of which are noticeably better than others). Acts 2 & 3 hold up pretty well: you've got enough skill points to really start to customize your characters, but not enough to push into the late game. Act 4, to say nothing of the endless epilogue stuff, is where things break down; by this point each character either has a build that is casually sweeping the field of multiple enemies (or all of them, like the bard) every round before the enemies get a chance to do anything, or you've discovered that the cool concept you built your character around doesn't scale properly into the endgame (e.g. the druid's summoning).As a programmer myself, I can absolutely understand the pain of having a ton of ideas you want to develop but not having the resources to get to them all. I hate when project managers make me cut a feature I really thought would be great, but it means that we have the bandwidth to get the features that do make it in done . I would love to see a sequel to Gordian Quest where the developers focused their efforts on really polishing a smaller number of their many good ideas.

_childDocuments_.review: I love my Golem, and my Golem loves me.Ever wanted to play Slay The Spire as Sisyphus and Bouldy from Hades? then this, my friend, is the game for you.I have complicated feelings about some of this game's combat design choices - some builds are unreliable and some, such as the guy with the bow, are OP as f*ck without even trying. And the UI can be a bit confusing or overwhelming at times, as having 3 full decks of cards AND 3 characters with full talent AND skill trees, fully equipped with items, that ALSO have gem sockets AND add ability cards to your deck while equipped... it's a lot to keep track of, and if you're an XCOM fiend like me and spend ages before a boss fight stressing over ever last equipment and talent, it can get annoying to navigate. Also the SP system, while brilliant, means the initial learning curve can be a bit confusing, and the help section is not particularly But it's in Early Access so there's plenty of room for tweaks. This game has already improved MASSIVELY since I bought it and it's not even finished yet. Overall, well worth the price. Random skill checks and modifiers on encounters make every fight tempting and the simple, cleverly streamlined leveling system is a real highlight.A personal taste gripe: I would like it more if you could cosmetically customise/randomise your characters and recruit more of them, a la Darkest Dungeon. Permadeath would seem like more of a viable, fun option - as is, they give you the option, but you are kinda screwed if your heroes die with Permadeath on, cos there are so few of them.TLDR; Played a Golemancer. Got upset when my Golem buddy went down. 10/10

_childDocuments_.review: Gordian Quest left early access this week!Choose 3 of the 10 unique heroes for your battle party (swappable throughout the game) and level them up through combat and exploration using character specific starter card decks.As they level, each of their decks can be altered or empowered through grid based skill trees you construct yourself -- which I really loved. Loot, insertable gemstones, and one use items also serve to empower your characters.Generally speaking, I enjoyed the art style and sound production, but the campaign's story was about as interesting as this game's title - not distractingly bad but also not memorable.   There's a campaign which I enjoyed playing through, a post-campaign endless dungeon mode which I have yet to dive deep into, and a stand alone realm mode that I haven't touched yet.This game is absolutely worth it for those who enjoy tactical/party based role playing games and/or card deck builder/battlers.

_childDocuments_.review: I very rarely review games, but as I bought this based on reviews and hesitated based on negative reviews, I thought I would this time.It's a good game, but has some flaws. Someone pointed out in a negative review that only 14% people beat the first act, and I feel like that's a valid problem after experiencing it first hand. I started it, got bored, confused, and frustrated, and quit after a few hours about half way through Act 1, and only went back after doing the rogue-like mode. Since you cannot really respec and the campaign is very slow and grindy and the character progression is extremely complicated with a lot of irreversible decisions (some of which you will need to make before you start playing at all), you can end up not having much with fun with it, and I'd actually suggest not doing it until you do the rogue-like mode to get a feel for what you enjoy and which characters you like and what actually works. It feels like the character progression was designed with the rogue-like mode in mind where you throw away your character after a single run, and doesn't feel like a good fit for the campaign for people that start there.Being limited to 3 characters also feels somewhat disappointing. The only spoiler I looked up was after about 5 hours in to see I'd unlock more character slots, and was disappointed to find the answer was no. It's another thing that makes sense for the rogue-like where can try new characters each time, but I don't think works well in the story mode where you basically end up with a massive unused bench of potentially interesting characters you won't get to use.There's also a bit of a tricky balance how the combat works. If you look at what the enemies are going to do, the game becomes somewhat too easy, and somewhat tedious. If you don't, you occasionally get just annihilated by some ridiculous move you were supposed to dodge. I feel like putting abilities in that one shots guarding characters from full health makes you play around knowing they'll do (which fair enough) but if you actually do that, the game becomes somewhat too easy and a little tedious.I enjoyed it, so I'll recommend it, but I feel like it has the elements to be a much better game than it is, even if saying that seems a bit unfair as while I can identify the problems I had, I cannot necessary say how to fix them or say they are entirely objective (story mode is too grindy with way too many meaningless fights, enemies depend too much on reading what they are going to, which gets tedious, character and story progression is too slow in story mode, and crafting feels incomprehensible and generally not worth it, exploration nodes get very tedious after awhile, etc).But, I had fun, and will probably keep playing. I feel like the rogue-like mode works much better than the campaign, even if the campaign is what I'd rather play. I'd recommend starting there, and if you like it, then try out the campaign, though I suspect it will feel too slow, easy, and grindy after the rogue-like mode for many.

_childDocuments_.review: One of the coolest rogue-like deckbuilders. You not only get your typical rouge like mode but also the campaign in the DnD style, with rolls, events and quests! Really cool concept and decently executed.Here are few things that are pros/cons depending on your preference. -Balance in campaign is completly off. If you plan and think about what your are building, you can breeze through campaign. I went with the STR Geomancer, AGI Archer, and INT Cleric and pretty much steamrolled highest difficulty with few rare card loops. With good RNG and card rerolls you can get ultra OP decks.-Rouge like on the other hand is feels really challengeing. To the point when it really made me think, which character should i choose to pair with the main one and how to reduce the damage taken to minimum. -There's a lot of customization options when it comes to skills, talents, equipment, cards, builds, attributes, runes, rerolls and so on. So if you want to min-max and make a broken teams, you can do it but it does take some time.-PvP i have no idea about, can't really check since i my code got revoked (the risk of buying from resellers i guess), but IIRC it's pretty empty, but if you have a friend you can play with i bet it's a lot of fun.

_childDocuments_.review: Pros:====1) Gateway game - not overly complex and fairly easy to pick up2) Fun, easy and has the right foundation for being replayable3) Very stable - I played non-stop for 6 hours without any crashes.Cons:=====1) Not for hardcore deck builders - game mechanics are less intense.2) Needs to provide better control for the card deck. Should allow gold payment to reset all skills.3) Definitely needs an Endless mode... YESTERDAY. Current game is too short and can be finished in a few hours.4) Forgettable campaign.5) Fix the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ gear. Most of the gear adds useless cards to the deck, which means they will be sitting in your inventory. Take a look at the feet gear in the game - you wanna draw Shift 1 over and over? A better idea would be for gear to add flat stats or even unique things like - insert a card here to master it or decrease AP cost. On the flip side, some pieces of gear is OP - anything that lets you regen 2 AP for free or retain cards at the end of the turn are pretty much mandatoryEarly access - balancing issues:=========================2) Pierre spellbinder seems to be super weak - needs to improve3) On the flip side, Ida the druid is overpowered - she can summon a wolf, a bear and unlimited # of hawks. Perhaps in rogue-like mode, this can come in handy, but in campaign mode, your level outscales the difficulty and she trivializes the content.4) Some items on Bertram the Ranger are too strong - I purchased a unique (legendary bow) and got a unique quiver and this added 2 double shot and 2 triple shot cards to my deck. This on top of the already existing double and triple shot cards. Mix in Surge (regen 2 AP) and almost every non-boss character can be bursted down in 1-2 rounds.5) What exactly do rations do? I ran out of them and didn't buy new for a bit and didn't seem to have any effect.5) The events seem to be generic and just added noise in the core game. Same with camping - potion of exhaustion is cheap, making exhaustion a joke. And shrines - they need more choices (for instance, elemental immunity or elemental weakness, master/unmaster cards for 1 battle, add temporary card for the next x-battle.

_childDocuments_.review: I´m sorry to give a bad review because the developers put so much work into improving this game and the graphics are really nice. But the battles are simply repetitive and very boring. Here they really managed to develop a deckbuilding game with only one successful strategy: to maximize damage, without having different kinds of damage. So maybe you do play against enemies with different strategies, but that doesn´t matter because maximizing damage is always the one and most successful way to deal with everything. I tried different difficulties, no difference. And the balancing is off: In the beginning winning or losing is almost entirely a matter of luck since you start with lots of garbage in your deck. As soon as you streamlined your deck, there´s hardly any challenge left for you to encounter. Basically there´s no sense in keep playing after level 20. This game has so much nice stuff, but at it´s core there is simply no concept for interesting battles.

_childDocuments_.review: Tepid thumbs up.  It's got a lot of really neat concepts, but most of them are super rough atm.  The skill trees are pretty fun.  The synergies could use some work, but at least have a kernel that's interesting.  Gear could definitely use some work (legendaries that are rarely worth using).  Oddly, the game maxes out my graphics card (1070).... which it really shouldn't.  So, yeah, lots of rough edges.  But the core of the game is fun: there's lots to improve with your characters, and the fights have the potential to be interesting.The main issue holding back a full recommend is the difficulty is tuned to be too dam easy, even on the highest difficulty level.  I found a pretty solid set of cards and characters straight off and was able to clear act 1 on the hardest difficulty with 99% of the fights resulting in 1-turn wins without the enemy even getting a hit in (yes, that's an accurate number -- they give you end-of-the-act stats).  That's waaay too easy for the supposed hardest difficulty.  Even the end-act boss fight was a total no-scratch yawn fest.  If there was something that was an actual challenge, I'd be beaming about the game.  The latest news says they improved reduced the power of characters, but they still have a long way to go.Things seem to be moving in a good direction, but I'm definitely concerned that they're more focused on more acts and less focused on balance.  What good are more acts if you get bored and give up before you get there?

_childDocuments_.review: While this seems like an interesting take on both tactical games and slaythespire style roguelites it is really just an unfair ramping of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ after the first "act". There is no sense of balance or progression at this point and the skill trees are far too randomly set up to make sense of. Difficulty is one thing, traps set to screw the player? Another entirely different thing. The balance issue imho is at the heart of why the game is thumbs down for me. Though many little things probably added up to this sense. However, if this is only Act 1/6 or whatever, they really need to pare down the standard encounters since it becomes a slog. Maybe Realm Mode is better for that.There's some Exp share, but it's not 1:1 with your benched characters, which is a shame.  It would incentivize me to actually play around with different party compositions, but instead I feel like I should just stick to one party the entire game, as those lost levels may make the difference late game.  I don't know if it actually does, as I don't know what the expected "balance" is at the end of the game.On Normal, the difficulty wasn't there. I kept my Cleric in my party in case things ever needed her, but monsters never did damage or debuffed. About 90% of her heals were wasted, and the remaining 10% weren't critical heals.There are random consumable resources like Supplies and Incense which are so cheap that it just feels like a small tax to use them. Refilling my supply just felt like busy work and added no tension to exploring. The weird thing is that there's already a mechanism to demonstrate that your dudes are exhausted, and it's literally called Exhaustion. I have no idea why Supplies are in the game.Each class has three specializations, but in reality it's basically three separate subclasses since there was very little synergy between them. The main issue is that every character has three stats, and each skill is (generally) tied to one of those. However, each of the specializations are generally tied to different stats, so doing two specializations weakens your character by not only giving you cards that don't synergize well with each other, but also splits your stats. In Slay the Spire terms, it would be like if a Shiv build and a Poison build needed different stats to make them better and there isn't a card that connects the two builds.One of the specializations, the Druid's animal companions, is laughably weak. For 2 action points, you get a summon that has a handful of HP and does about 7 damage every turn. The HP might be decent if tanking were necessary in Act 1, but given that the Scoundrel was doing upwards of hundreds of damage in each of his turns, and reduced damage by just straight murdering things, the power balance isn't quite there.The UI has some weird annoyances.  Not all menus have an X in the corner to exit out of them, so you have to hit the Map or Town buttons instead.  Ability ranges took a while for me to understand.  The game only takes into account your main hand weapon and ignores the off hand one when you compare equipment.I'm looking forward to seeing what the game looks like at the end, but the class balance being so off makes it feel kinda eh.Post release: None of the above complaints really got addressed.  I'm in Act 2 and the Scoundrel still clears out the encounters all by himself, except the rare bosses.  The explorations and campfire portions are extra tedious, given that most of the time they don't really give you anything of note.  It's just real tiresome to play.

_childDocuments_.review: *May 2021* This is shaping up to be both *promising* and *enjoyable* right now as a wonderful combination of four things 1. Turn-based tactical battles with a wide range of actions, synergies & tactics2. Hero development through stats, skills, talents & equipment loadouts, which combined together deliver a deck of action cards that each hero brings into battle3. Roguelike / endless mode gameplay, very much like Slay the Spire in its 'act' and 'branching path' structure4. Story mode gameplay, of which there are currently two acts, with more plannedComing in from other fantastic games with some similar mechanics like Slay the Spire, Monster Train, Trials of Fire, For the King, there is a lot that feels familiar. I might even pitch Gordian Quest as a bit of a mash-up of elements of For The King & Slay The Spire, but it is very much also doing its own things too.

_childDocuments_.review: I've bought and played this game for 3 days, played around 9 hours a day, and i could say with full confidence that this is my favourite out of other games I've played with similar type to this game (Slay the Spire, Griftlands, Monster Train, One Step from Eden). Here is my review of what i like about this game, and some things that i don't really like (ONLY ABOUT ACT I in NORMAL difficulty, as I haven't finished ACT II or used other difficulties yet).If you want a short conclusive review, skip to the end.Good things:-Extremely high customisation for the deck you play with each character.-You can play the class you want not traditionally, but still get the essence of the class. (You want a tank bard that soaks all the damage while buffing your party?, you can)-High replayability, mix & match the party, do different choices as much as you want and gain different runs.-Different difficulties with different risks, you want a chill run where you revive every time you get wiped out? you can; Want to feel a little sense of danger, but not lose an ally permanently if you didn't get fully wiped out? you can; Want to build and attach yourself emotionally to a character and pour your heart and soul into that character, but then do 1 small mistake, and lose that character forever, then cry in a corner questioning yourself why did you do such a mistake and blame yourself over and over for their death? ... well, you can.-Unique leveling system, you don't just automatically gain status upgrade and master cards by just leveling up, you have to choose what you want to gain when you level up, and which path you want to go from leveling up, which adds a layer of thinking of what to level up that would give you the best possible outcome.-Long run, but not tiresome, my first completion took me +- 14 hours, and to be honest, it did not feel like i took 14 hours to clear the game, because everything was just so fun and nice to play.-A layer to strategising of what to do because you not only see your oponent's intentions, you can see not only what they can do, but also the sequence of the actions that they're going to do the actions in, if you don't check what actions they can do and only rely on the numbers in the intentions, you might lose a party member or two, and proceed to cry in a corner, and ask yourself why did you do such a mistake... wait I've done this joke already.-A layer of mystery of what is to come, because unlike other games that I've mentioned before, you don't really know what you get after going to a certain point of event.-The battle style of the game is determined by the positions of both your and the enemy's characters, enemy's actions sometimes change accordingly to where your characters position is, and your character's actions is affected by which row and lane your character is positioned.No-nos (My truly subjective opinions are marked with "*", "*" increases on how subjective it is):-Act I doesn't really have much going story-wise as of this review.-No music outside of battles / in the map / in town (if there is I certainly do not hear it even with max music and sfx volume).-No specific graphic settings that can lower certain things but retain certain thing's graphics, actually, as of this review, i don't see any graphic settings in general; A specific graphic settings would really help with some lower end machines to be able to play the game smoothly without sacrificing all of the graphics of the game (Yes there are system requirments, but, my laptop does fit the requirments but the game still lags a couple of times).-* There is no "assign leader", giving an "assign leader" choice, so that the "leader" will be the one talking for my part in the story mode (reason why i think this is needed below).-* Wording of some spells should be changed, "all allies" should be "all other allies" if it doesn't affect the caster, and "an ally" should be "other ally" if the caster can't be targeted.-** Legendary items don't feel Legendary, said legendary items are easily obtainable, and a lot of the effects that Legendary items give just doesn't feel like it does the term "Legendary" justice.-** Big bosses & Final boss don't feel that different from other battles, the power level of these bosses just doesn't feel like "OH ♥♥♥♥ I NEED MY A GAME ON THIS ONE", honestly some of the elite / swarm fights feel more threatening than the boss fights, the bosses just don't do too much, sure they sometimes deal higher damage than usual or summon higher level creatures, but it just doesn't feel to threatening, especially for the final boss, let's take Slay the Spire as an example, when you reach the boss of each act, you truly feel like "oh, this battle is really not gonna be like the other ones is it" because they feel really different and way more threatening than the elites / other battles.-*** Druid class, oh boy, turning to a bear felt awesome, summoning animal companions is also awesome; But, only being able to turn into a bear and not other animals, just felt weird to me for a druid; As a druid it's weird that I don't have control over the animals as the animals will act like how an enemy does, to me it just don't really feel like they're my "animal companions", but felt more like a disney princess sang to get animals to fight for her (I know that the ranger's constructs act the same way, but to me it makes sense for the ranger because he BUILT the constructs to automatically attack, while the druid summons a companion, not an automated robot pet).-*** No ways to increase base AP, i get that having things innately increase base AP might beat the purpose of "Channel spells", but to me it just felt more restrictive rather than giving a layer of strategising, sure with adding more AP, a character that focuses on "Channel spells" might make "Channelling" useless, but i beg to differ and say that it actually could make strategising better with managing what and when you want to use your "Channel".Some things that might be a bug to watch out for (yes i will be reporting it as a bug):-So in the permanent death game mode, i lost my starting character, but i still have other party members so the game continues, but in the story mode the character that is talking for my part is still said character that died, which is why i think an "assign leader" choice is needed, so that the character representing you, will be the character assigned as a "leader", that way you don't have to agonise as the character that you have failed is still talking for you.-Sometimes the item comparison of equipped and in inventory doesn't show / compares it to equipment of other characters instead of the highlighted character.-When in shops the show equipment sometimes just would not work.-Un-equipping a potion makes it suddenly (clap clap) disappear (bows to the audience).Genuine questions from me to the people that have played this game:-What increases the max amount of bardic inspiration? is it just not modified by anything?-Does the summoned talents also affect constructs? or is it just for the druid companions?-Did you enjoy the game as much as i did? because i had an awesome time playing this game :DConclusion:The game is not perfect, and it is still in early access, but it definitely is a good game, there are way more to come, as of right now, there is already so much in the game that you could enjoy, so you should definitely check this game out if you enjoy games like Slay the Spire and of it's genre. 8.7/10

_childDocuments_.review: I got bored with the combat pretty quickly, and this game is 95% combat.I don't feel like I was making any meaningful decisions. Mostly I was just playing whatever cards did the most damage, either directly or indirectly through buffs. Most of the characters seem focused on doing straightforward single-target damage, which makes them feel vaguely the same. Not *really* identical, but not as varied as you'd expect a RPG party to be. There's something wrong when two different flavors of magic user feel identical in niche to a rogue.The main exception was the bard... who was notable mostly because she was very efficient at adding damage buffs to everyone else. Still, it felt like a slightly more interesting variant on doing damage like everyone else.Enemies tend to either select single attack or single defense actions, and any enemy that's taking a defense action is effectively taking themselves out of that round of combat, and you can safely ignore them. This felt decidedly off, that some enemies seemed to effectively doing nothing since all they did was play defense actions.There's a tactical map, which has some pretty odd restrictions, and often feels irrelevant. Your characters can move around, but are only allowed to move to spaces on their side of the map. Characters can attack anyone in their row or an adjacent row, even if they're well back from the front and are strictly melee, which meant there's little difference between ranged and melee attacks. Mostly positioning seems to be about managing who is going to tank any enemy attacks by placing them in front of that enemy.There are a few card combos, but generally you can't play them because you don't retain cards between turns. Card games which facilitate combos generally require that you have a persistent hand, so you can keep cards that are part of a combo against drawing the other cards.Ultimately, all the trappings of a RPG without the complexity and very different roles of different classes from a real RPG made me want to play a RPG instead of this.

_childDocuments_.review: This game feels like a combination of D&D and Slay the Spire, and in my opinion, it really works. The campaign mode has you freely explore a node based map while completing quests, leading up to a boss fight that allows you to move on to the next area. Realms mode is the roguelike mode, with a map structure that is more similar to games like slay the spire, and offers a greater challenge. I haven't played with all of the characters yet, but so far they are all a lot of fun and feel distinct from each other, with many ways to build every character, depending on equipment, stats, talents, and of course their deck.

_childDocuments_.review: So, as you can see, I played this game for 36 hours. 20 hours was the first run, 16 h the second one. And this counts only for the first act, because the other 3 acts aren't availible yet.The game is massive and has a good game depth. You have many options, 6 different characters with 4 different starting options and 3 cardschools.You can take up to 3 characters in your group and each one is different. But with a litte effort you can make the character completly your own. Wanna have a duel wielding hammer Mage? Just take the right talents, give him the weapons and conjure the attached skills to inteligence... Oh yeah, there are also gems to conjure your items / cards with. Got a good weapon with a skill your Warrior should use but it is a dexterity skill? Slap a red gem into it and make the card a strenght skill.I enjoyed my 2 runs with Gordian Quest and the dev's want to add a lot more to it.Is it worth? If you like card games, then pretty sure. In my opinion, the game could cost more, up to 100% and i think it will still be worth it.And just for the record: You can choose the difficulty. You like hardcore rogue-like and every death should be a death? Pick it.Do you want to have a good time and don't even want to lose anyone? Pick it.Do you are a Badass who wants to have a challenge? You can also do it!But, not everything shines bright... negative aspect for me was that you could only have one Campaign active. Do you want to try something else? You need to restart the game.This is normal in rouge-like games, ofc. But most runs in this type of games doesn't last up 20 hours. That was a little bit annoying.Conclusion: I very much like the game!

_childDocuments_.review: Played for 12 hours straight after buying it!..  Just finished the first Act and super excited to play more.  I was continually saying aloud things like "I really like this" when interfacing with all the mechanics and gameplay.I have played many deckbuilders, RPGs, rogue-lites, etc.  This one is the best in all regards so far; recommended through and through.I guess I can list some of the things I like:-Leveling is fulfilling.-Characters feel unique whilst still plenty of room for customization.-Talent web is fantastic because you get to build it yourself.  I never felt forced to pick a less than desirable talent.-Exhausting cards to upgrade success chances during events brings nice polish to deckbuilding.-Events in general have all been fulfilling with the right amount (or lack) of fluff.-I lost a lot of characters early on, but was able to push through and recover without feeling too behind.-Items matter, and a plethora of Legendary items makes gear choices fulfilling.-Plenty of control on adding or removing to your deck.  Easy access to deck manipulation is a big deal!-Gold is a limited resource; I always have a list of things I want to spend it on.-Pacing is transparent, ie you know when you will lose the game for progressing too slowly.-Although I ended the Act with one character doing 80% of the damage, the other two were still very relevant in other regards.-Not gonna lie... my absolute favorite part so far has been the 'Camping' events.  A nice little minigame of sorts with some great rewards available.Thing(s) I don't like:-I sometimes had to click 2-3 through party management where I wanted to only click once (yeah, it's a small gripe but I had to think of something).  It's still Early Access, so maybe even that gets cleaned up.-None of my friends are playing it yet.I tried for a good long while to think of some things I didn't like...  and I stopped early on listing the things I liked.  So, yeah, fantastic game!

_childDocuments_.review: Overall 9/10Let's start with the few cons :-Couple of bugs here and there, nothing major and still in early access, so understandable-Easy, the combat overall is not that challenging. Also, there's a few systems that are supposed to hinder your run, but are too easy to manage (supplies and exhaustion especially)-You can boost a team of 3 and clear the whole storyline with them, so no real use to spend gear and spend time in the skill tree for the other 6 characters (maybe add a system where you sometimes have to let characters rest up, like in darkest dungeon)Pros :-Deckbuilder, so almost endless replayability-Squad based, with each character having their own deck and speciality-Skill tree is pretty nice and original-Awesome synergies and a lot of builds to try (each characters (9) can specialize in each attribute (str, dex, int), example; the mage doesn't need to be built with int everytime, like most other games-Story is not too short, you have time to really optimize your decks and gear-Combat is satisfying, even if a little easy-Cool art design and cool characters-A campaign mode (20+ hours, act 3 still not out) and a endless run mode-Pretty addictingI really enjoyed my first 50 hours, now i can't wait to start another run and try new builds

_childDocuments_.review: I did not play this game that much, but gameplay wise it really put me off- You have to choose another party member, so you're essentially just playing as two characters every time. choosing a druid then a mage is the same as choosing mage then a druid later on. I really just want to play as one character.- You see everyone's entire hand as they play a card, instead of just the individual card they played, making it hard to follow- You have to target spells you can only self target. Clicking twice to do this is a bit unintuitive, and sometimes it's hard to figure out who you can target with each spell.- You don't know what anyone is going to do, as there's no intent system. If you wanted to make the best play, you'd have to look at everyone's hands and guess what they'll do, which is just not feasible or fun.- You get people on your party you don't control, and they make some really weird choices sometimes. Making them tank all the damage as much as possible would be the best option always, but sometimes they just move in place of your weak mage guy and put them in front of enemy lines, and moving him back wastes an entire turn- Some cards are worded weirdly- There weren't any choices story wise from what I played. Even if there are later on, it made it seem like it didin't. So all the characters get the same story, making it so the gameplay is what should carry the game, but as I said there were a bunch of smalls things about it really putting me off by it, so I feel no desire to continueComparing this to monster train, griftlands and slay the spire, in the same amount of gameplay for those games I could tell I really liked them. I didn't play this much so I won't give less stars, but 3 is what I'll give for now3 out of 5

_childDocuments_.review: StS is one of my favorite games of all time, so i'm always on the lookout for another game that captures the same magic. I've got to say, Gordian Quest comes very close to impressing me nearly just as much. After beating the four act campaign, I feel confident saying this is definitely a hidden gem if you're looking for a fun card-based RPG with deck-building, gear, skill trees, and party management. I've got so many positive things to say about this game: the art style is great, the character roster is diverse, plenty of enemy variety, terrific music. It just really nails all the key game-play mechanics that you need for a good game in this genre. I especially appreciate that the game gives you the ability to mitigate damage not just with blocking but also by avoiding attacks, which lends a nice strategic layer to the game as well. If I had to complain about anything, i'd say the only negative for me is that leveling in the campaign occasionally felt off, particularly near the end of act 2. But, the developers are active and still working on the game, so i'm sure this will eventually get balanced in the future. All in all, there's so much content here, and that's just for the campaign let alone the standalone realm mode. Definitely give this a try, I think you'll love it.

_childDocuments_.review: i really wanted to like this game - it has a very nice visual feel and interesting story - but the gameplay is just not good. As others have stated, it becomes clear pretty quickly that the best thing to do is just spam aoes to kill the enemies before they act. looking through the skill trees, it is obvious there is meant to be other tactics, but they are just implemented terribly. looking through the abilities, it seems they have sacrificed balance for flavor purposes. take fire/frost/electric damage. fire does 50% damage to adjacent, electric causes adjacent units to trigger their electric, and frost causes an attack penalty. additionally, a unit cannot have both fire and frost, obviously for flavor reasons. while on paper that might seem good, in implementation it makes fire significantly better than the other two, and makes frost just a trap build. theoretically, frost would be better against single targets (i.e. boss fights) but since the vastly overwhelming amount of fights are groups, and you cannot swap decks easily, frost is just bad. add on top of that the card pool for fire has better synergies and frost builds just are bleh.bad ability balance could be overlooked, if the other mechanics of the game weren't also just so terrible. the leveling system uses this awkward plate system where abilities you want to learn next are sometimes just not in reach, which means you don't really have a lot of control over what abilities your characters actually know. Or at least, that is how it appears at first. However, you can farm money to get books to get respec points, and then you have a small chance for each of your abilities to reroll into something that you like. which means you can actually build your character how you like, but you hafta sit through grindy battles that all play out exactly the same for a few hours just to tweak things how you like. Of course, you might be wondering, why bother with that grind, why not just accept the random abilities you get? because the way the game is "balanced" is that they obviously assume you have done this grind in order to get through fights, which means that if you don't do it, your team will just get wiped by random average monsters. starting in the second act (of 5?) average monsters start doing OHKO attacks. So if you aren't going first and killing them all before they act, your characters die and you need to start a new run. Since you need to go first just to get through, all the fights start becoming the same exact fight. Added to that, by the time you are done with act 1 you prolly have all the abilities your characters will ever need to learn. So you get through the first area and then its another 20 hours of the exact same fight, no new tactics, no new abilities. just damage going up, and monster hp going up.basically i think the core of the prollem comes down to the over-use of randomization in character growth. if players could actually plan their builds, the abilities and fights could be tuned to not just be rocket tag. the player and enemy damage could be lowered, and more creatures could be added in that require specific tactics.to put all this in perspective, in my last run after clearing chapter 1, my main character that always went first had over 74k damage done. the other two characters each had about 1k damage done. i had grinded a bit more than normal, so that i could get respec points onto the two side characters, because i wanted to see if different builds were viable, but it really didnt matter, the one character that went first just always did the same thing.

_childDocuments_.review: Gordian Quest is an amazing amalgamation of a CCG and an RPG. Less on the collectible side for the cards, and more on the story-driven, turn-based RPG side. Still, it's a combat card game that has elements of both genres and beyond. I can't compare it to games like Slay the Spire or Tainted Grail, yet I do see the heavy influences of such a card game. And I can't compartmentalize it to being a Rogue game either. It has its own blending of facets from various games in which we might all be familiar. As such this game feels comfortable yet unique and fresh.This is going to be a sleeper because the game's name absolutely sucks. If you made it to this store page for the first time, and are reading the reviews, then you at least overcame the publisher's lackluster performance to market this game. The only reason I discovered it was because of its reduced price from Steam's 2022 summer sale. And I'm glad I did, because I can't stop playing this game!I could review this game like I do so many others and complain about all of the little annoyances while highlighting the good qualities, filling up the maximum character count for Steam reviews. But I don't think that would do it justice this time. If you like CCGs, if you like RPGs, or if you like both, this game is still worth your purchase. There are plenty of game settings to tweak the game to how you prefer to play it. You can go all out hardcore or you can scale things back for a relaxing adventure. There is no wrong way to enjoy Gordian Quest.I only have two complaints that matter to me in the long haul, and that's the lack of voice acting and that the artwork makes almost every character and NPC look disgruntled. The former is easily fixed with partial voice acting such as repeatable, spoken greetings. We don't need the entire text narrated, but several random greetings each time you visit or talk to an NPC would be nice. Because the grunts and hrumphs are awkward. And as for the latter, don't get me wrong: I love the artwork as it's quality stuff. I'd just rather see characters with a more neutral or pleasant expression. The developer put in a few characters like that, such as a couple merchants, but still not enough.Otherwise this game is a blast! No crashes, runs smooth, and plenty of options. I'm enjoying the combinations of gear and cards (aka skills) and I really appreciate the freedom to socket and unsocket at will while in a town setting. I also enjoyed the variety of different encounters/events on each map. And then you even mixed that into a bit of a twist in the second act. Kudos. As for other reviewers complaining about camping or exploration, don't listen to them: nothing wrong with these events at all because players can easily skip them. Not to mention I enjoy them as something different. And finally, I have to say... the music is awesome!Keep up the good development work Mixed Realms! While you're at it, you should market Gordian Quest a bit more, because I don't think you're reaching everyone interested in this game with split genre personality.EDIT: Whoah! This developer really patches frequently. I don't think I've ever said this to any developer before, but |> A /\/\ N, we don't need updates that often. Seriously, it's a record so far in the month of July, 2022: 7/4, 7/7, 7/12, 7/14, 7/15, 7/18, 7/19, 7/20, 7/21, 7/22, 7/25 ... and the month isn't even over yet. Sometimes we just want to load the game after a hard day at work and not wait for a patch. But at least the patches were small and fast to apply.
