_childDocuments_.review: I really love this game, this is probably my favorite deck building game in the genre. I've played Slay the Spire, Monster Train, One step from Eden, Hand of Fate... and this game is the most enjoyable out of these games. I really like the idea of slowly building up my characters in a longer campaign. The skill grid and the equipment system are great, the interaction of different position/status ailments are cool, and the status scaling system is the best. It reminds me of Dota2 and gives a lot of potential to build my characters.However, there are quite some impactful flaws in the game right now:1.Difficulty seems to be a problem.... I've googled difficulty settings before I started the game and I believe Torment/Hard should be the default Hard/Normal. A lot of people is complaining about repetitive game play and I believe the game is way too easy for them. If the game is easy, combat becomes bland and meaningless.... There are a lot of frustration come from this game but for me, repetitive was never the reason. Because the game is challenging for me and I'm currently playing on Torment.2.A lot of different elements from different game style are merged into this game, sadly the RPG aspect is the weakest one. The main reason of that is the characters seldom speak. They never involve in the story, they only give robotic 3 words comments that sounds like textbook dialogue, they never interact with other npcs, they don't even talk to each other. They are all acting like bots.... Normally I wouldn't care that much if the playable characters are expendable like mercenaries in Darkest Dungeon or soldiers in XCOM, but if the game wants to build around 10 heroes saving the world they need to be alive. I'm not asking for epic storyline like Witcher or FinalFantasy, but atleast make them sounds like real humans.. right now they act like bots in the game.3.So many important mechanics in the game are unexplained, like the attack range of melee attack cards, the interaction of shock, I didn't even know you can put your own cards into empty slots of weapons until like 15 hours into the game. I had to respec my mage because I didn't know chill and burn cancels out each other. I'm not against learning by playing the game but this is too much. Also there are inconsistency in the game, why can't we see the full damage that is going to be done by shock or burn but we can see the full damage from poison for the full duration? And what does that card from Naran that "makes the enemy draw the same hand next turn" really do? Is that card only for PVP? What does that card plan to achieve when most enemies only have 1 card in their deck? Btw I'm actually stuck in act 2 atm... I just don't know where to go after I opened the water gate underground and beat 2 bosses that get unleashed. I've googled and I found people that were stuck at the exact same place.4.The gameover mechanics is unpolished. You get a free full party revive at the Inn if you got your party wiped in Normal mode, there is no point not to intentionally kill all your party members rather than trying to survive with 1-2 members and spending 200 gold to revive each of them. I tried Roguelite mode and that seems impossible because of those unexplained mechanics. You need to learn this game by dying and losing. In the end I just had to save scum. Roguelike/Roguelite game mode just doesn't seem to be fitting in a long campaign game unlike short runs games like Slay the spire.*Instead of reviving your full party in inn, what about something like a strong debuff? Maybe lower the max HP by 50% or lower your stats? What about putting obstacle cards in your deck like exhaust but you can only remove it by paying the revival cost (200g)?5.Map node system is lackluster. The fact that I can always easily go back to town means the Supplies and Camping system is pretty meaningless. Yes in dungeons you can't go back but you can always get wiped and get back to Inn. I've played 90+ hrs in this game but I've camped less than 15 times. The buffs from camping are handy it just doesn't worth the effort to play the camping system while you can spend the time leveling up or earning money for better equipments. The Camping itself doesn't seem balanced either. There are characters that can level up your cards or gain fate for you but others cannot...? Btw It would be nice if we can check the camping skills of our characters in the menu.*Is it possible to lessen the branch points of the Map and costing supplies on every step to make supplies more useful? If you don't have enough supplies you get a debuff or something. Or adding exhausts in your deck.6.The halloween event wasn't really fun. It was quite painful for me to replay the same event 10 times to get all the cosmetics... I appreciate the fact that the devs are doing free event to celebrate but 10 times is way too much. Games are meant to play for fun not work like chores. I would pay for a real DLC with real content rather than free events like this. It is sad to see this game get so many negative reviews because of bad decisions outside of the game itself.I really love this game and I really appreciate the devs are actually responding to this session. I hope they can listen, fix some of those major flaws and keep polishing this game.

_childDocuments_.review: I bought the game in the first days after the appearance of the game here in early access — I love that visual style. Sending hugs and great respect to the artist.Throughout early access, it was nice to see how the developers made the game from scratch, adding content to it. And now when the game has reached its release, I am sincerely glad that the developers have succeeded in all this.What can I name from the pros:— Excellent visual style and drawing;— Pleasant combat that does not bother even after hours of play;— Many unique heroes, each of which has three more unique upgrade branches. All this gives a very large variability in the gameplay style.— A good plot, although quite simple and non-trivial;— Interesting random events and a lot of mini-games that add variety. Something even reminds Darkest Dungeon;— The atmosphere of loneliness and despondency (in a good way), the last time I experienced this was only when I played Diablo 2, when only you alone are able to resist countless monsters;— The game itself as a whole consists of many interesting and pleasant details and mechanics, it is pointless to talk about each of them, but in general, due to them, the game is very addictive and does not let you go.Of course, the game has its drawbacks, and I really hope that the developers will find a way to get rid of them or minimize them:— Lack of dialogue voice acting. Seriously, there are a lot of characters in the game and the game looks so great, but the lack of voiced conversation between the characters is a real disaster.— Changed appearance of the characters. Yes, each playable character personifies a class, but there are a lot of armor, weapons and items in the game, of different quality, that do not fit on the character in any way. It is sad that in the game so much time comes to look at the characters who, for 4 acts of the game, do not change in appearance at all.— Not the smartest opponents, but especially allies.— Combat is not the easiest, I remember that it was quite difficult for me to figure out the builds and its features. It can be difficult for beginners, but when you do get it right, it will lead you to the plus that was described above.— In my opinion, the animations of the movement of the characters are not smooth, but this is a trifle.Otherwise, I am extremely pleased with the purchase and can congratulate the developers on the successful release of the game, I really hope to see more interesting projects and wish them good luck in their future work.

_childDocuments_.review: Gordian Quest is a really fun game, even for a 56yr old. I like the RPG elements, multiple variations on each character theme (complete w/ unique skill cards) and challenges. Initially, I found the "weaker" characters (i.e., NOT the Fighter or Cleric) just not working out longer term once the main quest countdown starts. After all, you only ever have 3 PCs that I have seen (plus some random NPCs at times), so you need a strong plan and a tanky damage sponge up front, two is better.There is an increasing pool of unique items to find in loot, with a "push your luck" aspect if you choose. The Devs have made some very nice improvements since it first released and honestly, I can say the other classes are mostly viable as a main character choice now. I tried the new Bard/Minstrel and she is fun. Very different and a... bit confusing as there are a lot of interactions and terms to learn so she "works" as advertised. I just need to spend some more time with the game.I would like to see the Codex include definitions for the item TERMS or descriptors as there are so many and you need to know what they do to make informed decisions on purchases and leveling up a character.Having said all that, the Devs are improving the game at a rapid pace and not a week goes by w/o some kind of bug fix release, etc. Some weeks it is multiple days.I like the artwork style and the in-game art is better than the title screen if you are worried. No voices, text boxes and buttons to push to get around like any typical game. Music is pretty good, I haven't gotten tired of it yet, although I hope there are a couple alternative tracks for in town as you spend a lot of time there. I do wish they would redo the story introduction voiceover. It is a terrible old man with a cliched wheezy voice that makes me cringe. Get a better talent guys, please!I would give Gordian Quest a firm 8/10 and improving while in Early Release. Give it a try and support the Devs. It is a lot of fun for the money and getting more so all the time.

_childDocuments_.review: I have tested and played lots of card games and gotta say, this takes the cake. It's absolutely stunning. Character personalisation is kinda Path of Exile meets Diablo. Itemisation is very cool. You can get skills, cards, items and you can customize and level up everything. This customization, nevertheless, its not like in Torchligh where you change the item for cheap currency and then it lasts for 20 minutes. Here, it comes with a price and then you can stick to it for a while. Loot and drop rate is exactly what you look for in a game like this. You can get higher rewards by adding difficulty in battles through shrines. The game is not focused in adventures and exploration, as you can expect from a card game, but it's there. The classes are not restrictive. Each character, which is a class, has four subclasses, meaning you have four decks to choose from. Each subclass will have an initial skill tree which you have to build yourself up depending on the choices you made inside that first tree. You can play a campaign normal mode or go roguelike hard where you have permadead. Maybe the only flaw is the learning curve; its kinda harsh at first, but understanding it later its well damned rewarding through its long chapters (I believe it has around five acts). Gotta warn you, though. If you're looking for something similar to Magic, Hearthstone or Yugioh, this isn't the right game for you. It's an RPG full of features of the genre closer to games like Slay the Spire and roguelite card games. It will take time until they make another one like this.P.D.: Update your graphic card, I had some trouble with the game before that.

_childDocuments_.review: Gordian Quest is basically a simplified D&D campaign told through the medium of a deckbuilding game.It has the trappings of that - along with the negatives - of that premise, as well.Against it are the parts of that premise that are a bit of a struggle: you start fairly weak and you tend to stay there for quite some time. Progress is sluggish, particularly for a deckbuilding game, to the point where you can go huge stretches of time without access to any of those neat higher-level abilities that make your class's gimmick really work. Until then you're working with (quite literally) half a deck.Along with that is the mortality. D&D was always pretty high mortality when you were low level and Gordian Quest is no different. It's quite easy to accidentally lose a character, at which point you can maybe go on for another fight or two before succumbing to attrition. The dearth of healing (outside the dedicated healing character) also tends to ensure that you need to play defensively or die to a thousand papercuts. Potions and setting up camp are all options, of course, but the former are fairly scarce and the latter burns through your provisions quite quickly, along with often leaving you just milling about while waiting for a character to rest or cook. It's both a fun mechanic and a frustrating one, depending on your mood.In its favour, however, are all the things that make those sorts of RPGs really fun.The classes are creative and bizarre, each one having at least three ways to play it (and a lot of ways to mix them) and so far as I can tell they're all pretty viable. You're encouraged to have a balanced team due to skill checks that inevitably require you to have a high level in whatever it is they're testing. The combat is fun and tactical and outside of the repetition of using the same low-level actions again and again it's pretty satisfying to finally get a combo together to eke out a win against a boss that is usually horrifically powerful.The art - both the animations and the cards themselves - are high quality. There are a slew of minigames to break up the gameplay, from dungeon delving to "exploration," to the aforementioned camp and interactions between characters. They all bring a slew of unique elements to the table and, honestly, the more they add the more interesting setting up your party gets.All in all I recommend it. There are a couple of bits that bug me but they're not quite gamebreakers - just stuff I wish I could find more convenient ways to deal with.

_childDocuments_.review: For a good while now i cant get enough of these "Rougelike-deckbuilder" games so when i see the tags under the Gordian Quest i know i had to check out the game and oh man was i not prepared.So first of all this game is massive what i mean is there is just so much mechanic that its mental , its quite ambitious and i feel like the devs kinda pulled it off.The game is like a D&D-rpg with a bunch of characters each having like 60+ cards and after you finally managed to choose a guy or gal you like you got sent into this Campaign with a board like moving system and after the first few fights you just get bombarded with mechanics. There is like a "make your own" skill tree leveling system , a right proper item crafting system with runes and sockets/socket coloring and RNG augmenting and all the good stuff (Maybe a bit of Path of Exile influence here? :P) and then there is all the D&D-like mechanic when it comes to the map , there are events with dice rolling and mini adventures inside your main adventure its crazy. _childDocuments_.review: for 20 bux this game offers a lot. If you like TCGs and want a decent amount of RPG level loot to play with I'd check this one out. Especially on sale. _childDocuments_.review: 9/10 - Even at maybe 45% done, this is the deckbuilder/RPG of your dreams, and a few niggling issues barely even detract from this brilliant little gem. Full review below:= Intro =I have a love/hate relationship with 'Spire' games. For every Monster Train, there seem to be a dozen mediocre ones, and most of them rely on endless, tedious runs of the same content with minor permutations. GQ sounded interesting, as it has a comprehensive single player campaign and some persistent qualities which definitely got my bacon sizzling.= Gameplay: 10/10 =Where to even start here? As things stand, two of the 4 main acts are done and playable (weighing in at maybe 6-7 hours a piece!), quite interesting RPG-style questing combined with deckbuilding, levelling, exploring and of course the turn based combat you should be accustomed to by now. On top of this, you have loot, crafting, dungeons...let's just say that this one swings for the fences.The 8 playable characters, each with 3 sub-classes to mix and match cards from are nicely varied and have their own 'thing' - although some (like the wizard and bard characters) are needlessly fiddly and obtuse to use, compared to the insanely powerful rogue and warrior and many skill sets, such as traps or nature magic feel rather useless, compared to say - nature summoning or assassination.Beyond the single player campaign (I've finished one act thus far), you have a realm mode, which is quite similar in design to Monster Train - you make your way down various paths to the 'end' of each realm, containing events, combat encounters and the like. Best of all, this has an endless mode (finally someone gets this right!).There is just too much to really go into here within the confines of the Steam review character limitation, so let's just call it 'bloody excellent'.There are a few minor issues, such as the aforementioned balance, but the only one that comes to mind is the permanent progression system, which is an RNG grindathon for petty permanent bonuses in the form of artifacts. This is just crying out for an additional progression system, perhaps some sort of character mastery or skill tree, or maybe some interesting, rare card unlocks.My only other gripe was the status effects certain enemies can use. Dispels are not baked into every class, and in many cases require specific gear. This wouldn't be such a big issue, if some status effects weren't essentially a run-ender the second they are used (preventing a character from attacking at all for 7 rounds...wat).= Graphics & Audio: 7/10 =Yeah, it's the same old' 'flash' style presentation that basically every game of this type uses, although it's implemented well.The audio is...decent, aside from the sound effect of monsters moving or entering the battlefield, which sounds like someone blowing loudly onto their mic. The music is perhaps slightly better than average.= Value: 9/10 =As things stand, you'll get more value out of this game at it's current point of development than probably 95% of 'Spire clones' out there. And again, it's not even half done. There really isn't much else to say here.= Overall =+ Finally, the RPG/deckbuilder I've been looking for+ Nice variance between characters and sub-classes+ Interesting synergies, without going crazily OP+ Incredible amount of content and variety+ Just a tip top little title- Balance is still a little wonky- Certain characters are needlessly obtuse to build and play- Permanent progression system is lacklustre- Some status effects feel unfair

_childDocuments_.review: Let me preface it by saying it's not the most gripping gameplay in town, but it's fairly enjoyable. It has none of the addictive traits of your usual Roguelike Deckbuilder.It's a nice game, but it shows you pretty much all it has to offer in about 5 hours. So it will be more of a slow burn I'll enjoy from times to times, compared to Hadean Tactics that I play regularly.You have two modes :- Campaign : A long playthrough where you develop three characters during a multi-chapter story. The story itself is fairly mundane so far, but the gameplay is good. You improve your deck, your character stats and their gear.- Realm : The standard Roguelike Deckbuilder. It's not very good simply because you start with very weak characters so it can quickly be a slog to try run after run just to get a little further. The slow pace of fights in this game also doesn't match the roguelike formula.Also, in a roguelike, you try to aggressively prune your deck to make it as efficient as possible, but there are very few options to do so here.

_childDocuments_.review: Nearly perfect game for me at this moment in life. Deck builder and character leveling make me feel like I have some control over the random progression, but the RNG keeps things interesting each run.Turn based, and progress saved on leaving the game, means I can play this for a few minutes between other activities or while needing to use up 15 minutes.Difficulty feels right to me. Some early bad luck can really kill a nightmare run, but once you understand the important of positioning (and reading enemies moves) your odds improve significantly. Doing a run solo on normal really helps you get a feel for character builds.The D&D feel to the game is an aesthetic I appreciate. For someone always stuck running the games it is a delight to get to have a taste of being the hero.The developers are also incredibly active and engaged with progressing the game. Check out their reddit forum and you'll see they comment on nearly everything. Incredible level of interaction for developers. I don't think I've gone two days without a patch improving the game in the 100+ hours I've played so far.If there is any critique I have at all it is that the Dex tree carries some abilities that feel mandatory on harder difficulties (free move once per turn, +1 card draw, +10 init) making it necessary to dip into Dex for every character. That may just be my style of play, but I have yet to be successful without dipping into those trees for nightmare mode.Thank you to the developers. Looking forward to seeing the final version of the game.

Right now, there's no incentive to not yolo into a fight, because you can just go back to town and heal with no recourse.  Meaning, you don't even spend money.  I imagine this will change in the final version or with other difficulty settings.  Your character(s) die, but with no perma-death... again, maybe on a different difficulty.   Overall, it feels pretty good.  It's got a little bit of the 'one more battle' feel, which is always a good sign.  I do hope the story changes between characters, because it does feel like it might be a little linear.  Not sure if I want to play the current story twice.  Maybe there will be a Slay the Spire type mode.  Anyway, good stuff so far and I'm exciting to see how this progresses.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall a very good game. It does suffer from some balancing issues, with certain abilities being rather OP and others feeling very underwhelming. The art style is great (though I wish the cleric wore more reasonable armor). It does suffer from a few issues that I think should be fixed. For one, its connection to the steam cloud seems janky. I often play on two computers, a laptop while away and my PC while at home, and this game has issues syncing up on both, so I've had several instances where a save simply didn't exist on one computer, which was quite annoying. Another, far more glaring issue is that there is ONLY ONE SAVE FILE. Like, really... what games do that these days? Please fix this, if nothing else. *Edit, nevermind, this is apparently not an issue at all, I just didn't see how it was actually done. The final issue is that the new characters are not available for recruiting in the first act. While you can select any of the characters as your starting character from the start, you're left recruiting the cleric and the swordhand, and then later the scoundrel and the sage. I'm not sure if you can get the druid later (I certainly hope so), but otherwise, the sonneteer, the warlock, and the golemancer only seem to be available for recruitment starting in act two. Given that I would like to build a party purely with these new characters (and start with them in act 1, because I don't like starting in act 2 where the sheer amount of skills you get at the start is a little overwhelming), I see this as a fairly big issue. Anyways, I hope the devs read this and act on it at some point, because I do love this game, and still do recommend it. *Edit - they did read it and cleared up a few of my issues! A sure sign of a dev team that actually cares about their product, thus reaffirming this as an even more positive review. Thanks devs! I look forward to future updates!

_childDocuments_.review: Great game.  Great deck building mechanics.  Great party building and character development.  You ultimately assemble a group of 3 (from several possible classes) with each class feeling distinct and different.  Excellent combat mechanics.  Strategic yet fast paced battles.  The combat, which is the heart of the game, is just flat out fun.  Lots of different and interesting things going on (between skills/talents/gear/socketing/more).  Plenty of randomization that makes every restart different enough to feel fresh.  The devs are active, communicate with players a lot, and the game has been improving regularly (as of this writing there's a juicy update on beta branch).  The game also presents one with plenty of challenges.  The graphics/animations are very well done, the UI is well done, all the info you need during battles if readily available and presented very well.I buy fewer early access games these days and return most if they're not immediately fun and engaging.  This game felt excellent when I first bought it and it's just getting better.  At the time of writing this, I already have ~40 hours played with just the first act to mess with (and I'm not the greatest at these games so I have yet to actually finish the first act - restart syndrome or something - the game has enough going on and enough "procedural" that restarting over and over and trying different things has been a lot of fun).Another thing I like about the game is that there isn't that much stuff that's locked up or dependent on failing repeatedly to get strong enough to have fun.  Some "roguelikes" expect you to die repeatedly and unlock/build up before you can really get anywhere and that is often not fun for me.  This game gives you some minor perks for making progress and failing, and you can unlock different variants on starter decks (without spending weeks of time), but it's nothing I'd consider critical to success - more like it adds variety (the starter decks) and a little bit of potential grease to ease the flow.I don't feel the need to compare every deck builder to StS (a game I love and can actually beat) or compare every new RPG rogue-whatever to DD (a game I enjoy but have never come remotely close to finishing), so the only thing I'll say is that as far as overall fun factor and quality goes - this game is up there and doesn't really feel that much like either.  The way you drag cards to play them is similar to StS, which I think is a good thing since that system is fast and clean.  I don't really see any tight comparison to DD outside of RPG elements common to many games.  I can only think people mention DD because of the overall fun factor and mix of elements going on.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is the quintessential example of a mostly positive reviewed game.Everything in the game is done on such level that for every cool feature there is a serious flaw:1) Classes - I haven't seen such diverse and viable classes anywhere else, they are fun to explore. BUT there are a few big "BUTs":* the characters are just dummies, and their personality is shown very sketchily, although they are drawn well.* there are 10 characters in the game, each with 3 classes for which the game does not provide training or a clear description of the mechanics.* the plentiful classes seems to encourage experimentation with combat mechanics, but there are only 3 slots in the party and the rest are left on the bench.* when you need a character from the bench, you have to build a deck for him blindly, and there's almost no chance of not ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ yourself because it's hard to gauge how effective the cards in a class deck are.* you can only pespec a character with a special artifact, which you still have to figure out where to find, so you can't experiment within one character either.* after level 30, progression ceases to have a significant effect on anything. * you don't get many synergy points and it's better not to spray them on several characters.Often, this means that the game motivates you to play with a once assembled party and once chosen class for each character.Okay, is there a Realms mode for experimenting with characters? No, almost every difficulty level in this mode is tiresome, forces you to play as safe as possible, and doesn't reward challenge in any decent way at all. In addition, for a rogue-lite mode, it lacks metaprogression, and each new run not only doesn't make further play easier, but also differs little from the previous one - in general, I consider this mode a failure. 2) Battles are dynamic, variable and can entertain even after a few dozen hours. BUT they can be randomly generated in such a way that they can either be over in 1 turn or impossible to complete at all - this is frustrating. The reward for most fights is more often than not randomly generated trash, and that's frustrating too.3) There are some curious game mechanics, BUT even more useless ones. There are so many of them that it sometimes becomes frightening, and the game itself does not highlight these mechanics in any way: random loot, gearing, leveling, several types of currencies, 4 types of merchants, 2 modes of exploration maps, several types of interaction with runes and item modifications, random events and randomly generated fights, shrines - all of this exists as if in parallel to each other and mostly exists only to quantitatively bloat the game.4) The game runs smoothly on Steamdeck, BUT there are ergonomics and visibility issues. For complex fights, you need to move to PC for better control. Also, in some places the game can lose control and stop responding to button presses, but it doesn't happen often.5) The soundtrack is good, although not outstanding, BUT only for the first 15-20 hours, then only Spotify.The game is either poorly balanced, or the game concept itself is carefully planned so that it's fun, but not so much.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't review games very often but this one deserves one. As a person who adores turn based games like Slay the Spire (25 hours) and Darkest Dungeon(70 hours) this one is the next on my list. First day I bought, I sank 4 hours without even realizing. The combat is fantastic with row and lane based action, with lots of synergies around positioning your units. You play with 3 heroes, who have their own decks, gear, weapons and items. Each item and weapon is actually a card that you can add to your deck; therefore you can mix and match these weapon cards into each hero's deck. During the fight each grid (usually 3 by 3 each side) may have different items such as chests, traps, areal effect and cover so you may use them to your advantage.Combat is pure fun. There are five beginning classes to chose from, so there is lots of possibilities, considering weapons, armor, bombs and potions. Each hero also has its own talent tree, which you can branch out differently.Besides these, the way you play is going through through the nod based map, where each nod has an encounter, shrine or a dungeon. These dungeons have their own node based branching maps with multiple floors and they usually end up with a boss fight. These remind me darkest dungeon missions. When you clear these nods, the map opens up in a circular way, but some events may trigger the nodes being invaded again. There are some minor problems which can be easily fixed though. One problem is that, since the units sit on a grid, when there are too many units, sometimes it is difficult to select the units behind the front ones. Also, the icons showing the conditions are a little bit small. When you click on the units though, you can see a summary on the left side. Enemies use similar card skills and use similar synergies; so you need to also break their formation. There are also various difficult levels and as someone coming from DD and StS, normal mode is not challenging enough. I will try the hard mode next. Town management needs a little bit more patching though, since it is not very clear what each building does. DD style progression would be nice.Overall, my first impression is quite positive. Since this is just Act I, you can expect to get around 20-25 hours once the game is fully developed. For the price of $16, I totally recommend this game to anyone who  likes turn based games.

_childDocuments_.review: My initial reaction to Gordian Quest was awestruck. The scope of this game is massive, especially compared to its other roguelike deckbuilding brethren. In fact, upon my first playthrough, I would have told you that Gordian Quest might actually be in contention for the best game in the genre. This game functions on so many layers, it's going to take you hours just to understand what the hell you're actually doing. There are customizable skill trees; a variety of classes with different subclasses; talent trees; crafting and upgrading; a whole camping minigame; socketable items with gems; a luck resource system; complex grid-based tactics; and of course: deckbuilding. It’s a lot to take in, and it’d be a lie to say that Gordian Quest isn’t pushing the limits of the genre. I just can’t say that the direction it’s pushing it in is something that I enjoy.Once you’re able to lift your jaw back off the floor after trying to digest exactly what is actually going on, Gordian Quest reveals its true colors. Like every other budding game genre, RLDBs (roguelike deckbuilders) seem to be nuancing off as the genre evolves, and there seem to be two directions that devs are pushing their games. One branch follows the footsteps of StS, embracing the deckbuilding as the game’s core gameplay loop, focusing on synergy and the card mechanics. And the other pushes the genre more toward a roguelike, where you’ll spend as much brainpower managing overworld resources than you will playing with your sweet deck. Realistically, most of these games are a blend of the two with a slight lean, but Gordian Quest leans way too far into the survivalist roguelike take than I care for. The only other game in the genre that I’ve played that felt less focused on the actual cardplay was Nowhere Prophet, which I also disliked. Gordian Quest feels very much like a roguelike with deckbuilding elements that serve as a small portion of a greater whole than an actual deckbuilding roguelike, and that’s not something I enjoy.Now, does that mean the game is bad? ♥♥♥♥ no. Gordian Quest is a great, well developed, gorgeous game, and it’s obvious that the devs have put a lot of thought into its design. It’s just not for me.TL;DR: Very complex, Very Pretty, Too much Roguelike, Not enough deckbuilder.
_childDocuments_.name: Gordian Quest

_childDocuments_.review: This is a beautifully done game. The thought behind the interactions between characters, the graphics, the effects, the UI. There are often times when I use a feature for the first time and I have an expectation and hope for how it works (i.e Respec) and that's exactly how it works. The game is a little easy though. I'd like more complexity and more strategic decisions. If you can stack guard you can disregard almost all effects. I also don't like the exploration minigame, I think it's boring. The monsters in the minigame should trigger encounters or something. I find that using defacto health damage, i.e lose 5 hp or 10-20% of your health isn't interesting. I think random curses are more interesting even if they end up numerically being something similar. I think that the exhaustion mechanic isn't fun to play with. If you exhaust a card it shows up later being a dud during a draw. If you exhaust a card it should be a problem when you draw it, and you either shouldn't be able to exhaust cards that aren't equipped or exhausted cards that aren't equipped shouldn't make it into your deck. You could have more DC rolls and only exhaust cards on failures. I basically never rest, even on torment. Exhausted cards are a minor nusiance when they could actually be a fun game mechanic that enhances the strategic decision making.For instance: There should be a mechanics to allow you to exhaust cards during combat, and when you draw the exhausted card it should reduce your inititative or cause another negative effect. It should be more intergrated into the actual combat system then just the draw a blank card, that's boring! :) You could make monsters that feed off of exhaustion, and also new cards that allow you to exhaust cards for some bonus or to play them immediately, and also have options to un exhaust cards in combat.I find in general the minigames aren't integrated enough into the core gameplay (the combat), the combat is the funnest part of the game and the minigames should orbit the combat and be more closely connected. But the game is also too easy, even on the hardest level- so playing the various minigames, resting, etc to gather a set of buffs which often aren't worth the time spent is tedious. I have to load the rest game, click the buff, move through the night, but the only thing I care about during the rest is chatting and building synergy bonuses.There should be a way to build synergy bonuses outside of the rest events, if you are playing too well then you don't get access to them. :(Otherwise, it's all very tight, the core combat mechanics are interesting. The tradeoffs, cold vs fire, channeling, how to build the team around your chosen mechanics and strategy are interesting and well done.

_childDocuments_.review: Game is very clunky. Its understandable since this is early access. As you dive deeper into the game, you will see that devs are trying to implement a lot of elements from different games. There are elements from slay the spire(deck building), from any rng game (equipment, pots), from turn based game (initiative and turn order). event rng dice roll with D20, and etc. This is great, for having this many elements in a single game. BUT! The devs are trying too hard making all those elements to fit into the game. For example, equipments that have card attached to it. i like the equip but the card attached is so bad that I ended up not taking that equip. Then skill tree, its cool and all but the fact that when you learn a "new skill", its when you get a card is just not good, both deck build wise and rng wise. Because once you learn a "new skill", you are forced to take a new card or replace your card with 3 other random cards. That means, sometimes you are forced to take "bad cards" aka cards you may or may not want/like. Plus the fact that you have lvl up to get to discard a skill to remove card is uhhhh, dont get me started on that. I am sorry that I am being picky but as a player who have 500+ hours in slay the spire, being picky is what you need to do after ascensions. Overall, I think this game does have great potential. I do like a lot of elements fit into a single game. For me though, I would pass on this game just because it doesnt synergize properly with all the elements. Lastly, there is a "bug", well I dont know if it is a bug or not but enemy will change the intent if an object is broken. In the "Take back the storehouse" "boss" fight, one of the enemy changed his intent after i broke the barricade. (This is my own gameplay of this instance:  If this is a bug, please fix it, because it made me feel that i got cucked. You never want to let your players feel that way, unless it is intended.Please dont take this post personally. Most are just my subjective view.Thank you for reading this post and have a blessed day!
_childDocuments_.name: Gordian Quest

_childDocuments_.review: First of all: I love the concept of the game. Having this RPG elements with card/deck management and tactical fight on a grid  (also I dont need the grid really). Second: The developer seems to respond to players, which is always a good sign and I really appreciate that.but... BUT... the game itself in its current state is beyond flawed in my opinion. And I tell you why.(DISCLAIMER: I played the live version aswell as the bleeding edge version, my critic is mostly viable for both, but I will point out if it only concerns one version... boys this review is going to be a big one)Most of the fights are easy as heck. Like really easy. In the beginning you have a some engaging fights and have to think about what you do, but 20minutes in you are absolutely obliterating everything. I cant stress that enough. And there are a lot, A LOT of fights. Most fights are done in my first round, dont even letting them the chance to do something. And when you are lucky and the enemy has reinforcements arriving, than you have to wait for it and wasting a turn. Beyond that if you manage to find a bossfight (I can remember 2 of them, only because the enemys were bigger not stronger compared to power level I had at that point) they reward you with x12 gold. Atleast in my case. My food cost more which I needed to get there. This food system doesnt add anything to the game at all other than having to run back and buy new all the time. Not in one single instance Ive run out of it or had to think what to do, just walk back to town. Annoying.Besides the stupid boss loot you get this precious legendary items.... casually every other battle. YES even on bleeding edge. When arriving in act 2 I was fitted completly in legendary and my inventory was full with it. Changing some of them for min maxing, not needing most of them at all. Like most of the equipment does, the legendary items aswell give you cards for your deck. Yeah... about that.In "bleeding edge" you have the option to buy void runes, and I recommend doing so, to remove the cards from items. Most of them are compared to what you can get naturally weak. Plain weak. (Besides this one AOE thing with root from a mage wand which costs 1 and does more damage than any other skills in a 4 square radius on the grid.... THATS over the top. I like it.)I was playing as a cleric, warrior and mage. The idea was to have a tank, a healer and a caster for the heavy hitting. Turns out the cleric heal spells are redundant. Either you deal that much damage that you dont get hit, or you get hit that hard, that the heal aint worth your draw. Coming from card games like "magic the gathering" I know how to efficiently build my deck, and REMOVING cards is the best way to do so in this game. There are per class maybe 2-3 good cards which are worth getting. After that try to remove as much useless stuff as possible. While you can delete cards from your decks provided by your equipment with void runes (bleeding edge) and talents on live (to a degree, not all of them, go play bleeding edge, seriously) you have more struggle to get rid of you main deck cards. (I hope there is no letter limit in reviews.... *sips coffee*)The main deck cards can be exchanged when you receive respec points. You can improve some cards, but you dont get rid of all of them (even the fire bomb on a mage is fun, you dont need 3 of them..... enemy go brrr). So the only chance of getting rid of this standard cards no one ever asked for is via skills in your skill.... tree? its not a tree... its like a skilldiamond... that sounds stupid.... skillgrid.YEAH. But there is a flaw too, while on live the "delete a card and be happy" nodes are pretty common, in bleeding edge they are rare. If you spend couple of skill points into your grid you receive a new one to set next to it, to advance your chances. THIS IS A GREAT CONCEPT. I really like it! Chosing one of 3 random ones is kinda okay if they would provide all different things. But they dont. Instead you get "mystery" skills on them, which you only see if you apply it. If you are going to SKILL something, then you have SOME SORT OF thought put in your build. You DONT want to random get something, especially if it takes 3 more levels to get the next one which MIGHT have the nodes you want. Especially if there are like 5 nodes on each which gives you new skills.... Why on earth you want to do that? I can run happy with 5 cards in my deck total. Having 100 cards and drawing all the time situational or "wrong" cards is tidious and inefficient (yes I am german, leave me alone, its in my bloodstream to be efficient). Oh and most of the talents arent very specific either, like most of the cards from items.There is also a camping mechanic in the game... .... yeah I did it once, would never do that again (No I dont mean sitting with a sniper on nuketown in the room behind the mannequin). It feels out of place and clunky even if I get the idea behind it. Not worthwhile the time. Enchanting... Yeah did that in path of exile, didnt do it here. This side mechanics are a good idea to add to the complexity but they fail to deliver. Sockets... yeah, good concept! But besides buying void runes to remove the spells you dont really find that many, especially that many good runes. And you dont need any of them to be successful at all.Finally its time to come to a conclusion: - Most of the cards underperform- Skilltrees (grids, jungles and other forms of that) shouldnt be random. at all.- Too many, too weak fights- Completly unrewarding and random loot- Food mechanic (srsly... why tho)- Camping / Sockets / Runes / Crafting / Enchanting - Good concept, but underperforming right now.- Too much situational items/cards. (look at slay the spire speedruns, you see how and why they get rid of cards)Oh... and I lost items while going from act 1 to 2. No idea why, but it doesnt matter really. More of the same.That should sum up everything wrong in my opinion. If the devs listen (which I think they do) and keep improving the game, this will be a gem. I hope they will.So if you unsure whether you should buy it or leave it - I cant tell you that. From my perspective, for people like me, I would recommend against it. But more casual players and people who like it soft, you can go for it.The game is NOT bad, its NOT buggy, its NOT bad performance, it just fails to meet my expectations which I summed up already. *sips coffee*(If anyone asked: this review 6462 characters long, not including this line here)

_childDocuments_.review: This is a really fun blend between a roguelike deckbuilder and an RPG. Campaign mode is my favorite, which is more RPG focused, but Realm modes is also popular which has a bigger roguelike focus. The mechanics are complex but really fun and it's nice to try out different builds with all the characters. There are 10 characters available and each character has 3 different schools of cards, so there's a lot of variation, and many schools have different viable builds within them. Pair that with a party of 3 separate characters and you get a lot of replayability with testing out different combos. The positioning with lanes and rows is personally my favorite part of the game, and that you don't need to play it as a roguelike makes it a lot better than similar games imo.

_childDocuments_.review: There is a lot to this card game... almost too much, almost.  I think it hits a good balance of letting the player decide how much time they want to spend messing with the mechanics, because there's a lot of game mechanics but you don't have to master each part in order to move forward. There are plenty of characters with lots of ways to customize your play style, though I only stuck with the same 3 so as to not get overwhelmed.It's very fun with excellent art but the sound design leaves something to be desired.
_childDocuments_.name: Gordian Quest

_childDocuments_.review: Just got to ACT III really like the art style, and the animations are simple but satisfying. Adding cards to your deck (at least in the first Act) doesn't over-saturate your deck, but I'm also going to try very lean deck builds. Story is neat enough so far. I've read maybe 70% of the text that has flashed up, and it was good from what I read. Combat is fairly simple and enjoyable. I'm playing on normal difficulty on my first run, and I've had a character die twice because I wasn't paying attention. The music and sound effects I heard were decent, but I haven't been paying attention too much due to other reasons, so can't say much about them (but nothing bad so far).I like how I'm able to go about improving characters. Leveling up is super simple, and spending the points is easy enough. Though, I would prefer to put more points into each skill grid before adding another. Maybe only getting a new one when I could fill out about half of the current one I'm on instead of every 4 or 5 levels.Loot and gear are simple and sweet. Pretty much every combat gives at least one piece of gear, along with some money or consumable. While most gear is meh (naturally) it's alright since I still get some value out of it by salvaging it at the blacksmith (not worth selling gear tbh. Would have to sell for 10 gp a piece at least to be worth selling). The gear varies nicely in terms of the bonuses they give the characters. Rates by rarity for loot are fine. Not getting too many rare items, and not too few.Overall, really enjoying the game. Give it an 7.5/10, and a good deal for the price ($17-$20 on sale or normally). Definitely recommend it for those into turn-based rpgs and deck building games.

_childDocuments_.review: A very nice discovery! The game is a successful frankenstein between Slay the Spire and Card Hunters. You explore locations going through "nodes", playing cards to defeat the enemies, but you also have multiple characters which level up and you can equip items to add cards to your deck. Add to that quest, shops, a story and d&d style skill challenges and you get a winning recipe! The art style is also very beautiful! The only thing that would need a bit more love is the music, which sounds a bit too MIDI for my taste.5 stars, MUST BUY!

_childDocuments_.review: I absolutely love this game. It's a wonderful combination of ideas - ideas you may have seen before. Roguelite deck builders aren't entirely uncommon. But I've yet to play one as put together as this one. The art is absolutely stunning. The gameplay is tight and enjoyable. If you've played something along the lines of Slay the Spire, an unavoidable comparison, you have the gist of what this game will be about. But there are many new twists that completely change the way it's played. You choose a starting character, but you will end up with the entire current roster of 6 heroes available to add to your team of 3. The battles are grid based so movement and placement become important. You get to deck (pun intended) out your characters with gear that adds new cards into their respective decks. The heroes level up and there's a quite robust skill node system that allows you to add new nodes as you play, adding new layers to the tweaking you can do for each hero. The rogue-like elements come into play on the map which includes several dungeons that have multiple levels themselves - and contain events that will have you making choices, and rolling dice to determine outcomes. With party composition have a clear impact on outcomes.All in all the game is absolutely worth a purchase in it's current state. There's a single act but different difficulties to choose from. And the developers are basically building the game with the community. There have been several updates already adding quality of life improvements. And new acts and heroes are planned with a seemingly solid road map and time table.Highly recommended!

_childDocuments_.review: Ultimately, the game entertained me for 40 hours, so I'll give it a thumbs up. This is a good framework but theres still work to be done.A big problem is that the game just isn't informative enough. Theres crafting, skill trees, loot, rune slots, exploration, combat, etc. but a lot of the basic information on these, you have to figure out yourself. For example, how do I get more Tier III cards? Does it require taking the same skill tree multiple times? Are they only unlocked at certain skill trees? How many cards are there from each tier? This is important because I kept rerolling card selection and getting the same thing results- makes sense if theres only 4 cards at tier II, but who knows?The difficulty is pretty unbalanced. I had to put the game on the 4th tier difficulty to get any kind of challenge and even then I rolled through Act I - III mostly on autopilot. Until I got to a boss who killed my entire full-health, guarded party in one shot midway through the fight. I dont know what hit me and there wasn't any information to prepare me for that fight (eg., if I should stack a certain resistance). So much for that 10-hour run.Ultimately the extreme grind was what kept me from picking it up again. Theres just too many of the same fights, and your run can be ended in a flash, it just didnt seem worth it any more.

_childDocuments_.review: Fun, card-based, rogue-like, RPG. The battles are fun, and while most were not that challenging, I did run into the occasional nail-biter. The story is simple, but the game tells it just fine. My favorite part of the game is the skill/inventory/ card system. Leveling up your characters means customizing your deck, while your equipment fine tunes your play style. I really enjoyed finding new gear and leveling up to customize my decks in a variety of ways. It was also nice that I got to customize my party and their decks to come up with some awesome combos. Going into a battle after learning new skills or finding a unique item was always exciting because you can feel your deck start to come together. I ran into one game breaking bug that a dev helped me through personally and quickly, so it worked out. I believe my experience with the game was well worth the minimal effort I had to put in to fix the game, and chances are they have patched it by now. I recommend it for anyone who enjoys team building RPGs.UPDATE: Have played Act I multiple times, and Hard mode definitely makes it more challenging and engaging. After 50 hours in the game, I finally started to recognize majority of the cards, and then they released Act II Beta, so I am diving back in!

_childDocuments_.review: Q) Is it good at the moment? Is the game fun?A) Yes, absolutely.Q) Is it perfectly polished?A) Nope! Though, it doesn't feel rough around the edges.Q) Does it seem like it will get polished?A) The devs are active and react to the community's suggestions and seem to be aware of what needs polish. So yes, it does seem like there will be polish.Q) How good might it be after polish?A) There's immense potential here. I can identify various things which need polish, and the devs have reacted to the suggestions in a very positive, promising way. (From buffing weak gameplay mechanics to improving the UI.) Q) Should I wait until 1.0 to buy?A) The game in its current version is fun and enjoyable to play. There's also fairly finished "acts" which work as scenarios to play through. So it's not even as though at some point a sign pops up: "We're not done yet. Come back in 4 months." Think of it as having seen a season of a show and waiting for the 2nd season to drop eventually. So, yes. I'd say it's okay to buy right now.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is amazing. When I'm bummed out that I can't play Tabletop RPGs, like D&D or Gloomhaven with friends, I can load up Gordian Quest and do a Campaign run. A great way to spend the weekend in quarantine. It's got depth, it's got challenge, it's got that instant-gratification of getting a random legendary for your character's build. It has all elements of a decent deck-builder, and character-progression RPG rolled into one. But sometimes I don't have 10 hours to sink into a campaign, I want something more casual, like Slay the Spire or Monster Train. Well, that's where Realm mode comes in! If you've played Slay the Spire, then you already know how Realm Mode works, because they're basically the same. Pick a team, pick a path, have encounters. Profit. Gordian Quest has a lot of elements of other games in the genre, but they also have a lot of their own quirks and twists on the norm. I highly recommend this game to anyone who like the Rogue-lite Deck Builder genre. Oh, and you can set it to Normal, Rogue-Lite or Rogue-like, to suit your preference. So, if you want super casual, with no perma-death, that's an option. Or if you wanna try Nightmare+ difficulty with no safety net? That's here too!Game aside, I decided to pull the trigger on this game for one reason. The devs. I had amazing customer service experience with them in Sairento, (one of the best, and most underrated hidden gems in VR), so when i saw that they had a game in this genre, I had to have it. I have not been disappointed. In play-testing the upcoming major patch, the devs have been very active in directly replying to fans, implementing bug fixes (insanely fast), and being transparent about their goals. I mean, you really can't ask for more than that. If you wanna play a game where you feel like your opinions matter, and are heard, honestly, this is it.

_childDocuments_.review: What a strange game. Lots of potential here but I'm not sure if a lot of it is unfilled potential.There are a lot of different game mechanics here, far too many. They aren't explained very well in help section. For example, you can camp, which I tried. I have no idea how this works, click on icons adds cards, seemingly endlessly. I ended up just advancing time until I got back to the main exploration screen and nothing seemed to happen.I wouldn't mind this if the game offered some level of challenge, but despite my understanding very little about the game there is zero challenge so far. I don't think the enemy units have done the slightest damage to any of my units. I always have the initiative, which results in zero challenge on normal difficulty.The developers solution to this lack of challenge is to suggest increasing the difficulty level. But there is essentially no advantage to doing this in the campaign, and this isn't a solution for lack of difficulty balancing.Update - as requested by the developers, I'm updating this review after playing the game to almost the half way point. The update to the increased difficulty happened just I was finishing the first act. Since I was moving to a new act it is hard for me to say exactly how the change affects the game but act 2 is definitely more of a challenge, which makes the game a lot more fun.The biggest remaining issue is the lack of more detailed tutorials which the developers are planning to address. In the meantime I have been watching beginner tips videos which confirm that there was a lot of mechanics I wasn't making use of.Looking forward to playing the remaining two acts.

_childDocuments_.review: Four hours in I would have recommended this game.  It has a really engaging base design but unfortunately it falls off a cliff.  The best way to describe the game is a party version of Slay the Spire (where each character has his own deck) but with more depth in stories, equipment, and pathing.So where does it go wrong?  I'll explain.1) Combat takes too long.  This is especially problematic when your party gets strong and many enemies are easy to defeat.  I'm currently fighting unchallenging enemy after unchallenging enemy and its so unenjoyable.  They say a run is supposed to be 4-8 hours but I'm at least 15-20 in on my current run.  Its possible that I'm supposed to be skipping more combat encounters than I am.  However, I think a core issue is that its a bit more open map and enemies can respawn via shrines.  So am I not supposed to use shrines ever?  In any event, I think Slay the Spire gets it right in that there are a FIXED number of encounters.  This game would be much better with a more linear format.2) Any deckbuilding game (even Slay the Spire) runs into issues.  Adding cards is supposed to be fun, but if you have a good core of cards adding cards only dilutes your pool making your draws less stable.  Furthermore, there are too many cards which are terrible unless built around a synergy.  The problem is that to go for that synergy, you first have to add a card, which makes your deck worse.  Then you add another that makes your deck worse.  Basically, you have to spend a ton of resources completely adding certain cards and removing others before you get a strong deck again.  I do like a number of the synergies but the process of getting there feels awful.3) The items and rune system seem amazing early on.  Then you keep playing and you're like, "I'm level 15 and I'm still getting the same items I was getting at level 1."  Items and runes do not get better throughout the game.  While I was super excited about runes early on, I now realize there are maybe 9-12 in total.  There was so much they could have done with these to alter builds and runs and just didn't.  I'm at a point in my run where every item I find is worse than stuff I already have.  You can get a legendary weapon at level 3, build around it, and never find anything that makes sense to replace it with.In short, what you end up with is that at a certain point in a run you have solid decks and solid items.  From that point forward, battles are time consuming and boring and finding loot isn't exciting because item drops don't scale with your level or enemy level.

_childDocuments_.review: The campaign is heavily padded with common encounters which quickly become tiresome because the enemies are terrible at fighting. Often, they'll spend their whole turn targeting unoccupied tiles, or giving themselves a little bit of temporary defense, or placing an easily-avoided trap doesn't do much even if you choose to step on it, or buffing themselves with a too-little-too-late effect. On the off chance an enemy does actually aim at you, you can just move out of the way. Even on the hardest difficulty, they still suck at fighting, they just suck with slightly bigger numbers.The most threatening non-boss enemies in my last torment run? Those that rolled the "thorns" buff, which deals a negligible quantity of revenge damage when you stomp them. They probably dealt the most damage out of any enemies, and they never dealt enough damage to matter.The difficulties are named Easy, Medium, Hard, Nightmare, and Torment, but they actually mean Journalist, Journalist, Journalist, Journalist, and Easy.There's some encounter diversity, but it's soon exhausted by the sheer quantity of busywork fights. The variety is further undermined by the inevitable incompetence that afflicts all enemies. They get steamrolled all the same. You stop thinking "how do I win this fight?" and start thinking "seeing as how it's next to impossible to lose this fight, how do I end it with the least brainpower invested?"Some cards have inconsistent phrasing or poorly-explained mechanics (Follow Through, Blast Wave). Many cards are functionally redundant or overshadowed by other options (Prowl vs Feral Leap, Somersault vs Fade To Shadows, Flanking Bola vs Lure, Assessment vs Strategic Instructions). Some are so bad they're not even worth drawing (Flame Shield, Battle Orders, basically all "X cache" cards), the only purpose they serve is to clutter your random selection pool and force you to use rerolls when looking for new cards to add to your deck.Inventory management gets tedious with trash loot; levelling gets obnoxious with skill grid micromanagement. Lots of promise here, not so much delivery. If you want to play a rogue-like turn-based deck-builder, get Slay the Spire. If you want a long-run, story-driven version of Slay the Spire, get Griftlands. If you want to play a drawn-out-like-sitting-in-traffic version of Griftlands, ignore this review.Additional Thoughts:The glory of Slay the Spire is in building decks that can "go super saiyan" in a variety of viable ways. Every encounter on your path is challenging, the bosses especially, and it's deeply satisfying to take your refined deck and smash through (or more likely, just barely limp past) that final boss that had been gatekeeping all your prior runs.Note that StS runs last a few hours at most. Gordian Quest tries to stretch StS's winning model into multiple days or even weeks - a fatal mistake. You might power spike in Act 1 or halfway through Act 2, and it's fun when that happens, but then what? You've already won, but the game makes you prove it for another 30 hours. Cue burnout and mindless routine-based play. The gameplay doesn't stay interesting, it doesn't evolve with compelling new mechanics, it wasn't particularly challenging before your character apotheosized, and it definitely isn't challenging afterwards.You could force yourself to switch characters just to keep things bearable, but those replacement characters start naked and at a baseline level that can no longer compete with standard encounters - not because they're particularly threatening, but because you're restarting with single-digit damage against card-sponge minions. The game tests your patience, not your ability.The "map exploration" mechanic was slapped on as an afterthought. It lacks sufficient depth to stand independently, it's not coherent with the rest of the game, and at best it serves as a minor distraction to break up a tedious gameplay loop until it inevitably becomes itself tedious.

_childDocuments_.review: An adventure that has everything you love about adventuring.You might see it as a card battler, but the level of character build complexity Gordian Quest offers is wide and deep. Every choice you make feels like it matters: card selection, deck building, upgrading cards, skill mapping and selection, gear crafting and selection, team composition, and the list goes on. Each of the nine heroes has three specializations and with the added complexity of gear, there are many viable ways to design each (and some even having unorthodox builds). While others might complain about the simple nature of the story, I found it a welcoming respite considering the breadth of everything else; there is charm in simplicity. One small gripe is that gear management feels slightly too much, even with the quality of life options. When you dive in for the first time, don't focus too much on trying to understand everything, keep your attention on the choices the game presents and enjoy the ride. You will always have the option to rebuild and rebuild and rebuild. Oh and developers: a glossary would help.Time to complete: 20-30 hours.

_childDocuments_.review: Interesting concept but it may not be what you initially expect. This is not a casual game at all. If you buy this game expecting a "Slay the Spire" this is not for you. However, I don´t believe that was the intention of the developers at all.At the moment of this review the game is still on early access. I think it is an interesting concept but it still requires a lot of work. One can feel the amount of love and effort invested in this game, but it may not achieve your expectactions in some ways. Let me explain:The game has a class system, with unique characters, progression and cards which is amazing!... On paper... What I mean with this is that managing the (slow) progression of three characters at the same time, makes the game a bit less engaging than I was expecting, since it is hard to get new cards to make your build. You can receive new cards, by talents (when you invest on a perk that allows you to do so), by objects (giving you cards that you are not really adding to your deck, since when you unequip the object you will loose that card) or by replacing another card with 're-spec' points. There may be other ways but I haven´t found them yet. Having to make competent builds for 3 characters using these methods at the same time makes it almos unbearable. I have the feeling it would have been more satisfying to invest that effort into making an amazing single character. At the same time that would have make the combat system unfair and frustrating.Additionally, there is literally like three textboxes ant that is the tutorial of the game. But the game has like 50 mechanics, menus progression forms, status, traps, a system for enchantments, shops, decissions, altars with modifiers, dungeons, etc... none of that is ever explained at this point. And that is a pitty.Other minor things like animations that would be nice to see in a smoother way, sounds and screams that are kind of repetitive, additional phrases by the characters with comments, etc...The character design and the art are amazing. I am really loving it.The mechanics of some of the characters are specially interesting and fun to play with.The decision system and the odds with the dice are well executed and fun. Multiple language translation. Other games are not translated apart from english and chinese, and that is a huge plus.If you really like these "build your own adventure" kind of game, this seem to be a pretty good one, in a way that the story is kind of there already, but the gameplay my change according to your character selection.At its current state, even if it has some minor issues, and it is possible that it doesn strike a chord for you, I feel I can recommend it. It wouldn´t be fair not to do it as I can see it has been made with tons of love and care and it is a good way to spend your evening!

_childDocuments_.review: Alright, I had about 4 hours of gameplay, enough to have a solid grasp and for an opinion. First of all I didn't buy this game because I want more Slay The Spire (game that I own but didn't hold my interest even 2 hours, one of purchases I regret).I bought it because they are trying to blend in multiple concepts, each one of those that make other games from which they are taken, unique and fun. They are not event trying to pretend that it's their original idea but they are creative about it.Now, there is a problem with this and I will credit to it being in EA. Despite abundance of mechanics and content already in, they feel very disconnected. In fact, a lot of things require either polish pass or they just don't work well and are better off removed, It's worth noting that I switch to bleed-edge build after and definitely see improvement in the right direction but I also do hope devs realize that more doesn't necessarily means better and more satisfying.The game clear tries to be it's own hybrid and standing out as one, and that's why I decided to give it a shot and enjoyed a lot, despite it's shortcomings so far. By no means discard this as " another" clone of Slay The Spire, because it's much more ambitious and diverse game that has everything for everyone - despite at the moment being a bit disorganised and shallow.And one more thing, the core of the game is very rock solid and with more polish and content refined, it's a game worth a try for every RPG fan out there with a deck-building twist.

_childDocuments_.review: Utterly soulless; feels like it was made with a "paint by numbers" philosophy without any thought. Almost every mechanic is superfluous. At best they feel useless, and at worst like deliberate attempts to waste your time. The game is not balanced and it feels as if even the most basic aspects of player experience were never considered.A fair amount of my time played is idle time, and the rest was me forcing myself to complete a run because I'd passed the refund window and hoped that things changed later. They don't. By the end of my "hard" first run, the average combat round amounted to all enemies being annihilated by whichever damage dealer rolled highest initiative, with my other two characters simply passing their turns (if more waves remained). It's trivially easy to end up with a deck size around 9-10, and with extra draw (also trivial to obtain) you essentially draw your entire customized deck every turn. I'm an average player and didn't even bother taking advantage of many options to enhance player strength. Maybe things get better on the higher difficulties, but it's not worth suffering through the core mechanics again to find out.

_childDocuments_.review: I have a few words about this game.I've finished the game in the hardest difficulty setting twice and it is easy for me to do it again and again with no challenge. If you comprehend the mechanics, the campaigns aren't hard in any difficulty - you have enough time to build your decks, keep useless cards to a minimum and choose your equipment wisely. Honestly? It doesn't have to be any harder because not all characters are created equally - Alphonse can decimate anything if build correctly with Assassination maxed, copied twice and with limited cards in your deck. Some other characters feel that they are in the weaker side but that might be just me, that's why I replayed without picking my favs. Playing with different characters = replayability.I also love the new Golem-controlling girl, but she's a pain to build right, and you really depend on getting specific draws of cards in order to specialize in her.As easy as the game can become in Campaign mode, the same can definetely NOT be said about the new game modes. They are hardcore, I've barely gone through them. The game itself is a masterpiece for people like me who prefer using their minds and explore different strategies all the time. At times, the RNG gives you a headache (building a Strength hero and drawing non-Strength cards or rerolling and still getting the same cards)Suggestions: 1. In skill rerolls, don't give the player the same cards, provide them with different cards when they use Fate to reroll.2. Create events in which heroes talk to each other, or the npcs - in camps as well, let's meet them a bit, understand how they feel. Also speaking to the foes they fight- Have them speak to the bosses. I don't say this is for everyone - provide the option in the menu to turn on/off the characters dialogues.3. Forgive me for saying but skill challenges, as of now are a joke. I never even bother getting equipment for them as the rewards feel bad and the tradeoff is horrible- Use a Fate to reroll a failed challenge that cost you 5-7hp ? I'll take the 5hp damage any time. If you want us to care about skill challenges, bring in Skill point rewards and the other rewards that appear in camping events. Losing 7hp is nothing, but losing a skill point? I'm gonna use that fate to retry, and I'm gonna equip gear to up my chances to get it.4. This might be just me, but I hate having to switch the direction of a random character I get after beginning the game. For example, I get the cleric and she has all STR oriented challenges. I constantly find myself wasting the first part of the campaign redistributing and cancelling her cards until I get her in INT gear/skills. When we get a new party member, the option should be given to select their focus: "Hello, would you like me to focus on "Healing, Divine Spells, or Taking and giving blows"The great about this game:The dev team. I read the forums, the posts and comments and I realized how invested they are in this and how they listen to their players. I had a bug in my game (a disconnected node) and A DAY AFTER I submitted a bug report it was patched and fixed. WHO DOES THAT nowadays? I mean really. Kudos.As it is still in early access, there's a lot of room for improvement as for now it feels to me as an unpolished gem.I had a friend ask me "Should I get this now or wait till it's out of Beta", my answer would be - get it now and start gathering those artifacts. Learn the mechanics and wait for the final release to fully enjoy and appreciate it. I know I am looking forward to see what the game devs have in store for us.

_childDocuments_.review: Gordian Quest is a fantastic game that already provides hours of content with the potential to be mind-blowingly good for fans of games like Slay the Spire and Darkest Dungeon. The team behind the game is friendly, communicative, and passionate about their game. I've already seen great changes made in the game base on pre-EA feedback.On a personal note, I think this game has the potential to be a Game of the Year 2020 contender once it's all said and done. It's basically all the things I love in games rolled into one and executed incredibly well.If you like card games, rougelikes, turn-based RPGS, and character building definitely give it a shot.

_childDocuments_.review: 4 hours in and am really liking the mechanics. I did run into a run ending bug where the map freaked out and I physically could not progress any further because of the bug, but seeing as it is meant to be played across multiple saves not to disimilar to games like Binding of Isacc and I did keep the renouned I had earned in the run so not a big loose.Mechanicly I would say it is like a hybrid between Slay the Spire and Darkest Dungeon, similar to both but at the same time very different from both as well. The way you earn more (or less) cards as you level up but also earn cards that are tied to gear is a nice mix. It is definitly not a 0.5-1 hr entire run like games like BoI and Slay the Spire, it is much longer, which is the only issue I see being that it is to long to be a bit sized game like Isaac but to small to be a single play through game so it falls in a weird middle ground. We have camping which reminds me a little bit at the camping from darkest dungeon but more extended as you can interact with the environment (like building a tent to sleep in, gatherin berries for supplies, etc...) which I really liked a lot. Also some smaller minigames like exploration where the goal is to plan a path through a map to gather the most resources or get the best outcomes. Of course not everything is perfect, for example I had a hard time figuring out the actions of my enemies in battle. _childDocuments_.review: A great card game with in-depth deckbuilding potential. But I think it really need an Occam’s razor to remove/simplify excessive systems that don’t synergises well enough with the core deckbuilding gameplay:Supply – I can go back to the town anytime via a portal and reimburse it for 1 coin each, which do I ever need to worry about supply? Never give me pressure like in Darkest Dungeon.Camping – again, not as critical as in Darkest Dungeon. In DD, I lose everything if I go back to town, here, no penalty at all, so why should I bother camping and making so many trivia decisions (12hr is way too long).Exhaustion – why should I go to an event node where I get an unusable card for sure in exchange of probably nothing? I would suggest, at least for campaign mode, set exhaustion as some debuff accumulated with battle (e.g. each character gain 1 exhaustion after 8 battles) and need lots of coin to remove, so players are encouraged to try different characters. Currently very little incentive given to players to try new squad during the never-ending campaign. I wanted to use a new character during Act 2, then I realised I need to sort out all his items, cards and 30+ skills points in exchange of a new team which is most likely weaker than my current one at start. So I gave up…Crafting – way too complex. The core gameplay of this game is deckbuilding rather than equipment-driven. 中文翻译问题，部分词缀意义不清晰，加上过于复杂的系统和简陋的教程，真的很劝退新手。
