_childDocuments_.review: Gordian Quest is a strange game, and I'm a little surprised that the reviews are not more mixed.Its the combination of roguelite, deckbuilder, tactical game, ARPG. The main twists that make it stand out from the majority of the roguelite deckbuilder genre:- You control not 1 hero, but 3 + allies/summons in a grid based battlefield. Each of them is upgraded separately, has its own deck, items, actions. On its own this would be enough to make it stand out the genre which mostly just copies slay the spire with some tweaks, but this games go further.- The skill grid is the BEST I've seen in any roguelike in my 24 years of game experience. You don't have a huge grid, but after each x skillpoints you can expand your grid with new grid parts, each time choosing between the 3 options based on the 3 available decks for a hero. Even so the best thing about the grid is that you spend the same resource (skill points) for getting new cards, reducing your max deck size, boosting your cards, getting stat points, unlocking talents. This makes them so much meaningful, and you can specialize your character a lot with these decisions.- The equipment system also holds an incredible amount of customization possibilities: each item can hold a fix skill or a card slot, rune slots and additional bonuses.This combos well with the skill grid, since you can get either permanent cards for your deck, attach them to equipment to make them stronger, or you can use "free" item skill, which can even be outside your normal class options. Your dexterity is high, but your intelligence is low? No worries, you can attach an intelligence skill to your equipment with a handy rune that makes it use dexterity bonus instead. You have a really useful card, want 1 more copy for your deck, but you need those stat points to get stat points and talents? Attach it to an item and use a mirror rune. Not only it will be added 1 more times to your deck, but you only need to upgrade and master the original copy.- There are 10 heroes in the game, and each one of them has 3 separate decks with 3 card rarities to build from. In a different game I wrote that this is usually bad for a roguelike deckbuilder, since the classes will only be varieties of the same 3-4 concepts, but here the developers did the impossible, and each character has at least 2 completely different but viable build. MASSIVE achievement. Not to mention that you have 3 of them in the team and the combos between them are also important.- There is a Strategy Point / Synergy system. Its not deep as the ones before, but basically each time you play a card you get SP which you can use to use stratagems and special skills. The stratagems doesn't count toward your deck size/draw, simply options to use when you have enough SP. The basic ones are pretty vanilla (get 1 draw, 1 movement, 1 AP etc), but each hero pair has their own combo moves. To unlock these you need synergy points on your heroes which you get from events, camping, and fighting together, giving a little RPG vibe.- The only roguelite element is the renown system. Basically you get renown for each fight and most quests. These points are shared between all game modes and all runs. You can buy/upgrade relics with it, of which you can use max 6 the same time. The good thing is that they don't give immense bonuses: 1-2 extra resist, hp, skill/stat point for a hero etc. Many roguelites goes overboard with these, making the game easier and easier, but here its a nice little bonus. Kudos!Now a little about the negatives:- the default game mode is the campaign. This is a shame, since it really sucks after the beginning. The story is not that great, you mostly fight against weak enemies and its pretty grindy. The progression is slow. But the thing is that the campaign mode is essentially just a really long tutorial: since the progression is slow and the resources are  basically endless, you can learn how to play certain heroes.The real game mode is the REALM mode. Here the resources are MUCH more valuable, every decision matters, and every fight can pose challenge. You are so limited that I had a run where I reached halfway without getting basically any items. Not good items, just basic equipment. I love itThe problem is that realm mode seems like an afterthought until you try it. I almost dropped the game after my first campaign out of boredom, thank god I didn't do so. Realm mode is the true game, but you need the campaign to enjoy it to the fullest. I highly recommend the developers to simply change the main menu, so instead of a list they appear next to each other with more info. I have a feeling many players dropped the game after/during their first campaign.- the game really lacks in the tutorial/guide department. After you learn the cards, get experience with the game and find all the "hidden" menus and mechanics (like how you can rightclick on a card node on a skill grid to see what cards will be options for that choice) its really good, but its a long journey to get there. This is a harder problem to solve, but expanding the help menu, providing tips'n'tricks popups when the game detects you haven't even opened a menu in the past 20 hours would really help. Hell, even the codex doesn't show which cards belongs to which decks, not to mention you need to realize that the color of the card border shows the rarity. Seriously the best tutorial for the game are actually the Steam achievements which will direct you to check the possibilities in the game. The best example is that my brother (also fan of the genre) had the exact same mixed feelings and almost dropped the game before I give him some insights regarding to the mechanics.In short: I love the game, its on my top3 list for the genre, really creative with its original ideas, streamlined, the graphics are nice, the realm mode is challenging, but if the learning curve and menu would be better designed the game would be much more popular in my opinion.

_childDocuments_.review: Ok, I'm not a guy who writes reviews, but!This game made me come here and start typing.To summarize it in one go is to say: you never stop wondering how this game not falls apart.Is has rich and most in-depth mechanics of all card rouge-likes. _childDocuments_.review: Roguelite with a ton of layers - deckbuilding, passive skill tree, events, gear system with socketing and upgrades. All the parts are well built and it's a really fun whole, but the complexity means there's a lot of stuff to manage and runs take a really long time (a "Quick Run" victory can take over 10 hours). You bring 3 characters (9 to choose from) and each has 3 combat styles plus a passive skill grid, so there's lots of build combos. Gear and socketing are really well integrated into deck strategy, the camping minigame is surprisingly fun, node types and path items make map planning more impactful. Overall the UI does a decent job of letting you manage all the moving parts, which is no small task. I also enjoyed campaign mode although it's only 2/3(?) finished right now, so the ending is a bit abrupt.There are elements that may give some players pause. It takes a while to get enough cards/gear/etc to sculpt your build, you spend a lot of time fiddling with stuff between battles, and you eventually reach a point where you've got the cards you want so your only upgrades come outside of that (gear/gems/passives). These aren't necessarily bad things, but they might not be what some people want in a game of this type.If you're looking for a long form deckbuilder with tons of systems to play around with and you're okay with slightly slower pacing, this game is very very good.

_childDocuments_.review: The gameplay is wonderful. A lot of ways to customize your builds with varied gear, skill and talent choices. The combat systems and dynamics feel balanced and well-designed. I like a challenge so I started right away in Roguelike + Hard mode with a few deaths and restarts as I familiarized myself with the heroes, enemies and hero customization. I'm halfway through a decent run at the moment and look forward to trying out more heroes in the nightmare mode eventually.You'll want to play this game for the gameplay; the story is good enough to serve as a motivational backbone for the heroes to go do what they do. This game is a true gem worth every dollar of its price.

_childDocuments_.review: Enjoyed this game immensely, it's a unique blend of deck-building meets dungeons and dragons meets darkest dungeon. It's a deck-building game that has RPG mechanics and storytelling, so there's this satisfying sense of character and story progression. As you complete quests and fight and get better, you see the town (the hub point in this game) expand. This provides you with more shop and NPC conversation options. This really does provide a satisfying sense of progression. From a gameplay standpoint, your objective is to complete quests and fight monsters so that can get gold and better loot. This allows you to equip your heroes with better items that gives them unique stats and cards that allows you to be more effective in combat. Interspersed in the dungeons are the "dungeons and dragons" moments where you are presented with a written narrative and must make a choice. These choices affect how your progression in that dungeon does though in my first play through, I'm unable to tell what different outcomes there are. The narrative is pretty good and provides a serviceable context to the world we inhabit and the enemies we fight.The art is appealing. The 2D characters and environment are well-designed and the overall UI clear for the most part and easy enough to navigate. The sound design is clear and crisp and provides a satisfying punch during combat. In summary, I think it's worth the price tag. 2 thumbs up, would recommend!

_childDocuments_.review: The game is relatively easy to get into, with a somewhat dizzying level of depth.  Multiple characters to manage, each with their own deck options and builds, equipment, consumables, crafting, etc.  First time I played I actually stopped because there was too much information for me to min max everything.  Fortunately you can go as deep as you prefer, and the character roster is big enough that you can choose what kind of play styles interest you.  The battles are interesting  with movement, initiative, and decent depth to strategy, though some types of encounters are a bit repetitive.  I've played through all the way once, though I got it before the later acts were available so played the earlier acts multiple times.  The success of Slay the Spire spawned a lot of these types of games and I've played most of them.  FWIW this is the one I've enjoyed the most!

_childDocuments_.review: I'm 3 hours in and have already rolled a 1 (the Skull) THREE TIMES in Challenge tests which is an automatic failure regardless of whether you burned cards to give yourself a bonus to the roll and Exhaustion. There haven't been many, maybe 4-5 tests and 3 of them automatic failures.I don't like d20 in tabletop, but this is being run on a computer that could implement any number generation method imaginable. Why not at a minimum change it to 2d10 and raise the challenges accordingly? We're (thankfully) not rolling d20's--nor ANY dice--in combat aside from Initiative, why are we rolling them OUT of combat?[Also no matter how poorly you roll for Initiative, you don't take damage unlike failing a Challenge...you still get to take your turn...if you live that long.]If this were a rogue-like where we're expected to die by RNG, then that would be different--the RNG *is* the game. And I like those games!But this isn't that kind of game. Why give us agency and full knowledge of the results of our actions in combat, but then implement this one thing that takes all that away?In my opinion, rolling a 1 is a bad enough penalty as it is. If you can somehow succeed (by Exhausting your character) anyway, then let the characters do that.Furthermore, is the 20 being an "automatic success" really the balanced opposite of a 1 being an automatic failure? A 20 is always going to succeed, regardless. So what's the bonus?If you want to keep the system as-is, a natural 20 should refund your card and remove exhaustion. Some tangible effect.Is this complaint really worth a downvote?No, but it is super annoying.Edit: I think most recently when I stopped counting I was at 4 skulls in 9 Challenges.(It would have been 4 of 8 but I used my one and only Fate point to reroll #8...and fail) I'm only talking about the Skull rate!This is in addition to just failing organically by rolling poorly.If you don't care about your gold, once the game gets going you can burn gold to get Fate (which is 50/50!)300 gold to get 3 Fate (on average) is a considerable sum.The one thing I will say is when you are on your first mission, losing 4-6 HP from a Challenge is quite significant when you might only have 15 HP.But sometimes those Challenge penalties are not as extreme. So you can save your Fate for the ones that are much more dangerous. [Although you don't always know the risks.]In Combat all information and data (aside from first turn Initiative) is 100% known; you can plan your team's entire turn down to the last 1 point of damage with zero surprises. No d20's rolled. No damage rolled. Nothing aside from random card draw turn to turn.But then...there's completely random Challenges.I still don't get it.And I still say that if the 1 is going to give you something negative, the 20 should give you something positive.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a good game, but it didn't seem so at first.When I first started playing, I expected this game to be something else... More of a roguelike deckbuilder like StS, but this is a bit more like Across the Obelisk than that, but still unique.Don't go into this game expecting a 30min-2h run here and there. This game features a full 15-30h campaign, which is pretty good. However, only after I finished it the first time I realized that the game actually plays much better on the hardest difficulty.Playing this game now with different characters on the highest difficulty is much more fun, rewarding and challenging than when I first played the campaign. There is little to no room for mistakes, but playing on the non-roguelike option lets you revive a hero (for a fitting fee) when visiting town. This mechanic helps when you feel like you've been cheated by some unlucky combination of enemy perks.All in all, this game is pretty good and I would recommend it for fans of deckbuilding adventure games, just go into it a bit more open-minded than usual ;-)

_childDocuments_.review: It just did't click between me and this game. Maybe your experience will differ.The game is a mixture of 2 genres: dungeon-crawler RPG, and Spire-like card building.  From the first it inherits in-depth character development with multiple stats, huge skill trees, and multi-level crafting system. From the latter dynamic combat based on drawing cards, and drafting random cards to add to your deck.On paper it seems like a great combination, but in practice does not play well.In typical RPG story-mode takes way to many hours, and it just sucks that deck-making decisions (or just bad RNG) haunt you for the rest of campaign. You either play on difficulty that makes all combat a joke, or risk being too weak to continue.In rogue-like mode, reading cards, skills and deciding the build takes way too long. It took me 8+ hours to complete 80% of a run. And I even skipped learning the crafting systems!Between runs progression is super unrewarding.To sum up - StS (and many of its clones) is fun because it is fast. I can try wacky decks, fail, learn, and try again (and unlock some stuff on the way). Dungeons crawlers are fun, when I can try different approaches (see Darkest Dunegon). Gordian Quest takes the worst of the two genres**unless you have 300h of spare time to put into this, then you will be able to see its full potential. I didn't.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall a solid and fun play. Rules are mostly intuitive, though a few terms could stand for better definition. As the game is in the alpha stages I expect a lot of changes, currently the difficulty seems to scale from trivially easy to "your party is dead start over" with very little warning. The art and music are both great, the style is consistent throughout. The story (so far) is a bit of generic "bad things are opening rifts to bad places, kill them" but really just serves as a backdrop for the battles, which are fun and engaging.

_childDocuments_.review: I totally get what the game was going for.  I like the art style, the rogue-like nature of it, the exploration, the choices, all of it.I also appreciate that the developers are so invested in their game.  I know they will respond to this review, and I apologize ahead of time for my criticism.  In fact, they did respond to this review, which I do appreciate it.However, there is just too much of... everything.  It reminds me of a YouTube show called, "Epic NPC Man", where it shows a character putting a point in something to put a point in something else to finally get a point in the stat they need.  That's what this game is like.  If someone wants many layered systems, this is a great game.  The problem is that it doesn't work for someone like me.  I like to plan and min-max.  There is not much planning here, so much of it is gambling or hoping a choice pays off.To address the question from the developers - I tried both modes.  I liked the campaign since I know it would end up to a grindy endgame, which is what I wanted.  But I was just overwhelmed with the choices (and possibly not being able to re-do those choices) with my characters.  So I just didn't make any choices at all.  It was the two types of skill trees that threw me.  More tutorials and a deeper codex on everything would probably help.After the fifth or sixth restart, I stopped.  I completely think it's a fine game, but there are just a lot of systems in place and I'm just left to wonder, "why"?  I would restart the moment I put a point into something I didn't want.  Yes, I could respec eventually, but it didn't feel fun at that point.  So I just couldn't keep playing.This game is on my backlog list, so I may very well try again.I have been a gamer for over 30 years.  I tend to play mostly PC games.  I also bounce around between games A LOT.  I may purchase a $60 game and play it for 2 hours or spend $10 on a game and spend 50 hours on it.  Even if I played a game a short time, it does not mean it is bad.  It just means another game caught my attention.  I also complain about flaws in games a lot, even about the littlest of things.  Keep that in mind when reading my reviews.  If I do not have a complaint, then the game must be special!

_childDocuments_.review: I have really enjoyed this game! I have had it for a few years and was playing it with my partner before life got busy; and we both really enjoyed the gorgeous artwork, the level of party customization with equipment and party composition, as well as the turn-based card combat! It was and is right up our alley.I was one of the people hit with the mass steam key revoking; and at first was really scared and thinking I had lost my game forever. While the whole thing has definitely shaken my confidence in Valve and Steam, the team behind this game were absolutely lovely to talk to when I sent an email to their support team and let them know what happened. Not only were they incredibly kind in their emails and explained exactly  what had happened to alleviate my fears; they sent me a new key within 24 hours and the game is happily sitting in my library once more ready to play. Would highly recommend this game, and the team behind it are absolutely swell people from what I have seen with my limited interactions with them.

_childDocuments_.review: I generally do not like to make reviews before finishing the game, but the Halloween event is one where I feel like if I ease the FOMO of one person who is on the fence about the game, then it's worth it. TL;DR of the game - deckbuilder card game at the core, with a huge number of shallow accompanying mechanics, most of which feel like a chore and none feel like they have much depth. Quantity over quality. You can get some fun out of it if you enjoy the genre, but don't expect anything too exciting.TL;DR of the event - looks like the developers are intending to keep up the interest in the game though events. While a good idea, the first event is just awful in every single way. The reward is a couple of cosmetics which is fine I guess. The gameplay is having to replay the same series of 4 missions 10 times to get all accessories. Same set of characters that are almost chosen to be terrible for the missions, with many skills being almost useless. Not to mention the random decks, some of which are even more useless than others + the characters being "high complexity" which really just means that unless you get to draw the right cards, they suck. The most insane part is that when the main appeal of the game are those many shallow extra character customization mechanics, they are not used in the event. And the missions are not even linked so no point trying to perform better in early ones - you'll just revive and heal to full in the next one. It's like someone intentionally took away the very few things the game had going for it. And to remind - 10x4 missions. Grinding of this base level is never a good thing in games.
_childDocuments_.name: Gordian Quest

_childDocuments_.review: A rogue-like deck-building RPG... right now in early access, and has bugs and balance issues, but I am having a great time regardless! Am a big fan of the developer's transparency and frequent updates during early access. Refreshing to see that these days. Can't wait to see where this goes -- has the potential to be one of my favorite games of ALL TIMEEDIT 5/26/2020:So I've now spent more than 70 hours playing just through the first Act, trying out each character in my quest to become a team of ruthlessly efficient killing machines.TONS of potential! And for a game that is still in early access, I've gotten a LOT of enjoyment and eagerly await more of the game to be releasedAreas for growth:1) items and item-granted cards. Often I find myself most efficiently killing monsters when I ignore all of the items that grant ability cards, since they "dilute" my deck and often don't coincide with my character builds. It isn't really until the items reach the two highest tiers that they are worth equipping. It seems like the developer team is aware of this as well since other reviewers have shared that feedback. I don't have a great fix for it though. That's why I'm not in game development :D2) badges/tags/status icons during battle can become quite difficult to see in the thick of battle if there are many units in closer proximity, especially as the game gets more interesting with different modifiers3) big fan of some of the unique items -- they feel powerful and getting the right one can make you nearly unstoppable. But some of them, in certain builds, seem perhaps overpowered, unless the difficulty level in subsequent acts increases substantially.There's also something to be said for the speed with which I can get in and out of the game, and play a quick battle or two, and then save and exit out.Keep up the great work, developers!
_childDocuments_.name: Gordian Quest

_childDocuments_.review: This is the first Slay the Spire clone I've seen that legitimately expands and grows the genre in exciting new directions. It takes the core gameplay loop of navigating zones, doing turn based card battles, and drafting cards for your deck... but adds in a crazy mix of CRPG vibes, randomly generated diablo-esque gear that adds temporary cards to your deck, D&D skill checks, and a really interesting randomly generated skill tree system-plus-drafting mechanic that makes even the same characters build differently each playthrough. The game is pure, mad brilliance.None of that, however, detracts from the fact that it's rough around the edges. That's to be expected from an early access title, but nonetheless: many in-game mechanics are poorly explained or work in highly unintuitive ways, the plot is utterly generic with paper thin characters, enemy variety is limited... I could go on. Thankfully, given that the game appears to be in very active development, I have high hopes that those issues will be resolved in time.When they are, this could very well be the clone that surpasses the original.

_childDocuments_.review: Frick yes.This is everything you like about your top hits like slay the spire or monster train AND everything you missed when playing them such as progression, team composition, items, RPG elements such as skilltrees and talents and even a bit of DnD mechanics. This game has got it all.Game is a bit easy so far, and even kind-of forgiving even when you do misplay. But I'm sure the devs will fix it before full release. And worst case scenario there's always the steam workshop. And yes, the game will have amazing modding potential.
_childDocuments_.name: Gordian Quest

_childDocuments_.review: This one is one of the deckbuilder game that I did not mind the repeatability of the fights. I finished the Act IV in 15 hours, I kinda rushed in the last quarter of the game, skipping fights and some certain upgrades and I did not get any hard times suprisingly. I am guessing that I finished the game so fast, still it took more than 10 hours to unlock other part of the game, and seems like it is the base of it. If you have some time and want to try, I strongly recommend it!
_childDocuments_.name: Gordian Quest

_childDocuments_.review: EDIT:  Thanks for replying, it's great to see developer taking the time to help players with their issues! I promised to update my review after playing a bit more so here goes: Maybe it's just me, but I don't like playing with open hands in a card game. Seeing the enemy intentions are fine, but having the ability to see all their cards makes the battles too predictable and easy. Enemies also seem to have trouble keeping up with the heroes, even "deadly encounters" felt trivial after getting few levels and unique gear. Speaking of gear, when the map opens up you get so much loot that I stopped paying attention to gear upgrades. All my heroes had multiple uniques around lvl 8.Cordian Quest has a lot potential as a turn based strategy game with RPG elements, but the gameplay loop is too long to call this a deckbuilder roguelite. and it's a bit too easy for my taste. There is lot to like though and I might pick it up later in development.ORIGINAL REVIEW:The game is nice, plays more like rpg than roguelite though. A bit easy too, at least the first 2 hours. I can't really say if I recommend this game yet, but for the price it should offer a lot of gameplay and deep deckbuilding mechanics. Will update my review after playing more.Couple suggestions to improve the flow of battle: 1. Show the attack target of all enemies by hovering over any one of them (like in Griftlands). Having to hover over multiple enemies to see who they're going to attack gets old really fast. Also show the attack indicator when hovering over the enemy model, not just the tiny attack icon.2. Please hide the decks of enemies and npc allies. It's confusing to see AI choose from a visible hand of cards. Just show the one card they play.
_childDocuments_.name: Gordian Quest

_childDocuments_.review: One of the best, if not *the* best, PURE Card RPG in the genre!! What I mean is, on top of being a fun and original card-based game, it's also a pure RPG, in that it has all the RPG elements and systems one could expect in a game bearing the term. I've played many of these types of games and there's a small few that separate themselves from the pack, and Gordian Quest is def one of them. Very good game! Thanks devs for your hard work in making it!
_childDocuments_.name: Gordian Quest

_childDocuments_.review: A Deckbuilder/RPG hybrid with huge potential that is tons of fun already. Still a few kinks here and there and some balance issues (as of early access) but nothing that spoils the fun. Bonus points for the devs being very active in the community. If you like these kinds of games you will like this one, guaranteed.
_childDocuments_.name: Gordian Quest

_childDocuments_.review: I am not too far in, but I want to give the game a thumbs up already. The campaign just started to get a bit harder on normal difficulty in act II. I am looking forward to play the skirmish mode on higher difficulties once I am through with the campaign.What I like best is the endless amount of different combinations of skills and builds. Deckbuilding is fun and deep. The meta gameplay reminds me of Darkest Dungeon.All in all, well worth the money.The complexity is a little bit overwhelming in the beginning though. For example I still to this day found no good explanation how those synergy points recover exactly, so I was afraid to use them in combat.
_childDocuments_.name: Gordian Quest

_childDocuments_.review: Wasn't having fun then, 2/3 party members are dead and I even if i was to win without them, they dont level when dead. The NPC ai was so bad, the wizard kept casting the first spell instead of the ones i needed and targeting full health skeletons.Not being able to control my turret was incredibly annoying. Arts nice.
_childDocuments_.name: Gordian Quest

_childDocuments_.review: Ok so i bought the game last night after pondering wether to purchase for a few days.Upon reading the reviews one of things things that persuaded me to purchase the game was how engaged the developer was in responding to community feedback both good and back taking all feedback in their stride.So as other have said the game is like a combination of several games for me its a battle brothers, Slay the Spire, Darkest Dungeon, Ring of Pain mashup taking the best of each. I am only 6 hours in so far however i can say it was the best money i have spent in months and i am finding the storyline engaging and fun. Currently i still have my original 3 characters in my party i have grown too attached to them to swap them out so far.One this i found surprising was the way that the map resets so close to the capital with new encounters in areas i have already cleared. Surely if we are winning the fight we would of secured the city and there would be no threat in the immediate proximity.That said the game is definately worth a purchase and if you enjoy the above mentioned games, alternatively if you have never played them before give it a try i swear blink and 6 hours has passed by and i know my Mrs will batter me when she gets home from work for not doing the house work.For me the game so far is a solid 9/10 and i will post an update once im 100 Hours in.
_childDocuments_.name: Gordian Quest

_childDocuments_.review: The positioning is not a fun new addition to the genre.  It is feature bloat that gains nothing but annoyance.  I'd rather play any other game in the genre than be bored.  Oh, and a run is like ten hours.  Not the point of these games at all.  In an hour here you'll just make it past the tutorial.  Any other game after an hour you're planning your next deck.Just get Circadian Dice.  Fast, customizable, classes, unlocks, actually fun.  No missing a turn clicking one square up.
_childDocuments_.name: Gordian Quest

_childDocuments_.review: Game used to be fairly unbalanced (some cards were really broken OP, others complete junk)  but it is getting better and better every patch. There's still some clunky mechanics like warlock's pools of blood but every class has at least one useful mastery so it's not too bad. Also this is way bigger in scope than most card games, it's closer to a medium-length RPG than a roguelike card game like StS. For the amount of content it has the price is quite low.
_childDocuments_.name: Gordian Quest

_childDocuments_.review: So I just completed the game on normal mode (part 1+2 because of EA).Part 1 in little over 6 hours, part 2 in little over 5 hours.I noticed I was going pretty well with my team in part 1, and my team then got transferred to part 2.I then became very overpowered quickly, because enemies had around 50-60 life, and my attacks deal 70-80 damage. This stayed for the entire 2nd part, which made it more like a grind, than an actual challenge. Overall the game crashed on me 1 time, no other gamebreaking bugs.Would recommend in sale or buy after game is completed for better balance and more content.Currently 7,5/10 would recommond.Edit: Thx for the response. Update: So I played a quick game after the campaign. Also a little to easy (it has 4 or 5 levels).After that, I decided to try and give solo-modes a go. I got to lvl 16. It took around 13 levels and 3+ hours of gametime to get to the challenging part. Even on solo-mode. So there is still quite a lot of balancing to do, but it was fun and it tool little under 6 hours before I finally died.That rush that I got after 3 hours, and that followed in the 2 hours after, thats the golden point to shoot for balance wise. Every encounter might be your last, but you keep on going.Overall verdict is 8/10 now. Will prob pick this up again after full release.
_childDocuments_.name: Gordian Quest

_childDocuments_.review: Fabulous.  It's a tasty mash-up of Slay the Spire, D&D, and Darkest Dungeon.  The character are attractive and likable, I like the D&D elements and unique card decks, and the freedom to choose where I go, which heroes to employ, and which strategies to use.  Fans of "Slay the Spire" in particular really need to pick this one up.
_childDocuments_.name: Gordian Quest

_childDocuments_.review: Reminds me of Gloomhaven a bit. But certainly it isn't Gloomhaven, and a nice mix of RPG with deck building, dice rolls, loot, and character and group progression with turn-based action. I played very briefly the quick mode, to get a feel for the game, and really liked the feel of it. Then tried the campaign version, and am very pleased with what I have seen so far. Fairly quick to pick up, without a lot of hand holding, so intuitive. Very fun so far. Wonder if there is intention for multiplayer? Oh, forgot, there is several modes of play, from easy to nightmare, so far those who like hardcore, this game seems to have it.
_childDocuments_.name: Gordian Quest

_childDocuments_.review: I saw some other reviews describing it as DnD meets Slay the spire, and i'll have to admit that it is a pretty spot on short description. If you're a fan of one, you'll likely be satisfied by this package. It's a solid experience through and through that offers a decent albeit none too exciting story which will see you through 4 acts. The bread and butter of this game is the combat however, at times it can become a bit much as encounters start to feel very similar once you've figured out your "optimal way to win" and you'll likely just spam that to oblivion. What I missed in this game was to care more for the characters, I feel like their stories and interactions with eachother was completely overlooked and also any incentive to try other heroes once you've landed in a trio you feel comfortable using. There was also some scaling issues which I found to be subtracting from the experience where act 1 felt super balanced and sleek and act 2 the complete opposite. Overall I had a few grievances but nothing major, i'd still recommend this to anyone that likes card battlers.
_childDocuments_.name: Gordian Quest

_childDocuments_.review: I like this game a lot, it offers the combat and deck building I expected and the RPG elements are really nice.Pros:+Good Art style, the fights are decent+It is really nice that you can pick classes and that you are not that heavily reliant on RNG to build a certain deck. The reason is that you have a grid-like level system where you can choose what reward to take. Card rewards only contain a subset of all the cards, that the game shows you beforehand, so it is much easier to actually get the card that you want.+The game is much more forgiving than other rogue like games, because you have multiple ways to go and can heal after fights, which is much less frustrating than "I am too weak for this at the moment, now it's game over"+I like the RPG elements like equipment, enchantments, potions, lootCons:-After like 3-4 hours of the game there is no real incentive besides leveling to actually kill all the enemies, because the rewards rarely matter anymore (With the exception of unique items). If i am in the "late" game, 25 gold as a reward feels really bad when the unique items, the only items I want to spend my gold on at this point, cost like 1200 gold.-The enemies need more special attacks so I have to actually care what they are doing. Currently the only thing I really have to pay attention to is to have a tanky fighter at the front and that is all, I have no need to even read the description of the card the enemy will use and I never get punished for it. I can stay at my place and do the same strategy every single fight, that's why fights become stale over time. I would want something like a trap ability for enemies or a channelled spell, that will do massive damage on my characters if it is not interrupted or dodged, so I have to actually move my characters around more. Abilities can and should be more drastic, even a "counter" ability, where an enemy gets massive amount of thorns for a turn would be nice, because I would be heavily punished if I ignore that and just attack him.And these are my personal balancing opinions, this is mostly meant for the developers and other beta players :-Passive cards are too weak. The abilities of the passives are not the problem, they are quite decent, the problem is that every passive card in your hand effectively reduces the number of cards you draw by 1, so if you have 3 passives, you only draw 2 cards per turn, this makes it nearly impossible to have a good deck consistency with classes, that have little card draw. I would suggest to either give passive effects a cost and make it like "play the card and keep bonus until end of battle" or to not make them reduce the cards drawn.-Playing the ranger with constructs feels extremely bad. In order to be effective with this, you need to draw the construct, then upgrade it, but a lot of the time you have to wait a long time for the construct itself and then also have to wait for the upgrade. In other classes this would be no problem but the archer has so many terrible card draw cards and often gets his deck polluted by low value cards like arrows. If you miss one upgrade, which is highly probable because it costs 2, you have to wait for like 4 turns to draw it again. I also think that the mastered version of the epic card that generates upgrades should give mastered upgrades. There also seems to be a bug with the mastered version of the multishot upgrade, because my tower still shoots only 3 times instead of 4.-In my opinion the druid in bear form is a bit overpowered because no matter how low you are as a player, you will get a 60 hp tank fighter for at least 2 rounds without taking damage yourself. But since this is one of my favourite cards and I really like the bear, I don't really mind. - This is a personal preference, but I think a lot of the time the cards that come with the equipment feel like a punishment. In the early game this is ok, because bad equipment should give me bad, unfitting cards too. But later I would want to have more variety and good cards, there are more than enough cards that you would actually want in your deck, even common cards. For example: Cycle cards like "Get Crit, draw a card" or "move, draw a card", summoning cards for towers, wolves etc. (but these should be class restricted). Maybe the best idea would just be to give the player the option to choose if he wants to add the card or not to his deck once he equips it.-Root doesn't behave like I expect it to do. If my heavy soldier uses a strong guard ability which doesn't let him move for 2 turns I would think that he just doesn't get pushed away by enemies. (Because the ability suggest that my soldier wants to stand his ground and prepares for a great impact and that's why he can't move)  This "feature" makes defensive root cards so extremely bad, because once my rooted front line tank soldier is pushed to the back he still can't move for another turn, this seems pretty illogical to me.-Some classes need better draw. The archer really struggles because of this, since he often relies on combos (like arrow + shot, tower + equipment, trap + forced movement). The cleric HEAVILY relies on his one good 0 mana cycle card or his epic draw card, if you don't get these cards, you will often have bad turns because your strong passive cards reduce your card draw. I rarely play mage so I can't say much about him.The soldier and druid have lots of great, common draw cards and don't really rely on combos, rogue has amazing draw cards, that's why these 3 are in my opinion by far the most consistent and best classes.
_childDocuments_.name: Gordian Quest

_childDocuments_.review: No Slay the Spire, but this one tries to have a more substantial story and *mostly* succeeds, though nothing much to write home about. Character design is high point, rather like Battlechasers, and most classes have something interesting to build with. Game drags on a bit near the end, but overall a 7/10 recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: I have thoroughly enjoyed this game, even with only 2 of the 4 acts completed.  It is an engaging squad based rogue-like that has challenging and rewarding battles and builds you can create.  As you master the mechanics and find some of the "cheap" combos, you can crank up the difficulty and play it at an appropriately tough level.  I'm patiently awaiting the next patch!
_childDocuments_.name: Gordian Quest

_childDocuments_.review: It's a rogue-lite, turn-based RPG, where an emphasis is placed on managing the health of your characters (like in DD). The game also features equipment (weapons, armor, trinkets) of various rarities (white, green, blue, purple) that you can equip your characters with and each character has an impressively-sized talent tree as well. You can also select one of several different starter-heroes at the beginning, although this makes little impact later on in the game, as you will encounter (and recruit) all those same starter-heroes later down the line.The game features no voice acting, which is a let-down so you'll have to do A LOT of reading in this game if you're at all interested in the story of the game and the backstory of the characters. And the music in the game is lack-luster, as I've played it for a while now but honestly can't even recall that the game actually HAS any music... and that's a sign that the soundtrack of the game is quite lacking tbh. I do however like the art style, as it all looks very hand-drawn and the hand-drawn models of the characters are ever-so-slightly animated, to bring them to life, which looks very cool imo.The game is currently in early access but I can totally recommend that you play this game already, although I feel that $20 is a little bit too much for this game (especially in early access), but if you've got the money to spare, then that probably won't bother you much. Overall, I fully expect this game to be a wonderful experience (like DD or StS). The devs are VERY active and this game gets updates literally a couple times a week, so it shows that they won't just dump the game like so many other devs do..For more reviews, visit my curator page: For my full recommended list of games:
_childDocuments_.name: Gordian Quest

_childDocuments_.review: Mixed Realms have come out the gate swinging! After releasing the wonderful VR experience Sairento, they have now developed a JRPGesque deck-building game Gordian Quest! Though it initially appears similar to Slay the Spire, the JRPG elements make each 'run' a much longer affair, where you can customise each character's deck (yes, characters - you have a party!) through skill levelling upgrades and randomised rare gear.It's just days out of Early Access, but this game already looks incredibly slick and polished, with few to no bugs. And they plan to add a lot more too, already planning to add an additional 6 characters to the existing generous roster of 6.If you like deep deck-building games, check it out!
_childDocuments_.name: Gordian Quest

_childDocuments_.review: It's a fun deck-building roguelike with some light tactical elements and a massive variety of combos to try. Campaign mode is large and time-consuming with immense scope for developing your team of 3 with individual decks, itemisation and skill development. Only 2 acts currently out of a planned 5, but in 5ish hours I doubt I'm even halfway through act 1 yet. Wonderfully consistent presentation and style, though I personally would have made the significance of the colours used a bit more clear. Respects your time - play continues as fast as you wish, and battles can be quick and painless if that's what you're after, or slow and methodical with mistakes punished severely if you'd prefer. My only gripes are the occasional single-click UI design and the placement of 'back' buttons. Mostly these are in the top right, but then for some reason, they're placed on the bottom left on a few screes. The GUI is just a touch counter-intuitive, but at least the escape key always works. Oh, and the camping sequence is one of the best representations of a adventurer's campsite shenanigans that I've seen in a video game. Sure, it is a little 'gamey', since it uses card-draw mechanics, but otherwise it felt like a real camp-out. I haven't had those vibes since Quest for Glory back in the early 90s. Only slightly undermined by the fact that by the time you get to camp out you've already spent several days traipsing about the wilderness *sigh*. Really cool game with a lot of potential that seems like it will be great fun even as it currently is.
_childDocuments_.name: Gordian Quest

_childDocuments_.review: This is the Deckbuilder for those who cannot live their powertrip long enough. If you like RPGs with turnbased combat and deckbuilders you will love this. The runs are a lot longer than most reference games in the genre: it took me a little over 10 hours to reach the end of the first act on normal setting with permadeath disabled. It's a great coffee-break game to hop in for a combat or two.10h is long but the gameplay loop is enjoyable, card variety sufficient and loot mechanics kept me interested. There is repetition and the game was rather easy which was not a problem since I enjoyed crushing the enemies. I still managed to wipe once and came close to it twice in the later stages which would have been annoying if I had kept permadeath enabled. Only the 1st of 4 Acts is in yet which would mean that if the pacing stays the same we could expect a complete run in the 30 to 40 hours range. Devs are very reactive to feedback, regular patches. Balancing is still ongoing.
_childDocuments_.name: Gordian Quest

_childDocuments_.review: A roguelike, deck-builder RPG? Dungeons and Dragons influences? Character advancement and party placement tactics?At first glance, Gordian Quest looks like everything and the kitchen sink. It has many different genres fused together as one, but it slowly unveils to be a love letter to the better aspects of these genres. Many recognisable influences come from games like Slay the Spire, Darkest Dungeon as well as Card Hunter to name a few. I happen to like these genres a lot. The town and party management aspects were nice, the decisions and quests I went through added to the world, and although it took some time to get used to the different class decks, I liked being able to customise what party I used to face the game, choosing to play a healing tank cleric, as well as a dps-control rogue and mage combo.This game does come with it’s potential improvements. The UI could be more streamlined, and in turn, it could help with the amount of information to absorb, both in story as well as mechanics. It helped that new characters started as ai at first, but balancing the different decks did require some mental gymnastics. Currently, it feels like positioning doesn’t play as much importance, and cards keyed to number shortcuts could make gameplay much faster.As much as it risked having too many cooks, everything in the game clicked. With rebalancing, debugging and improvements, in time, this game will shine.
_childDocuments_.name: Gordian Quest

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: Get this if you enjoy deckbuilding, character optimization, roundbased combat and crazy combos. Don't get this if you're looking for a roguelike runbased challenging deckbuilder.This gets compared a lot to Slay the Spire or other roguelikes and imo that's the wrong genre to compare it to. StS is a very typical roguelike about optimizing very limited and randomized resources during a fairly short run that handles optimization and fights over cards. GQ is a class based tactical RPG with fairly stable rewards that handles fights and character optimization over cards.GQ has some roguelite elements/options, but offers the option to grind xp out, choose your fights and gives a lot more freedom and stability for your character development, which will leave you overpowered if you min-max efficiently even on the highest difficulty fairly quickly. The game belongs more with tactic/classical round based RPGs like Final Fantasy Tactics, Disgaea, classical Final Fantasy games or the Dark Souls card game. Character building is where this game truly shines and where the majority of the depth lies. Essentially you are deckbuilding fairly thin character based decks to combo with each other. The game offers you somewhat plannable and often desirable rewards and I honestly think that a third of my playtime is just hovering over my level-up-board thinking about my builds and which wheel to turn to make it run better. It remains mostly interesting throughout the act and the level of optimization you can hit is pretty crazy. My high-level bard f.e. currently cycles fairly reliably 3x through her entire deck on the first turn.Characters have sometimes more sometimes less exclusive build options and can play and combo very differently. With the right builds characters can pull off ridiculous combos all by themselves and some unique items enable otherwise weak builds to shine. Add to that the characters can enable each other and the game offers a lot of replayability and depth already.  F.e. you can play a trapper and a force mage to trap the enemy field and then push enemies into the traps. Or you stack bonus damage on your rogue and use the druid to pass it to the mage who then uses it to aoe blasts the entire enemy line. Fights similarly to those of the aforementioned TRPGs don't really require this level of optimization and time though. Early on repositioning plays a large role on the highest diff and you need to plan your turns, but once you have a few levels fights get mostly about getting your cool combos into play, which is fun, but not that deep. I'm hoping that they'll do more with levelled enemies for quest/dungeon encounters and possibly with more mulligan options to make less thin decks viable, but we'll see.Noteworthy that the game is early access. And while it's stable (didn't crash once for me), a lot of content is still getting overhauled or is missing entirely (2/4 acts) as of yet. That being said the core gameplay isn't feeling unfinished. There are some elements/builds that are currently in need of further balancing/reworking, but the devs have promised to overhaul many of my gripes and seem to listen to the community.The core gameplay loop was fun enough to put over 90 hours in and I'll likely play more once their next update hits. In fact this is the deckbuilder that I enjoyed far the most of all the recent ones because it very much is it's own thing and works well. Considering that content wise from what was promised we're nowhere near full release I'm very interested to see where this will go.
_childDocuments_.name: Gordian Quest

_childDocuments_.review: UPDATE after ~14 hours:-Combat is still very fun, but decks aren't as varied as other games. This is in part because Gordian Quest is much more campaign-like and less rogue-like, as alluded to. This is a pro and a con. Once there's more meat and variety behind the decks, this will be more of a pro. For reference, I'm still on my first "run". I'd love a shorter game mode integrated at some point.-The devs are EXTREMELY responsive. They've released daily patches, respond readily on Discord, and more. This is super promising-Since it's still very early in the Early Access environment, you can see where variety is needed. Many equipment pieces in slots give you the same cards. Talents/skill tree need a bit more focus. I think this will come in timeBottom line, the core gameplay is fun, and this has potential to be a real treat once it's fine-tuned over the weeks and months.ORIGINAL REVIEW: So far, I'm 3 hours in, and really liking this game. It's still in Early Access, but here are some thoughts:-Takes the Slay the Spire combat system and adds depth with grid-based combat, positioning, etc. I like this as it makes combat a bit more thinky, YMMV-I love the art style and visuals. Gorgeous game. Some people have mentioned the UI is clunky, but I haven't found that beyond a couple minor gripes - you can't pause the game during enemy combat, it can be tough to see who an enemy is targeting sometimes, you have to hover over a card in the right spot or it isn't selected, etc. Absolutely nothing game-wrecking yet.-The card gain system is different than StS. You gain cards through equipment/loot (as in an RPG) or skill trees (as in most ARPGs). You still get end of fight rewards, but those are almost always gold and equipment. As such, your deck pool is more limited than StS, which can be a good or bad thing depending on your perspective. I do wish there were other ways to get cards and thin your deck. Right now, the only way to think your deck that I've found is through the skill tree-This seems more story based and less roguelite-ish so far. I'm 3 hours in and on the same story/run. An StS run is much quicker. The map is also different than StS - you pick where to go, can go back to a home town to heal and upgrade and craft (like Darkest Dungeon I guess). I assume the procedural elements are actual fights and map nodes, but it does feel like there might be less replayability in that sense. Still TBD though, as I'm still on my initial run-Expanding on the above point - there is a "roguelike" mode option, but it seems all that does is permadeath, at least according to the menu-I'm still finding new items, cards, etc, a few hours in. That's a great sign to me-Combat uses 3 characters at a time and they're all different. 6 characters so far. This is a good thing - opens up playstyles.-Events have you doing DnD style skill checks, which is a cool little feature. I don't feel it's a huge/core part of the game as yet, so wondering if this will be expanded uponThings I hope to see in future updates:-More enemy variety-More ways to get and thin cards?-More map node types (everything is either a battle or "event" so far)-Again, I'm eager to see how different replays are different. I'm worried that runs will feel very similar because decks are smaller, I assume the home base is the same, etc, but time will tell-More battle types? Terrain or something? I don't know, spitballing here, because I do like the combat-Really looking forward to future acts!All in all, I'm really enjoying this 3 or 4 hours in, and highly recommend it for StS fans looking for a different style of combat and overall meat.
_childDocuments_.name: Gordian Quest

_childDocuments_.review: Game is awesome, and the devs really care. They try new things, look for ways to shake it up and not make it feel the same, and MOST IMPORTANTLY, when things go wrong, they're more than willing to pull back and make things more user friendly again. If you love deckbuilding RPGs, this is an absolute stellar addition to the genre

_childDocuments_.review: PROS:Nice Art Style on some of the cards.Combat was fun but limited.Long campaign for a card battle game.RPG elements, like class skills and equipment.Cons:Game length can be either a plus or minus. Combat can become very repetitive within a hour or two.Not many class cards to choose from and I pretty much used the same cards most of my time playing.Monsters are also limited, you will be fighting the same ones over and over again. Overall I enjoyed most of the time playing, make sure you play on hard because normal difficulty was a cake walk. Didn't die once during my run.

_childDocuments_.review: Alright, this game rocks socks. I like deck-builders in concept, but this has hooked me in a way that a card game has not done before.It's just the right amount of light story to support the DnD-like framework of the actual gameplay, which is astoundingly good. Building out your characters, equipping them with gear and runes that affect/add cards, picking the team, going back to town to trade and enchant- it all just feels really good. The fights themselves are a lot of fun too, combining deckbuilding with a tactics/movement grid which varies in size depending on the location/size of the fight. I've heard two major complaints about this game, and they nearly turned me off of buying it, so I'll address them.First- 'this isn't a deckbuilder- you don't pick cards often enough.' The truth to this one is that you are certainly NOT getting cards after every fight. Each character has 4 starting decks you can choose for them, and from there, you will get the opportunity to add cards every few levels (you pick from a random selection from one of three schools per class, and you can reroll if you don't like the 3 choices you get), as well as based on gear, which you will find with reasonable regularity. It works. If you're looking for something that is pure 'build a deck,' maybe this isn't your game, but for me, it doesn't take anything away. It feels good, and it doesn't feel shallow. It's not Vault of the Void deep, but it's got plenty of depth for a satisfying challenge between gearing, cards, and tactics.Second- 'It's too easy.' There are five difficulty settings, and I'll level with you- Normal (2) is too easy if you've ever played a card game in your life. Hard has proven to be fun and satisfying. However, I'm not generally worried about getting wiped. There are two higher difficulty settings available, so don't be shy about picking those early. You can also select whether character deaths are permanent, and whether wiping ends your run (I don't recommend it- the game is long- it has a roguelike mode, but the main campaign is not a roguelike).What I don't like here is that there isn't a clear 'this is the way the game was meant to be played- hard but fair' difficulty setting. You can change the difficulty at any time, but I don't want to be thinking about micromanaging my difficulty setting based on whether the last fight felt too easy or too hard.So, difficulty- I would prefer that they tune it. I'm all for 'settings for everybody,' or more specifically, easy-mode for people who don't like challenging games, but I would enjoy having an 'official- game was balanced to be played on this difficulty' setting. It's pretty much impossible to die on Normal- this may ramp up after the first few hours, but 5 hours in, it was too easy. I have no idea what goes on in the nominal easy mode.Anyway, that's a big aside. Two colossal thumbs up for this game. I'm totally hooked, and I don't get hooked very often anymore.

_childDocuments_.review: Although I downvoted the game, I actually want to like it (as evidenced by my 72 hours of gameplay). It has nice graphics (in my opinion) and many card decks and roles to play—around 10 roles, each with 3 strategic sets of card decks. It seems like a lot, but they're actually grouped into a few core strategies: melee/ranged attack traits, support traits, and damage-over-time (DOT) traits. It's fun to discover each deck's potential, but the problem is... in my opinion, most of the decks are useless because the attack strategy is often the best choice. In a game like this, you don’t want to take too long in each battle; support or DOT strategies just drag out the fight and are likely to get you killed if you're overwhelmed (for example, by 9 powerful monsters on the field). As a result, only a few decks are really worth playing.Another issue is that the decks are designed to be very specific to each set, with hardly any synergy across them. So, even though the game offers different sets to choose from, you mostly end up taking cards from the same set. Each set has specific combos that don’t work well with other deck sets. For example, one of the Warlock deck sets revolves around applying "blood" to the player character as a mechanic, while other sets focus on applying "blood" to opponents, which means there's no synergy between self-applied blood skills and opponent-targeted skills. This makes deck selection less impactful and reduces strategic variety.Additionally, item improvements are too random. You often need to boost a specific attribute (like STR, DEX, or INT), and while items can contribute to this, their attributes are randomized, which means you often don’t get the stats you need.The result is that when you near the final act, you end up with the best card set that can no longer be meaningfully improved (due to the limited strategies available in each set). You have to spam the same gameplay loop repeatedly, which makes the late game feel tedious. I’m not surprised that fewer than 10% of players finish the game. So, if it's on sale and you like card games, this may entertain you for a while.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a deck-builder RPG in a similar vein to Darkest Dungeon and Rogue Lords.You build up a party of heroes from various different classes (and there are quite a few different ones to choose from that are interesting), each of which has its own decks and skills.You progress through the zones, battling the undead and bandits, eventually meeting with boss characters (those with better skills and more HP) to progress the story, level up and improve your equipment and decks.There's nothing particularly unique or different here - it's a standard deck-builder game, but it's pretty well done and the story is interesting enough to fill in the gaps between battles. I do like the different classes, which give you a lot of options for different runs through the game. There's also a short-run mode that allows you to do a 1-3 hour dungeon romp, along with the longer main campaign.Overall it's a thumbs up and worth a look if you like this genre of game. I give this one 7 skeleton warriors out of 10.

_childDocuments_.review: A really fun deckbuilding roguelike.  You get a lot of flexibilty with how you can build each character, since each character has access to three different card sets, and you can gain cards from all of them, so you can either focus one one or blend multiple.  You can take three character into a fight so there's a lot of room for cool combos and synergies.  The visuals are great and I really like the art style.  The sound and music is also really good, but the voice acting for the characters is sparse, which is a shame because I think a few more voiced lines could add a lot of personality to them.  My main complaint is that the game feels a bit bloated from mechanics that feel unnecessary (please remove explorations, they add nothing to the game and are very boring).  There are also some mechanics that seem like they're meant to make the game more survivial focused (such as exhaustion, supplies, and camping) but you're never far enough from town to make them worth using.  Maybe they're more useful in the realm mode and the later story chapters, but I haven't tested that for myself yet.

So the game is just mindlessly clicking the same cards for hours with no risk of dying and achieving almost nothing. Until you encounter some of the main quest bosses that counter your build and you'll lose almost instantly. Partly because you got bored of checking enemy intentions 5 hours ago.At the release of EA this was a challenging rogue-like with enemies having a bunch of unfair synergies. That was fun. Now it is just an easy story dungeon crawler.

This often does break the game at very high levels, but there's plenty to do before that becomes an issue.The devs have been fantastic at collecting and implementing feedback so far, consistently adding new content and game modes as well as making general improvements to the game. _childDocuments_.review: I agree with the guy who said that it's 'too many concepts' at once. I give it a 'meh' review, but rounding up (due to early access let's say), so to a positive. So let's start with what I don't like very much:- Some confusion about rows and lanes (will my skill affect it horizontally or vertically? Row is horizontal, but I remember I had confusion about that, I think it's opposite in the game, and not really explained in game), but it's a minor problem, or my lack of understanding;- Artifacts? Not sure how to use them in story mode, they say 'once activated', but in game help doesn't mention how to do that;- I think that 'assign new skill tree' concept is cool, but in practice I found it just annoying, having to do that extra chore on top of other things. I would prefer some 'set in stone' system really. Maybe something like Grim Dawn's devotion system - it's static, but the path you choose matters, so you might invest certain points differently, or aim towards very specific builds that need investment in other trees. Current system feels too RNG and not that meaningful. There might be just specific points you want to get, like later game extra AP per turn, but other than that, I don't feel a clear path in this. Every time I leveled up a character my thinking was '♥♥♥♥ do I have to assign new skill segment or not';- Either I am doing something wrong, or socketed gems are end-game. They're RNG in the shop, expensive to get, so building around them feels meaningless. I guess it's worth fishing for the ones that make you start with certain skill in the beginning of the battle, but rest feel much worse in comparison.- Camping system take so much time and again, I feel it's so tedious, I just avoid camps really. Even though you can get nice upgrades with this, it's just so tedious. Maybe it's just me, but let's say Slay the Spire camp system was simple fast and easy. You still had meaningful choices and it wasn't less fun because it was simple. I guess what I mean is, certain system that has several other independent systems build over it, does not necessarily mean it's good. Maybe for certain people that love that kind of complexity, it would be awesome, but for me it's not. If it only was less tedious, it would be great for sure.Positives:It has nice graphics, interesting gameplay despite of few chory or slightly ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ things. Despite of all the things I wrote above, I definitely had fun with it, it's not easy and at times your ability to think ahead and choose your skills/positioning will be tested. Story mode takes quite a bit of time to complete, but you never feel like it's boring, you'll get new quests and stuff to do. I remember I played till late hours because of 'let's just do one more dungeon'. Overall I don't regret buying this, and assuming some issues will be ironed out, I think it's not bad at all. I haven't played 'arcade' mode much (much closer to classic Slay the Spire), but from the looks of it, it's surely tactical and intense, and some systems that might feel tedious in story mode (skill trees), maybe they feel much better in faster game mode.About 7.5/10 for me.

_childDocuments_.review: There are two features that make a good card game, combos and synergies, the devs seem to think the answer is number and bigger number.In this game your character builds are defined by their stats, their equipment, their talents and their deck. Stats come in red, green and blue and affect the damage of your cards of the same colour deal. Your equipment has effects which boost your damage or boost your stats which also means your damage. Your talents are unlocked on the level up grid, the vast majority of which are a modifier which will amount to more damage.On your level up grid you can instead pick more health or stats, a new card, removing a card, upgrading a card or empowering a card. Picking new cards would normally be the way to a more interesting deck except the game lets you see all the cards you could get, you'll be hard pressed to find cards which synergise with each other, let alone your two other characters.Upgrading a card means increasing the number on the card. It never lowers the play cost, removes a limitation, adds an additional effect or improves a card beyond number going up. You can upgrade a single card 4 times for the biggest number but this has an adverse effect on your desire to create new cards since every card means you're less likely to draw the card you invested points in. Empowering a card does offer some genuine upgrades like changing an attack into an aoe or increasing its range (along with bigger number) however the game won't give you many options for this.The game's equipment system offers a further anti-synergy by having rare equipment give you a card. You can't decide what card, the card you're given has its normal cost and effects and along with being useless to your deck strategy, might be the wrong stat colour. If you want to avoid filling your deck with bricks the dev has unwittingly created a system where rare gear will often be worse gear.Since this is a game with lanes and movement I have to comment on that too. You don't know how many lanes will appear in a battle, might be 4 or it might be 2. If you're using characters or equipment which boosts your numbers by moving around you'll find yourself stepping on your own toes while repositioning since your normal characters have to spend a special sp point to move back into position, a point they could have spent on a more powerful card. This goes double if you play any characters which summon minions or are joined by an npc who will step off the front line to push your archer there instead.Since the devs are on another planet from what I'm looking for in a card game I'll lay out what I'd hope to see in a subsequent game:1. Keep the number of lanes static and let the player decide the exact position their characters will appear in the starting formation, not just the row.2. Put an indicator over the enemy's head what their next move will be so the player can plan around it instead of having to click the enemy portrait and see what cards are in their hand.3. Tie formation and positioning bonuses to characters and equipment not just cards. This will give the player more reason to care about gear and give the devs more room to work with than raw numbers.4. Give characters cards which synergise with each other. This could be simple like: Rogue places bomb, wizard creates gust of air pushing enemies into bomb. Or it could be an involved combo like: Golemancer adds boulder ammo to each character as a ranged attack card. Artillery commander plays cannon which also gets the boulder as it counts as a character, forest guardian summons Wojtek the bear who reduces the cost of all ammo cards for adjacent characters to 0.5. Dumb down your equipment system but make it meaningful. Characters don't need 13 slots of randomly generated +1 stats they need a few slots for artefacts which make a meaningful difference in game. Players of Binding of Isaac or slay the spire are familiar with this, a few effects which you can build your deck around and which synergise with each other are far more impactful than a dozen number changers. For example one artefact could cause you to reveal the top card of your deck and if its a different colour than the card you previously played an effect triggers while another could let you draw an additional card from the bottom of your deck then make you place a card on top each turn.I know creating interesting effects and interactions is much harder to balance so it'd mean fewer modifiers, fewer stats, less equipment and fewer characters but I think that'd be to the game's benefit. I bought this game with Alina of the Arena, that position based card game only has one character with starting builds separated by the starting artefact and two alternate cards yet its gameplay was immediately more engaging as reflected by its better review score.
