name: Airborne Kingdom
detailed_description: Tales speak of a mythical Airborne Kingdom, a floating metropolis that united all the nations of the world under its banner. One day, it disappeared, leaving its allies alone, and isolated. Decay and decline soon followed, with each left to fend for itself. Aeons later, a spark of hope emerges: A new floating city takes to the skies, to hopefully rekindle the tales of old and unite the struggling people of the world once more. Reconnect them and usher in a new era of harmony and prosperity. Take control of this new sky city and build it up from a fledgling town to a bustling metropolis stretching across the horizon. Roam the skies of the world, seeking out resources and opportunities below, find lost temples and deserted cities, complete quests, and usher in a new era of prosperity in the critically-acclaimed sky city builder, now available on Steam! Construct the sky city, a beacon of hope for the people of the world. Build housing and service buildings, research technologies, and gather resources to sustain its community. Face crucial challenges. Balance air drag with propulsion, lift with mass, and of course, the timid tilt. Attend to the people. Citizens require houses, food, medicine, and assorted creature comforts. Create the infrastructure to meet their needs and take the first steps towards making myth reality once more. Explore a vast, randomized world. Locate raw materials and process them into resources necessary to expand the city and seek out terrain-bound kingdoms to bring into the fold. Aid the struggling ground kingdoms. Complete quests to gain their allegiance, expanding your city's influence and establishing its legacy. Unearth the secrets of the first Airborne Kingdom, exploring the skies and seeking out secret shrines and forgotten ruins, learning its rich history. Build and optimize, explore and help, or just kick back and relax as the floating city makes its way through the sky. Tinker with the city in Creative Mode and create the greatest floating city in history, free from resource limitations or the pressure of time. Enjoy a vibrant art style and calming soundtrack, as you restore serenity to a world in need of hope. Seek out greater heights with previously released DLC content including New Game Plus and a Hard Mode
about_the_game: Tales speak of a mythical Airborne Kingdom, a floating metropolis that united all the nations of the world under its banner. One day, it disappeared, leaving its allies alone, and isolated. Decay and decline soon followed, with each left to fend for itself. Aeons later, a spark of hope emerges: A new floating city takes to the skies, to hopefully rekindle the tales of old and unite the struggling people of the world once more. Reconnect them and usher in a new era of harmony and prosperity. Take control of this new sky city and build it up from a fledgling town to a bustling metropolis stretching across the horizon. Roam the skies of the world, seeking out resources and opportunities below, find lost temples and deserted cities, complete quests, and usher in a new era of prosperity in the critically-acclaimed sky city builder, now available on Steam! Construct the sky city, a beacon of hope for the people of the world. Build housing and service buildings, research technologies, and gather resources to sustain its community. Face crucial challenges. Balance air drag with propulsion, lift with mass, and of course, the timid tilt. Attend to the people. Citizens require houses, food, medicine, and assorted creature comforts. Create the infrastructure to meet their needs and take the first steps towards making myth reality once more. Explore a vast, randomized world. Locate raw materials and process them into resources necessary to expand the city and seek out terrain-bound kingdoms to bring into the fold. Aid the struggling ground kingdoms. Complete quests to gain their allegiance, expanding your city's influence and establishing its legacy. Unearth the secrets of the first Airborne Kingdom, exploring the skies and seeking out secret shrines and forgotten ruins, learning its rich history. Build and optimize, explore and help, or just kick back and relax as the floating city makes its way through the sky. Tinker with the city in Creative Mode and create the greatest floating city in history, free from resource limitations or the pressure of time. Enjoy a vibrant art style and calming soundtrack, as you restore serenity to a world in need of hope. Seek out greater heights with previously released DLC content including New Game Plus and a Hard Mode
short_description: The sky city builder awaits. Create your own flying kingdom and lead it on a quest across an expansive world. Explore the varied landscape, build up a floating metropolis, aid struggling people below, uncover lost secrets and, ultimately, bring back the Airborne Kingdom legend.

_childDocuments_.review: Just finished my first playthrough after collecting all the wonders. I will say that like many others, the game is definitely a bit short and the lack of other scenarios does diminish the incentive to replay it for much more than just wanting to build a city that looks different or is a little more optimized. Additionally it's also not particularly hard. Even as an experienced City Builder, most games I end up having to restart multiple times early on as I get my head around the mechanics. The airship premise seems to come with a handful of ups and downsides.For one, it's really cool, and I love the style that comes with building a city in the sky. Additionally, I really like the nuances of the mechanics related to that. You have to manage not only having devices that provide lift for your city and the fuel to power it, but also have to manage things like propulsion devices to help your city move, and making sure your city's weight is balanced so that you don't tilt too far to one side or the other. The main downside though, and it's not really that big of a downside it's just a minor thing, but the mobile flying city premise also means that the pace of the game is entirely within the player's hands. Now this sounds like a good thing and like I said it's not like it ruins the game or anything. But the practical upshot of this is that the game can't 'surprise' the player like how lots of other city building games do. For example games like Frostpunk or Surviving Mars do things like throw storms at you or lower the temperature regardless of whether you're ready for it or not, forcing the player to adapt with changing conditions. Meanwhile with this game, the change in circumstances comes with flying to new areas, but because you control where you fly, that means you can always put off flying to the harder areas until you're ready for them, which I think is where a lot of the reduced difficulty comes from.All that said though, it's still a fun game, and I agree with the notions that it's a very 'zen' game to play if you enjoy building. However I would also love to see some kind of DLC or updates to the game that add more things to do. Maybe even new obstacles like weather could be added that cause various effects that force the player to adapt. And more building types would be nice in general. The people in your city feel like a fairly straightforwards resource, so adding more things like say the ability to get sick and having to manage healthcare or other forms of entertainment for your citizens or whatever could be fun additions to mix up the gameplay just a little more.Also one other minor annoyance I have with the game is that you can't manually assign people to different buildings. You need to have enough people to man the building when you build it, and if you want to reassign those people to something else, you have to deconstruct that building. I feel like if you could manually assign people to their jobs it would help free up some room for some more micromanagement. Overall, it's a pretty good city builder with a slight amount of indie jank that is long enough to at least entertain you for a day's play session. But you might need to be really invested in the premise to want to play it more beyond that. But as someone who is, I hope to see this game expand into something really special.

_childDocuments_.review: Airborne Kingdom is an interesting take on the Banished genre of city builders.  Where Airborne Kingdom is unique is that it has added both tactical and role playing elements.  Your character in this tactical RPG is your city.  Choices you make about the layout of that city change how effective you are at traversing the skies.  Traversal is in itself a challenge as well because your city is always needing new resources, but what is on the ground is limited.  So there is this need to constantly be on the move and planning your next route.  Balancing building up versus completing a quest for a city that needs help.  Quests unlock more tech which improves your city further.I play a lot of these city builders and I find Airborne Kingdom to be an interesting take on the genre as it offers new situations and new choices I haven't encountered before.

_childDocuments_.review: I have built a lot of cities over the years, and I've given my citizens plenty of reasons to flee them.Airborne Kingdom is the first city builder where I've lost people because the city was leaning too much. Before this became a review, my plan was to play an hour of Airborne Kingdom to get some achievements, but instead it ended up stealing most of a day, with me finally leaving my floating metropolis at midnight.I'm an easy mark for a city builder and rarely manage to escape their grasp quickly, but Airborne Kingdom lodges itself in its own niche thanks to some unusual experiments and its spectacular style. The basics are familiar and conventional: you build simple production chains and infrastructure to fulfill the needs of the city and its denizens, with the demands of both getting more complicated as you expand. Power, food, factories, morale-boosting diversions—there's loads to build, but you'll recognize all the categories. All this is happening in the sky, though, and that's a pretty substantial wrinkle.Airborne Kingdom doesn't feature any combat or even a whiff of conflict, at least not with other people. The war against gravity, though, never ends. Physics is a constant obstacle, and more than anything else it's that force of nature that determines your city's layout.You start out with just a little town center, gently bobbing away in the sky, perfectly balanced. Once you start placing houses, hangars for your planes and towering minarets, it's going to start sinking, so you'll need to generate more lift. And you're going to need to make sure it's all even.  Too much tilt and your citizens will peace out. And who can blame them? Nobody wants to live in a place where they have to nail down their furniture, or where they're greeted by a view of the ground, miles below them, every time they look out the window.They can stomach a little bit of tilt, but I can't. It just looks like a disaster waiting to happen. And it only takes one little building to push it over the edge. You have to find and directly recruit your citizens, their loss can sting, and you might end up left with too few people to work or explore, necessitating some unwelcome downsizing as you destroy buildings and try to plan your comeback.They're a precious resource, but it's coal that keeps your city aloft. All your most important components burn through the stuff, and unlike other resources it can only be stored in one location, limiting how much you can stockpile.Without that resource, the city's done for—sadly it's a bit too heavy to gently float to the ground. Physics ends up being an excellent replacement for terrain.Geography is a defining feature of a city, and thus city builders, but it loses its impact when you can soar above it all.You've got infinite space, but thanks to physics you can just keep expanding in whatever direction you want.You have to build methodically, and then make lots of little adjustments.If the city is lying a bit low, maybe chuck in a new fan or some wings.If all the new buildings are creating too much drag, some more propellers could give you a bit more propulsion.All of these things require resources, workers and space, of course, which might inspire yet more adjustments. These limitations have forced me to spend a lot more time considering how my city should grow, and it means no section is ever really complete—I'm always redesigning them.The result is something dynamic and organic, constantly shifting to meet new needs.I had a plan for how I wanted my city to look, and it now looks nothing like my vision.Instead it's something built out of my reactions to imminent disasters, my experiments, my experiments to fix the problems created by my previous experiments, and a few cosmetic flourishes.It's a bit of a mess, but I love it.  The world below still plays an important role. It's where all your resources are found. Absolutely everything you need to build with, continue flying and keep your people alive is found on the ground, and you can explore the entirety of the map at your leisure.To keep your city fuelled and fed, you'll have to constantly stay on the move, sending down workers in planes to gather up what you need.While Airborne Kingdom doesn't lean into its survival elements as much as, say, Surviving Mars, the relationship between the world and the survival mechanics is as strong as it is with a pure survival game.A settlement surrounded by waterInstead of giving you more places to build, the world exists to be explored.There are small settlements and cities waiting to be discovered and traded with, plenty of hidden bounties, and a few secrets that can be used to unlock wonders that will make your already very impressive city even more enviable.The map is presented as a literal map, with little embellishments like curling, torn edges, and provides just as much eye candy as the city. Despite dabbling in survival management, Airborne Kingdom maintains a relaxing pace.There are complications, crises and plenty of ways to ♥♥♥♥ everything up, but the first biome has all the resources you need in abundance, letting you build up a nice stockpile, and while scarcity can become an issue, you can return to a less challenging area pretty quickly and recuperate.For the most part, it's light and breezy.Those aren't typically adjectives I seek out in management games, but it's really kept me too focused on scouring the map and working on my own projects to notice that the challenges are infrequent and tension rare. Importantly, this pleasant pace gives you plenty of room to flex your creative muscles. You're not just building a city—you're creating a weird architectural marvel. While there are plenty of concerns that will shape your city, you're also free to follow your aesthetic tastes. This goes beyond building placement, too, since you'll uncover lots of paint schemes that you can apply to buildings individually, by type, or all at once. The only place the breeziness becomes a problem is when you're dealing with other cities.See, your ultimate goal is to create your airborne kingdom by forging alliances with all the cities on the ground, unifying the world.It seems ambitious, when in fact it's a doddle.You fly up to a city, find out what it needs, get directed to the exact spot you'll find that thing, and then—after depositing some resources—you're best buds.Nobody seems to have any concerns about this flying city appearing out of nowhere and making everyone join its empire, either. Once you've added a city to your list of allies, you never really need to think about it again. Your allies are always content. Airborne Kingdom never really explores its premise or lets you question your objectives. You don't need to make hard calls or worry about becoming a tyrant, because you're always presented as a benevolent force that everyone wants to be mates with.  A large cityThe ground-based cities also serve as trade hubs, offering up a long list of resources you can barter for.It's handy in a pinch, but I never found myself needing to go on spending sprees and only went shopping once or twice.The whole system really just seems to exist for emergencies, and there's no economy to interact with.You won't be creating trading routes or trying to turn a profit.The cities value different things, so you do need to think about where you're shopping, but it doesn't get much more involved than that. Overall this is a relaxing builder, with interesting art style, and one to play.

_childDocuments_.review: When I finished the campaign in Airborne Kingdom, I did something that I never do. I immediately started a new campaign. I know that’s a normal thing for a lot of people, but I’m very much a one-and-done gamer; usually when I beat a game, I’m fully satisfied to move on to something new. But not this time. Six hours in this game’s serene, storybook kingdoms simply wasn’t enough for me. I had to have more, had to build out a new flying city, and unite the world all over again. That’s what you want from the best building sims, that feeling that you cannot let go of the experience, and that is absolutely what is present here.Long ago, a legendary kingdom in the sky traveled the world, imparting knowledge and aid to the many kingdoms of the land. Their efforts brought peace and prosperity to all, until they vanished. In the intervening years, kingdoms fell upon hard times, and retreated into isolationism. The golden age of the world ended, but now you have the chance to bring it all back. The original airborne kingdom left behind plans for a new flying city, and you are to command this reborn hope for the world. Striking out from the arid deserts, you must grow your aerial burg, locate the twelve scattered kingdoms, and bring them together in some semblance of the peace and prosperity they enjoyed so long ago. Only then, will you learn of the fate that befell those who traveled the skies before you.Setting aside the absolutely fantastical optimism of a technologically-advanced society that DIDN’T use their powers for conquest, this is a marvelous premise for a game and fits extremely well with the serene atmosphere of the gameplay. Starting out, you have only the main building of your flying city. From there, you build paths, housing, workshops, and warehouses as you would with most resource-based builders. But given the unique nature of the game, you also have to place hangars for gatherers to launch expeditions from, mechanisms like wings and turbines to keep the city afloat, and different engines to help move the city across the world. Your chief concerns are food, water, and coal, and while you get options to use or process them more efficiently, you’ll always need to be replenishing your supply from the surface. Beyond that, you’ll need an assortment of other resources like wood, clay, and quartz to build your burg out. Some are renewable, some aren’t, but sourcing all of them will factor heavily into where you city goes and how it gets there.Another key concern that really spices up the building is the tilt of your city. Not only do you need to generate enough lift to stay airborne, you need to balance it out so your citizens aren’t living their lives at a permanent Dutch angle. Your options for balancing tilt are wide open, too, because you can try to build things symmetrically, or you can cluster all your thrusters at one end and all your buildings on the other like some kind of mortal see-saw, or you can try all sorts of other configurations. Your population will have new demands as it grows as well (as new citizens can be recruited from terrestrial towns), including lit roads, sources of faith, health care, and more. The mood of your city determines how easy it is to recruit new folks, and you can research all kinds of buildings that mix and match satisfaction of different needs, like tea houses and spirit healers. You’ll need to research all your new toys for your town, after buying the tech from the old kingdoms using relics found in ruins dotted around the map.I think this might be my favorite aspect of Airborne Kingdom, how smartly all of its systems are interconnected. Exploring the map is hugely important, since that’s how you’ll find the kingdoms you need to unite. But you’ll also find towns to expand your population, ruins that provide relics to trade for tech, secrets that allow you access to powerful wonders, and even workshops that give you new color customization options for your city. Certain regions have unique resources or, more importantly, lack certain staples like food or coal, so getting your kingdom ready for tougher journeys is part of the progression as well. It’s immensely satisfying to start out with a tiny, barely-functional village struggling with lift and stocking necessities, and eventually build up to a flying juggernaut that can survive comfortably for days without gathering expeditions.Each kingdom you meet will have a main quest for you to complete to earn their trust, usually a simple task like building them a structure or locating a nearby ruin. Further-flung kingdoms have more complicated requests, but none of them are particularly taxing. Between the quests and exploring, there’s enough to do to keep you busy as you tool across the skies and build out your own kingdom. It took me about six hours to reach the ending, and then I immediately jumped into the New Game + mode which randomizes the map and offers you new city centers to choose from. There’s also Normal and Hard difficulties for any new game, though I didn’t notice a huge difference between them. Either way, you’ll have plenty of ways to enjoy this gorgeous, storybook builder as you explore and expand. I’ve gotten pickier about builders in my old age, and Airborne Kingdom absolutely hits the sweet spot for me of interesting systems and relaxing development.Did you enjoy this review? I certainly hope so, and I certainly hope you'll check out more of them at  or on my !

So let's build this city in Airborne Kingdom.The game is a city-building game that involves managing, distributing, and collecting the resources that you have from the areas around you, and since it is a flying city, you can move around the map and explore the world. Also, you may meet some villages that may provide you with some workers for your city, and you may meet large cities and they will help you can get some resources and experience, and also will give you some very simple side tasks and most of them are either to provide them with some resources to build something or to rescue some people who are stuck in a place. The number of main missions in the game is very few and there are no special missions for your city or your residents or even random missions that may make you play longer. And also since the city you take care of is a flying city. You have to take care of balancing its weight between all sides and also put some fans to speed up its movement.The game is also a kinda survival game. You may face some difficulties due to the lack of some resources that help you to survive, such as water, food or coal in the world, and you must travel a certain distance to reach the places where these resources are available, or to buy them from the large cities around you. and you must check all your resources before you travel to new continents. This game may not be considered a relaxing game, your focus on resources, the weight of your kingdom, and your focus on satisfying your inhabitants is always important. That's why I don't recommend new people to start with this game unless they want some challenge.The experience tree in the game is so simple that you either combine more than two buildings into one or upgrade the ones you already have. As for changing the shape of your city, there are many colors to change the shape of buildings or the colors of roads and city buildings, and these colors you may get it through the cities that you will meet when you travel in the world.The world you meet is random each time you play, so you may not find many Guides for the game. Therefore, if you want to search for a specific building in the map, you should focus well on the screen in front of you. Also, the game contains 3 main continents in the game, and each of them has some advantages and disadvantages, such as a huge availability of food, but there is not a lot of coal. There is a side continent that has its own mission that you may not notice while you are playing which is a nice addition to the game as it makes you reorganize your city due to the obstacles you may encounter there.After you finish the game, you can start a new game, which contains larger continents and more challenges, and you can also customize your city center to give you some advantages, but I did not try it.The story of the game is very simple and will be mentioned at the beginning of the game, which is an ancient legend that there is an ancient kingdom that united all the cities scattered on the continents, but it vanished and disappeared and now you are trying to restore the glory of this city again.game graphic is close to the cel-shading and the design of the cities is similar to the Arabic design, and this thing suits it very well. As for the music, it is beautiful, but I do not think that it is considered good for long periods of time playing.A unique building game and worth a try for those who have experience with this type of game. But I wouldn't recommend it to people who are new or don't want to bother with resource management.aaaaaaaaaand that it <3

_childDocuments_.review: City builders are not my usual genre of choice, but I like to play one occasionally. When I saw Airborne Kingdom, I thought "huh, interesting aesthetic. And building a city in the sky? That's fresh". It immediately made me think of Miyazaki's "Castle in the Sky". What I didn't know at the time that the game is actually more like another of Miyazaki's movies - namely, "Howl's Moving Castle". Because the fact that your kingdom is floating is not just for pretty sights; you can - in fact, you have to - fly around the world while building your city!This might seem like nothing special, but in fact it completely changes the way you think about trade, resource gathering and story. Almost like it's not a city builder at all, more of a survival game. If that sounds a bit confusing, let me get into a bit more detail.Since you're constantly in the air, you need coal to keep your engines operational. In order to get coal, you need to find a deposit and send workers to the surface on little planes to gather it. You can either "park" your city over the deposit for quick gathering, or you can just do a fly-by and tell your guys to gather what they can while they're in range. Of course, this doesn't apply to just coal. You need also food, water, wood, multiple construction materials... and you can't just keep farming one thing forever, there are quite significant storage limits - and that forces you to be constantly on the lookout, hovering your mouse over the terrain, looking for harvestable resources. I loved that part. I can see it being tedious to some, as it requires your personal attention; to me, it was an excellent excuse to keep looking at the ground, watching the sights. You might've noticed I mentioned a story. Yes, this game has one - it's about using your status as a mobile fortress to help unite the fractured world. There are twelve kingdoms; all of them more or less isolated from each other due to inhospitable terrain and internal issues. That's where you come in: help them with their problems and guide them towards unity and cooperation with other kingdoms.If that sounds ridiculously optimistic to you, that's because it is. This game is incredibly optimistic in general. I'd describe it as "Anti-Frostpunk", mainly because a lot of raw mechanics are almost directly taken from Frostpunk - but the theme of the game is almost exact opposite. And I welcome this change. If Frostpunk is about making impossible choices in the face of utter despair, then Airborne Kingdom is about helping humanity reach its full potential.Another fresh thing is the ethnic theme of the game. It's pretty clear that this game is heavily inspired by Arabic architecture and culture - without referencing any religious elements. People of the world are presented as hardy, a little slow to trust, but cooperative, hopeful and revering their ancestors - albeit not in a way that curtails their progress. And that's great.I mean, whenever people from the Middle East are represented in (western) mainstream media these days they're seen as loud, rude, dangerous, regressive; antagonistic. At best, there's a wise, quiet Muslim scholar, or warrior-poet or some such. So it's a huge breath of fresh air to see that general ethnicity being represented in a completely new light. Not something you see every day, you know?The game can be a little slow at times. Or shallow. The city building is somewhat barebones by modern standards, but I don't really mind. There's an interesting lift and tilt system in the game; you have to make sure your city has enough lifting power to stay afloat, but also to keep everything balanced - nobody wants to live in a city where everything is tilted 10 degrees to the left. So as your city grows, you'll also be adding a lot of doodads and balancing things, like a balloon to lift that a little too heavy housing block; it creates this "living contraption" effect, again, reminiscent of Howl's Moving Castle.Airborne Kingdom is probably not as emotionally potent as Frostpunk, but even so, the game managed to surpass my expectations. Once I started playing, I pretty much got through the entire story over the course of 2-3 days. If you like city builders, give this one a go - if nothing else, it'll expand your horizons about how much room for growth the genre still has. Enjoy!

_childDocuments_.review: i would say this game is "meh", but steam wants me to either "yes" or "no" it.It took me about 14 hours to complete this game 100%, to get every achievement. and i paid about 16 bucks for it.i am a fan of the "1 buck per hour" - guideline, so in my opinion this game is just a tiny bit too short of that. nevertheless, it is an enjoyable experience, if you like calm and atmospheric city builders.therefore you should buy this game if you have money to burn, but not if you're on a budget.the game actually has a story and discoverable lore, something i greatly enjoyed while playing, and sometimes when i was close to running out of ressources, i got a bit panicky, for example i ran out of food, and there was noo food source around for miles, so i quickly deconstructed some homes to make a propeller to get to food faster, and in the end i managed to make it, but just because people don't really die in this game:when you inhabitants lack anything, be it food, water or comfort, their mood degrades, and people on low mood tend to leave.what is especially frustrating that, out of the 5 levels of mood the peeps can have, only 2 of those ensure that your peeps don't simply run off of your city. and THAT is a problem, as people are your main ressource to building stuff and gathering ressources. so it's easy to get softlocked when your peeps get a bit miffy.i would have liked it more if people would just work slower on lower mood, and only left on the lowest mood. why else should there be 5 levels of mood, if the last 3 are just the same?on the other hand, the quests are really great and unique! every city you sumble across has a questline, and they differ greatly from each other, demanding different things from you, and fit to their theme! something other games could learn about.but all in all, this game is relatively easy, and i played new game plus on hard difficulty, and have yet to go game over.TL:DR;game is fun and good but short and small

_childDocuments_.review: I really liked this game. The fear of actually falling from the sky made the stakes high, but the real charm of this game is exploring the beautiful landscapes of a harsh world.  I disagree with other reviews that it didn't have enough content -- I think it did much better by doing less in specific areas.This game is very aesthetic and it does it well. The map is artistically and fancifully rendered, and the different effects in the different lands, like heavy cloud cover, ice, and craggy mountain ranges force you to search for objectives and goals on the physical map. The customization options for your city are so numerous it is overwhelming, but you can quickly apply design presets to make your city look like a steampunk haven, a green oasis or a winter wonderland. Which is great because I couldn't be bothered to customize each building individually, although I think you could do a lot with that. The soundtrack is absolutely to die for and the camera tends to be easy to work with, letting you coast along with the city as you change the layout of the hedges. Despite needing to be cautious about running out of supplies, a lot of the charm of this game is in enjoying your creation chugging along.I think the choice not to make the game overly micro-managey was a very good one. Instead of clicking around in various menus, the game allocates people to tasks, assumes they are going for weekly checkups at the clinic, and makes sure the hang gliders make it back somehow. This means you can focus your attention on, you know, being the captain of a floating empire!!! I get frustrated with the opposite -- managers that have too much going on and none of it is balanced, and everything is full of bugs. This game picked a few strengths and built them out beautifully. Looking at comments from some reviews, most people's issues seem like decisions that were made for a reason. (It's fine not to like them, I guess) You can't disallocate staff from buildings in your flying city because you are meant to plan ahead and be efficient, and there is research that allows you recover all the resources from disassembling buildings. Before having that research, you need to carefully balance what you build with the utility you will get from it. In fact, most of this game is geared toward making you think about efficiency. There are more things to research than you will want to spend time on, because you are meant to make a choice and adjust your strategy to that. Navigation is also a central part of the game, so it makes sense that they didn't put in minimaps and shiny trails to your objective because that is literally the challenge of the game -- going where you aren't sure your objective is and wondering if there will be resources when you arrive. I did find myself wanting to mark the map myself, but you can get a wonder that reveals all landmarks on the map, so that feels fair enough to me.The masochist in me does admit the game has kid gloves at certain points. When people are dissatisfied and leave, it almost always makes managing the city easier, rather than punishing you for mismanagement. I think that it would have been more of a disincentive to have them take some resources with them. Also, in the north, when I got food and water bonuses from survivors, I noticed that they weren't "dumped" when my storage was full even though they should have been, as in what happens when you dismantle too many buildings. This made the north part much MUCH easier than I thought it would be, as I thought I would regret dismantling my water towers and food silos for more lift, and I ended up with free storage from the game. (Or possibly it was some kind of soft storage in the farms and water collectors? I'm not sure)All in all, I love that this game had such a nice take on the genre, and that they took the time to create a complete and finished game with interesting lore, smooth controls and beautiful graphics and sound and it is overall a real pleasure to play.

Sort of a Once and Done deal for me-A couple areas of the map are visually very hard to see. Even with clouds disabled-You can't unassign or reassign your population or "disable" certain buildings when not in use-Does get a little repetitive with very little to worry about other than keeping resources in supply-Sort of expensive considering the lack of replay valueOverall you'll enjoy it. _childDocuments_.name: Airborne Kingdom

_childDocuments_.review: I would love to be able to enjoy this game but there are so many essential features missing it is simply not possible. Playing feels like annoyances piled on top of annoyances, which is a shame because the concept is so unique.The most jarring one is being completely unable to unassign workers from buildings. Would you like to slow down your research so you can speed up a resource production? You can't! Instead, you must destroy your entire research building. Do you no longer need to produce a certain item, and would rather send these workers to gather something instead? I hope you enjoy having to bulldoze your production building to free up those workers, because that's the only way you can do this!The game also lacks a minimap, which is absurd when it revolves around navigating a large world.I'm very disappointed that the devs are announcing a new game while this one remains devoid of such major features.
_childDocuments_.name: Airborne Kingdom

_childDocuments_.review: Game is fun. It's like a nomadic airpunk version of Homeworld combined with a city builder, but there's no enemy air raids to worry about, you just have to make sure you don't run out of resources and down yourself. :)That being said, They NEED to add some sort of giant red flashing notification for when your kingdom is off balance, or some sort of meter at the top of the resource bar of the screen or something, because it's very easy to put your kingdom off balance and not even notice until 4-5 citizens decide to jump ship at the same time because of it, severely hindering your economy and population growth with very little notice. It's easy enough to fix once you realize. Also, the game still crashes on occasion, even though it's been fully released for over a year now. Hopefully they'll patch these issues before fully moving on to Airborne Kingdom 2, which I will be looking forward to.tldr; 8/10!

_childDocuments_.review: is a short, relaxing, and peaceful city builder offered at a reasonable price tag. If as a player you are looking for a challenging game, this won’t be it. With pretty graphics, plenty of building options, decent research, and the unique mechanic of balancing (literally) your flying Kingdom, it is an excellent introduction for newer players of the genre while still offering good content for more experienced users and anyone looking for a more peaceful approach to city builders. In Airborne Kingdom, we are on a quest to recreate the legend of an old Kingdom that was soaring up in the skies as foretold by the prophecy hidden in the tapestry.The gameplay while good, will not rock your world, your job is to build your flying city’s infrastructure while balancing the needs of its’ citizen. While you might lack resources at times, you won’t have disasters to counter, nor will you fight for domination. Rather,  you will have to manage your city, its own limitations and fly your base from place to place to gather more resources. While helping the neighboring kingdom and uniting it all once more under your banner. Building anything will impact the structure, look, and future design of your base. Being a flying city and all, you need to make sure that your city doesn’t tilt too much, isn’t too heavy as it will impact your flying speed, etc. You will be offered the tools to fix it of course through a generous technology tree and quite a few building options.Due to the very nature of a nomadic-flying lifestyle, you will always be on the move, resources being limited you cannot stock infinite amounts of them, as such you will need to be smart about your usage and try to plan ahead. Flying your city from place to place will let you explore your surroundings and send planes to gather resources, explore ruins and meet other civilizations mostly for trading purposes, and to generate alliances through some quests.Sadly, these quests are quite boring and repetitive. As soon as you encounter a new kingdom or civilization, they will tell you their needs, you will go to a certain location on the map, offer some resources up, build something for them and that’s it. On the bright side, once you will run out of things to do and add some longevity to the game, you will be able to keep building, playing, and starting a NG+.Graphically speaking, the game is pretty, the fantasy scriptures used in-game during the intro looks closer to Arabic than anything else and all the buildings have references to the Orient, in their structure or by their nature (the arabesque and minaret amongst other things), furthermore, all buildings have some sort of animation attached to them, whether it is wings, oars, or other means of propelling itself and keep it flying, it integrated itself really well in the idea of a flying city, this added a feel of some mysterious advanced civilization too.Finally,  is a short, relaxing, and peaceful city builder offered at a reasonable price tag. If as a player you are looking for a challenging game, this won’t be it. With pretty graphics, plenty of building options, decent research, and the unique mechanic of balancing (literally) your flying Kingdom, it is an excellent introduction for newer players of the genre while still offering good content for more experienced users and anyone looking for a more peaceful approach to city builders.

_childDocuments_.review: Very solid concept, executed decently. This game seems to appeal to casual settlement Gamers while those looking for more extreme challenged will be left hungry. Airborne Kingdom is a simple settlement game that any player can get into. For how long depends on the player. The fact that the player's settlement is mobile adds a very new (if not refreshing) sort of feature to the genre. The player literally directs their base as if they are directing units. Citizens naturally assign themselves to task and move around without player intervention. The  is heavily focused on this aspect as completing quests and missions will require mobility to complete. As the player explores and traverses the land (attempting to unite lost factions) new resources become available. The player simply clicks and assigns the amount of planes to harvest the resource. Coal, water, and food are key to running the kingdom, but to build and complete quests will require refined material. Building is neat and straightforward. The player attempts to distribute weight evenly in order to not tip the kingdom. Paths are required for buildings to be built and other neat decorative features become available as the player researches. Decor is essential to keeping citizens happy and from leaving the kingdom. At first it's easy to do, but as time goes on the needs become a challenge, especially when further research is required. Research can be sometimes long and tedious in the game and will require multiple academies to properly progress in the game. When the player runs out of coal the kingdom will slowly start going towards the planet. Once it crashes, that's it!The  are suitable to the game's atmosphere. The customizations for each building is a neat feature, with different themes or colours being available as the player explores the different biomes and lands. Paths can also be changed in addition to other functioning or resource buildings. Citizens can be seen walking around the kingdom and buildings have their own respective animations to signify to the player that they are functioning. The landscape itself is pretty and the variety of biomes is neat to see. Water can be seen moving, trees, birds flying, and clouds moving. The  are appropriate for the theme of the game, but for me personally nothing over the top. All basic and required sounds are included and don't annoy the player (which is always a good thing). Again, nothing that is adding more to the game, but nothing missing from it.So why the shallow rating then? The game is too casual for me and the missions are a little redundant. Run here, deliver resources, build the base, go back to another kingdom, deliver resources, then help them build an airbase. I do have to give credit to the Devs for trying out something different and approaching city-builder/settlement games a little differently. I liked it for a while, but the shine wore off. Some may like the pace of the game and the quests.
_childDocuments_.name: Airborne Kingdom

_childDocuments_.review: Not terrible or anything, but just very simplistic. The game loop is... simply... moving through a set of milestones, with no real variation on approaches - get more resources, give those resources to a city to build relationship, get more workers, use some to build more housing, get more resources again... that's pretty much the cycle. There is a little bit with unlocking new structures and more complex resource chains. But, essentially, it's very,  linear. The city builder version of a walking simulator.Airborne Kingdom could be OK if you just want a very chill builder, but I don't think it will have replayability even in this case.
_childDocuments_.name: Airborne Kingdom

_childDocuments_.review: A delightful little city-builder, with the twist that your city is a flying city. Carefully manage not only food and water for your citizens and resources for construction, but also the fuel supply for your city's engines as well as its lift, propulsion, and even its tilt angle. Airborne Kingdom is impressive in that it is totally nonviolent; you acquire territory through making alliances by completing quests. It plays a lot like Kingdoms and Castles, though the constant need for fuel to stay aloft also reminds me a bit of Frostpunk; Airborne Kingdom is much more optimistic, however.
_childDocuments_.name: Airborne Kingdom

_childDocuments_.review: This settlement builder really brings something others dont. You actively circle the terrestrial world managing your resources until you can manufacture enough yourself to do your sidequests which are all simple 'find the thing, click on the thing, and sometimes pay resources to finish the thing before you go.'I got hooked and polished it off in one 8 hour sitting. Is it perfect? Nah. But I enjoyed it a lot. It will likely live in my rotation of small-ish settlement builders that I will likely replay one a year or so.If your looking for a good weekend of a new game and like fiddly resource managment settlement games, then I suggest Airborne Kingdom. _childDocuments_.review: This is another of those games that honestly I'd give a neutral rating if one were available, but there's nothing massive wrong with it so it gets a thumbs up. The city mechanics are fine and the lift and tilt elements add something interesting to the city building genre, but there are so many small issues that the joy in the game ends up dying a death of a thousand cuts by the time you compete a run through the game. For example, the compass that you need to direct yourself around the map is worse than useless, it has more than one of each direction on a full 360 spin for one thing and aligns differently if you're even a little away from the town centre. Whenever you drop out of a menu the game refuses to return you to your previous viewpoint, which wouldn't be a big thing, but since you can't rely on the compass or freely move around the landscape often finding vital supplies is pixel hunting and being pulled away from it makes you want to scream.Lastly, half the point of the movable kingdom is that you can go and complete missions around the map, sadly those missions are just fetch and deliver trips which become tiresome around about two thirds of the way through.Still, its got a tech tree, city planning and interesting mechanics, so its getting a thumb just about up.

_childDocuments_.review: A game I wish I could give a neutral review for. This is like that school essay that you had to have so many words for, and you fluff the high hell out of it to get it as long as possible with as little content as possible.  That's more or less this game in a city-builder nutshell.The concept of Airborne Kingdom is pretty cool, and building a flying, tiltable, crashable town in the sky is a neat idea.  Sadly, that's where the fun in the game stops.  Gameplay involves flying the city back and fourth between major hubs on the ground, doing fetch-quests for them (the only type of quest) all over the map until they are all your friends.  There's no real mix-up to this gameplay, it's a literal rinse-and-repeat what you do from the start to the end.  You'll research and unlock new buildings to become self-sufficient and move faster/etc, but this is largely non-climatic and just feels like more of the same.Graphically, I was pretty disappointed, they could have done so much more.  The character models are just bland canned 'toons' with no detail and everything is pretty un-detailed in general.  A lot of the stuff just seems underdone.  For example a "wonder" that's the "Traquil gardens" talks about how the city of old had vines and plants hanging from under the town as it flew.  I was thinking when you got this wonder, the town would gain an Avatar (movie) like growing under the buildings and etc, but nope -- it's just a boring tree you put somewhere.  Kinda sums up the game. It was sorta fun, I finished it more because I wanted to say I was done than because it was pulling me in from fun.  The Hard mode run I did felt like a Normal run, so guessing Normal is way easy.  I would not pay full-price for this game as it is, I think it has enough entertainment value if you can get it for around $15ish. There's better ones out there, but this is so-so if you've played the others and see it on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: Relaxing little city builder if you like squinting at things through a fog of clouds.Rough around the edges, but the core building mechanics are solid.The city provides a collection of interconnected systems - collecting, generating, and managing resources, managing the layout of the city, balancing the useful aspects of buildings against their weight and trying to keep the city from being lopsided.What I like:- The building; even on "hard" the game is firmly in the casual category with it nearly impossible to fail once you understand the systems- The world; while its a barren wasteland, its a backdrop for a little power trip building a floating paradise and singlehandedly solving the problems of the lesser, landed cities.What I like less:- The quests; probably my biggest gripe - the landed cities are very repetitive and give two simple quests each like "spend x resource to help me build this" or "go over there and interact with that landmark and come back". then they become your ally.- The world; being a barren waste it gets rather repetitive with each interactable location being obviously for one thing and one thing alone: a city - which gives two quests, a small village - which can give people, a resource node, a cosmetic - which gives a new paint job for your city, a relic ruin - which gives tech points, a city quest area - only interactable once given the related quest, and a wonder fragment; thats it, things become very formulaic and world loses some of the luster towards the end.- Wonders; There are three wonders, and they are oddly balanced. Each is split in three fragments, randomly thrown somewhere in each of the three zones. This means that unless you are actively rushing them, they wont be assembled until the very end of the game at which point they are useless (and maybe not even then as they are easy to miss). But if rushed, they can be easily acquired mid-game (albeit with some patience as you comb the entire map). The boons they grant are also rather lopsided - The garden is by far the weakest, negating mood penalties from "dirty" building and city tilt. the "dirty" range is pretty easy to work around, and you don't ever want city tilt as it kills movement speed. The orrey completely breaks any exploration, revealing all locations on the map (if you happen find this first, its it makes finding the library so much easier) and finally, the library, this just buffs all output - buildings process faster, give more lift, thrust, etc. The library is a must, allowing for a significantly more streamlined city.- Research; gating new buildings behind having to buy plans from cities by spending relics collected around the world is great. But once available for research, there is no cost except for time to research it, and some tech you start with ready to research (stuff that's not linked to new buildings) - so basically nothing stops running a dozen of research labs at 3x time speed until all useful techs are unlocked while bouncing between a couple resource nodes to stay afloat. Basically the techs that remove costs for moving (and deleting) buildings need to be spammed immediately so that you can teak your city layout without having to worry. - Time speed; the game is slow, there is no reason not to always be on 3x speed- Dump item UI; you can select None, -1, +1, or All; if you are carrying, say, 150 wood and want to dump 50 of it, enjoy clicking +1 50 times- Alert UI; if you build a self-sufficient city, the game will continously warn you that your Food, Water, and Coal supplies are "almost full". The game also does not expect you to research everything and if you finish the tech tree it will forever flag the UI saying you don't have a tech researching.Aaanyways, in conclusion, the core mechanics are solid and well worth it if you want a small city builder with some simple exploration in a pretty, somewhat rough package.

_childDocuments_.review: A wonderful little city builder. Relatively light in the city building mechanics, it's almost more of a resource management game, but light there as well. Ultimately -- I think there are games that set out to be relaxing. For me, they often stray too far into the "Creative Mode" style of relaxing -- where nothing *needs* to be done and there are no consequences. I respect the existence of such games, but they aren't for me.Airborne Kingdom, you have to build with some considerations. You have to manage some resources. Some of those resources, if you run to zero, your kingdom will fall out of the sky. There are indeed consequences.BUT -- I never once ran out of that specific resource. I rarely felt challenged past a need to plan ahead a little bit. In other words, Airborne Kingdom straddles the line very nicely of relaxing, without becoming creative mode boring. For that, I loved it.

_childDocuments_.review: A nice and short quest-driven city builder game. The combination of exploration and city-building is pretty innovative, and very well supported by in-game mechanics in both intuitive and fun way: On top of the usual resource juggling, the fact that most resources are on land below means you have to explore, and you have to improve your ability to do so. When managing city layout, your main concern is the weight distribution, because your flying platform needs to stay stable. These mechanics immediately make sense given the setting of the game, and offer interesting challenges.The goal-driven nature of the game is a potential downside for those expecting a sandbox city builder in the likes of Cities Skylines. The game is closer to Frostpunk; the progression goes along a single road determined by the game, and each time you unlock a new technology, your city basically starts requiring using it, despite not having needed it before. When you are done with every quest that the game offers, you also have little reason and less ways to continue expanding your city. The game hits this mark about 6 hours in.Ultimately, the game seems to focus on a linear, stress-free experience. The challenges of the game mostly comes from attempting to get an optimal layout that juggles fulfilling population desires, adjacency bonuses and minuses, and shape of the city, and yet the cost of rearranging buildings is minimal (and later, completely free). The game stresses exploration as means to acquire resources, but resources are generally abundant enough (and regrow) such that you can stick around an area near-indefinitely. You should get this game if you want a short and sweet experience, and not a 1000-hour-playtime sandbox.

_childDocuments_.review: I bought this game on a discount, which does effect my views of the game.I very much enjoyed this game and the music is amazing!I do agree with the criticism that;1) You can't unassign workers without destroying it's buildings:2) There is no minimap, although I actually don't mind it too much, and you can't plot on the main map;3) The missions are relatively easy or too straightforward, not enough challenge. The arctic region was a decent challenge.4) It has an unfinished feel to it, like it's missing more content. This game can be completed a little too fast.5) There isn't enough replay value. There isn't enough to do post-game that has already been done main game.Otherwise, the fact that it's a flying city builder is refreshing to me. the game is visually beautiful, especially the floor tiles, despite it's low poly mountains and buildings. Also, the music is amazing!I would highly recommend getting this game on a discount or at least buy the music full price. The music is amazing!The specific songs that got me very obsessed are:"Journey's Lift Off""The Wind's Bazaar""Moonlit Cartographers (Part 2)""We Return to Our Home (Night)" and "We Return to Our Home (Day)"  by Paul Aubry

_childDocuments_.review: I want more . . .  I don't usually write too many steam reviews, but I am hoping the developers may see this and it may give them more of a reason to act.This game was quite good, but not great.Pros:Visually beautiful. While not the most graphics intensive game I have seen, the art direction in this game is phenomenal. While many of the models were simple, they all stood out and added to an overall grand panorama. The carvings and paint upon the desserts and mountains all make for a stunning portrait. The landscape looks vast, barren, and harsh, but not uninteresting or boring. The structures that you build your kingdom with all move independently along with the kingdom itself. Gears spin, wings flap, fans twist and turn. Between all of the mechanisms of the structure and the people running around and doing various tasks, the kingdom feels alive and is a sight to behold as you build it and  change it throughout the game. Even the little changes to the world, as you ally with other kingdoms and extract resources, were of note. Unique features: While not anything revolutionary, there are quite a few little features in this game that make it stand out. The ideas of managing the aeronautical stability of the kingdom was interesting. Actually visually seeing it tilt and lean from side to side as you stack heavy structures, or build powerful propellers, and how that tilt impacts your residents was very interesting. The constant mobility of the kingdom allowing you to send squadrons of smaller aircraft to gather resources that would slowly replenish, in an almost nomadic fashion.Balance of resource management: while not the deepest logistics system for a game, I felt a very solid sense of resource management throughout the entire game. Balancing workforce with food and water. Creating factories to refine more resources, only to have to use some of those same resources to bolster the kingdoms lift, propulsion, and comfort for my workers, and then being faced with more demand for fuel which would require more factories. The various needs of my people increasing in different ways as my population grows. The need for strategic construction in order to increase the efficiency of certain structures. The research system, which could give me access to revolutionary new building, or drastically change my existing building. I always felt like I was improving, but there was always something more I required. It was an excellent source of drive for me, that kept me playing, even during long treks between regions.Deep and well thought out world: The story of the game is light, but it is nice to see that every region, kingdom, and quest has its own distinct little narrative. Even the variation between settlements was interesting. All the little descriptions and written details build up the world all that much more.Cons:Shallow. The overarching story is weak at best, with no real people, places, or events of significant note. It doesn't do anything wrong, but it lacks depth and engaging material. Many of the quests are fetch quests. Several others are a sort of purchase victory, where you pay resources to progress a quest. While all the boxes get checked off telling you that you are saving the world, it never really feels like you are actually making any true change. While the construction and resource management were great, the rest of the game essentially boiled down to point and click movement and acquisition. It felt like a long scavenger hunt, where I would click to tell the kingdom where to go, and then click on various resources to pick up along the way, with no major threat or obstacle to overcome. Even in its stronger aspects, construction and resource management are fairly limited compared to other games. Most building raise one statistic and possibly lower another. The resources are all some sort of currency that are either used for fuel or construction. Very rarely do you ever build anything that can make a big change to the kingdom in any dynamic way.Overall, I really enjoyed this game, especially for the price, but I can't say its a great game overall. It left me wanting more. I like the theme, the setting, the systems. I liked a lot of what I saw, and it felt solid. It just felt shallow and limited. I want more. I want a more engaging story. I want a villain to chase or oppose, or a crisis to resolve. While the game does have you building a flying city, it never really feels like you are doing anything monumental. You spend a little wood and glass and iron to bolt on another farm, or house, or clinic. I like this slow build of an ever growing kingdom, but I want to crown it with a palace. I want more dynamic and unusual buildings and resources that require more thought than just simple addition and subtraction. I want more regions and a grander map. I enjoyed my 9 hours of play, but I would love for the game to give me reasons to play for 40 more.
_childDocuments_.name: Airborne Kingdom

_childDocuments_.review: it wasn't a horrible experience, but I feel like the novelty of building a flying city wasn't worth the very basic simple nature of this game. Some people have said that they found this game relaxing, but I push back on that and argue it's actually just boring. The mechanics that do exist aren't that fun to work with and the buildings you use and the ways you need to care for your population are super basic and boring. Nothing was fun about this experience, the soundtrack is pretty decent, but it gets old fast as it's basically the same track on repeat. I played the entire game in fast fwd speed and it still felt like a crawl. I'm sorry for being so harsh, just saying, don't buy this game on sale, just go play a game you already have like civ 6 or thronefall or dorf romantik, you'll have a more interesting time and you can still relax.
_childDocuments_.name: Airborne Kingdom

_childDocuments_.review: Well, for a long time I'm really torn.This game has issues, but do they outweigh the inventions and the things that make this game unique?Well I would like to compel you find out for yourself.This game is short, but not fast. You plan a city, as promised, this city can fly. You have to manage personell and ressources, income and storage. But this city still can fly. So you also need to account the balance, all the living space on the right and storage on the left will make your city unbalanced, and therefore your people unhappy. (I would be too if everything would turn halfway sideways).The again you could just lift the space up with a propeller. Buuut... of course that is a steam-powered engine. It stinks! And so you have to put it somewhere in the back, away from the living spaces... But wait, now it is forward tilted.That concept is great! You need to plan a city that is weighed out, not too heavy overall and fed with absurd amounts of coal to stay aloft. And suddenly those people want to eat and drink too. Overall you do the usual stuff, but moving around.That is the part where this game becomes an exploration game, rather than a city-builder. You need to find ruins, settlements and already existing kingdoms. It is a great refreshing new experience... if only... everything would not be so incredibly slow.I played it on the highest speed setting continously and still went away to grab a bite, came back and not really anything did change. The 8 hours it took me to finish this game could have easily been 6.. if the city would fly faster. You can improve it with engines, of course, but I had a hard time adjusting the ressources in order to get there. So slow it was... and boring too. Finished in around 8 hours on normal difficulty. I don't see a really worth in replaying it, but I may go to make an achievement run someday.

_childDocuments_.review: I finished the game in under 7 hours. At no point was I challenged in any way, although I did once almost run out of food because I wasn't paying attention. _childDocuments_.name: Airborne Kingdom

_childDocuments_.review: The game itself is really good. It's a slow chill game, much like similar games such as Banished. The graphics and audio are excellent. The voice overs are solid. The game play isn't completely intuitive, but you can catch on fairly quickly.This negative review has nothing to do with the game itself. It has to do with the information about the game, as presented by Steam. The problem is it has no controller support. And, due to a nerve issue in my arms and hands, I cannot play games using a keyboard. The information on Steam says there is partial controller support for this game. It's why I bought it after one of my YT subscribers suggested it. But, the game does not respond to a controller. AND, I was told in their Discord that there is no controller support. So, either Steam has the information wrong, or the developers gave Steam wrong information. Either way, this game is unplayable for me. And, I asked about this in their Discord. The feedback I got was excellent and fast. They let me know the game can be played with only a mouse--or almost only. I successfully played for a couple hours with no problem. So, the developers and game get high marks from me. And, if they change this incorrect information, I will happily change this review to recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: Airborne Kingdom

_childDocuments_.review: First of all, it's a good game with a new concept where city building is done up in the sky. It has unlimited options on how to design the city with some limitation on how the city grow. Found some minor bugs such as the need to restart the PC after closing the game to start the game again. Wonder why my antivirus quarantine the executable. Another bug would be the inability to put anything beside the oar. But why I don't recommend this game, is because it lack challenges and replayability. I finished the game, and collect most of the trophy in 14 hours (I restarted my gameplay once in the middle since I think I was wrong in how I play the game, so one playthrough should be around 10 hours).I hope the developer read my comment, especially this : Creating challenges and replayability should be quite easy. You can improve challenges via the trophy system by including parameters such as complete the scenario below certain time period, collect a certain number of people, hit max stats in areas such as resources or speed, etc etc. Replayability can be done by generating random map or adding maps and missions.

_childDocuments_.review: Really wanted to like this game, but in the end its just.. meh and too much money for the experience offered.I have just completed this game after 6.5 hrs - replayability for me is zero.The graphic design is nice, but there is no real challenge in this game.
