_childDocuments_.review: A lot of reviews complain that AK is short and lacks replayability. Compared to city builders as a whole, I agree that it can be finished pretty quickly, and can confirm I'm not eyeing a second run for a while.However, I think it's misguided to hold that against the game (or outright review it negatively), because this game is basically a hybrid between city builder and adventure game. There's a story with a clearly defined beginning and end, your progress in that story is extremely clear, and it managed to hold my attention closely for 7 hours. For the promotional launch price, that's less than $3/hr of being thoroughly entertained; I'll let you decide what your money is worth, but I consider this a steal even if it's a one-and-done.The adventure game infusion is very basic. You move your city around, find isolated kingdoms, complete a story-quest for them, and then pay a resource toll to claim them as allies. Do this to all of them, and you win the game. Many of them are in biomes with skewed resource balances that will have to be compensated for, which adds a good bit of depth to the city builder core. Many quests are as simple as traveling to and from a location, but when you burn through food, water and fuel just by existing, it's still an involved task.The city builder aspect is easily compared to Banished, and that's a positive thing, but with some fundamental differences that'll trip you up if you treat them the same way: labor is the biggest one, where, for example, if there's a Smelter that requires 4 workers, those workers are imprisoned in there, whether they've got the resources to work or not. The building cannot be disabled to divert the workers back into the generalist pool, the only way to get them back is to delete the building.If that sounds cumbersome, well, it kind of is. It was only in the last few minutes of the campaign that I realized the research to "get a full refund for deleted buildings" was intended to be a core aspect of labor management and not just a way to numb the pain when you screw up a placement. Then again, given how unreliably Banished's agents perform, I could just as easily view this design choice as a necessary evil.I beat the game in 7 hours on Hard... but I also don't think I played the game as exactly intended. There's lots of production buildings you can host to refine raw material yourself, but they're heavy, they hold labor hostage, and their output is pretty low. So instead, I made my city as fast as possible, built tons of storage, and kept all my workers free so they could descend on resource deposits like a swarm of locusts. Then when I was lacking on certain resources or refined materials, I could simply buy them at merchants without sweating the extreme markup that's supposed to discourage you from using them outside of emergencies.Was it in the spirit of the game to sidestep factories and farming? Probably not. Was it still fun? Yes, very. It's a good time pillaging a kingdom's surroundings into a barren hellscape, and then being constantly surprised that they will accept a skyport, instead of declaring war on you for ratf---ing their natural riches.Final mention goes to the art direction and the music, both of which are just about perfect for this game.  The soundtrack is worldly and epic, and would make you picture a journey to far-flung lands even if you weren't playing the game. The land beneath you is stylized like a renaissance map and looks great. Your city has a unique retro-futurist aesthetic that incorporates more globally-inspired architecture than usual, and there's also a ton of animated details like flapping wings or spinning propellers to make them even more visually interesting. GUI looks great too.On the whole, AK was a very welcome take on one of my favorite genres, and I definitely recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: Airborne Kingdom

_childDocuments_.review: It's fun for a very relaxed city builder/resource manager. I beat the main story in 7 hours and taking my time exploring. I never hit a point I was nervous or concerned in the game. Part of me wishes it was much bigger and I could have multiple cities and a much more complex build environment, but sometimes you just need an easy build game.
_childDocuments_.name: Airborne Kingdom

_childDocuments_.review: With art that can overcome technical limitations, and a storytelling so short you can write it on the back of a postcard, you will still find yourself looking for an answer in this game.First of all, there is no antagonist in this game, or even in the world building. There is nothing that can apparently challenge the sky city as it roams the landscape, stripping it of its resources. A prophecy is mentioned, and largely drives the story, but other than that the player is the only thing moving, acting and reacting in this game. Second of all, this is not a city building game, or a tactical game. People choosing this game while thinking of the glorious days of Stratosphere: Conquest of the Skies would not find a modern substitute here. All the resources that are necessary are outside of the floating microcosm, which sufferers no accidents or challenge once it is completed.This is a pensive, meditative exercise of going from point A to point B, while managing resources that are constantly diminishing. You will have to plot your course carefully, alternating your planes between different resources and "negotiate" (press a few buttons, really) with the locals.It's quite ironic that you, as the floating city, are represented as a saviour by the denizens below, while you drain their lakes, eradicate forests and eat all the berries at a prodigious rate to feed an ever growing monstrosity hovering above them.
_childDocuments_.name: Airborne Kingdom

_childDocuments_.review: Game has a lot going for it and I want to love it but ultimately can't recommend it for two reasons.1. Game hurts my eyes. The ground pattern is too busy and colors are washed out, making it hard to spot resources. This is probably on purpose, but still sucks. In the second zone it gets worse with a pervasive fog that gives me a headache to try to see through. Having lighting- or occlusion-based fog of war would be much better than plain old fog in terms of contrast.2. Rearranging your housing layout with each new upgrade to comfort/faith would be forgivable as "mechanics" except that moving ♥♥♥♥ bugs out 70% of the time where nothing works. The only fix is to press escape 3 times and then try again. If you're lucky, the same move command you've tried 4 times might finally work. It's often faster to dismantle and rebuild the building, except that costs more resources.3. Also, game crashes from tabbing out (in windowed mode!)
_childDocuments_.name: Airborne Kingdom

_childDocuments_.review: While overall it is not a bad game, the amount of content available and the level of jank of it's mechanics don't really justify it's price tag.How you build your city doesn't really matter, so long as you separate the "bad" buildings from your housing. People don't really move within your city, so there is no incentive to make it well designed.As such the gameplay is basically justMove city to unexplored locationHopefully find ruins that allow you to trade for new buildingsGather resourcesMake whatever building you happen to need (not enough lift? Build a propeller. Need more homes? Build a house)Now this would be all fine and good, if not for how poorly balanced the entire game is. Houses will make up the majority of your city because each house only fits one person, which causes problems because you need people to man the things that generate lift/thrust. In my late game city about half of my people were employed in lift/propulsion generation, which is a big problem because my city needed 3x more propulsion buildings to run at max speed. This has a nock on effect that it takes longer to go between locations, which means I need to be able to stockpile more resources, which makes my city heavier (and slower) still. And as your city gets bigger, your citizens will demand more luxuries, which means your city is less efficient again, and goes even slower. If you don't have these luxuries you will not be able to recruit as many new citizens and there is a decent chance that a sizeable portion of your crew will decide to just bail. Built too many path blocks without enough lamps? There goes 10% of your citizens.You can get better propulsion that requires less crew, but instead requires more coal. The problem is while you can build as much storage for all the other materials as you want, you can store a maximum of 200 coal. And if your city runs out of coal, its game over (or so I understand), and one of the regions is designed to have way less coal then normal, making it very dangerous to go this route. (You can turn wood into coal, but then you are using more people and adding more weight, which really negates most of the advantages).This two steps forward one step back design mentality makes the game more frustrating then enjoyable for me personally. I didn't hate the 5 hours I spent playing it, but there are so many better games at a far lower cost.
_childDocuments_.name: Airborne Kingdom

_childDocuments_.review: Airborne Kingdom is a beautiful game that challenges you to build your own utopia in the sky, a floating city far removed from the world below. It’s a city-builder that stands out for its unique concept, sure, but also for the relaxed way it presents its core gameplay. It doesn’t have you running up taxes on your citizens, negotiating with neighboring lords and ladies, or waging war on the next kingdom over. Nor will you need to worry about natural disasters or random invasions.The most challenging aspect besides feeding your people is keeping your ever-expanding sky city balanced, as you add more and more buildings, more and more weight, and it comes dangerously close to losing its equilibrium and plummeting from the clouds.You begin with a small nation, an engine, some propellers, a handful of workers and a single platform. But you soon add homes, and food storage, an academy and a hangar, granaries and factories. You’ll need to research new buildings and technologies, while applying counterweights and extra thrusters, more homes, more paths.Resources are gleaned from the world below, in the form of wood, food, water, and various materials. From your hangar you’ll send squads of foragers in tiny planes to gather essential supplies, as you travel from node to node. Eventually you’ll come upon other settlements, who you can trade with for blueprints and materials. You can also recruit citizens from these settlements, and opt to go on quests for them in return for rare schematics and treasures.At the heart of it, Airborne Kingdom is an incredibly wholesome game. Instead of violence, you spread peace, using your mighty flying citadel to scout the lands for relics and artifacts with which you can aid and win over the other cities of the surrounding lands – which is your ultimate goal. But as much as I enjoyed this aspect, I did find myself longing for a straight-up sandbox mode, just to see how big and busy I could make my sky fortress.Unfortunately the primary mode is all you get, and because there’s no real conflict or danger, I felt it better played in shorter sessions, when I needed to relax or wanted a break from the open world or high octane games I usually play. And that’s okay, because that’s what Airborne Kingdom intends to be. The artwork is beautiful, using simple shapes and pastel shades to bring its world to life, easily capturing the sense of height and scale required to make you believe you’re hundreds of metres above ground.And there is some danger, I suppose, if you over-build and unbalance your city, which can lead to unhappy citizens, civil unrest, and the aforementioned drop to earth. But if you’re careful, you’ll avoid this easily enough, and spend your time exploring the world, looking for secrets and hidden items that can increase your wealth or resources, or lead to new research opportunities and cosmetic skins for your city. There’s even a pretty decent photo mode if you’re into virtual photography and want to show off your burgeoning nation.Airborne Kingdom is rarely a very exciting game, but it’s absolutely lovely to look at, feels relaxing and pleasant to play, and manages to stand out in a genre that has been crowded for decades – which in itself is worthy of celebrating.Verdict: 8/10
_childDocuments_.name: Airborne Kingdom

_childDocuments_.review: It can be said that the creators took a little bit from games like NetStorm, Anno, Frostpunk, Impression Games (Pharaoh...) and made it casual, adding a touch of Adventure.This is an amazing game. Insanely beautiful and nice sounding. Pleasant and relaxing (on normal difficulty, I'll try high today). I would describe the game as mostly "travel sim" with a little bit of "survival sim". There is a city building here, but it is quite simple. There is resource management and production, but there are not many of them and they are simple. There are researches, but they are few. By the way, I did not meet any noticeable bugs, which is very pleasing. And here there is support for UltrawideHD!Unfortunately, there are also unpleasant moments: Descriptions of buildings and real volumes of production are different (as if there are problems with float calculations). The number of employees is sometimes displayed incorrectly. It's quite inconvenient to rebuild the city - there are no tools for this (for example, moving groups of buildings would be very useful). Towards the end of the game, vision range and movement speed begin to be very lacking - some improvements for this would be very useful, but they are not. The game seemed to lack some polish and a couple of ideas. All this slightly spoils the feeling of the endgame, but not significantly.
_childDocuments_.name: Airborne Kingdom

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty fun and unique city builder in the genre, but probably one of the only city builders I also don't have any desire to play again - feels like I accomplished everything I wanted to and there's nothing left to do.This game does many things well- beautiful art style (IMO), uniqueness, actually having a story line in a city building game gives a nice drive to it, interesting extra things to think about with building a city, such as the tilt of your city, the lift and thrust as well.I wish the game was longer, or had something that made me want to replay it, but I felt like I had a pretty much optimal city on my first play through. By the time the end of the story came there was nothing my city was lacking and I didn't really see how I could've done it much better.The tilt factor is an interesting addition and it can add an extra challenge when designing your city, but because I like to build quite symmetrical anyways I never really had to pay much attention to it. The only other thing I felt was lacking was the ability to pause buildings or assign workers so that I could optimize work flow from time to time, as you are fairly limited on number of citizens and workers.Great game, good style. A bit short - maybe wait for a sale for maximum value.
_childDocuments_.name: Airborne Kingdom

_childDocuments_.review: In this settlement builder, when your city runs low on resources... you move your city. Where the sky is the limit when it comes to your buildplan. Visually beautiful (with significant colour customisations and some minor texture plans), an ear-worm soundtrack and easy to learn controls.A 'complete' run through should take around 10~12 hours, there is a NGP and a free DLC that might cause you to rethink your cityplan.Overall a very charming settlement builder.
_childDocuments_.name: Airborne Kingdom

_childDocuments_.review: This was an interesting and enjoyable indie city builder to play, with its Arabesque theme & game mechanics. Similar to the game Flotsam by Pajama Llama Games, but whereas that takes place in an oceanic world, this is limited to the skies.Initially, I was wary of the game, as the idea of a floating city-builder struck me as difficult. These concerns were gradually allayed as I played through the game, having to restart several times as I was dissatisfied with the way my city was laid out. Balancing between both your city's speed and keeping it afloat so it did not tilt too much one way or the other proved to be less of a hassle than I imagined it would be. Having said that, some shortcomings ought to be noted as well. The inability to place Street Lights on paths, despite your citizens being able to traverse through a street light path, struck me as odd. The research tree could have been done with a bit more options, like boosts and reduced costs. Lastly, though this is not necessarily a negative depending on one's perspective, there is no workshop for mods. I suppose it's understandable since it's a fairly small team that worked on Airborne Kingdom, so they can't really be addressing issues caused by mods. Plus there was mention of potential DLCs later on, so we'll see. However, it would help the game's longevity & replayability if modding is eventually allowed.Credit should also be given to the Airborne Kingdom's soundtrack, which in addition to its Arabesque theme is nicely suited for a game of this genre. I have no real complaints and I managed to pass time with the game. In total, if you're looking for a city-builder with an interesting take, then check out Airborne Kingdom.
_childDocuments_.name: Airborne Kingdom

_childDocuments_.review: Airborne Kingdom is an interesting take on the fantasy of a travelling city. It definitely has a unique aesthetic with its Arabic inspired building designs and I personally enjoyed the mechanical, almost steam-punk nature of how your kingdom operates.However, while the overall aesthetic is interesting, its city-building gameplay is a bit too simple. There's not much depth and interaction between your buildings. The most you can do in regards to city-planning is to group appropriate buildings together to ensure that your workers have efficient pathing and production buffs are maximised. You can't customise worker behaviour nor create further ways to min-max efficiency beyond the few tools provided.Of course, a City Builder ≠ Automation game. But I would've liked to see a bit more intentional player interaction. As it stands the gameplay loop is quite repetitive,  You spend most of your time as a player watching your kingdom traverse the map (which does have the occasional unique landmark) as opposed to having to actively contend with city management.Another item that lacks polish, which becomes glaringly obvious when you have to backtrack so often, is the missing QOL features with the world map. For instance, in order to move around the map you have to right-click the land below. But if you want to travel long distances, you end up having to vaguely place your cursor across the horizon. It would've been much more convenient, if you could open up the map and place an active travel marker directly on it. As it becomes quite tedious to constantly click in a general direction, open up the map and realise you're off, and repeat again until you're headed to where you want.An additional point of contention, although some might argue that it's a design choice, is that the world map does not show the borders of the world and the map scaling is more expansive compared to the physical landscape. Both of these factors make the world map seem larger than it physically is. However, I personally found it bothersome to navigate with as it often led to me overshooting my desired travel point.All in all, I would still recommend Airborne Kingdom. It's not a lengthy game with a lot replayability, which means I'm much more forgiving with its issues. I ultimately enjoyed the time spent fully completing it and I think others would as well.
_childDocuments_.name: Airborne Kingdom

_childDocuments_.review: Very well made and relaxing city builder. Do not expect it to be a hectic experience full of micromanagement and problem-solving situations, do not expect the feeling of satisfaction of solving a traffic problem in Cities Skylines or the tension of juggling long production chains, Airborne Kingdom is not that, it hits somewhere else. This game is a walking simulator/city builder and as weird as that may sound it works and has scatched an itch at least for me. It is not a game about competition, about fighting or surviving the elements, it is about unity, cooperation and communication. The gameplay, while entertaining, is quite easy, allowing you to be creative, sit back and enjoy the ride. The visual design and music are absolutely beautiful, and everything is customizable,I bought at a discount but I'd say it is worth the original price. No bugs encountered so far, no pathfinding problems, no stress.
_childDocuments_.name: Airborne Kingdom

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of those interesting hybrid games that have come out recently. It takes the citybuilder and mixes it with a taste of survival/exploration. With an interesting sort of difficulty curve where as you spread your cities center of balance, changes in lift or weight create more drastic swings. Combine this with a mix of easily managed resources with some time based manufactured resources, it creates a balancing act on multiple different levels.Lovely music, interesting presentation, imaginative modeling, and some nice antfarm simulation. Story seems to be a little flat but is purely there for progression. I've enjoyed it so far. Only issue I've run into is the material collectibles don't show that they are aquired. This could lead to a situation where you find something you think is new only to realize you have been drifting in circles and already collected it. Not a huge problem, just would be good to add an "already collected" flag like the ancient ruins.
_childDocuments_.name: Airborne Kingdom

_childDocuments_.review: I'd say definitely keep an eye on it, I wish there was a "maybe" review or one that didn't count against it in the overall percentage, but honestly for $25, it's a pretty limited experience compared to other games around the same price.In the beginning, it has such a new and original feeling to it, breathing a new fresh air into the pile of other city building games. It felt like Highfleet without the impending doom around every corner, and for a while, that pretty nice. But eventually you could recognize the pattern in the simplicity of going from point A to point B, clicking on and collected everything in between, and snapping onto your ship the next tech you buy. And that just kinda finished it for me, I felt like I didn't need to play it all the way through to finish it; I was just done--saw what there was to see.I don't know, I'd say get it but always remember you can refund around or below the 2 hour mark and within 14 days of buying it.
_childDocuments_.name: Airborne Kingdom

_childDocuments_.review: I would not recommend this game because it feels almost more like a demo than a full game. It's sparse and is missing a lot of city builder complexity. The basic mechanics of a floating city are intriguing but in practice the game is so easy that it doesn't matter. When you add in that the couple side quests that exist involve just randomly exploring the map, hoping to find the right ruins, and the game feels so incomplete as to be unfulfilling. I beat it in 7 hours and I don't really feel like trying a NG+ or trying to chase down the last couple ruins because this game is well represented in the banner -- a bit of substance floating on a lot of inflated hot air. If you still want to play, definitely play on the highest difficulty from the start, but I wouldn't buy it without it being steeply on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: At full price and given the amount of content in this game, I absolutely  you buy it. However, and that's a pretty big however, I do recommend this game if you can get it for  half the price, perhaps even lower than that. Because Aiborne Kingdom is a good game. It's very well made, visually interesting with a great soundtrack, compelling mechanics and, as far as I could tell, no bugs. But it is a very, very small game, with zero replayability. The time I had on record at time of writing the review (under 6 hours if I recall correctly) is how long it took me to finish the game on a first playthrough while doing a completionist run. If you play at a normal pace, I believe it'll take you less than 4 hours to finish this game. For that, I believe firmly that the price is outrageous. This is an insultingly expensive game given how little game time there is, and especially because there is zero replayability value. I thought while playing that it was procedually generated, with quests that were also randomly created to fit the map. But no, the map and quests, if you can call them that (they're just gathering requirement, like "Bring me 20 wood") are part of a single, linear narrative that does not change no matter how many times you play the game.But like I said, this is a very enjoyable little game. So if you can get it for $6-$12 at MOST, and you love settlement managment and simulator games, you'll have a great time with this. _childDocuments_.review: It's a fun, but short, city builder / resource management game. There is no combat, and the only loose condition is if you mess up your resource management and either starve or crash. The city building is light, but fun. There is a lot of freedom in placing structures and you're primarily managing the literal balance of your floating city. There is also some level of interplay between laying out pathways and keeping certain industry away from population. The resource management is the meat of the game. You're balancing several survival and construction resources as you travel and explore. The game ultimately breaks down into thirds: first third of the game is the most difficult, with heavy balancing of resources to build and survive. The second third is when you're established enough to start exploring other areas and taking on more difficult missions. At this point you're mostly focusing on some optimization of your city and managing enough resource stockpiles to explore. The final third is just around optimization and exploration.

_childDocuments_.review: I got notified about this game when I saw a tweet a couple of days ago from one of the developers who plugged this game. I'd been on a bit of a city-building binge recently, and city-builders are some of my favorite video games. The game looked really appealing to me at first glance - a bit of a faux-Middle Eastern aesthetic, the fact that the city is flying above the ground, everything looks pretty good. And so I started playing it and before I knew it I was already halfway through the game.To be fair, this is a pretty short game, considering I finished it in just about 6 hours. It's a great game, though, and I'm really glad that I picked it up - it is incredibly, incredibly addicting and I lost track of time multiple times playing this. I think that the game, despite its shortcomings, is very solid in terms of design. Rock-hard solid. In fact, "solid" was the word that came to mind the most even when I was playing the game. Along with the general city-building genre convention of resource management, the novel addition of movement in the skies is a refreshing take on the genre, adding challenge, complexity, and a perfect balance to the rest of the conventions that the game uses from the city-builder genre. There are also new mechanics regarding tilt, lift, and speed, which I found really nice. The mechanics are almost perfectly designed, with just a good amount of challenge to not make it as stressful as, say, Frostpunk, but still retaining some sort of challenge on the way - around 2/3rds of the way into the game, I had a huge problem in that I lost a lot of citizens from unhappiness, and the fact that the game allowed me to turn it around and even survive when my food, water and coal were running low made the run very fun. I've heard other people call it too easy, so maybe take what I say about the difficulty with a grain of salt. Maybe it's the fault of the procedural generation, I don't know. If you do want a challenge, there is always a hard mode. In terms of game design, I would say that Airborne Kingdom is possibly one of the most solid games I've ever played, and I really don't say that lightly, since the mechanics all work together so well.The game also has an absolutely gorgeous aesthetic, with a papier-mâché/Middle Eastern tiles thing going on in terms of textures and models. The faux-Middle Eastern aesthetic works great, and is further harmonized with the very much new aesthetic of the buildings, which looks almost steampunk, in a way. The amount of customization in terms of how you want your city to look, too, customizing the motifs of the buildings and roads, is also really great. The soundtrack is great, too, with some top-notch tracks in there.I think that my main problem with the game, honestly, is that there's just not much to do and a very bare-bones string connecting the moment-to-moment gameplay with macro-goals. The general lack of buildings and other features is pretty disappointing, and left me wanting more, although it's probably a good thing that I'm saying that - it means that the developers did a good job at doing what they wanted to do for a short game. The story is also very bare-bones, although I get that it really isn't the main focus of the game, since what you're here to do is just to go through the very solid basic gameplay loop. I would have liked it, though, if they spiced things up and added much more variety to the different quests, since the only real difference in gameplay that I felt was the different availability of resources in different parts of the map. I do think that, as an indie studio's debut game, this is really enough, and they've shown a ton of potential in what they can do in future games.I would say that the game is worth it, and while I do think that the price tag might be a bit too high when it comes to a 6-hour indie game, I don't regret the purchase, since it's supporting a good game from developers with lots of potential.

As of 2024 they polished a lot of roughness, there may be still a couple things that could be enhanced (poor AI on getting resources / upgrades not so balanced / a too foggy fog of war), but they are just minor nuisances. _childDocuments_.review: This one is a pretty niche little game. It's a bit of an adventure/fantasy with city builder elements in it. It's a very lovingly crafted story line that has linear progression. I find it pretty damn good, super chill to play if you want the casual experience, with a slightly harder experience if you want something a little testier.Key features, I'd say are:. I'd call this a positive because this really harmonizes with the general atmosphere.. I really enjoyed this aspect. There's things to balance and take note of for the city builder aspect of the game that really doesn't exist in any other city builder. Without spoiling it, the addition of a 3d element to making a city in such a truly meaningful and impactful way is an absolutely wonderful spin on the city building genre. Highly creative and very well made. Honestly pretty well balanced too. is fairly unique. It's vaguely reminiscent of homeworld where, as you move your colony about, you'd collect resources on your travels BUT it's actually pretty satisfying to just watch them go at it once you give the order. 'specially if you built up a good dozen of them. is a pretty well taken care of factor in the game. You can tell the devs really gave it some thought on how to make it vibrant and special for each type of player with many different colours and materials and even whole theme's to use on each building. The amount of customization is pretty amazing without going overboard or becoming overwhelming, I'd say.Which leads into the next point of  and , which is honestly a pretty novel idea that uniquely suits this game and I don't think any other city builder on the market has ever tried exploring a multi-facetted system like this. You have to find blueprints for most of the techs. Pretty vital ones too and then you get to research them and then you can build them, so long as you paid attention and gathered up the proper materials.Like most other city builders the raw resources you gather can be converted into a higher tiered resource but this game takes it a step further in that there's really not much use for most raw materials until you refine them into their final form, before construction. It's unique because being a mobile city you don't always have those raw resources readily available, so logistically you have to plan your routes, think about how much storage you want (which is honestly a tricky balance when you're new) and have an actual plan to utilize those resources. You can't just stockpile quintillions of resources and never have to think about the resource again because warehouses come with an additional cost, above the resource cost and amount of space utilization. I won’t spoil it too much.The  is highly interactive and engaging and it brings a real sense of background or lore into the game. It’s very interwoven into the mechanics too and so part of the progression factor in the game is actually progressing through the story so that you can continue growing the city itself, which also presents it’s own challenges, that honestly aren’t as present or pressing in most other games.Another finite resource with a mobile city is human resources.  works differently than most other games. You have to travel and actively recruit. The more people you add, the more you need in order to support them and if you swing too far in one direction you’ll neglect other needs, which can really choke up your progression through the game.The only real negative is that because of the uniquely story driven nature of the game, the player reaches a point in the game where progression is no longer possible, especially since resources on the map are not infinite and do not expand as the players city grows bigger and more demanding. This also limits the amount of play style diversity and therefore replay-ability, hence the small number of hours compared to standard city builders. For myself a hand full of play through was enough but every once in a while I’ll come back to it and play through again (which is what brought me here to my review).In summary I’d highly recommend the game to anyone that’s obviously showing interest by viewing the store page. It’s great as a city building and shines in it’s adventure/fantasy driven progression system that could really appeal to a wide audience of open minded people that maybe also want something a little different to what the typical mainstream is offering.

_childDocuments_.review: I'll be honest it's probably unfair to give this game a negative review. I could definitely see myself picking this game up again at some point in the future and enjoying it, but as it stands now I'm just not interested.I have an ongoing quest to find a city-building or strategy game that scratches the same itch for me as playing a low stakes game of Civilization. Basically I would love a slow-paced, not stressful game where I can build a civilization and see it spread across the landscape with unique outcomes depending on the choices I make. I've never found anything that exactly fits what I'm looking for but I've tried a handful of strategy and city-builder games to try to fill that niche.Seeing this game on Steam and seeing how chill it looked intrigued me because I thought it might be in a similar vein, and to be fair, it kinda is.The game is a city-builder where you play a floating city that slowly expands. It has a chill vibe, and a cool Arabian aesthetic which is somewhat unique in the video game space. The gameplay is probably what you expect from a simple city builder with that concept, the twist is that you are actually piloting this city as you fly across the landscape. You find resources through your travels across the map rather than producing them yourself and there are interesting things you can find across the map as you travel.The main quest mechanic is that you need to travel across the map and identify all of the major cities that have permanent settlements and provide some sort of thing for them before moving on to the next one. The resource management loop comes from being able to journey while your citizenry grows and consumes resources while you travel looking for these macguffins that these other cities want.All of that is fine and works perfectly well. It also definitely fits the chill vibe I was hoping for with a game like this. The problem with it though, and the reason why I decided to mark this as a negative review, is just that I was so incredibly BORED while I did all of this.Although the aesthetics of the game are really wonderful and unique, and the idea of an impermanent city base is pretty cool, it's all very basic stuff and I didn't really feel like I had any interesting choice to make.The game does do some things very well, and apparently they're adding new content to the game, so I do feel like it may be worth revisiting for me at some point in the future, but overall I still have yet to find that game which perfectly captures the city-builder/strategy experience that I'm looking for.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is good, it needs a lot of polish, but it's got good bones. The city building is fun and intuitive (which is a lot to ask, it seems, of modern city builders), I like tooling around and gathering resources, doing little quests for the locals. It's lacking in QoL features though. I'd like to be able to selectively assign workers to jobs -- pulling workers off propulsion to go gather resources, etc, waypoints on the map would be nice, as would a 'always drive forward' / heading-and-speed navigation mode (I found myself figuring out a bearing and then clicking way off in the distance, which worked but was kinda clunky, it'd be nice to just pick a heading and set speed). I'd like to see more complexity, a bigger world, more options for how to approach the game (maybe I want to be a scavenger ship, maybe a self-sustained green paradise, maybe a pirate ship). Combat would be a welcome addition, although I don't think it's strictly necessary.Overall it's good and I look forward to updates.

_childDocuments_.review: After a night of playing, I think it's well worth its price. It does seem to lack replay value, it's probably only good for one or two playthroughs, but the fun value is very high for those who enjoy this type of game, especially if you appreciate atmospheric, Arabian-inspired aesthetics and soundtrack. The fact that you're building a floating city with special needs and special abilities compared to ordinary cities gives birth to some interesting new mechanics, though they're unlikely to stay fresh for more than one playthrough. I also appreciate the story, quests and exploration, though the first two probably aren't randomised. All in all, it's a fresh and interesting concept, which is mostly well implemented, but with not enough attention paid to replay value.Edit: After finishing my first playthrough, I don't have much to add. I enjoyed it a lot, it was three nights well spent, but at the same time I don't have much desire to start another game right away. I'm sure I'll return to it for another game in a year or two, though. Oh, it did occur to me that for people who really need a relaxing game every now and again, to balance whatever troubles they may have in life, this might be a really good fit.

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who played many building and strategy games, my first impressions on this game arent great.I will list the problems I ran into and prehaps write a full review later on.Menu, UI and options;- no options to change UI size, nor text size. - no options to invert or change mouse controls, only invert movement all together.- Title text is massive, explanation and mission text is hardly readable on small - medium screens.- Flavor/lore text is even smaller and in , meaning any lore about the world is the least readable text.- With text and UI not having any settings, this makes reading anything in the game a pain on even big laptops and mid-sized screens. Or for anyone who doesnt have amazing eyesight, or tired eyes.Controls and movement;- Mouse controls cant be changed in settings.- Left mouse is explained in the tutorial as drag-and-move camera, does not work at all. Its selecting only.- Middle mouse (scroll) drags to move camera (instead of left mouse) but is inverted, unlike every other movement. (left is right, right is left)- Right mouse rotates camera, but right clicking the ground also moves your kingdom there. This gets annoying real fast.Gameplay and progression;- Buildings can be upgraded, but upgrades are uninteresting. Upgrading costs no resources only time and workers.- Upgrades are either decrease cost (production/buildings), faster resource collection, or more storage.- Because all research cost time and people, and almost all upgrades reduce the time or cost. You actualy gain nothing from researching upgrades for most things in the game. You either research upgrades and get less resources while doing so, just so things cost less or produce more later on. Or you spend the time and people to collect and make resources faster instead, resulting in the exact same result.- The developers could atleast have added a research tree that adds some gameplay elements to the game.If you look for a simple building game then I suggest giving this a careful try, but make sure you dont go over the 2 hour refund time. If the above points I made remove most fun you could have in this game, its probably time to refund if you care about the money spend.Im disapointed the game isnt better, considering the potential it has. Aside from that I dont completely hate it... I think.

_childDocuments_.review: One of my all time favorite games.  It's a city builder and resource management on a different scale.  You not only have to navigate your city throughout the lands on various quests, you need to make sure that all your citizen's needs are met, be they basic necessities like food and water, or luxuries and comforts, such as lighting and gardens.If that weren't enough, you need to make sure your flying city, well... flies!  As you grow, you need to make sure your generating enough lift to keep the "airborne" portion of your title accurate.  And you need to make sure it can go forward to find more resources.  And god forbid if you overload one side over the other.  Listing is no fun in the water, let alone in the sky.Add in an awesome soundtrack, and tech system that makes you eager to find new things, and a large map with plenty to explore and discover on your own, and you've got one of the best games that $20 bucks can buy.  A definite must for the city builder gamer, looking for a little relaxation and winding down in a game after a long day.
_childDocuments_.name: Airborne Kingdom

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR - get it. It's fun.8 hours in as of the review, and I'm finding it very pleasant and entertaining. It's not as challenging as I thought it would be, but honestly I don't know of a very good side-by-side comparison in terms of similar games. On normal difficulty, you spend time trying to organize your city to look cool, but also stay balanced and be fast enough to accomplish your exploration, and make sure you have enough of each resource. Once you unlock a few of the good research upgrades, it's pretty simple to never feel like you're constantly having to grind resources or that you're in danger of running out, and you can mostly just fine-tune the balance of said resources. This is a distinct difference and why I say it's not as challenging as games like Timberborn or Frostpunk might be, because so far I haven't encountered an "end-game crisis" because I didn't manage my coal properly or oops all my people starved or there's some chaotic fire that wiped out half my settlement. Maybe that will happen if you're not careful or don't pay attention. All in all, I'm okay with the experience being a little bit more chill.The art style and visuals as well as the music makes for a very relaxing and visually impressive game. I would recommend this for anyone who wants to experience a beautiful and unique take on a city builder!Edit:Just completed the storyline, and I forgot there is also a hard version and a New Game +, which appears to have some interesting options for upgrading your town center and playing in a larger world. I will give the review an update when I play hard/new game + and see if it gets a little less relaxing ;)Edit+: I was right! Hard mode requires you to be a bit more proactive in managing your resources. A few times where you're like hmm, should I try to make it through this area or stay here and build up a few more food stores so I can go longer stretches without finding food. Also found I needed to barter for more scarce resources where before on normal I never needed to. Now, on to new game+ =D
_childDocuments_.name: Airborne Kingdom

_childDocuments_.review: A wonderful and relaxing city-building game with the added bonus of being set in the sky. Beautiful art style, gorgeous soundtrack, and just strategic enough that you can't get too comfortable with just letting time tick. Main story probably isn't the greatest in terms of replayability, but the option of creative mode and certain achievements you might overlook in the first run definitely extend beyond the main stories life. Along with the lack of replayability, the only major concern is how thick the cloud cover is, obscuring some of the smaller resources at first glance.Overall a great game and a definite recommendation.
_childDocuments_.name: Airborne Kingdom

_childDocuments_.review: Airborne Kingdom IS an awesome game. Its nothing really huge or pretentious. Its a fun little indie game where you build a flying city to reunite this magical world of "The Tapestry" You build and invent new kinds of buildings and improvements to your city that help you get bigger and move faster.. all while exploring the world and reaching out to form alliances with former kingdoms of a grand alliance. It has a very "eastern" kind of feel that is truly unique... its very simple and easy to understand.. If your looking for a simple, fun game that is really a step in a different direction.. you could do much worse then Airborne Kingdom
_childDocuments_.name: Airborne Kingdom

_childDocuments_.review: The concept of this game is good. It's very atmospheric and has a fun theme to it. Whilst I can't bring myself to keep playing it, I do recommend to try it. I personally struggled with the balance mechanism, and I don't really like the aesthetic of the 'buildings'; I find it hard to differentiate between them despite their being a customise building tool. All building games are repetitive but some just do it better than others, and Airborne kingdom doesn't do it well enough for me.
_childDocuments_.name: Airborne Kingdom

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: Great game, worth the price.Standard city-building type game with a simple tech tree. Positive feedback loops with gates, timings and spikes. Bread and butter stuff. The cool thing about this game is that your city can roam around the map and explore and discover things. This is also how you find new resources.The world is divided into regions with different aesthetics. Within each region, there are a handful of large static asset clusters that are distributed in dynamic (random) locations relative to each other. So each time you start a game, it may look like a new random map, but after a while you can start to pick out familiar asset clusters.There is a main quest to find all the kingdoms in the land and help them. There is also a side quest to build 3 wonders, which I accomplished after I beat the main quest. The wonders can be tricky to find, but they are very powerful and can make the main quest easier.You can also customize how your city looks by changing the colors. New color schemes are acquired by finding locations in the world.The music is good. The graphics are good. I have not had any performance problems. The game seems to be relatively bug-free after almost 20 hours of play. As mentioned above the gimmick of the city roaming around sucking up resources is pretty cool. The story is acceptable.
_childDocuments_.name: Airborne Kingdom

_childDocuments_.review: This is a great game if you enjoy city-building games.  There is no combat: you start off as a guy in a balloon and you end up running a bunch of connected zeppelins, or perhaps the flying SHIELD heli-carrier, as you do have to send down Sopwith Camels to collect resources from the ground.  You can make your flying city as large or small as you like, though the bigger the city, the more you have to worry about morale and desires and aerial drag.  There are 6 categories of things to research and 'lift' is one of them, and 'propulsion' is another, so there is quite a bit of variety: fins, balloons, propellers, and so forth.   I didn't take this part seriously in my first play-thru and my flying balloon crashed as it ran out of fuel.  However, there is no other way to die; you just travel above the world, doing fetch quests for cities and settlements.  Two thumbs up.Note: I got the game during the Steam Summer Sale for 50% off, and after a week or two or playing I'm still about only halfway through, so it's definitely giving me many hours of enjoyment.
_childDocuments_.name: Airborne Kingdom

_childDocuments_.review: This game is nothing but untapped potential. The devs have made a great world and fantastic system but failed to take it all the way to a fantastic game. I really did enjoy the game, but felt disappointed when I realized how shallow it truly is. 9 hours to finish the story, and I dont really see the point in subsequent playthroughs since all it really unlocks is a challenge mode of sorts. If you're looking for a more relaxed city builder go ahead and pick it up, I'm looking forwards to the sequel in the hopes it is a step forwards.
_childDocuments_.name: Airborne Kingdom

_childDocuments_.review: Very interesting take on the "Banished" genre, beautiful artwork lots of fresh ideas.My problem with this game is it's very repetitive, fly to new kingdom go grab the thing, return build a port and move on to next.I feel I've experienced all there is to offer in 3.5 hours.There needs to be far more content added to be worth the $20 or $25 price.
_childDocuments_.name: Airborne Kingdom

_childDocuments_.review: Excellent exploration game with a city builder component to it. I know that's not how the game is advertised, but that's what it is. I was able to stretch out the game play to just about under 20 hours to get all the base game achievements including wonders. Between the quests, resource gathering, and airship optimization I was kept busy while the game was relaxing enough to enjoy the lore. Looking forward to future content.
_childDocuments_.name: Airborne Kingdom

_childDocuments_.review: Hello,Not really a RTS/resources management game. In this kind of game you should have many roads to the same objective. Here you are incredibly constrained in the way you build your city. I fail to imagine a dozen radically different wining city plan.The resources management part is simplistic. For example you cannot specialise as the resource barter is almost always a bad deal (and the game say so). Meanwhile if you stabilise your city with a slight excess of coal, food and water it can over like this forever. There is no internal economic dynamic in your city that would alter the resources production mid and long term.It's more a puzzle type game.Have a nice day.
_childDocuments_.name: Airborne Kingdom

_childDocuments_.review: Fanstastic gem of game, one of the more unique and atmospheric city builders on display. A true breath of fresh air.This will be my third time purchasing this, first on EGS, then on Switch and now on Steam. Looking forward to tackling the new additions such as Hard mode and New Game+.Highly recommended for those looking for something unique with a fantastic atmosphere and a bit more chill vibes then the standard survival builder that is so common these days.
_childDocuments_.name: Airborne Kingdom

_childDocuments_.review: As it is now, I would not recommend this game. True I played it in normal, but the fame is super short with very little content and with zero challenge. I think the idea is great, but the "quests" are super boring and easy. You are asked to visit different cities and locations, which are marked on the map, while you are building your city. It took 8h for me but probably only because I wanted to research all buildings, but really you can probably finish the game in half that time. It needs to be more challenging..
_childDocuments_.name: Airborne Kingdom

_childDocuments_.review: So this is one of those games where "yes" or "no" are not good enough. I have more mixed opinionI have decided for "no" just because I can see many people have similar opinion like me and currently game is at Very Positive rating.At it's core it is good game. Good for chilling.Kingdom itself looks pretty good. Atmosphere of game is great.It is not very complex but it has fair amount of things to manage.UI is simple and provides you all informations you need.But it feels more like early access game.There is not much of content. All quests are just 2 variants. (Either "give resources x y z" or "find in area and bring back")You can chill and finish game in 10 hours easily and even in this short time game feels fairly repetitive.There is not much replayability. I don't see myself playing this game again any time soon.Surrounding is very simplistic. It feels more or less same. Yet performance of game is not very good.Controls are sometimes wonky. Moving buildings especially those stacked can be pain.There could be some QoL improvements like recall of gatherers etc.For 21€ it feels quite overpriced. If you want to play this game I recommend to wait for nice discount.
_childDocuments_.name: Airborne Kingdom

_childDocuments_.review: Seems more like a proof of concept. Not really deep. Linear progression. Sterile arts style not easy to look at. No attention to graphical details. Neither fun nor challenging. I had to refund. Waiting for the actual game with an actual economy, actual graphics/art and a replay value. This isn't it.Now that i think about it i understand why this was epic exclusive.
_childDocuments_.name: Airborne Kingdom

_childDocuments_.review: I did enjoy this game but feel it could have been vastly better with just a few small changes/adjustments.First of all, there are some minor things that annoyed me which i believe should have been patched out, e.g. still showing that red exclamation mark on research not being active even when i do not have anything to research anymore. A minor thing, but since the game is does not alert you about a lot of things it is annoying when it keeps alerting me about something i cannot even "fix".On a slightly bigger scale, i would have loved for the map to have a little more features....i really do believe it should show all the objects i interacted with, even without the wonder. I would have also liked to set a destination to move my city to directly on the map. I would have loved to be able to see resource nodes on the map with some filters, like...if i really need some wood i would like to be able to see the closest one i've been to on the map, instead of having to pause the game and keep turning in circles trying to spot one visually.On that note: I played the game twice. First normal mode, then New Game+ on hard. My second run was a LOT easier than the first. Why? Because i understood the game better and had more of a plan for a layout/technologies to go after? No. Because i had disabled clouds.This is just unacceptable and might be the biggest flaw in the game as it is: Clouds are "hidden" as a quality option, yet, they CLEARLY are a difficulty option with a map system like this game has. Especially in the Shallows. With clouds set to ultra i had to basically play that entire zone blindfolded - with clouds disabled i could simply see things.The game clearly has weaknesses in the long-term-difficulty - which makes it rather short. Something i hope they address in the sequel. But there are things they could have easily done for this game, too. I think a HUGE part of what makes the game so much easier later on is the ability to build as far as you want in any direction. It absolutely trivializes "challenges" like having to place certain buildings on certain edges, if you can simply create a new edge MILES away from your center and connect it with just one path. I would have set a maximum distance from the center which must be expanded (but not without limit) by research. I would have then added a generic "buff efficieny" building (like most already have in a specialised version) but with a 1,2,3 build limit (again, research) and then reduced the efficieny of all buildings MASSIVELY when not afected by that buff-building. With these changes, there would be a maximum of buildings you can place and  you would have to chose which to buff to optimal efficiency. That could have added more of a challenge to the 3 specialised zones.Having said that all, i still enjoyed this game and will definitly take a look at the sequel when it releases.
_childDocuments_.name: Airborne Kingdom

_childDocuments_.review: This game was wonderful to play, it gave a sense of being really well thought out and I very much enjoyed the combination of story, city builder and the different beutiful terrains. However, it does need an expansion and more difficult quests, it is a bit small and much more could be done within the framework
_childDocuments_.name: Airborne Kingdom

_childDocuments_.review: This game feels almost finished. There are so many obvious flaws, tho, that I doubt the devs intend to correct them. For example, buildings cannot be 'turned off'. Even tho a building cannot work because of a lack of resources, the workers will still go there and will not do anything at all. You cannot destroy some buildings, eg wings, which is a problem because you may want to upgrade to a different building that doesn't use workers ... so your workers are constantly being stuck in buildings you no longer need or cannot use.A game fundamentally about worker management that doesn't allow for worker management is not a good game, no matter how fun it is to look at.
_childDocuments_.name: Airborne Kingdom

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoy playing this game as its relaxing, but I wish there was moreThings I enjoy: ArtGiven Quests aren't too difficultGame itself is very neat and visually appealingCustomizing individual buildings between the preset designs, changing light colors, metals, etc.Things I dislike:Building level additions (2nd and 3rd floor)Map seems big, but feels small at the same timeCoal is capped at 120 ( unless im dumb and am missing something)No way to reset the Kingdom interms of customizing the layout (wish I could send every building to storage during a pause and redo my kingdoms layout (I understand reasons to why this may not have been included, but I wish it was)Things I wish would be added:A way to customize/ add individual floor layouts so you could potentially have paths at each building storyA lower deck: potentially to customize how the bottom of your kingdom looksOverall highly recommend this game if you want something to play while relaxing
_childDocuments_.name: Airborne Kingdom

_childDocuments_.review: The premise of the game is quite interesting and the artstyle is just beautifull. The controls are decent for a game like this and the soundtrack is really nice.Sadly, the story is very short and the games mechanics are too shallow to justify another playthrough.Goal of the game is, to ally all the ground-kingdoms and make the world a better place. An incredibly simplistic and boring story. The twist at the end just feels weirdly shoehorned in and doesnt make sense considering what you do, more to that below in the Spoiler section.Every kingdom gives you a quest and after solving it, you spend a few more ressources and its done. These quests consist of:- search for item XY in a specified general area close by- Pay x amount of resource and wait until stuff happens- one quest makes you bring their envoys/philosopher/whatever to three other kingdoms (basically go there, klick, come back and collect reward)This is just... meh...The city building aspect is rudimentary at best. At first it is fun building a city in the sky and unlocking new buildings, but the novelty factor quickly falls off. There is no complexity or challenge in building and sustaining the city.After allying with half the kingdoms, I already got a developer-message, apologizing for breaking the fourth wall and telling me, that my city size already exceedes what is needed to complete the game and that it might have an impact on the games performance. Charming little message, but the content is rather concerning for a "city-builder" after such a short amount of time, playing for the first time.Calling a settlement with a mere 200 inhabitants a city would already be a stretch, but calling it a kingdom? More like "Airborne (small) Village"So much potential wasted :(For 5€, this would have been ok, but there is simply no content or challenge in this game justifying a 25€ price tag...from here on,SPOILER-ALERT:After allying with all the ground kingdoms, you fly back to the tapestry ruin and... well... ascend! Because all of this helping other kingdoms in need was just a challenge for the worthy, to ascend to the heavens... the real heavens? Werent we flying around all the time? Mental ascension?Yea... so the illiterate dude that i picked up from some backwater village to work away at one of the rudders has worked his arms so hard that he now too has the mental faculties and morals to ascend to a higher plane of existence? Oh boy...Boredom hit me pretty fast with the "basic" way of playing the game, so I decided to just expand the city as fast and much as I can, tiggering the afore mentionend developer-message. Considering I was building a (for this game) giant city that depleted the natural ressources of every area at a rate that would make even the biggest of locust swarms collectively die of envy, it is rather ironic that this is, apparently, ascension worthy behaviour. I felt a bit like nestle, stealing the local populations water supply and then head of to the next oasis :D
_childDocuments_.name: Airborne Kingdom

_childDocuments_.review: A beautiful resource management game. The game art has a fairy tale like quality and I found the play experience unrushed, very enjoyable and actually very relaxing.Cant say enough about the soundtrack. It is perfectly paired to the visuals and the game art; definitely worth purchasing.The game has a huge potential in future expansions of the storyline and visuals such as gates to vast underground caverns, volcanoes, etc.Kudos to the dev team. Excellent work.
_childDocuments_.name: Airborne Kingdom

_childDocuments_.review: A chill city building game where you try to balance your city. Both in terms of resources, and weight distribution. Normal Difficulty is easy and doable. The wonders are at times very hard to find.Great game in general, though I find the camera uncooperative at times, especially when trying to find things.If explored relic and resources were added and toggleable in the map, that would make this game a whole lot easier.
_childDocuments_.name: Airborne Kingdom

_childDocuments_.review: A relatively simple but quality city-builder. The flying aspect is a good twist, and well-incorporated into the city building aspect. Music is excellent. Unfortunately, the game objectives are very repetitive, which is saying a lot considering the game is not long - I completed the main game in 7.5 hours.I bought it for $10. At that price point, I am quite pleased. I don't know if I'd pay much more for it though.
_childDocuments_.name: Airborne Kingdom

_childDocuments_.review: What a great game with an amazing soundtrack to just kickback with after a long week. If you have even basic experience in RTS, base building and economy BALANCING games (fun pun), then I would suggest you play on hard. I stand by the $1 per 1hour game value exceeded that (probably because I played on hard and took a bit longer than most). Its fun relaxing gameplay and only slightly challenging at times.  I would really love for this concept to be taken a step forward to a AAA title and more complex systems as I did want to just keep playing. Look forward to see what more The Wander Band brings out.
_childDocuments_.name: Airborne Kingdom

_childDocuments_.review: Wow,This game is chill and enjoyable. A great way to wind down at the end of the day.Astechetically its gorgeous, stylized and clean. You learn the visual language of the game and you spend a lot of time looking over the world to spot the various points of interest.The game let's you in easy and allows for multiple replays with more difficult rules and larger random maps.The story is light but entertaining and doesn't interfere with replay.The buildings and cities are customizable and you can enjoy hours of getting form and function to blend while you grow.
_childDocuments_.name: Airborne Kingdom

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly, I didn't think I would end up recommending this game but I am.Sure, is the content just a rinse and repeat? Is it too easy? Why yes, yes it is.The thing is, it is nice and relaxing, a tiny bit of technical difficulty, a bit harder if you try for the achievements but at the end of the day, its nice and relaxing. However I think this game will fall under love or hate so if you aren't sure, don't bother, you won't enjoy it but if you are interested just take the plunge and hope for the best.
_childDocuments_.name: Airborne Kingdom

_childDocuments_.review: One of the best city builders I've ever played. Played it on hard and it felt both cozy and demanding, thanks to the miriad of ways you can customize, compose, decompose and recompose your flying city, until toward the end you reach a state of near self-sufficiency and it feels like magic.But that's not why I loved it so much, what really struck my chords is its charisma: it does its own thing with such verve, and such beautiful music.
_childDocuments_.name: Airborne Kingdom

_childDocuments_.review: Building aspect is fun. It's fun managing the weight and balance. Also kinda fun gathering resources although it's slightly repetitive.But unlocking kingdoms becomes repetitive. It's traditional fetch an item for me type of quest. 3 kingdoms in and I'm already bored.Overall... I guess this has potential to become a great game. But so far it's more like a demo.
_childDocuments_.name: Airborne Kingdom

_childDocuments_.review: Beautiful artwork and music, as described by countless others. I don't feel like there's a whole lot keeping me coming back after the first play through, but I appreciated that I was able to play it my way and take several hours, with only a few moments of 'wtf?' when trying to figure out how to keep everyone happy - the tutorial is just a bunch of tool tips. Strong recommend when on sale.
_childDocuments_.name: Airborne Kingdom

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic game, very relaxing, so far only a couple of hours in,, but love it, can't wait to see where it goes, and of course get the sequel, great concept and fun building weird designs, even if it does list a little. Looking forward to where the upgrades, artefact designs and maps take me. Love being able to customise the design and lights in the buildings, looks great at night. 100% a great buy. Although I do wish you could manage your resources / workers a little better. i.e stop the adobe thingy for a while and use workers elsewhere without having to destroy it. Writing this I'm seeing so much more in the clip than I've seen so far, looks like there's so much more to it than I thought.
_childDocuments_.name: Airborne Kingdom

_childDocuments_.review: A very pleasant game, from its bewitching soundtrack to its Arabian Nights inspiration mixed in with Miyazaki's "Castle in the Sky" which seldom misses a beat and successfully creates an "out-of-time" vibe.However the overall lack of depth makes it an entry-level management game for a casual and relaxed experience, with limited replayability. Though the addition of the northern wastes portion of the map did provide some late-game challenge to address this issue.I'd venture to say the game was slightly overpriced at release and many negative reviews would have been avoided if the devs had priced it at 15-20 $/€.Overall I recommend this game heartily at a discount. As I write this review it stands under 10 bucks and if a poetic journey into an arabian fantasy world is up your alley, go for it.
_childDocuments_.name: Airborne Kingdom

_childDocuments_.review: Relaxing and fun City Build & Exploration game.I finished the main story in about 12 hours on Normal mode.I couldn't help but binge-play this to finish the main-story.I'd suggest you try to avoid binge-ing it like I did, and enjoy it with a relaxed mood.There's a "Frozen" area that I have yet to explore though, I plan to work on this after the story.Hopefully, they'll continue to add a few more of these bonus areas for us to play post main-game.Otherwise, there's not much replay value. Recommend you wait for a moderate discount.
_childDocuments_.name: Airborne Kingdom

_childDocuments_.review: This is lovely little kingdom builder for those who don't want to build complicated supply chains or constantly run against the clock in all corners of their settlement. The one basic threat in Airborne Kingdom is that you need to stay afloat and never run out of coal - and to feed your citizens, of course. Normal difficulty will however never escalate beyond "Oh, this is gonna be tight!"-moments unless you are reckless on purpose. Gather resources, build something, research improvements or new buildings and pick up settlers and make allies along the way. After 15 minutes you'll have seen about 80 percent of what this game is about.If you like games like The Wandering Village or Dorfromantik and just need a few teeny tiny hurdles to overcome, you'll probably like this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Airborne Kingdom

_childDocuments_.review: A cute little city builder. Decently pretty, very nice music, relaxing to play. It's a simple and  worthwhile example of the genre!It's fairly short (at least on the first playthrough). A lot of my 16 hours were spent playing with customization and waiting around doing research. Also, not much replayability IMO. You're building a fairly small village with limited configurations. I probably won't go back for New Game+, but if you really enjoy it you can. I played on Hard and never had any resource issues. The music is nice and relaxing.Minor gripes: I repeatedly experienced an annoying bug where edge scrolling became incredibly slow, which was fixed by going back to the main menu. Also, I recommend turning off clouds; in two of the games three areas they make things very difficult to spot from the air, which does more to irritate than increase the challenge. Speaking of challenge, becoming self-sufficient was very easy, and I never saw any reason to use the propulsion and lift methods that required coal. If you take fuel use and required workers into account, none of the advanced buildings are any more efficient than putting an equal number of workers into the basic tech.All in all I  enjoyed it though! A cute little game.EDIT: the developers added an entirely free new region to the game, which is enough content for me to come back for New Game+ and highly appreciated. Thank you dev team!
_childDocuments_.name: Airborne Kingdom

_childDocuments_.review: The story is short and It took me around 4hr to finish. The mechanism in this game is simple, all you need is to keep flying and look for the resources to keep on. The main quest in each city is not hard as I expect, pretty much can be done in no time.The soundtrack is nice to listen to, the pace of the game is comfortable, and the idea of the balance the weight is fun.
_childDocuments_.name: Airborne Kingdom

_childDocuments_.review: Airborne Kingdom is easily one of the most satisfying management experiences I've ever had. Rather than recycling the genre standard management of individual sims and their needs, the game focuses instead on a more original array of concerns, largely around managing your flow of resources - which involves not just where you've assigned your workers, but also where you've left your kingdom floating and what resources are nearby. The most unique element to manage is the tilt of your kingdom, which combined with the steady growth of your populace (and their need for housing) means you are frequently considering the location of your structures based on considerations that you've never had to think about in any other game. The simplicity and streamlining of so many mechanics really works in the game's favor - the relatively simple radius mechanics (light and discomfort) for buildings pairs very well with the tilt mechanic, while the lack of emphasis on individual citizens pairs with the attention needed for your actual kingdom, its position and its overall resource needs.On the whole, I deeply appreciate the game's commitment to its vision - you can tell it does exactly what it sets out to do, and doesn't weigh itself down with more mechanics or content that would dilute the experience (for example, many games would factor in sims' walking distance between locations, which is never a consideration in this game). The New Game+ feature was surprisingly fulfilling, and I thoroughly enjoyed the time I spent 100%ing it. I don't feel any compulsion to play it any more beyond that, but that speaks to my satisfaction with the experience.With all that being said, the simplicity does end up highlighting some interesting design questions that otherwise wouldn't be asked. For example, one of the endgame Wonders removes all negative happiness modifiers, which really just nullifies almost all of the interesting decisions with kingdom design - as long as your houses are clustered around a source of Faith, you can build your kingdom however you want. The screenshots on the store page show some really inspiring layouts for kingdoms, but there's never any incentive to build like that in the game, largely due to the tilt mechanics (and the resource cost for moving buildings); you'll probably end up building in a sort of blob, just expanding out whatever edge needs to be adjusted for the sake of balance. It's not until the end of the game where you can build with no real restriction, but isn't it a bit hollow at that point? My only other aside here is that it does seem quite off that so many small settlements you can recruit from are scattered across the map, but completing the main storyline gives you just about enough citizens to meet the ending criteria, and there's barely any reason to go above that population. My advice on hardmode is to never take any citizens until you've finished the main quest, and only then round out your population with settlements.I only spend so many words on my minor criticisms because I think it's interesting to discuss; it certainly didn't hinder my enjoyment, and if anything, it just makes me that much more interested in what these developers work on next. If there were any kind of successor to this game, I'd snap it up immediately.
_childDocuments_.name: Airborne Kingdom

_childDocuments_.review: A delightful story game. The city-building aspect has some new jazz with "tilt" and "lift" which were fun to play with at first. Once you optimize your city growth and self-sustainability the game becomes a matter of gaining more and more people so you can stop using coal and transfer that to people-power.I enjoyed my 13 hours in this game, short and sweet.
_childDocuments_.name: Airborne Kingdom

_childDocuments_.review: Really fun game, relaxing at times, challenging during others but not too fast paced. Managing resources and supplies well can be challenging, but 19 hours in and I didn't lose my ship once on Normal, only like twice did I get the alert that my coal was low and I started panicking. Just a matter of keeping an eye on your storage levels. Was exactly the type of game I was looking for, I could play the game and watch a show or text people and not worry about missing something. Going to step away for a minute or two? Just pause the world. Are you good on Coal/Food/Water? Step away and leave the game running on Speed 1 to let your workers harvest stuff. If you want something laid back, beautifully designed and a lot of fun I recommend Airborne Kingdom.The only complaint I have is there should be more Save Slots instead of just 1. If you are moving things around on your ship and you need to un-pause to have them build something, your happiness level goes down. I was at Jubilant and because I couldn't build comforts fast enough, all the houses in the area dropped to Mediocre. Then you have a very limited time before the people who only want to be there with a Jubilant or Satisfied rating take off and you don't have enough workers to build anything new. Would be nice to be able to try out different layouts for your ship without the risk of upsetting all your people.
_childDocuments_.name: Airborne Kingdom

_childDocuments_.review: Nice little game. I enjoyed playing it. I rly like the way they choose the map to generate in every new playthrough. Also the art style is simple very pretty. I also loved the way you could colour everythign like you wanted. _childDocuments_.review: I love the concept. The experience of building a flying city and taking it from place to place feels fresh enough that I keep gushing about it in all-caps to my friends. It took me ten hours to go through the campaign, and I had a lot of fun learning the mechanics. But on my second time through though, armed with a solid understanding of the dominant strategies, the gameplay seemed a lot emptier.  It was relaxing both playthroughs.The gameplay doesn't stand up to deep strategy and theorycrafting. This isn't SimCity - if you look up guides and build "correctly" the first time, you don't end up with a cooler bigger city; you just end up with something stale that you never have to fix. Skip the guides and learn as you go or you'll be bored - the city building is actually very forgiving.Overall I'd say it's memorable! It fulfills a niche I-wish-there-was-a-game-of. I'll probably think about "that cool citybuilder where you built a freaking flying city!" for years and years, whether I play it again or not. Can't recommend whether that makes it worthwhile for you on the price tag or not, but truly memorable games in this genre are in short supply.
