I don't have a budget rig but I haven't had issues with frames or stuttersEngaging.  There's always something to do, goals are well laid out but you can roam and explore too.Cons--------Can't customize the controls. Found right clicking to turn my camera and chose my destination to be clunky and wish i could chose what the controls are.Once a building is down it occupies your citizens even if it is doing nothing. I just found this to be a frustrating mechanic that broke the immersion at times.
_childDocuments_.name: Airborne Kingdom

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic game, checks all the boxes of a decent city builder while also being an adventure game thanks to your mobile city's ability to fly from place to place.  It starts out as an extremely casual, easygoing experience as all resources are very bountiful in the starter region.  However difficulty will increase pleasantly as the game proceeds and you enter regions with resource scarcities, while a growing population will begin to demand more different kinds of comforts.  It is relatively short, the goal being to ally with each of the 12 land-based kingdoms to reunite the world and each of them having only a single quest, but may still provide upwards of 10-12 hours gameplay.Overall I am quite happy with this one, and I highly recommend it!
_childDocuments_.name: Airborne Kingdom

_childDocuments_.review: A very relaxing game that you can largely take at your own pace. The art style is fun and the gameplay is that bit different from other similair titles. Maybe a bit samey because after 4 hours I have little strong desire to jump back in and finish the game, but may pick it up on a quiet afternoon to unwind! A great relaxation game (apart from the occasional scramble for resources)
_childDocuments_.name: Airborne Kingdom

_childDocuments_.review: Neat city builder with rather rare aproach (floating island games existed back in the 2Ks already but were always shunned), but its core difficulty lies with constant harvesting of resources alone (and keeping peeps fed). it has no combat and is exploration only in case you look for action. Zone two is also covered in thick fog and the third zone is worse.
_childDocuments_.name: Airborne Kingdom

_childDocuments_.review: A work of art. This has got to be one of the most beautiful games I have played in a very long time. Not only does it have an incredible graphical style, the sentiment of the story is truly lovely. The gameplay is fairly simple as city builders go but the balancing act you have to perform between workers, resources, and the literal balance of your city is quite enjoyable indeed
_childDocuments_.name: Airborne Kingdom

_childDocuments_.review: This is a really interesting game. I think it does itself no favors by locking the most entertaining campaign format behind the "New Game Plus" tag and requiring completion of the ~4 hour normal game. It feels really satisfying to eventually build a totally self-sufficient airship, or to create a more artistic design. I think the game is a bit on the easy end if you go all-in on min/maxing, but if you have some fun and build something fun, then this game really shines.
_childDocuments_.name: Airborne Kingdom

_childDocuments_.review: Airborne Kingdom — the sky city builder. Grow your unique town among the clouds, and fly it across a wide-open landscape. Explore the skies to restore serenity to the world below.

name: Paradise Lost
detailed_description: Buzz About the Game The war persisted for 20 more years only to end in flames when the Nazis launched nuclear missiles on most of Europe. In the aftermath, the heart of Europe remains shrouded in the mystery of complete destruction and deadly radiation, inaccessible to the rest of the world. You play as Szymon, a 12-year-old boy who’s just discovered a massive Nazi bunker while wandering the barren, nuclear wasteland of Poland after his mother’s death. He’s searching for an unknown man from a photograph his mother cherished. Who is he? Will you be able to find him? Descend into the retro futuristic bunker where advanced, industrial technology is intertwined with mysterious, Slavic pagan imagery and explore the underground city hidden within. Uncover the story of the bunker, from its takeover by Polish rebels to the ultimate fate of its inhabitants. What happened to them? Despite the desolation of the bunker, a mysterious girl named Ewa contacts Szymon through the bunker’s technology. If he can only find her, she might know the man in the picture. If he can find her, he finally won’t be alone…

_childDocuments_.review: This is a game I was both surprised and a little bit disappointed by. Ok, if im truely being honest, I didnt know what this game was going to be. It turned out to both be amazing in terms of story and visually compelling, but it lacked in audio(multiple audio cuts from the characters talking and overall audio quality was not great, CC is your friend) and there wasnt really any mechanics to the game, currencies to find, collectables or any of that, or being able to actually walk around in a semi-open world environment that it teased. Instead it walked you through a single path created by boulders, fallen rubble, building windows, and much much more. If you can get it for 5-10$ I would say its worth it, but in its current state not much more than that 6/10

_childDocuments_.review: This is areally bad walking simulator.It has extraordianry graphics but the story and the movement are really bad. You will learn more about the settings from the promotion matherial than the game itself. You can interact with specific objects during the game to learn more about the setting but there's very little to find, and the movement mechanic is atrocious (if it were good, it would have taken me half of the time to finish it).One specific problem i don't wee in other reviews is that it broke immersion sometimes, like the time where I was clearly supposed to interact with a lever before talking to my companion but i didn't push it, it resulted in my character telling that the door was stuck without me trying it before.Couple that with the fact that in the end it blocks out some interesting lore and forces you to miss out in some worldbuilding, it's a really bad choice.Btw, once you finish the game you can't go back to play a specific part of the story, you have to do it all again (it's not that long but it's worth mentioning).I'l come back in the future to see if anything changed and update this review.

_childDocuments_.review: A short yet interesting art piece.Paradise Lost was a very pleasant walking simulator with a story to tell. Diving deeper into the bunker only got more and more intriguing up until the end, however, I did find the story to become very predictable towards the end to a point where it felt a bit rushed during the the final stretch, you were bombarded with a bit of too much info when up until then it was partially up to the game and partially up to you to connect the dots, while I don't mind this aproach as I can see it being welcomed by someone that was struggling a bit to keep up it could have gotten spread out with an extra few minutes of gameplay.The only complaints I have is the lack of a save/load interface, I like to hunt achievements but I can tell the remaining I need are all based on the decisions made during the final minutes, playing through the entire game again just for those final decisions is a bit of a stretch for me, maybe if there was more decision material earlier on, aside from that I can only really think of some small optimizations when transitioning areas as my game did dip into the 30/40s for a few seconds other then that a smooth experience.Overall a great game that kept me engaged for an afternoon, interesting plot, good graphics, engaging story, lots of detail and good soundtrack.For slightly more then what I'd pay to see a movie it is well worth your money, support this gem and enjoy it!
_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Lost

_childDocuments_.review: * engrossing, atmospheric setting* neat alt-history, post-apoc take on WW2* lots to explore and soak in* interesting story* nice music and ambient sound effects* impressive art direction* save erases following ending (can be avoided if you know the right moment to restore your last checkpoint/level save to try a different set of options)* no manual saves, one way only* not much "game" if you favor a lot of interactivity, action, and/or puzzle solving* a few bugsI'll warn you now because the game doesn't -- following whatever ending you get, the game erases your progress. At least Nier: Automata is nice enough to ask you if you want to make that kind of sacrifice, but this doesn't and if you're an achievement hunter (or someone that likes to experiment with different choices and see where they go or what dialogues are said), you'll need to repeat going through everything again to get what you may have missed. I'll give it a thumbs up because overall, I felt this was a quality experience, but it's a marginal one because of this one "feature" and YMMV depending on how this might make you feel.That said, I really enjoyed my time here. The alt-history "what if" post-apocalypse world where WW2 stretched beyond the 1940s and ended in a nuclear winter leaves as many questions as the the mysterious bunker where the last, desperate gasp of the Third Reich lay hidden beneath the snow. It's into this setting that you're thrust into with little knowledge of the outside world or of the bunker itself -- your character is sure of their actions even if you, as the player, aren't. Eventually, your character's motivations become clearer through the experience, focusing your goals in as much of the same way as they do his in the story.Paradise Lost is a museum of crumbling glory and withered hopes buried somewhere in what used to be Poland that your walk will take you through. And you do walk -- slowly -- through it all (even 'sprinting' is only a slightly faster crawl). Because of design decisions like these, it can sometimes feel oppressive in its handling of the experience, but it's also one filled with details in every corner; cold concrete and polished marble welcoming in arrivals to this strange place can give way to wood paneled offices and V2 rockets on turning a corner. Papers with a mushroom cloud on the front page are the last look at a world long dead. Nazi horrors captured in text and silent memorials in the form of rusting weapons and experimental notes lay scattered about. Notes left behind add to the collective atmosphere of mystery and strangeness the deeper you venture into the bunker. The artists, writers, and musicians have crafted an incredibly detailed world to piece its story together.Much of the experience is delivered through a few flashbacks but mostly through notes and encountering something else later in the game that drives things ahead. Not all of your questions may be answered even by the end thanks to a few holes, but overall, it clings to its "museum" approach in relating its world to the player. It's mostly the questions and the sense of mystery that kept me moving forward -- what happened to everyone here? Why did things turn out the way they did? Did the bunker engineers really build that weird thing at the end?"Puzzles" mostly consist of decisions that you are prompted to make which can alter bits and pieces of the bunker around you. For example, reviewing an old record that you interact with may change something that you encounter later that was left behind by that "past" decision. And as mentioned earlier, saves are one-way -- you can't return to earlier areas and explore again if you feel that you've missed something. The ending is the same way but worse. I can understand that in a way, this save philosophy is meant to evoke a certain feeling of atmosphere and prevent "gaming" that feeling but on the other hand, I feel in this instance, it doesn't respect the player's time. It really didn't add much to the experience for me other than being annoyed at someone else tearing out the previous chapters of the book I was reading.As for bugs, I encountered very few. The worst bug was when the protagonist picked up an album later in the story and held empty air in their hands while comments about its contents played. It would have been nice to actually see the album, but that's the worst "game breaking" thing that I experienced outside of a texture glitch or two (like backwards text on a cement bag). Paradise Lost can be finished in one sitting (with snack breaks!) and as linear as the save system makes things out to be, each area is compact enough in presenting what they have to alleviate its relentless push for you to keep moving forward. In a way, that might be part of the message that it's trying to deliver. That even in this wasteland, the only thing worth doing to survive is move forward and never look back to forge a new beginning. But sometimes, forgetting the way back can be even worse.

_childDocuments_.review: Paradise Lost is at its forefront, a decent story driven walking game.The world is rich with beautiful scenes and atmosphere, and the underlying story is good.The story is strong and well told and the somewhat silent protagonist that you play as,is a refreshing design choice instead of having constant chatter the entire way through.The main issues i take with this game comes down to three points.First and foremost,The strongest feature point of this game in my opinion is the computer console (the EVE computers) in which you use throughout the game. It gives the player a glimpse into what happened in the past and that's fantastic. the problem falls within it's execution. During the instances in which the player interacts with these computers, you're given scenariosand choices. Each of the choices have outcomes that have benefits & consequences within the past and leave the player with the question of, did my actions actually affect the outcomes of the past/present or did they do nothing at all, and that is fantastic.The problem i find myself with though, is that Paradise Lost's (the book not the game) narrative purpose is the examination of free will, and censorship being placed upon ones free will and that limitation being a direct affront to God's intent for humanity. In that, person(s) being allowed to make their own choices based on the any and all information that exists to arrive at their own understanding and self determination. The Game simply betrays this core tenet of the narrative by putting a timer on most, if not all the computer related interactions. It gives you a split second to make a choice, and if you don't act then things happen anyways. The game makes a choice for you even if you wanted to pick the other option. This is a betrayal of free will. For a game that uses the title of perhaps one of the greatest works of English literature (Paradise Lost), and goes as far as even showing John Milton's name on book binding within the opening cut scene of the game. The game vaguely follows the narrative of the writing, or its intent.There are however, some points in the game which shadow certain aspects of the writings story points but only loosely. It could be argued however, that the minor references of censorship within the game could be a call to the intent of the Paradise Lost's writing as that was partly the underlying intent and purpose of Paradise Lost and Paradise Regained.Some may find this gripe to be petty or going out on a limb, but the The title of the game, The title, Paradise Lost, comes with weight and importance. Something this game fails to live up to.Secondly, The game feels empty, and from the narrative perspective of the game it makes sense. But from the player perspective, the game feels empty in relation to what you as a player are allowed to experience and see. I found myself many times during my play through, asking why i cannot crouch. There were many windows, world objects etc that i wanted to view but i simply couldn't because there was no way to crouch or zoom in far enough to observe them.Third,There are many points within the game where you as the player, come acrossdocuments or posters scattered around the world that are entirely in Polish or German.which is understandable given the setting of the game. The issue i have however,is that some of these documents, when scanned with a translator give important informationin relation to the overall background of the game world narrative. Additionally, there are documents that even the google image translator cannot identify to translate and that's not a fault of the game at all. But it would have been nice for those documents that the player physically picks up, to have the E examination option that almost all the other documents have and to provide a translation of said document.Smaller gripes i have, just to name a small handful (These aren't really major issues)-Many collision issues and other bugs that occur in forced game segments that are easilyrecreated and should have been an effortless catch in QA testing, such as floor pieces banging into the player while into an elevator. The green suitcase near the start of the game doesn't open even though you do the animation to open it. there are more, but i wont make this any longer than it is.- There is no visual evidence relating to the people involved in conflicts throughout the story(there are casings and holes etc. but how did all the bodies get moved?)The bottom line i suppose is the question of if this game is worth the money its listed for.at the time of writing the game is on sale for about $9.89 USD and full price is $14.99 USD.It took me 5 and 1/2 hours roughly to complete the game and I in no way rushed through it.Is almost 6 hours of this game worth nine dollars? i would say so, but is fifteen dollars worth it? I would say that its definitely a approaching being a high cost for content value at fifteen dollars. Did i enjoy it? yes. Could it have been expanded upon more in terms of game play and narrative? Yes.TLDR; its a short maybe 6 hour story focused walking game with a decent story line.+- It has some strange design choices which are a benefit and detriment to the game.+  It's characters are enjoyable, and the lore within the world is captivating.-  The game fails to live up to the pedigree of it's title.    6.3/10

_childDocuments_.review: Every time I play a post apocalyptic game I have a weird feeling that there should be a game which tells the story of an unsung hero. Who is that hero? He/she is that human being who goes into work AFTER the apocalypse, prints out the newspaper about the apocalypse itself and also delivers it to already sealed bunkers. No, this game isn’t about that hero, but this is another game which includes a newspaper lore object with the title “The bombs has fallen”...Paradise Lost takes place in an alternative universe, where the 2nd World War did not end in 1945, instead it became a stationary warfare. The extended timeline offered enough time for all parties to develop nuclear weapons and so release the hell of the nuclear armageddon upon our planet. This was actually the plan of the Axis, to clean the world from unwanted human races while hiding and surviving in huge, secret underground bases. Paradise Lost invites you to explore one of these bases and all its secrets.Paradise Lost is a walking simulator, an interactive adventure which lets you explore an underground facility built by the nazis. There is no action(fps or platforming elements), there are no puzzles, what the game is offering is just exploration and an overview to an alternate world with a lot of text based lore objects which helps you to visualize how life was in that universe and how the world changed.Bored about nazis? Well, the story takes place in their bunker, but the bunker was actually taken over by the polish underground resistance so while at the beginning you will find information about the world and about the crime of the nazis, later you will experience the life of the resistance too, but not from first hand, you will still find only documents and computer logs only. As the story progresses, you will figure out that the true personality of humanity showed up in this facility too: nazis might be gone already, but humans always need to monsterize others, need to find a new enemy or someone to blame, just like in our world. The unwillingness to cooperate on all sides made the facility just as lifeless as the nuclear winter did to the surface.Will you still be alone, or there are survivors in the facility? Curious about the fate of the bunker and the world? Then start playing the game:-)This is a story oriented exploration game, if you don’t like that, then you better look for something else, if you do like these kinds of games, then this will be a world you might want to explore.Rankings based on my own opinion:Story: 8/10Visuals: 7/10Voice acting: 7/10Atmosphere of the game: 9/10Linear gameplay? YesReplayed the game 3 times, not encountered any bug, character wasn’t stuck at any time, game never crashed and i checked every corner, tried to move to every possible location.Perfection time: ~3-5h. 1 playthrough enough but you need to back up your save file as some parts of the game need to be replayed and no manual saving in the game. The first you could find early in the game, where you need to choose how you will enter the base, and the other missable achievements awarded for the endings. You probably don’t want to replay a story oriented walking simulator 3 times just to see the other endings and to get the other ending related achievements. Once you finish the game your save file is deleted by the game, this is why you just can’t return to the end and select a different ending. So again: backup your save file!

_childDocuments_.review: If you like walking simulators which, at sprinting speed, simulate blowing off both your legs with a grenade while over-encumbered in Fallout 3, Then this is the game for you! Poorly optimized, unrealistic shadows and reflections, horrible controls, and frequent stuttering even on top-of-the-line PC hardware. Broken checkpoints and tediously long animations brings this slog of a game to an unbearable low.It's unfortunate, as this game *looks* stunning, and should be more enticing. I love how relaxing narrative driven "walking simulators" are, especially with the music, but this becomes to frustrating miserable, that I can't bring myself to continue. A top review says something like "...if you *were* able to walk faster than a snail with dysentery, you'd miss important story elements." but that's completely false. This game holds your hand so much, that 'Important story elements' are highlighted from a mile away, breaking immersion. There are other background pops that I'd love to get a better look at, but without a 'focus' or 'zoom' feature, all the interesting stuff just turns into background noise and repeating assets. This review also mentions a very common, game breaking, soft locking bug, and how to circumvent it. If your top positive review, your golden child, mentions a huge flaw, that's not great. A lot of the written narrative you have to read has some Deutsch sprinkled into the English, however, there are no language settings for this game. It would be nice to have the option of reading everything in meine Muttersprache.The game feels as if the developers spent their entire budget on level design and story, they then only had enough to pay for a sixth grader learning how to code on youtube to finish up the game. The game can be 100% in about four hours, or 30 minutes if you walked at the same speed as in Ethan Carter or Edith Finch.

_childDocuments_.review: This game has so much going for it. An interesting synopses, atmosphere, the still images look like a AAA game, the voice acting (so far) is way above most indie titles... sadly this game has 3 buts, and one is really big.The first is that it has the most painfully slow walking speed of even any "walking simulator" I have ever played. This is why I literally had to stop playing after less than an hour. It absolutely ruined this game. Everything else is not that bad, especially for an indie title. Second is that the game is way too gpu intensive for what it delivers. It will take more than a 1080 ti to run more than 1080p at 60fps. Now understand, this game doesn't really have dynamic environments, or even lighting really. Also, as I hinted at earlier, there is nothing that move at even relatively medium speed from what I have seen. Again though this is an indie game. That happens when people are learning a game engine. If the game is good, this is a non issue.Finally, the last issue is graphical anomalies. From objects popping through each other, to floating in mid-air, I would have had a hard time finding a screen-shot without some seriously odd issues. I reiterate though, this is an indie game. If you can play a Bethesda game you played $60 for and not be irate, this is passable. Except for the walking speed, every other issue can be summed up to an indie developer learning the ropes, and I am more than happy to support people starting out, especially when they show promise. But the walking speed... the walking speed was a design choice... I don't know what kind of person could play test this and say to themselves "yeah, its okay."Sadly, the walking speed alone makes this a "do not recommend"

_childDocuments_.review: A sub-par walking simulator, Paradise Lost will real you in with it's gorgeous environments and strong atmosphere. If you have the capacity to make it any father than that, I'd be surprised. For one, the game is slow. I have played many games within this genre and a slow walk speed is a staple. That isn't the problem. It's that every action comes with an animation. The same animation. Every paper you grab uses the same awkward animation. Every box you climb uses the same awkward animation. Every ladder you climb is agony, as you can clearly see the animation reset every two rungs. While probably done in the name of immersion, there is no quicker way to remind yourself you're playing a game than a constant need to break all flow to show an animation you've seen dozens of times already. Plus, the game involves mouse gestures which bring nothing to close the gap between player and character, instead only widening it.The story is also aggressively mediocre. There are barely any sideplots to keep up with and, despite the insane amount of documents you will pick up in the name of lore (and trust me, you will dread having to pick up another paper, watch the same awkward animation as the hand clearly never touches the paper, read gibberish, then place it back down with another slow movement), you learn almost nothing interesting about the world you are exploring. Also...Nazis? What is the point of this game invoking such strong Nazi imagery? Is it because Nazis are easy to hate? That you can justify including dark, horrible things in your story and, instead of approaching it with nuance and trying to incorporate themes into your story, you can just go "wow Nazis suck look at these terrible things they did (that we made up)." Nazis, are indeed, scum. But this game's story is middling and predictable at best, offensive at it's worse. All of this delivered with some truly lifeless voice acting that does nothing to elevate this dull script.Not only that, Paradise Lost is full of technical issues, from frequent frame drops to legitimate game-breaking bugs that make progress impossible. I applaud a small studio for trying to take on such a grandiose game, but it's obvious how outside their scope this product is. I hate to be so negative, but I'm also disappointed at how quickly my experience deteriorated with every passing minute. Avoid Paradise Lost, it does not deserve to be found.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a game for people that enjoy the slow discovery of unraveling a lengthy story. The negatives: Exploration is mostly limited with one-way zones and if you are the type of person that likes to explore everything you will be annoyed that there is no running mode when retracing your steps. The controls are a little janky, which if you are not careful can result in glitched animations when interacting with objects. The voice prompts are either glitchy or time out quickly, not sure if that was intentional. Also, after one specific autosave I was stuck frozen in the environment unable to move and had to restart a level. Controls aside, the graphics and gameplay are smooth even maxed out using a 1080 Ti on an SSD. The UE4 engine does have the usual surface gloss reflection issues, but otherwise the graphics are well done and there is plenty to look at!Some minor spoilers past this point: The story is based on an alternate-history premise where the US stayed neutral in WW2 into the 1950's before joining the war. Meanwhile US inventions such as the ENIAC and nuclear weapons spurred counter-technologies in Nazi Germany. Despite facing defeat once again, thanks to an additional decade and a half of technological advancement this Nazi Germany easily had the tools to do what the real one could not and triggered a nuclear winter with plans to continue the Third Reich underground using its doomsday bunker plans. The story is haunting and it is long, but if you enjoy a lengthy narrative story in game exploration form and can overlook a rough user interaction interface then this is a story/game for you!

_childDocuments_.review: Walking simulators are only worth playing if they have good writing that intrigues you and deals with interesting themes in a complex and engaging way. Games like Tacoma, Gone Home, and What Remains of Edith Finch are the current bar-setters in this regard. Paradise Lost, while featuring stunning, laudable art direction and an interesting premise, simply lacks the caliber of writing that I needed to stay interested in order to see it through to the end. It definitely seems to be aiming for something compelling, but ultimately it's a case of the writers chewing more than they've bitten off.You know prestige TV, like Mad Men, Breaking Bad, True Detective (seasons 1 and 3), and The Terror? You know how when you're watching those shows, you can just sort of  that there's something special about them, something really great in terms of the quality of the dialogue and the complexity of the storytelling and characterizations? Well Paradise Lost is a game that aims for that kind of quality, but whoever wrote it lacks the deft touch, patience, and insight needed to achieve such a height. It comes across like something that is aping good art, without having any genuine soulful expression of its own. For example, the writers seem to intuitively understand how interesting it can be to explore how a character processes the stages of grief, especially when framed against the plot of some kind of moral parable, but instead of subtly weaving this into the story in a tactful, clever way, the game heavy-handedly breaks the game into chapters that are literally named after each of the stages of grief, but then barely touches upon how the main character is dealing with their grief (or if it did, did so in a manner so indirect that it was lost on me--and either way, I felt nothing).The game is littered with letters and reports for the player to read, and these serve as the primary source of general exposition about what is going on in the game world. The problem is that the quality of these letters is generally pretty sophomoric. And I'm not talking about the game's English composition--the localization is actually pretty decent. No, I mean the  of the writing. There's no sense that these letters serve as anything more than blunt tools of exposition. There's no feeling of thematic cohesion, nothing that tickles the primal parts of your animal brain and touches upon the rich archetypes and tragedies buried deep down in there (the audio logs in all three Bioshock games are great examples of what I am talking about, as well as basically every moment of Edith Finch).Walking simulators really need to be bold and tell stories in daring, original ways. All of the successful ones are wildly imaginative in their premises, and keenly insightful in their thematic exploration. Paradise Lost, on some level, is aware of this, but it struggles to do more than erect the pretty facade of a good story. The game aims high without being willing to do the visionary legwork to actually reach that height.

_childDocuments_.review: Paradise Lost presents an alternate version of history but does not pack itself with enough narrative to remain interesting. Exploring a Nazi bunker is intriguing at first, when the story is not trying so hard to evade answers by excluding vital information. But when the story stretches itself thin, players have to wait until the lacklustre end for it to make sense. It is a shame, too, because the environments are designed well enough that they could have been part of a better game. Paradise Lost might have succeeded as a more traditional adventure title, with puzzles and non-linear exploration. As it stands now, even at its reasonably low price, this walking simulator is a few steps behind the pace.

_childDocuments_.review: If the optoin were available this would be a maybe. Make no mistake, there is little game here. It is a walking simulator with not much in the way of interaction. The character moves very slowly and some people will get frustrated by the pointless mini game activities to open doors and pull levers. On the other side it's a very interesting environment and story and the end is interesting and touching. You can make choices, but there wasn't much explaining the consequence of the one I did, so I'm not sure it would make much of a difference other than a different end screen maybe? I got it for about 10 dollars and it's normally 15. I would feel better at a 5 dollar price point for one big reason. The story is telegraphed and obvious within the first 20ish minutes of a 3 hour game and because you're playing a set character instead of playing yourself, there's no way to convey that you know what's going on because he doesn't get it. It's still interesting to see how it plays out, but with a 3 hour run time padded by slow movement, some more meaningful choices and interactions would have been nice. At the end of the day I enjoyed my time with it and in the years to come I might do another run and make some different choices to see if it affects the outcome at all. I'm  interested in seeing what the developer could do with a little more budget and with something a little more ambitious than a walker.

_childDocuments_.review: A game based in the history of actual Nazi programs that rewards players with knowledge of WWII and the crimes committed by the third Reich, Paradise Lost is a game that treats the Nazi's as villains without requiring you to shoot them as they rise from the dead. Real history, real stories, woven into set pieces that are beautifully crafted and demand your attention. Screenshot worthy, easy to finish in 5-hours without missing any story bits, and casual. You won't need to hide, shoot, or run away from anything, but the tension and unknown will keep you going. The lore is a bit confusing and there will be parts that contradict others. Don't approach the game with a fine tooth comb. You have to accept that some story bits will contradict others, but then again, don't all the best stories have multiple sides? Do you retell a story the same way every time you tell it? Humans are fallible - especially ones locked underground. At points emotional, tense, and once or twice a bit tedious (don't worry, it won't last long!). I would recommend this for anyone looking for an exploration game where the monsters of other a post-apocalyptic worlds aren't found.

Its art direction and premise, along with some of the backstory, are compelling enough that it might be worth a try as part of a sale or bundle, but not at full price.

_childDocuments_.review: Over 8 hours into the story… only walked about 100 feet.It’s basically Fallout, but the protagonist comes from the outside into the vault. The aesthetic of the game reminded me of the Metro Series games minus the action. It seems the devs wanted it to be an experience rather than just another action game. Paradise Lost has an intriguing premise, but this is one of those games you watch a stream or let’s play, and if you really want to experience it, wait for a deep, deep sale years later.Sadly the nutritional facts on a milk carton have a more coherent plot than this game. Unfortunately “story” is basically all Paradise Lost has since the game doesn’t have much gameplay outside of examining objects, pushing small buttons, and moving levers, if those can even be considered mechanics at all. Bonding narrative with the game mechanics is how entries in this genre elevate themselves to the next level so it’s disappointing to see Paradise Lost lacked ambition in this way. Even some metaphor-free environmental puzzles would’ve helped with the pacing and interactivity (as long as the painfully slow walking speed was sped up).Honestly the most incredible part of the game is that after two decades of Nazi occupation, there were still living Poles in Poland. The atmosphere is just amazing. The sense of the mystery involved in trying to figure out what happened, the attention to detail in the scenery and the darkness of the overall theme is astounding. Unfortunately many Americans won’t understand this game. Inhabitants of countries that survived the German occupation though will find many sad references to their past here. Too bad the gameplay itself isn’t as enticing as the setting and the environment.The world although empty, is strikingly beautiful. The dour depths of the vault in the game is wonderfully rendered, striking a good balance of awe-striking scale from the exteriors and detailed interiors. These grand bunker is reminiscent of Bioshock’s Rapture as it is a completely unrealistic feat of engineering yet the game uses those fictional elements to truly inspire a palpable sense of wonder. Average story and lore, slow paced but still interesting. If you’re a COD or Fortnite fan though though this game is probably not for you. If you’re in the mood for something slower paced with some very light engagement I’d give it a try.6//10
_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Lost

_childDocuments_.review: This is in no way a bad game, it has interesting concepts, a good story and Nazi Germany is almost always an interesting topic to focus on considering all of the different things they actually did in real life.  The reason I Cant recommend this game is because there is an obvious lack of polish and the fact that the entire story could have been told through another medium (Movie or Book) and lose no quality or miss any story beats.  The lore is in depth but the gameplay leans on the lore too much.  The ending isn't bad but there were so many other things that they could have done but avoided expanding on a lot of things probably due to financial constraints.  Which isn't their fault being an indie studio but some things could have been expanded in other ways.  The game offers minimal replayability consider there are 2 endings that are fairly black and white.  A lot of the twists are well thought out and well executed but on a second playthrough, that means nothing.  The audio is funky at times and the computer segments, while nice lore segments, are confusing.  Do my inputs have an effect on what has supposedly happened? How did the shelter fall?  Were these people in the bunker from the beginning or did they come across it after it fell and then poplulated it themselves? What happened to German High command? What was the point of the Drastic change in story direction after chapter 3?  They could have focused on plenty of other details of the world they setup but they decided to focus on the sibling story. The gameplay is atrocious.  Its not gameplay if you aren't engaged, Its an overgrown walking simulator without any real gameplay elements.  While the story does not require it, the medium that they chose does.  Like i stated previously, It could have been told in any other medium and not lost any fidelity.TLDR : Its an Overgrown Walking simulator that could have been told through another medium with interesting concepts but a lackluster ending.

_childDocuments_.review: Paradise Lost is an atmospheric, story-driven walking sim. It gives you that characteristic sense of immersion and claustrophobia that you get from a Metro game, only with a substantially different kind of plot and with no shooting. Fortunately, the plot and writing are strong enough to carry the game throughout its runtime. The most important thing to do in this game is to explore and read everything you can find, as they contain a ton of small details that both flesh out the plot and the world it is set in. You'll only get half the story if you don't read them. I started out on the fence about this game, but became emotionally invested about an hour in. It's short enough that you can finish in one quiet evening too, and I'm glad I spent my evening with this game.

_childDocuments_.review: This game has an interesting setting and premise but as a walking sim it isnt a lot of fun to play through.Its set in an alternate timeline where WW2 dragged on and ended in nuclear war. In the game you play a young boy who has recently lost his mother and ends up going to a massive abandoned Nazi bunker to try and track down some answers about his mothers past.The alternate timeline and setting are the most enjoyable part of the game. The bunker has a really cool aesthetic with a WW2 mixed with  more advanced technology sort of feel to it. You can find notes and recordings that fill you in on the purpose of the bunker and some of the things that transpired there.While the general setting was pretty good the actual gameplay was not. Your character walks really slowly and it sort of feels like this was done deliberately to artificially drag out the length of the game. There isnt really much to do other than walk through the levels and interact with the occasional document or item. Even some basic puzzles would have broken up the tedium of the gameplay. Another mild annoyance was that there are several items that can be picked up but are essentially pointless as the character doesnt comment on them and it just feels like these were dotted about to make the player spend more time exploring.The story was ok though I felt the dialogue and voice acting weren't great, at least in the English version. It sounded like English might have been a second language for the voice cast so maybe it might be better experienced in Polish.Overall I've hit recommended for this one, although if there was a neutral option that would have been more appropriate for me. If the setting and premise of the game sounds interesting to you then it might be worth a try, but if not it's probably best to skip this one.

The main character walks like a snail, it takes forever to get anywhere, so finding documents in rooms is tedious, not exciting.And I didn't like the way the game tells the story. It's scattered in dozens of different documents, diaries and letters, presented in a chaotic manner with a ton of unrelated content. That's probably why the ending had little impact on me – I honestly had no idea what happened. And that's a shame.

_childDocuments_.review: A walking simulator about exploring an abandoned WWII-era Russia military base.For most walking simulators, the main appeal is the story.  Unfortunately the story in this one is not great. You play as a child exploring an abandoned base, looking for information about his father, because reasons. _childDocuments_.review: The game's story is chilling when it leans into the horrors of Nazism - you will come across things like: A drawer full of children's spines; an entire office filled with human skulls, etc., and I guarantee it will disturb you - however, it fails miserably at trying to get us to bond with the characters. This is likely because it does a terrible job of explaining the reasons behind the character's actions, and the dialogue isn't great, especially considering context, or rather, lack thereof.While the story explains why we find no Germans in the vault - we never get a clear explanation as to how the "polish resistance" manages to infiltrate the vault in the first place and survive nuclear apocalypse, especially considering the security and the Nazi AI "EVE". Another plot-hole lies within what your Father does to your sister; he keeps saying it's to "save us" and "it's for the greater good" and so on and so forth - but given that he then leaves her behind and ventures outside of her influence, where she literally can do no good, and not only that but leaves her to live essentially a lifetime of loneliness, it's not clear what he means at all. What makes this worse is the game tries to convince us that forgiving our father is the right choice, even our mother hopes that he will "forgive her" for meddling with his plans. But what is his plan? We're never told; we're just supposed to believe this religiously-insane psychopathic murderer has good intentions. Ultimately the final dilemma of the game isn't really a dilemma at all, because the morally right choice is painfully obvious.The Game-play further disappoints; walking speed and interactions are so painfully slow (even for a horror game) that the run key basically is pointless since you don't run any faster, it just increases your FOV minutely. Tedious, unnecessary, and at times difficult to initiate interaction prompts further act as filler for an otherwise OK Psychological horror game. Also, don't bother picking up anything that isn't a letter since most of the other items serve no purpose at all. There are no real puzzles. Furthermore, in order to find all the lore, and the endings, the game is hard-coded so that you have to play at least three separate times; there is literally a section where you can only open two of three doors at one of the most interesting parts of the game, because they purposefully don't give you enough power.While the graphics and environments are theoretically gorgeous in a hauntingly beautiful way, ultimately software problems and bugs mean you will be only barely be able to play at High settings, if you can tolerate occasional stutter. TL;DR: Only worth playing for the story and graphics; for that reason just watch a play-through instead. Your experience will actually be way waaaaaay worse if you play through the game yourself, and you'll need to watch a play-through in any case if you don't want to do this multiple times for a few extra letters and lines of dialogue.

_childDocuments_.review: World War 2.One of the darkest Hours of Mankind.What if there had been no winner in 1945 and the war went on for another 20 years.And ended with no winner.With Europe totally destroyed by Nuclear Bombs.Welcome to PARADISE LOST!FIRST an important Hint.There is a bug that can be easy solved.When you return to continue your Game your Charakter can be stucked and did not move.Here go into the Options Menu, don´t change anything and press Accept.Now your Charakter will move on. Don´t ask me, why it is so, but it worked.That was the only bug i encountered and i played it to the End.SECOND an important Point.This is a Walking Simulator. NOT a Running Simulator.Yes, there is that typical Running Key to move faster, but it isn´t really faster.You have to go long ways through really impressive Areas. It can feel like chewing gum dragging long, if you are in hurry or just want to end this Game fast.In this Case, this Game is NOT for you. In my opinion this is willed, because this Game has an amazing and unique Atmosphere with so many detailsthat will be missed if you are just running through.NOW to the Game.As said before, PARADISE LOST is a unique Walking Simulator.There are no fights, just walking and exploring.You are playing a young Boy which mother died and he is now on his own.Destinny leads him to an old abandoned Nazi Bunker.From here an amazing and impressive Story starts, that i would also read as a book if its exists.I don´t want to tell anything about the Story, i went nearly blind into the Game, just with the knowledgeof a Review from a Friend, which was the Reason for me to play it.And i played it in one go, so impressive is the Atmosphere and the Story.One thing, this game will demand tough decisions from you and it also deals with hard topics from the Past.The Graphics are amazing atmospheric and so detailed that i stopped many times to explore Rooms and places just to find out howthey have had lived in the Bunker and what happened to them. If you are attentive you will find a trace of different People of the paston your way. What they did, where they arrived, where they lived. I like such Details, because they fascinate me. Speaking of Details, the Developer did very well researchment.The whole Bunker feels like 1940-1960´s with all of his belongings. From fonts to items.Each Area, absolutly each Area is amazingly done and feels real.That all is rounded up by a fantastic Soundtrack and wonderfull Speakers.PARADISE LOST feels like my favourite Game VALLEY. They have so much elements in Common. The Secrets of the Past, the Atmosphere and Soundtrack and yes (For the ones who played VALLEY) it really has a Fischer and Virginia, too.So, if you want to experience an amazing Story Driven Walking Simulator with an unique Atmosphere, then this is for you.Take your Time, use Headphones and darken the Room and dive into a fascinating Game.Thank you for Reading.

_childDocuments_.review: When I first saw the trailers I was intrigued by this game’s setting, being a sucker for post-apocalyptic deserts and historical fiction, so I decided to get it a few months ago but then it just sat in my collection for ages. Finally I played it and I am so very glad that I did because it has become one of my favourite indies. can be summed up as an amalgamation of some of the finest elements from , , and . However, it is also a “walking simulator”, which makes it quite different from all three of the aforementioned. At the same time it is much more interactive than the average product of this type and, although mostly linear, allows you to make choices that will result in some branching paths; this sets it apart from many other titles in the genre.It is also absolutely stunning. The environments here have been made with meticulous care, the atmospheric audio design really draws you in (even the protagonist’s sighs seem almost deliberately paced), all the art made for the game is striking, and the soundtrack is simply haunting. I was surprised to hear absolutely fantastic and truly emotional performances from the voice actors, as some of these more unconventional projects made in Eastern Europe tend to really fall short in that respect (even bigger productions like the newer  games tend to have pretty poor English versions and need to be played in Russian for the full experience).The world-building here is impressive as well. Sure, there is your usual outlandish Nazi science stuff that is par for the course in alternate history settings – along with a frozen post-nuclear wasteland, underground bunkers, and other things you might be used to. What is more exceptional is how believable, sci-fi tech aside, the game’s premise is. Nazi German plans predicted 80% of Poles were to be removed from the occupied country, most to be exterminated and the rest enslaved, which in reality the invading forces managed to partially achieve (about 17% of Poles living in German-occupied Poland were killed during the Holocaust with ~6 million dead and almost 2 million forcefully resettled).Up to 200.000 infants were kidnapped from Poland and sent deeper into the Third Reich for medical experiments and slave labour; the ones “lucky” enough to be born with blond hair and blue eyes had their identities secretly changed so that they could be Germanised, raised by the SS to become members of German society. In occupied Poland itself schools above primary level were shut, use of the Polish language restricted, educated and influential groups executed, able-bodied persons forced to carry out hard labour for the Nazi war machine, and the local population frequently massacred. All of this is historical fact.What  shows is the truly horrifying vision of a world where the war continued well beyond the 1940s, allowing fascist leaders to carry out all sorts of other sick plans as part of their twisted Generalplan Ost, until the global conflict turned into an atomic exchange. Consequently, the narrative – quite respectfully – deals with the grimly serious subject matter of genocide, racist pseudoscience, inhumane experimentation, and other relevant topics that most players will find disturbing. Intertwined with this is a more personal story of a surviving Polish boy who ventures beneath the ruins of Kraków. The excellent audio-visual presentation makes this a poignant experience.Some will be put off by this straight away purely because of the gameplay. That is fair enough, it is not for everyone. There is a “run” button, but it increases Szymon’s movement speed marginally. This is not a game to rush through, though, as the way it is built from the ground up implores you to explore everything it has to offer. Most players will be done with this story in about 3 hours, but you might be able to stretch it to as much as twice that if you go for all the endings. The only issues I’ve had with the game were of a technical nature: an easily dealt with glitch and one more immersion-breaking bug. Some have also reported frame rate drops, but I have not come across this.The asking price is low, especially considering how expensive games have gotten in general, but I understand people being cautious about spending any money on a less than 6h product. On the other hand, it would be criminal to not pick it up when it is on sale. If you appreciate a smarter and considerably more atmospheric journey than most of the first-person games out there then you should definitely give  a go.

_childDocuments_.review: Paradise Lost is a great example of a game with good graphics and nothing behind it. I love walking simulators like What Remains of Edith Finch, Everybody's Gone to the Rapture, Firewatch and others, but this is probably the most dull and superficial I have ever played and hated. There is literally zero gameplay; you move your character from A to B listening to the story, pulling some levers and pushing some buttons. A boring atrocious experience with a really slow walking speed.About the story, you can get the whole picture after 30 minutes. They basically spoiled it in the trailers and even in the game description. It's neither good or original, they tried hard to make a mix between Firewatch and Metro but written by a team of unexperienced writers and an invisible game designer. Ah, there are also two awful endings based on a couple of choices you can make at the end.The environments look good but if you look at the 2D assets in the background it just feels like being inside the Unreal Engine viewport. Level design is not very intuitive; you don't really know why and where are you supposed to go. Until I gave up, I was often exploring empty rooms where the only action I could make was opening a drawer just to find... nothing. I could have probably finished the game in 3 hours if it didn't waste my time with useless exploring.I also got a game-breaking bug in chapter 4. My character started floating and couldn't enter the elevator, so I had to reload the checkpoint and play again those 15 minutes.The game identity suffers a lot. At first you find some documents and papers written in german that you can't understand because there is no translating interface; then you hear some recordings in polish which, again, are not translated, so you can't understand a single word; and then you find tons of documents that are perfectly translated in english, which don't make any sense in a nazi bunker. Jesus, just make all the documents in their native language and let the UI translate them.The voice-overs really killed it for me. They used Polish voice actors trying to act in English. The result is awful, with forced intonations and reactions (you can hear them from the trailer). It would have been better if they spoke using their native language + subtitles. It's a shame the game doesn't even have Polish voice-overs. Dialogues also tend to overlap on each other often, which is quite disturbing.After I finished the game in two sessions I got headache and nausea. Maybe it was from the motion slowliness, maybe from the constant headbobbing, maybe from both, I just know that I went to sleep thinking: "damn it, tomorrow I'm gonna write a f* negative review!"

_childDocuments_.review: While I experienced the same glitch as others when it comes to getting stuck (this happened whenever trying to start at a midway checkpoint and the only remedy is restarting the chapter), I found this narrative rather engaging. Yes, the walking speed is slow, but I felt okay with that because there is so, so, so much detail to take in around you. I found it really cool to see the dedicated content creation effort.I'm infinitely curious about other story arcs and endings that would happen. At one point, I thought I was going to explode, but I managed to get through the run and shut it down... it left me wondering, is there an arc where you do explode? What choices had serious change consequences, and what happens if I choose some things differently? Such as looking through certain areas where you can only go through so much before some doors lock down and some areas can no longer be looked at. Unlike other reviewers, I do not think this was linear at all... I made some choices to intentionally deceive the "partner" in the game, and I fully expected a certain outcome that was but was not actually true in the end.What I *can* say is that I think this story, like this dimension of the universe, would make for a fascinating adventure game where you might choose between the Polish, the German, and the other groups (not naming due to not wanting to spoil lol). Beautiful imagery and no clarity on what all actually happened that led us to this moment, there's enough ambiguity that I'm almost tempted to try going to the start and choosing other avenues. The biggest gripe I had was that some of the choices indicated by their wording that it would lead to certain outcomes and the results didn't align with expectations. That's not to say that I don't like surprise twists or anything... but I couldn't tell if making selections in the memory tubes made a difference, and final choice I made, I didn't expect it to be effectively me choosing a death line. But perhaps that's a solid good thing in the end... Definitely a great game for those who like a curious and not-so-easy to figure out moral dilemma story. I hope it expands to other titles leaning into the same reality.

_childDocuments_.review: The idea of the game is nothing new, it's another alternative history tale. But the story aspect is done really well and I enjoyed it.I'm obviously not a nazi supporter in any way but I must say they had really cool aesthetics so the symbols and other stuff is used in games to this day, even some fantasy or sci-fi games adopt similar style. And I must say exploring the nazi bunker was fun. The story combines sci-fi and some history which in the end leads to a story about nazi experiments on people. The main plot becomes quite predictable soon but the bunker is fascinating and terrifying.Although it would be nice to see more games about soviet atrocities too.The game also tells a story about human nature and only proves my opinion about humans – they're selfish beings. Even at these times where nazis are a thing, when people supposed be united they instead start fighting each other and of course there are religious fanatics, everyone's fighting for their own good.Gameplay is simply walking in a very linear path with occasional detouring into some rooms or facilities to read the documents or listen to audiologs. Oh you will need to press the buttons, open doors and pull levers, a lot of levers, sometimes even pull it to the side, not down or up. Amazing.Seriously gameplay is average at best. I love walking simulators, I really do but I prefer when there's something happening when I walk, either someone is talking or you listen to some audiolog or something or admire the scenery at least. While the areas here look pretty, there's not much to see, 10 seconds is plenty and when you do that you walk and walk and walk *yawn*...oh did I fell asleep? No, still walking to that lever over there, I will need to pull it, yay! Oh wait, there's a door...*2 minutes later* oh i'm almost there, I wonder that door opens into outside or inside? Will see soon...Walking is very slow, on one hand you want to explore every corner, on the other hand you're afraid you won't find anything there and then you will need to walk back V-E-R-R-Y S-L-O-W-L-Y. I mean too slow, it's like a hundred year old grand-grandpa walking in the park and dragging a pile of bricks behind him.There are computers also. These are boring too, you just stare at the screen where computer does its thing and listen to some dialogues, there's nothing else going on, no cut-scene or anything just a boring computer screen. Of course it's nice to learn about what's happening, but ffs give me something to watch or do while it's talking.Graphics are pretty nice. All the areas and rooms look good, every area tells a story about nazis and bunker's inhabitants. There are some open areas which are beautiful but mostly it's closed environments. The diversity is quite good when it comes to areas and each chapter you see something completely new.There are some cut-scenes in the beginning of the game, they look average but I still expected more of those.Performance is average. It's very inconsistent, sometimes I was getting 90fps, sometimes 45fps, mostly fps was somewhere in the middle. For the game with nothing going on around I expected better performance. Played on 5800x, 2070s, 32gb @3440x1440 at nearly max settings, had to tone down one setting because fps was horrible.There's native ultrawide support but it's buggy. When you load the game and want to continue playing you end up in a state where you can move. But since i'm a genius I thought, what will happen if I hit alt+enter and voila! I can move again, so hit alt+enter again to go back into 21:9 and everything's fine. Same thing happened twice while playing too. Not a big deal but annoying.One more thing regarding technical side. There's no chapter select! So if you're an achievement hunter then back up your save when you reach the end and read the guide. There's more than one ending and when the game ends it wipes your save file and you need to start over, so keep that in mind.I usually am not needy when it comes to voice acting, I play a lot of smaller, niche, low budget games so i'm used to “ok” voice acting, it's enough for me. But here? The voice acting is bad even for my ears. I'm sorry but devs could've done much better, it's not some rpg with million words, you have a handful of sentences to voice. None of the characters sound believable, they're just reading their lines.There's some nice music, more like ambient music sometimes but it fits the atmosphere perfectly and accompanies the terrifying mood well.Overall a decent game, it has tedious gameplay but nice areas to explore and good story which saves this game. I recommend buying this on sale and only if you enjoy walking simulators and story driven games.

_childDocuments_.review: I really loved this game. _childDocuments_.review: Wow.Just wow. The game is a walking sim like no other. I cannot believe how much attention to detail went into this game. It is absolutely beautiful.The atmosphere is downright terrifying in some parts, and I didn’t miss chase scenes or jump scares most games like this include. They spent a lot of time on atmosphere, voice acting, characters, scenery and story rather than gimmicks. Quickly into the playthrough you’ll start comparing it to another famous horror game, but it still seemed new and fresh and kept me going. I wish it had a save point so you can go back and play the different endings yourself.It faces some hard hitting topics, and part of the horror is the reality of what happened under Nazi rule. They kept it light versus what we know the Nazi’s were doing, but it isn’t hard for our imagination to push those things further and see things that weren’t said. I wish everyone could play this game with onlookers. We did eye color polls, and went way down that rabbit hole discussing eugenics, folklore, and belief in the supernatural. I was surprised how many of my twitch family had recessive eyes, and they added up to equal the dominant ones. It’s scary to think after so many decades, we still have issues with race and inequality, but games like this remind us to keep fighting against racism. The gameplay is good as far as walking sim, but some in my stream said they didn’t like the occasional mechanic to interact/move things. I did, but in this type of game we’d be fine with a simpler click. I thought it was nice they did a new design, but it’s kind of pointless if they always work and you cannot fail an action. The isolation of the game and the feeling put into everything really came through, and it was an awesome experience. I might or might not have bawled like a baby, but you’ll never prove it.Pros: world buildingvoice actingcharacter developmentstreamlined, didn’t get lost or not know where to go without giving away too muchCons:Hard to read some of the letters. One was right in front of a lamp and yet the paper was so dark. You don’t need to add typed text like other games, but maybe you can make it so the page is lit well enough to read easily.The click and slide was annoying sometimesNo save points to replay the endings

_childDocuments_.review: I may come back to this review and edit it after giving the game a pause for now. _childDocuments_.review: Paradise lost is an interesting walking simulator. I picked it up as a research for a design project I worked on. The brief of the project was high tech post apocalyptic tribalism aesthetic. And this game plot and setting fit quite well into that.There is a fascination that I have with media and games that are envisioning the disturbing alternative history in which nazis would prevail. How much further could their war technology advance? What horrible crazy plan could they come up with next? Wolfesntein: The new order blew my mind in this regard because I never really taught about it that much. But while Wolfenstein envisions crazy robots and battlefields that sometimes can look like something straight from the Terminator movie, Paradise lost goes in other direction. While nazi high technology looks similar and could be straight from the Wolfenstein series, there is no action, no bullets flying around and nobody chases you. In fact there is just you, exploring the facilities as some kind of archeologist. Everything is intact, as everyone have just disappeared in a single moment, leaving all the lights on.It is a serene experience that focuses purely on the exploration of alternative history where nazis would build a huge city underground where they could shelter and thrive. The magic lays in the uncovering of all the beautiful and horrendous details of the world that nazis built for themselves.There is also a tribal part that I mentioned at the beginning. But I am not going to spoil you that. Uncover it yourself.

_childDocuments_.review: I got the game mostly because I love story and exploration games such as this and the visuals looked impressive as well as the concept.The GoodAs mentioned before, the visuals are incredible and definitely add to the atmosphere. I think it would have added if ultra-wide support was there (please devs consider adding this) but even on a single monitor it really felt as if I was there exploring this massive underground bunker. I think this game would be interesting to see in VR, but alas.Controls were simple and got the job done but not as easy to use as some VR games. Although, it was easy to see where I needed to interact with things so that made it easier. It would have been horrible if they did not have the system and I would need to move the character around clicking on everything due to the kid's slow, plodding movement.The story would be the best thing here. While not a revolutionary story it was executed well and I liked how they tied it in with the five stages of grief for each level of the bunker and used them as the themes for those areas. The story flowed organically and was in concert with the environment revealing just enough to keep you interested and moving forward. Thankfully there were no glaring plot holes or items that jarred me out of the story.The BadFor a 12 year old boy, Szymon plods along like an elderly elephant wearing clogs. I mean, come on I wasn't the most active 12 year old but I sure as hell zipped around and ran enough in normal activities. If it wasn't for the strong interaction system the game would have been near unplayable as getting Szymon from one side of these large rooms to another could take what feels like 5-10 (probably around 2 but still).Dialogue scenes are also non-skippable. If you run through the game again, you'll need to sit through the many dialogue scenes and bear it Oh and the Auto-save system... Yeah I could do without that noise. It is annoying, like most auto-save systems are, but the worst of it only comes to bear when you finish the game and let the credits scroll, it will friggin' delete all of your saves! Yes, you read right, all the saves go poof and you need to play from the beginning. Thankfully this can be mitigated somewhat by loading the last checkpoint, but you cannot let the credits come to an end before either loading the last checkpoint or restarting the level in order to see some of the other endings.It is short. Really short, took me about 7.9 hours and that was walking around an soaking in the local color  as it were. Also, with how slowly Szymon moves you can forget speed-runing throuh game.OverallEven with some of the small negatives, I would recommend this to anyone who enjoys a great story combined with exploration of a gorgeous environment. For action fans I would not recommend this since it would feel like a slog/walking simulator,

_childDocuments_.review: I just finished Paradise Lost and I'm sitting here trying to figure out what to say about this game. I enjoyed the game and it's story but at the same time I am also irritated with the game. Without spoiling the story, you play as a boy trying to find someone in a photo that your mom had while in a post apocalyptic world.Sadly you don't get to really explore this world because this game is just about a single path all the way through. Aside from a few choices here and there and the occasional dialog that occurs when you find a specific letter or object to interact with. Honestly I'm not even sure if the few choices throughout even have an impact on the story. Now I'm pretty sure your choices in the final chapter will grant you a few different endings. However once you have completed the game then it seems like your only option is to have another play through because once you are taken back to the title screen your only option is new game and the load your last checkpoint is now gone. Which sucks because I would have been interested in additional endings but I'm not interested enough in this game to complete another play through just for another end.Now for the nitty-gritty part of my review. As you can see I gave the game a thumbs up, because it was an enjoyable game to play. It's definitely a good separation from your normal games. It's just a relaxing walking sim with no way to die and no way to get lost. However I would love to have been able to see more of this world and find out more of the story (which I may have missed some letters that gave me the information to fill the holes in my experience). I would also like to note of some awkward audio issues that happened to me, only a couple of times. Like hearing a waterfall that is very loud, as it should be, but turn a corner and you no longer hear the water at all.Do I recommend this game? Yes, I do, but only if you think you would enjoy a game that is spent walking around an empty bunker where the majority of the story comes from finding a white dot, walking up to it, and then clicking on the dot that may or may not fill in some story for you. If I had to give this game a number value then I would give it a 7/10. It's fun, well thought out, some awesome environments, and a good story. I just feel like there is something missing. Maybe I missed some stuff in the story by not clicking the right button on an elevator. I really don't know if this is what the developer intended for the story or if I missed some (what I feel) important parts of the story. Maybe I am supposed to fill in these holes or answer my questions with my imagination, but for that it is definitely a 7/10.

_childDocuments_.review: There are a few cases where you'd wish there was a "neutral" button as well when writing a review, and to me this is one of them. What I like about this game:Its story is not exactly complex (given that you can easily finish about everything it gives you in about 8 hours that's kind of to be expected). But it's intriguing enough to leave an impression, strongly supported by the nice visuals and sort of minimalistic score. Especially that last aspect really met my taste. More often than not I was underwhelmed lately by dramatic overscoring, which, you know, can also destroy the atmosphere. There are only hints of past violence, no actual fighting of any sort. There are no cheap jumpscares. I can see how this game feels boring to a lot of players. Personally I am one of the people who read all of the diaries and notes of hidden lore in games like Fallout 3. The subtle alternate worldbuilding caught me, though it could have been just a bit more elaborate. What I didn't like:Some negative reviews state that the walking speed is too slow. While I agree that it could be a bit faster, and the difference between walking and running is ridiculous, it wasn't quite as bad as I feared. Still, a proper running mode for at least a few seconds (you're playing a child after all) would not have hurt the experience. And that's especially because of the second issue, which is much more severe: while I only experienced one actual crash, there is quite a number of collider glitches where you can get stuck in place if you took a step in the wrong direction, with no other option than to load the last savepoint. Sometimes this actually happens during in-game scripted events, which is all the more frustrating as you literally cannot prevent the game from placing you in a position where you might get stuck. Adding in the fact that the savepoints are scattered kind of arbitrarily (i.e. quite far apart in some instances) that might actually mean walking the same paths and doing the same things twice or even three times, which is definitely killing the fun. And once you have uncovered the story the game has about zero replay value to offer. That is a relatively obvious problem, making it an absolute d*** move of the developers to decide that the savegame gets auto-deleted after you have taken the final decision in the game -  so to see what happens if you pick a different choice in that last moment you're supposed to replay the entire game. Honestly, that's a deliberate, absolutely unnecessary slap in the face.The good thing was that I was warned by reading the negative reviews, so I made a copy of the savegame just prior to that last moment and could easily restore the deleted file to explore the other endings. Unfortunately there's really not much in terms of endings to explore anyhow. Given the second video above I guess that some more content might have been planned, but was never added, which is sad really. TL/DR: Give it a try while it's on sale if you like a nice little story and some food for thought. Don't buy it if you expect anyething like Fallout or Wolfenstein, it's absolutely nothing like that. And make a backup of your save file before you actually make your final decision in "Acceptance".

_childDocuments_.review: Paradise Lost is one of those games that feels more like art than a traditional game. If you enjoyed Dear Esther or Gone Home, this fits the definition of a walking sim. If you're into reading up on the lore behind Fallout Vaults and their eerie backstories, then you'll love this game because it's like exploring one big Fallout vault with a dark story that keeps unraveling.I was enraptured from the start. I didn't look at the store page, I just saw this in my library under 'exploration' and decided to boot it up. That's why I didn't realize this was an alternate history where WWII unfolded differently. I thought this was our world, and when I saw papers in the vault with Nazi stamps dated in the 1960s, I shivered. "What happened? Are these underground folks under the impression that the war is still on?" It reminded me of that old soldier, Hiroo Onoda, who hid out in the Philippines, thinking WWII was still ongoing until he was found in 1974.So, you have the Nazis and their horrible programs running, then some competing factions whose own beliefs end up dividing them. Meanwhile, you're suspecting something is off with the girl you can't seem to find, although she keeps promising she's safely hiding just around the next corner.The game had emotional depth and an intriguing premise. I loved reading every note scrap I could find and seeing the world build out & each area was so well-decorated! You could feel the difference between the 'rich' and the 'poor' in the rooms of the individual inhabitants and in the city itself.My only complaint is with the UI. The 'targeting' system for picking something up seemed clunky. I often had to click multiple times to get a reaction until I learned how close I needed to be. The reticle 'lighting up' didn’t always mean I could grab the object, which was annoying.Who hasn't dreamed of finding an underground city? In this game, you can! If you don't mind reading and walking sim-type games, check this out!
