_childDocuments_.review: Paradise Lost, from a mechanical standpoint, is your average walking simulator. It is a fairly linear game that neither provides you with a ton of exploration nor stimulating puzzles that require you to rub some brain cells together. However, from a narrative standpoint, there are many things that Paradise Lost does right:1) The environmental/world designs are simply awe-inspiring and truly evokes a sense of wonder. PolyAmorous created a believable world that truly feels like it had once been lived in and you can see the evidence and traces of the bunker's denizens. Certain points in the game will make you feel exactly what the Hobbits felt when they first saw Rivendell.  2) There is a compelling reason for your actions and your purpose in descending into the subterranean bunker. The game doesn't wrap itself around pretentious philosophical introspective mumbo jumbo like some walking sims do. Every bit of narrative or dialogue in this game is delivered to you straight. 3) The world 'lore' is fleshed out really well. Not only is this game pretty to look at, a lot of attention was paid to the lore of the world. As you explore new areas and read notes, you begin to understand when and how things started to fall apart, the emerging challenges, and the struggles and conflicts that arose as a result of leadership failing to address those challenges. But most importantly, Paradise Lost paints an incredibly compelling picture of what desperation looks like. A lot of questionable choices were made to resolve problems and the deeper you explore the bunker, the more you see 'scars' in the world that mark these drastic decisions made out of desperation. Overall, I would recommend Paradise Lost for the price of $10 (promo sale). It should last about 3 hours. While I don't foresee it will have much replay value, I personally felt very engaged the first playthrough. The characters aren't exactly the best I've seen, but they aren't exactly lifeless either and the more you play, the more you start understanding who they are as people. A part of me does think that a lot of potential was not realized by turning this game into a walking sim, but nonetheless, I really do think the devs did a good job with this title and look forward to future titles that will also deliver this sense of wonder to me.

_childDocuments_.review: Short version:Pros:+ Looks good+ Interesting setupCons:- Excruciatingly boring- Story felt like a nothing burger- Uninspired gameplay- A “look, don’t touch” world- Subpar voice acting- Tedious exposition“Long” version: is a first-person narrative-driven game developed by PolyAmorous and published by Walkabout. You play as a 12-year-old kid in his search for closure inside a WWII bunker.I installed this game on a whim. I did not know what it was and I reckon I got it in a bundle somewhere. My point is that I had no preconceived notions of the game and went into it with an open mind. Here are my thoughts.First, the story.While the premise is very interesting, the story lacks substance and comes across as a pseudointellectual attempt to be deep and meaningful. The pretentious dialogue and empty world did not help, either. Most of the context and world-building can be found through countless letters scattered throughout the game, but I will be honest, after the first 15 or so, I started ignoring them. It felt tedious and unrewarding.In terms of gameplay,  is a walking simulator.While it is not my favorite genre of games by far, I have had my share of amazing experiences with story-driven games like  and even . You basically go around very gorgeous rooms and outside areas, only to not be able to interact with anything. This “look, don’t touch” approach is usually questionable and I would have forgiven it if there was any semblance of gameplay in this game, but no, it is devoid of anything fun.Graphically,  is stunning. The art direction is absurdly strong and the developers really captured the claustrophobia of some areas, while really nailing the overall imposing nature of the buildings. Beautiful visuals alone are not enough to redeem this lackluster experience, however.Sound effects are solid- there is an eeriness to the things you hear while playing, which I appreciated. You will realize that nothing will ever happen while playing, though – all that atmosphere and build-up to get nothing in return.The voice acting is quite bad – again, the writing did not help at all and I feel like the voice actors are not experienced enough to convey even basic emotions, let alone some of the pseudointellectual sludge that is shoved down your throat.The soundtrack felt so generic that I do not even remember it. I can say, however, that I rolled by eyes when it built up, as it was a pathetic attempt at pulling at the player’s heartstrings. Hard pass.Unfortunately, I am not a fan of this game – in fact, I would go so far as to say I dislike it.I loathe giving bad reviews but I really feel like  is a very visually striking game that is, ultimately, a disappointing experience. Its pseudointellectual demeanor, the insultingly tedious gameplay and the amateur voice acting make me not recommend this game at all.Final score: 4 out of 10.If you enjoyed this review, please consider following my .

_childDocuments_.review: I must admit that the premise of the was rather interesting. I'm also not afraid of the so-called walking simulators per se. But oh boy was I bored. And sad. Not because the story would've been emotional in any way, but because of the missed opportunity. So the starting point is a nuclear wasteland in the 80s some twenty or so years after the Second World War ended horribly with the Nazis using nuclear weapons. The protagonist, Szymon, is at the entrance of a WW2 bunker that once promised a safe and prosperous future for the chosen members of the Third Reich. Szymon has a picture of his mother and an unknown man and Szymon is on a quest to figure out who the man in the picture is and what happened to him. Sounds exciting, right?The first moments in the bunker reveal the vast space built underground and I have to say that the milieu looked authentic, albeit too clean and empty. But I was hooked. For the first 10 minutes that is. After that playing felt like a chore and I only ended up completing the game because I sort of figured out it would not take more than a few hours. With hindsight, those are hours that I can't get back. Should've stopped after my gut told me so.Well anyways, I finished this boring game with tons of missed potential. The premise was interesting and the levels were (at least the levels for the first half of the game) intriguing. I would've liked to see more of the offices and see more clear signs of life (even signs of past lives). But no. All I got was a playable character that is so slow it takes forever to walk from a to b and there isn't really anything to do. There are plenty of interesting stuff here and there, but only the chosen notes can be picked up and read. Well of course I also could click left mouse button near some console and the click it again after seeing a finger near a button/switch. And that's it. That's all there is to actually do. I mean how come the guy can't even descend a ladder more than one step at a time. It's just so tiring.Oh and yes, the story. The ending is apparent after the first 20 minutes of playing so no surprises there. There isn't really that much dialogue and the nonexistent dialog is unnatural. The characters should be asking questions and discussing many other things that are clearly more relevant to the situation and would've been more interesting and engaging. It's just clumsy chit chat. That means that the story is more about what has happened before rather than what I as the player is experiencing while exploring this bunker that should've given more. And the primary source of the story are the notes laying around. If I had skipped those there would've been nothing. So what about the notes... At first they seemed coherent and believable, but as the game progressed things became weird, unbelievable and just too fantastical compared to the setting. The story told with the notes kind of ruined what the setting was about to deliver.There was something interesting though. There are couple of points where I could see a computer log/recording replayed and through these it was also possible to get snippets of what has happened. But the content wasn't really what was interesting, it was more the look and feel of the recordings. That I liked. Partly.  Because weirdly I got to make decisions about what had happened while viewing the recording. At first I thought that it would be some kind of time travel, but no, it was not and it did not seem to matter what ever choice I made. At least it didn't feel like I was really making any decisions.So my recommendation is to avoid this game. There are always better titles out there like Firewatch and What remains of Edith Finch. I would even recommend going out and walking aimlessly for 4 hours. That's gotta be way more exiting than this. Or maybe go to a library and read a book for once. Reading thrills the mind in more ways than this game.

_childDocuments_.review: There's so much wasted potential here that I wouldn't even call this a game. I know, melodramatic. Let me explain. When you start, it's amazing! The plot is a deep mystery that you uncover piece by piece, and everything is wonderfully out of place. Where am I? What are those doing underground? All in all, I played for 74 minutes because of that mystery. Sadly, the gameplay is so dull, repetitive, and frustrating that an awesome storyline cannot save it. The walking is probably the worst I've encountered in a video game. You. Move. Very. Slowly. All. The. Time. Seriously, I've seen elderly boomers walk faster than my character. You cannot run, crouch, climb, jump ... I think an ant moves faster than me in this game. Once, it took me 1min 40sec to cross a room. (If that seems short, hold down your W key and do nothing for 100 seconds straight. Then do that over and over again for an hour.) But that's the thing--it's not really a game. There are no puzzles, no important decisions, no quick decision-making, and no conflict or combat. All you do is very. Slowly. Walk. From one item point to another. There was a locked door and I thought, "Maybe I could climb those boxes to get around it, or blow up the door with those grenades ... ah, I just have to walk to that white dot, then walk to that other white dot, and then wait for an NPC to open it." You're completely passive. (And for a game that features snail-pace walking, it's surprising how much vertigo and motion sickness it causes. )Then there's the plot--which I still don't know after playing for over an hour. I think my character is a kid looking for his dad, but I had a mom so maybe I'm looking for her? If you replaced the main character with a dog or remote-controlled drone, I don't think the story would change at all. The mystery of what the setting entails is again amazing--but there's no story. It's like if a science fiction author created an alternate history that rocks and forgot to create characters or a plot. If this is on sale for cheap, give it a try. The initial 30 min or so is mysterious and clever, and it's fun putting together all the pieces to realize what's going on in the setting. But if the price point is above $6 or so, I'd skip it. The controls are frustrating, the gameplay is non-existent, the plot is either obtuse or missing, and you have more interesting decisions if you read a Choose Your Own Adventure book.

_childDocuments_.review: Come one come all! Witness the adventures of Szymon, the world most arthritic boy, and Poland's 7th national treasure! WATCH as he slowly crawls his way through an abandoned Nazi bunker! CRINGE as he struggles with his unmoving sausage fingers to open doors, play with inverted mouse for extra challenge! GASP as he overcomes his body's lack of cartilage to sprint, attaining the electrifying ground speed of an obese turtle! (Except for when the devs disable the sprint key, somehow worried that Szymon might hurt himself by going too fast?!?) CURSE as you wander too close to a white dot and accidentally leave a place you were not done exploring! SHOUT in amazement as his arthritis creeps into his voice box and delivers the most wooden lines that has ever reached a human ear! CHEER as he encounters a story that is the most predicable that has ever been told, free of both thrills AND chills!Roast aside, it really kills me how much love and effort have been put into Paradise Lost's excellent environmental storytelling, level design, superb sound design, and music, only to be brought down by not getting the basics right. Basics like satisfying movement and User Interface (the one-way transitions could have easily been telegraphed with a different coloured circle!) are ESSENTIAL to immersion, but so many of these types of games get absolutely wrong. If the player is frustrated or worried, they're not paying attention to the story or the emotions that the scene is supposed to bring out. There's a wonderful experience here, but I just wish I could have it as a different character with working arms and legs.I would recommend Paradise Lost to people really into looking at all the pretty levels and soaking up the delightfully mysterious atmosphere. However, it's poor in pretty much every other aspect, so I would tell literally anyone else to look elsewhere. Even people looking for a good so-called 'walking simulator' should buy the excellent What Remains of Eidith Finch. Those looking for good narrative experiences AND good gameplay should look into the recently released Pale Beyond.A minor nitpick at the end, but

_childDocuments_.review: I did not love it 100% for a few reasons:- Bugs/getting stuck when loading a checkpoint/save.- The actions were clunky/cumbersome - like always having to use the action multiple times.- Poor controller support/move+look speed - I ended up playing most of it with KB+M, though I would have preferred a controller.- The voice acting was just ok.I did enjoy it all the same however:- The setting was very interesting and the backstory/alternate history was a new take for me.- The visually were pretty good, and the walking simulator allowed for good exploration/lore discovery.- A somewhat predictable end, but the choices you can make at least gave some diversion from a purely linear story.

_childDocuments_.review: It's grand.I really enjoyed the sedate pace it sets, and the environments are beautiful.  The attention to detail and level of craft is really something else.  The only complaint I would have against the environments is the fact that the same paintings are used repeatedly to the point where it breaks the immersion.A far bigger problem is, although the conversations your characters has, and the notes/articles they find, form an engaging narrative enough to pull you through it, the main reveals are telegraphed from a mile off.  The game is far too obvious in it's eyebrow-waggling as you go along, a little more misdirection would have been welcome.  There was probably one additional reveal I didn't see coming, but even with it the emotional impact was a bit stunted.  And I for one thought the moral choice was far too weighted on one side as being the obvious choice at the end, but turns out according to steam achievement percentages I picked the lesser chosen choice.  So I learned at least that steam users are predominantly psychopaths so there's that.And beyond that there's some bugs.  Like the audio not always matching the subtitles.  And often times if you're listening to an audio diary, then the protagonist's comments on that dialogue at the end will appear to also sound out of the same place in 3D space as the audiodiary, which is either an oversight or the protagonist is an aspiring ventriloquist.But although I seem down on it, I did enjoy my time with it and there's enough length here to justify the expense (at least when half off), and the quality remains consistent throughout.Recommended for walking simulator buffs who like alternative history and WW2 setting.

_childDocuments_.review: Played the whole game, but some glaring issues made the experience considerably less fun than it should have been. 1)  Headbob/Camera Movement - So the developers say they added a "Headbob disable" option, but at least in my fully updated copy of the game it did not seem to do a damn thing.  This game easily has THE WORST First Person camera movement I've experienced in ANY First Person game I've played.  And I've played a ton of First Person games, especially First Person Narrative and Horror type games.  The main issue is that the camera moves slightly upwards when you start moving and when you stop moving it goes back down to its original resting position.  This means that if you move around with a lot of "start" "stop" type motions your camera is constantly going up and down with every start and stop option.  THERE IS NO WAY TO GET RID OF THIS IN THE OPTIONS and it's a completely disorienting, awful use of the camera in order to make the game "more realistic."  Flat out, it sucks.  I don't even get motion sick from these types of things generally, but it was so disorienting that I imagine anyone with a sensitivity to these issues would be completely unable to play the game.  I had to go out of my way to "constantly move forward" in order to avoid this terrible start/stop motion.  2)  The mechanics are literally terrible and uninspired.  Oh you want to open a door?  Sure, make sure you're standing right in the right spot, then click, then you have to hold click down after a UI element pops up, then you have to move your mouse forward, or backward, Left, or Right (whichever way the lever/door/etc. opens) and then hold it there for half of a second.  This means that literally every door you have to open takes an extra 2s to open, which is incredibly frustrating.  There's no reason it shouldn't have just been, i dunno, any of the other door opening/lever pulling mechanics that have been introduced in almost any other First Person game.  3)  The movement was incredibly slow.  No run option.  Constantly slow walking.  Pads the gametime by an extreme amount.  I don't understand this personally as I'm the type of player that's going to take my time and explore all nooks and crannies regardless, but no speed increase sucks.  The Good:The story is not bad, although a bit obvious.  The environments are fairly gorgeous.  I only kept the game because I got it for $7.  Would not recommend to buy for more than that and if you have motion sickness, stay away.

_childDocuments_.review: Okay so let me start out with the positives... this game is gorgeous, with great art and design of environments. This game has fantastic music. The story could use some better dialogue and pacing but was interesting and showed that the writers wanted to create a very lived-in world, which I appreciate. It's a quick walking simulator that tells a beautiful story, and you get to make a few decisions along the way to determine the outcome.With that said, I can't recommend it. Everything above is true, and the game really shines from all of it, but it is entirely overshadowed by the abysmal walking speed in the game. It takes about three hours to finish this game, but with a regular walking speed it would probably take less than two hours. So much of your time is just crossing rooms very slowly. At one point I found myself stuck in a room (I kept missing the exit) and whereas a normal game would have had me running around for maybe a minute or two, I was trapped for at least 10 minutes because crossing the area took so long each time I tried a new possibility.The only reason I can think of for this is that when the game was finished and ready, someone higher up told them they couldn't release a game that was only 1.5 hours. So the only way to quickly add time was to slow the walking speed... then slow it again... then slow it again... until they had a 3 hour game.Next time, just release a 1.5 hour game. It would have been nearly perfect.To the developers: If you add an option in the settings to change the walking speed to twice the current speed, I'll retract this review and leave a positive one. No joke.

_childDocuments_.review: Addressing some of the most common criticism I've seen,An action game. All action moves (climbing up, down, shimmying across a ledge, etc) are performed automatically after walking up to the prompt.A puzzle game. There's some very light puzzling going on, but I'd say they're rather more like "interactions" with the environment. Other than a couple of branching paths, the game is pretty linear.Think Bioshock + Metro 2033 + Gone Home.It's a narrative heavy exploration + observation game. Or, a "walking sim". We all know at this point what the genre is and what it isn't. This game focuses on what it wants to do, and does it marvelously. The main mechanic is observation. The visual storytelling is superb, rivaling Bioshock at its best, the environments are impressive and varied, and careful exploration is always rewarded.Every scene is a joy to explore. The music is great at setting the mood as well. I thought the walking speed was just right for the type of gameplay that is being encouraged, you're not meant to get anywhere in a hurry. That said,The game bites off more than it can really chew on its grander themes, its lore and world-building. The personal story of the protagonist is compelling, but the bigger story of how things came to be is confusing and weak. I've seen mentions that there's documents released outside the game that should fill in the gaps better, but I really don't want to do homework to play a game.The voice acting. Dear god the voice acting. The adults are fine, but the kids' voices are dreadful. Especially the one character who, sadly, gets the most lines in the entire game. She reads her dialogue so awkwardly, like she learned the script phonetically, but doesn't really understand the words she's saying. It's a shame because it really brings the emotional weight of the writing down.I'm very glad I played this. I love environmental storytelling, and I really loved seeing it applied so carefully to grand stories like this. Go into it knowing what this game is offering and what it's not, and you might love it as well.

_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Lost

_childDocuments_.review: This is a walking simulator, and a slow one at that. The environment and setting are solid, but the game is let down by its gameplay (or lack thereof) and its voice acting. The latter of the two, it has to be said, is quite abysmal even for a video game. It might be better to phrase it like this: If you are making a walking simulator and the main story is to be carried by two voice actors and their characters' relationship and emotional journey, then you better hire the best talent in the business and not just two randos you found at a bus stop in eastern Europe. And if you can't manage that, then there ought to be some interesting gameplay outside the regular walking and reading notes. What I am saying is this: The game fails as a walking simulator with an immersive story, and as it couldn't manage to succeed at that it might have been saved by being a more engaging gameplay experience - but it just isn't.
_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Lost

_childDocuments_.review: The good:- nice environment art & designThe bad:- everything else, including...The ugly:- bugs which won't be fixed because the devs and publisher have already abandoned the gameThe concept is interesting by itself, but it's also kind of cliche. Story and narrative is very weak. The atmosphere is there, but that's thanks to the excellent enviro design. Character animations look very poor, but there's also very few characters that you'll actually see during playthrough.The game is super linear and the only story branching is at the very end when you have to decide on 2 things. You'll have to play through the whole game if you want to discover the other possible outcomes, although I think it's just a different scene at the end and different ending achievements unlocked, so maybe just check it out with a let's play on youtube?Rendering glitches happen quite often.Turn off headbob before starting the game (turned on by default) - there's a nasty bug where upon loading you can't move your character from it's positio if headbob is left on. It happened to me when I was 40 minutes in the game. There's no manual save system so first I tried reloading checkpoints - landed in the same spot with same problem. Tried to restart level. Landed at the very beginning of the game! Was afraid that I lost all progress just now, but I quickly went for the reload checkpoint option and got back to the 40 minute progress mark :D Then I looked for answers online and found the hint to turn of headbob.I mean - the devs and publisher must be aware of this. It's criminal that they did nothing to fix it or at least warn players (even disabling the headbob effect as the default setting would be a welcome duct-tape style fix).The game crashed on me 2 times during long playthroughs, no particular reason, just a "fatal error" and exit to desktop.The walking speed of our character is like a slow stroll and you can't do anything about it. I think this was a deliberate move from the developers - the game would end much quicker if we could run as there's really not much there.
_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Lost

_childDocuments_.review: Paradise Lost is one of the spookiest games I've played that  a horror game. I kept waiting for a jump scare around every corner, but it never came (although I did jump once towards the end of the game, but it was totally my fault).This might be one of the purest "walking simulators" I've played. The locations are seriously stunning, but sometimes a little too dark. I really could have used a flashlight in more than one spot. There aren't really any puzzles, but ocassionaly you'll be tasked with finding an item to progress passed a door. My only real annoyance was how slow the animations are. Watching your character slowly climb over obstacles again and again slowed down some already slow-moving sections.The story was touching, if a little predictable. I think if you're a fan of the genre, this game has a unique setting and is overall an interesting enough mystery to keep you hooked. I played it all in one sitting at just under 3 hours, which I think is the way to experience it.
_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Lost

_childDocuments_.review: One of the best on-rails walking sims I've played so far. The story is good, the pacing is solid, visually it's stunning and at no point did it feel like it overstayed its welcome. Do wish the protagonists hadn't been children though, it makes all conversation less engaging. _childDocuments_.review: I'm not gonna explain what a walking sim is, however I do have to mention that plenty of negative reviews are mentioning things that are, well, literally what constitutes a walking sim (walking (duh), little interactivity, slow immersiveness) as if that's bad - when it's literally the genre. So yeah, if you dislike these aforementioned things, this game is probably not for you.But if you're well aware of what you're getting yourself into, this game's pretty good. I think the story's pacing is a little off, the "big" reveal is strongly hinted at very, very early on in the game if you care to read all the notes/listen to the audio logs scattered about (which you should). The plot is nothing revolutionary or unheard of, really (Nazis committing atrocities, shocker), but people just dig Dieselpunk (myself included) and alt history. And then I guess there's also the "revelation" that other peoples can, in fact, be inhumane as well.They should've hired at least one native German speaker to go over the German text ingame because some of it is, uh, of questionable quality. I guess it's fine unless you can actually read it. Also the English voice acting was pretty average. The visuals and optimization, on the other hand, are great and what you'd expect from the underlying UE4 tech. Some reviewers are experiencing bugs with the save system, can't say i've come across any during my playthrough. Make sure to read up on how to experience all the endings beforehand since there's a point of no return and your save gets deleted afterwards (which seems unnecessary now that I think about it).

_childDocuments_.review: I liked and enjoyed the game all in all. If you are very patient, enjoy a basically walking sim, following story without much influence from your end, and can overlook the few frustrating bugs that it has, you will enjoy the game as well. Make sure to get it on sale and you are good i´d say.That being said, i would recommend it even, if it weren´t for a few problems/bugs i experienced, that going by the discussions forums, have been there since even before it launched on Steam. They make the experience... a bit unsatisfying at some points. Examples:- The headbobbing many people have been complaining about can be turned off by now, didn´t bother me much.- There is no running-option in this game, besides it says there is. The speed for running is the same as walking, can be veryyy annoying throughout the game.- There is no Save option! Not even talking about manual Save-slots, there is Autosave yes, but it doesn´t mean crap if you can´t use it. Why?- Because each time you do load up the last auto saved Checkpoint, you can´t move anymore, end of story. You are stuck in place and can´t get anywhere from the loaded Checkpoint. What you have to do, to be able to move again is, you have to restart the entire respective level. This was the most annoying and frustrating bug this game has to offer, and again, going by the forum, it´s been there for a while and hasn´t been subject to a fix by the devs. Big minus here!- There is no Chapter selection whatsoever. Reason why this might be annoying? You can´t get all the Achievements in one playthrough. Now if you don´t inform yourself in before hand, you won´t know that, before finishing the game at least once. As there is no Save-option and neither a Running-Mode... you have to do everything all over again, as slow as it is and just target the parts, you missed the Achievements in, within the first playthrough.- At least one place, at the very End has a collider bug that just let´s you float upwards forever and as there is no save loading, bingo, you have to restart the level. There was another place this happened as well in the second Chapter but i saw people said, the devs fixed that over time. At least something.All things mentioned above, have been reported multiple times, by who knows how many people, and the game has been out for a while, not just on Steam but on other Plattforms as well. Brings up the conclusion, either the Devs are not really interested to fix things or they just don´t care about it, as it kinda works and people buy it anyway.Other than that, texture wise, atmosphere and scenery, the game just looks amazing, bis plus here. They did put a lot of effort into details, even if the repetition of items/assets is quite high here and there but it is not disruptive to the over all looks and the picture the game creates.Horror/Thriller Faktor is getting higher towards the end but it´s nothing to bad, nor are there any jump-scares per se or similiar. It´s a tragic storyline you could say but you already see that it´s not all about sunshine and rainbows in the Trailers, so thats that.

_childDocuments_.review: Full disclosure, I got a review copy, but that was just for streaming. I'm not obligated to write this review.In total, it was about 4-6 hours to really explore everything (it says 8 hours, but I was distracted by chat stuff for portions), but wow— cool spin on a couple classic concepts. Felt very Fallout, Bioshock, The Turing Test, and yet snagged it's own place among them. For an indie team, one of the best lighting I've seen in any game in a while. Story was engaging and voice acting was better than average.If you play, read everything. Think about what everything means. Try to guess what's going on, and keep updating that thought as you get more info. There is a lot to unpack in this little package, and while most of the story is told through experience and scattered documents, it is quicker to play the game than describe what all is going on by the end.I'd much prefer polished, quick experiences like this in a 1 playthrough burst than long, drawn out games that are long because of a lack of content. I wish "run" moved a bit faster, but I didn't mind taking my time to explore the art/lighting— it's absolutely fantastic.The music was atmospheric and great when it was there, but it wasn't there often. This added to the mood, but I'd have taken some background ambiance to add to the scale of the rooms, but did I mention how nice the lighting was?Definitely a recommend for me.

_childDocuments_.review: Winter, 1980. Szymon, a boy raised in a post-apocalyptic wasteland, discovers an abandoned Nazi bunker. I solved it by going to the settings and disabling head bob as soon as my save game loaded. The walking pace is really slow while the environments and events kept me engaged. _childDocuments_.review: Overall, a decent game with an interesting story, but two glaring issues in an underutilized world and clunky game mechanics. Collectibles giving the perspective of different prior inhabitants would have been welcome.  With an alternate World War 2 as a backdrop, this world should have been more fun to explore and understand.The game mechanics were the other issue.  They felt a bit too slow/clunky for a game that's based on exploration.  Some of the animations, such as climbing and descending, could have been sped up just a bit.Other than that, the game had an enjoyable story with a well-designed (albeit somewhat lifeless) world.  Much of the collectibles that were there were interesting, I just wish that there was a bit more.  The music did enough to build a bit of an atmosphere.  Nothing really outstanding, but I'd give the game a 6/10.

_childDocuments_.review: Not the kind of experience I usually go for but it surprised me. It's a short narrative game with stunning and well detailed scenarios. The gameplay is not the strongest.It contains some design problems that can affect the experience a bit, such as the UI/UX for dialogue selection or that the interaction with buttons is not intuitive. Although I experienced some critical bugs where I was forced to restart the level and also disable head bobbing in the first level because it gave me a few glitches, I decided to give it a positive review because I loved the immersion, animations, sound design and story. _childDocuments_.review: Paradise Lost is a good name for this game. Over the last decade walking simulators have gone from emotional/thought provoking pieces (Dear Esther) and comical/satirical (The Stanley Parable) to coming of age stories (Gone Home) and even straight up horror (Outlast). The bar is constantly being set higher and higher for video games and walking simulators are not exempt from that. In my opinion a good walking simulator has the same impact as a great movie or television series or novel. It is great to walk through the woods in Firewatch or swim through the ocean in Abzu to release some stress. That feeling is completely lost when the immersion of a game is ruined. When the keybindings make the game hard to play, when the voice acting is flat, when the story isn't engaging, and when the characters personalities aren't developed the sense of paradise I have with the game is lost.I do not recommend this game for anyone looking for a new interesting walking simulator. The game lasts about 4 hours from start to finish, and does not have any replay value.

_childDocuments_.review: Tips: Turn off head bob. As other reviews have mentioned, leaving it on will result in you getting stuck to the ground in some occasions when loading a checkpoint/save.When dialogue plays slow down/wait for it to play out before moving forward. Moving forward into new areas too quickly and triggering new dialogue will skip the current dialogue.Review:Its a very beautiful game with very good worldbuilding. The atmosphere is very fitting for the tone of the game. The game isn't a masterpiece by any means but it manages to convey a pretty touching story. I feel like there was a lot more potential for the game to be expanded upon though in terms of story and gameplay. The controls are simple though it seems to be made for controllers more so than keyboard and mouse, but you don't need to anything complicated so these controls are fine.My only main gripe was the bugs. For a narrative based walking simulator, having to reload checkpoints when cutscenes have missing items or when animations bug is very annoying. It ruins the immersion. At the very least checkpoints are fairly common so it isn't a big issue but it is annoying.

_childDocuments_.review: I have just completed this game.  I looked around carefully at all locations and read every note which I could find.  I was fascinated by the detail of this world.  The story line drew me in and I found it difficult not to just keep going.  It is a wonderful game.  A note of caution: it can be somewhat depressing in places and I did find myself saddened by some of the history revealed. The game autosaves.  Generally speaking, I prefer being able to save on demand.  I have had to give up on games because I couldn't complete the appropriate part before the autosave.  However, the autosaves in "Paradise Lost" occur frequently so this is not a problem.I experienced two problems.  The first time I returned to the game after a break, my character would not move.  This problem was solved by unchecking "head bob" in the settings (don't forget to "apply").  (I've no idea what "head bob" is!)  The second problem was when I could not move my hand from one button to a higher button when selecting which one to press.  My mistake was to move the mouse slowly forwards; it needs an enthusiastic shove.  These two problems seem to be fairly common.I took 6.8 hours to finish the game. _childDocuments_.review: First off right up front: This is not a game for the kiddos. Not that anything unsavory happens but this game has zero action.It is a interactive story. A video game book. OR as the gamer bois say: It is a walking simulator. The story progresses by having you push "W" and move the main character forward. Occasionally you will have to skillfully press either the "A" or the "D" keys. If you can remember you can also press "SHIFT" which gives you a slight speed boost- but not much. Otherwise you keep your eyes open for circles on the scenery. These mean you have something to left click on to perform some action from climbing, descending, reading paper logs, letters or memos and even picking up use full items to be used at other locations.    That has to be the most depressing review I have ever written...Even so, I enjoyed "Paradise Lost" from beginning to end. It IS a story NOT a game. I rode the rails and looked at the beautiful world the devs created. It is a bleak landscape of a "What if..." world where Nazi scientists had set up an underground bunker to ride out the war.They brought some prisoners with them and using the systems throughout the bunker they fight back.   The topics about what the Nazis are doing are adult in nature and are reasons I wouldn't recommend this for kids. The writers do a great job telling a story that (for me) crept up on me and had me interested before I realized I was.It has a few small choices that may get you to replay it to see what changes and I read it has four endings, I may revisit it later to see them but not in succession.I had two glitches playing. One is the "can't move" bug. If you exit the game and come back, your character is stuck and can not move. It is an easy fix just go to the game options settings and hit "accept" (like if you changed a game setting and "save" the new setting.) And that fixes it- you return to the game and can move. It is a pain in the tookis but an easy fix.Second I returned to an area where your character picks up a book and the second time I ran it the book did not show on screen. You could still interact with it and the story progressed but the book was missing.So if you want a chill sci-fi story you can "play" for a few hours you may like this one.If you are looking for the next "DOOM" you won't. -Mr GrAnD

_childDocuments_.review: This game is riddled with bugs, technical issues and odd design decisions such as a terribly slow walking (or running) speed and no way to go back and check if you missed anything (besides loading a checkpoint). _childDocuments_.review: Disappointing to say the least.The game has many flaws and little strengths.- It's pretty, if you don't look too close. There is a serious like of polish which with a walk speed that slow allows you to notice this kind of details. - The walk speed like many other pointed out is a bit too slow but fortunately there is not much needs for back and forth.- The game is short, only took 3 hours to beat (in two sessions). So I don't recommend at a full price.- There is little to do other than inspecting a few documents and looking at the pretty environments. No real puzzles or meaningful interactions.- Many collisions issues, especially around ladders and some triggers require to be so close that they disappear from your screen because they are out of frame. Given it's the main and only way of interacting it's kind of ridiculous.- Lastly, the writing is abysmal and the timings are off as well. Notably around choices, many time they appear on screen and you get pressed to answer before even having the time to read your choices. Also some story points give choices as well, but given they supposedly re-tell some past events it doesn't make sense.Overall, I don't recommend. _childDocuments_.review: Paradise lost is a story about person who is alone in an apocalyptic world and happens to come across another person who needs help. _childDocuments_.review: Paradise Lost is a walking sim set in a dystopian alternate past. The graphics, music, and atmosphere are amazing, and the story is sad but moving.Works on Linux (Steam Compatibility Mode: Proton Experimental) without any glitches.Others have pointed these things out, but I think they bear repeating.  The game is a walking sim with some simple puzzles.  You can look around and explore (but that ability is limited) or you can just push through.It's not really very long.  I went through twice in less than 9 (combined) hours.  Some areas I took my time in, and then restarted the levels for achievements, or just because I wanted to go back and explore some more.... silly, I know... but I did it anyway, and don't regret it. I imagine I could speed run the game and finish in less than 3 hours.As others have also noted, the movement is quite slow.  There is (listed) a button (shift) to make you "run" but in all actuality, it doesn't make you move faster.  What "shift" DOES do is ZOOM in on something you're looking at.... not a lot, but sometimes that does make a difference.... especially when you're just looking around.I really wanted to be able to explore more.  It'd have been nice to also be able to move faster.  Also, I found the HEAVY footsteps and regular sighs of.... boredom?....exasperation? ....to be annoying and out of place. ...especially because they (the sighs) seem to happen regularly, and don't fit the situations at all.  The heavy  "CLOMP CLOMP CLOMP" of the footsteps were also out of place, like the main character was a 350 Lb man wearing shoes with plywood soles instead of a teen probably weighing less than 100 Lbs (sorry, I can't figure Kilos, even though that would be more appropriate.)Some reviewers complained about the voice-acting being bad. I disagree.  The voice acting is just fine for the characters countries of origin and story-background.  The voicing isn't "typical American" style...it's not super emotional with lots of pitch and speed changes... but it is totally typical for the characters who seem to be of Slavic, Polish, Russian, and (maybe) German descent, but trying to speak in American English... maybe that will be different if you play the game NOT in English....I very much enjoyed the game, and think my money was well spent.  Sure, I got it on sale, but I'll rarely pay full price for a game.... sorry, Devs .... and usually won't buy unless it's at least 50% off ...again, sorry Devs.... but I think this game is with the price.Overall, I think the game was great.  I'll dock you a bit for the slow speed and lack of ability to really explore and a point for the weird controls ( I shouldn't have to do all those combo moves just to open a door or drawer or ...whatever...)I give Paradise Lost 6 pairs of liederhosen out of 10 possible.

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoyed Paradise Lost. The story was interesting, the end was touching, the music was fitting. The only minor negative things that I would mention is the walking vs running. There's virtually no speed difference and it was a bit frustrating. The controls are sometimes a bit clunky. Overall, I highly recommend it if you can put up with some minor frustrations. The story makes up for the negative impact. All achievements trigger properly.

_childDocuments_.review: I think what irks me about this game is something that will set me apart from most other negative reviews. In the end I am not upset about it being a walking simulator (an extremely slow one at that), but instead I am upset about two things. I will spoil the game, so please duck away here if you aren't interested in being spoiled. The TL:DR is I don't recommend it.Okay so spoilers:In case the developer ever reads this, I hope this doesn't come off as meanspirited. I am sure you guys did a fantastic amount of work on all the details of the game, but in the end I just don't think its a great game. First of all, the game is set in an abandoned alternate-history Nazi bunker. That sounds like a cool premise. Why is it abandoned? What happened to the people in it? Whats the over all story? These are all great questions: Unfortunately the answer is given within 15 minutes of playing the game, because this game isn't at all about the Nazi bunker, it's about the Polish resistance fighters who somehow overcame the entire bunkers defenses in like a day of fighting, despite the Bunker apparently being full of battle-hardened well-equipped Nazi soldiers. The entire story centers around what these Polish dudes and dudettes get up to in the bunker after all the Nazis are killed, and this is extremely uninteresting to me. Not just because I feel like I got duped, being that all the promotional material I saw was about this secret nazi bunker, but also because the story of the Poles is so extremely one-note and predictable that I more or less guessed the ending the moment the story goes from being about the Nazis (again, like 15 minutes) to being about the Poles. I just really didn't care about the Poles' story, and it completely dominated the entire runtime of the game. Okay so second, I just don't believe the world at all. The bunker you go through is so extremely otherworldly and yet at the same time so extremely sparse that I just don't buy that it is a "real" or (perhaps more accurately) credible place. All the little set piece areas you go through feel like that, set pieces, and at no point was I convinced this was an actual place that had once been full of people. You know how Rapture from Bioshock seemed like a real place? Like everything was strange but believable? Paradise Lost is the exact opposite, it is completely unbelievable in its scope and scale, it never seems real at all. I think what is most puzzling is that the entire world seems like it has never been inhabited, and yet the bunker was at some point, supposedly, teeming with life. They more or less handwave that away at the beginning of the story, but that just ruined it even more for me.All in all I just don't care for it, and I think even at the reduced price I got it at it was a major disappointment. Plus at 3 hours this game is very very short, even for 8 euros.
_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Lost

_childDocuments_.review: Hi Adidas here, I'm the crazy man in his 40's who maintains the "Walking simulator Fan Club", so I played dozens of these games so i can say with relative authority that I have a good idea of what makes a good game vs a mediocre one. I write my reviews as I play the game to make sure not to miss anything, and pride myself in having the most detailed walking simulator reviews on Steam."Paradise Lost" is "Dear Esther" meets "Bioshock" and had a baby that looks like "Firewatch" set in a very interesting, hyper detailled steampunk revisionist 'Nazis went underground' setting. What struck me was the incredible attention to visual detail. For an indy title, it's impressive to note:a) The carefully crafted movement animations (passing under a train carriage, going down a ladder, squeezing oneself through old archive files: all of those have been animated by hand specificalliy for that sequence). b) The HUGE amount of effort put into making each room/chamber/factory unique and a REAL pleasure to discover (each room serves a purpose and is carefully layed out). Even the entrance reveal is quite something to behold, but then so are each and every room in the hotel scene, feeling 'lived in' with hundreds of 3d models used to make realistic interiors. As per my screenshot, you'll see the back of cupboard cheaply made doesn't look like the wall that supports it, the draping next to it, the carpets, etc. Sometimes walls are made of 4 or 5 different beautifully hand drawn textures. It's very , very well done. I haven't seen a single 'generic corridor' in this game. c) Every scene tells a story. For example, there's a little workshop of miniatures you enter with a painting set and so on. You wonder why it's for - and realise it was to build the next room - everything is a model of what's to come. It's not just a 'nice to have' - it what makes this game - this game and no other game. Major props for that.d) In a strange but understandable decision, they went for an effect where your body is visible when looking down, which was certain hard work to achieve from the developers, no doubt. When you hold an object, your hand rotates with the movement of the mouse. It's very clever, but it has some consequences in the form of geometry bugs and oh-hum controls.Put together, these three element give the game a very cinematic nature, and makes you want to see 'what's behind the next door' - it's really easy to finish the game in one sitting.A walking simulator needs a good story. This one has quite the concept (hidden nazi base under Krakau), and relies primarily on exploration for exposure. Two stories are told via both a voice over (i don't want to spoil it) and notes left around. The notes are very well crafted, original artwork has been placed everywhere and the game really shine in that regard, rivaling (and sometimes beating) AAA titles.Plot wise, we're talking straightforward scifi, so don't expect 'David Lynch' ambiance from "Everybody is gone to the rapture" and , if you watched movies and read books before, the plot twist is given in the first quarter of the game if you pay attention (if you speak German, even earlier). Nonetheless, I quite liked it, as it wasn't so 'black and white' as most games. If you pay attention to the notes littered around, you'll find there's a warning hidden inside the game about not repeating the past. It's subtle and well done.It's not all 'milk and honey' however, especially as the voice acting is poor at times, terrible at others, the dialog quite frankly sucks, and the game hyper-linear (litterally you could argue it's 100% 'on rails. But it's a walking simulator, it's meant to tell a singular story and therefore not that big a deal - just frustrating to have to click things in a certain order and a certain order only. Thankfuly the story is not as binary as 'nazis bad, poles good' - this is far more about human nature than ideology, as the real world is. I found it captivating. There are a few , sadly too rare, moments of interactions that puts you in "tough decision mode" - especially as the game world feels so 'real'. Yes, the game looks gorgeous, but because of the quality of its art and textures, not the complexity of its engine (no HDR, no fanciful Ray tracing).It is let down by bad optimization (a right that can play CP77 1.0 on ultra at 70fps at 5k was struggling to keep up with high 50's on medium at 1440p here), but that' a common problem with unreal engine 4 and 2080rtx GPUs. Just set AA to medium and shadows to low and you should be good to go. Likewise, the HDR is (by the admission of the Devs) broken: it has an option but it never enables. This makes things a bit wonky on my Odyssey G9 despite using the best connection possible (ultra short DP cable). In other words: everything looks too reflective especially in the dark , where a rail handle will shine like a series of christmas lights just because a lamp is somewhere in the room. If you have a G9 or a similar option on your monitor, disable 'auto luminance'.Finally, the game doesn't support 32:9 aspect ratio, unlike most modern titles.Most of you will be frustrated by the painfully slow walking/moving speed at times, simply because you'll forget to push a lever somewhere and will have to walk all the way back. 3, 4, sometimes 5 times, until you 'restart checkpoint' and get stuck on geometry.The game certainly benefit from a patch or two due to some game-breaking bugs. The forums are littered with complaints regarding 'being stuck' and sure enough it's extremely easy to 'get stuck' on polygons.There are multiple of these bugs acknoledge by the devs that feel the game was never play tested (evidently not the case, but still - half my playtime was walking back and forth trying to find 'what i had missed' when what was needed was a reload.) If you do buy the game: make sure to disable 'headbop'. Just ... trust me. Solves about 90% of the bugs.There is also no manual save mechanism, and even though checkpoints are frequent, it's well known gamers dislike this model as it forces them to manually back up saves should the game crash or be given a chance to 'try something different'. No such luck here.Sadly, this seriously negatively impacts the enjoyment of the game, and 6 months on from the bug report, I doubt they will ever be fixed.Outside of these complaints, the game is a very solid entry in the genre, but only once you get used to 'how it wants you to play it'. The major downsides are the lack of innovation and the bugs.Yes it looks GREAT, it's probably the walking simulator, if not the game with the most visual detail I've seen in years, with some rooms feeling genuinelly 'lived in', and no two assets reused, and extremely complex geometry. It sounds good, the story is okay and the bugs are almost forgiveable. Quite frankly, if a game needs a remake in Unreal Engine 5, it's this one.But where "The Occupation" added a layer of activity to the genre, or "Before Your Eyes" made you cry your eyes out, "Paradise Lost" "only" offers incredibly clever , well crafted interiors over and over again after X hours which is a shame given how much blood sweat and tears the developers have clearly put into this game. Definitely a buy if you're a walking simulator fan, especially at the low cost during sales. Even more so if they ever patch it and rid the game of the bugs once and for all, but I've read it woudn't be possible as most of the bugs come from the fact the game allow you to see your body and would require a fairly extensive rewrite. Shame. PS: I do look forward to their next game!PS2: Save your autosave file at the end of the game if you want to see both ending and get both achievements. The game DELETES save files when you finish it! However, be aware both endings are identical.

_childDocuments_.review: I bought the game with the knowledge that it'd be more of a story game rather than an interactive game. However, it has a ton of flaws that shouldn't be there. - You walk slow as a snail, and holding SHIFT to sprint increases your speed with 0.00001% at most. - It plays animations for every obstacle you want to climb / descend, each lasting 3-6 seconds. This gets very frustrating when you want to explore. - The only interactions you can do are with doors or papers you can read. Why bother having a feature that forces you to hold left-click and dragging your mouse in 1 direction? There are no difficulties or any random mini-events to these interacts. It's just an obstacle to make the game slower than it already is.A can give credit to the beautiful environmental design. It has a ton of details and it was easy to immerse yourself in it. I can't say I'm too crazy about the story though. It's set in a post-WW2 event which is entertaining, but the storyline about the character itself was pretty bland and boring.I'd give this a thumbs up soley for the environmental design, but there are too many things with this game that drags it down. If you want a game that you can play when you're bored and if you are a fan of immersing yourself in the environment, go for it. But if you're looking for any sort of gameplay, don't bother.

_childDocuments_.review: It is a dark walking simulator, somewhat in the spirit of Amnesia: Machine for Pigs, SOMA, and Bioshock. It is thematically related to Man from the High Castle and Fallout. Yet, as for a proper walking simulator - no fight, no hiding, even no scare scenes.PROS:- The visuals are stunning, both in terms of style and quality.- Good story-telling in general (contrast with the first part of Amnesia: Rebirth).- The story unfolds gradually, making it consistently captivating.- The world is fascinating, feels consistent, and well-designed. - Characters are believable (it is my issue with most games).CONS:- Short (3-4h gameplay).- One character voice acting could be better.- While I did appreciate that some things are not clear (it adds to the mood), some parts felt that either -would benefit from being expanded (even if only through notes) or cut out.- While voice communication is interesting, it does result in a strong relationship as in SOMA or Firewatch.OTHER:- I saw a few negative reviews stating that the walking pace is way too slow. Even though I am very impatient (and used to demonically fast-paced games such as Doom Eternal), the walking speed was good (provided I always "run", i.e. use SHIFT). A minor inconvenience, not a deal-breaker.

_childDocuments_.review: If you're looking for a linear, story-driven game that also involves exploring a mysterious location, you should take a closer look at Paradise Lost from developer PolyAmorous and publisher All in! Games should take a closer look. Paradise Lost is set somewhere in Poland, in an alternate reality. In this one, the Second World War lasted a few years longer and the Third Reich had its first nuclear weapons from the late 1950s. However, lacking reliable missile technology to use these limited weapons for attack, they become part of a contingency plan against advancing Russian forces. Their use is intended to temporarily stop the enemy and evacuate key parts of the population to huge underground bunkers, where they can make new plans. In the role of twelve-year-old Szymon, we discover the bunker. A photo of our mother makes it clear that something connects her, and therefore us, to this mysterious place. In search of our roots and the secrets that this place hides, we penetrate deep into a world full of mysticism, megalomania and cruelty. Our journey takes us through several very different levels of the gigantic facility, where we learn a lot about its turbulent history.However, we are obviously not completely alone here. Through a communication system we get in touch with a person who accompanies us on our journey through the underground realm with advice and action.What exactly did the Nazis have planned down here? What became of you? And what connects us ourselves to this place? Only those who penetrate to the last level will get an answer to all questions.Especially at the beginning, the game world of Paradise Lost feels very oppressive and also eerie. After a short time, however, the creepy factor quickly begins to give way to a feeling of morbid fascination.The game world of Paradise Lost tells all kinds of stories. It shows the megalomania of the Nazis as well as their cruelty, but also reports on the fears and hopes of the people who were evacuated to this facility. Our way leads us through all kinds of different environments, like production halls or living areas. The deeper we penetrate, the more mysterious the place seems to become. All areas have a striking attention to detail and imposing design in common, which increases the immersion of the game immensely. The visual imposance and the oppressive atmosphere of this place is marred by the somewhat dusty graphics, the choppy motion sequences and the limited freedom of movement.In Paradise Lost we move around the bunker complex in the first-person perspective all the time. To learn more about the history of this impressive place, we can find notes and tapes everywhere, which tell us more about the life and plans of the inhabitants.This knowledge also influences some dialogues we have with the mysterious stranger, via the internal communication system. The more we know, the more often additional dialogue options are available to us. However, these flexible dialogs do not affect the actual gameplay. Our path is very clearly marked out and offers only limited room for exploration.At some points, we have to flip switches or search for certain objects in order to progress further in the game. Real puzzles or challenges don't arise from this, though.There are also neither quicktime events nor fights in the game. The experience is completely focused on exploring the bunker and its story.Technically, the game works very well on the whole, even if our character's animations seem a bit clumsy at times. There is one annoying bug in the game and that is when you load from the last checkpoint you can no longer move. Unfortunately, I had this bug as well and the only thing that helps is restarting the level. All in all, the game doesn't make any demands on the player's skills, but it offers everything necessary to experience an intense story.My playtime for Paradise Lost was about four hours. I think it can be done faster.

_childDocuments_.review: (PL) is a linear narrative adventure set in an alternate timeline during the 1980s. World War II didn't end as we all know: Nazi Germany developed weapons of mass destruction and used them against their enemies, plummeting the world into a desolate nuclear winter. This story is about Szymon, a young Polish boy that sets out into the wastelands for personal reasons, and finds an abandoned Nazi bunker he intends to explore. What he will find, will change his life forever.Visually speaking, and as kind of expected from a narrative adventure, Paradise Lost hits the mark in full. The sprawling bunker where most of the adventure takes place, is rendered out in a realistic way, inspired to the architectural trends of Nazi Germany at the times. The equipment seen lying around such as weapons, engines of war, tools and so on is also historically accurate, which is a good plus for immersion. Light effects and textures deserve a special mention, as they bring life to each environment in a consistent manner.The desolate, eerie atmosphere expected from an abandoned underground complex, is transposed very well in Paradise Lost, albeit it's way less terrifying than it should be - especially from the perspective of a young boy. Nevertheless, the setting feels immersive most of the time, and that's what counts.The tracks in the background correctly emphasize discovery-related moments or transitions to new areas, which by themselves already make a solid impression on the player. Voice acting is passable, with actors simulating accents in a decent manner when speaking English as non-native language, and even cursing in their own mother-tongue in more heated situations.One of the biggest issues with the story, is that it spoils the main narrative hook way too early, so most players will already understand what's going on there and then. Afterwards, the game becomes much less interesting because of this fact. Also, there are some inconsistencies regarding facts: for instance, after a battle raged in the bunker there should be many dead bodies or at least traces of blood or struggle, but there are none to be found EVER. There are more of such issues, this was one example of several.it is made clear that Szymon can read and understand German pretty well, as most documents he finds have been written by Germans but auto-translate into English or whatever language is set. Some others, and also text on walls, instead are untranslated for whatever reason, so unless players happen to speak German in real life, they will remain a mystery for them.Even for a narrative adventure, Paradise Lost proves to be very uneventful and linear. There are almost no tense or otherwise "heated" moments during the adventure, which sets a bland pace most of the time. Environmental interaction meets bare minimum standards, especially today in 2021 when the genre has evolved and introduced minigames or anyway diversions to break the main gameplay loop most of the time. So, by today's standards especially, PL proves to be way too linear, without anything to diversify the gameplay.Is performed on foot most of the time, and on occasion by using machinery such as elevators. Szymon can either walk or sprint, though the difference between the two stances is minimal, as the general traversing speed proves to be low at all times. Levels are structured in a very linear manner, often with only one available route and some one-way drops that make backtracking impossible. There are a few optional rooms to explore in some areas, though they are never extensive parts of any level - they contain additional lore or indirect clues to know more about what happened.Happens when the protagonist approaches a white-dot marker, which indicates the presence of an interactive item nearby. These objects can be doors, machinery, computers or also documents to read. Sometimes, a specific item will be needed to perform a successful interaction, such as a key or a component for instance. Generally, the level of environmental interaction is very low even for this type of game, with sparse documents here and there but little else except primary-quest related items.

_childDocuments_.review: is... frustrating. It has a number of compelling ideas, and its art direction is impeccable. However, a combination of frustratingly rote and slow gameplay, wooden storytelling, and mechanical bugs ultimately leave it disappointing.It's a little tricky to pin down the source of my disappointment, but much of it stems from the way the game realizes its setting, I think. Set in an alternate history where the second World War didn't end in 1945, the N*zi party began developing nuclear weapons in underground bunkers before launching a nuclear strike that led to nuclear winter. It's extremely bleak, and the combination of fascistic pomp juxtaposed against subterranean caverns and tunnels feels like the best of both  and the  series. A good start, for sure, but the excitement quickly wears off once you realize that the post-apocalyptic setting is little more than set dressing for the main character, a little Polish boy named Szymon seeking answers about his late mother's past.Now, using ornate and larger-than-life settings to elucidate a protagonist's inner struggles isn't a bad idea, even if it's played less than subtly in-game. (The game's chapters are literally the stages of grief, in a creative choice that feels almost obnoxiously on-the-nose.) What makes it feel hollow, ill-suited to games as a medium, is how little actual input the player has in the traversing of the tale.  is a walking sim's walking sim, and the linearity of the experience is emphasized all the more by a lack of exploration or puzzles. A good rule of thumb for the quality of a walking sim is that, as a player, you feel as if you are not missing out on a potentially more mechanically and narratively rewarding experience by stripping out mechanics, and  often feels like a duller version of .But, I thought to myself for the first leg of my play-through, perhaps the writing would make the slugging walking speeds and unintuitive interaction controls more tolerable. And, perhaps to a WWII buff or a die-hard junkie of alternate history stories, that would be true. I... did not find that to be the case. Setting aside the wooden and awkward voice acting, 's story feels both slow and unfocused. In spite of the aforementioned influences of , , and , the human undercurrent of the story is effectively shifted entirely to the background.  told its story primarily through audio logs, and so  does so as well, eschewing the much needed horror and mechanical depth that made the experience noteworthy. From , it lacks the dreamlike magical-realism that shifted the genre into something closer to , and from  it lacks the warmth and casual verisimilitude of its cast. It's not a game without charm, but the ideas on display have been more effectively explored in so many games that  feels cold and dead by comparison.What few aspects to the game I enjoyed felt mitigated by their implementation. The game has simply delectable environmental and art design, with painstakingly meticulous animation... that serves either only as window-dressing or else actually slows down the proceedings, both in terms of Szymon's movement speed and in terms of frame rate; the optimization of this game baffles me, as playing with literally every single setting failed to illicit a comfortable, consistent frame rate. I appreciate the ambition to invoke John Milton's poem of the same name and to loop it into the story, but the trajectory of the plot makes it feel like an afterthought, a deliberate effort to try to elevate the game's actual plot past the pulpy territory it resides in. Even when I was in a more patient mood, reloading checkpoints caused the main character's collision to malfunction, requiring me to "reset" his position by opening up the settings menu. For the life of me, I cannot  what's causing this.Look, I get it. There are cool ideas on display here, and I don't  to bash this game. I didn't set out with high hopes, but I did approach  with an open mind and a willingness to be surprised. Instead, the game squandered every opportunity to impress, only managing to land squarely on its face out of the starting gate. Get it on sale if you feel you absolutely must, but otherwise, consider playing one of this game's many,  influences instead for a better time.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is currently in the Humble Choice for February 2022.   If you are interested in the game and it's before March 1st, 2022, consider picking up the game as part of the current monthly bundle.A slow walk through remnants of the Nazis.Paradise Lost takes place in an alternate history where Germany did a lot better in World War II.  It’s also a walking simulator of the worst kind.  It is a game that takes the walking part of the genre title way too literally and lets the player move at a snail’s pace, but don’t worry there’s a sprint button that walks at a snail's pace if it was on ice.  And if you’re not sure that would make the snail faster, that’s exactly the problem. This is a slow game, made slower because of the slog.  Many interactable objects have to be triggered in the right position and looking in the right direction.  The letters left behind are relatively uninteresting, and often drop German, possibly Polish, dialect whenever they care to.   I gave up after about 40 minutes because I was getting bored with it, and annoyed because players are trudging through a Nazi bunker, but not in an interesting way.  Forced to walk slowly through locations that should infuriate most people for what they stood for, doesn’t make a good game.  This reminds me of the walking speed of Everybody's Gone to Rapture and that’s a bad thing.Pick this up if you want to walk through nazi bunkers, and follow a story.  The chapter titles talk about the stages of grief but doesn’t give a meaning for it yet, and I’m pretty firm on no longer being interested.   Paradise Lost makes me think this game is trying to say this is some form of hell, and I’ve heard there's some Slavic mythology here?  But I didn’t see anything worth continuing for. _childDocuments_.review: I was looking forward to  as soon as I saw the first trailer. This is a very interesting game taking place in an alternative version of our World War II history. If my understanding is correct the Allies were eliminated and the Germans managed to create nuclear weapons that were eventually used against Europe. And the end result is what you see here: a nuclear wasteland covered by snow on the surface. Our protagonist is a boy called Simon who leaves his home (shelter) where he lives with his mother in order to find an underground bunker where he's supposed to find more information as to who his father was. The game consists of 5 chapters during which we navigate in mentioned bunker and to include some dialogue so as not to present us with a boring game Simon is aided by Eva, somebody who seeks the boy's help while he's down there.But the bunker has a lot of German texts and documents from officers. How come? This was a retreate for them and the Polish resistance managed to successfully eliminate the opposition. To know more about the story and also of the inhabitants it's worth reading every document and listening to all audio logs. Some of the underground locations look fantastic and if there are screenshot aficionados among you you'll appreciate the scenery and the attention to detail that was put into the creation of even a single room.Now,  I played just after  and I noticed the same issue here: high system requirements and occasional FPS drops. As a plus for me this is one of those first person games where we can see our body / legs when looking down. Now, the emphasis here is literally on walking and by collecting keycards we can easily make progress. We press buttons and pull levers regularly but there is no real puzzle that would make us stop and think. It's alright as this is all about immersion.Beside the occasional FPS drops there are some other minor issues with . Reloading the game can often result in Simon being stuck. The headbob option I recommend that you turn off in the options menu. This did the trick for me otherwise you have to start a chapter all over. Also, when you can interact with objects there is always a circle appearing in the right direction but pressing the button may not have a result as you are not close enough yet to the object you can interact with.The above are just minor issues. Overall, I had fun with . It gives you a solid 3-4 hours of gameplay time and it has several endings. The voice acting is also great. If Simon could walk at a greater pace or if running was possible I would do a complete 2nd walkthrough.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a very typical walking simulator. Long dead, foreboding environment, haunting, yet slow character-centric story, beautiful visuals, boring gameplay.It's basically Bioshock, if you removed all the characters, combat and social critique. Now, without those elements, Bioshock would probably be not great, but okay, just like this game. It's okay.Paradise Lost doesn't offer anything new in its genre. It has an interesting setting, but a painfully slow narrative with no puzzles. The story's conclusion is the only moment where character choice plays a role and it ain't stellar stuff. Both main characters are sort of uninteresting, and so unlikely that their struggle is hard to empathize with since the whole story feels so alien. In all honesty, how the Nazis wanted to run the bunker and the eventual uprising was far-far more thrilling, than the rather meaningless story of our protagonist. We do see some of this more interesting narrative through notes, logs and audio recordings. Piecing it together is rather fun, because not every element is presented to us in a linear fashion and there are a lot of world building pieces that don't directly support the main story, only enhance it. All these are visually really nice, the graphics quality is consistently great.The environment design on the other hand, has a few ups and down, it started out really strong, at first it felt like the designers actually thought about making a believable place first and implemented the gameplay once that was done. Like the way people would arrive to the bunker is shown incredibly well and with great detail. We see where the luggage and belongings go, how they are inspected and disinfected, where the paperwork is done, the class system. Unfortunately later levels feel thrown together and random. Why is the meat factory right next to a medical wing? Why does a public bridge made for walking also include rails that go nowhere? How can plants survive in the cold with no sunlight? Lot of small elements made the whole world really unbelievable.Only encountered a single game breaking bug. Interacting with items was really difficult and felt like pixel hunting. The are no mechanics or other gameplay elements, besides watching monitors. Not exactly an engaging way to tell an interactive story... Every action has some type of longwinded animation, that feels just tedious and overly long. The walking is incredibly slow as well.Paradise Lost is definitely an okay game, but I wish there was a meh option, because this kinda falls into that category. If you like walking sims, it's probably more than okay. The environment design is the game's main highlight, and if that's enough for you, maybe buy this on a sale.

_childDocuments_.review: Szymon is a 12-year-old boy, left alone after his mother passed away. Exploring the nuclear wasteland that was Poland created from an alternate reality WWII, he stumbles upon an abandoned massive Nazi bunker that had its own city and civilization deep underneath the earth. Learn about its origins, the reason for its existence, what happened to the original occupants when it was eventually attacked and taken over by Polish rebels, and the colony they created inside from the ashes; and perhaps, make a home for yourself here too.I had a really fun time playing Paradise Lost, I also however, love walking sims and haven’t experienced the bugs mentioned in other reviews. Aside from a visual glitch that in no way affected myself or the story, I had a great time! 3+ hours to complete with four endings and decent replay value. I highly suggest when you start the game you turn off head bobbing and severely reduce the camera sensitivity. There are no jump scares, nothing terrifying, nothing ever chases you.
