Something to note: In chapter 1 you have an option to walk through the station gates directly or take a detour through boxes and luggage – I suggest you go through the gates the first time and on your second playthrough; should you choose to do so; go through the luggage for a more fulfilling experience. _childDocuments_.review: I took my time exploring and beat the game in around 6 hours, which includes replaying the first chapter because of a bug. The bug I encountered appeared to be game breaking, as anytime I loaded my game (from a restart or from a checkpoint) my character would just run in place as if they were stuck. Once I knew how to bypass this bug it becomes trivial. Getting your character to be able to move again just requires you to change your game from windowed to full screen (or vice versa) to get unstuck. Otherwise the game runs smoothly and looks great. The environment looks great and the atmosphere is very immersive. The story is interesting and made me want to follow it through to the end. However, the game play is almost non-existent. This is essentially a movie where you just hold “W” to make your character progress and click on the white dots you see to interact with any objects of interest. There are a few dialog choices that I assume affect the story and will give you different endings. I was hoping for more in-depth game play where you solve puzzles and interact more with the environment. It’s a very passive game and is more or less just a walking simulator, or should I say snail simulator, because the character walks excruciatingly slowly. If the character’s walk speed were set to anything sane then the time to beat would be cut in half, as most of the game is spent waiting on your character to make it from one side of the room to another. I wish I could give this game a neutral score but, I would still recommend this game for anyone looking to experience beautiful and interesting environments, and hear a unique story.

_childDocuments_.review: I love walking simulators, I like to walk around at my own pace, read letters and listen to tapes very realistically lying around (who doesn't leave tapes conveniently placed inside playing devices right next to where they recorded themselves talking?). And on that front, Paradise Lost delivers: it has a good story - albeit not completely groundbreaking if you've played some similar games. It has a character who has a valid reason for wanting to discover more, and a good pace unraveling the story bit by bit. It's a right amount of creepy, but no jump scares - perfect for easily startled horror lovers like me. The sound design is quite good and the voice actors are okay - the pace is a bit clunky and I found myself clicking nervously when they where talking, hoping to skip some of their interactions, or at least continue exploring while they where talking. (Not a good sign when you think how I looked forward to each tiny bit of dialogue in Firewatch). But the visuals are STUNNING. I took a lot of screenshots and really enjoyed just standing and looking around, especially in the fourth part. There are a lot of excellent ideas, really well executed.Where the game doesn't deliver, or just not quite enough to make this a full recommendation, is basic gameplay. I don't necessarily want a walking simulator to be an adventure game, I don't expect puzzles to knock my socks off. Really, just walking and discovering a story is fine by me. But if you do introduce puzzles, make them count, make them significant. It's like with pen and paper roleplaying: don't make the player roll a die if there's no consequence. There were instances where the dialogue announced that a door was blocked and how to unblock it, before I even got to the door - I would have liked to get the possibility of looking and thinking by myself. Another time I picked up an item, not knowing what the item would be for. I actually never found out, so I probably skipped something there, and the item just disappeared after some time. Which is fine, it's just a bit frustrating. Even more frustrating is the character's walking speed, especially if you need to find your way and have been going around a room three times already, hitting against boxes and fences just as high as the boxes and fences you could climb over just one room back. It just seems a bit arbitrary. Most drawers you can't open, and then there is one you can open - and there's nothing in it. Why allowing me to open it then?It's nothing keeping me from playing the game, but it's making me grumble all the way through, making me very aware of the game mechanics, where a more elegant solution would have immersed me completely.And for the love of AI: do add controls to be remapped, or at the very least show me in the setting which buttons do what. I spent way too long trying to reach an upper button, hitting every key, arrows, shift-combinations possible. I finally figured that I needed to lift my mouse very slowly, no keys needed.So it's still a recommendation, but try to be patient when you play Paradise Lost.

It's a compelling mystery though certain elements are easy to guess and the ultimate destination is not entirely satisfying. Player decisions don't *really* matter that much and the mechanics are repetitive, so I might recommend this for very casual players. I finished in 3.5 hours, taking my time, reading every letter discovered and generally spending my time enjoying the experience. _childDocuments_.review: Theres several things you want in  a good walking sim, solid story and setting, rewarding exploration and pretty visuals, so how does Paradise Lost stack up? lets take a look.On the Pretty visuals side Paradise lost certainly delivers, with its retro futurist style the bunker is interesting to explore and provides a surprising variety of environments for what is basically just a big cave. But thats all well and good but without some solid exploration theres not much use for the visuals.So the good news is that there is some value in exploration, apart from the stacks of papers and notes scattered about the main path, there are a handful of side areas and most interesting of all secret rooms. But theres a few problems here, the first and biggest is the painful movement speed, its a slog just to get through the game but going off to explore especially later on as the real story begins to unfold, but walking off the beaten track is discouraged by the fact you'll have to walk all the way back after. The other problem is that the exploration isn't very rewarding, yeah there are notes on side paths but so often they are little bits of flavour and don't seem all that important to the main story. I say seems because I get the feeling that I'm missing stuff but after a couple runs through the game I at a loss as if its me or the story that has holes.Storywise the games got it going on in at least one department, its got an alt history thing going where during WW2 the germans were able to develop nukes (because the US was still neutral so they had less pressure on them and more time) but after losing to the USSR the germans built massive bunkers and nuked the hell out of their territory causing a nuclear winter, the world is a frozen wasteland and your character sets out to find the man in an old photo after the death of his mother. This leads you to the bunker and the beginning of your explorations.  Where things went south for me was that I was able to guess the story right up near the front of the game, its super obvious from just one note on the main path, but that doesn't mean you should avoid notes after, they just flesh things out more as you go along, though it is annoying that the main character is ignorant for so long. But thats not all thats wrong, should you miss something important like a conversation or note with important info the game will just treat it like you did which could cause some confusion when it comes up and you'll be all wait... what? (I can't get into exactly what without spoilers so...)But before we wrap up a few annoyances, apart from the slow walk speed, anytime you have to open a door or press a button you have to do a weird little mini game thing, where you click and drag a circle and drag it to a bar and hold it until it fills, which why? its annoying just open the door, the games slow enough already. Second the game has multiple endings which sounds good until you find that theres on chapter select and the game deletes your save at the end forcing a replay if you want to see the other ending (which is just requires choosing a different dialogue at the end of the game, nothing while playing) and with the slow, slow walking and the fact that replay adds nothing to the story (that might just be me guessing right at the start what the story was, so no need to reinterpret notes in  a new light), if you're after 100% achievements or just want all the endings then backup your save.Overall I did like the story but the other elements were constantly annoying me, spoiling what small enjoyment I got from the game.

_childDocuments_.review: This is really not what I planned to write in my review.This game, despite it's  really has some great qualities, and an amazing story...But I simply can't give a positive review to a game that . I would categorize this game as: an atmospheric walking simulatorYou start in a weird world/parallel universe, and gradually discover it's history and backstory through clues in your environment, and notes you findThe musical score is well timed, and perfectly fits the mood.The world around you is huge, and weird, and amazing, and strangeAlthough this doesn't mean the graphics are amazing.They're pretty good.But far from an AAA game graphics.The annoying part of the game - is the game-breaking bugs (obviously).Which appear in the game even if you don't do anything special, and just play the game as it's intended to be played.For example: You can't load a game if "Head Bob" is enabled in the settings.There are also pseudo-bugs: Like the fact the game "freezes" every time you find a microphone.But in fact it's just waiting for your input (to roll the mouse wheel).But unfortunately it's not properly explained - so can lead to a lot of frustration, reloading, and people thinking it's a bug.The second most annoying part of the game (after the bugs) is the walking speed. It's slow. Very.And "running" only marginally improves it.However this "bug" is actually a feature.The game is a slow walking simulator.There isn't much to do in the game except that. There is no action. There are no puzzles. There are no choices to be made.You walk. You watch the environment around you. And you read the notes you find.That's pretty much it.If you could simply run through the game - there would be not much game left...The redeeming quality of this game - is the story and the atmosphere.The story is very original, and really draws you in (especially if you are like me, and love alternative history)And the atmosphere the game builds around the story is great as well.You're not told anything point blank, or have endless walls of texts to read.You're told very little, and need to piece together what happened from the very few notes, items and clues you find through your travels.And simply by observing the world around you.If you are able to overcome the bugs and design flaws of the game - there is a real gem hiding inside it...
_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Lost

_childDocuments_.review: With no neutral option I must vote "No"This is a perfect example of a good maybe even great idea for a game which got wasted due to bad executionStory is fine, although a bit predictableGraphics are very goodAudio is also on the positive sideA lot of optional elements building the lore(yet this part seems incomplete, see the comment in cons section)Plenty of checkpoints so you don't loose progressUnfortunately the game feels rushed and incompleteGame mechanics slow the progression as much as possible(slow walking, pointless multi-click interactions for simple actions, no skipping dialogues/animations, no manual saves/chapter select and saves get deleted once you finish the game[Without resolving to some tricks you have to replay it 5 times to 100% it])Bugs - Every time you load the game you have to go to settings and just accept the existing ones to unstuck your character, menu doesn't pause the game[cutscenes], I also encountered a few freezes[at least there are plenty of checkpoints], minor graphical glitches like a bracelet becoming invisible when picked up for examination, or items moving one through another during interactions)Multiple references which the game doesn't even try to explain, nor do they affect the game in any way(Game could have used the story to familiarize players with some less known aspects of WW2 and the eastern front, instead they feel more like easter eggs for people already familiar with them). Aside from the historical references, same goes for most of the lore related interactions - they are completely optional so you may complete the game barely discovering a few most basic aspects of the story.Very linear(one slight path deviation possible, all other choices barely have any consequences up until the very end of the game)Many passages are one way, making backtracking impossible even if a perfectly fine way back should be available.To sum up:The game has a feeling that something much bigger was planned and in the end it got cut down to bare minimum, slowed down as much as possible to give the impression there's more content and even then the final product wasn't even properly testedYou might still want to play it for the story, yet the experience will be spoiled by the game mechanics. If you're ready to get past the UX problems you should still be able to enjoy the game, yet unfortunately a game which is enjoyable only on such condition doesn't deserve a recommendation.

_childDocuments_.review: A breath of fresh air. It is nice to not constantly having to scavenge for ammo, health and collectibles. This game was a nice change of pace. A walk-through with some faults but not enough for me to quit right after starting. The puzzles to me were a little too simple, needed to be a little more challenging. I read some reviews about how you lose the main plot and perspective, I did not find this to be the case. It kept me intrigued enough to press forward wanting to know the final outcome. The plot does become obvious after note reading by the 3rd level. Again, still wanting to get to the end. The environment and art work is beautifully detailed. A classic feeling of 3rd Reich ambiance and architecture. Sound effects and music did make me keep thinking that around any corner or door opening something may give you a jump scare. A few more interactions and choice making in dialogue would have been nice, but not necessarily a must. Voice acting, while not superb, did have a tone in accent and dialect that would be different in this alternative reality, I found it interesting and melodic. The price I paid of $10 was worth it, probably would have paid a little more. Would recommend if you are looking for a slow paced story driven walk-through without any anxiety that will not break the bank.

_childDocuments_.review: Tentative recommendation. I enjoyed the story, though the twists were expected from the first control room reveal. Still, it's clearly inspired by Bioshock with a hint of Soma thrown in there. No enemies, very relaxing (mechanically), with a creepy post-apocalyptic atmosphere. You'll get frustrated at how the characters all act like idiots in the backstory, but it's to be expected in these kind of games. This one does a clever thing with the story to explain why everybody conveniently left notes detailing their fall.Only real downside is how slow the character walks. Seriously. It's actually sped up in the trailers, he walks at half that speed, and literally every door requires you to "push" it open with the mouse. You'll get sick of these mechanics fairly early in.Also, for me, I hate chromatic aberration. You can't turn it off.

_childDocuments_.review: So. This is very much a 'recommended' with some huge caveats. First and foremost this is most definitely a walking simulator, which shouldn't be a dirty word but is definitely an acquired taste. If that ain't your taste move along. There is a lot that's good about this game, first and foremost the story is pretty great. That's it's strongest and really only component, but it does it magnificently well. The writing is coupled with truly stunning environments that are very immersive and have a real feeling that it was a lived in space. The art in general is all very high, with each chapter feeling completely different and visually gorgeous in it's own way.There are no puzzles and the game play literally consists of you moving from one area to the next progressing the story. Given there are some mechanics that involve you clicking or clicking and dragging, but  in honesty it is just an elaborate way of inputting an 'interact' button. There are certain sections that will require you to get a certain item to progress.. and here is the biggest downfall of this game.Good lord is it slow. I mean SLOWW You walk along at such a mind numbing pace, which I get it you are meant to be taking in the scene and being immersed but.. I MEAN SLOWWW I feel it actually detracts from the experience, by the end I was getting exhausted by the pace and saw an area not twenty metres away that looked interesting but chose to simply keep moving in the direction I knew was the next check point because journeying that twenty metres would have aged me fifty years.There is a sprint button, which I genuinely think has been put in the game as a pisstake because your speed increases by so little that I'm pretty sure I was moving the same pace and the FOV just changed a little. This is on top of dialogue and sequences that you MUST play to completion, which along with the slow walking pace can lead to some incredible frustration as the point was made five minutes ago and you are still waiting for the voice lines to finish or a computer terminal to load.Those issues really do press on the player after a while, and would have been a thumbs down from me if not for having such a great story and beautiful art. If you enjoy immersive walking sims, I say give it a go but be prepared for a slow burn.

_childDocuments_.review: As far as walking sims go, I enjoyed this one. Was it perfect? Of course not. It's riddled with minor flaws but if you can get this for say €5 it's worth a go.What I enjoyed were the detailed graphics, the original setting, the slow unravelling of the story using notes, voice logs and other hints. The game has a surprising amount of detail & thought put in the locations and the story is for sure a very interesting one.I didn't experience many bugs - just twice where I got stuck in scenery. No crashes or anything else. Nor did the walking speed bother me. I believe a walking sim is a walking sim, not a running sim. The whole point is to take in the surroundings & to absorb everything. This is not the kind of game for people who want to rush through. Since the game is very linear, it's not like you'll be doing a lot of backtracking - the game does rather value your time despite the walking.There are some annoyances though. The game kind of loses itself in the last third in some ways. Whereas the first part is mostly logical with beautifully rendered Nazi-era settings, the last third is rife with pagan areas, huge trees, etc. which just feels weird. I could kind of believe the first areas could exist but the last third is a bit ... out there.I could tell that the dev was Polish because that last third seems to be heavily steeped in Polish folklore. As such, while I felt the story had huge potential & the ending was still satisfying, they could have gone a much different & better way. Having a Nazi underground that got destroyed by a Polish AI going rogue would have made more sense than what they made out of this. I feel like they tried to overly complicate matters to the point where you kind of lose investment into the setting. Once you figure out the Nazis were killed in no time and the rest was basically a struggle between Polish survivors, it just doesn't feel as "cool" anymore. Worst of all, the "big" reveal at the end was extremely predictable. In fact, the moment Ewa contacted you, I knew what the twist would be because several documents had already given hints. So all in all, it's a 6.5/10. A great setting, fun story, but too steeped in Polish pride & folklore, not enough Nazi setting, not enough made use of the potential. It would have made a far better movie than a game to be honest.

_childDocuments_.review: I can understand the reviews being mixed for a few reasons.What I liked:-Eerily beautiful, post-apocalyptic atmosphere. I enjoyed looking around and taking in my surroundings.-Graphics and details are wonderful.-Story is interesting, despite being a bit confusing.-True form of what a walking simulator is supposed to mean. You simply walk and click. For someone who isn't into first-person shooter games and into more of a narrative simulation game, this hits the nail on the head.What I disliked:-You can't run. The SHIFT key only really changes your FOV by a tiny bit. Maybe gives the impression that you're walking faster, but still ungodly slow.-Although I said the story is interesting, I'm still left with questions...a lot of them. Also left curious as to how the story did do a bit of a 180 in my opinion. To go from Nazis to a weird crazed man obsessed with an odd "religion"...I don't know. It just felt forced and confusing.-Dialogue was lackluster. It's hard to develop some type of connection with the characters.All in all, it took me just under 4 hours to complete. It's a good game for an easy time killer and a way to escape realty...albeit into a dystopian, Nazi invaded Europe, but hey. Despite the cons, I'd still recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: One day I was simply browsing through Steam and looking at games which contained popular user-defined tags for games that I had not traditionally played before such as those with “exploration” and “walking simulator” identifiers. Having a higher-end desktop computer (latest version of Alienware Aurora R11 with a top-end NVIDIA GeForce RTX graphics card and ultra-wide curved monitor), I was also looking for titles that had been released recently (2019+) along with a “mostly positive” (or better) user-rating. I’d played a few titles from “smaller” developers and was interested to see if my past experience with these type developers was just fortuitous or if I could find others that could deliver the same good gaming experience. In short, I was experimenting and wanted to know if other solid, well-built products were being released by lesser known / smaller developers that I was not familiar with. The story, for me, was engaging but I’m a huge world war 2 history buff and have often thought and wondered, what would the world look like today if the allies had lost that war. Some have said the player character moved too slowly throughout the game but I found that to be refreshing in that it gave the player a chance to explore the world built by the developers. It helped me get into the character more as a good RPG should do. I personally did not experience any “bugs” or “glitches” as one might expect to find. The game play mechanics were simple, easy to use and quickly acquired mainly because this game is designed to be a bit more story / narrative driven. In conclusion, I’d highly recommend playing this game even if this is typically not the type of game you usually go for. Overall, I found it to be refreshing and something I plan on playing through again at some point. If you’re looking for a good, solid made game with a good story and relaxing game place, give this one a try. I honestly think you’ll be surprised and impressed; I was!

_childDocuments_.review: Well, there was a legitimately interesting game here.. sadly I couldn't even get through the opening cutscene without the game having two bad frame rate stutters, and if they can't even get that right you know you are in for a bumpy ride.So, the game has issues like the SS had a few bad apples.  For some reason the game has headbob, which is incredibly annoying, and makes it feel like your vision is always being dragged towards the bottom of the screen, although this can thankfully be turned off. What can't be turned off is the incredibly slow movement speed. I do not jest when I say that I have seen people in mobility scooters with 4 flat tyres eat the inches up faster than the player character. Running doesn't seem to do anything beyond slightly zoom the screen in to give the impression that you are running without actually increasing your speed. Thankfully the game is a walking simulator, so there's no reason to be running, but it still feels incredibly frustrating to move so slow. The thought behind this was presumably to encourage the player to feast their eyes on the visuals. The fallacy here is that the visuals, whilst nice, have this very odd blur and flicker effect about the edges. I've seen it in a few other games, Amnesia: a machine for Pigs, Maid of Sker and Bloodborne. (So two bad horror games, and one of my favourite games). Most objects seem to have very hazy edges, and with some of the smaller ones, such a wire or cables it seems to be in constant motion, and the effect can be sickening.  Bloodborne  got away with this by being in third person, so the rough edges were a lot less of an issue. I am legitimately at a loss why you would put such effort in art direction and then give all the objects hazy edges that make me feel sick. To make matters worse, texture pop in is a very frequent problem. And I'm not talking "wall is blurry till we get close" (Although there is plenty of that), I'm talking "Wall on the elevator forgot to load in until halfway down the shaft." Most of the in game documents also range from difficult to read to flat out impossible. Besides having ridiculously small font and bad lighting, the text is often stricken with the same flicker effect, rending it utterly unreadable. All in all, for a game that's trying to be a visual feast, said feast seems to be made mostly from Marmite and Asbestos sandwiches. A final issue before the big one is interfacing with objects. Everything you can interact with has a little white UI element hovering above it, which besides shattering immersion also makes you a lot less likely to look at the art direction because most people (Myself included) are likely to walk into a room and just beeline towards the interactive objects. This is a minor issue however, the big issue with interaction and why it gets a whole paragraph in this prolonged whining session is that it's both very unclear and very inconsistent where exactly you have to stand to interact. Sometimes you can do so whilst about a foot away, sometimes you need to be rubbing your face on it, sometimes it's in between. I am at a loss that the developers could mess up something as simple as "walk up and click", as with almost every one I found myself forced to do a little jig back and forth repeatedly clicking until the game acknowledged that I was there. You might say that because I'm Irish doing a little jig is fine, but I disagree. Normally people would at least buy me drink(s) before expecting me to dance, and I generally don't expect to be made to do so by a walking simulator.I digress, the biggest issue actually loops back to the pop ins. Upon getting to Chapter 3, I entered a building to find that all of the doors had failed to load in. This allowed me to walk to the next area without doing anything meaningful in the first, only to find out that here doors had loaded in but I was unable to interact, making it impossible to move forwards. Three checkpoint reloads, two level restarts, and a final restart of the game after verifying the integrity of the game files only to find that upon restarting, every single object in the building had failed to load in, leaving me wandering barren and empty hallways. At that point I gave up. I shall try again in about 6 months in the hope that the developers actually patch this mess. There seems to be a legitimately interesting story here, but everything besides that ranges from disappointing to awful. 2/10. Barely counts as Game

_childDocuments_.review: I wanted to love this game, I really did. And I do... for certain aspects.  This game has some charm, if you love a good story, then I do recommend this game, though there isn't anything too complicated, other then trying to figure out where to go next at some points but most of it is pretty straight forward, but if I had to put a grading system to it, it would look something like this:Graphics: AWorld Building: SStory: B-/C+I also ended up running into a few issues, a floating bug near the end as well as an FPS Eating portion that I had issues with, a simple restart of the game cleared it though, but that but was a issue was I started floating and was unable to continue, and ended up going back through the game. You can make choices but honestly, not much of your choices matter, (other then the illusion of choice), as well as the game actually cutting you off from a portion of the lore of the world near the end, for some weird reason (Too many levers cause an overload but there isn't a way to avoid it so you have to continue without learning whats behind door number 3)((You'll see what I mean when you get there)), and this fact irritated me as I found that there isn't a chapter function built into the game, since to go get that information with different choices I would have to start back at the beginning only to play the game all the way to the end. Also, developers: I found the lack of skeletons or graves rather disappointing, as well as I noted a few plot holes with certain things that should probably cleared up, but I don't think those are as serious.All in all, I do recommend this game on the world building alone. The bunker is vast and the world feels as if it was lived in, as if you want to follow in their footsteps to figure out what the next bit of lore would be. Thank you guys for making a wonderful game. I did enjoy the story, and I hope to see something from you guys again.

_childDocuments_.review: As others have said, movement speed being increased would definitely improve the gameplay aspect. I'd even understand if they limited faster movement to periods when no dialogue is happening, but it does drag the experience down a bit. There were a few performance issues I ran into in a later chapter, but that may just be my system. Now that the negatives are out of the way, here's why I still recommend it. The story, admittedly maybe not the most unpredictable story, but still a very cool concept. This game has lots of great environmental storytelling, and speaking of environments the effort put into every part of every room was incredible (which did help the slow movement speed feel more bearable). Honestly the quality of the environments and scene-dressing were on par or better than the best AAA games. So, considering the size of the studio that made this? I am willing to overlook a lot of the bugs that would ruin any other game.

_childDocuments_.review: Paradise lost is an interactive narrative adventure game in which you assume the role of a child exploring around a nazi bunker in an alternative universe where things did not go quite as planned. If you are able to look past the technical shortcomings of the technical aspect and the lack of polish (no pun intended), there might be an interesting story for you to discover.Curator Page:+Intriguing set pieces+Inspiring setting+Thoughtfully crafted environments +Amount of background story elements+Jaw dropping music-Hit or miss voice acting-Gamma and contrast in dark sectors-Tanking framerate-Subpar texture quality-Walking/ Sprinting speed too slow-Relatively short in just under 3 hours-Lack of quality of life settings-Navigating through doors and ladders is a choreParadise lost is a great example of a game that has an incredible amount of potential, but evidently falls relatively short in the technical department, as well as the quality of the moulding of everything coming together.Starting off with the positives. I really enjoyed the setting of the game and the tremendous amount of potential it has to offer. The environments are crafted with creativity and attention to detail, from the destroyed statues and the rubble surrounding them, to the offices and the way they are laid out with the various objects on the desks etc.The story is well put together with great detail in the side stories, that help the player create a more accurate picture of what happened for the world to turn out the way it did. I typically do not care enough to read long texts that I find in games in general, but this one peaked my interest because of the setting.Lastly, the music left me wanting a soundtrack. Certain actions cues the music in just the right moment, with just the right melody. If I had to choose one thing about this game that I loved the most, it is the audio design in general, but specifically the score.On to the negatives we go. The voice acting can be give or take on how well it is done. For the most part it is simply satisfactory, with the main two characters struggling quite a bit. The contrast is done extremely poorly. There second half of the game relies heavily in atmospheric environments and after tinkering with the gamma and brightness, I was not able to generate adequate results. This resulted in my inability to very often be able to see and navigate through the environment correctly and effectively.The framerate often tanked to an unplayable, single digit frames per second. Optimisation for such a small game is done terribly and I think that the developer must absolutely spend some time in optimising the game through patches.The game's length is quite short, under 3 hours. It would definitely be a lot shorter if the walking speed, and the sprinting speed, were not so incredibly slow. You cannot toggle sprint so I find that straining my pinkie to run almost at the same speed that I walked was almost not worth it. Lack of quality of life options such as the above, an FOV slider and lack of ultrawide support do not help in painting a good picture either.Lastly, the most annoying part about the game is absolutely opening doors, climbing ladders and the lot. There is an extremely unnecessary prompt that you have to follow every time you open something such as a door or a drawer. It got old, quickly.I feel genuinely bad being this critical about a game that has such great promise. From the moment I read the setting of the game, I was hooked and very excited to jump in the game and explore around. The reason why this game does not give the same impressions like other walking simulators do is due to the lack of polish it presents the player with.The above, in combination with the considerably high asking price, are reasons enough to recommend against purchasing the game. If however you find the game on a deep sale or in a bundle, and you are fascinated by the setting of an alternative outcome of world war, then by all means, do not hesitate to pick this game up and immerse yourself.

_childDocuments_.review: Very slow progressing game, and not because of the story, but mainly because of how painfully slow the character walks.  Even when you press the so called 'Run' key all it does is slightly zoom the view a bit, but there is no improvement in character walk speed.  As far as the story goes, I knew who the other character you interact with was from the very beginning.  It just seems like user interface in this game is designed to slow you down in some way, for example, to open a door you have click the mouse button  when you get close, (which is fine) but then you wait for a couple of seconds until a small little graphical display comes up showing a circle with a dot in the center, and a semi-circular bar either at the top or bottom of the circle, which you then have to interact with by left clicking and holding the mouse, and then dragging the mouse towards the direction of the semi-circular bar, and then wait for it to fill up.    Every letter and document that you pick up seems to take a long time.  I don't mind short games, as a matter of fact I perfer them on occasion, when I just want something fun and interesting I can finish up in a few hours, but I can't stand games that drag out the UI actions just to extend the length of the game.Finally, and this is more of a odd peculiarity, but for a so called Nazi (Vault-Tech) Bunker, there is one thing blaringly missing... No, its not the swastika, those are all over the place, which makes me wonder why you chose to put those in but not a single picture of "The Fuhrer"  Overall, your not missing much if you skip this one, but if you really love walking simulators and underground complexes, maybe you'll enjoy it.

_childDocuments_.review: Raj Utracony - można by rzec, symulator chodzenia z dość intrygującą fabułą, ale od początku. W grze wcielamy się w 12-letniego Szymona, który odnajduje bunkier SS skrywający nazistowskie tajemnice. W miarę postępu fabuły, czytanych listów, dzienników, rozkazów, dowiadujemy się coraz więcej o wydarzeniach jakie rozegrały się w tym ogromnym schronie. Przemierzając kolejne pomieszczenia i korytarze poznajemy dziewczynę o imieniu Ewa, która kontaktuje się z nami poprzez głośniki i śledzi nas na kamerach rozmieszczonych w bunkrze. Sam bunkier i tajemniczy obiekt pod nim, historie odkrywane po drodze, wszystko to jest wykonane bardzo ładnie, przemyślanie, dokładnie. Lokacje są szczegółowe, wypełnione przeróżnymi przedmiotami, które opisują cel tego pomieszczenia, sposób i styl życia mieszkańców. Fabuła również jest dobrze zaplanowana, historia wciąga do tego stopnia, że chce się iść dalej, by dowiedzieć się więcej. Gra też prezentuje się bardzo ładnie graficznie, jak wspomniałem, świat jest szczegółowy, dokładny, dopracowany. Całość spinają klimatyczne odgłosy w tle, które dodatkowo dają poczucie ogromu i tajemniczości tego miejsca.Dobrze, z wymienionych przeze mnie (moim zdaniem oczywiście) zalet, są też wady, które, według mnie, gryzą oko i ucho gracza. Jak wspomniałem fabuła jest bardzo dobrze i spójnie zrobiona, niestety, w moim odczuciu, miejscami zwalnia do tego stopnia, że robi się nudna. Drugą wadą, a raczej ja tak to odebrałem, były dialogi między chłopcem a Ewą, które czasem wydawały się nienaturalne i robione na siłę. I na koniec, trzeci, najbardziej niepasujący mi element układanki - Polskie wtrącenia w wypowiedziach, nagraniach, rozmowach. W moim odczuciu psują one nastrój, wytrącają słuchacza z równowagi. Uważam, że voice acting w grze powinien być jednolity, bez wtrąceń. Mimo wymienionych wyżej wad, podkreślam, że jest to tylko moje odczucie z gry, polecam ten tytuł, gdyż jest on bardzo dobrą produkcją.******************************************************************************************Paradise Lost – one could say, a walking simulator with a very intriguing story, but… from the beginning. In the game we take the role of a 12 years old Szymon, who finds an SS Bunker, where Nazi secrets lie hidden. As the story progresses, as we keep reading through the letters, journals and orders, we learn more about the history of the huge shelter. While traversing the countless corridors and rooms, we meet a girl named Ewa, who contacts us through speakers and follows our movement with cameras located throughout the entire complex. The bunker itself and the mysterious place below it, stories uncovered along the way - all of that was made very nicely, thoughtfully, carefully. Locations are very detailed, filled with items and their tiny secrets, which indicate the purpose of the room, way of living and lifestyles of their inhabitants. The plot is really well planned, the story can get so absorbing that you want to keep playing just to find out some more. The game’s graphics look good, as I mentioned, the world is full of details, precise and polished. All is bound together by fitting sounds and background noises, which add to the sense of enormity and mystery of this place.Alright, with all of the listed (in my opinion, of course) pros, the game has its share of faults, which, by my standard, irk the average player. As I mentioned before the plot of the game is very well made, but the pacing has its bumps - at times it slows down so much, that it can be a drag to get through. Another issue, at least for me, were the dialogues between the boy and Ewa, sometimes they felt unnatural and forced. Lastly, the least fitting puzzle for me – Polish language inclusions in statements, recordings and conversations. I found them distracting and annoying, I feel like they spoiled the mood. I think that voice acting in games should be unified, without inclusions which sound unnatural.Despite the listed faults, and I would like to underline, that these are my personal feelings, I recommend this title, as it is a really good production.

_childDocuments_.review: Worth $5 AUD. This is a recommendation that comes with caveats.It's fine. The story doesn't do anything interesting, you'll have clocked all of the twists by the first control room and none of the endings are particularly interesting. It's interesting that you're initially set up to believe  It's a good change, since what little nuance the game has would have been sapped completely if they had remained characters at the forefront of the plot.You can't change your FOV so get used to feeling like you're a horse with blinders on. The sprint key is useless, doesn't change the speed. Everything else is slow too. I'm going to assume radiation has turned Szymon's bone's to mush because there's no way a human, especially not a teenage boy, is this slow. This is the same problem I had with "Everybody's Gone to the Rapture" except the actual item interaction itself was faster and I could adjust the FOV and walking speed with mods to make them more human.The voice acting is pretty bad. It's obvious that the voice actors aren't native English speakers, and if they are they are the worst native English speakers, so why have them speak English? It's a game about Polish people, voiced by presumably Polish people, why not let them speak Polish? This is working under the assumption that the incredibly wooden voice acting was caused by actors being forced to speak English, but the actors just might have been terrible in the first place.Where the game shines is visual atmosphere. Another thing the game needs is a dedicated flashlight and zoom function. You get a lighter in-game, but it's only active for a few minutes at the start of the game and cannot be brought up again. I would have liked a flashlight and zoom so I could look at the details for the world. It's quite beautiful, with lots of small details but because the mechanics forbid it, you are unable to do anything but move along.Actual length of the game is 3-4 hours, however this is artificially inflated by the slow walking and interaction speeds. I would say the developer intentionally did this to make sure the two hour mark was hit so you couldn't refund it. Why not keep a normal speed, but add more content or lower the price? Makes the game seem more like a cynical scam, similar to games that try to make you feed machines more quarters, or super-hard NES games to force people to rent more games, when those were relevant.It's very linear. I don't consider this too big a problem in a walking simulator, but it means that beyond one mission where you can clean a camera (optional) and finding random documents and audio logs you're just opening doors slowly in a big hallway.

_childDocuments_.review: First i would like to say that I really enjoyed this game!The story is involving and the graphics are simply astounding The attention to details is the best I've ever seen. And this from the studio's first release! They obviously have some really experienced artists, level designers and art directors onboard.As for most of the negative reviews referring  to the game as a slow paced walking simulator with a less than inspiring story, are really missing the point. And it quickly becomes apparent that most of them are not within the intended target audience. A story driven exploration game is all about taking your time to explore, ingesting all the details and scattered information. Both the story and the alternative universe in which the story is set really leaves you wanting for more but at the same time the ending feels conclusive and rewarding. _childDocuments_.review: The movement speed is unfortunate and there are a number of technical issues (reloading a save locks your movement until you open the options, additionally I became stuck on a few objects and fell through the map a handful of times). Despite that, this walking sim game still delivers a story interesting enough for me to recommend it. It's a quick play, perhaps really only taking about 4 hours for a complete play through, but the world that is spun in that time is intriguing and bleak, yet is experienced through the eyes of two children who have not seen much of their post-nuclear-apocalypse world. Because there's no combat or puzzles, I'd suggest getting the game on sale due to fairly low replayability.

_childDocuments_.review: As other reviewers have stated, the graphics are stellar.  The story is fascinating, but too early you catch on to the true nature of someone the protagonist speaks with through various intercom mechanisms.  The big surprise is lost, but you have a remarkable environment to explore and the notes, letters, etc. you are guided to pick up and read tell a very interesting story.  Now for the 'thumbs down' rating.  For me, a deal killer is the protagonist getting frozen (cannot move) when loading a save point.  There are posts that discuss how to address this, but it's a core issue in game mechanics and I'd rather not have a checklist pegged on my whiteboard above the monitor so I can recall the steps.  The game also has certain action paths that will effectively get you stuck without any opportunity to get out and continue.  I just encountered one such scenario now which caused me to exit the game.  The developer could have provided a way out by activating a door, but that was not the case.  Oh, and the 'slow walk' (all you can do is a leisurely walking pace)...  That is maddening, particularly if you are re-starting a level and want to get back to the point where you screwed up.  Not happening.Overall, among the best graphics I have seen with an unheard level of detail at this pricepoint, but the wonky parts mentioned above totally kill the game IMHO.  Once fixed I'd say this would be a great game at 4K resolution, but in its present stage I'm afraid only Leopold Von Sacher-Masoch would find it appealing.

_childDocuments_.review: I wasn't sure what I would get when I bought this game. It's an amalgamation of isolated softcore 'horror' and questioning of the player's moral code. I'm sure there are multiple ways for this game to end, but I'm confident I choose the right path. This storyline is very heavy, but it is a story that I thoroughly enjoyed with both tears and laughter. I hope that one day humanity will understand that there is a better choice, one where all people are considered as equal so that this may never be the fate of the human race. Now on to technicalities, this game doesn't exactly feel complete. The... 'action points' as I will call them are buggy, they don't let you interact unless you're in a correct position and I actually got stuck a few times. One of the desks in Level 4 my character clipped into the desk while reading a note and I had to reload the game... I feel like that should've been fixed before release but I know nothing is perfect. The graphics are also troublesome, it's almost impossible to read anything unless they are set on high or above but doing so decreases the performance on my machine. However I figured out about halfway through that you can press 'E' to make notes easier to read.I got lost many times trying to advance the story, there are many dead ends and things that don't exactly feel like they were necessary to the game. There is a lot of reading, and I think it's better to show rather than tell so people can get their own impressions rather than reading note after note. All things considered, I congratulate the development team, the writers, and all else involved on a job well done. While I think the replayability of the game is absent I'm sure there are some people who want to get all the endings and fully enjoy this creation. Great design, great soundtrack, excellent writing, but graphics quality and maneuvering could be better. Please add the ability to sprint at some point, it is difficult to backtrack at such slow speed. xD
_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Lost

_childDocuments_.review: Unplayable buggy crap full of glitches. I couldn't even get through first chapter (Denial) because after load / continue of the game I remained stuck on the same place and couldn't move. I restarted 'Denial' level several times, but never had enough time to get through it and always remained stuck after load / continue. None of help on the net worked for me. Game is a gold plated buggy trash, not worth of playing at all in its' current state. Ok, now for the overall feeling I had for that small part I actually saw:Music choice, relevance for given area: 10/10Graphics: 7/10  - distant objects and big structures looks really cool and creates lots of 'wow' effects  - closer objects not that much (terminals, buttons, boxes/shards/flasks)Gameplay: 3/10  - running is not really running. I could barely notice change in movement tempo.  - sensitivity of movement vs. rotation doesn't go really well (rotates too fast, even when I set sensitivity to minimum), walking is like a snail  - objects makes obstacles even if they are not made out of solid materials (for example opened paper box on the ground must've been glued or what)  - whole collision detection system is strange, feels like I'm not even close to the object (a table for example) and I already cannot go closer.  - object selection is too sensitive on player location, I spent "ages" before I could actually open / grab object.  - interaction with objects is also weird. When you have to move a lever, it takes miles of movement with mouse to get it on the right place (but this could be because I had to decrease sensitivity of mouse movement)   - aforementioned glitches and inability to continue with the game -> this is a major problem, otherwise it would get 6/10maybe really really maybe if developers fix the bugs and game become actually playable I give it a second chance, but it will be probably easier to watch the main story on youtube and forget this joke.

_childDocuments_.review: This being a walking simulator, the only thing that impressed me was the art direction. The visual aesthetic is phenomenal, and there are plenty of gorgeous sights to see. However, every other aspect of this game was--to be blunt--crap. Everything for an engaging story is there, from futuristic Nazi tech to the downfall of an underground society and finding out who that person is you've been talking to the whole game. Yet, none of it is pieced together in a way that feels captivating, and the five stages of grief theme that it's going for is almost comically on the nose, with the chapters literally being named after them, appearing in fade-to-black transitions in big, bright letters at the start of each one. Every single damn thing you do in this game is slow. There's a feature-length's worth of content, but because the kid you play as walks like he just got out of bed, the game takes nearly three hours if you've been bothering to read the notes and listen to the audio logs. There's a sequence toward the end where suddenly it's treated as if time is of the essence but your character doesn't make ANY attempt at picking up the pace a little, like they developers couldn't even be ♥♥♥♥♥♥ to do that for what I would assume is an urgent "hurry the ♥♥♥♥ up" situation. By the time you get to the end, no matter what choice you make, you'll be less than satisfied; the writers could have built it up in a manner which yielded much more impact. Not a terrible game, but overall mediocre.

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoy walking simulators, and this was a good one, despite its short runtime.Graphically, it's definite up there; beautiful, detailed and lush environments are speckled with doodads and era-appropriate greebling. Some landscapes are absolutely massive and downright impressive. The caveat is that only a few items in the environment can be interacted with. Other than gawk, there's no much to do and little to discover.Sound was overall pretty good. A few sound effects were a little out of place or need a little gain correction. Doors, for example, almost always sound like you're slamming them open, which is a little jarring. There is voice acting, but it's... let's say serviceable at best. The actors lack any real intonation and some dramatic lines are delivered very flat.As other reviews have mentioned, the general pace of this experience is hindered by your walking speed. Does it takeaway from the experience? No. Are there corridors you wish you could just sprint through? Yes. Quite a few, actually.Story-wise, the overall concept is great but the execution is a little on the nose. You'll likely guess some of the story's punchlines within the first few minutes. There are 4 possible endings, but only differ by a few voice lines and it all ends very flat.If you're into walking simulators, this is worth a look, especially for the world-building and visuals. The overall experience is okay but nothing that'll stick with you, especially considering you'll complete the experience under 4 hours.Oh, and if you're wondering, no, this game does not contain any jump scares or anything scary, so you can kick back and just meld into the environment.
_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Lost

_childDocuments_.review: Could not last more than 20 minutes before I almost fell asleep.  The story is slow and the main character walks even slower.  You have to wait forever to get to the next point of interest.  If they wanted to tell a story then make a video of it to watch, but don't call it a game, when all you do is walk around an read letters and pull levelers.  The path is COMPLETELY linear.  All paths are blocked except where you are supposed to go.  They doesn't even appear to be puzzles to solve. HOW IS THIS A GAME.  Steam should refund everyone's money for this piece of crap.  It's an embarrassment to call this a game.  Walking is not playing a game!

_childDocuments_.review: Beautiful graphics and highly immersive atmosphere- You will want to go out of your way to see as much of everything as possible. The story is slightly predictable, but is well written nevertheless.The walking speed of the character could have been faster, and an option to skip dialogues would also have been a plus.As of november 2021, I got a bug where the character got stuck in place after loading a save game, which forced me to play a full chapter, play to a save point, and then load and restart that new chapter. This sound worse than it is, since the chapters are short, so it's very manageable. Those things aside, I loved a lot of things from this game, and I will surely play it again in the future.
_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Lost

_childDocuments_.review: I'm not sure how I feel about this one.  I knew going in it was a walking sim where you are mostly just piecing together the story.  Much of the story is told through notes  you will find and audio recordings.  I was pretty thorough in my looking around, so I don't think I missed much but I still felt like I was only half understanding things most of the time.  I'm all for environmental storytelling, but I feel a bit more exposition through flashbacks or something would have benefited this title.There are a few places in the game where you basically have to choose which path to continue exploring which will gate off the other option.  I guess this is to incentivize repeat playthroughs, but it only makes very minor differences in the outcome from what I've read.  Often times this game feels like it has stubs of cut content in it.  Items that you can pick up but can't do anything with and seem to have no purpose, storytelling or otherwise.  Drawers that you can open that are just empty and do nothing etc.  Maybe some of that stuff could come into play with different paths, but I don't see myself revisiting it anytime soon.  The walk speed is extremely slow, which I don't mind for the most part because this game is about enjoying the environment, but doesn't allow for you to just zoom back to a section you want to check out again.I guess this review seems kind of negative even though I recommended it.  I did enjoy it, despite it's shortcomings.  I wouldn't recommend it at full price, but for the few dollars I paid on sale it was well worth it.  The levels are beautifully crafted and rendered.  The game looks absolutely phenomenal and everything has a great ambiance.  The music and sound design are well done.  Even the voice acting is quite good for the most part.  I just feel like it needs a little more "game" to go with the beautiful environments.  But if you want something relaxing to just explore for a few hours, you could do a lot worse than this.

_childDocuments_.review: I wanted to like this game, a walking simulator set in WW2 would sound like an interesting way to savor a story at the end of a tiresome day. But hell, is it annoying…Lets get the first thing out of the way, the run, there is a run feature but … its hardly noticeable. Half of the time I thought my SHIFT button is broken or something, thing about your normal walk speed is 1.0, well the running is 1.1. I get this is a walking simulator and you should enjoy it at walking speed, so here is the question WHY THE BALLS DID YOU INCLUDED? Just remove the run and increase the walk speed, or fix it and make it feel noticeable. And devs took the lazy way, meaning if you look down you see your character’s torso and legs, guess what, same animation plays for walking and running, didn’t even made a different animation, they just increased stats and FOV slightly changes. Speaking of speed, after playing Dear Esther or Dagon, this one feels way too slow, everything from interactions (which take extra mouse/buttons pushes for no reason) to the walk/run speed. Even for a walking simulator, gameplay gets too tedious.Lets talk about the rest now, story. I didn’t mind the story, its alright, but it feels like it finishes too abruptly. Without spoiling too much, at first you set on an adventure to find certain someone, as story progresses however you run into someone else, you find that someone (at which point you decide a few things to get the ending) and that is were the story ends. It is like you have forgotten the goal you set on the journey for. There are numerous notes/documents scattered across the game, haven’t read all of them, so it might explain it there, but what the main story suggests is that he is dead; how he died, or is he truly dead, never says. Now it does have multiple endings so the others might answer this, but I’ll be damn if I’ll play this again, besides you cannot save close to the end and chose another ending. The end I took, I was supposed to escape the facility, and it just ends there, did I actually escaped, what happened after? Those and others are never answered…Audio and voices acting. The main character’s line delivery is... well lets just say a dead sock has more enthusiasm that him, we get that he is a kid but come on… did the devs tell him how to act or give pointers or just told him to read a prompt cuz it sounds like that. The other character ain’t doing better either, the best voices were those recorded for certain audio logs you find scattered in game. Music and SFX are fine, they do a decent job to immerse you in the world. Gameplay, ohh boy… well I already mentioned it feels too slow, in addition to that there is a constant bug were if you close the game and re-enter the character is stuck, to fix this you gotta press ESC, go to Settings, accept all (I didn’t changed anything and worked), return to the game. Many complained about it.. so here is the thing, I played this in 2023, that is 2 years after the release, so by this point there is no excuse not to had this fixed. All these small issues could have been fixed by now, but it seems the devs just threw this game out and abandon it… Well if they don’t not care about the game why should others, I do not recommend this.

_childDocuments_.review: Even for a walking sim, the game is too. Damn. SLOW. It's like they made the player move at a snail's pace on purpose to pad the runtime out. _childDocuments_.review: Visually stunning (I took way too many screenshots) and the ambience is great but that's pretty much it.It's terribly buggy, especially the 3rd chapter - figuring out how to fix the whole big lounge-like area to be able to go through it (and not fall through the non-existent floor the moment I step through the invisible, supposedly closed door) was a chore since I had no idea which room is supposed to be open and which one should be opened later in the still more or less playable area - all of the doors disappeared; the optimization is terrible; you can't skip any dialogues or cutscenes; the animations are weird and stiff (like when you climb ladders and ledges, jump down... or do pretty much anything else); the walk speed is so slow the game gets boring after a while - sometimes I didn't even want to bother straying off the main path to explore as it would take too long to go back; all you're able to do is just walk around and do some simple tasks like pulling levers or opening doors, wow.As for the plot - you get to know it mostly by reading long-ass notes and letters, so yeah, I almost spent more time reading them (or at least some of them) than actually playing the game and honestly - it wasn't worth it. _childDocuments_.review: While i will admit i agree this game was a tad too short and could have benefited from a little more to do in the interest of exploration, i have to give this game a solid 7/10. I found the comparison some have made to Bioshock absurd only because this game isn't touted as a super sci-fi futuristic secret world of miracles- by all accounts this base is really a failed long term investment by the Reich. The look and feel of the place is done extremely well, with dust and scattered papers, discarded weapons and remnants of battles long over, collapsed buildings, etc. Again, this place is no rapture. You do indeed get to see some really interesting scientific things throughout the base as well, or through documents and files left about. That is in fact how majority of the story is told after all- and that's okay. My issue is that there's too little of it. While there were many interesting or even disturbing things that were revealed through some notes, not a lot of the "Why" questions(The ones that don't directly matter to the main storyline) aren't answered. For instance, we know WW2 is vastly different. Much like Fatherland(1992), the US remains neutral into the 60s. Nazi Germany seemingly holds out like they did in World War 1, only for 20 years. Now, while i can understand to some it's "Who cares, it's just a what if?" Well, to you i say: I care. I mean, they held out for 20 years, devised this rather idiotic plan to stash what is essentially Aryan children from Himmler's programs underground to be trained, return to the surface and wipe out the remaining enemies- that is AFTER Germany says "♥♥♥♥ it" and nukes everyone on their hitlist- and from what it's looking like, the Germans got hit with the bombs too. So that's just one example- in short, the only main issue i have is Too many good ideas that aren't followed with enough- or any- enthusiasm.

_childDocuments_.review: Paradise Lost is a visually pretty walking simulator that delivers a disappointingly bland and predictable narrative.Where the game really shines are its detailed and impressive environments, environmental story telling and how it manages to maintain that sense of isolation as you explore the abandoned locations. Unfortunately its narrative commits the cardinal sin of delivering too many hints that practically spell out the major story beats way too early in to the game thus taking away any sense of mystery.That being said, I find it difficult to recommend the game, as it takes a blunder in what I would say is arguably the most important aspect of a walking simulator - the narrative - rather than being invested in the events, it simply failed to hold my interest as I slowly trudged towards the completely predictable ending.

_childDocuments_.review: Paradise Lost is a zero-challenge, incredibly detailed immersive story, sometimes (accurately) called a “walking simulator”. They’ve come far since Dear Esther, which was some arty visual thing with insufferable, pretentious dialogue. Paradise Lost has more worldbuilding and visual storytelling, with some absolutely exquisite environments on par with those seen in the Metro games – the world feels alive, real and lived-in.Also note that you’d benefit from being able to read and understand German in this game – some of the details – signs, documents, dialogue, etc. will provide extra information on the world. I expect that being able to understand Polish would help too.Overall, this is an excellent game for people who love worldbuilding and exploration. If you are looking for an exciting Nazi-themed *game* (in the traditional sense of the word), go play the Wolfenstein series.

_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Lost

_childDocuments_.review: Paradise Lost has a very interesting setting and premise, and a not so interesting way to experience it."It's winter, 1980. Szymon, a boy raised in a post-apocalyptic wasteland, finds an abandoned Nazi bunker." is an interesting idea, but the game opens with so many flashbacks and slow, climing on-off :boxes, platforms, train wagons animations that it ends up being slow even for a walking sim. Many people complain about the walking speed, which is fine IMO, even if the running button only equals to a jogging, or really brisk walking. You don't need to sprint everywhere. But the game fails to fill up the time between notes, voice recordings or radio chat(Ewa). Voice recordings can only be listened to where the recorder is, for most of the game the voice can only talk through stationary loudspeakers or microphones. It's also a connected issue: as the story starts to unfold (or rather, clean up. It's really simplistic and pretty much handfed) you start finding critical notes. Ewa addresses what's on the note in the second you pick it up, not as it would be logical - after you put it down. The game tells - through Ewa - such revelations and connections that are pretty clearly written on the paper, but gives you no chance to read it, or think about it. The game even goes "it must be hard to accept *****, sorry" just a few seconds after finding it out. LET THE PLAYER THINK. LET THE PLAYER BREATHE. While the environment is not as copy-pasted and sterile as many walking sims create their world, the game's tempo just doesn't really work out. Slowish to progress through the game, but somehow still feels like the game just info-dumps you. I miss the radio chat from SOMA, or the sound diaries of Bioshock. They built character for Catherine or a general atmosphere for Rapture, respectively. Both aspects felt more natural than barely talking at all, then just vomiting up information but strictly constrained to the "main plot" and nothing else. Ewa is not a character, but a plot element, and that hurts the game.Story-wise one of the plot twists / secrets is blatantly obvious, but from the tone of the characters at the reveal it's utterly shocking. It's hard to empathise. In some weird, twisted way the whole game reminds me of Bioshock.  I think are much better ways to utilise a videogame's options, even if you're making a walking sim. Add your note inside the moving elevator, not in front of it. Don't make me click twice to use a single-button microphone. Adding direction-related prompts to levers is also a moot point if I need to click once to even get that prompt. This is not how you make your game more engaging. This is how you pad a game with mechanics that add nothing. There is not a single time when you "use" the directions to do a puzzle or anything.Overall, Paradise Lost feels like an interesting twist on a story I already heard, and I would have rather read a "what if" type of novelette, than to play about about 7 (net) hours, looking at everything to find so little.

_childDocuments_.review: Paradise Lost is a slow-paced story narrated walking simulator based in an alternate universe Poland where you play a young boy called Szymon. The mentioned slow pace artificially drags the whole game length to around 3-4 hours. I speedrun it once after the first playthrough for the rest of the achievements in about 2 hours. The controls are simple: WASD, left and right mouse click and shift for running. Running makes you walk 3% faster, even while holding down shift the whole gameplay feels clunky and slow. The somewhat easy puzzles are somewhat fun and are quite a relief to multiplayer shooter action. Various audio boxes, letters, notes and other collectables are put in random places. The exploration is the main part of the game, who wouldn't want to check out every single inch of an alternate universe/history Nazi bunker? Most of those letters are boring, while the audio logs give some nice background information to the whole plot.The sound design in Paradise Lost is magnificent. From the soundtrack to the ambience, everything fits perfectly to Szymon's odyssey throughout the cold bunker. Nearly every 3rd corner is rigged with some sort of ambience sound like in Horror games. You expect cheap jumpscares but the actual product is an atmospheric goosebump moment. Walking through a long lost battlefield inside of train wagons accompanied with chill violin music while MG42 and STG44's lay on the floor with empty bullet shells gives more than just the chills.The performance was surprisingly well and surprisingly bad at the same time. I am impressed that a small Polish studio can make cutscenes that are rendered to allow my 21:9 ratio monitor to see everything without black side borders. On some points in the game, I had minor stutters and the environment felt blurry or badly made. Some shadows, for example behind the German Reichsadler in the beginning, are badly formatted like poorly made PNG or fake vector files. Or in English: the "staircase" effect appears with blocks of pixels building up the black background for these so-called shadows.I was honestly impressed by more than just a handful of stunning moments of artistic choice in Paradise Lost and I have made way too many screenshots on my way. The dark and dead bunker corridors are more and more redundant the deeper you delve into the story. The water and light effects are beautiful yet some hyper polished stone reflects minor details that were out of the line of sight. My 2080TI was somehow around 90% usage due to the graphics for some reason. I am unsure if that 90% were actually needed or were just a byproduct of bad coding. I do not care as the end result on my monitor were gorgeous.Without any spoilers, I want to mention that the overall story of the game is not that bad besides some minor plot holes that are filled by reading -every- single note and what not. If you speak or understand German, then some minor details will come up earlier than the plot wants you to. Halfway through the game, you could already guess what's to come, but nonetheless, it's better than some visual novels, and way more fun.As much as I want to say that it's a good game, it's imperfect. It has many flaws like the head bop checkpoint bug or the clunky and very slow-paced movement. The minor framedrops can be due to my high-end monitor and may differ for every user.Overall I would give Paradise Lost a solid . I know it is a walking simulator, but in comparison to for example  it's very very slow and clunky. To change those "negative" points the whole game would need to be changed, so that is out of the box.I honestly like the whole concept and idea of the game. A somewhat futuristic but also old setting inside of a giant Nazi bunker with multiple layers of different technology and themes per layer.

There is very little "meat" to the game as you would expect from a walking sim. You basically just push 'W', you occasionally interact in the most simple kinds of ways with levers, doors and stuff and you simply  watch things unfold. There aren't even any real puzzles or anything. Paradise Lost is all about experiencing the story, listening to the audio logs, reading the notes and advancing through the game. Verdict: If you're in the mood for a simple game like an in-between snack then have at it. Just don't expect too much.

_childDocuments_.review: A Desolate Journey of Isolation - "Paradise Lost" ReviewRating: 8/10"Paradise Lost," developed by PolyAmorous and published by Walkabout, is a first-person exploration game set in an alternate history where World War II did not end in 1945. As a young boy named Szymon, players venture into the mysterious and desolate underground bunker, uncovering a narrative that intertwines personal stories with the broader consequences of war.Storyline : 8/10The narrative of "Paradise Lost" is its standout feature, offering a poignant and emotionally charged exploration of loss, survival, and the consequences of unchecked power. The alternate history backdrop adds depth, providing a unique lens through which the player can view the repercussions of a prolonged conflict. The personal journey of Szymon is both compelling and thought-provoking, making each discovery within the bunker a revelation that adds to the richness of the narrative tapestry.Atmosphere and Environment : 8/10The game excels in creating a haunting and atmospheric environment within the underground bunker. The attention to detail in the art and level design contributes to a sense of immersion, and the desolation of the setting is palpable. The visual and audio elements work in tandem to establish an eerie ambiance that complements the narrative's tone.Gameplay and Exploration : 6/10"Paradise Lost" leans heavily on exploration and environmental storytelling, with limited interactive elements. While the lack of traditional gameplay mechanics might disappoint those seeking more active engagement, the deliberate pacing and focus on storytelling align with the game's narrative-driven approach. The puzzles, though not overly challenging, serve as subtle conduits for advancing the narrative.Graphics and Sound Design : 8/10Visually, "Paradise Lost" is striking, with detailed environments and atmospheric lighting that enhance the emotional weight of the story. The sound design further immerses players in the experience, with a haunting soundtrack and ambient sounds that evoke a sense of solitude and mystery.Alternate History Concept : 8/10The alternate history premise provides a unique perspective on the consequences of war and unchecked technological advancements. The blending of real-world historical elements with speculative fiction adds depth to the narrative, encouraging players to reflect on the ethical implications of scientific progress.Conclusion : 8/10"Paradise Lost" offers a thought-provoking and emotionally charged journey through an alternate history tinged with despair. Its strengths lie in its narrative depth, atmospheric design, and the ability to evoke a range of emotions from players. While the lack of traditional gameplay elements might not appeal to all gaming preferences, those who appreciate immersive storytelling and exploring the echoes of history will find "Paradise Lost" to be a captivating and melancholic experience. It's a testament to the power of interactive storytelling in conveying impactful narratives within the gaming medium.
