_childDocuments_.review: The game looks and sounds wonderful with colourful backgrounds and a haunting melody playing throughout. Voice acting ranges from okay to excellent and special effect noises are loud, brash and attention seeking. It all culminates into quite an exciting experience.Perseverance is needed as some battles almost appear impossible at first but you’ll need to think about your enemy’s strengths and weaknesses and tailor your team to win. Your party is customizable throughout the game and the line up can be changed also. You’ll be able to equip different items, potions, special skills and reassign your skill tree and attribute points. I spent quite a lot of time configuring characters to try and beat bosses. Some boss battles took me numerous attempts to win. It feels very rewarding to finally beat an opponent.The puzzles are quite difficult in places but mostly enjoyable to work out and in the main they felt logical. There is a lot of exploration plus loads of hidden treasure, secret passageways and items to find. As you progress, you’ll acquire special party skills which aid you in solving some of these puzzles. The story was okay. It kept the adventure ticking along. I mostly enjoyed the banter between characters and learning more about their backgrounds. Each party member had a back story which was discussed and developed throughout, and at the end I felt like I knew the characters quite well and wanted them to succeed.The Sun King Napkiraly has been abducted and consequentially the land of Operencia is plunged into darkness. It won’t be long before the Underworld is unleashed bringing about the fall of mankind. After a recurring dream you are compelled to set out on a journey to release the Sun King. Operencia is split into three main areas. Battles, exploration and puzzles.Each party member has up to nine active skills they can use in battle with three basic skills identical to all characters. The rest are unique to each party member. Each character has a skill tree with three branches determining their skills. Each battle arena has three combat lines – Front, middle and back.  Some skills and weapons are more effective depending on the distance of the enemy.Each character has a varying number of hit points and energy points determined by their core skills and the way you configure the character’s attributes. Other attributes include intelligence, wisdom and vigor. Certain weapons and magic skills can only be wielded with a certain number of points. Solving puzzles, defeating enemies, locating secrets etc. earns you XP, EP and HP which levels you up. At each level you get one skill point and three attribute points to spend.The interesting thing about this game is that you can re-allocate all the points you have accrued at ANY point in the game changing the character completely and the way they fight. This is crucial for success, and not just their attributes but their skills, weapons, armour etc. There is an automatic method to fit out your companions to their maximum potential if you so wish.Using unique abilities uses up energy. Without energy you won’t be able to use any skills and must rely on you three basic skills. You can refill your energy bar through potions or other characters special skills, or after battle at camp fires. Battles are turn based and you can gain initiative and the first blow by sneaking up on enemies. Enemies can stun, fear or place you in a state of sleep meaning you will miss your turn. Enemies can drain your energy or taunt you meaning you have to attack that particular enemy. There is a lot of variation in tactics and sometimes you’ll have to fight three battles in a row before you can replenish your potions, health and energy at camp fires. Luckily you can save the game at any time.There is always a map available to help you navigate the area you are in. As you move, the map is revealed, making it easy to pinpoint where you haven’t been. Once discovered, objects of particular use will be highlighted on the map.Movement is tile based although you cannot move diagonally. The camera is completely free and can be moved around at your discretion. It is surprisingly easy to move around at pace using the camera and map as a tool.On each level there are chests, secrets, percentage of map and campfires to reveal. Secrets include gaining access to locked doors or finding secret passageways; Campfires let you replenish everything at the cost of one firewood. You can also fast travel anywhere, and change your line up. You can buy and sell goods with the merchant and even brew potions in a mini game.You can find chest keys which open certain chests revealing goodies, collect gold, potions and weapons along the way.There are thirteen levels to explore and some areas are inaccessible until later so you’ll need to return with a special skill or item. There is a wealth of information in your journal detailing monsters you have encountered, notes you have found, dialogues, and a really useful guide detailing everything you’ll need to know.Puzzles are an integral part of the game and you won’t be able to advance without solving some of them. Puzzles include searching for objects around the map, pressing levers or avoiding traps, re-arranging mixed up pictures or just navigating across inaccessible areas.Throughout the game new skills are revealed. There are seven in total. Spade (Finds chests); Feather (lifts heavy objects); Stoneheart (builds bridges); magic beans (grows plants to climb); nimble boots (can run fast); magic wand (can freeze objects); rooster (can go through holes). You will use all of these or a combination of these to solve puzzles.  The visuals were gorgeous and the game felt very colourful for a dungeon crawler. Characters were drawn beautifully and enemy encounters were interesting. With over fifty different types of enemies, battles never seemed repetitive. Each enemy had their own battle stances, personalities and special moves.There is a beautiful orchestral score playing throughout the game which fits into the look and feel of the game perfectly. Battles are loud and exciting and dramatic music and effects are played at all the right times to create mood and atmosphere.Curator Info: This game was received for free through curator connect.

_childDocuments_.review: Operencia is an old-school "blobber" style RPG. I'm on the final level of it and at this point I'm just finishing it to finish it. The game began very promising, it's colorful and nice to look at, and your party banters frequently and amusingly throughout, there are fun secrets to discover, and early on the systems for combat and character advancement are interesting enough.Unfortunately, the end of the game is where things start to fall apart. While the exploration remains strong, combat become much more of a slog; enemies gradually gain more HP and become mostly immune to your powerful insta-kill attacks that you've invested in, and you party's damage output doesn't really rise enough to match it. Some can charm or sleep your party members with little chance to resist and very few powers that can remove these conditions, causing many irritating lost turns. Others will immediately open a battle with an area attack that KO's your weaker party members  before they can act. These setbacks, while often not enough to cause you to lose the battle, mostly just cause them to drag out needlessly and grow boring.That's a shame, because the game makes a great first impression, but the late game fighting really hurts it and the story, while charming in a folklore-ish way, isn't enough to keep me invested.

_childDocuments_.review: I love this game.  ! I`ve played through it twice , -( and a half way through once,  when I chose permanent death , and everyone of course died :(  )Here is what you get :The Good : The story is based on Hungarian folklore, and is very well written . Great customable options to choose from the start. Different areas to go to, outdors, dungeons, castles , dungeons , etc - and you get fast travelling between them , early into the game.Puzzles - great puzzles ! And nice secrets to find !Character customisation is great, and you have the option to change it at any time , if you should want to .Lots of dry humour :)Combat is turn based, and since you have so many different skills to choose from, you can make it into a lot of fun .Lots of items to find , and a vendor who travels with you . Lovely graphics !Lovely music ! The little ! tiny ! not so good ;Item findings, and the vendors collection - it isn`t always that balanced, imho. And you might be in great need for a good armour or weapon. Mostly armours  - especially for the mages. But when that`s said ; late game item sets are Fabulous ! Next little ! tiny ! complain is :It is a bit tricky, - (at least it was for me ) - to figure out all the mecanics of the game . I had a few ! " Oh ! I can do that ! I wish I knew before ! "Lastly , a suggestion : Playing a mage as your main character is recommended, since another mage wont show up until rather late in the game. But really, Operencia is fully playable without a mage .

_childDocuments_.review: I am about 11 hours into the game and have been enjoying it so far. If you enjoy dungeon crawlers like Legend of Grimrock, Wizardry and similar titles there is very little reason to not pick up this game. It "feels" short so maybe try to get it on sale.Great quality of life information:  The game allows you to reset all your skill points and stat points at any point to try new things. Talent trees and everything can be swapped around and redone at any time and any place outside of combat. Early into the game you get the ability to fast travel to any map or area you have been to before. This allows you to not have to get too concerned about making sure you have every nook and cranny checked for secrets on the way through. FYI: Some secrets require later items to gain access to.Biggest thumbs down so far for me:A large portion of the enemies in the game can summon minions. The minions act as soon as they are summoned which means there is no lost "action economy" for the creature. He uses his action to summon and the summon immediately acts. You do not get extra experience, loot or gold for killing summoned monsters. Sometimes a normal pack turns into a long boring drawn out battle because the summoned creatures use skills to protect their summoner. Which means you need to try to kill the monster faster than they can summon. This can get very tedious and I only had it happen a total of 3-4 times in the 11 hours. Every time it did happen just took me out of so much that I can basically remember each time.That's all I really have to say. Thanks!

_childDocuments_.review: I am happy to give Operencia: The stolen sun the thumbs up. I thoroughly enjoyed the story, which is loosely based on Hungarian/Slavic folklore, and the challenging puzzles and fights. That being said, Operencia is not a game for everyone, so let's dive into the good and bad and see what's up with it.The GOOD:1. The Story and the world - the story is great, with voice-acted dialogue and very high stakes. The Sun is gone and it's down to our motley crew of heroes from all walks of life - from peasants and thieves to knights and demi-gods to go and find it.  Along the way they will face a variety of challenges and fights which will really test their mettle. The maps are beautifully crafted, colorful and detailed, as well as pretty big and full of secrets, puzzles, and hidden things, which demand careful and prolonged exploration. Enemies lurk everywhere - so be careful and try to surprise them - or be surprised yourself! And about that...2. The Combat - the combat is extremely engaging and should not be taken lightly as it is extremely challenging as well. Tactical thinking and party composition is paramount here unless you want endless amounts of frustration during your gameplay. As the adventure progresses, you will have 4 main + 3 extra heroes to swap in and out between fights which is absolutely required. The developers created a number of different areas which demand that you rotate your roster - as you will find that some of your heroes do better than others on various maps. And about that...3. The Heroes and their abilities - I am in love with the fact that instead of classes, you have 6 companions that you can find, each of them with different skills and then you have 3 archetypes for your main protagonist to choose from (Warrior, Hunter, Mage), also with their own abilities. While the basic Melee-Ranged-Spellcaster system is still in effect, the heroes you are given will keep you tinkering with their skills for a good long time. And about that...4. RE-SPEC!!! - no, RE-SPECT to the devs who, while making the combat extremely challenging, allowed us to re-specialize the heroes - BOTH SKILLS AND STATS (!!!) at will and at any point of the game. This is so good and so liberating, 5. The puzzles - the puzzles are creative and interesting, with sufficient amount of challenge. Additionally, the devs actually encourage backtracking and revisiting areas that you have already completed (usually to a certain extent). You can be sure I will talk about this some more soon...The BAD:1. The MAPS - while I enjoyed the exploration aspect of the game, I cannot say I enjoyed the huge amount of backtracking involved. The ability to leave notes on the map was sorely needed, as sadly, I was forced to resort to online guides to remind myself where what was on the next play session - especially if you want a completionist playthrough.2. The Puzzles - some puzzles are a clear exercise in frustration until you discover the patterns AND get used to the game movement as you might find yourself stepping a tile too short or a tile too far and botching the whole thing.3. Replayability - while starting with another Hero class might sound enticing, be aware that everything in the game is static and there is no randomized loot. You will always find a specific item in the same spot in each consecutive playthrough.4. More Heroes and rebalancing - Get this, unless you start as a Mage, you will not find another decent nuker in the game. Some heroes come close if you spec in Intelligence, but not close enough to satisfy your elemental damage needs. A second nuker close to the Mage in abilities was sorely needed. Also, I am somewhat underwhelmed by the Hunter protagonist, as I felt Sebastian was better in almost every aspect - but it could be down to me not speccing him right. more testing is needed...NOTE: I saw many people having issues with framerate drops, bugs, etc... I had none, probably because the game has been sufficiently patched during the last year, and in all fairness, I do have a relatively beefy laptop.Conclusion:At 50-60% off, as the game usually goes nowadays when on sale (10€) it is a great buy. You can expect to triple or quadruple your money in gameplay hours, which is greatly appreciated. While I had my fair share of emotions with the game - ranging from appreciation to flat out raging at the infuriating aspects of it, the game kept me coming back for more and that's a good thing in my book. While in my opinion, it embraces the notion that "a hard-earned victory is way sweeter" a bit too tightly, it is still a very solid game with great visuals, engaging story and interesting combat. I felt thoroughly entertained. Damn my girl knows me too well to get me this game...All that taken into consideration I am issuing Operencia: The Stolen Sun the following verdict:

_childDocuments_.review: Is this game a masterpiece? YES. At least for fans of classic dungeon crawler RPGs like me.One of the most influential gaming experiences for me was Interplay's Bard's Tale: Tales of the Unknown from the mid-80s. It introduced me to the RPG genre and provided me with endless hours of fun. Operencia is the first game that evokes a similar feeling in me again, 35 years later. It is a dungeon crawler with tile-based movement and turn-based combat. Like Bard's Tale was. The only striking difference is the quality of the graphics. Operencia is gorgeous. And, contrary to Bard's Tale, your mouse allows you to look around freely and interact with hotspots. Additionally many QoL improvements make the whole experience more casual. For example, you don't need to draw your own map on graph paper anymore, there is an automap. The game is saved easier, not only when you reach the Adventurer's Guild. If you prefer it the old way, you can turn off the minimap & the objective markers and then turn on permadeath. I like a challenge, but this is a bit too hardcore for me.After creating your character out of 3 classes you begin your adventure in a cursed underwater castle where you find the first (of 6 possible) of your additional party members, an old thief who was just robbed. He writes a journal of your adventure, which you can read anytime. There is also a guide available, detailling stuff you discovered and new gameplay mechanics. Quite helpful if you don't want to write down everything. And there is a LOT of lore in the game. I would not recommend the game to anyone who hates reading. Character management offers you an equipment screen, one for your talents, one for your skills, one for your attributes. Quite complex, while the character creation of your main character was ok but not of Baldur's Gate complexity. You manage your whole party, but your main character is a young hero/heroine who had a recurring dream and sets off to adventure just because of this. Quite an idiot, if you ask me. The other characters comment on the story or your decisions or make fun of you, but you decide on their equipment, upgrades and of course you give them orders during the fights. Fights are turn-based with the usual options, like attack, defend, use spells, skills or equipment.The party can be healed when resting at campfires spread over the gameworld (even in a wet underwater castle...) as long as you have found a bit of firewood before. You can also save your game at a campfire, and there is an auto-save at certain moments during gameplay. The gameworld is big, besides the country of Operencia there is also the Underworld and an Upper World. To advance you have to find and solve puzzles, from pulling levers or finding keys to some more advanced ones. The first puzzle for example consists of moving mirrors to seal an exit of the Underworld.The production values are rather high, apart from the stunning graphic you get to see many cutscenes, there is a lot of voice-acting through the game, my ultrawidescreen monitor shows the game in perfect 1440x3440 with 144 Hz, if you don't want to play with m+kb you can also use a controller. Best Bard's Tale inspired dungeon crawler RPG available at the moment.

_childDocuments_.review: TL:DR; Pretty but unrewarding, slow progression and a game more focused on exploration than combat.Have to recommend due to:-Very pretty-Runs well, no crashes or bugs-Nice atmospherics for immersion, sounds music voice acting all well done-Nice lore, using a mix of central european myths and legends adds some good quality and feeling to the background However, game lacks depth. It's very simplified and there is little to no customization. There is no way to gain xp or gear beyond what you are provided by the very limited number of enemies, and leveling even at level 3 feels slow and unrewarding. It feels like an RPG with training wheels on that is targeted at a younger age group than I was expecting. Difficulty is set at the beginning of the game with no option to change during, so if it feels a bit easy or hard the only way to change this is to start from scratch. Explanations of what some of the buttons or effects do is lacking, eg the 'optimize all' button changes all your equipment to the supposed best fit-out, but doesn't explain why having a second weapon or shield equipped is not optimal (?). Some design choices are odd, such as having enemies move around the map in real time, going so far as running after the player if spotted, however all player movement and combat is grid and turn based.

_childDocuments_.review: The best I can describe this game is "cargo cult dungeon crawler": the developers wanted to make a plane (an old-school first-person turn-based RPG) but only had the knowledge of working with straw (mobile ARPG tropes). The result flies just as well as you would expect a straw plane to fly. For example, the developers apparently heard that a dungeon crawler should have puzzles, and even made some effort to make puzzle designs visually and mechanically varied. But all this effort goes to waste because of how easy puzzles are: most of the times you are told explicitly which item is needed for a particular puzzle, and even when you're not, the game is so linear that you rarely have more than two possibilities to exhaust. The result is that instead of puzzles (proper dungeon crawler design) you get fetch quests (mobile ARPG design). And if that wasn't enough to kill exploration completely, they landed a final blow by introducing quest markers and incessant party chatting to ruin the pacing. A similar fate befell combat and character building. You get the classic melee/ranged rows, but they're meaningless because any weapon or spell can hit any row, only with somewhat different efficiency. Instead of fast-paced combat based around attrition and resource management, you get the rote MMO setup where everyone is a mage - i.e. has a small set of active abilities limited by cooldowns - and each round you just use whichever ability has returned from cooldown without much thought. On the upside, HP and energy don't regenerate on their own and you need limited camping supplies to rest, but on the downside, there are just too many of them strewn around the levels. Oh, and they are the only resource to manage since the game doesn't have consumables.Yes you heard right - there are no consumables in the game. Instead, potions take the form of "skills" that can be used a limited number of times between rests. I'm in two minds about this mechanic. On the one hand, the potion brewing system where you have to decipher a recipe by solving a logical puzzle is the one thing I liked about the game. But on the other hand, consumables in RPGs typically serve as a way of compensating for you character's weaknesses - either when you're exploring a level-inappropriate area, or you have built your character improperly. So the lack of consumables means you can't make mistakes when developing your party, especially given that there are no random battles and you can't grind for levels. The developers solution to that? Free respeccing at any time, just like - you guessed it - every run-off-the-mill ARPG. Only while it make sense in ARPGs with their randomized and constantly respawning hordes of enemies, in a dungeon crawler with only fixed battles, it takes all fun out of character development as well. The sad thing is that the game had potential to be fun if only it had a competent systems designer - the Hungarian folklore that informs the story is interesting, and so is the visual design of the levels. But as it is, it has no meaningful exploration, no meaningful combat tactics, and no meaningful character development. If you're looking for an old-school dungeon crawler with modern visuals, you'll be better served by 7 Mages, Might&Magic: Legacy or Legend of Grimrock 2.

_childDocuments_.review: "Alas, some buried treasure!" This game starts off in promising fashion with a well put together tutorial that has you playing a party of highly experienced characters through a short adventure so you can get a bit of background to the game and familiarise yourself with the controls and gameplay. You then roll up your own character, choosing from either warrior, hunter or mage classes, and after a short intro, find yourself exploring a mythical sunken castle. You find your first companion quite early in the game and at this point, the game is quite enjoyable. The Hungarian lore of the game is interesting and refreshingly different, combat is well balanced, the level design and hand drawn cut scenes are nice and colourful and wonderful to look at, and the game looks like a well polished product. However, by the time you reach the third main area in the game (the Deva Fortress), the difficulty seems to take a tremendous spike with some ridiculously tough opponents, and you then start really noticing how bad this game's combat mechanics are. I tried two playthroughs, firstly as a warrior and then as a mage. The mage I found could do better AOE damage but was flimsier than a wet paper bag. Regardless, I gave up with both at the Deva Fortress as the combat was just getting too frustrating.So what's so bad about this game? Mostly it's the combat system (*** MINOR SPOILERS ***).1. Lack of party formation in combat.During combat, enemies can stand either right in front of your party, slightly further away, or the furthest possible distance away. Your party can attack any enemy on the screen with melee or missile weapons, but melee weapons are most effective against close enemies, and least effective against the furthest enemies. However enemies can seemingly attack anyone in your party of up to 4 characters without penalty, as your party seems to have no order, so mages cannot take cover behind sturdier fighter types, for example. Also, you cannot close with distant enemies - they just remain where they are. 2. Useless normal attacks. Your characters' basic melee or missile attacks are really pathetic and do very little damage, so you have to use your special abilities when you want to do decent or AOE damage. The problem is that these have cooldowns and also use up your character's energy points, and these run out really quickly. The only way to restore energy is to either do nothing but defend for a turn (and this also has a cooldown so can only be used every 3 rounds) or else rely on other characters who may have a special ability that restores energy. Conversely, enemies seem to be able to spam their special abilities as they wish and are only restricted by their cooldowns.3. Broken mechanics.Your characters seem to miss most of the time even when their chances to hit an enemy are 70% or more, and some special abilities don't seem to work as they should. One companion has an ability which lets them go into stealth mode, yet they still take damage when an enemy performs an AOE attack. What's the point then? Another companion has this ability that lets them shoot a hail of arrows from their bow, and even though the ability description says "it MAY damage other enemies nearby", it only seems to damage 1 or 2 enemies in a group. Also your starting companion has a number of abilities that inflict poison damage yet at least 80% of the enemies in the first few areas are either resistant or immune to poison!4. Lack of defensive options.Lack of healing and defensive abilities in combat. The game has a weird potion system where you have to craft potions yourself and each character can only equip one type of potion; eg. you have this healing potion which you craft but you can only craft 2 at a time and only 1 character can equip and use it in combat. Another potion can be used as a bomb but again only 1 character can use it. Why can't I craft a number of healing potions and give them to all the party members to use in combat? Playing as a mage, you have virtually no defensive special abilities you can use - they are for inflicting damage. This makes it difficult to keep weaker characters alive in tougher battles as enemies tend to target the characters with the least hit points. 5. Enemies taunting your party.Your characters have virtually no chance to resist enemy taunt abilities, so you can have these battles where 1 fighter who can taunt your party stands in front of a group of enemy spellcasters. Fighter taunts your party, and everyone can only target the fighter with their attacks, unless they use an AOE ability. Great fun as the spellcasters at the back then pelt your party with spells.6. Ridiculous difficulty spikes.In the third area, there's this frustrating battle which caused me to rage quit the game on two playthroughs. Basically you end up fighting two guys and a stone golem. Both these guys have more health than anyone in your party, are able to heal themselves, do more damage than any of your characters, and can summon more stone golems. The stone golems themselves have massive physical and elemental resistances which means they take about half damage from anyone who attacks them (a normal non-critical melee attack from your warrior will do probably between 4 and 8hp damage to the golem, who has about 150hp, and a fireball from your mage will maybe do about 10 to 15 damage), and an AOE attack which they can use periodically which can knock off about half the hit points of the weaker party members. Defeating them means any summoned golems vanish, but the golem they were originally with remains, and by then, your party is just too decimated to defeat it.On the plus side, the game has some nice music, immersive ambient sounds, well polished visuals and a wondrous fairy tale feel owing to its rich Hungarian folklore. It's just such a shame that the combat mechanics are so frustrating. Sitting there chipping away at a 150hp stone golem for a couple hp of damage on most of your party's attacks is just no fun when it whacks your entire party with an AOE attack for 20 to 30 damage.

_childDocuments_.review: is a grid movement, turn-based dungeon crawlers set in the land of fairy tales. It is quite a decent addition to the genre overall, but didn’t really break any records in terms of complexity and depth. It’s fun, brief, well-made and polished. Any fan of turn-based dungeon crawlers should try it, with the expectations of a lighter experience compared to the classics.The Good:The Bad:Now I will talk about different parts of the game in greater detail. Specs: Ryzen 3700x and GTX 1080 and 1440p monitor.The game mostly runs at 60 FPS in almost every location including combat, however when there are a lot of particle effects like using some magic spells, or this one area in chapter 5 that has elemental particle effects on-screen, the FPS dipped into the 40’s for me.Other than that, the game runs pretty well on the highest setting, and my experience has been very polished so far. Don’t even notice any minor bugs. First of all, there is a customizable difficulty option in Operencia. They are chosen at the start of the game, and cannot be changed later.The next part to talk about is the combat. It’s turn-based, and the combat takes place in a different field from the dungeon like older games or JRPGs. When you reach the tile in the dungeon where the enemy is, you enter the combat screen. If you approach them from behind, you will ambush them with initiative bonus. The combat field is very simple. It’s in first-person view, and the enemies stand in 3 layers of area: near, medium, far. Your type of attacks correspond to the effectiveness.Each of your characters have different skills and a single item slot you can equip. Some enemies have different resistances, and the strategy lies in resource management and figuring out enemies’ weaknesses. In hard difficulty, there are quite a mix of easy and really hard encounters. There are also a limited number of enemies in the world. Once you defeat an enemy, it disappears forever, which means the number of EXP you can gain is limited. You can’t grind but you can be underleveled if you choose to not fight enemies.Which brings us to the next point, the character system. You build your character with a set of 3 different classes: Warrior, Ranged, Mage. Each class has different skill trees. You also have basic attributes like STR, INT, VIGOR, AGI that correspond to your character’s status and skill damage. Each time you level up, you will gain 1 skill point and 3 attribute points.Now this is the weirdest part of the character system. You can respec anytime, anywhere without any repercussions, including your party members. You cannot change class, but you can undo all skill points and attributes and reassign them freely. It seems like the game’s balance itself is designed around this system, because some encounters are impossible with the wrong skill sets, and I had to reassign some skills in order to defeat a boss or even regular encounters.Now I will talk about exploration. In my opinion, the exploration is the best part of this game. The dungeons, while they aren’t enormous, are filled with tons of cleverly hidden secrets and puzzles. Unlike The Legend of Grimrock, the secrets aren't overly reliant on “find this slightly off piece of bricks to reveal a hidden door”  instead, each door has a unique design, and puzzles that make up most of its secrets. The story puzzles are pretty entertaining too. They aren’t ridiculously hard, but fun to do.You also obtain various artifacts that can open up new paths, similar to Zelda or Metroidvania type games. In campfires, you have the option to go back to previous areas you’ve visited and unlock secrets you cannot obtain before you get certain items. The items you get from secrets are usually worth it, as the most powerful equipments are usually well hidden. You also have a store where you can buy or sell excess items, but compared to items you find in treasure chests, they are pretty weak. The game’s graphic itself are nothing special technically, but it has great, consistent art style and paired with the fantastical locations in the dungeons you visit, it does make a pretty game. Enemies' models are quite detailed, well-animated and sometimes their animations telegraph their next attacks or stances. The skill effects are also well done and there are quite a lot of them. While it obviously is not a high budget game, the visuals do a very good job making the game look appealing.The sound design is also pretty good. Soundtrack is decent, nothing to write home to, but each area’s theme song fits the locale. Different skills and attack types have different, recognizable sound effects. Different tile types have different sounds when you step on them, you can also hear enemies roaming in the world. Skeletons will crackle, robots sound like metal pistons pumping, etc. The ambient sounds are also very well done, from the sounds of insects in the wilderness, birds, or machineries, each area has their own unique set of sound. In my opinion, the story itself is really meh. It’s not terrible, but it doesn't really do anything to impress me. I do like some of the characters in your party, and they will often banter and joke around, and I really enjoyed those interactions. The story definitely isn’t why you're gonna play this game. All things considered,  is a pretty fun game, it does some things right but doesn’t really excel in most aspects of the game. I would recommend this to a fan of dungeon crawlers games, and I also think it is worth a try for a non dungeon crawlers fan looking into a new experience. The simplicity and various difficulty options feels like it would welcome newbie players well.

_childDocuments_.review: Thank you for this game!It delivered well everything that was promised: beautiful dungeons, cool classic but varied puzzles, great soundtrack and a well balanced challenge in an overall good story.The big strength I see are :- The fully flexible respec/restat at any point of the game. It erases the stress of "I can't try this because if it's ♥♥♥♥ i'll have to wait 5h before I can change it, if I can at all" of other games. I had a lot of fun changing comps and builds.- The potion system is well thought. Crafting them through a little riddle mini-game, and having auto-refill charges on rest is another idea that solves the well known issue of player hoarding powerups until "the right moment", which never happens and you end up with 9999 potions in stock.- The voice acting was rather nice. Some felt a bit too forced (looking at you Kampo) but at least it was not bland.The 2 things I would say are vastly improvable are:- the early game balance of casters : if you don't pick mage first, you don't get one (which is rather a support) before half the game, or have Joska with poison spells (with the 2 first maps full of ennemies resisting.... poison :D). Actually i fully recommend any player to play mage first run. It's fun, powerful and other classes are way better covered that this one.- having a combat log. Many times i took damage or had my turn skipped (probably due to CC) without being even able to see what was happening to me through the animations.Those are details though, and I can only recommand this game to everyone. It was a blast!

_childDocuments_.review: As a great fan of the Etrian Odyssey series for the Nintendo DS/3DS, I was looking for a similar experience on the PC. To be short: Operencia is not on the same level in terms of the total experience/package. The purchase of Operencia was also fueled by wanting to check out other works of Zen Studios, as I'm a great fan of their high quality Zen Pinball games. Operencia is not a bad game, but I would never recommend it to anybody when they would ask for a dungeon crawling experience. This is another game that suffers from poor choices in terms of game mechanics, wrapped in a shiny stylized package for the overall audiovisual design.Pros:+ Stylish handdrawn artwork. The world design is also done very well and convincing. The visual presentation is up there with the very best in the high-fantasy genres.+ The Unreal engine makes this game look very nice. Quality textures and accompanying glittery effects for all kinds of spells and environmental interactions.+ Fully voiced dialog. Mostly done very well, with the exception of the Asian party member.+ A few memorable musical themes, aided by convincing environmental effects like nature sounds and echos while people talk in certain spaces.+ The environmental puzzles are varied, and make sense most of the time. There is more here than just placing colored blocks in the right wholes. There are a few head scratchers here and there though, and the pipe based puzzle in the last dungeon is just annoying.+ Skill points and abilities/spells, can be completely restructured at every point in time.Cons:- Mediocre storyline: form a party, fight through dungeons and defeat the final boss in the last dungeon.- Very generic enemies: ghosts, mages, rats, robots, skeletons, spiders, etc. The usual, and only the usual. Especially the robots in the Copper Forest areas, look pretty ridiculous and have these long silly robotic animations. There is also one line in the game, where a character states something about fighting the same enemies over and over again. Therefore it seems to be that these game designers are not taking themselves very seriously.- Not too many spells: only six can be active per party member, with not many more available for them in total.- Slow and methodical saving process. Almost in the style of the type writer with ink ribbons from the classic Resident Evil games. You literally have to save before/after every fight. There is always a chance your party will be wiped out, even on normal difficulty and having high levels and the best possible gear.- Some annoying difficulty spikes throughout the game. Normal difficulty should also be called Hard difficulty.- The final boss in the Glass Palace is nearly impossible. An extremely annoying fight, due to the difficulty spike and the insane amount of enemies. This is the main reason why only a small percentage finished this game.- Leveling the party does not feel very rewarding. It literally feels like the party is stuck at the first few levels, because the same enemies will keep popping up and they will also wipe the floor with your party when not careful.- The gear management for your party, is pretty much non-existent. Most of the time, it is reduced to pressing the "Optimize" option.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is an absolute gem. I haven't seen a REALLY good dungeon crawler since Grimrocks - and this is it. Finally!However, the "mandatory" Grimrock comparison isn't really valid. In fact, tile-based movement is just about the only thing Operencia has in common with these two masterpieces. Which doesn't stop it from being a masterpiece in its own right, as far as I'm concerned.So, what do we have here?So, movement is tile-based. But the camera is completely free: you can look around as much as you like, and sometimes, something gets placed in a "special" way. Don't panic: the game doesn't abuse it (or provides hints).Locations are 3D and have multiple floors as well as different heights within a single "floor". Pits also exist, but they are few and never used to access anything that you can't reach otherwise. Occasionally there are elevators and other means of vertical travel.All of it looks gorgeous and diverse. Music is awesome too, with a unique theme for each location - if a bit repetitive at times, since it plays constantly without pauses.In Operencia, you only create your main character. The rest of your party consists of unique characters who join you as the story progresses. There are 6 companions in total, and max party size is 4 (main + 3 others). You can change party at campfires (universal "hubs" for everything from saving to alchemy and trading), but the story and narrative assumes that they all travel together. So, inactive characters get full experience and participate in dialogue.There are no classes as such. Instead, everyone has a skill tree with 3 branches. Most (not all) of these are unique. What's NOT obvious about skills is that they do get more effective as you level up (e.g. get better success rates). There are also 6 attributes (strength etc). You get 3 points per level, but bonuses can also be gained via skill trees and, of course, items (up to +10 bonus).There are also FREE redistribute buttons! Yes, you can respec your characters anytime, as many times as you like. If you play with hard combat, you'll probably have to do it multiple times. Leveling up "correctly" doesn't matter that much in the first half of the game, but things get a lot more painful later, and not everything can be "fixed" by items (especially if you can't even wear them).Operencia has a mildly intriguing setting based on Hungarian (and other) folklore, with a tiny bit of history in the mix. Three worlds, World Tree, Sun God, dragons, griffins, fairy curses, stars from heaven in human form, Attila the Hun - you have it all. The story has most of the standard "unexpected" turns and revelations. But it's neither dull, nor confusing. Constant lighthearted party banter helps too (there's a lot of it).If you are one of those taught by Grimrock to walk around wall-hugging, looking for hidden buttons - relax. There are just 3 buttons in the whole game, and they are hard to miss. There are some illusionary walls, which can also be noticed with relative ease because they are semi-transparent. Light sources located nearby make it even easier. Other secrets are either puzzle-based, item-based or artifact-based.This is one of the best features of Operencia! As you progress, you'll find unique items which give you new abilities. You'll need them to progress, but they are also used for secrets. And a lot of these require artifacts which are obtained later in the story (sometimes MUCH later), so you'll have to backtrack to find them all. This adds a bit of a "metroidvanic" vibe to the game, which adds a lot to the fun, so I won't spoil any details.Old locations can be revisited once you finish the first 3. Then, you are completely free to backtrack, with just one obvious (and temporary) exception. The game does give you a lot of "no-return" warnings, but really, you can just ignore them. No matter what it says, you CAN go back. Only the final battle is, well, FINAL: once your start it, you win the game or you die (no post-gameplay).Puzzles are there. Not nearly as much in Grimrock and not nearly as challenging. There are standard ones which you've seen a hundred times and probably hate by now. There are unique ones. Some rely on artifacts. None are particularly hard, and the worst part is that the devs somehow managed to make a great old-school game without respecting their players' brains - so they made your companions give lots of unwanted hints, ruining about 90% puzzles which were easy to begin with...Alchemy is... weird. When you find a "recipe", instead you get a riddle describing various properties of the ingredients. You need to solve it by arranging these properties correctly. You don't have to collect the actual ingredients. You just get the potion with a limited number of "charges" (yeah, I know it should be "doses" - go tell the devs), which can be replenished by resting. Oh, and you'll need a cauldron first.There are some autosaves (depending on your difficulty settings). To save manually, you have to visit a campfire. There, you can also do other things (more unlock as you progress), but primarily - rest by spending "firewood" (limited resource) to replenish your HP, energy and potions. Contrary to some of the game's wording, you DO NOT need to spend firewood to save!Unlike Grimrock, where you kite monsters in real-time on the same maps you are exploring, Operencia uses a classic turn-based system. You see a monster on the map, you approach, you switch into combat mode and the monster becomes 3-5 monsters... The only thing that matters before the combat is whether you approach from behind to ambush, or get ambushed yourself. Ambushing side gets an initiative bonus for the first turn.In battle, enemies are positioned in 3 lines by distance: close, medium, far. This is unchangeable: killing the frontliners does NOT move the rest closer! You can attack anyone with any weapon (e.g. far line with a dagger), unless someone *taunted* you. The distance just scales the attack's damage according to its own "efficiency graph" (visible in UI).Your party does NOT have front/back lines. The enemies attack whoever they want, the best way to prevent it (well, except AOE) is the infamous Taunt ability... Problem is - for the most of the game it is YOUR ENEMIES who spam Taunt against you! Only a couple of skills can counter it, and they have ridiculously high energy cost and cooldown, making a lot of fights infuriatingly hard, sometimes impossible without just the right setup. Hello unlimited respecs...There are also rechargeable "party skills", but they are unlocked gradually as you progress.Combat UI is severely lacking in terms of giving information. Tooltips mention "weapon damage" without ever saying what it is. Enemies are labeled "Elite" without telling you what it means (hint: you can't instakill them). Attack animations mix with idle animations, damage/immunity flyouts are quick and color-coded, so it's easy to miss what happens and hard to understand why: there is no combat log whatsoever!Still, somehow, the combat manages to be quite fun between all the frustrations. I played with "hard" combat and had a good challenge, but never really got stuck. I even managed to clear out the final location with just one rest (right before the final battle), and I still had 8 spare units of firewood. There really are more than enough other ways to conserve and replenish your resources if you pay attention to all of the game's features. But if you just rest after each battle or two, I guess you'll run out quickly...Good news: mobs don't respawn! if you love dungeon crawlers, you should definitely play this. Operencia can be very frustrating at times, but it is totally worth it!

_childDocuments_.review: Im leaning towards positive because the game is overall great... but if you are getting it because of VR maybe take pause.100% of my gameplay was in VR.The game has great graphics, great performance, the story is nice and entertaining, the voice acting is awesome, characters are kinda likable and enemies are greatly designed.Played with an xbox controller and it worked perfectly, the turn based gameplay, and grid like movement, helps the control feel perfectly fine, VR gives a great sense of presence and of course immersion.The only issue i have is that it feels a bit... Grindy? like at some point you do something and "a doors unlocks somewhere" and you have to go back and search where it opened, and i dont mean go back 2 rooms, but the whole map undoing puzzles and going basically to the beginning, where, granted, it was pretty clear there was a room i couldnt access yet... i did it once, then the next times i saw that msg if it wasnt clear what where the door was, i ignored it and the rewards because, it was too much of a pain to transverse through the level (in VR?).And then there are these puzzles where you have to search for clues, and you need a "light" that only lights up for X moves and increases intensity the closer you are to the clue, sounds ok written up, but, it was a pain to do them, and those where not optional.looking semi aimlessly for hidden clues that, feels like they its there to artificially extend the playtime.Personally id be grateful if they could cut those parts and make the game 1/2 its lenght.Aside from that, the game is really well done all around, i enjoyed thinking my moves, and tactically attacking enemies, boosting my abilities and getting stronger.i definitively didnt like going back to the map looking for a door that opened somewhere.I think on flatscreen this isnt much of an issue, but on VR, its a pain and feels ungratifying and a chore to do, i felt it was a waste of time at some point, just plain didnt enjoy it.I still recommended this, because its well above the average quality of a usual VR game, and even with its issues, the game is worth your time if you are interested in turn based games in VR.

_childDocuments_.review: The good:- Nice real time dungeoncrawler with turn based combat- Combat balancing is ok- Enough secrets and things to find to tickle to explorerer nerve - if you have any- Decent story- Clear mechanics/functionalitiesThe bad:- No clear story conclusion to any of the open threads- Several VERY annoying bugs (Boy scout achievement; Game breaking bug that prevents progress; Item management bug with keys; Master Thief achievement bugged occasionally)- No reply/support on steam forum + and the bug was reported back in 2020 so...i guess it won't ever be fixed- Equipment amount could be better (more useful variety instead of tons of junk)- Comfort functions are severely lacking (inventory management, etc.)- 0 re-playability /0 story choicesthe Tl;dr:If you like a classic dungeon crawler and you are not flying off the rails because of bugged achievements (like I am!) you could buy this game - though i would still advise to get it when it's on sale.You will get around 40h for your money, if you play till the end. _childDocuments_.review: I give up.  I'd have to rate the "normal" difficulty on this game as "insanely impossible".  I love this sort of game, and and usually great an maximizing my skills and leveling, but this is just atrocious.  The devs don't seem to have wanted to waste money on balancing at all.  As an example, it's not uncommon to *ambush* an enemy, yet still have them wipe out your party on their FIRST attack (that's assuming you gathered all the secrets on the way, and effectively "over-leveled"). _childDocuments_.review: EDIT:  So I just beat this game not long ago, and there are some Achievements I missed so I'll probably do another run of it in the future.  There is a great walkthrough guide out there if needed as well, as there are a few places one might get stuck.  Overall, I give this game a 9/10 (I couldn't romance Joskar so I'm sad XD)I love this game!I'm a big fan of turn-based RPGs, and between this and Bard's Tale IV, I'm getting the kind of tactics I love.Pros:* - Awesome characters!  Not only are they all voiced, but they have funny dialogue as well as interactions which make them feel real and not just some pictures on a screen.* - You can redistribute allocation points in your skills and stats at any time!  So even if Mezey is built like a powerhouse when you first get him, you are more than free to make him a magic user if you wanted to!* - Puzzles!* - Beautiful environments and music!Cons:* - When it comes to camping, you need to really think!  Firewood is used to Rest (otherwise at a campfire you can just Save or look through inventory etc).  Since Firewood can be a rare commodity, you need to really decide if you want to rest or if you can hold on a bit longer.* - Though you find items scattered around the world in chests, the only 'shop' in game is dependent on not only finding a particular character, but also on what part of the game you are in.  It doesn't replenish (only at certain times) and money can be hard to come by.* - No way to skip a turn.  This is more of a nitpick, but in battle you either fight, use a skill, or wait (using a skill or waiting have cooldowns).  Sometimes you just want to skip your turn but you can't.* - Item usage.  This might be controversial to some, but though I enjoy the process of figuring out how to make a potion, you can only set one potion to a character, and some only have one or two uses.  And that's it.  The only way to get that back is to Rest at a campfire.Lots of tacticalness to this game.  So if you love RPGs and turn-based ones, come check this game out!

_childDocuments_.review: Finally, the ordeal is over.  After hunting down every secret and achievement in this game, I feel like I can finally lay this abomination of mediocrity to rest.  And what better way to lay the tombstone than to write a review?You might be wondering at that term I used—"abomination of mediocrity."  After all, if the game is mediocre, how can it produce such revulsion?  Well, there is a point at which, after an extended period of failing to do  particularly well, the atrocious whole becomes greater than the sum of its bland, uninspired parts.   is that game.  It begins (and ends) with the lack of actual content.  Ignore the Steam playtime.  The in-game timer tells me I have about 20 hours put into the game, which seems fairly accurate—I didn't often load saves or die.  Of those 20 hours, I spent perhaps half actually progressing forward in the story, playing the game.  The other half were spent ferreting out secrets and fully exploring maps.  Some of these elements aren't actually the fault of this particular game.  They're the fault of a lack of innovation in the genre.  is trying to be a first-person dungeon-crawler RPG, and die hard fans of this type of game want nothing more than to have the same experience they had when they first played  on their Commodore 64 back in 1985.  I imagine that last statement might not be very popular with certain people, but hear me out.  I said that  was  to be that game.  Unfortunately, of the above-listed categories, it succeeds only in playing out in the first person . . . and there's little reason even to include that element.   is not a dungeon-crawler, nor is it an RPG.  It's a puzzle game.  A puzzle game imagined in the worst way, complete with repetitive backtracking, the unimaginative use of items (as if the game is trying to join the  franchise), and items concealed by their microscopic size, rather than by clever artifice of any kind. Let's start with the lack of dungeon-crawling elements.  If you truly wanted to torture yourself, you  turn off the map and break out the grid paper, but that still wouldn't save this game.  You feel less like an explorer and more like a cartographer in this game.  There's no real  to explore.  Half of the game's dungeons put the exit right in front of your face—it's just inaccessible due to some convoluted, nonsensical hoops that you'll have to jump through.  I'm not actually a big fan of this genre, but I think even true dungeon-crawler enthusiasts will be turned off about the exploration in this game.  The same is true of the secrets and the items they hide.  Gold is useless, except that you need it for an achievement in order to buy out the shop's entire stock (you don't actually want any of the items that it sells), and most of the items are too.  It's not uncommon to open a chest and find an outdated piece of gear that was obsolete three dungeons back.  There's nothing worse than finally discovering the last secret in a map only to find that it was some junk that you didn't care about. In regards to the RPG elements . . . they're just so badly balanced and designed.  You get a character who's a healer.  Useless.  You can heal outside of combat with potions, and the game lets you rest so often that it just doesn't matter.  Keep in mind that I'm playing with extra-difficult enemies and a mode that lets you rest less often turned on.  Yeah.  You get characters who can inflict status effects.  Who cares?  You can count the number of different enemies in the game on your fingers, and half of them (the important half) are immune to anything and everything that is of any use.  Everything else falls prey to the insane number of instant-kill attacks that they put in this game.  You can re-specialize your skills and stats freely.  While I'm usually a fan of  flexibility in this department, this game crosses the line . . . and then proceeds to run about twenty miles too far.  When I say  I literally mean at any time outside of combat.  It gets to the point where you'll just be switching your entire build between levels or even between individual fights to cheese the game.  It makes enemy resistances meaningless.  Every good build consists of just enough survivability for convenience, with everything else mono-statted into damage output. Every fight is a suicide-rush to kill the enemy before they kill you, and then you heal up afterward.  You don't  to play this way, but combat is so tediously long otherwise, I really wouldn't recommend that you do anything else.  The game just isn't a competent RPG.Every endeavor you undertake in this game is ruined by the fact that there is ultimately no reason to do it.  For example, in order to brew potions in the game, you have to solve a logic puzzle.  The puzzles are far too simplistic, especially since there's no penalty for failure or guess-and-check, but they were the only puzzles I actually came close to enjoying.  Oh, but look.  All but perhaps four or five of the potions are useless in this game, so at the end of the day, you feel like you just Googled a logic puzzle to kill some time.  There's no meaningful reward.  I'm no achievement-hunter, but I ended up doing a 100% achievement run on this game because there is literally nothing else to keep you going. The game is also plagued by demo-dementia.  That's a condition where your design philosophy is to spend 50 percent of your work on the front-end 10 percent of your game, because you want people to buy it.  As you continue development, you figure that no one is going to play past the first dungeon anyway and "forget" to put any effort into the rest.  In the first dungeon, you have some feeling of accomplishment when you find a secret.  Since you don't have any gear, everything you find feels like an upgrade, and they're generally decently hidden.  By the end of the game, a "secret" is literally using a dungeon item at the designated place.  That's it.  No puzzle, no searching, nothing.  Half of the "secrets" are just things you have to do to get past the level.  Sometimes two, three, or even four "secrets" will be in the same place at the same time! Lastly, let me comment on the storytelling.  The developer is a Hungarian studio, and the lore and story of this game is the usual Slavic-Hungarian mishmash (yes, I'm aware that Hungarians aren't Slavs, thank you) that people from Central and Eastern Europe seem to think the rest of the world needs more exposure to . . . while the rest of the world yawns in tacit boredom.  I do find that statement more than a little offensive myself, so I apologize, but . . . ugh.  Everything is there, from the unpronounceable (and thus unmemorable) names, the ridiculous and crazy stories, to Baba Yaga, to owls with huge metal genitalia (I wish I was joking).  Then throw in Attila the Hun for good measure, and voilà!  We have   I felt like I was on an acid trip for the entire game.  Unfortunately, the surreal quality of the game is only compounded by the bad localization and apparently low budget.  There are entire sections of mangled text, and if I saw "Alas!  Treasure!" one more time after digging up the routine "secrets" with my shovel, I was going to strangle someone.  Maybe my party was crying "Alas!" because they knew it would be something useless.  The game ends on a literal black screen (see "demo-dementia" above) while the "true" villain cackles into the darkness about how this was all according to plan as if setting up a sequel.  If that's what's intended, I can only beg . . . please don't.

_childDocuments_.review: Hello.This is fine game for people who love dungeon crawler. You will get about 20 hrs of playtime for one full run if you know what you are doing. The puzzles and secrets are not too hard and often reward you for your efforts.The potion system is fairly unique and a nice addition to the game.Combat tends to be on the harder side and you need to learn and understand the combat mechanics in the later parts of the game or you get crushed. The characters and the banter is very enjoyable as is the fairytale like setting. Normally I do not care so much about the story in such games but here I watched every cutscene and listened to every banter.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't know that this has grabbed me well enough to finish, but after 10 hours I'd certainly recommend it:* The Hungarian mythos is refreshing and well-done; reminds me of some of Steven Brust's writings.* Characters are engagingly written; I find myself looking forward to the next bit of campfire dialog.* Decent mechanical fusion of first-person real-time blobber with turn-based separate-screen combat.* I'm not hugely fond of the skill selection & extremely fine-grained stat system, but they work.* Even on "easy" mode the difficulty starts ticking upwards in chapter 5.

_childDocuments_.review: A longer review, will follow, as soon I have beaten this game.First of all, I usually prefer my dungeon crawlers in the style of Eye of the Beholder/Grimrock-Style.This game has a different battlesystem, which is turnbased and allows no movement mid-battle.But it introduces 3 lanes (close, mid, long) which will affect on which skills to use best, since certain skills suffer a penalty if used on a lane it's not suited for. Therefore this game sometimes demands tactical thinking. You also have to be mindful about whicht enemy to kill first and at certain occasions you also have to decide wether to kill of the enemies one by or or trying to kill them all at the same time, because they might spawn additional enemies. The boss battles can be challenging, too, especially on the hard difficulty ^^The design of this game looks really nice (I've played only 7 hours, yet, mind you) and the locations reached from Underwatercastles, tombs, dark mystic forests, ruined castles etc. In most parts the environment looks really beautiful and there are lots of secrets to be found within each location.Sometimes you need to revisit past locations, because you might be able to get past certain obstacles with a new item you've found, so it offers progression similar to metroidvanias, but I can't tell for sure if it's mandatory to revisit the old locations. Anyhow, there's loot to be found anyways ^^What I admire most of this game is the whole atmosphere, that profit alot from the tales and discussions between the characters. Some stories are rather sad, others are quite funny and I love how they sometimes say mean things to each other ^^I'm not even half-way through the game but I've played 10hrs, already and I expect the game keep me entertained for a longer time, for sure, though it's  hard to guess how long it'll be. But from what I've seen I believe 30 hours might be a good guess. Maybe more or a bit less.If you like dungeon crawlers with turn based combat and a nice atmosphere, you should be having fun with this game ^^

_childDocuments_.review: A mostly, old school party based, dungeon crawler in the vein of Bard’s Tale, Wizardry, Might and Magic, etc.  For those who aren’t super old, the most similar game that is somewhat newer would be The Legend of Grimrock, though this has turn based combat.  This is a more modern take on the genre though, with the ability to look any direction, smooth movement and a much more story and character focused game.  Your character and party will often interject, commenting on dungeon features, story beats and just small talk.  The story and characters are all fully voiced, and the voice acting can be quite good (with some exceptions).  The gameplay itself is the usual for this type of game with exploring, fighting creatures in your way and a handful of puzzles per area.  The puzzles are mostly well done and intuitive, but there are some where the objective or clues are just too obscure.  One near the end was also a way too long / hard slide puzzle that killed the pacing.  Many puzzles also require artifacts you will find later in the game.  Once you unlock it though, getting back to those points is pretty painless.  The combat is turned based, with each party member and monster acting based off their initiative.  Unlike the old games, each character gets skills with cooldowns they can use in addition to their basic melee and ranged attack.  Beyond that, there are a few original things like a potion creation mini-game (you just have to figure out recipes you find, no experimentation) and an unusual fantasy setting based on non-D&D / non-western fantasy.The positives are the characters, dungeon design, atmosphere and mostly the puzzles.  A lot of life is breathed into the game via the voice acting and storytelling with some very excellent voice acting from some characters (unfortunately this also makes the bad ones stick out more).  The characters are all unique, gameplay wise as well.  The first companion you find is a rogue, but if you start as a rogue your skill trees are pretty different.  The same goes for all others, making each character unique.  The puzzles are usually pretty short, and easy enough to figure out the concept and solution that you won’t get annoyed or frustrated.  Of course, there are some exceptions as I noted elsewhere, but there is the internet to help if needed.For negatives, the game has a weird combat system where abilities use energy, but you don’t regenerate energy at all unless you camp (which uses limited wood) or defend during battle.  Defending has a cooldown and can only be done once every three turns.  Abilities tend to use a lot of EP’s, so you will find yourself defending a lot, which gives combat a weird feeling and is not particularly fun.  Not a fan of that system.  Also, the fact that camping uses wood and you have no clue how much wood you will find or how long the game is, can make you too conservative.  I ended the game with a lot of wood, but I also used the defend mechanism way more than I would have liked.  The game balance is a bit all over the place as well.  There are a few, very annoying enemies with abilities like energy drain or unlimited summoning that can be hard… but more so, they are just annoying and not fun.  Some of the abilities available to you, also feel off.  Your rogue will be your only source of healing for almost half the game for instance.  And if you don’t’ play as a mage, you will be lacking area of effect spells for a long time as well.  For the story, while well delivered, it was not my cup of tea.  You will be talking to gods, and hearing tales of tears making lakes and other over the top types of story beats.  While original, I prefer a more grounded setting.So, is this worth a buy.  For me it was, but I think it will be hit or miss with many people, even those who like dungeon crawlers.  If you like, over the top and well delivered stories, exploration and puzzles and aren’t as interested in character building and combat, you will probably like it.  If you are used to this genre being very combat heavy, with well balanced and fun combat and that is mainly what you are looking for, this game might not be for you.

_childDocuments_.review: There is quite a bit of good about Operencia: Stolen Sun....and some not so good.The best of the game is its fantasy setting and decent presentation visually. Its a good game to escape into with a pleasant, although somewhat linear, story based primarily on European folk mythology. There are no typical RPG elements such as dialogue choices or character creation. All dialogue is linear and scripted. There are 7 set characters comprising staples such as Rogue, Tank, Magician etc. 4 of these can be used to create a party. My first bugbear with the game is that stats for each character seem really unbalanced. For instance the strength stat, one might assume, would lead to greater damage dealing in combat, however this often isn't the case. You will routinely find yourself frustrated that your low strength magician can swing a melee weapon for equal or more damage than a high strength warrior even with critical multipliers taken into account. The balance in combat often feels off and not in line with the stats accumulated. Some things feel nerfed and some feel over powered but in an inconsistent way. Battles take place in an arena style where enemies are placed either close, mid range, or at the back to the front of your party. Its odd though that one might expect ranged attacked to be required for distant enemies and melee for close by, but this is not the case. Curiously melee attacks are absolutely as effective or ineffective at long range as any ranged attack. It doesn't seem to matter how you attack at times which negates a prime area of combat strategy. Special attacks, requiring an energy bar, are dull and too few in variety and often don't yield any greater damage than a regular attack. Enemy resistances are also dodgy, for instance I encountered a weak to lightning enemy, attacked with lightning only to find that a follow up regular attack, without critical, was far more damaging. There are also some combat mechanics which lead to frustration, for instance the 'taunt' mechanic whereby an enemy (always a tank) will make it so your entire party can only attack him. You wail on him for what seems an eternity, almost kill him and then another enemy tank casts taunt as soon as the previous ones spell expires and you start wailing all over again with the new guy. It feels as though battles are deliberately made longer by such irritations, I believe probably, because the devs couldn't get the balance right in terms of combat multipliers vs enemy strength and your gear.  Gear itself is another frustration in terms of lack of balance. Its not that there isn't enough gear, its just that you quickly reach a point where it feels as though it doesn't really matter what gear you wear. The devs must have had a problem with this because a really weird 'optimize' button exists on the inventory which will, with the click of a button, place the best gear available on your character. As hard core an RPG player I am I'm ashamed to admit I quickly reached a point where I clicked optimize as a staple because the gear just wasn't interesting and of much practical benefit in terms of one piece over another. Which ever gear you wear you will rather irritatingly require rest after most battles by the way of a camp fire which requires a piece of wood either purchased or found in the environment. This does quickly become a hindrance to flow although potions and some abilities can replenish health and energy in between battles. The problem is though, without fully resting, starting a new battle will result in said potions not being available or alternatively a heavily depleted energy bar.Puzzle elements, on the whole are well done with a few tough ones interspersed among the more obvious. Music is derived from eastern European themes and is well written and atmospheric. Sound is OK overall however some choices of sounds in game are questionable and seem out of place.  Voice acting is mostly solid but dialogue is often extremely dull and frequently rather irritating in delivery. Rinse and repeat one liners in battle grate fast (such as one character inexplicably shouting 'BEWARE' at the start of battle and another quipping 'You won't even get a hit in' which just sounds so lame. The voice matching to characters is also curious and something just seems off. Its as though these were the only guys available to do the work on the day of recording.So after all that why recommend? Well, despite a few uneven moments and frustrations, Operencia is a real labor of love and the devs clearly care deeply and respect the mythology in the game. Its a good game in many ways with some polish and flare but one which, with a bit more work on combat mechanics, could have been a great game. The experience is lite overall but, although the game doesn't reach anywhere near a Grimrock I/II level of greatness, there is something there which will pull you back in to find one more hidden secret you missed....Buy it on sale and enjoy escaping into a fantasy world but don't expect the ride to be completely smooth.

_childDocuments_.review: I played this on xbox years ago via gamepass and since it isn't on there anymore I saw it was pretty cheap so bought it to try to play it again. And after a few days back with it and with how poorly balanced the game is and how obtuse some of the puzzles can be I cannot recommend this game. Which is a shame because the stuff I remembered liking like the world, characters and metriodvania style backtracking work really well. But the terribly designed puzzles, dungeons, and fights especially late game make this a truly unfun experience. On normal in the final dungeon if I get two characters confused for any amount of time its easy 75% chance I wipe. The excuse of "poor optimization" or teambuilding is invalid when the game does a terrible job of explaining anything and there is a hard mode for that type of optimization. Additionally Puzzle/Dungeon design especially late game become so confusing and hard to figure out what specific item I need to complete x or y. Some items don't highlight if they are interactible so sometimes I'm just whipping my mouse around hoping I see something to interact with. The last 3-5 hours of playing have been a lesson on when to give up a game. I already beat it once and I remember the final boss being a slog then even with rose tinted glasses. I cannot keep playing, If you don't look up optimal teams/strats I hope you get lucky on team builds and RNG but the best way to get lucky is to find a different RPG.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: Recommended, but with significant reservations.Pros: - Beautiful and varied environments and effects- Engaging, tactical combat- Plenty of access to loot that helps you customize your characters- Generally satisfying boss battles- Great soundtrack- Mechanically, it is a big plus that you can re-specialize your characters at will, even if it is pretty ridiculous- While the game is linear, the ability to go back and visit past locations to find remaining secrets means that completionists and treasure-hunters will have a fun timeCons- Late game battles become extremely obnoxious (will I get hit by status effects this time, or not?)- Story is quite tepid, nonsensical, and with random trope-pulling as needed- Certain important points about the game are not well explained (finite amount of rests, beginning character choice is quite important)- "Secrets" in this game are all over the place. Some are very obvious, some are very obscure and not even logical. Some give powerful loot that is basically necessary for some classes- Gearing your characters is fun, but ultimately is just about stat and resistance boosting. - Gear sets are few, and are quickly made irrelevant by progress- The traveling store is 80% useless. Most armor/gear is not as good as what is found in the world. Aside from buying the all-important firewood and a handful of items, there is little point- Inventory management matters not at all. Aside from your list growing longer, there's no consequence to keeping every last item you get in the game. You can sell all this for gold of course, but see my point immediately aboveI played the demo for Operencia and was immediately sold. After purchasing and making it about halfway through the game, I began to see serious problems with game design. Now, on the doorstep of completing the game (about 38.5 hours), I don't know if I have the moxie to push through.The combat gets very frustrating. Exploration essentially becomes a balancing act based around how many groups of enemies you can dispatch before needing to use your next precious piece of firewood. Add to this the late game tendency for enemies to counterattack frequently, confuse or stun your characters, and deliver other powerful status effects, and this adventure game quickly becomes a fantasy chess match where you have to precisely calculate when to perform which actions in combat, and which steps to take outside of it.If you're really craving a graphically stunning, modern take on the grid-based first person RPG, then this is worth a look, and maybe you'll find it less frustrating than I. For those who want more freedom in combat or exploration, I don't think I'd recommend this. I don't regret buying it, but I probably won't ever play it again.

_childDocuments_.review: Gameplay: Its what can be expected from a grid based dungeon crawler. If your looking for more modern looking take on the old Bard's Tales and TSR D&D titles this is like those. The puzzles and challenges are rather simple and easy to get through. Combat is similarly easy to sort out and will have you breezing through most of the encounters in short order.Visuals/Art:The design and art style is well done, everything seems to fit together and works well. It uses a mix of cut-paper style animation (in cut scenes) along with 3d models in 3d dungeons. The "VR" mode is interesting for about 10 minutes. If your trying to show your friends that you didn't waste your money on your shiny VR rig this isn't really the game to show them.Story/InteractionUnfortunately, this is where this game takes a big nosedive and ruins the quality work done by the rest of the team. The voice acting can be overlooked as not horrid but not good either. The writing is what really turns this into a turd. Every other line of dialog out of the characters are snarky one-liners. The developers may have thought this was cute or endearing while in actuality it made me want the monsters to win. The characters come off as a collection of annoying ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. Nothing is really done with the story to develop the characters you must suffer with. To say that the story/dialog is lazy and poorly executed is being kind.  I really would have liked to finish this game, I've always enjoyed gridders but the writing in this one is so bad that I just can't suffer through it.

The voice acting is somewhat mediocre, sometimes it is well voiced, sometimes not. All in all, it is worth to try out. My only complaint is the 1 year Epic exclusive.
