name: Shadows of Doubt
detailed_description: A procedurally-generated sandbox stealth game with a whole city of secrets at your fingertips! Shadows of Doubt is set in an alternate reality in the hyper-industrialized 1980s. Think like a detective and use a variety of gadgets as a private intelligence investigator, gathering evidence and making money by solving cases, finding and selling information and more. Play your own way in a fully simulated world with hundreds of citizens. Discover, meet and tail individual citizens, each with their own name, job, apartment and daily routine, in unique, procedurally-generated cities. Each case has different culprits, clues and experiences for  you to test your investigative skills. Explore anywhere in the city! Every nook of every trashy bar, every place of work, every seedy hotel room… This dystopia is your oyster. Break into apartments, rifle through secret documents or hack security systems - even a discarded receipt can be the key to cracking a case. Trace the receipt back to an individual location, scour CCTV footage and match the time up to the receipt to find out who it belonged to! The entire world is fully simulated . Each citizen has an apartment, job, daily routine, favorite things to do, places to go, and people to interact with. They live out their lives independently, in a world that moves on with or without you— uncover this knowledge and use it to your advantage! Become a private investigator in a truly unique detective experience. Think like a detective to solve the cases around you: check call histories, find passwords, read private emails, speak to persons of interest, watch CCTV footage and more to retrieve evidence and build your case. Store information on your investigation board and link evidence together as you piece together the full picture. Features Become a private investigator and track down a serial killer in a fully-simulated sci-fi city. Think like a detective and use a variety of gadgets to gather evidence and solve cases in this truly unique detective experience. Meet individual citizens, each with their own name, job, apartment and daily routine, in unique, procedurally-generated cities. Take on new cases to earn cash, purchase new gadgets and equipment, and customise your apartment. Gather evidence to build your case - scan fingerprints, check call histories, read private emails, watch CCTV, and find key pieces of evidence to gather information and accuse your suspect. Play your own way - pick locks, break down doors, sabotage security systems and bribe citizens for information, or stick to the law and play by the book. There are multiple ways to approach each case. Explore every room in every building, and talk to every citizen. Lose yourself in a detailed sci-fi noir world.

_childDocuments_.review: This is exactly what I've been looking for in a detective game.  It could use more polish and variance definitely to always keep things different and fresh, but a procedurally generated detective game is something I have been looking for for ages, with the closest game being Noir Syndrome, but Shadows of Doubt is on a whole other level of complexity for finding culprits.I wish the game had more graphical options to reduce graphic settings further to improve stability and performance (some lighting options and surface reflection options are a bit much).  I don't need this game to be pretty, just fun and run nice.  I can't wait to see additional stuff they add from the roadmap.If you enjoy gathering clues to try and find a murderer in a city of 300-1000+ people each with their own unique traits, fingerprints, etc.  You'll probably have fun with this game.  You definitely learn new ways to get information as you experiment with stuff and I always feel like I am learning new stuff every time I boot this game up.  (The HELP menu is also a great teaching tool for learning the ins and outs of everything)

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: a fun experience you won't get elsewhere, but the devs have put their head in the sand and may have walked off leaving the game half baked. Get on saleI'll start by saying the game has a lot to enjoy, its a very unique experience and a great time can be had playing it. However, while the game has had improvements in way of bug fixes and some new content from the early days of Early Access, it has not reached a point where I or many others would call it "1.0 ready".By far the biggest concern for me is the increasingly non-communicative devs. Its certainly not been radio silence, there's been lots of dev updates; but the community has been very vocal about dissatisfaction with the push to 1.0 release and have brought many issues and desired features frequently to the front, with no acknowledgement from the development team. I do not believe that every desired feature should be included; the game has a specific vision and rough gameplay loop in mind, and some things such as the ability to kill npcs really conflicts with the mechanical core, however many quality of life changes for the sake of immersion, easily implemented, have been ignored, namely having the ability to smoke - something you'd consider almost central to the gritty neo-noir detective aesthetic. It certainly would take little to add, and would make a lot of people happy. Consuming alcohol is possible, and the game lets you watch poisoned murder victims vomit themselves to bloody death, so taking a silent stand against a simple crowd pleasing move seems strange.I think many people hyped themselves up with the ideas of what could be, and would talk about more and more features that might never have been feasible, and I suspect the hype may have ran away with the game, beyond the means of the devs to match. That doesn't, however, justify the overall feeling that the devs are washing their hands of the game and moving on. Communication is key with games such as these, and for some time now the devs have not been communicating with their playerbase; they've simply been making statements.

_childDocuments_.review: Just play a default map and stay away from the city builder/editor (the feature is half-baked).  If you have graphical issues turn down the rain rendering.  This game has two major issues that are compounded by these two settings.  A population over 350 will start causing serious processing lag. The default maps are smaller then the ones you can create in the editor so stick with those. Every person is going about their lives. Each one a further drain on resources as they run around littering, turning on and off devices, interacting with each other, etc. This problem is further compounded by rain.The rain not only causes NPCs to react, (running to get out of the rain, opening umbrellas, having status effects applied all of them...) but also has the heaviest impact on graphical rendering.So, keep the population low, play a default city, reduce the graphics of the rain (if needed), and you will likely enjoy this game!

_childDocuments_.review: A fascinating experiment in randomly generated detective gameplay. You earn money by taking up jobs. Private detective work, like taking surveillance photos of persons of interest or uncovering romantic affairs. Assist law enforcement by taking up bounty jobs to arrest violent offenders. And there is always guaranteed to be exactly one serial killer on the streets to investigate. Strange quota for a town to keep, but it certainly keeps things interesting.There is a lot of immersive sim DNA in the game, too, with all of the mechanics interacting in subtle ways. Every NPC has a name. Fingerprints. Relationships. A job with a work schedule. They observe events and can be questioned as witnesses. They can even be bribed for information or access. A neighborhood full of skyscrapers is fully generated with businesses and condos, fully lived in by the aforementioned NPCs. No false doors anywhere. You can literally go anywhere in this neighborhood. Legally or otherwise.You have to maintain your health. Buy food and water. Keep warm. Bathe to keep from getting smelly. Ideally, make a home, which you can decorate as you please with whatever you can afford, including with functional devices like phones and computers.You won't find an overarching story line, but the emergent gameplay is intriguing enough to anyone who wants to feel like a private eye. I doubt you will find another game like it.

_childDocuments_.review: This is so close to being great if not for a fatal flaw. It's easy and fun to get sucked into the atmospheric hustle and bustle of the city and crimes committed in it, hurriedly exploring it's nooks and crannies while tracking down criminals or running from the cops, and mapping out clues. The developers got so much right. But it fails at the most important thing: investigating. If a case isn't nearly impossible to solve then it quickly gets repetitive with little variation in the strategy required. Unfortunately I can't recommend Shadows of Doubt because this detracts too much from the experience after a few hours.This issue is due to the city, it's inhabitants and the cases being procedurally generated. I can't help but wonder how much more varied, incrementally challenging and wondrous it may have been if they had crafted just one city, it's inhabitants and all the cases instead. Will be keeping eye out in case this ever happens.

_childDocuments_.review: I usually don't write reviews for games, however, this game in particular really caught my attention and I really want to share my thoughts on the game. First off, I love the idea and concept, I enjoy playing this game. I even find myself getting lost into it, spending hours of time playing it. The attention to detail, how every npc have their own life. It's very well done, I applaud the devs for their work on this game and how amazing it is so far.Secondly, yes there are some bugs and etc, but I can overlook those easily since it's not game breaking or anything. I'm sure plenty of reviewers have mentioned it and the devs have already started patching those thing up.Thirdly (this is the one that made me want to make this review) This game has so much potential, I know the devs already have some ideas on what type of add ons they want to put into the game, like new case types. I totally agree with that, variety in cased types would definitely make the game more interesting. However, I believe the devs should expand on the already amazing npc A.I. Now I'm not talking about fixing or changing anything. I'm thinking about adding onto it, I noticed how there is a lack of options when asking npcs questions related to cases. I most recently experienced a case where a victims significant other was no where  to be found, I found the significant other much later. The number one question I wanted to ask the significant other was "where you during these hours?" but, that isn't an option in the game. So I have a suggestion.Now devs, you don't have to take this suggestion if you don't want too, however, I believe this can enrich the experience more if you can implement more advanced questions. Such as "Where were you between the hours 'blank' and 'blank'?" As well as "Do you know anyone who had a grudge against the victim?" Questions that any investigator would ask and I believe it could make the cases more interesting since having this level of complexity would give each case more of a story. Of course this game is generated so it's always different, but I believe there could be a lot to play with here. It can give cases more distinctive experiences between each other. That is my suggestion and hope the devs take it into consideration (If they happen to come across this review that is) All in all, this game is great and I think the devs should double down on this game, I'm even planning on streaming this game on my youtube channel. I find the game that enjoyable and want to share it with others. So great job on this game and definitely keep working on great projects like this one!

_childDocuments_.review: Loving it so far. It's finally a detective game where I feel like a detective and my hand isn't being held half the time.You'll be searching for fingerprints, researching suspects, looking through security footage and questioning witnesses. Some cases can involve multiple crime scenes with multiple murders, the killer can keep killing if you take too long. You're able to follow leads, such as going to the victim's workplace to match the murderer's fingerprints with a coworker, visit a location they were seen at just before their deaths to look for their potential killer on the cameras and whatever else leads you to the killer. On top of that, there's other odd jobs you can do such as stealing documents, getting photographs of people and recovering stolen items.Overall it's a really solid experience so far and I'm excited to see where this game goes in the future.

_childDocuments_.review: Very fun game with an interesting concept and a fair amount of replay value.There are some bugs - I fell through the world about 3 times during my 14-hour playthrough. Sometimes you're instructed to pick up a briefcase for a random sidequest, but it generates in a particular unreachable or unfindable location. No huge deal, you just close the case and move on.The game is quite deep, but it starts to feel formulaic near the end of your playthrough. Eventually you'll know what to look for in even the most mysterious murder cases. If you want a challenge, do not use the government database computer unless it's as a complete last resort. It makes it trivial to build a profile on practically anyone in the city, and the game will just straight up tell you "this fingerprint on the murder weapon belongs to Devon Jenkins, he lives at 601 Eriksen Terrace and works at the Midnight Pawn Shop".You'll find about 15 hours of gameplay time here before you get bored, maybe a little more if you mess with mods or if you find the game enjoyable enough to replay it. It's also still being updated with more content!

_childDocuments_.review: After taking a break for a while to see how the game developed, this is very disappointing. Performance was never **too** great, but playable even on lower end machines. Having upgraded and used this game as a for a testing to see if my PC had issues, and if I wanted to play yet, the performance is very upsetting from where the game came from in early access. The game play itself is very addicting, as generating new worlds to solve even the same kind of crimes is extremely fun. It seemed (at least to me) to be the first of it's kind as an extremely detailed, "no evidence is too little" detective simulator.  You can sneak, break in by slamming into a door that someone is opening because you knocked on it, socially engineer, and even bribe your way into most places that require authorization. You can buy and create a home for yourself, genetically modify yourself to fit a specific style of game play, etc.  But sadly I cannot recommend as the variety and fun is outweighed by a mansion of performance issues. Just to give an idea of how not optimized this game is, it runs worse than Cyberpunk as it currently stands. If you like the idea of this game, wait until these problems are fixed, and I promise it will be worth the wait if it gets fixed. I'll update this review if and when it is fixed, but for now I sincerely don't recommend the game.

_childDocuments_.review: Get plopped into my first city. It's dark and it's cold. I walk around the corner and spot a convenience store. I decide to step in to get warm and talk to the employee working there.Ahh they have bourbon! Now that will keep me warm on this cold night. I step outside and glug the entire thing, throwing the empty bottle back inside the open door of the store.I'm very woozy now and can barely stand up. I stumble around occasionally dropping to the ground and then picking myself back up. I throw trash cans, trash bags, and boxes out of my way as I try to get my bearings. I stumble in and out of a bookstore. While the inebriating effects of the booze aren't wearing off, the warmth they provided is, so I stumble over to a burning barrel to get warm.There's a guy standing nearby. I can sort of make him out amidst the swirling voxels spiraling in front of my face. Then I hear gunshots. I look over, and there is a man in a trench coat standing there with a gun in his hand. He fires a couple more shots and the guy goes down, blood pooling around his body. The man walks away as if nothing happened!My first case has now started, and boy is it going to be an easy payout since I witnessed the killing first hand. I stumble down the street after the man.  He gets suspicious of me and starts to run away. I stagger behind him as he weaves in and out of buildings. I wait outside a bathroom stall as he relieves himself and then continue the pursuit.After several minutes of chasing and one bathroom break, I have finally had enough. I decide it is time for my fists to put an end to this, but it's really hard to land a solid blow when you can't stand up straight. I take a few swings and land a punch, but then I realize I had forgotten that this guy was packing, and he pulls out the same gun that offed my barrel buddy and plants some rounds into my chest.I wake up in the hospital and manage to escape. Looks like I am going to have to track down this guy the old fashioned way. I go back to the crime scene and collect prints  and a wallet from the victim. Guy's name is Carlos Somethingoranother. I investigate his apartment and his place of work, but I am not finding anything linking him to trench coat dude. I find another lead which is the name of his landlord. Maybe she has a thing for guys in trench coats. I get to her apartment and try to pick the lock when no one is looking. An alarm goes off and I am trapped inside a hallway with a turret that shreds me like mozzarella cheese.I end up back in the hospital. I escape again, and I go back to the convenient store and buy another bottle of bourbon and glug it down. I could get used to this detective life...

_childDocuments_.review: It's a good game, buy it if you like stealth/detective rpg type stuff.Wanna know how I know it's a good game? Because despite getting frustrated into force closing it about 5 separate times in the last couple days, I kept re-opening it to load my last save, and try again. Even now, after I already completed my First Big Case™ and quit the game, I can't stop thinking about skulking around town and sniffing out the next big scoop. I want to go put on my best ♥♥♥♥ Tracy impression as I go rough up some goons and fast talk a couple of no-goodniks. It's not even about the character upgrades to increase your health or inventory slots, or the Social Standing ranks you can get, and all the juicy perks that come with them. I just want to jump into a vent and Inch High, Private Eye my way through a building to get the drop on the local riffraff. And this game lets you do it. The city isn't so much as procedural, as generated, set up in advance before you ever load in. You choose some starting conditions like size and adjust the how-conveniently-placed-all-these-paperclips-are sliders, and the game generates apartments and people to live in them. And then businesses for them to work in, friendships, relationships, enemies and lovers, you name it. Each npc has a life they live outside of whatever Sam Spade shenanigans you're getting up to at the present moment. There's some jank around the edges if you play for more than 30 seconds. You can watch npcs bust into a sprint, then stop, turn 180, and walk calmly back down the staircase they just winded themselves climbing. Drunkards will stumble and flop around, occasionally ragdolling themselves through walls and doors. They don't seem to mind though. If you played Skyrim and snuck around at any point, you'll probably be familiar with the 'ol "hide behind the basket you're holding in front of your face" trick. But it's all in good fun right?So anyway. I like this game pretty well. Left-clicking to both close a drawer and accidentally steal the thing inside the drawer you were trying to close is a real kick in the teeth, ain't it though?

_childDocuments_.review: 1.0 Review: This game is so good, but it's so disappointing to see the state that it's declared as "finished" in. The ending is lackluster and the core system is extremely repetitive. There aren't that many branches for you to take and you can feel just how much AI is used in its design. The game feels like a mass of loosely put together elements that are supposed to create an interesting story. The game lacks a plot or some kind of story to keep it all together. Otherwise, the advertised "unique nature" of each case is unique in just the changing of the name. The gameplay is extremely repetitive and nothing changes.  You can tell there are SO MANY unfinished features or ideas that the game had in mind but just never finished. The game loop has remained the same from when it first released in early access to now. The same way you gather evidence, the same way you arrest people, and the same exploits are available. The most frustrating part of the game is when you are trying to turn in evidence, and it's 100% the evidence you need, it counts it as incorrect or missing. This is especially true with murder weapons. You could go all over the city trying to find the murder weapon of a case and it simply cannot be found. Another issue is when you find a weapon that has the suspect's fingerprints on it and was found in the victim's house and it doesn't count it as the murder weapon. Meanwhile, there is no weapon on the suspect's body or in the suspect's house. Extremely frustrating. You never need to actually solve any murders to decorate your house since you can just go on a robbing spree in three apartments and have enough to purchase the penthouse in the most expensive building. The game is extremely buggy as well. It's all because of the procedural generation that takes place. The pre-defined rules are not enough to prevent any mishap. Too many times have I been crawling in the vents only to find out that there is a wall blocking any further access into the vents. Memory leaks are a HUGE issue as well. From the way that files are saved to the way that the game runs, its clear that there are some core programming issues at play here. The game NEVER FAILS to freeze up on loading up to just the menu. It also lags out when you've been playing for over two hours. Saving the game is also a big issue because of the freezing during both the creating of the save and the loading of the save. Additionally, the size of the save files is ENORMOUS, good luck trying to have multiple saves because of the sheer storage. If the game was 10 dollars, then I would feel more comfortable giving the game a good review, but as it stands, 25 dollars for an unfinished buggy mess of a game is too much to ask for. It will keep you entertained for about 15 hours but that's pretty much it. I've played the game at almost every major patch and it just doesn't satisfy the consumer's expectations.

_childDocuments_.review: Disclaimer: I spent 10+hours with the demo version earlier this year so this review isn't based purely on 90 minutes of play time.The Good: First impressions in terms of atmosphere and player freedom are very promising. Procedurally generating a city block with this much granular detail is no mean feat. The fact that you can interact with every object and NPC is initially exciting and a bit overwhelming. The tutorial case throws you in at the deep end and you really DO feel like a detective who is painstakingly combing through the crime scene, generating leads, following clues, tracking suspects, sneaking into premises etc. So yeah, that first few hours is genuinely impressive as a glimpse of what an immersive detective sim could be. The Bad: The core game loop starts to feel repetitive very quickly. This is mainly due to the proc gen nature of all the cases apart from the tutorial. I really enjoy detective stories, whether they are novels, tv shows, movies, podcasts, but the thing that I'm drawn to is often the characters, setting and events surrounding the case as much as it is the nuts and bolts of the crimes themselves. If Sherlock Holmes solved the same crime in the same location using the same method every time then it would get pretty old pretty quick. Shadows of Doubt's main problem for me is that there's no compelling story surrounding any of the generated cases atm. It's just similar bare-bones scenarios with the same kinds of leads to follow each time. Personally, I think I'd much rather play a game that had just a handful of crafted, unique cases for me to solve (but still with the freedom to approach each one in my own way) rather than an infinite amount of procedural cases that feel just that.I'm also not that keen on how systems like survival and combat are handled (although this may just come down to personal taste). Thirst, hunger, tiredness etc. feel tacked on and the shoddiness of the combat system makes it feel like the developers would rather you play the game without resorting to violence. It makes me wish that there was a mode of the game where I could play as a police detective rather than a PI so that I could just focus on solving crimes but not have to worry about the other aspects of the game (maybe with the option to break the rules and sneak into somewhere without a search warrant; rough up a suspect for evidence etc.).I really want to love this game - it's the kind of thing I've been dreaming of playing for years and years - but I can't recommend it in the current state. I'm hopeful that the full release will address the main issues I have with it and look forward to playing the finished version.

_childDocuments_.review: Alright, kid, you've stumbled onto a case that's as thick as the fog rolling off the river at midnight. You've got two stiffs, a couple of tickets to nowhere, and a name as elusive as a cat in the alleyways. "Aoibhe," it's got a certain ring to it, but it's as insubstantial as the smoke from my last cigarette. You want my advice? You got it.First things first, you've got to start piecing together the fragments. Every clue you've gathered, every scrap of information, it's all part of a larger picture. Pin everything you've got on your detective board. Fingerprints, physical attributes of the victims, known associates, hell, even their salaries could be relevant. Shadows of Doubt ain't a game for the impatient or the faint-hearted, it's about threading together the strands of a complex web​1.You've got a name, "Aoibhe". It could be a red herring or the key to solving this case. Either way, it's a lead, and in this business, you don't let a lead go cold. Hit the government database in City Hall or any other government building. Plug that name into their computers. It could give you a face, an address, or more information that could help you dig deeper into this mystery​.Remember to keep your tools handy. Finger print scanners, handcuffs, they're your best friends in this business. Use the scanner to collect prints from the crime scenes, the victims' offices, hell, even their lunch boxes. Never know what might turn up​.Be ready to break some rules. If Aoibhe is hiding behind locked doors, you've got to pick those locks or bust them down. If you're lucky, you might find yourself inside before they even know you're there. Be careful though, always turn off the cameras and be ready to make a quick exit if things get hairy​.Don't forget to take care of yourself, too. The streets of this city are as cold and unforgiving as a loan shark's heart. Keep warm, keep fed. Rest if you need to, but remember, the clock's ticking. Every second you waste is another second this "Aoibhe" stays in the wind​1.This case ain't going to solve itself, kid. Remember, in this city, the shadows are deep, and doubt is your constant companion. But keep your wits about you, follow the leads, and you just might bring some light into the darkness. Good luck, detective. You're gonna need it.

_childDocuments_.review: I feel terribly conflicted. Shadows of Doubt attempts something no game has ever attempted before; an actual procedural immersive detective sim. And it nearly pulls it off. Until you realize that ever case is solved by sneaking into the government data base, and spamming your fingerprint scanner everywhere. SoD has an amazing framework, but fails to fully realize its immersive detective sim vision, with severely lacking content and underbaked game mechanics. The dev claims that community feedback is important to them, however this rushed 1.0 release does not reflect the feedback I’ve seen on many forums and discussion boards. They’ve announced that their main intent is to only patch.  While an absolute heartbreak that this game will never reach its full potential by the devs own hands, perhaps the Steam Workshop community can help bring one of the best possible noir detective sims I’ve experienced to its full potential.Until then, temper your expectations, and realize you’ll most likely get several hours of mild enjoyment, but most likely never pick it back up again.

_childDocuments_.review: Excellent puzzle/deduction game in it's early access stage already. I've not had any big bugs yet, the only things I've really noticed is that 1. sometimes a character will be caught in a loop. But errors like that can be solved by saving the game and reloading (or sometimes by a friendly punch). 2. the random cities can have rooms which become inaccessible and 3. running at 20-40 fps on a 7700k/1070 with lowered settings, there's some work left to be done there to optimize the game.At this time most of the cases come down to either one of two ways to solve a case, though the mechanics for these are very much enjoyable. The only other option currently available to solve cases basically involves knowing all the inhabitants of your random city, which feels like you're cheesing it. Next to the main murder cases, you can also do side missions which vary from finding thieves, arresting wanted criminals, taking pictures of people, humiliating people or vandalizing someones home.The game really needs something to create a long term appeal. I can't wait to see the developers add some depth to the game. Perhaps add motives to the mix? Or accomplices? Or strings of cases telling an overarching story? The world building so far is great and it offers quite a few opportunities for that to happen.At the time of writing this, I've played the game for 49 hours. So I would definitely say there's enough content here to justify the price of admission. And hopefully it'll only get better once we get closer to the real release.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is so fascinating in this state because, while truly every feature in the game just fully does not work at least 15% of the time, it's still just such a magical well-crafted experience that I'm fully enamored with it anywayThe randomized detective game is a holy grail, and obviously it has a limited bag of tricks that eventually you get through no matter what. But I think where Shadows of Doubt succeeds is two key core decisions:First, the core of the game is a fully-simulated social city, which makes investigation feel real. It feels very different than games where characters fill a predefined template of criminal and witness and red-herring roles, vs in Shadows of Doubt where the world happens organically: a crime happens when someone reaches a level of animosity in their simulated life to _do the crime_. It's a lot harder to metagame, and thereby more immersive: your conclusions have to be rooted in the facts, because the crime was rooted in the facts, too.Second, the investigation part of the gameplay loop is fun enough on its own, which helps a lot to extend the lifespan of that bag of tricks. You spend most of your time in Shadows of Doubt playing its stealth infiltration game, in new varied areas—but it always feels very connected to and motivated by the deductions, with plenty of freedom and variety in how to pursue them. If this game were just the deductions, or just the stealth, each one alone is nothing special… but together they reinforce each other very well, and give Shadows of Doubt a lot of genuinely fun and fresh-feeling playtime.That said, while I'm excited for what could come in the future about more richness and more content… the bugs are where the focus has to be next. The UI has a lot of rough edges (I can almost never interact with the map correctly), the simulation has trouble with consistency (often shops that are "always open" have no staff working there), things and people clip through walls a bit too often, and there are some holes where it feels like a feature is supposed to be but isn't (no one seems to buy loot items?).But you can feel the magic here, and  the gameplay loop is already a lot of fun if this is exactly the game you crave.

_childDocuments_.review: The first hours of the game are fantastic. When you don't know how the systems work and interact, there's a joy in discovery, and you even sometimes feel clever for figuring something out with an obscure clue you were given.But eventually that novelty wears off, as the limit of the procedural generation reaches its limit on unique scenarios to give you, and suddenly it becomes a routine. There's a few hours where the world is cozy enough you want to linger, and so you grind through the routine of taking your evidence, and figuring out what you need, but you no longer feel clever, as there is no more discoveries to be made, no unique scenarios that cause you to put your thinking cap on.Unfortunately, the game has an end, and the grind it took to get there was a little more than I enjoyed. The final stretch felt like a chore and I almost walked away without completion. Which, after having reached the end, was not worth the push.I do recommend for those first hours alone. It was a solid 12 hours of wonder, 6 hours of comfy routine, and 4 hours of agonizing chore.

_childDocuments_.review: Shadows of doubt has an interesting visual style and immersive setting, clearly taking inspiration from the likes of Blade Runner and Deus-Ex. The voxel world is well crafted and cohesive despite being procedurally generated. It's main game-play revolves around being a private investigator in a dystopian city, hunting down serial killers. There are also different side missions to complete and cyber upgrades for enhancing your sleuthing abilities (or just making you taller).A great surprise for me was that you can buy and decorate your own apartment, you can use it to shower, store items and sleep. Being able to personalise it helps you really feel like you have your own space and get more immersed in the world.Whilst the game is early access but don't let that deter you, what is here is great albeit a little unpolished. There are some bugs and performance issues but if you have a system that can comfortably run the game, I would definitely recommend giving it a go. It has its quirks and there is a limited subset of case styles that generate for the side missions, but this game is already deeply satisfying and ripe with potential.

_childDocuments_.review: Shadows of Doubt is surprisingly good. I was skeptical of the premise, but after watching LGIO's video I had to pick it up. Now I'm behind on work and I blame all y'allThe randomly generated nature of the game is just too intriguing. It does mean that weird stuff can happen, and sometimes a job just can't be figured out - for instance, if the target you are supposed to steal from gets killed by the murderer :O - but that's just how it works out. I wish my computer was beefy enough to play on a very large mapIt's also important to remember that, except for the tutorial, there isn't a planned out clever solution to every case. Sometimes you just have to put in the legwork - spending (in game) hours finding and going through workplace and residency documents, then referencing government records for each individual one-by-one, just so you can try to find somebody with the right shoe size who MIGHT be the killer. In this sense, I feel like this game represents what it's like to actually be a detective than any other experience out thereThis game does leak memory worse than any game I have seen in this decade, though, so occasional restarts are currently required for the best experience

_childDocuments_.review: Don't play this if you intend care about things like "Search Warrants" or "being nice." You'll spend most of your time breaking into places and stealing things, and all semblance of repercussions becomes null after you leave the premises. It's Procedural generation, you'll end up with a "Delancey Street" and also a "Delancey Ave" topped off with an apartment called "Delancey Heights" that is nowhere near either of those roads.World props like Food Trucks seem to pop back in too late, there's some optimization issues with "very large" maps, which are essentially 5x5 city blocks. Investigations usually call for finding "the specific" breadcrumb trail, so far its been fingerprints on the murder weapon each time, and going to the victims place of employment to find a match and info there. UI/UX kinda feels scuffed, navigating between inventory, map, and evidence board. Inventory is limited to four slots, Can't seem to find a way to pawn off expensive stolen goods. my virtual apartment is a hoard of diamonds and questionably-radioactive syringes.Why the Positive review though? Despite all the flaws the game is still fun. The detective work is rewarding; finding an airduct three stories above the crime scene that leads inside so the Robocops don't get mad at me is great, usually because I'm Breaking and Entering into someone's apartment to do so. It's a good and proper sandbox, with a fun concept. It needs work, but its an Early Access title. The core mechanics are good, which is an earmark that the game won't be permanently in development. Get the procedural gen sanitized, optimize the loading seams, and maybe a couple more tooltips on different world functions, and it's a solid game. Worth the sale price, this is more fun than a $80 dumpster fire from any AAA studio so long as you're not addicted to PvP hate-gaming, balance patch notes, or anything with common-to-legendary item tier'ing.

_childDocuments_.review: Recommended, with the caveat that this fascinating early-access experience is still pretty buggy, so if you don't have the patience for that, you'll probably want to wait. That being said, the open-ended nature of the gameplay means it's probably not possible for you to get locked out of progress, since any case that isn't able to be resolved can just be dropped, and another one picked up.Emergent storytelling games are my favorite kind of sim, and the potential in this one is enormous. Currently a lot of the clues and interpersonal dynamics in the game are pretty shallow, but you still have a wide array of ways to approach obtaining the information you need, and assembling it together, to fill in the blanks in your ongoing case files. The 'sync disks' (body mods) are also pretty buggy -- I have a lot of them, but half of them seem to have stopped working at some point. They seem fun, though, and hint at ways to flesh out your detective to change how you choose to play.I'd love to see more depth, but what you'll find here is already intriguing and fresh. I'm really looking forward to seeing how it develops.

_childDocuments_.review: Very questionable 1.0 release when the game doesn't really feel like a fully-fledged game.The game is far too easy. The gameplay loop always boils down to the same simplistic steps: investigate the crime scene, find the leads, investigate the leads (which is primarily just busywork than it is solving a puzzle), discover who the bad guy is (usually a coworker, friend, family member, or a lover/stalker), then doorbash the bad guy and arrest them.This formula very rarely ever changes, and gets infinitely easier as you fill in your records with details of the citizens (or, like everybody else, search up every name in the police database to solve practically every case you get automatically). Although, you do have to pray that you don't get a crime scene that happens outside and isn't a Sniper-type case, otherwise it becomes nearly impossible and you're better off doing literally anything else until the murderer strikes again in 24 hours.As for side cases, a lot of them are identical to each other, but that also assumes that you can even start the side case by not having your only lead be "they sniff farts and their last name ends with the letter 's'" (otherwise it's an instant skip).There are still a lot of worthless character upgrades to get, meanwhile there are upgrades that pretty much break the game and make it even easier than it already is. The balance is extremely weird.There are still countless bugs and performance issues that plague the game.The camera system continues to be largely useless for various reasons - you have better chances of finding the culprit's fingerprints on the underside of a trashcan than you do looking at the cameras that are pointing directly at the victim's apartment door.Talking to citizens continues to be largely useless for various reasons - there has never been any useful info given when talking to citizens in the immediate area of the crime scene if they saw or heard anything suspicious. The only purpose they realistically serve is  giving me the details of a suspect assuming I have enough supplementary details about them or a picture of them. Aside from that, the conversation system only  to have a lot of depth to it, but it is a completely worthless system. The citizens always say the same thing and none of it is ever useful than just breaking into the usual places and fingerprint scanning everything until you find a match to whatever you found at the crime scene.The "design your own apartment" system is extremely pointless other than for vanity and submitting to the developer showcase. You hardly ever go back home except to sleep because that's pretty much the only thing you can do at home. The only three benefits are that you can buy the police vending machine to stock up on handcuffs, buying the food/drink vending machines to fulfill your needs, and buying a shower until you get the character upgrades that make you immune to the "stinky" and "cold" debuffs. All the other furniture cannot be used and/or gives no buffs or other tangible benefits. You can't even cook food in a stocked kitchen, you still have to go to a diner or vending machine.Overall, Shadows of Doubt needed more time to bake, but this 1.0 release is saying many things that we all know what they mean.

_childDocuments_.review: Shadows of Doubt is an investigation style game, one where you play a detective in a dystopian world akin to Blade Runner and oddly enough Bioshock as well, before the collapse of Rapture.  A case is usually randomly started, and you'll have various methods to accomplish your goals. The only issue is that there's definitely a "meta" to figuring out your culprit.  The biggest issue with Shadows of Doubt is that once you've solved one case, there's very little in the way of changing how you investigate, and those methods will usually enable you to arrest the suspect before they're even able to kill another person.  I do love the atmosphere of the game, and the general uneasiness I feel when investigating a murder.  While each case plays out the same, I've encountered several unique cases including a serial killer trying to leave behind puzzles to leave hints as to their identity, which was funny as the anagram didn't matter as I solved it before they could murder again.  Honestly, there needs to be extra variables involved in cases.  I wish I could directly communicate with the developers, as I have a lot of feedback.  I want to see this game start a Renaissance of Immersive Sim games, and so far I loved it.  As it is right now, it is a skeleton of what it can and will one day be.

_childDocuments_.review: The call came over the radio, "A suspected murder, the victim, a 32 year old single white female, dead in her apartment from a single gunshot wound to her spinal cord". My god. Detective Sundance slowly removed his sunglasses in the middle of the night and sat bolt upright in his armchair. He knew this town was going bad, like a portion of synth chicken left out of the fridge too long. Sundance knew how fragile life could be. In fact just that very same afternoon he wandered the streets pelting passers by with a fire extinguisher and then looting their unconscious bodies for loose 1 dollar bills. And so Detective Sundance left his single room apartment, on one of the middle floors of what could only be described as a slum. This town was slowly turning to madness. As he entered the apartment of the victim, a sickly aroma of perfume mixed with gunpowder filled the air. Examining the body, Sundance found a note with the scribblings of a madman on them. A single underscore, followed by a full stop and then four underscores, an i with an accent on top and then a final underscore. Sundance once again, in the middle of the night removed his sunglasses. "My god, we've got a lunatic on the loose". Turning towards the front door he spotted a city directory. Thumbing through it like a chimpanzee attempting to reach orgasm, he found what he was searching for. J.Martín. A name that would forever haunt his dreams. He quickly scribbled down the address on a scrap piece of paper he found on the nightstand alongside what looked to be a tube of lipstick and the pin code for the victim's very securely locked safe. He left, in search of J.Martín.It wasn't too difficult for Sundance to find the perp's home, the building they lived in was opposite the victim's, on the same floor no less and with windows directly facing each other's apartments. Sundance knew that J.Martín had seen something through that silvery pane of crystallised sand that drove them to madness. Upon knocking on the door and waiting an inordinately long amount of time, probably so the resident could climb out of their iron maiden, the door opened to reveal what appeared to be a woman suffering from some form of dwarfism. Questioning this person, it turned out to be none other than Julia Martín. Knowing that she was the murderer due to her insane way of talking and refusing to answer any questions besides the one for her name, Sundance swiftly spun on his heels 180 degrees, clasped a metal bucket that was laying next to the elevator door and launched it at full force directly at Julia Martín's skull. With a disgusting thud, she fell to the floor, folded, like an origami deckchair. Sundance quickly cuffed her and took her prints. She was indeed the killer. Sundance once again removed his sunglasses from his face in the middle of the night, "mother of god" he exclaimed. He quickly filled in his paperwork and ran at full speed out of the building and to City Hall.No one really knows what happened to J.Martín or why she did it. In the end, Detective Sundance only cared that there was one less lunatic roaming the streets at night.

_childDocuments_.review: I've played thousands of games across consoles aplenty and through decades of PC game development. This title stands truly alone among the masses. The concept, the mechanics, the depth of complexity and simplicity of cheesing, this game aces it all. This title is a savage reminder that it's lonely at the top, as your character is a reflection of the game. The more successful you are is irrelevant. In a "living" city, filled with people, you're still a lone detective. Cole is alone, surrounded by games that tried to master any one element of the several perfectly orchestrated elements that comprise this game.

_childDocuments_.review: It’s 12:04 am. You sit at the local diner with a cup of coffee and your notebook out in front of you full of sticky notes and information on places and people of interest. There’s a constant drizzle outside and the temperature is close to freezing tonight. But it always rains here. You go through the info, trying to piece together the puzzle. Wife, uninvolved. Friends haven’t heard anything. The killer cut off all the surveillance 10 minutes prior to the murder. No hateful colleagues or spiteful ex lovers. You checked it all. Then a cold chill runs down your spine, you get a notification that a second person was found killed. You know it was all your fault. If only you had figured it out sooner, you could have saved them.This game is something else. The graphics work. The atmosphere is wonderful. It is creepy and charming, cozy and haunting. You solve murders your way. Bribe people, sneak in, beat people up. There’s a good progression system too.  If you like mysteries, if you want a well-priced game that you can play endlessly. Get this. If you want a game where each persons lives are simulated, along with the complexities of their lives. Get this game. If you want a game where you just punch people and steal their stuff. Get this game. Everything about this oozes charm. The devs are wonderful. The discord is open and welcoming. It is a deep simulator where you can role play out a complex detective at ease.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm unfamiliar with the history of the game in regards to promised upgrades, so I'm recommending it based on what I played. For a procedurally generated open-world detective game, I'm very impressed. The atmosphere gives off strong Noir and Cyberpunk vibes, and it's one of the few detective games where I'm actually doing detective work. The cities it generates actually feel like cities, with apartment buildings and restaurants laid out in a way that makes sense. While the story doesn't really hit hard due to its generated content nature, it's infinitely replayable and always gives you unique scenarios. The addition of buying apartments and being able to decorate them is also a nice touch.
_childDocuments_.name: Shadows of Doubt

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like this game but I can already tell the game just feels shallow.The tutorial mission is great. It has the player chasing down leads, discovering clues, interacting with the world and even had tense moments where you had to think fast and make a quick decision.But after the tutorial the game just falls of a cliff. Almost all of the missions you pick up after the tutorial are a complete joke. Procedural generation might lead to near infinite possibilities, but the reality is that 99%+ of those possibilities are just shallow quests with no real story or any thought behind it, the computer has just randomly decided that person X did action Y, no motivation, no underlying story, no big secret reveal, just a randomly generated glob of pixels doing a random action.Which is a shame, because the tutorial was great, it tells a story of how characters interact and you can piece together their relationships, their actions, and their lives as you dig through their personal spaces, their emails, and their phone calls.   You see a world develop and a story play out. If every case was like this, it would be an amazing game. But as it stands, after this game it's not worth the player's time to do any of the random missions, which is the entire game after the tutorial.

_childDocuments_.review: Game is early access and it does show; the performance could be better but considering what is happening in the background it actually runs quite well. _childDocuments_.review: It is frustrating and unfair when you run across some bugs. Objects can clip through the floor if you place them incorrectly. Some objects will be dropped in unreachable places if you were to drop them from your inventory menu instead of physically throwing it. You are also prone to clipping through floors, and if you didn't save before hand, you'll just lose your progress. You can break windows and jump out of buildings, but you will find it difficult to enter buildings from the outside because of weird texture alignment. Handcuffing a unconscious person will prevent you from taking prints from them, quests that have you throwing objects or leaving objects near places will not register at times. After losing progress about 3 times, I just couldn't stomach much of this anymore. Well it is an early access title, but it's still immensely frustrating.

_childDocuments_.review: Quick foreword:I don't not recommend it because its bad. The game is actually really immersive and fun. The games in a funny position at the moment where there's not enough content to sustain it long term. So if you want to invest and get it now for cheaper (supposing the price increases at the full release) you can do that. Other than that, just wait.Now onto the actual review.Shadows of Doubt is one of those games where I can look at its positives and still have a tremendous amount of fun. For about 12ish hours. There is simply not enough actual substance to the game. You don't really work towards a greater goal outside of retirement so after a point when you finish your first handful of murders you can actually just stop playing entirely as you've experienced all that is fresh about the game.I'll try and list a variety of mechanics or lack there of in a list.Citizen memory functions as a detriment to everything Detective, you can't inquire specifics. You've got a handful of questions you're forced to ask and so you can't ask, "How do you know the Victim?" then explain to them they've just be shot. In fact, NPCs can't actually work out that a citizen has died, so they'd just tell you when they last "saw" them. Which on that topic, NPCs can remember EVERYONE. I ask one guy from one building:"Do you know John Smith?""I saw them on 202 Kovak Heights on Tuesday at 11pm"While this can be helpful, its both unrealistic and it does make things very easy.Player Memory works in a similar manner. Your Detective brain is so overwhelmingly good that you can remember EVERY. SINGLE. NPC's. FINGERPRINTS. So theoretically you can cheese the whole game, by going apartment by apartment grabbing the NPC tenant info and then going through the government directory and log every single citizen in the game. So when a murder happens you can identify prints immediately.Difficulty seemingly does nothing. No, I'm not kidding, I've only played this game on "Extreme" difficulty and have yet to get a case that doesn't hold my hand with how lenient it is. I had a cases that just give the killers name to me on a note at the crime scene.The Murder generation process is slightly broken, while this hasn't personally happened to me, but sometimes murders don't "generate". The game functions like this: Player solves Murder -> A timer plays and then a random civilian becomes a murderer -> The murder occurs -> A second NPC discovers the scene and it gets reported -> New Murder Case! However that body is occasionally not discovered. So what happens then is the game is stuck in limbo. No new murder can happen until that body is found. There is seemingly no workaround for this outside of completely restarting.Money! The game has inflation that rivals pre-WW2 Germany. You can rack up Tens of Thousands and not spend a dime. You get roughly $1800 for completing a murder case, food costs about $4 and thats all you really need to spend money on. You can buy apartments (for little to no reason) for the cost of a murder case or two, but once you've got the ability to actually buy apartments, you have plenty enough money (unless you're playing on Super Quick game speed in which case you won't need an apartment anyway).Theres a plethora of defunct items in the game too. ATMs and credit cards. Blood Types. Guns. Cigars. Video Tapes. Security Cameras half the time. At least half the medicinal items in the game and most building equipment. I'll go into a couple of these.When you or If you, buy an apartment you can fill it up with items like fridges and sinks. However you can't cook, you can't actually get food from your apartment properly. You have to put an actual vending machine in your kitchen to get food, likewise with a coffee machine. At least the TVs work and look pretty.There is an actual phone tracking system in the game, you can use this in the "story/tutorial" mode, but in Sandbox where you'll be spending your time, you don't need it. Whenever you get phone numbers you actually get their addresses too. So whats the point in calling them if you can just go their house? There's a lot of mechanics like this, where there are neat mechanics but there's some other mechanic that is much easier to do that over-shines it.Now I don't want to be presumptuous but I have the strong feeling that the core framework of this game (both mechanically and its coding) is bad. On the surface it works but there's aspects to this game that should be super quick fixes or mechanics that should already be in the game. Like SMOKING. Or civilian re-population that just aren't in the game. These are things that not only work inside the games lore, (it does have that btw, its not half bad too, though rather shallow and underutilised), but also the game needs (more so in the re-population department there). You can effectively soft-lock your game if you play for too long by having all your civilians die. Its a strange feature imo.Now before I go onto one of the larger personal grievances I have with the game. I need to mention, the performance in this game is DREADFUL. There is no reason this game runs as poorly as it does. I've got a 3060ti and 16gb RAM with an i7 and its barely touching 50fps on the highest settings. It drops to around 20fps in hotels. This is a damn voxel game. Minecraft with shaders and over 400 Mods runs better than this. Now. The biggest Grievance. The actual Murders and Side quests. With economic inflation, following your first murder you don't need to do side quests. There is actually more content in the side quests than in the actual murder cases you get. The Liars and Cheats update ONLY ADDED SIDE QUESTS. These side quests do not have any impact on the murders and so they feel almost as detached as the Krypt in Mortal Kombat. You can effectively play this whole game on Very Long game length (which is well over 30 hours long btw) and not touch them once. Not to mention they're also slightly hidden away too. (Bit of an exaggeration there but the game knows they aren't important either). But the point I'm making is, THEY SHOULD BE. Make them have an impact. There so much potential for a cheater to turn into a killer.Adding onto that, the Murders themselves are so bare-bones (There is a limit to what the game can feasibly generate tbf) but a simple investigation on the body/home and a single subsequent investigation can often times net you the killer with ease. At a point you can begin to link the murder names to the type of murder it is and most of the time skip that subsequent investigation. Off memory there are like 5? murder types at most. Which if you're lucky you can get done in the space of about 6 hours. After that you've got hardly anything left to do.I'm aware the only thing I've spouted are negatives but for as long as there isn't enough content in the game, no matter how random it is, it will get boring fast. And considering the next major update is apparently the 1.0 Update I'm concerned with the future development of the game. There is too little right now in the game to go full release. And if its a case of rushing out the 1.0 update to get this game "Finished" then I strongly make the counter case of DO NOT BUY IT.

_childDocuments_.review: What a gem.I'm not big on pixel graphics games, however this holds up very well with some of the most immersive design and good use of lighting that even I can appreciate the art style.The gameplay is where this really shines, incredibly deep detective simulation where everything can play a role in the crime scene: Is there fingerprints on that toothpaste?What size shoes did the victim wear? Do they match up with those boot prints?Where does their spouse work? Whats their working hours? Perhaps I should drop by.Whats the last telephone call they sent/received? Maybe i'll trace itYou get the idea.This might be one of the most masterfully crafted gameplay loops i've experienced and I can honestly see this game being a huge hit.

_childDocuments_.review: Shadows of Doubt is an awesome detective game where you find yourself in a proceduraly generated city with cases to solve as a private investigator. It is up to you on how you want to complete jobs and solve cases as they are presented to you. There is no story, only you and the sandbox world full of citizens going about their daily lives. Collect all the info you can on anyone you can as even your friendly neighbor can end up being tomorrow's murder case.This game is worth more than the asking price even though it is in early access, I have only ran into few small bugs here and there that can be fixed with a "turn it off and back on" procedure. Hope they continue to work on this game as well as add new types of cases. The dev. team should be very proud of this game and it will continue to gain popularity online, especially with us YouTubers.

_childDocuments_.review: Yeah, it kinda hurts my heart to give this game a bad review because I really like the concept. But I'm tired of constantly giving "neutral" reviews here on Steam.There is a good concept here, really, but in all my attempts to play the game and conduct an investigation, I encountered several problems. There are bugs, like the one where the option to ask about a certain person never appears.For instance, I tried to solve a murder and arrived at the location where the police were trying to open the door. At the same time, the assassin casually walks out as if nothing is happening. Of course, I arrested the person, but I couldn't talk to the police or progress with the case. Perhaps I should have let the guy go and pursued him later, I don't know.In another mission, I took a job posting that required me to find someone sitting on a bench in a particular street. Firstly, it was incredibly difficult to locate the person, especially on that confusing map. The game doesn't provide clear directions or an easy way to understand the layout, which is frustrating. Eventually, I found the person sitting on the bench, but when I wanted to ask about someone named Melvin (or something like that), the option simply didn't appear.I also attempted a different job where I had to help a woman find her stolen bottle of wine. I went to her apartment and spoke with her and her partner. I found three fingerprints, two belonging to the woman and her partner, and a third one that I assumed belonged to the person who stole the wine. So, I had some good leads and a few names of their co-workers. But guess what? None of the names matched the third fingerprint. Frustratingly, I went back to her apartment and checked her address book, which had around 30 names listed. I checked every single one of them, including people from the same building and other buildings, but none of them matched the third fingerprint. How am I supposed to find out who stole the bottle and where it is?So... yea... good concept, but too much problems, maybe after a lot of patches, come back in a year and will probably be a better game.

_childDocuments_.review: REVIEW 3.0I've changed my review again, having seen that they are planning to bring this out of Early Access before the game is finished in my opinion, which is something I suspected they would when I first purchased the game. It's still devoid of features. Whilst the base game and features are all there, it all feels very empty of actual content, there's still so much missing from this game to make it a true detective game. There's far too much reliance on guesswork or finding fingerprints. As I've stated previously, motive plays zero role in this game. They're planning to do a Missing Persons update when they release 1.0, which is great, but it's still going to suffer from the same issues that plague it currently. This lack of content and variety makes the game boring, a bit of a chore, and with little replay value. It absolutely stinks of them rushing it out for console, releasing 1.0, then adding a load of features that should be in the base game as 'DLC'. REVIEW 2.0I've changed my original review and I now recommend the game.There are still quite a few problems and issues I have with this game, but at £16, I've sunk a few hours into it and I am quite enjoying it. The new updates have added new case types, the game is more interesting and it's more fun to investigate the game. I am concerned that they're planning to come out of EA soon and release version 1.0, as I don't think the game is in a complete state still and I'm worried they'll abandon it. Some of the issues I have still are the clunky controls and inventory system. I also think there's still not enough variety with cases and the motives behind the murders don't have any bearing on your investigation - I think should be one of the requirements when solving the case. As well as naming and providing the murder weapon you should be able to choose the motive, whether it's a work dispute, infidelity, or a random killing.There's also some silly, easy cases to solve. The killer had left a note at the crime scene which was an anagram of his name, it was something like _ . _ _ _ _ _ _ and the letters JHOSLOV, so I literally went through the city directory and found a name that fit. It took less than 2 minutes to figure it out. It's things like this that break the immersion. Notes at the scene like PUT A PIN IN IT but nothing else alluding to this during the investigation. Put a pin in what? Are they a whistleblower? Were they going to tell the killer's partner they were having an affair? Again, it breaks the immersion. I still take issue with the fact it's trespassing for me to be in crime scenes but City Hall are happy for me to investigate? I like the sync disks for upgrades but some of them feel pointless or overpowered, so I don't end up installing them or even taking them with me. For example the one that gets NPCs to be more likely to provide information is really good, but it makes the game too easy.It's too easy to make money and level up your social credit as well. There's also bugs, objects not loading in, graphical glitches, the floor disappearing from underneath your feet. I get these bugs every time I load the game so I imagine other people are as well? It wouldn't be hard for the developer to replicate the problem and provide a fix.  I just hope they don't stop supporting this game once they come out of Early Access. I've got a feeling a lot of the features that are missing will be included in paid DLC in the future which would be disappointing.  REVIEW V1.0Is it an interesting game? Yes, absolutely. Definitely one of the more unique games I've played.I didn't play it for very long before refunding it. For me, I can't recommend it currently even though it's in early access. There are several reasons for this:Controls are clunky.Inventory system isn't particularly great - you start off only being able to hold 4 items (I am aware this can be upgraded) - but it's extremely frustrating. I don't want to have to go back and forward to the same apartment multiple times just to pick up stuff I've found like Syncdisks. It's tedious and not enjoyable.The map has no variety. A new map is generated whenever you start a new game but they all feel the same. The rooms and apartments all have similar layouts.The npcs have no variety. They all say the same things and do the same things, which takes away from the immersion. No case variety.The cases aren't particularly difficult to solve - often time there is no motive to the killing. You can maybe find one by reading the emails of the victim but it's not required to solve the crime. The murderers often leave cryptic messages or patterns behind in blood - why? Most of the time it's not relevant to the case. You just scan for fingerprints usually and find someone that knows the victim (co-worker most of the time) and get all their fingerprints until you find one that matches.There are also other issues as well, like you get a mystery notification telling you there's a new murder case - how do we know this? Are we psychic? If we're allowed to pick up the case file from the Town hall for it, and essentially authorised to investigate it, why do the police try to kill you as soon as you enter the crime scene? Am I allowed to investigate it or not? Everybody seems to have the same method for storing passcodes - leave them on a note in their bedside draw or work desk. Why? It's daft. The npcs should use codes maybe relevant to them like their DOB which we can guess or try to brute force, but don't force-feed us clues like 'count up from 3'. There's no repercussions for any illegal activity - you just run away. You're an investigator yet you can murder people whenever you want with no repercussions at all. You gain social credit from solving cases but you don't ever seem to lose it. Don't get me wrong, the game has bundles of potential and it's a great concept, it's just unpolished and lacking in content/variety. The game's description says it's been in development for many years, and it's been in early access for 6 months now. It's concerning that it's been in development for years and there's such little content. I just don't feel like it'll ever be in a state where it's fully completed.

_childDocuments_.review: Now I haven't been playing this game for a while, however, I believe it to have amazing potential to be a great game. I would recommend buying the game now while it's cheap, however, I would not recommend playing it, because even in the tutorial there are plenty of bugs and glitches that make the game a lot more difficult than it should be. So far the most prevelant one I've come across is an issue with the loading screen. If you click off the game for even a split second while it loads the game will stop loading entirely, and I have been forced to sit and wait for it to continue. It can also be really bad if you didn't save and cannot exit the game or else you have to start over from your last save point, or if you haven't saved, you start from the very beginningAnother issue i have is the security. The game claims you can turn off security yet when I have tried to it often doesn't work. The game often ignores the fact you have turned it off and continues as if nothing happens. Now, I have a few general issues with the game itself that are a bit annoying overall. Number one is the dead ends in Vents. The vents in the game are already long, winding and confusing with an exit rarely coming along. Pile that on with the dead ends and it feels that it's impossible to escape, that and the apparant stink and cold status effects you pick up while crawling around in them and you'll be stuck for ages looking for a way to get to the place you want to.The game has difficulty settings and I've tried them but it seems no different from one another. It's a big map I get it but easy mode doesn't change any of the difficulty with security, encounters, or vents. I get busy a lot in my real life so I often play games on easy mode so I can experience them with a simple breeze without having to worry too much about getting stuck on fights, puzzles or other such. However this game doesn't offer much of a change when it comes to difficulty. Meaning I haven't actually had the time to enjoy the game because with how busy I've gotten in my real life, it makes it hard to get deep in and enjoy the gameAs I said, buy the game while it's cheap, cause i absolutely expect a price raise when this game fully comes out with all the bugs fixed

_childDocuments_.review: There are those games that come along once in a while. Games like Kenshi, Elden Ring, Half-Life.. That pushes the gaming industry forward and actually takes risks in crafting an experience that hasn't been done before. This is in fact one such example. Shadows of Doubt is an engaging and thrilling game where you play as a Private Investigator/Detective in a noir cyberpunk-esque randomly generated city. Solving Cases is the main drive of the game and its up to you on how to tackle these cases.Without a shadow of a doubt this is definitely a must play game that everyone should experience at the very least imho.If you need further proof: The first time I played, I bought the game at around 10 am and played until 9 pm (Thank goodness its a saturday). I couldn't bring myself to stop playing.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm changing my review to a thumbs down following the 1.0 release. The devs have been very slimy about their release, and due to their announced lack of content post-1.0, this game is essentially dead on arrival for me.  I recommend avoiding ColePowered Games in the future.I first bought this in Early Access in July 2024 and remarked that while it was very fun at its core, the game felt incomplete alongside numerous gameplay polish and bug issues. I expected to sit on this game in Early Access for another year receiving content updates and bugfixes.I was shocked to see the announcement of 1.0 later that month. EVERY community around this game (Steam forums, their Discord, and reddit) had the consensus that this was too early for a 1.0 release. Shortly after that announcement, the devs released a statement assuring people there would be further support and content updates after 1.0:"To reassure everybody, we have no intention of abandoning the game at 1.0. We've worked incredibly hard to develop Shadows of Doubt alongside you during Early Access, listening to your thoughts and feedback to introduce new content and address bugs and issues, and I'm incredibly proud of the 1.0 release."However, one month later coinciding with the release of 1.0, the devs stated in their blog: "We’ve finished making the content we wanted to include in the final game." They followed up that they would be focused on polish and bugfixes.It is unfortunate because this is the bones of an amazing sandbox game - and it could be saved by the modding community, but the announcement of no more content updates has probably killed the hype.
