_childDocuments_.review: It was another cold January night in Charlotte Heights, and the chill hung in the air like an estranged father hangs off a balcony smoking a cigarette. Money was tight, I had no leads on my current case and I had sync drives to feed, so I took a chance on a random job on a corkboard. "Throw some food in a guy's face", seemed simple enough at the time, maybe this was the break I'd been looking for. But everyone knows things are never as easy as they seem in the city of sins.6:45, I rang the number on the ad. The voice on the other end directed me to a payphone across the street. "Be there at exactly 6:48", his raspy voice screeched into my ear. I should've taken that as my sign to leave while I still had the chance, but Mama Hutchins didn't raise a quitter. Maybe a fool though, as I made a mad dash down the stairs of Gomez House in a desperate bid to make it in time. And as luck would have it, I happened to show up right on schedule. The same voice, now with the worn-out speakers of a payphone long past its time adding to the grating of nails against my skull. He directed me to a briefcase nearby, said all the information I needed was in there, and hung up without another word. Looking inside the briefcase, I felt the familiar sting of disappointment hit my gut as I saw the information I had to work off. Or rather, the lack thereof.34 years old. Skinny. Partner works wait staff. Lives on the 7th floor of Gomez House, the very same building I'd been holeing myself up in for the past few months. I find myself stuck between a sigh and a chuckle, as it strikes me that maybe it wouldn't have been such a bad idea to go to that building get together last Christmas, maybe mingle a little bit. "Need to focus on my work", I told myself. Well, now I was going to need all the focus I could get if I had any hope of cracking this case.I quickly gathered the necessary materials for the job: a disposable camera and a hot dog, and spent the rest of the day staking out all four apartments on the 7th floor, biding my time until the owners left their dwellings and rendered themselves vulnerable to my watchful gaze. The fates must have had too much fun toying with me since it wasn't until I was on the very last one that I got any inkling of who I was after. And much like an inkling, I gracefully slid into the apartment under the cover of darkness to snoop around for even a slight glimmer of information on my target, and a slight glimmer I did indeed find. Antonio Walker, a saucy little nonbinary accountant with a rap sheet longer than my deleted browser history, it's no wonder why my client wanted them wienered down so badly. I also came out with another name: Queensworth and Associates, an upscale accounting firm on the other side of town, my target’s stomping grounds. I prayed to the divines that I'd be able to simply waltz in and wiener them and be done with the whole thing, but to my ever-growing disappointment the place was locked up like the giant’s castle around the golden goose. But I was going to get my goose, that was never a matter of any doubt.I thought about simply waiting outside, wiener in hand ready to ambush them on a bathroom break, but by this point my patience was running thin. I needed them like a horny teenager needs a bare-chested boy band alt skin of his favorite League character, and I needed them then and there. So I went home and slept until the inky blackness enveloped the city, and came back to begin my heist.I slipped beneath the all-seeing eye of the security alarm, taking a risky long route to the break room. I wasn't quite sure what I'd find in there, perhaps some half-eaten donuts nobody took the responsibility of throwing away or a crumpled-up love letter for an unrequited office romance, but Lady Luck finally turned a face card in the form of the security office code lying straight on the counter.Bearing my golden ticket, I slipped back the way I came towards the security office, making my way inside and beelining straight for the employee records. Their schedule, exactly what I needed, lying in wait for me right at the front. I decided to celebrate my newfound victory by pilfering the rest of the office, hoping to find some other piece of information on my mark that could be used to further exacerbate the woe of their wienering, but instead I found something much more potent.Two diamonds, nearly the size of my own eyeballs and cut cleaner than a prom night line of synthcoke. a score like that would set a man up in sync drives from here to kingdom come, I'd be hard-pressed to give up that kind of opportunity. But in my haste, I had neglected to leave any room for anything else I’d want to bring home from this adventure, and my pockets were already full to bursting with my codebreaker, handcuffs, camera, and my trusty wiener. I made the tough decision to leave both the camera and the wiener behind, confident that I'd have the time to pick up new ones on my way to ambush the sorry bastard the next day, and quietly retreated out of the building fortune in hand.I sauntered back to my apartment with my newly acquired treasures, pleasuring myself on the idea of being able to have synthmeat every meal until the end of time, when all at once I was confronted with a horrifying spectacle. Antonio Walker, my target, standing right before me completely vulnerable. And me, wienerless and wanting. In that moment I understood what it meant to be blinded by greed, to be so enraptured by material possessions that you lose sight of what's truly important. In that moment I, Roman Hutchins, knew what it felt like to have everything and nothing at the same time.I checked my watch. 3:36. Their girlfriend gets off of her night shift at 4, after that she'll answer the door for them and I won't have another clear shot until they get off of work. I had to act fast, I dropped off my gems in my apartment and ripped out the door back to Queensworth to reclaim my waylaid wiener. I deftly dodged past the cameras and alarms to come back to the security room, where my long-lost compatriots lay in wait for me. After a brief but heartfelt apology, I checked my watch again. 3:52. Time was a luxury I could no longer afford. I ran straight through the alarm in my haste, taking 3 solid backshots from an automated turret on my way out the door. Haven't done that since college, but I guess it's just like riding a bike.With my deadline hot on my heels I raced back to Gomez House, bolted straight up the stairs to the 7th floor, and pounded on the door like I was Nintendo serving a Cease and Desist to a Brazilian startup company. I stood there in agony for what felt like an eternity and then some more, hoping and praying I made it in time. And then it was like the gates of Heaven opened up for me, inviting me into the loving arms of the kingdom after. There they stood, in all their agendered glory, Antonio Walker, the fated recipient of my wienering.Time froze. The wiener left my hands at a breakneck speed. The look of horror spread across their face like a bad case of herpes. And I was in the front row for the whole spectacle. Then all at once, the wiener hit their face, I snapped a picture of their indignity, and hightailed back to my apartment. By the time I realized it was over I was already halfway through turning it in over the phone, and much to my surprise I was rewarded for my efforts with a brand new sync drive, on top of everything else I had gained. Not what I expected, but how could I refuse?Then after that, I slept. I slept for what felt like ages, and when I awoke I was a new man. One unfettered by the draw of riches, with a new outlook for my line of work. A man of honor and integrity, with a renewed sense of appreciation for the journey rather than the destination. And of course, a man who now makes security cameras stay deactivated for twice as long as before. Maybe materialism isn't all that overrated, I suppose. 9.5/10

_childDocuments_.review: I picked this game up after watching Rimmy's playthrough of it, which inspired me to get a copy and try the game for myself.Being an early access game, my expectations were placed on the lower end for good reason, as I was already aware of the plethora of bugs and missing features that still needed to be released. Despite these missing features however, the game succeeds in being both fun and charming enough to offset the inconveniences of early access,The Pros:Although the exploration factor is just a small part of the overall game, it succeeds in exposing the player to the carefully constructed setting bustling with just about enough activity to not make the map feel devoid of life, while not being overbearingly suffocating in its presentation.NPC interactions, though limited, are an appreciated feature in the gameplay in of itself. Wherever it's available, however, NPC interactions are almost essential towards the core factor of the gameplay - the Investigation.The investigative factor of the game remains the core of its gameplay, and can satisfy a wider audience of both veterans and newbies to the genre. The game relies on both your memory and your attention to deliver the best results, and makes it both noticeable and rewarding to do so.Although the game's progression rests on the cases you solve, there are many side-jobs that one can carry out if they want to live their story as a humbler or more oddball private investigator. While they might not always present the highest reward, they do add additional flavour to the games progression and world building..The experience and upgrade system follows a trend I find rather unique in games of this fashion. Experience in this game is defined as 'Social Ranking,' which is befitting to the themes that this game carries in its take on the classic cyberpunk. The use of Syncdisks and Vials for unique upgrades also allows players to bypass the usual problems of rigid level-based progression systems.An optional extra which I wholly appreciated in this game was the 'Player Home' mechanic, providing a homely, safe haven that contrasts the cold, darker atmosphere in the urban world. Here, you can keep stock of your goods, boons and self-defence weapons and reflect on the way your story is going so far.The Cons:Being an early access game, Shadows of Doubt suffers heavily from a lack of optimisation. Despite owning a relatively good spec build, consisting of an AMD Ryzen 9, RTX 3080 and 32 GB of RAM, I still experience FPS drops when playing in fullscreen. This often leads to long loading times and in some cases even freezes and crashes the game. Fortunately, this issue does not seem to affected windowed play.Another graphical issue I've encountered is screen tearing despite having VSync enabled. A solution I found towards this was turning off the FPS Limiter option, which seemed to fix the issue.The presence of bugs is also a given, and the only major bugs I've really noticed are map clipping issues which lead me to fall into endless voids. These often lead you to reset into the map with a leg fracture, which makes this bug extremely inconvenient at the worst of times.Smaller bugs I've noticed include bugging out of the Decor Editor, which often requires you to reload the save to temporarily get it to work again. This normally occurs following an FPS drop, but has on the off-chance also happened continuously with no warning.Aside from graphical bugs, the melee combat tends to be somewhat clunky and sluggish, making escaping from most fights a more preferable option unless you have a good melee weapon, and while guns do exist within the game world they act also like melee weapons, defeating their purpose entirely despite the AI being able to wield them.Although Shadows of Doubt has potential, the inconveniences and performance issues plaguing the game's stability put me on the fence on whether to recommend this game or not. Being an Early Access game, you're effectively paying for an unrefined but mostly functional product; something which is not always the case with games of this type today.I would recommend diehard fans of these types of games to buy it if they are willing to play it while the development cycle continues. Otherwise, if you are a more casual player, I think your best course of action is waiting for the game to get polished and fleshed out a little bit more before buying it for yourself.

_childDocuments_.review: UPDATE #1So most of the major bugs (Like glitching trough the floor, softlocking your game) seem to have been fixed, though I cannot say that with 100% certainty. It has not happend yet, so that's a good thing.As for the murders. They still keep happening at a pretty slow rate. you can go 1 or 2 days without a murder. There are sidequest/jobs you can do in your spare time, but these very often seem either bugged or just very difficult to solve (Example: My mark was a 24 year old person working at the hotel. I checked every single backroom and every single employee file, digital and on paper. There was no 24yo working in the hotel. I found 1 25yo with the same description, not the correct person. Very strange.)Other then that the repetitiveness is still there, although a few small things have been added like a some new dialogue options and I got mugged for the first time (Which means very little as you can just run away, but a nice addition). However every case still has the same steps to follow in order to solve the murder. I really appreciate this game, but i cannot enjoy it for more then a few days a year just because it is always the same stuff.Performance seems to have gotten a small boost, but not that much.Original Review:This is a pretty tough game to review. I really want to love this game. I kind of do. It is very ambitious and has some cool RNG cities. Is it fun? Oh yes! It's a very unique game and I like it. So why the negative review?Well, the game is simply full of game-breaking bugs. And I mean really game-breaking. I had to delete entire worlds with hours of progress because it started bugging out. Hitboxes of floors would randomly dissapear or getting stuck and get teleported into a strangers home are the most common examples. A friend of mine also had 2 worlds where almost no murders happened. That's kind of an issue for a murder mystery game.I also got softlocked out of the tutorial twice. Once because of an alarm that I accidentally triggered was impossible to turn off again locking me out of a building permanently and the other where the RNG build of the world placed my only escape route out of reach, causing me to always get caught by the cops. Lucky this is not an issue in sandbox as it's non-scripted.The rest of the game is really fun, though it get's repetitive quickly (90% the same dialogue for every NPC, usually the same steps into solving every murder etc.), it's still remains fun and has a good difficulty to it. Maybe even too difficult at points.If you can live having your world break at times and have to start over, then you might really enjoy this game. It's very open world, though the worlds are small (unless you have a really good pc that can handle the larger worlds), but expect there to be bugs and expect the game to not hold your hand in anything at all.This game has HUGE potential, but at the moment the gameplay just feels repetitive and technically unreliable.

_childDocuments_.review: This game has the unique ability to make me feel like I truly accomplished something. The unscripted, procedurally generated, cases have to be solved dynamically; this makes for an extremely rewarding game loop. This game has no audible voices, no sense of self, as you hardly know anything about the main character, yet somehow it is one of the most immersive titles I've ever played. Let me explain, to the best of my ability why that is: In a nut shell, the world exists. I could stop there, but I'll elaborate. The world exists...apart from you. What I mean by that is, that the world, it's denizens, and their personal lives, all exist apart from you. For example, Brenda may live on the 11th floor of the building across the street from yours. She has an identity. She has a last name, fingerprints, a shoe size, a husband, a job, an inappropriate romantic relationship wit her co-worker. A phone number. She makes 48k a year, and was recently denied a raise. She frequents a Chinese restaurant a couple blocks from her house. She has migraines and is a meat lover. This is all stuff that is true of her, and might not be true of anyone else. But the reason you're sneaking around her apartment collecting all of this data is because she sent an email to someone a few days ago, an angry email, threatening violence. She doesn't seem the likeliest of suspects, her shoe size doesn't match for instance, the perpetrator was a large size 13, and the victim was killed in a gruesome way, the body encircled by a bloody, demonic, pentagram, but it's the only lead you got. That is, until you discover a human skull in the end table near her bed, and next to it, a pair of men's shoes...size 13. Her husband's...Still that's not enough to go by. You quickly pull his full name off the lease papers they keep in their closet. Alfred Bennis. His business work schedule is pinned to the fridge. It appears Alfred works at Johnson Enterprises. You decide to go to her husbands work place at night time to rummage through the employee records. You find Alfred's file, his finger prints, and a nice clear portrait of his face. You wonder if any of the victim's next door neighbors would recognizes him. Now that you have a picture you head back to the scene of the crime and knock on the door across the hall. An old woman answers, she comes across as a tight lipped lady who doesn't want to put her nose in other peoples business, but you insist, adding with your inquiry a few credits to persuade her to take a look at the picture. She confirms that she saw the man in the picture leave the apartment in a hurry, around 8pm.... An inspection of the victim's body had indicated an estimated time of death at between 7:40pm and 9pm. BINGO! You have a suspect who was spotted at the scene of the crime, who wears size 13 boots, and is affiliated with the victim through his wife. Now, you could keep gathering evidence just to be absolutely sure. Hack into his emails, rummage through his locker at his work to see if you can find the murder weapon, see if you can find footage from street cameras that shows him stalking the victim. Should you submit your case resolution, and find that you were WRONG...well, then you must have missed something. Were the size 13 boots even relevant? Didn't a cop with big feet go tromping through your crime scene before you got there? Did you ever check the trash at the victim's apartment for any evidence.  Well, maybe, you'll get a second chance to catch the murderer after he kills next victim....  And next time, you'll be ready. All of those personal details, connections, and forensic findings not only make the world more believable and immersive, it makes the cases more difficult to solve; you aren't fed leads that prompt pre-written dialogue, you don't have shining clues conspicuously glimmering on the bed. You have a massive haystack of data to comb through with your own deductive reasoning and an absolutely ingenious little evidence board to map out your connections and visualize your logic. THE CASE BOARDI could have written only about the case board. It is single-handedly my favorite part of the game. But let it suffice to say that I was struck by the innovative use of the case board system in a video game the same way I was struck by the Nemesis system in Shadows of Mordor. It made me ask the questions, why isn't this mechanic being used in way more games. Shadows of Doubt is onto something, I can't wait to see what more the developers do.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: Fun game with a solid foundation, already better than some fully released open world/simulationist sandbox games. But there are issues like poor optimization and bugs,  and needs more dev time in general for it to really shine. Would recommend if you're okay with  some tech issues.A really incredible game. It solves a problem of detective games (case resolution being hand-holdy or simple) by marrying it with a problem of open world games (insufficient player motivation) in order to get something greater than the sum of its parts, a detective game that's flexible and robust enough to meaningfully support distinct leads and alternate methods of approach with effectively no guidance or "rails" — outside of some in the tutorial mission, which I would recommend playing just to get a good grasp on the game systems. In general, the fact it succeeds at the promise of the trailer is wild.Biggest and most abject problems right now is optimization and bugs. I'm technically below min specs at the moment with a GTX 970, but this game chugs and frames hang, meanwhile I can run Elden Ring (with the help of MSI Afterburner) smoothly. I haven't run into too many bugs, although I ran into a big one where when waiting, stopping waiting then getting up can randomly teleport you into a nearby area, causing unintentional and often hard to remedy trespassing — cancelling directly out of waiting dodges this bug. I'm aware bugs and optimization are both a high priority on the dev's to do-list, so they may improve, but it's worth noting that they're a bit rough at present.Aside from those, the social systems are minimal at best. Which is fine in that it's functional, the game works, but I feel like dialogue with more distinctive personalities and more ways to convey information to the player (e.g. getting case information in a noir-style conversation rather than from a dead drop briefcase) would really fill out the experience. Although it is understandable that this probably wasn't an early priority given the complexity of implementing things like procedural evidence generation.Pick it up. Looking forward to seeing how the game develops & hope the devs get enough cash to really turn the game into something incredible.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a victim of it's own success.Everything that is listed in the game's description is true and the developers HAVE delivered on the product that they promised in the store page, albeit, there are bugs. Most of the bugs are silly or end up adding a quirky humor to the gameplay, but a few really break the immersion. (Why has EVERYONE in the city decided to never go to work again? Etc...)The issue arises with the fact that the game is really fun and it really works to make you feel like you are a P.I. solving crimes. It does this really well. So why is that a problem?Because the core gameplay loop works so well, it becomes really easy to envision a game that is everything it already is and MORE. The dialogue is fairly basic - there's room for lots more well-crafted and varied dialogue. That wouldn't be hard to add, right? It kind of seems like a P.I. should be able to smoke a cigarette...that would be fairly easy to add, right? What if we added things like Taxis to the game...that would be easy to add, right? What if someone committed a crime against you, (Like robbing your home while you were out.) That should be easy to add, right? Would it be possible to investigate a cold case? What about using Chat GPT so we could interact with the NPCs by asking our own questions? What about a cooking system? What about...etc, etc...The issue is that the game has the POTENTIAL to be not just a good game, but a truly genre-defining game worthy to be held alongside classic titles like the original Deus Ex.The potential is there, and it's really easy to see the potential. But the devs never promised to deliver on most of what people are complaining about.Did the devs deliver on what they set out to do?Yes. The game is a solid 7/10. The only reason it's not higher is due to the bugs.Could this game receive tons and tons of DLC and expansions?Yes. The potential content that could be added to this game is staggering.The real question is whether or not the devs actually *want* to take the game to the next level that the fanbase so desperately wants. If they don't want to, then I hope they honestly put the effort in to help the modding community have the tools they need, because this could be a game with an active modding community for a decade at least.This game is easily worth the full price.

_childDocuments_.review: Shadows of Doubt is a dream game. The ultimate detective game where you decide how you want to solve cases by discovering clues all on your own and following leads you prescribe. The procedurally generated world is its own entity- a living city in which its citizens have their own lives, needs, and daily tasks. Random crime can upset the balance, though so can you, by interacting with the world however you like.The world will react to your every action, good or bad, and reward or punish you properly. Murders happen, and if you don't find who-dun-it, they will continue to happen. Use anything you can at your disposal to build your evidence case: fingerprints, emails, motive, weapon used, confession. Bribe, sneak, trespass, interrogate, threat, steal if you wish- just try not to get caught committing a crime yourself. As of now, the game is not finished, but it's still a gem. I'm wishing the best for the final product, for there is absolutely nothing else like it.

_childDocuments_.review: Firstly, this review was written by  who borrowed the game from my account and cannot post it via theirs. All words were written by them.Shadows is really genuinely one of the best Immersive Sims I've ever played. An entire 6 blocks (and more, if you generate a larger map) that feels intricate and believable. Your jaw is guaranteed to drop once you open a phonebook and see the names of every citizen and business on your little dystopian island. And it's not a shallow simulation, either; Citizens have schedules, Likes, Homes, Jobs, Friends, Family, Medical history, purchase history, bank accounts, emails - most of which are entwined in some way. The game constantly surprises you with the amount of little creases and clever details. Shadows feels like a Bethesda engine game taken to the next level and wrapped around a murder mystery theme. The game is packed full of little mechanics built to immerse you in your role as a detective. Reading the newspaper report on the murder the day after for clues; Canvassing friends, family and neighbours, each with their own opinions and disposition; Sneaking into an admin room at night to steal phone records.The game is remarkably well paced despite its random nature. You feel like you're in your own little detective novel. From taking time to do side jobs while you work on the case you can't crack - then finding sudden inspiration from it, to running to the killers home before they strike again - only to be seconds too late. Even with lack of polish in early access, the simulation runs incredibly smoothly. NPC's path well, show up where they ought to and generally behave as you would expect. The only issue is they talk and act like little clockwork robots in current patch. The devs say a writer is working on the writing right now - whether this is just lore or dialogue remains to be seen.The game captures the feeling of being a Noire detective better than practically any other game on the market. For example, my third case included a professional killer that left nearly no clues. The killing was related to a late payment - but what were they paying for? After reading through the medical records of the victim, I noticed they had a lot of a particular brand of medicine that was not prescribed by their doctor. After checking the black market doctor - I found a matching print in the employee record. I felt really clever for making this logical deduction myself, without relying on brute force. And the game allows many ways to deduce the killer - You almost never feel like it's impossible to catch them.Judging by my playtime and what I've said so far, you might wonder why I can't recommend it - Simply, you find yourself running up against the limits of the random generation very quickly. In about 12 hours of playtime, I had 6 out of 8 murders play out in one of two exact same ways - A disgruntled debt collector, or a corporate killing. The former of which always includes a note as a clue (A game of hangman with the killers name) that makes the case trivial to solve. It makes the murders feel very gimmicky and a little depersonalised. Other times, the game generates next to nothing, and you're left scratching your head wondering if the simulation has bugged out, or if you're just stupid. Add on the characters talking like little robots, the experience begins to feel very game-y and limited.The game has side-jobs that are a little less gimmicky E.g. A stolen item or a corporate espionage. These jobs will randomly choose a few facts about the victim, and leave the rest up to you. I ultimately ended up preferring these side-jobs to the murders. The murders became routine quickly, and you can deduce the killer easily based off of the "type" of murder. Side jobs don't have these, and require you to lean on the games more intricate systems to solve them, which is where most of the fun is.The game also has some survival mechanics. Survival mechanics can be used to enhance and add stress and pacing to an experience; this is especially true of cyberpunk. Scraping up credits to make rent and deciding whether to spend your pay on food or drink can be used to make a setting feel dystopian - As of right now, they're just annoying to deal with. After your first case (the game spawns in many high value items in safes - money is not an issue) you will no longer feel like money is a problem. Thus, eating and drinking start to just feel like an annoyance. Getting cold is particularly irksome - If you have to stand outside and use one of the outdoor terminals, good luck using the cursor as your detectives head shakes around like crazy. Don't get me started on the drunk status effect. All the effects are trivial and all of the effects annoy - which diminishes the tension and immersion.These aren't fundamental flaws, though. A lack of content is just the nature of early access, and the survival mechanics are well founded in principle. Shadows has an immense potential but I cannot recommend dipping in early if you're looking for a lot of content to play - you will start repeating yourself very quickly and the edges are very rough.I do recommend trying the game to play the first pre-generated tutorial case and perhaps some of the side-jobs. It is an excellent showcase of what the game is capable of - and is what the final game should aspire for. Great writing, Interpersonal in a way that feels less like clockwork. An intricate case with many leads to follow up on with a clear motive for murder. If every case in build 1.0 captures the feel of that first case, the game will be amazing. Hopefully I can come back at launch and change this review. I'm looking forward to it, even! Just give the game a little bit of time, I think.

_childDocuments_.review: Shadows of Doubt is everything I have ever wanted in a game. SoD is an incredible detective game where you actually have to do the thinking for yourself. Why are there so many? And sometimes not even on the doorknob)*Arriving too early at a crime scene will sometimes cause the AI to freak out and run around in circles.* The AI will sometimes get permanently stuck in a loop of moving furniture or turning on and off light switchesThere are also some aspects of the game that don't make sense to me at all.* You receive a murder case from the city hall, but the police won't let you investigate. _childDocuments_.review: Shadows of Doubt: A Bold Concept That Falls ShortShadows of Doubt ambitiously strives to carve out a unique space in the detective simulation genre, presenting itself as a noir-inspired, procedurally generated playground. The allure of such a game lies in its promise of fresh, unpredictable mysteries and a world teeming with life and depth. From a distance, the striking visuals and compelling concept may pull you in, hinting at a world where each corner hides secrets waiting to be uncovered. Yet, beneath its polished surface, the game struggles to deliver the depth its premise implies.While the game excels in creating a visually rich environment, the cracks begin to show in its execution. After just a few hours, it becomes clear that the procedural generation, though ambitious, results in a world that feels surprisingly monotonous. Every building you enter, every character you encounter, starts to blend into a repetitive sameness. The initial thrill of stepping into this dystopian sandbox quickly gives way to a sense of hollow repetition. There's an undeniable lack of diversity, both in the environments and the personalities that populate them, leaving the world feeling less alive and more like a stage set on repeat.The gameplay itself, while intriguing at first, suffers from a lack of meaningful consequences. There's a certain freedom in the game—exploring NPC homes, solving cases, and navigating the city—but that freedom comes without much weight. Killing innocent civilians, for instance, carries no real repercussions, eroding the sense of immersion and accountability that could make such a sandbox world truly engaging. Even dying or losing a fight lacks tension, as you're simply carted off to the hospital with little more than a shrug.And what of the core of the game—solving cases? While the detective work can be satisfying initially, the game falters when it comes to sustaining interest after the first few cases. Once you've solved a mystery or two, the realization dawns that there isn't much else to do in this world. Roaming the city quickly becomes a dull affair, as the environments offer little in the way of unique experiences or compelling activities.In the end, Shadows of Doubt presents an intriguing premise and an eye-catching world, but it stumbles in its execution. The game promises depth and complexity but delivers a surface-level experience that quickly grows stale. While it's admirable that the developers aimed for something new and different, the result is a game that feels like it hasn't quite figured out how to fill its own vast, empty spaces.

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of the coolest game engines I've ever played. The level of immersion and sim is simply incredible. I will be playing this for many more hours.If you like stealth/stealing/questing in Bethesda games, this is effectively infinite of that. The meta progression within a save file is very compelling as well. Owning your own apartment and furnishing it is a nice treat after you complete some cases and have the extra cash. Your character also earns social status and can get upgrades through DNA splicing (or something to that effect) which keeps you playing on the same save and city even after completing your first few cases on a character.Only real flaw is the bugs regarding some of the generation and overall performance. I've started a new save stuck in a wall, and have fallen through some floors. Fixed by just generating a new city. The game will hitch randomly while loading sections of the city and there is some jarring pop-in even if you have powerful hardware. This rarely affects the actual gameplay though, as there is little in the game that requires fast reflexes (besides countering melee hits, which is a bit finicky also). This should also improve over time from more optimization.If I start going more in depth I'm going to be typing for half an hour. If you're interested in immersive sims, procedural generation, detectives (and procedurals), emergent gameplay, puzzle solving, stealth, cyberpunk, or any mix of those, this is the game for you. There is so much here already, and seems like it will only get better with time.Highly recommended. I hope there is modding and workshop support in the future because the foundation for this game would create some fantastic customized experiences with mods.

_childDocuments_.review: I love games where I can wander around freely and explore every nook and cranny. Usually that means ignoring the main objective and it feels like I'm not really supposed to spend so much time looking around. But not in this game – this game heavily incentivizes you to explore and check anything you come across. It feels very immersive and rewarding. It’s so fun that you can explore literally every part of the map. No building or apartment is off-limits.Admittedly, this game does have a lot of bugs, but I haven’t come across any game-breaking ones yet. I’ve just learned to work around them, or I go back to my last save file if needed.My only real gripe with this game is the building mechanics. I would love to decorate my apartment but the way it works is pretty frustrating. I wish it was easier to pick up furniture and items you’ve already placed – just by clicking on them, without having to search for the right thing in the catalog first. I also wish there was a way to change the colors of my furniture after placing it. It’s difficult to match colors before placing something and you lose money every time you sell and re-buy an item.

_childDocuments_.review: Games honestly really fun, the core mechanics are solid and that creates a really fun an re-playable game play loop for those who enjoy it. _childDocuments_.review: TLDR: 10/10 would drunkenly stumble around a victim's apartment and beat up bystanders to escape the enforcers again.My first case:Someone slides a note under my door, asking me to find someone. I have nothing to go by but their name. (Yup, the default handcrafted tutorial scenario, gotta start somewhere). I use the directory to find out the adress tied to that name and go there. On the way, I find a bottle of bourbon in the street, which I pick up (very important detail). I eventually find the building, I go upstairs, find the apartment. No one answers so I let myself in and find a dead body. I begin investigating, death by bullet wound, low caliber, the weapon is on the kitchen counter, there is an expended cartridge in the living room, there even is a supressor in the victim's safe. Seems like an open and shut case. I make my way to the bedroom and find a codebreaker on their desk. As I go to pick it up I realize my inventory is full. (Mind you at this point I had fully intended for a serious playthrough.) So I figure, in order to empty an invetory slot, I should down the bottle of bourbon I picked up earlier, and I do. Halfway down the bottle I put it on the desk and realize my mistake. I do pick up the codebreaker with my newly freed inventory slot but I'm absolutely plastered. I go back to the kitchen to start taking prints, stumbling and falling over every piece of furniture in my way. I somehow manage to reach the victim's body and take their prints, then I begin looking for prints elsewhere like on the gun. This takes me a ridiculous amount of time as I'm unable to hold the print scanner steady. Eventually I do succeed and it turns out the gun on the kitchen counter was full of the victim's prints, In fact there were no other prints in sight. I decide to dig up the trash can for something useful and after digging out a few milk cartons I find a receipt for a diner, and a crumpled note about a weapons deal. There's a lead! But now on top of being drunk I was also smelling like a trash bag.I decided to borrow the victim's shower for just a little bit, and on my way out of the kitchen I see the safe again... RIGHT! THE SAFE IS OPEN! I do my best to scan for prints on the safe and sure enough, those are not the victim's. After a quick shower I decide to take a look at the phone to see the calls listing, but I do something wrong andtrigger an alarm. I rush for the kitchen once again, remembering a vent I can escape from. I attempt to climb onto the counter to reach the vent and fall head first onto the floor. I get up, and try again, and I fall again. I too drunk to climb onto the damn counter! Eventually I hear banging on the door: "ENFORCERS, OPEN UP". I was wise enough to lock the door behind me which gave me enough time to go into hiding under the victim's bed, just as the cops busted down the door. I laid there for what felt like forever, waiting for a chance to make a run for it. While waiting, I accidentally found the victim's diary under the bed. The victim was clearly worried about something, two names were brought up. One seemingly a friend, the other sounded like an unsavory type who had roped the victim in some shady business.Some time had passed and I was feeling less drunk, but a headache was also starting to make itself known. There were only two enforcers i nthe appartment, but one of them was guarding the door, preventing me from leaving the bedroom. At some point however they were called over by their colleague in the bathroom. That was the openning I was waiting for. I ran as fast as I could to the kitchen and jumped in the vent. The definitely heard me so I had to get out of those vents fast. One tiny problem, I had no idea where I was supposed to go. I crawled around for a bit trying to get to another vent that would allow me to reach a lobby, but I accidentally ended up in someone's apartment. And they weren't too happy to see a stinky drunkard come down from the ceiling.I had to beat up the both of them, in self defence of course. But their front door was locked. I tried looking for the key to no avail. One of them woke up before I could find it, and they ran straight through that front door, leaving it open for me, but raising the alarm in the process. I sped out of the apartment and down the stairs as the gun turrets were looking for the culprit and someone made it out unscathed. I took a breather on a bench at the port, then headed over to city hall to grab a case form. Then I had to pick a lead.I had a few options before me, I could investigate the diner for which I found a receipt, I could also ask around the victim's workplace, another option was the phone number that last called the home of the victim, and finally, the arms deal note had an address on it. I opted for the safest one and went to the victim's workplace to ask around if anyone was aware of anything shady going on. When I got there, I talked to the receptionist and negotiated a guest pass, only to realize I was talking to the receptionist of the wrong office. My victim worked nextdoor. So I went nextdoor to the right office. It was noon and only the boss was there but he proved rather uncooperative. I waited for him to leave and snuck in.I used the codebreaker from teh victim's apartment on the first cruncher I found and got the admin codes. Turns out that first desk I hit was the friend from the diary. I skimmed through their emails which confirmed the story. The victim was stuck in something shady, and couldn't leave safely. The friend had reasons to believe someone was coming for my victim, I guess they were right. I also found an email from my victim to their arms dealer, and that email had their full name. By that point I was pretty sure the dealer was the murderer, but all I had was circumstancial evidence.My next move was to check out the adress for the arms deal, some decrepit basement full of shady people. I was clearly not welcome here, and I decided to bounce before one of them showed an itchy trigger. Defeated, I decided to visit the victim's friend, his adress was in the victim's address book so I didn't have to work too hard to figure it out. As the elevator door opened, my heart sank. The murderer had found him before me, and tied up his loose end.I didn't know what to do, I guess I still had the diner to investigate but that didn't seem like a promising lead, and unless I had a full enforcer team to back me up, no was I could take a look around the arms deal address, and we all know that wasn't gonna happen. Then it hit me, I had the murderer's full name, I could just look up their adress in the city directory, and arrest them there! And so I did. As I reached the 3rd floor of the building, someoen had just come home and shut their door. I knocked on another one, and asked the person who lived their if they knew this person. They informed me that they were neighbours, and directed me towards the door that had just been closed.This was it. I steeled my resolve. No mistaked could be allowed here. First I lockpicked the breaker box to shut the security door, I wasn't letting them get away. Then I knocked. I tried asking politely first, about their name, if I could have their prints, if they knew the victim... Naturally they told me to mind my own business, and closed the door in my face. I couldn't go home like this. The only proof that could tie them to the murder was the prints I found, since I didn't ahve the weapon. So I had to get their prints. I busted down the door and fought them. Got a pretty nasty leg injury but that was it. I passed them the cuffs, took their prints, and sure enough, they matched. Case solved.I limped back to city hall to hand in the case form, and went home for a good night's sleep. I couldn't help but feel like I could have prevented the second murder, but at least, the murderer was now behind bars.

_childDocuments_.review: I showed up to a crime scene and found a bullet hole through the window. It was pretty hard to spot -- it was up high, covered by the curtains. Knocked on doors, asked to check out people's apartments. One guy on floor 5 had a flattened cardboard box on the ground in front of his window; I looked out the window and it had a perfect view to the victim's apartment.Searching the rest of his apartment, I found a receipt for a rifle and ammo. At this point I was pretty sure I found the killer.I searched his job but found no rifle. Went back to his apartment, and there was a rifle on the ground. Had his fingerprints on it. I was so excited that I arrested him and submitted the rifle that I had found as the murder weapon.Results: I got the killer right but the murder weapon incorrect. I went back to his job to try to figure out what I missed. There, I saw a note on the wall that said "Rifle for sale". Two fingerprints on it: the killer and one of his co-workers.Turns out this is what happened:Killer owned an antique rifle, he sets up deal to sell it to a co-worker.Killer bought a new rifle, used new rifle to shoot victim, then sells new rifle to co-worker an hour later.Using the sale, killer kept the antique rifle AND passed the murder weapon off to his co-worker.10/10 game.

_childDocuments_.review: Edit: I've solved a case! It's the best game ever! Also turns out if you knock on a door you can bash it in as someone's opening it for free clue-searching! It's a bit silly but it works!It has a great atmosphere and is very immersive. The way you connect clues with red string is brilliant. That's it however. If you'd like to explore a little in a noir environment it's good. If you want to have fun it's a chore.Why doesn't the gameplay work though? Well, on paper it's great: you go around and find clues and put it all together in your brain and you figure everything out. In practice in 99% of cases to get clues you have to go into apartments whose inhabitants never leave and never let you in and when they sleep they wake up when you open drawers/turn on the pc. The stealth mechanics are atrocious and nails-on-blackboard irritating. Worse yet, you need to crawl around in darkness with a pathetic flashlight to not wake everyone up. And there is no brightness slider. You're in the deepest depths of Tartarus in this one. If there was a way to distract people out of their apartments or give them sleeping pills that'd be great. I am not aware of those mechanics however.Because all the murders and clues (and everything) is procedurally generated there's no clear way forward on an investigation. You need to thoroughly comb through every inch of the victim's apartment, all the people they know from their address book (sometimes there's 20 or 30) and the places the victim and all their friends work. Having to ride up and down 20 floors on an elevator is incredibly annoying. Sometimes you need to do it 50-ish times in a single investigation in multiple buildings. Lock-picking is annoying, you're always out of lockpicks. Turning cameras off is annoying: it's trivial and always exactly the same except you need lockpicks. If that's called fun gameplay, I'm out.There's also bugs but it's early access, those will probably be fixed, fair enough.I'll keep playing it because I really want to like it and it feels like it really has the beginnings of something great but at the moment I wouldn't use the word "fun" anywhere around it.

_childDocuments_.review: It's  good, despite the few occasional bugs. Also, the case structure is a little repetitive, but I was never bored in my playtime so far.After 43 hours of playtime, my first character, Josephine Moore, was finally ready and able to retire to The Fields. It's said to be a better place. Better than the megacorporate hellhole island that Starch Kola rules with an iron fist...Shadows of Doubt is probably the best detective game and immersive noir sim that is currently available. Your character won't simply narrate the solution to themselves like in many other games that feature "puzzles". There is no handholding once you've completed the tutorial case. The only "handholding" comes in the form of being able to set a waypoint to any discovered location and certain information being automatically connected to a certain person or location.Josephine's days usually began with her wandering around town, going to Trinity Fox Tacos or Rosaunnes Restaurant to grab a bite and a can of Starch Kola. Her police radio always primed and ready to pick up information on the latest murder. Sometimes she wondered if it still functioned correctly, as the printing press was able to print and issue newspapers with an article about the latest victim just as quickly as her police radio gave the message that a murder had happened. But that doesn't matter in the grand scheme of things.Only once in her time in the skyscraper-town of Okinawa had she been the first to discover a murder victim before the Enforcers. They usually were very quick, but on that one case, she got lucky. It happened right before her eyes, on a busy marketplace. The screams from the bystanders witnessing one of their peers just drop dead to the floor must have alerted the Enforcers. The killer was able to blend into the chaotic crowd, which quickly dispersed into multiple directions, and so Josephine decided to focus her attention on the victim.She quickly grabbed the finger prints of the corpse, took a photo and rummaged through their pockets, before the Enforcers would come and make access to the corpse that much harder. Nothing useful aside from the wallet of the victim. Name, adress and a key to their home were now in Josephine's posession. As she was ready to ask a nearby pedestrian if he had seen anything weird, she noticed a crumpled up paper under a foodtruck. And next to it, an empty syringe. , it read and below it where a bunch of scrambled letters. Using her Print-Scan 800, she added the fingerprints on the killer's love letter to her caseboard.Occasionally sipping on her coffee, Josephine approached the door to the victim's apartment. Annoyed at herself, that she didn't manage to pin the killer right on scene, she flung the half-empty styrofoam cup down the flight of stairs she just came from. Then, she whipped out her trusty print-scanner and methodically analysed every fingerprint she could find on the door. And there it was: One of the last legible prints on the door handle matched those on the crumpled paper the killer left behind as well as those on the syringe. Now Josephine only needed to figure out who those prints could belong to. A neighbour? A colleague? She headed for the building's security room to review the camera footage.....Seriously, this game is so fun and not only will it be satisfying when you solve a murder, but you'll also feel incredibly smart, because  were able to figure it out. Not the game.I only have two or three negative things to say about Shadows of Doubt:That said, if you like the idea of being a private investigator who barely scoots by the law (and sometimes wades through literal poop water) to solve murders, this is the game for you, even in its current Early Access state!

_childDocuments_.review: I went into this expecting a small and repetitive- if interesting- experience. I was pleasantly surprised by the evidence and case system. The corkboard allowed me to put together cases in ways that other investigative cases would never allow, and the custom sticky-notes let me put a bit of fun flair into it as well. The multitude of upgrades (in the form of disks) allowed me to gradually have an easier and easier time finishing cases, though the one complaint I might have is that buildings that have CCTV systems visible and able to catch you breaking the law do not always have security rooms in which to access them, though that is the nature of procedural generation, and only once did it lead to me having to drop a case for lack of leads.Overall an incredible experience for the price. Once you have an understanding of how the game mechanics work, most larger cases are a relaxing but engaging pattern of finding the evidence, collecting as many identifying features as you can for your target, and then going to town hall in the hopes of finding their additional information to close the case. Alternatively, you can also go on foot, inquiring through the crowds until you find a lead. It is also important to note that this is an early access title, and a shockingly complete one, at that. Definitely worth the buy as it is, but if you're hesitant about committing to an EA title, then I'd recommend keeping an eye on it and buying it when you think its right.

_childDocuments_.review: Shadows of doubt is a game for people who are fascinated with procedural generation, and motivated by stealth, and .  It is a fresh and interesting take on crime solving and I think the presentation is precisely what I've been waiting for for a long, long time.  The voxel graphics allow the game to get right into the action without taking itself too seriously.  It's set in the future but simultaneously the past which is interesting:  Phones ring.  There are phone books and registries.  Lots of paper littered throughout the world so you can theoretically approach situations like you would imagine cops do.  Looking through drawers for clues, bits of paper with passwords scribbled on them.  Now, granted, the procedural generation makes things a little bit predictable, like every shop will have a picture of all of it's employees, and there will definitely be a password for the computer terminal you're looking for scribbled somewhere, and everyone's password is the only password you ever need to find for that person - which, actually now that I think about it, is actually pretty realistic...  Still, your approach needs to change based on where your targets are and what their personality is like.I think this game is fun right now, on it's own.  I think if they were to expand on the systems, this game could become something amazing.  It's amazing now, and I just want to shout out to the devs - you guys did a really good job and I love this.  Well done, I'll recommend it to my girlfriend.

_childDocuments_.review: One of the most unique games I've played.Procedurally-generated murder mysteries in a procedurally generated city. Lots of gameplay systems interacting with one another. The process of solving the mysteries is tricky at first and especially with this being early access, you can't be 100% sure that it won't bug out. But it's in a remarkably good state, and there is a lot of fun to be had as it is.When it comes to solving mysteries it solves the standard detective game problem that you can keep rubbing different items together and end up getting the answer. There are hundreds of characters and locations so it is simply impractical to solve a case using that method.All your good sleuthing stuff like scanning for prints, crawling through air vents, tracking phone calls, sneaking into their workplace at night or bribing people to let you scout around.Only thing that is (currently) lacking is cases don't seem to generally have a motive. I work out who the killer is from their prints but have no idea why they did it, as I can't ask and they don't seem to reveal motive outside of the tutorial so far for me through their email correspondence.

_childDocuments_.review: I love this game. But I can't justify buying it for $20 in it's current state.The amount of game-breaking, soft-locking bugs I'm running into this patch makes the game unplayable. Here are some that I run into frequently:Citizens won't follow work rotas, either not going to work or returning home when they're supposed to (sometimes not doing either.)Citizens randomly walking in air and clipping through walls.Citizens getting stuck in a loop of opening a door, locking it, unlocking it, going back inside, and repeating the process.Alarms in the city hall being permanently on alert no matter how many times I disable them or sabotage them, which means that when I die I get respawned in the ward and then instantly killed by the security guns (which starts an endless death loop.)Sometimes I'll take damage and the screen will go pale showing that I'm clearly still damaged, but it won't tell me what effect I have so I can't heal myself back to full health correctly. Sometimes I'll try every drug and splint and bandage I can, but my game treats me like I'm still about to die.Aside from the bugs that desperately need attention, more generally, I believe the game to be repetitive. I understand that's part of the deal with generative content, but I would love a story mode with handcrafted, challenging murder cases with diverse puzzles. I really love the tutorial, for example. Most cases feel like you have to track down the target by breaking into their home or workplace.I wish dialogue was more robust. I am a detective, yet I can't really interrogate anybody. I want to be able to say more than a handful of things to the people in this world. I want to ask them where they were at x time on x day, who they were with, etc. On the same note, I feel like shops are very lifeless at the moment. I want to be able to ask shopkeeps about their customers, who was there at this date, what did they buy, who were they with, has anyone bought a knife from you in the past couple days, etc. I know there's gun dealers who have records of their customers, but I'd like for the legal shops to be more interactive. I'd also like to see the citizens go to social events and have leisure time, like going to dance clubs. I'd like it if they could actually go to club meetings since so many NPCs are in them. I want them to have hobbies and interests and do activities that reflect those hobbies and interests. I want them to go to locations other than work and home. It would add to the immersion and bring many more interesting potential crime scenes and suspects.Some other various things...Let us throw away items more easily - Especially briefcases! I don't like throwing them on the ground, and I don't like having to throw them into the sea either. Can't we just throw them in the dumpster?Performance issues. I lag so badly when it rains and when I'm walking outside.Please make something we can wear permanently to get rid of the cold effect. If we could buy clothes, like a scarf, that would be great. I'd gladly give up an inventory slot dedicated to a scarf or coat to get rid of that annoying shaky cam. An umbrella for rainy days would be great, too.Also having more options to sit and pass time would be nice - especially if we could speed up how quickly time passes. I often need to leave a building to find a place to sit and by the time I find an appropriate location I'm far away from the location I want to be at.Again, I love this game, but it really needs polish right now. I honestly wouldn't recommend buying it in it's current state as I get soft-locked SO often it doesn't feel playable. I would have recommended it a few patches ago, but now it's just too frustrating.I will update this review next patch. I very much want this game to succeed.

_childDocuments_.review: In some ways this is my dream game - a wide ranging and complex procedural simulation PLUS a detective game PLUS Deus Ex IMSIM gameplay. That promise, and the places the game comes VERY CLOSE on delivering on it are what's kept me engaged so far - but they have a lot of work cut out for them in early access to deliver on it.The Good:- The breadth of the simulation so far is genuinely impressive, the number of people, their schedules, and the ways they are all connected to one another is all very cool. The way crimes emerge and pieces of evidence connect them is a genuine development feat - and solving these crimes feels like real, actual detective work. It's absolutely unique and the fact that the game is delivering on this core promise so well already makes me very excited to see where it goes from here.- I really like the presentation- The tools that you have so far are well-thought out- I'm a sucker for crawling through vents and rooting through people's emails, and the fact that literally every room in every building is explorable and populated with this stuff is incredible- The amount of STUFF in the game is incredible. Procedural murder solving, an apartment you can decorate, various side jobs, sneaking, fighting, etc. it's very impressive for a sort-of solo dev effort.The needs-improvement:- It's buggy as hell. Obviously it's an early access sim game, so that's going to happen, but I think I've gotten used to devs doing much more polished, more promotionally-oriented EA releases and this isn't that - it is VERY unfinished and the game breaks all the time. In its current state, I would say there's a 25% chance that any given action/interaction in the game will just completely fail.- Sometimes this bugginess is funny - NPCS will start going buck wild and attacking eachother - but often its frustrating - frequently I'll get jobs that give me one or two details about an unnamed target, and either their residence or workplace - but nobody matching those details works/lives there and the job is incompletable. You also clip through the environment A LOT, and plenty of other wonkyness.- Case/Content variety - after playing a few hours the limitations of the existing content REALLY start to show. There are a limited number of kinds of crimes to solve (and a few brute-force techniques that will almost always work).- One of the limitations of the current system I'd like to see changed is that the victim ALWAYS knows their killer personally, even in a contract killing - which means their killer's name is always in their address book, giving you a no-fail (if tedious) path to victory every time.- The same goes for other content, like emails, the various details and goings-on in NPCs personal lives, etc. After a few hours you really start to see the wireframe and my brain just started filtering out all the great flavor because it's all the same. Everyone's inbox basically consists of the same scam email, the same 3 ads, the same 2-3 emails they can have with a partner, and the same apology email from a rival/spurned character. It's a great start but there needs to be a LOT more content variety to keep players reading.- More tools/ways to interact with the world - while there are a TON of different, interactable objects in the world right now, most of them are really just physics objects you can throw to create a distraction. The actual, functional objects are cool (camera, handcuffs, fingerprint gun) but I was so deeply disappointed to discover a black market firearms shop, plot and execute a break in, only to find that you can't actually use any of the guns or ammo, they're just melee objects/throwable distractions.I'm really, really excited about the game and I can't wait to see where it goes over early access. I really hope the developer takes their time and doesn't rush the game out of EA because the potential here is sky high - it will probably just take a lot of time to fully realize it. What's already there though, is extremely cool.

_childDocuments_.review: Man, I really hate to do it, but I have to put my review in the negative category. Now don't get me wrong, for the price tag, you are getting some decent game.SoD had such fantastic potential to break into a niche that is pretty much untouched and uncontested. An immersive sim/sandbox about being a detective with little to no help except your own wits and some tools? Sign me up. Sadly, all the games systems and mechanics just never got fully fleshed out. They are there, but not expanded upon. You will primarily be searching for a few key pieces of info, and repeating that loop over, and over, and over. You will not ever find the motive of criminals in a meaningful way. You will be scrambling to find fingerprints most of the time, and typing on computers a lot.I could go into more details, but this would be an essay at that point, and you don't got the time for all that.That is all you are getting, decent. I was waiting until a 1.0 or a steady state to write a review for it, because EA is a bit unfair. The devs have stated that they are essentially, not developing the game further, but only maintaining it at this point, along with adding workshop.I wish the devs the best in their next endeavor, because I genuinely think they have the capability of making something great, I am just not sure why this was dropped so suddenly it seemed, when SoD had such potential to be a real gem in gaming, especially in the detective/immersive sim genre.

_childDocuments_.review: This game has the potential to be something very special, but right now it's still very, very early access and I would consider this a "wait and see" review.What this game does really well are the clues it gives to solving a murder. After the tutorial, the game doesn't hand hold you at all. Like a detective, you have to be thorough in your searches or else you could miss some key evidence, and there's lots of different types of evidence to find and many things to interact with. Identity cards, fingerprints, receipts, notes, address books, last known caller etc. You can also interact with most objects you see in the game, although a lot of these items don't seem to have any use to them right now so it feels a bit shallow. However, the evidence pin board feels really good.The game itself, whilst foundationally interesting, feels a bit hollow quite quickly. For example, conversations with NPCs are reduced down roughly the same 4 questions, most of whom won't give up any info, including their name. You can write this off to the setting you're in perhaps, but dialogue immediately feels like just an often frustrating, repetitive checkbox rather than something interesting. There's currently no personality with any of the NPCs as they all answer questions in the exact same way, which is a shame in a game like this. Whilst bribery is an option (albeit very basic and unrewarding), intimidation or blackmailing isn't which is something I think could deepen the immersion. If I am faced with a stonewall of a suspect who may have key evidence, doing a background on them and finding out about something potentially shady they've done and using it against them to potentially get key evidence would make for really interesting cases.There's also no way to play this game as a straight laced detective. You're going to have to break the law regularly to solve cases, and there's really no incentive not to. This isn't necessarily a problem, but as it stands, it's fairly easy to get away with anything. For example, once you're in someone's apartment, you can pretty much take whatever you like as chances are you broke in there and once you leave the building your "wanted level" disappears and the guards aren't a big threat, even if you weren't all that stealthy. Even if you rob someone, or steal their house key, it seems like the victim never reports or reacts to these things. If you rummage through someones house and take their key, after a certain amount of time the locks should change, or once reported, security is increased in the area meaning you'll need to be more stealthy or take a different approach. The world doesn't really react to your actions right now in a meaningful way. NPCs also tend to suffer from short term memory loss. I broke into a suspects house and we got into a brawl, they broke my leg so I limped out the building until I lost my wanted level. Upon returning to the same building minutes later, when they saw me it was like the interaction never happened. No mention of what happened, no reporting me to anyone, it was like we were meeting for the first time when we spoke. This feels really immersion breaking. There's really very little consequences for playing things wildly right now. If you're violent and there are witnesses or the victim is able to sound an alarm or call someone and report you, the security cameras and guards of that building should be a lot more hostile towards you, making it more difficult to get in and get the info you need, at least until that case is solved or certain time has passed.I can't speak for the main story as I haven't played much of it, but the procedural murders can feel very... Procedural. In one case, someone was killed outside their apartment building, the killer left a note that spelt out their name but with the letters scrambled. I just went through the public directory, got their address and immediately found them, their ID, fingerprints and the murder weapon. From some other reviews, their cases seemed a lot harder, and variety in difficulty is a good thing, but with this murder there was no clear motive, they didn't know each other, no witnesses and the self-incriminating note that wasn't remotely difficult or cryptic. Without motive, there's an emptiness to the cases. Reading between the lines and trying to figure out a motive is half the fun of being a (virtual) detective and in itself can help the player figure out where to look next based on a "hunch" or when they're lacking the leads to know where to go to next. Alongside this, I've experienced a few gamebreaking bugs. For example, sitting on a sofa outside someones apartment, waiting to break in after they go to work, once I got up, I was teleported through the wall into the building and stuck between the wall and a safe. There are no autosaves, so I had to abandon that game completely. I also got drunk off bourbon and the camera shake was so unbearable and broken I had to quit. I tried to wait it out or eat to see if it helped but it didn't work. It was unecessarily punishing.The Twitch integration so the audience can be citizens sounds great, but when I tested it, it wasn't clear whether it was correctly linked or how I could check.Overall this game really *could* be something special, but only if it focuses its attention to in-depth social interaction, varying personality traits and more pre-written cases. The procedural elements are great for creating routines for the citizens and basic information, but beyond that it starts to feel very shallow when it comes to solving procedural cases. Using the procedural elements alongside very specific pre-scripted missions I think would be a lot more satisfying and can add depth that's hard to achieve with procedural generation alone.

_childDocuments_.review: Best detective game ever made. First off, It is a chunky game doing a ton of work in the background which takes a lot out of even beefy systems. However the AI driven murders and procedural generation collide to make every case feel different and while the primary processes remain the same putting together your board and chasing leads feels great. Even when they all turn up dead, pushing you to long shots for figuring out who all entered and left that building and who is in there with that size shoe or who left that one out of place fingerprint. While waiting for businesses to close or you to have your next eureka moment, you can take on side jobs that also offer great content.I have seen bugs, I have seen issues, I see room for growth. But at its core no game deliverers what this serves. It is a technical marvel and Cole should be very proud of such an accomplishment.

_childDocuments_.review: Shadows of Doubt is weird.The first case (that was proc-gen'd) i did was pretty enthralling. But it's kinda cuz i'm dumb and didnt check the city directory thoroughly enough to find the name that matched the jumbled up clue. Because, as it turned out, the killer lived on the same floor as two of the three victims.The reason i didn't think of this is because it would be very, exceedingly stupid to murder two of your neighbours. But that's how it happened.So i made a couple new worlds, but the issues i had with the first one continued. On my most recent world, the first murder was done by their next door neighbour, and i found this out because the fingerprints at the crime scene matched up with the fingerprints on the neighbours door. next murder was in broad daylight by the place the victim worked at and had a business card nearby with prints on it. I ran to their workplace, took the prints off of the receptionists desk and immediately matched them with the crime scene.The third case, and this is where I started to realise the problems fully, was a murder clearly motivated by romantic obsession. and the murderer wrote their first name on the wall. so i looked at the address book, found the name, and went NEXT DOOR and arrested them.Is it just my worlds? luck? The game isn't particularly good at hiding who did the crimes which it probably should be given the murder mystery thing. if there's a business card clue, it's probably a coworker. if it's not clear by the method of the murder, don't worry the suspect has written their name down somewhere. And if all else fails, literally just check next door, not even on a different floor.The jobs tend to have a little more variety and detective work because they let you have way less information. You have like, height, hair and the building they live in and you go off of that. And it's way more interesting but even that can get tedious.I'm not trying to dog on the game that much, it's early access and the developer is obviously committed to improving and completing the game. But in its state right now I think it'd be wiser to maybe wait a bit before pulling the trigger on this  purchase.

_childDocuments_.review: was absolutely blown away the second I stepped outside and witnessed the rain and bloom and- wow. The graphics including the style are absolutely beautiful.They give the game and its genre so much charm- it's hard to stop playing.It's also hard to stop breaking into people's apartments, steal their valuables while you are  witha guest pass or beat them into submission only to leave them handcuffed in the shower. :)From the beating heart of the city- to every individual person living in it. They all have their own jobs, routines, apartments and places to be. You can explore those places; legally or ; and slowly piece together who a person is. Cases can be randomly generated and people tend to get stabbed in the most public of places. While investigating a murder you might stumble across another body. There's weapons to buy, new equipment to use and a bunch of mechanics to make your detective work easier.Locking doors, finding keys, using door wedges, breaking down doors, hiding underneath objects, knocking people out, looking through safes and cracking them, breaking security systems. Lots. To. Do.If you're into solving murders while exploring a living and breathing city with constantly changing people- And since this is only the beginning of its release there will definitely be more down the line.Without a doubt.

_childDocuments_.review: Yes!:Why it is good?:Imagine a crime-tabletop-puzzle game but brang it into a sandbox-FPS/RPG of active NPC's: with active jobs, routines, affairs, traits and the sporadic will to commit murder in any moment.  (There will be always 1 murderer simultaneously or none, but never two; however they can stack victims overtime) This is what it is.    There is no game like this which makes it a must play for detective nerds. FLAWS: Some few cases's evidence, can be procedurally messy as: "body has knife injury" but then there is bullet shells in the floor, so gun was the actual murder weapon and the injury didn't matter at the end. (rarely, but it can happen). Or "find this guy: shoe size 4" (only info) and you might end up as "the prince tracking for cinderella" or just dropping that case away. BUGS:- there is some glitches here and there, but nothing game breaking. As: a chair teleporting you next room, falling from the fabric of reality due speeding through a door, objects overlapping and/or over-spawned items. - BUGGY ACHIEVEMENTS: Some achievementes  have a delay to trigger, some will when you re open the game, others as food consumption wont stack properly, making "100 coffees" being 250 or so, (all food trophies are a pain)FUN FACT: murderers will be freed eventually but dead people will continue to deplete population (you wont notice tho. The end game could have 6 or 10 (ingame) days. and murders happens once a day; and there is 250 citizens in the smaller city)Comments and... complains?:- V-Mails need some work. They are almost the same and mostly trash-mails for every single NPC.  Rarely useful in the investigation process.   Aswell for the shoe-prints, you rarely take them  in consideration nor are present as evidence.  - Club's membership are pointless to mention, as they don't show as real places nor as visible feature on any NPC documentation, nor gossip.  Very weird info note to be present. (maybe unfinished game feature)- People has Umbrellas and you don't. *Sniffs*- There is blood type but no dirty cloth mechanic nor sample tests... It's ok (maybe not yet).- You cannot build relationships (I can understand why tho). But it's weird to be some kind of nobody at anytime; YET convenient!. (There is still social Level, which eases the info gathering from people by trust)- Knock out achievementes is supe, SUPER  stup*d :/  It only exist to make you loose your sake and timeGame is clearly not polished, but IT IS FUN!. (if you enjoy snooping around, of course). Best fake detective experience I have had with a game.Cheers!
