_childDocuments_.review: Shadows Of Doubt is a noir detective game set in an entirely procedurally generated chunk of a city, filled with appartment complexes, shops, cafes, bars, and offices, that are populated by hundreds of fully automated NPCs, who all have jobs, friends, go shopping, have work times and home times, partners, an appartment, as well as about 20+ indentifying traits to them raging from fingerprints to income, and from size and voice to handwriting style. Whenever a murder happens in this city, any of these hundreds of NPCs could be the murderer, and it is your job – with very little handholding from the game’s side – to find out who it is. This game was such a fresh surprise to me in so many ways, I am still a bit in awe of some of the ideas and the immersiveness the developers create in general. Shadows Of Doubt has tons of mechanics I always wanted to see in a detective game – the corkboard with red string that helps you track down suspects lets you put any info you find whatsoever on it – even if it’s a completely irrelevant napkin you found on the street; and the ways to get your information are endless: breaking into homes, breaking into offices, crossreferencing police databases, employee records, asking random people on the street for information, scanning an entire building for a certain fingerprint, calling a phone number and then breaking into your hotel’s basement to see where they redirected the call to, reading a persons private emails, etc. – it’s truly a joy how much creative control the game gives you over how you want to find a piece of evidence. Shadows Of Doubt is also incredibly good at nailing down the noir vibe of the setting – the constantly rainy or snowly weather, the “survival mechanics” that make you survive on fast food, coffee and cigars, breaking into people's homes to take a shower, the dubious legality of your job – if you play the tutorial, you even are divorced and homeless at the start of the game! I had so much fun immersing myself into this miserable little detective character I had created, and the game certainly makes it very easy. While Shadows of Doubt is somewhat formulaeic, the people, locations and circumstances of what you are supposed to do and what information you are given differ so much from case to case, that I found it almost a bit reassuring, that certain things are ‘always the same’ so to say – there are about 30 or so different email texts people send each other, so it’s easy to rule out if an email is important or not, NPC AIs are not very smart, every person seems to have sticky note somewhere for their *one* passcode, and after a while you have figured out that every person keeps Document A in the bedroom closet and Document B somewhere on their kitchen counter. But it’s reassuring in the sense that you start to get a bit bolder in how you play the game – breaking into a house while the person is sleeping instead of waiting until they go to work, knowing how to trick cameras and avoid alerting security systems makes the game a lot more fun than if the game would be too realistic and punishing in these scenarios. In the tutorial, when I wasn’t yet familiar with all of the systems, I found the game brutally punishing and pretty hard to play, but it’s really just a matter of getting familiar with the game mechanics.There are tons of other things I find absolutely wonderful about Shadows Of Doubt – the jobs you can additionally do to earn money are creative and a great spin on the base mechanics and feel quite different than the “main” cases; The fingerprint mechanic should win an award for something, you can literally go to any surface in the game and pull out your scanner and you might get the fingerprints of people who recently were there, which actually realistically maps to light switches, post boxes, doors, etc. more than it does to random walls. The city is just big enough that you don’t really get lost in it and the game's sound design and visual design are both stunning and even further nail down the vibe of the game.My only 2 complaints would be that the game isn’t really performing all that well (I can’t really blame them, they’re simulating like 200+ NPCs all at once), and that the cases sometimes require you to catch a really specific clue that you may have not thought of (e.g. one case is based around the fact that you think of scanning a really specific item for fingerprints, which isn’t unintitive, but if you don’t do that you find no other connection to the murderer whatsoever) – this is made a bit harder by the fact that the game doesn’t really care about “motive”, so your only goal is to find out who it was, with the game not generating evidence for motive at all – which is a bit confusing, since the tutorial case implies that there *will* be motive to the murders. Generally, if you don’t mind the game maybe being somewhat clunky and a bit buggy sometimes, and if you like the premise of this game I can really recommend buying it. It’s mechanically innovating, beautiful, and has a true commitment to the detective noir style.

_childDocuments_.review: This! This is it. I have never been more excited about having such a great experience with a game which I have never seen a playthrough of. The weird thing is that I have been searching for such a game for a while, and as I said: this is it. I love the fact that everyone in the city is just living their own lives and that there is a lot that is happening all around you. I really enjoy that you have to use your brain to solve these "small murder puzzles", and it is amazingly satisfying when you catch the killer. I enjoy the small details such as having toothbrushes, and that the AIs brush their teeth. It is absolutely amazing, and I can't wait to see more of what the devs are going to do with this game. I don't know if the devs will see this post, but after some hours of playing there are a couple of things which I noticed/would like to see more of: - I had one world where all the side quests seemed to be connected to people who I just identified. This made is too easy to solve and took away the fun of completing the quests. I don't know why this happened as there are a lot more people in the city who could have been the person of interest in these side quests.- I would really love it if it would be more diffiult somehow. Not difficult as in the murder crimes only, but also if it wouldn't be as easy to rob people. For me, it takes the fun out of it when it is too easy to steal e.g. diamonds. Maybe there could be some mechanic as to randomly get searched by enforcers in the street, or that the people who lives in the buildings kind of follow you if they allow you inside because they dont trust you to walk about by yourself. If would also be nice to have more difficulties in entering a persons building, and that MORE people would deny you to come in even though you bribe them. I would generally just love it to be more difficult, having a bigger variety of murderers, murder weapons, types of murderers. Maybe some that go after a specific type of people, maybe multiple killers and double murders happening at the same time. - I would love more conversation. Not only as having more options of things to say, but that the AIs have more lines. Maybe they would have different personalities somehow. It makes it somewhat boring to chat with them when all the AIs have the same thing to say even in the side quests. Also it would be amazing to be able to get to bond with these AIs. Maybe have friends or lovers that would make meaning of buying places (this also could maybe provide some buffs/debuffs).I absolutely love the complexicity of the game, and would love to see it getting even more complex. It is absolutely truly an amazing game which I am enjoying both before writing the review and will continue to do so after posting the review. This is truly IT. Thank you for this game.

_childDocuments_.review: It's times like these where I wish Steam allowed a "Mixed" or "Neutral" option for recommendations in reviews. Shadows of Doubt is an extremely detailed, intricate game that relies upon multiple layers of gameplay coming together to form a cohesive experience. Sometimes, and usually often enough, that does happen. You will get a notification about a case, stroll over to the crime scene (almost always an apartment), use your fingerprint scanner on every atom in the room (and wonder who's been Exorcist crawling up the walls and ceilings), rifle through belongings, find details, then follow up on locations and people mentioned in those details and belongings until you hit upon the correct suspect.That sometimes works.Here's what happens when it doesn't:I get a case where a man was shot in his kitchen. His body was laid near the wall, with strange writing on the walls. Passing beyond the kitchen and into the living room, on the wall directly across from the body, were bullet holes. I scanned through every inch of the rooms, looked through boxes of documents, found his workplace, ID, blood type, and birth date. Went through his computer, and found an email he sent, worried about a non-binary person who was bald. I go to their workplace, question everyone, and get nothing. I scan every inch of the workplace, and get nothing. I break into the apartment security room and review the footage from around the time he was killed, and get nothing. I even resorted to randomly scanning apartment doors for matching fingerprints to the ones found at the murder scene, and still got nothing.Every single way I could think of to solve the case was shut down by a lack of evidence. Do you know how I eventually solved the case? I went through and printed every single NPC file from the police database, wasting probably around 40 minutes of my time in total after giving up multiple times from boredom. Eventually, by pure brute force, I found a match, and had my suspect.Shadows of Doubt relies very heavily on its systems working properly with each other to form a logical conclusion, but that just doesn't always happen. There are times where, by no fault of your own, you will have ZERO opportunity to organically solve a case, and you will either be reduced to "cheating" with the database spamming, or simply closing the case. I really, really enjoy this game, and I sincerely wish for the best for the developers in realizing their dreams for this game, because what's there already is insanely impressive and mind-blowing. But it isn't perfect by a long shot, and if you play this game, you will eventually get frustrated by how the game is structured.

_childDocuments_.review: I actually like this game more than I dislike it, but I would struggle to recommend it; it just wasn't ready to leave early access - it's plagued with bugs of all kinds (graphical glitches specifically are boundless) and performance is infamously poor. Taken into consideration with the fact that, despite genuinely achieving to be the most immersive detective experience in gaming yet, it's still as shallow as Rockstar's 'L.A Noire' was more than a decade ago - let me explain: random generation never works how developers intend - it can make every experience different (for better or for worse), but it can never make every experience fun. Look no further than Starfield with it's thousands of unique but boring planets! In Shadows of Doubt, there are no motives, only a handful of crimes, and just a dozen or so notes and emails, which means you will frequently and inevitably stumble upon the same content, and fast. As you can probably deduce, this results in each case playing out more or less exactly the same (especially kidnapping cases): you will search the crime scene for 'the same' evidence, chase leads in 'the same' ways (which, admittedly, is the most enjoyable part of the game, featuring well-thought out and decently innovative systems), and arrest the culprit (or not). So, while each case will be technically different, it's trivial and, bluntly, they all feel the same. It's not fun. I would have much preferred the developer focused less on soulless procedural content and instead perhaps on a single, handcrafted city with longer, more detailed cases because from paper to execution, even though the foundational systems of an incredible, immersive detective experience are there, Shadows of Doubt is significantly less interesting. It needed more time to cook.

_childDocuments_.review: At the time of this review i have completed the tutorial case and one procedural sandbox map/case. among a few side gigs.TL;DR Is it worth? Yes absolutely. This is one of the best early access games you can play right now. IE if you told me this was a completely finished product i would believe you. and the dev team has been incredibly quick in resolving many of the issues on launch. This isnt some "press x for detective vision" ""detective"" game. the only tool given to you to figure out crimes is a fingerprint scanner (which you have to find out yourself who they belong to) and your own wits. but within the framework of the game you are giving many options to complete your tasks as you see fit. You really do feel like you did some honest to god proper sleuth work once you fit all the pieces together and solve your first crime. Its actually impressive the ways you can go about tracking someone down. For instance: fingerprint, footprint scanning, checking surveillance footage, checking telephone call histories, asking citizens around if they know someone in a photo, checking their place of employment, looking up names in directories, finding purchase receipts etc etc. The pin-board system is fantastic. the game automatically connects pieces for you if the game knows its connected and you have the options to make your own connections if you know something for instance but havent "proven it" yet. but as said the game is very good at making these connections for you. outside of murder cases you can take on various odd jobs mostly found on notice boards of restaurants/stores/city hall. they include cuffing dangerous fugitives (bounty hunting i guess) trashing property and taking photo evidence, finding briefcase hot drops for other jobs. tailing persons of interest and some more i have yet to do. You can spend your earnings on upgrading your detective kit, buying nonlethal weapons and stun grenades, food/medicine. Augments/synthdisks that give you various perks. and buying apartments that can be decorated and furnished with quite impressive customization. I played on Normal difficulty and the ai ranged from working as intended to derp and weird pathfinding or "routine patterns". Ai has abusable short term memory loss. which probably is necessary for progression for some instances. stealth works mostly as intended with a few quirks with the human npcs. nothing terrible but youll know what i mean when you experience it. performance wise i only experience a few stutters when bring up the map/connection board constantly or running into a high density area. otherwise things were pretty smooth. in way of bugs the only one i experienced got patched out the very next day. There is plenty here to justify the asking price and there is more to come in the future roadmap. also devs let me actually use the guns you can find/buy in the game. blz. and add vhs players. i had one in my inventory for too long thinking it was usable evidence lol. 9/10 would throw steaming hot coffee at someone for a quick paycheck again.

For example, without spoiling, a case pops up and tells you to visit the scene. Well I don't know where that location is, so???? I get so tired of looking for the damn places because I just want to play the game. There's also a few bugs, which is understandable considering the game is in early access. _childDocuments_.review: Edit: I absolutely love this game, and it pains me, but I have to change the review to negative.There's so many things I enjoy about this game. It's a fun detective immersive sim, finding out ways to solve the cases is satisfying when sometimes something clicks, or if you even by accident receive new info by asking people around. The core of this game is great and I really wished to have more games like this.But this Early Access and 1.0 release are extremely disappointing. There were one or two types of building added, two or three case types introduced, and that's it. It literally feels like nothing. The game is full of bugs, and I could argue that there's even more than what I remember when I first play it when it released. It used to be buggy, sure, but now I keep getting stuck on benches and other things on the street, because models didn't load in time and are invisible for a while, both outside and inside, and the map takes few seconds to actually load from a blank state - neither of those used to be a problem. Few additional cases didn't change much - there's still no endgame, no real goal or a prize besides just getting social credit to max level only to press the end game button. There's never any struggle for money, because after a case or two you have enough to just buy stuff you need and keep on going. Murders, the funniest parts, are actually quite sparse and it can take a few IRL hours to get a new murder case after finishing previous ones. Murderers still don't have any motives and plenty of times it can either be very easy or nigh impossible to finish a case (screw you, sniper killing people on the exactly same spot on the street. You won't be missed.) Some cases are still unsolvable - good luck finding the target knowing that the person has blue eyes and shoe size 10, exactly nothing else. Interaction with NPCs is pretty much always the same and after a while it just gets tedious. To solve the case you start just paying people to let you in their houses and searching through all their papers to get info you need, then go to next flat to do the same, repeat until done. Or maybe just get a sword that one-hit KO pretty much everybody and just go around the flat, then to the next one, and so on. If you do it well enough, even with all the alarms, blockades and angry people trying to shoot you, you can be fully capable of checking out an entire skyscraper this way, then just run away without a care, because if you just run it's extremely easy to get away with everything, and once the pursuit stops, you're basically clean, you'll just need to wait out few ingame hours and not go to the building you were in for everything to drop and disappear. Or you can use the easy way and use a computer with govt database which lets you literally learn the details about everybody. Takes a while, is boring, makes the game even less boring, but it is a solution, and then you can always know whose these fingerprints are and where they live. I just choose to not use it, but it's there and feels like you absolutely didn't earn that info you're getting out of it. The game can lock you out from certain things if you're unlucky enough, for example if a murderer kills the only person working in a store, you'll never be able to use it again, because the game won't adjust to that. All that just to get to the one of the most dissatisfying ending I have ever seen. You made it. Good job. Yay. End credits. I absolutely LOVE this game. This is at least one of my top 3 of all times. It's exactly what I always wanted and hoped for. I was so hyped to see it grow, to watch stuff added, cities made alive and deep, I wished to see brand new city types, more cases, more ways of doing things. Meanwhile after a year and a half I got an option to buy an artbook or a console release, with a pretty good chance it's been now abandoned forever. It pains me so much to see that happen. The only thing I can hope for are mods, because modders are incredible people, but it's not what this game could be. It turned from a noir detective love letter sandbox greatness with perspectives into a shell of what it could be. Noir a lot of times start with the detective main character being on the bottom, only to rise up. But in this case, I'm afraid it's not that kind of story.**OG EA review: It has it's Early Access issues. Quite a bit of bugs - I managed to fall through the floor and die few times as well. That being said, it's one of the funniest games I've played and my current obsession. I can't wait to see more of this fantastic noir cyberpunk world in further updates. Figuring out who the culprit is from a scratch with a bare minimum of information, following different leads and that dopamine rush when you suddenly figure it out - the last missing piece you needed. It's awesome.

_childDocuments_.review: I'd like to preface this review by saying, while I recommend this game in terms of its gameplay loop and the overall premise, I cannot stress enough that you should probably wait for a later release before purchasing. If you ask me, this game is very fun, but the price tag is a bit much for what is currently implemented.Obviously, the game isn't fully polished yet, that's to be expected as it is in early access. That said, upwards of $20 USD may not be as worth it as the game is now. Nevertheless, I still want to support the developers because, aside from the lack of polish and the unfitting price tag, this game isn't bad at all. It just needs that extra dose of finishing touches which I'm sure the devs are hard at work on. I recommend this game, and if you want to support the developers by purchasing this early access, there's nothing wrong with doing so. However, I just feel like it may be best to wait for the full release so the remaining kinks can be ironed out. Then, $20 USD will likely be worth it.Essentially, you are placed into a procedurally-generated city with procedurally-generated citizens, and procedurally-generated crimes take place which you must investigate and resolve to climb the ranks of society and earn your way into retirement. That is how it is right now, at least. Overall, I think that is a brilliant concept, and Shadows of Doubt works with it in a very engaging way. The emphasis on stealth in order to access crime scenes in private areas is satisfying to get good with, and I will confidently say this game does a good job of making you feel like a detective doing whatever it takes to find the truth. The random generation of the game's environments also means that for every different city you play through, the obstacles for each case and your tactics for overcoming them have to be ever-changing and adaptive. There is an emphasis on not trying the same few actions over and over that Shadows of Doubt does a great job of indirectly teaching the player; many different crimes happen across the city, and each one is completely different. For what has been implemented so far, I have to give credit where credit is due. The developers are on top of their game in terms of making the gameplay and environment immersive and engaging, and Shadows of Doubt is great at teaching the player that the ability to adapt and overcome is essential for solving cases.That said, as you could have probably guessed, I have some problems with this game. Problems that I'm sure will be worked on going forward, but problems nonetheless.First and foremost is performance issues. I cannot tell if it is just my PC or if it is because of this game, but running larger cities is extremely taxing on my frame rate and the general performance speed of my system. Early on, I tried to generate a medium-sized city (which is the second smallest size option, small is what I had chosen up until this point), and I'm fairly certain I encountered a one-time bug that caused the game to completely softlock while generating the NPCs for the city. This only occurred once, to be fair, but I wished to voice that in order to transition into the next problem I have.Shadows of Doubt is (pardon the pun) undoubtedly quite polished for a game in early access, which shows how much work has been put into it up until this point by the developers. Still, there have been plenty of instances throughout my playtime that reminded me, "Oh, right. This game is in early access." There are minor things, such as the NPCs and their dialogue. Even from the very beginning, I've always felt that talking to the citizens in the game always just felt...stiff. Every NPC seems to use the same sorts of responses to stimuli; they all say the exact same few rude things when they're unwilling to give information, and when describing suspects or events they witnessed, their dialogue feels so template-esque that it sometimes makes me think of a Mad Libs that was filled in completely seriously. This issue isn't a make-or-break for the game, it's just a small nitpick, but it does kind of make interacting with citizens honestly boring to an extent when you know they're either going to give a template description of a person, or they're going to say some variant of "go away, I don't trust you."On top of that are the glitches and bugs I've encountered, which range in severity quite wildly. It could be something as simple as physics making throwing an object end up not working out, or an important piece of evidence left by a criminal being stuck halfway inside the sidewalk in such a way that it is impossible to examine. Then there are bigger ones that absolutely require attention, such as when I attempted to walk into the city hall building at the same time as an NPC, and the resulting collision bugged out and forced me through the floor outside the map. I fell, blacked out, and ended up in one of the hospitals just because I attempted to walk through a door. I will be keeping track of these bugs and reporting them as they happen, but I just needed to mention it.With all of that said, I think I've dragged this review on long enough. Yes, this game is still in early access, which in my opinion does make some of my current problems with it forgivable. And to be fair and give the game some credit, what was done right was done brilliantly. Shadows of Doubt is genuinely very fun and engaging, especially for someone like me who enjoys games with procedural generation that let you explore the environment like this. The procedural murders, crime solving, evidence collection, and working your way to the top is really a bonus for me, but a damn good bonus. Problems, however, are still problems, and Shadows of Doubt is FAR from perfect. In conclusion, I can recommend this game based on its gameplay, the immersion, and its general concept. I cannot recommend this game based on its price tag or the current level of polish. If the good that I discussed here was anything that you found interesting, please! Buy this game and play through it a bit! If you like games about solving crimes, or games that prioritize stealth, you'll get a kick out of this for sure! But, if you would rather wait for a later release or a reduced price, I think that's also a very fair judgement to make. Either way, these developers have made something beautiful, it just needs a bit more time.

_childDocuments_.review: Shadows of Doubt is an impressive game, but is not for everyone. The concept is unique, but might ask too much of the player. You're a detective in a city solving cases. As you work through cases, you build out a web of connections for your victims inching closer to your suspect. When it comes together it's an incredible experience.However, it is a very buggy game. Often, citizens will get stuck just going in and out of their front doors. Sometimes UI elements will bug out and you lose your entire clue board. You'll spend about half the time just working around the game's jank.I think it's a game for people who play too many games. Its novelty is worthwhile for those willing to meet it more than half way.

_childDocuments_.review: I sunk nearly two days worth of playtime into this game and it's only been out for about a week. It scratches every itch I never knew I needed as a gamer.To sum it up, if you took the go-anywhere, do-anything game design philosophy of Deus Ex, give it the atmosphere and aesthetics of games like Papers Please or Orwell: Keeping an Eye on You, and make it fully procedurally generated like Minecraft, you get Shadows of Doubt.In particular, it epitomizes the "One-Block RPG" idea penned by Deus Ex's creator. If you don't go into the buildings, the game world seems small: there's only between 9 and 20 buildings in the city. But in these buildings, every back room, nook, and cranny is explorable. The largest of these buildings can have up to 21 floors (up to 19 above ground, as well as a basement and the occasional flooded sub-basement). There are bars, diners, factories, offices, slums, Chinatown-style restaurants, living quarters that go from downright abysmal on the lower floors to obscenely pristine up in the Eschelons, pharmacies, laundromats, parks, illegal arms dealers, gambling halls, loan sharks, hospitals, police precincts. clinics where you can upgrade yourself.You can play pool in the bars, buy and customize your own apartments as much as you want, take on all number of side-quests from both reputable and shady clients, or if you want to go the upper floors and businesses and engage in a little bit of burglary. The main drag of the game is obviously being a detective, taking on investigations and pinpointing your perp, whether it's a serial killer ready to strike again, a wanted criminal on the lam from Starch Kola Enforcers, or some poor sap who you've been paid to clown on with a well-thrown Big Mac. Sometimes the cases are open and shut- you get the perp's name or address and go there to do what you need to do. Sometimes you only get their fingerprints and the floor they live in, or their phone number, and it only takes minimal leg work. Other times you only know their first initial is T, they don't wear glasses, and they like chess. Or that they're skinny and their salary is 100,000 credits. That's when you have to really dig deep and scour the whole city. Sometimes solving a murder is simple. The killer might leave an anagram which an astute puzzle solver can figure out in 2 minutes by cross-referencing the address book, or, since one of the hundreds of AI citizens has to actually go out and commit the murder, you might catch the killer in the act and apprehend them while they flee. Other times they get offed on a busy apartment building landing, or out in the streets. Sometimes the suspect is one of the victim's neighbors and coworkers and it's some easy legwork- other times it could be an acquaintance of an acquaintance, or someone random altogether. You can solve a crime any number of ways. You can interview anyone that knew the victim and see if they slip up and confess by accident ("Why yes, I did last see them in their apartment at exactly the time they were murdered, why do you ask?") or give you a physical trait of the true killer to go off of, you can check sales ledgers of stores that sell weapons to see if any of your suspects purchased something suspicious, you can check CCTV footage, you can check fingerprints. You can finish any mission completely by the book (other than getting to the crime scene- right now there's no option to get into a crime scene without trespassing) without picking a single lock, breaking into any homes, or pissing anyone other than the true killer off. Or, you can be a master spy, silently slipping into homes, unscrewing lightbulbs, shutting down security systems, and avoiding detection in the name of getting what you want. You could, if you were so inclined and had the ballistic vest and handcuffs to spare, mercilessly break into the apartment you want to search and beat the crap out of the suspects before cuffing them, guilty or not, but that's a good way to get an entire apartment complex shut down with a security alarm for in-game days. There are problems. The game isn't quite optimized yet? You need a beefy computer to run it with a decent framerate, and there's definitely a memory leak where the performance drops like a stone and reloading saves becomes impossible. Sometimes the AI will break if you interfere with it too, and heaven help you if the AI that glitched out was the designated killer because then there's no murders to solve. Some methods of obtaining suspect information (read: the Enforcer computers you can get into at City Hall) are an absolute game breaker, giving you Orwellian information about literally anyone in the city; I have to actively refuse to use it when I play because of how easy it makes the game.But this is early access- this is the first WEEK of early access. I can talk about the issues that are going on but they're probably going to get ironed out. I can talk about the features and changes I'd love to see, but not only do the developers have an Early Access Roadmap talking about all the content they're still going to add, but they're going to look into mod support (so maybe hello SoD Workshop one day?) It's more than worth the $20 price tag.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a decent game and I find it fairly interesting, but it feels a little barebones, especially on the dialogue side. No one in the entire city seems to want to talk to you about anything, which I can kinda understand because of the setting and everything, but there's no point in attempting to use most of the dialogue options - I choose the option for finding out if they've heard anything strange recently, and 100% of the time I get the answer "Nothing". There is VERY LITTLE variety to their responses, they either know "Nothing", or they don't want to talk to me. On the other hand, if they have any information on the people I'm looking for, they do give more information, but it's still a little dry. If it's possible to assign personality traits to people and give each trait their own pre-written responses/speaking styles, as well as lighten up a bit on their asocial behavior, I think that would immediately make the game's dialogue system that much more engaging. They don't have to give me the murderer's exact location at this very moment or all of their features, just say something interesting. Otherwise, I have no reason to use any of the options given besides asking people for their fingerprints or asking them if they know a person.I very much like the idea of the game and how it mainly plays out - you start a case, you make your way to the designated area and start from there. The game doesn't hold your hand at all, you have to think for yourself on what to do in every case. Need to make a police arrest as a side job? Sure, here's what's known about the suspect. Do with that information what you will. Usually there's *just* enough information for you to get an investigation going, for example their number and one physical trait, maybe their workplace, maybe something else entirely. There's a lot of possibilities, and the best part of it all is that you have to just figure things out.Fair warning to the next part of the review, it may be a bit spoilery. I'll try to mark out the specific game mechanics as such in case you want to give this game a whirl and figure things out entirely by yourself.As an example of the aforementioned side job type, I was given the suspect's . Having only this information to go off, I decide the simplest thing to start with is to just  Case closed.This is one of the many ways a case could go. Other times it may not be as easy as that, and all you're given is the victim's body, a murder weapon and the killer's fingerprints. You'd think that would make things super easy, right? WRONG! I went to the victim's workplace,  asked random people if they know , and not a single one of them matched the murderer's fingerprints. In the end, I'm left with 0 leads for me to follow as I'm not smart enough to figure out what else I could use, and the case is as good as dead. Or at least it would be, until I realized I can just  I'll talk about that more and why I think that's probably a bad thing a bit further in the review.The game is a little too easily exploitable, and adds to my feeling of the game being barebones. I'll list a few examples, as I hope for them to be adjusted:Getting into a fist fight is no problem no matter how many people are attacking you, just keep backing up and punching them and they will never be able to hit back. Perhaps possible to solve if your walking speed gets restricted when your fists are out, when you're walking backwards or when you're in combat in general.Government database allows you to brute force every single living person's fingerprint and all their other details (I restricted myself to only using it if I have the suspect's name and no further leads to follow, cause otherwise it's boring and defeats the point, all the info is "memorized"). I have no good ideas on how this can be nerfed or adjusted otherwise.Lights out means you have free reign to do whatever you want, even if you stand directly in front of someone while inside their house or any other area you trespass into. Similarly, if you make a loud noise, you're free to run away as fast as you want, and if they see you they won't take note of it, even if something's open and/or missing.Next, it feels like there are no consequences to the things you do in this game. No one reports you to the police no matter how heinous your crime. As long as you run a little bit and wait for the security systems to reset, you're free to do whatever you want. Everyone forgets what you had just done to them 5 minutes prior. At worst, you may get knocked out, put in the hospital and asked to pay 20% of your money in medical bills, and off you go back into the world.It's also very buggy at the moment. I've fallen off the map 3 separate times and clipped through buildings like 5 or 6 times. Decorating your apartment is very annoying as well - if I place something from my storage and then attempt to purchase new furniture, it completely bugs out and doesn't allow me to press anything. It also disables my inventory.Performance is not really great outdoors, but it's playable enough for me. Your mileage may vary heavily.Despite all that, I still think this game is worth a shot to anyone interested - you'll more than likely figure out if you like it or not within 2 hours of playtime.

_childDocuments_.review: A procedurally generated mystery machine? Sign me up! This is the game I've ALWAYS wanted. As someone who loves all the Sherlock Holmes games (I've played a mix on here and Xbox), loved LA Noire, Heavy Rain and other sorts of mystery games, this was a dream come true. The problem with the aforementioned games, is that the outcome of the cases doesn't change. Your approach may change, but it's generally the same solution and clues each time.This game, while there isn't much of a story other than some quick narrative to kind of bind everything together, makes sure every case and setting are unique each time! It's a thrill having to raid people's homes for clues, follow their work schedules to know when they're home (or not ;) ), interviewing suspects, plotting evidence, sifting through government records, scanning fingerprints all to pinpoint down to one suspect who may or may not be guilty if you missed an important clue!Also, you're not only investigating murders, there are other side jobs available to you, like recovering stolen items (one of my favorites), taking pictures of people, arresting people and more. Also for the aspiring Feng Shui person, there's the ability to decorate your apartment!Now, that doesn't mean the game is 'perfect' (yet anyways). I've run into a few bugs (as happens in Early Access), from minor things like apartment numbers appearing backward, not being able to hand in a case (fixed with a reload) to major bugs like people not appearing in photographs or CCTVs (which can be used as evidence, and like mentioned before certain side jobs)But other than that, you get a full blown detective experience in a world generated with a population of quirky citizens (some are nicer than others) that is unique to you! No one who plays this game will have the exact same experience and the amount of things to do in the game will keep you addicted.I do really hope they continue working hard on this game for I am loving every minute. I would like to see even more variety of clues, and things tightened up a bit. Sometimes cases can take only a few minutes to solve, then some you can raid the suspects house and still come up without the item you're looking for.I highly recommend this game, especially for fellow Sherlockians!Note:If you enjoy this type of game and want something a little more basic and quick, check out the 2D pixel procedurally generated mystery game called Noir Syndrome. I loved that game when it first came out, and have always wished for a more in depth game like it, and it came true with Shadows of Doubt!

_childDocuments_.review: Got this game before the price hike in hopes that the 1.0 update would be huge and exciting. Reality check, it is a slap in the face. A lot of bugfixes (good) but barely any new content. When 1.0 was announced almost everyone said the game was not ready and the devs should reconsider, meanwhile the devs have not listened and only responded with "We're still going to support the game after launch!" If they wouldn't reconsider over a massive decision such as that, how are we to expect them to listen to the people when it comes to adding content? My trust in the product has gone out the window, as should be the same for anyone who invested in this game during EA. I admittedly did enjoy what time I have put into the game, though, the lack of variety in cases eventually gets repetitive. The sloppily-done procedural generation only goes so far. Most things are too easy to cheese; sync disk upgrades, while very nice, need re-balancing; a lot of cases are too lacking in information on the suspect to be completed, and the computer in the town hall is far too overpowered. This is just scratching the surface of issues with this game, and the best the devs could muster for 1.0 was mostly bugfixes. Would not recommend the current state of this game, and I do not trust the future for this game.

_childDocuments_.review: It was another rainy night in Charlotte Heights. I was finishing a stale coffee at the Indigo Hare as I was checking the post board. Someone had posted a job, looking for a person to be discretely found and photographed. Straight forward job, paid suspiciously well for what it was, but I needed the money. I dialed the number on the notice. The voice on the other end minced no words, "a payphone in an apartment block two blocks away will ring in three minutes, answer it" *click*. Figures. I hurry over there fighting the rain. I hear the phone ringing as I open the door to the apartment lobby.Picking up the phone, I hear the same voice on the other end. They tell me to take a photo of the mark and slide it under an apartment door. More information on the target is in a briefcase under the payphone I was currently using. The client disconnected and I opened said briefcase. "Target's first name starts with the letter 'M', they are 25 years old, and their partner's first name is 'Tiffany.'" Not much to go on, but I've done more with less.My first stop is City Hall. Public access crunchers don't have the access I need for government records, so I... *ahem*  one of the enforcer offices after noticing one of the officers left their pass code posted on a notice board. One quick records search later, only two "Tiffany's" are on record in the district. One resides at the apartment block where the payphone was, the other at the apartment block where I'm expected to drop off the photo. It was an even chance to be one or the other, so I looked into the payphone address first. I let myself into their apartment, but other than a few   items that I relieved them of, I discovered that this Tiffany's partner had a first name that started with an "A." Not my mark.I worked my way over to the other apartment, rode the elevator up to the 16th floor, and knocked on the door. No one was home, so I picked the lock and made my way inside. I needed a name, a photo, something to confirm the mark. After nearly tripping the alarm and disabling a second, I confirmed "M" was indeed this Tiffany's partner, and even managed to locate his passcode for his Muncher. I accessed it and bingo, photo and name. I had also located a work rota for Tiffany. Working on the theory that they likely have similar rotas and Tiffany was expected home within the hour, I let myself back out, found a bench, and waited.Tiffany made it home first. I waited two more hours with no sign of "M" when I caught wind of a murder across town, a job much more up my alley. Intent to return to this job once I wrapped that case up, I bumped into "M" two flights of stairs down. Figuring at this point I no longer cared about discretion, I had a murderer to catch after all, I slipped my camera out of my pocket and snapped a quick photo of "M." Turns out, "M" does not appreciate the art of photography, or may be that they're in hiding from someone, because after I snapped my photo they drew on me and sent a few rounds my way, grazing me. I bolted down the steps and found a spot to lie low before "M" gave up the chase.I threw a few credits into a medvend on another floor, bandaged my arm, and slid the photos under the apartment door four floors below the mark's apartment, then I was on my way to check the murder scene.

_childDocuments_.review: Sadly, I have to echo what everyone else is saying: it's not ready, and now we know it probably never will. Price has been increased after an EA period of a year and 4 months gave us basically nothing noteworthy (1 new killer type and some perks for increasing your social rank) without addressing any of the core problems the game has, including bugs.It's entertaining for what it is and definitely unique, but its problems will be staring straight at you within minutes of starting your first game and only become more serious the longer you actually try to engage with the few systems you have available. The biggest one is that there's no real consequence for anything you do. Spend a whole playthrough committing crimes left and right, get seen by literally dozens of people as you forcibly barge into random people's apartments and beat them up and steal everything they own, and nothing ever changes because your 32k+ credit fine vanishes the instant you leave the building and sit on a bench around the corner. Solve a case and more pop up within a few minutes. Let citizens get murdered and new, equally bland citizens take their place.Bully someone literally every hour of every day for a week straight, kidnapping them in their own home with handcuffs and pretend you're feeding them to keep them alive while you torture them in cold blood, and absolutely nothing happens. You'll walk out the building, turn a corner, sit on a bench or enter a different building, and it's all instantly forgiven.Nearly every item in the game is completely useless because every problem can be solved by brute force without consequence. Gadgets like rubber grenades and doorstops are never worth using because you can lockpick every door between you and your target and instantly KO everyone by throwing chairs at them from the start of the game far more easily and reliably than you would by using them. They were designed in a vacuum because they sounded cool, without any actual consideration for the game they exist in, nor any reason or acknowledgement whatsoever (even superficial) for you to roleplay using them.Another major core issue is that all murders (and minor jobs for that matter) completely lack motive. All crimes are of opportunity, as killers simply pick targets randomly with a bias for convenience from proximity. Emails detailing things like infidelity or denied raises are completely meaningless fluff and never factor in as clues unless by sheer coincidence they generate with the killer's name. This means the vast majority of murders are committed by either the victim's partner or a co-worker, and since motive isn't a factor, all that's really useful to you is hard evidence in the form of fingerprints and physical attributes. Anything else you may find is junk to pawn off or fluff. As a result, there are no real narratives and it is false to claim the world is simulated beyond the simple fact that NPCs move to and from places. NPCs *do* have to physically move somewhere to kill their target, but that's it. They don't do it for any reason, nor are there any consequences for it. There are no conspiracies to unravel or relationships that matter. There are no hate crimes, revenge killings or anything of the sort - it's pure RNG. There is no personality to the killings; they don't get more brutal or sloppy if the killer is a neurotic speed freak with anger issues or cleaner and more obscure if the killer is a charismatic corporate type. They don't choose weapons based on context or personality. It's just RNG with no substance, which means nothing for you to actually do detective things over.There are a myriad of other problems I'll gloss over as they mostly exist because or are exacerbated by the core issues I already presented: performance isn't great, city generation is very glitchy, NPCs are so terrible with schedules that work hours might as well not be written down anywhere since they'll basically never open or close their work places at anywhere close to the right time, your apartment will frequently just eat items you leave in storage, there are numerous bugs with how the case file will attach attributes to specific NPCs (often creating redundant copies of the same person using the same infromation), sleeping takes absolutely forever, upgrades are terribly balanced and not incorporated into the world in any way (there isn't a single NPC you can observe using any of them nor are they even part of the written fluff).After 16 months of early access, none of them were really resolved but the price was increased and the game pushed out for console money anyway. The game is fun for a while, unique, and probably worth it on discount, but I'm not going to support a forced 1.0 pump and dump in good faith.

_childDocuments_.review: Shadows of Doubt is probably one of the most unique and innovative games I've played in a long time, and I've been incredibly impressed with its entire concept and gameplay loop.The idea of procedurally generated murders in a detective game is really cool, and opens layers of replayability and ongoing fun that I really enjoyed. I learned about the game shortly before its early access release, and decided to give it a shot shortly thereafter, especially after seeing a lot of glowing reviews. I was not disappointed, as I think it combines a unique gameplay concept, executes its aesthetic well, and has a great mix of activities available to keep you busy in the game.I think the thing it does best is its gameplay, which is a loop of solving murders that occur in the city you live in; you have to navigate around obstacles like whether or not you'll be allowed to examine the crime scene, and figure out what tidbits of information to look for. There's many ways to play, from full stealth to a more brute force approach. When you've solved a murder, you can return to your other daily goings-on, which may include solving smaller side-jobs, or doing a bit of your own investigation and snooping (or theft, depending on your playstyle!)I think its gameplay pairs well with its aesthetic, which I think the description of the game describes as a "Hyper-industrialized 1980s." That does sum it up fairly well, though I think it combines a lot of elements and focuses more on making itself a part of the genre of "Detective game," which is to its benefit. I loved every minute of being a private investigator in the city, and I find there's always some new detail about the way the game operates that makes me happy to discover. I really enjoyed my playtime, and could definitely see coming back, especially as this game is still in early access! I had nearly forgotten that fact, as it feels very complete. I ran into only one issue in the game, which was the way the rain would affect my framerate, but I was able to solve that by tinkering with weather settings, and I'd hope both that the issue will be solved in the future, and that it wouldn't deter players from an awesome game.Can't recommend this game enough, absolutely give it a try if it appeals to you! It's a lot of fun!

The amount of options to solve almost every case is rich and the world is very atmospheric. That's about it on the good parts.Now, where shall I begin wih the red flags? The game is a buggy mess that lags even on RTX 3080/R7 5800X3D machine, but that's not the main problem, really.UI/UX and navigation are atrocious, like a Dementor (yeah, read another book!) it sucks any sort of fun and enjoyment out of the game. There are no way to track clues on a map in a remotley predictable way. Clues managenent and reading through information about your victim is a puzzle by itself, more difficult than the most cases at hand. Look, when it's a huge problem to find your own apartment or almost anything relatable on the map, you have an issue. I do hope that the dev will hire someone to actually plan the damn UI, let alone draw one in a workable maner. UI scale on a 4K display is tiny, the interactive elements are either too hard to see or stand out too much. Inventory management is kinda ass and feels broken.There are also tons of game-breakling bugs. Tutorial case can softlock you (like, a lot). What else? Well, I really thought that the scale of the city would be much bigger, but that's EA game for you. Right now it's 4 by 4 blocks, feels very cramped tbh. There is also stark lack of sounds, soundtrack (and music direction) and first-person animations.At this point this game is more like a paid demo for a proof-of-concept. Some things do seem to function, but that's it. It's broken, boring and simply frustrating to navigate around almost every mechanic or concept here.Wait for more polish, at least in the UI department.

That can happen anyways but at least in that situation it's due to a mistake you made or a dead end trail.There is a very solid game here, wishlist it and keep an eye out.
_childDocuments_.name: Shadows of Doubt

_childDocuments_.review: This game is pretty good! A detective game that I've always wanted, everything is randomly generated! You can decorate your own apartment, plus there's a survival system. This game takes some time to learn, and there are many ways for you to go about on solving the murders and cases. Cons/Disappointments/Nitpicks: Art direction and Art Style is not really my thing, but eventually as you play i got used to itYou need a beefy computer to play this game, or else you'll encounter lag spikes I wish I can customize my own character I would like more content, more things to do >Is this game worth full price? Hmm, I'd say get this game on sale
_childDocuments_.name: Shadows of Doubt

_childDocuments_.review: Great! Even in it's current Early Access state you can get a lot out of it. The main gameplay is solving murder cases. They happen organically in a large noir city. Check out the detailed crime scene. Gather clues. Place all your clues on your bulletin board (Honestly one of my fav features from this game. It's so fun.), and investigate your leads all on your own. The game doesn't give hints or tells you where to go. If you're a bad investigator, you will fail a murder case and that'll be that. Very engaging. Needs more content. More varied murder scenarios. More challenge. Maybe a hard mode where you can't user certain databases that make some cases trivial. Different murder cases to help with the repetition. If this game has interested you at all, you owe it to yourself to check it out!
_childDocuments_.name: Shadows of Doubt

_childDocuments_.review: The game has so many interesting ideas going on that I was immediately captivated just by the concept alone, but as the novelty wore off I came to realize that it just isn't actually that fun to play.Once you learn how to solve cases all of them are either trivially easy (any case that can be solved using the government database, which the devs somehow still haven't bothered balancing) or pretty much impossible (find the one person in the city who has blue eyes and shoe size 7.) The stealth gameplay is mainly based on trial and error, and a lot of slowly crawling through vents. Or you can just wait for the tenant to go to sleep, that works too. When caught the tenant will just chase you and try to punch you for a bit before going back, while onlookers (including police) have zero reaction. The exception is when you get caught in a government building and the game bugs out so the alarm never ends, which happened to me more often than not. Falling through the floor was also a regular occurrence. I decided to come back in a year or two when the game was more feature complete, because the bones are all there. I was surprised to learn that apparently the game is leaving early access in September, and the price is increasing in August, for what is still a glorified tech demo.
_childDocuments_.name: Shadows of Doubt

_childDocuments_.review: Detective game play is fantastic, and coincidentally makes for a good thief simulator too.  Solving crimes is pretty rewarding and with the procedural generation you'll sometimes get easy cases and other cases might stump you for awhile before you finally solve them, but you'll certainly come away with great stories you'll want to share as other comments will attest to.
_childDocuments_.name: Shadows of Doubt

_childDocuments_.review: great idea, great premise. Falls short in a few categories.murder suspects literally roam the streets with guns drawn. preform a murder infront of enforcers and scamper off completely scott free. but if you punch them to save someone you get a 5 star wanted level by the entire street.Falling through floors or walking through walls. Constant cant escape it one building has at least one floor and one wall with 0 collision Inability to use firearms, despite having 8mm ammo and the gun that uses 8mm and the silencer to go with it. nothing can be used other than to throw or bludgeon with. yes its funny to pistol whip someone but if 4 goons jump me for my money and my life in a back alley as i try to access cctv cams let me kneecap them. (or become a vigilante/murderer myself)You can go so hungry and thirsty you'll die in about 4-5 hours if you're not constantly chugging Kola and hotdogs down your gob. Pawn shops not recognizing their own merchandise i stole and sold to them. Diamonds trophies watch's all from their safe/store and im allowed to sell it back to them and make way more money than if i ever did a job.your starting apartment also has a tendency to be the building that you wind up falling through everything.This is everything i found out in my meager 4.5 hours of playtime, for 20$ if you love this niche it's so worth it, if not wait for the bugs to be fixed and the 1.0 launch. I'm coming back to this game later but for now its a no from me.
_childDocuments_.name: Shadows of Doubt

_childDocuments_.review: Can't recommend this amazingly creative game. It's full of potential that I believe will never be realized. 1.0 is out in a month but the game feels like its still in the primary stages of development. While progress has been made since launch, I do not believe there have been any "major content" updates. There is so much left to do to make this a true immersive sim. Releasing it now is a mistake. The game is LITERALLY BROKEN RIGHT NOW. You can beat the game because its open ended, but much of the time you have to abandon your cases because of lost NPCs, broken geometry, and crashes. I'm so disappointed in this choice.EDIT (Post Launch): Still buggy, still broken, still falling into the world or getting stuck on geometry, still issues with unsolvable cases due to dead NPCs, still getting the same cases over and over, auto travel still broken, perscription information still unused, etc. I'm over the fact that no new content or context is being added. Now I'm just pissed the game is still so buggy.
_childDocuments_.name: Shadows of Doubt

_childDocuments_.review: Just wow, what a cool concept executed well. The way the world feels and how you interact with it. Over time how crime scenes evolve and police cordon off the area.. It is all just very immersive.. and a bit eerie, thinking I am going to run into a serial killer when looking through a dark apartment.This has got me very excited for the future of this game. I did have an issue with the AI not registering me coming out of a murder scene and a few bugs so far. I also would like to see less mini guns stashed in each apartment building and more police response to alarms. However I can understand if this is by design to show the style of the city you play in. This game is definitely recommended for anyone who wants to experience a good detective sim and in my opinion, this is a bargain at the current price (£15)
_childDocuments_.name: Shadows of Doubt

_childDocuments_.review: A 75% buy.It bears to remember that this is absolutely not a complete game yet. While the game is alot of fun and solving the murders is what i like to see in a detective game. The low number of cases available severely limit its replayability. Once you have solved a case and a similar one pops up again, you know what to do and thus the game gets stale relatively quickly. However, it is alot of fun for around 10 or so hours. It needs a lot more cases though.What it also lacks is world building. While everything is simulated, the NPC's are incredibly basic, offering very little in terms of interactivity. You cant make friends, you cant make enemies, crimes you commit against folks are forgotten quickly. Many items in the game dont (yet) have a use. The survival mechanics  feel a bit pointless as they are relatively easy to deal with. Performance of the game also limits the city size to small for most computers, its crashy and DOES NOT have autosave on quit. That means an ironman like run isnt possible and isnt recommended as frequent saving is very important due to crashes.While there is a lot of negativity in this review, i still like the game a lot. It has with alot more work quite a bit of potential.
_childDocuments_.name: Shadows of Doubt

_childDocuments_.review: I've just straight up been playing this game for 3 days. Got a bit of strangeness here and there, but those should be easy bugfixes. Its easy to get lost in all the gathering of info. I can imagine this game could become one of those long term timesinks for me. _childDocuments_.name: Shadows of Doubt

_childDocuments_.review: I took too long. The enforcers are already guarding the door to 503 Rose Building, the scene of the crime. There's a vent above, might lead into the apartment. I'll just have to be really quiet. With the blessing of my manlet-be-gone sync tech and a cardboard box I casually reach up and pull myself into it. It's cold in here, good thing I brought coffee. I tumble around, but eventually find my way into the victim's bedroom. I sneak into the kitchen where a gnarly scene awaits.The dame is laying face down in her own blood. Yua Morita, 33, office manager, shot to death. Scantily clad, might have known her killer. The wounds suggest a high calibre rifle. The kitchen is narrow and cramped, had to be point blank. Diary's under the bed. She thought that she was stalked by a male of average height. Believed him to be a headhunter first. Too broad.I find her passcode on a note. Nobody remembers anything in this city. A v-mail from her doctor blames her medications for the paranoia. Hope she didn't pay the 45 crow consultation fee for that. She asked the building management for video evidence, but no cigar.I start looking for prints. After finding dozens of the victim's I happen upon an unidentified one on the rim of her toilet. Bingo. I grab her address book and head to her workplace, Offinex Enterprises. It's late, closed hours ago. I pick the lock, dash under the cameras, and disable their security. I find their roster in a filing cabinet. Check the prints. No matches. Won't be that easy, eh?I head to the city hall and check the prints of everybody in her address book. No matches. Was the killer a stranger? I take a detour to the local fence. I don't know the password, but it makes no difference. I kick down the door, grab the sales records, and book it. I hide around the corner and conceal my face with the newspaper until it's clear. I check the prints of everyone who bought a rifle or ammo. No matches. Huh. A stranger with an old gun?Four days pass, still nothing. I take a side gig to feed my crippling Starch Kola addiction. While scanning the mailboxes of the complex next door, I come across a familiar set of prints. It cannot be! The mailbox doesn't have an address on it, but there are only a few dozen apartments in the building. I scan every door until I find my prey. Multiple matching prints. I barge through the door and draw my truncheon, but I'm alone in the apartment. I find her papers in the closet and... Oh no. An enforcer. The very one who guarded the crime scene. The fool must have taken a bathroom break.I head back to the victim's apartment. Must have missed something. It's already cleaned up, body's gone. Funny, I can see the enforcer's flat from here. Wait... I check the windows. They're pristine. But were they four days ago? I failed to verify. Maybe that shot wasn't as point blank as I thought.I open the files from the arms sales. Only two average height males. One is homeless. The other, Rishi Rege, lives in 402 Pickett Heights. Right across the street. Clear line of sight. There's no time to waste. I pry open the elevator door and jump down the shaft. That Vigor tech was worth every crow.I knock. A woman opens the door. She rejects my initial request for entry, but can't resist when I sweeten the deal. When she wanders into the bathroom, I drive a wedge under the door. She doesn't need to see what's about to happen. Rishi's waiting for me in the living room. Doesn't even deny the deed. Goes down in a few strikes and the cuffs click. I look around the rooms. Handwritten notes suggest he's a peeper. I find his sniper rifle in a walk-in closet. There's only one thing left to do here.When he comes to, I ask him why. She didn't close her blinds, she asked for it. At times like these I'm glad I don't carry a gun. Might have bludgeoned this nutjob to death with it. I head to the city hall and fill out the resolution form. There isn't enough evidence to confirm the murder weapon, but it's only a minor cut from my pay. He's nailed either way. Case closed.It's a game where I spent 10+ hours chasing down the wrong fingerprint and I don't regret a moment of it. There's some clear jank here, but it's still an easy recommendation.
_childDocuments_.name: Shadows of Doubt

_childDocuments_.review: The smell of cigar smoke and sound of ice clanking against the wall of a full whiskey glass fade away as you listen to the story told by this mysterious figure. It was a dark and cold January night, the wind was howling and the streets crawling with citizens from all walks of life. A chill came over me, the kind of chill that can't be fixed by a burn barrel. My radio static clicks and clacks *Murder reported 1601 Tian Building*. I start running, despite the aching in my joints from the bitter cold, I need to beat the enforcers to this case. I burst through the lobby door only to see an Enforcer running up the stairs just ahead of me. I scoff. *Smarter not harder* I call the elavator and on my ascent pass him by. He's moving slow and out of breath, but my truncheon and I are kicked back, all warmed up and ready to kick some pixels. I knock on the door. Surprisingly the vic isn't alone. Could it be a lover? The perp? Or did I just plain have the wrong address. Footsteps approach, the lock clacks.Calm as could be, a little too calmly, the door is opened by a man. He starts to walk out, he doesn't wanna chat. *Another puff of cigar smoke floats through the air* with no enforcer in sight I cuff him, take his finger prints and send him on his merry way. He can't hide from me, no one in this city can. The enforcers approach the door, my time is running out, I slip in through the door un-noticed by the guard outside. But much to my surprise there's another enforcer already inside. He spots me. I run for the bathroom, barricade the door and jump into the air vent. I enjoy a good chuckle as much as the next PI, so I watch as the enforcer struggles to barge down the door and see the look of disappointment on his face when he notices I'm nowhere to be found. Alarms sound throughout the building. I scale down and break out just one floor below. Alarms don't scare me, I'm half deaf anyway from being shot at up close so many times. I bolt up the steps, truncheon in hand and knock the guards out. I'll be in and out before they wakeup and they won't remember a thing. I succeed.The living room is a mess, a bloody syringe lays on the carpet with a sloppy fingerprint left behind. It's a new one. Not yet in my database. A true good ole fashion mystery. The body lays in the corner slumped over. The taste of the blood tells me she was poisoned. *Smacks tongue* cyanide I mutter to myself. I ID the Vic and soon after discover a business card in the corner, under a cardboard box. It has scribbled on it "DIDNT MAKE THE CUT. DO BETTER, YOU ARE DONE"I search the house and find where the Vic works, I rush over to the Crimson group. Break in after shutting off security and find the employee board. A man catches my eye. "head of QA department." Lucky for me he hung his own picture. The print is a match. I sprint down to city hall, pull his information from the database. I race to his apartment, it's early in the morning and I need my 8 hours of beauty rest. It's early, I'm not in the mood to play games. I knock on his door. He says he's coming. 5, 10, 15 seconds pass. I bang even louder. Nothing. Did he off himself? Did he escape somehow? Is he preparing his weapon to kill me at the door? I'm not giving him that chance. I burst through the door using my good shoulder. He is running at me from the bathroom. I knock him out cold and cuff him. He's confused, doesn't know what happened. He doesn't want to speak to me. It's ok I have all the evidence I need. I find the vial of poison on him and make my way to city hall, massaging my now sore shoulder. I turn in the case file, collect my crows, and hit the sack. Tomorrow is another day, another murder to solve. ----------------------------This game is one of the best I have played in a long time 10/10 buy. Endlessly playable.
_childDocuments_.name: Shadows of Doubt

_childDocuments_.review: My first case involved a murderer who chose to kill all his colleagues. I spent almost 3 game days to track him down. He killed 3 victims in the meantime, which was like half of the company employees. Poor company must have gone bankrupt! :D I already started to think that my case is bugged, because I didn't seem to have any chance to track who it was. And then it came - a proof came by looking at CCTV camera installed right in front of the victim's door! Emmanuel Davies was his name! I even managed to arrest that guy myself - right in the office where he worked (and which was almost vacant due to his killing rampage).Now I have a second case - victim shot dead by a rifle. Neighbours said they saw a suspicious person hanging around at the time of murder, wearing glasses. So I checked CCTV cameras again and saved photos of all glass-wearing people who entered the building around the time of murder. I have  4 suspects. This will be a tougher one...I played the game for around 20 hours now, but I already love it! There are some minor bugs but honestly, those are expected from game like this. My biggest surprise is that I can manage to play "very Large city" without any problems or stuttering issues. I can definitely recommend the game as it has very unique atmosfere. I absolutely love the procedurally generated interiors - they look so cozy and immersive! I only with tere will be more building types in the future, more architecture styles (I can imagine Burton-like Gotham city Gothic towers for example). This game has a ton of potential and I hope it will be even better in the future.
_childDocuments_.name: Shadows of Doubt

_childDocuments_.review: A fun detective game where everything is entirely simulated. This can cause some errors with certain object placement, vents, and items in certain areas, but I've never experienced anything impeding progress. The variety of missions leaves something to be desired, but the procedural nature of the odd jobs and murder cases makes every case unique and with varying levels of difficulty to solve. I also wish there was more in the way of interrogating suspects. As it stands you are more of a freelance private investigator with no police jurisdiction, so all you can really do is ask people simple questions about their name, anything suspicious, if they know the person you're investigating, or their fingerprints and hope that they don't tell you to touch grass.Other than that, It's a fantastic game and I can't wait to see where the devs take it from here!
_childDocuments_.name: Shadows of Doubt

_childDocuments_.review: This game has so much potential. It is still very rough around the edges. A lot of work still needs to be done to polish it up and add some more variety to the game. But I'm having a blast playing it. I think I'll get to the point where it gets old because it can be a lot of the same jobs over and over again but there are many different ways to investigate in order to solve cases. Adding multiplayer would be the absolute best feature imaginable for this game but as a developer myself, I understand how difficult of an undertaking that would be. Single player is still worth buy the game for $15 or $20.

_childDocuments_.review: i'll hold off on writing an actual critique as this game is in VERY early access, but just to summarize: as of april 2024, there's barely any actual content in the game, the game is VERY buggy, it's VERY repetitive and at time even tedious and it runs VERY bad. i capitalized the very there because these are not minor issues, after 10 hours of playing i'm basically all done and am really bored. the steam page and videos about this game may lead you to believe that there's a very indepth system present of procedural generation and crazy detective mechanics, but there's no such thing, you can't even shoot a gun or kill anyone. hold off for now, this is slightly more than a tech demo, but it's still a long ways away from being good.
_childDocuments_.name: Shadows of Doubt

_childDocuments_.review: It's a neat game, but it is mostly in a prototyping stage in my opinion. The cases are too monotonous, lack complexity, and require a LOT of anti-exciting busywork most of the time. IMO, it really needs something like an "AI"-Director, that constructs more complex cases with evidence chains and events. It also suffers from quite a few bugs that must be ironed out to avoid frustration (especially in the UI/case relevant object persistence department). In terms of UI/UX there are quite a few features that could be designed in a better way, or that are just janky. The kinds of evidence and the way cases are structured gets boring a LOT faster than it should, and it feels like this game is leaving a whole lot of potential on the table because of that. The whole criminal investigation aspect needs massive expansion and improvement. Motives, kinds of relationships, the kinds of crimes that could be investigated... this thing could be glorious.All that said, this is one of the coolest little games in a long time. I'd still say Sid Meier's Covert Action is the best game in this genre, but that's mostly because it had proc-genned plots and investigations that were pretty cool and connected to what was happening in the world, which is not the case here.
_childDocuments_.name: Shadows of Doubt

_childDocuments_.review: A simulation game that manages to capture what it's like to be a seedy private ♥♥♥♥ in a city that knows how to keep its secrets. Bribe witnesses, gather evidence, and eat all the synthetic meat you come across to catch the killer.The downside is, that it accurately captures what it's like to be a seedy private ♥♥♥♥ in a city that knows how to keep its secrets. You'll be chasing any lead you can get; reading every email you can find, looking at every minute of security footage you can access, and sometimes simply working through every name in a victim's phone book in a desperate effort to find a lead. Sometimes, you'll be at a dead end. The only thing to do then is to pack it in, because the trail has gone cold. This can be tedious busywork, much like being a real private detective. It's not glitz and glamour, kids. You'll be digging through trash and selling out to the corporations just to get an edge, and taking unsavory jobs just to make ends meet.If you can stomach that, this is a game that encourages creativity, patience, and curiosity in a way I haven't before seen in a game, and I'm hungry for more.
_childDocuments_.name: Shadows of Doubt

_childDocuments_.review: I arrive at the murder scene to find a policeman warning a young lady (just inside the doorway) to vacate the crime scene. Thinking this person is awfully suspicious, i decide to have a quick chat with the lady and ask a few questions, locking her in place as we chat. During my questioning (which was getting me nowhere) the policeman turns around and plugs her in the back of the head a couple of times, killing her for trespassing. (she continues to tell me that it's none of my business while lying dead on the ground)After searching her body and finding a pistol, (the murder weapon) then searching the crime scene, i find out that the lady who was executed by the policeman for trespassing was in fact the killer!Case solved within 5 minutesThis game is great!Knocking on doors, waiting for the occupant to answer then barging through the door KO'ing the occupant is my favourite thing to do.

_childDocuments_.review: After the game has been in development for so long, I expected there to be more "completion" to the official release. The game is still a buggy mess in terms of world generation, animation, and character pathfinding. After generating a new world today, items were spawning within each other, the NPC's were glitching through walls, the lighting of rooms were still faulty, etc.I get that this is an indie team and that coding video games may be hard but this "release" seems very rushed and half-heartedly put together. With a release like this, I worry for the game's future development and upkeep and I can't help but think the developers might abandon this game soon. If nothing is addressed about these issues within the next couple of months, I'm refunding the game.
