_childDocuments_.review: At its heart, Expeditions: Rome is a great CRPG with amazing turn-based combat, all set against the backdrop of the late Roman republic. Just to get it out of the way quick: The game is great, and while I have some criticisms to make, that doesn't mean the game isn't one of the better games I've played in a while. This is almost certainly my 2022 GOTY.The Good:  - The turn-based tactical combat is done about as well in this game as it has ever been done in any game. The decisions you make during the combat are almost always meaningful, particularly while playing on the harder difficulty levels. It is incredibly satisfying to take on forces much larger than your own and come out on top.  - The game features interesting RPG companions with their own unique personalities, in the tradition of titles like Dragon Age. Unlike games like Dragon Age, here you get to take all of your companions with you on the main quests, so you never feel like you are missing out on one of them.  - The RPG dialogue and story decision points mostly feel very meaningful. There are multiple endings and multiple ways for things to play out depending on the decisions and dialogue choices you make.The Meh:  - The game clocked in at 46 hours for me which, for my tastes, is a little on the long side of things. There is some flab that could have been cut, which I'll get to later.  - You essentially have two teams to go on missions with you. On the one hand you have the A-team, which consists of your main story companions, all decked out in the best gear. Then you have the B-team, which is a team of faceless mooks that you hire at the start of every Act. The game essentially forces you to use the B-team during "pacification" missions (these are the missions you have to go on to fully take control of a province during the campaign). At the end of each Act, the game typically has a large set-piece battle where you combine your A and B teams together (which is cool). The problem with the B-team is that they are generally less leveled and geared than your main A-team, which makes their missions artificially tougher than they ought to be. On top of that, these guys have no personality so, unlike your companions, they just aren't that much fun to be around and play with. In theory, I believe they were going with an "X-Com" kind of vibe with the B-team, where you grow attached to these other squaddies and you have those painful moments when your favorite or most useful teammate gets killed during a mission. In practice, these guys don't have enough personality to care about and you don't even end up learning their name, let alone get attached to them in any way. It is an attempt at something, but it falls a bit flat.  - The game has crafting, but it never felt like an interesting decision to make. Every new Act means the equipment in the area goes up a level, which means its time to craft new stuff. Again, it falls flat and feels unnecessary.  - You get the opportunity to upgrade your legion camp as the game goes along, but here again it never feels like an interesting decision. You just upgrade as you go and you never really have to think about getting one upgrade over another. Another game system that falls kind of flat.The Bad:  - The UI is a bit clunky and doesn't communicate everything that it needs to you. The game is filled with status effects and little combat modifiers, but I'll be damned if I found out where the game told me about half of them. Moreover, I should be able to know when the enemy archer has a line of site on my characters or not, but the game gives you no indication. I can't even count how many times I thought I was in full cover, only to be shot in the face by an enemy archer during their turn.  - The game consists of overworld maps, where you move around armies and take your character's main party to various locations, and then the detailed scenes of the various locations that your party arrives in. Those detailed scenes are often very large, and often very empty. Many times a quest will have you go to one of these scenes, force you to walk all the way across it to talk to some NPC, and then walk all the way back to the exit. The game could really use a "leave area now" button. Moreover, at the end of combat you have to go around and scavenge the bits off of the bodies of your fallen foes. This process takes forever, is rarely rewarding, and feels like it could be totally streamlined out.  - The voice acting is generally excellent, so this is kind of a personal nitpick, however, they made this very odd choice of mixing in the Latin pronunciations of certain words that we would otherwise anglicize in our daily lives. It is incredibly jarring to be reading a subtitle in your head such as "Julius Caeser and the Legate came up with plans on how to use their Centurions to command their legionnaires", and then the voice actor gets there and says "YOU-LIUS KAI-AYE-ZAR and the LA-GAH-TAYE came up with plans on how to use their "KEN-TOURY-ONAYS" to command their "LEGGY-ON-ARAYS". Like I said, it is jarring, and by the time they get to Act three most of the voice actors can't even agree upon how to pronounce the new names and words that are coming up (seriously, "Vercingetorix" must be pronounced five different ways in the game).The Ugly:  - If you've read other reviews then you know by now that the legion combat on the overworld map is just terrible. It consists of picking one of three random cards for four separate phases of battle. Whoever has the most troops left at the end wins. The cards you get to pick from are totally random (you can't craft a deck), and most of the time the differences between the cards are negligible anyway, so it never feels like you are making a meaningful decision. Unfortunately, you do more of these annoying legion battles than you do just about anything else in the game. The worst part of these battles is that they are so clearly a missed opportunity for an actually good, well thought out battle system that I'm sure these developers could come up with, given that the main tactical combat system they made is so good. It is just a shame.  - The "random encounters" are infuriating. While traveling on the overworld map with your party, you will frequently be waylaid by random encounters. Some of these are interesting and at first they add flavor to the proceedings, but by the end of the game you'll find that 90% of these encounters boil down to "x,y party members are injured", which functionally means you have to stop whatever it is you were doing with your party, march them back to your camp, and then wait the 30 hours for them to heal up before you can go back to doing whatever it is you wanted to do in the first place. Like many things in the game, it feels like an artificial speed bump to slow your progress, and it becomes incredibly annoying as time goes on.Okay, enough grousing. The game is almost perfect, so go buy it. It has some issues, mostly pertaining to extra fluff that they've layered on top of the otherwise excellent CRPG and turn-based combat bits. This extra stuff only serves to slow the game down and drag out the run-time. The final Act of the game basically does away with all the extraneous bits, and it is absolutely the best paced part of the game. I hope they learn from that for the next entry in the series, which I'm absolutely going to play now regardless.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall: Tons of fun. There are a few elements that I found tedious/take away from the experience, but well worth dealing with those. I will be doing another play through some time to try out a few other decisions/endings.This game really shines in its two main elements: combat and diplomacy/storytelling. The combat is similar to XCOM and can be pretty challenging (especially at first). Once I got the hang of it I really had fun. The siege missions are especially fun. As far as the storytelling goes you make so many little and big decisions throughout the game and there is often never a "right" or "good" answer. It does not hold your hand and tell you the consequences or potential outcomes and each thing you say. It feels like you are truly paving your own story. In the end, there are 7 major endings but the combos of all your small decisions probably can give you countless endings.  I would argue that the legion combat and resource management could be completely stripped from this game. In my opinion these things added very little and were annoyances getting in the way of playing the parts of the game I enjoyed. I just skipped through every legion sequence picking tactic that was obviously the best. Perhaps these things wouldn't have been so bad if the map and UI weren't so god awful to use. Those are truly the worst part of the game. I spent way too much time scrolling around the map trying to find something because it was impossible to see a thing. Make a zoomed out map with persistent icons and don't make me go back to the outpost just to do a simple task.  Besides those things, great game.
_childDocuments_.name: Expeditions: Rome

_childDocuments_.review: Decent game, but it felt like it was released a few months shy of being complete. The combat is the best feature of the game, but it is not as frequent as one would hope. Instead, there is a lot of walking around and rote tasks to complete in order to get to the next combat opportunity. There are many quality of life improvements that could have been made, including picking up loot (why make us walk to each corpse after a battle? just automatically collect it), getting rid of extra loot (could flag inferior items to remove tediousness of getting rid of loot), getting to a certain destination to continue the story (why not save 2 minutes of walking and loading screens if there is only one place we can go to?), having the camera automatically move to the best angle, and more... This game could have been phenomenal, but there were too many small things that ultimately detracted from the best elements (combat, plot/story, real consequences behind choices, and the setting).

_childDocuments_.review: I'll keep this short. Game had an interesting storyline, while shaky in Act 1, really started to pick up steam in Act 2, and fell flat in Act 3. It was to a point I just didn't care anymore to finish it. Main villain's ploys are laughable at worst and just easily see through where you can guess what is about to happen without seeing dialogue choices.Choices made by the programmers of this game for mechanics boggles the mind. It is suppose to be a military type campaign but does nothing to incorporate strategy elements. You have options to unlock "strategies" as battles commence against rival armies but you have no choice in which ones to select for the various phases. Its all random. Further in order to do anything you must send your entire legion on the map to gain resources. The ENTIRE legion. Wanted to build a farm, construct a mine, everyone in the legion has to go do it making continued conquest and the system itself just slow. What I don't get as well is the choice to specialize your companions and soldiers. By the time you get to the end game you have already filled up a particular skill tree for them and start bleeding over into others. Thus other than differences on the overall category of soldier type (defensive, archer, high attacker, healer) there is no uniqueness to anything and all just become bland copies of themselves. Even for the unique companions it is the same thing.Crafting is available in this game but unlocking different armors, and designs to customize equipment do nothing special. Minor differences such as a +1-3% is all the difference it makes. As well, you would expect different weapons and armors for the various cultures you are visiting in the world to have some key differences but that also isn't the case. Weapons/armor for the Gaul tribes does the same as the Egyptians. You may get some different visual appearances but big whoop.In all if you must have this, buy it cheap. Otherwise, take a pass.

_childDocuments_.review: the most important aspect of a game. Pros:+ Great story telling+ Charming and diverse cast of characters + A very well researched adaptation of Roman warfare and culture+ Reading the tool-tips in the options menu was very entertaining. I'd like to commend greatly whoever made those at Logic Artists because it gave me a hearty chuckle.Cons:- Core gameplay loop- UI / UX- Missing a lot of QOL- Legion Battle SystemWell it starts out as fairly typical (and very enjoyable) Turn Based Tactical RPG. You create your main character, watch some cut-scenes, chit chat with people around you, partake is some cool missions with objectives that you can choose how to complete. I really thought I was going to enjoy the game a lot at this point.Unfortunately, after getting into the  portion of the game it just lost a lot of it's charm and became slogging chore to do anything. You eventually take command of giant armies via the legion battle system which just boils down to a numbers game with some fancy animations that actually don't mean much. After the first couple it's just easier to auto-resolve and skip the animations. You don't place units in any way, or make any real strategies, you just pick the formation that leads to the least losses or more loot depending on what you want and skip to the end. If you have a sense of imagination maybe it would be cool to create a head-cannon of whats happening on the battle, but it's just not a system that peaked my interest much. Of course, these legion battles are only a third of what the game has to offer, but even the tactical battle system fell off for me in the end. You have wayyy too many to manage. All with their own gear and perk trees, it was cool when I had 5 companions, but with 10+ it was just too much for me to handle. Especially due to the UI/UX I mentioned. The UI itself is alright. It's very in theme and stylish, but for lack of a better term it just looks flat and un-intuitive to maneuver. Compounded by the fact that after a battle you have to manually click on every dead body to gather the loot which you end up scrapping most of to craft better stuff anyways. I just stopped having fun. Loot wasn't a reward, it was a chore. My companions that I really enjoyed took a back-seat at camp, and I just felt spread thin on what to do. I received this game as a gift from a very generous doner, and I'm really glad I had a chance to try this game, but I cannot recommend it, especially at a price of $45. If you're REALLY REALLY into the Roman / Greek war history, and are okay with spending a lot more time managing instead of fighting- this game might be for you, but it simply wasn't for me.

_childDocuments_.review: Pros:  The small attention to detail and object design in the world is impressive (too bad you can't admire it from close-up though).Cons:  Combat gives NO experience. You gain NO experience from killing enemies. Did you catch that? It doesn't matter if you kill 1 enemy on a mission or 1000000 enemies, you'll still gain the exact same rewards from the mission when you complete it. I honestly cannot for the life of me understand why the devs would design their game like this. Think of a single bloody game that has levels, but DOESN'T give you experience for killing enemies (besides this one).... .... The 'attack of opportunity' (AoO) system is . I've NEVER played a game where the AoO system works like this. It hugely benefits melee characters and makes them quite a bit more powerful than ranged characters. The battlefield is hex-based. So unlike XCOM2 or DOS2 or Wasteland 3 where you can move freely, in this game you can ONLY move on hexes and it VERY often results in you facing an enemy 1-on-1 in a corridor, because there are many corridors that are only 1 or 1.5 hexes in size... so you literally have 5+ people queuing up behind the character, just passing each turn, because they can't act or attack at all until the guy in front dies. Combat ends and enemies run away when you kill a certain amount of them (5-10). That means you literally lose out of loot, since your loot simply runs away.  Bleeding, Harried, etc. isn't applied if the target character has armour. This MASSIVELY benefits the shield-bearing class, since they are basically always immune to all status ailments. So even if your skill applies Bleeding 100% of the time, it WON'T apply Bleeding if the target has armour from their shield. The game has TIMED, channel-exclusive, twitch drops. You have to watch over 30hours of twitch on various different channels, before the 31st of January 2022, in order to collect all the drops. So you're not only forced to watch specific twitch streamers for 4hours+ each, but it's also timed exclusive so after the 31st you can't get those in-game items again. You can't zoom-in NEARLY enough for the 'zoom' function to be actually useful. This game could have benefited MASSIVELY from being able to zoom-in very close, but for some reason, the devs made it so that you can't hardly zoom-in at all. The classes are MASSIVELY linear. The 'shield class' can't dual-wield OR use crossbows OR two-handers... likewise, the Medic and Archer classes can't use shields, etc. This is a gigantic limitation, especially when you compare it to DOS2 (or many other TRPGs) where the classes aren't severely shoehorned into specific shapes like this.You cannot change the game's resolution when playing on 'borderless windowed' mode. The game costs 45 bloody dollars. That's the same base-price as DOS2 and nearly the same as XCOM2 or Wasteland 3, but the game  that either of those games have. This game simply doesn't have the right to ask 45 bucks.... it would be like Sims 4 asking $300.... it's simply too outlandish. The options in the character creator are abysmal. Only 3 different faces, and 3 different hairstyles..... that's just lazy. There's no other word for it.... lazy devs. The cinematics are that typical lazy type of 'static image, that's slightly animated'. It's a very, very lazy type of cinematics and I would have MUCH rather preferred to see in-game cinematics instead of that lazy 'static image' type of cinematics. There was no pre-load available before game lauch. Any game that is as big as this one (20GB+) and available for pre-order weeks in advance, SHOULD offer a pre-load. This is pretty much industry-standard by now, but for some reason, this game didn't offer a pre-load, and that's a big con to people who still have rubbish internet.It's seriously not even close.... I would play XCOM2, DOS2 or Wasteland3 a hundred times over, before I play another hour of this game. It has WAY less freedom, WAY less content and WAY less RPG-ness than XCOM2, DOS2 and Wasteland3, and it has no right charging $45. I wanted to like this game, since I'm a big fan of the genre and have over 400hours in the above mentioned games, but this game simply isn't worth being mentioned in the same breath as those games. Not recommended, .Here's my first hour or so of the game: My wishlisted games if you wanna be a bro: For more reviews, visit my curator page:

_childDocuments_.review: A 'game' like this is all about connecting with the characters.  Equipping the characters, building them up with equipment.  And then composing the characters to do missions.You essentially have 2 teams.  Your companion characters, which all have stories and thatpart of the game is okay.  Then you have the 'B team'.  Selectable disposable charactersthat form your praetorian guard.  In total all characters is about 14 characters big, whichleaves 8 for the 'B team'.  Now given a mission, you will select the best characters youcan which means your companions.  That means you will always select the 6 companions to doany given mission.  The game designers identified this as a problem, so they force you to do some missions with the 'B team'.  You can only pick 1 companion character to do these missions.  My point is that party composition is largely a non-affair.  Your six primarycharacters are all prescribed (like a lot of RPGs, so fair enough).  Forcing you not to usethem though, after equipping them with all your best gear....  And then you might argue,how about some good stuff for the B team?  Well its an RPG.  You are supposed to careabout the character and his load-out.  And now the game is forcing you to screw that up?You don't care about the B-team.. Why would you?And then there is the final mission of Act 1. all your characters are disarmed.  The dialogsuggests you have hidden your weapons. But I can't see how you access and equip them in the middle of combat.  The game is about choosing characters, equipping them, and then composingthem in a team.  The character group is prescribed and the equipment is all gone.  All othermissions thus far are trivial, and now its a slog to retry this mission over and over againwhile fight mobs with swords using my characters fists?Like I say, fantastic level design...There is more....I'm now at act 2. and there is a mission where you go to the after life and meet this catcharacter, who offers you a choice.  The idea is that you can choose to go to Elysium andbe a good person, or go back to the real world and be a bad person. You are offered 2 doors,one yellow and one red.  Guess what happens if you pick the red door?   That's right, the gameends right there.. Game over.... What kind of game does this?  Its laughable..  You don't offerthe player an absolute ending and call that a choice....  Its a forced reload.  What does redmean to you?  Is that bad moral character or death?  Yellow?  Elysium or daylight?What is good is the Roman theme.  Which is what I suspect is getting all the positive reviews.There is a very great lack of games, especially RPGs that address this time period. Also, someof the tactical choices are good.  The idea that shields are a foil for archers.. That spearmenshould be behind the sheld line.Now that bad tactical choices..  The medic in the team is a triarchus, the spearman.  When in formation, you expect the shield dudes (princeps) to take the hits and the spearman behind himto deal the damage.. However, the spearman is also your medic.  You are forced to choose, whetherthe triarchus will be a medic or a damage dealer.  Then there are archers. They always hit.  If the archer has poison arrows, then in order to surviveyou must either have antivenom equipped as a tactical item, which is a mission itself to obtain,or all your non shield guys need to hide.  The game has a habit of shooting my veles (light troops)who don't have any shields with poison arrows which will hit.  Consequently my veles is going downand the only tactical counter to this is not to use the veles character.. Move forward with yourprinceps and clear the archers.  Wait a minute....???!!  You mean my heavily armed tanky dudeis the guy who's going to be chasing down these light moving archers guys who live on the back line?Okay, but what about just enduring the poison?  Well my veles gets shot 3 times, and runs back to the triarchus, my medic, who, can't buff his hit points at all if he's poisoned. I don't expect thebandage to cure him of poison, but I do expect a hit point buff.. But no, my veles has taken 3 poisonarrows trying to do his job, which is to run around the back and harass the archers, but is now on theverge of death and can't be healed by the medic who is standing right next to him, bandage in hand.Okay, what about my archers?  Yeah they deal damage alright.  not as much as poison arrows, but theoverwatch mechanic is the most powerful in the game.  My companion archer can shoot 3 times during overwatch, which means that tactically the recipe there is a one trick deal.  Overwatch... all the time. The enemy light guys just fall apart.  So my conclusions to the tactical composition of the team when not using companions? Loads of princeps, veles are useless.  Since the princeps are tough and immune to archers, its the only practical way ofdealing with poison arrows.  archers are cool if you can hide them.Caltrops... oh boy... you throw down a blanket of caltrops that inflict bleeding damage on any charactersthat pass through them... Unfortunately the enemy mobs are smart enough to avoid them.  And the caltrops will still be there when the immediate mobs are dead, so I end up hurting my own guys more with caltrops.Its another useless mechanic.2nd act there is a weird ability for dead mobs to come alive for a single round and while being invulnerable,get to attack your dudes.  There is nothing complex about this mechanic.  Its a free shot... They are invulnerable, so overwatch is no help.  The only guys that handle this well are your tanky princeps butthey handle all damage well.  I can't figure out what the intention of this actually is?  How does it modify your game play?  How does it introduce anything interesting... on the contrary, it puts you in the situation that once all the enemy guys are dead, you need to tortoise for a turn just to make surethat none of the dead guys will rise again, and pummel your softer dudes.Okay... now onto the strategic game... This comprises conquering territory with your legion..  legion battlesare a really lame card game of 4 rounds, 3 card presented and supposedly your choices affect the outcome ofyour legion battle.  I haven't lost one yet, but supposedly if you did lose, you could just try again.You pick a general from your praetorian guard to lead the battle.  Not sure how he affects anything either.And he is a centurion, and not a legate, which is your character... that's right... Your character does not lead legion battles...  He's more of a AWOL small action trouble shooter than a strategic thinker it seems.  The strategic game comprises:  Well... pick a territory to invade.. find the capital - move your legionthere... Then do the pacification mission - a small action where you can only use the B team.  Once that is done, you get the territory.. Then you move you legion to the mines, lumber yard and tanneries.  Theorder does not matter.. Once you have these you can go back to your base, and expand on it.  Thenonce you have purchased certain upgrades, the armoury and forge, you can finally build better equipmentand upgrade the stuff you already have...  So for those not paying attention, the short version; you canonly upgrade your gear half way through the game, after doing this really dull and even dumber sequenceof 'strategic' actions.  RPGs are about gathering and equiping gear... Why restrict item upgrades for half the game?Legion morale seems to be of importance, and the only real cost to expanding on the strategic map. There is nogauge indicator for morale.  I haven't actually tested driving moral down and checking... but supposedly thatwould be bad.  But, ... quite marvelously, there is a method to increase legion morale.  You move one of your praetorian dudes into the baths and that buffs legion morale by 4 every 32h.. and I've run out of space for my comment......

_childDocuments_.review: One of my favorite games of the past few years. It successfully combines isometric combat (XCOM), territory control (Civilization-esque), and RPG 'choices matter' in a single package. Isometric combat in other games rely on sci-fi or fantasy elements to make it interesting but this game pulls it off with the limited resources of that time period. Each class has a variety of abilities that allow for different playstyles with synergies between the characters that add strategic depth. The game rewards good tactical gameplay, taking advantage of the terrain where possible, and maximizing the synergy between characters. The end of each act has an epic tactical battle where this really shines.The story is compelling and the voice acting is superb -- possibly on par with BG3. Cleopatra's voice was dripping with the condescension and attitude I expect from a Queen of Egypt. Each of your characters have unique personalities and stories and there are great romance options.The moral choices were especially interesting in this game. Some games have moral choices that are very black and white good/bad/neutral. Here many of the choices are morally grey and there's possibly no right or wrong answer. The ending has a montage of how your choices affected the lives of the people you met over the game which was a nice touch.The weakest link in the game is the territory control aspect of the campaigns. After conquering the first 4 territories it starts to feel very 'rinse and repeat'. The army battles boil down to a numerical tug of war card game where there isn't much strategic depth. The encounter stories while exploring the map were interesting but by Act 3 they started to feel like an annoyance.Overall an excellent game that proves tactical / RP doesn't need laser guns and magic wands to be interesting.

_childDocuments_.review: Very much enjoying this. I would say the tactical combat occupies a bigger part of the game than the RPG story/dialog/puzzle elements. Also a little unusual in that you're basically conquering countries that would do fine without you, so doesn't have that feeling of 'aha i am saving the world one piece at a time aha'. But still a great game nonetheless.Combat is very enjoyable imho. One caveat is the enemy turns take way, too long. Would be great to have a setting like other games where enemy animations in combat can be 2x or more faster. I've been using Cheat Engine to make the animations faster so i don't spend so much time waiting.My only other nitpick is that more polishing would be good on a) the legion management on the main world map (need to keep moving the cursor on and off landmarks to make the upper left reset to the list of legions and what they are doing) and b) item crafting and modification (not enough filters for troop type, quality etc)

_childDocuments_.review: Excellent combat strategy game with its own rule-set.  The experience is daunting at first but worth the effort.Biggest Like: In many fights, you will have friendly assistance.  These units will be marked green and they are amazing.  Other games provide mediocre AI assistance, at best; these guys are pros.  There haven't been any moments that made me wonder why the AI did what it did and that is a rare thing indeed.Biggest Dislike:  The constant in and out loading screen of handling the affairs of my army. It's not a long loading screen, but in order to do certain things it's necessary to be near one of the tents located in the current garrison.  Therefore, the time cost of some decisions is two loading screens.  Periodic interruptions that don't break the game's fun but do delay it.I've played for almost 30 hours and just completed Act I.  I strongly recommend this game to strategy gamers who appreciate a good challenge.  There is a lot of quality here.

_childDocuments_.review: With over 70h ingame I've finished the game last night with a very positive feeling. Its quite different from what I've expected at first, and even the great extended demo doesn't give a full insight of the humor and various aspects this game holds. Without spoiling anything, you might see a game over screen for being reborn as a cat :D I really appreciate the effort put into this game, the localisation and voice over, the historical details as much as the lines and final narratives. The game doesn't get boring at any time, as it doesn't feel artificially stretched, and the variation in quests is another positive thing. Decisions matter, eventhough some only seem to do so. But that's part of the fun, right? However, there aren't any loose ends when you've finished the game and that feels very satisfying. Graphics here and there could be better, and the character design would profit from a little touch up, as well. Siege animation is the only thing I skipped, as this isn't really appealing. The one thing that really, really urgendly needs a fix is the combat speed, at least the enemies move. You're often outnumbered, which is fun to play, but it can be really annoying to retry a fight if you could easily wait 3-5 minutes just waiting until the enemy is done. However, this shouldn't stop you from buying. I wasn't sure if its worth the money at first, but it surely is.

_childDocuments_.review: Compared to the relatively short Expeditions: Viking campaign, this game is more like HI I'M BILLY MAYS FOR EXPEDITIONS: ROME. Because every time I think, OK, the game will end now, BILLY MAYS shows up and says BUT WAIT, THERE'S MORE! 50 hours into the game and there's quite a bit to see and do throughout the game ... as long as you're operating with your small group of legionnaires. In this small group setting you do get some up close and personal combat using a variety of weapons, as well as a skill tree unique to each warrior class that unlocks more upgrades as you earn experience. Want to craft torches and throw them at your enemies just to watch them burn? OK. Tip your arrows with poison? Go ahead. Learn how to do a spinning whirlwind attack with a giant Roman spear? Sure thing. There are a lot of different offensive and defensive tactics that you can set to give each member of your praetorian guard unique fighting abilities in combat.I like how the game was broken up into separate acts, as if it's some Shakespearean play about Rome only, so far, no one's done my dirty like Brutus did to Caesar. Except for that one guy. Between each act there's an interlude, like an intermission in a long movie where you could go get a snack at the concessions stand, only here it's walking around Rome completing missions by talking through various issues. And occasionally drinking too much. OK, and killing a few people who need killing.The game does take you through multiple campaigns across multiple continents, with each setting presenting its own unique challenges and enemies alike. And cats. Seriously. Cats are a thing in ACT II. Just go with it. Another interesting element is being able to use a forge in your encampment to build, upgrade or modify weapons and armor and then equip your centurions as you see fit. Or disassemble them down to their constituent parts in order to make other weapons or armor. No, you cannot manufacture cats. The biggest complaint I have is the legion combat system. A bunch of markers symbolizing your legion on a map. You pick your leader, pick an (attack) card, any card, and with the same randomness of Blackjack, your card and leader choices are played out in an animation reminiscent of that old electric football game where you turn it on and the players buzz in random circles around the field. BUT WAIT THERE'S MORE. You can have a legion that is up to 3x as big as the other army, and you will still incur sizable losses because there's no way to know before combat starts which is the most capable centurion to lead the battle. It just seems really random at times.This is where I would have liked to actually lead the legion, like in Ultimate General: Civil War, where you form up the different elements of your legion and you order them to attack the opposing army, one cohort at a time in real-time. That would be fun. Instead, it's more like that electric football game I mentioned, which was all the rage back in the 1970s.BUT WAIT THERE'S MORE. Is the game worth the price point? Yes. Yes it is. Aside from the shortcoming I saw with legion combat, the rest of the game is very polished and fun. I'm 50 hours into the game and there's still quite a bit left for me to do and see before the end game. Also cats.

_childDocuments_.review: An incredibly well crafted game, with lovable characters, an engaging storyline, a convincing atmosphere and a fun, intuitive yet endearing combat system. I fell in love with expeditions game and this one did not disappoint. A great choice if you like tactical RPG set in historical settings (with a lot of creative liberty, of course, but still, it tasted like Ancient Rome). A resolute, definite recommandation from my part.

_childDocuments_.review: Tactical strategy turn based game with unique mechanics specific to the game. The demo itself showcases a lot of the gameplay elements within the game and was the primary reason why I decided to buy the whole pack. The only element the demo didn't seem to touch on in any depth is the region capture system. The campaign, story, characters and voice acting is top notch. The only thing that lets the game down a bit is the UI and clunky inventory system, and sometimes turns take too long waiting for enemies / allies to complete their moves.Highly recommended; it's a guided campaign experience with turn based strategy where you pick your own party and even play simulated legion army battles as though you are a commander of a Roman legion. Not much to say other than to pick up the demo and try the game out to decide if for you or not - as it lets you play and capture the first region.----After having spent another 80 hours in the game-----Still highly recommended. Very interesting characters and politics, and some story hubs with side quests to develop your companions further. Dialogue remains top notch all throughout, and the intrigue gets deeper and more interesting the more you play. This game perhaps has one of the most interesting siege mechanics available - being able to assign companions and praetorian's to fight simultaneous battles that affect each group separately. Truly something to behold. The game spans several different historically significant campaigns (i.e., Egypt / Gallia (Gauls)), each with its own enemy specialty and weapon preference - meaning you'll need to change your tactical items to compensate. Some regions were a little lengthy though, and the map legion combat will at times detract from the main story experience rather than enhance it, taking on the feel of busy work after a while.Quite frequently you'll come across random events whilst journeying across the world - these tend to be text based, but are very interesting and occasionally lead to battles.High level characters feel absolutely incredible, from indestructible tanks (Principes) to slaughtering machines (Veles with Reaping). Combat remained interesting and engaging all throughout, and very rarely did it feel like a slog, save for some of the large sieges.The UI still remains a bit clunky, even after learning it. This is particularly true for the crafting page, and the inventory leaves a lot to be desired. Functional, but could be better.Not enough can be said about the top notch voice acting, and dialogue / writing. Daresay it rivals AAA quality.

_childDocuments_.review: I rarely write reviews, but I felt that Expeditions: Rome warranted a formal message of approval. In the past week I played the game for almost 100 hours, over the course of two separate playthroughs. The story is good enough to keep an avid RPG story-centric player such as myself enthralled with the handful of choices and paths presented, to the degree that I believe there is about 3 playthroughs worth of content here. There are one or two points throughout the game which are disappointing, but overall I am very satisfied with what is here.In terms of gameplay, combat is good and what you would expect from an Expeditions game. It feels significantly improved over its predecessor Expeditions: Vikings and each class seems to have a more refined identity. I have personally found the Veles class to be exceptionally strong. If you enjoy turn-based tactical combat, you will enjoy this.Graphics are not the best I have ever experienced, but throughout my play-time I never had any glaring issues that took me out of the experience. They are more than passable and quite fit the theme and setting. Speaking of which, was particularly well-done for the historical-fiction route that they took. The greatest problems I experienced were a fairly consistent amount of crashing (not enough to be a large problem, about once ever 3-4 hours I would get a hard crash to desktop, but otherwise non-existent), and the pathing of your party. Because the game always has you walking around with a group of 6 (and you can't split them up) you will occasionally get stuck or will not be able to reach a source of loot (a body or chest). Beyond this, the game has a few perks and faults that I cannot remember at the writting of this review, but after playing it for 100 hours I can confidently say I highly recommend this game and it is well-worth the price to any individual who enjoys RPG or turn-based combat titles, you will get your investment returned. A special thanks to the developers for making a quality product and a sincere hope that you will release some form of expansion/dlc/additional content for this game and/or new titles under the Expedition series.9/10 highly recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: Really great fantasy spin-off pre-imperical Rome. If you're a history dork like myself, you'll have a blast listening to conversations and subtle pokes at irrelevant (to the game) historical moments and their alternate outcomes as well as the main story. Even things as subtle as "crossing the Rubicon" are done right in this game, I love it, and most people probably have no clue how cool and important to Roman history that is.Aside from that, gameplay-wise, it's a blast. I love the combat, wish there was more, but what is there is great. Playing on Insane can result in some fantastic moments of butt-clenching glory. I'm a huge fan of most RPG's with turn-based combat like DoS, Pathfinder, etc. It has it's own unique elements that are fun, but ultimately stays simple at core in a very good way. It's one that anyone can enjoy, newcomer or veteran alike.Only negative is that some things feel a bit empty. I would like to have seen more in a certain spot that sits between Act 1 & 2, and I find there are some big missed opportunities that would have made this a legendary game. However, that's mostly me as a history nerd wishing there was more. What is there, is very very good.
_childDocuments_.name: Expeditions: Rome

_childDocuments_.review: I just finished my first play through of the campaign. It took 85 hours, which seems to have been the right amount of time. It's an epic game, very ambitious, and I believe it was very well done. It seems to have taken the weaknesses of games of a similar genre and found ways to improve them. Having a set of companions who can actually lead their own missions with other, less central characters, was a very smart way of growing the gaming experience without either watering down or having to develop more and more background stories. It came off nicely, as you had your circle of closest friends and another, wider circle of fellow soldiers. It helped you feel like a man of rank and station, and elevated your companions to their own stations, too.The way the story is broken into separate military campaigns is brilliant, too, in that they help to expand the passage of time across many years, give a history lesson on the role of the military in Rome's republic, and break up the game play's grind with a series of political events. It gave a sense of a significant weight to your actions as a military leader, because you knew a day was coming when there would be consequences as you faced the Senate without a sword.The story is attempting to bring to the player a sense of greater meaning regarding the causes of authoritarian movements in a Democracy by putting your character in the shoes of someone whose choices have historic consequences. I found that the game had me thinking about the events we see in our current day as a parallel to history. I appreciate the commitment the story telling gave to teaching how easy it is to justify the steps from freedom towards tyranny. The game play has a helpful way of making you feel like a general for big battles via a card game like series of phases, but you get to  play skirmishes in a very mechanics-oriented combat system. You can meta-game your way into a team that works great together if you want, or just throw characters into the fray. Every character class has an important role, and the specializations of each class give you a chance to try different things. This is augmented by the fact that you end up with quite a few characters to experiment with, which is something most other games would require many play-throughs to pull off.The game isn't perfect. Crafting doesn't hold the place that it could have, for example. But when compared to its strengths, such "complaints" don't seem worth the trouble. I will probably play through it again sometime, but not right away. Like the X-COM games, I'd probably appreciate a second play through a year from now. That being said, I'm not sure what other game I could find to fill the time until then. There aren't many games these days that can even come close to this one.
_childDocuments_.name: Expeditions: Rome

_childDocuments_.review: This game gets deeper and deeper as you play. In a style somewhat similar to XCOM with just a hint of Heroes of Might and Magic, you lead a Legion of Roman troops as you battle across several continents and campaigns. A political game of chess, the story is decent but overall second fiddle to the great combat and deep gameplay. Light crafting, unit management, large scale battles with multiple fronts and even army-based battles played out with cards (or strategies as the game calls them). There's a lot more here than I initially thought playing the demo. If you like XCOM type games you'll love this. Biggest tip I can give you is to pay close attention to what you need to capture on the battlefield in order to upgrade and build more utilities in your base. It takes strategy to pick the right resources to gather and the right upgrades to pick and these are essential to becoming a powerful force.

_childDocuments_.review: I was expecting good combat, and it is very satisfying; I played on Hard and found it to be very punishing of mistakes during the first two acts but still allowed you to clean up a map very quickly and efficiently if you know what you're doing. Fights are fast and intense; every move and turn matters. However by the third and fourth acts my characters were overpowered enough that the challenge had more or less faded.  What I was not expecting was how much I came to love the companion characters, who all have fascinating personalities and storylines. Even Caeso - who I thought was just going to be generic lawful good guy - ended up being a total bro with some very human moments, dare I even say a Garrus like figure. Before playing the game I thought it was mainly going to be an impersonal simulation but make no mistake, it is a story based RPG through and through that will be a real treat for those who love both that and Rome.

_childDocuments_.review: Is Expeditions: Rome worth your valuable time and money? If you have even a passing interest in History, CRPGs, or tactics games like Xcom that answer is a  As a historical CRPG, with extensive reactivity and fun gameplay systems, this was a rare treat of a game that I highly recommend.For me, RPGs live and die by two things: The quality of their stories, and the fun factor of their gameplay systems. Expeditions: Rome (E:R) goes above and beyond in both accounts. : E:R's story takes place during the years of the twilight of the roman republic. For those unfamiliar with the history, it's a heavy drama-filled period of time, full of intrigue and compelling characters. E:R very quickly sets up the premise that because of you, events will play out very differently than actual history. And the game is much better for it! If you're worried that this game will involve too much reading, or be too heady with detail, worry not! E:R makes the very smart choice to change things, and distill details for the sake of a good story and fun gameplay. Dialogue fast-paced, written well, and is 100% voice acted! Everyone from your closest companions to the random merchant you meet gives excellent and authentic performances. The main characters you encounter are great. Your companions in particular are wonderful, have vibrant personalities and will constantly comment and bring life to the game.  The antagonists are just as good, and display enough depth to make you both hate and understand their actions at the same time. Your choices matter a lot in a roleplay sense, and you feel pretty important as a character. Quests very often have multiple outcomes, and your companion's approval constantly shifts depending on your dialogue in a way that makes you think about your actions but does not feel restrictive. One particular thing I enjoyed was how your choice of gender matters for the story, and for more than just romance.  The closest thing I can compare the game to is XCOM, with a bit of Total war auto-resolve thrown in. On the ground level, I thought the turn-based combat was easy to learn and extremely fun to master. Encounters always seem fair, have unique objectives, and harder difficulties really force you to make use of all your resources. Depending on your builds, however, your main team can easily steamroll through the game by the end. It also has a solid crafting system that was fun to use. Often, you're forced to use a B-team of "mercenary" like NPCs that are not bound to the story like your companions. I found this to be a great innovation, as this B-team is never quite leveled up or equipped well as you and your companions, forcing you to change your typical strategies. These characters can permanently die (if you allow it), and that lends some much-enjoyed tension to these encounters The other half of the game takes place on the strategic map. Building up your legion is relatively easy, and since there is no time limit, you can very easily always outnumber your foes by buying more troops through infinite sources of income. In the middle of my playthrough, the much-criticized "legion battle system" has been updated and vastly improved. It's not the most fun part of the game and is basically a fancy total war auto-resolve system, but the tactics you choose during the legion battles feel impactful, and you're given a lot of information on how you can affect things.Took me roughly 60 hours to beat the game hard. The soundtrack is fantastic, to the point where I bought the album for myself. The graphical presentation is solid, and certainly above average for most CRPGs. I encountered only one minor bug (on two occasions) with the sound that was fixed by a reload. +Fantastic historical fiction story with meaningful choices.+Full, quality voice acting+Exceptional characters+Fun turn-based tactical +Graphical presentation+Music+No bugs This is worth your time and money, even at full price.

The combination of turn based tactical combat is like a combination of XCOM and a crpg like Baldurs gate where you get well developed story companions as well as rng companions who can differ every game. It was very cool to combine that style of gameplay with the overall military campaigns that let you command a legion and conquer new areas for Rome. In the end I was challenged, entertained, and surprised at how much I cared about all the characters. _childDocuments_.review: Very well done. I can honestly say that the story is pretty well done. It is engaging and fun to see what happens next.Very few bugs. All of the ones that I encountered prevented me from moving, or my legion from moving. They were few, but potentially game-breaking. I managed to re-garrison my legion and it "fixed" the problem. Only for it to happen again and again. I am sure that it is something that will be fixed. I would hope so.All in all, a very fun Roman simulator. As for battle, it is a bit of a challenge, and always varying a bit. New opponents and different combinations. If you are familiar with games like X-Com, then you have the gist of it. The major battles are really good the first time or three, then get HIGHLY repetitive. So much so, that you just auto-resolve it all. That sucks. The sieges are fun. _childDocuments_.review: Expeditions Rome is my kind of game.From the original XCom UFO Defense on PS1 to Divinity II... to whatever.  Tactical RPGs, Tactical Squad Based Fighting Games are my thing.And honestly, I do think this game is done really well.  There are minor "complaints" such as the large scale, card based army battles are stale.... and too easy to matter.  Literally, I am not sure if it's possible to lose them or not after 150 hours of play time.But still, playing a squad based tactical game, I knew there would be some minor base building, world building stuff... And I like how it's done.   I found the text based travel events to be engaging and interesting.  They were also varied enough that I didn't start seeing repeats until later in the game.The combat was unique in that often times you had to defeat a set number of enemies, rather than "defeat all enemies".  This is pretty innovative, and avoids the danger free end of combat mop up that is so often present in these games.  Enemy squads can remain at relatively full strength even when you are on the verge of victory.Varied mission styles, sieges, multi team coordinated attacks.   I Love This Stuff!!!So.  Why the negative review?Why in the *%^# would you design a mission where the only outcome of my character and team is failure.It's completely game breaking for me.  To me now my team has failed.  I have lost all interest in finishing the game with them.  Further more, I know that there's no alternative, so I have no interest in replaying the game to try new roster development in preparation for that battle.If you "had" to do an auto loss fight, make it a text based event like is used so much throughout the game.To me it has ruined the entire experience, and I won't recommend the game to anyone, much less friends and family.Unfortunately, such a poor (in my opinion) story event completely breaks the magic of believing my team can push through anything by working together and relying on each other.  Any future victories would be hollow, and thus pointless.As such, I will give away the ending of the game.  Your team gets auto-slaughtered by an angry mob of Gauls.  You then take control of your largest rival, and his team.  Who I promptly also let die at the hands of said mob.  Thus the end of the game is you are just another of the semi-forgotten names in Roman history that people will occasionally look up on Wiki whenever a new Rome TV show, movie, or video game is released.

_childDocuments_.review: Deceptively simple gameplay alongside an engaging story with likeable (and remarkably unlikable, in a good way) characters. The decisions you will have to make, while numerous, are sometimes limited to the point of being infuriating. Your player character is incredibly naive and is regularly outmanoeuvred and taken advantage of in the most blatant of ways with no recourse until the trap is sprung. It often feels like you are role playing as a moron with 5 wranglers keeping you from the glue amphora.The classes are distinct and most subclasses have their usefulness. The principes veteran subclass (based around crowd control and disabling) and the early levels of the sagittarius subclasses are entirely useless.Legion system does seem a bit arcane at first, but once you figure out the only thing that matters is keeping generals alive and morale high it's super straight forward. Ultimately everything else is expendable and easily replaceable.Crafting system is sometimes frustrating. If you're like me and want to keep everyone in Roman gear you will sometimes go dry for better equipment until you get improved schematics as a drop. When you do finally get them you will have to endure the crafting time + queue system to regear your 20 praetorians (if you can actually remember what is needed for each individual) and pray you get good abilities on your weapons. Hopefully you've gotten enough crafting materials while waiting for schematics otherwise you may find half your team naked because you ran out of heavy components.Everything else is pretty good. If you have any interest in the time period or you're just looking for an approachable and easy turn based experience you'll probably like it.

_childDocuments_.review: Can not recommend game (though the start was quite good) and what will most likely never change, as I have the impression they (devs/publisher) will not fix it, as the previous games in the "expeditions" series had the same problems.1) GFX is good enough (equipment differences, distinguishable characters, architecture, wold, all fits)2) SFX is also quite good (well it all sounds as it should)3) BGM is good (I realy like the soundtrack)4) The tactical combat works as it should... movement points, action point (so just one attack), various skills like cover and hunker down and aid and blabla. It is not just pure "kill all enemies" (ie I had a fight where I just had to destroy some crates, did this and the fight was over).Now, all sounds right, but why not recommended?1) Lack of documentation and instructions (like your legion leading 4 centuriones are droping approval rating and you do not know why. because you cant see their personality, so move them to praetorian guard, check the personality, get back to the tent, move them back to centurio group, and then just play and hope for the best, because sometimes the actions you do do affect them just as your party, and sometimes not.)2) World events... while it is good to have something happen, the options presented are somehow "unfulfilling". It seems nothing is based on your skills and the outcome is purely random. Like you come across a lake, decide to go for a swim and the morale of your troops increases by 1... yay. The next time you come across a lake and you decide not to go for a swim and the morale decreases by 10... wtf? Or some local ride along, they abducted the daughter of someone and they are chasing after the abductors. You stop them, the abductor could not pay the dowry and so he abducted her... and your options are: pay the dowry, attack the abductors, attack the chasers... And all events are like that, when something good happens, the benefit is minimal, when something bad happens, you are realy heavily punished, and sometimes you just have to pick one from equaly stupid and bad choices.3) But what realy got me, and will most likely go on your nerves: the legion battles. So you have 5200 soldiers and enemy just 900, its phase iv (last) of the battle and out of a sudden the legion is hit 10x for 150man loss... and you will just scratch your head "what did just happen?" (this goes hand in hand with 1... you are told how the battle works in general, but lacks any detail and the player can only assume. up to now I still have not figured this out and just fumbling in darkness. wish I knew how many attack phases there are round, so far it was just random, because then I could calculate on my own when a strategem speaks about 10% more agression... and so on).Edit: a couple hours later...Sadly nothing much changed. I am still addicted to this type of game and will most likely finish it. On the other side the frustration factor remains and actualy even increased.On the pro side: I figured more "concepts" of how to play the game, but not thanks to good tutorials, good codex, dev explanation on their website, or some usefull guides on the net, but try & error. And while I am quite happy about it, it is also frustrating, as many of this things had to be explained somewhere.On the negative side: my legion now have all strategems available, and even some realy good "one time" use strategems. But the battles are still pure random. The game offers you random 3 strategems per battle phase to choose from, and most of the time the 3 are quite, very, useless. I have dozen of battles behind me, which means hundreds of phases, and the number of time this game offered a usefull strategem that would fit the situation and help can be counted on one hand. Like its phase 2, enemy down to 600 man and you could realy use that scorpion strategem (kill 600 enemies), but noooo, you get player defense -%, risk to commander/centuriones, morale - .... and when the phase starts you get hit 10x for 100 casualties. Uff. Why arent all strategems available during the proper phase? Would the battles be too easy then? Isnt exactly that the reason for higher difficulties? It seems more and more devs think that this increases the challenge, nope, it incrases just the frust factor. There is no challenge in that.The second thing is, the tactical combat also started tobe questionable. Like the one siege... distribute your characters and praetorians to 4 groups to tacle various objectives... ok sounds good... the objectives are described, so you distribute your people to fit the siguation... ok sounds good... and then it starts... and you find out the frontal main assault team would be better off with some speculatores, and the speculatore (infiltrators) teams who actual had a sneaky objective, would be better off with some princeps, because there is a ton of enemy groups every 2 steps and you cant sneak past them and have to fight them and there is a round limit to achive the objective. So the princeps may be slow, but at least they survived.Constantly shaking my head here...Edit 2 after another 40hrs... game is still extremely stupid and is actualy getting worse. You are warned not to trust, you know its an ambush, but every freaking encounter in ActIII you can do absolutely nothing and spring the trap over and over and over again and it is getting tiresome. The options for the player are very limited and not worthy of the title "roleplaying game". Mostly the game offers 3 choices but in reality its just one, disguised as three. Or you can trust or kill... and because you have no proof yet to kill... so the game forces you into a bloodthirsty warmongering path. Very RPG like... not. Thats my last update. Going to finish this abomination and go play marbles.

_childDocuments_.review: Expeditions: Rome is a great game, with tough choices, and compelling combat. As an RPG, you'll find a lot of weight to your decisions here, with choices that matter beginning with gender and following throughout the entirety of the story. Combat is standard turn-based fare, no re-inventing the wheel here, but what's there is well executed, and I enjoyed the combat throughout. The game's biggest shortfalls are the strategy layer, and quality of life issues. The strategy layer is frankly quite boring, roaming the world and commanding armies is not exciting, and feels more like a tacked on mini-game than a core gameplay pillar. Quality of life issues are here in the form of spending too long walking around, and sometimes spending far too long waiting for the opponent to take their turn. That being said, Expeditions: Rome is much more than the sum of its parts, it's a compelling narrative experience, with a solid story, well-written and interesting companions, and quality turn-based combat. I recommend this to any fan of RPGs or turn-based strategy games.

_childDocuments_.review: Just completed the game clocking in at 110 hours on hard mode. Was really fun! This was another total surprise hidden gem that will go past a lot of people. Still early, but this will surely be a strong contender for game of the year for me, and I am really looking forward to the game that will beat it! So firstly, the MAIN focus of this game is built around the tactical turn based combat encounters, quite similar to x-com but in a Rome legionnaire setting with swords, shields, bows, daggers and pikes. Do not go in expecting a Divinity Original Sin with pickpocketing, complex side quests, RPG mechanics or a large world or something like that. This is not a typical CRPG. But built around this solid foundation of turn based tactical combat, there are several things:Didn't have any game breaking bugs. But this game really does not like alt-tabbing out. The game crashed many times if I tried to switch to another window. There were also rarely some small bugs especially in act 3 where the battle overlay UI would not appear, or I could not open some chests even though I got the prompt for it. A quick reload solved these issues. I would not recommend Ironman mode until they fix this. Save often. Otherwise, performance is really good!Not a lot honestly. The one thing I really wish existed was a simple QoL UI improvement. Whenever you start an encounter - you have to select 6 people. This particular menu doesn't really show what weapons they are carrying or armor etc. You are supposed to just "remember" what they have equipped. To find out, you would need to quit out and go back to the character screens. A simple equipped inventory summary would have been nice in the selection screen itself.Oh, the game could also use a lot more character portraits. They also don't look a lot like the in-game models and that kind of grinds my gears a little.Lastly, I'd recommend playing this on hard difficulty or above. Normal or below would just be too boring in my opinion. This is really a strategy game, and the fun in this game is in making builds, trying out different strategies, positions, team balance and moves. None of this will matter if you just go around one shotting everyone. Don't give up. There is always a solution and is very satisfying when you pull it off :-)

_childDocuments_.review: 80 hours in and I am still enthralled by the game. I pre-ordered based on the setting, game type, and discount and have not been disappointed. However I have had no problems what so ever from Expeditions: Rome thus far. There are aspects of the game that could be made better from having more in depth game play, like the big battles. All in all I give it a 9/10.

_childDocuments_.review: It pains me to give this a negative review, and I did enjoy the setting and parts of it, but it's just...a very simple CRPG with some absurdly stupid writing at points.I never play these games for tactics - I play them purely to enjoy a roleplaying experience with choices that matter and companions to enjoy being around.I will try to sum up the good parts and the bad parts below:+ The bug-free release was amazing, I beat the entire game in +/- 3 sittings and have not had a turn-end freeze bug or anything of the sort that's usually expected on launch.+ The music and visuals are awesome, upgrading your items (which takes a bit of grinding with your outposts) actually changes how they look.+ The combat is fun but gets a bit boring at times because of its simplicity. I didn't expect XCOM levels of tactical depth but what we have here is pretty basic (although the enemies moving in groups when they have nothing to do nearby and the fact your action points reset when you destroy militia/civilians was a fantastic mechanic).Now for the maluses which hinged the review firmly downwards.- Nonsensical writing at points. You will be outmanoeuvred by your opponents no matter what steps you choose to take. Your companions (specifically one of them trained in intrigue) will suddenly become stupid and miss a glaringly obvious trap purely because the writers needed them to. They, despite being battle-hardened praetorians by the end of the game, suddenly all commit incredible mistakes and outright telling them  to do a stupid thing before they attempt it will still force you down the path of "writer needs drama to happen". Adding to that, the game assumes a HUGE amount of things, railroading you hardcore and skipping the interesting stuff for more and more and more drama. - The pacify region mechanic forcing you on a side-quest with only your recruitable mooks and one companion is one of the most stupid game-design decisions the developers have taken. The quests have around 3-4 variants and will repeat every single act until you're sick and tired of doing them.- The absolutely most interesting character, Raia, in act 2, is not a companion and not even romanceable. This is a negative, she has all the abilities of one and even gets an ending slide but was probably cut or forgotten about midway through development.- The companions themselves were nothing special. You've got the generic soldier dude, the sneaky one, the angry barbarian, the mentor and the smug fighter. Typical D&D.- Commanding a legion is not as fun as it sounds. The game frequently forgets you have a huge force at your beck and call and some side-quests even have a few of your own legionnaires actively try to kill you because they're looting stuff, which makes ABSOLUTELY ZERO SENSE.- The skill trees feel unrewarding. Combat is simple, as I stated before. You'd kind of expect more.It's good to tide you over until Baldur's Gate 3 comes out of early access, but it's not worth buying at this pricepoint if you're not already an avid fan of CRPGs or the Expeditions series.

_childDocuments_.review: Very Enjoyable game. The turn based combat systems and mechanics are tight. The pacing and gear progress is well balanced and enjoyable, plus the customisation is fantastic. If you want to micro manage everything you pretty much can, all the way down to gear bonuses and stats. On top of that, the RPG side of the game is great. Enjoyable (If somewhat predictable) story line. All in all a thumbs up from me.

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely the best ARPG I've played in a long time.  Expeditions Vikings was a good game, Expeditions: Rome is an amazing game.  In terms of historical accuracy - It's basically a multiverse take on history, so shut up about it not being 100% accurate.:::SPOILERS:::Following the unfortunate death of the young Gaius Julius Caesar, you take his place in history following the murder of your father.  The game takes you through four Acts:  Asia Minor, Africa, Gaul, and finally Rome.  The choices you make will DIRECTLY EFFECT the course of the game and the people around you.  Every single decision will have an impact; great or small, on the game.  Let me restate that for dramatic effect:  EVERY DECISION WILL HAVE AN IMPACT.  You may think you are making the right choice at the time, but who knows what will happen down the line?  Spare someones life, it might come back to haunt you.  Kill someone who you think deserves to die, there will be unintended consequences.  Think very carefully about what direction you want things to go in.There are a lot of fun twists and turns in the game.  One of the only cons I found was that legendary equipment isn't very legendary.  You will often find grey items that are better than your orange legendary.  Camp management is a fun little side part of the game.  If you enjoy it, make sure to have a Praetorian working at your Arsenal to upgrade your tactical cards.Really enjoyed this game, almost wish there would be an expansion but the game ends very solidly and satisfyingly.

_childDocuments_.review: I hope the developers feel proud of their work because this was truly a delightful game. Every time I have found different endings and possibilities, this game offers so much replay-ability!! I really hope there's a 2nd part in medieval Europe, it could be spectacular. Thank you endlessly for such a gem.

_childDocuments_.review: With Expeditions: Rome, you can expect an immersive and intense gaming experience. The game offers a unique blend of strategy, role-playing and exploration that will keep you engrossed for hours.The gameplay of Expeditions: Rome is both challenging and rewarding. You must carefully manage your resources, form alliances and make difficult decisions that will affect the outcome of the game. The battle system is also very well done and offers a good balance between strategy and action.One of the best things about this game is the story. It is a complex and compelling story full of political intrigue and personal drama that will keep you hooked from start to finish. The writing is excellent and brings the different characters and their stories to life in a way that is truly captivating.The game also features beautiful graphics and sound design that help bring the world of ancient Rome to life. The detail of the environments and character models is impressive and makes it easy to get lost in the world of the game.As you progress through the game, you can customise your character and develop different skills and abilities. This creates a sense of responsibility and achievement as you watch your character grow and develop.Overall, Expeditions: Rome offers a positive gaming experience that is both challenging and rewarding. The game offers a unique and immersive world that is sure to capture the imagination of any player who loves strategy, role-playing or exploration.

_childDocuments_.review: This is an extremely good tactical RPG. The classes are very diverse and can be built to fill different roles. The base game mechanics are simple enough that a new player to the genre will not struggle to learn the game, but at the same time there is enough complexity to it that an experienced player can optimize his party to build some rather devastating combos. One of such combinations is to use mostly princeps to crowd control large groups of enemies, then have the spearmen create huge chain kills. Expeditions Rome is not without its flaws though, none of the characters seemed particularly interesting, and there are no dedicated cutscenes. Legion missions can be repetitive, but the developers are aware of this problem and actively work to make them better. The overall stroyline is interesting enough to keep your attention, mostly by allowing you to interact with famous characters like Julius Caesar and Cleopatra.  The game greatly benefits from its historical setting. Overall, deffinitly one of the best tactical RPGs I have played, and I've spent alot of time in this genre with games like XCOM and Fire Emblem. Expeditions Rome is worth the price and will not dissapoint you.

_childDocuments_.review: A really good combat-focused turn-based rpg. It’s certainly more like XCOM rather than traditional fantasy RPGs like Pathfinder or Divinity. Because of the leaning towards combat and battle maps rather than a fully open world, it’s a lot more digestible when you only have limited time to play.There are a number of QOL improvements needed, but the Devs have already solved half my original issues from when I started as of writing this review.Pros:-great combat-In-depth gear system-clear and engaging story-easy to pickup and playCons:-confusing mechanics like the legion battles-gear crafting upgrade mechanics like swapping item traits are unclear in how they’ll affect the item in the end

_childDocuments_.review: I really liked Logic Artists' first strategy game, Conquistador. Vikings was a big, fat meh, suffering from lack of focus and seemingly running short of budget with placeholders left and right. This game is... God knows what this game wants to be, I presume not even the developers really know what they wanted to make. Wide as an ocean, shallow as a pond is a perfect phrase for it.Wants to be a CRPG with lite strategy elements, and seemingly every trendy game elements are included, like crafting, have your own camp and followers and such. But oh my god, it is so poorly designed, so bloated, that I just gave up playing. Quality of life is almost nonexistent. Highlights/lowlights:- This strategy mixed with CRPG is an amazing idea. Too bad, that most of the strategy part is just shallow, annoying and cumbersome. Large-scale fight is nothing but using cards with slightly different outcomes; may change in the future, but ♥♥♥♥ me if I keep playing, since ->- This game is just painfully slow. Combat is slow. Character development is slow. Progress is slow. Everything feels ages to achieve, even developing your characters. You are constantly held back by tiny tutorials, just the whole game feels like a chore to play.- There is no map for the CRPG exploration part. Seriously, some areas are really like a labyrinth, not being able to have an overview is a pain in the ass. Easy to miss places, NPCs, etc.- It's easy to misclick and mess up your actual fight. There is no undo, though. In a TBS. Da ♥♥♥♥...- Speaking of fights, the encounters are so painfully slow and tedious, that it's impossible to describe.- Quality of life is terrible, e.g. you will be swimming in items very quickly. All of them look mostly the same, since a Gladius can have different quality tiers. Yet, there is no option to scrap the unused items, you have to do it manually.- I swear the designers sometimes really had no idea of what they are doing. Your closest companions have their own storylines, missions, so you kind of get invested in them. Yet, some missions explicitly forbid you to take them on the given battle, because... because... no idea why. Instead of it, you get random generated units, hired from a large pool with zero personality.- Vikings had a morale system which was ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and seemingly the developers can't depart from it. Your decisions affect their mood/loyalty, but come on... you have like a dozen praetorians. Are you expecting me to memorize each of their personality and keep in mind their current level of loyalty to balance my replies in interactions?I loved Conquistador, had it's shortcomings for sure, but it was obvious that the budget was tight. Vikings had many shortcomings, but I considered it as a result of lack of budget, again. This game seemingly had a big budget, yet problems remained from the previous games. Sloppy game design (I mean it's game development 101 to be focused and include things which are actually fun), lack of focus, bloated elements and zero respect toward the player's time invested. You fooled me twice, there won't be a third time.
