_childDocuments_.review: Overall Rating: 3.5/5 Playtime (first playthrough): ~60h, Level of difficulty: insane (highest)Story & Feeling: 4/5Gameplay & UI: 3/5Graphics & Music: 3/5Price & Content: 4/5Story wise it's an "okay"-Setting and overall an "okay"-Game if you ask me. If you like storydriven games in a medieval setting - this is a game for you. Also or especially if you like the history of rome and the development of the roman empire. The game itself is very straight forward - decisions matter but in a way, where dialog options have nearly no impact while some decisions have a huge impact but in a straight forward context. Sadly it wasnt possible to romance more then one character, which for me was a bit disapointing - since in that age it was quite common to have serval relationships at once. All in all the characters you see mostly look like the same, so the number of models is limited.I have to say, the biggest downside for me was the absolute aweful camera movement. No scrolling in or out, so hard to find enemys to aim for. Also: No minimap in the game is a huge discussion. I would have expected more from a title released in 2022. Its still isometric combat, so camera movement is high priority. Also a negativ for me was the change of clothes everytime you leave rome - you have to figure out which character was wearing which armor or weapon - it was a pain, and: Why didnt tools get refreshed when you join a new act? This was also a pain for me. Campainmode didnt really matter in that game and was rather boring - not even a challange on highest difficulty. Characterdesign was good and also not so much RNG involved (looking at other games like this). So it was good to be able to calculate what's gonna happen. Crafting system was "okay" - didnt really used it so much - I was mostly focussing on the legendary Weapons and Armor.Not much to say, graphics were "ok" for an "A"-Game. Also Music was quite okay - no negatives here. Had some crashes when using burning arrows on ground with oil - but otherwise pretty stable. Make sure you have the latest driver.Ok for me - playtime 60h on highest difficulty - hardest fight was the very first one where you have absolutly no gear (startet es a triceps), probably easier with a princeps for example. From that point on, highest difficulty was not really a problem - not even on first playthrough. Bought the game for full price, I thing its a good balance between money and time spend on this game. Would I play again: Probably not. Replayability is quite low, considering other games like this on the market.Is the DLC worth?: You get another character class. Decide if you like it - if you do, then my recommendation would be to buy DLC before first playthrough. If you already played the game or if you are half way through, I would recommend skipping on the DLC.  I still give it a thumbs up, cause all in all its an "okay" game. But for me nothing special in any way.

_childDocuments_.review: Personal GOTY for 2022. I don't believe anything will beat Expeditions: Rome for me this year, not even the next seeing the roaster of games coming up. This game isn't for everyone though and I must admit I'm extremely biased as a SPQRaboo (if that even exists), ever since playing Caesar 3 and Rome: Total War as a child. It doesn't help that where I lived for most of my life has strong historical ties to the Roman (attempts at) conquest of Caledonia. TL;DR, played quite a large part in my childhood and everyday life-- so there is bias.  Positives: -Core gameplay is great. Apart from balancing issues that I cover in my criticism below-- it's fun and satisfying. The animations are chunky and powerful, the abilities are useful and can be a godsend, the maps look amazing, the loot is always worth to looking out for. -Strategic world map is brilliant, it adds another layer of gameplay on top of core turn-based combat and fits in very well in about every regard. It rewards exploration while keeping you on your toes in regards to food, water, medicine and morale. Legion battles are fun and not tedious, although I do wish they did a little more with them. -Music is outstanding and atmosphere is on point. Creating my character with 'LEGATUS' blaring through my headphones gave me goosebumps like never before. Going through the world and hearing 'VICUS' ring in the background as I explored nooks and crannies was pure bliss. Hearing the beating of war drums of 'BITHYNIA' upon fighting made me want to dedicate my life to inventing a time machine and popping off back to the Iron Ages.-Story and quests are expertly written. You can feel the love, dedication and research the developers put in to make it just right. I'm not exaggerating when I say despite the game being great all around, story is arguably it's strongest point. It has characters that I wanted to physically strangle upon hearing their voices-- that's a new thing for me personally. Development in the story is simply top-notch.-There's replay value for at least 2 play throughs, if you only care about the narrative. If you want to get all the achievements like myself, you're looking at 3 or more. Each play through being 50-70 hours each, depending on pace and if you want to get absolutely everything and cover all quests.My main criticism lays in regards to its companions, bugs, RNG and the absolutely monumental difficulty spike in act 3.-Companions are great, and despite not agreeing with some, such as Bestia, they really grow on you and aid with the story.My problem is with their implementation. Apart from some decisions, your choices are skin-deep as most of the time they'll stick to pre-set scripts. This is truly a bummer as they could've pulled a Roman Mass Effect, but apart from some that are really *ooft* situations, they feel benign. Only changing their relation with you, which is a number and status-- maybe an occasional comment in the camp. It's sadly a wasted opportunity. But there are sections in the game where your decisions and what you say to your companions are paramount. -Bugs aren't game breaking but do prepare for some jank. Such as getting soft-locked after a screen transition, or in case of one of late game unique pikes-- outright having broken animations. Luckily the core mechanics didn't bug out for me even once, which is a great thing. Again, not game breaking, but can be annoying as mostly cosmetic.-You don't prepare for battles-- you prepare for the RNG that will decide your fate at the start of near-each and every battle. This is most apparent at latter stages of the game. If the stars align just right, or 'just wrong' in this case-- you will be crushed upon starting due to how positioning appears to work. If your enemies start close and they go first-- pretty much only consumables and throwables will save your hide. This RNG issue is the main reason why I'm demotivated to play as the Gladiator class for the achievement, as a huge part of the class relies on that random number generator, which can make or break battles at random. -Advancing from act 2 to act 3 is comparable to going from a brisk jog to crawling through a maggot-infested bog filled with rusted razor blades--  It's tough, let's just say that-- not 'good-tough' but still fun. Like I said at the start, an absolute GOTY for me-- with some unfortunate missed opportunities and balance issues. Get it. Even if not on sale, you won't regret it. I guarantee it.

_childDocuments_.review: I had a really fantastic time playing this — though it’s not without its faults. In short, I used to love Roman history (to the point of studying Classics), but I don’t get much time for it these days. Then along comes this game, and it’s an enthusiast’s delight: little historical details (even down to the Latin), beautiful landscapes and renderings of ancient cultures, and a gripping storyline loosely based on Caesar’s life.  Plus the individual turn-based combat is very fun, and the characters are well-done!There are some minor gripes: the legionary battles (on the campaign map) felt a little arcane, campaign playtime sometimes drew out (with a lot of repeated events), and there’s a lot of rifling around through boxes.But at its best, this is a fantastic and lovingly-crafted historical escape, and I loved just having the world to explore. Definitely my game of the summer

_childDocuments_.review: The combat system is pretty balanced, and the actions you do in battle feel like they matter. Not only that, your talents and talent paths feel impactful and you have to think before making a move or committing to an action, some battles can be very challenging but there's always a way to overcome. Even on Insane difficulty it felt balanced and not completely overwhelming. It was a decent challenge overall, the character stories are interesting and not bland, the alternate history perspective is within the realms of possibility and the decisions you make matter.The only lackluster part of the game I felt was the legion battles, which feel pretty easy to win even on high difficulties, and are a bit more like a chore and not very meaningful towards the overall gameplay/story. But they at least give some filler to flesh out the greater "macro" picture of how the story takes place. Also, it's Roman so bonus points for that. I'd recommend for anyone that likes CRPG's.
_childDocuments_.name: Expeditions: Rome

_childDocuments_.review: Expeditions: Rome is a party based RPG with strategy elements. The player character is a Legate in the Roman army and must lead a legion of soldiers in wars with Greece, Egypt and Gaul, while also protecting your family from dangers within the Roman senate.I haven’t played the previous games in the Expeditions series, so my review will focus on the qualities of this specific game, without comparing to previous games.For most of the game you’ll control a party of six characters as you perform quests, talk to NPCs to advance the story, and fight enemies. Combat is turn based and if you’ve played Xcom or other similar tactics games, you’ll have a good idea how things work. Your characters have action points to move around a hex grid and attack enemies, on the player’s turn you can move all of your characters in any order, which allows you to make the best use of their abilities, and then all enemies take their turn.There are four character classes which use different weapon types: sword and shield, dual blade, archer, and two handed staff or spear (this class is also the healer). Characters can unlock various skills when levelling up, but their main attack moves are determined by which weapon they have equipped, and each weapon type has a few different options. Equipped armour and trinkets also provides some stat bonuses such as extra health, increased movement range, and damage resistance. Positioning is very important. Each map usually has some narrow chokepoints you can defend to reduce how many enemies you’ll fight at once (obviously you’re always outnumbered). Two handed weapons usually have a longer attack range, allowing those characters to stand safely behind shield wielders. High ground provides accuracy bonuses for archers, while buildings and trees can block their line of sight. Characters who attempt to move away from adjacent enemies will trigger attacks of opportunity, and archers can use an overwatch ability.Many attacks will inflict status effects such as bleed, burn or poison which all do extra damage over time, or you can stun or knock down enemies to prevent them attacking next turn. If your characters lose all health, they’ll go into a bleeding out status, and you’ll have a few turns to stabilise them before they die. There’s permadeath, but its not as brutal as Xcom.Most enemies use the same classes, weapons and abilities as your characters. Enemy AI is quite good most of the time. They’ll gang up on weaker characters and look for opportunities to flank you. Their biggest dumb moments usually involve fire. There are a couple of ways to set tiles on fire (enemies really like doing this), and it seems like enemies put a higher priority on attacking you than staying alive, so they’ll happily charge through and stand in tiles on fire, taking burning damage, if its the only way they can get to you.Most missions require you to either kill all enemies, or a specific number of enemies causing the rest to flee. There are a few missions where you have to destroy enemy supplies, steal an important item, or defend a friendly building. And there are a couple of large scale battles where your party, along with friendly soldiers, take part in multiple stage missions to siege and capture a city. Those siege missions also include defensive barricades to block movement, while friendly and enemy catapults bombard the map with huge boulders and fireballs.The other main part of the game involves moving your army, which contains thousands of soldiers, around the map to fight against enemy armies, capture territory and resource buildings needed to upgrade your camp.Unfortunately this is the weakest part of the game. As someone who has played hundreds of hours in various Total War games, I think the battles are very basic. You’ll select a commander to lead the battle, choose a few tactics which have positive or negative effects, and then watch a 2D animation of symbols representing swordsmen, spearmen, archers and cavalry just kind of move around briefly while numbers appear showing how many soldiers either side lost.You can’t select individual units and order them to attack specific enemies, and the tactics you have to choose from in each battle seem to be randomly selected from a larger pool. Thankfully these battles are really easy so you can fast forward through all the animations to save time.The story is very well written and features lots of interesting characters. One good thing about the strategic map is that it enhances the story by giving more context to your party missions, and helping to understand how they fit into the bigger picture of the war.As you travel around the map you’ll also encounter lots of random events, which involve your companions. This could involve being attacked by wild animals, ambushed by enemy soldiers, or simply relaxing by a lake.Some quests and random events allow the player to make choices such as whether to kill or spare an enemy leader, and convince a character to help you by using threats or coin. All dialogue is fully voiced, and the voice acting is really good.I didn’t notice any significant bugs or crashes. Framerate is less important in turn based games, but it was mostly stable for me anyway. It took me 55 hours to complete the story, which represents great value for money.Expeditions: Rome is one of the best games I’ve played recently, with very enjoyable, tactical combat and an excellent story. I wish the legion battles had more depth, but even so this game is a must play for RPG fans and its worth picking up for full price.

_childDocuments_.review: An incredible historical tactical CRPG taking place in republican Rome, right before the founding of the empire, beginning with the third Mithridatic War. Has an interesting and memorable cast of characters, the diversity of which accurately represents the diversity of the Roman empire, interesting and varied combat where you can experiment with different options and strategies, and a gorgeous and beautiful depiction of the settings through expert visual and sound design. I can see this being slept on as the genre isn't as popular as others, but if you enjoy games like Wasteland 3, Xcom, or other tactical/turn based crpgs, you won't regret giving this a try.
_childDocuments_.name: Expeditions: Rome

_childDocuments_.review: Great addition to your library if you're a fan of Tactics/Turn-Based RPGs. - Great story- Likeable and memorable cast of characters- Engaging turn-based gameplay (once you get the hang of it)- Surprisingly addictive overmap gameplay- Freeform skill system (every class has access to all their skills, no subclass specialization)- Some points in the story feel a bit railroad-y (but not enough to say its bad)- Character models are a bit too bland and same-y (especially for ancillary characters)I haven't bought a western game in some time due to all the shenanigans that have been plaguing them, from technical problems to scummy developers and everything in between, so to be completely honest, I went into this game ready to find things that I might dislike, even if I did like Expeditions:Vikings and the initial demo. However I can pleasantly say that even if the game did stumble in a few places, it way exceeded my expectations and proved itself enough for me to rank it as possibly the best Historical Turn-based RPG I've ever played, up there with Dragon Age: Origins (for Fantasy) and the Xcom games (for SciFi)The story is nicely crafted to steer you along and for me it kept motivated me enough to finish it all the way through. Best part is that if you play as a female MC, people keep talking smack about you and its very satisfying that you actually get to prove yourself and rub their smug faces in it (whether through intellectual means or via force). The companions are likeable enough. Some stand out but most are serviceable. The antagonist though, I can't remember the last time I harbored so much hatred towards a single character, and I think thats great writing as it shows that the devs/writers really gave a lot of thought to spur you, the player, in order to continue by taunting you through his smug punchable face. I've only finished one ending but I look forward to find all the possible ways that I can shove his face in dirt in all the other endings.Gameplay-wise I'll say it needs a bit of getting used to. The game forgoes initiative and instead adopts the "everyone can move and attack at any time" angle in between the team's turn cycles. So you have to rewrite your a brain a bit if your used to thinking several steps ahead in order to maximize damage and positioning. Here you can move a character, switch to another character attack (or not) and then switch back to the previous character and continue attacking. It messed me up a few times at first because not only do you have to take that into consideration, the skills are also built to take advantage of this system. Several skills forcefully move an opponent but does no damage, which at first I thought were just to be used as support moves. It wasn't until I forced a character that was surrounded did I realize that you're supposed to make use of your characters' "Attacks of Opportunity" using that skill, i.e; surround a peon then force move that guy and watch him get pincushion stabbed by all your allies at once. The game has several stuff like that that isn't explicitly explained to the player, so that might be a negative for some people.The overmap is a nice time filler game loop that is surprisingly addictive. I've played good games with awful overmap gameplay and this is one of the better ones. Captures that "just one more turn" feel in its simplicity.Overall a really great game that is well worth your money

_childDocuments_.name: Expeditions: Rome

_childDocuments_.review: Have you thought about Rome today? :3Expeditions: Rome is a turn-based rpg that blends elements of both tactical and cRPGs. Think XCOM but with a crpg story. The story begins with your character's family being the victim of Roman politics and fleeing to be protected by a family friend, who just so happens to be a consul. The story then progresses as a history what-if scenario, where you fill the role of Caesar in history, as he dies unceremoniously in mission early on. You participate in the campaigns of Asia Minor, Egypt, and Gaul. You make various decisions in these campaigns, such as whether to keep local leaders alive, handling internal legion issues (decimation go brrr), and how to handle politics in between campaigns in Rome. The order of the events doesn't match to the history, but it was an intentional artistic choice to fit the story. As a history nerd with a degree, it's a more than valid decision. Got this during the summer sale and wasn't expecting much but was pleasantly surprisedPros:*Music is solid, though I wish there were more tracks :)*Despite using only just swords, shields, etc. The classes and weapons give a lot of variety for character builds.*Game rewards using the environment and consumables to drastically impact the battlefield. Bonus for making consumables easy to replenish.*no time limit on completing story objectives, you are fighting wars that take years after all!*Full voice acting. The quality of the voices varies, but the main cast of characters are really good.*Though it is a matter of taste, I liked that the story took roughly 60 hours to complete*The main 5 companions are pretty interesting and fairly reactive to the main plot*Pretty faithful in the history of the period, with lots of little details mentioned (at least to my understanding of Roman history)*The story is impacted based on your character's gender (it drastically changes interactions due to the patriarchy and intense sexism found within Rome)*Character portraits actually change based on the skin tone you pick!Mixed:*Game has a bit of learning curve. Once you get used to it though, the game was challenging without being too obnoxious (my playthrough was on the game's equivalent of hard)*Wished there was more content for the companions as they only have 1 or 2 quests at most*A few bugs present though nothing particularly game breaking. Sometimes the AI wouldn't do its turn locking the game but a reload usually fixed it.Cons:*Game felt rushed towards the final 2 acts (4 in total)*The legion management and battles felt tedious and not particularly interesting. Battles are glorified text events and keeping the legion's morale up felt too annoying. Despite the tedium, it wasn't difficult conquering territories.*Sieges are god awful. Luckily, there's only a handful of them. It comes from an issue of the game occasionally throwing dozens of enemies at you. In theory, very cool and it is satisfying watching your praetorians systematically wipe the floor with them. In practice, these encounters take a long time because there's so many turns each round*NPC allies are very goofy and often cause problems (especially ones you have to protect killing themselves by running into fire constantly)TLDR: a gem of an RPG that uses history in faithful way with mostly satisfying tactics and story. Despite the issues, I enjoyed it a lot, crave more, and made the history nerd in me very happy. Lowkey, my dream game as a kid. Roma invicta! 9/10

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic game which any fan of a tactical strategy RPG in the same vein as X-Com can enjoy. This is a hidden gem that was easily the best game I played last year. I loved the alt-history aspect of the story which kept me engaged the whole way through. The characters are well-written and I grew to like them all a lot by the end of the journey.I was having such a blast the first 10 hours or so, it actually made me go back and play the previous two games Expeditions Conquistador and Expeditions Viking which I also greatly enjoyed.Seeing the transformation from their first iteration with Conquistador to now Rome is quite an amazing feat. The quality and gameplay improved immensely over their years making these games and it really shows. The quality with this game is top-notch and it's a shame more people don't know about it.I highly recommend this game and even the previous two games in the Expediitons series. I can't wait to see their next Expeditions game if they ever announce another one!

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR : Turn based combat good. Legion/region "minigame" kind of repetitive after a while. Story is ok/good, would recommend if you enjoy Roman settings. Granted I picked this up for about half the price, I think this game is worth playing if you are, like me, somewhat into ancient Rome and the likes.The tactical, turn based main part of the game is pretty fun, and was enough of a challenge to keep me intrested the whole time. Story isn't the best among this type of game, but it's again more than acceptable. It follows, yet diverges enough from this period of the roman republic to have its charm, and to include our little trip in it quite well.I must admit that I got quite bored of the conquest/legion minigame, that just didn't feel fun after the first few times. Could've done with a bit more diversity on the pacify missions, or maybe a bit more in depth side of the legion management.While i didn't enjoy this enough to make me want to replay it multiple times, the combat and the setting made up for the parts I disliked, so that'll be a recommendation from me.

_childDocuments_.review: I've enjoyed all of the expeditions series.  They play similar to XCom in tactical play.  The graphics are good and I have not experienced any game ending problems.  Sometimes the story choices do not contain the choice I would like to make but the story is engaging and enjoyable.  For this particular installment I love the ending story telling wrap up that encompasses the many choices you made throughout the game to give the story your direction.  I'm not sure how replayable the game would be other than to make more choices to change the ending, but I did play through XCom several times just for the fun.  This is comparable.

_childDocuments_.review: These Expeditions games are getting better with each incarnation.  I discovered Vikings recently and played it start to finish; very fun game.  Then I tried Conquistador.  I suspect the story for that one is great but the interface is terrible, so I bailed on it after an hour of playing.  I'm surprised Expeditions made a sequel after that one, but I'm really glad they got their act together and made Vikings.  Now I'm on Rome.  The interface continues to evolve and unlike most sequels, gets better with every new instalment.  The combat for this requires strategy rather than mashing a button.  I'm really enjoying the story so far, and I'm not going to comment on specifics for that as I don't want to spoil anything.  Anyway, give the demo a try and see if you like it before buying the full game.  That's what I did.

_childDocuments_.review: Wonderful game, full of excellent gameplay comprising both strategic and tactical elements, although the latter received the most focus. The tactical play is turn-based, which is my preference, and highly influenced by your skill development and also greatly by equipment. There is a fundamental equipment crafting & upgrading and dismantling for crafting resources. The strategic map also has exploration elements.The graphics are excellent for this style of game.The story is deep and all dialog is very well voiced. Key decisions made during your campaigns have significant effects. The story is woven together with your essential gameplay in a masterful way--I don't think another game intertwines all aspects of gameplay with the dialog and story.Finally, the handling of a female "legatus" is extraordinarily well done. Without making the female just a male general with a fairer look, the developers leaned hard into this decision by the player and their attempt to remain historically...sound. It affects the dialog in many ways, beyond mere appropriate gender pronouns (don't worry those are present and well done; very few omissions, and I appreciate the duplicate dialog writing and recordings that had to be made all over the place!Rather, the developers made the brave choice to both recognize how Roman society placed women and to make it a significant, viable, non-bland choice. I don't think I've played a game where gender choice felt so natural and handled so well, while remaining very true to what we know from contemporaneous authors (while still not being a history book, suspend your disbelief, thanks). Your character will be treated differently in dialogues and how certain choices are presented will reflect Roman mores very well, while not all undermining your ability to build your story. This said, it is a game and not an Oxford history course; certainly far more enjoyable, in my book.Phenomenal game. Tonnes of inspiration from real historical happenings, but in its own order and with it's own flavors.

_childDocuments_.review: Expeditions Rome ended up being one of surprising all time favorites. Though its XCOM-esque combat was a little unrefined and a touch more boring than XCOM in the modern day, its mostly due to the issues of converting the mechanics to the setting. Still at a game-play level is perfectly fine and I certainly found the legion management system genuinely delight.The thing that most pulled me in however was its full use of the historical setting. While it of course is a slightly more fantastical variant, its both up front about its artistic licenses and is more willing to be honest than a lot of games. I love late republic Rome as a history nerd, but often find the idea of it in games a bit troubling. Games often ignore realities of Rome not one to one with our modern cultural biases. It as a sexist, cruel, slave obsessed empire without an emperor. Yet also not the Rome white supremacists view it as, a nation of competing politics, of convoluted laws and traditions. One with a multicultural reality despite the racism of Rome and one with ambitious and driven women despite the intense sexism of the day.  The biggest example that struck me was the immense amount of writing and narrative devoted to the story dealing with playing a woman. The whole first act has you acting as a hidden shadow Legate because women lack the dignity in roman law to even have a first name, you certainly have no legal right to run a legion. It comes up constantly in the game, often to punish you, sometimes to bind you closer to people like Caldia. Rome is sexist, and its presented harshly, not in a way that celebrates it. This can be seen in other aspects. The way racism is depicted in how senators talk about your majority black legion (which is very realistic for legions formed in Africa before someone gets on my case about it) or slavery. Slavery was so deepy ingrained in Roman society that you can not escape it. You are a roman legate, you are a Patrician, there is no way around the fact you are a slave owner, and instead of pretending it away or minimizing, you see it constantly and interact with it.Its of course not one to one, and part of its historic brilliance is it diverges directly from our time line by shooting the most famous historical character in the mouth before he had the opportunity to do anything even remotely famous. It gives you room to make up new names and faces and let people be and die or do things totally differently or out of order.And yes some things are flattened to make the story work certainly, and in the fourth act some elements feel… a little a historically contrived. Also like maybe the game should stop sucking Cato’s ♥♥♥♥ so hard the guy was not perfect. Yet it all evokes the right elements and lights up the imagination in my mind. Is nothing else it got me to rewatch all of Historia Civilis’ youtube videos.All in all, the game is a fantastic fun, mechanically not quiet amazing but like as a fictional historical Rome game, certainly hits better than idk Rome 2 Total War. Can’t believe the last big continent wide historical game is that hot mess-Anyways, play a woman, honestly adds so much flavor.

_childDocuments_.review: The first game I've tried from this series.  I completed the game with my first character and have started work on another one, trying a different class.Some pro's and con's to the game.CON'S- Certain parts of the game get repetitive to draw the player's time out more.  It's pretty clear to see when you're campaigning.- Some of the side missions and encounters recycle the same map.- Equipment Upgrade system requires a camp upgrade that you can only get late in the game.  So a whole aspect of the gear system, upgrading existing equipment to a higher tier, is not available until the game is almost over.  I wish it was available earlier.  You can loot and craft replacement gear but I want to be able to take what I have and upgrade it as I play sooner.- Non-essential NPCs get a cheap portrait where they're shadows.- There is an annoying bug where the game randomly reassigns skills away from what you organized.  You have to keep a close eye, particularly for Syneros who is your only true, dedicated healer.  It's very bad if you have your main healer participating in a fight only to find out the game switched out his healing skill.IN THE MIDDLE+/- You eventually command a Legion.  There's story and missions you have to do related to your Legion.  There's also command of that Legion during a pitch battle, but it's not quite what I thought it would be.  The Legionary battles are sort of like a card game.  If you're imagining something like a strategy or tactical wargame of units on hexes, or Total War, or even Dynasty Warriors style, that's not what you're getting.PRO'S+ Nice looking battle maps.+ Great looking artwork:  Your character, party members (Centurions and Praetorians), special characters, and the tactical "cards" in Legionary battles look really nice.+ Great voice acting.+ Had great fun with the story.  The game is set in a fictional take on the late Roman Republic and you'll see early on in the game that it's different.  You see familiar characters from the era like Pompey, Caesar, Cato, and many others.+ Fun story and honestly I wish the game would just keep on going with more.

_childDocuments_.review: If you like oldschool strategy RPGs like Fallout or Baldur's Gate, you'll feel at home with this game. It approaches historical fiction in an interesting way, blending the stories of several different historical figures into your protagonist and allowing you to make meaningful and nuanced decisions that affect the outcome of the game in ways that feel plausible - Rome existed for a long time, and no matter how you act or what you do, the decisions you make generally result in something that actually happened at some time or another in the country's history (even if the exact year or people involved are slightly off). You want to romance Cleopatra? Marc Antony did that. Become dictator for life? Gaius Octavius. etc.The gameplay itself (combat) is pretty fun and satisfying for the most part. It's strategic and cinematic. One thing that bothered me is that during the second act you get access to tier 3 weapons and armor which is the final tier, so during the entire third act it's pretty rare for you to find or make gear that is better than what you already have, making the process of opening treasure or looting bodies etc feel pretty unrewarding after a certain point. Also, maintaining two gearsets plus skill trees on 14 characters is a bit tiresome. However, having that many characters, and being able to dismiss and hire new praetorians allows you to experiment with the skill trees without feeling too committed if you think you've made a mistake.Battles where the enemy gets to move first feel extremely unfair, and there are several of them where half my party was dead before I got an opportunity to move. Usually starting over and repositioning solved it, with two exceptions - one, where you are supposed to lose which was quite frustrating because I didn't figure that out until several attempts in - and one where you're given the option of staying hidden and allowing two opposing factions to fight each other before getting involved, in which the npcs walked over to my starting position and discovered my party on turn one before I could move no matter where I placed them or how many times I restarted.Small gripes aside, overall I really enjoyed my time with the game. The nuanced dialog system made me really think about who I was talking to when choosing my answers, and having party members with different personalities approve or disapprove of your choices felt reminiscent of Dragon Age: Origins in a good way. The gameplay is solid and satisfying, and the story is historically inspired and competently executed. 8/10 would conquer again.

_childDocuments_.review: A wonderful combination of role-playing game, turn-based tactics and overworld strategy with an engaging story, good characters and a fascinating historic setting. I did enjoy the world and story for the most part, with recognizable historical figures having cameos left and right, including the obviously historically accurate appearance of Asterix and Obelix in a side quest. :-)I played on Normal, which was the perfect difficulty for me to mainly experience the story and win about 95% of encounters or legion battles without having to reload. Rushing towards the Forge was a good idea, although to my embarassment I only noticed about halfway through the Africa campaign that you are supposed to click on recipes in your inventory to learn them. Ooops. Well, regardless, overall the user interface was well-polished and the gameplay loop was engaging for several hours per game session, so absolutely no complaints from my side.Some minor criticism concerns the length of the third chapter, which was a bit long for my taste. At that point I had more-or-less easily crushed all of Gallia's territories, but still had to go through several hours of main quest, riding back and forth and seeing everyone act as if the entirety of the country was not already under Roman control and as if we had any trouble feeding the legion.Overall I had a great time for 50 hours and got an ending I am happy with for my main character and his companions. Time and money well spent on this.

_childDocuments_.review: I own all 3 Expeditions games and Expeditions: Rome is the best of the lot. I'd give it 8.25/10. warning: spoilersPros:- Beautiful equipment display and scenery whether at peace or at war- Interesting backstories and personalities for your companions, voice-acting is excellent and consistent across encounters- Random quips from your praetorians during combat and random events can be excellent at times and liven up the gameplay- Music is fitting and got me into the feels of medieval conquest and upholding the stature of Rome - Decent alignment with history and explanation provided as to why Egypt and Gaul campaigns were swapped in the timeline- Titus Pullo (from HBO's Rome and apparently Julius Caesar's records) appears as a selectable praetorian- engaging rhetorical turns of phrase employed by Cato and Cicero during senate sessions- has a truly amazing quest game-play involving a gladiator, a sceptical soldier, and cats- tactical combat is solid. I quite like the combination of available skills, class synergies, and unique equipment- legion conquest is functional and gives a highly satisfying ring as you enhance your legion's capabilities and speak to your primus pilus- Roma InvictaCons:- you can be highly inconsistent in your interaction choices just to game the morale of your companions (they should be able to form a more permanent impression of you rather than just letting you flip-flop your tone between conversations)- being a firefighter in a late-game event was extremely tedious having to move the characters back and forth. It made me feel like I was solving a mathematics problem of fire exposure vs rate of water supply rather than playing a game- SPOILER ALERT: you are made to feel like a terrible person (Syneros going as far as to call you 'lesser man' and your companions generally abandoning you) if you go down the path of Octavian and overthrow the senate --> I feel like the developer(s) may have inadvertently let their more modern liberal democratic bias seep into the game (I certainly hope it wasn't an intentional attempt at soft influence, that would just be offensive) which isn't fitting for a historically themed game- we should have had at least had one clearly imperialist companion who pushes for the Legatus' ascension into power based on competency and glorious conquest (any one of the more enthusiastic praetorians could have filled this role and it just felt a vital missing piece in the game)- not enough is done to show the corruption in ancient Rome (widespread bribery, decadent behaviour, the concentration of political power among a select group of patrician families who generally lookout just for their own self-interests) despite it being mentioned in the trailers. We did not even get a single quest targeting corruption in the senate and I felt the background information was insufficient to bring across the severity of the situation at the time- no mention of a continued relationship with Cleopatra in the Octavian ending which just makes you her one-night stand even though that would clearly not have been the case as per the historical conduct of Julius Caesar- it seems strange to me that we have to choose between maintaining Africa or Egypt at the end of Act II, Rome clearly has the capabilities to subdue and administrate both regions- should allow for re-specing maybe at the cost of denarii in case we added a skill point that turned out to have very little utility (an easy to implement but crucial function that was missing in this game)Overall, a great 1 playthrough game (you can just reload the start of ACT 4 to see all endings), and I am very glad to have experienced it.

_childDocuments_.review: As an SPQRaboo, this game ticked many pleasant boxes.The story, characters, voice acting, music, historical architecture -- all great.However, in the later acts the story felt more rushed. Some important events that your character goes through are glossed over. They could've worked those out further to provide some more depth and involvement with your character and your companions.As far as historical accuracy, it did a good job.Early on, something happens that shows how E:R's timeline diverges from our own history.They do play around with a few character's age. Some would've been infants at the time the game takes place, so it's not entirely correct. Some characters, like Crassus and Pompei, should've been more prominent, IMO.But I'm still happy with the inclusions of Cato and Cicero (although Cato seems a bit too cooperative in this game).As far as performance: great, didn't encounter many bugs, if any. Also a special mention to the writer who wrote the funny tooltips in the Settings menu.

_childDocuments_.review: An addictive top-down tactical rpg that mixes the party mechanics of classics like Baldur's Gate with compelling historical fiction and interesting army-management mechanics. Very well-written and exciting storylines, with meaningful alternative endings that you can play out. The army management is less successful, as others have mentioned, but I still found it fun throughout the game. Highly, highly recommend for the immersive story and consistently fun, often challenging gameplay. I will definitely play it again, and I rarely revisit these types of games once I've finished a campaign.Also, a bonus for fellow women who like historical combat-based games is the ability to play a female character and face some interesting, well-considered implications as a result without the common game-dev insistence that no woman ever picked up a weapon before 1985. Indeed, the game addresses the tensions between Ancient Greco-Roman patriarchy and neighbouring cultures like Scythians, Berbers, and Gauls which afforded women wider and sometimes martial roles. These considerations add an interesting dimension to the story that is often overlooked in historical games.

_childDocuments_.review: Ave, Legatus. In a nutshell? This was an incredibly fun game that I easily recommend. This is especially true if you like this historical setting, engaging and fun turn-based combat and an interesting and unexpected story and getting to meet with several historical figures.Expeditions: Rome sets itself in a historical late Republic setting where you play as a Speculatore (scout/recon element), then turn into a Legatus (legion commander) but clearly shows that it doesn't follow actual historical events to the letter, allowing the player to make major decisions. This game really had some great moments that had me sit back and consider what I would do in that particular situation, with no simple answer I could give. What exactly is the value of a General? Would you make bad choices to come to the right conclusion? Are you a defender of the Republic or just after your own personal goals? While the combat did keep me playing it was ultimately the story and characters that sucked me in enough to play for 50 hours. However, I don't want to give details on this because I think it's best if you just experience it. That said, the voice acting was great and I think the characters and their development was enjoyable to see.The combat system in this is fantastic, it felt fluid and fun and character abilities you have change on a basis of what weapons they have equipped as well as skills you level them up in. There are 3 different skill trees for each class and the game allows you to have 5 voiced and close-to-story companions called Praetorians with several other named Centurions available to take on missions including Marcus Aurelius, Titus Pullo, and Lucius Vorenus. You may choose to bring tactical weapons to help enhance your soldiers in combat, including the famed Pila, Greek fire, posca, torches, bandages and several others. These items could be replenished for free if you set a soldier to doing it on the larger map and passing some time, otherwise you could pay with resources and money to have them come back immediately. Where this game REALLY shined with combat was the larger scale battles that took place in each different region. Your team comes up with a plan and a massive battle encompassing many different stages would take place. You would get to decide who gets to take on which assignment and then get into an often challenging series of encounters (imagine 4-5 battles in a row) where equipment and even health would not replenish. These were great highlights to see in the game and were especially fun with the fact that your Centurions could die and be lost forever (Praetorians deaths result in a game over, and this option is able to be toggled). While I have tons of praise for the game, there are also several areas that were not as great as they could have been. The open-world map is generally just a to-do list. Larger scale battles take place between your legion and enemy forces but only really show an overview map with some numbers appearing based on decisions you make with tactical cards in different phases of the battle. You can upgrade and research more tactical cards to use in battle or get single-use cards that are very powerful, but overall these battles are just not interesting or engaging to watch. Aside from that, you command your legion to walk around the map and conquer strategic points such as farms and mines to gain resources to upgrade your camp. This really felt more tedious than anything as you'd constantly get attacked by enemy armies with some prophetic way of telling you where you'd be attacked days ahead of time. These battles never really felt like they offered a challenge, and really made the larger scale map feel like a chore. Also, why can't I use outpost management when I'm where the legion is garrisoned without having to load in every time? QOL changes like this could improve the experience at least a little. Overall though, it's a pretty polished experience with only one bug making my combat more difficult but not difficult enough to lose (note that I played on Caesar - Normal difficulty).In summary this is a strong contender for my GOTY 2022 already and it's only ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ February. I can't imagine if someone made a crossover mod to siege battles from this tying in to Total War: Rome II just like someone did for Crusader Kings and Mount and Blade Bannerlord. This review is sponsored by the Capitoline Brotherhood of Millers. The Brotherhood uses only the finest flour. True Roman bread for true Romans.

_childDocuments_.review: It feels like I've been waiting my whole life for a game like this.  I'm a huge fan and life long student of classical history, especially that of Roman history--to play through such a 60 hour epic was a true treat. In this game you take the role of a Roman Legatus, whom you create, like in games such as Baldur's Gate etc. You can choose gender, class, and there are some decent customization options for looks as well. Your character essentially becomes an alternate history stand in for Gaius Julius Caesar, as you conquer Pontus, Egypt and Gaul. Along the way you make impactful decisions, gather a party of-very well voice acted-nuanced (but not without their cliches) companions, who really add to the story with their side quests and commentary. The combat is turn based strategy, and can drag a bit as you cannot speed up enemy or npc turns. It became especially tedious during sieges. The second aspect of the game is conquering territory on the map, which you explore (without a time limit). Large scale military battle are done in a separate map, where you decide on what 'actions' to take, guided by a 'power' bar. I found it to be a smart way of doing it. You get more actions by upgrading your legion camp, and getting more strategies. I've heard that this is the last expeditions game. It's sad to hear, but really if this is the last it is a very good way to end it. Rome is very much an improvement over the other two expeditions games, which includes Vikings, another game that I loved. Games like this are unique, and rare and deserve to be appreciated. I hope to see an expac for this game in the near future. Expeditions: Rome is a solid 9/10 for me.

_childDocuments_.review: [Played on Insane Ironman with Combat Deaths on]A fantastic journey inspired by the story of Julius Caesar, it takes us through many varied regions, characters, plots. The historical fidelity and climate is superb, I would call it the best Rome-themed game out there! Superb voice acting and very high quality locations, there was a surprisingly huge variety of uniquely-crafted locations even for random battles.Quest choices are meaningful, combat is quite interesting (though some builds could use a hard nerf!), legion command system, while incredibly flavorful, was superficial in the end as all legion battles are too easy no matter what your preparation level is. Certainly something to improve!The single thing I disliked in the game is the completely randomised crafting/equipment, of not only all the stats, affixes (bonus stats) but also weapon skills, meaning there is no rhyme or reliable way to get what you aim for without dozens or hundreds of dismantle&crafting cycles. Does not help the problem that regular quality items could have superior stats to highest quality, pristine versions. Makes comparing any loot a chore to sort out as you have to compare hundreds of items case by case.

_childDocuments_.review: For the first time in recent memory I've purchased a game that appears to be ready to play, does pretty much everything the advertising says it will, doesn't require a 50GB update or patch every time I want to play it, and seems to be complete. There are of course subjective issues ( SALWEY? ) but this is one of the best games for the money that I've seen in the last several years. It doesn't come across as a beta version which was released too early or needing additional DLC to work right but still has expansion and improvement potential. It would be nice to have an option to have the entire spoken language in Latin (with subtitles of course :) ), spoken by folks who didn't sound like their other job is a London taxi driver, for example. Anyone who's ever seen the Netflix series Barbarians where the Romans speak Latin and the Germans speak German will understand what I mean. It adds so much to the feeling. Nevertheless, my sincere congratulations to the programmers and developers for an excellent product. Hopefully this approach is the future of computer game publishing and not a deviation from the future norm.

_childDocuments_.review: Many say this game is like "X-Com". I don't think so. It's far more like "Divinity Original Sin 2". The characters are not as deep as in Divinity, but they are good. The english voice acting is very good, the german one is okay. The fightings have a lot of stats to look at and the use of the enviroment (high ground) is as important as the use of objects  (Greek fire, pila, water,etc) and allows tactical desicions to turn the tide of a fight.Now, the game comes with a major flaw: The battles! Oh Gods have mercy! The clash of our legion with an enemy army is absolutly poor made. Little symbols that wave back and forth a bit and a few arrow sounds. That's it. The battle plans are pointless and you can take a counter cavallery tactic, even if there is not a single horse symbol on the battlefield. No clashing iron sounds, not a single legionarii romani visable and the three phases in that the battles are divided in, become tedious after the first battle. Only the command cries of the centurio in charge are good again. It's sad, that this part of the game is so rubbish made. It's my legion, that I command for the good of Rome, for Jupiters sake! I want to watch my men fight for Rome, if I'm not able to command them in person and not some cheap symbols that tells me nothing and that don't give me the feeling of wachting the clash of some thousand men.I can only hope (and maybe sacrifice some doves at the temple of Mars) that the successor  (if there will be any) has this corrected and gives us propper battles. I don't need a Total war experience, but come on, such things where made better 25 years ago.Some minor things are a bit clunky. - You will be running around a lot on realy buitiful made maps, but you can't part your group. This means the whole cluster is running with the main hero and if there's a ladder or some branches, you have to wait for every single one of the group to climb this up or down. - If you send the heros a longer way and there's a ladder and a way around, you can bet that one dumb hero is using that damn ladder. That costs a lot of time and nerves. - You divide looted stuff into crafting parts with an right mouse click, but no one tells you, to HOLD the mouse button down. I had to watch a video to figure this out. - To kill untrained enemies gives the hero the attack action point back. Why? And for what? Why untrained, why not the more dangerous trained enemy? Weird design. - You can't brake off a movements. If you do a wrong click and your hero is running through fire or oil or crosses the guarding zone of an enemy and dies by an opportunity attack, then you will hate this game.   I haven't finished the game yet, but I rate it positive even with the great battles that will make you cry of the wasted potential and the minor flaws.

_childDocuments_.review: Well, here goes my review. And I don't recommend the game, sorry to say. (Edit below. The edit is still bad)I'm a huge fan of the Expeditions series, and love what Logic Artists does, but I feel they dropped the ball with this one. I am not enjoying myself, and this is due to some design issues, in my opinion.First off, the good:The tactical combat is very cool, and much deeper than this game's predecessor. I love the different classes and routes you can take with them, and the combo's you can make. Very enjoyable. I also like the setting, and the way they expanded on the former Expedition's possibilities. The idea of the Legion and sending Praetorians on side missions is good, in essence.But as I keep playing, I stumble upon more and more confusing issues, which suck the fun away for me. I actually think of stopping, but I'll keep going a bit more to see if I can get my money's worth out of it..First off, the obvious: Legion battles are too abstract, too confusing, and it doesn't feel like you have a lot of control over them. I like the idea a lot, but I have 0 connection with this aspect. It feels like something mandatory you have to click through. Akin to Pathfinder Kingmaker's horrible, horrible Kingdom aspect. I want to play a tactical RPG, not manage obscure, vague, unclear tasks I feel I have no substantial control over.Then, the legions again. As I conquered and pacified a region, I want to take over the strategic assets (mines, tanneries,..). I can only do this with my legion, of 2000 men strong. Really? Why? Can I not send my own char and his strong Praetorians to basically command the tannery to work for me now? This makes no sense.Then, onto the Praetorians. Basically, I have my own main char who is the boss. He can't do all the tasks himself, I get that. So when I need a region pacified, I can send a Praetorian and some goons. But, for some reason, my main char can't stay behind at the fort and manage stuff, he has to travel along. This makes no sense. He can't come along for the fight because he's too important, but he hàs to come along to.. do what? This is not explained, and does not seem natural.The Praetorians, then, can also be used a Centuriones, fighting along your Legion. Which means your Praetorians are actually used for quite some roles: Fight alongside you, command a posse of goons for side missions, fight as centuriones and be posted at buildings for whatever that building does. This is not explained quite well enough, and is quite confusing as well. There are just too many different layers in this game that overlap, mlaking it blurry. The differences should be better laid out.Lastly, the way main quests are prioritized feels wrong. At one point, I had 3 main quests. however one of those was prerequired to be able to do another of those missions. This is mentioned once earlier in the game, but with all the confusing stuff coming at me, I did not make the connection. This had me wandering along the countryside looking for clues, untill I selected another main quest which was 100% required to do before you could progress. Honestly, this should have been more clear. You should not have a main quest open, only for it to be unable to finish unless you finish another. There's a lot better solutions for that. It only serves to frustrate and confuse.I want to love this game, and I get what LA is trying to do. But it just feels wrong, bloated, unfinished, and all in all confusing. They have made a lot of improvements on the tactical part, that bit is quite impressive. But the strategic bit is just... unnessecary, vague, and not well developed enough to feel a connection with it.I anticipated this game for years, but I'm quite dissapointed. I expected more.Edited:I gave the game a few more hours of honest chance. But I gave up. I managed to overcome the things that haven't been explained (after hours of trying stuff out and getting help from the "friendly" community), and some of the things that are not worked out (well or at all). But now I'm starting to see the combat is just not entertaining enough to keep me hooked. I don't even get the chance to use a steady group to fight. I can manage soldier deaths and replacements, but forcing me to use specific chars or blocking me from using specific chars... That's just a major ♥♥♥♥ move. The game lacks depth, and is a major dissapointment. LA: I don't know where you dropped the ball with this one, but hopefully this feedback (and that of others) will help you things together.I mean.. what the hell happened? Why put in legion battles that are not fun, or finished, or explained, or interactive? Why all this ambiguity concerning the praetorians and all their uses? Why can I not use my main charachter for more than half of the things going on? Why are the battles so lackluster, and completely not innovative? Why must there be such "surprises", which are not fun or challenging, but just annoying? Why couldn't you be bothered with explaining all the stuff you chose to put in the game? Why didn't you bother with more tooltips? Why are you forcing me to use part of my crew or blocking me from using part of my crew? Man. I've been gaming since 1988, and few games let me down as much as this one. It's good to see a lot of people are enjoying it, but I'm not buying LA games any more, if this is the route you consciously chose.

_childDocuments_.review: Expeditions Rome is a good strategy based game. The game itself could be divided into 5 blocks of gameplay: The first block is the map movement where you move as a squad of your chosen praetorians and tackle the challenges the game offers you, whether it is capturing strategic resources or cities with your legion, digging out chests for loot, replenishing your water supply, etc. The map varies depending whether you out for conquest or in the city, the latter being much limited and a simple travel point screen. When you are playing on your campaigns the map is quite big and offer its own set of bonuses and challenges.The second block is your camp where you craft items, assign praetorians to work on certain benefits. It is where you recruit generals for your legion and for your praetorian guard. Every character your recruit for your own guard must be managed on terms of equipment and skills so that it can serve you accordingly into battle.The third block is the decision making you do when you talk to characters, choices matters and they shape the game around you, eventually your choices shape the ending depending on certain key moments. When you create your character you have three traits to choose, depending of which of the three you choose it will influence your dialogue choices in key moments.The fourth block is the combat with your praetorian guard which relays on good observation using your surroundings to your advantage and striking the enemy in a smart way. You have elements you can use to your advantage like fire, oil, poison and others. Every character has a skill three combined with weapon choices, for example an archer cannot be a healer, the classes are predetermined and cannot change. However the archer can equip a pick or a sword as a second weapon which is quite handy when your enemies get up close. The fifth block is the legion combat system against your enemy. At the moment of writing it's a card based kind of system when you use the card that gives you enough points in favour of a desired outcome and you resolve or auto resolve each combat. After a while it gets annoying. I read they are currently trying to implement a more entertainment way to approach it.I believe it's a good game worth playing but it can get a bit annoying after a while with some mechanics. I'll summarize what I liked and what not.+ The graphics are quite nice, not on par with DOS2 thought.+ The combat gameplay it's interesting, where you can attack in any order you like and move your character afterwards given you have movement points available.+ The sound is quite good.+- You can only romance one character so choose wisely ;).- The camp upgrades are not rewarding enough. I maxed out everything in act 3 and I thought I could buy supplies in my camp but the merchant still sells you the same three things: slaves, food, medicine. - Depending on the map you find yourself it was hard for me to acquire basic supplies like linen for bandages, quickfire for torches and other components to either craft supplies or replenish them.- For my personal taste there are a myriad of items to equip which left me confused which character should equip what, I didn't find it so straightforward. For the same reason I didn't use much of the crafting.- The dismantle mechanic was very annoying, to the point I would not pick up items, you have to dismantle every single item by holding RMB. A mass dismantle option would be VERY WELCOME.- Upgrading your current items is blocked by camp upgrade, which I found a bit annoying but when maxed out I found out you could upgrade to a max of lvl 3 that item, very annoying indeed.- Another annoying mechanic of the game is that you can only heal others with bandages, you cannot self apply them.- There's not an Italian translation nor audio, as an Italian this saddens me beyond reliefI believe most of the things can be improved and tweaked by the developer in future updates, I still recommend the game as I had a lot of fun with it and it's replayable. This was my first run and I'll be starting my second after I finish this review.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall a good game with a lot of love and care put into it, but lots of padding (unintentional or otherwise) makes each act feel less enjoyable and kills replay-ability. The story is good, engaging and has some generally good side quests (though 90% of the time, things end in combat). The attention to historical detail is reminiscent of Ryse: Son of Rome, and it really immerses you in the world of Rome and its conquests, even if the story and characters themselves are fictional. The main story is great and about 20-30% of the side stories were very enjoyable. Your sidekicks are really well done, with a lot of party banter and flexibility in how you manage them. The branching storyline and myriad options for ending the game are great, with Fallout style ending 'slides' to show you how you shaped the world and people around you. Even if all choices lead to the same set of outcomes for you personally, there's a lot of options for how the story plays out in terms of who lives/dies, what becomes of certain NPCs and your companions, the state of various conquests, and your own personal fate. The models and locations are sprawling and and beautiful and the first time visiting a number of locations and just admiring the detail was wonderful. Combat animations are interesting and varied, and the combat itself is fun - it's tactical combat in the vein of XCOM and offers a variety of classes and enemy types, as well as interesting combat situations. It's the strongest mechanical part of this game, and offers a lot of variety and challenge. Sadly the conquest  and camp management mechanics are dull and hard to enjoy, with a lot of repetitive busywork and hard to decipher mechanics (still no idea how to prepare for conquest battles, the enemy numbers just got bigger with each act and I just tried to keep up by grinding out bigger numbers on my side. Then when we battle, I just try to counter their big numbers with my big numbers - it's as boring as that sounds. There's nothing at all emergent or engaging about this. I really enjoyed all of this; it's clear a lot of love went into this game and I appreciate the developer for putting so much attention to detail into things. That said, I won't replay this game again because of how much padding there is that adds zero joy to this game. My main issue is with the pacing of the game, which gets worse with each chapter, because:1. Large size of each location map relative to the amount of content in it - a location may have 3 people to speak to and each NPC is positioned a minute away from one another (there's no way to speed up the running animation). Additionally it's hard to find NPCs in a location even with highlighting on because you have to swing the camera about to spot some of them2. Often you need to go to a location, do something for 10 seconds then head to another location to progress a quest. Some quests have several of these steps in succession and the loading screens between world map and locations quickly become tiresome and made me abandon some of what were clearly boring fetch quests3. After party combat you have to go pick up everything manually, running around the map and then to the exit. It does lump together nearby searches but again you have chests scattered across the map and it takes ages to run and pick up everything. Just let me exit and choose all the loot from bodies that I want in one place. If you want me to go chest hunting then fine, don't include those so it's a reward for those who want a worn dagger and some vinegar badly enough 4. World maps get bigger, harder to navigate and the conquest stuff gets more tedious and difficult rather than genuinely more challenging or complex - lots of go here, occupy this or fight for this and wait for a clock to tick down. The conquest stuff was mainly box-checking to progress your party's story line in every act, there never was a feeling you were impacting or changing the lands you were in5. WHY DO YOU NEED TO MANAGE YOUR WATER SUPPLIES (OR EVEN SERVI AND RATIONS) - THEY'RE ALL JUST BUSYWORK AND HAVE LITTLE IMPACT ON THE GAME OTHER THAN JUST SOMETHING TO MANAGE. It's resource management to keep on-brand with "Expeditions" but narrative-wise, the Roman army in a foreign land is not quite the same challenge as Vikings venturing to England or conquistadors carving through the new world. In one act, there's a brief moment of ludo-narrative harmony when the Roman army finds itself short of supplies for good reasons but once addressed shortly after as a plot point in your party's story it goes back to being more busywork.I'm still going to give this game a thumbs up because I did enjoy it but just be mindful of how much busywork there is to do to enjoy excellent story (with a great villain and lots of interesting NPCs). A lot of the padding can be removed without impacting the quality of the game but for reasons I don't quite understand, game developers still spoil so much of their highly impactful work by mixing up pacing with padding.Hoping this game still winds up a success as I'd love to see them do a game set in feudal Japan (like Shadow Tactics or  Ghost of Tsushima) or during the Heroic Age of Antarctic Exploration, and hopefully without all the filler next time!

_childDocuments_.review: The premise of the game is actually fun and the overworld map mechanic, the army clashes, as well as party management is all ok. Nothing new but none if it sticks out as out of place. The one big gripe i have with the game is the random status effects in combat. Combat, as often the case with turn based games, can take a while. Which is ok because the core concepts they have, armor / resistances / flanking / glancing strikes etc, are all solid. Instead of leaving it at that they decided to implement conditions like panic. Why ? We are supposedly leading a group of Praetorians, trained roman soldiers, hardened in battle. Not some 1st week recruits. So 10 minutes into a fight, your tank stubs his toe and starts panicking, (No more actions taken). Your Sniper goes Berserk and starts attacking his teammates...This isn't Darkest Dungeon...These mechanics are not just unnecessary, they turn otherwise tactical fights into a random mess. Which is a shame, as the rest of the game seems solid but the party combat is to drawn out and happens to often for these kind of random factors to be any fun. This is obviously a personal oppinion, if you like these mechanics then you might enjoy the game.

_childDocuments_.review: I would start by saying, buy on sale. A fun time killer, this is. Over all its rather simple. The tactical rpg combat is challenging and fun, even if it is Divinity simplified. The Story is predictable, and the dialog options are not exactly brilliant, but they have very humorous moments. Oddly, i gotta give props to the writters for creating something of a semi-historical game, that is, a young kid could actually walk away with a good deal of knowlege and understanding surrounding the end of the republic. The "warfare" element is oversold, being not much more than a numbers and card game. Yet i enjoy it as a break from the rpg tactics map which can get a bit monotonous or frustrating given how much time it can take. So yeah, if ya can get it on sale, and ya want a time killer, give it a look. Dont expect gold.

_childDocuments_.review: Found the combat pretty enjoyable, lots of options, things to try, skills to hone and break. Can't say how historic any of the world building is, but felt pretty flavourful, enjoyed exploring the world mostly. Third act, a bit less so. Had a nice way of motivating me to get all the upgrades for my camp.As is unfortunately common, suffers from a few hard railroading points. Not the worst, even if technically you're always being tugged to the path there were many places where it felt at least that I could roleplay and pick my solution to things. A couple of points where your character is maddeningly dumb purely for story convenience, or is unable to express discontent. Best example is surrounding a fight you need to lose. So, this fellow you know is out to get you and has secret loyalties in the region introduces you to a guy he assures you is trustworthy. You're led into a trap by this fellow, character forced to be convinced by him. And the fight on normal anyway, is rough but not impossible... except for eternally spawning reinforcements. Just, something about taking out both ringleaders but having to sit and wait... Also a frustrating assassin you're just not allowed to take out, nor in fact your mortal enemy despite opportunity. I almost laughed when I was finally allowed to fight said assassin, had him downed, went to use my, finish downed opponent button, but was forebade... and then next turn he got up to escape. Really breaks the immersion. Those moments which really needed better written narratively, or given slight alternate paths to allow player freedom aside, otherwise pretty enjoyable entry to the genre

_childDocuments_.review: Gave this game a pretty solid shot based on a love of SRPGs and curiosity.  It started out fairly decent, but there was a lot of irritating stuff that hindered my enjoyment.I'd probably recommend this game despite what I disliked about it to someone who was really into Roman history.  But all of the detail they put into it from that didn't really do much from me.I had some glitches with the overworld UI where labels wouldn't show up on things and I'd have to mouse over where I thought things were in areas to find where to send my armies to.  But even when the overworld worked it wasn't particularly compelling.  Just "use resource to unlock next bit of the tech tree" with your legion then conquer next area.  The legion battles aren't particularly thrilling either, I just pushed any button and won them with little to no detriment.The action economy in battle is a little weird too.  There's limited use tactical items in battle that don't cost actions to use, but you have to spend resources to refill them at your base every once and a while.  Except, it's kind of trivial to keep them all at full strength so you just spam them constantly.  There's a mechanic in place where you get action points back for killing blows on minion type enemies, but it's not always easy to tell which ones are minions and even then it'd probably be better if there weren't so many useless enemies on the field.Also, I hate the "pacification missions" where you can only take one named character (and not the main character) and the rest you have to fill with generic, weaker soldiers.  Very tedious.I played past my refund eligibility and don't really regret it because it was interesting seeing a somewhat unique attempt at the genre.  But I don't believe I'd recommend others get into it.

_childDocuments_.review: The game is great, I love it, but it is soooooooooooo buggy.  The highest level strategems in legion battles almost never give the correct bonuses, which can and will lead to the deaths of many centurions in the 2nd half of the game.  The enemy's bonuses during legion battles are sometimes randomly doubled for seemingly no reason, which also leads to the same issue.  Both of those things have happened in the opposite direction, giving me more bonuses than I should have, but that's happened maybe three times while it happens to the enemy nearly 100% of the time.  The music regularly either stops completely or plays twice at the same time just slightly out of sync if you reload an autosave in the middle of combat.  The gladiatorial arenas lag horrendously even on lower settings, and will just outright crash after a few minutes about half the time if you're playing gladiator mode and not just visiting them in the main game.I've had two playthroughs ended fairly early on because my game decided that crossing the water to go to Asia Minor would instead send me back to the tutorial and make me unable to interact with anything.  Couldn't get past that no matter how many times I reinstalled or verified game files.  I've also had a few instances of several unique items just not spawning in the world.  I have only managed to get through the game one time, because every other attempt has been ended by a game breaking bug.  Despite all that though, I sill love this game.  The story is great, the gameplay (when it doesn't break) is great, and I love the style.  It needs some major bugfixes though.  I have heard that not everyone has these issues, but it seems widespread enough from looking at the bug reports that it's more likely an issue with the game than anything on my end.
