_childDocuments_.review: *Slight spoilers*OK, I have got to be fair and redo my review.  I admit that I was frustrated by running face first into a wall at the end of the 1st act, when the difficulty took quite a spike. I tried again and eventually was able to make it through that part by changing my strategy quite a bit. So, what is this about? I bought this on a sale, and I soon was kinda sucked into the game and had a lot of fun. It combines RPG elements with turn-based strategy. You travel around, talk to people, do quests, make moral decisions and then either do turn based battles with your companions (XCom-style) or have your army (legion) fight an enemy army. The latter part is nothing to really write home about - you see a bunch of name plates move around, you choose different moves (some more risky than others)  and hopefully will beat the enemy after your third turn. The fights with your companions are much more X Com style - you have a certain amount of moves, you have different attacks and abilities you gain through the skill trees. There is no overwatch (there is a certain ability some chars have that are similar), and you can do attacks of opportunity. Speaking of skill trees, these are... not exactly inspiring, IMO. There were no abilities that had me go "Wow this sounds so cool. I need to work towards this ability". There are some useful ones (demoralizing enemies for example), but I didn't find these abilities to be too enticing. However, the game is fun. It DOES get repetitive eventually, and you will spend quite som,e time watching the moves of your enemies, which may take a while. I also SOMETIMES felt as if the enemies had more range... it felt like they could cross like a third of the map and STILL attack, but maybe I am wrong here. Just be prepared for spending a long time watching the enemies move, as there will be a lot of them. What kinda discouraged me at one point was the end of act 1, where you have to endure a string of battles with two different groups of companions. It was, I believe, 5 different battles, and I failed miserably as you don't auto heal fully in between. So at the 4th stage, my chars were really low on HP.However, this was where consumables came into play. You can collect and craft stuff like bandages. I didn't notice at first that there were some at the start of some of the stages. Once I found these, I was able to heal at least a bit and move on. Also, sometimes, there will be friendly NPCs you can activate by moving close to them (at least in that string of fights) and they'll move on their own and attack your enemies. You will also often get reinforcements (just like the enemy) which is a nice touch. You're a military leader after all. So... I finished act 1 after failing miserably and it DID feel nice to actually finish that. I am looking forward now to moving on, because even though the game does have weaknesses, it still is fun. Pros- Looks nice- You learn some things about life in the Roman Empire- X Com style combat, sans the fantasy/Sci Fi elements, a bit more "gritty"- You can level and develop your companions- Somehow addictiveCons- You'll spend quite some time watching your enemies move, with no fast forward option (like the recent Warhammer Chaos Gate has)- You need to rely on (and craft or collect) consumables, which is not everyone's cup of tea- End of act 1 is quite a difficulty spike- Sometimes, it's hard to find/see objects on the map, like for example stuff you can pick up during combat or in between- Not entirely intuitive in the way it teaches you things, you should/need to fiddle around with things and try out different options, for example when you build your camp. - Skill trees don't feel really enticing, a lot of so-so abilities in these. - Can get repetitiveVerdict: A nice X Com style game in a historical setting, combining the history of the Roman Empire with a slightly different storyline (diverging from the way things went). Can be addictive, but also has some flaws. If you are unsure, wait for a sale or check out some longplays on YT.

_childDocuments_.review: Expeditions Rome was a dream for a fan of Roman History, particularly the late republic that this game emulates albeit in an alternate timeline. My love for the period propelled me through the janky/uninspired bits of the game, though for someone not already invested in the history, events and historical figures you’ll encounter I feel the game doesn’t have much to offer the standard gamer.Gameplay wise the game flows between over-world war making and being a turn based CRPG. The latter is the superior part of the game, particularly the story/dialogue based content that I found myself craving more of throughout my play through.The over-world aspects of the game sees you marching your legion(s) around Greece (Act 1) Africa (Act 2) and Gaul (Act 3) in which you’ll have to both attack enemy settlements and defend your own, while managing supplies, morale, and troop numbers. By far the war making is the most tedious aspect of the game, the battles are uninspiring, mundane and generally felt like a chore even with me pressing auto-resolve more and more often. It doesn’t have a particular challenge beyond the fact that for the most part you’ll only have one lone legion in which to fight the war. The CRPG half of the game like I said involved dialogue segments, and turn based combat. The combat is fun, for the most part, with distinct skills and classes, the game challenges you to think smartly before you charge in unprepared. The only blemish on the combat is that, especially late game, battles take forever as the the game forces you to watch each individual enemy turn with no way to speed things along. Often times the excellent combat would be interrupted by me watching the enemy accomplish little throughout a twenty minute turn where dozens of enemies were on screen. The story and dialogue is its strongest aspects, primarily when the game sets you loose in the eternal city where you’ll switch between controlling your followers and controlling your custom character as both they, and you, navigate their lives. We meet the likes of Cato, Cicero, Pompey Magnus and even a young Caesar, with many of the figures of the era playing a role. Ultimately I’d recommend this game to any fan of the Roman Republic or even Turn based combat though you’ll have to be prepared for the rough/mundane aspects of the game as it’s far from perfect in the execution Of its ideas. Regardless a lot of passion for the time period went into this game, and I trust soon I’ll play through the game a second time with the DLC Gladiators class. Roma Invicta!

I don't know what a "Twitch" is, but I do know that I paid for a game to play.  I DIDN'T PAY FOR SOMETHING THAT I NEED TO DO SOMETHING TO WATCH OR DO TO GET A MINOR CUSTOMIZATION CHOICES.   THAT IS WHY GAME DESIGNERS HAVE A JOB (like English literature majors)  THAT DOESN'T INVOLVES "DO YOU WANT FRIES WITH THAT?" The second SERIOUS design flaw is making a game that you have to make a secondary party from your NPCs to pacify regions using only one of your Praetorians from your main group. _childDocuments_.review: This is a game to buy if you're a fan of the Expeditions series, and of the Roman setting. If you are not one of these, I cannot recommend it. Like all of itsExpeditions: Rome inherits the exact combat system of its predecessors, and is actually in many ways much worse than them. It features some of the most unbalanced class dynamics I have ever seen in a turn-based RPG, with the Archer and Veles classes so massively outclassing the two other classes that by the mid to late game, if you are not using only these you are basically handicapping yourself.They still haven't added a way to speed up enemy movement, so battles with 30+ enemies will have their turns taking several minutes to finish. RNG is as massive a factor as ever, with many battles being decided purely by your fortune with the dice.With all this being said, I highly recommend AGAINST playing on iron-man or Insane difficulty in general. These things do not make the game harder, they just basically lock you into abusing the broken classes to survive, as you're going to be so outclassed otherwise that you'll be save-scumming into oblivion. I repeat, insane is not "hard", it's just frustrating. Having RNG play such a big part is just never fun.The setting is at least done well. You get to get the feeling of commanding Roman legions and playing with the politics of the time. Obviously it's not historically accurate, since it has to give space for player agency, but I can at least say that most of what happens is somewhat realistic.All-in-all, even with its shortcomings, this was a really fun game. But they seriously need to start innovating more with their formula, because right now the only thing that has really changed is the graphics. I still say that Expeditions: Conquistador is the best in the series. It honestly has better combat too. I still miss the prep phase.

_childDocuments_.review: High Quality RPG with tactical combat set in classical Rome. Well done fully rotational 3D and zoom scroll with an adjustable pitch angle UI. You can tell effort was spent on creating the 3D models and environment objects. Think of Age of Decadence except you have a whole squad. Swap armor, weapon, and helmet and the appearance of your soldiers reflect the changes. This is one of the few games I can play using maxed out ultra graphic settings. Considering I have a GT1060 card in an older i7 this is quite a feat these days. It looks good. The RPG elements are linear and told through well written text and voice acting to further present choices for the main character's fate. Some choices matter. These scenes are not animated, although artistically rendered nicely in 2D.  I suspect this left more resources to be applied in creating the detailed tactical world scapes. The regional maps do give a semi open world feel, although objectives are mission oriented.Combat is xcom style tactical. You control 6 soldiers, but some battles will let you control more for large scripted brawls. Very similar to Expeditions Vikings. This game is much bigger than vikings so more time, more content. It has crafting and resource gathering to create higher quality armors than what is typically scavenged. You also get a base camp to manage your Praetorian Section and Legion. Oh, you also maintain a legion on the side. Legion battles are abstractly fought in a rock paper scissor dice roll card laying fashion. Over all this is a great game.

_childDocuments_.review: I would give it negative rating because the entertainment was barely average, but I spent a lot of time in this game and that means I was somewhat invested. Unfortunately it's completely dragged down by a horrible design, lack of interesting content and average writing.The game takes place in the Roman Republic, but in alternative history, where Gaius Iulius Caesar didn't get a chance to destroy it. Sadly, you're just a pawn in the story, no matter what you do, nearly everything unfolds the same way. You get to meet historical characters, but don't expect in-depth dialogues or anything of substance. Even your companions don't have much depth, they represent archetypes, often cringy, never interesting. The RPG part is very subdued compared to Expeditions: Vikings, most of the locations are either cities with merchants, or a few room buildings/dungeons for battles. Gametime is then fluffed up by the strategic part, which is a disaster. Bored to death, you spend 80% of your time managing your legion because you have to peddle back and forth to do little things which have minor impact on the battles. It's baffling why the devs thought anyone would enjoy it. Same goes to upskilling and managing your party, it starts as interesting but half of the perks are pointless, so you end up just clicking on things. Crafting is even worse. UI is terrible and confusing, game is still pretty buggy. Oh and those random encounters - they are too frequent and too pointless.OK, so what's good? Combat, especially before you get overpowered (I played on Hard). The unique setting and the fact we have historical RPGs, which should be a thing. And the main antagonist was actually quite compelling, rarely slipping his mask, he was the only well written character in the whole game and hoping to see him squirm at the end of my gladius was the main reason why I didn't give up on it.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a good game. You should buy it, if you like turn based tactical games. If you do, crank up that difficulty level a bit, as it's rather easy. Especially, is you have some Veles (aka Rogues) that can just kill several opponents (I once did up to 10 with my main character) in the same turn. The class balancing seems a bit off.The game tells you a fictive story in a world that's mostly consistantly built. It's an interesting setting and the story telling is okay most of the time.That said, the conquering of the regions is quite boring/easy and I dislike the random events and automatic and frequent attacks against some sector of yours. Especially in the third act the game loses player agency and forces you to do weird and stupid things. I think, they've spent less time on the end part of the game. It felt repetitive and less good, than the previous chapters.In your camp you kind of have some limited base building. You can improve your army that way and build better items. I would however recommend to the devs to build on that in future games and make it more complex and add some quests and make it feel more homey/personalized. The thing is that all camps mostly look the same, if you ignore the upgraded parts.It is a good game, but there are many things that need improvements.

_childDocuments_.review: I initially wrote this game a bad review, but I decided to keep going to see if my opinion changed. It really hasn't. Expeditions: Rome is a mess of bizarre anachronisms, weird alternate history, and mediocre combat, wrapped together in a sometimes-decent but overall incoherent and dull story where you, kind of, play through the career of Julius Caesar as an OC, except out of order, and not really. All of its sins could be forgiven for its uniqueness as a cRPG set in Ancient Rome were it not for its wargame overworld system, which is unbelievably tedious and is effectively a click-through simulator that is, unfortunately, mandatory for progressing the main story. Crafting mechanics, base management, survival systems, and much more have been shoehorned in for no clear reason. Level, quest, and encounter design are very poor. Most fights feel pointless and don't progress anything. I once slaughtered some Greek merchant's guards for no reason; when he confronted me as to why, my character could only reply, "I dunno, they looked sketch lmao." That was the best the writers could come up with, and that moment repeated again and again as I continued playing.This should have been a game about playing as Caesar's XCOM, but instead is about leading an army; it doesn't make any sense that you, a legatus, are leading troops into endless fights.I don't understand why this game has such good reviews. It isn't horrible in aggregate, but every one of its constituent parts is extremely mediocre. It doesn't do anything well. It might be worth playing for vibes alone, but given the huge number of anachronisms in gear, art, setting, characters, language, and story events, it's barely a historical game in any real sense, that's a pretty hard sell. I would still consider it on sale were it not for its length; this game is absurdly long, and I cannot imagine wrestling with the horrible legion wargame for another 50 hours. I'd sooner go play Imperator: Rome, and I hated Imperator: Rome.

_childDocuments_.review: Great game but buggy as hell on Windows 11. I spent already several hours to fix problems: Adjust windows firewall, reinstall graphic drivers, data integrity checks, computer restarts, etc. At the moment I have another game crashing bug and I can not continue at the end of Act 2. Every time you enter a new area or load a save game you have to pray that the game works. Literally none of the dozens games I played in recent years crashed so many times. Not even Cyberpunk 2077 in December 2020 or the early access of Baldurs Gate 3. However, I am confident they can fix it in the upcoming months. It seems to happen only on some Windows Systems... The following review does not take these crashes into account... Who should buy it?If you like RPGs or round based tactical combats. I am talking about games like Wasteland 2/3, Expedition Vikings, Divinity Original Sin 1/2 or the latest X COMs. If you like history it is a plus. Who should not buy it?If you are mainly a hardcore tactical combat nerd and you want a big challenge, you might don't like it. I started the game on hardcore and it is still much more easier than Divinity or X Com on the lower difficulty levels. If you even prefer games with the depth of Jagged Alliance or X Com Terror from Deep, don't buy it. Moreover, the game is also not for you if you expect a historical correct story about the last days of the republic. It's an alternative history scenario. They also changed armor and fighting styles. By doing so the studio could implement classes which are similar to other games. I think it's a plausible design choice and they did a good job. But if you go crazy about historical accuracy, don't play it. What is great?- Historical setting, no dragons, Orcs, magic and other ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. They took the best documented period of ancient rome and some of the most famous historical persons show up.- Choices which have an impact later on. The choices/RPG part has not the depth of a Wasteland 3 or offers the choice of a branching tree like in Tyranny or Fallout New Vegas. But it is done in a good way.- Round based combat, could be more challenging, especially in the end game. But still good stuff. What is not so great?Mainly some Design choices (all rather minor points): - The whole menue is a bit cumbersome and not intuitive. Especially replenishing tactical tools or the crafting system. However, once you know the mechanics, it is ok. One menue where I could access everything would be much more better.- You have to dismantle sometimes objects to get the resources. This is done with a simple right click. But I had to google to figure this out. You also don't have an option to dismantle several objects at once. - Please implement a progress bar on how much praetorians like you or not. Having only text labels like (Hesitant, Disgruntlet, Loyal, Pleased, etc) are not very good. It would be also great to know what type praetorian I hire. An honest one or an Arrogant one? If you play an honest character you don't want to hire a greedy hesitant praetorian.- The fights are too easy. Especially the world map. It's nice to have an additional strategical layer. But if you just click on everything you can hardly do anything wrong even on hardcore difficulty. Usually your Legions will always win.

_childDocuments_.review: Expeditions: Rome is a remarkable game.  As a Romanophile, I was skeptical about it, with so many games (even the most illustrious Rome: Total War series) getting things outright wrong about ancient Rome.  This game does, too, but. . . it's not so much that I don't enjoy it.  This game takes some artistic and historical liberties to incorporate your character into a somewhat (you know, "based on a true story. . . or in this case,  true stories") historical arch.  You fit in and run around conquering via legion(which is not the crux of the game, so it's no surprise that it's not that fun) and fighting tactical missions with small groups of party members (your "Praetorians").  The former adds complexity to the game with interweaving upgrades to your legion outpost, which leads to upgrades for you and your Praetorians, but the latter is the meat and potatahs of the game.  And man, is it fun.  Upgrading your comrades' equipment, playing out their story through the plot of the game, interacting with them, and finding fun combinations between them and their own abilities and other Praetorians' abilities is extremely fun.  Leveling them up opens up whole new combinations and strategies, and it's just really, really friggen fun.  Figuring out how to most effectively use your abilities is extremely enjoyable and challenging.  I'm probably about halfway through the game (sixty four hours!), and still get excited every time I sit down to play the game.  I love it, and it ranks up there in my top ten.  But again, this is my nerdy hobby.  I would recommend this to anyone who likes some of their other titles, such as Desperados III.  The RPG element is also very fun, and you would think the relatively small skill trees and historical limitations on the RPG side of things would get stale, but they just. . . don't.  You can tell that they put a lot of work and passion into this game, and honestly, it shows, because it's a stellar adventure.  Pros:  See above.  Cons:  Steep learning curve.  I always play on "hard" when I start a new game, and it was rough, but figuring it out is half the fun.  Don't get discouraged.  Some of the "RPG" elements that might appeal to hardcore/grognard fantasy RPG players are lacking or aren't there, but I feel it's a necessary sacrifice to get a more historically accurate story, as well as a tactical system that isn't broken or easy to game.  There are "drops" you can get from watching twitch streamers play, but there are always zero streamers playing with drops enabled, which blows.

_childDocuments_.review: Brilliant gameplay, story and characters. The developers have truly learned a lot from their mistakes in the previous Expeditions games, and this time, they created a masterpice. Finished in under a week, I was completely sucked in by the fascinating storytelling, unique atmosphere and stories, varied gameplay. Worth full price. No bugs, completely polished and full of content.Always hard, often unfair, yet never boring nor inconsequential, Expeditions: Rome deserves high praise, as this levels of excellence in a turn-based tactical game is very hard to come by. I would have to give 10/10, if I had to, as only very few games made me so involved in what is happening and made me care about the characters and the outcomes of my actions. And they all do matter. There are minor mistakes or stuff I don't prefer in the game, sure, but they all pale in comparison to the sheer greatness of the story and gameplay.Congratulations to the devs - this is a huge success, and they made at least one fan real happy with this entry.

_childDocuments_.review: A very good RPG/tactical turn based combat game. I love the fact that it was mostly kept realistic and with great attention to historical detail - without magic and fantasy elements. Made me truly immersed in the world of Ancient Rome - down to the more-correct-than-usual Latin pronunciations (as far as we know). I do think it slightly begins to outstay its welcome during the last fifth of the game (especially because some segments simply require characters to walk across a beautifully rendered map for no reason) and the legion battles provided cool historical flavour but were neither challenging nor truly compelling. But aside from that, graphics, voice acting, story and meaningful choices combined with an excellent and addictive combat system to make for an enjoyable and memorable experience.
_childDocuments_.name: Expeditions: Rome

_childDocuments_.review: Game starts very slow. - Dialogue is basic video game writing just to move the plot. - Inventory management is a chore because of infinite space and numerous, mostly inconsequential, weapon and armor options.- Combat revolves around quick damage bursts so enemies don't one-shot your party (I played on Insane difficulty).- Legion mini game is simply redundant, and is there as a huge time sink.However, at the end of Act 1 the game simply does a 180 turn for the better. - Writing becomes much better, consequence of many interesting characters being introduced and all contributing to the plot, world building and party development.- Level 2 weapon abilities are way more fun and you can devise your combat strategy based on smart use of powers.- Art style is beatiful in Act 2.- Legion mini game is still terrible, but at least it's quickly over if you know what you are doing.All in all, Expeditions Conquistador is in my top 10 games of all time, it's that good. Viking was weak in every aspect. Rome is in in the middle and then from Act 2 onwards it becomes a very good game and worthy successor to Conquistador.
_childDocuments_.name: Expeditions: Rome

_childDocuments_.review: Each release in the Expeditions series is fantastic and Expeditions: Rome is no exception.What is it? A historical-ish turn-based RPG. No magic spells (using bandages instead of spells or healing potions), characters from history (although ages and such are not quite in line with real history), and a story that can parallel the rise of Julius Caesar (depending on your choices).The combat is tactical and full of meaningful choices. One feature this game has that I wish more did is setup at the start of battle. Generally, you are given a zone and you can position your characters freely within the zone. Some other games seem to always put your main character up front in battle, which can discourage people from playing "squishy" characters. Not so with this game! Build yourself as an archer if you wish and you will be able to position yourself behind the characters with shields!Outside the turn-based combat, you have a legion that you can command around to conquer various areas. The legion battle system works. At the time of this writing (February 15th, 2022), there are mentions of this system being updated, so it may get better in the future. Right now, it is perfectly functional, although it is not as exciting as the combat between characters. But it works and is a different mechanic to play with.I don't want to spoil the story and characters, but it feels like a game set in the waning days of the Roman Republic. The characters don't act like snarky 21st century hipsters; they seem like real people who lived in that world. Thus, you will have to make choices that may not line up with your modern sensibilities (such as the fact that I found no option to free all of your slaves). I'm not complaining; this is a good thing. The developers took the time period seriously!TL;DRIt's good.
_childDocuments_.name: Expeditions: Rome

_childDocuments_.review: I have to recommend this game based on the sheer unique and exciting game style it presents.  It offers both a meta and micro style of play combined with well written dialogue and historically accurate descriptions.  The game was well done and it shows.The caveat I have is the game isn't very challenging (on default difficulty) and it's quite long, making certain progression feel trivial and unexciting.  It feels like playing an XCOM game on 'Story Mode' or more like a tutorial with a story.

_childDocuments_.review: What this is not: An accurate portrayal of historical events and personas from the Late Roman Republic.What this is: A well crafted story game with likable characters based off of ancient historical events that, while not necessarily historically authentic, is enjoyable, heart wrenching/warming, and impressive in its own right. If you have even a fleeting interest in Roman history, specifically in the Late Republic, this is a must buy. If you enjoy turn based RPGs with a large open world to explore, give it a shot. If you love choice driven games where your decisions not only matter, but have a real effect on the characters and the world around you this is a must buy as well. So pronounce your V's like W's. Remember all C's are pronounced like K's. And above all, Roma Invicta!!!

_childDocuments_.review: Tough review as I don't think this is as tight as Expeditions: Vikings, but if it was just the same as that game I'd be disappointed.  It's bigger,  more expansive.  The entire legion commanding thing is too much and not quite enough.  There's just not enough gameplay to it and it occupies too much time.  And the whole problem would be solved if vendors had more cash.  At the end of act 1 I was running around Rome with 500 denarii and missed a lot of content because I figured there'd be a place to sell my hundreds of slaves. No time crunches anywhere is a saving grace and really, it sort of exposes the tedium to the above mechanic.  You can just put the game on five speed and wait for a week to pass for vendors to refresh.  The new recruit pool isn't big enough and after a while the only people left have absolute trash specs with no way to respec but it's a 35h wait to refresh that small pool.So really I only have two issues that both come down to, they're a bit tedious and could be polished up a bit.  Otherwise, this is a turn based RPG set in historical Rome using a hex tile map.  If that is your thing, you are just trying to be convinced to buy it I guess?  Well, yes, do that.Really the best thing about these games is the writing.  Hilarious and true.  The game teaches you a little Latin and about Roman culture during loading screens.  Saying much more would spoil the plot but it's great.  I am just in Act 2 as well; this game is not small or short at all.  9/10 I think the larger map battles should have more gameplay than pick the card that minimizes the largest negative number

_childDocuments_.review: Let me preface my recommendation that this is only because it's a 5/10. There is a great story here with lots of choices alongside interesting characters, sadly and severely hampered by poor game  developer decisions.* Poorly balanced skills. You *have* to plan your builds ahead or you can brick your characters. With the hireable Praetorians, this can be circumvented, but Heaven help you if you muck up your character build or those of your Companions. This is because of the absolutely baffling decision of:* No option to respec/retrain. Given that there are really bad skills this can set you back. You and your companions are used in most of the pivotal fights and if you have made some mistakes with your build you are going to have a bad time. I knew ahead of time so planned my builds, but for someone who hasn't done their research this could really cause issues,* Excessive power of environmental effects, Apparently Legions should have been armed entirely of torches , Greek Fire, and caltrops. Gladius? Waste of time. Fire is especially egregious as merely throwing a torch at someone is enough to set them aflame. There are ways around this with other Tactical items and skills but it's even more tedious and annoying than in Divinity: Original Sin 2 since almost every enemy seems to have these and they outnumber your skill and tactical item uses,* Mass combat. Wow, what a missed opportunity here. I wasn't expecting Rome: Total War 2 but just a card-based system? Even Sid Meiers Pirates! had a better mass combat system and that was 20 years ago. Just watch your unit icons shuffle meaninglessly back and forth over a terrain board. This is a turn-based combat game and the wide variety or Roman Legion units could have been used in a similar fashion here on the strategic battle map,Anyway, if you can persevere though the tedious tactical combat system, there is a great story here with quite a few different outcomes to experience. Too bad the game dev team wasn't the equal of the writing team. If they had been, this could have been a 10/10 for me.

_childDocuments_.review: I first came across Expeditions: Rome through Steam's discovery queue. Though I am a fan of Roman history who enjoys media like Sierra Entertainment city-builder strategy game, Caesar III and Historis Civilis YouTube channel, I wasn't particularly captivated with it like I am now as the current trailer only shows cutscenes. Months later, I ended up downloading a "demo" of Expeditions: Rome because I wanted to leave my Dad a bundle of games to try out. I booted the game to test it out expecting Diablo 2 but with a Roman setting and somewhat weak plot. I completed the game in about 100 hours chuffed to bits with both the journey of it all and I was especially amazed with how it all ties up at the end. It left me thinking about the implications of my choices in the game and I'll leave it at that.Expeditions: Rome trailer does not do the game justice in how graphically impressive and mechanically sound the combat is. Combat is polished in the sense that you'll physically see a slash attack decapitate a target from a semi-precise point of contact all the while Caeso is making some quip about enemies not being able to get past his shield. Even if you're not immersed in the role the game setting puts you in, I would implore people not super familiar with turn-based CRPGs like me to try the demo.Much of the main and supporting characters are written very well. If you like dialogue with a lot of witticisms, you'll enjoy it a lot. It's the type of game where you wish you took the time to pause and screenshot one of the many witty character lines. The characters have interesting arcs to them and I found myself relating to at least one of them. The main and supporting characters are primarily voiced, and voiced extremely well if I may add. I swear, Syneros sounds like he is voice acted by Christopher Lloyd, the old man from Back to the Future, but ah it's a different guy.On the matter of immersion, playing through the game felt like I was playing a accurate reenactment of how ancient Europe was at the time instead of doing high-speed action stuff that happens to have X historical setting. You're put in situations where you have to interact and listen to what servi, peasants or citizens have to say about their world which exposes you to ideas like slavery courier services being pretty cheap, how legal disputes between 2 patricians are solved and of course, how foreign people feel about the occupation of Romans in their homes. You have situations where even if you're going the pure angel route, you'll think to yourself: Am I the bad guy?There's a lot I can gush about the game but I risk spoiling details best left discovered. Interesting systems like having a 2nd squad of prateorians and dealing with the army conquest system (it's not the best but I wouldn't call it ♥♥♥♥ and ball torture) are better covered by the other reviews here. Expeditions: Rome is a game leaving me wanting more and for all the right reasons! It's a "If a sequel came out, it would be a insta-buy for me" type of good game.I'd give this game Cleotitties/10

_childDocuments_.review: When I bought this game, it was only because I was interested in the idea of a roman rpg, so I pre-ordered it a week or so before launch. It has quickly become one of my favorite games of all time. When I began I assumed that it was going to be what I had imagined, but it was so much more than that. At first I was absolutely sure that it was going to be a basic military game but I soon came to love the unique companions and characters in this world. After the first chapter I simply could not stop playing it! The combat was far more fun and quick than I had thought, I would test new strategies with new abilities in every fight. Mission after mission, campaign after campaign, all made me more in love with it. Although I sing high praise to the combat I actually still believe it could have had far more freedom in player choice. The game's options offered lots of freedom and roleplaying and the ethos you pick at the beginning of the game offer lots of replay value but I always felt that the beginning of each act was completely cut off from the other acts. Your choices aren't basic good or bad decisions and often offer great moral dilemmas, not to mention that many options have great consequences during your campaign but I still felt like it didn't matter how I won a war in any of the campaigns since it would hardly even be mentioned at later points. In my game I became the governor of Egypt and felt like everyone in the game world was impressed by my character's actions, but by the next war in the game the only thing close to a reference of my victory was being called the conqueror of Africa by my superiors-at the start of the campaign and never a point after that. Another thing that I felt was left desired was the historical figures. Pompey, Antony, Casca, Brutus, Decimus, Crassus and many other esteemed politicians and generals around the time period the game takes place in either had only rare mentions and appearances or had no existence in the game at all. Another thing is that I wish Rome had more civilian encounters. You only go to Rome a handful of times and the only thing you can do in Rome is do a few side quests and buy an artifact (later on a unique dagger) and basically nothing else. I would have loved to go around building personal alliances in my own career, and maybe buying highly expensive treasures with the massive amounts of loot from my campaigns but it never really worked that way. Another thing is that by the third act in Gaul the quests and world get fairly dim. Quests in Egypt and Asia Minor are wonderful to play and unique with many places to find treasures and markets to buy things from while Gaul has a single village and a "stop the soldier from harassing the farmer" quest. I think that act 2 is by far the height of the game and I seriously enjoy the various options you have in the campaign. I would also like to mention the many unique weapons and armor in the game. Be it the helmet of Scipio Africanus or Tutankhamun's lost dagger you can find tons of unique gear in the game world. This review is already long enough but I'll wrap it all together in a simple way. It is one of the best game's I've had played in a while. I was completely immersed and obsessed with all the random encounters you can experience and the numerous paths you can take. My only complaints are that it would have been potentially more fun and perhaps cool if the game world was fleshed out beyond just 4(5 technically) locations and if there were more historical figures you could engage with. Seriously, if you love strategy games and especially RPG strategy games you need to buy this game.  Sorry if my review seems long or chaotic in any way but make no mistake, my opinion is high of this game.

_childDocuments_.review: I like this game a lot, it improves on the formula set in Expeditions: Viking. I like the Roman era a lot and the aesthetics of the game are much appreciated. +Combat is nice and tactical, forcing you to sometimes take your time in a fight. Story is alright I suppose, with varying outcomes (which is always nice). I reallyyyy like the voice-acting in this game (especially that of Syneros). -The legion management is not fleshed out as much as I would like, it feels like an annoying chore most of the time. Fighting with the legion is outright dull and very repetitive. (+)I found it cool that you could recruit new soldiers to your party, enabling them to both serve the party on the map as well as the legion itself - kind of neat! All in all, a solid game with tactical elements and a somewhat engaging story (I liked the one in Viking better) with a few less developed features. _childDocuments_.review: It has been years since I could say with confidence that I genuinely love a game. But it's absolutely true for this one. It's a very interesting blend of tactical CRPG, resource management sim and visual novel. The story is very engaging, the characters are all well written and superbly voice acted (even correctly using the Classical Latin pronunciation of Names and words!), and the setting is presented with much attention to detail. Some liberties had to be taken, of course, so if you are one to nitpick, you will probably get frustrated. But if you can overlook certain things and are interested, even casually, in the classical period in general and Rome in particular, then you will probably love this game too. There are so many story paths to take and multiple character builds to try out that I will probably replay it for years to come.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm sad to give this game a negative review but that's... how i felt after putting the game down, the game was fun at first and the combats were cool, legion mechanics felt like they were very well done at first glance but they just feel like a waste of time after the second fight, you're literally just clicking on what does less damage to you and more to them, no tactics involved at all.Let me give more details on that.The combat is very repetitive and unbalanced at times,  enter an area, instantly in combat, clear the whole thing, loot the corpses and leave never to come back in that area ever. Looting enemies seems to either be bugged or just straight up not done well, clicking on corpses sometimes doesn't work and i watch my soldiers standing on their bodies like psychopaths instead. It feels like a waste of time to loot, just give me a keybind to loot everything or just give me everything directly after the fight is over.Combat seems to punish slow players like me, if you try to be on the defensive, enemies will outnumber you very fast, throw torches and pilums at your face, and trust me, they know how throw.My biggest complaint about this game is the companions, i really enjoyed having my small group of soldiers tearing enemies apart... until they introduced the random companions that you WILL have to use for some missions, no way around it, and even when you can use your main group, you'll still have to deal with those random companions, gear them, make sure they can actually do damage to enemies. It's just not fun, and it seems to be an issue for a bunch of people.Now the legion stuff, how to explain, this is probably one of the most useless mechanic in a video game i've seen so far, capturing areas on the map is literally just clicking, sending the legion to that area, waiting on the world map for 4 ingame hours (note that there are no timed events, at least not until the point i stopped playing) and voila, you have an area for yourself just staring at the open map.Now legion combat, sounds cool right? nope! the fight consist of 4 phases, during each phase you have 3 options, you have to take the one that deals the less damage to your legion troops, morale, xp, ect.. but guess what? just select the one with less red text and you're good to go! that's it, you're the best legate that ever existed.The water/nourishment/morale mechanics didn't do anything at all, especially nourishment, i've never seen the bar going down, so i have no idea what it actually did so you can just ignore those stats completely, it adds nothing to the game.The game ran just fine, no real bugs or crashes on my side, but i did see some negative reviews talking about crashes so check them out if you're also struggling with those.
_childDocuments_.name: Expeditions: Rome

_childDocuments_.review: This is what the Expeditions games have building towards for years and it is something really lovely to see. I hope this is not the Swan Song for Expeditions. But at the same time this is a high note and really the best version of Expeditions since it began. Really worth playing if you like CRPGs and Rome. I can't think of anything else like it.
_childDocuments_.name: Expeditions: Rome

_childDocuments_.review: While i loved Expeditions: Vikings, one of my favorite CRPG in terms of role playing, i sadly can't say the same for Expeditions: Rome. The combats feel slow and not intuitive, and the world map is honestly tiresome. Everything about the management of our army is boring at best. The story is ok but not really engaging and the characters lack depth.The game is beautiful though and i wouldn't say it's a terrible game, it just never clicks with me.
_childDocuments_.name: Expeditions: Rome

_childDocuments_.review: This is a very, VERY solid and story-heavy Tactical Turn-Based Strategy RPG. Outside of a few minor bugs (I have not had anything gamebreaking, nor even a CTD as of this review), this is one of the more polished big studio releases I have played in a long time. Every choice in dialogue has its consequences and the actual battles are (often, not always) difficult but fun. Figuring out ways to maximize status effects and stacking buffs/debuffs to take down enemies early on is very useful, for multi-stage battles will put you at a major disadvantage if the early engagements are long slogs where you lose a lot of HP and consumables.The audio design is pretty superb, and music is compelling while never being grating or annoying. Voice acting is pretty great in most cases, visuals and graphics are good for this genre and the setpieces can be really gorgeous. The only thing that aggravated me is the lack of tooltips, so sometimes you have to figure things out for yourself (which apparently the devs have said those will be added in) and inventory management can be a little tedious at times. I can live with that.Love this game so far, and I have only reached the end of ACT I at 15.3hrs gametime, so I forsee this game to certainly provide more than adequate bang for your bucks.
_childDocuments_.name: Expeditions: Rome

_childDocuments_.review: Best one in the series and a great game in general. Love it.This game was a tight experience from beginning to end. The combat is great, but the story actually ended up really getting me into the game. By the end, I had to keep playing to see where all my decisions were going to lead. The number of possibilities is impressive too. After finishing the game and seeing how things went for me, I see just how much variation there could be. Awesome Game. Solid from beginning to end.
_childDocuments_.name: Expeditions: Rome

_childDocuments_.review: One of the biggest surprises of the time. The game has a Roman theme that takes you from Greece, to Egypt and Gaul. It's an alternative timeline where your character kinda takes the place of Julius Caesar in a what if scenario. The story is engaging from the start and the combat is excellentPros:-Combat-Companions-Difficulty-Story-Choices that affect the story-Character buildsCons:-Legion combatHighly recommended game
_childDocuments_.name: Expeditions: Rome

_childDocuments_.review: Solid game. Great combat, the story is also pretty good, and the mechanics for improving/conquering/building things up is very nice. Only downside for me is the itemization; too much generic/rubbish items that just clog the inventory. Also too many crafting options, for objects you'll likely never bother to make. Wish there was a better way to specialize your crafting, so you didn't have to rely on picking up skill books that taught you a bunch of new items at once.Highly recommend it if you're a fan of games like XCOM.
_childDocuments_.name: Expeditions: Rome

_childDocuments_.review: Took me a second attempt to get into but I loved this as a history nerd. You basically replace Caesar’s place in history as you climb the Roman political ladder from an exiled noble trying to hide from enemies in the Mithridatic Wars to leading legions in Asia, Africa and Gaul and possibly crossing the Rubicon itself. The companions and settings are fun and diverse and its interesting to see what changed in the game compared to history both with or without your involvement. Combat is quite fun coming from a AA space with every act having an extremely well done battle or siege as a climax.There are some filler elements such as army battles and region pacification missions that force you to not take your full story NPC squad that stretch the game a bit, but the pretorian squad based combat is a great Classical Era version of Xcom. Soundtrack is amazing as well for what it needs to be, I find myself sometimes putting on the siege tracks when at the gym.While the writing on a whole is good the large exception is anything having to do with your Roman Rival antagonist directly. Rather than take any of the real figures of the time the game creates an OC that is constantly brilliant and untouchable until the last battle of the game. You have no choice but to walk into ambushes set by him or his allies and nothing you do can counter him. While this is likely there so that the story can happen with limited world states that need to be developed for, I feel like there would have been better ways to plan around that. On the other hand, playing as a woman character is actually taken into account and I feel extremely well done as a plot point rather than hand waving like many similar games do for more or less the same experience. Game ends with great slides showing the new state of the world that feels as solid as classic examples including fallout or Baldurs Gate. A bit better than the sum of its parts, I hope Logic Artists gets more budget to polish their future titles more as I love diving into the small genre of historical CRPGs, I wholeheartedly recommend this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Expeditions: Rome

_childDocuments_.review: At first glance, it may seem to you that this game doesn't offer anything new in regards of tactical gameplay since it's very limited in weapon & character class variety, however after a while you see that this simply is not true.each weapon comes with different skill sets just like ultima online did back in the day. and being able to swap 2 sets of weapons in game creates a nice tactical depth. the game is so well balanced that each encounter requires different tactical approach. I recommend playing it in hard difficulty.Much better than the previous expeditions games. This game is not like divinity or baldurs gate 3, it's like x-com 2 with spears.Post-Campaign Edit: What an amazing story. This game exceeded my expectations by a mile. A must have for tactical RPG lovers
_childDocuments_.name: Expeditions: Rome

_childDocuments_.review: It does a good job of immersion, despite just ignoring historical accuracy. I don't consider this a detriment since it plays extremely well to its strengths. The characters are alright, the story is alright, but the environments and the turn based game-play are excellent. I didn't run into any crashes or bugs. Lets see, what else is there to say?The strategic legion battles are a bit boring, and get repetitive, but for the most part they are quick. The tactical unit battles play like a mixture of X-Com and Divinity and besides the immersion of the world I feel like this is where it shines. It will take a little learning but when you managed to pull a plan off and wipe a field with a combination of group attacks, buffs, and debuffs is really satisfying.
_childDocuments_.name: Expeditions: Rome

_childDocuments_.review: Loved 'Expeditions: Vikings', but this one tries to be a bit too much of everything. The map conquest battles are really, really boring and have next to no player agency: even on hard mode it doesn't really seem to matter what choices you make during the battle, you don't really lose any. And the larger tactical battles with your characters involved sometimes hinge on dice throws for a catapult to hit, not on your tactical ability. Story felt very 'railroady', with the only fun part some moral dialogue choices. But without the gameplay to back it up, this results in a clunky interactive novel.TLDR: Do choices REALLY matter in this game? Not to the gameplay it seems.
_childDocuments_.name: Expeditions: Rome

_childDocuments_.review: So, after 66 hours of play, the world is at my feet, the legions adore me, the Senate is afraid, and the people of Rome greet me with flowers. Was this trip exciting? Oh yeah! It also has some strange moments, so the conversation will turn out to be long, get ready. Expecting just a good successor to X-COM, on release I got a multi-layered tactical turn-based rpg with a great storyline, the real impact of your actions on the future of this game world, solving many plot obstacles is non-linear  and a lot of interesting game elements that begin to unfold as your skill increases. The creators bring a wide variety of things to the mosaic of their game, almost all of which work perfectly. Actually, big questions arise only in the global strategic part of the game, and then only in the third act, where there was a little lack of sense of proportion (and judging by the list of fixes in a future patch, this will be polished)Setting. Ancient Rome, man… Ancient Rome. How much we miss more RPG games on this inexhaustible theme of adventure. Legionnaires rattling their shiny armor, senators having sharp conversations with each other among the majestic white walls, the smell of wanderings and conquests, conspiracies and wine. The plot in the game is simply excellent, and you feel like not just a participant in it, but its architect. The player then throws in military campaigns, then returns to Rome, and it is still unknown where the risk of his life is more serious. The secondary characters are also well developed, with their own interesting stories, often stretching across the entire game, while also fitting in well with the larger epic story unfolding in front of you. As the game progresses, you will inevitably encounter a large number of major historical figures, often reshaping history as you wish. The choice of the player here really affects everything; even minor things can backfire in the finale, drastically changing the fate of the characters. The final act of the game is also variable, I managed to see two completely different huge final parts that last for many hours, which are perceived and played with another feelings, not at all looking like reskins of each other. That is, even after a huge amount of playing time, the creators in the final cared about an unbanal plot, about finding something new and interesting for the player. It deserves respect.The turn-based combat here is very intense and develops along the way. The game was completed on the penultimate difficulty mode with "death in battle" turned on, and if at first there were no difficulties, then the further, the tougher everything became, reaching its climax in Act 3. Interesting maps with the possibility of non-trivial vertical movement, cunning and very vile enemies, the impossibility of characters escaping with impunity from a direct combat encounter, a variety of skills and tactical items, everything here is pleasing to the eye. Rare items of equipment and weapons in this game are really RARE, like in the legendary Witcher 3; when you find them, the path to which is usually very difficult and not obvious, you experience real joy, because this is a reward not for a stupid grind, but for overcoming difficulties, for your ingenuity. The global strategic part of the game is quite satisfying, developing your fort and legion quickly becomes an interesting activity, and fighting with opponents does not bother you. The only exception here is Act 3, where there is too much of everything. There are too many enemy forts, too many negative random events, when you literally cannot take a step so that you are not poisoned - killed by wild boars - fell off the bridge with critical injuries - fell on Nemesis, etc. This is very annoying and frustrating, especially considering that the Gallic act has quite a strong plot, and possibly the most hardcore turn-based combat encounters in the entire game. It's good that after that comes the most powerful final act, in which the global strategy retired, and only tactics come into play.The expedition to Rome was a success. The epic decision of the fate of the world organically intertwined with small stories, respect for the established traditions of the genre was soldered with interesting ideas and innovations. This great game gives you the opportunity to make great achievements, give more Ancient Rome to all of us!
_childDocuments_.name: Expeditions: Rome

_childDocuments_.review: Expeditions Rome: The Fate Of Rome, And The World, Depends On YouThe Short:  Thumbs Up.   “Are you not entertained?”   “Yes, I Am!”Story: A+RGP Element:  A+Characters: AGameplay:  AHistorical Depth and Detail:  A+World-Building: AGame Freedom And Choices:  AComplexity:  As complex as you wish to make it. Rewards investment, but doesn’t punish simplicity.Graphics: B- or C+ --not the strength of the game, but rather the old reliables.Voice Acting: A+Game/Story Resolution:  A++Replay Potential:  ImmenseThe Long: Once Upon A Time In Rome . . . .Expeditions: Rome is the third game in an evolving series of Expedition games by the Danish developer Logic Artists, the first of which was Expedition: Conquistadore (2013) and the second Expedition: Viking (2017). Both games were good games, with a great deal of attention put into doing justice to history and integrating history into an engaging story of What If? Building off the strengths of those games, and correcting some of the weaknesses, Expeditions: Rome is a truly epic adventure set across the breadth of the Roman Republic in the period of the life of Julius Caesar (BC100-44).The game begins, in fact, with your character crossing paths with a young Julius Caesar. But for reasons I won't spoil, history places you in the general position and upon the general path that, in our world, he walked. As your story unfolds, you are unwittingly drawn into events and machinations far larger than yourself, and set upon the path of Legate -- the commander of a Roman legion. In this capacity you will participate in three great military campaigns -- Asia Minor, North Africa and Gallia (Gaul), with intervals spent navigating dangerous intrigues in Rome. As Legate you will be responsible for maintaining, equipping, leading, organizing and directing your legion(s) both in garrison and in battle, developing its troops, equipment, training, morale and capabilities. All of this could easily be a game within itself.But, at the same time you and a circle of close companions -- each very well developed characters -- along with a wider group of Praetorians (essentially your chosen bodyguard) will explore vast territories, interact with historical figures, accumulate experience and skill and engage in numerous political intrigues along the way of both conquering these regions for Rome, and playing a game of high-stakes cat and mouse with a quite capable nemesis who has their own ambitions set on rising to rule Rome. This aspect of the game could stand as a game in and of itself, and as such, is better than many historical or fantasy RPG's.A third element of the game is the acquiring of materials, equipment and wealth as you go, the most important of which are the four basics upon which you and your legion depend -- food, medicine, slaves and gold. Unlike many historical games which shy away from slavery, Expeditions Rome, like Rome itself, is integrally connected to and dependent upon the servii (servants; slaves) both as a form of wealth and the underlying social/labor class. How you treat the servii in your own service and which you encounter will play a major role in the story and the game itself, and relationships between you and individual servi are complex and layered, as they were in Roman life. Aside from these four essentials, you will also encounter and acquire a great variety of materials, goods, artifacts, trophies and equipment of all kinds. You can both equip captured armor and weapons and talismans, and eventually have your legion smith and artificers improve and craft more. The range of armour and equipment spans the breadth of the Roman world and its adversaries, and is very nicely rendered. You can dress and equip yourself in the manner of Greek city states, Berber tribesmen, Egyptian soldiers, Germanic tribes, and mercenaries and spies and rangers and cut-throats of all kinds. All of this corresponds to the proper equipment types based on the historic roles and functions of different ranks and classes of soldiers in the militaries and on the battlefields of the time. The research into the aesthetics, doctrines, tactics and dynamics of the battlefield, be it at the scale of armies or the scale of individuals and small units, is painstakingly done and highly representative of the realities of the time while also allowing flexibility for story and a high degree of variability in how you choose to employ and use these various specialists together to achieve your goals. The possibilities are nearly endless.All of this is accomplished -- and this is something exceedingly difficult for a game of such detail to achieve -- while also preserving a certain elegance and simplicity to the process which only overwhelms to the degree and depth you wish to pursue. You can keep it easy and minimal, or dive right into all the possibilities to wring every last ounce out of the opportunities, without compromising the basic story or game progression itself.At the heart of the game, the story itself is compelling, complex and layered without being byzantine and baffling, and one which should invest you progressively in both the greater drama unfolding in the history of Rome, as well as the lives and relationships of your companions. Aside from the writing, the voice acting is first class, something never a given for any RPG. The graphics are good and sometimes quite beautiful, but they are not cutting-edge, and the isomorphic top-down style of presentation is an old and proven standard of the genre. So, if flashy graphics and first-person perspectives and the ability to choose multiple camera angles is your thing, Expeditions: Rome is not likely to impress you all that much. The game, the world, the history, the characters and the story are the meat of this game.Lastly, and where I especially find that Expeditions: Rome excels, is in resolving the game. So many games have you invest many hours to achieve a goal or victory, and resolve it all abruptly with a "You win, Yay!" or a simple selection of cutscenes. After everything you've done and invested, it is a monumental let -down. This is definitely not the case with Expeditions: Rome. Expeditions: Rome ends with a full narrative of the consequences of your actions and relations to history across the breadth of the empire and in the lives of the major characters; it follows the lives of you and your companions beyond the scope of the game itself, within the world you have made. Unlike one or a mere handful of endings, this story-telling depth exists in the form of seven different major endings, and within that, more then 100 individual and historic outcomes on a smaller scale. In short, it is unlikely that anyone but the most obsessed and hardcore gamer will ever play out all the permutations. This level of resolution is more than just rewarding; it is worthy of the scope and scale of a game that puts you at the center of a tumultuous and pivotal period in the history of one of the greatest empires and civilizations in history.

_childDocuments_.review: Expeditions: Rome is incredible, one of the few games I'd have scrubbed from my memory so I can experience it all over again, an excellent blend of baulders gate and xcom, whilst maybe not being as deep as baulders gate it certainly puts itself at the top of the trpg list. This game has been on my wishlist for a while and now that I finally got round to it I'm blown away and then some by how fantastic this was, it's more crpg than I was expecting but the star of the show is it's deep tactical combat, it's both mechanically sound and visually satisfying, when my first attack of the game cut an enemies leg off I knew I was going to be in for something special. Whilst I do think this game has incredible combat with a variety of options at your disposal some classes are a little more broken than others but this isn't a massive deal breaker. The main bulk of the game sees you command your legion across several campaigns from roman history, you fight for control as you need to supply not only yourself but your legions that you command. You are in a constant tug of war as you fight for dominance and rally troops to your cause, all whilst par taking in fantastic tactical turn based combat from small skirmishes all the way up to multilayered sieges involving a mass amount of onscreen characters, never has a turn based game felt so alive and epic.This is all wrapped up in a fantastic alt-history retelling of romes most famous times, whilst maybe not as deep as a game like baulders gate or pathfinder I still felt that the many branching choices had a profound impact on my story all whilst leading to a fantastic conclusion. Whilst also not the strongest characters in a game I still came to adore my party and the budding romances that blossoms from the battlefield, all dialogue is voice and whilst the writing isn't the strongest it's certainly still entertaining.My only major complaint is how boring the legion battles are, the main combat is your traditional xcom style trpg combat but another aspect is legion battles. Legion battles aren't well implemented and I found myself mashing auto resolve to get them over as quick as possible. I couldn't even tell you how they work because I never bothered to invest much thought into it other than pressing auto resolve, just picture a bunch of pictures and icons on screen all moving around which is a poor emulation of a massive scale battle and you'll get the picture. All in all whilst is has a few shortcomings they are not enough to drag the experience down, this is a fantastic game and one I can't recommend enough. Ad victoriam.
_childDocuments_.name: Expeditions: Rome

_childDocuments_.review: On Normal it's pretty fun, there's some difficulties but nothing impossible. The game has a system to increase or decrease the relationship with everybody based on your answer, I thought it was a great dynamic. While so far - I'm at the end of Act 3 -, It feels like you have some event you can avoid and some you can't. Some of the choices have much massive impact, while some don't. The fun in this game is there you're never exactly sure when that is.The game starts in the Minor Asian part of the continent, you are looking to avenge your father who was a big shot in Rome. At first, the game presents itself as a place where you'll have choices of playing a politic character, an all out warrior, a calculated warrior. What's great is you can go full corruption mode, or super stoic and just.  I feel a balance of pretty much everything goes far. It does have some weight to it if you're going on a extreme as you may highly displease your comrades I feel the game has some balance issues, but if you're not a pro-min-maxer looking to rig the game, I feel there's some class that's particularly OP while some that ... well just doesn't make it. While you discover which ones are good vs the bad ones, you'll have at least a bunch of your squad that will suck but can be worked back in shape by the end of Act 2.I feel like this game is a solid 7/10, soft 8/10The negative is that it gets pretty grindy and I feel playing the second time playing doesn't have a great excitement vs Divinity which has a similar style. Bought it on sales- wouldn't pay the full price.
_childDocuments_.name: Expeditions: Rome

_childDocuments_.review: In short:+ Great story with many choises and consequences, will replay it again to see the diffrent outcomes.+ Companions who you grow to like and care about.+ Amazing voice acting, didn't run into a single bad VO perfomance in my whole playtrough.+ Graphic wise it looks impressive for a game of this type, also didn't have any perfomance issues.+ Had zero bugs or issues in my 60+ hours playtrough.+ Very fun combat system, but some (there were not a lot of them but still) of the encounters bordered on unfair (when you get surrounded on all sides at start of battle and enemy has the first turn there isn't anything you can do besides pray to RNG).+ The big siege battles were probably the highlight of the game for me - even though in some massive battles the AI turns took way too long.As for the cons:- The biggest one for me would be the legion battle system, didn't find it fun at all, got repetitive way too fast. Also it was too easy, there was almost no risk of losing.- Uninspiring/generic soundtrack... and that would be it for the problems i had with this game.All in all, one of the most fun i had in a c'RPG in the last decade or so.
_childDocuments_.name: Expeditions: Rome

_childDocuments_.review: Throughout my entire playthrough I was so excited just to see where the heck this story was going, the conflicts escalated, a new game mechanic was added, and I was constantly comparing the real life events of Roman history with my actions as the NEW important factor in history.I ask anyone who's interested in this game to play as a woman as your first playthrough. Im floored at how actually relevant  outside of roleplay purposes both in universe and the decisions you can make, you're treated differently, some with respect and others with condescension or dismissive at your skills. You're creating history being the first woman to become a Legate to the point they have to create a new term that fits your new post. I've played every "Expeditions" game and enjoyed them but felt there was something lacking somewhere in them all but they cracked the code on this one. The voice acting was excellent, and gameplay was addicting I love how theres this Tyranny vibe where your early decisions can get weaponized against you later on in the game and how the politics of Rome becomes just as important as your wars in other lands.I can't praise this game enough without spoilers, this is easily my favorite CRPG in almost a decade and I implore anyone even if their not interested in the setting to buy this you won't be disappointed.

_childDocuments_.review: Solid tactics game with some really epic fights. Does a lot right in terms of putting you into the lead of a large conflict while also taking it down to personal story level. Game can be slow at times as conquest doesn't happen quickly. but patience is paid off later in the game as you get some upgrades and are rewarded with some really epic fights and decisions. Loved Expeditions: Vikings and now will recommend Rome!
_childDocuments_.name: Expeditions: Rome

_childDocuments_.review: I rarely write reviews for games I enjoy. I figure the money i hose at the developers is enough. But this game is good, really good. Sure, it's a bit of an alternate history fan wank, where ~certain personages~ never make it out of the history books. And yes, it's super-weird to see pre-Marian soldier types in the post-Marian era (maybe the Marian reforms never took place).Still, it's got a lot going for it. You'd have to be a history lover to sperg out over those ~kinda~ mistakes. The game handles a lot of what it does well. The combat is an invigorating back-and-forth that never feels like a curb stomp on either party's behalf. The story is, well, Roman history; what makes it stand out is how tactfully and intelligently something like sexism is handled. Make a female character, see what happens.Its biggest failing is that it can be a bit opaque at times, with tooltips that zip by and leave you wondering what you're supposed to do. You'll waste maybe ten minutes on things like that.Anyway, buy it, and ignore the pants-pissers whining about Logic Artists making NFT games -- THQ Nordic controls the IP now, so the game will get some love post-release.
_childDocuments_.name: Expeditions: Rome

_childDocuments_.review: A step down from Expeditions: Viking. Too much filler, with various non-interesting gameplay, like managing legions, world map interactions, etc, constant loading screens, and very little party based gameplay compared to their previous gameplay.The combat is also far less interesting and more like a puzzle game, with you constantly having to figure out how the developers intended it to be done.

_childDocuments_.review: In Expeditions: Rome, you take on the role of a young Legatus, a rising Roman commander who finds themselves at the heart of Roman political and military turmoil. Following the murder of your father, you’re sent to distant frontiers to prove your mettle in war and navigate a brutal political landscape. Your journey takes you across iconic regions, including the shores of Greece, the deserts of North Africa, and the lush forests of Gaul. The plot’s foundation is historical, but it explores alternate possibilities, allowing you to shape the future of Rome as you see fit.The story is structured across three major campaigns, each with its own unique challenges and story arcs. These campaigns are filled with political intrigue, alliances, betrayals, and complex moral choices that influence not only the fate of your legion but also the perception of Rome itself.The core of Expeditions: Rome is its tactical, turn-based combat system, which offers deep and satisfying strategy akin to titles like XCOM but rooted in historical settings. Players manage their Legatus and an elite squad through battles that balance skill, positioning, and use of cover. The combat here feels precise and rewarding, with an array of skills and equipment allowing players to customise each encounter based on the enemy and environment. Flanking maneuvers, skill-based attacks, and environmental hazards add complexity, keeping every battle dynamic and engaging.Key elements that enhance combat include:The turn-based system makes each encounter feel like a carefully orchestrated game of chess, especially as battles grow in complexity with the addition of higher-stakes missions, environmental traps, and difficult enemy units.Customisation is a significant feature, beginning with character creation. You can shape your Legatus’s appearance, gender, and backstory, adding a personal touch that enhances the connection with your character. You even get the option to select the rhetorical style between 3 perks: Ethos (power of authority), Logos (logical arguments and reasoning), Pathos (emotional manipulation. The progression system allows you to develop both the Legatus and your squad members, all of whom have unique personalities and skill sets. The companions each have backstories and loyalties influenced by your choices.Beyond squad-based combat, Expeditions: Rome introduces grand-strategy mechanics through legion management. As a Legatus, you are tasked with overseeing a full Roman legion, which involves:Every dialogue choice in Expeditions: Rome carries weight. The game allows you to shape your character’s personality and ethos, which has ripple effects on your relationships, your allies’ trust, and even the outcome of battles. Dialogue options are nuanced, offering diplomatic, honorable, and sometimes ruthless responses, each impacting the story and your reputation within Rome. These choices can alter not only the trajectory of the main plot but also how your companions and legion perceive you.The narrative settings and historically inspired characters, including familiar figures from Roman history, create a grounded yet imaginative world. From the coastlines of Greece to the forests of Gaul, the historical atmosphere is immersive and meticulously crafted. The game incorporates the politics of the Roman Senate, adding another layer of intrigue as players must navigate alliances, betrayals, and political rivalries.The visuals in Expeditions: Rome are detailed and fitting for its historical theme. Environments are lush and varied, with meticulous attention to the landscapes of Greece, Rome, and Gaul. The game shines in its character animations, especially during combat, where attacks feel impactful and realistic. While not groundbreaking, the graphical fidelity is more than adequate to pull players into the world, with visual flourishes like glistening Roman armor and vividly rendered battlefields. Occasional optimisation issues may occur, but they don’t detract significantly from the overall experience.Expeditions: Rome is a thoughtfully crafted blend of tactical RPG and grand strategy, offering depth, immersion, and historical intrigue. Its richly woven narrative, complex character dynamics, and impactful decision-making set it apart from typical tactical games. The attention to historical detail is commendable, creating a world that feels lived-in and authentic. While a few technical and pacing issues persist, they are minor setbacks in an otherwise ambitious and rewarding experience. For players who enjoy strategic combat, narrative depth, and immersive role-playing.Rating: 9/10
