_childDocuments_.review: I'm a big fan of the Expeditions series, having played ever since the first one came out (Expeditions: Conquistador). I like Expeditions: Rome. However, even though I like it, I still think it's the worst one in the series. First off, I think Expeditions: Rome reaches too far beyond what it's supposed to be about: expeditions/exploration. Expeditions: Rome is not about exploration, it's about conquest. The game is split into three acts, and in each act you  conquer a foreign territory (first Greece, then Egypt, then France). In addition to your small party of followers that you use to complete quests, you also control a legion of 4,800 soldiers that you use to conquer territory. Your party and your legion move independently and it almost feels like you're playing two different games at the same time -- one game where you're exploring the map with your party and meeting with local leaders to secure alliances and progress the plot, and the other game where you're moving your legion around to conquer land and paint the map Roman. This two-games-in-one system doesn't always make sense; for example you can ignore the main quest while conquering all of Egypt, and then after you've conquered all of Egypt, you meet with the pharaoh for the first time to start progressing the main quest, and he boasts about how his huge armies (that you already wiped out) are going to drive you out of your territorial foothold (that you already expanded to cover all of Egypt). I understand that the developers wanted the player to be able to complete the quests and the territorial conquest in whichever order they prefer, but the result is a total break in realism and immersion. I prefer the style of the previous two Expeditions games, where any allied forces you control are assumed to follow your party, and thus exploration and conquest happened hand-in-hand -- the developers did not improve the series by adding a separate army/conquest mechanic and changing the focus of the game from exploration to conquest. Secondly, the game difficulty needs to be balanced better. I played on normal difficulty, and I found the game to be uncomfortably difficult during the first third, well-balanced during the second third, and then way too easy during the final third. The frustration of the game being too easy during the final third is compounded by the many large battles you fight; you'll play battles where there's 20+ enemies and 10+ allies and it takes nearly five minutes just to watch the enemy and allied troops resolve their turn after you pass your turn. It's hard to stay engaged when you already know you're going to win the battle and every time you pass your turn you need to wait five minutes before you can play your next turn. Apparently I wasn't the only player who got bored: if you look at the achievements, 33% of players have the achievement for beating the second act, but only 17% of players have the achievement for beating the third act and finishing the game. In addition to the inconsistent difficulty of battles, I was also disappointed by a lack of challenge in the army/conquest mechanic; I never lost a territory, and my legion won every single battle except one (and even when I did lose that one battle, there were no consequences). In sum I think the army/conquest mechanic should be more challenging, and the battles during the final third of the game should be more challenging. Third, the game is buggy. Most of the bugs are not game-breaking (e.g. the legion battle audio keeps playing after legion battle ends, or you find items with missing names and icons) but there was one point where my game outright crashed, one point where I had to restart the game because I couldn't click anything, and one point where I had to load an earlier save because a side quest spawned a location in an inaccessible part of the map.Finally, there are quite a few mechanics in the game that seem pointless. For example the game has a morale system, and warns you that party members will leave if their morale falls low enough. Yet throughout the game my party members always had good morale. It was a waste of time to build and fully upgrade the bathhouse, which boosts morale, because no party members were ever disgruntled enough to use it. Similarly, a lot of the bells and whistles around the army/conquest system appear to be meaningless: you can win legion battles handily without building walls or a storehouse, and many of the stratagems that you can use during legion battles lack any context where they would be useful -- for example there's no reason to use a stratagem that allows injured legionaries to recover because injured legionaries will recover automatically after 24 hours or so and meanwhile the enemy will always wait at least one week between attacks. Overall I feel like the developers were too ambitious, putting too much on their plates, and the result is an oversupply of superfluous features.I know it sounds like I didn't like this game, but I did. I just think the previous Expeditions games were better. I enjoyed the 55 hours it took me to beat Expeditions: Rome, but if you're new to the series I recommend Expeditions: Conquistador or Expeditions: Viking -- they're better games, and cheaper too.

_childDocuments_.review: Plays a little fast and loose with the timeline, which is a shame, but ultimately a minor issue as far as I'm concerned. The overworld conquest portion is passable; it feels good expanding your territory and building infrastructure, but the battles get tiring after a while. It's just choose 1 of 3 random cards per phase, for 4 phases, and try to balance some numbers, rinse and repeat.The core gameplay is excellent, however. Combat feels fun and tactical. It also comes across as more fluid than Vikings, somehow, but I can't point to any comparisons other than my own gut feeling, so might just be me. I'm feeling a lot more drawn in than I did playing Vikings, at any rate.The story and interactive dialogue are likewise interesting and, aside from a few timeskips and the occasional lapse in believable logic, feel quite immersive and connected.Overall, a thoroughly enjoyable experience, at least if you're more of a layman in terms of Roman history.

_childDocuments_.review: Based on my experience playing trough the free demo and about 10 hours into the game, continuing  from where I left off in the free demo:The devs have listened to criticism from their previous expeditions titles and this one has a more fleshed out class/skill system that feels better. There might be fewer skills than in vikings but the classes and their skills feel distinct instead of different iterations of the same thing. Each of the 4 classes have their role to play, as do the three "paths" that you can go down within each class. While you can double or even triple dip into the paths, each has an impact in how you play the class, for instance do you want your archer to be focused on longer range? On interrupting enemies? Or also be capable in melee? Or a mix or all 3?The gameplay itself is solid and engaging. The skills, movement and RPG mechanics feel solid and intuitive. There's no surprises on why something happens, you have a good overview of all relevant stats and get the feedback you need to make informed choices in combat. The only area where I feel more information could be provided is in the army battles, where rolls are made and based on them you get a certain outcome. To begin with it's not entirely clear how that works, but after a few you start to get an understanding for it. It's the only area where I felt the tutorial wasn't comprehensive enough.As for the story, so far there feels like there's many choices to make that impact how you proceed and go forward when playing. It makes you feel like you're actually in charge of the army and your companions. You're given options on how to proceed with a quest or issue, and you implement the one of your choice. Overall it feels very solid. They have also removed any time limits, you can take as long or as little time as you want to solve things the way you want. While I personally didn't have an issue with the time constraint in Expeditions: Viking, especially as they introduced a way to disable it fairly early, it feels good to know for sure that you won't be punished for taking your time and it gives you the opportunity to experiment freely.I personally like the story and setting, which I also did for their previous title Expeditions: Viking. The story in both games have been solid and engaging, with focus on letting you choose how to do things.The game also has a crafting system which feels good. There's plenty of opportunity to customize and craft the gear you want and plenty of reason to keep making more or modifying existing ones. There's even the opportunity to deconstruct gear with unique effects and attach it as a charm to existing gear to give what was an ordinary piece of gear the effect of the unique item, just in case you prefer a specific item over the unique one for any reason. For me at least, that was a very welcome addition as I tend to care more about appearance than stats in some cases.It's well worth a buy, and best of all there's a FREE DEMO!!!!! Just download it, give it a try and see if it's the right game for you or not. I miss the days when demos were the industry standard rather than the exception. I feel that for a dev to release a demo today, they have confidence in their product. And from what I've seen so far of Expeditions: Rome, that confidence is well placed.

_childDocuments_.review: I am a roaring Romeaboo, so it would not have taken a lot for me to love this game, but this is one of the greatest finds steam's algorithm has ever dropped into my lap. XCOM-style tactical combat with a surprisingly thoughtful story driven by strong, likeable characters, all set amidst the late-roman republic in which you are given the chance to re-write history. There are definitely a few issues - the AI throws interminable waves of enemies at you in many sections, and you are forced to painstakingly watch every individual move it makes for what seemed like 100s of individual enemies. There is also the 'illusion of choice' common to many RPGs, where you are forced to make stupid decisions to progress the plot, and some of the more interesting political conflicts from the time are skimmed over or barely touched. That being said, these seem like minor issues - there are still several meaningful choices to make, even if they are on a smaller, character-level scale. For anyone who loves Roman History, this is a dream and a must play.

_childDocuments_.review: Short version:  Shallow legion battles, limited praetorian choices, seasoned veterans that fall behind in levels between acts, tedious reloading to get decent skills. I'm very early in Act 2.  There's plenty of praise elsewhere, so I'll focus on gripes.Legion battles are extremely shallow, mostly choosing obviously best choices for a battle you can't lose.  The defensive battles in Act 1 were simply swatting down small suicide attacks launched by a king who's supposed to be a military genius commanding forces vastly larger than yours.  Boring and nonsensical.Hiring praetorians (non-story companions) is frustrating.  Even with a Recruiter specialist, there's a fairly small, fixed pool.  Refresh a few times and you see the same guys over and over: same name, class, portrait, attributes, and loyalty.  At least the skills are randomized, so you can retry for better choices.  I ended up with praetorians with identical portraits.  The game should allow portraits to be reassigned.In Act 2, my praetorians from Act 1 are two levels lower than new recruits.  Worse, they lost all progress.  One guy was 99.3% of the way to level 7.  Now he's at the bottom of level 6.  My seasoned veterans are at a disadvantage.  But if I hire new ones at level 9 (trying to avoid one or two with weird facial expressions) it's a lot of reloading to get skills decently assigned.If skills came unassigned, players could start this archer as a sniper and that archer as a hunter without tedious rerolling.  And if you invest several points to get a skill that doesn't work as you expected?  There's not even a limited respec.  You just have to live with a mistake developing a story character.  Restarting now would be too painful.  There's not much replay value.

_childDocuments_.review: Verdict: It is quite an enjoyable game pushed to recommended by an excellent setting. Get it on sale if you want a made-up story from the Roman Empire.Positives+ Steam achievements (70 - requires 2 playthroughs, hardest difficulty, Iron Man active, combat deaths active and 10 require DLC)+ Steam trading cards (8 to make a badge)+ You will see a lot of historical figures (Caesar, Cicero, Cotta, Mithridates, Pompeius etc.) + Well done Rome turn-based RPG with elements of strategy + Quite an enjoyable story of revenge and political machinations, although it is quite basic with a lot of 'But .. Why?!' moments+ A lot of armours with several different themes (Rome, Greece, Egypt and Galia)+ It really shows there was a lot of research done + Your party members are each unique in their values and how they want things to be approached + Random events are quite nice, but once you do them all you are going to see 1-2 on a loop + Classes feel different + A lot of active and passive skills+ Legendary weapons and armour have unique effects + 4 endings + 4 companions + 1 optional + 4 classes (Princeps, Veles, Sagittarius, Triarius) + 1 from DLC (Gladiator)+ Each class has 3 unique skill trees Negatives- Crafting of equipment is RNG-based - all weapons and armour have a range of bonuses - The strategic part is not the strongest - Siege battles are more annoying than anything else and enemies know where you aim catapults - The characters of your pretorians and companions seem like a needless addition - combat gets quite repetitive after Act 1- Inventory management is a pain in the ass honestly and there are too many stats that you don't feel like they have an effect on anything - Conquering new regions was not exactly as fun as it boiled to - picking the best cards, replenishing soldiers, doing a side mission, repeat - The story drops the ball after Act 2 and somehow loses a grip - No zoom-out function and command queue on the overworld map - An incredible amount of waiting (injuries, enemy turns, no automatic loot after battles ...)- You don't see the effects of most things - You cannot respec your characters which makes experimenting much harder
_childDocuments_.name: Expeditions: Rome

_childDocuments_.review: Rome has literally done nothing wrong, ever, and now neither do you. Every single character is written great, eliciting the exact emotion the writers want you to feel for them. The game play can be wishy-washy at time, such as some timed objectives gaslight you into thinking you need to fight just as much as move, but you'll never find yourself losing for any other reason than you put yourself there.
_childDocuments_.name: Expeditions: Rome

_childDocuments_.review: In my opinion, Expeditions: Rome was indeed fun. The game had a gameplay style similar to the Fire Emblem games without the massive amounts of characters. And adds the ability to dictate class level-ups, allocating points however the player sees fit, instead of the "evolving" system of Fire Emblem. Add in the fact that dialogue options matter, which leads to multiple endings, and this game can be played multiple times without feeling as though it is repetitive. I played on normal difficulty and was surprised that the game sometimes felt genuinely tricky without feeling unfair or impossible to handle. However, this game is not without fault. My main issue is that most of the fights you will have are small, with only maybe 8-12,13 enemies on the field and 5 or 6 of your characters against them. I wish the game had more large-scale battles to make the atmosphere that the game's sets feel much more prominent. I did not think I was at war with Egypt or the Gauls. It felt more like little skirmishes. In the end, the game was still quite enjoyable, leaving me wanting to play again with a different character. (I bought the game while it was on sale maybe around 20 USD. As of posting the game is 44.99 USD after playing I would pay for full price, but if you are not fully sure if you want to send that much money I would advise waiting for a sale and picking up Expeditions: Rome)
_childDocuments_.name: Expeditions: Rome

_childDocuments_.review: Expeditions Rome is a satisfactory turn based CRPG. It is no life changing experience, but what it sets out to do it does well enough.Overall I would give this game a 7/10. If you are a fan of the genre and turn based combat + the set piece of Rome speaks to you, then you might feel like this game is a 9/10.PROS:+ Solid combat system+ Some interesting gear pieces+ Good enough plot to keep you interestedCONS:- Most of the systems outside of combat are not very deep, and quite surface level- There are not many choices that matter, and your character is a bit stupid at times when walking into ambushes for plot reasonsNEUTRAL:- The conquest system where you command your legions is quite tedious, but I feel like the game is still better for it, as you wouldn't get the fantasy of being a Roman commander without it.
_childDocuments_.name: Expeditions: Rome

_childDocuments_.review: I only needed to play the tutorial to know this game is AMAZING. Best way to describe it is a Divinity Original Sin 2 but set in Rome. There are games like it, but none of them in the Rome setting. It is the setting and feel that has made a SPLENDID game.Character customisation is nice. I love the idea that Titanicus Verginius Jeff will forever change the history of the Roman Republic. It is also awesome to tell people "my name Jeff".Combat is splendid. I've played multiple games like ER, but none have made me think as much. It has a unique twist on action points and replenishing them that adds a whole new level of deciding your battlefield roles.I really enjoy the voice acting in this game and am mighty impressed that all the voice actors have committed to replicating the old Latin sounds. I can picture Latin students would get a kick out of it.The game deserves enormous credit for being accurate with its history and not blindly appeasing woke mobs. There are only a couple or a few discrepancies but any rational being could easily move on as they are insignificant. I just need to say it again the the combat is spectacular!The campaign map is a great experience and I'm loving the ability to command Legio Victrix. Reminds me of glory days in Rome: Total War.Fantastic game!

_childDocuments_.review: Expeditions Rome definitely lives up to the hype.  I easily got lost in to playing this game for over 3 hours the first time playing.  The game dynamics are creative for you get to create a character and the choices you make in the game matter.  The game play for fighting is easy and the graphics are pretty easy on the eye. _childDocuments_.name: Expeditions: Rome

_childDocuments_.review: I am 34 hours in and this game is constantly (pleasantly) surprising me with new things.  The dialogue is interesting, story compelling, combat is entertaining and there is a lot of customisation involved for your party from their class type with different skill trees, armour and weapons which have stats and perks.  Party members also have individual personalities and qualifications which determine how they react to your decisions and how well your Legion fares when they lead it in the larger scale battles.  If you liked Divinity, the combat is very similar and the world map has a Mount and Blade feel to it.  Feel free to jack up the difficulty, for my first PT I have it on medium difficulty and my party feel much stronger than most enemies but I still occasionally come across a battle I need to re do due to bad positioning on my part and enemy tactics.

_childDocuments_.review: Excellent turn-based RPG with not so often seen setting - ancient Rome. You can be savior of the Republic, or one who will destroy it.Plot is is quite good - you travel around world conquering for Rome and stopping plot to destroy your family. _childDocuments_.review: 45hrs in, and I love the game more and more.It might have been the kind of game I was looking for at the moment, but this CRPG taking place in one of my favorite parts in History is just what I needed.Rich story, so many choice, and so many tactical possibilities during skirmishes.I was wondering how the game would handle a female character in such a setting, especially regarding what the character is brought to achieve, and it was so delightful to see that the NPCs are reacting to that.Except the main character's, all texts are voiced over. _childDocuments_.review: Expeditions: Rome is a really fun CRPG with some gripes that will either make or break the experience of the player.The good: All stories and interactions are completely contextualized, you feel like a Roman on a campaign. This is underlined by a great aesthetic and a lot of variety in which you can individualize yourself and your companions. Although some have called the item and crafting system bloated, I think it works fine, as the randomly generated items really incentivize experimentation and it was a fun experience to find weapons with abilities and stats that completely changed the way I approached fights. The game gives the player tools to tweak weapons and armor however they like. If you find a certain piece of armor you absolutely love you get the tools to upgrade and tweak it to bring it all the way to the endgame, although sometimes re-rolling/re-crafting is necessary if you are going for a certain build for a character. The story is fine. Reviews have stated that the antagonist magically has the upper hand every time but this is also contextualized with the mess that was the late republic. It further drives the player to really consider the big endgame choice. The character stories are what I liked the most. They are morally grey-ish and you weight your own relationship with them against the actual actions. There are romancable characters, but this is completely optional. Your dialogue choices don't end up having much of an effect besides the relationship/morale system but give enough freedom to express your character and it's possible to stay consistent. You can be a Idealist trying to do your duty, a mysoginist and a mass-murdering barbarian slayer all rolled in one and consistently act it out. Gameplay is hex based turn strategy. Although its not the deepest system it delivers fun moment-to moment gameplay as you solve the the puzzles resulting out of the Action-Reaction turn based combat. There is room for experimentation and new enemy archetypes get introduced in every chapter of the game. The game is mostly bug free outside of some visual and physics glitches. No important triggers or any quests broke during my playthrough.The Bad:There are a lot of Quality of life features missing. You cannot exit maps without walking to an exit point, this is a waste of time and every safe zone should have the option to just get out whenever one likes. There is no way to speed up movement outside of enemy turn speed either. Inventory management is a mess and not functional at all for the kind of RNG loot system they went with. Tooltips are missing and information is not always given to the player, so you cannot react to new enemy types when you first encounter them, you have to see their moveset and abilities to form a counter strategy, at which point it may already be too late for one of your characters. The metagame, so the handling of your legion(s), is a neat idea but ultimatively underdelivers. The system is obtuse and lacks any form of feedback or information necessary. You click things like "10 % Defence" or "10 % Agression" but you have absolutely no idea what these changes will do. Like most of the game it's also too easy, I have never, I repeat, NEVER had a single legion clash that didn't have a 100 % success chance while playing on hard. The metagame also ties in with the generic missions that you do to liberate provinces. Some of those missions are unique but most are interchangable with random encounters. The world map needed more things to do and be intergrated better into the systems that feed it. One of your characters gets bitten by a snake and you treat his critical condition at one of your outposts. This entails loading into the camp, clicking 3 buttons, leaving the camp, letting time pass and then loading back into the camp to get the character back into your roster. Why the devs didn't include a way to assign characters to tasks and interact with the camp in general from the worldmap is beyond me. I believe I watched what amounts to a movies worth of youtube content in the time alt-tabbed during the loading screens. Naturally this same process needs to happen for crafting, refilling your consumables, aquiring legion manpower, trading ressources etc. If the intent was for the player to not miss events or character interactions in the camp itself, then a better way needs to be found, as this whole process didn't respect my time at all and will break the will of anyone who doesn't load fast or has an SSD by act 3 at the latest. Conclusion:The game is undeniably fun to me. As someone who has played a lot of CRPG's it was a cool experience and you don't get the chance to roleplay as a Roman often in videogames. The combat was satisfying but bogged down by the repetitive nature of the generic quests that tie into the metagame. The story was fine and some of the writing is quite witty. There is undeniably a lot of content in here and a lot of systems to explore. I still recommend buying full-price if the pro's outweight the con's as stated above, but on sale it's a definitive recommendation. The studio behind this game has a talent for CRPG's and if they focus a bit more on quality of life features as well as the metagame their next title might be even better.

_childDocuments_.review: I went into the game without knowing what it would be like besides the starting content shown in the demo. After playing the game I've noticed that the turn based party combat reduces significantly as the game progresses and you spend a lot of time choosing a spot for your legion to attack which involves choosing 3 combat cards to win. I can't say I enjoy the legion combat, but I enjoyed the moments of walking through a city and completing quests or solving puzzles. I look forward to completing the game to see more of the party based combat and decision making, but will be rushing through the legion combat.

_childDocuments_.review: I loved this game, until I eventually hated it.PROS:+ Interesting tactical combat, with plenty of options and combinations+ The game has some ridiculously gorgeous isometric locations, and overall the visuals and voice acting are worth the price+ Companions are a good company+ Spear of Achilles. Because nothing can beat Bestia Tabat killing 10+ enemies on the first round.CONS:- Overall game length. The game overstayed its welcome after first 30-40 hours, really.- Act 3, in particular. Repetitive scenarios, silly narrative twists, extra length. And terrible visibility on combat maps, compared to other acts.- Almost all world map mechanics: Legion battles, territory/resource control, pacification and "random troubles". These sound fine in idea, but in practice, it's a mess. All of these mechanics were a constant pestering annoyance, and a massive mandatory time sink. Artificial restrictions such as having to backtrack to legion camps for almost any action/decision, or hoping for a favorable RNG event / card, only made it worse.- The endgame nearly robbed me of satisfactory conclusion, after all the effort to get to that point. Most endings are of "good, but..." type.  The "choices" the player has to make there are really just choices on what to sacrifice, and that is a questionable way to end such a long campaign.Overall recommended, but I'll never ever touch this game again.P.S.: Instead of a DLC that adds *more* to the game, I'd consider a DLC that removes half of what was there already. Player time is valuable, Logic Artists!

_childDocuments_.review: Not sure what they were trying to do here.  Building your fort is abstract and boring, Battles at the legion level are boring and consist of 4 choices to determine the outcome.  Smaller battles are decent, but some of the attack choices don't make sense (why does a gladius ONLY have a double weapon attack?!  Why can't I just use it?).  Don't get it, not worth it.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall I would say the game was quite enjoyable. The turn-based combat, especially the staged combat encounters were the highlight of the game, and provided some decent challenge at the highest difficult levels. The game was beautiful, and the effort put into the voice acting was appreciated, even if the writing was a bit whatever. I did not play through the game with the DLC but may come back and try it again as there are some decent variations in how the story could go.In terms of the negatives, the game really loves having you run around for no reason, I have no idea why there isn't a button to let you just leave areas whenever you are ready to leave and why people can't send couriers to each other instead of you having to travel to talk to specific people over and over again for no real reason (i recommend having something on a second screen to do while you are forces to run around between loading screens for no reason). There is high level legion combat in the game which i appreciated the idea of, but the execution fell quite flat. Even on the highest difficulty it felt like there was no way to lose the battles which given endless resources and time made that aspect of the game trivial and a bit more of a chore.

_childDocuments_.name: Expeditions: Rome

_childDocuments_.review: A low-budget, tactical CRPG that does not deliver in any category I can think of.  Graphics and design are ok I guess, but nothing to write home about.  Writing is awful.  The whole point of a historical game is immersion and they completely missed there.  Modern social issues aside, it is impossible to tell real historical insights from stuff they just made up.  I just started skipping the dialogue after an hour or two, and then what's even the point.  They tout this as "choices matter" but in 10 hours I have yet to make one.  Mechanics are utter garbage.  Its that "armor and health" crap like Banner Saga, but less deep and less realistic.  Very little actual freedom to design characters they way you would expect in an RPG.  The ability system feels like they adapted a card game rather than a table top rpg.  The items and equipment even moreso.  Might actually be charming if it wasn't so full of arcane, nonsense mechanics.  I had to google a lot of things the game didn't explain correctly or at all.  Between the long battles that I have to redo 4 or 5 times to figure out the secret, the bloat of wandering around the kingdom on your horse trying figure out what's going on, and the long cringe-inducing dialogues, there's really nothing left to enjoy here.

Legion management got a bit boring at times, just point and click and you take over cities, but the combat scenarios and story was fantastic. _childDocuments_.review: If I could rate this game neutral I would but steam doesn't let me. So I'll just voice a few grievances I have about the game:Expeditions: Rome consistently expects you to know stuff it didn't tell you. Oh you didn't go to the senate and talked with one guy after the first 5 year time skip but before continuing the main story, which is an incredibly small window of time? Well congrats you just missed out on an incredibly important improvement for your character!And then 8 hours later you find out you missed it because you *need* it and googled when you're supposed to get it. And then it's the moral dilemma of "do I want to continue a gutted run" or "do I reset and play the ~8 hours again"I chose option 3: Play something else that actually respects the playerAnd while this was the first time something of this scale happened the game expects you to know stuff at a smaller scale too. Especially in fights you constantly need to reload because of things you couldn't have known the first time. Also on the note of combat, I played on Normal and every fight was either so easy it's boring or a borderline impossible task. I don't think anyone on their team was responsible for balancing.This game is a CRPG that takes a long time to beat. If you pursue sidequests one playthrough takes around 55 hours on average. That isn't a playthrough time you can just do over and over again to learn everything. The devs expect you to do it anyway. Just play something else that is respectful of your time. Honestly it's sad because I really loved the time I spent in this game, it's just held back by bad Game Design decisions that accrue over time to just suck the motivation out of you. I want to continue playing this game so bad because I really enjoyed the story and world, but at the same time the Game Design does it's best to make me want to quit and just play something else.

_childDocuments_.review: I experienced a game breaking bug while playing in ironamn - inasne so it's not like I can just go back to a previous save. I chose not too speak with Geminus to attack a city from the harbor, this caused this quest chain to break causing you to get stuck on a ship with Geminus when trying to cross islands. I read that this bug has been in the game since the Demo days which is just unacceptable from any developer. It's so disappointing and disheartening after putting all the time and effort too get this far in the story. I really hope steam honors my refund request.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a game, not a historical text.Great game. Lots of fun and details.Battles are tactical and challenging without being unreasonably brutal.Game activities are varied, from small squad tactics to larger battles where you "armchair general" your entire legion through a battle.  Game looks good, sound good, and runs well.Haven't come across any game breaking bugs.This is a game, not a historical text.Loot is varied and there is a lot of it for the loot hounds. Almost too much. It can get overwhelming when you have eight versions of the same sword each with slightly different stats and differing skills ( the skills available during battle are combination of weapon attached and character attached ).  You don't need to obsess about the differences to proceed in the game, but it's a nice layer of detail for players who enjoy fine tuning their strategy. This is a game, not a historical text.The developers obviously put a lot of effort into researching and designing the game. It really shows in the play and the visuals.  The in game voices and sounds are  well done.  It's entertaining and engaging, and well worth the full asking price , BUTif you are looking for a historical text, this is not it.If you are the kind of person who will obsess about a historical inaccuracy  rather than enjoy a well designed, fun, and engaging game, then you should probably avoid this.This is a game, not a historical text.  A very fun and enjoyable game.You have been warned.

_childDocuments_.review: NO SPOILERSI feared that I would never be able to get the same satisfaction as I once had while playing Divinity: Original Sin 2... This game very closely captivated in a very immersive manner, the same way Divinity once did.For those who are on edge or unsure, a couple of pointers that may help you to make up your mind.1- Very immersive setting, highly inspired (but not wholly accurate) from events in history. Remember, it is a game of fiction where certain details are  detached from reality. But on the whole, this game will make you feel as a Roman like never before. Huge plus for enthusiasts of the era.2- Decent challenge along the way. The game manages to find things interesting, even after 30 hours, I felt that I was under some pressure to make the best of the bad decisions I had made earlier on, and I am a veteran XCOM and Divinity player... Punishment is real, but forgiving (except in some serious cases). Customization allows for the game to play out in the way that you prefer.3- Integrity of the events, well this is a personal favorite of mine. Some actions and decisions taken hours ago may lead to unexpected outcomes, but more importantly, the dialogue is very deep and you sometimes really need to listen to what people are saying to get the significant hints out there.4- Cleopatra...5- Base, legion, morale, item, resource management... Though not deep, it adds a certain flavor to the game that other RPGs in the same category do not present. 6- Soundtrack. All real gamers out there know that the soundtracks are important as they are the best way to enhance the atmosphere and the sensation a game is offering. This one hits the spot just right, having played games for well over 20 years, I have grown resistant to such tricks. Yet, this game broke through my guard and actually touched my soul with the timing and quality of its soundtracks... 7- Characters... Personally, I somehow got connected to a few characters without realizing... When you actually take a pause in the game and stare at the wall blank for 5 minutes straight, you understand that the game already made a good impression on you with its characters.8- Opening up: This one is a very, very welcome feature. After playing the game for 10 hours, I thought I saw all the game had to offer, alas, I was mistaken. 15 hours in, a new feature pops up, 20 hours, an expanded game mechanic presents itself, 30 hours, things get slightly chaotic and you realize you are not as safe as you once thought due to certain dynamics changing... The game does a decent job at spicing things up and prevents itself from getting stale quickly.9- The plot. As of writing this comment, I am far from completing the game, I am probably at around 40-50% mark and I am totally engrossed in the story and I am seriously looking forward to see what happens and how I can affect/change/partake/witness it.10- Cleopatra...11- A tiny detail, but I loved the studio behind this work. They are quite open to criticism and they even mock their own past mistakes and choices in their previous installments. They listen to their audience and shape their game based on the gamer profile. This is a magnificent game compared to their previous ones, which are also decent but far from being as good as this one. This already shows that the devs can be reliable and worthy of support. This part has to be clarified as well... As with any game, there HAS TO BE certain drawbacks, anyone who denies it is lying. As much as I love this game, I still find certain parts in need of some polishing.1 - Overwhelming introduction of mechanics early on. The game has a strong filter early on and tests how willing you are to play the game. In mere minutes, while you are trying to get used to something, game gives you something else to consider straight away. And this happens a bit too rapidly early on and can indeed feel like it is becoming heavy. If you can persist, the waves die down and you can sail in peace as you get familiar with all of them as hours pass away. Still, a bit daunting at first.2- Certain key properties are not practically accessible... This can be my biggest complaint, something trivial, but with constant repetition that the game includes, it can slowly become tedious. You will want to access a particular component of the game, but you need to make a transition and go through a loading screen to access that one small thing that will probably take a few seconds of your time. You then have to go through the same loading screen again to back at what you were doing... Not a big deal, but stings after awhile.3- Speaking of repetition... Things will get repetitive, this is probably true for all games out there, but you get to feel it in this game a bit stronger somehow. They are amazing and interesting the first few times, challenging even, yet after awhile, you will feel not that into that particular event and may not wish to participate... Though the rewards are generally satisfying, the amount of time it takes puts it off. Luckily, the game does not bombard you with those, though you will still probably go through a few of them.4- Refund unlikely due to the amount of hours the game needs for it to totally open up and show you what it has to offer in full detail. This game might not be to the liking of everybody, obviously, so a refund feels like a safe bet. But in this particular case, it may not be a valid option to rely on since the game will still need a lot of your time to expand more and more to give you an even better sense of satisfaction and challenge.It is good. Get it... If still on doubt, wait for sale, then definitely get it, and try to persist through the early game. Although it may be tempting, try to refrain from watching streams or YT videos about the game as it may contain spoilers. You may not wish to ruin the setting for yourself as even some dialogue can give important information regarding the plot and events. Well, I recommend seeing how it unfolds and gets you grasped in its story. If not, well, you can always ignore me and see how the game is from a few sources and decide for yourself of course.Edit: Corrected typosI will keep the comments open in case anyone wants to ask a specific detail (I fear I cannot go into much detail if it has to include spoilers from the game) so that I can answer to the best of my abilities.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a gorgeous, beautifully written game and, unlike 99% of games, choices you make actually really, really do matter.  It's the first game where I wasn't just spamming 'skip' during conversations because A) the writing was, overall, very good, B) the voice acting was superb and engaging--absolutely terrific, and C) the conversations just naturally engaged me.  About B), though, the voice acting might be the best in any game I've played, ever. Without a doubt it has the best VA of any non-AAA game.  And speaking of choices...one of the most consequential choices you make is when you're creating your character and deciding whether your character is male or female.  If you play as a female, you're constantly undermined, doubted, and running into obstacles with the roman law of the day.  Dialog and circumstances are totally different depending on what sex you choose, and it makes for two wildly different experiences and very high replayability value. I'm both glad and astonished that the devs  leaned all the way into imagining how this story might be different and how both scenarios and dialog would play out depending whether the main character is male or female. I played as a female and it makes for a completely different experience from almost all other historical games that decide to maintain "blindness" to the main character's gender choice (if the choice exists). It's a prime example of how much thought was put into this game--and so much was.  This game is fascinating and several cuts above the rest.  Other stuff: the learning curve is a bit high if you're new to tactical turn-based games and even if you're not so new...there are a lot of mechanics and learning them all might take one whole playthrough.  I was realizing stuff about combat mechanics up until the very end.  My only gripe about this game is super trivial and hardly a gripe...sometimes when there are tons of enemies and you're waiting for them to take their turn it can take a while.  One time I microwaved a tamale and the fighting was still going on, LOL! Anyways, wonderful game, 11/10, totally recommend!

_childDocuments_.review: This is not a bad game, but I don't recommend it because for the price it offers too little to many great games out there.The game starts off well. I enjoy the new combat mechanism, and the classes seem balance at first. However, at about the end of act 1, I realized that the system is not good. You don't actually have a lot of options here, here is the detail:- There are a lot of combat statuses, but it's not worth applying those. To get the best debuffs (knocked down, stun..), it first requires to apply other kind of debuffs. Therefore, you can only apply the debuffs by coordinating 2 characters, or spend 2 turns doing that. This makes debuffs useless because there is only 1 AP and since skills with debuffs usually deal less damage, it's better to just go plain damage and kill it instead of wasting AP and turns on debuffs.- The above is especially true, when apply to a new mechanism in this game: the untrained enemies. Most of the enemies (not sure about the later part of the game, I just got near the end of Act 1) are untrained that when killed, refund the AP. Therefore, it's better to use the high damage skills to kill the most of these enemies in every turn.- Another bad thing about statuses is that, you can only apply it when the attack causes the damage. That means you cannot bleed the highly armored enemies, cannot lower boss's resistance and damage if they have high armor and shield (most of the time they do, they're bosses anyway). This, will leads to the next point.- The armor and shield, it matters at first, then you realize that critical damage bypass shield and armor completely, and there is a class in the game that have access to guaranteed critical hit since level 1. Mid Act 1 there is a boss with like 10 armor or so and it would take at least 4 turns to shred all the armor, enough for him to kill your whole team. Since his armor is too high you cannot deal any damage and thus no debuffs, the most viable way to kill him is to use critical hit.- The battles usually put you in the position where you're out numbered, tight spots and thus killing the enemies fast enough is the highest priority. If you do it right, the battle should end in 1-2 turns. If it last longer than that, then your chance of survival will be lower. Therefore, only classes that do good damage matters. That leaves you with only the archers and assassins (archers have access to a skill that can attack twice per turn, and an overwatch ability that can also attack twice per turn, and assassins simply have damage +50-100% in the first 2 turns - which is actually the whole battle most of the time).- With all the points above, after the deduction, you have like only a few options to build the party. I'm not sure if this is because I played on the highest difficulty or not. I'm planning to play on lower difficulty after this, because the highest difficulty is not that difficult, it just limits your options to play and enjoy the game.Another main mode in the game is the legion management. It's like a tiny implementation of an 4X game. You control your legion and use it to capture sectors, its resources and do the legion missions. It's very hard to lose these legion missions and battles, and the whole point of the legion is just for getting you more components to spend on crafting - which in fact can be much simpler if there is a proper trading system. In this game, you cannot trade your equipment, it must go a long way from looting, dismantling, learning recipes, crafting... I don't know if this is an implementation choice or at that time in history, people actually don't trade items. Anyway, the whole crafting system is more cumbersome than necessary, it slows the game down too much.Another big annoying thing: the game doesn't have a mini map. Yes, it's true, NO mini map. I don't know if it's technically too hard or it's intended that way but it absolutely make me enjoy the game less.One last big thing and it's also the final nail in the coffin for me, it's the price.At full price, this is even more expensive than Pillar of Eternity (1/2) when they're first released (I'm in Vietnam), about the same price as Divinity Original Sin and much more expensive than a lot of great indie games out there. Yet it offers too little play time. I haven't finished the game yet, but from the stats it's about 50 hours to complete the game on average. Comparing to other games I mentioned, this is too little value, cost wise.Imo, the game worth only a third of its price, so wait until it sales 60-70% if you want to try.Update:- As I changed the difficulty to lower, I also have a more refreshing look on this. The combat, still lean heavily on dps builds, now is manageable with any builds, and thus I can use all my main companions and play my main char as any class I want, instead of using mercs and build my MC as DPS class.- The story is really good, the choices and consequences are there to explore, and since this is not a popular game you won't find much spoilers there. The most mind blown thing for me is the gender of the main char. I finished more than half of the game just to know that one of the main branch was decided since the very beginning of the game: at the character creation screen, when I chose my character's gender, so yeah, at least the game has some replay value. I'm gonna try the male char in the future after I forget most about the game I guess.All the other annoying things above are still there, but since the breaking deal for me is cost-value ratio, I changed my mind since I play this more than I thought I would. You can have about 150-200 hours here if you do all the side quests and finish the game as both genders. Still, I think it's better to buy it on sale, 30-50% off is a good deal.

_childDocuments_.review: At first game was less interesting than other games of this genre or even than Expeditions: Vikings (not THE best game in this genre). It is sad cause I actually had much more hopes for this one. -Party management system isn't well made. For some missions you must take party-member + centurions, for others main-characters + party-members. But you have only one party on map so all this happy train travel to location only for message that this character cannot be used on this mission. Why? Because reasons - that's why. Also you always can forget some of characters on camp assignment and no way to retrieve them except travel back. -Inventory. Inventory management itself isn't very well made too but... it can be forgiven. But rewards system... Items you receive from game or must craft don't have much sense immersion-wise. It just another mechanic put in game very ungracefully. Legion (2500 person strong) made victory against plenty of enemies and will loot... 2 slaves and  17 coins. My party win against some ambush and I will loot hundreds of coins and plenty of items. Another thing - availability of basic items. Playing as a commander of Legion you expect that with thousands under your command you can count to have spare pilum or caltrops. But no. Even simple water jug must be crafted from salvage and garbage. Your super experienced blacksmith doesn't even have option to craft basic things until you will give him a recipe. And better still he can't do this alone so party member must be left in camp as a helper... Why do I have blacksmith at all? Why I can't have even simple water jug in my camp or can't buy any of that items? -Story-wise - dialogues doesn't have much choice and consequences and game is far away from many others. Some story behind missions just don't have sense and again added without even thought about immersion. If you will achieve your goal on map - all enemies will run away even if they had you outnumbered and outgunned. As example - if you must burn some crates on map and you can just run to them and burn them and ignore every enemy along the way. Even if you are surrounded - you will win. -Skill and class system - is pretty basic. For some classes skills doesn't give something you want to achieve at the end of the skill tree. But Reaper skill is overkill. With it character can make kill chains with 5+ enemies.At this moment character creation system is awful graphically - you have only one character model for male and another for female and you can change height for this model ant that is all. So male have giant arms and wide chest and female have pretty wide hips. Some basic choice of faces for character included and portraits is okay. -Difficulty on hard is pretty nice, more on the easy side. But no complains on this part.-Engine is pretty and as whole game is nice-looking.-No game-breaking bugs so far.  All in all - it is worth playing but it is far from masterpiece. _childDocuments_.review: While it's not as historically accurate as how one might think, how the game presents itself, or as the game description implies, Expeditions: Rome is a great game in my opinion. For anyone interested in why it's not "historically accurate", refer to this article here, it's well put together and explains in great detail why the game isn't historically accurate: Anyways, besides the issue of historical accuracy, Expeditions: Rome offers a lot of great things:1. Great voice acting2. Memorable/Unique companions for the most part3. Funny little historical jokes/references4. Good sense of progression5. Good graphics/settings6. Very rare, albeit annoying bugs. Not game breaking. I experienced one bug in all my playtime so far where my companion got stuck in a corner of a map so I couldn't loot the area and had to leave without looting. Considering I only experienced one bug in my time so far though is pretty good imo.7. A lot of playtime and replayability with different endings. At the time of this review I've spent 42.8 hrs on the game in the span of 4 days, and I'm not even close to halfway (though to be fair I had to restart my first playthrough due to some regretful decisions I made). 8. Resource grinding isn't too bad, just scrap a lot of stuff and make sure to toggle on the option to highlight lootable containers/corpses by checking keybinds. However, there are some cons that my or may not be a deal breaker:1. Not very historically accurate at all (see article linked above)2. Classes that characters can spec into are unbalanced. Veles (Assassin skill path) and Sagittarius (Sniper and marksman skill path) are much more powerful than the Princeps (Tank) or Triarius (Support/Sub-dps) class. The gladiator class is so weak it's not worth it. Killing enemies quickly and efficiently is how to win battles and therefore the Veles and Sagittarius are more valuable due to their damage output. 3. Army battles, aka battles involving your legion, are just squares/circles with symbols on the screen and tactical cards being used to influence outcome of battle. It become stale to watch battles play out as symbols on a screen quickly. Wish they either made a different system altogether for legion battles that was more interactive or at least put more effort into visually representing the armies. Overall: There are a lot more pros than cons, and if you can get by the historical inaccuracy, unbalanced classes (it is a singleplayer game so it's not too bad), and somewhat average legion battles, the story is very engaging with its visuals, voice acting, and main cast of characters. I bought the game on sale and I would recommend doing so, as I do think that a $44.99 game should have a way better legion/army battle system. Either way I recommend trying it if turn based combat rpg games are your thing.

_childDocuments_.review: If only steam had a rating for meh: despite the fairly high degree of polish, the excellent character writing, the truly fascinating historical period of the setting, the undeniable care that the studio put into the project, the fundamental deficiency of the combat system remains painfully obvious and cripples the entire game. The strategic management of this game feels like a refreshing macro perspective, until you realize that it is literally a dashboard with some numbers with vague and inconsistent meanings. Upon the arrival of a new region, once again, you click upon a red dot and you click the button to send your spreadsheet into battle against the AI's spreadsheet.You choose a few random cards that are reputedly 'tactics', which moves some bars around, but whatever meaning those bars have? You have no idea. And after you win, you inevitably (almost) find yourself dealing yet another pacification mission, running back into the first legion's camp, where you have to speak with this specific person, and then, at the end of all that, you get a generic combat mission. And this repeats itself, for around 20-30 hours. It seems like Logic Artists, after designing the combat mechanics and such, felt the need to waste the players' time through lengthy, boring sieges, the same encounters but vaguely re-skinned, and again and again ad infinitum. As if grinding away a few hours of my time with yet another catapult section justifies their painfully mediocre game design. And despite the setting, despite the writing, despite the (somewhat) organic feeling character interactions... The time spent in Expeditions just leaves an odd taste in the mouth, like lukewarm tap water in an too warm afternoon. Probably best enjoyed in the same mood that which compelled me to write this meaningless review.TLDR: Underneath polish and decent writing: boring combat mechanics that feels the need to justify their existence by wasting your time.

_childDocuments_.review: PC Specs: Intel Core I7 -10700KGigabyte RTX 3090 Gaming OC64GB Kingston Hyper X FuryExpeditions: Rome, the third in a series of historically-accurate RPGs from Logic Artists. If you've played the previous two games, you'll feel right at home here. And if you haven't, well, you'll still feel right at home, because let's be honest, how different can a game set in ancient Rome really be?GameplayExpeditions: Rome is a turn-based RPG set in ancient Rome, where you get to play as a Roman officer leading your army on various campaigns. The game is pretty straightforward - you move your units around, attack the enemy, and try to capture their stronghold. And if you've played the previous Expeditions games, you'll feel right at home here.The combat is enjoyable, and there's a nice balance between strategy and action. The game has a good mix of ranged and melee combat, and you can customize your units with different weapons and armor. The game also has a good variety of enemies to fight, from barbarians to gladiators.GraphicsThe game's graphics are good, with detailed character models and environments that capture the essence of ancient Rome. The game's visuals are also bright and colorful, which adds to the game's immersive atmosphere.SoundThe game's sound design is good, with realistic sound effects that add to the game's immersion. The game's music is also enjoyable, and it can make you feel like you're actually in ancient Rome.Pros:Enjoyable turn-based combat.Good mix of ranged and melee combat.Customizable units.Good variety of enemies.Good graphics and sound design.Cons:Feels similar to the previous Expeditions games.ConclusionIn conclusion, Expeditions: Rome is a fun game that builds on the success of the previous two games. The turn-based combat is enjoyable, and there's a good mix of ranged and melee combat. The game's graphics and sound design are good, and the game has an immersive atmosphere.However, the game does feel very similar to the previous Expeditions games. If you've played those games, you'll know exactly what to expect. But if you're new to the series, then this game is a great starting point.Overall, Expeditions: Rome is an 8/10 game that's definitely worth checking out if you're a fan of turn-based RPGs. And if you're not a fan of turn-based RPGs, well, what are you doing here? This game is not for you.

_childDocuments_.review: An Xcom/CRPG hybrid. Combat design is like Xcom but with a lot less enemy variety, so it's just functional. The writing is structured like a CRPG with acts and branching dialogues, and is generally pretty strong as long as you don't think too deep about some parts. A pretty good and enjoyable game overall, feels like the streamlined summer flick of CRPGs.Downsides:- Companions barely have interactions. If you drop by to talk to them every chance you get, you'll find you don't have anything to say for hours straight.- The Archer class is hilariously overpowered and can clear the entire map in one turn with two very easily acquired weapons. They can ignore every mechanic put into place to keep archers in check. It's actually bewildering how this slipped by the balance team.- The tank class feels pretty useless, because alpha striking is a lot more effective than actual tactics in this game, much like XCOM.- The legion mechanic is barebones and poorly designed. Because legion experience adds flat power and only goes up when you kill more units than you lose, it's a snowballing effect. After a certain point, you don't even need to think about anything. During battle, it's RNG which tactics you get, but it's all a numbers game and you just have to pick the ones that give you stat boosts.- The bulk of the game revolves around the legion mechanic and conquering territories, but the pacification missions you need to undertake are really lame.- There are way too many unique items that let you just ignore some detrimental gameplay mechanic for free.But so long as you go in without expecting a masterpiece, you'll find that it's a pretty fun time.

_childDocuments_.review: Exceptionally immersive and thoughtful.I'm partial to turn-based tactical games with hexagons. What can I say?; I bought Steve Jackson's "Melee" when it was released (and still have my copy: I'm that old!). The Expeditions series honors that kind of tactical puzzle at its core and if you like the puzzle (who to move forward, where to position, which skill or weapon to unleash?), the series is excellent and really only gets better in each iteration.But this iteration is simply a breed apart. The dedication to historical detail, coupled with a strange "what if" quality is totally immersive. Roman military campaigns are treated with meaningful realism, but also friendly game-light abstraction, while the strategic battle addition gives players a game-within-a-game. The companion characters are people you actually want to get to know, and not just click through dialogue (that's really really hard to pull ff and almost always otherwise fails). The pieces are all in place.The plot moves in a semi-linear way forward with only a very few key decisions in the culmination of each sub-campaign, in ways that change the endgame... until the endgame, that is, and then the branching narratives get super-interesting. I think players would really benefit from actually role-playing their character,  throughout to provide a kind of coherence that they will need in the end game to stand by WHO YOU ARE to make the hard late game decisions, so that they make sense to the player. Your choices depend on actually being true to how you embody the character. Very few games encourage this. In this sense, the game is actually best if actually role-played, which for many players is not typically a priority. Even so, Expeditions: Rome yields best to players who do, investing themselves in the pretty-well written narrative.Beyond this, the play s terrific. You will get map after map of complicated tactical fights, with a variety of characters, whose specific abilities can be used in tandem, at least for smart players. Each fight is unique, with a difficult map, opponents with skills that you have often not seen before, and often a moment of surprise, midstream, which will take you a moment to regroup and puzzle out. This is what you sign on for in this game series, and it does not let down.The larger "strategic" system is more primitive and repetitive. You slowly acquire territory, turn "cards" in legion combat, and play the unsurprising odds to win on the battle field. I found this addition exciting and fresh, but I wouldn't argue it is especially revolutionary. The larger scale system does break the rhythm in a good way, however, and is thematically spot-on and challenging. All fine.Most important: this is a BIG game with a lot of hours of play, some of which are a bit "rinse and repeat", so the end game needed to be a payoff. I certainly thought it was. I felt the finale was earned by all of my slow work through the complex landscape the game provided leading me there.Rome is the best offering in the Expeditions franchise - and I've played them all. If you like this kind of thing, this is a thing you are going to like. I did!
_childDocuments_.name: Expeditions: Rome

_childDocuments_.review: I've played all the Expeditions games; Conquistador, Viking and now Rome. In my opinions its the one I've enjoyed the least, despite spending over 150 hours on it. It is a very ambitious third game for sure, much bigger than the previous installments in the series, but sometimes bigger doesnt make games better. For me it felt excessively lengthy, and overly repetitive, which is my main issue with the game. The story is also not as good as Expeditions: Viking, which I thoroughly enjoyed. By the end I just wanted to get it over with. I would recommend buying Viking, or even Conquistador instead of this.

_childDocuments_.review: Expeditions: Rome is the sequal to Expeditions: Viking which makes the game significantly less enjoyable. The characters and squad-based gameplay are good. Most of the rest of the game is boring or poorly implemented. First, the world map. Simply put, it's very difficult to actually get your companions to get somewhere. You double click on a location, your companions start moving. Unfortunately, random encounters start. These start fairly innocuous. Picking berries or finding an abandoned camp and you can decide to rob it or leave it. Unfortunately, in Africa, these random encounters can include random battles like walking through tall grass in Pokemon. These happen frequently and are very boring after the first three times because typically you're on your way to a mission and can't afford to fight a battle against random bandits which can potentially injure your companions. Also, when you actually arrive at the location, you'll be irritated because you can't get your cursor to click on the exact pixel which allows you to enter the location. Thankfully, there's no time limit on the game, but it's very frustrating to have to do this every single time.Let's talk about the story. Expeditions: Viking was simple, but compelling. Build up your village to prevent it from being wiped off the map by your rival. In Rome, you build up your legion to conquer territory in Asia, Africa and Gaul. It sounds more interesting, but I promise you it's not. Building up a village and seeing it turn from a collection of burned-out huts to a fortress/trade hub is great. When you build up your legion, all that changes is the tents get bigger. But you get to conquer territory. Sure. That's actually the worst part of the game. When your legion marches out, it can go and conquer territory or build infrastructure. You need the infrastructure to upgrade the legion and forge which allows you to upgrade your companions' equipment. So, you're going to spend a LOT of time upgrading infrastructure. That's simply a timer and has no real gameplay mechanic. Let's talk about the real conquering. When your legion attacks an outpost, they reach the enemy settlement and then you select a commander. Then, go get a coffee, run some errands, do anything other than watch the boring legion battles. You can barely affect the outcome by using "cards". That's fine, but you might as well not even have the option considering how boring it is. They know it is, because they have an "auto-resolve" button. Of course, you can't actually use that button because the AI doesn't understand the only thing that matters is "legion defense" and will pick dumb cards which will get a lot of your legion killed.Overall, the main problem with this game is a lack of focus. The story ins't as compelling as it should be. The gameplay is very repetitive which gets boring after the first act, making the second act a chore (after about 20 hours). The implementation of the legion mechanic should have gotten more thought. Honestly, I do still like the game, but it doesn't live up to the previous title. I'm serious when I say the story relies on you being a Romeaboo to keep going since you don't have a clear objective which pushes the story forward.

_childDocuments_.review: After two full playthroughs (male or female makes for quite a different experience), I can only surmise that this game isn't finished. As in, this isn't the final iteration of what is supposed to be the finished product.As the 3rd entry in the series, it strays way too far from what makes it an Expeditions game in the first place. Being an army leader that goes on multiple conquests across the world, always at the behest of others, is simply not how these games go. Even the devs seem to have realised this, at least in part, as they are reworking the main "gameplay" aspect of said conquest (which basically always amounts to randomized nonsense really).It's clear they were blinded by ambition, forgetting what made their games great and then running out of money / dev time to properly finish things up before launch (missing portraits and ability icons, fewer personalized squadmates, story railroading, ...). The UI is terrible, unreliable and frequently in it's own way. The plot feels underwhelming and undercooked. What few personal side-quests for your companions there are, are really short and rather limited. The story get the wind taken out of it's sails on multiple occassions (inexplicable time jumps of several years in which no-one ages and nothing really happens). Not to mention the excellent prologue in Vikings, which was a step from Conquistador, is completely absent in this entry for some reason.Sadly it all amounts to a jarring, lackluster and bizarre experience for someone who loved both Conquistador and Vikings very much. With a major overhaul of a core feature planned as mentioned above, as well as some DLC on the way apparently, it seems best to stay away from this game untill all that is done and polished to a shine.

_childDocuments_.review: Definitely my personal GOTY. Expeditions: Rome is the best entry in the series by far. It's a great mix of TRPG and CRPG with shockingly high production values and overall polish. The visuals are beautiful and the game runs quite well for the most part. The more large scale battles can dip down occasionally with all of the fire and particle effects, but I've only encountered one glitch that was easily fixed with a save reload. Every single NPC is fully voice acted except your character (which I prefer in RPG's). The portraits are all large and detailed for every major character. The soundtrack and sound design as a whole are excellent. It's epic in scale and attacks sound really meaty especially when you gore the enemy. Environments are varied and full of detail. You find yourself leading a conquest in Greece, Africa, and Gallia, with breaks in between each act where you can address personal matters in Rome. Bells and whistles aside, the core aspects (imo) of a great RPG are almost all there. It's important to remember that this is NOT a pure CRPG, so don't expect much exploration. If you're expecting Baldur's Gate or Divinity, this is not exactly that. It has elements of that. The overworld map is mainly just for leading your legion which is unfortunately the worst part of the game. There are a few small towns/cities you can explore a little with only a handful of fairly simple side quests to complete. All companions have their own questlines you can solve as you see fit and they're all well-written, but not that challenging. The customization is very in-depth. It's not fantastical at all (mostly), but they still managed to pull off a good variety of classes, skills, and weapons that other fantasy/sci-fi TRPGs fail at. You can choose between the assassin, soldier, support, and archer class. While that may not sound like a lot, each class has three unique skill trees per class you can mix and match to your liking with weapons that have their own unique skills as well. Trust me. No two praetorians of the same class will play the same. The combat, unsurprisingly, is the highlight here. If you're familiar with XCOM: EU, this will be familiar, but it's the synergy between classes that really sells it. Supports can attack over the heads of soldiers blocking enemies from the front. Archers can use soldiers as a form of cover with the Bulwark skill. Supports can use Inspire to give the assassin his action point back to flank an enemy a soldier is attacking to reduce their resistances (slashing, piercing, bludgeoning) to 0% to do full damage and setup the archer to use Assist to attack the enemy and trigger attacks of opportunity from all adjacent allies around said enemy. Hopefully, that gives you an idea on what I mean.The narrative is enthralling to the say the least. It's full of political intrigue, humor, drama, revenge, personal relationships (including romantic), and it's the kind of story that we don't get often in most self-proclaimed RPGs. It's a story about YOU, not some punk rocker AI stuck in your head. You control your own ambitions and you hold the lives of your companions in your hands. Your multiple conquests will only succeed if you lead them properly. You determine who leads the nations you conquer, what companions will follow you, and even hold political influence in Rome. I won't spoil it, but the endings are great.However, there are flaws and they almost sap the fun out of the game entirely. Random annoying events will occur when time is passing in the overworld map. They are varied and they mostly suck. It's mainly the many events that cause injury, take away resources INCLUDING WEAPONS AND ARMOR, and throw you into unavoidable combat with a random selection of companions. These wouldn't be so bad, if the negative effects were based on some sort of decision you made, but they don't. You just get told some of your companions have been hit with some terrible injury and injuries can be brutal. They sometimes take days to recover from and you don't want to fight with an injury. The debuffs are too painful. The other major issue is with the atrocious legion combat. The actual, boots on the ground, squad-based combat is phenomenal. The legion combat is not. It initially was complete nonsense with little to no control and boring as hell. They patched it based on the feedback to make it better. Now it makes sense, but is still boring, with a little more control, and lots of random nonsense. All you do is select a centurion to lead the attack and go through four stages of selecting one of three "stratagem" cards while mashing the spacebar to skip through the boring visual of icons shuffling on screen. This part of the game was so clearly an after thought, it makes me wonder why they even bothered. The game would be 100% better without it. It's not hard at all. Just pick the cards that keep morale up and risk to centurions/commanders down. These battles take up at least half of the game and it unfortunately brings the game down from being a masterpiece.If you can look past these blemishes, you'll have what I feel is the best Ancient Rome game ever made. After the disappointing launches of Imperator Rome and Rome 2: Total War, this game actually lived up to expectations and exceeded them. While this game may not execute the grand strategy mechanics as well as these games, it does execute its narrative and micro managed large scale battles/sieges like no other. It's a strong recommendation from me. I give it a 9/10. It's worth the money. My 90+ hour playtime was just for one playthrough.

_childDocuments_.review: This Expeditions game is such an improvement over Vikings. I played the game on the hardest difficuly and it lasted around 75-80h for a single playthrough. There are multiple regions to explore and they are all very different from each others and beautiful.There are some downsides. The army battles dont matter. You will always win as long as you have more power than the enemy. The cards dont matter, except the loot and centuriones ones. It is just a meaningless system at the moment. The twich drops will eventually become lost to everyone once all the streamers stop playing the game (if you are a streamer, the twitch integration tool is incredibly well done. Use it). Another downside is balance. Its just all over the place and some builds are incredbily OP at the moment. _childDocuments_.review: Just like Expedition: Vikings, Expedition: Rome is an onion with many layers, depth is revealed as the game progresses, new mechanics, maps, items, skills and followers appear as you proceed. _childDocuments_.review: Very interesting turn-based strategy with a focus on melee combat, interesting combat roles and some insane class abilities - all connected by a story with a somewhat freely interpreted historic context. From the tactical combat side I found it interesting that blocking and breaking through bottle necks on the map has a big importance and is supported very well mechanically - you really notice whether you have two of your shield bearers blocking an alley or not. A definitive highlight are the epic siege missions with multiple stages, where different parts of your group have very different goals (this is in my opinion the main excellent feature that future strategy games really should have a look at). Also, turns out fire is really dangerous - especially if it is on your two shield bearers mentioned above that were supposed to hold the line.The most obvious points of critique are all the side features, which are quite clunky - the resource management on the big map is rather meh, legion combat is a lot of systems thrown together for mostly just the bigger number winning and the loot system is very random with a too much inventory management (although the last point keeps cropping up again and again in RPGs, so that probably is just my personal dislike). Also the difficulty of the missions is sometimes very inconsistent.The writing is on the one hand quite good with interesting character moments, but every now and again it feels quite heavy handed. Also for some of the story decisions I still feel like I wasn't given the necessary context of the situation why only A or B are possible options, yet I found myself well entertained throughout.

At the meantime, you can do some side quest and know your companions in Rome, you also know a lot of historical characters and befriend with them. The gameplay is swithcing between RPG and Turn-Based battle, with 4 classes for you to choose(if you buy the DLC, you can got a new one).
