_childDocuments_.review: Found this to be a pretty good first person puzzle game.They've obviously taken a lot of inspiration from the Portal game with the science gone wrong in a massive futuristic lab setting, not to mention the various references to Portal dotted throughout the game. But it does manage to stand on its own two feet with the use of light to create paths through levels where stepping in the shadows will kill you.The puzzles strike a nice balance of being challenging but not too frustrating. Often a bit of experimentation and trying different things will yield the solution.Something thats a nice bonus is that the guy who voices Agent 47 does the voice of the scientist in charge of the lab in this game and he's pretty good in the role too. Whereas in Portal you had Glados making caustic remarks and belittling you as you played, in Lightmatter you effectively have Agent 47 doing the same thing, and its pretty cool.Overall I enjoyed it and I think this game is worth playing if you enjoy first person puzzle games like Portal.

_childDocuments_.review: This review is based on the demo (Levels 1-15).I found Lightmatter to be an enjoyable first-person puzzle game. While there are some parts where your movements are necessarily timed against a moving environment, for the most part the puzzles are solvable at your own pace.Given that each puzzle boils down to manipulating cones of light in such a way as to give the player safe passage, there is a surprising amount of depth to it. There was more than once where I was stumped, only to realise the solution with a metaphorical forehead slap.Having said that, a fair number of unnecessary deaths for me occurred due to strangely large gaps on the rotating platforms (levels 13 & 14). They required jumping at the last possible moment to clear them. While death is rarely punished harshly, costing maybe a minute's worth of progress if you're unlucky, it is annoying that the platforming be so tight in those sections in what is primarily a puzzle game.A final point to mention, when you get to the end of the final level of the demo (level 15), there is a part where Virgil, your erstwhile guide & CEO of Lightmatter Technologies, tell you to "empty your pockets to proceed". Interacting with the button at the gate kicks you out of the game and to Lightmatter's Steam page where you can buy the full version of the game. A very cheeky way to convert players from potential to actual customers.However, this means that you can't get a proper ending of a playthrough of the demo. You're forever stuck at those gates, your choices being to buy the game or quit out!Positives:- Clean graphical style- Intriguing story- Virgil is a super-condescending arse (this is a good thing, trust me!)- Thought provoking puzzles- Mostly chill- Shade thrown at Aperture Labs!Negatives:- Some of the jumping sections are suspect- Possible lack of variety on puzzle mechanics?- It would be nice if there was some incidental interactivity with the world. There are objects scattered everywhere but they are superglued down- They don't let you finish the demo properly! 😆TL;DR: I enjoyed my time there, give it a try and see if it's something you'd like.

_childDocuments_.review: There is no exploration, there is no place for your personal questions about anything. What could have been an interesting setting, is just a bland, generic gameplay land, as you rush past interesting looking objects, which you can't examine at all.You have just WASD, spacebar for jumps, E as use button, then left and right mouse buttons, that's all.- empty, fodder filled locations- bland, grey palette, making the world feel dead- mocking narrator, who thinks his poor jokes are clever- in 10 seconds explained threat of "black glue", which is any area with a shadow- threat of shadows is so "BIG", that you just sink in them and then respawn right where you stood 2 seconds before...you don't even feel like you've died, it feels as a joke, no explanation given HOW you've survived it- for a game about Light puzzles, you don't have a shadow...and when you step in front of a light as part of puzzle solving, the light magically passes through you- the balls on devs, who compare themselves with such games as Portal...yet when they reminded me of Portal, I immediately missed the quality of Portal's story, as well as Glados, who was far more interesting narratorIndie game = automatic high praise from the simple minded people - Sadly this game is just bland, unexciting, fails to make you interested in its own world, it shouts explanation at you about sci-fi themes that would have been worth of deeper exploration and yet they don't bother to do so. I really can't complain too much about it because I'm having fun and it's a nice experience so far.I do have some gripes though.  I have to say I got stuck on one puzzle because you have to set a lamp right on the edge of something and couldn't get it to work. I really had to adjust where I was standing minutely using a controller just to get the right spot where the game would let me drop my lamp. I thought I just couldn't figure it out but had to watch a YouTube tutorial to figure it out. I didn't think that level was designed super well. I like the art style. The game seems pretty demanding for what you get though. Playing it on high settings in 1440p at 60fps using an RX 580 pushed it pretty hard. I'm not sure if it's just the light and shadows being demanding? I'm sure I wouldn't notice much of a difference turning down the settings. Controller support is great. Only downside I saw so far is that I couldn't change the resolution in game with the controller and had to use my mouse and keyboard. Very strange. The other settings were easy to change just not that one.You can cap your frame rate at 30 and 60 or do unlimited. Not sure why there's no 120 or 144.  It seems to be trying hard to be like Portal. There's an Aperature Science reference and it's trying to have some sort of witty demeanor. It's nowhere as funny as the Portal games and comes off as trying too hard. Overall I'm enjoying the game and am eager to play more of it! I was initially concerned that this game would be scary but it really isn't so far. It might sound like I'm griping on it a lot but I'm eager to try more  I'll likely update this review as I play more. Note: This is a review copy I received for being a Humble Partner.

_childDocuments_.review: Lightmatter is yet another game that wants to be Portal, this one perhaps even more so than most. You are in a facility run by a man named Virgil, who has activated his new perpetual energy source, Lightmatter. Naturally, everything went wrong, and you are cast into a world of light and shadow – where the shadows will kill you if you touch them.Better stay in the light, then!The game takes place over the course of 38 levels, all connected together in a single large facility. These are similar to Portal’s test chambers, except that the challenges are not created by Virgil, but rather the environment.Virgil is a somewhat cartoonish figure – a genius inventor whose regard for the health, safety, and welfare of his workers is somewhat questionable (though he does seem to at least not WANT his invention to have negative side effects). He’s very driven, but also a bit paranoid and crazy, and in denial about the fact that his invention isn’t going to pan out because of the whole “shadows that devour all organic matter” thing.The game’s puzzles are decent enough – generally pretty short, and usually relying on the player having some critical insight about how to proceed in moving around lamps and light posts to illuminate their path and activate switches.  Most of them have 1-3 points where you have to be clever, and the puzzles are simple enough not to be tedious but difficult enough to make you stretch your brain a bit to solve them. However, the game doesn’t really have much in the way of unique mechanics – the game is very much centered around carrying around objects and rearranging them, with the shadows are lava being the game’s only real “innovative” mechanic.One of the game’s biggest problems is that it is a bit too obviously inspired by Portal, so it ends up coming off like a pale imitation. Virgil is somewhat funny, but not as funny as GLADOS or Cave Johnson. The game’s puzzles are okay, but the mechanic of the game is nowhere near the cleverness of Portal’s central mechanic, and indeed, overall, the game feels very standard from a mechanical standpoint, and lacks the variety of something like Portal or even The Talos Principle, with only a very limited number of puzzle variants. And while the game does manage to make 38 levels out of these mechanics, it isn’t particularly memorable – it’s all okay from moment to moment, but never really manages to go beyond that.Thus, all in all, it is hard to actually recommend Lightmatter. It isn’t that I wasn’t entertained while I was playing it – it was decent enough – but it feels like an ephemeral experience. There isn’t anything about the game that was memorable beyond its basic premise, the puzzles are okay but nothing to write home about, and while the game looked reasonably attractive with its limited palette, it doesn’t really wow. Even the story feels a bit too standard, with the game following a fairly standard overall progression, down to the final level being longer and timed with “mission control” being furious with you and trying to stop you/kill you/whatever, as is the case with oh so many of these games.Lightmatter is one of those games that I’m going to forget I ever played in a year or so outside of looking back at my Steam achievements and being like, “Oh, yeah, I vaguely remember that game.” But even now, having just finished playing it, I’m having a hard time remembering most of the first half of the game, and even the second half of the game is fading fast from my conscious mind.

_childDocuments_.review: Very fun and original 3D puzzle game; reminds me of other great titles like Portal and especially Talos Principle, but perhaps not as graphically beautiful as those games.  They even threw in some skill based puzzles towards the end where you navigate quickly moving shadows.  Nothing like the action sequences in Portal but still fun.The story line is actually pretty interesting (if somewhat vague) - even making a few passing references to Aperture science.  The dialog is minimal and it doesn't take you away from the action (no cut scenes).The game did crash 3-4 times during my 11-hour play through but it auto-saves often enough that it wasn't too big of a problem. If you like 3D puzzle games this is definitely one of the good ones.  Wait for a sale if you don't want to pay $20 for an 11-hour game.

_childDocuments_.review: Lightmatter is a simple puzzle game where darkness kills you. I almost gave up on the game at the beginning as it starts as a walking simulator but it gets interesting after that. My only complaint is that the game runs at stable 60fps however it feels jittery, it's not smooth, vsync and/or frame limiter makes no difference. _childDocuments_.review: No, it's not as slick as Portal.No, its not as challenging as The Talos Principle.But it gives it a heck of a go.Really great as a first outing and recommended on moderate sale. The game is about 5 hours.Only major complaint is technical, and it's not a small one either. The game seems to have some kind of FPS limit of 50, except the game claims it can run uncapped. My overlay will indeed tell me I'm running at 200fps, but the camera still moves at 50. It's not a deal-breaker for this kind of game really, but it wasn't pleasant. Last issue of note is no control rebinding.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: The idea behind the game and overall presentation is good, yet it is a huge disappointment. Why? It's short, and what it's worse, it ends the moment it starts to be interesting and challenging as the results, I feel it wasted so much potential to be a very good puzzle game. The game has 38 levels. It sounds like a lot, but unfortunately, most of these levels are very easy introductory puzzles to new mechanics that take a minute or two. And that's because most of the time, the game uses only one of the mechanics it has in each puzzle. And only for its last two puzzles, the game finally mixes all of them, creating an exciting challenge that ends quickly, leaving the player wanting more. The game definitely should have at least a few more levels like that.From a technical point of view, the game is fine. It crashes from time to time (but this might be a Proton issue), and support for ultrawide screens is kind of broken (it crops cuts parts of menus).Don't want to give it a negative score, but I recommend getting this one on sale.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: Can't add much to what's been said, every puzzle action with a quirk will stand in the shadow of Portal. This one embraces it and throws in enough easter eggs to say "Hey yeah we know, ok?". On it's own merits the mechanism is at least interesting, the puzzles have a sharp difficulty ramp in the middle, though sometimes it's just a mindset thing as I could roll through quite a few levels before banging my head into the wall. The ending does see a brief switch away from puzzle to action platform and that I think may prove challenging for some, I found it reasonably difficult, in keeping with the game. Otherwise mechanics are clear, and very much like Portal, it is very 'on rails' but that is the nature of all this genre. The atmosphere is quite amusing, voice acting is over-the-top but exceedingly well done, and mainly by David Bateson (I mean, c'mon Agent 47 yells and sneers at you throughout the game, fantastic). So yes, have to say it, it's Portal with Flashlights. It's a good game. Not much replay value once the puzzles get cooked out, and honestly with the short play time (3-5 hours, I found it on the shorter side but I did rush it), I would save this one for a steam sale. It is a good game, honestly, I hope to hell they release a community map development system. That was a shot in the arm for Portal and amped the game value. However, I don't know if this will generate the same cult status but I would enjoy playing around with the mechanic further. Or if not? This was a decent standalone title, highly recommended for fans of sci-fi puzzle-action with the caveat that unless you truly value the atmosphere, humour and mechanic, I would wishlist this and look for a price drop. To the developer, congrats, you really did a fantastic job, thank you for the demo and I look forward to your next work.

From the base concept, to the story execution, to the constantly refreshing puzzles, Toe to tip  it was a tight and fun experience. There were a few frame drops here and there, but most were barely noticeable, and those that were didn't last long. And that's the only criticism I can think of, other than it going by so quickly.

_childDocuments_.review: A short but entertaining Portal clone whose puzzles revolve around light instead of portals. From the white walled puzzle rooms to even the red colored backrooms that you're not supposed to be in, this game draws quite a bit from Portal. Don't take my word for it, as the main businessman references Cave Johnson and there are multiple Portal references in the game. While Cave Johnson has an amazing range of humor and personality, the evil businessman in this game is a lighter version of Bioshock's Andrew Ryan. Its all about business and the 'greater good.'I beat the game in about 3 hours and I feel as though it was the right length in terms of gameplay being entertaining before getting boring. Would I recommend the game at full price? At 3 hours, absolutely not. But while its on sale or from a humble bundle? Ya, I think it was entertaining enough for that value.7.5/10.0
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: This game has to be the greatest tragedy I've ever witnessed.I took my time with this game and completed it twice. Every single puzzles were really well thought out and well paced. None of them made me feel like I was cheating the game, and I couldn't cheese any of them either. That alone is quite the achievement for such a small indie studio.Immediately, I felt the huge inspiration on Portal and The Talos Principle, two franchises that I love to bits and will cherish until my very last breath. It's sad The Talos Principle isn't getting the huge recognition it deserves as to me it's on the same exact level as Portal. But I digress.Lightmatter's visual style is unique and incredibly well thought-out, blending a cold and menacing atmosphere with a novel gameplay mechanic: light keeps, shadows destroy. Get yourself ready to die in this game as this will happen a lot. But instead of being a punishment for not solving the puzzle, it becomes part of the process. Death in this game is a minor setback and an example rather than a problem.Alas, despite how much this game does right and how much love was poured into its making, Tunnel Vision Games unfortunately is no more since four years now.I've listened to everything the developers had to say in the developer commentary mode - one which is presented just like how Valve does! So many of the feelings I had from this game were confirmed by the developers themselves: from the inspiration to the game design. While Lightmatter threaded into Portal's footsteps, it still forged its own path as a puzzle game.The process of introducing each new puzzle elements and mechanics to the player were basically identical to how Valve would in Portal and Half-Life. There are no tutorials, there is only context. The only two concepts the game teaches you directly are how to jump and how to interact with objects. The rest is up to you to figure out: climbing ledges, using portable lamps, lighting up a path with connectors...Dev team, if you are reading this: thank you. This is one of the greatest puzzle games I've ever played. Listening to all of you explain the process of making this game was a delight. From how the narrative came to be, to how the environment was built, was all inspiring and simply amazing. You poured your hearts and souls into making this and it clearly shows.I wish the future was brighter for Tunnel Vision Games. I would have loved to play a future puzzle game from you all.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: Lightmatter is a bit of a one-trick-pony. Overall, I enjoyed the game's unique puzzle mechanics but ultimately the game wasn't terribly deep or long. I finished it in about 6 hours. In other words, after understanding the mechanics of the game and solving the first puzzle, it's pretty much rinse and repeat. But the puzzles do get progressively harder and some are quite ingenious.The obvious inspiration for this game is Portal as is evident by the Easter eggs hidden through out. But the real comparison to me is to The Talos Principle, which I consider to be much more polished and deep.This game is like fast food. It's tasty and initially satisfying but leaves you wanting more. Overall, I'm more positive than negative though, so I recommend trying the demo and seeing if you like it.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: The game is locked to 50 fps regardless of your specs and settings. If you're used to 120+ Hz monitors I guarantee this will look legitimately unplayable to you.There's some obscure hack that may change this but it also crashed on me 20 minutes into it. The actual content looked great so far but the technical implementation is in a horrible state.EDIT: the fps unlock hack works well. However the game has crashed 8 times now (wiping some progress every time) and I'm only about 1/4 into the game. These crashes are unrelated to framerate.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: On the one hand I did enjoy the game. The art style is simple but effective. The story is a straight forward narrative but interesting enough for a single play through.Unfortunately that's all it really has going for it. This is a one and done really simple puzzle platformer that won't take more than a couple of hours to complete and it has no replay value at all. Levels are small linear corridors with a few things to interact with, move a few things around and then solve a couple of jumping sections and move on. Basically a couple minutes of tweaking around while listening to some prerecorded narrative talking at you.I could probably recommend the game for under $10, but at the $20 price point, it's going to get a no from me. Way too short and simple for this price.Just to put it in perspective, if you are really good at puzzles you could finish the game and refund it before the refund timer is expired, and even if you were slow at puzzles I don't think it would take you more than 4 hours (and that's likely you redoing the same jumping puzzles due to mechanics failures for extended periods of time)Of course, you don't really need to read my (or any) reviews. Go ahead and play the first 15 missions of the game for free. But do be aware that it's nearly half the game, buying the full game is only 38 levels in total. The first 15 (free) took me about 30 minutes to finish.Just to be clear, the only reason this is negative is that it isn't worth $20. It's actually a pretty neat game, it's just so short that it isn't worth this price.---EDIT:I played through it again working on achievements simply because I already own the game. I stand by my comments. This should be like $5 tops and that's being generous because I like the voice actor that narrates the game.---

_childDocuments_.review: Many a game have tried to emulate Portal’s format and delivery, but none do so as openly and obviously as Lightmatter, an indie first person puzzle that will take around two hours to complete.You are, for all intents and purposes, a faceless protagonist, waking up to the wailing of sirens in front of a misleading exit sign. A few drops and tumbles later, you find yourself at the doorstep of a mysterious underground laboratory, while the shadows that surround you glow eerily…From the first steps you take in Lightmatter Industries’ sprawling facility, you get a strong vibe of familiarity: Virgil’s snarky voice is this game’s GlaDOS, the quick succession of puzzle rooms predicts a short, but intense experience; exposition is delivered mostly through radio banter and audio logs. Lightmatter doesn’t try to hide its inspiration; the game is littered with references to Aperture Laboratories.The first aspect that sets Lightmatter apart is its look: a tame cel-shaded design is nothing to write home about, however the way things are rendered in the dark displays an interesting concept - objects and walls have outlines and the shadows are all hard, highlighting the lethality of the space. The level design is streamlined, but dense in props and decoration; its richness in detail more than makes up for the almost monochromatic saturation. Perhaps the best aspect of the game - its sound design - completely overshadows its highly derivative story. The eclectic use of synths, drones and digital ambient are perfectly fitting for the setting and change the tone and tempo of every beat in the script: just like in Portal, the rigid initial structure breaks at one point, abandoning the series of tests for an escape sequence and a kind of bossfight. While Portal never gives up using its titular mechanic up until the end, Lightmatter’s final ten minutes consist of a glorified running simulator with minimal platforming elements.The minimalistic cast, consisting of two voiced characters, works as intended. David Bateson of Hitman fame does the heavy lifting as Virgil, the facility’s owner, while Natalie Hitzel provided the voice talent for the tape recorders you collect throughout your journey. Their function is mostly to deliver exposition and a couple of twists, and while their work is engaging, they weren’t given much to work with in the script. Compared to J.K. Simmons hilarious unraveling as Cave Johnson, Virgil is a vaguely creepy milquetoast villain perpetually providing non-working bridges and scolding you for his own incompetence. As the game’s title suggests, the gimmick here has to do with light. More specifically, the shadows will kill you, so your objective will always be to build a path of light leading to the exit. When traversing the 38 levels that make up the campaign, you will have to move lamps and, later on, photon connectors in order to achieve that goal. They start out simple and ramp up the difficulty, introducing new mechanics every few rooms, but considering you only use two types of props and their limited functionality, I can’t help but feel there could have been more done with the whole “darkness is lava” philosophy (a certain other indie game called Contrast comes to mind). The hardest any puzzle ever gets is making the lamp positions extremely specific, but I can't imagine anyone ever getting stuck running this. Which is fair, the point here isn’t to get you stuck, but rather to move at a pace where the intrigue can unravel organically. Still, there's a certain kind of satisfaction you get when overcoming particularly difficult or tricky puzzles and Lightmatter has zero chances of delivering that sensation on account of its lackluster design philosophy.There are only so many permutations to the “moving lamps around” game design doctrine, so if you’re looking for more depth in the same genre, The Talos Principle might prove a more worthy diversion than Lightmatter. What this game promises are a bunch of entry-level physics jokes tying together a paper thin plot all dressed up in competent visuals and marvelous sound. Replayability is conditioned by a few achievements collectionists will spend an extra hour getting and an alternate ending you can unlock by idling at a key moment. Only buy this if you're so in love with Portal you could potentially befriend its mentally challenged third cousin for a copycat nostalgia trip.

_childDocuments_.review: A fun and clever first person puzzle game. You could say it's a Portal 2 ripoff, and in many ways it will remind you of it: story, level design, progression system, the great voice acting, and many in-your-face direct references to it.Still, it's a great game if you're gonna copy one, and a fun puzzle game by it's on merit. The only shame it's that 3-4 hours long, a bit too short. If you get it at a discount you'll have your share of fun with it.

_childDocuments_.review: First and foremost this is a first person puzzler, except the puzzles are hardly challenging and there is very little variety. You'll race through the first half of the game with barely a pause, mildly entertained but wondering when it'll pick up, and then before you know it you're at the final level more bemused than amused. By then you'll be tired of the bland aesthetics and eager to finish the game. And this is where Lightmatter really kicks you in the nuts. Because instead of taking a cerebral approach, the game pitches you into a punishing session of tedious platforming. You'll die (a lot) and grit your teeth and swear, all the while wondering why no one warned you that the game ended like this. I hated it.And the game crashed to desktop with tiresome frequency. Thankfully it loads up fast.Lightmatter is not entirely without its charms. The story and voice acting are decent enough, and hats off to the devs for all the Portal/Cave Johnson references. It's also an easy 100% achievements-wise so if that's important to you, and you like first person platforming, maybe you'll get more out of this than I did. Just wait for a sale.Lightmatter... it started out 10/10, was still a respectable 6/10 by the halfway mark, but staggered across the finish line a lowly and unloved 4/10.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: Lightmatter took me 9 hours to complete both endings and while I wasn’t really satisfied with either ending, the journey to get there was a lot of fun.  Lightmatter isn’t shy when it shows its love for Portal but it is really heavy on the mechanics from The Talos Principle.  Instead of jammers, you’ve got spotlights and instead of connectors you’ve got photon connectors.  ----------------------+  great antagonist.  Virgil is no Cave Johnson or GlaDos but he is suitably condescending and megalomaniacal.  I hated him but in a good way.+  intelligent saves (for the most part).  You will be consumed by the shadows….oh yeah I didn’t mention that standing on a shadow will tear you apart on a sub-atomic level did I?  You will die in Lightmatter.  A lot….if you are anything like me.  Luckily if your puzzle solving was on the right track it will start you off from roughly where you just died.  If you exit out of the game though it set me back to the beginning of the whole stage it seemed.+  fluid movement.  You move in a very Portal-esque butter-like smootheness and have an ample jump.  There are some platforming moments in the game and you will be required to do a bit of gymnastics.  But generally the game is focused on the puzzles.+  puzzles.  Lightmatter puzzles ramp very well and scaffold you along the way.  They mostly fall in the range of just challenging enough to not feel too casual but there are some way easy ones and there are some that will really have you scratching your head until you hit that “oh, I’m an idiot” moment and realise the answer was right in front of you the entire time.+  easter eggs.  If you like finding these little moments in games, Lightmatter is stuffed with them.  As you would imagine there are Portal ones galore and many more.  I won’t spoil them here.+  writing and voicing.  Virgil and a woman we hear on some audio tapes are voiced excellently.  There is also a ton of idle monologue.  What I mean is that when you are solving a puzzle or are loitering in an area, Virgil will switch on his mic to berate you in a number of witty ways.  These don’t seem to repeat and its little things like this that make a game for me.+  options.  There is a slew of options.  A music player to sample the voice and the level music.  Level selector to go back and hunt for missing achievements.  There is also an unobtrusive speedrun stat tracker for all you speed demons.  + you got something to say devs?  Yes, yes they do.  I am a sucker for a great director's commentary and there is a TON here._________________-  expectations.  I expected another mechanic to be thrown in, like mirrors to reflect light, or a flashlight you could actually aim 360 degrees around a room (you can’t aim the spotlights, merely send light straight ahead).  So when not even a 3rd item was found to spice up the puzzles, I felt a bit deflated.   -  crashes.   FIXED__________________So there you have Lightmatter.  It’s a pretty smart puzzler that has some great moments and uses Talos Principle mechanics but sticks to a more humourous Portal kind of story.  The games that it pays homage to are better though and I found Lightmatter to be on more of a Turing Test or Q.U.B.E. level of quality.    Definitely a thumbs up though and worth a play.Edit:  Developers came through quick on fixing the crashes as promised.  Also they continue to add minor fixes for visuals, controls and running the game.  They recently added a ton of directors commentary which is really great to listen to.  Thanks for this great game and your continued work on  it post launch.

_childDocuments_.review: Played the free (first 15 levels) Lightmatter.  It was a very enjoyable 3 hours to do this... I'm guessing that the full game will take 10 hours to complete.  Appears to be a single play through - unless you are into Speed Runs.  Since I am not, this is a once and done - so the value per time just isn't there for me at $19.99. _childDocuments_.review: Lightmatter is a fun -and sometimes maddening- puzzle game.  You basically have to figure out how to light your path through an underground facility whilst being (mostly) guided by the creator of the facility.  I won't elaborate as to not spoil the game.   It is kind of along the lines of "Portal."   You will see a number of reviews that make the same comparison.  It's fun, and worth the $20 for what you get out of it.  I do wish the ending was a bit more elaborate as to the main character; it would have been nice to see some more development along those lines.   All that said, buy it.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: The puzzles were fun, the platforming wasn't horrendous, and the main character was interesting. The game tries so hard to compare itself to Portal, I just want to give it a pep talk, because I really do think it stands well on its own. Which is strange to say, since the thing I found most interesting about the story was something I don't think was intentional at all. Spoilers and some literary analysis below.As soon as the discussion of James started coming up, I started reading Virgil more and more as a gay man, which honestly added a very interesting layer to the game. I don't usually like it when games make the villains gay, but having it be sub-textual helped, as well as Virgil being the only character that we ever heard the point of view from. There's something in the story of a privileged gay man believing he will forever be the underdog, betrayed and persecuted from all sides, blindly seeking corporate glory with the thin excuse of saving humanity. It makes his motivations more three-dimensional to me. It was honestly enjoyable to see so deeply into Virgil's point of view, and yet so vehemently disagree with it. He wanted to save the world by killing the few he thought he could get away with. It honestly reads as a story about the dangers of gay assimilation, to me. The dangers of becoming what you have once faced yourself.Basically, if you like to analyse media and like Portal or the Talos Principle, give this game a shot. It undermines itself by hamming up the references like a LOT, but the gameplay is solid and the story is unexpectedly nuanced.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: Personally, If you're feeling bored i would recommend the game.The game is great at best, but annoying at worst. I really like the idea of the 'shadows are lava' mechanicBut some levels just had this strange difficulty spike, and then the next level would just be easy.Some areas I like more than others, the greenhouse area looked amazing, while some area looked dull, like the furnace room. just the furnace room, i hate the furnace room.The optional levels are really well made, and actually give a lot in terms of story.And the attention to detail is amazing,  Of course i'll need to address the elephant in the room. The game doesn't have good optimization, and you will never get a smooth framerate with an average computer. I turned down the graphic settings in order to make the framerate just above tolerable for me.Overall good game, just needs a little improvement in some places.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: This is really two games in one and chances are if you like one part, you won't like the other.  What I consider the main part of the game is a puzzle type game, reminiscent of the Talos Principle, which I loved.  The closing portion is a fast-paced running, jumping game for which you want a gaming controller and probably will need to take several runs at it.  I got most of the way through (I think) when the game crashed and lost my progress.  I never felt the motivation to do it all over again so I guess I lost out on the back story.  Overall I thought it was enjoyable though.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: Tried the free demo and then immediately bought the full game. (The demo is also reasonably long.)The game's core mechanic of shadows = death is a fascinating concept that's executed well and allows for a creative variety of puzzles, presented alongside stellar voice work and an interesting, well paced story.The gameplay is extremely reminiscent of portal (which the game references a couple of times) but still maintains it's own unique identity.I thoroughly enjoyed playing, definitely recommend if you're interested in puzzle games/liked portal 1/2.10/10
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: I'm enjoying this game a lot. It's just what I like: puzzles with minimal "moving parts" that require a lot of switching around. No puzzles requiring fast reactions (at least so far and I think I'm close to the end), just a lot of thinking and setting the pieces just right. All that thinking means this is not something you can play after a hard day at work. You need a well rested brain, especially towards the end. I got a -25% coupon for the DLC that unlocks the game, and I think this is worth what I paid.Edit: I finished the game, and didn't like the last parts. There were a lot of well-timed jumps needed, which is what I hate in games, but fortunately failing (which I did a lot) doesn't set you back too much as long as you don't exit the game. And of course, if I can do it, most other players should have no major problems with those parts.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: A wonderful tribute to Portal, and a masterpiece of a puzzle adventure, combining fun, clever gameplay, and an interesting story with fun characters. Although it can feel a bit on the nose with its' Portal references, considering how much this game evokes the spirit of the game, it's excusable. I managed to beat it in 4 hours with my peanut brain, but I assure you that's the perfect length for it.If you enjoyed Portal, that's definitely the game for you.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: Opinion:-The game is amazing, thou on small scale. Would gladly wait for a second game on a much bigger scale!-The game gives you a Portal 1 vibe (they even reference Portal). But they differ in the correct place. Portal uses... wel, portals and Lightmatter uses... light... .Introduction:-Light is everything here, shadows are the void. Navigate your way through the research center by moving lamps, conencting lightbeam rods and use parkour. Don't forget to use your brain.Pros:++ Portal like feeling but with a different fun concept.+   The story is fun like what comments the scientist makes on whatever you do or ?are? .+   Learn to make pathways with limited resources.++ Some forget that a demo can change the persons opinion. Luckly there is a demo here (6 levels).Cons:~  Though fun, it was shorter then expected-   Most visuals/items/views are bland to the eye or not important to either story or interraction.Conclusion:This game is a sprout of a fruit tree. You know it can grow, it has the potential and you can be sure it will be a sturdy tree that gives a lot of fruit. Although it is comparable to a massive tree like Portal, it is a special game on it's own.Try the demo and judge for yourselves.A good 7.5/10 for me
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: Very good mix between Portal 2 & The Talos Principle. The story and the voice acting are really good. If you like puzzle games, you will like this one for sure. The difficulty is perfect (a little bit too easy sometimes), I almost didn't have to search for solutions on the internet.However: the game is too short in my opinion, the ending is not great, and there are lags in the latest part of the game if you have a bad or medium graphic card. Moreover, I would have liked to see 1 or 2 characters like in Portal 2. (we see nobody in the game).Conclusion: I recommend it but don't expect something long.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: Nice concept, puzzles and story. Overall fun. A few hard puzzles.Short game (5 hours). Some parts were too walking-simulator-like for my taste, they were weird to have with the game's graphics (was I supposed to take my time to enjoy them?).Ambiance is Portal-esque done right. Gameplay though, I'd say the game is easier than Portal 1/2.Horrible performance (low fps) in some areas, even with the minimum graphic settings.100% achievements is easy. I probably wouldn't have even needed a guide if all the bonus achievements weren't based on .
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: This hidden gem took me around 5-6 hours to beat, and for its short length, it is a simple, yet challenging portal-esc puzzler. There aren't many game mechanics at all, but the game does make use of them to create some (at times) tricky puzzles. Personally I only had to use a guide for one level, (this is coming from a person who SUCKS at puzzles) so you shouldn't have too much trouble progressing if you're more interested in the story.The references to Portal and the snarkiness of Virgil make his dialogue entertaining to listen to as your travel through the depths of the facility. In addition, the lack of loading screens (Instead utilizing passive unloading of the game environment) help greatly with immersion. The mountain base feels like one singular complex instead of an infinitely spanning facility connected with elevators like in Portal 2.My only complaint is that the game tends to crash during play. (Especially during the long levels. Looking at you, level 22) However, since nobody else seems to have the same problem, I'll attribute it to the older PC I was running at the time.However, if you're looking for a challenge, this isn't the game for you. For these people, try out The Talos Principle. It has a large array of difficult puzzles.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: After trying out the free version of the game (30-50 mins of gameplay) I've taken a break only to get my wallet and write this review. What do we have so far?- nice art style: yes- great sfx: yes- smooth mechanics: yes- engaging gameplay: yes- intriguing storyline: yes- sarcastic narrator who thinks you're a potato brain: yes- cake: yes- Aperture Science: almost- cat(s): possibleSubtotal: absolutely beautiful Portal successorp.s. dev team, you have my full support and love
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly I think this game is hella underrated. While it definitely requires some pricey PC specs to play comfortably, the game is a sweet ride downtown. The art style, the characters, the story, the puzzle mechanics, the secret achievements, and especially the references to other games all made this a W in my book.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: This game had me giving shadows the side eye for days! Clever and unique, with nods to my favorite games. Some of the puzzles will have you thinking in dimensions you never considered before. Your guide through the whole game is exceptionally believable in their role too. The style of animation/design is somewhere between cell shading and realistic that fits the light vs. dark atmosphere perfectly.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: There's games that are inspired by Portal... then there's games that want to be Portal, this is the latter. It doesn't make the game bad but it does make it a little bit cringeworthy. That being said the puzzles are all about removing the dark with a couple of methods of light manipulation all whilst being berated by an omnipotent gamemaster (like Portal).The core gameplay is good and the story is above average (like Portal) but the game is wayyyyy too short (like Portal) and I guess you could try and speedrun it for some replayability (like Portal) but its a one and done game (like Portal)Recommended on sale.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: Fun little puzzle game with a unique concept. Reminds me a lot of my time playing Portal with the laboratory setting and quippy antagonist. That being said I can't recommend buying this at full price, I'm not particularly clever at solving puzzles and I still finished the game in less than 4 hours. It could really benefit well from being at least twice as long or make some of the puzzles require a bit more brain power.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: Hi-rez first-person puzzle platformer.  You are trapped in a facility that's developing a new technology, except something has gone wrong, and now touching any shadow will kill you.  Use mechanisms to move platforms and portable lights to chase the shadows away.  Escape the facility.You are ostensibly a guest at the launch of the new Lightmatter technology.  Or, more accurately, you wake up on the floor of a heavily damaged building.  You see the last tram leaving the facility without you.  That leaves only two people in a building that seems to be falling apart around you: you, and Virgil, the CEO.  He's not actually with you, but he has cameras to watch you and a speaker system to speak to you and guide you out.You can get a pretty good feel for Virgil from the blurb on the store page. "This invitation includes a one hour tour through my facility, a ten second glance at the launch of Lightmatter, as well as five seconds of eye contact—with me."  The game involves running through corridors, jumping over gaps, avoiding shadows, and listening to Virgil.  It's okay not to like him...he doesn't think much of you either. "Now, move to the elevator....Excellent.  You've already exceeded my expectations of you,."Due to whatever the Lightmatter project has done, which seems to involve making a form of solid light, shadows have taken on a more tangible form as well, and consume organic matter...namely, you.  Touch a shadow and die.  As you progress, you will need to manipulate your environment to ensure you have a lit path.  Using buttons to move platforms can sometimes remove shadows.  There are also portable lamps you can position, though you can't jump while carrying one, and I suspect you can't leave an area with one.  Dying from touching a shadow doesn't cost you much progress, so there's little risk in experimenting.The puzzles are interesting.  Virgil does get annoying, but I assume that's a feature.  Though I'll be disappointed if I don't get to punch him at the end of the game.The game does come with a very unfortunate launcher.  Others have said it doesn't add anything to the game and is just an annoyance.  My experience with it was stronger: it displayed bigger than my screen, cut off on all four sides, and I couldn't actually get to the game with it.  I had to go into the installation directory and find the executable to use directly. (Perhaps Virgil designed it.)Other than the launcher, though, I'm generally satisfied with what I've seen so far.  I got it a HB bindle, but the current store price of $19.99 isn't unreasonable for the amount of work that went into the game.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: They freakin' did the unthinkable! No puzzle game has ever really hooked me, but once I got a few minutes into Lightmatter, I just couldn't stop playing. I loved the fact that the mechanics are so simple, but the levels so brain-wrecking, instead of advanced mechanics that take forever to understand but boring levels.If you're like me and puzzle games aren't typically your jam, I'd encourage you to give this one a try. It very positively surprised me :)
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: Lightmatter is a first person puzzle game all about light and how it matters. Shadows kill you, and that's basically all the gameplay mechanics there is! You get exactly two tools to fight these shadows: a spotlight and a sort of beam that connects to other beams and forms a path of light. They are intuitive to use, but the beam comes in quite late, giving you only one tool to use for most of the game. Lightmatter feels slightly repetitive because of this, but also because the game world is quite dull. The graphics style is certainly unique, but the world itself doesn't feel alive. It's the same environments over and over, nothing moves and you barely see any signs of life in the world. The story is driven by two characters only. The player is silent and gets constant intercom traffic from this crazy scientist/CEO. The voice acting is amazing, but the comedy feels like it tries for a Portal and Stanley Parable mix. Unfortunately, it misses the sweet spot those games hit. It feels a little forced and I get the feeling the writers couldn't decide if he had to be menacing or funny so he ended up being neither. It would've worked better if they focused on the mental side instead of the condescending sarcasm. There's a few audiologs throughout the game but they're forgettable.As for difficulty, Lightmatter is just right for most of the game. It makes your brain work hard enough but without melting it, except for one or two puzzles. Expect between 3 and 5 hours of playtime depending on how good you are at puzzles. What I found disappointing is that in the last ten minutes, the game introduces some really well done first person platforming. This never appeared in the hours leading up to that point, even though it could have really mixed up the slightly repetitive puzzles if it had been sprinkled throughout the game instead of getting it all at once in the ending sequence. All in all, Lightmatter is a fun little puzzle game. For it's full price, I can't recommend it because it's short and the story is a bit more miss than hit, but at a 50% or more discount you definitely get your money's worth in puzzles.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: tentative yes, the light mechanic is good, and the puzzles in the back half are pretty good, but the middlish ones before the second major mechanic is introduced are a bit sloggy. The game is very inspired by portal (they aren't hiding that) but i think it could've done with 1 or 2 more ways to interact with the light, but not bad
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: A great puzzle game, I found it more similar to the Talos Principle than Portal (seems to be what people compare it to).While the game has unlocked frame rate, it has a weird 50 FPS lock on the camera itself, which makes the game a stuttery mess. You can fix it yourself by checking out the discussion here since devs seem to have abandoned the game:
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: Lightmatter is one of the best puzzle games i played in a while, it's basically the love child of the portal franchise and the Talos principle, it is delightfully written, and designed, it's scattered with Easter eggs, and has a unique style I've never seen in a puzzle game, I see it as a tribute to the portal franchise and a damm good one. HIGHLY recommended.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: Excellent puzzle game. Not too hard, not too easy. If you're a hardcore puzzle gamer, you'll finish this game in a few hours. If you're a casual puzzler, count about 8 hours. And then achievement hunting can begin ;)The story is simple but well executed, the sass from the CEO is legendary.Really enjoyed playing this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: Lightmatter is a really neat little game. Taking me under 4 hours to beat, it’s not particularly long, but I do not think that is a bad thing, since the puzzles are well designed and it ends before it overstays its welcome. The game pretty much has 1 mechanic: shadows kill you. It’s easy to understand and the high contrast art style makes it very clear what will kill you and what will not. Using this simple concept, they have managed to make many interesting puzzles. Some of them I flew through, but there were a number of them that I had to stop and think about.While you do the puzzles you get talked at by a somewhat comedic CEO, who feels like he wants to be a Portal character. Really, between all the references and callbacks to Portal, this whole game feels like it wants to be Portal. I do not think that is a bad thing, because Portal is amazing, but sometimes it feels a bit weird how hard this game tries since I do not think it has any relation to Portal. Of course this game is not as good as Portal, but it is still very good.My biggest complaint would be it felt way too sensitive. If even one toe gently grazes the darkness, the dying animation will start and there is nothing you can do. At times this can be very frustrating, even if it is my fault for touching the clearly marked darkness. There is also something weird with framerate. The game says it’s running well above 60, but it feels like its running below 60.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: Lightmatter is a pretty short and fun puzzle game, the story is pretty simple and easily enjoyable. However, as much as I had fun while doing the puzzles, the game is quite buggy, there were two instances of bugs I found, one of them kept making my game crash constantly, and to fix it, I had to change the FPS Limiter settings to 60 instead of Unlocked. The second problem I encountered was that during level 19 my game ran into a problem were the screen would flicker with random colors and I couldn't see anything, to fix I had to re-download the game. Besides those bugs, the game is quite fun, I would suggest playing it if you like puzzles.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: Only on sale, for a very low price, or if you can find a key elsewhere for 3 to 4 bucks)Some of the puzzles are very basic, because there are only 2 tools to solve puzzles with,but their combination SOMETIMES makes for an actually really good experience.The writing is mostly weak. Some humor is ok, but it's mostly unfunny and mentions portal too often to leech off its glory.And in the late stages it's just a dumb platformer...
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: Similar yet unique in its own way!First. A lot of people say that this game is really similar to the Portal series, and I can somehow agree to that.1. You are similarly set in a broken down research facility.2. You need to move from one room to another through the use of some physics-related mechanic.3. There is a single powerful force that oversees you and can manipulate your environment.4. There is an underlying story that exposes the corruption of the power.5. At some point in the game, you veer away from the course that the "overseer" intends you to take.6. The overall feel of the game has some dark, sinister vibe to it.So that's some of the similarities. BUT! We can't say that it's a direct copy of Portal. Yes, they are of the same genre, but the totality is different. While Portal primarily focuses on momentum, kinematics and kinetics; Lightmatter goes for optics - light's physics, trajectory, etc. You can't use the same method of thought for the two games.Now. Focusing on Lightmatter. It's a very well-crafted game. The graphics are "cartoony" but well executed. The dark areas look menacing. The level layout is well-made to get the player into the controls and movement, as well as the first few obstacles which introduce the mechanic of dying when stepping in the darkness. The physics and the controls aren't wonky or overly-sensitive. The degree of difficulty of the puzzles are also well-done and won't frustrate players right of the bat.As for any negatives. The only thing that I'd say is that sometimes, the voice-over can be too much. It's a great way to tell the story, but it feels a little too "in your ear" rather than "coming from the overhead speakers in the facility". But that's it.Overall, I'd give this game a 9/10. And I'm sure anyone who plays the demo would be immensely urged to purchase the full version.Please do check out my gameplay video of this game:Thank you very much!
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: Lightmatter is an absolutely fine 6.5/10 puzzle game.  Not particularly good but also not badIt's short at around 4-6 hours to 100%, the puzzles for the most part are easy and don't really ramp up in complexity like they do in The Talos Principle or Portal.  The only puzzle I had trouble with was the final and I was far more annoyed than satisfied when I stumbled into the solution.  That said it's fun enough to play through, it looks nice and the voice acting is surprisingly good.  Get it on sale.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: I've been going through my library looking for games to 100% and this game caught my eye again. I first played the demo back when it came out and forgot about the game until now.I am happy that I found this game again because it is a very fun experience. The mechanics felt great, the game looked great and the voice acting both for English and Danish is superb. I do think that the game is flawed but I don't expect the absolute most polished game from a small team such as this and for some reason the game looks lower FPS than it really is. I think it has something to do with how they programmed the way you control the camera because when the game took control of the camera it looked insanely smooth.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: Why is this the demo but also required for the full game? Just have a separate demo.Crossposted with my review of the full game - Summary: A puzzle game trying to be Portal, and it does an okay but not great job. Worth buying on sale, maybe too short otherwise.Pros:+ Good level design if a bit linear and the difficulty ramp up is good.+ Story is a nice plotline if overplayed at the end, and the dialogue is funny.+ Runs well, looks nice, no crashes.+ Autosave is good.Cons:- Quite short for the price, only took me 3 hours for my playthrough.- Only 3 puzzle mechanics (flashlights, beams, and buttons to move platforms) meant the puzzles ended up feeling pretty similar to each other, especially when I thought they were hinting at other mechanics to come (e.g. the plants) and then they never showed up.- Overly linear. The devs want to force you to see everything they've built, so there's not a lot of things to discover. Similar to portal you crawl through some maintenance parts of the facility and find secret tape recorders, but they're all out in the open in linear order which doesn't really make sense given the story.- References to Portal are fun but kept reminding me I wasn't playing Portal which is a better game.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: A truly good puzzle game. Story is easy to pick up on and enjoy the theme and get in the place of the character.BUTWhen you are stuck there is no help , I would imagine after a specific time there would be a hint but there is none.+The graphics are simple but modern and good looking.+Funny/entertaining dialog +A hella of a good puzzle-No help when it is needed-Couldn't even get pass the demo of the game-Passing a puzzle/level isn't rewardingWell if you have the time and patience this is a game for you.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: Lightmatter is a fun, albeit rather kind of short (4-5 hours) puzzle game. The puzzles are fun and challenging, but not so difficult to the point where it's frustrating and unenjoyable. The narrative is enjoyable and it's interesting to listen to the one sided conversations. The game took me 4-5 hours to get through, and then another roughly 2 hours to get the bonus achievements, though partly because they require re-solving some of the puzzles and waiting for the achievement to trigger. The concept of "Play the first hour and then decide if you want to buy it" is a phenomenal option, in my opinion. You play enough of the game to get hooked and interested and then might be more likely to buy the full game after, without having to download anything else. It's like a demo, but your progress saves and it is identical to the base game.I recommend this game to people who were fans of the Portal series, as it is rather similar in feeling.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: Would Definetly recommend, copped it in the Humble Bundle, believing it to be a B-Tech Portals Rip Off, but it exceeded my expectations, with unique and memorable puzzles and mechanics that always stayed fresh and never became frustrating (Though still with alot of problem solving, which is a hard balance). This is a top tier game and deserves so much more praise. Its story, art style, mechanics and even voice acting, come together as one wholeheartedly amazing experiences. Get this game now! That is an order! And Dev's give us lightmatter 2 plz ASAP, ik time constraints, but i just want more of this game!!!!!!!
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: It would be a neat gimmicky puzzle game, with a twist on the "floor is lava" taht clearly takes cues from Portal.But didn't take cues when it comes to a being well intagreted puzzle-platformer. It starts as a almost entirely puzzle game.At the finale they decided to turn it into a platformer, despite the fact that  minimal twitch skills were required up to that point. It has a four-stage stucture with several savepoints and several challenging parts. Then it crashed and put me back to the start of the sequence, despite the fact I almost finished.Neat game, but be prepared for this final twist.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: I can't seem to be able to finish this game. There are no more checkpoints towards the end and it keeps on crashing. After repeating the 10-15 min of playtime from the reactor shutdown checkpoint to when it crashes for a couple of times, I'm fed up with it. That, combined with the overall tendency to crash on a random basis and, and being fed up with the dialogs, leads me to not recommending the game. It has its moments, but for the last 5 hours, it just made me rather frustrated.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: My recommendation comes with a major caveat. This game is short, the ending is mediocre, and it tries to be Portal without any of the real spark that that game had. But, it's got some interesting puzzles and fun mechanics, the story is good until the ending, and the genre of good puzzle platformers like this is pretty slim.Buy it if you want more Portal-esque gameplay and don't mind paying $20 for a couple of hours of fun. Wait for a sale if you have any concerns about entertainment to time ratios. Pass if you're looking for an actual solid ending or real challenging puzzles.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: Short but fun game with interesting narrative. Basically game took some mechanics from The Talos Principle, narration style from The Stanley Parable, blended with their gaming idea and made pretty fun game.  There are many easter eggs, mostly from Portal games. Downside is that it can be beaten in 4-5 hours.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: This game was an utter pleasure, you can jump, use (carry and place, push buttons and levers) and WASD. What seems simplistic will challenge your braincells sometimes more, sometimes less when you try to trace your path through deadly shadows to escape the Lightmatter facility, where Virgil is your only companion through crackling radio communication. It's a very nice puzzle platformer with a nice narrative, mostly requiring brainworks and sometimes also courage. Would recommend anytime! If you try it, I wish you strength, conviction and lots of light on your path.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: Very good puzzle games. Wears it's influences on it's sleeve for sure, and the portal references are kind of cute at first, but felt a little forced later on. But Virgil was a good antagonist and all the voice acting was very solid. The puzzles were challenging but not headache inducing or too punishing. Generally just a really good puzzle game with a cool idea executed well throughout and with enough variety that it felt just right.Will it go down as a classic like portal or the like? Not really. But that doesn't mean it isn't a great puzzle game in it's own right.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: Did you like Portal, and have you already played Portal 2?This is a first-person puzzler. As one of the intro stages says, imagine the floor is lava, but instead of lava, it's shadows. So you walk around shining light on areas, to get to the exit of the room. Step on a shadow, and die. The gameplay is great, the puzzle solutions are fair, and a lot of the quality of life issues are great. Checkpointing is friendly, the narrator's hints are well timed. It is a perfectly well made game, and the length is perfect for a weekend.This is not as good as Portal/Portal 2, nor is is the greatest imitation I have played. Lightmatter does not bring much new to the genre. It plays a lot like Portal - you are a silent protagonist, there is a GLaDos/Cave Johnson style narrator, a lot of the aesthetics,  and pretty much every joke from Portal 1 is referenced. There are so many, there should be an achievement for finding them all. So, if like me, you've replayed Portal too many times, this is a good game for the weekend. Well made, enjoyable. But I'd also recommend you check out Antimatter, Talos Principle, and some time on Google because there are number of games in this genre for you to explore.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: As other folks have mentioned, this has a similar feel to Portal and actually had a couple of references to Portal in the game.  I really enjoyed it and was able to beat it in about 8 hours.You are in a big factory that produces a substance called lightmatter.  Basically a source of light, but the factory is being overrun by shadows which leech your life, so if you step in a shadow you die.  In order to get out of the factory, you have to use lamps and different devices to manipulate the light and create paths so you can get past the shadows.  As you progress you are monitored/guided by one of the founders who is speaking to you over the coms and providing some backstory.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: A wonderful puzzle game with a simple concept taken to the extremes. Lots of fantastic dialogue and story which worked very well with the visual style. Clearly Portal inspired, but in a way that feels like Aperture's crazy cousin rather than a spin-off or lame clone. Thoroughly enjoyed and hoping for future content just like this!
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: Recommended on sale, as it's a little on the short side, although long enough. This is a good first-person puzzle game. Not as good as Portal / Portal 2 (but then what is?), but far from the worst I've played either.The important things, the puzzle designs, are done very well, and use interesting mechanics which I hadn't seen before. None had me stumped for ages or reaching for a guide, but they weren't all obvious either, with several requiring a bit of thought and experimentation.The game has three phases where slightly different mechanics have the focus. They all work fine, but be warned that one requires some dexterity. It doesn't go on for long, and I got through it without issues, but if you're a puzzles-only person who struggles with first-person movement in a hurry then it might cause problems; for anyone else, it's nothing to worry about.I feel like the main puzzle mechanics could've been combined a bit more instead of being largely segmented with only a small overlap, but it's also nice to play something without loads of filler and repetition.The story / narrator-antagonist-helper side of things is the usual. Portal seems to have completely defined this genre and everything else has to emulate it, for better or worse. It does the job here and also doesn't get in your way, but it's nothing new on that front.Graphically, it's a very stylised, flat-shaded / untextured look to things and almost monochrome. I found the rooms looked a bit samey from place to place, which was sometimes disorientating if I respawned, as I wasn't sure which direction I was heading in anymore. Very minor issue, though, as you're never in that large an area and won't be lost for more than a second.Performance is... weird. The game seems to have an issue, mentioned in some threads, where the graphics engine runs at 60 FPS or whatever, but the actual camera movement (turning, walking/running) updates are reportedly capped at 50Hz or something. I immediately noticed movement and turning felt jerky, despite getting 60 FPS, but I did get used to it after half an hour or so and it didn't spoil things.Ran fine with maxed settings at 4K on my 1080ti. I also tried it briefly on my Steam Deck and it ran very well on that as well (felt smoother, in fact, maybe because I limited it to 30 FPS and no longer had that mismatch between framerate and movement updates). I didn't play for long on the Deck, though, as I was outdoors and found the game's environments difficult to see properly, what with them having a lot of areas in very dark lighting. Not the game's fault at all, and everything is easy to see back indoors on my monitor.Level design is good in terms of serving puzzles, but bad in terms of selling you on the idea that you're in a real place. Everything feels arbitrarily put together just to create the geometry needed for the puzzles, rather than a place that makes sense in terms of people using it to do work and experiments. Lots of games, especially puzzle games, have that flaw, so it's just a minor thing.In summary, if you want a good first-person puzzle game with some fresh mechanics, this should be somewhere on your list.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: Overall a good game but I am sorry, the story is too short (around 2-3 hours gameplay, if not stuck) for this price, lower than $10 is much better.  Also, if there are more gamemodes it should be much better, like (portal 2) multiplayer workshop level design, etc. it might worth $20.I would recommend this game because of all the effort and it is still a good game, well designed levels and storyline.  However, there are a lot of empty space in the storyline, which needs to be filled up.  For now, it feels empty after finishing the campaign (especially when there are even nothing to do after finishing it).  Really hope that there are more stuff to do after finishing the campaign, just like other $20 games.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: Lightmatter is an unusually interesting game that gives off Portal vibes, and is executed sufficiently.Lightmatter keeps it's gameplay to a simple concept -- Don't touch the shadows -- and builds its entire game around that. It keeps a relatively low to medium difficulty curve throughout most of the game, but I needed to use gimmicky solutions in a few puzzles. That said, the puzzles are interesting, and the environment is well-developed to make you think you're traversing through a laboratory, which really ties you down to the game's story.The only few gripes I have is with when and how the game introduces new mechanics. You are left to your own devices for a long time for some mechanics, yet you only have a handful of levels to explore another. The game's final level throws in gimmicks that have never been introduced beforehand. While the simple core rules of Lightmatter let me quicky process what was happening, it could have potentially been introduced earlier, and in more levels.Nonetheless, Lightmatter is an impressive game that I'll put up there with Portal. The default price might be too steep for what the game offers, so look out for when this game goes on sale.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: I was very impressed with the demo. I like this concept of using light to solve puzzles. I found the mad scientist fun and the game has a definite Portal vibe. It ran very well for me with an RTX 2070.  My only minor complaint is the jumping. It feels a bit off and that made one of the puzzles in the demo more difficult than it should be. I was shocked at how long of a demo this was at over an hour of content. You have plenty of time to understand the style of puzzles and the dark humor of the game.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: Wow, I'm so blown away by this game. I had the chance to see it a bit during development and helped approve the Portal references. I thought it looked good, but had no idea it would be my favorite 1st person puzzler since The Talos Principle. Absolutely brilliant mechanics and they're explored just the right amount. Nice mix of platforming with right the right tightness in timing and spacing. The dynamic music perfectly sets the mood. Visual style is squeaky clean. Voice acting is great and the dialog is well written. It really don't get much better than this. Hats off to the devs and I hope they do more in the future.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: Definitely RECOMMEND!This game was TONS of fun!  I have seen and heard a lot of comparisons to Portal with how this game plays.  I can't say if it does compare in style to Portal as I have never played Portal, but what I can say is that the puzzles were unique and interesting and the mechanic with the lights was something I personally have never seen before!Another great thing about this game is that there are secret for you secret hunters out there. I finished the game but I definitely didn't end up getting all of the achievements.  Definitely some things hiding out there for the secret hunters/100%ers out there!Check out the full game or some of it below if you don't know if you are interested in getting it or not!
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: I am a fan of the Portal franchise and this is very clearly inspired by it, especially by the second one with the whole CEO/Creator voice-over shtick and I absolutely love it. As someone who has been starving for a Portal-esque game, Lightmatter definitely scratches the itch. The puzzles are fun, if not a bit too easy at times, but still satisfactory to solve. My only criticism would be that the story ended up being a bit confusing, there were some glitches here and there and it was somewhat short, but overall I definitely recommend the game!
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: A really interesting puzzle game that definitely reminds of Portal in a lot of its style. This is obviously the developer's intention, what with the blatant references to Portal that often felt a bit  on the nose for me, but the game itself is a lot of fun!While not very long (I finished in under 3 hours) it's definitely a fun experience. And with the great business model of allowing an almost full hour of demo (a quite substantial portion of the game), you can easily see if this game is for you!Also, as much as I like GLaDOS, having the main antogonist be a human being with emotions (a  of emotions), really helped to make the story feel more personal. It being rooted in actual current day issues also added to round out the story and make it feel believable, even with all the science fiction. All in all the story helped the game stand apart as more than just a Portal re-do with different mechanics (and even that would've already been fun). But now, what we have is an interesting and fun puzzle game that while definitely inspired by a classic, still manages to stand on its own.I definitely recommend at least checking out the demo!
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: Leaving a thumbs up or a thumbs down is pretty difficult for this game, because it's all in the price. - Lightmatter has good-ish story. The endings were crap but the rest of the journey was nice, atmospheric and funny. Great voice acting too ! It just had too many "Hey, 'member Portal ?" moments for me.- The gameplay is good, at least what's here. Only 3 puzzle mechanics and no hard puzzles at all. Seriously I didn't have to look up a guide or anything and only 2 or 3 puzzles took me more than 5minutes to figure out. I finished the game in 3 hours.- Graphics are awesome, props for the great art direction.- Performance was mixed on my VEGA56 and Ryzen 1700X, at 1080p. That's really odd and the graphical fidelity doesn't warrant such poor performance. But as always for performance, maybe it's just me. The option menu was dissapointingly sparse. You can't even rebind the keys. That's absolutely unacceptable, and pushes what would have been a lukewarm "thumbs up" to a "thumbs down" review from me. I'm looking forward to what the devs will do next, it's evident that they have the raw talent to make something great, and when Lightmatter shines, it shines bright. Unfortunately, there's just not enough here and the lack of polish really makes the game hard to recommend.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoyed this game. As others have said, it's clearly a love letter to other games in the genre, while maintaining its own unique feeling. The stylized art has a simple beauty to it and I found myself admiring the little details and easter eggs hidden around the rooms. David Bateson's performance really helped add a lot of charm to the narrative.It is, however, $20 for a 4 hour game. That's including the 21 minutes spent to get the bonus ending. While I did enjoy every moment and am happy to support indie devs, it might be an issue for people looking to get more bang for their buck. The puzzles give way to fast platforming towards the end of the game which might also be a turn off. I still highly suggest giving this one a try. Is it the best puzzle platformer I've played? No, but it has a charm that I find myself wanting to tell all my friends about.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: One of the more interesting puzzle games I've ever played.  The mechanics were unique, simple but versatile, and a challenge from start to finish.  It got harder, without getting impossible.For a game with nothing but voice actors, the story was amazing.  This was truly science gone wrong, and ambition gone even more wrong.  The most unsettling thing about this game is knowing there are people like this in the real world running all kinds of nefarious experiments in secret.It was reminiscent of Portal (in game Portal references aside), but a much darker feel.  The back half of the game was tense, and did a good job of ramping up the desperation to escape.Solid puzzler.  Would highly recommend.
