_childDocuments_.review: Gamers who enjoy puzzle games will find that  treads on well-worn ground with interesting level-design that makes good use of the shadow and light mechanics. The game itself isn't particularly long (4-5 hours) and the puzzles themselves are of medium-difficulty requiring some critical-thinking, but generally forgiving of mistakes.As with all games with the "protagonist escaping big-brother in a lab" motif, comparisons to the venerable  series will naturally be drawn. While  does de-emphasize the platforming quite a bit, it stays true to the more important aspect of having well-made puzzles that fully explores the core mechanics. The puzzles themselves are mostly self-contained rooms, relatively in scope, and each exploring some aspect of the mechanics.The soundtrack, if you call it that, is largely comprised of just dialogue between you and your observer "Virgil". The silent and matte grey environment leaves only Virgil's dialogue as audio, who is a bit chattier than one would like. While GLaDOS's snide dialogue and Wheatley's badgering was largely accepted on account of their comedic qualities, Virgil's dialogue isn't quite as entertaining.: 6.9/10

It reminds you of cell shading from the game XIII, but with the polish of a new decade driving it. The pace, music and atmosphere is absorbed by the timetested (NaissancE) , but despite that still original puzzle-gameplay and fits into the presented world like a letter to it's envelope. It all just makes sense!The story itself is intriguing and told though the lens of a charming, but seemingly insane, narrator. Think of Cave Johnson (Portal 2), but with his own quirks and soul! _childDocuments_.review: In the furthest reaches of the , on the northeastern shores of the Elder Continent, lies the city of Varchas. It is a complex structure of light and mirrors meant to make sure its citizens "walk in the light of Mihir" at all times, as stepping out of it, into the shadows, marks you as tainted (Taamas) and gets you expelled from the city. It’s a metaphor for exemplarity, for keeping pure in a place tainted by darkness, that works in contrast with the general theme of the game, where light makes you vulnerable, allows you to be “examined and understood”, and ultimately kills you.Why am I talking about  in a review to a first-person puzzler inspired by  and ? Because while playing  I always thought Varchas was a cool poetic construct, it worked well as an ideal of purity, but it would never work in the real world. How could you live an entire life never, not once, stepping into a shadow? Well,  makes it work in 3D and does it pretty convincingly. It’s a cool anti-Thief experience where you have to forget everything the stealth-game tradition has taught you over the years, namely that you are safe in the shadows, that they protect you, enshroud you in a veil of darkness and make you invisible and unknown. No, here you have to stay in the light at all times (and endure the constant anxiety of feeling vulnerable and exposed, enhanced by the fact that there's a creep there watching you on camera and commenting on your every move), because the shadows will kill you instantly if you step out of the light, they will literally swallow you like a deep black tar pit (and let me tell you, as a Thief fan, who always felt shadows were warm and protective, the first time that happens in the game is a horrible experience!). And if  and  as an inspiration for the clever puzzles haven’t already convinced you, I’ll happily throw in  as a hint of what you can expect from the game’s witty and wonderfully reactive dialogue.

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoyed my time with Lightmatter (one complete playthrough), but only because of the extremely low price I got it from on Humble Bundle.First off, what the game does right. There are countless Portal clones and inspired games out there, but this is probably one of the better of those. The controls are simple, the graphics are great, the voice acting is awesome, and the puzzle mechanics are very unique.Getting into what makes me not recommend this game, it's only about three hours long, with zero replay value unless you wanted to speedrun or listen to developer commentary. This is pretty ridiculous for a twenty dollar price point.There are only two puzzle mechanics, and they're very close in terms of function: the lights and the power nodes. These puzzle mechanics are only mixed together once or twice, and this is near the end of the game. Mixing these two mechanics was really the highlight of the game, but it was too few and too late. There really needed to be some kind of third element to the game (light switches? swinging lamps? something?) and they really needed to start mixing things up early on. Even Portal had dozens of hazards, interactables, and enemy types. This game has lamps, conduits, and the floor being lava. That's literally the whole game.The game really wants to be Portal instead of doing its own thing. Aperture is even referenced two whole times by the main actor in regular dialogue, something that doesn't make much sense in terms of lore with the Portal/Half-Life universe. The main guy also has an Andrew Ryan thing going, especially when he starts accusing the main character of being a spy. Really took me out of the experience. I don't mind references and the like, but at least be original with the writing. The game basically takes place in Aperture Labs.Speaking of which, there are only two voice actors, and one of them is delegated to voicing maybe half a dozen or so audio tapes that don't really add anything surprising to the back story. The main VA is pretty swell, at least up until the ending of the game, but he's not enough to keep things interesting the whole ride.The puzzles are far, far too easy. You get a checkpoint every time you make any amount of progress, most of the puzzles are blatantly obvious, and even the smallest amount of trial & error can have you beating each puzzle with maybe one screw-up. A first time player with some basic FPS platforming skills can beat this game without issue.There are no difficulty settings, bonus maps, or alternate game modes. There is a "speedrun mode" and developer commentary, but these are just the base game with a timer or someone talking over the game. For twenty bucks, three hours is far too little playtime.FPS platforming is terrible in 98% of games, including this one. Some stuff looks like you could never stand on it, or it is in shadow (which you cannot touch - think "the floor is lava"), but yet you can jump right on it. Other times, you'll be slipping off ledges that seemed perfectly okay. The game relies on platforming and jumping far too much towards the end. The shadow mechanics and such are cool, but expect to die at least once before realizing your light source will pass behind an obstacle.All-in-all, get it on sale or through Humble Bundle or something. If you've played Portal, you've played a better version of this game, in terms of scope and style.

_childDocuments_.review: I guess Portal and the genre it spawned is pretty old now—come to think of it, I first rented the Orange Box from a Blockbuster. Yeesh. Anyway it's obviously old enough that Lightmatter, yet another first person Science! puzzle game, can call itself a "love letter" to the genre.  Drawing direct comparisons to one of the best games ever made is a most dangerous game that Lightmatter has no issues playing, with repeated references to Aperture Science, Cave Johnson, turrets, cubes, cake, everything. Fortunately Lightmatter doesn't suffer for it because the game is a perfectly fine example of the genre; it's not exactly mind-blowing, but it is a fun way to puzzle out a few hours.The premise of Lightmatter, like most of these games, is simple. Shadows will eat you; just like that one episode of Doctor Who (they even reference it as an achievement). You need to lug around heavy floodlights to shine a clear path to each exit. It doesn't seem like a concept with long legs, but credit to the devs for wringing out a lot of creativity and depth to their chosen premise. They also do it without cheesy gimmicks—there are only two different kinds of lamps used in the game, where a lesser puzzle game would keep adding new types as they ran out of ideas for puzzles with the old ones.But what elevates Lightmatter above many other example of the genre is that the puzzles are really clever, not complicated. A lot of puzzle games mistake complexity for challenge, throwing a million things to keep track of and a pile of trial and error. Some of the solutions in Lightmatter fall into this trap, but a lot of them rely more on outside-the-box thinking or clever exploitation of the mechanics—fun little a-ha moments that make you feel real smart when you piece together what you  need to do. It's not a challenging game and I was never stuck for more than a few minutes on a puzzle, but Lightmatter at least feels smart and makes you feel smart—something not every wannabe Portal does.(The final level is also genuinely exciting and threatening, something many puzzle games stuggle with.)The presentation is pretty great, using a timeless, high contrast, cel-shaded comic book style that looks terrific and really makes the danger of the shadows stand out. There's also a customary snarky voice over the loudspeakers in the form of Lightmatter's egomaniacal CEO; while the dialogue isn't hysterical or anything, it's perfectly entertaining and David Bateman does a great job exuding that Agent 47 sinisterism without just retreading his most famous role. In particular there are a lot of good reactive moments—for example, when I yanked a spotlight away too quickly and a door closed on my face, there was a single, quiet chuckle that was hilarious.In short, Lightmatter is good! It doesn't quite rise to the top of the puzzley-Portaly-pile, but it's certainly a great example worth puzzling with for the genre connoisseur.

_childDocuments_.review: Beautiful first-person puzzle game with an interesting story to uncover. It is also relatively short.  The 30+ levels flew by, and I was hoping for more when the game ended.Overall, great game worth a play, but considering the difficulty and length of the game, perhaps wait to get it on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: Lightmatter  belongs to the first-person puzzle genre and  really follows the same successful formula that we first saw in Portal and defined a whole new genre. You can say it is a "Love letter" to a long forgotten genre,that for sure blew our minds back then and definitely couldn't have enough of it.You wake up inside a facility called "Lightmatter Technologies" and you don't know why you are there.It seems that they were trying to do something "big" there,but something went really wrong and now the facility is infested with shadows.A mysterious voice from someone called "Vigil",who is the CEO of Lightmatter Technology,will try to help you to escape and save yourself.Will you make it?...Is everything as it seems to be?Clearly following Portal's formula and sharing game mechanics from both "Portal" and "The Talos Principle", Lightmatter achieves to give us another brilliant puzzle game,but with its own unique personality.Here we don't have portals as the main game mechanic.Instead of that ,we have Light and Shadows.You can say it's an alternative point of view on portals.You will try to escape room after room by solving puzzles.You will try to light the way through the darkness in every room, so you will find the exit and escape.Lightmatter's puzzles are neither super hard nor too easy.I think they have the right amount of challenge in them so you can say they are really satisfying.Some of them are really brilliant.In Lightmatter we have a narrator that will try to guide us through the game.The excellent voice acting from David Bateson combined with the great dialogues,the jokes,the sarcasms,the references , are a big plus to the whole atmosphere of the game and you will never feel bored.I think Lightmatter is an indie gem which , although it borrowed a specific formula from Portal ,in the end it proved that it can make something special,with its own personality,something unique and memorable.I highly recommend it for the fans of this genre and for others too.One of the best things that happened to this genre after "Portal" and  "The Talos Principle"!

_childDocuments_.review: (written after an all-nighter used to play the game) Gameplay mechanics are very simple, almost bare-bones puzzle game system, yet pretty uniquely utilized (unlike in the case of a similarly oriented ). I say "at times", because really 90% of the time I was essentially speedrunning the game and I am very dumb, so it's really pretty easy. I'd not really delve deeper in the story, as it is rather blurry and doesn't give the player much anything. Overall  is a fun game for one afternoon that I would actually like to see get a level editor, because the campaign is criminally short and the before-seen system of logical contraptions works in a pretty novel way, so it's really a shame we don't get to see more of it.

_childDocuments_.review: Lightmatter is a first person puzzle game which takes place inside a research laboratory where the development of a light based energy source has gone very wrong, causing shadows to be deadly. You spend your time moving light sources in such a way that you are able to safely traverse the facility. The puzzles are well build and generally offer a challenge without causing frustration. Vigil, the CEO of Lightmatter Technology, talks to you during your journey throughout the facility. His narcissistic personality and his condescending manner of talking to you breathes life into the game and regularly makes you laugh. It is very clear that the developer have tried to go for a portal-esque vibe. The writing doesn't quite reach that level, but it did pleasantly surprise me.I was gifted the game, but I do want to remark that I think the retail price is little high as I managed the finish the game under 3 hours. I did really enjoy my time though.

_childDocuments_.review: I would definitely consider this game a "hidden gem". It has great mechanics from start to finish and, whilst not particularly groundbreaking, the story is engaging and sensible enough to justify the game play.THE GOOD+ Clever and formulaic puzzles which will challenge you but rarely make you feel like you need to "brute force" them+ Minimal, but nice art style that fits the theme of the game (it's all about light, so too much detail would incumber the actual game play)+ Good enough story+ Great voice acting+ Decent length - took me a little under 5 hours to 100% and I was "ready" for it to finish by that time+ Free demo of the first part of the game so you can try it out+ Is unashamedly heavily inspired by Portal (minus the portal mechanics), so if you like Portal then this is trying very hard to appeal to you and, in my opinion, succeedsTHE BAD- Puzzle variety/complexity is limited and whilst there are multiple mechanics taught throughout the game there are only a handful of endgame puzzles that really challenge you to use everything you've learned- The developers have disbanded, so there will never be a sequelMaking that last point a negative in a review is probably a little contentious, but that's how much I enjoyed this game. I genuinely feel bad knowing there will never be a follow-up or another game from this talented team.As I said in the last positive point, this game is going hard on "what if Portal but with beams of light?" and that might rub some people up the wrong way. To me, however, it just felt some clearly inspired devs tipping the hat to a game/developer they clearly look up to and, in the progress, making a very good puzzle game that is a great experience even without any Portal references.

_childDocuments_.review: Lightmatter is a puzzle game where you have to play with light sources in order to avoid strange, dense, man-eating shadows. The game follows a the-floor-is-lava approach where the ‘lava’ can be made harmless by illuminating it. This creates a lot of different opportunities for puzzles based on the movement of different illumination object (lamps and such) in order to, well… not die eaten by shadows.The story of Lightmatter proceeds mainly thanks to the CEO of the Lightmatter company, which will not only guide us through the gigantic structures and laboratories, but also explain to us what Lightmatter is and why we are in the current flesh-eating-shadows situation. This character alone brings a portal-like sensation to the game, which is also set in the same universe (the CEO will, in fact, cite Aperture Science and its experiments multiple times during the course of the game), taking the same role that GLaDOS had in the portal series: a character serious at time, sarcastic in others and with a general disregard of safety (or human lives).The CEO is also the inventor of Lightmatter: a new and renewable source of energy which, according to him, could save humanity as a whole. With photon crystals, he built the CORE, basically a perpetual machine which generates more energy than it consumes (and breaks a physic law or two by doing so). Everything goes wrong during its inauguration though, and you find yourself trapped in the facility, surrounded by strange, dense and pitch-black shadows.As I already said, the way puzzles work is by forcing the player to light paths that are otherwise filled with shadows. This usually involves moving equipment from one way to another, while also having to deal with bridges, switches and, you know, puzzle stuff. Puzzles do work and are enjoyable, but the difficulty curve is tuned a little too much on the easy side and this makes all puzzles, except the very last ones, a little too simple. When progressing in the game another aspect about puzzles becomes obvious: they lack new elements. The game introduces lamps at the very beginning, photon cells (basically light-activated switches) and then photon connectors, special portable turrets than can create “wires” of lightmatter, creating corridors of light. These three elements are only used together in the last levels, and are too little for 3-4 hours of gameplay. Light-based puzzles inspire lasers, mirrors and, why not, batteries! Why are these simple elements not part of the game?Talking about what actually is in the game, though, puzzles are quite solid and well thought, have a good flow and are rarely frustrating (and that’s also because of the low difficulty).Graphically the game looks nice and, even though it uses for the most part very dark, gray-scaled colours, its graphics do the work. Sadly there are not particularly good vistas on graphically-memorable moments and, even if we are talking about a game set in an underground lab, something more could’ve been done. It’s not that the game is graphically bad, it’s just… good. Luckily the simplicity allows for good performances even at higher resolutions, and the game can be played even on older GPUs.Lightmatter is good puzzle game that could’ve been an easy Autosave if it wasn’t for the lack of content regarding the puzzles. With it, though, Tunnel Vision Games proved its worth, so hopefully we’re going to see a more complete Lightmatter 2 in the future!

_childDocuments_.review: This is a demo masquerading as a full game. The ACTUAL game is listed as DLC for this game, which is deceptive and intentionally misleading. The fact that the DLC is called "Lightmatter - Full Game" should be proof enough that this should have "Demo" in the title. The demo ends with a quite literal paywall at level 15/38, where , and interacting with the terminal opens a link to buy the "DLC" on steam. I would not be upset about this if the devs were honest in their presentation, as the game was fun while it lasted. This is not a free game with $19.99 DLC, it is a free demo of a $19.99 game. If this is made more clear, I'll probably come back and but the game.

_childDocuments_.review: Lightmatter was an interesting, if short, little puzzle game. Topping out at 5 hours (maybe 6 if some of the puzzles stump you for longer than they took me), I can only recommend this game on a pretty deep discount. I typically aim for at least $1/hour of entertainment and it would be real disappointing at its full $20 price tag.Aesthetically its neat but also fairly bland. There's lots of interesting stuff around but you can't interact with any of it and a fair bit of it will be out of reach in the shadows anyway. Puzzles only really come in two varieties and, while the puzzles that are there are pretty interesting, you only have 2 (and maybe a half) mechanics to interact with so once you understand the mechanics, there's not much challenge beyond thinking about the few very limited things you can do with your light sources.Things of note:- The story was fairly neat but pretty straightforward- Sound design is good- Game reads pretty well (its mostly black and white)- Controls are responsive- Did run into a single, seemingly random crash (jumping in place to look at something from a different angle) but it auto saves at each 'chamber' so you don’t really lose much if it dies on you- Not sure why 'shift' is also 'jump' and can't be unmapped, had to retrain my brain to stop using it when I was trying to sprint- The game menu also doesn't support ultra wide monitors, the menu over-scales and clips outside of bounds so several times I had to go into window mode and resize the window to access specific menu functions- Was disappointed lights you are carrying blink out of existence when you cross a checkpoint. I know why the game does it but, if you're going to force object destruction, the game should follow the rules of its own universe and have an in-game reason for them to be left behind rather than suddenly disappearing.So, recommended short puzzle game if you can get it $10 or less.

_childDocuments_.review: == REVIEW ==I haven't played a game as challenging, gripping, and even kind of philosophical as this one since Portal 2, and that was a while back. Before you immediately judge it as being a rip-off of the Portal series, just have a play first. The story is similar in ways to Portal 2 (I don't think that's too much of a spoiler), but the gameplay is very different and refreshing from the bad games that are popular right now. The graphics are beautiful and the plot is second only to the Portal series.== PROS ==+ beautiful graphics+ great story+ interesting mechanics+ level difficulties increase throughout but generally aren't too impossible+ at least 2 hours for your first playthrough (I'm guessing it's probably speedrun-able to around 20-30 mins?)== CONS ==- surprisingly low frame rate (I was getting 50-60 FPS on medium settings on a GTX 1060)- the ending wasn't as satisfying as I hoped (you'll see why if you get there)- some of the levels are too hard in my opinion- a little bit buggy (crashed once during my playthrough) but I am writing this on release day== SCORE: 9/10 ==This is genuinely the best game I've played since Portal 2 (the only game I would give 10/10). If you liked the Portal series and are fed up waiting/hoping for Portal 3, THIS IS THE GAME FOR YOU.

_childDocuments_.review: A wonderfully infuriating game.  There's an early level, my first time working on a "hard" puzzle, and I was so convinced that there was something wrong with the game that I was considering looking it up.  When the answer came it hit me like a wrecking ball.  It was so simple, but also not obvious!  That moment was when I truly began to appreciate how amazing this game is.  It's atmospheric, artistic, has a good plot, the voice acting is amazing (can't stress that enough), and when you're not loosing yourself taking in the beauty it makes you think so hard your head might explode.  And that early "hard" puzzle was stupid easy compared to later stuff.Very chill and laid back.  At first....  ;) For its length and price this is probably the best game I've ever played.  It's not super long, but it isn't too short either.  Don't look for videos of it if you ever want to play it, it'll only spoil everything by handing you the answers.  That being said, this game is so much fun that even knowing the answers I can easily see players going back and trying to speed run.

_childDocuments_.review: Lightmatter is a puzzle game in the vein of Portal - and even makes a few cute references to Aperture Science's shenanigans during the course of the game. The end of the game does include a less-puzzle-y, more-platformer-y section, but for the most part it's playing with light beams to avoid stepping on shadows while you, as the silent protagonist, are alternatively badgered and cajoled by the narrator/facility director who is reminiscent of Cave Johnson.

_childDocuments_.review: this game was fun. i would put it in the same subenre as the talos principle what with its fascination with managing objects' sightlines, albeit without the clever philosophical writing that that game is beloved for. it's quite a bit easier, but if you liked the style of the puzzles in that game, you'll also like what this has. the writing here is serviceable -- it's the standard sort of power-and-rebellion narrative you'd expect from a science fiction game with no character models.however, it's weird that the primary point of comparison is the talos principle given that this game exists squarely in portal's shadow. at one point i came across a radio playing a remix of still alive less than half a minute after the ceo character referenced cave johnson by name. this was the most egregious example, but it's hardly abnormal here. the game is, in general, filled with constant, direct, desperate references to daddy portal-senpai. it's difficult to overstate how distracting this is. if steam reviews were a better place for long-form media analysis, i could probably spill a lot of ink using this as a case study for how constant references can ruin otherwise decent writing. some of the moments that were trying to be emotionally impactful fell flat simply because i had been trained to scan the environment and dialogue for references to portal so i could ignore them. it's not a good idea for your game to remind your players of a better game they could be playing instead. and it's all portal all the time! this all wouldn't have bothered me so much if it diversified its taste a little (maybe putting a reference to the talos principle here, the turing test there, the witness somewhere else), but as it the developers had tunnel visioned on that one particular game to their work's detriment. and while it is filled with allusions to portal, it doesn't actually commit enough for me to be able to read it as fanfiction. portal references don't bother me as much in, say, aperture tag, because that game is openly a fan work set within the same universe. but this isn't that. it wouldn't make sense to read this game as being set in the same universe, but it also sure as hell wouldn't make sense NOT to read this game as set in the same universe. it feels really sloppy.i am recommending this game on the basis of gameplay, but please only pick it up if you can handle constant, semi-diegetic references to a much better game.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: A blatant homage to Portal that still manages to find its own way. The main character foil is less Cave Johnson and more Samuel Hayden -- absolutely dripping with hubris, yet at the end of the day he's still working to help humanity, including your own sorry ass. Other than hammering you over the head with a few explicit references to Aperture Science, the humour is mostly wry and subdued, and on the whole the game has a more serious tone. Fortunately, the voice acting is more than good enough to carry it with aplomb.The puzzle design is good. It kept me challenged and engaged without getting me stuck, except once toward the end. It doesn't quite attain Portal's sense of "puzzle character" -- making the solutions to "out of bounds" puzzles in late game feel spontaneous and improvisational compared to the neat, compact solutions of the test chambers -- but the Lightmatter facility has a lot of character in its own right, and some great attention to visual detail. I often stopped to observe my surroundings and wonder what purpose they served in the normal functioning of Lightmatter, and I was usually rewarded.It's worth noting that this game has (apparently) two endings, and as of this review there are two achievements that no one has been able to find, or at least no one has decided to write up how they did it. I was able to find one "out of bounds" area that didn't give me an achievement, but which contained some rather mysterious extra objects which made it clear the devs intended it to be found. So there are some clear indications of hidden depth. My playthrough only took about four hours, which might not be enough for its price tag, but I might very well come back and play this again.

_childDocuments_.review: Journalist, the shadows are deadly!Think "the floor is lava", but with shadows that devour biological matter.You play as a silent, nameless protagonist, tasked with navigating the Lightmatter facility. As you make your way through the facility, you will encounter puzzles centered around manipulating light to create a safe passage towards the exit. The protagonist is silent, but the CEO of Lightmatter will keep you company. His voice actor does a pretty job and is fun to listen to. The game is pretty short, it took me just under 3 hours to beat the campaign, but it has some replay value because there are secret things you can do or find to unlock achievements, and there's an option to enable speedrun stats if you're into that sort of thing. It's a short, fun game with puzzles that get more and more challenging towards the end, it has good voice acting and I really liked the visuals.

_childDocuments_.review: A lot of reviews say that fans of Portal will like this game. I would recommend a lot more caution.While this game shamelessly rips off its genre, aesthetic and narrative style from Portal, what it fails to capture is actually having any significant number of interesting puzzles. Meanwhile, it crosses the line from "inspiration" to "desperate referencing" by making direct references to Portal twice in the narration, which is really off-putting.As far as the puzzles go, there is a real lack of depth on meaningful mechanical progression. The core mechanic is "the floor is lava". Standing on a shadow is lethal. You can place lamps to light shadowed places, move certain geometry around with buttons (or light-activated sensors). Later on, you get a different kind of lamp that chains light between them. And... that's it.If you spend about 10 minutes thinking about what puzzles you might make with these mechanics, you've probably spoiled most of the game for yourself already. There are maybe three puzzles that are not extremely obvious an linear, and the rest is a incredibly basic fare. This is not Portal, where there are "ah hah" moments regularly. This is a barely-fleshed out, bland puzzle game with a story you've seen before.If using beams of light to manipulate things sounds like an interesting design (and it can be!), you'd be way better off playing The Talos Principle instead. It has mechanics that are basically the same as the lamps (but with the addition of color for added complexity), plus many more puzzles, better puzzles, metapuzzles... just... much more content. It's twice the price, sure, but it's 10 times the game, and it goes on sale regularly.Overall, I just can't recommend this. In a genre as saturated as "narrative first person puzzler", this is at best "fine". That's a hard sell when there are actually excellent games like Portal, QBeh-1, Talos or Outer Wilds to play instead.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: Lightmatter is a lightweight puzzler that covers the basics of the genre. It compares to Portal but lacks the same finesse, humor, and complexity. It revolves around two main devices: lamps and photon connectors. The former is simple but used well enough. And the latter is interesting although ends up being clunky. The player’s guide, Virgil, lacks much personality or humor, but he’s still better than complete silence. It may not have a lot of mechanics, but that doesn’t make it a bad game. It uses what it has well and does it all with pleasing visuals. Lightmatter may walk in the shadow of giants, but at least it brings its own light source.

_childDocuments_.review: Great linear single player puzzle game. Wonderful story, great main voice actor. Beautiful shadows. Overall over 30 puzzles.Some small improvements I would have wished for:- Would have wished at least a 1,5x speed option on the (optional of course) developer commentary though. ;-)- Also, my GPU (3070) ramps up when tabbing out of the game. (This seems to be an issue with many games and is probably engine related.)- Sometimes it was difficult to assess whether I should wait while dialogue was still playing, in order not to trigger the next dialogue. But with a bit of patience rather than running through the game that's rarely an issue.Looking forward to the dev's next game.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: If you liked Portal, you will like Lightmatter.Lightmatter was a delight to play. As a big fan of 3d puzzle platformers, this game definitely holds its own. The art style and colour palate is simplistic, but not rudimentary as to break my immersion. The music is incredible and really adds to the overall feeling of importance and impact that the player is supposed to feel while navigating the machinery and offices of the facility. The story is intriguing and constantly draws you along through curiosity using a trail of breadcrumbs and a disembodied voice. The game definitely has a Portal vibe and shows obvious and on the nose signs of inspiration drawn from Aperture Science. I thoroughly enjoyed the classy way the game makers used a paywall to unlock the full game. I played the free demo until hitting that paywall, and instead of facing a black screen with "Insert Credits to Continue" Like I was expecting, I was faced with clever dialog and a literal door. Being redirected to the payment page and being able to jump right back in after purchasing the game to an open door was quite satisfying and felt classy to me. I had no issues paying the price I did for this game. The game has built in tools for the speed running community and so I think they will have fun with this one. This also adds some replay-ability.Ever since I played The Talos Principle by Croteam, I have felt a real emotional response from a female researcher's recordings laying out the background story for me. It is quite immersive and really encourages me to want to see the story through and find justice for the voice.The puzzles in this game are not necessarily difficult, but I did find that some of them stumped me for a bit until I finally figured out that I just hadn't explored the area enough. Just like in The Talos Principle, you unlock different methods with which to use the main game mechanic. Honestly, I would have liked to see more methods explored and unlocked, but for what I got I am happy and look forward to potential DLC in the future. I do also feel the the game ended to early and abruptly, leaving me wanting more.TLDR: If you liked Portal, you will like Lightmatter.Pros: -Simple, Clean, Non-distracting art style-Immersive music and ambiance-Clever game mechanics and platforming-Unique StoryCons:-On the nose Portal references-Game duration a bit too small
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: Blown away by this game.Got it and played it through in a single day... Couldn't put it down.Comparisons to portal are inevitable (and he game includes more a few nods to Valve). Usually the contenders fall flat, but in this case... They're in the same weight class.There are a few classic logic puzzles early on, but those are developed into something ever-more complex and ingenious.The shadow mechanic is used beautifully to present endlessly varied puzzles.Perhaps my only criticism is that it has an over-reliance on timely platforming, but the controls are crisp and responsive, so it's not much of an issue.All in all, I'm very happy with the purchase.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: A very aesthetically pleasing game that most definitely takes cues from Portal. For experienced puzzle game players, the puzzles are a bit on the easy side, but the challenge should be just right for most. Tons of fun little easter eggs and attention to detail that give the game charm, but way too expensive given the short length of the game. I recommend picking Lightmatter up on on any sale under 10 dollars.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: First person puzzlers changed after Portal. Every game in the genre since has needed to somehow deal with being in the series' shadow. Lightmatter does this by directly acknowledging the series. It name-drops a couple of times, and has objects directly inspired by the two games. It leaves the game in a weird position, clearly trying to be in the same universe but also trying to distance itself (probably for legal reasons).Aesthetically, Lightmatter is very nice. Taking the same run-down laboratory palette as Portal, adding cel shading to give a cleaner look and to help with the distinction between light and shadow.There are some beautiful moments in the game. I have one in mind from about the turn in the story. Anyone who has played knows this moment.Story wise, there is one. The game uses it to defuse the strain of puzzle solving and to propose a philisophical question at the end. Just prepare to be railroaded down the story, even if you'd make different decisions in those situations.With the platforming, the controls are nice. Once you get used to the movement I had no troubles. The final level is basically a big giant platforming segment (think trying to reach GLaDOS in Portal 1), and I had no troubles with the platforming itself (just knowing where to go at some points).Is the full version worth a buy? Sure, if you like first-person puzzlers. My first playthrough took 4 hours, and that's with getting stuck in a few places.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: This game isn't very long or very hard, but does challenge you a little and the story is fun enough.I'm mostly writing this review to point out that the entire game, which was made by a Danish developer, was written entirely in English and THEN translated to Danish and subsequently voiced by a well-known Danish voice actor.I just find this interesting and kinda funny. :) I have no idea why a game would include a Danish language version with a well-known voice actor if that wasn't the original language it was written in, but it clearly wasn't since most of the jokes and references are funny in English but not in Danish. ;)
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: Full disclosure I was given a key by the Dev's to do a pre-release review.This is my honest opinion of my play through.(Non-Spoiler Review)The platforming is well done and the controls are very tight. I never felt a missed jump or landing was due to the game it was just me walking off edges while exploring or miss judging a jump. The puzzles were fun and made me think and I never felt scared to try something and get it wrong as the game saves quite often and loads you back in moments before you messed up.I had one puzzle that had me stumped longer than I would like to admit but the AH HA moment felt good. During the puzzles you have someone giving you story elements over a loudspeaker helping you lose yourself in the game and giving a valid reason as to why you are doing all of this.Some special extras the Dev's include a speedrun timer (Enabled in the extras menu) with stats like deaths and total jumps (was a fun tidbit to see), and some special nods to other great puzzle platformers.Is this game right for you……….. Do you like figuring out puzzles and manipulating light? Do you like running and platforming? Are you looking for a new game to speedrun?If you answered yes to any of these I think you will enjoy your time in this game. I mean the 1st hour is FREE so why not give it a go!!!!!
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: I was impressed and delighted by Lightmatter. Familiar format, novel concept, strong visual style, variety of levels and pacing. Overall excellent execution.I wondered before playing whether the shadows as a hazard would add a bit of a horror or unsettling vibe to the game. But this was not the case (and I played right before going to bed). There are no section that are pure black, light sources are always very clear. And if you stand in the shadows you have about a half-second as the screen darkens, and then you are back in the light again ready to try again.A couple of crashes, but neither disruptive. Not sure about the launcher, just skipped over it and went straight to the game.Biggest disappointment: It is finished and I still want more. Will definitely go back to 100% this one. Looking forward to more from this developer.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: This is a super cool game! The concept is super simple and easy to grasp, yet exciting to play through. The storyline is linear, doesn't require much attention or thinking; there are many philosophies and quantum physics concepts embodied in it. That being said, it's still a very exciting puzzle solving game!! Some puzzles can be a little bit more difficult in my opinion, but overall it gives me challenging problems to solve while enjoying the game. Definitely recommend if you want a quick puzzle game!Genre: chapter based adventure, puzzle solving
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: To be clear - this game is a tribute to Portal 1&2, and (in the puzzle mechanics) the Talos Principle. And it's slick, fun, and well paced. I had some crashes (particularly at level transitions), but I'm sure these'll be patched out in time, The change of pace for the last level... naah, I not going to criticise it. It's a bump, but I think it's a good call.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: Concise and rich.No filler puzzles, each one was fun and either played with a new concept or did a spin on a previous one. Each element has easily predictable behavior, which makes it easy to draw the solution in your head (something that a lot of indie puzzle games struggle with). Puzzles aren't extremely difficult, but still fun to solve.Voice acting is entertaining and never gets in the way. Consists mostly of good jokes and sarcastic exposition. They were clearly inspired by portal 2, but did so tastefully, without just copying its style. Though, they could've easily made it without the , but I wouldn't say they overdid it.The story is short and simple, with enough depth that you don't get bored of it and to be sufficient as a background for the technology you wield and the jokes you hear.Overall, a very good game!
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a nice mix and match of Portal and The Talos Principle. If you have played those games, you'll feel instantly at home. It doesn't reach the playlength of both games, but it is cheaper since release so it evens out,The interaction with the antagonist (taunts etc.) are more Portal-like, while the mechanics of the puzzles are more Talos-like. Most puzzles can be solved with just a bit of thinking and careful checking of the geometries. A few leave you scratching your head for a while, but none of them feel unfair.There weren't any bugs serious enough to be worth to be remembered, so the coding quality is of the same tier as the writing and design. Well done.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: This is a simple puzzle game, but as a fan of Portal, Talos Principle, and Cube, I enjoyed it. It's not as good as any of those three, but I did enjoy it. One thing it got right was the pacing at the end. Picking it up again after a while to finish it, I was getting to where I was ready to be done. The game made it sound like I had a long way to go but the puzzles were over. All that remained was some fast paced platforming, needing to stay in the moving light pools. But with some good music, it felt like being behind the walls in Portal. It was exactly what I needed to finish the game on a good note.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: So, the one hour demo turned into about three as I explored every nook and cranny, enjoyed the fantastic music, the great voice acting, and generally soaked up the atmosphere. Much like others have mentioned, the play reminds me of Portal, though these levels are designed more similarly to the ones containing Portal's companion cube than the actual portal mechanic. The narrator is the owner of Lightmatter Technologies, and his dialogue is a nod to GLaDOS - entirely his own, but with the same caustic dismissiveness. There are other small Easter eggs toward Portal as well, and coming across them is a delight.The game never felt buggy (though some people have reported a problem with crashing around level 25 - I haven't made it there yet, but keep your eye out), and honestly the only bad thing I have to say is that it's really difficult to tell what level you're on without going back to the title and selecting the most recent one from the list. That aside? The art, the music, the dialogue, the achievements, all golden.I started this to unwind from my first week of a new semester (which, if you're playing puzzle games to soothe your minds kids, my advice is don't; you're only going to make yourself crazy), and I realized about two hours in that I didn't have *nearly* enough coffee for this. I haven't felt this jazzed for a new release since Stardew Valley, and frankly if I didn't have to eat, I'd still be at the game now.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty damn good puzzle game where the goal is to literally light your way to the finish. All of the levels were fairly well done, controls are as basic and they could ever be, and the story was interesting. Very post-apocalyptic, which I enjoy!I'd love to see this game with a bit more color. The lack thereof certainly lends to the overall atmosphere of the game, and I very much vibed with it, but I'm left wondering what it'd be like with more color is all.Most of the achievements are obtained via story progression, but some are absolutely ridiculous and I'm not even sure how some people came across them. That's my only gripe with the game, honestly. Of course, referring to the community is always an option, so take that as you will.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: This was fantastic. Clearly influenced by Portal and The Talos Principle, but also at times Half-Life (at least, its more puzzley elements). The puzzles are great, the voice acting is incredible, and it provides a surprisingly strong story without pausing the action. And while it fits the mold of "yet another first-person puzzler", the mechanics are unique enough to make it stand apart as its own game. It's not terribly long, and I'm fine with that; think Portal 1 rather than Portal 2. Steam says I got about 6 hours of gameplay out of it, and that seems worth the money to me.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: Recommended for fans of puzzle games. Similar to a budget version of Portal and has a similar story but can still be fun. Puzzles range in difficulty from simple to obscure but usually can be figured out with a little repositioning. It is fairly short at only a few hours, so I would recommend getting it on sale if you are interested.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: Interesting FPS Puzzle game.  Its built pretty well, death is instant but respawn is quick and automatic, you don't lose much when it respawns you.  It has a lot of narration from one character and a lot of portal references with some humor.  Pretty good game that you can play through in a couple of hours.  Shame Tunnel Vision Games won't be putting out anything else.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: A bit expensive considering the gameplay only lasts 3 hours. They picked a quality over quantity approach. None of the puzzles are repeating or a mash of previous puzzles. It gives you a puzzle that you've never done before, and a solution is wildly different each time. I almost kind of wish they had padded the puzzles out a bit more.I only ever got stuck once, a puzzle where i had to sit back and re-evaluate my life. But even the puzzles where i wasn't stuck, i wouldn't say they were easy. Each one made me rethink how i use things. It's not as simple as blocks and buttons, you're not solving with mass you're solving with light. Depending on where you put it, it can push one button or multiple. Not only is it your button presser, but you're ability to move.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: A friend of mine gifted this to me and If I heard of the game before hand I would have 100% purchased it myself. The concept of being able to manipulate light to stay out of the darkness was really fun, I hope this game gets steam workshop support or more levels, this has a lot of potential. Only thing that was a bummer was the fact that the game felt a little short and the fact that the last level completely destroyed my frames and I had to turn down the settings a few notches to be able to even do the platforming. I would definitely recommend this game for anyone who enjoys portal like puzzle games since it has its humor and style of game play.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: Played the first hour, decided to buy the full game, glad I did. If you like puzzle games/ones that kill you if you fail/arent fast enough and puzzle games that progressively get harder/make you think more youll like this.Pros:Pretty decent storyif you achievement hunt like myself they are pretty easy to get and 100% (no speed runs or no non-death requirements)few hours of gameplaysome levels are very pretty for the simplicity of itif you like cats you can hunt one down and have bunch of screenshots of a cat XDthe easter eggscould restart when I needed to and didnt have to restart a whole level if i diedCons:I would wait for a sale as I think $20 is a little muchfew hours of gameplaysometimes the puzzles/levels feel repetitive, could have been harder as it felt you could speed run it sometimeshow much people try and compare this to portal (just because it has portal references and small aspects does not make it anything like portal XD)game is too forgiving sometimes when you die (isnt always a bad thing but it helps if you want a challenge)all together 8/10
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: So far it is awesome! A lot like playing Portal for the first time. I'mma buy it.Edit: yeah it was very good.To elaborate on why I enjoyed it. The tests the game put you through became difficult, but with enough time and fiddling you discover it and the level of accomplishment is really high. The humor however was critiqued by a few people. Yet, I enjoyed the witty remarks and the almost friendly narrative of the CEO as he does try to help you, but keep his business from going completely under... So he comes off as more of a misguided friend.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: Its a buggy mess that constantly crashes and i wasnt able to get throught the first puzzle because the game forgot to load the exit section... The narrator is just constantly rude towards you without any motivation. maybe gets fun later on but feels like they try to be "funny" in the same way portal is except its just annoying.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: Lightmatter is another short and sweet puzzler that I can tuck away in my memory as a puzzler with a good few head-scratchers sprinkled throughout. While not terribly long, at about a completion time of 4-5 hours, I find the premise of the game absolutely alluring. The game is at its peak when absolutely surrounded by shadows, with only a single lamp or light-tether to keep you alive. That is when the game's whole theme hits full force. The voice acting cast only includes two characters, one of whom only appears sporadically throughout the second half of the game. However, the accompanying voice that follows you through the game's entire length does a phenomenal job of line delivery and character portrayal; he really makes a strong figure to latch onto. Every time a line of his would play, I would stop in my tracks to hear what funny or critical banter he would have to deliver, just for fear that it would cut off if I kept moving. (It never did, they do a great job of preserving the VO, it'll even continue to play if you die during, which I don't see other games do. Much appreciated detail.) (no plot details included in this spoiler, only minor nondescript details pertaining to the ending): Where I would say this game falters is in its messaging. When I finished the game,  The game also has some story beat setups that don't really have a reason as to why they pay off. For instance, the game nearly had me believe that there would be a boss fight of sorts, a chase sequence, something of the sort, only for my expectations to be subverted in a way that left me more confused than surprised. Things like this, and other minor details caught my attention once my playthrough was over. I would give Lightmatter an 8/10 overall, the game's mechanics, execution, and style are all impeccably on point, I only wish that they fleshed out the ending a bit more, and maybe added some length throughout. I don't know if this will be a continued offer, but at the moment they're allowing everyone to play the game's first hour for free - if this is a continued offer, I would definitely suggest giving it a swing, even if just for the first hour, as there are definitely some fun puzzle mechanics contained within.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: This game brought back memories of when i first played Portal (i also enjoyed the portal references within this game). This kind of game is the reason i love first person puzzle games and i hope that the developers of this game go on to make another. You will not regret spending the money to buy the full game. depending on your speed it is only 4 to 5 hours long but worth every penny.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: A fun little puzzle game, remniscent of games like Portal, Talos Principle or Cube. It all revolves around the idea that shadow on the floor "is lava" and you have to stay on lit floor to progress to the exit of the room. You can manipulate the shadow by moving objects that cast shadows, carrying and stategically placing lamps and later on beacons that serve as conduits of a kind of energy beam.Many of the puzzles are Towers of Hanoi kind of puzzles where you have to bring all lamps and beacons from one place to another, In the last level you also have to do some jump and run action to avoid moving shadows or jump onto and from moving platforms - but nothing really hard even for a casual player and death is meaningless in the game as you respawn immediately at the point where you made your fatal decision.There is a token background story behind the game, but you don't really need to care much about it, as it's neither as intriguing like Portal's GlaDOS or deeply philosophical like Talos Principle. The art style might be a bit bland to some with a lot of asset repetition, but it serves the whole concept of light and shadow pretty well.I recommend this to anyone who's in the mood for a brief puzzle game that doesn't take up too much of their time. It's not necessarily a "must have played" though.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: This recommendation is only for the demo. It's interesting, but a few things discourage me from trying the rest of the game.+They created an in universe explanation for this game's paywall and it's kind of funny+I'm surprised there's no depth of field option, but I'd rather have it like this then having DoF you can't turn off+The game creates checkpoints every time you leave a dangerous area, preventing tiny shadows you couldn't see from wasting your time-The solutions to puzzles can be very obscure, especially when key pieces are obscured by the dark.In the second to last puzzle in the demo, I was stuck at the ramp for awhile since it wasn't clear that a certain wall was actually transparent. I almost couldn't solve the final puzzle in the demo until I realized there was a tight enough angle for the lamp to cover both switches.-can't turn off bloom-The guy talking to you is obnoxious, constantly telling you that you're too slow when you've only been there for a few minutes (on top of blaming you for everything wrong that's happening)-your own shoes (and body) don't cause the ground beneath you to become organic matter eating shadows-taking jabs at aperture science was a bit too arrogant and wasn't deserved
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: wow, good game!i like puzzle games like that, played a bunch of them. now decided to go through my backlog of games on steam and right from the start i knew i want to finish this one.too many references to portal, like namedropping aperture science, straight up having companion cube and a turret in an office, talking about cake... feels almost like a case for "silence brand crab"but over all, a good one!
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: We get it, you liked the Portal franchise.The game is decent, the voice acting is good, the graphics are interesting.But the game tries  to be Portal, it made Cave Johnson and Aperture canon in their universe. So I hope this was worth it devs, because here's my thoughts framed as a comparison to Portal.The game is short. That in itself is acceptable, if the time spent is dense with enjoyment. This is, unfortunately, where Lightmatter falls short. It does not have a lot of mechanics. Lamps, connectors, doors, switches, moving platforms, and whatever terrain could either get in the way of light, of items, or of you. The possibilities given by these objects are few, and exhausted too soon.Too many levels end up solved with the same trick. Only maybe two or three felt like a challenge.The design of the game world could've also been made more remarkable. Some areas that were supposed to feel important felt like little more care was put in them than the levels themselves, and that's not putting the bar very high. This issue means that the world didn't really translate the importance of what you're doing. Nothing visually stands out enough, except a couple explosions and . Outside of story-important areas, there was really not much to see. A lot of places felt samey. I think I counted at least three separate staircases that block you from climbing higher with the exact same stack of carts.Nothing moves, no humans are around, machines only move if they're moving platforms or spinning fans most of the time.In Portal, you're the last human in a world alive with machinery. In Lightmatter, the world feels dead. Machines have no personality, the world has no personality, and frankly most dialogue, though excellently delivered, was a big nothing sandwich meant to sound like Cave Johnson while occasionally dissing Cave Johnson.The music didn't help either. Pretty dull soundtrack, doesn't really change depending on what's happening. Portal had extra bits thrown in depending on whether you're flinging yourself around, toying with lasers, dashing across propulsion gel... Lightmatter doesn't. Frankly, even the finale left me barely hooked.In fact, the ending was just unimpressive overall. Music wasn't there, game gives you hope of more interesting scenes before shoving you back into more of what you know, you don't even get to see the thing the bad guy wants you not to do happen. It just fades to white. My favorite part of the ending was literally that you finally get to see another person walk around for like... five seconds.20 bucks is too much for such a dull experience that pretends itself far too big. Buy on sale if you want this game, but honestly? Not really worthwhile on sale either.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: This is a crazy great 4 dimension puzzler that deserves a better mind than mine! I dip into to it when I'm feeling smart and it makes me regret not taking more spacial geometry and architecture classes. Great fun and humorous taunting reminiscent of Portal(2). I refuse to look for hints, so it may be on my drive for a long time! Play it & tell me how YOU do!
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: I finished playing Lightmatter... and my god... it's truly amazing. I am in lost of words to be honest on how I can even describe my experience, it felt like Portal's and Half Life's stories and puzzles mixed together, and created a wonderful baby which was this game. I seriously recommend playing this game, it is truly an experience to behold.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: Pales in the light of Portal.It's a  light matter maybe, but after uninstalling, it leaves behind 3 folders in subfolders of AppData (C:\Users\Username\AppData\). It didn't ask if I wanted to remove those as well. Had to check for and delete them manually. How did I know they're there then? Experience....I know what to expect these days. One is named Tunnel Vision (the dev) and two are named Aspyr (the publisher), iirc. I appreciate being able to play the first hour to try before you buy, but do clean up after yourselves please, devs.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: Waking up in some sort of energy plant, everything seems to have gone horribly wrong and you must find a way to escape. You find help from Virgil, the owner of the facility, who recognizes you from a tour group, but it is up to you to solve the myriad of puzzles to advance further. You notice that the facility seems rather empty where there are lab coats and other random clothing articles strewn about. There is a danger that you are initially unaware of as you continue to navigate the maze of empty and lifeless halls and shafts, but Virgil warns you as you continue further and further along, "Stay out of the shadows..."I've played the game up until the end of the free levels, and I intend to purchase the full experience when I have the chance. Although the game is not necessarily a horror title, the environment at times can be very unsettling with an ambient soundtrack that accompanies each level. The gameplay of this title consists of solving puzzles in a Portal-like fashion, as each puzzle concludes with you leaving through a door to continue to the next level. Despite this, I believe the transition from level to level is more fluid than Portal because you are able to see more aspects of the facility as you progress instead of being forced into a cylindrical elevator. The puzzles in each level are of an appropriate difficulty, where the game will gradually introduce new elements that are key to being successful as the game progresses. I never thought a puzzle was unreasonably difficult, but there will definitely be times you may be stuck!I may have compared this game to Portal (As Virgil makes a direct reference), but it is a unique game with an intriguing story with an immersive atmosphere. I highly recommend this game to those that might have played Portal or who may like puzzles in general. The game may be puzzle based, but do not feel intimidated if that is not your typical style to play in. There is a perfect balance of story, atmosphere, and gameplay which allows the player to not be overwhelmed with the presented challenges.In short, I highly recommend this game and hope more people enjoy it as much as I do! I will also leave another review on the full game's page after I complete it entirely.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: Game play seems alright so far, however I have the really annoying glitch where the jump button will just stop working, killing me countless times, if I Alt-Tab out of the game and go back in it sorts itself out. Also had a glitch where the screen resolution went square instead of widescreen after hitting Esc to pause and had to reset all my Graphic options to sort it back out.Also, I got it on humble bundle but looking at the cost full price, it does not seem worth it to me for the few hours it takes to complete.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: A charming light-physics-based First-Person Puzzler, Lightmatter is another entry into the oddly specific genre of "escaping a poorly-run scientific research facility while a voice on the P.A. demeans you". The levels are seamlessly designed, running smoothly from one into another without any glaring breaks in the narrative, and the colorful character of Virgil is a wonderfully detestable antagonistic force that does his very worst to "help" you along your journey. There were some real thrills in here- every input is a triple-check to make sure you're not accidentally plunging yourself into the unforgiving blackness, and I found myself gasping at every narrow miss, especially towards the end-game. I would recommend this brain-tickler of a game to anyone that enjoyed the original Portal.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: This is a fun puzzle game! It has a simple mechanic but a lot of character and a good narrative. I finished it in a little over 6 hours, but for the cost it's not bad value for money. If you're into unlocking achievements then there's probably a lot more that you can get out of it, I only managed to get 11 out of 23 in this time so I could replay it and be much more curious. Give it a go!
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: Nice shortish first-person puzzle game with a cool mechanic. Movement feels very good. Controls are great. Some slightly clunky interaction, but overall very satisfying. The visuals awesome, the light/dark stuff is great.I was expecting way more puzzles though. And way less endless corridors and silly timed platforming.Antagonist is way too obviously evil. The story could have been a little more ambiguous and at least given you some choice.I'm looking at missable achievements and a guide for them, and most are just plain stupid. Like "stare at it for a minute or two" or "wait 21 minutes in the lever room" -- are you serious? I looked through every corner and looked at most everything, and I still missed almost all of them. It took a few seconds to trigger antagonist's comments about stuff, why would I expect to spend MINUTES on these.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: I can say a lot of things about this game.It is a competent but not groundbreaking first person puzzle game.The story is interesting with a sympathetic antagonist even if the overall beats have been done before.The level design in particular is excellent and I never found myself stuck on any given puzzle for more than a few minutes.But all of that is secondary to Virgil delivering one of the best damned one-liners i've ever heard."I am a man of obsessions, do NOT make yourself one of them."Damned fine bit of dialogue right there. Well done.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: It was a fun ride. It was a bit short, but I really enjoyed the narrative. If it were any longer I don't think the story would have been as interesting. The puzzle rooms are well designed and rewarding as well. All in all, I would recommend this at full price of $20, so when it is on sale, its a steal.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: In many ways, Lightmatter feels like a spiritual successor of Portal to me, and that's not just because of the many references to that game. You have a similar setting in a laboratory that has conducted some questionable experiments for the greater good and are followed through the game by a snarky overseer who comments on your every move and mistake. Is it the most original setting? No, it definitely isn't. Is it still fun? I would argue that it very much is.The puzzles never feel too complicated to be frustrating. Still, I did get stuck at one puzzle and managed to break the game by getting on a moving platform I wasn't supposed to, which in return meant I had to redo that section since you have to go back through it eventually. Still, despite the puzzles not being too complicated it did feel quite satisfying whenever I solved one of them.The fact that you can play the first hour or so of the game for free is also quite a nice change from other games. If you don't feel like paying for the remaining few hours, that's fine. Don't buy it then. And if you think that you would enjoy the rest of the game, consider buying it. Since playing the first 15 levels or so is entirely free however, I would highly recommend anyone to at least try that out. Whether you buy the full game afterwards is completely up to you. I had a lot of fun while playing it though, despite its short length.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a somewhat hesitant recommendation since nothing about Lightmatter particularly stands out to me, but it is a fun enough first person puzzle game.Admittedly I wasn't paying much attention to the story; something about Lightmatter, as you would expect.You play as a dude who gets trapped in a facility when it malfunctions, and you have to follow the rather condescending instructions of a scientist to find your way out. You do this by lighting up dark areas with lamps and connectors to progress, because shadows and darkness kill you. Levels get more complicated as you go (though not too complicated, the game isn't terribly difficult overall) and in the last couple of areas you have to follow existing, moving lights; for me it was a bit much trial and error in these last parts, but considering I ran in a circle about five times at one point without realizing, maybe don't use me as an example.I enjoyed the game and the length is fine as it might overstay its welcome if it were longer than it is (3-5 hours). The music is actually pretty good, though I will say that the constant whingeing of Science Man got a bit on my nerves after a while - which has nothing to do with the voice acting which is fine, but with the fact that I'd rather not be talked at almost non-stop while trying to solve puzzles.The first hour of the game is free  to play so you might as well give it a try and see if it's for you. (Why it specifically says "first hour" puzzles me slightly but in my case it was accurate.)

_childDocuments_.review: Lightmatter is a short, yet immensely enjoyable game that has managed to scratch that first-person puzzler itch that I didn't know I had since probably Portal 2. That comes with little surprise as this game is heavily influenced by the Portal series with easter eggs and references all throughout the game. Lightmatter is very unique in its presentation and art style, which is also part of the principal game mechanic. The "Aha! moment" you get after solving a puzzle is something that is not easy to achieve in game design, yet this game does it with ease. Every level is its own set piece that challenges you to find a solution, but also tells a story and develops the world. All in all its a great game and I absolutely recommend this, especially to Portal fans.

_childDocuments_.review: This game wants to be Portal.It wants to be Portal really really badly. From blatant name-drops to huge references -- apparently Valve even let them put Still Alive in there somewhere.The problem is that this game is not Portal. First, it's not in Source, but in an engine with much less fluid and fun movement, which in a game about only standing on specific spaces on the ground is a significant loss. Second, the humor is nowhere near as biting -- there are some decent moments, but it flipflops between taking itself more seriously with the audio logs and taking itself far less seriously with the humor. When Portal tells a joke you believe that everyone up to the writers is taking it seriously, and that adds to the humor. When Lightmatter tells a joke half of the joke is that they're telling a joke, which makes it far less funny.That's not to say there's nothing here -- if this was standing on its own it would be decent, if somewhat mediocre. But the people making this game made an active attempt to compare themselves to the pinnacle of first-person puzzle games. If you're going to aim for the king, you better not miss.And even if they're not trying to dethrone Portal, even if this is just in good fun, constantly trying to make your audience think of a better game when they're playing yours is not going to make your game look good by comparison.

_childDocuments_.review: I don’t think it’s any secret that Portal is one of the biggest, if not the biggest, influences for puzzle games of this day and age. The Stanley Parable, Quantum Conundrum, and Antichamber are a few examples of the long list. The majority of these games sadly don’t live up to the polish and enjoyment that the Portal titles gave, but some do truly stand out and make for memorable player experiences. Lightmatter doesn’t entirely fit into either of those which works in both its favor and serves to bring down some really high potential.Lightmatter is developed by Tunnel Vision Games and published by Aspyr Media. You may know Aspyr from publishing many games to Linux and Mac, along with publishing Windows games such as Observer and Borderlands 2. You play as an unnamed character, who came for a celebration of the Lightmatter Technologies launch. Something has gone terribly wrong, though, and shadows are now eating people alive. You must use the tools at your disposal along with light itself to find out what happened here. You’re guided by Virgil, voiced by the talented David Bateson (Agent 47 of the Hitman games) who helps you through the facility.Virgil serves both as the game’s most significant and worst storytelling aspect. He serves his purpose absolutely, being your source of backstory and knowledge of what’s going on. He even cracks a few good jokes here and there that got a laugh out of me. The problem with him, though, is that he tells you too much. When I had gotten a quarter of the way into the game, I noticed myself getting annoyed and wondering what this had to do with the actual plot. For example, several scenes have him guessing who the protagonist is. This would be great, but without a reveal of the character’s identity, it feels pointless. Not to mention that all this was crammed into a pretty short game, which I’ll get into later.Despite the negative things I have to say about the story, a fair amount of what he did say added to the experience. There’s a fair amount of backstory to the characters and Lightmatter Technologies. You learn a fair amount of who Virgil is and who his allies are, along with those who doubt his new technology. As the player, you will be left to choose who you think is right, up to having different endings. It does give a bit of player agency, even if one ending does require a secret way to do so. It’s by no means perfect, but it’s compelling enough to where you’ll be interested to see how it all ends.This is in many parts improved by good gameplay and some beautiful visuals. The game does an excellent job of keeping the gameplay fresh despite not introducing many new mechanics. It’s a point that I’d typically criticize, but I don’t find it as much of an issue here. You even get an interesting new mechanic later, which only improves the gameplay tenfold. I would’ve liked to see the two main mechanics used a little bit more together, but it isn’t going to harm your experience much. As said, this works really well for the cartoon-based style of the game. It uses a cel-shading technique similar to Borderlands and Team Fortress 2, which will allow it to hold up pretty well years down the line. It’s a brilliant design choice by the developers, and one I have to commend.All of this is wound together by a great score. I’ve always been a fan of synth music, and I find it fits really well in Lightmatter. There’s even a page on the Extras menu dedicated to the different songs used in the game, which is a plus in my book. The options menu serves its purpose as well, offering a lot of graphics options, control sensitivities, gamepad support, and different languages. There’s definitely a lot of accessibility here, so those who care will love that.And then there’s my final gripe being the length of the game. For my playthrough, I went a bit extreme by getting every achievement since I’m an achievement hunter. That entire experience clocked out at about four hours. I’m a person who values typically quality over quantity, but $20 for three hours without achievements seems a little extreme to me. I usually expect around six to seven hours out of a game at that price, so it’s a bit disappointing. Thankfully though, the three to four hours you play are going to be quite enjoyable thanks to the amount of polish. There were maybe one or two bugs I experienced through my entire playthrough, so it’s clear that a lot of effort was put into playtesting.Lightmatter is a game that takes advantage of its mechanics and visual style to create a compelling experience. I have no doubts in my mind that you’ll want to see this game to the finish, especially to hear the excellent soundtrack that accompanies it. With that being said, it’s hard to ignore the backstory being quite excessive and the story being shorter than what it should be. Despite that, this is a game that you won’t regret experiencing.You can find this review and more on . Thank you to Tunnel Vision Games and Aspyr Media for providing a copy of the game to review.

_childDocuments_.review: Lightmatter is an excellently executed environmental puzzle game in the vein of Portal and The Talos Principe, with a strong narrative to support the whole experience. The artstyle is unique and beautiful, the puzzles are top-notch, but not  difficult, and the voice acting is incredible.
