_childDocuments_.review: Well, this truly is the "little brother" to the "Portal" series, as it takes place in the same in-universe and uses a lot of similar game mechanics, but it also mixes things up with elements from "The Talos Principle" etc, mainly the light beam puzzles that seem to be lifted straight from that game. In no means is that a bad thing, though, since the gameplay is fairly challenging at times and quite simple at others, depending on how good you are with puzzle games in general (and how much you enjoy them).The narrative story of "Lightmatter" does require you to listen a lot, but it does not make you stop while listening, unlike a bunch of other games do (you can rush towards the exit and not be afraid the dialog will be cut short at any moment). If you are willing, you will notice (and possibly enjoy) the little references and breadcrumbs here and there that may seem familiar, if you have had prior dealings with Aperture Science.Overall, it is a fractured 8.5/10 from me, since the experience is quite short-lived, if you are really good at puzzle solving and blaze through the game on your first try. In my case, there were a few situations where I was quite lost for a while until it "AhaAAAah!!"-d on me and I am very OK with that. Next, please!

_childDocuments_.review: Short review:Basically the opposite of Thief: The Dark Project.Long review:Haha, only joking. If Lightmatter were the opposite of Thief, that would imply it's no good. But it is. In fact, I'm very impressed with this game. I've played a handful of 3D puzzle-platformers and the like recently (Portal 2, The Turing Test, The Talos Principle, Kairo, etc), and Lightmatter is one of the best, certainly the most focused and dedicated to its single established theme. To sum up, it's a game where in order to escape from a nearly destroyed science laboratory, you need to stay in the light and avoid shadows, which dissolve you immediately. You do this by manipulating portable lamps, and later on, connecting crystals to light sources to create new paths of light. It's similar to the connectors in The Talos Principle, and its works like a charm. The game is split into separate puzzle chambers, and the game never feels overwhelming despite the complexity of the puzzles. The game gets a lot of mileage of this simple idea without overstaying its welcome.One thing that definitely does do that, though, is the narrator, Virgil. Oh boy, the dialogue itself is well written and the story is fine, but man does he never shut up! It's a bit verbose.That aside, a few things really elevate this game. First is the striking visual style, which certainly gives Lightmatter an edge over The Turing Test. The game plays its light versus darkness aesthetic to magical effect, creating an appealing and atmospheric mixture of subdued purples, blues, white, and black. Sure, there's not much interactivity in the lab, with most objects being either well in the shadows out of reach, or just there to fill space. But Lightmatter does look brilliant. Second is the level design. Lightmatter does linear design superbly, guiding the player convincingly through a large space while not being too restrictive and on-rails. The chambers require a mixture of timing, jumping, and traditional puzzle-solving, and all these elements come together to make something that's hard to master but very hard to put down. I loved playing this game for the six or so hours I spent on it, and I think there's enough potential here for some expansion material or a tangentially-related sequel.Apart from the game crashing to desktop a couple of times, that's all there is to say really. Enjoy it, savour the delightful visuals and puzzle design, and don't let the shadows devour you.

_childDocuments_.review: A neat light/shadow concept that visually carries a short but fun game.I don't like to compare games in reviews because apples and oranges and eye of the beholder or whatever. But this game takes direct inspiration from Portal and Talos Principle. Portal in narrative and setting and Talos in most of the puzzling. So yes, another "Portal clone" or "Portal wannabe" with the whole "stuck in a facility with a narrator" thing. It is indeed getting very tiresome to deal with this setting for every FPS puzzle game but to their credit they openly leaned into it. The narrator even talks about Aperture Science. So at least they were being open about it. And well, the reason people keep coming back to the concept is that it works.The use of light and shadows in this game is a seemingly great concept but most of the puzzles didn't provide a ton of challenge. If you've played Talos Principle, the concepts come to you quickly and easily. It uses the projectors/spotlights and refractors concept. While the setting environments are elaborate and big in scope, the immediate puzzle "rooms" or locations are far too tightly designed. There is not an inch of real estate that doesn't directly lend itself to the current puzzle. If you see there's a gap you can jump, you have to jump it to complete the puzzle. If there's a protruding balcony in the corner, you will be placing a spotlight on it at some point during the puzzle. It's too straightforward in regards to layout. It becomes too much of a clue. That's not to say you won't get stumped once in awhile or stop to scratch your head, but a few environmental red herrings would've padded the difficulty in a good way. The puzzles could've ended up larger and with more pieces as well. And one wholly unique puzzle piece/tool would've given the game's puzzles their own flair. But ultimately I felt like I was playing a collection of easier~midrange Talos levels.The game does show glimmers of independence with the light/shadow mechanic here and there. Underwhelming platforming near the end is actually welcomed as it explores the concepts more beyond the Talos tools. But the gameplay, nor the puzzles, ever fully live up to the potential. Or maybe they did, and the light/shadow concept was merely a new way to present something old. Still though, I had fun and the game does have a good style and scope when it comes to the narrative. The visual style fits the light/shadow gimmick and the environmental visuals outshine the layouts by a lot. It is a truly complex looker despite simple first impressions. Visual design is the strongest part of the game. I do think something got left on the table and it needed that one extra piece of the puzzle to stand out. But I had fun. A short length saves it from ever becoming a chore. Worth a playthrough if you like the genre.

_childDocuments_.review: Very solid puzzle game that borrows heavily from Portal and Talos Principle but doesn't quite reach that superb quality of either (but comes pretty close).Great puzzles. Great concepts. Great story. Tight movement.Minor complaints that keep this from being grouped in the same class as Portal and Talos Principle:Weak Endings.The game could have used one more mechanic to feel more fleshed out.Last level relies heavily on platforming (won't be too hard for most) when none of the other parts of the game did. My dad would love this game but be unable to finish the better ending since he can't do twitchy platforming. Half of the achievements are really, really dumb: Half consist of finding or staring at an inanimate object for one minute (one can only be done on a certain day of the week). Really??? Sit there and do nothing 21 minutes??? Please. Push a button and hope that RNG shows you what you need to see for an achievement; repeat if unlucky (took me 10 minutes). At least there is a complete achievement guide if you are a completionist.We're in 2020 and still can't remap controls in some games. All in all, I'm really glad I picked this one up. Easily worth the $12 I paid. 9/10

_childDocuments_.review: Lightmatter is a gratifying puzzle game that takes a rather simple premise and runs with it for about three hours without getting repetitive or frustrating.The best part is that the game is “free-to-try.” You can play the first hour or so for free, and if you like what you see (and if you like first-person puzzle games – you will), you can then purchase the rest. I love this model, especially for an indie studio’s debut title. It sure made my decision to play the rest of the game much easier.The game could use fewer Portal references and a more robust story, but fans of first-person puzzle games with a soft spot for megalomaniacal voices in their ear will enjoy it.Bottom line, Lightmatter plays, looks, and sounds fantastic, and leaves you wanting more. Hopefully, developer Tunnel Vision Games is listening.

The simple but effective story is told via radio and tape messages. The path through the levels is strictly linear and interaction with the environment is limited to the core puzzle gameplay. Graphics are simple, but provide a unique style. Fans of 3D first persion puzzle games should check it out.

_childDocuments_.review: The puzzles are not too difficult, of course they get a little more difficult towards the end, but shouldn't be a problem for most people and in addition, platforming passages add variety.Some of the achievements are funny and interesting, but a little unfair at the beginning, because with the rare achievements you just have to wait and look at certain objects.I like the story that was being told and the references to Aperture Science are really great. The developers have created a nice little game that is worth playing.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: Lightmatter is a cool light puzzle game, well worth the experience. I really like the personality and story this game takes me through, and I really love that there's no generic "clearly this is the bad guy", and everyone's escalations, from their own perspective, make sense. It's a short game, but very much worth it, as the puzzles can be difficult and can make you really think.And as an additional bonus, the game has developer commentary! And it's got a menu to let you listen to any of the voice lines again that you want! And it's got a speedrun mode if you're into that! Great job! Love extra care for the postgame.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: The level progression is an absolute blast and very similar to Portal. But the ending is the worst! The aims of the characters helping you are not clear cut and you, the player, has no clear cut reason to go all the way at the end. The boss must be stopped, sure, but it all seemed rushed and leaves me with a bunch of questions. :(
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: Lightmatter is a great example of "short and sweet", clocking in at around 4 hours for me. Overall, if you're not afraid to spend 10-20$ on a finely-crafted singleplayer puzzle experience, it's worth checking out.Puzzles are of course the heart of Lightmatter, and they do their job. All of the puzzles are contained in relatively simple and small areas, and have a single "aha!" moment, None are overly difficult (with the longest taking a half hour or so), but I wish the three main mechanics were combined in more ways. Nonetheless, I found solving each puzzle to be satisfying.Story-wise, Lightmatter doesn't have the most thought-provoking or funny story you'll see around, but it was enjoyable enough as the background to the puzzles. In particular, the character who speaks with you throughout the majority of the game is voiced very well, and has dialogue that feels natural for his personality. There is a side-character who's voice acting feels more forced and "video-gamey", but they have so few lines that it didn't bug me too much.I'm a big fan of the "drawn" look Lightmatter has, with thick black lines around each object. On the audio front, I'm a bit less onboard. There are a few great songs during more emotional or exciting moments, but the ambient music is quite repetitive and boring, to the point where I just turned  on my own music in the background.As I said above, Lightmatter isn't going to be a game that you get massive value out of. I think there's something to be said for shorter, polished games though, and it certainly delivers there.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: Lovers of Portal, The Turing Test and Talos Principle, look no further! Here awaits your latest expedition into the future of saving the world. Trust in Lightmatter. This astonishing power-source shall finally remove the barriers humanity has faced and shall allow us to-If you are reading this, Virgil has gone insane! He's locked me in a room an- finally reach the dizzying heights that humanity has been destined for since it first learned to harness power.As the creator of Lightmatter, I am only glad to- We need to shut it down! It's killing people! I didn't realise it was this bad, but if he turns on the main core, we're all going- guide humanity into a brighter future. A future illuminated, by Lightmatter.Endless credit to the writers and voice talent. This game, although short, encompassed all the things I loved about megalomaniac science CEO's as well as a grim satire of upper-management.The puzzles are good and the characters are enjoyable. I can think of no ways to improve this game as it stands and since I'm a picky git, that's about as high praise as I can give.I can only hope that there's a sequel in the works...
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: A very good first person puzzler from a small and passionate team. You use light to manipulate your surroundings and create paths, as shadows will kill you instantly. The narrative is simple, but good enough to keep you going until the end.The game controls well and the concept has been executed almost flawlessly. The only two complaints I would have are about the length and complexity of the game. It took me 4.5 hours to finish, with a bit of afk time, but I wish it was a bit longer. The puzzles themselves are also generally on the easier side; I feel like more could have been done with the concept in terms of puzzle complexity and difficulty. Still, for what it is - a quick and simple fluid first person puzzler with an overarching narrative - the game is great and a definite recommendation.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: Disclaimer: I received a key by the publisher to show off the game on my twitch stream.It took about 6.5 hours for me to play through the game on stream, as with any puzzle game playtime will vary depending on how stuck you may get. I am definitely not great at puzzle games but like to keep my mind challenged so play them a lot.Visual style is simple but looks great and the levels designs worked really well. Both music and voice acting perfectly fit the narrative and setting. The story was interesting and easy to follow and personally there was only 1 puzzle I really got stumped on with it taking close to an hour to figure out. Challenge of the puzzles slowly ramps up adding new mechanics as you progress. The game also has some nice nods to other media, with portal references really standing out.If you enjoy puzzle titles like portal this is definitely worth a try. Especially with the "Free to Try" model the game has on steam which will ease you into some of the beginning levels for free to see if its something you would enjoy.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: This game was a fun one to play, with challanging but not impossible puzzles to solve, using a very unique mechanic I personally haven't seen used in puzzle games. The story was interesting and fairly engaging. I personally say if you have the money on hand, buy the game and play it, it's not a bad trip.And if you like Portal, prepare for some name drops of Apeture Science and some Portal music. Sure made me laugh the first time it happened
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: Lightmatter is an entertaining puzzler with a unique and well executed concept. I've completed 2 playthroughs, the first being around 4 hours long. However, those 4 hours are filled with the smooth voice of Agent 47 as Vergil, plenty of Portal references, and puzzles that are just hard enough to have you really think without being so hard you need to resort to a guide to beat the game.I disagree with the way the devs have this game listed on Steam, hiding the true game price inside DLC in order to push Lightmatter onto the "Free Games" section on Steam, but that's my only gripe with the game. Considering that, I still do recommend playing Lightmatter.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: Amazing game that combines the "stay out of the dark" of Lit with FPS platform puzzles of Portal, with homages in every direction. The only thing it lacked was a "bounce light off mirrors" Zelda-ish puzzle.The plot is funny, dark, and unveils itself slowly with minimal exposition- each character is well rounded and quirky, despite only two characters having speaking lines and another being a cat. Even the nameless, faceless, voiceless protagonist has some secrets to hide if you're paying attention.I feel the game captures the idea of "dangerous new technology" incredibly well, especially since we are so close to the mind and perspective of the mad scientist behind it- the technology has amazing potential, it has some neat tricks and Virgil, our partner as we delve into the depths of Lightmatter, brings up all the possibilities inherent in the technology. At the same time, it also causes shadows to eat people, and his obvious egomaniac tendencies make you think maybe it's not exactly as "green" an energy as he keeps insisting.  It makes me think of Steamboy the animated movie, where one character holds up this revolutionary new steam technology as being able to revolutionize the world and make everything better, and then less than 15 minutes later is casually using it as a weapon of mass destruction.My one regret was not being able to slug Virgil in the face after all was said and done, especially considering he manages to get the "last world" no matter what.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: A Portal rip-off, and proud of it!You find yourself in an abandoned, semi-ruined research facility, being guided by a disembodied, egotistical voice, getting past logic puzzles (light beams instead of portals). Sound familiar....?Lightmatter doesn't just know the shadow it is living in (did you see what I did there?), but revels in it. The voice of Virgil complaining about "those monsters over at Aperture Science" is hilarious.The puzzles are good, without being enormously challenging. None of them had me stuck for more than a couple of minutes. But don't let that put you off - I thoroughly enjoyed Lightmatter. It is a good game.And don't let those bastards at Aperture Science tell you otherwise!!!
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: Really great game!Voice acting 10/10, really got to appreciate the characters.The game is short, managed to finish it in 2.9 hours, but it's a really entertaining game, never played a Puzzle game like this one.Puzzles were really interesting, most of them were easy, at least for me, though there were some that got me scratching my head for quite some time.The history is really interesting, I would have loved if we got to know more about the world and the background.The narrative was really on point, it was great!When it comes to graphics or aesthetics, it's really difficult to rate it. The aesthetics in general were really good, specially towards the end of the game. But overall, I didn't felt like there was much to appreciate on it, I found my self speed-running the scenarios because of it.I do really recommend the game if you are bored some day, pretty entertaining.Gratz to the team for coming up with quite a unique idea!
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: Game was your typical indie puzzle game length, good price point when bought on sale.  Dialog was funny and entertaining without being too much, and I liked that it wouldn't get interrupted or restart if you happened to die.  The environment was a disconcerting mix of very detailed yet noninteractive, so I ended up spending a lot of time examining things without any benefit.  The achievements were also not my favorite, as they involved finding certain objects and then standing by those objects for 2-21 minutes depending.  Just felt like a way to pad gameplay time...
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: Story and presentation of the world are pretty amazing.The portal references were too obvious IMO, wish they didn't outright mention Aperture, should've been more subtle.A lot of the puzzles give you that aha moment, and while some of them can be very hard, they're mostly very doable.Visually it's very cool, but the game crashed and froze a lot for me (and I mean a LOT - though this might be different for you).I like that there were no loading screens, with there being loading zones instead. Sure there was a slight stutter, but it made it feel like you were actually moving through a facility rather than a series of rooms.Overall, I really, really liked it.

_childDocuments_.review: Well, it was quite short, but fascinating adventure.+1) Game has a really good story line2) Portal fans will like this very much3) Some puzzles forced to think some while-1) There is no tutorial in the beginning, even controls are intuitive2) The final of the game is just hidden, why dont devs show us what happened after3) Gameplay time. (like in Portal)2) Coop mode with another story line will be really greatFinal mark: 8/10. The game is worth buying & passing.

_childDocuments_.review: Portal-like where you have to strategically place and manipulate lamps and light-emitting orbs to remove shadows to progress because if you walk on shadows you die. _childDocuments_.review: Very meh, but not bad.Did not like the puzzles much, failing sometimes reset the puzzle and sometimes not which was confusing. Most puzzles were in my opinion boring, where you know what you need to do, but executing it requires just moving platforms back and forth in the right order or whatever. They didn't make me feel clever, just like trying every option until one worked.Story was fine, and the ending platforming sequence was fun. I think adding some platforming between puzzle levels would have helped with puzzle burnout.The story and buildup felt way too derivative of portal. A problem with most of the games in this puzzle genre though. However, in this they really highlighted it by making all these references to portal all the time. Once would have been bad enough but they kept doing it. Why would you want to remind the player of a way better game all the time?The one thing I liked was that Vergil kept changing his mind on who you, the player, are. But I was disappointed in how little they used this gimmick. I would have liked more/funnier jokes about journalists and "health inspectors" and so on.

_childDocuments_.review: Lightmatter is a decent puzzle game no doubt inspired by Portal.Where the main concept is "shadows are lava" and by illuminating them you negate the effect.While you get a nice introduction how to solve the puzzles a lot of them feel like task in the end because you know how to solve them you just need to bring everything to the right place. _childDocuments_.review: I loved this game!  So many games claim to be "the next Portal", but this is the first one where that felt true to me.  No, it's not quite as awesome as Portal (I don't know if anything can be), but this comes awfully close.  I love the puzzles, the storytelling, and the overall vibe of the game.  It was just plain fun!  Plus, bonus points for all the Easter eggs.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: A visually stunning and lovingly crafted tribute to the fps puzzle genre, with implicit and explicit references to Aperture science made throughout, in case you were in any doubt as to what inspired the developers...Some very smart light-based puzzles along with the odd dash of mild parkour will get your brain-sac pulsating in an environment where the shifting shadows will melt you faster than you can say 'farting photons'.It's not a long game (I ambled through it in under 5 hours), but it still left me satisfied and I know there were a number of secrets that were missed hidden in the dark recesses of the beautifully crafted levels, so I may well replay it later on.The voice acting by David Bateson (Agent 47 - Hitman) is also superb, perfectly cast as a power hungry and condescending scientist, watching your every move, cajoling and taunting you from some distant location, ever-present yet never feeling overdone or hammy.Thoroughly recommended to fans of the genre, the price point is about right I think, but if you can get it on sale then all the better. 4.8/5 slices of pie
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: I got this as part of a Humble Bundle, and being a fan of Portal and other puzzly type games I was quite excited to play Lightmatter.    I'm also a big fan of the Stanley Parable, which I feel is somewhere in the DNA of this game buried deep too.Basically explained (in-game) as a variant of "The Floor is Lava", the portals from Portal are replaced as the primary puzzle device by lamps which cast shadows.   Similar to some other Indy games from a few years ago in which the shadows were dangerous, this game pits you against "gravitic anomalies" which are (basically) any surface which is completely devoid of light.You make your way through a series of very Portal-2-esque locations, solving puzzles to get past light-based triggers, doors, and so on.    The puzzles are well designed, solvable through either lateral thinking or brute-force, so you don't often get stuck for long.    There are a few run-and-jump sections where you have to be a 3d platformer. These can be a little annoying if you're not super-precise with the jumping, but the game insta-resurrects you, so it's not a major problem to die.  You'll die a lot, and thankfully the devs haven't put in any silly achievements about getting through the areas without dying, so there isn't that to have to chase.    The achievements themselves actually are a bit silly.. Needing to stare at a burger for 2 minutes, for instance.   You have to try to work out what to do in order to get some of the achievements, and the only clue is the achievements' name.   Don't bother, just check out the forum post where someone's listed them out, and save yourself a LOT of hassle.  You'll thank me later.The music's good, the voice acting is brilliant, and the soundscapes are fantastic if you play on headphones.Any physicists will baulk at the idea of there being a lamp in a room and somehow scattering suddenly stops at the edge of cubic objects, so the front face and wall behind the box can be brightly lit, but the shadow between the box and wall is blacker than Vanta Black... It just can't happen as long as you have reflections, scattering and lambertian surfaces.   Also, the surfaces turning into "gravitic anomalies" sounds like black holes....  which would do all kinds of damage... So, you have to take the actual physics of this with a pinch of salt.    :)Get this and play it!  It's really cool.

The game pace is also great, it mixes some easy but fluent platformer in this puzzle game, a change of speed which helps us relax every now and then.Problems1. Crash twice.2. There are some easy deaths after introducing light matters.

_childDocuments_.review: Very good puzzle platformer. Not quite as hard as some others like Talos Principle, which can be considered a pro or a con, depending on how hardcore a puzzler you are. I'm probably about average, and I completed it without having to look anything up, which is always a plus. Great voice work, and the game doesn't overstay its welcome. It ended right when I wanted it to. Definitely recommended if on sale - not sure I would have paid full price.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: Well, might as well get it out of the way sooner than later: yeah, it's hard not to make comparisons to Portal. It's the same genre, has a similar setting, an eccentric person pursuing potentially dangerous science talks to you over a radio, and it's a whole ball of fun.Granted, It only took me a little over five hours to play through (over the course of a few days, I imagine it'd take longer in one sitting to process the puzzles and what-not), but if you're the kind to achievement hunt you'll probably want a second go.That said, I agree that the game could probably be extended without feeling stretched too thin: in particular, there's room for more levels incorporating the whole of Lightmatter's elements. However, what is there is quite fun and teased my brain a great deal. The story, too, was quite fun to see unfold over the course of the game: simple as it might be, it was paced very well.Overall I definitely recommend it. Will you get a dollar-an-hour value out of Lightmatter? No, almost definitely not. However, I think you'll still get your money's worth by any other metric from a good story, fun gameplay, brain-teasing puzzles, and the occasional Portal reference.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: Very Portal-esque vibes. Took around 8 hours to finish the game 100%.Puzzles get harder the further you get into it with new Mechanics being brought into the mix.Story is pretty good with the occasional Portal reference being a nice addition.Performance wasn't perfect, didn't feel like a consistent 60fps which seemed weird as the Graphics shouldn't be that demanding. Might be a personal problem but worth a mention.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: Weakly recommend. Worth it for $5, maybe not much more. This game wears its inspiration, Portal, right on its sleeve. Although there's nothing wrong with that, you'll quickly get tired of the 100th Portal reference, of feeling like you're trapped in a subreddit of 14-year-olds who just discovered "the cake is a lie" memes, of the same "I'm telling you how to navigate this world while also insulting you constantly, you moron, you absolute dunce who can't even figure out you must press W to move forward and SPACE BAR to jump, god I hope you die here in DemeaningToThePlayer Industries. Oh, you're alive? Well now press CTRL to crouch if that's not too much for you, you complete imbecile."The puzzles are almost entirely versions of the "you have a wolf, a  goat, and a bag of lettuce and you must cross the river" puzzle: find a piece, move it here to clear a path to bring another piece over, and now use that to bring the first piece to where you need it. Visually, it's a very cool mechanic, but as the game continues it doesn't move much beyond that. The additional changes to the puzzles as you continue feel pretty similar: more pieces to move around, but the pieces are still all the same basic shape. For every great puzzle there are 3-4 identical levels, where you'll feel like you're doing the basic same thing you just did in the last room.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: Fun game. Not especially long, but I enjoyed it. I spent far too long on a couple of the puzzles, but that's just something that can happen with puzzlers.The light vs shadow mechanic is interesting. The story itself is kinda fascinating.  Love the voice acting and dialogue. Also, great music!NOTE: Appears to have two endings, although I only took the default route.Quite a few references to Portal (Aperture Science), very much enjoyed those.  I felt it was worth my purchase.

_childDocuments_.review: A really fun puzzle game where you explore the breaking lab of an insane feat of man. I completed one puzzle really quickly and felt incredibly smart since it seemed super difficult looking back then took about 10 minutes to find a broken window to get the elevator.It also seems to be inspired by something, but I can't quite put my finger on it what with the distracting talk of neurotoxin cake and this "Aperture Science" thing.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: Cute, and the individual puzzles are with only a few exceptions very short and not particularly difficult (It's a ~2 hour game, there's ~40 puzzles, you do the math), but it holds together all the way through and the light mechanic is a lot of fun; play the demo, please, but for $20 you could do worse. There are an excessive amount of Portal jokes (I wasn't looking for them and I counted seven? and I know I missed at least two more based on the achievements I don't have), but the plot doesn't rely on them, so it's not game breaking. The random precision platforming sequence at the end was hell, in a bad way, though. I understand what the developers were going for, I think, but either there should have been a lot more precision platforming earlier in the game (the vent sequences would have been a good place for them), or they should have an option to skip it for people like me, who deliberately checked that there wasn't going to be anything like that and got blindsided by it.I do wish the 'true' ending was a little more.... conclusive? Because it's just Virgil whining at you some more, and I still had questions. Speaking of Virgil, he's an excellent villain, and I struggled through the end just to find out what he was going to say about it, and while I was disappointed it was in character. Also I firmly believe his first guess was right, and you are an OSHA inspector, and boy is he ever going to fail his inspection.9/10, overall, and Lux is my baby now.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: While the concept for the game sounds fantastic, the execution wasn't really the best. Almost all puzzles are very easy to solve, except for 3 by which I got stuck. By 1 only because I didn't saw that I could jump across the gap because of the broken railing there.The other two puzzles were "difficult" (and tbh all of them) for me because the guy couldn't shut up for a hot minute and let me do my thing. I cannot multitalk, and when someone talks to me while I try to solve a puzzle, then I get distracted by that talking. So I had to turn the voice volume to 0% multiple times throughout the game.Apropos the narration. I don't know what else to feel than dismiss about the fact that there are multiple references to Portal. Game, build your own identity without making oblivious references to your inspiration.The story in itself it fine, nothing big, nothing small. Perfect for a puzzle game like that, because I think a puzzle game doesn't need to have a big story.I think the game would have been better as a (puzzle) platformer, as the final act was more fun than any else before, lmao.

It has a nice unusual art style with nice sfx. The game mechanics are good and solid and overall an engaging game play. A good experience and worth the money. Hats off to the devs ...now do more :)

_childDocuments_.review: Most comparisons will be to Portal, but that's not a bad thing. If you like Portal or the sequel, this game should appeal to you. Think of it as Portal meets Alan Wake. You are trying to avoid darkness and a lot of "floor is lava" style puzzles are in store. Game isn't too long, roughly 3-4 hours and has voice good voice acting to keep the story going.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: This puzzle platformer is a quick and entertaining romp through a stylized underground facility using a series of tools centered around the manipulation of light and light-related objects. For the most part, the puzzles themselves are quite straightforward, and (with one notable exception near the end) tend to be spelled out pretty clearly with environmental cues if you look closely enough. At times, the writing of the character serving as your guide/narrator can be somewhat grating, but is mostly a mildly amusing twist on the GLaDOS concept out of Portal. Honestly, the developer of this game REALLY seems to like Portal, considering how many references are in it, including several lines from the pseudo-antagonistic character that place Lightmatter's existence within the world of Portal and Black Mesa. Unfortunately, aside from these comments, the story as a whole comes across as a standard (almost stereotypical) egoistic mad scientist bent on trying to exert his will on the world around him and beyond assured of his own superiority to all of those around him. While in Portal this affect of the omniscient narrator was diegetically explained by the fact that it was a machine literally in control of the entirety of the Aperture Science facility, this game has no such explanation and thus can come across as a bit contrived at times.Overall, it is short but a fun use of a few hours of light puzzle solving with a minimally engaging story, but if you're mainly interested in a novel platformer with a fun and curious concept to play with, you can't go wrong here. It certainly isn't Portal, but it could potentially be its own thing down the road if the developer ever expands on this!
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: Decent game. Not as hard as the free portal stories: mel. But you will have fun with it. Voice acting is "veeeeeery nice" and subtle enough with its permanent indirect insults. Amient sounds are soothing.Puzzles are decent - and less hard then said portal stories: mel or the talos principle.You completely play in confined areas,The devs definitely did a fine job here.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: Oh boy where to start.First off, the utilization of having an hour to test the game is something that I love and think more games should do. Then the story continues to grow, I find myself getting more and more invested in the puzzles and story. Sometimes I would have to walk away from a puzzle to think about it, but my goodness. This game scratched the Portal / Puzzle solving itch I know they were looking to scratch. Second off, the way the story makes you a silent protagonist fits so well in the situation you find yourself in. If they are working on future content- I would love to see a custom map maker of sorts, I know its a lot of work to build that system but I would love to see the community content that comes from the systems that are implemented within, I also fear that same content from the crazy people that play video games. I HIGHLY RECOMMEND. Please give this game a shot. I can't wait to see what comes of the future of this developer. (p.s- art style is soooooo unique and I absolutely love it)
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: When this game came out I played it for about an hour and half, forgot about it for about two months and decided to finish it once and for all. To be honest, I'm glad I did, (This is April 2020 when I'm writing this review). It's a pretty solid game, if you have a decent computer the game will look very pretty, but to the ones that don't, the low settings are okay. The game does not take long to complete, about half a day if you're going for all of the achievements, but the game has an interesting story and complex puzzles that really make someone think. It also has plenty of easter eggs, mainly to Portal and they're quite fun to find. My only criticism is of the achievements, most of them are about going to the right area, or staring at something for a minute, or dying in a certain place. I feel like the achievements had more potential, "Record of Six" was not a hard achievement but it was a good challenge to keep in, maybe if there was an achievement for speedrunning the game or not dying a certain amount of times to give the game a little more extra difficulty for the ones who want it. It deserves an 8/10 because the story, art design, and puzzle and level design are well made, however the achievements were a missed opportunity. Don't get me wrong, I enjoyed every second of this game and I highly recommend it to anyone that enjoys first person puzzle games.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: Generally I like this game.I love visual style. White and dark lab interiors look great. I also like music. It fits puzzle game nicely. And I've enjoyed solving most of the puzzles.What I didn't like were not-so-subtle Portal references. You don't have to scream "Hey, we love Portal and it's our inspiration!"  It gets annoying fast. Also the game is a bit too short. But I prefer short polished game to a long messy one, so it's fine

_childDocuments_.review: A worthy descendant of Portal. Except for the ending (last level is platforming, story ends meh), but you can skip that (unless you crave for the achievements).Gameplay is very well polished, ambiance (visuals and music/sound) effects are subtly... effective (duh!), puzzles are very good (none of them becomes long or tedious). It helps to know that dying is never a big deal, you won't lose much progress, if any, so you can go try things and die and quickly respawn; I wish more games were like this.And there's a demo! Too few studios do those these days.4/5 recommended

_childDocuments_.review: I must say i am bloody surprised by this Portal-like game.For an indie game like this one to go almost further than a genra defining game such a Portal, it was astonishing.I love the voice acting making an immersive dive in a darker and more moraly ambigious universe filled with references to his older cousin.Sure, the replayability is a bit short, allowing you play almost twice through the 38 leveled campaign in almost a bit under 10 hours.Sure, some achievements are here only to grow gametime (looking at you 21 minutes of idle) yet all of this is extremely rewarding and *redacted for spoilers*Add some community creation and mods and this game would be a solid 9 or 10.Honestly, you'll love this.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: Wheatley Called...The one positive I have is it looks nice if you are standing still. Animations are stiff but I don't even factor that in for the measure of fun. You have very limited control options and are not able to re-bind keys. Not a huge deal since your actions consist of walking, jumping, and interacting. No running, which can be reasonable for balancing earlier puzzles but a detriment for trying to expand later. Every puzzle I have solved so far led me to say "huh, that was it." No Eureka moment or reflecting upon the cleverness of a set-up. There are some ok-ish implementations of moving machinery or platforms.The first 5 minutes nearly killed the game instantly. You wake up to a smarmy British man who belittles your intelligence and gives expository monologues about what happened and what to do. Your first mission is to turn on the lights. Doing this does not give any insight or teach any of the games mechanics other than the interact button exists. Your reward are more monologues by this unlikable head honcho.Now you are introduced to work lamps (lights on a stand). You can pick them up and walk with them but you can't jump with them or angle the lens. Nothing hints about the functionality of the lamps, you just figure it out. As far as I know that's it, that's the rest of the game. Two of my biggest problems with this game aren't even relevant to the mechanics:1)annoying speaker guy2)tapes left by people talking about "head scientists in the field of science". Anyone who uses the term "science" to explain anything other than "the field of" or "progress in" probably has no idea what they are talking about. Maybe in 100 years when people start getting hired for reasons other than merit, but not today.

_childDocuments_.review: This game seems like a good little puzzler, albeit that the story line is not particularly engaging, at least for as far as I've played it.But, it's 2020 for goodness sake - why are new games still being released with no option to re-bind controls, and with the default controls no good for left handed players. You're losing out on 10% of the market.I'd be tempted to buy this game if I could re-bind the controls.

_childDocuments_.review: Worth playing once for the interesting concept.Unfortunately the puzzles aren't particularly challenging, and they don't seem to build up to satisfying levels of complexity the way Portal does, for instance. There are a couple particularly good ones, but most of them fall a bit flat and leave me thinking, "Was that it? Just had to get this lamp here and now I'm done? Oh well." When the puzzles did stump me, it really felt like I was just dumb, rather than that the puzzles were clever. More of an "Ugh" moment than an "Aha" moment.The story was adequate, but I found the characters incredibly overwrought and unlikable in a not-fun way. Despite toying with some "ethical" ideas, there isn't ultimately much complexity to the plot or the characters, and you don't get to make any choices. I don't come away wishing that I had heard more dialog, or wanting to revisit this facility. My computer is pretty bad so I didn't get to experience the visual effects to their fullest, and I found the platforming aspects of the game very clunky and frustrating. That's most likely a personal problem though.Overall, this is a pretty fun one-time play, but it doesn't have anything so magical that I would want to revisit it.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: Lightmatter is a portal-inspired puzzle game where shadows kill you and you must use light to solve puzzles and progress. While the story and references hearken back to that of Portal, the puzzle design is unlike anything I have played before, it helps to think of the puzzles in reverse to figure out where you want light to be by the end, but I still found myself struggling on a few puzzles.The full game takes around 2 hours to complete so I don't think it's worth picking this up at full price, but it frequently goes on sale for 60-70% off which is most certainly worth it, I hope they make a sequel eventually because I do think there is more to explore in this world.In lightmatter shadows kill you and the only way to stay alive is by staying in the light, It's all very perspective based and you must find the correct angle or placements of lights to help you solve the puzzles, you are given many things to do this throughout the game like lamps and what is called a photon connector, which is essentially a laser that emanates light when in line of sight to a source, these along with having to deal with temporary lights and moving platforms allow for some pretty unique puzzle design. The narrative is pretty similar to portal with an unseen antagonist speaking to you throughout the game, he also references characters from the portal universe many times, I personally enjoyed it but I saw that some others didn't. The ending tries to be intense but it usually just ends with you dying and nonchalantly respawning with little progress lost, the voice acting here is great but I think it falls short in the puzzle department.The achievements are pretty fun and you can get them all within 1 playthrough if you follow a guide, if you happen to miss anything the game features level select allowing you to get very close to where you need to be for each achievement. The only bad achievement is "Burger Friday" that requires you to complete a task on a Friday.The sound design and music are pretty repetitive throughout up until when the finale music kicks in. The standout part of this game however has to be the voice acting of the CEO, he plays the part perfectly and brings a great intensity to the role.Free demo available. Features level selection. Features Ingame speedrun stats overlay. Keyboard, mouse and controller support but seemingly not rebindable. Voice over supported in English and Danish, subtitles supported in many languages. Dyslexic font option. Game has crash issues occasionally. Portal-inspired puzzle game where you must use light to solve puzzles and progress. Worth buying on sale. Unique puzzle design. Interesting story. Stellar voice acting. Level select. Fun achievements.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: This was really good. Up there with Portal in quality, though the constant references to Portal I could have done without. That said, it's easily the best first-person puzzle-game I've played since Portal 2. It uses a very different gimmick, but pulls it off (mostly) really well. Definitely worth checking out.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: Short but sweet game where you traverse through a facility solving puzzles while an intercom voice gives you backstory with a quippy style.No this isn't Portal, but its still a good way to spend a couple of hours. The game knows it is cloning the DNA of Portal so it throws as many Portal references at you as it can, from dialogue throwing shade at Aperture Science to hidden items like a P-body and cube, and even achievements about cake and lies.These puzzles aren't going to strain your brain, especially if you have played Portal or The Talos Principle. At times i found myself standing around listening to the guy on the intercom tell the story because i was worried I would get through the next puzzle too quick. Only once was the answer not immediately obvious, and even then it didnt take long to figure out. But I really enjoyed the style of the puzzles and appreciate the work that went into them. I feel like I'm Marge Simpson, I just want to say they're neat.Worth a buy to spend a rainy afternoon blitzing my way through puzzles while an interesting story unfolded.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: If you liked Valve’s Portal series, you HAVE to try Lightmatter. The game is honestly amazing and feels like it’s in the same universe of Aperture Science. The main antagonist talks so much ♥♥♥♥ about Cave Johnson, it’s amazing. The first 20 levels or so of the game you can do for free ( I think they market it as the first hour of the game is free ) but I got so invested that by the time it came to pay, I already had my wallet on me. The puzzles are hard, the secrets you find are really fun and the achievements were on point. I absolutely loved the ending and I hope they make another one. Took me 7 hours and 2 days to finish ( I wanted to actually enjoy it and take my time ) and it was DEFINITELY worth it.

The puzzling built into the game is challenging at times and let's be honest the guy over the P.A. system is so damn condescending that I couldn't decide if I hated him or just wanted to high five him for the witty banter.Overall the creators did a good job and I'd like to see more, maybe figure out a way to add some DLC with more game play. _childDocuments_.review: If there's one thing you can say with certainty about Lightmatter, it's that the guys who made it really *loved* Portal, and wanted a game that was 'like' Portal, but where the floor was lava.  The consequence is a game that actually has some ~ok puzzles, I did end up having tutorial one just because I literally could not find one awkwardly placed light on the third floor of an elevator, but other than that they were actually mostly pretty good. But surprisingly the little sections of platforming at the end of just dodging the shadows was satisfying and fun, perhaps even more so than the puzzle elements earlier. I don't recall whether I got this in a bundle or how I came across it, but in the end I think this was an enjoyable little 4-5 hour game.

_childDocuments_.review: Fun game with increasingly more difficult puzzles. An original design that reminds me of Portal, perhaps not as compelling a story but a great one nonetheless. If you love puzzle solving and mystery, I cannot recommend this game enough! We need more games like these! (Only 4 hours playtime which is the time it took me to finish the game) My guess is between 3 and 5 hours depending on the time you take to solve the puzzles.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: The best game of 2020 so far.Lightmatter is a puzzle/platforming game in the same vein as Portal and The Talos Principle. The main mechanic of the game is similar to that of the floor is lava where darkness is akin to what lava is. I.e, stay in the lighted areas and not touch dark areas or die. There are two main tools to carry around and help you create a lighted safe path towards the exit in each segment. The first is a lamp that shines light in a straight line and the other is an orb that will pull light rays from a special light generator or fellow powered up orbs as long as it is not blocked by any obstacles. Fans of the Talos principle will no doubt have a sense of Déjà vu.It contains some of the most clever and well thought out puzzles that I have ever played. Even more impressive is the fact that the development team consists of relatively young graduates from Denmark who used an unorthodox and wholly innovative creative process to plan out the puzzles: Lego blocks. I am still trying to picture the process in my head and hopefully they will release some behind the scenes snippets of this unique creative process. The team definitely a fan of the genre as there are some easter eggs/mentions about the floor is lava, Portal and a possible Hitman one (rubber duck)Hitman fans would be delighted to know that David Bate, the voice of agent 47 is the main narrator of this game, providing the voice for Lightmatter Technologies CEO Virgil. David pulls off a very convincing CEO which shows his talent as a multifaceted voice actor. That being said however, this game still lacks some polish which would no doubt be polished out in the upcoming patches:- There was a glitch in the area when you encounter the dangerous dark areas for the first time where the exit door did not spawn and I spent a good 20mins back tracking trying to figure out what I missed until I hit the "retry" button and this time the exit door was there.- Another glitch with the very first orb was once I carried it, I could not put it down, I had to "retry" again to fix the issue.The final act is a slight letdown for me as it doesn't contain anymore amazing puzzles and its mainly a platforming segment. An ability to save would be great as I can foresee some players getting frustrated by this segment. All in all, if you are fan of puzzle games, recommending this game is a no brainer for me. Its sits up there with the very best of its kind alongside: Portal, The Talos Principle, Inside etc
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: If you like Portal, you will like this game. It's the same type of puzzle but with light and shadow.There is a CEO like cave johnson following you all along with his voice. It's really nice to hear him talking. As you play, he make joke and everything. I really recommand this game. It's worth the price. The content and the time is equal at a run on Portal 2. 10 Hours of playing mostly with a lot of puzzle.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: It's a game that seems like it tries pretty hard to follow in the Portal series' footsteps, even having a few direct and indirect references to that series placed within the game. Despite that initial setback, it's an extremely charming game with a really cool mechanic that I feel is used well in various ways throughout. The story is pretty simple, but that's not always a bad thing. I feel the one thing that could have been improved upon is how the puzzles are ordered throughout the game. You really got the coolest, most complex puzzles/puzzle elements in the middle stage of the game, and then return to timing and platforming towards the end, but I won't fault the designers for that if they were trying to stick to their narrative. The puzzles right before the end where the giant doors would start closing to shut off more and more of the light in the room was still cool as hell, and introduced the right amount of hurry for that part of the game story.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: Clever, short, and not-terribly-challenging FPPP (First Person Platform Puzzler) consisting largely of un-timed puzzles where the main goal is to light up your pathway to the exit (more The Talos Principle than Portal) combined with the occasional platform-inspired "jump" your way to the exit instead -- especially in the final act. Although a bit heavy-handed at times, the story, voice acting, music and overall art direction make this an easy buy for puzzle fans on the fence.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: A "short" game playing on light and darkness. I enjoyed the story, the sound and the graphics. Gameplay was great and I had a lot of fun.It's like portal (same idea of puzzle chambers) but a whole new spin on the genre. Never a dull moment, the puzzles were clever (not too hard and not to easy either) and the 3D platforming was excellently implemented. Do give it a go. I've finished it in about 6 hours and still have achievements to get.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: Bought the game on sale, wish I could buy it at normal price.After a 4½-hour playthrough of the game, I felt a joy of puzzle solving I haven’t had since the last time I played Valve’s Portal 2. I had the language on danish (because I’m a Dane and Lars Mikkelsen’s voice is satisfying as f**k) and I enjoyed it the more I went down the rabbit hole. The story is great and has some good plot points, the level design was challenging but possible (the point of a puzzle solving game, duh) and I love all the lovable references and hits at Portals legacy.The art-style and content of the levels could perhaps have been more detailed, but it’s simple and it does the Job. It was nice when they introduced the standing lightbulbs that gave the puzzles a unique feeling, but the gab until you could use the normal lamps again felt a bit stretched. A mix of these features earlier on would have been nice.In Conclusion: If you have played Portal or Portal 2, you will love this game. It’s not a copycat, yet it’s easy to see that its heavily inspired by Portal, but it’s unique and the people behind it can be proud of it. Oh yeah, be prepared for all the kettles that’s placed all over the place. You can’t miss them…
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: I haven't bought the full game so I can't give a full review, but the time that I did play for I enjoyed. There are definite elements from Portal (and the games are in the same universe apparently) but it has some cool mechanics. The puzzles were good, and maybe I'm just bad at puzzles, but challenging too. I'd suggest you pick this game up if you're into fun, interesting puzzle games.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: Obviously heavily inspired by the Portal games, not just because of the puzzles but the dry humour as well (not to mention the references within the game). A thoroughly enjoyable game; challenging at times, but never truly punishing. A bit linear and a little frustrating with the amount of static random objects that you cannot interact with (I have been spoiled by open world games), but those are minor complaints. Ultimately, I would recommend this if you are at all into puzzle games.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: Puzzles are well done, challenging, and come up with some pretty cool scenarios to work through. The story turned me off though. I know the "narrator" isn't supposed to be well liked, but he spends the last 1/3 of the game yelling at you to stop doing everything you do. When a game makes you feel bad for playing it, it's hard to enjoy the experience.It's a close call, but I'm not recommending this since the unique story is what I came to the game for and it did not leave me satisfied.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: Lightmatter is a somewhat short, charming little puzzle game comprised of bending light to navigate the shadows in a crumbling facility. The puzzles may make you stop and think for a moment, but they aren't too difficult, and they're quite fun to figure out.With a simplistic art style and good eye for detail Lightmatter achieves its unique aesthetic. The achievements are simple and silly, good for achievement hunters!If you're worried about whether or not you can run it, keeping the graphics low should keep it smooth.I recommend taking the free hour before buying the game and buying on sale.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: Nice game.It’s pretty smooth, though there is a bit of a lag spike during area transition. The puzzles can be both simple and mind boggling. And the game definitely knows how to paste itself. Overall, good stuff for anyone looking for a pseudo-comedic puzzle game.It can feel a bit short for its price though, so some people might prefer to wait for the more-than fair discount.Though on a personal note, I found that one Portal reference was kind of funny. The other 4 might have been a little overkill.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: It’s a nice little first person puzzler. You’re an unnamed protagonist who might as well be a crack OSHA agent deployed to an energy generation facility. Problems are to be solved deploying light against fatal shadows. Modestly funny, makes so many nods to Portal it could get a neck injury. I enjoyed my time with the game.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: The prologue of this game was free initially, so i tried it and was sure would not really buy the game, but i clearly was wrong. This game with the sci-fi touch and humour (which is not too crazy but alright) got me hooked. The levels are quite good, some are thinkers but most of them can be solved with ease once you get the hang of it.  A new concept of puzzle game where darkness is not so friendly.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: This game is educational not for its content but, like a reviewer said below, for its price point. We're reaching an inflection point here where the cost of producing the game that people expect is running into a hard ceiling of the 50/60$ for AAA titles that people have been used to paying since 1990. The difference is that the titles in 1990 required maybe 2-10 people to produce over the course of a year. Now they require thousands of people and tens of millions of dollars over the course of many years.Why does this matter? Because Lightmatter inadvertently stepped into this balancing act. The game is a good game, its got a decent story, decent mechanics, decent everything....except decent doesn't get you a high price point if the playable content isn't there. The primary mechanic, for those who haven't played, is that you manipulate spotlights to provide safe passage through a level. If this sounds familiar it's because it is...it's the exact mechanic of the laser in the Talos Principle. And this is where the price point discussion comes back into this. Lightmatter, for 20$ nets you 30 levels where you MAINLY use the spotlight. Talos Principle for, let's just call it double the price at 40$, nets you over 120 levels - 4x the level content (and if you buy it on sale, you can get the DLCs, etc...for free) not to mention numerous additional game mechanics  to help aid you in manipulating the laser light, NOT just a laser beam. That's the problem with Lightmatter, it's not enough "game" for the price it asks. If 40$ gets you 120 levels then 30 levels should cost 5$; but beyond the harsh math, the lack of mechanics/content within the game and the substitution of platforming for "puzzling" (which is just lazy) simply do not justify 20$. Even IF the developer added 120 levels, but changed nothing with the game mechanics, it wouldn't be worth more than 10$.Maybe this game would have been worth 20$ back in 1995, but, as consumers expect more and more content while keeping the 60$ hard ceiling, games delivering below that threshold get labeled "overpriced".And, sadly, that's what this game is currently.

_childDocuments_.review: I speak about aspects of the game in this review, but do not have spoilers.Lightmatter was an amazing game. I think people claiming it to be a Portal rip off need to take another look at Portal, the mechanics are very different. Even if it were, I don't think another Portal is such a bad thing as they don't come out very often. That said, it's clear that Lightmatter took a lot of inspiration from Portal and some voice lines make it clear that the two games exist in the same universe so to speak.With that out of the way, Lightmatter is an exceptional game. The puzzles are challenging, the pacing is great, and the story is exceptional. I think the game did feel like it lacked a bit of necessary budget to make it truly phenomenal. For example, the story seemed a bit rushed like more content could have been made to make it feel more complete and a bit longer. Also the ending sequence and scenes were great but felt like a lower budget settling for something more grand they could have done given more time/money. What I think they got right with the budget they had though is they did not compromise on quality for the part they did do. The story, voice acting, game mechanics, and graphics all had a notable attention to detail that made it clear this was not a cheaply made and rushed project. This is appreciated in a day where most games feel incomplete, even AAA titles which have what seems like an unlimited budget.Overall, Lightmatter was a fantastic game that immediately earned a spot on the short list of games I truly love and recommend. I think if you try it out you won't regret it and you'll definitely get your money's worth. Here's to hoping they see great success and come out with a higher budget sequel. For the record, I would be willing to spend much more money for a version that goes longer and deeper.

_childDocuments_.review: I haven't played puzzle games since Portal 1 so that says a lot about what games I like.However I received a "free gift" which, basically was a clever PR invitation from the developer/publisher to check out the game.- You get a free trial, a lot of games are missing this very basic offering. Try the game for free, buy it if you want to continue- The puzzles are extremely well put together. Not too hard - not too easy. You will find yourself in situations where you get frustrated over how easy the solution was, but you just didn't think of it.- It reminds me of "Prey" in the sense that shadows = bad. Also, it's like the game we played as kids "The floor is lava".- The cartoon'ish grahpics fits the game perfectly and the soundtrack is very ambient, chill and relaxing. Almost reminds me of Mass Effect when you navigate around the ship or citadelAgain, this is not my kind of game but I purchase the game and I intend to finish it.I like the way they advertised the game through ones inventory as a free trial and I feel like, the developers really tried to create a unique, fun puzzle game and I wan't to give them credit for that.Very interesting game. It's a good purchase.

_childDocuments_.review: An alright puzzle game with some issues. The concept is interesting but a lot of puzzles felt repetitive due to the limited mechanics, especially towards the end. The story was mostly forgettable, voice acting was decent but boy howdy I hope you never played Portal 1/2 because if you did you're gonna have an extremely hard time taking it seriously.There are, at minimum, five separate Portal 1 or 2 references in this game. Possibly more visual ones that I missed, and most of them are unavoidable, being told to you directly through audio. There's a massive difference between an easter egg or paying homage, and straight up ripping the player out of the story because all of a sudden you're just telling me a direct reference to another game. Some people might enjoy it, I did not. tl;dr can't recommend for $20, might be worth at $10 during a sale. Definitely play the demo, if that intrigues you the rest of the game is alright.

_childDocuments_.review: Great art style, and the controls are solid using a controller. There is some strange fps the game seems to be locked to. My counter says 144 but its just obvious it is not that high. Nevertheless the art style and effects were fantastic. Everything nicely polished, and loved all the Portal references.The light / shadow mechanic was fun and very well implemented. It did in fact remind me a bit of Talos Principle. If you enjoy fps puzzlers, this is a great one to try. But, by the end, it became a platforming run with an angry, not as humorous as before, voice that sort of ruins what otherwise had been very entertaining up to that point.  I would get it on a sale because of that, its short length, and some sections being a bit repetitive. And despite what some reviews say, no, you do not buy the game twice. You download the demo, which has some play time, and to continue further, they ask you to purchase the full game which comes as a DLC. At least that's how it worked for me. Which is an interesting way to introduce you to a game and I believe more developers should try that approach. It lets you play enough to see if it will be interesting enough to buy and keep going, or if its just not for you.

_childDocuments_.review: A quality first-person platformer. My favorite thing might have been the aesthetic - as you can probably guess, light is a big part of the game, and the light and shadows look great. I found all the puzzles to be challenging and interesting, and none so hard that I needed a guide.My one issue is not a real complaint, so please don't read it as such: I am pretty tired of the "antagonistic PA system" that so many games in this genre utilize. Glados was amusing, but not super hostile until the last half of a pretty short game, and The Talos Principle had its own spin on it. But then with Quantum Conundrum and now this one, I can definitely say that I prefer not to be berated by a scientist while I solve puzzles.Again, though, this is good stuff; and it even has a demo, so really you've got no excuse for not at least trying it!

_childDocuments_.review: I originally played the "demo" portion of this game back in 2020, and for years I stubbornly refused to purchase the full game out of frustration at the occasional difficulty of the puzzles (although admittedly the puzzles were fine and I was being petty). Since then however, every couple of months I would remember what a unique experience Lightmatter had been and I wondered if I should swallow my pride and finish what I had started. With the 2023 Winter Sale I decided to do exactly that, and with my save file in Steam saved I picked up where I left off and finished what turned out to be a charming, Portal-like experience clearly made with a lot of love and respect for the Valve classic. If the early game grabs your attention the way it did mine, don't hesitate to purchase the full game, especially as the final acts feature some of the best voice work. At $20 its a bit steep, but the game goes on sale often so you wont have to wait too long before its south of $10. I really quite enjoyed this one and I think you will too.

Only downside is the length, I really wish it was longer, or at least some DLC so I could support the devs.Overall, a fantastic and fun game.

_childDocuments_.review: think of this as a very tentative recommend. the presentation here is really nice, but the characters presented are essentially TV Tropes caricatures. one of the reasons portal worked so well was the witty writing, and the writing here is just trying too hard. the puzzles don't really give you "aha" moments so much as "oh, right, duh" moments. i had to consult a video walkthru a few times, and eventually, i just got bored. there's some neat ideas here though, and the graphics are beautiful, so you could definitely do worse than this. just keep in mind... there ARE laser puzzles. and laser puzzles are always the worst in first person puzzle games.

Lightmatter is a very chill puzzle platformer, with a simple, yet beautiful artstyle that really matched the theming and the gameplay mechanics very well. the gameplay is, as the narrator of the game says, "the floor is lava, but with shadows" by manipulating light sources oy have to find and navigate your way through the levels. the puzzle of the of the levels vary in difficulty. some I breeze through, while others had be scrathing my head. as i said at the start it is a very chill game, and I found very relaxing in general to play it. the story and jokes is a bit so so. the developers do not hide their love for Portal, and Valve. and the jokes can be a bit on the nose and tiresome. but still it is not a dealbreaker ind anyway.  play this game if you just wanna relaxe and chile out for an hour or two and have easy fun.

_childDocuments_.review: First of all, great game. Four well spent hours. I didn't rush through the game, but enjoyed running exploring the environment, finding easter eggs. Good sound design, and the music was suitable for the game. Played the danish version, with Lars Mikkelsen as Virgil. He did a great job, but I can't imagine David Bateson would do anything less. Unfortunately not all voices where translated yet, which where a bit strange. Had minor performance problems and a single crash (no problem, started up right where i left), but nothing to break the immersion. The game is clearly inspired by Portal, which it does not hide. So if you like a futuristic puzzle game, and have a temptation to explorer, I would definitely recommend this game. I know I'll take a playthrough again sometime, to explorer even more.

_childDocuments_.review: I think the game is overall good, solid 7-8/10 but let me show ups and downs. I am not a puzzle expert so this will be a casual gamer review. Ups /\* The game has a nice story. Maybe a bit too cliche overall, but i like it and wanted to see what will happen.* Easter eggs, mostly portal. * Both VA's are pretty good. * Puzzles were good. Mostly not too hard and not too easy. * Aesthetic. It fits the game very well. * I like the ending. Actually, i probably love it. Downs \/* The game resembling Portal, toooo much. Virgil is Glados, but sadly not even close dialogue-wise. Especially early levels of the game, it was only annoying to hear his talk. Thankfully, later in the game he talks more about the story then general disdain.  The map feels like Portal 2. I mean, the concept is basically destroyed underground facility. I think they overdo resembling Portal. * Virgil's dialogues are far from elegant. It is way too obvious "arrogant villain" talk. * I think one more mechanic could make the game lot better and complex, which is a good thing for a puzzle game. I personally enjoyed the game. _childDocuments_.review: Look, what's that? Youtube offered me a video on some game called 'Lightmatter'? Haha! Copying Breaking Bad's 'Greymatter'? Let's see how these guys fail...hmmm...Yes, it's indeed grey. Pfff. Let's see. Nothing is more important now... That voice is familiar. AHA! That's the guy from Hitman games! What's his name?...Look! He is in a video about finishing work with these Lightmatter people. Using that man for this game was a clever choice. This gets me interested.The game logic is a simple idea. Play with lights where shadows can instantly 'kill' you. This looks to be a puzzle-platformer something.  Like Portal, yet very different idea. I cannot remember now how long I am looking for a good one. Let's see how this fella does in the video. Not bad. I guess he/she practiced several times. :) Ah the video ends in the middle of the game. I want to see more. How much is it on Steam? Very well! There's a free to play 'demo' and even the complete game is around €16. Cheapo-s! Let me try...Different shades of gray everywhere, rarely other colors like red, or blue. Plus the black material (aka. shadow ;) ) which devours you as soon as you touch it. And of course the light. Sharp lights everywhere. This looks too simple in the beginning, but no matter. This is the game's strategy. Like these shadows the game itself pulls me in more and more. The puzzles are getting harder so I don't care about colours really. Man! This is getting more interesting, or I am getting older and I cannot solve them that fast. As for the controls, everything is simple: back, forth, left, right, jump and one for using things. Why make it complicated, right? We're not shooting here with 42 guns. This makes the puzzles possible in many cases.Finishing more and more levels after each other. Nicely flowing and even though the surrounding objects are not too detailed, they are nicely fit into the game's style and the story around it. I' m starting to like it. Sometimes red light breaks the mood and now I am seeing some blue as well now.I get to the end of the demo and even the process to buy the full game is very cleverly integrated into the flow of the play. Maybe too easily! Eh, I give the money ;) I want to see the next level. The story - as expected - slowly revealed by the above mentioned voice. It well comes together with the play. I suspect some plot-twists as well. >) Many times I think: Here comes the end, because cheap games does not run long, but no. There's another change in the flow. It's still continuing. But it's time to exit for now. The summary? IMHO it's very well worth the money. Maybe even more. Well planned puzzles. Nice little story around it. Not a demanding game.It well represents Antoine de Saint-Exupery's quote: "Perfection is achieved, not when there is nothing more to add, but when there is nothing left to take away."High-5 for the creators!... I want to finish the whole game. Maybe refresh the review after it.

_childDocuments_.review: I just wanted to share some quick thoughts. I love this game. It is a Goldilocks for pacing and length while perfectly balancing serious thought-provoking ideas and humor. A complex narrative is woven through challenging puzzles that leave you feeling competent and satisfactorily ignorant. I also adore the art direction with its industrial design and use of grayscale with color highlights. My favorite part is the game escorts you through the discovery and development of a new way of energy production and I believe it is ultimately a much-needed allegory for nuclear energy. Admittedly I'm partial to this kind of game so go ahead and form your own opinions by giving this game a try, first hour is free!

_childDocuments_.review: Really fun little puzzler. Pretty short and my first run was 4 hours without using a guide. All the puzzles are very solvable with a bit of thought and very satisfying when you work them out. For me the ending sequence was *maybe* a little flat, and there were a few bugs creeping in at time (temporary inability to jump, a few crashes etc), but overall the mechanics are excellent and I heartily recommend it if you're looking for some Portal-like fun. GLaDOS would be proud.Also, some wonderful (if not subtle) Easter Eggs in there ;)
