_childDocuments_.review: Pretty decent little puzzler.  Cool concept, good pacing, and of an appropriate length.  The one thing I do want to mention - a lot of the puzzles feel a bit like sliding block "make the image" puzzles, though not that frustrating.  If you strongly dislike those, keep that in mind.  The scientist narrator, Virgil, is a real treat, well-written with excellent voice over work.  Same voice actor as Agent 47 from Hitman, David Bateson (among other things).  Incidentally, the Danish version I saw in the credits is Lars Mikkelsen, so it probably is great in Danish as well.  For what it's worth though - the English version is the original, Danish came later.  Worth a play, was a great get from Humble.  One complaint, it seems to have some stability issues and has issues running at a proper frame rate (looked to be locked at 30 to me, which it isn't supposed to be).  Didn't stop me from enjoying it!

_childDocuments_.review: A very nice first person puzzler in the vein of Portal. The theme and narration can seem a bit derivative, but the gameplay, based around light and shadow, is fresh and fun.New ideas (sadly not that many) are incorporated regularly and make the game always interesting. It's the perfect length for what it is and it's not overly difficult.I would love to see a sequel with the concept pushed to its limits! Recommended if you liked Portal.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: Recommended to fans of casual first-person spatial puzzle games. The general premise of illuminating your way to safety is interesting enough, but the puzzles are rather straightforward. The last section of the game departs from puzzling into a "run and jump" sequence, which is also fairly simple with good checkpoints. Total runtime is approximately 5 hours. For a first-and-only title, I was impressed by the overall polish of the game. Outside of expected small stutters between levels/loading zones (and one crash, also in a loading zone), the game ran smoothly, and I never personally fell out of the map. I did briefly lose a lamp when it fell through an elevator, but--much like Portal--the autosave allows a reload at the start of any level, which meant I never lost progress.Speaking of Portal, the developers apparently got permission from Valve to set this game within the same universe. There are multiple overt calls to lore, which has the potential to delight or annoy the player, depending on your tolerance for that kind of thing. I personally didn't find it all that appealing.

You made me laugh, I admit it :DI'm looking forward to buy the game as soon as possible - I'm kinda hypedKeep up the good work!

_childDocuments_.review: Overall rating.. 6/10. To sum up, "Not enough meat on the bone."I can see the structure that could become an amazing game, if it had more features and more levels. It has two "tools", which can be explained with Talos principle's jammer and connector (fairly similar in concept). And the fact you can't jump with them makes for not so really smart puzzles, but oh well, that is just my opinion about it. There were some clever parts and clever puzzles, but for most of the levels you could get through them quite easily. One or two puzzles got me stuck for an interesting reason - I couldn't see the rest of the level from where I was standing and that got me confused. I cannot say, if that is my own stupidity or poor level design. Otherwise, there are really not much of in terms of memorable puzzles. It's sad that the colors mainly divert from blueish white to black, making it all look quite the same. Yeah, no. In the beginning the announcer was acceptable, in the end he was annoying. There is some form of background story, but there is just so little of it. And there is not even a satisfying ending. We don't get to know who we play as. In other games, it wouldn't matter, as there is no emphasis on who we are, but rather on the gameplay, but when the announcer asked, who we are, why don't answer it? Just like the puzzles, the story is not memorable. Unfortunately. The part where he references aperture labs and "Artificial intelligence" (among other things) brought a smile to my face. It's more like collectibles, and standing and looking at something for a given amount of time, reaching a story event or finding a "collectible".  They don't feel satisfying to get.I have a hard time picking between recommending the game or not. The game doesn't deserve to be fully praised, but also not be fully buried in a pit. It's like a bland meal with few bits that actually taste good and somewhat satisfies your hunger for puzzle games. If you even a little bit liked this game, go play Portal(2) and Talos principle. Q.U.B.E. is also very good first person puzzler that is worthy of your time.

_childDocuments_.review: F**in' 10/10. I've legitimately been disappointed at the lack of intuitive first person puzzlers. seeing this, as one might assume, made me very happy. It's difficult in some areas, but not in a way that leaves you feeling like any failures weren't your own fault. Generally a creative concept, a fun genre, and a great nod to games like Portal.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: All in all, this is a fun puzzle game with minimalistic graphics, an interesting game concept based on shadows that devour organic matter and a decent story. However, I am somewhat disappointed that there are only two types of lights and some moving platforms, which have to be used to solve the puzzles.In my opinion, this game does not play in the same league as Portal, but if you enjoy puzzle games, you should definitely give it a try.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: First off I wouldn't recommend buying the game at full price, but rather to wait for a sale. Or you can do as I did, and get it with humble choice.The game play reminds me of the portal series, and the narrator reminds me of the narrator in the Stanley Parable.The graphics aren't bad, but don't expect ray tracing.The story is interesting and engaging, even if it is short.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: I wouldn't have bought this without the demo. Frankly I really respect the decision to give away such a large amount of the game like this and would love if more companies could provide demos of their games. As for the actual game, it's full of clever puzzles and cleverer writing with a decently intriguing plot sprinkled throughout. However, it has some drawbacks. For one, this may be the fault of my aging PC but the stunning visuals come at the cost of optimization. Even on the lowest settings the graphics are lovely and the framerates are poor. This especially became a problem during , as the more intricate environments only dragged the framerate lower and made precise movements impossible and frustrating. Plus, the writing does take a hit from  and it really distracts from the otherwise crisp and well-told story with plenty of revelatory twists along the way.Overall, fantastic game with incredible execution and a respectable price, with some minor slip-ups in writing and requires a powerful pc to experience properly. Perfect for those left hungry for more by Portal 2.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: I had fun. Short and sweet. The puzzles are good, some needed some thought. I found they mostly trended a bit easier, but that's okay.The last 10 or 15 minutes suddenly becomes less puzzle and more running and jumping a lot, which is an odd choice. I didn't mind, because I'm good at that sort of thing, but keep that in mind if you are not.I enjoyed the writing. The progression of names is a funny detail. Imo there's a few too many Portal jokes, but not a big deal.I want to know how they implemented their lighting. The core mechanic is cool and I'm impressed with its execution.If you like puzzle games, and the idea of getting talked at by an unstable science man sounds fun, give it a go :)

But overall it's a very enjoyable game if you like the difficulty being in the puzzles, and not in the mechanics, and the storytelling is ok

_childDocuments_.review: This is a very interesting game that does a the same thing as a lot of other games but in a completely new way. You remember when you were a kid and you would pretend the floor was lava and if you touched it you would die. Well this is the video game version of it! The puzzles are tricky enough to keep you interested but not so tricky as to make you rage quit from the game. After you complete a puzzle you feel a sense of accomplishment as you move onto the next one. The story is not the most amazing thing but if you can get over that and just play the game for the mechanics and puzzle aspect than you will have a good time. I highly recommend this one for anyone out there into puzzle/platform style games.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: It's decent Portal inspired game, but it's fairly clear the devs ran out of puzzle mechanic ideas.The basis of the puzzles is creating paths over shadows (which will kill you if you walk over them). There are two main puzzle mechanics- uni-directional spotlights on stands that you can move around to shine on shadows, and crystal bulbs on stands which will create light in a path that you can carry and move around. The issue is, the spotlight are introduced, then after a large number of levels moving platforms are introduced, rinse and repeat for the 2nd mechanic of crystal bulbs.There are only a few levels where these two mechanics are combined, and shortly after they are, the game ends. This is very poor pacing, and I'm sure the devs would have done it differently....if they just had more ideas they could've implemented. They were so desperate to mix things up, the very last level of the game ditches everything and turns into a platforming section, which actually isn't terrible, but isn't great either and it's not at all puzzle based.Now I have to say I didn't dislike it, but it doesn't impress. A full playthrough takes about 5-6 hours. I got the game for free on Amazon, and otherwise I wouldn't have played it after the free trial. It really isn't worth $20.

_childDocuments_.review: VERY very good game , it even refferences aperture science at odd times and that makes it funny too , it has a SUPER very interesting puzzle mechanic which is the first time i see such a mechanic , it shows you the ins and outs of the lightmatter facility and gives you a full tour , you should buy this game and have fun, and dont forget to empty your pockets at the gate for that new elevator!
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: A fun puzzle game that takes a lot of inspiration from the Portal series but still manages to be its own thing. The game is short, you can complete it less than 4 hours on your first playtrough. The artstyle is very simple (minimalistic) yet it delivers good atmosphere and thus lets you focus on the important visual queues for the sake of fluent gameplay. The game is as simple as you can immagine when it comes to game design. The controls are easy and even though without a tutorial the difficulty and audio-visual queues make up for it. The story is barebones but not bad. It has just enough to keep you interested until the end. The voice acting (mostly 1 person) is quite good and entertains you while you complete your tasks. The downside of the game is the lack of gameplay elements. You only have 3 mechanics in the entire game next to walking and jumping. The game becomes much more difficult during the later missions but mostly due to the parkour-like segments. The story comes down to a "we have portal at home" vibe. Psychotic scientist talking to you on the radio and monitoring you while you complete tasks in order to leave the giant laboratory. At the same time you collect radio messages from past employees hinting at something sinister. Finally you have a huge parkour segment where you don't listen to orders and try to defy the big bad, etc. If you liked portal, you will probably enjoy this, especially cause of all the easter eggs and mentions of the series in this game. But the game might come off as a knock-off to some. Overall I enjoyed it for what it is.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: Got the game on the grounds that it was FREE. Wasted an hour playing for me to get to a spot just for the game to legit be like "pAy mE $20" If you want to complete this game be prepared to pay for it. I can think of a million other better things to waste $20 on. Edit: The original ad for the game said "Play for free" Voices clip out, I fell thru the map at the four way bridge, Not to mention multiple inconsistencies with the shadows hit boxes. This is in no way a $20 game.Edit of edit: I win Shoelessbeats. I win and you lose.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: This is a very decent puzzler game, short enough that you'd want more but at the same time challenging enough that its short span - maybe 4-5 hrs - doesn't wear out its welcome, and leaves the potential for more mechanics in the same vein. The concept is rather simple, borrowing on the "floor is lava" idea: step on any floor that is in shadow and you die and restart at the last checkpoint. You have to jump, time moves with moving equipment, manipulate lamps and platforms to move light sources and shadows around, and the like to get from an entrance to exit across about 40 different puzzle rooms. Room checkpoints are frequent, and in the longer ones, they're in "parts" that you can't easily and accidentally undo your previous part. This may not have as many "a-ha!" solutions as Portal but there were enough to make me feel pleased at getting through the puzzles. Game makes it very clear what is a deadly shadow, what you can interact with, and generally good at marking your exit point, with some smart level design choices.Story is done all through voice overs as you solve the puzzles so there's no disruption as you progress. It sets up the narrative and why shadows are deadly pretty well, and again, the potential of a sequel. Only real downside is I felt they could have explored a few more potential ideas with the lighting concept since that's core to the engine, but I appreciate the balance of length vs. challenge, particularly as there's a bit of reflex needed to solve some of these.(Disclaimer: Had played demo when it was available, but played out the full game via free copy through Twitch Prime)

_childDocuments_.review: It was fun... until it broke.Game crashed in between two puzzles, and after rebooting game, gamepad controls didn't work, despite getting the pop-up that said gamepad controls were loaded.I was all prepared to give this game 5 stars, but it doesn't work anymore. Maybe I should have stopped after 25 minutes instead of going for the full 30.First crash: during anecdote about losing a leg.Uninstalled, reinstalled, had to unplug and re-plug my gamepad to get it working again.Second crash: during joke about Aperture Science.

_childDocuments_.review: Short (~4 hours or so) puzzle game that's not fully realized and sorta left in the past after the closure of its developer. It's a game for those wanting a first person puzzle time waster for a couple of hours, but will ultimately have its players forget about it after a couple of days/weeks.At its core this game is a bunch of logic puzzles ranging from simple, which makes up the most of them, to slightly harder ones. The puzzles never gets as challenging as they could be, and even at their most difficult the player is rarely juggling too many balls in the air at the same time. Towards the end the game also switches gear, and abandons the logic puzzles in favor of basic time limited running/jumping. The puzzles are also unsatisfying themselves, and never really left the player with a new realization of the base mechanics.The story is a simplistic one -- you play as a character of an unknown (and ultimately irrelevant) background that's in a science facility when an explosion rocks the complex and the evacuation leaves you behind. With the help of the CEO of the company, you need to navigate the facility and its puzzles while avoiding dark areas; essentially the unlit floor is lava which when touched results in an instant death that sets you back a couple of seconds. During the progression of the game you will reveal more and more of the situation in the facility and the events that lead up to it.What looms over the game is its own constant references to a much better and realized game -- Portal. This game cannot stop referencing Portal, whether it's through narration that puts Aperture Science as a competitor to the fictional Lightmatter Technologies, or through props from Portal. It even does this through more obscure references or similarities between the eccentric CEO of Lightmatter Technologies and Cave Johnson of Aperture Science.Sadly the game is not excelled by the comparisons or "homage" to Portal -- if anything it brings it down a few notches by reminding the player that while they're wasting four or so hours with this game, they could've spent the time playing a much better game: either of the Portal titles.On top of this the PC version suffers from a critical design oversight/mistake from the developers that will with the closure of the studio forever remain unpatched: the camera updates at a rate of 50 Hz/FPS. Any frame rate above 50 FPS will experience a noticeable stutter when looking around, and the only way to alleviate this is to play the game locked to 50 FPS on a VRR monitor, or V-Synced on a 50 Hz display.Yet even so, the game suffers from lack of optimization still -- even my RTX 3080 had additional aggressive stutters in some parts of the game even when locked to 50 FPS.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: Not too shabby for a first-person puzzler that runs with a premise as straightforward as lights versus shadows. The story/setting is very consciously like Portal, but with lamps, and Andrew Ryan instead of Glados or Cave Johnson. Overall, it’s just the right level of difficulty for a game that’s a few hours long, and the story, while derivative, is a nice driving force that ties all the puzzles together that’s also voice-acted quite well.

_childDocuments_.review: Solid puzzle game with interesting mechanics. There are plenty of fun sequences, and not many that feel samey and boring. The story is a bit meh, and the visual style is very gray and flat, although it's also kind of cool. It would have been cool to see more of a story than "shut down the reactor", and maybe a few different light mechanics rather than just the "shadows are lava", but this game did make me want to play and finish it.Solid short puzzle platformer, get it if you want a few hours of diversion.

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoyed playing this game.  Somehow reminds me of the Portal games, but has a unique puzzle mechanic. I wasn't surprised to find little tributes to those games.  I particularly love Virgil keeping me company as I progress through the game.The puzzles are challenging but neither insulting (too easy)  nor depressing (when I can't solve them!).Visually interesting - really sets an atmosphere.

_childDocuments_.review: This game tries way too hard to be portal. The aesthetic is blatantly copied over, though the visual style they used is nice. Virgil is just Cave Johnson combined with Wheatley and completely faceless. The puzzles are decently difficult, but you can get through the entire game in under 3 hours. I was disappointed by the ending sequence just being parkour and zero puzzling. There are only two puzzles that combine all puzzle elements into one, which is unfortunate because the game does have real potential.What makes this a no from me is the incessant referencing of portal. Portal gets namedropped 3 (4?) times and the game pretends to be in the same universe as Aperture Science, which just feels incredibly forced and uninspired. There is also a more subtle reference in a radio playing the portal radio tune, which is nice and I would have liked to see more of that instead of just namedrops.

Trial and error finally finds the solution is the best feeling ever. Like solving that one math problem that gets you all the time. But really wished to see more of the story, the things are told to us that we never get to see. Maybe things are better off to be remain unseen.

_childDocuments_.review: Its a nice game. Not fantastic, but good enough. It took me six hours to complete it with all achievements, so take that into consideration when buying it.The only strange aspect of the game is that it is a puzzle game, but its final challenge is a dexterity run instead of a puzzle. Not what I would have preferred but it was fun nevertheless.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: I suck at puzzle games. Period. I do however know that, so while I will mention the difficulty I personally felt, I won't effect my overall review. Well... Perhaps, but I promise it doesn't have a negative impact at least. --------------------------------------------------------- The games is quite easy to understand. You solve puzzles with light, but it's not that simple. Everything touched my light is a safe area while everything dark or shadowy hurts you. It is your goal to light areas up so you can traverse the lab you are in so you can find a way for the "dark matter" to leak out into the world.This is mostly done with construction lights. Because this in a lab where they test how the "light matter" works, there is more to it than just that. It is heavily inspired by portal, so the light can trigger switches and you have to traverse test areas too and even broken down lab rooms that no longer works as it should. Sound like portal right? They even indicate more than once and not subtly that it IS in the same universe.--------------------------------------------------------- I think there are 30 or so puzzles to complete and as mentioned I am stupid when it comes to puzzle games. However, I actually managed to complete it without any guides. I raged a lot. Told myself the game was broken, but it wasn't and I am stupid. I therefore think the games difficulty curve is near perfect. You learn how it all works in a steady pace and never make an 180 at the rules they set. I've learned that if I can beat a puzzle game with "aha" moments and don't get frustrated it is too easy. After a discussion with some other players, it seems that it actually has a quite nice overall difficulty. --------------------------------------------------------- This game is made by Danish developers, but they need to cater to an international market and the game is by default English. Don't get me wrong, the English voiceover is great and fun. The humour is very much like Portal. However, if you speak or understand Danish switch it to Danish! The voiceover is Lars Mikkelsen. Some might know him as Mads Mikkelsen's brother. He's a great actor who doesn't get enough credit. (He had a role in The Witcher Netflix series).--------------------------------------------------------- I just wanted to do a short review for this game. Partly because it is a Danish game and partly because they really got that Portal feeling down. The game is short and doesn't overstay its welcome. If you like puzzle games I definitely think you will like this one. If you don't like Portal-like humour and don't like puzzles I can't see a good reason for you to buy it.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: Super creative implementation, the puzzle design and visual design are both fantastic. Although, the game is a little short, the developers have clearly gone for quality over quantity and it has resulted in a very enjoyable and unique experience. I would recommend this game to anyone, including those that do not usually game.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: Interesting mechanically but I think there was room to expand upon the concept - there are only really two main mechanics with some acrobatics mixed in. The puzzles were mostly intuitive, I only really got stuck on the second to last level. The voicing was also well done. A lot of the missable achievements are just staring at something or waiting for a set amount of time, not the most interesting and not particularly difficult either.

_childDocuments_.review: This is like Closure, except 3D. Closure was a good game.I just wanted to amend this review now that I've completed the game to really double down on a glowing recommendation.This game is fantastic. I thought at first that the direct references to the Half-Life/Portal Universe seen, heard and spoken throughout the game were un-earned and maybe a bit pretentious or arrogant, but after listening to the commentary and experiencing the quality this game has to offer, I'll happily accept that connection in my headcanon of a world where cancer-causing physics-augmenting moon dust, alien superempires, and crystals capable of defying entropy coexist.Closure was a good game.This is a  game.

_childDocuments_.review: Recently i bought a steam deck so i decided to try some games i've never touched in my steam library.Boy this game is great, although it wasn't really recommended for the deck it held itself pretty good.Really loved the game, from the voice acting, to the mechanics all the way to the puzzles, it's surely a game that everyone that loves this genre must try.I would have loved if there was more than two endings, but i won't complain about that too much.10/10

_childDocuments_.review: I randomly came across this game because a play-through video popped up in my YouTube recommended, I thought the game looked interesting so I checked it outPicked this on on sale for $10, very enjoyable, very Portal like vibes with some references sprinkled in, the playtime was a bit short, I managed to blow through it in about 3 hours but the puzzles were challenging, the game felt polished, the voice acting on the antagonist was great, realized after that it was the same guy who voiced Agent 47If you're looking to get your puzzle game fix this is worth a look
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: Gameplay is pretty fun (but not as much as Portal, for example), humor is self-aware and IS the most entertaining part of this game, graphics are simplistic but clever not to show people, so everything looks good enough to not think about it as cheap.Linux-related - Proton (Steam Play) Experimental running perfect, no tweaks required. Probably will run as good on Deck (but I don't have one)(Someone gifted me this game because he received it in some bundle and didn't need it, so I cheched box "received for free" just to show that I write this review without paying for game full price, and that may slightly affect this review)
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: Solid gameAbout 3-4hours of content. Puzzles are not too difficuilt, but i love that the game does hold your hand on them, but the solution is usually before you, or just off the corner of your screen if you visualize where you need to go and how to get there.  The game usually introduces the mechanic before making you use it. A lot of thought and love went into the design and the story. The achievements are not quite clear and don't always make sense but they are just fun enough to be worth the hasle.Spiritual successor to portal? Most definately, not as overdone and polished, but it takes the portal style and adopts it, not perfectly, still feels a bit forced and the logical straightforward paths get replaced by fast moving wireless platforms, well, at least no solid light bridges.... wait...Yeah, a bit confused with this game, but generally had a great time.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: Really, my main complaint comes down to the length.  I'd say I'm average at puzzle games, and I only got about 3 hours out of it.  I don't think it'd have the replayability to make me want to come back, either.The options, especially accessibility, are good, but there are some odd exclusions.  The game has a font for dyslexic people, something I've never seen before, yet lacks the ability to rebind keys.  Yes, it does have different preset layouts for other keyboard layouts, but still, that's a really odd exclusion for a PC game past the '90's.The gameplay is simple, but fun.  I'd complain that it doesn't give you a tool to keep with you for use, like how Portal has the Portal Gun, but the game is short and well-paced enough without it to not need it.  The difficulty ramps up evenly throughout the game, with no really notable spikes.Graphically, the game looks nice.  I never noticed anything that looked even as bad as "okay".  I like that the shadows look like a sort of liquid, almost.  Kind of like a thick oil.  It looks like something that you could fall into and never come out of.The story is exactly the sort of thing you'd expect, honestly.  The Glados stand-in does his job pretty well, though.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: It's a fun puzzle game with mechanics similar to the Talos Principle, however it's very short ~3 hours long.  There's a bit of story but it's nothing to write home about.You could collect the achievements to extend your gameplay, but some of them require you to literally wait >20 minutes of real time doing nothing, so don't waste your time collecting them.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: This game looked like maybe a fifty-fifty to me when I bought it earlier today, but after just completing it I must say I've decided it's more than just that. Lightmatter is a puzzle game that, just like other great puzzlers, uses a brand new way of approaching challenges. Using light to make paths in the dark is something that I never thought I would see in a game, but here we are. It also had a story that made me want to keep playing so I could hear more, although if I'm honest, it was a bit short of one. The graphics were part of what made me enjoy the game so much. It felt like portal but in an early, less textured stage of development, which I enjoyed a lot. On a related note, the game was incredibly laggy, and it was difficult for me to get myself to lower shadow quality hence the purpose of the game. Also, in some of the final stages, some of the puzzle elements just wouldn't work, and I was forced to restart the level (like if I pressed a button, nothing would happen, but after restarting it would trigger something). One last thing was that it seemed like once something was introduced into the game, everything else would go away completely for a while. This review was mainly just a small list of complaints I gathered while playing, but everything else was incredible, and I would love to see a sequel, maybe in a city or something.Gotta say though, there was some serious disrespect for Cave Johnson :)
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: Fun puzzle game set inside a large research laboratory.  The game uses lamps and photon doo-dads to solve puzzles ~ navigate the building avoiding the deadly shadows. To my mind the tools are too limited to create challenging puzzles and the story and maps  are too similar to Portals. It adds up to a game that could have been far more exciting than it is. Both Portal and The Talos Principle are better games. However, games like this are rare, and for that reason alone it deserves consideration. It's not a bad game, it's just not a great game.  If you just want one or two puzzle games then the first choices have to be the games I mentioned earlier, but if you really like this genre then yes, by all means buy it.  It's fun. There is about two to three hours play but be warned that there is a certain amount of jumping at the end. I mean it's not on a scale of Destiny 2 where it takes days to learn, but nonetheless some folk hate platformers, lol.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: Interesting quick game, less than 4 hours to beat it and do the time waste for the alternate ending. The demo is the first 15 of 38 levels. You can complete the first 15 in under 30 minutes and race to do it again if you want. Although, there is nothing different no matter how many times you run it. It does have 'Speed Run Stats' under extras, but the only way to know you did better is if you record it yourself.  Several level after the demo content, there is another style of light to use for puzzles as well as a combo of that new style and the lamp. The art style suites the game well, as the sharp edge of the light actually matters, but does make everything kind of drab looking. Before the first Aperture Science joke the game already had a Half Life vibe, then we meet Virgil and the way he "guides" you along really gives it a GLADOS and Portal feel. Especially when you "stumble," more like only one way to go, on the path through tunnels with "secret" messages that you can't even accidentally miss. However, several jokes later and even the presence of the turret bot and companion cube, there is no doubt Tunnel Vision Games likes Portal. I do feel there could have been more puzzle opportunities, but with the Portal references, to include the 'Still Alive' song on a radio, I was half expecting a portal gun to pop up to help direct the light.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: A very enjoyable first-person puzzler with some platformer elements.  There are no enemies, just puzzles that you solve with lamps and other forms of light, because shadows kill you.  It's a very unique concept and the simplistic visuals (which are just how we perceive this world due to lightmatter technology), make it easy to understand.  Once you get how the mechanic works, the puzzles really aren't too challenging and have an intuitive flow, but there are plenty of headscratcher moments.  The game is heavily inspired by Portal and there are plenty of references, bridging the two game worlds together.  I also see inspiration from Talos Principle and Stanley Parable.  The narration is well done, adding humor and drama, while informing about the world.  I beat the game in about 7 hours and immediately wanted to complete all the achievements.  I'm interested to see what this developer comes up with in the future, they seem really cool and are very responsive on steam.  I bought this game on sale for $13.77 (including tax) and it was well worth the price.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

_childDocuments_.review: Lightmatter is the atmospheric, first-person puzzle game inside a mysterious experimental facility where the shadows will kill you. Watch your movements closely through the sprawling tunnels and rooms or be swallowed into the vast darkness. The game tells a sci-fi story about a maniac inventor who has created the ultimate power source called Lightmatter. Players must explore the facility in an attempt to discover the hidden plot, while facing challenging puzzles that require mastering different light sources to survive.
_childDocuments_.name: Lightmatter

name: NEOVERSE
detailed_description: NEOVERSE is a time warping multiverse game consisting of thrilling adventures that are packed with great and exciting challenges; combining roguelite, deck building and strategy gameplay all in one. It puts your skills to the test. Set off on an adventure with unique heroes to save the living realms regardless of time and space. “Be the savior of Neoverse” Create your own Strategy with 300 cards and over 100 skills Choose from 3 charismatic characters, each with their own unique abilities and specialities. _childDocuments_.review: A decent Slay The Spire clone with some rather serious balance issues and odd mechanics. If you haven't played Spire, go play Spire. If you have, here are the core differences:1. Combo mechanic. Play certain card types in order, get a 2x-to-next-attack buff.2. No defense decay. You can stack defense over multiple turns, although some enemies have a buff to instantly drain all defense at the end of a turn.3. Bingo mechanics. Kill an enemy with an exact damage amount for some extra gold; perfectly defend vs an enemy's attack to stun them the next turn.4. No map, relics, events or random shops. All runs are 15 battles long where every fifth is a boss. Between each you pick the tier of the next battle and see what reward it's going to give you. Some of these rewards are skill points you can use to get relic-style upgrades on a skill board; although most of them are pretty boring and there's nowhere near as much gimmickry or fun variations as Spire. 5. Nowhere near as balanced as Spire. Two of the three characters have cheese builds and the level of cheese extended to me being able to beat an Ascenscion 10 run on my second try with a character (being able to buffer lifesteal to the point where you can fill your entire healthbar in one attack is a bit broken, it seems).Aside from that, if you're here from Humble Monthly like I am it's a decent use of a pick and seems fairly stable. It was an enjoyable use of a couple hours for a few runthroughs but I don't think I'll be returning.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm going to directly compare this to Slay The Spire (STS) because it is most definitely a clone with the following differences:The biggest 2 differences:1 - you always draw to 5 cards on your go until you run out of mana OR hit the bottom of your deck, an unusual mechanic to come straight from hundreds of hours of STS but a significant change of pace none the less.2 - This game has combo's and not just within cards, each turn a combo bar is present, and if you play cards in the combo your next hit = x2 dmg (depending which toon) attacks are red, defends are blue, instants purple upgrades yellow, its simple and a nice change of pace. The moment you miss a combo, whether on purpose or not it resets offering a new combo. Little differences i wrote down while playing in no particular order:If you kill an enemy with the exact damage you get bonus goldYou can move the camera around the fight arena! serves very little purpose but a nice addition none the lessThe shop is available at all timesAs is a whole new RNG skill tree thing which is kinda RPG i guess, deserves more explanation than I can giveEach game is 4 waves of 3 choices of fights with their own respective quests (which continue throughout your game) followed by a boss 3 times over (so far, I haven't got whatever is required to take me past the 3rd boss)You can unlock equipment outside the game which does various stuff to affect future runsBuffs / debuffs degrade -1 per turn, often only active the current turnThere's some cool attack animations especially on the boss fights but unfortunately I'm usually just staring down at the cards to noticeThere is a Tutorial video which is sufficient to explain the gameCons / Improvements needed: (Tbh I struggled to find many at this point in time)You can't sort your deck by mana costI'd like an option to see the bottom of the cards as standard rather than hovering since I can't tell what colour they are at a glance until I learn from memory I suppose?!There is a glaring spelling error on the front page of the first toon that says "have anegaive effect" which should be "have a negative effect". Don't judge me on my spelling on this review though lol, but I'm not selling a product.Overall 10/10 for entry in this genre, I needed something else to tickle that itch, but STS is still the undoubted King.TLDR: My play time will say it all (purchased through humble choice may 2020)

_childDocuments_.review: It's good?Gameplay Loop:1) Select from 3 heroines (2 are locked from the beginning) 2) Select your mode (2 are locked from the beginning)3) Select your starting deck (4 per character)4) Equip gear5) Fight a series of battles until you meet the boss5) Shop5) Upgrade skills6) Fight bossWhy I recommend this game:* First off, the heroines are lifeless and it scares me everytime I look at them in the eye. It leads the game to have a feeling of being cheap. * The non battle systems are quite different from it others of it's genres. For instance: -You can shop at anytime. Even during a battle. -You can upgrade your skill tree anytime (skills = relics). The skills tree system is also interesting. It’s a 5x5  grid that you can buy any of the skills but the 5th one. To buy the 5th one you must buy the preceding 4 in an horizontal, vertical or diagonal line. The skills are also randomized. The choices you make will be different each run.  - You get 3 equipment slot. These slots can completely change the game. You equip them before starting the game. - The starter decks can play very differently.* The battle system goes to 11 it it's craziness: - You automatically draw cards everytime you use a card until the end of the deck. This REALLY confused me at first.  - If you get your armor = your enemy’s damage output then you block the attack and stun them until the next turn. Even bosses. - If you kill your enemy so that their HP = 0 exactly you get extra gold. - There’s also a combo system. If you play the type of cards in the order presented then your next attack will have double damage. - You also select which enemy you will fight every round. Each of those fight will have a mission that you can meet to get a big bonus (more gold, more skill points, etc). These missions are not battle specific. The mission reward can also be turned in anytime. Meaning you can use them during a battle. This does change your strategy quite a bit.* As noted above, the game have far less RNG than other games of the genre, This does make the pretty easy (I have ~80% win rate on the highest difficulty). However, all the systems work together really well. It's is definitely more than the sum of it's parts. * The big plus is the runs are quite short and quick. It’s a good change of pace if happen to play game like Roguebook, Tainted, Griftlands, etc where the runs can take multiple hours. I gave this game 3 trophies out of 4

_childDocuments_.review: At its core, Neoverse is a Slay-the-Spire-esque "roguelike" deckbuilding game where you play cards to clear combat encounters across three acts of increasing difficulty, each one capped off with a boss fight. It aggressively invites comparisons to its dark fantasy predecessor, being more similar than many others in the same narrow genre.However, despite the fact that it saves a lot of effort by way of imitation, Neoverse is a rather different experience to play.For one, Neoverse is more forgiving. Some negative reviews complain about the difficulty spike of the bonus boss, but while that encounter does require more care and preparation than anything else in Neoverse, it's still nowhere near the teeth-grinding frustration that you get in many games with "Roguelike" elements that expect you to fail over and over until the RNG winds blow fair and you're able to assemble that perfect winning combo. I'd go so far as to say that until you start pushing the harder content like higher-level Transcendent Universe runs or Challenge Mode, the game is actually pretty easy... at least if you have a good instinct, either learned from playing or transferred in from familiarity with the genre, for what to do in general. But, I would say instead that Neoverse feels much more 'fair' than most other members of the genre.The core reason for this is that Neoverse is much less random than Slay the Spire, or most other titles that aspire to the "Roguelike" tag, supporting Neoverse's focus on tactical card-play over run-management strategy. For example, permanent buffs in Neoverse, equivalent to the Relics that can be acquired rarely and largely at random in Slay the Spire, are designed as skills. You use a specific resource (skill points, of which any run will get a steady trickle with options for more) to purchase whatever skills you want out of a grid generated at the start of the run. You can see all the skills that will be available to you, including the capstones you need to buy out a row or column to access, plan ahead, and cherry pick what you want. There is some randomness in what's available, but any run you should be able to make something like any build.Similarly, while cards and consumables do still drop from the combat encounters, Neoverse features a permanently available shop, which maintains its stock until the player pays to refresh/reroll it, allowing you to save up for what you want if necessary and carefully sculpt your deck. This gets even easier with one of the optional starting items, which lets you pay gold to remove or upgrade cards, otherwise fairly restricted actions.There's no map movement either. Each act has five battles; each of the first four rounds you pick between three entries, different in their difficulty (at least one base-difficulty normal battle and the rest normal or more difficult and rewarding elite or high elite battles, as I've seen) and in the "Quest" (a minor task you can do, usually in battle, like playing three attacks in one turn, or rarely outside like "reset the shop) and quest reward that you'll pick up if you go that way. The boss battles offer quests, but you get an fitting act boss whichever door you pick. Removing the navigation, as well as the random spite of Slay the Spire's '?' nodes, takes a load off and lets the player focus on playing cards.Speaking of playing cards, let's talk about what Neoverse adds to the formula: the "Battle Tech" system. These are little tricks you can pull off in combat that are always 'available', barring an intentional disabling on the part of the player, which will make your life easier. To Parry, for instance, you need to have the exact armor to take no damage from an attack: block it all and not a point more and the enemy taking that swing at you will be stunned and lose its next turn. Precision is the same concept in reverse: take out an enemy exactly, with no overkill, and you'll be awarded a small but meaningful gold bounty. Lastly, Combo is probably the most important in actual gameplay -- if you play cards of specific types in an indicated sequence you're rewarded at the end with the fact your next attack played in the same battle will do double damage. Pulling off Battle Techs is important for success in Neoverse, and represents a very different sort of experience to Slay the Spire's "Whatever gets me through the turn" basic sequence of play.Some of Neoverse's choices that make the Battle Tech system work also serve to reduce randomness -- for instance, armor here persists from turn to turn, while more critically in Neoverse, you always draw a card if able when you use one and free a slot in your hand. Because of this, and the fact that you start with five 'cost' worth of resource to play cards rather than 3, you cycle through your deck much faster, given that you still discard everything at end of turn. Also fitting the overall focus on tactics over randomness, there's more of a focus in general on cards that "Consume" (remove themselves for the rest of the battle when used), and therefore thin your deck even as your number of owned cards for the run creeps upwards.On the other side, Neoverse's focus on tactical cardplay compared to Slay the Spire means that the game designers clearly wanted you to beat every encounter, even the dreaded bonus boss, more or less "fairly". It is still possible in Neoverse to assemble a deck that gets into an infinite loop and wins every battle the turn it finishes its setup (potentially turn 1)... but it's nowhere near as easy to get a degenerate loop going here as it is in Slay the Spire and it's not really as rewarding either, requiring a couple very precise resources. On the other hand, that does also mean you have more freedom to explore different builds and card choices rather than trying to reach for stylized perfection.When it purely comes to the gameplay, I think I prefer Neoverse to its predecessor. It's lighter, tighter, and the battles themselves are fun and enjoyable without totally losing the roguelike "need to make sure I don't paint myself into a corner" experience. However... there are elements in which Neoverse is weaker, or could be weaker depending on your tastes.For one, the CG art looks good... but not perfect. The monsters look like monsters, the girls look like girls, the robots look like robots, and they all look pretty good (gribbly, here, being a kind of good when it's intentional) at least most of the time. But on a whole, it might not have as much personality as Slay the Spire's art style, which is simplistic in points but always distinctive and evocative.Another one is the flavor. Part of what made Slay the Spire so engaging is that it took place in a mysterious yet consistent fantasy world, and the runs you took were windows to that universe. Neoverse, on the other hand, is more of a kitchen sink. Each act has a theme, I suppose: Act 1 is a post-apoclayptic ruin, Act 2 is mixed period Fantasyland, Act 3 is a sleek and mechanized future, and the area surrounding the bonus boss is an eerie misty sea. However, these themes don't go together, nor do the champions. I suppose Claire or Helena could be at home in Act 2 while Naya might find Act 1 or 3 familiar, but in any case they don't belong to the same environment as most of the game nor the same environment as their fellows. There's also no lore text in game, meaning you can't really discover anything of the setting or story past the opening crawl. I suppose the crawl does at least explain why the champions are running through problems where they're out of context, but it still doesn't make for the same kind of immersive experience. On the whole, I'd highly recommend Neoverse if you like Roguelike deckbuilders or, given its relative difficulty, if you want to try getting into them. It's not all things to all people, but it is a darn fun game, and one I'll probably keep playing even having cleared all the achievements.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm really very happy with the purchase of this game and it has quite an interesting gameplay, despite the fact that in essence it is a typical roguelike like Slay the spire and stuff like that.Pros:— Cute graphics— Non-irritating music— Lots of interesting mechanics: items, cards, leveling skills, etc.— 3 different characters with different gameplay.— Fanservice lovers can look at short skirts and bouncing breasts.Minuses:— The unreal engine did not benefit this game as much as it could: the game is not very well optimized.— The opponents are just free (well, or paid) assets from the unreal engine store.— The game does not even have a basic tutorial, beginners will have to tinker with effects, abilities, choices, opponents and mechanics.— Unfriendly interface, even after playing the game many times, everything seems very complicated and inconvenient for me.— Outrageous difficulty: sometimes the whole race can seem like a cakewalk, and sometimes even with a good deck of cards and abilities, you can lose miserably. The bosses of the universe are simply unbalanced.— Lack of atmosphere: ancient Greek minotaurs and gods, ninja assassins, horror monsters, robots and drones, orcs and vampires. All this is mixed into one heap under a very dubious reason, and because of this, the feeling of some kind of connection is lost.The disadvantages of this game are very serious and if they were corrected, then the game would be just great, but for now I can just say that if you find the strength to understand its mechanics, then you will open a good game, and if you don’t have enough patience, then you have not lost anything serious.

Because of such randomization, I find every run to be different and entertaining--sometimes with frustrations because of missing the cards I wanted to synergize with XD. In every run, I was surprised to find new synergy either with cards or with both cards and character skills. To fight the real boss, players need to go into the ascended universe of the adventure mode--like a prestige/new game+ mode--with a cube purchased with trophies. _childDocuments_.review: Let’s face it, you’re here for one of two reasons- either you’re wondering whether this is worth one of your humble monthly picks, or you’ve played it and are wondering how such a great little game has flown so gracefully under the radar.Neoverse owes a massive debt to Slay the Spire, as do all roguelike deckbuilding card battling dungeon crawlers (Jesus), and certainly at first glance its real stand out feature is the sexy anime ladies. In truth it’s only really the main characters with this style of design, and the monster designs are all sadly rather generic. I actually think it would have been to the game’s benefit if they’d really leaned into the cheesecake – sure, it might have turned off a few people but it might have given the game a stronger personality. That’s not to say the game is ugly – there’s obviously a lot of love that was put into the presentation and animation, and there’s a lot of technical expertise here even if the art direction isn’t anything to write home about. However card battlers live or die on the strength of their mechanics, and Neoverse is incredibly solid. While there’s no doubt that a lot has been lifted from Slay the Spire, it offers a lot of its own twists to the formula. You might as well compare Legendary to Dominion – sure, they’re both deckbuilders and Legendary’s core mechanic is based heavily on the genre created by Dominion, but you can’t in good faith say Legendary is a rip off. The mechanics here are clear and well explained, helped by an excellent UI. If you’re worried about a dodgy translation (and going by the store page that’s a legitimate concern) don’t worry – there’s obviously been a lot of passes here for balance and I never once struggled to determine what a card or enemy could do.There are two main modes for the game – Adventure, where you slowly build your strength before possibly taking on the last boss, and Hunter where you essentially draft cards to add to your starting deck before taking on up to 20 battles. This is arguably the more interesting after you’ve been playing for a while. There’s also a feature called Transcended Universe where you can give the enemies advantages and yourself disadvantages – the worse it gets the better your score.And there’s plenty to keep you going here – repeated runs will unlock cards, skills, equipable items and costumes for later runs. In the end I got ~35 hours out of it before I’d largely unlocked everything and finished the game properly with all three characters, and that’s a solid amount of entertainment for 15 quid (or more realistically, a humble pick).

_childDocuments_.review: If you enjoyed Slay the Spire or Monster Train then there is a lot to like here. Sometimes going for the combo is a matter of losing the battle but winning the war.  Overall I recommend this game, it is a solid 8/10 but with the caveat that the art style is a massive hit or miss.

_childDocuments_.review: This is essentially Slay the Spire with training wheels. The game plays almost exactly the same but it gives you a ton of control over your build, which makes it really consistent and easy. This may not sound like a downside but the challenge from games like Slay the Spire is trying to build a deck and make selections around what you're given. Neoverse gives you almost everything you would need or want for a build because it throws rewards at you like you're a Vegas stripper. The main source of this problem is the shop because it is literally available to you at all times. Even while you are in combat, you can use the shop to buy cards, items, and skill points. The shop is waaaay too accessible. There are some really good ideas in this game though, such as Precision and Parry. You get rewarded for perfect lethals on enemies and I think this is great because it was an added challenge I was already giving myself on some of my Slay the Spire runs. It can cause some tension as you're trying to figure out how to deal the last bits of damage perfectly. Parry is also a great system that lets you stun enemies by building up the exact amount of block required to counter their attacks. The reward for this is that you stun your enemy on their next turn. This idea of asking the player to perfectly plan out their turns can actually make what would be an otherwise monotonous fight into an interesting puzzle.If you struggle with playing Slay the Spire or other deckbuilders like it, Neoverse might be a great starter for you. It's got the same gameplay loop that makes the others entertaining but if you enjoy the challenge that the others provide, then you should probably avoid this game.I also have gripes about the aesthetic of the game, but that's very much a small gripe to have. Afterall the gameplay is the most important aspect of a game. Hell, I didn't like Monster Train's "mobile game" aesthetic either but I got over that and that game is excellent. The animations can be entertaining but you could literally strip this game to just be numbers and words I'd probably enjoy it all the same since that's mostly what I'm looking at the whole fight anyways. For my tastes the characters are unnecessarily sexualized (although I get that some people would be into that kind of thing I think you're actually limiting your audience by doing that), a large majority of the enemies are unmemorable, and the backgrounds are very generic. Like I said before, you could literally blackout everything except for the UI and I would literally not notice a difference.I think the game could really use restrictions on when the shop is available to you. Don't allow me access to the shop throughout the entirety of a run. It makes the card rewards from combat seem pointless because most of them suck or are things I've already grabbed from the shop earlier in the run and no longer need. Limiting access to the shop means I have to really consider my options when a card reward shows up. As it is now I skip 90% of them. The game could also use some more mechanically unique enemies. The enemies I remember are the ones that have very interesting mechanics like the enemies that give you a card that if you don't waste mana on and play it, the entire group of them get more powerful. The first time I fought them I didn't really understand what was going on, but I soon realized what I needed to do and that fight became memorable because I made mistakes. Unfortunately most of the fights run down to just me playing defends until I take no damage, and then attacks with the rest of my mana. My final suggestion would be to also create some out-of-combat events like other games. Give the player opportunities to make decisions that aren't combat related but also allow them to still do something to progress in some way. The game isn't atrocious, but as a fan of the deckbuilding genre, it's too easy and there are better options when it comes to having fun like this.

_childDocuments_.review: I am going to put my criticisms first, and then tell you why you should buy the game anyway. So if you just want the positive, skip down.OK, it is Slay the Spire with nice graphics. Reminds me a bit of Etherlords though by saying that I am really showing my age! The characters are....well...bouncy, which may turn you off (or on) depending.Yes, there are differences, but they are not big enough to lift this out of the status of being a clone. I mean, the starting decks are exactly the same (except for the two special cards each character gets). The card upgrading system, having room for 3 potions (whoops, I mean items), "force" for strength, "shield" for dexterity, it's all there.It is not as good as StS either.  The creature variety (in terms of how they operate in combat) is not on the same level. A lot of them look and act pretty similar, to the point where it is hard to tell them apart or remember what each one does. The three classes share a lot of cards in common, which makes them less interesting. The skills don't affect the game play as much as relics do in StS--you won't be molding your deck around possessing a certain relic as you sometimes do in StS.That being said...I knew that it was the same going in, but I've played over 500 hours of StS. That's way more than it usually takes me to get bored of a game, but still, I did get kind of tired of it. I bought this game because I wanted to play StS with a few new wrinkles to freshen it up. I was not disappointed.There are some major differences in the way acquiring rewards occurs. You can get skills and buy from the shop at any time. You choose what skills to get, so you have more control (though you end up getting most of them anyway so that ends up being moot). There a few big game play changes in combat too. Defense points stay around at the end of your turn, so you are never stuck with worthless defense cards in your hand. You draw a card every time you play one (until your deck runs out). There is a combo system that adds a lot--you have to consider the value of continuing a combo vs. what card might be best to play in the situation. The first class you can access could easily be a mod someone wrote for StS, but the summoner character has some way different (and very cool) mechanics.I give it thumbs up. It might be a rip off, but it adds enough new stuff to revitalize the system--at least for me. I certainly won't put the same kind of hours into it, but it is totally worth the price (and I got it on sale, so even better). If you like StS you should try this interesting variant. If you haven't played StS and you like this, do yourself a favor and pick up StS too. The graphics are way worse but the game play will blow you away.

_childDocuments_.review: Without a doubt. _childDocuments_.review: What I expected was "♥♥♥♥♥♥ Slay the Spire with waifus." What I got makes me want to kiss the developers on the lips. It is like Slay the Spire and in that it's a deckbuilding card game where you advance through a series of fights organized into three acts, each one concluding with a boss fight. You can pick between three different characters, each with their own resources and different styles of playing and builds. But instead of Slay the Spire's scarcity where you have to assemble a deck out of the scraps that RNG  throws you, Neoverse gives you so many ways to build your deck and tune your run for your preferred type. The characters have options for different starter cards, the shop is available all the time to buy new cards and items from, and the characters have randomized skill trees that let you pick and choose permanent buffs to grant them on the run. And then, to top it off there's equippable items that both change your character's cosmetic appearance and gives them different bonuses. There's a little bit of RNG but it feels so liberating and fun to be able to just make the build that I want. Additionally, the lowest difficulty level is beatable with bloated, undertuned, ♥♥♥♥♥♥ decks which actually gives you time to learn what works and what doesn't instead of killing you halfway through the first act leaving you scratching your head. Don't get me wrong, I like Slay the Spire, but god is it a breath of fresh air to play a game that lets you goof around and experiment and feel like you're making the ultimate badass deck, and waits until the higher difficulty levels to force you to really master the game's mechanics. I feel like I'm having fun instead of struggling to master the game. I love it. Thank you, Tinogames.

_childDocuments_.review: A few years ago, it felt like almost every indie game was a Darkest Dungeon clone, and before that, FTL clones.  It seems this go-round, there is no end to Slay the Spire clones.  Actually, it's much worse than the preceding DD clone season.  As I write this review, about 20 more Slay the Spire clones have been released as early access with at least 60 more on mobile platforms.In the tabletop space there is a concept known as the Heartbreaker RPG which is loosely an amateur/independent entry into the field that is lovingly crafted, well-meaning, but otherwise unremarkable in execution and therefore nobody plays it, thus making all that hard work rather heartbreaking.  This is how I feel the majority of Slay the Spire clones are and will continue to be.  The foundation of the gameplay is sound, but each new entry doesn't seem to bring much to the table other than a personal twist or some minor adjustments to the formula.  The main reason, I feel, is that while Slay the Spire is a very good game, almost everyone feels like it does something wrong and maybe they could do it better.  There's always some aspect of it that someone doesn't like and as the old addage goes, "if you don't like it, why don't you make your own, buddy?"  I've just never seen so many try their hand all at once.So... why choose Neoverse over all the others?  I have no idea.  I haven't and will likely not play every Slay the Spire clone out there.  In fact, I admittedly don't really enjoy Slay the Spire all that much in the same way that I don't enjoy Solitaire all that much.  If you put it in front of me, I'll gladly play it and I would never go so far as to say they're bad games.  They're just... games to play when you're bored.  Deck building as a concept is pretty done in the analog world so it doesn't really excite me in the digital world, though I can understand that it is a relatively new concept for people who don't play games at the table and therefore can be very exciting for newcomers.  Marrying it to a dungeon crawl/roguelite is a pretty nifty idea, too.Personally, I find Neoverse more enjoyable than Slay the Spire for one reason only, and that is floating defense.  You can spend your turns in Neoverse really building up your armor and it carries over each round so long as the mobs haven't chipped it away (or played jerk cards that simply remove it entirely).  It significantly changes the strategy enough that I prefer it over the starting-from-scratch approach that Spire takes.  Other than that, anyone familiar with Slay the Spire will not be surprised by anything here.  I find it's a lot easier and rather than finding your relics, you can simply purchase them as upgrades.  As a result, the game is noticeably easier and less intense, but I've never really found this or any of the Spire clones in the category of 'thrilling'.  The more obvious differences are the graphics and character models which are serviceable and less Lovecraftian aberrations and more mutants and robots... and the occasional scantily-clad woman.  Whatever.Like most of the Spire clones out there, I don't think many of them are bad.  There's just a lot of solid ground work in place that keeps them from being bad.  Which one you play ultimately depends on the little variants that they bring, be it floating defense, some kind of theme, or grouping it with levels, tower defense, some FPS minigames, or whatever.  As far as Neoverse is concerned, I enjoy it for the specific reasons mentioned above. I honestly believe most of the clones out there can simply be reviewed with "If you liked Slay the Spire, then YMMV with this one."

_childDocuments_.review: Slay the Spire but with boob jiggle and some really terrible features. Still kinda okay, but I'd suggest just sticking to Slay the Spire unless you're a diehard fan of the genre. Even then, it's probably skippable.The biggest difference is that once you play a card, you draw a new card to replace it unless your draw pile is empty. This makes 0 cost cards very desirable and makes cards and card draw not an important resource. 0 cost cards always have limited uses or side effects that keep you from going infinite, so that's not too huge an issue. However, this change makes deckbuilding feel less like a precise art and more like throwing together all the good stuff and digging for whatever you need that turn.Sometimes the buttons for items (which are like potions from Slay the Spire) don't work. Most notably, you can't seem to discard an item while looting, despite the button to discard not being grayed out. You also can't click any of the item buttons when there's an enemy behind the button. Probably just early access pains.Instead of relics you get skills you can freely buy with skill points from a grid that is randomly generated each run. Skill icons are not visually distinct, especially before they're purchased, so you have to mouse over all twenty-five skills and read them all every run. Bit of a chore.The game's most glaring flaw is the ill-conceived "precision" system. If you kill an enemy by doing only the precise amount of necessary damage without going over, you get 50 extra gold. Not only does this add a whole ton of rigmarole in terms of needless math and power tracking, but it also encourages you to stall fights until you can get the perfect number. When you break the game and make an overpowered deck, which is usually the high point of deckbuilding games, you just feel bad because it just makes it too easy to overkill stuff. Also, there's an enemy in the game that can spawn minions endlessly, so you're effectively encouraged to stall that fight literally forever so you can get precision on all the summons. It's difficult to overstate how badly precision sucks the fun out of the game. Who thought this was a good idea?There are three characters, and as of this review I've only played the first two. The first one has a heat mechanic which is interesting but feels limiting at times, and a radiation mechanic whose balance is all over the place. The second is very sustain-based, which makes choices in fights feel less consequential since if you make a mistake you can just heal up afterward and be fine.The graphics are pretty but lack personality and flair. The card art has a stylistically grainy quality to it and, while high quality, is often aggressively unappealing to look at.So basically it's Slay the Spire cloned with a naive understanding of what makes the game good and how to improve on it.

_childDocuments_.review: NEOVERSE takes the unpredictability of roguelite combat and fuses it with the calculated decision making of a collectable card game. Unlike the grander schemes of strategy seen in titles like Magic: The Gathering and its dueling prospects, NEOVERSE takes a much more rapid and action-based approach to random-encounter battles in something more akin to a dungeon crawler. This will all be very familiar to fans of Slay the Spire and while similarities here are glaringly obvious in mechanics, NEOVERSE carries a slight edge of its own personality through the unique space opera theme and high fidelity 3D presentation.NEOVERSE has a blissfully simple and seamlessly easy to hop into card battle formula driven by a baffling-ly simple to use drag, drop and click control system. Attack value shows your attack damage, defense cards show the armor value blocked, and your current manapool is clearly displayed to give an indication of your remaining moves. All of the special details and status effects that come with more complicated cards are clearly explained in text, and beyond a quick minute long video explaining all this there isn't really a need for a tutorial.The easy to understand mechanics here don't keep NEOVERSE from becoming difficult, however, as you pass through the introductory first chapter and particularly on bosses things become challenging to the point where every card and every turn counts. The addition of mechanics introduced through new characters and their various deck setups keeps the variation in difficulty nice and diverse with all sorts of ways to play, from simple brute attacker setups to more meta healing systems and even health draining Vampire card decks.Where NEOVERSE really excels far and beyond its card battling competition is its sleek 3D presentation and interesting sci-fi environments. Of course many will be quick the judge the space waifu gimmick but aside from cosmic space opera babes being the eye-candy there's a very well realized sci-fi setting here with some seriously attention catching backgrounds, and even more impressive twisted mechanical enemy designs. The various visual effects of each attack skill card give a huge amount of flair to the already lightning-paced battles, and the distinct look of each of the three character's attacks adds a lot of personality between them.The soundtrack is more-or-less forgettable, so far, and if it isn't a placeholder I'm sorry to say it doesn't do much outside of the slightly memorable title theme. It isn't terrible, it isn't necessarily interesting either, it's just sort of there. Not really worth mentioning beyond that.The combat in NEOVERSE is definitely a good feeling. Its quick, its smooth, its relentless but it also gives the player as much time as they need to read and "feel" out the cards and their purposes along the journey. That's good, because combat is all NEOVERSE has and while that's fine, I'm hoping to see some more story and backdrop for our detailed heroines and their mysterious space opera setting in the future. Highly recommended entry point for card-battling roguelite players and old school deck-building veterans alike, hopefully the game can do more to differentiate itself from the other popular deck-building roguelites on the market during its Early Access period.

_childDocuments_.review: Neoverse is a roguelite deckbuilder which has an unusual mixture of sci-fi and fantasy themes. The player will travel across a multiverse fighting against robots, giant insects, humans and demons. The gameplay has a lot of similarities to Slay The Spire, but also enough differences to make it feel like a fresh game.Combat is turn based with your moves being represented by cards such as attacks, defends, and constants which give you a passive bonus during the fight (like Spire’s powers). Playing cards costs mana and you automatically draw a replacement card every time you play a card, which means you’re not limited to whichever cards you originally drew on that turn. You can see what action the enemies intend to take on their turn which allows you to plan ahead.Neoverse has a few unique combat mechanics which gives the player lots of interesting tactical options during each fight. A precision attack is when you hit an enemy with the exact amount of damage needed to kill it (so if it has 5 health, deal exactly 5 damage), and rewards you with bonus gold. A parry is when you have the exact amount of defence needed to block an enemy attack (they would deal 5 damage but you have 5 block), which stuns that enemy, leaving them unable to perform any action on their next turn. And a combo is when you play cards in a specific sequence indicated on the UI (for example attack, defend, attack, defend, but it changes every time), and this makes your next attack deal double damage.I also like that you keep surplus defence at the end of turn (unless an enemy has the armour destruction ability), which means you’re not punished for drawing all your defend cards on a turn when the enemy doesn’t intend to attack (something that regularly makes me curse the RNG gods when playing Spire).There are three characters to choose from who use unique card decks which offer different playing styles.Naya is an aggressive character, attacking with both sword and gun. Attacks generate heat, defends reduce heat, overheating adds a useless card into your deck but there are ways to deal extra damage when you have some heat, making this a risk/reward mechanic. She also has some cards that apply radiation which works a bit like Spire’s poison, dealing damage at end of turn and then reducing.Claire is a paladin, armed with lance and shield, and as you would expect is a more defensive character. Some defence cards generate punishment which reflects damage back to enemies when they attack you. She’s also a religious vampire (yeah, this game is a bit weird). Some cards generate faith, which if you stack enough creates a powerful holy card. Other cards apply the vampire effect allowing you to regain health based on damage done to an enemy.Helena is a mage who can summon one of three different creatures to fight alongside her. At the end of your turn, the griffin increases your defence, the lion attacks a single enemy, and the dragon’s fire breath damages all enemies. The minion’s ability can also be triggered by playing certain cards. She’s currently my favourite character because its fun to build a deck which summons a dragon and then orders it to attack multiple times every turn. Dracarys!Each run in the normal adventure mode consists of 15 stages which are all fights. No shop rooms, no random encounter rooms, no campfires. There are normal enemies and elite enemies and every 5th stage is a boss. You can access the shop after every fight to buy new cards, consumable items, or skill points. Skill points can be spent to buy passive upgrades (similar to Spire’s relics) such as 1 defence for every card played, regain 1 health for every enemy killed, reduce cost of a random card to zero mana every turn, and many others.Every stage lets you choose between three possible fights, each of which gives you a different side objective. It might be win without losing health, win in 5 turns or less, play 4 defends in one turn, etc. These objectives can be performed during any fight (not just the fight that gave you the objective) and when complete you receive a reward such as skill points, a medkit, an evolved card (more powerful version), remove a card.There are also two alternate game modes. Hunter mode has 20 stages, the enemies are more powerful but you regain 20% health after every fight. You can still use the shop and skill upgrades at any time but every 5th stage lets you access a black market with more valuable upgrades. Transcended universe is Neoverse’s version of ascension mode, with progressively more difficult modifiers added at every level. As each successful run lasts around an hour, testing your skills by seeing how far you can climb up the transcended universe levels is where the bulk of the game’s replayability lies.If you enjoy games with deckbuilding mechanics or turn based combat, Neoverse is definitely worth checking out. I’ve already played for 18 hours and I expect that number will rise much higher, so I think you can easily get value for money at full price or a small sale.
