_childDocuments_.review: Well, it's a Spire clone. There's a bunch of funky mechanics, including a randomized skill tree, in-combat bonuses from match armor to damage perfectly, killing an enemy without any overkill, or playing particular sequences of card types. It's not that the game is *bad*, or that it brings nothing to the table... there's just not really any reason to play it over any other Spire clone. I think the problem is that the cards themselves are boring. Each of the three characters has, from what I can tell, 2-3 archetypes/decent decks? The mechanics don't have interesting interplay between them, so it doesn't feel like there's all that much to discover and runs tend to be either full archetype deck or failure. Get it if it's on sale, I guess. Or don't. There're better options.

_childDocuments_.review: The is a very polished deck-building game with beautiful graphics, complex card synergies, and randomized skill board generation. Each of the three characters has its own unique card synergies that are fun to play. The randomization of skill boards, missions, and card availability creates a unique deck every single run. Because of such randomization, I find every run to be different and entertaining--sometimes with frustrations because of missing the cards I wanted to synergize with XD. In every run, I was surprised to find new synergy either with cards or with both cards and character skills. The deck building and skill development of this game is definitely complex and entertaining if you are into this kind of deck building game.

_childDocuments_.review: Neoverse. It's like a roguelike deckbuilder, and if you're scratching your head thinking, "What the hell is that?" Don't worry, I was too.So, picture this: you're slinging cards, clearing out baddies in three acts, and, of course, capping it off with a boss fight. It's like déjà vu from some other dark fantasy game, but Neoverse thinks it's special. Now, it's not a complete copycat; it's got its own vibe.First off, it's a bit of a softie. People complain about this bonus boss being a tough nut to crack, but honestly, it's a walk in the park compared to other games where you're expected to fail more times than you blink. Neoverse gives you a fighting chance, and that's a breath of fresh air.Why, you ask?  Neoverse likes you to plan your moves, not just hope for a good hand. There's a shop that doesn't run out of stock until you say so, and you can shape your deck like a sculptor working on a masterpiece.No wandering around a map, either. It's like a menu – pick your battles, face some challenges, and enjoy a boss fight dessert. No fuss, no frills. And let's talk about cards – it's not just about playing them. Neoverse adds this "Battle Tech" thing. Parrying, precision strikes, combos – it's like a dance of destruction, and you better be good at it.Sure, there's some armor and bounty jazz, but the game wants you to earn your wins. None of that luck-of-the-draw nonsense; it's all about strategy. Oh, and the game's pretty quick – no dragging on like a never-ending novel. You cycle through your deck faster than a squirrel on caffeine.Still, if you're into roguelike deckbuilders or just want to dip your toes in, Neoverse is a fun ride. It's not perfect, but hey, what in life is? I'll probably keep slinging cards in this digital carnival even after snagging all the achievements.

_childDocuments_.review: While this is very much a Slay the Spire clone, I honestly enjoy this game more than Slay the Spire in terms of mechanics. There are bonuses for dealing or blocking exact amounts of damage as well as a combo mechanic that adds an extra layer of strategy. There's also a little bit more progress that sticks around between runs in the form of farmable gear that itself adds a bit of variety to gameplay. It's not as balanced as Slay the Spire, and overall, there's not as much polish. The localization in particular is very bad, to the point that a handful of the tooltips are misleading. But given that there's no actual dialogue or plot, this isn't as much of a dealbreaker for me as it might be in a more story-heavy game. If you can tolerate the fanservice, which is more gratuitous than the store page suggests, then I'd say it's worth it.

_childDocuments_.review: In general, I am pretty cautious of rogue-lite games. I like making progress in a game, and losing all that progress tends to be incredibly frustrating. With Neoverse, the game itself was so enjoyable for me that I wasn't even all that confounded by losing. I typically learned something about my card strategies, pinpointed cards I wanted to pick when given a random selection to choose from, and which cards and skill upgrades to get when I got enough money/gems to do so. There are enough cards that you can do some pretty clever and satisfying attacks/defenses/buffs with varying combinations of cards and skills.The RNG element of the game only left me totally screwed one time when I came across a very early enemy that wiped the floor with me, though I can't recall the specifics, and this was after I knew how to play the game. That said, this only happened once, and it wasn't right near the end, robbing me of my efforts or anything. Also, you do get one death that won't give you a gameover. You can restart one battle that you die in, but no more after that. When you die, you start the game over, but any new characters you unlocked, or new cards/skills you unlocked will remain findable/purchasable again on future runs, and these unlocks often greatly increase your odds of winning.Speaking of winning, I've completed three runs so far; once as each character, and it was quite exciting. I've lost at least 2 or 3 times as many runs as I've won, and though I grumbled a bit, I never got livid or rage-quit. The game has no story, the opening cinematic is less like the actual game than almost any game I've ever played (which takes some doing), there's no dialog or character interaction, and when you win, you just win; no ending or real fanfare. This game is all about the gameplay, and as someone who typically veers away rogue-lites, that's quite a feat.I would like to add that each of the three characters aren't simply different skins/appearances. No, each gal plays very differently from the other two ladies. Although there are a few overlapping cards they all can obtain and a bunch of similar skills, their cards are different enough that I didn't play any of the women the same despite me being notorious for using the same strategies in games when I find one that works. Not only do they each play differently, but each gal has three different starting decks which cater toward three somewhat different playstyles on each individual character, and there's a "deck of the day" (fourth one) you can select as well.I'm going to uninstall this now, but I can easily see myself reinstalling this game and making several more runs to try and get through the game sometime using the various other standard decks for the ladies. I am shocked at how much I want to play this game considering this isn't usually my genre. I am basically having to make myself stop playing so I can devote my time to other games I need to play (or replay in the case of some old favorites).If you're unsure about getting this, maybe watch some videos of it online to see if it looks like something you would enjoy, and - as with most games you're not dying to play - grab it when the price drops on a nice sale, perhaps. Take care! =)

_childDocuments_.review: Scroll down for full GameplayNOTE: The game is reviewed on its own merits, but I will be making comparisons to Slay the Spire (STS) as the playstyle is very similar.Neoverse is clearly inspired by the likes of STS but simultaneously offers new and compelling takes on the gameplay. The core concept remains the same, you pick battles, get rewards and ultimately fight bosses and a special boss. Neoverse does introduce some new ideas like being able to shop at any time so your gold is never useless or effectively solving the “bad hand” situations known in many deckbuilders.The game gives a lot of control to the player and is far less reliant on RNG than similar games of its type. I simply loved that aspect of it.While it may not have the longevity of STS, it is a worthy entry to the roguelike deckbuilder subgenre and I greatly enjoyed my time with it. + Good deckbuilding aspects. Not super deep, but deep enough for it to be fun.+ Has another layer of decision making thanks to the precision, parry and combo mechanics (details in the gameplay)+ Using shop at any time. Yes, ANY time, even during the battle. Don't know what item (potion)/card you will need? Just wait until you need it and then buy it. + Randomized skill tree gives variety between while also leaving enough freedom of choice on what you want to focus on.+ The UI is great. You will have all the necessary info displayed to you without feeling cluttered.+ 3 characters to pick from, each with their own unique decks and very different mechanics. * Comparing to STS, Neoverse is easier. Experienced players will likely find success quickly. Thankfully, there are 15 difficulty levels (like ascension in STS) to compensate for the base difficulty.* It may not have the longevity of STS. Still, it does have plenty of content for at least 15-20h.* Anime girls. I will leave it at that. - Mixed impressions about the art style. While the 3D models are fine, it feels a bit messy how it’s all put together. I particularly didn't like the art on the cards. Sometimes they are traditional 2D drawings, sometimes they are made from a 3D model and sometimes they seem to made from an altered photograph.- Similar to the art direction, the game is lacking in the sound department as well. Some sounds are absolutely missing, like some mechanical enemies dying, but there is no *clank* sound when they hit the ground. It's not a huge issue but it does feel *off*. The core concept has not changed from other roguelike deckbuilders. Battles, bosses and special boss. You build your deck along the way. * Precision, parry and combo mechanics give another layer to decision making. If you kill an enemy by doing damage equal (but not greater) to its health, you will activate precision and get bonus gold for it. Parry is similar but with defense, i.e. when you have block exactly as the amount of damage received, that enemy is stunned. Combo doubles the damage of the next attack if you play certain cards in specified order (attack, defense, instant etc). This allows for setting up for some massive damage combos and opens up new opportunities (especially with gear)* No bad hand draws. If you played STS you will know how frustrating it can be do get a hand full of defense cards when no enemy is attacking. This game completely solves that problem in two ways. Firstly, block does not expire, so you can spend one turn building up defense and the second turn attacking. Secondly, when you play a card, another one is immediately drawn from the deck, so you will still have a chance to get the card you need. This only works if you have cards in your deck, so you will need shuffle cards to activate it in some situations.* As previously mentioned you can buy items anytime. Gold is at no point unusable.* Skills (like relics on STS) are randomly determined during the start of the run with core skills always being present. Skill points can be purchased or acquired through rewards. What skills you get and upgrades matter as it can as compliment as much as define your playstyle.* You remove/upgrade cards mostly through mission rewards which are special tasks you need to do during a fight. The great thing is that missions can be done in any fight and rewards can be received at any time too. Which might matter if your reward is “upgrade all attack cards”. You might want to wait until you complete your deck for that ;)* Later in the game you can buy gear, which change up some things slightly (like making combos easier to do or introducing a new special shop). This opens up new ways of playing.In conclusion, Neoverse is a great entry to the roguelike deckbuilder subgenre. It may not replace STS from the throne, but it innovates in so many ways that it makes it a worthy contender. Highly recommended!

_childDocuments_.review: I had a dear friend that constructed an angel-white-deck for Magic The Gathering that was supposedly super effective. Good on him because I knew jack-all about card games at that point in my life! Later on when more of them went digital the cool kids started ranting and raving about Slay The Spire and Monster Train. The genre just never really "clicked in my brain". Yet here I am many years later having enjoyed what I played of Marvel Midnight Suns. When I saw Neoverse I thought I would give it a try as well!The best way I can describe Neoverse is imagine a turned based J-rpg with beautiful visuals akin to Final Fantasy before that franchise went "All action". But instead of exploring the world or learning the lore you just move on from one random battle to the next in an infinite multi-tiered monster closet. In place of the menu commands for your actions there are cards. Very quickly you add more cards to your deck with some of them having better synergies between each other than others. You also create extensions and combos by either parrying perfectly or doing just the right amount of damage to enemies where you defeat them without over-killing them. Some vaguely defined hoopla will explain how man-kind pushed dimensional portals and time-travel too far causing multiple-realms to layer together like an apocalyptic wedding cake! There are three attractive heroines that come from these varied scenario set pieces and they all specialize in a different set of skills. There's a cyber-punk-assassin-ninja girl that uses guns and a radioactive charged sword. There's a holy paladin Templar infected with a bit of vampirism. Lastly there's the summoner that mixes up her game-plan between a dragon,a griffin,and a lion. Each of them have "three grooves" that start you off with unique decks.Bosses and enemies are randomized and eventually you can up the difficulty or play other modes for greater rewards. Equip-able objects,purchasable perks,and items will get you through some tough situations as well so be sure to "stock up" when the opportunities present themselves. Neoverse is fairly generous with its' in game currencies and as you get better with deck-building encounters that seemed like insurmountable tasks beforehand will become doable with the right use of equipment,complimentary skills,and strategies.Considering 5 people put all this together I'm fairly impressed! There were probably some asset flips used but that has never bothered me too much. I'm more concerned with a game's fun factor and considering the fact Neoverse has  me appreciating a genre I'm usually lukewarm towards that is quite the accomplishment!Obviously an evolving narrative,interactions between the heroines,and actual character growth would have gotten me more invested. Marvel Midnight Suns handles those aspects competently so if the Neoverse developers want to get more ambitous with a future sequel "that" would be the route to gravitate towards!Pros+Fan-service. (Which is smart to have when your game is not backed up by a decent story!)+Deck-building that is actually immersive and enjoyable. Easy to learn but oh boy is it hard to master!+ Looks very nice! Definitely junk-food for the eyes!+Varied enemy types and varied bosses will keep you on your toes.+Much to unlock including new cards,new equip-able objects you buy with trophies,new modes,and even additional outfits.+In game store and upgrade-able talent-board are available even in the heat of battle!+Playing different colored cards in the right order displayed on the screen will extend your combo. Pretty self explanatory even for a newbie like me!Cons-Despite the randomized nature of Neoverse it is still quite repetitive in certain ways.-A bit of DLC gouging. (But at least those dlcs give you in game trophies you can exchange for helpful side equipment or cute familiars!)-Leaves a lot up to your imagination. I do mean "a lot"! Not every game needs a decent plot-line or even fully fleshed out characters to be good but it would have helped here.-Certain difficulty spikes seem unfair. Then again, I am not exactly a pro at deck-building.

_childDocuments_.review: Neoverse is a card battler rougelite game. Meaning you start of with a deck with basic cards like attack and defend etc. Then you slowly build your deck and skill tree. 3 characters to choose from that each have their own archetype. I'm mainly going to just talk about the basics. Characters:Naya: Uses shooting cards or radioactive (bypass armor) cards. Overheat system, 5 overheat stack = hindrance card - you take 3 hp dmg.Claire: Uses faith cards (build 5 faith stacks and gain a random card (not random if you equip wings) that heals/atk/defend/or gain punishment. Uses punishment cards = enemy takes dmg equal to punishment stacks. Vampire cards = heals equal to the dmg inflected not negated from armor.Helena: Summoner, 3 different types. Tiger = single dps (Attack card type focus). Dragon = aoe (Instant card focus). Griffin = defense (Defense card focus). Uses command points to use their effects.Skill trees:Each character has their own skills reflecting on the unique cards they use. Resets and randomize every run. Gear:You can use trophies you earn from playing to buy gear for your runs. Some gears only work in adventure mode.Battle system:Draw 5 cards and keep drawing until you run out from your deck then reshuffle next turn. Start with 5 mana, can be increase later. Combo system match the sequences of cards to do 2x dmg (or defense with a gear). Parry = your armor equals to the monster dmg and then stuns them next stun. You can't get parried.Precision kills = your dmg equals to the monster remaining hp. Gain bonus gold. Modes:Adventure: Choose 1 of 3 starter decks (3rd deck changes daily, but may require you to be on a higher transcended universe (adds negative effects to the run) to use), gain a bonus effect if you at least clear the 1st boss from your previous run. There is a total of 15 (18 if you equip the unknown stone) stages, 4 normal/elite fights then the boss then repeat. Each boss stage rewards a trophies (more is gain on higher transcended universe level). Each stage you select which mission to take on which will lead to different rewards. After dying or finishing you can choose to save your deck for challenge mode.Hunter: You have the the basic hunter upgrades attack and defense cards (attack does aoe and defense stronger than basic defense card) then you select few more cards to make your starting deck. Has 20 stages, with every 5 level being a boss level and rewards a trophy. After every boss level there is a shop that is able to remove/upgrade cards and other things.Challenge: Cost 10 trophy to enter and you use a saved deck & skills from adventure mode. Has 10 stages, all of them being boss fights from adventure mode, but tougher. Each stage rewards a trophy.That what the game is. I like it since its a new run every time with some little changes.

_childDocuments_.review: I will point out that Neoverse is in early access and I will give a final review once completed. Is Neo worth the price of admission and how would I describe it. To me it is an ambitious beautiful jtcg rough anime delight and one of the most beautiful intros from an Indy developer Tinogames Inc. that I have seen for a long  time.  It presents some great pros and some challenging cons so let's ride the wave and get to it. PROSPresentation: First think I noticed was instead of cards and lousy depictions of your heroes, you get a great third person perspective, gorgeous layouts, crisp clear functions and colors and terrific graphics and effects. They even think of the impaired with its smooth presentation. Just a great start in my book.Game play: For just a three-character hero start, you have clear distinctions in differences, abilities, skills with 100’s of possible combinations and plenty of card support with few gaps that really comes down to smart card construct and execution. AI: Great inventive enemies that can have their own strategic purposes and combinations that were well thought out. They don’t make the mistake of an AI bias system card draw, no dice rolls, which can upset TCG lovers out there, but how you construct your deck is central to your success or failure.Aesthetics: Each character has its own skill trait with boost selective enhancements that are fun to add. It has several game modes to appease all levels of players which was wise of Tinogames to do. They picked out the best of what they liked from other TCG games.Depth: It has a lot of Slay the Spire inspiration in it. There are stores, a unique tech tree, mutation of cards, and combination trigger that really glue you to the game play. Plus, for me. CONSDistract: In a market where you’re up against Hearthstone, Magic the Gathering, Duelist and the 100's of other games. I would caution parents that exploitation of skimpy outfits can represent the wrong aspect of the game and can hurt you with certain demographics. They should focus on the game mechanics, more characters, male too, and a variety of buildable based template formats. I know its common place in many games, and most won’t mind, but as a review I can only warn. Slight con for me. Balance: Character skills can get exploited to expert players who may find the replay ability once discovered a turn off. Some may feel many combinations to be a broken mechanic. However, as you add more content, more characters and abilities, enemies. The replay ability may improve. Incomplete: It is a one player game even if your totals are up against other players. It will be interesting to see how they address multi player additions to the game. They may in time add a function were your seeing two, maybe three playing as a team vs the system or other players, but the lack of pvp functions hurts. A small con for me.Replay: Another part is the incentive from a campaign or story mode function can also hurt replay ability with Neoverse. They may indeed add a unique way of presenting this to Neoverse that sets it apart, but for now a small con for me. Coding: There have been some technical issues, bugs, lack of language adaptions and flaws. The game is a constant work in progress I caution to make sure your system can handle the game requirements. In time they will sort out.My first impression is Neoverse is a rare gem in Early access to find. It will be interesting to see the final version of Neoverse and additional content done the line. It will all come down to that next build of characters, new cards, and new player modes, effects, enemies, storylines, and yes costumes down the line, that make the Indy developer Tinogames a great success story, but for now, it is as advertised. I do think it is worth the price of admission to support this new Indy dev and a beautiful template to build upon. See the video game play above discussions to see if its to your liking. Neoverse is a nice addition for any TCG lover and a game to watch in the future. Look for my final review then. My final score 3.8 out of 5

_childDocuments_.review: Developer responded quickly to complains about unbalanced enemies, and fixed them within a day! Here's what I think of it after the patch. It's a really good game, the graphics are pretty, and the gameplay has a LOT of depth. Each character has a unique style, and changes the game completely. I do still have one tiny complaint. Drone Echinoid's are still too strong. It gains 10 armor each turn, it's immune to debuffs for the first 5 turns, it causes decay if it has armor at the end of it's turn, and to top it off, it deals 2 damage to the player each time it's attacked. It's really frustrating, and you basically can't defeat it...I hope it gets adressed soon, but other than that it's definitely worth the money!*Edit* I've been playing it more and more, and I'm finding it even better the more I play it. Turns out that enemies gain random buffs, and sometimes it totally screws you over. I've reached the final boss in some runs, and in others I died in the second world to a normal mob. It's a roguelike so it's understandable that RNG sometimes gets the better of you. The thrill of picking random skills and getting the ones you want is what keeps drawing me back. I'll be writing character specific reviews as I play each one.- NAYA -Naya is a very unique champ so far. Instead of pumping out large amounts of damage, she relies on stacking radiation on enemies. Radiation is the equivalent of poison in most other games. At the start of the enemy's turn, it takes damage equivalent to radiation, and reduces radiation by one. She also has a decent amount of defense cards, but you'll often find yourself coming short with defense if you don't stock up on them. Some cards with more powerful effect will increase your overheat stacks by a certain amount (1 is deducted at the start of every turn, or whenever certain defense cards are played). If the battle ends, you lose 1 more point of overheat, and your maximum hp is reduced by the remaining overheat points, so make sure you don't have any when the fight ends. It's recommended to evolve radiation cards first, as well as skills that will help in adding more radiation. Some enemies have stacks of immunity, which prevents you from stacking radiation on them from the get go. You normally have to try hold out and defend until these stacks vanish before you can really do damage to the enemy.

_childDocuments_.review: Slay the Spire Meets Soul Calibre.Deck building games always bored me..... until I played Slay the Spire - then I became hooked, well obsessed would be a better word. I played that game to death, then went out hunting for and clone. This game *is* a clone. Indeed, a blatant rip-off - which was just what I was looking for! Started playing thinking 'Well, it is a knock off, so it will not be as good as StS - but it may tide me over until StS2'. So I started playing it and after an hour - started to like it more than the game it copies!Like everyone else says - it bring enough new ideas of it's own to make is stand on it's own legs. Also, as everyone else is saying - the graphics are wonderful. I played SlS thinking - 'this proves that gameplay trumps graphics every time' (which is still true) - but with this game you get great gameplay and great graphics. If you like StS - you will like this game - and (like me) you may even like it more.....and any game that has an ability called 'fire of uranus', gets my vote!

_childDocuments_.review: Neoverse is another Slay the Spire clone with a focus on gameplay mechanics. However, the game lacks in polish in terms of overall feel and immersion.Pros:-Fun gameplay, very similar to Slay the Spire in terms of core mechanics.-Addition of some cool mechanics that reward the player for doing things like killing enemies with exact damage.-Bonus missions that give bonus rewards based on completing extra requirements, which adds extra goals and depth beyond just see and kill enemies.-neat exp and store system that are accessible at all times.Cons:-Game aesthetic is all over the place. Environments feel random and enemies often feel super out of place. The game looks like they just put in some character/enemy models that they thought looked cool without actually thinking if it made any sense in tandem with the environment or game in general.-Unlike slay the spire, there is no map overlay that you follow, instead you just get thrown into a menu that presents 3 options before every fight, and that's everything you experience about the game outside of combat. Makes the game feel just like a bunch of random fights instead of an immersive experience.-There's a neat opening cinematic, but it really doesn't feel like there's any real story or worlds that you're traversing through. It's just random enemy to random enemy, and then you jump through a portal after boss fights.Overall I think that the gameplay mechanics are tight and fun, but the game just feels so soulless. I want to like this game more because I think the gameplay is actual good, but as a player I'm often more motivated by interesting characters or plot or aesthetic, all things that this game has none of. You'll either love the mechanics of this game and play it a ton because thats all you care about, or you'll be like me and finish one play-through and quit because it lacks in every other area and I don't feel like it offers enough to differentiate itself from better games in the genre.Rating: 5/10

_childDocuments_.review: Great roguelike card game with high replayability valueThis game borrows concepts of rogue-like card games like Slay the Spire, Monster Slayers and from Hearthstone. The only difference when compared to all these mentioned card games is that it is set in a 3D setting where you can see your character dishing out attacks or defending and activating some power cards. Tha animations are great. At present, there are only 3 characters each having 4 decks suited to a variety of playstyles. The game has 3 modes of gameplay such as Adventure mode. Hunter Mode and Challenge Mode. The last two modes offer a lot of replay value. It has RPG mechanics such as the skill tree system and ability points which is there in all the modes. There is also a gear system which can alter the look of your characters and also the gameplay depending on the selected gear. There are costumes which offer pure cosmetic change to your character. I have faced some minor issues like game freezes or lags in between battles or the store select screens.Overall, its a great roguelike card game that is worth playing and coming back for more.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: too easy, bland, and unoriginalBeing a direct ripoff of Slay the Spire (StS) does this game no favors. If you have played StS, then just keep playing that, as this is a shallow imitation hiding behind anime aesthetics. I'll just compare the 2 biggest things I noticed; difficulty and "art".Difficulty: Way too easy. Throughout the game you can select 1 of 3 mini-objectives every battle to unlock bonuses; a neat idea that needs fixing. An example: "deal 35 damage in 1 turn and receive a 20% heal". That sounds all well and good, but you do not receive the bonus upon completion, you use it whenever you want (between fights) meaning I as able to save 4 or 5 heals until the final boss, and no matter how badly damaged I was before the fight, I knew I could heal to max before and be at no disadvantage. Also, your character carries their block over between rounds in a fight, meaning you technically are never at a disadvantage when you draw your hand, because if its all block cards you can just play them all and next turn do all your damage with no worries. Another bizarre choice if being able to enter the shop at any point, especially during fights. Fight not going your way? Just pop in and buy a health item. No health items? Refresh the shop for 100 gold and BAM, now there's 3 and you're good to go. If the game had made it harder to get money, then maybe this would be okay, but its actually incredibly easy. Whenever you get a perfect kill (deal the exact amount of damage it would take to kill), you get 50 gold or so (I don't remember), and this will build up quickly unless you're playing blindfolded. There's way more examples, but this is already too long.Art style: Its anime. Crossed with random stuff. This feels like they bought a bunch of random art assets and then justified it with "Oh but you go through portals sometimes to different dimensions, so yea, robots in the future dimension, and demons in the fantasy dimension." I'm not saying they didn't make the models and whatnot, just that it seems like they didn't have enough ideas in the same genre, so they just made a bunch of random stuff and justifications. It blows my mind that people actually say these characters look good too. They're so painfully generic they'd only look good if they were Skyrim mods, and even then that may be a bit rude to the Skyrim modding community.Now to be fair to the game, it is quite possible it really opens up after hours of play and trying the other characters. It's possible. But after playing one game with the first character, and easily beating it, I couldn't help but feel that it wasn't going to show me anything new/worthwhile if I kept going. One of the main attractions to StS for me is trying new builds of characters to see what works and what doesn't; so why bother experimenting in a game that offers no challenge? To see if I could make it harder by handicapping myself? Maybe it is meant to be played blindfolded, that way its possible I might actually lose, and then I wouldn't have to look at the boring art and characters. Now I'm almost sad I refunded it; should've tried that.

_childDocuments_.review: I'd describe this game as "Slay the Spire Express."  It streamlines and makes more consistent all the familiar Slay the Spire mechanics.  For example, Neoverse does away with the Shop, Treasure, and other non-battle nodes.  Instead, Neoverse has a persistent shop and a persistent skill tree that you can access at any time, even in the middle of battle.  You can buy cards and consumable items at the shop and permanent upgrades at the skill tree.  It's a good idea, since it not only makes the run faster, but also means you cam focus more on the actual battles instead of trying to navigate your way to a shop or treasure node.I was able to find this game on sale for 1 euro, and for that price it's a steal!  The base price of $20 is a bit high, but you can usually find this game on sale on Steam or some other Steam key selling site.

_childDocuments_.review: Neoverse is a cards-based roguelite RPG that's really easy to get into. In this game, you'll set off on various expeditions, one after another, all the while improving your character as you go along either by upgrading their skills or purchasing new and better cards. There are 3 different characters by the way, each with their own deck of cards and specialty skills.In expeditions, you'll need to go through a series of events. There are 7 different types - 3 of them are basically combat events where you'll battle normal or elite enemies, or even a boss; while the remaining may allow you to upgrade your cards or grab a free heal (DNA lab), collect new ones for free (Supply Crate), experience a random event where the outcome you get depends on the action you choose to take (Event DB), and the Data Store, which frankly is the game's in-game store which sells cards, power-ups and skill points, that you can access whenever you're not in an event. Instead of randomizing the events you get, I like how the game lets you choose one of two events every time you've completed a previous event. You'll even get to see what comes after said event, allowing you to, for example, plan which battles to take on and which to avoid. The gameplay in this game is also intriguing to say the least, mainly because instead of having your drawn cards permanently on hand, whatever cards you have left in your hand will be discarded after your turn. This makes planning your move for the next turn a tad bit difficult (in a good way) but not completely impossible. Boss fights can be quite tough though mainly because they usually can deal a huge amount of damage - damage that you might not be able to defend from; and has several skills which will either hamper you or bolster their stats whichever stat it may be. In fact, my character met her maker during the second boss fight - the boss has like 400 health, deals 40 damage per hit (My character only has 90+ health and she's only dealing a fraction of the damage the boss dishes out), and has a rather high Damage Reflect. I should also point out that - and the game doesn't really mention this - if you die in this game, it's pretty much permanent. You'll actually have to start a new game but at least your upgrades will remain.P/S: I'll update the review as I put in more hours to complete the game.Personally, I find NEOVERSE to be a very entertaining game for a card-based RPG. The game's fun in a strategic way and of course, the game looks gorgeous too! If you enjoy roguelite turn-based RPGs that feature cards, I think you'll find NEOVERSE a unique addition to the genre. (Note that although many reviewers have drawn comparison to Slay the Spire, I have not played the latter game, so to me, NEOVERSE is rather unique)So to sum up, here's the TL;DR version!+ Gorgeous graphics+ The card-based gameplay feels unique, is very easy to get into and can be pretty fun - i.e. instead of keeping the unused cards you have on your hand for the next turn, your "leftover" cards are discarded.+ The tool tips are incredibly helpful - be sure to read them!+ Sufficient variety of events+ Challenging boss fights+ No limited to deck size (from what I can see) - Might not be a pro but it does add another level of strategy to your gameplay, especially once you start to accumulate more cards.- Tutorial can be a bit more interactive but it's still fine. - The storyline seems to be limited to only the menu screen (read the scrolling text). Would love to get some more background about the world, the character, and the story through the expeditions

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to recommend this game, but I cannot. There is glaringly obvious artificial difficulty worked in. When an enemy attacks, you'll draw nothing but attack cards. When the enemy enemy defends, you'll draw defense cards. If you play you should notice the pattern almost immediately. I wanted true RNG, not an orchestrated algorithm like this to make the game more annoying rather than fun. At first I thought it was a coincidence, then after several games and lengthy play sessions I realized it wasn't. Graphics are good, the characters have neat little personalities and when you misclick they can make exasperated comments and gestures. I like the overall vibe the game has, and it is fun. Until you realize it's not relying on RNG to give you a challenge, it's literally stacking the deck against you. I wanted a fair fight, and didn't get one.

_childDocuments_.review: Let me preface before I get critical by saying I really do like this game. I am someone who is very experienced in roguelike deckbuilders and have dominated StS and Monster Train. I also played this game in offline mode on planes and travelling on my steam deck than way more than 5 hours. It runs extremely well on Steam Deck btw. The thing that ruffles my feathers is that this game could have gotten into that caliber of this genre of Griftlands, Monster Train, and StS. There are great ideas here that if executed properly, would have created that same itch that StS gives. Unfortunately, it feels like there are some corners cut, glaringly with an uninspired, uncohesive card pool that hold it back from getting triple digit play time. You can see the inspiration in some of the archetypes like the summoner/stance swapper character and the vampire and faith archetypes for claire. Then Naya, the default character is basically just a less satisfying version of the silent from StS. No, seriously. She has 0 cost shoot generating deck basically akin to silent's shiv archetype or radiation builds, which are this game's version of poison. Unfortunately, even before getting into the 'ascension level' system of this game, it gives way too many resistances like artifact from StS to non-boss enemies for builds like radiation to be remotely satisfying. Stance swapping as much as I like the summoner ultimately just boils down to spamming aoe or single target damage or block depending on the situation. Runs don't feel unique enough because no playstyle really has any meaningful payoff. StS has crazy run-shaping cards and artifacts and this game just doesn't. It feels like it wants to but it doesn't. It's got a really cool skill grid system in each run, but ultimately none of the skills are never big enough to offer a massive motivation to build a particular way. And seriously, the card pool is so boring. There's a few exciting cards here and there but there are so many cards across different rarities that do the same thing. The legendaries are worse than the uncommons with some. When I'm picking this game's versions of challenges/paths, I just really don't know what to shoot for when the card pool is so janky.I will definitely check back on this game at some point, but it is not in early access, and the last patch 1.4 was in Q4 2020 so I am not holding my breath on any massive overhauls.

_childDocuments_.review: Sitting on the fence between recommended or not, but ultimately I cannot recommend this game yet because of balance issues. The way the decks are randomized in every game, and the mix of cards offered to you can essentially make or break your game long before you get anywhere near the end, making player skill a moot point in some fights. You can also wind up cruising along several of the fights just fine, reach a Boss at full health and with several evolved (upgraded) cards, before BAM! nothing you do matters because the boss hits you with just so much damage and too few of your defense cards turn up. Having the last 2 hours of progress wiped out due to bad luck? Not fun.In the end I can only recommend this game to players who want something to casually while away their time, and who don't mind a heavy luck factor. If that's you, this game is great, good graphics, fairly intuitive combat systems. As for me, I'm not going to touch it again.

_childDocuments_.review: It's like 1 stop from being a mobile card game imo. It's got excellent mechanics... and that's it. I suppose the attractive women are supposed to attract a certain, but there's almost no depth in story here. No cinematics, unlock more cards as you grind through the game repetitively, and that's all there is. _childDocuments_.review: "A Delightfully Addictive Romp Through Time and Space."First and foremost, Neoverse's greatest strength lies in its captivating setting. The game thrusts players into a mesmerizing world where time and space converge, offering a delightful mishmash of futuristic technology, mythical creatures, and ancient civilizations. The rich lore and vibrant visuals breathe life into this fantastical realm, immersing players in an adventure that is as engrossing as it is visually stunning.But it's not just style over substance with Neoverse; the gameplay itself is incredibly addictive and rewarding. The core mechanics of the roguelike genre are expertly executed here, with each run offering a fresh and exhilarating challenge. The strategic depth is commendable, as players must carefully manage their resources, craft powerful decks, and make split-second decisions in the heat of battle. The thrill of progression is palpable, as each successful run brings with it a sense of accomplishment and satisfaction.Furthermore, Neoverse excels in its variety of playable characters and deck-building options. Each character boasts unique abilities and playstyles, allowing for endless experimentation and replayability. Whether you prefer to unleash devastating spells as the sorceress, wield mighty weapons as the warrior, or harness the power of technology as the android, there's something for everyone to enjoy.That being said, Neoverse is not without its flaws. The game can occasionally overstay its welcome, especially during longer play sessions where the repetitive nature of the gameplay begins to set in. Some may find themselves craving a bit more variety or innovation to shake things up and keep the experience feeling fresh throughout.However, despite these minor shortcomings, Neoverse remains a blast to play from start to finish. Its addictive gameplay, captivating setting, and wealth of content make it a standout title in the roguelike genre. Whether you're a seasoned veteran or a newcomer looking to dip your toes into the world of roguelikes, Neoverse is sure to provide hours of fun and excitement. Don't miss out on this thrilling adventure through time and space!

_childDocuments_.review: For a Slay the Spire clone this just wasn't interesting enough to keep me interested. Neither the mechanics or the graphical style is appealing for me.When a well reviewed card battler goes on sale and shows up in my store I tend to pick it up and give it some playtime to see if I'll like/love it. It doesn't have to be Slay the Spire or Griftlands to keep me interested past the second playthrough - this one just didn't cut it. The flavor of a fan service JRPG anime style really is right up my alley; I am that type of degenerate but if that's going to be your flavor then your graphics can't be chunky in places. If you're trying to sell me on your style then your card images need to be... well... not something I could throw together in photoshop with a google image search and a filter.On the other hands, if you want to appeal to me with your mechanics then you need to make it interesting enough that after two playthroughs I feel a reason to keep playing your game. My first playthrough with the primary character I found an easy near infinite damage loop that trivialized foes to the point where the difficulty would have to increase some 50 fold (similar to an ascension 20) before I felt in danger. So why keep playing when the game doesn't offer that... On my second run I played a defense deck that won too easily. So the mechanics are too easily abusable without the type of scaling difficulty that other card battlers have kept me playing. In single player games we want to do broken things but not when it trivializes content too quickly.So all in all.The graphics aren't compelling -- The fan service isn't fan service enough and the cards look ugly.The balance feels way off and makes the content uninteresting. There are many games I recommend picking up when on sale to give it a spin; this one is a skip. If you want a card battler there are better options. _childDocuments_.review: This is a deck building card battle game with RNG elements. In my experience, 100 trophies from one of the DLCs was enough to buy the optimal gear for all three characters and you can enjoy the game without having to waste your time grinding.There are several modes of gameplay but generally the goal is to battle through a series of stages using your deck of cards that have various effects such as dealing damage, generating armor or character-specific resources, inflict debuffs, etc. After each battle, you gain rewards in the form of skill points and gold which you can use to buy new cards and more skill points. The cards available in the store and the skill board is randomized in every playthrough so each run through the game offers a different experience and therefore high replayability. Due to the high degree of RNG in terms of skills and cards that can be acquired in each playthrough, the difficulty is determined almost completely by chance as there are certain skills and cards that are essential for each character to perform decently and can make the game remarkably easier or gamebreakingly difficult depending on whether they show up in the current run. The most powerful cards and skills have to be unlocked by using each character on multiple playthroughs before they even have the possibility of showing up in a run. There are three characters - Agent Naya, Paladin Claire and Summoner Helena, each with their own set of cards, unique playstyles and mechanics. Upon starting the game for the first time, you can only play as Naya and you have to reach certain stage checkpoints in a run to unlock Claire and Helena. Naya is the undoubtedly the weakest character of the trio and your first few playthroughs will be extremely challenging and frustrating to the point that some players might just give up. However, Claire and Helena are definitely much more fun to play and definitely worth the effort to unlock them. Each character has two additional unlockable outfits that can be obtained by clearing Transcendence Mode and Hunter Mode respectively. _childDocuments_.review: This is a surprisingly fun game. While at heart, it is a card game, it makes it fun with all sorts of effects.There are some rather overpowered cards and builds with very few counters to them. The exact skills you have access to seem to be randomized each run.You will need to beat the game multiple times to unlock everything and you can gain bonuses to later runs.The starter character runs two main mechanics: Overheat and Radiation. Overheat is mostly negative, but some cards do take advantage of overheat. Radiation is effectively similar to poison in other games in terms of dealing damage over time. While others can take advantage of the Radiation mechanic, the starter has additional ability to take advantage of radiation.The second character is probably the strongest of the three and her mechanics are: Counterattacks, Life Steal, and Healing+Random Card effect (10 Heal, 10 Damage, or 10 Armor). If built well, she can heal through basically any damage dealt and can kill enemies as she bunkers down.The third character is sort of unique in that she has four main mechanics. No Summon, Defense, AoE, or Single target. While hybrid options do exist, it seems overall better to specialize unless you get somewhat lucky.As of the current version:Probably one of the best cards in the game gives you a random constant each turn. The biggest counter to this is negate buffs that only a few enemies have (only stronger enemies with a large pool of hp seem to have this and they usually hide it until later). Other examples of strong cards include one that gives you 2 random constants and yet another gives you a single constant out of 5 random choices. These have their own limitations, such as having to use them the first time you encounter them in a battle (they are removed from battle if used and after the turn if unused). These can be countered somewhat by cards that prevent you from playing them or through sheer bad luck if you run out of mana and they show up.These cards are heavy game-changers as they effectively allow you to reduce the size of your deck.Now, Defensive builds that run based on Armor are somewhat countered by piercing damage (direct damage in many TCGs) and effects that do extra damage to defense or remove defense entirely.On the other hand, healing builds are relatively hard to counter except by force, which can allow for one shot attacks.Force builds are very powerful and basically only countered by buff/force removal. Force builds are especially potent with multi-hit attacks.  1 damage 5 times sounds like 5 damage, right? Well, wrong. 1 damage 5 times procs "reflect damage" 5 times. It also procs "counter with stack and reduce stack by 1" 5 times (believe me, taking 15 damage per turn is better than taking 5, then 9, then 13, then 17...). However, force works on the damage value, meaning 10 force and 1 damage 5 times ends up beign 11 damage 5 times.Point is: Everything has SOME sort of counter or limitation and many cards have some level of synergy. Now, sometimes counters are very rare, but at least they do exist.Missions are also nice. Sometimes you want to pick a battle that gives you less gold because it comes with a mission gives you some effect you want. Missions are not lost after the battle and you can choose when to collect (outside of battles), allowing for more strategic value. You can save that 100% Healing for a boss battle, save the delete card for when you have a different deck build, and that upgrade all defense cards? You might wait until you have more defense cards to use it.Basically, there is a lot of choices you can make that influence how the game plays out, making it feel less random. Which is very nice as many Card style games out right now make it so that skill is less important than luck. Here, like many of the more popular card games, it is somewhat more skill based, which makes it actually fun.

_childDocuments_.review: A game very like Slay the Spire. But it's 3D as you may tell already. First impression of the game was that it was easy on the first adventure mode I did. I wasn't used to winning on my first ever try from games like these. Tho, it did take me 3 hours.. And here I will start with a negative with this game. pacing. That is the thing tho... In StS, you can play that game as fast as the game lets you.. In this game it constantly "do" things that makes you stop and think for a second, that doesn't happen as often in StS. And I don't necesserily mean in a good way. Here are the things that will make you stop. ----You will constantly draw new cards, this can happen in StS too, but atleast with StS you have choosen to make a deck that will draw a lot. In StS if you can play 4 cards with none of them will draw a card, you can just play those 4 cards, and end your turn. This is a thing that will not happen in this game, you constantly stop and check what card you drew. ----You may have a chance at a "precision strike" (Killing the enemy at a dmg that will precisily kill them i.e it has 5hp, you do 5dmg, you get a precision strike which grants you gold(I believe it granted Skill points at a earlier time))You constantly stop and check if you can use a card that will enable this, instead of just using whatever card that will kill it. ----You may have a chance at a parry ( Like precision strike, you just need to block AS much dmg an enemy does to you to get a parry, this rewards you with a stun on that enemy for a turn) You constantly check if you have the means to make a parry, instead of just boosting yourself with shields to a whatever amount you can. ----You may have a chance at a battle tech combo. This is the real pacing killer. as a mention in detail on the bottom of this review, as it became a rant and longwinded.*However, after I started ignoring, parry, ignoring precision strikes, and ignoring battle techs. (Sorry can't ignore card draws here) The enjoyment and gameplay speed, increased dramaticly. The only time I don't ignore them, are at maybe some boss fights, and when I have a mission to actually achieve these things. But that is fine, ocassionally doing them ads to the variaty in a good way actually. Constantly chasing them tho. No. Don't even bother. unless you really really want to min max everything. Ignoring them also gets you a few surprising moments when you do manage to trigger them, without you actually trying to, it happened much more often then I thought they would. Classes are made interestingly tho, there are 3 classes, but basicly there are 9 classes TBH... each class has basicly 2 sets of strategies. You have the gun blade girl, with (Radioactivity, basicly poison) and gunslinging (a lot of attack damage) The priest, with praying abilities(Lots of healing and protection), and... vampirism... okay? (life steal)And then helena, which is basicly the robot from StS, but with only 1 orb slot, and not fun. No. Helena is bad atm in my opinion, in her gameplay design. when I first saw her cards, I suspected something like multiple animals (orbs from StS) but no. you can only have 1 animal, and when I tried Helena, I just did not have fun. Its a.. deck building game very like Slay the Spire, if you liked Slay the Spire, you may like this if you want that game but.. something somewhat different. If you didn't like Slay the Spire gameplay, you won't enjoy this.. unless bouncing titties, and 3D graphics, is what sells it to you. I like it tho, even if it has some issues. I still think Slay the Spire is the superiour game. but you can only play StS so much before anything different to it, is enjoyable for a while atleast. And the pricetag on this game? How can you not try it if you crave more StS gameplay!*--- "Battle tech" the point of it is that it will give you a random set of combinations of different cards the game wants you to play. if you do. Your next attack has double damage. The problem with this feature, is that if you are going for them, it slows down the pacing of the game biiig time. And here is a few reasons why. You have to stop your card spamming and see what combination you need, and if you can do it. If you find that you can't do it. You still may want to go for it, as each time you play a card you also draw a card. (imagine each card having "1+ draw a card" from StS terms) This means that you may draw the cards you need. Which means that you constantly has to check where you at the combo, and what card you need to play to continue the combo. Also if you play a card that isn't part of the combo, it will reset and make you a completely new combo, which means remembering the combo you need to do, is a completely pointless effort to make, it is probably better to never change the combo until that combo is actually done. but I can see issues with that implementation too. Me trying to do this, with almost every single chance I got. took most of the time when I played this 3 hour first run.. To the point where I am now completely ignoring the "battle tech" feature, as it doesn't exist. tho you will occasionally trigger it anyway. which is nice I guess. But ignoring it, has sped up the gameplay considerably.

_childDocuments_.review: Neoverse is a 3D rendered deckbuilder/card game, very very similar to Slay The Spire, and it shares many of the same features. On the upsides the visuals are better from a technical standpoint, but thematically it's a bland, generic mix of robots and anime girls.  The core of the game, building a deck and fighting battles by playing one card at a time, that's not so well done.  Your hand isn't very important because you draw a card when you play a card, so your turn is decided by how quickly you burn through your resources... and if you choose zero costs cards, you don't burn any resources.  There's little else in the way of strategy, as RNG is king here. The game features no proper level design or game/story flow/plot, as they opted to try to use samey repetitive procgen algorithms as a substitute for adding such content to the game.  As a result, the game doesn't actually have any content worth mentioning, just endless, boring, repetitive, soulless algorithmically generated sameyness.  Developers must learn that procedural generation is not an acceptable substitute for content. The game bizarrely is DLC bloated, making this seem a lot like a cash grab mobile app that you have to pay for just to play.  It's not as good as Slay the Spire, has more faults, and it's just not fun.   If cards is what you want, try Slay the Spire, Hearthstone or Magic The Gathering.

_childDocuments_.review: YouTube Link:Neoverse is an underrated, turn-based roguelike deck-builder that delivers a fantastic gameplay experience. The focus is squarely on the mechanics, and it’s easy to see why—the gameplay is rock-solid.You start with a basic deck containing simple attacks, guards, and a few skills. As expected in deck-builders, each card has a mana cost, and your mana (usually 3 per turn) is depleted as you play cards. The real fun comes as you progress, adding new cards to your deck through rewards from battle, completing objectives, or purchasing them from the shop.There are three playable characters in Neoverse: Agent Naya, Paladin Claire, and Summoner Helena. Each has a unique card pool, offering distinct playstyles with strengths and weaknesses. What stands out is how different each character feels—they each bring their own strategic depth, and mastering them is incredibly rewarding. As you play through runs, you unlock new starting decks with different themes and strategies, offering even more variety.Each world is made up of five stages, with the fifth always being a boss fight. Completing stages can reward you with skill points, new cards, and stat buffs, which you can use to further customize your deck and abilities. The key here is that rewards can be earned anytime throughout the game, so you can choose when to complete specific objectives.The game’s replay value is high—there are plenty of unlockables, including new cards, costumes, and skills. For those craving a bigger challenge, additional modes are available to push your deck-building and strategic skills even further.Neoverse is fun in both short bursts and long sessions, offering plenty of depth and replayability. The only real downside is the lack of a tutorial, which can make the learning curve a bit steep at first. That said, once you get the hang of it, the game’s addictive nature keeps you coming back for more.

_childDocuments_.review: For a deck builder game, this one holds up. There are 3 characters to pick form, each one with a different playstyle and set of cards to build a deck. It listed that each character has 3 different deck to pick from, but for the most part they all play slightly the same in the end. The random Trait tree keep the game fresh every game since there isn't really a set build to follow, aside from to mapping out how to get the strongest traits and hoping there is enough cohesion in the tree to make it worth going after.My favorite mode in the game is the Hunter mode. It is kinda like a drafting format where you are given standard starter cards then you "open a pack of cards" and pick 1 card from that pack, the rest of the cards you didn't pick get discarded  then you get another pack of cards and pick 1 from it again. You do this till you have enough cards to make a deck to play with. I recommend picking it up on a deep discount. If you see it at 85% off, just give it a try if you like Deck Builder games. As for the DLC, unless you like an outfit or don't want to forever be stuck wearing the Clown Mask equipment, I don't recommend getting them if you are just starting the game. The DLC comes bundled with 100 Trophy items. Trophy are used to buy game altering equipment for your characters and can be used to buy retries for a failed run.

_childDocuments_.review: The miniscule story is ludicrous, and only told through fading text messages in the title screen. Four of the eight costumes per character are only available as DLC, which is a silly money making scheme.That's about all the negatives I have. Now for the good stuff:Neoverse is a deck-building card game with decent animations, and various interesting mechanics. The game features three play modes, and three different characters with quite distinct ways of approaching the game. Each character comes with two different play styles, which greatly impacts what skills, cards, or advancements you want to buy throughout your run.This game is no competition for Trials of Fire, because battles are less beautiful and surprising, and there is absolutely no story, reducing your investment in the battles to the satisfaction of picking the right card combination for a tumultous finishing move, followed by the unlocking of a new power move or special item.Don't expect a masterpiece. But if you like deck-building, and are not avert to sword swingers in sexy costumes, you won't regret entering the Neoverse.
_childDocuments_.name: NEOVERSE

_childDocuments_.review: I had a weakness for blondes so... yeah. This was my introduction to "slay the spire" archetypes... aka a tactical rogelite singleplayer card game. I was shocked at how fun and beautiful the game is. You can tell the developer put his heart into this masterpiece. I know many will complain it's too similar to slay the spire... but it does have some unique changes. As an example, you can choose different starting decks. You can alter the character's gear and unlock it. You can even upgrade the character with passive bonuses that substitute relics.In a lot of ways, this is just an improvement, both visually and tactically, version of slay the spire. But trust me, it's got plenty of unique and interesting ideas that will keep you invested.Now, the game is a bit easy unless you try out ascended worlds, that's where the real fun begins. It's a really enjoyable and wonderful game, and you should check it out.Although it's not being worked on anymore, it's definitely worth playing. Give it a shot!

_childDocuments_.review: This is a solid 7/10, maybe 8/10, that shines in its visuals and some of its unique twists on the genre, while not having the deepest deck building or varied cards. That's not to say that there's nothing to experiment with, or that the deck building is entirely bad, but you really can't compare it to Slay the Spire, Monster Train, or even Tainted Grail (which also has so-so deck building but is great in about every other way). It's more that you've got 2 archetypes per character, and there really aren't many meaningful variations on the archetypes (that I've discovered in about 10-15 hours of play, anyway - ignore Steam saying 5).To be honest, I'd describe this lovingly as "A great low budget game". There's the occasional typo. You can tell it's translated (not terribly but not particularly well either, which leads to some funny instances).  It doesn't have the depth of the best titles in the genre. However, it's stylish, there *is* a lot to see despite the relatively limited build options, and hell it's just fun. One thing to note is that it's very well animated. The animation actually stands out as being surprisingly good all considered.If you haven't played Slay The Spire or Monster Train (didn't love monster train but most people do) then you should absolutely play those first; They're objectively better. That said... There's just something about this game I really like. It's charming. I can't put my finger on it, but it's just more engaging than most deck builders. Maybe it's the 3d environments & models with the smooth animations, I don't know, but I personally think it's great despite its flaws. Is it worth the asking price? Depends on how strapped for cash you are, but if $20 isn't a big deal to you then yeah, I'd say it absolutely is. If it's between buying a game and eating for the next 3 days... Maybe you get it on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a decent addition to the card-type games out there.  The graphics are decent and can zoom and rotate anytime during battle.  Reminds me of Spire but combined with a JRPG like Final Fantasy.  Again, very rogue-like with random availability of cards and items.  Later on different levels of difficulty presents itself.Success, usually is best accomplished on a regular basis if you focus on a theme of what type of cards you wish to play with, instead of spreading out in many different directions.  You simply do not want to pick up every card you can unless it will be useful, for the most part.  Lean and mean is the way to go unless you do not have the shuffle ability, when you hand is empty and cannot draw more cards.The 3 characters vary considerably.  One focusing more on Shooting or Sword, another on Summoning of Guardians, etc... and there are variations of each of these types, like radioactivity, and such.For the price on sale, truly a bargain! _childDocuments_.review: Hello prospective buyers and curious others.I do recommend this game. It is what is called a rogue-like deck-building game and it is exceptionally well made. It may draw comparisons to other similar games in the genre, of which I have played a couple, and I would say it holds up well against them.It is nice to look at, which is always a plus. I've only yet played a single character so I cannot quite say with certainty that the mechanics are as deep or interesting as in other games, but so far I've not seen any evidence to the contrary. It has what I enjoy about these kinds of games, cards that synergize well with each other and give you the chance to express yourself and your skill through careful strategic choices. It is these kinds of choices that I really enjoy, and particularly so when everything comes together with a little luck and some smarts. This game is fairly priced for what should certainly be many hours of enjoyment. This South-Korean made game could use some lore or story elements as the environment begs for speculation but we the player are completely left out of the loop of what is happening in this world! It would also be pretty neat to have a mode where you play three campaigns at once, one for each of the three characters and maybe even have systems that allow you to trade and send cards that each one finds to the other characters. And then have some kind of post apocalyptic story going on all the while with the goal being for the three to reunite or something like that. But then if the game had a great story I would expect the price tag to rise equally. So for what you pay, you will get a very well made, polished, nice to look at and fun rogue like deck builder akin to many of the other games in the genre. Enjoy

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty fun game. A lot like slay the spire but has a few cool mechanics and a completely different aesthetic separating it from being just a clone. The battle arts mechanics are cool and feel good when you get them off and the class concepts are pretty cool. There seems to be tons of content too, so a lot of replayability if you are really into the game. The game is very easy on normal difficulty, I beat the last boss on my first try with each character, but there are modifiers and NG+ type modes to extend to the enjoyment. The default difficulty was so easy I sort of just considered it a tutorial on how to play the different classes. This probably has something to do with all of the extra mechanics that help you along the way compared to other card based roguelites ( the battle arts, skills, shop being accessible at any time, defense staying at the end of turns, etc) but I wouldn't say this is necessarily a bad thing at all. My biggest complaint with the game has to be the inconsistent models for characters and enemies. Its not the worst I've ever seen by any means but if you pay attention to it it makes the game can often look like a cheaply made Unity Store asset flip. The card designs are also very inconsistent, some looks great while others, many others, looks like stock photos with a couple filters over them. I can't really blame the developer(s) for not being amazing 3D modelers / graphic artists though and overall the game does looks pretty good.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is really fun, if you're a fan of card games: Magic the Gathering, Yu-Gi-Oh, Hearthstone, Pokemon--you'll likely find this game to be enjoyable, and if you don't--well you only spent a few bucks on it. The gameplay is straight forward enough, choose your waifu, choose your deck, fight through 5 stages of enemies. The fifth stage is always a boss battle and you can choose normal difficulty or elite difficulty for each run for different rewards. The deck system is really impressive and the strategies you can employ are various, but each of the three heroines have a certain style. You have a sword and pistol user who plays like an assassin, a shield maiden who is oriented around defense and winning battles of attrition, and the mage who...well I haven't played with her yet at the time of this review but I'm sure she'll be a debuffer of sorts.The shop is always available to get you out of tight slots, and if you end up with a card you don't like sometimes the game will allow you to choose missions that will allow you to do so--provided you complete certain prerequisites such as doing x amount of damage or playing five instants. The challenges and the enemy types keep the game interesting and if you're looking to melt time in an airport or during a lecture, this is the game for you. Just the right amount of fanservice, strategy, and replayability.

_childDocuments_.review: I got Neoverse in a recent Humble Bundle and I am enjoying it quite a bit so I thought I would drop a positive review.This is a fast-paced roguelike deckbuilder very much along the lines of Slay the Spire.  You select one of three characters, pick a starter deck, and run through a series of increasingly challenging turn-based battles.  After each battle, you receive random rewards and new cards for your deck.  You can further customize your character by visiting the item shop or purchasing skills from an upgrade grid that is randomly generated each run.  Most runs end after three "worlds" of 5 battles each, but if you have the right setup, you can go on to challenge the extremely tough final boss.The art style in this game is unusual and there is no story to speak of; the characters are all busty anime babes and the mish-mash of enemies definitely reminds me of the strange types of things you might fight in FF7.  Despite this, everything feels fun and flashy and campy like a straight-to-dvd hollywood flop, and its not such a bad vibe.The three characters all have very distinct builds and playstyles.  The athletic gunner is designed around poison and high-risk-high-reward attacks, the heavy-armor paladin can turtle and receive divine blessings or attack with vampiric health-leaching mechanics, and the long-robed mage is built around managing summons.  Each of these characters receive unique cards that can lead to some pretty satisfying synergies.This is a really replayable game; there's loads of things to unlock.  There are three modes.  Each run only takes about 30 minutes to an hour, and it takes a while to unlock all cards and abilities and costumes and accessories for each character.  When you master the basic run, you unlock increasingly harder difficulties for the standard story mode, which adds to replayability.  Any successful deck in story mode can be saved, and transferred into a much-harder "challenge mode" where you can pit it against harder enemies.  Finally, there is a gauntlet-style "hunter mode" that puts you up against more enemies at once, but with a modified random deck that is better suited for facing multiple foes at a time.Overall, this is a winner in my book.  It's light and breezy and fun, but with enough challenge and enough variable difficulty to satisfy all levels of gamers.

_childDocuments_.review: A neat but janky little roguelike deckbuilder, with some interesting ideasThe game offers a nice set of interactions and combos, as well as some auxiliary mechanics to change up your play. The basic building blocks are very simple, but there are enough moving parts to go around. I wouldn't describe it as much of a challenge once you get those moving parts in motion, but doing that is usually entertaining enough that I stay investedIn terms of presentation, the sound is good, the visuals pretty nice (though the playable characters' designs take some getting used to, they're... pretty tasteless, honestly). The in-game text provides the information you want in a clear, understandable and consistent manner, though the phrasing can be awkward at times (at least in the english version, I don't know the other languages on offer well enough to make any statement on those)The game can be played with the mouse, keyboard, or gamepad, or any combination of those three. The non-mouse controls do work decently in their own right, but sometimes require you to use WASD (for keyboard) or the left stick (for controller) to move a cursor around on the screen unless you're also using a mouse, so it's clear the game was designed for mouse (or perhaps touchscreen) play first. Still, I can't fault the developers for providing options and making sure they degrade gracefully. As far as I can tell, the game does not offer a way to rebind controls though, which is a shameAll in all, if you can deal with a bit of jank and some less-than-tasteful character design, Neoverse is a good time

_childDocuments_.review: I wanted something to scratch the rogue lite deck building itch while I waited for StS to come to android and neoverse does a decent job. It's not a bad game but when Slay the Spire does such a good job, I have a hard time recommending this game and would give Neoverse an average rating if I could.I wasn't really interested in the artstyle or animations so I put the game on speed mode and just burned my way through. I believe the DLC is just for cosmetics?The game is separated into 3 stages (acts) and you have 5 or so fights before coming to end of stage boss fight. It's essentially StS with training wheels, the shop can be accessed at all times, it's very easy to customise builds and there are very few penalties that restrict your gameplay. The game is also very clear on rewards, what special requirements are needed to gain those rewards, enemy attacks and movesets. Rewards are not automatically claimed so can be used strategically, e.g. using health regen before boss fights. You also gain trophies from runs and these can be used to obtain gear. Gear are items that permanantly provide you character with a buff or effect depending on the gear chosen and is not consumed, making future runs slightly easier.There are some interesting features, such as camera control during fights, which are nice but mostly useless to the game itself. I never understood the heat mechanic, but I still managed to beat the game.
