_childDocuments_.review: Why they decided to show everyone blonde in the splash art is beyond me. Naya has black hair, Claire has red, while Helena is the only one that is naturally blonde. You unlock those skins after being a run with those characters on ascended 1.That out of the way, I purchased this game and all DLC a bit back when it was under $15. At that price, it was definitely worth it. It's Slay the Spire but with waifus. I hope more content is coming, perhaps even a new character, but the game that is here is incredibly delightful --and, of course, beautiful.For $20 plus the cosmetic DLC's? Eh... I say wait for it on-sale again if you have any interest. Otherwise grab Slay the Spire.
_childDocuments_.name: NEOVERSE

_childDocuments_.review: A pleasant surprise.  It has the same type of addictiveness and run time as Slay the Spire (a typical run is good for around 2 hours), with it own unique cool card combinations and constant deck building fun. It’s not too difficult as I already beat the end boss on my first run. Maybe it’s a tad too easy, or I’ve just become too good at these games. As for longevity, this is the only caveat but at less than 8 bucks this is even good value for money if I only make only 2 more runs.I was surprised by how smoothly it played, how good the cards looked and how well it was designed. It has waifu galore written all over it but I didn't mind. When looking at footage I was turned off by the artificial and overly bright look of everything (lots of pinks and purples), but I just turned brightness down and I think it looks just fine. I don’t mind the lack of story, I don’t play games like this for story but there is a bare bones background tale there. There’s sort of a wild Final Fantasy vibe going on with weird monsters, sci fi tech, some mythological monsters, gods, mutants and so on. The typical JRPG fare where nothing’s too crazy. But this is actually way more engaging as you’re constantly using your brain, making so many choices, where mistakes aren’t uncommon. Personal opinion of course, but if only FF games had combat systems this interesting! I can see those turn-based JRPG games evolve by using more mechanics like this. Really good solid gameplay and never a dull moment. The colored combo chains remind of Destiny or Fate, which is unfortunately ruined by savegame corruption.In this game you get more choice than in Slay the Spire, because very single card gets replaced after playing it, so you always have a full supply. This makes it more interesting IMO. You never run out of something interesting to do.  The full 3d dynamic looks good and it didn’t turn out to be too demanding on my modest PC. Nice music completes the package.
_childDocuments_.name: NEOVERSE

_childDocuments_.review: Probably my favourite deck building rogue like. Three different characters that build different decks. It's easier to build different decks in this game than some others I've played.I kinda wish the enemies felt more varied. _childDocuments_.review: I don't know much about card battle games, I just find this a fun game to sit down and play for an hour here and there.Is it a deep game with lots of strategy? I would say its seems deep. There are lots of cards with different effects, and winning means making a decision about which is the best card to use in the moment. You make combos and build your deck as you play, making decisions about power ups to buy and including new cards, You need to take into account various buffs and debuffs that both you and the enemies have. So I guess I would say its got a lot of strategy. Are there better card battle games? No idea, because I don't play other games in this style.What do I like? I like the different play styles of the three characters. I like that you can have lots of costumes to keep things fresh visually. Mostly I just like that I can treat it as a low stress game that I can just sit down and play for a bit every now and again.

_childDocuments_.review: I will start by saying that I do not like Slay the Spire (STS). I have tried playing it multiple times and I just don't enjoy it. I know that many consider STS the best of this genre, but for me it just falls flat.However, I have enjoyed the majority of STS clones I've played, with Neoverse being one of my favorites. There are a few new elements that Neoverse brings to the table which really make it stand out for me.1. Your shield carries over from turn to turn. In STS, it sometimes feels too random when I draw all my shields on a turn when the opponent isn't attacking and then don't draw any shields when they are attacking.2. Precision and Parrying. In Neoverse, you. get a bonus for defeating or defending against an opponent exactly. For me, this adds a nice puzzle element of deciding what to play when.3. Combos. You'll get a double attack bonus if you successfully play card types in a specific order. This gives another fun challenge and puzzle to pay attention to.4. Quick access to store and upgrades. Unlike STS, where you can only get new cards or upgrades at specific locations, in Neoverse, you can access them after any battle. I love the options to constantly craft my deck and work towards upgrades.5. Missions. You can choose one of three options for each level. Each level will have a differing difficulty and give a specific reward if you meet specific conditions. The conditions do not need to be met in that round but at anytime during your run.All in all, I find there is more going on in Neoverse that makes it more compelling to me. I find it relaxing, yet challenging. The one area where I really feel that Slay the Spire is superior is in its graphics. Although I very much enjoy the graphics in Neoverse, they don't quite seem to fit the gameplay. The 2D art of STS reminds me of an actual card game and fits the genre much better.
_childDocuments_.name: NEOVERSE

_childDocuments_.review: Start by saying this - I am not generally a fan of deck-building card games. _childDocuments_.review: The short: a solid deckbuilder game that takes advantage of the digital format to give you a dynamic, rewarding experience each playthrough. Good difficulty curve, great combo systems, and few if any gameplay hitches or bugs.The long: A lot of fun and chill at the same time! The three characters each have their own play styles and even then, you can modify your decks to give those playstyles their own tendencies. Resource management is everywhere from playing the decks to modifying them to obtaining the right items at the right time.Comboing cards is very gratifying and any given turn might take 10 seconds or 10 minutes, depending what you're planning and how much you've played a particular variation of a deck. The difficulty curve is solid: you might die a lot but you'll always feel accomplished and rewarded for your next playthrough. Once you get through a character, there are daily deck challenges to keep you engaged.The graphics run smooth and are pretty, too, and you definitely get the sense of being a multi-verse hopping butt-kicker.Only negative I can think of if I really try: occasional weird language choices\typos. But, bug management seems solid and I look forward to the possibility of more content! (Even if it's "just" swag...)(My free copy was a gift from a friend.)

_childDocuments_.review: A fun deckbuilding roguelite similar to Slay the Spire whose gameplay has changed quite a bit through since Early Access.The gameplay is very similar with some notable differences which make it easier but not too easy that you can steamroll without much thought. I bought it Early Access since it was on sale not expecting much and normally don't like deck builders particularly because I've never been good or had an interest. However, it convinced me to give deck builders a shot since it was genuinely fun.  At a glance it may look like a low-quality fanservice-y game with the designs but it is surprisingly competent for what it aims to be with decent player character models and animations, interesting monster designs, deck variety, and gameplay mechanics. Backdrops  are also relatively detailed and the UI is also relatively pleasing to the eyes while being easy to understand and use.There are three characters each with three deck focuses that you can focus on before starting a run. There are no rest points, but each path determines what challenges you will acquire and they can be completed at any point in the run. These come in the form of playing a certain number of cards, renewing shop, turn limit completion, etc. Completing them will allow you to claim health recovery, card removal, card upgrades, skill points, etc. Some can be claimed immediately while others only outside of combat. The shop is always accessible but will require you to pay to restock. Shields carry over each turn for both you and the enemy meaning cards that can deal a lot of damage or destroy shields are a must since you will encounter enemies that can tear it easily. When in combat you start off with 5 mana. You will continue to draw the next card every time a card is used until your draw pile runs out. This allows you to easily setup combos. Combos aren't just the card synergy but also buffs that get triggered when you play card types in a certain order. These can aid mana costs, damage output, or provide defense.  Instead of relics you have equipment and skills. Equipment can be purchased before every run using trophies which are earned after killing each boss of a world(?). Once purchased they remain permanently available. You can equip three at a time and each provides their own boost and/or penalties. These also alter the appearance of your character. Skills are only available mid-run and bought using skill points. They can provide immediate bonuses, passive bonuses for certain card types, or stat buffs. This has a bingo-like system where you can only purchase skills on the outer-right/bottom row/column only if there are unlocked skills that form a line corresponding it.The game is worth the full price. If you can't afford Slay the Spire, wanted something slightly easier, or wanted prettier graphics then this is a fantastic alternative.

_childDocuments_.review: Neoverse is basically  anime girl version of "Slay the Spire" - it is a solid roguelike deckbuilder with three different characters- each with two generalised playstyles. The game plays as you would expect; with a series of waves and risk/rewards balanced based on user risk choice and a little luck of the draw. Throughout you earn perks and battle rewards which take the place of relics and provide ample boosts to your strategies.  In comparison to Slay the Spire, Neoverse offers a much more consistent and user driven progression- with pretty much everything down to exacting choice by the player. Often the player is given multiple different options which help them select or reject cards based on purpose. There is also a "gear" system which allows three additional perks to be slowly saved for and added to the set.As you would expect from Slay the Spire- or Ratropolis (if you are looking for a roguelike tower defense deckbuilder, really not a bad option either)- the more you play a character the more card/skill variety you unlock up to a total of five. In my playtime I was able to unlock 2/3rds of the unlocks, with most of them directly impacting the character you are using. Once you have finished unlocking your deck's potential and obtaining special booster items- the game then offers the "Hunter Mode". While not an "infinite" experience, its 20 levels with set progression milestones and more limited selections really force you to work with what you have to crush the randomly buffed opponents. This longer length also allows you to reach a level of power avalanche common in games with relics- allowing for some truly impressive lategame card combos.Overall this game is a great option for those who have entirely played out Slay the Spire and want something new that scratches that itch. I totally recommend it- one of the nicest Humble Choice surprise pickups to date.
_childDocuments_.name: NEOVERSE

_childDocuments_.review: A lot of people compare this game to Slay the Spire which it is - but while it doesn't have quite the depth that STS has, I actually enjoy it more. First - hot women. I find no way of being upset about jiggle physics. Second - I love the way the different girls work. My personal favorite being Claire, the "shieldmaiden" of the group. Her Punishment mechanic (reflect, basically. Every point of punishment does one point of damage to the next enemy to hit you.) combined with the Vampire mechanic (you can guess what that does) makes for a TON of damage output and while you are getting hit as you're not building up the amount of Shield some other characters do, you're healing for every point of damage you're outputting, which is a TL;DR - Fun game, fun classes, girls that jiggle, addictive.
_childDocuments_.name: NEOVERSE

_childDocuments_.review: Blew away my expectations. A lot of content - multiple gameplay modes, characters, outfits, items, skills, bosses. The deckbuilding is done incrementally over the course of a playthrough so you never know what kind of deck you'll end up with. At first that put me off because I normally like to plan my strategy ahead of time, but the almost "rogue-lite" nature grew on me. It has a low barrier to entry for a card game - no need to memorize hundreds of cards up front. All effects and card abilities are well documented. Increasing the difficulty and retrying a run is a lot of fun.

All 3 of the playable protagonists offer a unique playstyle. _childDocuments_.review: It actually took me awhile to get into this game, but once I did I enjoyed it immensely.  it’s definitely a unique addition to the roguelike deckbuilder style games.  Assuming you know the general style of these types of games, here are the unique/notable features:-3 unique characters.  Unique as in nothing I have played before with several different thematic ability/build types.-Combo system where playing certain card types in order give a damage bonus and procs certain skills-Extra gold from "precision" (AKA exact damage) kills-Parrying to stun enemies if you block the EXACT amount of damage they do-A grid-like skill tree where you spend skill points you win from battle OR BUY-No events or story nodes.  No nodes at all-just select one of three battles each with a unique quest-reward and difficulty-Futuristic/robotic enemy and skill style is very coolIt's unique and fun.  Not a ton of grinding to unlock difficulty and stuff. Highly recommend for fans of the genre.

_childDocuments_.review: Very interesting combos, interesting playstyles to build into. I like the precision/parry/combo ideas, they are really fun to play around. Balance could use some work.I only plan to unlock the character skins and beat the game on Transcended (increased difficulty) a few times, unlike similar games where I am motivated to beat the game on the hardest difficulty. Having said that it will still probably be a solid 15+ hours of playtime.
_childDocuments_.name: NEOVERSE

_childDocuments_.review: I guess this a Slay the Spire clone. I've played and completed a lot of StS and I can see the similarities. But there are a lot of differences as well. For one, the developers of this game made no effort to polish their game. The first screen I encountered when loading the game has a really obvious type. The tutorial video is next to useless.I've read other reviews that say this game is easier than StS. Not for me, but maybe that is because I enjoyed StS and was motivated to play it. I found Neoverse tough, at least in part because so much is left unexplained. With more polish and better balance, this game might be somewhat enjoyable. As it is, I didn't enjoy playing it at all.
_childDocuments_.name: NEOVERSE

_childDocuments_.review: After playing fair bit of Claire and learning her combos and strengths... she doesn't have any massive weaknesses. Honestly... she heals,heals from damage,does damage to enemies that hit her and gets op cards from her faith mechanic. Really really strong. But still you can die due to your own mistake or misplay... her only "weakness" is she has no real dots I guess.The summoner girl is pretty strong in hunter challenge if you get lucky with skill tree.The main difference between STS is that you draw a new card from draw pile after you play any card and reshuffle happens at the end of your turn rather than at the start/drawing (happens at start if you don't have enough cards to fill your hand). So basically if your draw pile is empty you can't play any cards anymore. If your draw pile is full of 0 cost cards you can play all of them. Very handy for combos :DIt's like slay the spire but 3D and weird. Does have the "Oh ♥♥♥♥ I made an op combo" feeling tho.
_childDocuments_.name: NEOVERSE

_childDocuments_.review: It's extremely similar to Slay the Spire with nice graphics.  For a StS clone, it is complicated, deep and worth playing as its own game, with many interesting choices to make per run. It's not as hard as Slay the Spire, but still poses a decent challenge. I defeated the true final boss after 16 hours or so once I started to understand builds for each character, but there are extra hard modes that would make it even more challenging. I've mainly lost interest now I've beaten the true final boss, but fully clearing the higher hard modes with all characters would probably take a lot more time and effort.
_childDocuments_.name: NEOVERSE

_childDocuments_.review: Picked up this game with the Humble Monthly Bundle. I am a huge lover of Slay the Spire, and deckbuilder type games in general, so knew I would get some enjoyment out of the game.So far I have not lost a run yet, although I did have to retry my 1st end boss battle. I've beaten the game once with each hero, and twice with the summoner hero, as she's just quite different to most "classes" of heroes in this genre and a lot of fun. Griffon does seem a bit OP at this low level though.If Slay the Spire was a difficulty 10/10 game for new players (especially early game with few unlocks and little experience with the cards) I would rank this at around a 6/10 for new players. I cannot comment on how the difficulty ramps up as I have simply not played enough.If you tried Slay the Spire, but found it a bit too difficult I would suggest this as a slightly easier intro do deckbuilder games.Just always remember: Don't add random cards to your deck just because you can and they're free. A smaller deck is a more consistent deck. Only try to get cards that compliment your current deck, or are just too good to ignore.

_childDocuments_.name: NEOVERSE

_childDocuments_.review: This may look and sound like a cheap knockoff of Slay the Spire but it is anything but cheap. The gameplay is very similar, and I would say, more accessible at times. There are many different mechanics at play here that arent present in Slay the Spire, though the overall gameplay experience is relatively the same. I would go so far to say this one is slightly more accessible even than the game it is copying.           It has very nice graphics and relatively easy to understand mechanics, though you do have to play a few times to fully understand what each of those mechanics does. Some examples being Overheat, Decay, Faith, Vampirism, punishment, paience,  and the mechanic for leading a guardian beast in battle. It does little to explain these mechanics, though there is an info bubble when you hover over them while in battle that is sometimes a bit vague. When coupled with gameplay it starts to make sense how these things help or hinder gameplay.          I found myself replaying the game over and over when I tried it out from the humble monthly yesterday. It was one of the ones that i thought I would enjoy less overall, but decided to give it a shot to see if it would go into the play pile or the toss to the side pile. I was pleasantly surprised that i felt the monthly was worth it this month based on this game alone.
_childDocuments_.name: NEOVERSE

_childDocuments_.review: I give it an OK/10.The premise is good and while it's clearly a clone of Slay the Spire, it does try to play with different mechanics. If you like that game, this is probably worth a run or two, but it doesn't deliver anything like the same level of polish and simplicity as its inspiration.It's extremely easy to exploit the game and get infinite gold, which translates to "instantly" (right after infinite mindless grinding) getting all of the skills and cards that you want, as these can be bought at any time. That prevents the game from being serious or challenging, but it does mean you can play with all of the toys and make broken combos more easily, which, for many, will be an attraction, rather than a drawback.

_childDocuments_.review: It's basically a reskin of Slay The Spire with no map, less content, and more booty. If you're into rogue-ish deck-builders and playing dress up with anime girl avatars, then you'll probably like this, at least until the novelty wears off. On the plus side, it's pretty polished for an indy game. Graphics are good, UI is fairly clean, some character models (not the girls) have pretty interesting design, especially a few of the robot models. I did not encounter any noticeable bugs on my first two playthroughs, and I enjoyed the experience.On the down side, it's not nearly as challenging as other titles in the genre, like STS or FTL. Path planning is a core mechanic in roguelikes, and it's completely absent here. This leaves Neoverse feeling a little hollow. The girls (read player character avatars) are the same uninspired, voluptuous hoe-hum anime girls we've seen since, well forever.Bottom line, I would have preferred to see more actual game play content, instead of a cavalcade of impossibly small bikinis, miniskirts, and halter tops for which to go kicking a$$ across the multiverse so adorned. I received this game as part of my Humble Choice subscription, so it has pretty high value for me. At full price, perhaps no so much. Still, it's fun and I liked it, so it's a thumbs up from me.

_childDocuments_.review: NEOVERSE is a great roguelike deck builder with 3 diverse characters and interesting gameplay. Much like another popular roguelike deckbuilder, you unlock new cards and skills.  In addition, as you defeat bosses, you can gain trophies to buy gear for future runs.  There is replayability with different modes and daily starting decks.The game isn't particular unforgiving - some battles are difficult, but there isn't an overall feeling of defeat as you progress.  You have more choices on how difficult it will be, and in addition, choosing tougher battles gives better missions with better rewards.

Some awesome mechanics like the combo systems (where you spend card categories in a certain order to get a crit buff) make this game especially fun too.

_childDocuments_.review: Humble Choice really blessed me with this game. It scratches the same itch that games like Slay the Spire, Lophis Fate, and Monster Slayers does. So on that basis alone I have been enjoying my time with it.What I like specifically about this game are some of the Quality of Life improvements and twists on the genre. My pet peeve with Slay the Spire, and to a much lesser extent Lophis and Monster Slayer, is the randomness of 'when/if I can buy things'. In Neoverse the shop is always available both between fights and during them. Enter a fight and think 'Damn, I wish I'd spent money on that healing item at the last shop?' - not a problem, buy it when needed. Hoard the gold, spend it wisely.Other common genre functions, like removing cards, are options which come from missions obtained in between fights. Missions don't have to be completed immediately - they remain active until their completion requirements are met. Nor do you need to cash in the rewards immediately - if you get a mission where the reward is 'heal 30% max HP', you can save cashing it in until just before a boss fight if you've managed to take a heavy beating before then.It's the QoL improvements to resource management which I particularly enjoy in this entry to the rogue-lite deck-building genre. Definitely worth playing for fans of the genre, and an easy entry point to those wanting to try this style of game out.

_childDocuments_.review: Do you like RPGs?Do you like card games?Do you like having to deal with enemies that are either too easy or too irritating to deal with yet you still want to assert your dominance?!Well this may be the game for you. As many would say, it carries a similar gameplay experience to "Slay the Spire" however, with the 3 selective characters (all with their own unique themes), this brings it to another level:Agent Naya - featuring quick and cunning abilities to outwit your enemies. A personal favorite of mine.Paladin Claire - the might, shield and resolve to guard against all attacks and return just as much.Summoner Helena - the friend of creatures that yield to her beckoning, her companions provide an excellent array of choices to control the battlefield.I can go on and on of how addicted I was whenever I picked up the game from time to time. It's an amazing rogue-like card RPG that holds an arcade experience (my personal view). Truthfully I'd suggest this to anyone who has an interest in card games. I love the amount of potential you're given to create interesting decks and because it is a rogue-like arcade experience, decks are almost never the same. Even skills for each character are diverse. Unfortunately, I'm not looking to write a full on in-depth review but I'd give this game a solid 8.5/10 for how much it yields after early access.To all those that are new to card games or rogue-like RPGs, give this game a try. This may pique your interests for other card games or rogue-like games. Best of luck to you.To all those who have decided to buy the game to try it out, I say to you, "Welcome to the NEOVERSE!"

_childDocuments_.review: It does have its rough edges and issues here and there, but the team is constantly working on it. There isn't a week that goes by that there isn't an update, a fix, or a change. The easiest way to sum this game up is Space Slay the Spire with Waifus, so I feel the best way to review this game is by saying what's different from the two:--- Defend Points don't go away at the end of turn--- The Relics are Passive Skills instead, and you can only have a maximum of 25--- You cannot lose Skills or trade them--- You can upgrade a little over half the skills--- Its possible to break the game with each of the characters (break as in faceroll the game)--- No mod support (I don't know if this will be added later or not at all)--- Instead of Daily Climb there is the Hunter Mode, which is harder and rewards future runs depending on how well you do--- There are no in-game events (There used to be in a very early build, but they've been removed)--- Completing Ascension 1 and getting to stage 10 in Hunter Mode you can unlock costumesI personally haven't encountered any bugs (at least that I'm aware of), and they've been constantly updating. I've been playing every now and then between builds, and they've changed the game mechanics about two times so far. I'm a little iffy on the current mechanics, but I'm looking forward to this game being fleshed out!

_childDocuments_.review: Some evenings, I play Slay the Spire with my brother on a Shield.  Last night I couldn’t help but talk about NEOVERSE during this, and most of my comments were geared towards how I liked the mechanics of NEOVERSE better.I love the tactical nuances of trying to get Precision by taking an opponent out by reducing their HP to exactly zero.  You get a skill gem for that, so its worth going after, as skill gems are how you upgrade / acquire your passive benefits, which are analogous to Relics in Slay the Spire.A similar thing goes on with shutting an opponent down by making your shield exactly equal to their attack.  Doing this will stun them so they don’t attack next round, and it’s an interesting decision that will make you not use cards you might otherwise have played mindlessly.Since your shield doesn’t go away at the end of a round, you don’t have rounds where your defend cards are useless, which happens often in Slay the Spire.NEOVERSE is mostly about tactical decisions.  But each fight gives you a new target to shoot for (eg win without taking any damage) that can be accomplished any time thereafter and gives you a reward, like more skill gems or start with extra shield or something.At each stage, you’re presented with 3 options for fights, each with different challenge / reward combos and ranging through Normal, Elite, and High Elite difficulties.  At the end of each chapter, you’ll have a Boss difficulty battle, and you’ll be presented with 3 different rewards for it.As far as cards go, you have Constants, which are like Powers in Slay the Spire.  But these cards are not eliminated from your deck, though many of them will.  You also have Instant, Attack, and Defend cards.When a card is played, it is immediately replenished from the draw deck, but you don’t automatically reshuffle if you run out, so it’s possible to run out of cards in hand (which is one of the challenges you can get in a combat). This will make you go fishing for cards, with a specific purpose in mind: to trigger a combo.  Each combat, you’ll be presented with a combo of different types of cards to be played in succession.  Playing a card outside of that combo will reset the combo.  Triggering the combo makes your next attack do double damage, and another card is added to the combo chain.  Chains will go up to 5, and then reset back to 3.This also presents you with interesting tactical decisions, because you may want to hold off on attacking so you can more greatly benefit from your 2x, all the while factoring in how to reduce an opponent down to exactly zero.Mechanically, this game is richer than Slay the Spire.  It doesn’t present the narrative of moving through levels and picking a path, and it doesn’t have ? rooms where decisions must be made, which also elevates narrative of Slay the Spire.As far as the classes go, you’ve got 3 and they’re each very distinct, with 4 different starting hands to allow for a different focus on gameplay.  While the characters in Slay the Spire all seem male, these are all very clearly female.  Others have derided the game for having ‘anime waifus’, but I think this is an unfair characterization.  Each character will have skills available for purchase that relate directly to the mechanics of their class (eg Summoning, Radiation, Vampirism).During the course of play, the store will always be available between battles.  You can pick up cards, items (equivalent to Potions in Slay the Spire), and skill gems.  You can pay to completely reset the store.While you will heal to full health after each Boss fight, there is no other standard way by which to heal yourself.  Some cards will give you heal, but this is usually small, which the exception of one of the classes which focuses on vampirism and healing.  Aside from that, you can get healing rewards by completing challenges, and much like the completion of the challenges themselves, the rewards can be taken any time thereafter (out of combat).While still in Early Access, this game is already very polished and fun to play.  I recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: I hadn't played in several months, since late 2019. So I was pleasantly surprised to see some of the major changes in the game recently. There's already a lot of reviews covering the basics, so I'll instead talk about what I like about the new systems and other changes.To begin with, the balance has changed a lot. There was a time before where you were utterly discouraged from using some mechanics that you'd expect to be common for card games, such as shuffling your own deck, because too many monsters had punishments for shuffling, like having your buffs removed or blocking certain cards for a turn or two. On that note, there were also too many common monsters that easily removed buffs. So there was essentially no way to make a buff-based deck, because back then, the majority of the cards that gave you buffs were one-time use, meaning once they got removed from your character, later during a round, there's no way to get it back. You'd have to rely on passive skills to give you buffs, if you could even access them, since it's random each run.Nowadays, shuffling is not so heavily punished (in fact in my first run since I came back, I didn't find any monsters that punished me for shuffling), and so far only bosses seem to be able to remove buffs, which is fine. I feel like there's a lot more power for the player to actually come up with clever strategies, rather than just relying on the 1-2 effective ones per character that didn't rely too heavily on buffs or shuffling.There's also a new equipment system, which is persistent between runs. You earn the currency to unlock the equipment items by defeating bosses in each run. The equipment gives fairly drastic bonuses, making the game somewhat more interesting, depending on what combination of equipment you choose (you can choose up to 3).All in all, the game is still in active development, and the developer has been busy. I already recommended it before, but these recent changes make it easier for me to recommend it again.

The lack of mapping gives the game a unique feel but it for sure does not try to hide its influences to much. It has fun game mechanics and plenty of ways to build out your deck.  This game should for sure be getting more attention given how well it holds up against others games of this style currently having their day in the sun. _childDocuments_.review: hi,have to say i am positively surprised by this game. was looking for a card game which hasn't got a lot (any) questionable algorithm mechanics like in some f2p card games out there. I like the freaky art style and the impression playing a turn based old school rpg fight system combined with a card deck system. the combination of managing your deck and unlocking skills for your battles, adding items and cards to your deck during or after each battle gives a nice depth to the system. also in the beginning of each "journey" you can choose between characters and within same several deck orientations which varies the starter deck. during the battles you can unleash combos or other effects by playing a certain sequence of cards which adds more damage for your next turn. solving missions during battles rewards you with several things in addition. first I thought this all is a crazy mix of things that might not fit and are a bit overwhelming in the beginning but after a short time playing it makes sense and gives more depth to the game. I don't know where the game will finally end when it will be out of early access but I think I got my moneys worth and see myself playing this game many hours. cheers

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely Fantastic. 10/10. I've always loved rogue-like games, and the combination with card game-play definitely suited my taste. _childDocuments_.review: I feel like this game was made by someone who played a lot of slay the spire but never really got good enough to beat the higher ascension levels. Feel free to correct me if you know the developer or are the developer. I will be comparing this to slay the spire a lot. If you don't own that game, you need to get it if you are interested in this genre. It is the best one I've played so far and the reviews for it seem to agree.The poison mechanic in this game is bad and can only really be built around by being lucky enough to have the skills for it in your randomly created skill tree, which will act as your relics that you get to choose, even though half of them are garbage.The way the deck/drawing works is amazing in this game. You don't need to draw extra cards because as soon as you play one it goes to your used card pile and replaces itself unless your card adds a card to your hand. This effectively lets you play defends when you need them and attacks/constants (powers) when you want them. However, if your deck would hit zero cards in it, you stop drawing unless you play a card with the keyword shuffle/have the skill that does it. Very fluid, however there are times when your opening hand is just ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ defends and you play 6-8 of those without doing a single point of damage or playing a constant, so the RNG is still there with having to build a deck skillfully.THE REST OF THE REVIEW IS IN THE COMMENTS SINCE STEAM HAS A LIMIT. START AT THE BOTTOM AND GO UP FROM THERE. Let me know if I have something wrong or you disagree. I could be argued with about some of the mechanics.

_childDocuments_.review: Short version: You liked Slay the Spire? Give this one a chance. I was expecting to be unimpressed and to get a refund before the two hour mark. Twelve hours later I feel that this game is worth it, whether on sale or not.  Long version: I really enjoyed Slay the Spire. I thought this would be more of the same with different graphics, but while the basic mechanics are similar, Neoverse has plenty going for it. There is a lot of variety between the three characters, with each having two main starter sub-decks, a hybrid deck and, later on, an "expert" deck (just basic cards, so tricky at first, but allows more customization down the road). Overall I felt like I had a bit more control over my builds than I did with StS. Some of the builds allow you to pile up the buffs and I really enjoyed the healer/paladin character and how a defensive strategy was entirely feasible even against powerful enemies. The moves of the characters are satisfying and match the cards. The enemies are well-designed and quite diverse, so that awesome technique you developed for one adversary can quickly fall apart against another, so you need to balance your deck to make it all the way to the end. Luck helps, as always, but good tactics and unlocking some of the better cards will help you tackle the tougher opponents within a few hours. I failed about 4-5 times before making it to the final boss. Took about 12 hours. Plenty of replay value though. So far I have only played the normal difficulty mode, so there are plenty of challenges ahead.

_childDocuments_.review: EDIT: My original review (below) failed to take in to account that this is an early access game. The developers are listening to complaints and making fixes. That being said, if you buy this game be aware that though it is interesting and well-made it is not nearly as polished as Slay the Spire. It has lots of potential but also lots of warts. I have confidence that over time it will get much better. But for now be prepared for both fun and occassional frustration. I have revised my recommendation to Yes based on the rapid balance fixes implemented by the developers.---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------If you are burned out on Slay the Spire and you're looking for something similar...this game is unfortunately not for you. This is a meager imitator. It tries hard but ultimately it fails. It is slow and boring. The balance is off. Too many enemies rely on simple debuffs rather than interesting mechanics. It is possible to get into stalemates with enemies--where you cannot kill them and they cannot kill you--so it just becomes an endless unwinnable loop.This game has potential but right now it's not worth the purchase price. Maybe in a month or two after the developers have received some feedback and have tweaked the balance and added some quality-of-life improvements.Developers, if you're reading this: The Drone Piranha is obnoxious and game-breaking. You either need to allow it to respawn only once or lower the HP trigger on the respawn ability to 15 or 20 percent. As it is now, a Faith build cannot kill it but cannot lose to it.

name: Fae Tactics
detailed_description: In Fae Tactics, follow a young magic user named Peony on her journey across a vibrant world full of mystery and danger. Summon allies, cast spells, and befriend a motley crew of characters as you dive into the growing conflicts between man and magical beings known as fae. Long ago the world of magic was separated from the natural world by Elemental Gates. One day the seal on the gates was broken, flooding the natural world with magical fae creatures once thought to be myths. The worlds merging was imperfect and much of the land was torn apart. The devastation claimed the lives of most of the population of natural and fae creatures alike. Those that survived have forged new lives in the ruins of the old worlds, but growing tension between man and fae threaten to finish what began with the opening of the gates. Unique menuless turn based tactical gameplay. Manage the magical elements of your party to counter the enemies elements. Befriend a colorful cast of allies! Level Up and customize their abilities. Battle all kinds of Fae creatures and collect them into your team. Find powerful and unique Spells to help tip the scales in your favor. Traverse a variety of colorfully detailed environments in this isometric wonderland. Unravel secrets as you explore the various conflicts in the world in any order you want!

_childDocuments_.review: For this review, I'm going to compare Fae Tactics (FT) with Final Fantasy Tactics (FFT).The initial disappointment for me was the lack of a job system like FFT. However you still get a lot of customization options for each character via traits, weapons and scrolls. Traits affect your basic stats (e.g. Attack, Health). Weapons and scrolls allow you modify and add more abilities (Accuracy, Regen, MP drain, etc).Parties are limited to 6 units - 3 leaders and 3 fae. Leaders are main story characters. Fae are summoned units you capture when you kill and pick up their summoning cards. However you can't have 2 identical fae in your party (unless you use a mimic fae). This makes FT a lot harder than FFT because you can't just build 5 Dual-Wielding Ninja-Monks and steamroll the game. ^_^Battles are heavily elemental based (Fire, Water, Earth, Wind). Before each battle, you're allowed to study the enemy units on the battlefield and prepare your units. You are also allowed to select a maximum of 3 spells. Easily winning a battle means selecting the right elemental weapons, spells and fae. There is another type of Element (Arcane) that is mostly neutral and you could just build your entire party around it, but it would be suboptimal in certain boss battles.The UI and controls are pretty good. The game is way more forgiving than FFT in terms of testing moves and showing attack results. Every attack will show you the expected damage and chance of missing. Also the entire game can be played with one hand via a mouse. There is no 3D rotation in FT though, the game is strictly a 2.5D isometric game. But the battlegrounds are well designed and I never felt the need to rotate the camera.The music is excellent. Even in negative reviews of the game, FT's soundtrack is often praised. It's on par with any big budget Final Fantasy game.The story was better than I expected. Characters were all interesting, and there were plot twists along the way. I had expected a generic throwaway fantasy story, but there are certain moments where I thought - hey that's pretty cool.In conclusion, I enjoyed the game a lot. But don't expect a FFT clone. Instead enjoy the game for its own unique characteristics.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a long review, here's a tl:dr.Solid game with tactical depth, worth the money. If you were/are a fan of Final Fantasy Tactics, then get this game up. If you're going to purchase this, think about going to the Humble store directly to purchase it.Before I give my opinions, I'll give a basic explaination on how the game works. If I miss something, sorry, this isn't meant to be a guide.GameplayThe gameplay concept is simple enough and standard for most turn based tactical RPGs. The bad guys have characters speckled across the map and you also have characters in squares on the map. Every character has a speed or initiative value, which determines turn order. Each character takes their turn to do actions until you either fail or the win condition is achieved. Each character has an element associated with them. Fire, ice, water, earth, wind, electric, arcane, or physical. Most elements are weak to and strong against other element types. For example fire is strong against ice, but is weak to water.CookingThe cooking mini game is simple. You have a grid of 16 squares and you play the game Memory. Click a square to try to match it somewhere else in the grid. There's a timer counting down once you start. Each match you make adds a stat to the next battle. Hp, increased attack, or many other options. You can enhance these bonuses with your camping points, which you get in the grid as well. Party ManagementThe party management menu is very simple. Each character has two gear slots. Their weapon and a scroll. You can obtain scrolls from enemy drops and chests on your missions. There's a large amount of scrolls that can be found that have bonuses like more hp for certain types of allies, jump higher, or move further. Weapons change the element of the character and quite often, their whole playstyle.Each of the main characters gain a trait point when they level up. You can place that point in one of three categories; offense, defense, or utility. Each category has two things that it increases the value of, but the second is different for each character. Example: both characters are spending points in defense, character 1 gains HP/MB (Hit Points/Magic Barrier) and Defense for each point spent while character 2 gains both HP/MB and increased resistance. These second bonuses are gained and increased for every 5 points spent in that tree. These points can be freely redistributed at any time when you are not in an active battle.SummonsObtain talismans to summon creatures at the start of the battle. These characters work just like your main characters, but you don't get to equip them with anything. At the start of combat, the summons you have equipped will be brought into the battle, and if they die they are out for the remainder of the battle. You can get some really interesting combinations.Now on to what I think about the game. I'll give each category a score out of 5.Gameplay - 5 - Really good and deep combat gameplay.Story - 3 - Average story that doesn't break any molds and can get a little dark at times.Sound - 4 - Music is nice and the sound effects are very well done.Graphics - 3 - It's pixel graphics.Options - 2 - The available gameplay/sound/video options are very limited.Replay Value - 3 - Mostly a one and done playthrough.Stuff I Didn't Like1. One of the draws of this game is supposed to be the "menuless" tactical RPG experience, and for the most part, it's well done. However, it's also one of the biggest problems for me. Access to information is done very poorly here. I received an item around hour 2 of my playtime that gave +1 Teamwork. I was 15 hours into the game when I got access to see what Teamwork actually was. Unless I'm missing something pretty big here, the only way to know what a keyword means/does is to have a character with that keyword as part of their kit. Another example is one of my characters had the ability to Cripple opponents they hit. The only way to find out what that actually did, was to proc the cripple on an enemy and mouse over the tooltip for the debuff. In a game that's all about positioning, knowledge of the enemy, and how to tactically distribute your tools, not having access to keyword information is a pretty big failure.2. You have no control over the placement of your characters at the start of a battle. 99% of the battles you fight aren't ambushes, so there is no reason that in a tactical game I shouldn't have the ability to place where I want my characters to start. In games like XCOM it's fine to not have that because your starting position isn't deadly. The number of times one of my summons was killed before I even had a single turn because it started within range of an enemy that got to act first is absurd. This should never happen. There is also a bug as a result of this where you can summon your characters off the map, which prevents you from continuing the game.3. This is a personal preference and not a flaw in the game, but damn I am tired of pixel graphics. I played my Nintendo Entertainment System 30 years ago, I'd like something more than an 8-bit PC game please.4. Level grinding for summons. I feel there is a big missed opporutnity here. If you want to use summons that are earlier in the game, you're going to have some griding to do to catch them up. I don't mind grinding out levels for main characters, but because the summons setup is so diverse, it can pigeonhole you pretty bad into using specific ones because of the level differences. Picking up ultra balls in combat with the summons does help to catch them up, but I would have much rather seen the possibility of summon talismans dropping that would boost the level of that summon if you already owned it.5. No rotation of the map. So many times it was a challenge to select the right square or character because they were hidden behind something else. Fortunately this didn't punish me gameplay wise as it's pretty easy to cancel movement and you have to confirm an action, it was just very frustrating.Things That I Thought Were Done Well1. Every battle is an evolving puzzle to solve. The first several hours were REALLY easy and I quickly found a strategy that I thought was the go to strategy that would win everything. I was wrong. I must admit, I got frustrated and mad at the game for getting all up in my butt like a boar hog on a corn cob, but I learned that I had to adjust my strategy. Once I did, I steamrolled that battle that was wrecking me. Now I'm in the habit of adjusting to solve the puzzle for each map and it's increased my enjoyment a lot.2. Each character is unique and flavorful. I love all of the characters in the game, so far. They are cute, funny, weird, and heartbreaking. Only being able to take three of them into a battle is a really hard choice for me. Each character has it's own strengths and weaknesses and since the traits are not locked in, you can create some really interesting and fun builds for the characters.3. Depth of team composition. I can make some really good and flavorful teams. Not only are the characters themselves unique and powerful, you can complement them extremely well with your summons. Not using a dedicated healer? Get a summon for that. You can adapt to the battlefield extremely well by using your summons correctly.4. Combat is fun and engaging. Not really a lot to say here, I dig the meaty feel of a bird in boxing gloves punching the spit out of a dynamite throwing unicorn squirrel.5. Enemies feel dangerous. With the right setup for the map, you can cakewalk your way to victory, but if you underestimate your enemies and try to brute force your way through, you're going to have barrel of whoopass opened up on you.6. Side systems like cooking and crafting are nice additions. They aren't complicated and not something you have to focus on. The parts for crafting come naturally. The only caveat to the crafting is the increased summon limit feels absolutely required to have.

_childDocuments_.review: I wish that I liked this game because I'd been following its development and waiting for it for a long, long time... but I don't.I play a *LOT* of turn-based tactics games, but the more I play this one the more I'm certain that it's a flawed game; I've now reached a point where I believe all the mechanics have been fully introduced, and absolutely none of them have been that intriguing.My major complaints:Minimal progression for units. Each "real" unit (of which there are quite few) has three stats, and each level you get one point to distribute. These are your Trait Points. They are all subtly different within their categories (offence, defence, "special"), but they're not different enough to be interesting. One character may get Crit Damage and Attack for their attack line. Another may get Back Damage and Attack. Others might get Accuracy and Attack, or Def Breaker and Attack (what does Def Breaker do, you may ask? Who knows -- there's no manual and there's no way to mouse over these undefined traits to get any information).No real itemisation. Monsters and chests can drop scrolls (of which there appear to be 42), and these scrolls all give a small bonus: +10 Accuracy, +3 base Attack for all (element type) units, +1 Move, +1 Teamwork (though of course, who knows what Teamwork is? Not this gal, because it's yet another totally unknown trait that in fact does *not even show up on a character's stat screen*). Each character can equip one scroll. Much later in and very rarely as some story quest rewards, you can switch your main characters' weapon types out for different ones, which will generally the element and swap out a mechanic. That's it. That's all there is.God-awful AI. Invariably, the battle begins with you grouped up at a given starting point, with enemies all over the map. This seems fine, but the monsters that aren't within a certain range of you (5 hexes, maybe?) don't do anything. They will simply self-buff, buff allies, or pass, until you get close enough to trigger them pursuing you. This allows you to take battles at your own pace, utterly trivialising them, unless of course there's --Ally AI. Your allies do not share this caution. In fact, your allies will at almost every available opportunity simply charge in, completely and utterly heedless of any enemy opposition, and make an exercise of turning their backs whenever possible. At times, they will not even finish off a nearby enemy you've weakened -- they simply pursue a new one, leaving you to waste an ultimate, get attacked, so on and so forth. This is extra obnoxious, because - of course - if an ally dies, you start the engagement over. This is compounded *EVEN FURTHER* on maps with a boss fight, because if ANY character gets fully KO'd on a boss fight map, you lose and start the fight over. I have spent two hours on one map because it begins with you being given two allies -- both heedlessly reckless -- who will then proceed to charge in and get themselves comboed to death by wedging themselves in amidst as many melee enemies as possible. Often times, there is literally nothing you can do. You can go in with healing spells, healing units, whatever it is you would like to have, but it won't matter -- they will frequently position themselves so incredibly poorly that at times it only takes a single attack and the accompanying combo attacks to kill them.The bulk of your army has no progression. In Fae Tactics, a big part of the game is you taking a look at the battlefield and deciding which units you're going to summon out of those available to you (on death, enemies have a chance of dropping a summon talisman that lets you summon that specific unit later). On paper this is very cool! In practice, though, there's no progression for those units at all -- not only can they not equip even one of the 42 talisman equips above, they don't even get stat points when they level up.Uninteresting upgrades. You get scrap items that you can use on the map screen to craft new always-on pieces of equipment, of which there are maybe about 10. One of them is simply there to gate progression (upgrading your bike unlocks new areas), and the others are simple +x% chance for Y or +n to units of (element type). You eventually unlock a cooking minigame on camp as well -- this is also not particularly interesting. It is a 4x4 card match game where if you get too many 'bad' cards, it ends. This is, of course, entirely luck based. Your reward for successful matches? +x% to Y stat. Not riveting.The map is bland and frustrating. Over time, you unlock new locations which may or may not have story quests. Those story quests may change or disappear over time, however. Again, on the surface this is an interesting idea. But how do you know which ones are going to disappear when? You don't. You simply save before a (usually lengthy and frustrating) battle and hope that the other thing you were interested in is still there so that you don't have to reload and do everything all over again. Additionally, because there is no real 'overworld', your exploration results in nothing more than a new location showing up in a list of locations, so it doesn't feel like you've really 'progressed' anywhere. Since there's also no shops and since there's no units to recruit outside of story events, there's also nothing really interesting or exciting about unlocking a new town.Uninteresting tactics in combat. Your units get three actions, aside from moving: they can attack, they can pass with a self-buff, or they can buff an ally. That's it. Hopefully you find the attacks that your units make fun and interesting, because if you don't... well, too bad, because absolutely nothing is ever going to change about them save for numbers getting larger. Your units do get what are essentially 'ultimate points', and when that meter fills up (from attacking, being attacked, or buffing allies) you unlock an enhanced attack or enhanced ally buff. Generally, these are not interesting either. Boss enemies also get these ultimate points, generally just fast enough for them to one-shot any ally AI you happen to have on the map, so that's fun.No real spellcasting. The story makes a big deal about how you're a spellcaster -- something rare for a human -- and the game blurb even mentions spellcasting, but what it actually is is you select three spells/spell-like abilities per engagement, and that's all you get. These also drop from chests or enemies. There's no mana -- they simply refresh every <x> turns based on their power level, and you can use them anytime it's your turn on any character. Despite turn-based magic being a decent idea, I also don't find this particularly compelling, nor is the process of tactical selection enjoyable; what invariably happens is you are forced to select all three spells based around what you think might keep the ally AI alive long enough for you to play intelligently and end the battle.Fae Tactics is a game with a lot of interesting ideas that executes all of them fairly poorly. Maybe a future patch will fix the truly atrocious AI, but given how long this was in development I kind of doubt it. Even then, I still don't think I'd recommend the game -- it'd simply change it from a thumbs down to a neutral.Regrettably, it looks like we will have to continue to wait for a new entry in this genre that's worth playing.

_childDocuments_.review: The whole game took about 30-40 hours without trying to 100% it on first try. It took me nearly the same amount afterwards on new game+ for 100% the game.The game is a SRPG\TRPG game in the vein of FF Tactics and the earlier HB bundled Fell Seal.  This was a recently released game and was quite shocked that I get to play it already in Humble Bundle. It has the same gameplay style as most SRPGs but it still has its own charms and rules. I never felt it was stale even replaying the game as soon as i finished the main story.  Replaying the game also lets you continue with your level and stats intact but the enemies are also leveled up.This is one of the few games that i didn't speed run on the new game+ and it still felt Great replaying the game. There are some bonuses from the storyline that pays off in the end that there were already some hints happening at the start that i didn't notice until i replayed the game.The artstyle reminds me a lot of PS1 Legend of Mana. (That needs a remake or remaster) Story is memorable and having different character endings shows everyone's stories end nicely. Pros- Great Story and Artsyle- Just the right difficulty with some HARD bosses sprinkled that will require you to change "tactics"(heh) - I REALLY appreciate Epilogues for games that have character storylines Needs improvement-There are still some bugs but haven't encountered game breaking ones. _childDocuments_.review: Ever since the Final Fantasy Tactics serie has gone away, fans of the tactical RPG genre have been starved of good games. While some series pretend to carry the mantle, they usually fall flat in one or more ways. Disgaea is more about grinding big numbers than tactics, Valkyria Chronicles is stuck with the infamous "scout rush" that make you play with only one unit, etc.Well, despair no longer, because Fae Tactics is here! It's great, unique, and a true tactical RPG.To be fair, the game's start is a bit rough. It tooks me several sessions to go through the tutorial region. Not because it is long, but because the missions are very limited. You have both very limited options but you're also drowing in various UI symbols and tutorial explanations that don't always make sense the first time around. But once you manage to push through this first region, you will get to play the full game and start seeing how great it is.A normal battle of Fae Tactics gives you 3 "leader" units, and 3 "summoned" units that are summoned by the main character, Peony. The leader units are stronger than the summoned units, but if you lose your leaders, the game is lost, whereas summoned units can die without affecting the mission. Already, the variety of Fae Tactics starts appearing. Not only do you get to pick your leader units among a list of people you acquire through the story, you also get to pick summoned units among the list of creatures your Peony will learn to summon. And thus, you will soon learn how sometimes it makes sense to tank with a big leader unit, and sometimes it's better to let a summoned one in front to avoid an early game over.But this is only one among many of the interesting game systems that Fae Tactics offers. While it would take too long to detail all of them, the two major ones are the ranged vs melee system, and the elements system.First, the range system: ranged units obviously can more easily hit targets, and also more easily hide. But to compensate for this advantage, Fae Tactics has created a combo system. Whenever you attack an enemy, if you have a melee unit next to that enemy, that melee unit will also get a free attack on that enemy, whereas a ranged unit only attack on its turn. So you will have to figure out when it makes sense to use ranged units that are easily defended, and when it makes sense to send one or more melee units so they can attack several times in a single turn.As for the elements system: each unit (be they friendly or not) is either a physical unit or an elemental unit. Physical units are rarer than elemental ones and function as a neutral type that has neither advantage nor disadvantage. However, elemental units gets assigned one element from the list of seven possible ones, and it has major implications on how the unit works. Not only will your attack always do critical damage if you attack a weaker element (for example water over fire), but they will also be weaker on elements you're not good against (water on electricity). Moreover, it goes deeper as your element also affects the capabilities of the unit. For example, wind units can haste other units so they will move faster and farther on the battlefield.Thanks to these 2 systems, and also several others game systems that mesh well together, Fae Tactics offer a wide variety of options to tackle the various missions of the campaign. Do you want to rush the enemy ? maybe you want to summon some wind units to hasten your units. But what if the enemy is mostly made of earth units ? maybe you will want to switch to fire units instead. Or maybe it would be better to use units that offer big healing or defensive buffs to tank ? The choice is yours, and it will often depend on what you face.Because what you face will change a lot. The campaign is quite long (I'm about 30h in, though i'm taking my time), and it is very well made. While the AI isn't perfect (it will make mistakes from time to time), it's deep enough to offer a good challenge. More importantly, the missions you will face will vary often enough so you don't feel like you're doing the same thing over and over again, and also it will push you to try new strategies.Some missions will have a neutral map, giving no advantage to either side. Others will start you on top of a mountain, for a massive damage advantage. Or it could be the reverse, and you will have to figure out how to climb without getting decimated. Even more important than the terrain, the enemies teams will vary a lot. Sometimes you will have lots of canon fodder, other times it will be an epic boss battle. The elemental system will also affect the game in many ways: there is no single team that is the solution to all the missions, you will have to be smart enough to adapt to each challenge. And even when you think you've got the basics down, the campaign is well made and will offer many surprises along the way...I think you get the idea: the game is rich, it offers plenty of varied challenges, it also pushes you to do well (there are various XP bonuses if you manage to not lose a unit, or if you finish the mission in a certain way, ...), and is also great at letting you experiment: You can always adjust or reset the stats and equipment of your leader units between each battle, so feel free to experiment to figure out what works best for you.I'm gushing about this game, because it very much deserves it, but I need to be fair and also acknowledge that it is not perfect. There are some minor issues that can sometimes impair you. I've already talked about the disappointing starting region. But this is luckily forgotten and forgiven once you're past it and the game gets going for real. But there are also some more long term issues.Chief among them, is the lack of an in-game guide explaining the vocabulary. Sometimes the game will tell you that an item provides "+1 xxx", without telling you what the word xxx means. While you can often infers or test what they mean, the info is often spread out, and I've had to refers to an external guide a couple of times just to understand the exact meaning of the word or ability.Another minor annoyance is the lack of more speed options. The game offers a x2 speed option, but I've been playing with it constantly on, and I've often wished for an even faster speed, especially when I'm just redoing the first turns of a battle I've already failed before.Those issues are never enough to stop my enjoyment of the game, but I do wish a patch would fix some of them.On the whole, Fae Tactics is a fantastic game. It is fun, it is varied, it succeeds in a genre that so many bigger studios have failed on, and I'm so happy I've picked it up on a whim.It also avoids being frustrating by allowing you to pick which mission you want to go for next, so if you've been stuck on a specific mission, you can always back off to the map, and try something else, until you're stronger and/or comes up with a better plan for the mission you abandoned.If you've been craving for a tactical RPG, you should definitely try Fae Tactics. Don't get put off by the so-so tutorial missions, and you will find a great game that will offer you dozens of hours of tight tactical gameplay.Additional note: If you find the game too easy, i recommend trying to go for the "No units lost" end of round bonus on every single battle. I've played the game that way, and it made it tougher, and more interesting tactics-wise. Be prepared for a tough challenge and many restarts on some of the trickiest battles.
_childDocuments_.name: Fae Tactics

_childDocuments_.review: I'm not sure why people keep comparing this to Final Fantasy Tactics when a lot of the core systems from that game are missing in this one. It's an interesting tactics game in its own right and I think the comparison will hurt the game in the long run, especially if people buy it under the assumption it'll play the same way.PROS:• A lot of unique monsters with their own unique abilities adds a neat layer of strategy and a collectible element to boot. • The pixel art is really good. Even the idle animations of each monster and npc lend a lot of character to the designs.• Combos are FUN. Chaining attacks into other attacks is immensely satisfying, and there are times where I didn't take note of my own unit placement only to be pleasantly surprised when multiple attacks start coming out.CONS:• Bad UI design. It's atrociously low res. I thought this was only going to be an issue with the demo but it seems to have carried over into the release build. I play on a 1920 x 1080 display and so many of the UI elements are clearly low res rasters that it becomes very distracting. The in-game pixel art scales very well but everything else becomes a blurry mess. Feels like a flash game from the early 2010s sometimes. A lot of information is obfuscated and the bad UI problems mentioned before make it a slog to go through menus. A lot of info can be compacted into a much cleaner layout (the summon monster loadout menu is a particularly bad example of this).• Lack of choice. Again, this is where the comparison to other tactics games hurts this one, as it lacks many of the customization features that have become hallmarks of the genre. There's no job / class system and summonable monsters can't be named or learn new abilities. Equipment is boiled down to a single passive item slot. Spell choice is limited and new spells seem to only be found randomly by killing enemies.  You can't manually place your units before the start of the battle, leading to moments where one of your summoned monsters might die instantly from bad placement. • Unsatisfying growth. The traits bar only offers tiny incremental bonuses, and since there aren't any unlockable skills or abilities hidden behind the point system leveling up feels generally unsatisfying. I don't know what a 0.6% increase in reaction ability means, and I certainly can't feel it.

_childDocuments_.review: Let me preface this review by saying that I weigh aspects such as gameplay MUCH higher than other aspects (like story), so keep that in mind.Some people might look at this game and go "Wow this looks like Final Fantasy Tactics!". To be clear, this isn't FFT (if you want that, go check out Fell Seal). Instead, Fae Tactics is its own breed of Tactical RPG, which, while it might be simpler than an FFT-like game, puts the pieces together in a fun and compelling way.So how does this work?Each battle you can deploy 3 "Leader" units and "up to 3 Fae summons". At the beginning of the game, you only have 3 leader units, and won't find more till you progress in the story a little bit. As for the Fae, you will acquire a couple initially (which Fae you're given at that point is determined by the birthday that you entered at the beginning of the game / which astrological sign that corresponds to your birthday) and get more as you play. Obtaining more Fae is quite simple -- during battle, sometimes Fae will drop a card which one of your units can pick up -- adding it to your collection.You also have access to 3 spells which you can cast on the battlefield. The idea is: you select which three you want before battle from your spell collection and that's what you get to work with. Spells have cooldowns (like 3 / 4 / 5 turns etc) and  on cooldown. Furthermore, you can only cast 1 spell per round, and the spells can be cast anywhere, regardless of where your main hero (Peony) is on the battlefield (somewhat similar to the Heroes of Might & Magic series, if you're familiar with those). Because of these factors, which spells you chose to take each battle actually makes a pretty big difference; yes, you can take 3 powerful spells, but be restrained by their cooldowns, or perhaps take a small variety of cooldowns to be able to get benefits sooner and more frequently."So you said this wasn't FFT, so how  you customize your units?"For the Fae summons, they are basically "canned" or "pre-determined" in terms of their stats / specials / etc. In themselves, they aren't particularly customizable, however, you have so many Fae, that the idea is "using the Fae you think would be best for this encounter that I'm on right now".For the Leader units, they have two equipment slots: Scroll slot for minor stat bonuses, and a Weapon slot which fundamentally affects how that unit plays. Lastly, they have "Trait Points" (1 / level) where you can assign them to three categories of Offense / Defense / Special, which have varying effects based on which specific Leader unit it is. Note that  -- quite nice in my opinion."If this isn't FFT, how do abilities work?"Fae Tactics utilizes a more-streamlined system of contextual actions. Basically, with your units, they have:The point is that there aren't menus of "selecting your action", instead, you just move your units, tell them to do one of the above actions, and go for it. (Side note: yes, there is a "delay turn" action as well)Small mechanical spoilers:Miscellaneous notes:Closing thoughts:Overall, I'd say this game is quite worth it, especially at a base price of only $20 USD. For those concerned about gameplay time, give or take a little bit, the devs claim that it's about a "60 hour campaign", which I've heard confirmation from other players that that's pretty accurate. There is NG+, but it doesn't really "add much new", so, whether you care about that or not is up to you. Just because a game is perhaps "simpler in nature" (especially when compared to FFT-type games), that doesn't mean it's "bad". In fact, I would claim that the various moving parts of Fae Tactics come together quite well and will lead to an enjoyable gameplay experience.If you'd like a more-extensive and in-depth review of this game, I would recommend checking out a friend's Steam review / review site article found here: Note that there might be an aspect or two which he mentions which may have changed since he wrote that, as the game has already gone through a few patches addressing bugs / balance concerns (such as making sure units' exp doesn't fall behind others as easily).
