_childDocuments_.review: Fae Tactics is a major disappointment and failure in nearly every aspect of SRPG design.I do not recommend this game.The game fails to deliver a consistent or balanced experience on any aspect.You have you 3 slots for main characters and 3 slots for summons.  Summons are your pokemon, and 90% of them are utter, irredeemable garbage.  They are the trash mobs you fight throughout the games, down to the exact stats.  The difference being the enemy gets to field 10+ of them, while you get 3. They (with few exceptions) hit like wet noodles and die to the lightest of hits. They exist not to really be unique, fun characters but to provide your main 3 with buffs and proc combos.Your non-dog main characters are also mostly made of tissue paper,  but thanks to the trait system (extremely bland +% to stat on levels), they are 2-3x stronger than your summons.  They also go into a downed state on death instead of instantly dying, making them 10x tankier than your summons.Each character only has 3 actions: an attack, an assist (use on ally), and a wait skill (if you do nothing). The game has more of the trappings of a puzzle game than a SRPG, but the massive amounts of RNG heartily undermine that.  With extemely strict action economy, the fact you can have % of status, % of miss, and % of possible attack undoing reaction all together.  Back attacks are the only way to get past the RNG.  I have had matches where I had to restart the battle on the first turn because if I missed an 82% hit, I fell too far behind and died.The gameplay quickly devolves into a game of have your tank MC tank cover literally everyone summon every turn or they'll explode into treats.  Sure, there is no permadeath, but the ridiculous end of battle rewards less reward perfect play and more make it completely necessary.The better play you do, the more exp and drop multipliers you get.  They stack multiplicatively.This is what near-perfect play rewards: 16 xp is nothing, but 216 is a full level for everyone.  If you let someone die, then every single party member effectively lost 1/2 a level.This wouldn't be so bad if the story scaling wasn't full of unpredictable jumps.  You have access to multiple areas and missions at any one time.  There is no notification about the level of any of them, and they do scale with the number of story missions done.  This means you can go do a lvl 17 mission and the next one you go to is lvl 27.  You die. Overcoming that level barrier is not possible.Levels themselves feel out of place and meaningless in the game.  The trait system is extremely barebones and meaningless.  If you need the dog to tank, you put everything in tank. If you need the bird to kill and debuff, you put everything in atk.  There is no thought or meaningful customization there.  Otherwise, levels are just +stats.  Your only unlocks are reaction skills at level 5, ultras at lvl 10, and EX attacks at level 20.  All those attacks unlock THE INSTANT a character hits that level.  The unlocks happen for enemies the second a character hits that level... even midbattle.  You can have enemies just suddenly gain abilities midbattle because one of your characters level up.Ultras are super attacks main characters and enemy leaders get by doing any action or getting hit. They are ungodly strong  and break the game in half.  On your end, they can wipe out hordes of enemies.  On their end, they will oneshot basically of your guys.  They are built on hit, and enemy leaders are tanky.  Normal leaders have 2-4x as much hp as your guys, while full fledged bosses will generally have 10-30x as much hp.  They build whenever the enemy gets hit too.  Have fun. Some are map-wide.There is a system for prebattle buffs.  It is a 100% RNG match cards game because relying on RNG to prepare for a fight is what you need in an SRPG.There is an upgrade system which uses drops to give either fairly small, meaningless upgrades or game altering ones.  Expanding the number and quality of summons you can get or +60% spell dmg are locked behind it.  The system does not really have a purpose other than to force you to pick up these drops to ensure you have the strength needed to win.The parts do have a secondary use.  There are story sections that require certain numbers of the drops.  You will not know the story mission requires drops beforehand nor how many it requires.  You won't get a second chance if you miss it either.  if didn't you have 10 wires and 5 mana crystals when the game decided you needed them, you just miss an item that could be incredibly important.The game is terrible at explaining anything.Did you know that the starting date you choose affects your starting spell and summon selection?Do you know what the teamwork stat does?Do you know the dmg or the status inflict rate on Ex attacks is?Do you know what each reaction ability does?Do you know what the enemy ultras are?Did you know that the cracked lava tiles will disappear, killing any non-flying unit on them EVEN THOUGH THE TILE ISN'T MARKED AS A HAZARD TILE?Do you want to know how much dmg enemies do or their chance of hitting you?The game will never tell you any of this.  It does not explain key words. It does not explain anything, ever.How do you get more summons, spells, and loot?  You pick them up from enemy drops.  You have to pick them up. Any loot not picked up is lost at the end of the match.  This means you get to start assigning people to loot duty in an SRPG.  It is more a tedious exercise than anything else.  The final enemy you kill can also drop loot, but because the fight ends on their death, you can never pick it up. Gone forever.About half of the missions have NPC allies that you have to protect.  The NPC AI is completely braindead and loves to get itself killed, which is an instant loss.Boss fights introduce a new mechanic: if a single main character is defeated from the downed position, you automatically lose. The with ability for bosses to summon allies and attack in the same turn, it is not uncommon, but also not infrequent to instantly have a main character die from full health in one or two enemy moves without any player input.None of these are fun mechanics.You cannot choose the starting position of your units.  You cannot see where your summons will be placed UNTIL AFTER YOU START THE BATTLE. This means you can have to restart a fight because your melee summon was placed in a spot where it cannot reach anything, while your ranged one started closer. You cannot see enemy stats or abilities at the start of the fight.  There is no way to plan around previously unseen units as the only information the game gives you beforehand is their element.Elements are not actually deep or strategic.  If a map is mostly 1-2 elements, you choose whatever counters it and a weenie with a good buff.  If the enemies are a lot of eles, then you just choose your strongest dudes and buffs.  All elements really do is require you to look at the page-long rock paper scissors chart.In a game with so many different threats and bars to watch/manage, it has absolutely no UI support ot help you.  You have to hover over each enemy leader to see what spells they have and their CDs. You cannot see how many more attacks an arcane unit has before it gets an autocrit. You cannot see if anyone is in threat of being combo'd. You cannot see the dmg on your non-targetable spells. There is no easy way to see what can threaten whom, as you have to hold right click over an enemy to see its threat range, which is incredibly awkward when dealing with many enemies.The story is patchwork and generic.  The characters have very little development and are not interesting.  The story solidly exists, nothing more. The game has absolutely no QoL and half the mechanics directly fight against the puzzle/SRPG elements.The game is a mess of poor balance and instant kills.Do not buy.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a very fun and charming take on a tactics game, but don't let the cute graphics fool you - there is plenty of challenge here as well! Considering that Final Fantasy Tactics is one of my all-time favorite games, this one definitely scratches a different kind of itch. I like that you can collect and level up monsters (fae) to summon as allies at the beginning of each battle, rather than the standard job/class grind that other FFT-esque games follow. Also, managing which talismans (spells) to take with you into battle, and carefully planning out how to use them, is an interesting way to help control the field.Overall, Fae Tactics feels polished and well-balanced, hitting just the right spot for those who want to stay engaged in a not too complex, but still very satisfying game. I feel like I've already gotten my money's worth, and I'm not even halfway done yet! Would obviously recommend to anyone who enjoys tactics games! :)Update: Now that I have finally finished Fae Tactics, I can easily say that it is one of my favorite tactics games ever! So happy I gave it a chance! :D

_childDocuments_.review: General Overview:  Fae Tactics has tons of care poured into it, but it’s certainly not for everyone. I had a great time with it, but I also don’t have a ton of experience with SPRGs. I can say that the game has a ton of fun and interesting elements, but it’s faults can’t be ignored. Oh, and for all things holy be sure to turn on 2x battle speed in the options.Notable game mechanics:Even by RPG standards, there’s a lot of different mechanics at play determined by RNG, especially outside of battles. Equipable items, loot drops needed for upgrades, the useable units themselves, and more are determined by what randomly happens to drop upon an enemy’s defeat. This can be somewhat mitigated via grinding for what you want, but even then, there’s no guarantee you’ll get a specific drop.Speaking of grinding, it’s almost entirely optional here. Enemies tend to scale to your current level, making the only real purpose for grinding is farming the aforementioned drops. I was able to get through the whole game without going into a single free battle. The enemy recruitment mechanic is another central mechanic. In any given battle, 33-50% of your units will be recruited enemies, with the other half consisting of story characters. The enemies you can recruit are based off of the ones you defeat, but there’s no guarantee that a defeated enemy will drop its recruitment card. This mechanic is fun, though it can be very easy to get comfortable with a few favorite units. The tradeoff for this mechanic is that there isn’t a lot of customizing individual units as a result. Each character (story and recruited enemy alike) is somewhat locked to a certain playstyle, especially early on in the game.Things I liked: The game’s difficulty is hard, but usually fair. You’ll quickly be up against enemies that have you beat in both numbers and stats. Even regular encounters can end in a loss if you’re not careful about allied unit placement and enemy weaknesses. Like any game with RNG elements, you’ll occasionally lose a battle due to an unlucky roll of the dice. However, I always felt like such a loss could have been prevented had I done a better job of organizing my units (barring any level featuring teleporting totems). Additionally, many common pitfalls of SRPGs are thankfully absent. While there is a traditional “evasion” system, it can be mitigated by having units attack enemies from behind. Additionally, enemy reinforcements don’t attack the same turn they arrive, critical hits are based on type rather than RNG, and allied NPCs not named Marcus are surprising component. Overall, 95%+ of the game’s story levels are fun and fair to play. But fair warning; when Fae Tactics has a poorly designed level, it’s usually a REALLY poorly designed level. (Disclaimer: I played on the normal difficulty)The branching path system is a really nice touch. If a particular mission looks daunting, you’ll often be able to go to another one and come back when you’re ready. There’s also a ton of secrets and collectibles to find, including secret missions, rare items, and even entire story characters. The Story is fun. It’s does a good job of knowing when to keep things serious and when to be lighthearted. The plot twists aren’t blatantly obvious and there’s rarely a character that comes off as dull. Despite the “visit new area, do X, and leave for the next one” structure of the story, there’s a surprising amount of worldbuilding baked in as well.The soundtrack is great. That’s that. Things I disliked:Probably my biggest gripe is that Fae Tactics will occasionally omit telling you critical information. The biggest offender is that I was never able to determine what an enemy’s “ultra” skill would do before they actually used it. There were a few other instances of this outside of this, but they weren’t super common. The first few hours are rather rough. The game does a good job of explaining the core mechanics, but there’s so much to take in that some details can slip through the cracks. A glossary of keywords and mechanics would have been a godsend. (Though there is an easy-to-reference guide for unit weaknesses and resistances). The graphics are fine, but nothing special. There’s a good amount of repetition in the enemies and assets, but it comes off more as a limited budget issue rather than a lack of creativity issue. The cooking minigame gets old very quickly, but the stat upgrades it gives are significant enough that you won’t want to pass it up, meaning that you’ll end up doing it after every set of battles.TLDR: Pick up Fae Tactics if you’re looking for something fresh with a lot of love put into it. Pass if you’re not ok with the occasional poorly design level or improperly explained mechanic.

_childDocuments_.review: Essentially, Fae Tactics is a beautiful, varied TRPG that plays much faster than most TRPGs due to streamlining how you give commands and a few other aspects.I played on normal rather than hard, so that may affect certain things. Normal felt challenging enough to where I had to think about things for most fights and changed teams often, but with proper planning and examination I was able to one shot about 80% of fights, so it felt like the perfect difficulty for me.Pros:++Lots of vastly different playstyles(once you get to about mid game). Utilize AOE stealth, set up huge burst damage like back attack + water bonus + antiair + elemental weakness + rage + height advantage, tank things with taunts and healing and buffs, leverage mobility and range advantages, set up melee combos, stack buffs on your team, bring a squad of faeries who buff other faeries, teams that help a certain character combo off, etc.With that alongside the elemental weaknesses, I utilized a ton of different teams throughout my playthrough, which I really appreciate.++Much faster than most trpgs, although could be a bit faster, but the control setup allows it to be faster and in certain ways easier without resulting in an overly simple game. The basic flow of choosing between "Do i attack, use a wait effect, buff an ally, use an ultra, or use an EX move?" is quite great- the fact that the game emphasizes support moves more than most games adds considerable nuance.The relatively fast play helps make it easier to just hop into another battle. It would be even better if it had a rewind function, and a few more relatively easily implemented improvements though. But in contrast, a lot of TRPGs are bogged down by various types of slowness.++Lots of nice subtleties about the combat. Got an annoying debuff on a character? Put a buff on them to overwrite it, there's only one slot for major buffs and major debuffs, so you can use that for counterplay. Fights can vary a lot, shifting which approaches are viable. I'd say 3-4 of the fights are just sort of annoying, but the rest were reasonable, good variety. ++Nice art/sprites, beautiful varied designs of creatures+Bunch of nice systems that compose your team+On normal at least, you dont have to grind at all. I went through about 70% of the game without doing a single free battle, I only started doing them to capture more summons. Your characters and summons have their levels rubber banded quite well. Progression feels nice as you unlock more spells, scrolls, and upgrades.+Newgame+!About even:~Story is pretty decent overall. A bit of it is very good, most of it is about average. I would say the worldbuilding is better than the story.~Almost nothing is missable, and you have tons of leeway for the missable stuff, aside from one encounter where what you should do(and the fact that something missable is even there) is not as obvious as it should be, but at least there's NG+. Look up a spoiler free guide and youll be fine.Cons:--Early game team variety is pretty weak. You'll probably rely on a couple of things quite heavily.  It can be a bit of a drag, especially if you get into a grindy battle or run into certain difficulty jumps. The essential problem early on is you dont have a lot of things to customize your team with, which is probably why some reviews complain so much about the lack of customization- by midgame you have a lot. It's not FFT levels of flexibility, but you can still do a ton of different setups.I think they should've given you some more scrolls/weapons/summons early on to flesh out your early game strategies. Once you get past early game, I dont have much to complain about besides a few fights being kind of annoying, or some inconveniences or clarity issues. Regardless, here's some minor downsides:-There are about 3 parts where the final boss in a section is quite unusual, so you may have trouble beating them. This would be fine, but if you decide to cancel the battle to go get more equipment or do other story parts, you'll have to redo the prior fights first, which is just annoying. One of the bosses is a 1v1 fight with a particular character, and it seemed to me you can only win if you have at least one of about 3 different equipment scrolls. That fight seemed like a lot more of a static puzzle than the more flexible strategy environment most people expect from games like this.-2 of the first 3 main characters dont really talk, which weakens the player's early attachment to the story and characters.-Some minor annoyances with progression, like RNG for capturing summons can be annoying. Or if you do want to grind, getting high amounts of EXP can sometimes be annoying with certain forms of lopsidedness.-Some mechanics could be explained in a more easy to find way. It can be easy to forget that you can just hit space bar to bring up the elemental weaknesses.-There's about 2 missions where AI controlled allies(who i had to make sure didnt die) put themselves in serious risk. I never actually lost those missions because of that, but I almost did.-You arguably get too strong late game, but that's mostly just an inherent risk of highly customizable TRPGs without turning them into overly-rigid puzzle games which would suck the fun out of the options.Also, I gotta say, the developers clearly put a lot of passion, thought, and effort into the game overall. Valdis Story is a similarly impressive game from them- it is a feature-heavy metroidvania with lots of playstyles. I cant wait to see what they make next.Overall, it has great variety, great combat nuance, it plays faster than most TRPGs which makes it much easier to get into and stay into, its beautiful, and you dont have to worry about wasting time grinding. But the early game can be samey and feel limited, and there's a few annoying fights and some minor annoyances and clarity issues.
_childDocuments_.name: Fae Tactics

_childDocuments_.review: Fae Tactics, as the name already connotes, is a Tactical RPG game with such amazing pixel art that puts other similar games to shame. Although it's not very famous since it's just published by Humble Games, Fae Tactics is one of those games; yup, the ones Humble just publish secretely without anyone noticing and they become instant underrated gems and you play them thinking they're going to suck but instead you become super addicted to them.Fae Tactics puts you in the shoes of Peony, a witch, descendent of both human and fae... These halfbeings are mostly viewed by the pure races as conniving, and trifling so they are immediatly given the cold shoulder, and rightly so. However, Peony is different... All she wants is to help people, and care for her motorcycle. As she travels the wilderness with her two faithful 'starting' companions, Peony will become entangled in a plot bigger than the kingdom and she will have to sacrifice a great deal to save the world.Gameplay-wise, the only thing that I really despise about this game is how it tries to shove a million mechanics down your throat at the same time and it's got this thing where if you don't use most of the basics it tries to teach you, you'd lose. Only after 4 hours in did I realize that you can deal more damage to enemies with your ranged creatures by standing on higher terrain lol. Peony can also summon creatures she fought before at the start of the battle, much like main characters these summons level up and are quite useful if you stack their Wait power on someone, but unlike the main characters you cannot level up their attributes. One of the best summons that you get early on is the Gremlin Witch, her self-wait power boosts her assist power, and her assist power heals your characters. You can also get scrolls that you can assign your main characters that increase attributes or defenses. Your main character gain purple orbs during battle, allowing them to unleash their full potential once their purple bar is full... And that's where you should be mindful in your team composition as some "full potential" powers are really pathetic, especially in certain boss battles; so open your eyes and read before taking any character to battle.All in all, Fae Tactics really lives up to its name; it's got Fae, and the Tactics get sometimes overwhelming but the game itself, with all its amazingly likeable character is a cutesy experience. In my opinion, the game deserves an .
_childDocuments_.name: Fae Tactics

_childDocuments_.review: Fae Tactics is enjoyable. I actually came into the game only slightly more positive than neutral. I expected it to be competent but I did not expect to be enraptured, and yet I was. I kept finding myself wanting to do one more stage and even now, with the game finished, I am finding myself going through stages trying to hunt the items I missed hoping to extract a little bit more of the joy I got from playing it out. I want more and I will play it again soon, and that alone is usually enough for me to recommend it to people who enjoy the genre. What makes Fae Tactics different is that I want to recommend it to most everyone who has the slightest bit of inclination to play a tactical turn-based RPG due to how effectively it manages to balance simplicity with depth. Even if you have a low degree of tolerance for convoluted rules systems you should be able to get into Fae Tactics. If you are someone who likes lots of crunchiness with a variety of options to explore then Fae Tactics should satisfy you. It is a crowd-pleaser and frankly exceptional. Get it. Play it. Enjoy it. Pros:Excellent stage design, with a variety of goals and challengesCharacter development continues to the end of the game and beyondHigh replay valueEnjoyable story and settingCons:Somewhat imbalanced characters, gear, and spellsSlow startTough to keep characters at equal strengthLack of keyboard options can make some actions tediousIf you want a larger explanation where I go in depth you can see my review at Turn Based Lovers which you can see here:

_childDocuments_.review: Valve’s “recommend / don’t recommend” is basically worthless for anything other then an AAA title or absolute disaster.  It doesn’t really help with smaller titles like this were there is a lot to consider, but I’ll do my best.What’s the easiest way to make your “tactics” thoroughly unenjoyable?  Way out ahead of any other issues are orders of entropy, making movement a slog and extremely illogical zones of control / collision objects.  Before even trying to justify Fae Tactics on its strong points, we need to look at how critically and unforgivabley it fails in these regards.If your attack has a 20% chance to do double damage, 15% chance to miss, 10% chance to be reflected, 20% chance to be blocked, and a 35% chance to add a depuff … where are the tactics?  The game would be far more accurately named “Fae random results”.  The range of outcomes actions can have is far too varied for your planning and decisions to feel meaningful.  Even counting for mitigating as much as possible by position and taking advantage of the rock-paper-scissors mechanic, there is no way to know what your attack is going to actually do.  That’s not a huge problem when that means “it might do somewhere from 20-30 damage”, but here you’ll be looking at the best-case scenario as enough damage to one-shot most enemies, a knockback that takes them out of position and gives you a huge advantage, and applying a meaningful status debuff, while the worst case is the attack being reflected back at you and killing you outright.  The result is never satisfying; it’s feels cheep when a good dice roll trivializes an encounter leaving you with no feeling of accomplishment, and it’s infuriating when you’re tactical flawless play results in a game over because your team rolls so low they do no damage and the enemies turn is a endless series of super-critical.  No matter how much you enjoy and find value in the rest of what the game has to offer, you will always be fighting this and it never goes away.The combination of a insane “first movers disadvantage” that can result in even the most powerful units you have dying in a single turn if they move out of position and painfully bad “z axis” movement, moving from one side of even a tiny map to the other is a slow crawl that feels more like work then entertainment.  At the same time, there are no zones of control and no units can create collision objects, so unless you’re standing against a wall any monster can simply walk though you for a devastating back attack, and you can do the same.  Even standing against a wall, you always turn to face attacks … meaning a ranged unit can flip you around and subject you to back attacks from all the units around you.  It’s … silly, plan and simple.  It constantly pulls you out of the experience as you’re never looking at a real “battle”, but instead your focus has to be on these unrealistic mechanics.  There are common problems in the genre, so to say this is something that Fae Tactics does exceptionally bad is perhaps unfair, but it doesn’t do it better or even as good as other entries.More then anything, that’s what it comes down to.  The game is cute, has its charm, the pixel graphics are fantastic, and summons and spells provide unique and fresh systems.  There is fun to be had here, and your enjoyment is gong to largely depend on how much you enjoy that charm and how forgiving you are of the flaws.  That is … in a vacuum.  But when you start to ask “why should anyone buy this over Wargroove or Disgaea or the other heavy hitters in this extremely saturated genre?” … I don’t have an answer.  There is more uniqueness, more charm, and better overall mechanics to be found elsewhere.So if you own every turn based tactics game there is already and you just want more … sure.  This game doesn’t suck, you’ll have some fun and you’ll get your fix.  But if you’re looking at Fae Tactics because you want to get stated in the genre or you are looking for a follow up to the one or two entries you’ve already tried … it’s extremely hard to recommend.  Disgaea 2 PC is better on every possible level and it's $7 cheaper.  And when I’m saying that about a game that came out in 2006 … that really brings how little Fae Tactics brings in means of innovation and polish front and center.

_childDocuments_.review: This game got good reviews so I had high hopes.  The pixel art is amazing, but let me break down the battle loop for you.Start battle - even at 2x speed this is exceedingly slow:Enemy 1 moves 1 square casts buffEnemy 2 moves 1 square casts buffEnemy 3 moves 1 square casts buffx until 10 enemiesBoss casts spell to summon another monster - moves one square - casts buff2nd Boss casts spell to summon another monster - moves one square - casts buffRepeat for every turn you will play, minus the 2 enemies you are fighting at that moment.  Those 2 enemies will then 1 shot your summoned characters.  You kill them but prepare for 5 turns of slowly moving your characters towards the enemy as you wait forever for all the buff and character summon spells to finish.  By the time you make it there the enemies have exponentially increased slowing each turn even more and have stacked 100 buffs on themselves and you have wasted 10 minutes.
_childDocuments_.name: Fae Tactics

_childDocuments_.review: Definitely one of the most interesting SRPGs I've played in a long time, and as a fan of the genre I really appreciate that this game aims for something different rather than simply trying to emulate Final Fantasy Tactics / Tactics Ogre (like so many other games do).The thing that sets Fae Tactics apart is how mechanically lean it is. Each of your unit’s moves are determined by context; if you target an enemy you will attack, if you target a friendly unit you will assist them and if you choose to wait you will get a passive buff. As a result, you don’t have a large range of skills to choose from; instead there is a much greater focus on tactical positioning and setting up combos with other units. Despite the art style evoking Final Fantasy Tactics the moment to moment gameplay feels closer to something like Fire Emblem.This streamlined philosophy extends to the other game systems; there is no real micromanagement of unit equipment or large skill trees / job systems to explore; rather, the focus is on selecting a group of fae creatures with complimentary elemental types for the battle at hand. I personally found this singular focus on the tactics rather than the “RPG elements” synonymous with the genre refreshing, but I suspect it will rub some people the wrong way. I’d recommend this game pretty universally on its mechanics, and the pixel art is so incredibly charming as well! High up on my list from 2020 so far.
_childDocuments_.name: Fae Tactics

_childDocuments_.review: Ever since I played Final Fantasy Tactics: The War of the Lions as a teenager, I have been on a never-ending odyssey in search of tactical games that can give me a similar experience to the aforementioned title. While playing Valdis Story, another game from the devs, I heard about the development of Fae Tactics, and it immediately caught my attention. I knew instantly that it was going to be a game that would satisfy my desire to play a "tactics" game, and it really did. Thanks to a very entertaining story, although confusing at the beginning, a great variety of mechanics and a rather curious repertoire of units. It's an eye-catching game that does well in capturing the essence of the genre, in my opinion.The story of Fae Tactics revolves around Peony, a young witch, who hates to be called that, accompanied by a faithful canine and a little bird of a very particular species. This group travels the world in search of something that at first is not revealed to us, and makes it seem as if we are simply advancing aimlessly. But that's because the journey begins slowly and gradually expands in several directions, presenting us with several plots in parallel, and sometimes intertwined.I must admit that it took me a while to get used to this, I didn't understand very well which mission was the main story and which wasn't, but at some point I realized that most of the stories that were presented to me had their own importance. Some of them were necessary to get new characters for the group, others to improve their weapons, unveil secrets of Peony's past or an NPC; and I ended up enjoying this tangled but fun process a lot. As a final fact, depending on what you do, several epilogues are unlocked, which I think is a fantastic addition.In terms of gameplay, we'll have a preparation stage, where we'll be able to equip our characters, level them up, eat, etc.; and then choose a mission and move on to combat mode. In this mode we'll be presented with various maps with enemies scattered around the area, environmental traps such as lava or poisonous plants, and sometimes with some objective such as reaching a specific area to win. The combat itself is the classic of the tactical genre, but with its own touches, as we'll have a maximum of three "leader" characters, protagonists so to speak, and three Fae summons that are the product of Peony's magic, which by the way will always occupy one of the three character slots.What I felt most curious about was the system of waiting and support, and that is that each character has an ability corresponding to these two actions, depending on their element. For example, wind creatures can wait and raise their agility, or use their turn to grant a movement bonus to an ally. This makes for an interesting twist, since in addition to the classic healing unit, which would come to be the water element, everyone can fulfill the role of support in some way. Having also the typical elemental advantages and weaknesses, we have an additional layer of strategy and dynamism to the battles.On the other hand, we can’t miss the level-up system, and every time a leader character levels up we can choose between three stats to increase: offense, defense and special. Leaving aside the usual, what stands out in defense is the mana barrier: a layer of energy that defends us from critical damage (elemental weakness, such as water attacking fire), so it is important to maintain ours and reduce the enemies' quickly. It is usually erected innately, and also with the support ability of earth units.Apart from levels and stats, we'll have several scrolls that we can equip to our leaders, each with its own passive bonus, such as increasing the attack of all ground characters or increasing the damage to isolated targets. There are also a large number of spells for Peony, and Faes that we can invoke in combat. It should be noted that all this must be obtained by playing, defeating enemies and opening chests, or occasionally by story. Around end-game time, we’ll unlock another passive system, and if we also count some improvements outside of combat and the weapons of the leaders, we can say that there are quite a few mechanics to play with. By the way, Peony's base armament allows her to use any element depending on the scroll they have equipped, perfect to cover our weaknesses more easily. All in all, a deep and more than robust gameplay.Fae Tactics' artwork is no slouch either, presenting us with meticulous pixel art for the environments and units. The sprites are very detailed and their animations are fantastic. The designs of the Fae enemies and allies vary to some extent, and the character portraits are nice but somewhat monotonous, as they do not have different expressions. To solve this, the characters sometimes show a text balloon with animated "emotes", such as a crying or blushing face, and the truth is that they look cute. All this is wrapped up by a beautiful soundtrack, with catchy and very diverse tunes.In conclusion, Fae Tactics is a game that presents a wide repertoire of mechanics, entertaining and very well thought out. The playable characters are remarkable from the moment they are introduced, and are further developed throughout the game, with plots that unfold in a very captivating manner. The tactical strategy, the story that ranges from emotional to disturbing moments, and the wonderful audio-visual delight, made for a very enjoyable experience. The truth is that I loved it, what more can I say.
_childDocuments_.name: Fae Tactics

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoyed this game for the combat.The monster collection, the skills, everything is great. Combat is challenging, even on normal.The story? oh boy.. the story is atrocious. Very hard to get through and the characters are paper thin in terms of complexity and design. TLDR - play this for the amazing combat, stay away from the poor writing/story presentation/overall lore.

_childDocuments_.review: Game is decent.However game features enemy level scaling with the number of story encounters you complete. This ruins any sense of progression. There should not have been enemy level scaling. If you want to gain an edge due to level scaling you have to augment your stats. In order to augment stats, you have to craft items, which is fine. However to get those items for crafting they have to be picked up in battle after an enemy dies. This effectively causes you to lose a turn picking up one item each time. Worse yet, story encounters end once you defeat the main enemy unit of that encounter, who often drops an item. Items should have just been auto grabbed at the end of battle. "Monster catching" is a mechanic in the game, however to do so you have to pick up the monsters card after defeating them. And just like before, this too uses up a turn. Compound that with the fact it's rare an enemy drops their card. It's completely random. Which means little chance to experiment around with different monsters unless you get lucky. Should have been a mechanic to collect monsters. Difficulty and battle pacing is everywhere. You'll have some encounters that are a breeze, some are appropriate, and then some that can be a bit brutal, but for those it feels less about strategy and more about being woefully out classed in regards to how much damage you're doing. And so those battles just drag out. Not difficult, more whittling down numbers since you can't get an upper hand. This again is compounded with the fact you have to use up turns just to gather items and cards. There is praise to be given. The story is good, dialogue is fine. Has a lot of SRPG tropes that never get old (more damage higher up you are, more damage when attacking from behind, group attacks, etc.) Multiple story threads going on at once, and you choose which routes to follow. Felt very PS1 Legend of Mana. All in all it is just decent, would not recommend, there are much better SRPGs out there.
_childDocuments_.name: Fae Tactics

_childDocuments_.review: After playing many tactics games to relive the FFTA memories I had as a kid, I found that this game unfortunately falls for many of the pitfalls that drive me away from tactics games. The battles have narrow passageways without many unique ways to traverse them, so you spend many of your turns just advancing instead of thinking tactically. There are items scattered about the map to collect, so you end up wasting 3 turns going to pick up the item, putting you at a disadvantage and of course, it's not very interesting gameplay. The enemies outnumber you, and are HP sponges, meaning the proper tactic is always to abuse the AI and draw out one enemy at a time and gang up on them. Units don't have classes - this was fine for me, and felt like a unique idea. Each character had an ability to buff another character, to buff itself, or to attack an enemy. There really wasn't much feeling of growth or customization compared to class-based systems, but it felt decent enough. Element rock-paper-scissors. This is always a disappointment - Tactics games are supposed to encourage you to use the map and the unique abilities of your units to your advantage. But instead, you just bring water when the enemy is fire. Enemies can revive their leaders. This was the point I uninstalled - One round sequence went like:Kill enemy leader -> Revived -> Kill him again -> Revived -> he party wipes 4 characters in one hit. What should I have done? The strategy that worked - abuse the AI to split them up as I kite them around the map.Story had me interested enough to at least read the dialog, but I don't want my tactics games to feel like a slog. Let me be creative, let every turn feel impactful and pose unique challenges to me instead of lots of big health bars.
_childDocuments_.name: Fae Tactics

_childDocuments_.review: Updated Review: I've decided that Fae Tactics core gameplay loop is enjoyable enough to give it a positive rating. This game does come with some heavy caveats. Do not play if you're not ready to be frustrated by some massive difficulty spikes. Do not play if you are looking for a strong narrative. Do not play if you can't forgive poor UIs.For every 2 good things this game does, it does 1 thing horrendously. The core gameplay is fantastic. If there was more effort put into the narrative and a lot of the UI elements and presentation, this game would probably go down as one of the greatest Tactical RPGs of all time. As it is, though, it's just an enjoyable but flawed game.Old Review - My disclaimer: I've been waiting for this game to game out a long time, as I'm a massive fan of Endless Fluff's previous game, Valdis story. The fact that I have to leave a negative review pains me very much.As much as I've been enjoying this game, I just can't give it a positive review until they fix what is one of the most glaring oversights and points of frustration I've ever seen in a game. The majority of Fae Tactics puts you through battles across 3 different maps with no saving in between.Just now, I played for ~1 hour and struggled through 2 of the maps. They were pretty long and difficult fights and one of them took me multiple attempts. I had to put the game down, but there is no option to save in between these fights, so I lost all of that progress. Once I saw that I have to get through the first 2 maps all over again I instantly lost all motivation to play the rest of the game.I'm perfectly fine with the game being very challenging, but it's just unacceptable to have to redo those challenges simply because you ran out of time to do yet another 20-30 minute battle. It's a simply fix and the fact that it's not already in the game is just an absolute disrespect to players time.
_childDocuments_.name: Fae Tactics

_childDocuments_.review: + Great pixel art style and presentation; nice music, story and characters seem interesting enough+ Incredible potential for depth, which unfortunately for me goes overboard and turns into a negative...- Way too convoluted with too many mechanics for me:Instead of being able to sculpt your unit with growth, skills, or classes, every unit has an element.Fire does crit damage to earth/ice but takes crit damage from water. Which is not to be confused with ice element which does crit damage to earth/water. There's wind/electric/arcane as well. Each element has an assist skill, a spell cast on an adjacent unit. These are proving annoying as I don't want my squishy healer-assist right next to my melee unit. Each unit has a wait skill, which is nice as it's a self-buff usually, rather than wasting your turn with 'wait.' It can be annoying though, to decide between assisting a unit or buffing yourself. They're nice to have because you're constantly barely inching forward to try to specifically aggro the first mob. If you overextend by one square your first unit gets hit by 4 mobs and it snowballs pretty poorly. If you want to heal them you are putting your squishy in attack range of those 4 mobs. Restarting a level--a seemingly frequent occurence--starts to feel especially wasteful on time, even on 2x speed. You have to watch every unit move, cast a buff, wait a full second or two of neutral animation before and after each unit. Multiple times, before you get to engage in any combat. Maybe I've lost some patience for tactical RPGs, I don't know. I desperately wanted a 3x or 4x speed after just a few hours.I have my 3 main units, then I have summons which are extra units but I can only bring so many, based on summon capacity and their cost. I have to choose between several weak ones (who can wind up useless or getting one-shot) or one strong one. Sometimes the higher cost ones don't actually feel better. I may be misunderstanding the strategy but I often regret the summons that I choose. Element of your units/summons become extra important because if enemies have mana barrier, it's a shield where if you use the wrong element the damage is halved. This sounds cool to me on paper, but ultimately winds up in more awkward shuffling of units in strange ways, due to the nature of needing units adjacent to each other to cast assist skills. All this annoying movement is compounded by the fact when a defeated enemy drops an item, you need to move a unit onto that space to pick it up. Yet again, where I want to place my units feels obnoxiously convoluted. I don't want to put units in bad spots to pick up an item and eat unnecessary hits, yet I also don't want to leave one unit alive at the end to spend a bunch of turns picking up scattered items.While you're doing the aforementioned inching-forward-fearfully, the units are likely casting mana barrier on one another--repeatedly, even when they already have it--which makes it so you REALLY need to crit (elemental weakness) otherwise you do half damage. Which puts so much emphasis on element type that you can be really restricted on what unit can attack which enemy. Add on curses, reaction skills, insta-kill places like bridges or cliffs, and it just feels over the top on the complexity. Someone described it as a puzzle game more than a tactical RPG, there seems to be a pretty particular way to do things, especially boss battles. The ways in which this game is difficult feel like they're wasting my time, rather than the winning strategy feeling gratifying, for me at least.If you really like difficulty and tons of mechanics and complexity, this could be great for you. This game does have a lot of cool stuff in it.I loved FFT, I loved Disgaea, I loved Banner Saga, I loved Fell Seal... I don't even *like* this game. I really wanted to. I don't enjoy fire emblem, so maybe I just don't like overly difficult tactical RPGs, I'm not sure. This is my 3rd of 4th attempt to sit down and give it a shot, and each time I've left disappointed and frustrated.
_childDocuments_.name: Fae Tactics

_childDocuments_.review: If Final Fantasy Tactics and Legend of Mana got together, had an unforgettable night of passion, and conceived a child, Fae Tactics would be that child.  Legend of Mana's art style, music, sidekicks, and elemental affinities inside of FFT's grid based strategy.  As a veteran of so many FFT inspired games, I'm thrilled I keep losing, because it makes you rethink everything.  Party, Summons, Scrolls.  In a universe where games offer you either no challenge(XCOM) or are designed to destroy you over and over (Othercide, The Last Spell), Fae Tactics lives in that beautiful place in between.  A rewarding challenge.Really makes you wonder what other PS1 era love children the world is missing.  A Valkyrie Profile with Spyro the Dragon's gameplay?  A Bushido Blade Vagrant Story?  A PaRappa the Rapper Parasite Eve?  So many possibilities!
_childDocuments_.name: Fae Tactics

_childDocuments_.review: Somehow this game compels me to 100% it. It's difficult to the point where it taunts me to get better and it also has some artistic style to it. The story and world-building is nice, but I didn't really like the ending. The characters grow through their special missions where you learn more about them and they get stronger, and will even talk with each other outside of combat.First the good, the game can be quite punishing. There's not much point in playing a strategy game if you aren't going to think, and this game will let you know when your strategy and preparation isn't on point. The game will give you all of the tools necessary to beat it. What's hit or miss about that is that the tools you need are in a different section of the game. The game was designed so that you would hop around story lines and regions, then you'd get something that would give you the power you need; this is probably not the game for people who like to make linear progression.But there are so many missteps that it can be hard to like it. The most obvious thing you'd notice after playing an hour is that battles take way longer than they should. Even when playing at 2x, the total time taken by the enemy every turn is at least half a minute, that's because every enemy has an assist skill and animation, and they will use it. This assist circle-jerking also has another problem, stat boosts stack infinitely. On one hand, this discourages turtling and encourages efficiency, on the other hand, it gets so bad that a fire monster will one shot a water leader despite me trying to rush to minimize their buffing.I think one of the absolute worst designs is the forced teammates. Being forced to use a teammate isn't bad, lots of story based strategy games do it, it's the missions that they're forced into. Almost every single time they force you to take someone, at least half of the map or even 100% of the map will have enemies that are strong against the forced teammate. Not only will they be a liability, they will be completely useless and do no damage. Then at the end of the mission, you get the weapon that would have given you the advantage in that scenario. Forcing me to carry sandbags so I can upgrade them sucks, they should be involved in their journey towards power.I'm still marking this game as recommended because I still like the game and the challenge, but I feel like these things should be addressed in future games.
_childDocuments_.name: Fae Tactics

_childDocuments_.review: Ehhh more of a neutral  recommendation. A lot of the game is original is cool, but boy are the parts that are bad, really bad.1) The boss fights take way too long, but they're not that difficult. Once you find your rotation and the right stuff to do, you have to repeat it way too often and lasts forever.2) There's a skill in this game called "Flux" that shouldn't exist. Have fun chasing things around after 1 hit, especially on maps with limited movement.3) The AI for NPCs is cancer. There are certain maps with objectives that NPCs also need to meet along with your units. I've had NPCs get stuck in AI loops with enemies more times than I'd like to admit and had to restart whole battles.Recommend for only true turn-based tactics lovers who don't mind the grind. Play at your own risk.
_childDocuments_.name: Fae Tactics

_childDocuments_.review: I had high hopes for this game that advertised customization, party building, and varied abilities.  Instead, I found a highly repetitive grind with palette-changed friends and foes that are slightly different from each other with the most basic of customization options available.  Min-max with these basic characters in order to get clobbered by completely unfair circumstance and highly inconsistent AI.Uncontrolled allies regularly switch between idiotic decisions to hyper-efficient team wipers with no warning as to who's going to pop off when.  Random chance is cool and all, but not when losses cost you both time and progress of what feels like entire battles spent tip-toeing on egg shells.  If your NPC ally decides to buff a character you're about to rely on, they override your current buff you were planning on taking advantage of.  If they attack an enemy that's next to your melee character, that means your melee character is forced to waste their super move they've been charging for the entire battle (couple this with a poor turn order allowing an enemy walking into range for this combo, and this behavior is completely unpreventable).  I binged this game hoping to find more depth the further I progress, because it definitely doesn't include all of it's "features" until you hit specific checkpoints.  Each of these features doesn't give you more fun things to do or options, just increased tedium.  You play mini games and craft items that promise you buffs, but are so negligible that you never feel them take effect.Oh, and bosses can get so buffed up even though they're your party's level that they kill every unit of yours in a single attack.  Which is really funny, because all they need to do is kill a SINGLE UNIT in order to end the battle in defeat and force a retry.  If you don't take the retry and feel the need to return to the map to grind more, you will lose all progress (hours of effort) you have made in the chain of battles up to that point.Oh, and additional enemies can be spawned randomly in any location with zero prior warning.  This both disrupts the incredibly important turn order and can catch your units completely off guard by an unlucky element match up.  My "favorites" are totems that protect every single enemy on the field that explode for AoE damage when destroyed.  I regret how long it took to find out all of these quirks, as there are many better modern SRPG's out there better worth your time and money.  Don't make my mistake.

_childDocuments_.review: My thoughts on the difficulty (specifically normal mode, not hard): I don't think it's as difficult as everyone else is making it out to be. However, if you're coming from other tactics RPGs and approach Fae Tactics with the same game plan (generally, find a working team composition and grind to make it stronger), you're going to have a hard time. At one point, I was fighting a particularly hard group of bosses with one enemy leader that would chain-lightning through several of my units, killing everyone almost instantly. After trying to brute-force the level several times and getting frustrated, I decided to spec everything out specifically to deal with this leader, while playing careful around the other enemies I was now weaker to. To my surprise, my new strategy worked brilliantly! Sometimes the best choice is to come back to a mission later once you've unlocked some other equipment/creatures/abilities, but sometimes you just need to try a different plan.When you find a few different methods that work for you, the game feels very fair and rewarding to play. While unlocking new abilities and creatures through grinding/progressing doesn't make you strictly stronger, it does expand your tactical possibilities and provides new creative ways to fight.Other thoughts:The game feels very fresh and refined; the controls are super clean, numbers are relatively small and easy to understand, combat elements are all impactful and noticeable. Status effects in particular are especially well implemented compared to most games, IMO. The pixel art is beautiful and very charming! However, the text font doesn't fit the aesthetic and character portraits feel pretty lifeless. Every part of actual combat is gorgeous, but menus and chats are not meeting the same standard.The story is nice so far, IMO; nothing remarkable, but it hasn't been detracting from the experience for me at all. Far from the worst Tactics RPG story you could imagine.Overall well worth my time and money already. It's been a while since I've had such a strong drive to play a tactics game like this!

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR for People who cant oncentrate on Text for 2 minutes:If I had to rate the Game, I'd give it a 9/10, 4/5 or 91/100. The Gameplay is fun and stays fun, the Characters are all very likeable and the Story/Worldbuilding is decent. Well spend 70 Hours of Game. Recommended from me.Here is the longer version:Fae Tactics is one of those Games that you never heard of that turn out to be criminally underrated when you actually do play it.I just finished it and I can wholeheartedly say that this were some very well spent 70 hours of Playtime. I almost fully completed the Thing too, but ultimately were too lazy to go for full 100 percent.The Mechanics of the Game are simple yet intriguing and even if you are not usually at home in Tactics RPGs, this will not make you feel like an Idiot. You can choose from 3 Main protagonists and 3 Monsters you find along the Way that can fit into the Battle you currently face. You need to think, but your Head doesn't need to hurt afterwards. Its very decently balanced and most, if not all of the Fights feel pretty darn fair and if you screwed up, you can usually pinpoint quite quickly when and why.Which brings us to the "screw up" part which has no repercussions. If you lose the mission, you can try again and its just that simple. Very nice cause its not frustrating you with going through like 8 different screens. It just says "retry" and badaboom baddabing, you're back in the Game.The UI is easy to understand and althought it feels very simple, there is depth to it that gradually comes to you. The choice of multiple Spells and Monsters you can collect feel rich and - although the "re-using skins with different attributes" is strong in this one - also rewarding cause they each bring something that feels like you wanna check it out.Sadly, once you adjust your Mind a few monsters are SO good that you don't necessarily need the others anymore. That is to say that Balancing is partially bad, yes but ALSO that you can make it a bit harder for yourself by playing around, cause the Game allows for you to do that. There are some difficulty spikes particularly around some later Bossfights but all in all those are Rare and still feel doable.One Mechanic I especially liked was how one Character could only ever be infected by one Status effect. If you overwrite it with a different one the old one is gone. So you can overwrite Blind, for example, with an Attack boost. Its a fun mechanic that adds actually alotta depth since there are some Statuseffects you can enter the Fight with, but can't as easily re-apply so you have to consider when and how to actually overwrite and such.The other one I enjoyed was how the Characters had an Ultra Attack that could be used as support or Offense Move using a special gauge you filled up during combat. As you are forced to either use the Ultra now and waste it or not attack at all, it makes you manage that Resource - but that never felt boring or annoying to do, and moreso something that you want to take best advantage of. Well executed IMO.I heard people complain you can't find some stuff without proper guides, but as I found every Weapon, almost every Spell and Monster and every optional Crewmember + did all the Optional Sidequests in the correct Order without guides: Id say the Game does a very decent Job at dropping Hints. But only if you dont just completely skip every dialogue.(But then play something else, the Story really is worth reading it.)Which brings us to the Beef. The Worldbuilding and Storytelling which is - Phenomenal would be too much - but definitely very, very good. The whole game Captures a vibe thats really intriguing and draws you in. With its Art direction, Music and Storytelling it feels coherent and does not overdeliver on what it is or something. You want to know more about the World, you actually LIKE to do those Sidequests, because there are cool things happening and interesting Characters to meet.Its a very likeable World all in all and I salute to the Writer behind it for really keeping me motivated. However, there are drawbacks ofc.The Story is - Fine. Really, thats not meant as an Insult, its fine like an actually good Story. There are Elements that made me lose my ♥♥♥♥ temporarily for how well written they were, and others just made me go "meh" on how it felt very generic. The Problem moreso lies in the Holes, which for me were easily spottable, sadly. HOWEVER - if you allow yourself to roll your eyes quickly and look past those, its quite unique in many aspects and very enjoyable. Peony is luckily not one of those annoying brats that just feel like they didnt understand how existing works. For some it may be a bit cheesy, but it has - good - Fantasy Novel aspects that I honestly would have clapped about when reading it.Big pluspoints for including different endings depending on the Things you did during the Sidequests and that Epiloque Bit at the end that made me smile.Play it and you know what I mean. Prolly makes you smile too. There is also a new Game plus to collect what you missed but... honestly, I think this is more of a onetime burner. Not really offers enough to justify a NG+. Feels like this was more of an "why not".All in all, I had a Blast with everything the Game gave me. Sure, some of the Plotholes could've been better, a few more "original" monsters instead of reskinning the existing ones with new attributes but at the end of the Day, this was a great experience that led me to the Credits with a smile on my face. And honestly, thats kinda why I play Games. So Kudos to the Devs. 9/10 from me. Would've been 10 if the NG+ would have followed the Idea introduced at the End.

_childDocuments_.review: A really beautiful game that is heavily weighed down by poor gameplay design decisions.Pros- Simple presentation with surprising amount of depth for the combat systems.- Interesting approach to reducing menu navigation in combat that mostly feels smooth.- Gorgeous artstyle with unique designs.- Substantial amount of content, whether it’s story missions, equipment choices, or variety of enemies/companions.- The flow of combat feels good, with gorgeous animations and punchy sound effects that add to a really satisfying feel when attacks hit.- Catchy soundtrack that fits the theme and mood of the game to a tee.- Distinct story setting that features a lot of surprisingly mature and dark themes.- Memorable characters that get decent character development. Cons- Limited choice once battles start. You are essentially limited to three essential actions for the most part – attacking, assisting allies with a buff or heal, and waiting (to activate a self-buff). Also while there are some workarounds, you are essentially unable to assist allies unless you’re right next to one of them.- Lots of gameplay kinks and irritations that add up, such as being unable to pick up items from the last slayed enemy and being forced to use your ultimate skill on low health enemies when your character happens to be part of a combo.- Maps and combat encounters seem to follow the design philosophy of making things as frustrating and annoying as possible for players. With lots of choke points blocked by traps, map-wide effects that reduce movement which just serves the purpose of prolonging battles, enemies starting off at high ground while being able to snipe at you, pits that enemies are able to shove you into leading to instant death, large expansive maps where enemies are randomly teleported to after being hit, flying enemies flying over pits and staying there out of reach from your melee units, so on and so forth.- Game uses a very basic form of enemy level scaling, where they scale to the highest levelled member of your party, making levelling almost feel pointless and even detrimental at times.- Boss monsters are heavily unbalanced. Almost all bosses are able to cause heavy damage and possibly one-shot your party members while having large health pools at the same time. Furthermore, bosses are able to cast spells and/or summon reinforcements as extra actions on top of their standard attacks. Many of them also have special abilities, such as getting buffed as the battle goes, laying traps all over the battlefield, or teleporting all over the battlefield just to list a few. Most of these battles feel like a slog, and there are almost no cases where you do not feel like you are at an overwhelming disadvantage.The game seems like it has a lot of potential, with really fantastic presentation that leaves a great first impression. However, the lack of finesse in handling the gameplay just kills a lot of enjoyment one would have had with it otherwise.

_childDocuments_.review: Fae Tactics is a turn based strategy game with a simple base, but complex set of interactions to keep it interesting and a strong story. To quickly summarize it all: the combat is exceptional with little reliance on raw stats, while the writing is charming and well paced. In other words, this game’s really good.At its most basic form, combat follows the systems of most turn based strategy games in a pretty standard way. You’ve got a party of characters, each with a bunch of stats and abilities to differentiate them. Damage is directly proportional to your attack stat while defense is a flat modifier in reducing damage taken. Statistics such as evade and accuracy are listed as percentages directly, and you’ll see the exact numbers in attack previews. Initiative determines when the character goes in the turn order, while various other numbers will describe how the character moves and how far they can attack from. Lastly is a typing system, which determines critical hits and resistances. Fire will always crit against earth, just as earth resists lighting. With these in mind, the numbers game is intuitive and easy to play. What makes the game special is how it transcends this basic gameplay with a number of novel systems.The combat of Fae Tactics has its systems set such that the player can always overcome enemies with vastly superior statistics through the use of force multipliers. The most common of these is the mana bar, which functions as a buffer to one’s health bar. The key difference is that damage dealt to characters with any mana at all is halved after calculation, allowing your comparatively frail characters to survive otherwise lethal blows. This on its own would be a curse due to the large mana pools of enemies, and as such it’s countered by critical hits. Critical hits aren’t random, and more importantly ignore any damage reduction caused by a mana barrier. As such, it’s a system you need to leverage. If you’re not paying attention, someone’s going to Ko’d by a critical and you’ll be on the back foot. Once you understand it, you can set up your units such that their health bars are never touched.That said, you don’t need a critical hit to overwhelm a mana barrier. While ranged characters can threaten massive areas from relative safety, melee characters can provide an immense amount of pressure for and/or against the player. Melee characters will always get an attack of opportunity on any enemy struck adjacent to them, meaning that being in the right place at the right time can score you the weight of several extra turns. This makes initiative and movement critical to maximizing your damage potential without directly increasing the numbers.Of course, the game gives you plenty of ways to influence the numbers. You can reach that fabled 100% evasion or have obscene amounts of attack or hp through the various buffing systems available. You can tear down mighty enemies by dragging their defense far into the negative. I personally tried too hard to prepare team wipes where I’d set up Peony to knock out most of the enemies in one massive attack. Of course, this can come at the cost of a good team composition. While you want to have the typing advantage for guaranteed criticals and resistances, each element has a few other properties associated with it, most notably an enchantment and curse. Units can only be influenced by one enchantment  one curse at a time, new statuses overriding the old. Enchantments can change stats vastly, such as haste nearly doubling movement, dance making units impossible to hit with projectiles, ice barrier negating criticals, and rage boosting attack by 40%. I, for one, can’t live without haste; so I’d always have a wind unit regardless of the enemy typing. To counter enchantments, you need only to apply a curse to override it. Curses and enchantments directly impact your ability to leverage other systems, and keep typing from being a battle of rock-paper-scissors.Units are differentiated by more than just their stats too. Every unit will have anywhere from four to a lot of different traits which define them further. Peony has standard movement, ranged attacks with direct fire, powers up on kill, crits on every third attack (because of the arcane element), can sometimes reflect ranged attacks, and gains the “chain” property for her next attack when passing a turn. This is distinctly different from an owl which has flight movement, melee attacks that hit the target and the tile behind them, and gains attack when passing a turn. The main thing is that different units don’t just have different numbers. Rather, they interact with the basic systems in unique ways.The combat’s not without its flaws, or rather, flaw. Notably, the game is slow to get started. Movement’s low since you don’t have haste and you don’t have all your cool abilities yet. Of course, that’s to teach you the systems, but it’s still slow. Further, the combat animations, while beautiful, are also rather slow. Fortunately, the options menu lets you double the speed to speed things along, though they’ll still make fights take quite a while longer even when they’re faster. Of course, the combat picks up once you finish the tutorial, and it stays good right up until the end credits. As for the animation speed, it’s fast enough, though it could stand to be faster. At the very least, the animations are nice to look at.Overall, the combat’s special in more ways than I can describe within the character limit of this review. That the game can do things like simulate a can pretty convincing boxing match is impressive to say the least. But I digress. The part that makes it neat is that the game gives the player a lot of tools to customize with and systems to leverage. To this end, the player wins because they were able to leverage the systems in place. Not because they were lucky, though luck helps. Not because they grinded for better stats. The game gives the player a fair challenge with consistent rules and asks if they’re clever enough to win with the tools available.Unlike games such as Fire Emblem, characters aren’t allowed to die in battle (though summons can) whether that means a temporary retreat or a game over. Worry not, there’s a great system there to ensure that death is fair, though there’s not enough space here to get into it. Anyhow, everyone has a role to play in the story and you can bet on there being missions exploring how each fits into the bigger picture. As that suggests, the story is fed to the player one segment at a time. During the introduction, you’ll only have one thread to pull on, but that one thread quickly leads to more and at any given time you may have upwards of seven or eight fragments of the story to follow. The story is a collection of short episodes that happen within the world, revealing glimpses of the connected tale as you see more.The world is well built and supports this story nicely. To this end, prior events and a handful of bad actors work to drive conflicts. As with the combat, there are a number of systems that work together to define the world and its operations. How mana works. Where fae come from, and how that can be a problem. History works to define the world’s present and influences its future. With such a world, problems exist between people with varying degrees of scale.It was impressive how much mileage they were able to get in using emoticons to display how characters were feeling. Throughout the game the characters go through a lot and you can see them react accordingly. There’s not much more to say other than that the writing is very good.Fae tactics is an exceptionally good tactics game with a great story. It’s got tons of systems working together to grant the player an immense amount of control over combat without making it inaccessible. The game is fair. Not easy. This game’s a good one and I’d recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: A massive disappointment! Been eagerly following this game, loved the art, and was interested in the team building. What I got was a few neat ideas wrapped up in great art but with terrible, terrible execution.First, combat is really tedious. Largely this is due to the assist system, where every unit has an assist ability they can use to buff others as well as a wait ability to buff themselves. The result of this is the combat is often filled with 2 or 3 enemies sitting in a corner granting each other more and more stacking shield buffs, when you finally get to them they each are sitting on 100+ extra shields you now have to chip through.Second, the "menuless" obsession resulted in the units having no real development or build choices. Every unit has one each of attack, assist, and wait actions, and Leader characters (main characters, those that aren't summoned) have an ultra ability (this charges up as they attack or take damage), the ultra ability is really just a slightly more powerful version of their attack or assist abilities and is used automatically when next you attempt to use those actions, you can't choose to save the ultra ability for later, you must use it. All of this means that your characters are pretty boring and don't improve or change.Third, this game wanted to be clear, and present everything without a menu but the game we got is insanely obscure. Abilities and stats are hidden behind weird names and never explained. I highly recommend you just google the terms. Seriously, what does assist power or team work mean?! The game has no interest in telling you what your basic stats mean.I can't believe how horrible this game is to play. Everything is so slow and drawn out. For example, you get this spell that grants a small bonus to attack to each of your allies. Using it results in a 4 second animation that has to play over the head of each, and every character. One by one, slowly going through them all. Another example is on hit effects, say you have defense breaker, bonus mb damage, and you steal buffs on attack. Each time you attack someone each effect has to play one after another, slowly animating out. Another example are all of those lush, gorgeous animations that the game wants you to STARE AT, you will spend a lot of time just watching enemies slowly faff about the battle field buffing each other. Much of this I blame on the horrible AI, to make the game harder they just had to add a bunch of enemies to each stage, but the result is that battles take ages as you have to watch them all wonder around the battle field one by one doing nothing.This is the most disappointing game I've played since Broken Age. Really depressing.

_childDocuments_.review: Well, my initial review was way too long to fit in Steam's character limit, so consider this an abridged version of my thoughts.: This will be a long review, because I genuinely think this game deserves better than what I currently see in the reviews. Ultimately, I found Fae Tactics to be a satisfying tactics game experience with a few flaws here and there that detracted from enjoyment, but not to the point where the game ever felt unfun. The more I played, the more I enjoyed the game. Its strengths lie in varied and fun map design and boss fights that force both proper pre-battle preparation and in-battle strategizing, while maintaining a fair yet challenging level of difficulty from beginning to end. Its weaknesses lie in a refusal to offer the player any glossary of terms or accessible tooltips that make learning the relatively simple mechanics more difficult than it should be. I want to be clear –  I thoroughly disagree with other reviews that peg the game as “frustratingly difficult”, and the devs have made some changes recently that address some of the complaints I have seen in other reviews (such as the “wet tissue paper” summons issue I have seen some complain about – though I didn’t really think that was an issue to begin with, I did end up liking the change for increased survivability on summons). The game isn’t easy for sure, but I believe it presents a fair challenge. Just don’t expect to stomp every encounter without thinking, and I would certainly advise new players to avoid playing hard mode on an initial playthrough.I’ll dive into what works and what doesn’t.::This is cut short due to Steam's review character limit. The game needs an in-game glossary to explain keywords/mechanics, emoticon faces occasionally intrude on emotional story moments, cutscenes are unskippable, main character is forced in every fight (which reduces player choice for leader units). None of these is game destroying, but they are certainly annoyances that the game could do without.Fae Tactics is a tactics game that excels in map design and fair but challenging difficulty. The story and music are passably decent, and it commits the sin of lacking explanation for things that can make the first 10 hours or so slightly annoying. I thoroughly disagree with the complaints I have seen that the game is “too difficult” or that friendly summons are “too weak”. I found normal challenging but fair. I almost never had to replay a map, and was able to make it through many boss fights without losing a single unit. Friendly summons don’t match the power of leader units, but they are invaluable for support and chip damage.I wish steam let me write a longer review, because I still have a lot more to say. If you have questions about the game, feel free to post a response here or message me.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm a huge fan of turn based tactics games, and I was so excited for Fae Tactics to come out. The art style is amazing, right on par with styles I love in the genre. While I'm a fan of titles like XCOM or Shadowrun, isometric dynamic terrain like Tactics Ogre or Final Fantasy Tactics are really my cup of tea and titles that fit that niche are hard to come by. Fae Tactics, however, I think still has some kinks to work out. There are so many interesting elements. The leveling system is an interesting take with the ability to constantly re-spec, the spell and summons systems contribute a facet that makes it feel like there are more puzzle elements which I like, but with all the interesting systems, it just doesn't land on a satisfying experience. There are far too many situations where a battle goes from potentially tactically interesting, to why are those enemies just hanging out over in the corner? To, alright, I'm on the home stretch, but suddenly all of my summons and party get KO'd in one round when five mobs take their turn in a row. Some battles enemy power/HP varies wildly, combat can go from turns of traveling across the map with low player movement, to sudden ambush of too many mobs, series battles will end in seemingly unwinnable final boss stages that sink hours of time and frustration and I just generally found myself realizing, I'm not having fun playing this. With the current balancing, Fae Tactics feels to me to struggle with normal-is-hard-mode syndrome. We've got such an interesting constantly changeable stats system, why no difficulty change setting? I'll keep checking in to see if the game play feel gets less frustrating as it gets further from launch, but for now it's a lot of interesting mechanics that don't add together to make a fun time.
