_childDocuments_.review: If you enjoy Final Fantasy Tactics and similar games, specially Final Fantasy Tactics Advance, it's a pretty good bet that you'll enjoy Fae Tactics as well. The unit building may seem shallow at first, doing away with the typical skills/equipment adopted in similar games in the genre, but eventually you unlock a big enough number of options for outfitting your Leaders, as well as selecting accompanying Fae to summon into battle, that the preparations screen be enjoyable by itself. You get a look at the battlefield before putting your team together, and checking on your opponents and building a counter team often feel like a puzzle.The storyline is quite different from your FFTs and Tactics Ogres, however, moving away from grand war stages, towards fairytale inspired monsters and races. It's all pretty whimsical, much like FFTA was at times, which can be hit or miss depending on the player. The setting is interesting enough, but the plot might be a bit too open-ended for it's own good. You can progress the plot missions in pretty much any order after the first set of missions, which is cool, as taking a different route changes the order of acquisition for the steady stream of unlockable units/weapons the game throws your way, but the narrative looses a bit of cohesion, and a lot of momentum. The characters in your party are pretty cool, tho, and Peony is a pretty adorable protagonist.My biggest gripe with the game was that the first few hours, before I had enough units or more varied weapons to make meaningful decisions, team-building choices felt very shallow, making the battles feel samey. This is definitely not the case, and different team combinations get very unique eventually, but it did make me almost drop the game.This is a big recommendation on my part! Will definitely keep an eye on Endlessfluff Games going forward =)
_childDocuments_.name: Fae Tactics

_childDocuments_.review: AT A GLANCE: 22% Would Recommend / PREVIEW: A lot of promise, but it's still not ready.I thought this title had potential after the demo, if it adjusted the difficulty some, but after 2.5 hours in it just decides to dawn a new coat of difficulty and start confusing you more than ever. It's never consistent and only starts its annoyances as you desperately run around the battlefield for resources only for some combo attacks to kill one of your leaders and, for some reason, you fail the entire mission. It just doesn't feel like the events were thought all the way through past the first 2.5 hours of play. Heck I'm trying to consider coming back to this title, but since any mission can either be an instant failure or just boringly easy: I feel like I should just spend my time elsewhere.
_childDocuments_.name: Fae Tactics

_childDocuments_.review: Great game!  I love that you can play this game tactically in several different ways.I love that the ui is streamlined. Easy access to respec, Press space to see info what element are strong or weak against. I also made good use of the high ground bonus.  Warning:  It can be a very challenging game. I have learned that if a boss fight seems impossible at first, it's because you have not found the right combination of gear,  summons, spells, or selected heroes. Some fights gets easier when you have unlocked new characters. I recommend you to unlock the secret characters. Best tip about this game:  hard boss fights is usually about lowering the boss defense.  My fav character for lowering defence was Payachin.
_childDocuments_.name: Fae Tactics

_childDocuments_.review: I liked one of this dev's other games, Valdis Story, a lot, and I wanted to like this game a lot too. It looks great, and there are fun mechanics and fun variety to the characters. The writing isn't very good, just like Valdis Story, but the characters are fun and charming. You mostly play for the gameplay, anyway.The main problems I have is that as you get further, the fights get longer, in a bad way. In a game like Final Fantasy Tactics, each mission is one map. One map that's designed carefully to present an interesting challenge. This game often throws 2-3 maps at you for one mission, and there are already a lot more missions than in Final Fantasy Tactics. The design of each map starts to feel indistinct and uninteresting.A big problem with the combat compounds the lack of interestingness in the fights: the elemental system. It has way, way too big of an impact on your success. As you unlock more summons and characters and you have more control over which elements you bring to fights, the "strategy" of the game is reduced to "bring the right counter elements, and make sure those guys attack the enemies that they counter". Having the elemental advantage makes enemies so little damage to you, and you do so much damage to them, that it outweighs every other consideration. There's not much thinking beyond "make sure you hit the right guy, and keep your guy out of range of an element that it's weak to".
_childDocuments_.name: Fae Tactics

_childDocuments_.review: Pros:- Art style is great- Good soundtrack- Animations are amazingCons:- Gameplay is extremely simple. There are no weapons, classes and abilities. The characters only have passive abilities, basic attacks and special cards which you can only choose 3 per battle.- All battles feel the exact same, there is never something new.- Most interesting battles there is an OP ally NPC unit who can oneshot (or almost) any enemy. Your job is just to survive, stay in the corner and wait for the NPC kill most of the enemies.
_childDocuments_.name: Fae Tactics

_childDocuments_.review: An amazing little gem of a game. The story and characters are both lovable in many ways, the art style of the game is stunning and the soundtracks are just absolutely wonderful!The combat system in this game is simple enough to be easily picked up yet complex enough to reward experience and skill, unit stats are very well balanced with the flow of the game and you are wholly responsible for how hard or easy the game is by your own choice in progression.While I think the Enchanting/curse category could use some improvements, the game itself is very very worth your money and time, there's no argument there.The only major issue I had with the game was the game's over reliance on you giving your own characters the "Haste" enchant, without the haste enchant you might as well cut the legs off all your characters and watch them squirm and try to drag themselves across glue on the floor because the default movement range on almost every character is nonexistent. What's that? You want to experiment with other enchants or just go your own way without having enchants on your units at all? WELL TOO BAD, HAVE HASTE OR DON'T PLAY :DLike, in the early stages that are very very small, having a movement range of 3 or 4 tiles is perfectly fine. But once you get anywhere beyond the first couple of stages, the stages start to be medium to large sized, and then you notice your characters only have a movement range of 2 tiles in a map that's fifty tiles across and you start to wonder where the hell did your parents go this wrong?In conclusion, the gameplay, graphics and sound design overall are absolutely bloody amazing, but the combat system's over reliance on haste enchants kind of ruins what could've been an astonishingly customizable and varying combat experience.
_childDocuments_.name: Fae Tactics

_childDocuments_.review: These endless FFT comparisons are driving me insane. It's been over 20 years since that game came out, and the genre is far, far larger than what tiny amount Square Enix has released. If anything, the game is far more like Luminous Arc in minute to minute gameplay. The game is not very much like Final Fantasy Tactics, and it's not trying to be. That's not a bad thing.This is a game that gives you an immense amount of tools right out of the gate, and expects you to actually make use of them. Your protectors aren't going to dull incoming damage to nothing like an MMO tank, your heavy hitters aren't going to be one-shotting everything left and right. You need to set up combos, utilize effects like chain and root to strike entrenched enemies and disable guards, and make use of the extraordinarily versatile units you're given. Once you get the hang of things, you'll be rip-and-tearing through enemy formations like butter.
_childDocuments_.name: Fae Tactics

_childDocuments_.review: This is a weird situation.The mechanics are fairly simple, you have elements strong/weak against each others (not in a traditionnal triangle but close enough), melee that can trigger "combo" attacks when an adjacent enemy is attacked by another unit, back attacks that bypass evasion and reaction, height advantage, all fairly common and basic mechanics.The health is a bit interesting, with 2 separate health bars (and a third for the "downed" leaders).Defeated enemies usually leave items on the ground (food that heals/buffs, crafting materials, sometimes scrolls).All in all it's not barebones but not exactly filled with complex mechanics either.There are no real classes, levels matter fairly little outside of unlocking special moves at level 5 and 10 (you gain stat points that you allocate but the stats themselves are boring), outside of a scroll you can equip to your 3 "leaders" and global bonus from crafting there are no equipments, you have a mini-game to gain a small boost between battes, but nothing exciting.It's not like you don't have to use strategy, pulling enemies to where you want them, setting up before engaging and quickly dispatching as many enemies as possible are pretty important, abusing combos, elements and back attacks (especially against bosses) is key to winning quickly and without losing units.It just lacks that "something more" to make it really great.At the same time it's only 20 euros, there is quite a bit of variety in the maps and enemies (most normal enemies can also be your own units to add to your 3 leaders) and it's still fairly solid at the core.As long as you don't expect final fantasy tactics (some of the basics are the same but it's not as deep with the classes, abilities or story) it can be a fun tactics rpg to play, but if you expected to find a successor to that graal of the genre, this is not what this game is.
_childDocuments_.name: Fae Tactics

_childDocuments_.review: A beautiful and compelling tactical RPG with great music. A lot of games have come along claiming to be the next FFT, but Fae Tactics is the only one that matches the quality of that classic while also being original in its art style and mechanics. Another coup from Endless Fluff -- I'll be paying close attention to anything they do in the future.
_childDocuments_.name: Fae Tactics

_childDocuments_.review: This game is really great. Fantastic art/music but the gameplay really shines.My Main gripe with srpgs is how painfully slow the gameplay is, final fantasy tactics, tactics ogre etc are all glacial in the pace of combat. Fae tactics really streamlines alot of those issues for a satisfying and well paced experience. the maps are pretty small so you dont waste multiple turns just marching slowly across a huge map filled with trash mobs.the characters builds can be changed on the fly and respeccing takes like 10 seconds, encouraging you to experiment and chance up your builds as opposed to sticking with that works because it would take like an hour to retool your team and it might not even be better. The combat is nice and fast paced, characters can only take 1-3 hits before going down so you wont be spending ages slowly chewing through trash mobs that cant fight back but require multiple turns to take down.Finally the mechanics are "easy to learn difficulty to master", so you can pick this up and play effectively very quickly. Its full of interesting tactical decisions while omitting pointless bloat in the form of multiple systems for energy/limits/soul power/anger etc etc.So yeah overall if you prefer faster style tactics games (think advance wars or fire emblem) and find "normal" SPRGS too slow (think disgaea, final fantasy tactics etc) check this one out.
_childDocuments_.name: Fae Tactics

_childDocuments_.review: There is a lot to love about this game and I highly recommend it. It deserves a much longer and thought out review than this but I don't want to stop playing long enough to write that yet and many other people have already done so.I primarily want to address the the complaints I saw most about this game which were the UX/UI and too many clicks to complete a turn &c.Click count specifically is a huge gripe I have with games and it will often be enough to completely prevent me from playing a game I might otherwise like. Fae Tactics does typically take about 4 clicks to complete a turn but after completing a battle or two I got into the rhythm I found that regardless of click count I can still cycle through turns fast enough that it doesn't really feel like a drag on the battle pacing almost at all, and certainly far less than other games with similar mechanics. On top of that, the 2x battle speed option is very well appreciated.As far as the UI, I do wish there were some tool tips on varies stats/abilities but after playing a while and experimenting you are able to learn a lot of what at first is a little vague.This game peppers in new and interesting mechanics within the first several hours so if you really "want to like this game" like so many of the negative reviews here say, I would recommend spending more than 15-30 minutes on it and see if your complaints aren't quickly forgotten like mine were.
_childDocuments_.name: Fae Tactics

_childDocuments_.review: This game is way better than it has any right to be.But be prepared to get through the first hour or so before it starts to really open up.PROSVariety - You can change up your spells, summons, party members and equipment.The game encourages this too so you never get stuck doing the same thing unless you really want to.There's also a lot of variation here, plenty of choice in each category even near the start of the game.Light hearted story without being obnoxious - If you like JRPG style stories (without the anime tropes) you will enjoy this.Easy to give orders - They've streamlined button input so that its really easy to give orders without having to go through menu's. Each units turn takes like 2-3 clicks max.Art and sound are both excellent. Attacks and spells sound punchy while the pixel art, animations and art direction all work together to create something unique but still immediately recognisable and really quite pretty.Attacks are also mercifully quick so it keeps things moving which is always nice. (you can even speed up animations in the menu)Maps are compact and don't outstay their welcome - Each one will take like 10-15 mins max meaning you are always making decent progress even if you only play an hour or so a day.SO-SOBoss' get super attacks that are often giant AOE attacks (Area of Effect), they also can get spells which are AOE's and when they both hit on the same turn it feels super rough.You can absolutely plan around this but it's easy to mess up. At worst it just means you retry the level or just lose a bit of XP. You can always grind it back though.You have to learn a pokemon style "A-type" beats "B-type", "B-type" beats "C-type" etc elemental strengths and weakness' table that is a bit of a pain really.Party size is a little limiting - Not actually a bad thing though, it just means every move is more important and you will have to make tough choice about who you bring.CONSNot a good intro - Honestly takes about an ~hour before you get to a point where everything starts to come together.This is because the first hour is essentially a tutorial and until you unlock everything it can feel extremely simplistic. (even though it really isn't) That being said, It's not a bad time but it does give the wrong impression for sure.Can't rotate the map - While 95% of the time this isn't an issue, occasionally it means you can't quite see things right.It never got to the point of being frustrating.You don't pick up items after battle - if it's still on the floor it's lost forever. Not happy about this really.**Advice: Equip the "Phantom Hand" spell,  it's extremely useful, it can open chests and it will save you many wasted turns trying to pick up items.Overall I'd say a quality streamlined take on turn based tactics.Yet despite that you don't feel any loss of complexity and offers it a unique spin of it's own.
_childDocuments_.name: Fae Tactics

_childDocuments_.review: Although I recommend this game, It's kinda hard to wholeheartedly do it. It almost scratched my Fire Emblem/tactic itch, but not quite what I was looking for
_childDocuments_.name: Fae Tactics

_childDocuments_.review: This is a master class strategy RPG that proves that a billion stats and skills aren't required to make a good game. In this game you have variety, and in that variety its where you truly feel the game. There are two dozen spirits, each of which have a varient. Each of these spirits have their own stats and their own combination of abilities. As the game progresses you eventually get to use each of these spirits or otherwise encounter them. Alongside your entirely unique party, each with their own ultimate attack,  ultimate assist, regular assist, regular attack, wait skill, EX-attack and even 2 extra unlockable weapons, you have the ability to pick and choose for your battles WHAT you want to do. That is what this game is all about. Its more like chess than anything else, except where you can see the enemy's pieces before you even choose yours. Did I mention that who you bring to certain battles, or how you play those battles has an effect on the story? There are two secret party members who both require you to pay attention to the story in order to get them. There are entire storylines that require you to not kill or not let certain NPCs to die to do them.This game is amazing and while the initial sheen may wear off and it might not be what you wanted (A super in depth strategy RPG), give it your time. Its well worth it.
_childDocuments_.name: Fae Tactics

_childDocuments_.review: I really REALLY REALLY wanted to like it but just.. I can't. WAY too many one-shots. Way too many extremely annoying, arbitrary mechanics.This is one of those "tactical" games that, at the end of the day, is far more a puzzle game. It's less about decisions and more about rebalancing your team for every fight to min-max all the fiddly Rock-Paper-Scissor type rules and such very arbitrarily. It's not that it's "hard", it's that you will just be one-shot constantly with absolutely no recourse. Or you fight a boss who summons towers that buff her that never wear off and teleport ANYWHERE ON THE MAP when you hit them even once. Maps are a good 30x30, and most units more 3 spaces or so. It's really just tedious and not fun.And it sucks because I see a lot of really neat ideas. Beautiful pixel art, lovely music, some decent ideas, but it's buried under maps that are setup far more like a puzzle than a tactical game. Heals and such have no cost so you one-shot a foe or they just get healed to full instantly, over and over. Any unit can heal a boss when they're down, no delay, no way to interrupt. It's satisfying when you can line up several melee characters or whatnot and chain a combo or something but.. that was the only part that was satisfying and you're wildly outnumbered map after map loaded with one-block-wide paths that one enemy blocks while flying and ranged units attack you freely, it's just.. needlessly heavy handed in a way that makes you constantly shuffle your team and rely on one-dimensional strategies rather than good decision making.

_childDocuments_.review: Really want to recommend this game, but there are so many little annoyances that I'm not sure I'll be going back.  -Basically everything is controlled by the mouse.  No hotkeys, no shortcuts, and nowhere to rebind anything.  -To add to the above problem, there is entirely too much clicking required to get anything done.  There's a confirm screen for every action, and you need to be constantly clicking the mouse to do basically anything.  For example the cutscenes are really long and there's no way to skip them, and the game requires you to click to advance every piece of dialog, even when that piece of dialog is just an emoji floating above the players' head.  -The player is kept in the dark about everything.  There are no hover-over tooltips for anything, and finding out what something like "Teamwork" does can be pretty esoteric.  I'm three hours into the game and I have no clue where to find my characters' reaction abilities.-So far, I see a lot of the combats I am in turning into dogpiles with the goal of just bursting down their units one by one.  I'm really not a fan of games where it's possible and even common for one of your members to get one-shot by an enemy.  It dumbs the strategy element down tremendously when things can be resolved so quickly.  -You can't place your units at the beginning of the battle.  They just start in some random formation, so you have no input in regards to how that critical first turn plays out.  -You can move and then perform an action, but I can't perform an action and then move?-Enemy evade is way too high.  I'm normally a pretty chill dude, but this game had me saying "SERIOUSLY?" out loud a lot when my dudes would constantly miss 80% shots.  It has a lot of redeeming qualities, but I'm getting a little miffed dealing with these trifles, they make the game less fun overall.  The core gameplay is great, and the whole thing where each unit has 3 things they can do is a really fresh take on streamlining the otherwise bloated nature of the genre.  If you play a lot of games like this (turn based grid based squad rpgs) you will probably get a few good hours out of it.
_childDocuments_.name: Fae Tactics

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of those situations where I would rather have a 'neutral' recommendation rating. I'll make it short and sweet (the opposite of what the game does).This game is quite fun - you have many options to build teams, and the story is interesting. Look to the many positive reviews to learn more, I agree with them.What leans me towards not recommending it however is that everything takes forever and you only get a 2x speedup to the battles. Every animation takes multiple seconds, then the character stops in place for a second or so, then it moves on. This is amplified by anything that hits multiple units - it goes through it for every unit. This makes battles take double to triple the time they should. So while I recommend this game for the gameplay (look to all the positive reviews, they are spot on), most battles felt mind numbing from all the needless waiting.

_childDocuments_.review: 5/10OK, what this is NOT: final fantasy tactics, tactics ogre, fire emblem, xcom, disgaea, advanced wars, yggdra union.What this IS: a banner saga like with cute monsters/pokemon, kinda remenbers me gungnir (from atlus), but less interestingWhat i really liked- graphics and look of characters- certain level of strategy, every character have its uses- monster that you dont use level up toowhat i didnt like- history is beyond boring: a girl looking for her mother for no specific reason, helping every person (risking her life) that she enconters for no reason/reward,- no equip, itens, no money, no skills besides the default ones and almost no customization of characters, you just get many diferent ones but they dont learn new things and the craft sistem just give you passive habilities though the game- no important/interesting characters besides the main one- history is pretty bad (it may become better in some point but im playing this for some time and i just lose my interest)- no reason to grind (which may be attractive for some players)- ok battle system but nothing awesome/different.- no rewarding feeling (since you wont gain rare itens/skills)after 5 hours i will stop playing it because it is boring, no motivation to keep going for all the mencioned reasons above, Buy it if you like banner saga and cute little monsters, dont buy it otherwise.

_childDocuments_.review: Is good.The gameplay starts simple and gradually tacks on complexity and depth. The story is basic, but has its deep moments. The mood seems cute and often slaps you with dark tones of despair and death, making you think about your actions (granted you care).Tactics wise, there are many different characters, summons, spells and loadouts to choose from and approach the situation with. Provides many hours of enjoyment. My only personal gripe with it is that I wish it can run faster. The seconds add up and I don't like having my time wasted.Overall its a good game. Its worth the full price tag. Lots of content. Has replayability.

_childDocuments_.review: I can best sum up this game as a modern synthesis of many classic JRPGs; Its got the team building of Brigandine, the monster collecting of Pokemon and the co-op attacks of Disgaea, laid out in the isometric style of FF Tactics. This is all wrapped up in an adorable art style that reminds me of Legend of Mana which sets it apart from, speaking candidly, most Indie-RPGs that are just flat out ugly to look at.Veterans will know what to expect but notably it introduces an innovative mechanic to the genre's action economy in that there is no such thing as a wasted turn. Beyond direct consideration of hammering your opponent's face, players have to consider that ALL units have Assists (buffs which can be applied to allies) and can even gain buffs just by using the Wait button, over and above being able execute combo attacks and Reaction abilities just by standing in the right place. It adds a nice layer of depth that rewards long term planning during a battle in contrast to the genre's typical emphasis on pre-battle unit customization (which is also present in this game though not to the same complexity as FF Tactics). The story is also quite engaging; The Save the World plot acts as vehicle to carry the well-written personal story arcs of the seven main characters while the three side characters add some levity to the game. The World-building also deserves special mention since its able to weave a compelling post-apocalyptic magical setting with a strong internal mythology that references the studio's first two games without bogging you down in walls of text and in-game exposition. The only flaw I can see in this game is New Game+; The game is initially capped at Level 60 but the underlying mechanics are already somewhat unstable given its propensity for recursive buffing and further uncapping the stats leads to some truly oppressive boss fights that can last upwards of an hour since their defenses could grow to a point where they effectively take zero damage from all attacks.Also there is an unresolved bug that prevents a certain collectible monster from spawning during its appointed encounter. Its not game breaking and getting it is not necessary to complete the game's achievement but it is somewhat irritating. I bought this game on sale while waiting for Evil Genius 2 I would heartily recommend it to anyone yearning for the good old days of pre-Gacha waifu harem JRPGs.
_childDocuments_.name: Fae Tactics

_childDocuments_.review: I previously reviewed this game with a thumbs-down, citing the ridiculous hitpoint bloat of some bosses and numerous fights that feel like they were never once playtested.Sure enough, those fights were fixed or patched to be less unfair, which at least shows that the devs care enough to do so.There is a lot to like about this game. It has a lot of charm with its sprite graphics, an excellent elemental rock-paper-scissors system that encourages but does not mandate choosing a counter-element, and the story line is... there, I guess.Character customization is limited but meaningful, even summons can be customized to some extent by changing the main character's equipped item. Gold star there.The game could really benefit from some sort of reference or glossary to unintuitive mechanics. As-is you just have to trial-and-error them. For example cannon range works differently than the range of any other unit. The diagonals are 'free', meaning that range 4 can actually be up to 7 spaces away. This isn't the only item, and while the game does a generally good job of introducing you to new mechanics, there are some that just make you shrug, facepalm, or otherwise shake your head.Another example is that there is a soft 20-turn time limit on every match before enemies start repeatedly receiving buffs. The time limit isn't much of a problem for the vast majority of missions, but it's never mentioned anywhere and can be annoying during some boss fights.There are many fights where you must babysit AI-controlled allies, which is mostly fine until the game starts ramping up the difficulty and you have to rely on them in any way shape or form. I played on hard mode due to extensive past experience with these types of games (note: you can't change your mind after choosing without starting a new game) and the escort situation has made some missions less than fun. Still, not back-breaking so far. There is a mechanic where a downed leader (i.e. anyone who isn't a summon) can be helped back up before they die for good, which is nice. But if they die over water or empty air or other terrain where they can't be 'downed' then they die instantly. Some maps are quite heavy on those sorts of terrain, and the AI never gives consideration to that terrain.But the best part of the game is the mechanical design. Each element counters and is countered by one or two other elements, except water which has 3 extremely common weaknesses and sucks. But that still leaves like 9 other interesting elements. This counter mechanic takes the form of critical damage. Unlike in other RPGs where crits are random, in this one you do critical damage to elements weak to yours. My best guess is that it amounts to about 50% more damage. BUT! Some units also have shields, and non-critical damage does half to shields. The brilliance of this is that there are other ways to do critical damage, such as the main character's ability to do critical damage regardless of typing on every 3rd attack. This means that you aren't hard-locked into only ever picking units to fight with who are super-effective against the ones that you're fighting. You only need to break through their shields with crits, and you can do that in more ways than just using their vulnerable element. So if you take a liking to a particular summon, you can bring them along with you anywhere even if they're at a type disadvantage as long as you play smart.This combined with an excellent initiative/speed system and the beautiful and *extreme* simplicity of how the game handles combat commands without ever sacrificing depth of strategy makes the basic game mechanics of the game the best part by far.But, there are still some other issues.There are limit-break type moves which replace your other actions, which I'm not terribly fond of. You gain charges by attacking and also by being attacked, and managing these super moves becomes over-centralizing in my opinion. Worse is that, with tough single boss enemies, you get punished for trying to kill them which really limits your tactical options against them in an unfun way.But I think the biggest flaw of the game is simply that the AI isn't very smart in general. If you compare it to FFT, the gold standard of the genre and a game that came out 23 years ago, the AI is far less clever even though the game mechanics are much simpler by comparison.I think the bad AI is also what necessitated so many of the game's poorer design choices. A turn limit to prevent stalling out the short aggro ranges, a massive numbers advantage for the enemy in every single fight past the first few, and a gotcha super move mechanic that at times can make combat feel like a lifeless puzzle rather than a strategic and adversarial experience.All things considered, it's a good game and you'll probably like it at least a little if you enjoy the genre. But I can't help but feel disappointed, because it could have been a fantastic game.
_childDocuments_.name: Fae Tactics

_childDocuments_.review: Fae Tactics is a great turn-based tactical game. It might not be as intense as Into the Breach, nor as minimalist as Bad North, but its bright, colorful environments, strong story with likable and interesting characters, wonderful music, and well-designed encounters give Fae Tactics a unique brand of charm otherwise lacking from its alternatives.Let’s start with the gameplay. The core gameplay loop is quite simple in theory, but the game’s mechanical systems allow for a lot of variety in how you approach the encounter. Each day, you can take an action at a specific location, which then either triggers a cutscene that advances the story or an isometric, turn-based combat sequence that will also advance the story. You can also free battle to farm resources to upgrade your Talisman and collect more summons if necessary. Each encounter will spawn a board and various enemies of various types. Yes, this game has an elemental typing system which is complex. Each type has specific weaknesses and strengths and a unique assist ability you can use on your units to enchant them. Some of these are not made equal. Because turn order allows you to potentially strike before taking damage, and movement is necessary to get into range to do the damage (and units are generally painfully and pitifully slow), haste is a god-tier buff. Likewise, each unit in the game has a special “wait” ability, which, for leader units (main characters or enemy commanders), can vary based on weapon equipped. For example, the main character, Peony, can “wait” (neither assist nor attack, usually a default action that will occur when positioning) to buff her next attack with Chain, which will hit all enemies in range, when equipped with her default item. When she equips her ice spear (her best weapon btw), her wait skill is reflex, which makes her reactions more likely. In this case, her reaction hits the 4 tiles touching hers (no diagonals) with an ice move that has a high potential to freeze the enemy and gives her a permanent +7 defense. Each party character has 3 weapons that can be unlocked, giving them different typing, wait abilities, assist abilities, and reactions. There are also a number of gems that can be unlocked, that give your characters additional buffs or effects. For example, my personal favorite was to equip Ice Spear Peony with the Stigandir scroll (+3 movement, +1 initiative; guaranteed first move + 6 tiles) with the gem that gives you blink movement. This essentially turned my Ice Spear Peony into a teleporting flanker I could use to easily reach the middle of a group of enemies with her Ultra move primed and detonate the equivalent of a nuke in the middle of the enemies. Each character has a place on your team, made especially pertinent based on what encounter you’re dealing with. You really are rewarded by thinking through the strengths and weaknesses of your characters and combining their plethora of skills and abilities into a team that is ideally suited to that encounter. Change your party, their equipment, and even their gems around as needed. Hell, you can respec your skill points at will, so if you’re getting rolled you can even make characters tankier for that one fight at the cost of some damage.The talisman is yet another layer of mechanics which empower you to think about the best composition, although slightly more limited due to balancing. The talisman has 2 things it gives you: spells and summons. Spells are relatively simple: you can activate one per round at any time one of your units has their turn as a bonus action; although the spells originate from Peony, it does not need to be her turn to cast them. For normal encounters, I recommend the kiss spell, as it is a fairly powerful heal every 2 turns, the hand spell, as it lets you collect items on the map without having to end your turn on them, and silence, which does damage in a 5 tile radius around Peony and has a chance to silence, which prevents enemy leaders from using their own spells and removing their MB shield regardless of how much they have. The other spells are way more situational, but can occasionally find use (entomb, for example, is strong against teleporting phylacteries).Summons are enemy units that you’ve defeated and gained the ability to summon by picking up their respective business card that they drop after defeat. You can’t gain the ability to summon all the non-leader enemies you confront, but you can gain the ability to summon most. Like with spells however, not all are created equal. The Bone Servant  (and coincidentally one of the most annoying enemies to deal with). This is because his passive makes him take 80% less damage from any attack that is not a back attack and his wait ability lets him protect all allies that are 3 or 4 tiles around him. In the vast majority of encounters, I ran 2 wind summons + Bone Servant for haste buffs and protection. Fights where this combo was not viable required somewhat more thought and planning. Most of the story unfolds in “cutscenes” where the characters talk to each other. I find these broadly well-written (barring some minor grammatical errors like a period instead of a question mark) and the characters have distinct and interesting personalities. Some of the dialogue can be a little cringy, but remember: Peony is a 15 year old girl. Cringy dialogue is per the norm for that age in real life, so I think it adds to the character. Also species/worldbuilding designs and artwork are peak. Very creative and the sprites are awesome.The world itself has a lot of intrigue and mystique. You do learn a lot about the game through expository dialogue, but it was always properly contextualized; characters weren’t talking about the mechanics of magic for no reason, but they would explain elements of the cultures and the world’s history when other characters asked. Because the characters come from such diverse parts of the in-game world, this sort of cross-pollination of cultural knowledge and exchange makes sense, and is probably how society should conceptualize and approach diversity in real life. I’m not going to even spoil it, but the end twist was really ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ good. In retrospect, it was foreshadowed very well, but I was not expecting it at all. Likewise, while you don’t start with a good grasp of why you’re doing what you’re doing, you come to learn in time. This game is not 5/5 mainly because combat is . Enemies take forever to do their turns, and there are a lot of them. Please do yourself a favor and turn combat speed to x2. Why there isn’t a speed even faster than that, I don’t know — one should be added (at least for enemies taking their turns). This is the largest factor holding me back from NG+, and is something I’m sure has filtered a fair number of people. Slow combat is great at the beginning for appreciating the art, visuals, animations, sounds, but by the 20th hour I just want to execute my strategy quickly (x4 speed quickly).Finally, I’d be remiss to not comment on the music. Beautiful, quirky, full of character and charm, and very effective at communicating the characters’ emotions. The ominous “♥♥♥♥ is about to go down” theme is perfect for setting the mood. Likewise, I found the emojis in this game to be charming and perfect for effectively communicating the tone a character would be speaking in. Where Coromon’s emojis felt sappy and cartoonish, these actually tell you what emotions the characters are experiencing and contextualize how the dialogue should sound. Highly recommended. One of the better tactical games out there for its sheer depth.
_childDocuments_.name: Fae Tactics

_childDocuments_.review: After recovering from a mild Into The Breach addiction, I started craving a little more depth when building a team in my next tactical RPG. Fae Tactics fed me exactly the kind of experience I was craving. Tailoring your crew from stats to minions had me test driving play styles I'd prefer to avoid in other tactical RPGs. When I had my ass handed to me by bosses looking like Satan's seahorse, I never felt cheated. I knew I failed due to my choice of team comp and build decisions. Awesome game, worth every penny. What are you waiting for, help this little girl destroy the world!
_childDocuments_.name: Fae Tactics

_childDocuments_.review: Update: Have finished the game. My review and recommendation still stands for those who like tactical RPGs and don't demand that they all have FFT/TO level of complexity. It's a quality game if you're willing to accept that.While not the most complex tactical RPG out there, I am having fun with the game. I've not been bored with it even with it's simpler systems and mechanics. Some may not like the assist system, but I think it's one of it's more interesting quirks. It gives the units something to do if they can't attack and adds a utility consideration to which units to add to your summon list. The same is true for the wait skills - sometimes it's better to wait to activate the skill, such as Peony's Chain ability. Spending a turn so she can hit any enemies within a certain range of her target can be worthwile...and maybe risky depending on the situation.The menuless system works pretty well, though that's in part due to the simpler nature of the game. A complex game like Final Fantasy Tactics couldn't work menuless. That said, it does it's job and makes controlling the battle smooth once you get used to it. The one quibble is that it's not clear (or I missed it) on how to NOT use your ultimate when your unit is ready to use it. A "one click for basic attack, double click or shift-click for ultimate" would have been nice. Combos are possible when melee units and ranged units work together on an enemy. This also works with Peony's Chain skill. So, if you have a melee unit near three targets and Peony with her Chain active hits all three, the melee unit will chase all three hits. This works for as many melee units are near a target, allowing damage to pile up quickly...both for and against you. I always love combo mechanics in RPGs, especially tactical RPGs. Seeing actual teamwork "simultaneously" and not just each character choosing same target on their turn is refreshing.The spell casting is done by Peony (and enemy leaders) and her spell list is set by choosing three spells for her to take into the battle. Spells have different cooldowns and can be used any time during your phase, but only once per phase. They also have cooldowns and start in cooldown mode. Enemies leaders follow these rules as well, even if there's more than one. There's no equipment in the traditional sense. Each main character (leader, in game's terms) can equip a talisman that provides a certain bonus to themselves and/or the team. Talismans can be found in treasure boxes as well as from killing enemies. This is also how Peony's spell choices increase. Foes may drop a spell scroll, and, in the case of an enemy leader, it's often one of the spells they were using against you. In addition to talismans and spells - food items and enemy cards can drop. Enemy cards are how you add to your roster of potential summons.I especially like the food items. Some can provide a shield (magic barrier) that absorbs damage. Some raise HP. Some give attack, and so on. They can put in some unexpected change in the battlefield. Initially, I kind of missed equipment - probably because I'm used to seeing it basically everywhere else. And talismans don't "replace" the choosing of a full load of items - more like the accessory slot, but, like accessory slots, they can make a difference and do provide some changing up your team based on your tactics and summons.Stat progression occurs using a trait points system. You get a point to allocate each level and you can change them as you wish between battles. There's no job classes or such, this seems to be the proxy for it as you can "create a job archetype" in some sense. A "warrior" could max out on attack with some HP while a pure tank could go HP and perhaps some special, depending on their reaction ability. Some will find this over-simplified, but I thought it did what it needed to and being able the change at will is a nice (and essential, given that there are no jobs/classes to change) touch.The problem...it's leaders only. That's a mistake. Recruited creatures (remember the enemy cards?) can't get trait points. This makes the system not just more simple...it makes it too limited. This is easily one of the biggest gripes I have with the game. I hope there's a future update that allows non-leader units to access the trait points or some system where they can be "attached" to a leader to inherit their traits...something to give them more progression and some customizing.The camping minigame is...something. Matching against the clock is a different way to approach a cooking mechanic, though I'm not sure how much I enjoy it. On one hand, it does beat grinding for the ingredients, but then that could be time (and more incentive) to explore free battles and maybe find more creatures, including those that don't show up in the mainline story battles. Granted, I'm probably still early in the game, but that's why I'm of mixed mind about the not having to search for ingredients.Crafting is where hunting down materials comes in as well as bonuses for winning battles without losing any units. Crafting lets Peony create items that have persistent effects. There doesn't seem to be too many of them, and if that's the case, that's a bit of a missed opportunity. This system could have at least replaced "traditional" items especially if it had some limitations (some items may be always-on and active but others that provide unit boosts - pick/build two for next fight).The art style is colorful and enjoyable. The graphics have been clear on what's happening and generally on the interesting side, and the sprites are nicely designed. The music is very good as well, doesn't get annoying, and have some variations.The game has been very stable for me to this point. Haven't encountered any crashes or other technical issues so far.Overall, at least at this point in time, I'm recommending this game if you're willing to try a different, more simple take on the tactical RPG genre. It's not nearly as complex and in-depth as some of the classics in the genre, but the price is reasonable and it is enjoyable.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is real nice, I enjoyed every bit of it, down to the quirky comments, the gameplay to the music.My only nitpick with the game is that you can't make it go faster than x2.The game desperately needs a x4/x8 or "skip animations completely". _childDocuments_.review: It's good! Right off the bat, do not go into this game thinking it's FF Tactics or Fell Seal. It's a tactics RPG, but doesn't actually share much in common with either of those. So long as you recognize that, and go in ready to learn this game's unique take on the genre, you're in for a real delight!I played the Demo for this a bit ago during that whole Demo extravaganza Steam put on, and of the many, many Demos I played during that time, Fae Tactics stood out as one of the best. Exciting gameplay, engaging story, and a charming aesthetic. It really has it all.The basics of the combat are as follows: each of your units has three types of moves, one that targets enemies, one that targets allies, and one that targets themselves. It's extremely intuitive, simplistic, but in a good way. For the most part, targeting enemies is an attack that deals damage, but targeting allies can have a wide range of effects, from healing to buffing. Self-targeted skills also have a wide variety of things they can do. After that, units also have different passive skills that change how they interact with other units. For example, one of the main party members, your dog Chico, has a reaction attack that triggers if an enemy adjacent to him is attacked. So if you place Chico next to an enemy, you can create a series of chain attacks for bonus damage. It's all delightfully well done, and leads to some truly thrilling moments when you can line up multiple allies with reaction attacks together to create some incredible combos!There's a lot more nuance to the game - like traits that can be leveled up and reassigned at will, summoned partners, and magic spells - but all of it is explained well in the main game. Bottom line, if you like tactics RPG's, this one is worth your time!

_childDocuments_.review: Half a decade ago, Endlessfluff Games made one of my favorite game ever, a metroidvania called Valdis Story : Abyssal City. This game offered :- an emphasis on tight and sometimes unforgiving gameplay (where Hard mode really means Hard, and Normal doesn't mean Easy)- numerous mechanics that, while sometimes not very well explained, offered some real depth to your strategies (huge shoutout to the community for sharing experimentation and knowledge about the game)- a stellar artistic direction well-served by beautiful animations, but menus that lack in the ergonomics department- a simple yet compelling story with a good balance between darker themes and an heroic feeling- and the only thing not made by the two devs themselves, a beautiful soundtrack (Zack Parrish for Valdis Story, and Sam English for Fae Tactics, two very, very talented people)If I insist on what made Valdis Story's identity, it's because each one of these elements is present in Fae Tactics, and very much like its predecessor, it's not a game for everyone. Probably the biggest criticism that can be made is the fact that this game has quite a few missables, and I'm not only talking about collectables, which there are a lot, between Summons (ally units that you get from drops), Spells (powerful battlefield-wide effect with X turns cooldowns), and Scrolls (passive abilities you can equip on your Leader units), elements that give a real "pokemon" vibe to the game, but about weapons or even characters that you can miss if you don't do the correct actions at the correct time.But is it necessary a negative? If you like to experiment and discover, or even share knowledge with other players, I think you'll have a good time. If you want to just sit and play, and don't like repetition and sometimes failure, then maybe not so much. In the end, I was managing my expectations about this game, because too often had I been disappointed when riding the hype train. However, I'm pleased to say that Endlessfluff Games made me once again fall in love with one of their games.
_childDocuments_.name: Fae Tactics

_childDocuments_.review: Very fun tactical rpg. Despite some reviews I read about the game online, this game does not have a hard time limit to complete and missions do not disappear if left for later. There's one event that's timed in regards to unlocking a character but it's very clearly displayed as such.If you're going for a completionist run, try not to miss any chests in story missions. While there are ways to grab certain spells from enemy leaders, not all spells can be obtained that way. So take a good look of the whole map before completing it.I would recommend this game to anyone who enjoys tactics games.
_childDocuments_.name: Fae Tactics

_childDocuments_.review: This game is really, really good. But here's what this game isn't : Final Fantasy Tactics. If that's you're expectation, you might be in the wrong place. There are many ways to make a good jrpg-styled strategy RPG and this is one of them. Music is top notch, pixel art and animations are excellent. Portraits could use diversity but that's the smallest of gripes.The gameplay is very straightforward and somewhat open ended as the game allows you to play some mission in the order you want. Your success revolves around planning fights properly using the right party. The game has a pretty complex setup of elemental strengths and weaknesses that takes a bit of learning and your units have a ton of different passive abilities that influence they ability to function properly. The game could definitely give the player better access to information about what some stats do; that would be my biggest issue with the core gameplay aspects. Everything else is really solid. The pace is fast, the story is interesting even if the writing is a tad sloppy at times. I'm really enjoying my time with Fae Tactics and would recommend it to anyone who likes Japanese JRPGs that aren't just FFT.
_childDocuments_.name: Fae Tactics

_childDocuments_.review: I want to write a good review for this game, but there are just so many frustrating mechanics, that while at it's core is a decent tactical game, is fundamentally stressful in nature.Primary issues:- Collectable items & scrolls appear as drops from enemies, however if you don't nab them before the end of the battle, they are gone forever. Ex. You just downed an enemy, and it drops an item you're looking for. One of your reaction skills kills the last leader, and the battle immediately ends giving you not time to pick it up- Win conditions on missions where you encounter allys require you to protect them, even if they are blindly running low health into a pack of enemies, completely ruining the ability to play the game with tactics. Who cares if you have protection and healing, the AI doesn't care, it wants to ruin your mission.- Level curves for fights are ???? I'm not sure if it's based on your units, or your highest unit, but the way leveling works in the game, fae and leaders with protector level up way faster than everything else giving your team an incredibly skewed level curve, putting you at a disadvantage against enemies- Level designs purposefully attempt to overwhelm you with enemies, typically that are higher level than you, but just have generally bad AI- All enemy leaders have cards, but only your one leader has cardsThat's most of what I can think of off the top of my head. I'm probably going to keep playing, but mostly because i feel invested now, and i'll work around the bad AI. Some of the pros of the game:- Writing is campy- Interesting elemental system, with main character being able to easily transition between elements- Other leaders have items that allow them to switch out how they work mechanically as well as their elements- Summoning system is mostly fine, allowing you to pick a wide variety of units- Leaders also feel individually powerfulAnd some mixed elements:- The crafting system I have mixed feelings about. It feels like it's supposed to replace a basebuilding-like element that gives you permanent buffs. However as my first gripe described, getting these items is a chore, since you'll need to scour battlefields mid-battle to pick these items up, wasting precious movement and turns.- There's notes about how if you wait to long quests will change or disappear. I can see why they would want you to not grind everything up, but it gives a stressful urgency to what feels like it should be a mostly chill game
_childDocuments_.name: Fae Tactics

_childDocuments_.review: Fae Tactics successfully boils the tactics rpg genre down to its essential elements and creates a deep and engaging system that emphasizes adapting to challenges while using all of the mechanics at your disposal. There are no skills to learn or equipment to buy, but there's a load of units, scrolls, spells and load outs for you to change depending on what you're facing. This is a game where you *cannot* have a single group you use for every fight. This alone puts it leagues above every other tactics game I've played, including FFT.  The music is evocative and the world obviously has a lot of love and care put into it. I wholeheartedly recommend this game. That is not to say this game is perfect. Bugs were prevalent throughout my playthrough, most of which amounting to polish bugs, but one amounting to a game breaking bug that forced me to change my party to adapt. (Rhyfel's counter attack bug)Another issue is the game's battle pacing. Damage calcs, buffs, debuffs and curses are all displayed individually. Initially this isn't a problem, but as the game progresses and the battles become more complex; you begin to watch the enemy act more than play the game; and that's a serious problem.Lastly, the game's dialog and plot, can be stilted and jam packed full of exposition, but I can forgive this since this game was made by what appears to be a two person team. I get the feeling the devs had a lot they wanted to tell with very limited means to do so. Despite its faults this is a labor of love, jam packed with content, challenge, unit variety and even replay value with 3 secret characters and multiple endings. This is a purchase you won't regret. They didn't "simplify" the tactics game formula, they streamlined it and I look forward to how they iterate from this title.
_childDocuments_.name: Fae Tactics

_childDocuments_.review: fae tactics puts the player in the position of the perpetually pogging protagonist, peony. ...and when you realize that's all her portrait expression is, the game is utterly and unshakably cursed. but on the other hand, how silly it is kind of adds a bit of charm to it?this about sums up the game in a nutshell, but for some reason, i will continue typing.as a trpg veteran, in terms of mechanics and core gameplay alone, this is absolutely the best iso-trpg i've played. -the element system is clear and powerful. -every unit generally has multiple actions worth considering the trade ofs of doing each turn. -on normal mode, i cut through most battles on the first try but consistently felt pressured and satisfied by the difficulty. -many iso-trpgs are suffocatingly slow, but this has a speed-up option; 2x felt great.-inventory management is minimal yet meaningful-rotating different units and characters in and out felt cool-the monster-catching felt meaningful and very well integrated-there is a lot of freedom/non-linearity with all the side missions-also wow this is a whole-ass 40+ hour game even on speed up-changing pogony's element is pretty neat-it's hard to overstate how good the sound effects are making things feel very rewarding. this doesn't fit in this paragraph but it needs to be said.in sum, the core of the gameplay is amazing and feels great.it is lacking some polish. most of it is lacked in inconsequential places. if time and resources were a factor, they prioritized them well. but it is noticeable.most notably, the writing is particularly unartful. i still enjoyed the story. i actually liked most of the characters, and more than i expected to. the perennially empoggened protag (pogtag, if you will?) had about two braincells, but she rocked them hard. the writing is predictable, but not boring. the dialogue, however, was occasionally distractingly bland (or un-edited). this is definitely the weakest part of the game, but it is not a deal breaker. cohesive world-building and likable characters shore it up well enough.all in all, the game is pretty poggers.
_childDocuments_.name: Fae Tactics

_childDocuments_.review: This game got stuck in my head since I saw the trailer, both due to the graphics and the catchy music. I found myself recalling that music several times afterwards and months later finally gave in. After going through an entertaining story, character progression, summons, elements, talismans, gems, awesome 2D graphics and soundtrack, I thoroughly enjoyed the game.I think a smaller number of game systems would have been enough for the game to be plently of fun and interesting battles, or a simplified element strength/weakness matrix, but nonetheless the extra complexity didn't get in the way and the having the extra collectibles was nice (although I didn't catch'em'all).
_childDocuments_.name: Fae Tactics

_childDocuments_.review: My favourite of the isometric tactics games by far. The art and aesthetic is great, the story and characters are excellent and well designed, the world is interesting and compelling, and the combat is the right balance of fun and challenging. The creature collection aspect really adds an extra layer of fun and tactical possibilities and keeps you coming back for more.Big fan, big thumbs up.

_childDocuments_.review: For those with a shorter attention span, I'll put the important stuff first.  Fae Tactics is one of the greatest turn-based tactical RPGs out there.  What you have to look forward to:I'm a huge tactical gamer, having been hooked on the genre from my young teens in the late 90s and playing through a wide variety of classic and modern titles alike.  I've played this game twice through, once playing blindly on Normal difficulty back before the V1.009 update, and a second time on Hard difficulty at the current version of V1.010.  Interestingly, my second time playing the game was noticeably easier than my first play, despite playing on the higher difficulty.  This is partially due to just having more experience with the game, but also because of how well the game was rebalanced in the V1.009 update.  There are still some summonable fae that are much more broadly useful than others, but the number of viable options for every strategy is much more robust now.  The new gemstone equips are also incredibly influential, offering ways to tweak movement types, stats, or simply start a battle with one of a number of rare buffs.  It definitely left me feeling like a kid in a candy shop with how many effective options I had at my disposal by the end.The elegance in design of the game overall can't really be overstated either.  You can only ever do three things in a battle: target an enemy to attack, target an ally to buff, or end your turn without doing either to self buff.  The amount of variables to how those three things change from one unit to another is beautifully set up, and the progression of complexity is a very easy curve that spans the entire length of the game, with the single exception of the gemstone questline (which has a level of complexity to the enemies that exceeds that of the final boss).  I've never seen another turn-based tactics game play so quick and punchy, yet still require so much strategy to both the preparation and execution of a battle.  Really, hat's off to the developers.Now to the criticisms, which are pretty sparse to begin with.  Originally, I remember having issues with certain UI elements not having any explanation or tooltip, but that is pleasantly no longer an issue in the current version.  The other minor gripe is with how late some of the cast's final weapon quests pop up.  Some characters have their full kit available by the halfway point of the game, but others are so late that you'll have access to the "point of no return" final story sequence before the character's final story quest is even able to populate.  It leads to some cast members feeling like they have much more diversity than others, at least in the initial play.  It's worth noting that New Game+ opens the game with all prior equipment available from the start, including weaponry, scrolls, and gems.  More notably, there's no indication at all in the game that many character questline events (needed to unlock new weapons) require you to get kills and/or utilize their Ultra up to some hidden requirement.  This only really becomes an issue if you choose not to use a character outside of their mandatory quests, though.  The requirements generally seem to be rather lenient, as I managed to get all but two characters' full weapon sets blindly on my first run.  Now that all of the cast is more balanced in effectiveness, I found myself regularly swapping between all cast members on my Hard run, and every character quest popped up without any grinding as a result.  There's also no indication of a potential romance between two characters (a requirement for their "A" endings and one achievement), unless you just happen to have the first character in your active party during the second character's introduction battle.  Considering that you can easily recruit the latter before the former, it's quite easy to completely miss and even permanently lock yourself out of those particular endings and achievement.All in all, these criticisms easily pale in comparison to the mountain of praise I have for this game.  Truly, I can't recommend the game enough, especially to veterans and fans of the genre.  So please, treat yourself.  I insist.  You deserve it.

_childDocuments_.review: Ignoring everything else about game design, what really put me off was the lag.Each stage the game gets slower and slower, as if data is piling up in the background with nowhere to go.I don't know the exact cause of it all, I'm no coder, but there is no reason that a pixelated game should struggle this hard to run smoothly.Had to request a refund after about an hour.
_childDocuments_.name: Fae Tactics

_childDocuments_.review: I bought this expecting a game like Final Fantasy Tactics (which I love!), but was pleasantly surprised!Instead of deeply customizing characters, this game gives you dozens of different units to play with, Instead of giving your characters 20 actions they could possibly take, this game gives you 3 meaningful ones. Units have big strengths and big weaknesses, so you have to carefully choose which units to bring, and what to do with them in battle. I haven't played the normal difficulty, but the hard one punishes you for your mistakes. If you let your fire summon near a water enemy, it will die in one turn! That said, no battle seems too hard, every time I lost a battle I could see exactly why. It also made an spectacular job with how transparent the mechanics are. Everything you need to know is on the screen, or in the cheat sheet that you get by holding spacebar.Overall, a great game! Music is great, visuals are great and gameplay is great.
_childDocuments_.name: Fae Tactics

_childDocuments_.review: This game was absolutely wonderful. My only complaint is... I wish it was longer! I'm looking forward to trying to 100%, which I normally don't care for with most games. I also really enjoyed the story, which I was surprised by.A really great way to tap into some FF Tactics nostalgia while still keeping it super fresh. I can't recommend it enough if you know you like this sort of game.

_childDocuments_.review: So far I am really enjoying this game, the game play is great and the art style and music is also fantastic too, among other things that I could spend some time going into. However, I have come to a point where I believe I have run into a bug that is making it impossible to continue and is hindering my enjoyment of the game. I have not found any way around it other than maybe killing them in a different order but I am unsure if a similar bug would happen with one of them too. _childDocuments_.review: Great artstyle, generally solid combat encounters, and the overall base game design is really solid. Story is kinda generic, but I really like the characters so it's certainly good enough. Takes the very typical isometric TBT gameplay and simplifies some portions while adding a couple of new mechanics for an experience that overall feels like it really hits the mark in terms of trimming fat while still maintaining complexity where it's needed.
_childDocuments_.name: Fae Tactics

_childDocuments_.review: Fae Tactics is a unique monster collector/tactics battler with some innovative concepts around unit equipment customization, support abilities, and even the concept of a passive action that takes place when a unit doesn't otherwise do something on their turn. There's no story to speak of here and a relative lack of unit variety, so it gets pretty grindy over time, particularly when forcing you to complete multiple maps' worth of fights back to back or replay a map when one of numerous units gets knocked out. It's worth messing around with some.
_childDocuments_.name: Fae Tactics

_childDocuments_.review: I can tentatively recommend this game. It's good! Not great, but good. Battles are rather slow, you have to take a lot of time to position yourself advantageously while the enemies steadily buff. Character customization is low, but fluid; if you die to a powerful enemy, next time you attempt that level, you can just put your points into tankiness instead of damage and try a different approach. The elemental damage system alright, though a bit over-complex in places. The elements of the enemies on the battlefield will usually determine which support monsters you play for your team. The special effects of attacks are numerous and pretty random; you often won't feel in control because you've only got a 35% chance to freeze that enemy in place, and it doesn't go up; but you may knock him back with the same attack, or crit him, so the total chances of something good happening are decent. However this means that, as stated by other reviewers, Fae Tactics is light on the 'tactics'. Position your characters and hope for the best.Don't compare this to Final Fantasy Tactics. There is no depthful, robust character customization. There is no grandiose, Shakespearean storyline, although the storyline it has is passable. If anything, it's roughly on par with Luminous Arc: serviceable in all regards. But, there is nice art, a light-hearted atmosphere, and overall a fun feel to everything. From this point, I don't see myself going back to it after I've drunk my fill, but it's a fine distraction for the COVID times.
_childDocuments_.name: Fae Tactics

_childDocuments_.review: This is a great game.Fae Tactics is an incredibly well polished isometric tactics game. The game itself is relatively compact in that there aren't an excess of systems to keep track of so there isn't the menu hell you tend to find in this genre. While there aren't many mechanics to keep track of, they are all important to the game and work very well together. Learning the systems and how to best capitalize on them between each map is super fun and rewarding. The game progresses naturally and there's no need to grind or anything unless you're hunting a specific drop. The characters and writing are cute and funny, which match the generally lighthearted aesthetic of the game, although there are a couple surprisingly hard hitting moments in some of the character's stories.There are a few small issues such as the occasional typo and some very minor bugs but the fun gameplay, colorful art, catchy music, and all around good time to be had with this game make it absolutely worth it.
_childDocuments_.name: Fae Tactics

_childDocuments_.review: Every battles feel the same:You regroup your units under the Dog's Protection (that is OP), so none of your units except the Dog will take damage. And you stomp the map just like that. You heal the Dog with the Bird, and even without any heal, the Dog can just use his ultimate to heal himself.There is no tactics at all, only 3 possible action for each unit (wait, attack of buff allies). Nothing customisable there.It's just a game about stacking on the Dog, and getting enough DPS to kill ennemies leaders (if you lack DPS, you're going to lose, because they heal a lot, and have one shot ultimate skills).My main character is lvl 14 or so, and still have only 30 HP. The monsters deals at least 50 damages to her. So if the Dog doesn't protect her, she is dead...

_childDocuments_.review: It's really hard to come up with whether I like this or not. Its one of those games where an in-between rating would be good. I loved huge parts of it (look at my playtime). The artstyle is great, the maps are really well designed, the combat system is interesting with many varied encounters. The story is interesting in parts as well as is some characters, however the boss battles become increasingly more unbalanced as the game continues (to the point where it starts feeling like you and the boss are using two different combat systems) with no ways of modulating difficulty. You can try some different builds but they aren't that different. There's also the fact that the main mechanic of summons is random drops on the battlefield which means you have no way of influencing whether you get better ones. I spend 45 hours in the game and maybe around 25-30 hours in I got my last summon with about 50% of the complete deck & I never got another with with a WILDLY unbalanced deck with allright (for most battles) deck of water & ice, some arcane, totally crap wind (I had like 2 & not very good), about the same with fire and a few earth cards. Anything except water & Ice (and fire if the elements lined up) wasn't worth bringing to a fight near the end game. I still kept trying, and did make it to the final boss but with frustrations mounting with every boss fight. Bus after the boss stage 2 wiped out my entire team in 3 turns (by itself mind, not with other creatures) & having to restart from stage 1 I booked it & watched the finish on youtube. I'm not sure IF I could have completed it, but by that time I had had it with the unbalanced combat system.So should you buy this game, I don't know. It depends. There's a lot of good stuff here & if you are willing to be open to maybe not finishing the game, there's a lot of really good combat encounters here. At the same time as I said the boss battles become increasingly more unbalanced with each boss But I can't honestly say I didn't have a good time with the game either. I had a blast with it for most of the playtime, even with the frustrating bosses. It only got really bad near the end. But again that's up to you - even for me I hate that I couldn't finish it.

_childDocuments_.review: I want to like it but it has such jank controls compared to other SRPGs like Disgaea I can't deal with it. Up moves right, right moves down, etc. You're better off with a keyboard/mouse but that's pretty lame because in order to finish your turn you need to confirm your facing....so the cursor will move from where you positioned your character and now you have to select your character again just to end the turn. That's a sloppy, simple fix that should have been implemented ages ago. Menu bar needs to stay on the character that just moved.

_childDocuments_.review: Fae Tactics is a Tactical-RPG, like Final Fantasy Tactics, the yardstick of the genre.As a reminder, the basics of the gameplay are to move these units on a map covered with squares (movement imitated to a certain number of squares), attack the enemies and then position yourself to one side for the next turn. Indeed, it is important to position yourself well because an attack from the side or from the back will do more damage, and it is also valid on the opponents.Where Fae Tactics stands out is offering a summoning system at the start of each turn. These are actually additional members of your team made up of monsters that you have defeated and whose card you have acquired. You can set up your allies in advance or do it before the start of the fight if necessary. This is different from unit management in other titles, but it is true that it amounts to about the same in the end.But that's not all. There is also a magic system, where you can set up three different powerful spells, and which you can cast with any of your units before its movement phase and when magic is available (i.e. when the cooldown is finished). This is interesting because it adds a new possibility to a character's turn. Here too, you can set the spells in advance or before the start of the fight.A final point of gameplay that is innovative is the passive skills of units, both allied and enemy. Each character has a passive skill that activates when the character does not take an action (you can still move him before). When you validate the end of your turn, your skill is triggered. This can be a zone of protection within which each unit located there and being attacked will not suffer damage because it is the defendant who will take, a self-regeneration of MP or shield points, an increase in combined attack chance, etc. Suddenly, this increases the strategic dimension, because it will sometimes be necessary rather to delay a turn to have the passive skill bonus before making an attack which will be more devastating.In addition to this, each time you level up, you will earn a point to place on a line of your choice: offense, defense and special. This allows us to customize our heroes a bit, in addition to the weapon and a scroll.Fae Tactics is a pixel art style 3D isometric game. Don't expect fine graphics that can't be seen a pixel! However, the game is very beautiful, very colorful, and the animations are neat. In any case, no problem to make it run, whatever the machine!The soundtrack is also very nice, reminiscent of music from the 16-bit era. They are very pretty and set the mood well, catchy during fights, with a western air, and more relaxing during dialogue phases.Fae Tactics really convinced me. We are certainly in a tactical like we can see many others, but the title brings some welcome subtleties. The pixel-art style is very nice and the soundtrack looks like a western too.
