_childDocuments_.review: Very solid tactical RPG!  While there are some complexity issues and far too many mechanics at times, it's a solid adventure with challenging bosses, and a fun cast of characters.Visually it looks nice, characters and enemies are presented in an isometric viewpoint, and terrain is simple but effective.  "Sprite"work has a good amount of detail and animation frames.  Sound is done well, distinct sound effects that don't get too old or annoying.  Music is very catchy!There's a whole element system, with advantages and disadvantages, you can view this table at almost any time by holding down the left trigger on the controller (I'm not sure what it is on keyboard).  These elements matter a lot, toward mid game enemies WILL begin doing ridiculous damage with elemental advantage and you will do scratch damage without exploiting this element system.  You will need to carefully balance your team for every fight (and especially for bosses) or you will get destroyed.  In addition, day of week matters, as each day has a particular element it boosts.  Going against enemies strong on that day can be a death sentence.There's a good bit of customization with your 7 characters (plus 3 hidden/optional/secret characters), each one has different weapons that allow them to do different roles.  This will become necessary as you will have to shift things around character and weapon wise to do certain quests or to gain an advantage in certain fights.  You have up to 3 different weapons for each character, scrolls that can boost certain elements, improve any of your stats, or provide debuffs upon hitting foes.  Later in the game you'll also have the ability to equip gems which will trigger spells on some attacks or provide unique boosts.  Finally, Peony has 3 spells with turn cooldowns that she can use (spells can be used on any ally you control's turn, once per round), and can summon up to 3 allies.  Some of these allies can get alternate forms with different elements and different attacks or support skills.  There's quite a variety of things you can do.In combat, you can attack, use a support skill on an ally (which usually provides a buff or healing), or use a wait skill (which can give a self buff or prepare for a special effect next turn.  It's important to know when to use each of these.  Positioning matters quite a bit as well, melee units can trigger chain attacks on a target (of course some foes and bosses have anti-melee options) when it's attacked within range (this is good as in a lot of tactics games melee is really bad).  Direction facing also matters, you get an advantage against most foes by attacking from behind, unfortunately that also means that at the end of every units turn, you have to decide on a direction.  This adds a considerable amount of time to the overall gameplay.One thing to note that isn't really mentioned anywhere is that Peony's starting weapon changes its element based on what scroll you have equipped.  If you equip a scroll that boosts earth allies, her weapon also becomes earth.  If you use a scroll without an element defined, it defaults to arcane.  This means that Peony can always have the elemental advantage.  Note that her assist skill will also change to match what summons do with that element as their assist.Story is solid, the beginning starts with Peony searching for her missing mom, and getting tangled up in a whole bunch of messes as she tries to help out.  This changes by mid-game, and becomes a bit darker with more mature themes.  There is a single ending, but there are different variants based on whether you've completed all character sidequests or not, and a few other decisions that may have been done.The drawbacks of the game are that you get a new mechanic practically every battle early, it overwhelms you a bit yet still doesn't tell you some important things (like Peony's element changing weapon!).  Some fights drag on a bit, especially before you get the characters and summons necessary to exploit certain weaknesses.  Teleporting upon being hit foes are also really annoying.  There are also several timed events, and you can lock yourself out of certain optional characters or endings if you progress past certain points.  This means you'll need to try again on NG+ after a 45 hour or so game.Overall, the positives outweight the flaws, and I definitely recommend it to anyone interested in tactical games.

_childDocuments_.review: Really smart and self contained tactical strategy game. I really love how simple their "weapon wheel" is. _childDocuments_.review: Good game.The creators (who are just two people) set out to make a game like Final Fantasy Tactics, Fire Emblem, and Advance Wars without as much menu navigation and samey overload as games filled with armies of generics and two dozen classes.They have mostly succeeded, with a set of distinct characters and a battle mechanic based around character abilities and summoning additional monsters to the battlefield, but you only get a limited amount of characters and summons per battle so you have to be strategic about what you bring. It's a great balance of being simple and has just enough strategy to be interesting.The story is fun and engaging enough. There is also beautiful pixel art in battles and menus with higher definition art. The graphics are like playing Tactics Ogre or FFT on the PSP, except at 1080p.Overall this little indie game has one of my favourite TRPGs and is well worth a look if you're into the genre.

_childDocuments_.review: 7/10 SRPG with a gorgeous art style, I was surprised by how much this game grew on me as the story went on, because 10 hours in I wasn't really attached to these characters, but this game has a surprising amount content and story and I loved how each new piece of the story wove back into different characters backstory. I think the game is far too simple for too long, because gems (additional equipment which proc spells), most summons, and other weapon choices are obtained slowly throughout the story it makes the end game very fun, because you have more options and powerful characters to play with, on the other hand the start of the game feels far more bland, and if I wasn't so enchanted by the pixel art I would have never gotten to it. Still, I'm glad I did stick around, and was happy to support an underrated indie game like this, looking forward to the next one!
_childDocuments_.name: Fae Tactics

_childDocuments_.review: A lovely time with turn-based tactics. Very much an elemental rock-paper-scissors approach, executed nicely. Visual style is charming, music is excellent, characters are interesting, and the story packs some genuine punch. How dare you make me feel things about a bird with a water laser (among others)!Singular actual complaint: there's only one "talking" sprite per character, with expressions instead being represented by little bubbles over the "battle" sprite's heads. This can make some of the dialogue feel a bit at odds with the characters' default expressions (mostly main character Peony).Game balance is a little wonky in places, including the occasional allied NPC attacking things they really shouldn't, but it never feels like a pushover or an impossible challenge (on Normal mode). It's very satisfying to set up big wombo combo attacks and stack movement buffs to silly degrees. (Definitely need to make use of the melee attack-of-opportunity feature to do well.) Can be played entirely with a mouse (no keyboard needed) or a controller.TL;DR: 10/10 charming tactics game, would yeet a troll off a cliff again

_childDocuments_.review: Extremely underrated game. Best SRPG I've ever played. Great, fast paced combat. Fun, colorful graphics. A somewhat interesting story, with endearing characters. Almost every enemy you fight can be "recruited" and summoned in battle as secondary party members (alongside your primary named party members). There are many elements each unit can have, which are strong or weak vs other elements, and preparing for battle by crafting a team of the right elements, with the right scrolls to buff them, equipment and spells is fun and rewarding. There's 0 grinding required. I never once did a single "free battle", only the story missions.Also, although each named party member can unlock and change between 2 or 3 "classes", there's no constant class changing to learn a bunch of passives to put on your units like many other SRPGs have. Their level stays the same (you don't have to re-level each class) and they don't carry any skills over, which is great in my opinion. I always hated that part of SRPGs. I preferred units just being one class and hated the busywork of constantly swapping every unit's classes to learn new skills. So the lack of that, to me, was a huge positive.It's a really fun, no-bullsh*t SRPG that doesn't waste your time. Give it a go, it's well worth it. Hoping for a sequel someday.

_childDocuments_.review: Rating 8/10 Minor spoilers ahead (nothing crazy, mostly general things that don't outright speak on the story beats)Fae tactics is a charming tactical RPG that is somewhat of a fusion between a monster collector and a traditional tactical RPG.Story wise isn't anything groundbreaking but it was enough to keep me interested the entire time especially closer towards the end. I really just want to be able to see more of this world as a whole more so than how this particular story played out. Not to say it was bad, but considering how amazing the feel of the world building is and some of the concepts that were sadly pushed to the side or not touched on, i want to know more but there isn't really more to know unfortunately unless we get a sequel or if you play the prequel to this game. (which is an over decade old match 3 game, i will probably play regardless) the things this game sets up are genuinely interesting and it's sad to see the lack of follow up they put into interesting threads of world building.The game is both linear and non-linear at the same time. There is a set story and a set line of events of which you must go through. this, alongside interesting side stories, makes the world feel quite alive. However, the fact that you can do a good chunk of the story out of order either makes you miss out on key story details, or making it far too easy to predict what is going to happen because you have a character who is much more knowledgeable than the rest of the party in an early scenario because you obtained said character from a later part of the game. this kind of ruined a couple surprises for me as i ended up obtaining the water memory before the wind memory, when it feels like it should be the other way around but due to how the game is formatted, it's completely feasible to have this happen. This made some plot twists a lot less interesting. Speaking of the memories, i really think there should have been a memory for the electric element as well, not only to elongate the run time of the game, but also to add some more importance to how lackluster and worthless the element felt throughout the game (more on that soon) along side this it feels really bad missing out on certain story beats and not only missing out on more lore for a character but an entire set of bonus challenges all because you made a rash decision during the finale of a certain encounter early into the game and thus lost access to an area vital to two different story lines.The game play is what kept me going through the rougher parts of the early game. On the surface level it's a fairly simple tactical RPG compared to a lot of what is on the market at the moment but if you involve yourself with the game's systems and really learn what there is to work with, it very quickly becomes quite complex and engaging with how modular team building is. Before every fight you can switch out most party members and most summons alongside different equipment that you earn throughout the playtime of the game. The element system as a whole is fairly solid in concept, but falls flat in a few directions in terms of balancing and somewhat in lore. The electric type as a whole could have been removed from the game without changing much in the slightest. about the only thing this changes is a particular endgame story for a character, and slight balancing with how it relates to the water element and the arcane element. without electric, it would make sense why wind counters water because wind would more so have been a sky element as a whole. water having three weaknesses really makes it feel quite niche in most places especially early where the majority of the threats are wind and one of your starting team members is a water. the electric element feels like it was added late into development because they didn't want arcane and basic to be too similar, and to add counter play to the machines of grunhold. the problem with this though is the fact that there are so little early game electric units and only ONE electric summon and to obtain it you need to obtain a unit you don't see until way later. and aside from that, there are only 4 (by technicality) electric weapons, and 3 of them are secrets and 2 of them are one secret characters, the 4th one you get by equipping arcane peony with an electric scroll. you can't get most of these weapons to help with the grunhold scenarios overall making the electric weakness feel worthless for the most part. and for the most part, it really feels lacking because of all this. and alongside of this, a few leader units felt absolutely worse than others by the design philosophy of their game play being a bit underwhelming and not very good, especially on harder difficulties making what they want to do quite difficult.The game's difficulty is a bit frustrating. I played the game mostly start to finish on hard mode hoping it would add more complex enemy variety to every stage. instead, as far as i can tell the most hard mode does is make enemies do a ton more damage. which would be fine if not for the fact most major enemies have ways of damaging the entire party in one go and you end up spending a majority of the next few turns recovering while the boss continues to beat on you and buff itself. As of writing this i haven't been able to beat the final boss on hard. the moment i shifted the difficulty down to normal, i beat it in one go flawlessly due to not being one shot every round. I would have much preferred having more complex enemy line ups and abilities that slowly choke you down into an unwinnable scenario by sheer pressure rather than being overwhelmed by damage numbers alone. there were times that i was getting combo one shot from neutral damage max mb with hp near the thousands by the final boss despite having two protectors on the same team covering the entire party. meanwhile on normal this never happened, and it was an utter cakewalk because the enemies didn't do nearly as much damage. this and the electric element are really my only two real grips with the game playoverall fae tactics is an incredibly charming game with a world that deserves much more love and so much potential for a great series of games. The way the game handles a few balancing decisions is a bit questionable, but overall a fantastic experience. once i can git gud and beat the final boss of the game on hard, NG+ is next to get everything i missed out in the main game for the best possible ending

_childDocuments_.review: Imagine if Pokémon was like FF Tactics...wait- Pokémon Conquest already exists.That comparison still works tho, it is a combination that works very well. Collecting creatures that you can swap around for different combat scenarios is very engaging. They just really nailed the core gameplay on every level. All the different buffs, positioning, spells, elements, chaining attacks together, it just works really really well. I never felt lost, or confused about why a thing happened. Normally there's a pretty simple reason for each situation that can occur, and that makes gameplay glide along smoothly.Hell, it took me five months of playing this game off and on before I beat it—something that I never do. If I stop playing a game for whatever reason, it usually goes unfinished. Not this one though. I kept coming back, because it's just so damn fun. And every time I did, the core mechanics were never lost on me. It was like I had never even stopped playing. I think that goes to show how well-crafted this game's mechanics are.I really enjoy the smaller, shorter maps—compared to something like Fire Emblem, you can play through several chapters without feeling tired or burnt-out. I don't think it's necessarily better than how FE does it, it's just different, but I like that approach.I will say I wasn't exactly engaged with the story. It wasn't bad, but because of the game's nature, every plotline feels like a sidequest. Which is...very strange? I'm not against the idea, I kinda like it, but you're constantly jumping between different plot points at your discretion and skill level—it was like I was trying to piece together a puzzle that was slowly deconstructing itself as I built it. There were some standout moments I really enjoyed, like Payachin's storyline, or that moment with Peony and Claudia near the end. Although I will mention there was a surprising amount of burying gays, or queer people just flat-out being villains. Definitely a strike against the game for sure.Anyway yeah, Fae tactics was pretty good. Give it a shot if you're in the mood for a tactics game with monster taming.

_childDocuments_.review: This game looks simple and boring at first, for a tactical turn based game you usually expect jobs/classes, equipment, items and this game has none of these, and yet through clever mechanics it managed to create a very deep game.It has been a while since I had a game of this genre where I had to think before battle, i usually just use the same setup in every battle, in Fae tactics I felt the need to tailor my team to each and every battle as felt smart as a tiny change in tactics was the difference between complete defeat and an easy victory.The game lets you change your entire setup before starting the battle, from character builds to summonable units and equipped scrolls and spells, so you don't have to save before battle and load to switch strategies, and since you can see what you are up against while setting up you can tailor the perfect team for each fight, and believe me you will need it.

_childDocuments_.review: If you love good gameplay STAY AWAY!!!! The problem of the game in short: the battle mechanics. The mechanics are extremly simplyfied. So much that it makes no fun. You cant choose any actions. All you can do is select weather you want to target an ally or an foe unit. Then your character performs an support or attack skill. This is very problematic. Good tactical RPGs let you choose from a wide range of abilitys to perform. Its fun when you can choose weather you want to target your own or the enemys. Sometimes maybe you want to hit your own units with an attack spell like fire, because they can absord it or something else. Here you cant play around and try different combinations of skills. Your characters have just one support skill witch is incredibly borring. I have just played this game for about 7 hours and dont want to continue it becaue every battle feels completly the same. Your options are just too limited and that in a genre where you usually have so much options that they completly overwelm you. Think about games where you have about 20 jobs and every job has about 15 skills and lots of weapon slots. What leads to millions of combinations for your team composition. I played over 200 hours Final Fantasy Tactics A2, over 150 hours Advance Wars 3, over 150 hours Fire Emblem Awakening etc.. They where all not perfect but kept me entertained for over hundred hours. But this game was borring after maybe 3 hours. I really wanted to like this game. Its art style is just perfect. The monsters have so much charme. It reminds me of similar tactical rpgs like Final Fantasy Tactics. But the animations make it unique enough to give it its own identity. The problem of the game is its game are just it mechanics. Which is so sad. Another problem is its ridicusly difficulty. You can die really easily even on the normal difficulty. Even if you grind enough. I have seen enough reviews that warned me about this on youtube. But ignored them because of the beautiful art style. But I have to aggree its to hard. Enemies can spawn new enemies. While some of your Fae leave the battle if they get k.o. So if a battle gets longer the enemy can always get reinforcements, while you loose units over time.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: 9/10 One of my favorite games.This review will remain spoiler-free with the exception of the "Story/Setting" section, which will include information learned in the first ~10 minutes of the game. Skip that section if you care THAT much.My playtime is actually right about 100 hours; I put in 40 on the humble app on one playthrough and the save transferred when I bought it here. Outside of one weird achievement I messed up I have at this point completed the game through two playthroughs. Fae Tactics is an indie tactical RPG heavily inspired by Final Fantasy Tactics. It draws influence from other RPGs, even having a number of systems reminiscent of Pokemon. Its pixel art serves as another nod to a particular era of gaming history. The setting is unique, the story is solid, and the gameplay is fantastic. While it is not without faults, those that it has are very minor in the grand scheme of a wonderful total package. Those familiar with TRPGs will understand Fae Tactics right away. If you haven't played this type of game but you may be interested in this one then you have some learning to do: expect lots of systems and time spent thinking. Preparation done outside of battles is often more important than what you do IN the battle! One interesting difference is that the game is mission based, but not linear. Enemies scale with your progress and you have a set of missions that need to be completed that open up more of the game, but you can choose what map to do whenever, even ones with no relevance to any story beats if you want to just grind or farm, as long as it's a map you've already unlocked.Of note to everyone is the aforementioned Pokemon-style influences. Every unit has a type, and the types do more or less damage based on the type it's attacking. Each element also has a buff and a debuff (called curses) associated with them. But wait, there's more! The game includes a system for obtaining "talismans" of enemies that allow you to summon that enemy type as your unit.At any time you'll have between 4 and 6 units on the field unless you choose to weaken yourself for whatever reason. 3 story characters (or leaders) and a number of enemy units based on the strength of the ones you want. Stronger units = less units. This is quite a bit less than most other modern TRPGs, and the maps are smaller as well to accommodate the lower unit number while keeping the action going.You also get spells you can use every so many turns, being able to choose 3 to take into each fight, strategically picked to give you an edge on that map of course. Or just take the one that lets you grab items on every map like I do. Did I mention there's crafting? It's a system integral to opening up the world as well as buffing your combat capabilities! The game uses pixelated graphics reminiscent of it's influences. The difference to me is that older games used art styles that were able to work within the limitations of the systems they were on. Lots of little imperfections and problems spawned from those limitations. The devs of Fae Tactics chose pixel art as a style, but rendered it on modern systems. The result is a game that, while it evokes nostalgia, has sprites and backgrounds without those little imperfections, and are beautiful, colorful, and lively! Seriously I love the art in this game. The game takes place in a post-apocalyptic magitech world. That's a very unique and awesome setting that immediately makes the game feel special. You play as Peony: a teenage girl travelling the world with her wacky companions searching for her mother. Don't let the bright and colorful art and presence of magic fool you though, this game gets d a r k. They get away with so much because of the art style, it's actually funny. The game is rated 10+, with the story getting pretty deep into things like genocide and religious fanaticism. Hell I don't think I've ever played a 10+ game with frequent fully nude character sprites before (why would fairies wear clothes?) but the pixels don't really "show" anything so it's fine.Speaking of fairies, this game draws from a LOT of different folklores and digs pretty deep while throwing in a few creatures of it's own. Sure you've got your common fantasy fare like elves and succubi, but there's gremlins and plenty of other lesser known creatures too. The devs also put in a lot of references to weird things like 80s movies which were pretty funny to recognize. The music's solid, it feels adventurey or actiony when it needs to and often does feel like something from an older RPG. I think I liked it more at the start, but there are pretty few tracks so I found myself wishing for more variety after a while. Outside of the music variety thing there are a few minor issues I have with the game: for starters there's no borderless windowed mode. I like borderless windowed mode, it just makes switching in and out of the game easier. For some reason the sound effects slider frequently changed its own volume when I went into or out of a battle so I'd have to readjust it which is quick but still kinda annoying. There's really a lack of settings in general which doesn't bother me too much outside of the borderless windowed thingDespite being highly rated everywhere I look, the game is not super popular so it's difficult to find information about it, and the game only tells you certain things through loading screen tips. Because of the lack of info, I made a mistake on my second playthrough and missed one of the hidden achievements when I thought I had done everything for it. Kinda sucks but I'll play it through again later to get that last chievo. I h*ckin love Fae Tactics. It's a unique but recognizable take on the TRPG genre with fun systems, great art, a surprisingly solid story, and a lot of character. 40 hours for a playthrough is absolutely perfect for this kind of game in my opinion, and it has quite a bit of replay value since your route through the story can change and you keep your levels and such in new game+. If you like tactics games and you haven't played this, you're doing yourself a disfavor!

_childDocuments_.review: A fun turn based tactical RPG. Combat follows a sort of rock-paper-scissors elemental weaknesses, and has some differing strategies and depth to it that make it fun. _childDocuments_.review: I went into Fae Tactics with little expectation. I'm not big on strategy games but after playing a couple of similar titles figured I'd give it a shot and I'm honestly glad I did. This game is a hidden gem. Initially the game starts out a little slow and tutorialises you on a fair few things before really giving you much of a plot hook. After the initial period everything is solid. For me personally, I tend to care little for story in games, it's great if it's there but it's not a big requirement for me however I found that in Fae Tactics the characters really grew on me and the story is especially fun (And rather dark) given it's structure is a little more complicated in that you follow narrative strands that all wind up feeding into bigger plot points or character arcs. It's really well done. The gameplay is solid too with characters (And summons) doing one of a few things per turn, you can move and then do one of the following: attack, wait (Which usually has a skill) or assist a team member which gives them a buff. Your main party can use ultimate attacks after gaining charge which can then be used for extra strong buffs or attacks as well as using a portion of this meter to do special attacks. There are a lot of options here. I also briefly noted summons which are an exceptionally fun thing in the game. Every enemy you see, including some of the stronger boss fae can be added to your roster and used as allies. It has a very pokemon feel to it which works great with the included type matchup system. The type matching system is generally good but could have done with some slight changes to make some types a bit better balanced.There is some talks about the game being difficult that I see and honestly, the game can get hard sometimes. The game doesn't really have an order in which you do things so you can wind up fighting bosses that you may not be fully prepared for. The key however is that you can usually build a strategy around these obstacles and honestly this was probably one of the more fun parts for me.The areas that you play in also tend to have gameplay implications, mushrooms that poison you, flowers that explode, water, lava and pits that characters/ summons may be able to navigate but can also be used as insta kills if you knock enemies into them. It's great using these hazards to your advantage though the game could do with telling you what hazards do as it tends to just state "hazard" without explaining the range or type of damage they deal. Speaking of areas, the art on show for the locations is absolutely perfect. Look at any screenshots of the game and you will see what I mean. I wish the character sprites were a little more refined but overall visually this game is a delight. Sound wise everything works. Sound effects are dramatic and crunchy when they need to be and telegraph exactly what is happening. The music is also a really solid point too as it tends to match the areas very well and is interesting and great to listen to. Overall it took me 50 hours to get through the game and by the end I didn't really want to go past the critical point to finish the game up but I had run out of things to do overall. Definitely worth the asking price and worth trying out especially if you're into the genre.

_childDocuments_.review: I was looking for something to scratch a final fantasy tactics itch I had been feeling without the recently released tactics ogre price. I bought the game during steam sale, but wouldn't be mad if I had payed full price for it. Fae Tactics definitely delivered and exceeded what I expected from an $8 purchase. I was drawn to the game by its great pixel art style and found the story and characters to be very engaging and endearing. Some other reviews have seemed to complain about a lack of jobs system but the game provides a good deal of tactical flexibility between party members, the Fae you choose to summon, the ability to redistribute character trait points, and your equipment load out. It also ignores and stream lines some of the more tedious aspects of some of other games in the genre (i.e. you aren't going to be buying and swapping out/selling boots , hats, armor, and you aren't going to be grinding for money or levels). In the 60+ hours I've played, i have yet to feel the need to grind for anything. That's not to say the game is a pushover. While there have been battles that I breezed through, there were others where I just got annihilated and had to adjust my approach, strategy, and/or equipment load out over multiple attempts to squeak out a victory. None of the battles have felt impossible and there are various story lines to follow if you don't feel like repeating a particularly challenging battle.

_childDocuments_.review: This game really scratches the itch left by Final Fantasy Tactics, with complex strategy options and a good deal of customization. It starts out relatively simple, especially for veteran tactical RPG enjoyers, but ramps up to some reasonably difficult fights that require research and multiple approaches. Game balance is good so you can solve most encounters a few ways.The story is quite good, it won't leave RPG fans disappointed. The art is charming and inventive, and the lore is not dumped in your face so you can let the world mature as you go. One complaint is how so many important keywords and mechanics are just never explained, leaving you to smash out what they do through trial and error. Prepare to read the battlefield thoroughly and hunt for tooltips, or at least skim through a general guide once you start to get stuck. There are also events and rewards that become locked if you don't do the right mission order, with no indication this happens. In some ways, this evokes the old-school RPG feel of keeping a notebook and discussing with friends wtf is going on, but modern gaming has shown that not telling you things is not fun.Overall, I found it easily worth the price and time, and I think it is both a great title for tactical RPG fans and players new to the subgenre.

_childDocuments_.review: Shallow character progression, limited tactical options, and a litany of small frustrations make this a bore. Grid-based tactics is a tight and competitive genre, with games from decades past tending to hold up both in visual charm and gameplay appeal (FFT, Fire Emblem, Front Mission, XCOM, and so on). Polish is lacking here, both in terms of overall design and execution. Here is one example:The turn order is displayed at the bottom left of the screen. A conspicuously absent element of polish is that the enemy selected by your cursor is not highlighted automatically in the turn order display; you must manually open the turn order menu and scroll to find the enemy you had in mind, jumping to fixate all around the map, and then visually double-check that you've got the right one by looking at the turn order display. Many enemies are generic and share identical portraits, without names to distinguish them. Information that should be visible at a glance is a chore to find.Characters' movement range is limited, making progress across the map feel slow, and the ability to react and regroup limited. Turns feel slow as a rule. You will at times find yourself spending multiple turns running around shallow pits or lava streams instead of jumping across, which the excellent Final Fantasy Tactics rightly allowed over 25 years ago (and Tactics Ogre before it). Perhaps the idea was to make flying units more appealing?; but it is a design decision that creates only the smallest measure of depth, at the price of frustration and unreason. The same can be said of the decision to restrict a reasonable movement radius to characters currently possessing the haste status. The logic should have been ironed out in playtesting, as decisions that were possibly supposed to add tactical depth or balance have not really succeeded at doing anything but sapping the fun (and time).I would describe it as a 6/10 GBA game. The unique summoning and card elements are only unique from a distant, pedestrian view: the truth is that instead of having five or six highly customizable, skill and gear-equippable, visually distinct, named units, Fae Tactics battles give you three characters who might pass for guest units in other games, and three summons who have no more customization potential than a scroll-summoned animal or zombie in another RPG. It is lightweight without being fast, and slim without being elegant. The menu-lite battle design was a costly decision which didn't ultimately result in a superior UI. The map visuals have variety and aesthetic appeal, but the system didn't ultimately support memorable moments as in other tRPGs: involving large height differentials, or fighting in chokepoints, stairwells, corridors, and so on. There were exceptions, but flatlands abound, and marching against cannons was tiresome.If you want a somewhat obscure tactics RPG with a whistling soundtrack and Western vibe, try Wild Arms XF.

_childDocuments_.review: Edit at 77 hours: completed the game on normal. Excellent experience, the story feeling was like completing one of those classic RPGs (somehow Lufia II comes to mind).  Thank you to the devsEdit at 38 hours: the gameplay remains interesting, with varied boss and challenge scenarios. I feel the story and characters get even better as the story develops. Review at around 20 hours:At first I was distracted by how colorful everything was and how the team members look like pokemon creatures. So much that I moved to other games for a while. After finishing fell seal and into the breach, I was really itching for some tactics gameplay so I gave it another chance. And boy did it deliver.This is clearly a labor of love by the developers. The battles require good preparation in the form of summons, weapons, traits and spells - suffice to say without proper preparations it is very easy to lose hard. Elements especially, flying/swimming units, melee/ranged, assist, wait and ultra skills can turn the tide of battle. It doesn't have a job class system like typical tactics games, but it doesn't detract from the gameplay. The many monsters you can recruit and summon make battles interesting and selecting the right summon into battle is vital, which is part of the depth. There is also a level up system with allocating points to specific traits (each character have different points that can be allocated, for instance the main character can increase move while the other characters cannot).The music is great, the characters are interesting, the bright and colorful world, menu, etc are charming. The story and character interactions are surprisingly serious given the presentation (Although it is decidedly not grimdark or dark fantasy). If you like tactics games, I recommend giving this one a chance. I spent around 140 hours in Fell Seal and estimate around that same ballpark for this game.

_childDocuments_.review: What I like about this game is that at any level prep screen I can scan the level and there are multiple strategies I can choose from. There's no over centralizing mechanic that can let you forget other mechanics. The mechanic the game is centered around are the type matchups, but that encourages you to find new strategies rather than allow you to use the same strategy the whole game.     Leveling up is satisfying since you gain skill points you can choose to unlock skills, but at newgame+ you are usually maxed out on skill points so you only level up to scale with the enemies.     But the real progression of the game is through unlocking stuff; beat levels to unlock spells, more equipment, weapons, & units and beat enemies for crafting materials, equipment, or summons.     This makes it a good idea to browse maps for enemies types that can drop an advantageous summon, but that leads to an annoyance I have with this game      That annoyance is that you can't skip cutscenes. If you want to browse levels like I said, any story map you check forces you to watch it's cutscene, and if the story mission you exited to search levels for was a multi-mission one you have to watch the cutscenes again.      Fortunately, this rarely happens on the normal difficulty, you can usually beat a level with what you have with good playing.     Unfortunately, playing newgame+ does not let you skip cutscenes, at all, so yay.

_childDocuments_.review: A really fun tactics game with a couple weird little twists on standard mechanics I really like. My favorite is the way that they handle the ranged/melee dichotomy, with ranged units being more flexible because they can place their attacks, but melee units getting an ability that gives them a free attack any time an adjacent enemy gets attacked, which gives a lot of fights a really dynamic feel because you can pile on melee attackers to do a huge amount of damage really fast if you know what you're doing.It does have a few poorly-balanced encounters though. There's one fight so frustratingly hard that I highly recommend just cheesing it (there's a boss with unreasonably high health and damage but no mobility, so just outrange him and kill all the minions and it's easy), and another fight that's almost as hard and really annoying that I couldn't even figure out a way to cheese, plus a handful of fights that are sold as really terrifying but are honestly kind of easy.Overall it's a pretty good game though. Charming, mostly fun, and solid in length without overstaying its welcome.

_childDocuments_.review: Fae Tactics:The Good, The Bad and the OutdatedShort version: 3.5/5 - would recommend to Tactic RPG fanatics. It gets enough right to be a decent game but also uses enough outdated or bad design choices to annoy me.Longer Version:Fae Tactics is a decent, if deeply flawed, Tactical RPG, similiar but still different to Classics like Final Fantasy Tactics or lesser known ones like Luminous Arc.It takes lots of the good parts of these kinda games while still falling into the same ridiculous pitfalls that frustrate players with this kinda game.The story follows Peony on her quest to find her mother and later, to destroy 4 powerful magical artifacts.The game uses a menu-less combat interface. You get the selected characters stats on the upper right, the turn queue on the bottom left. You can move, attack, support or wait without having to use menus. Rather efficient in that regard.The animations are very well done, showing character on every unit, even mook units. This is not always a pro though.The soundtrack is a good mix reminding me personally of games like Wild Arms and Disgaea.The main Problem the game has is balancing. Part of the game is to collect the cards of enemies to be able to Summon them for battle. The problem being that the cards you get are always inferior to the enemies you actually fight. This comes from the simple fact that, instead of changing enemies based on the map, Enemy STATS are changed to suit the map. Random increases of stats across the board, being able to attack without height limit etc. its all here. While this is excusable for challenge concerning Mini Bosses and Bosses, when the most basic mook unit has 5 movement when you fight it, but the same unit only has a movement of 2 when you SUMMON it, it feels like a crutch to safe time instead of properly balancing the story maps. Not to say that other Tactic RPGs dont do the same, but that is not a proof of this being good but a emblematic of a much bigger issue with Tactical RPGs in general.Status Effects (Curses in this game) start out very useful but become completely useless a good 1/4 through the game where even with negative status resistance, you will never, ever land them, while enemies will land their 50% chance statuses 100% of the time. In other words, Curses are great against the player, worthless against enemies. Once again, while this is excusable for Bosses/Mini Bosses, when even normal enemies simply wont get status effects no matter how high you stack your chances, it just makes another tactical option completely useless.Also the game has EXP for unused Units. Unfortunately the units only get a certain percentage of whatever EXP you get. And your summons each level individually. This can lead to grinding that for all intents and purposes shouldnt EXIST. At the very least one would expect the summons to scale to Peonys level but no.On top of that, you cannot actively change the starting positions of your team. Each slot has a pre-set sortie spot on each map and the only way to "move" characters is by switching the slots around. Okay for Main Characters, annoying for summons that only appear after you start the battle.Due to this, most of the difficulty comes not from enemies having good strategies or interesting patterns, but simply being able to outgun, outrange and outmove you on every opportunity. The problems just get exacerbated on higher difficulties, where the aforementioned stat boosts get much higher.And this is before we get into bugs like your volume randomly resetting and other odd stuff. Generally excusable, as the dev team seems to be quiet small.Pros:-A colorful cast of characters.-Easy to understand, hard to properly master-Lovingly made animations and music-Lots of customization options-Lots of summonable allies.Cons:-There is only a handful of summons that are actually useful.-Drop RNG is horrible-No skipping cutscenes, making repeat playthroughs a chore.-Having to wait through every single animation of every enemy unit is tiring after the 100th time and the game could really need a "skip animations" feature.-Heavy reliance on quantity over quality in terms of enemy design.I honestly can not 100% recommend the game to anyone but the most starved Tactics RPG addicts. But for those few, its a worthy game for the collection.

_childDocuments_.review: The extent of the mechanical depth of Fae Tactics is evident since the first time you mouse over a character, the complexity of the combat is embedded within the characters themselves in the form of elemental affinity, passive skills, reactions, assists, etc. Due to all the important information being readily available, the combat is highly based on hard counters. There's even a permanently available elemental chart which can be brought up by holding the space bar.On a similar note, Fae Tactics also follows the honored SRPG tradition of allowing the player to recruit enemy monsters to their party. I think this is a nice addition to a game that otherwise lacks a traditional progression system. As an example, the player might not get new skills from a level up, but completing missions can potentially result in a new party member, spell or equipment upgrade instead. This is a trade-off more than anything because the usual job system is completely absent. In terms of presentation, the game is colorful and flashy, I'm not a fan of most character designs, but I do realize that's subjective. However, what does deserve a lot of well earned praise is the sound design, the soundtrack is delightful to listen to and there are distinctive sound effects for buffs, debuffs, kills, different movement types, etc. I could almost play the game blindfolded, it's awesome. On the other hand, I don't have the same degree of praise for the story. Without spoiling it, there's a decent mixture of lighthearted and surprisingly dark moments, and it's clear that a lot of thought went into creating different locations, cultures and characters. What stopped it from being great in my opinion is that the main plot is highly compartmentalized, each "chapter", so to speak, goes over a new character, their personal struggle and the culture they inhabit, only to be basically forgotten by the time the next character is introduced. All things considered, I don't think the writing is bad overall, perhaps a few more campfire interactions would have fixed my problems with the storytelling. To conclude, I think Fae Tactics is a good addition to the library of any SRPG fan. It's easy to understand, colorful, and the biggest problems I could point out about it were purely subjective. It's a really sweet game overall.

_childDocuments_.review: Fae Tactics is far from being just a FFT clone, it has it own twists to the isometric formula, a lot of personality and simplifies menus and action for accessibility and fast gameplay.The games uses a lot of the classic JRPG tropes one come to expect of the genre but they are used effectively and makes you enjoy a new, yet familiar, experience and not just another tiresome repetition of cliches.The story of the game is build around its characters, so it has a slow start until you’re introduced to the first few additions to your party. Once that happens you can clearly divide the game into “character arcs” with our main character “always ready to help” Peony as the link that joins all these stories. When the tutorial ends, we’re face with different “Story” missions to take, and a non-linear approach to advance through the game down different paths, helping the last centaur avenge his tribe, join a cocky prizefighter in his fight against a mafia boss or avoid them all together and keep looking for Peony’s mother. This non-linear approach makes replaying the game an interesting and enjoyable experience since you can see how different characters react to events by recruiting them in different order. Obviously by the end of the game you are going to have the same core party and played all the main arcs.There are some optional story arcs and characters, and the last update added extra missions as challenges were each fight is a though boss fight that rewards you with extra equipment. One those side stories has some of my favorite scenes, the Story of the Gremlin King. That arc could be considered “filler” in a way, it doesn’t advance the main characters or the main plot and you don’t obtain anything special by completing it, but every interaction between Peony and the Gremlin King is a beautiful piece of dialogue that packs a lot of meaning behind every line, making a secondary character like the Gremlin King feel alive and sympathetic. And this is were the game story shines, everything feels alive and full of lore, and you get to experience it all through the optimistic eyes of Peony.The game wants you to feel the emotions of traveling this world. And it does a great job at transmitting these emotions, it is not just the presentation, everything is handled with care to make sure that you feel something. There are moments of fun, there are jokes, there are gags… but there are also moments of introspection, moments of sorrow, moments of tension and fear, and beautiful heartwarming moments. And all this with a simple soundtrack, beautiful 2d graphics and short but great dialogues were each word matters. This is a game with a lot of heart, a really f**king lot of heart.With that all of that said, one question remains, how does it play? The game employs an initiative based turn system with order determined by the speed stat. Now one of the core features of the game is that there are two types of units, the main characters function as “Leader” Units, they have a full set of skills and allow for certain customization with different equipment and passive trait points. On the other hand there are basic units called Fae, that Peony summons to aid her in battle. The Fae don’t have reaction skills neither allow for any customization but are summoned at the start of every fight no matter how many times you lose them. Fae are not only an interesting addition as expendable units, but also add a bit of a “catch’em all” feeling since to get a new summon you need to obtain the “Fae talisman” as a drop from said Fae.The reason why you would actually want to get all the different Fae to summon is that different Fae have different summon costs based on their skill set and that the game uses an Elemental system to determine Weak and Critical Attacks, for example a Water unit will always deal critical damage to a Fire unit, but the same unit is going to deal minimal damage to Wind, Eletric or Ice units. Critical attacks became important when enemies start having Magic Barrier (MB), this barriers reduce incoming damage from any non-critical attack, so having the right set of elements for a fight makes a big difference. But this is only the tip of the iceberg, the game has a lot of mechanics to unpack, and giving them all away can feel pretty daunting. But the game does a good job of slowly introducing the different mechanics, for example reaction skills and ultra attacks are locked behind low level requirements so basically they don’t appear until you have enough battles under your belt to understand the basics of the game, later they became second nature since you are going to play around 30 hours to finish a playthrough. All in all, the game is accessible and features a good amount of interacting mechanics to give the battles a good tactical and strategic depth with a lot of options to try different party compositions.Sadly there is no game without flaws and the ones on Fae Tactics while few can became a turndown for some players. The most important flaw but that is not immediately noticeable is that you cannot skip dialogue scenes, at first this is a non-issue because every scene is new and interesting, but with the option to play NG+ or try another run on Hard Mode, the inability to skip scenes or even set them to auto-advance so one can go do other stuff while the scene plays, gets in the way of your enjoyment of repeated playthroughs. The other low points is the long tutorial battles, they have little plot development to get the game going and are really simple demanding the most basic and streamlined tactics to finish them, certainly a non-issue on the first playthrough but when I have to think of passing those 6 battles again before getting into the meat of a NG+ mode, man that made me wish for a “skip tutorial” option. Another minor issue is that bosses, while always build around the idea of using certain strategies to beat them, relay to much on big HP pools and/or big MB pools, with the added mechanic of Apex, a shield that nullifies critical damage and armor reduction until destroyed, this makes boss fights get really long in some cases, on one hand long fights give a chance for things to get interesting mid-fight if you get too cocky, but half the time you have totally nullified a boss and are just chipping away at their HP until their inevitable death. The last thing that bugged me was that you can’t set a resolution for full screen mode, it always uses the resolution set in the OS, my issue with this is that I like that my pixel art games have integral or pixel perfect scaling, something that Fae Tactics lacks, choose the wrong resolution and you’re gonna start seeing all sort of artifacts in the animations and menus, nothing the general user would notice but really something to irk a pixel purists.Fae Tactics is a game I can recommend to anyone, the game is accessible but with a lot of different mechanics to play around, the plot and characters are fun and enjoyable with really well done emotional moments and a great pay off in the end, the art is colorful and cheerful, and animations are beautiful, the issues of the game mostly appear on repeated playthroughs and could be corrected in the future. This has been a game I enjoyed a lot, I could see myself coming back if a content update or DLC appears in the future, and I really wish to see what other stuff Endless Fluff produces.

_childDocuments_.review: (copy pasted from Twitter thread)So I just finished Fae Tactics and and I have to gush.It's been a while since I finished a ~40 hour game in less than a week (even when I had the free time to), let alone one that was not a new release.If you're looking for something interesting and new in SRPGs, this is it!At the core is a wonderfully simple system. Each has 3 possible actions to end their turn, an attack against an enemy in range, an assist to an adjacent ally, or a wait skill, usually some sort of self buff.Your team is 3 leaders and 3 summons. When leaders reach 0 HP, they have a few hits before they're out. They can be revived or healed by an ally, or wait to stand up. Every time a leader attacks, gets hit, or assists, they get a point toward making an ultra attack/assist.If a unit attacks an enemy that is adjacent to a melee attacking ally, that ally gets to make a combo attack.Summons are out when they hit 0 HP.There's a simple element system for crit & weak hits. Some physical characters get special crits and 'arcane' element crits after 2 attacks.Best of all the level design was very well balanced. On normal difficulty I only struggled with boss fights and never had to take more than 2 extra tries. I never had to grind. Winning usually felt like a matter of balancing offense, defense, and the element systems.The SRPG cardinal sin of long fights doesn't apply here. On 2x battle animation speed, I noticed that it took about 15-30 minutes to finish a battle and auto-save.I have two small criticisms.It's unclear how to unlock some events. Some characters felt underdeveloped because I didn't complete their stories.Mechanical keywords aren't defined everywhere they're used. For some equipment, I had to look around to understand what benefit I got.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is now up there with my favorite tactics rpg such as Final fantasy Tactics, Disgaea and Tactics Ogre. This game does something very different than those I listed where you have a large roster of pre determined characters with a specific set of skills but they all level mostly on pace and you can modify your party every fight. This allows you to have a game that doesn't require level grinding, but looking at your enemies strengths and weaknesses and making the right party for every fight. Buffs and debuffs are VERY powerful but your enemies fight on the same terms as you. So making sure they don't buff and you debuff them is vital. Numbers can go up or down indefinitely (like an enemy can have negative defense if you play right).The elemental system of weaknesses also builds on the games strengths and everything is relevant all the way to the final fight. In terms of story and writing I'm not a great critic wont say its the greatest story or writing out there but it kept me entertained and engaged and wanting to know what happens next and of the world at large.

_childDocuments_.review: An excellent tactics game. Although on its surface much simpler than other tactics games due to a streamlined stats system and the context-sensitive actions (meaning there are no menus and you can play the game through purely mouseclicks), a lot of depth emerges from the party/summon system and the elemental systems.The game is side-quest linear, with a single main line of quests and a good number of side quests depending on who's joined your party. Enemies scale with number of missions completed so it's hard to grind your way out of challenge, but the level-up scaling is not particularly good, forcing you to always think about the team you bring to each mission and the weapons you equip your team with. Your main party has three equipment slots that can change their elemental type, attack type, and add various abilities, and your summon party of (disposable) fae are fixed, but you have the ability to unlock a large number of different summons in order to adjust your toolbox for any given mission. Tuning your party for an encounter right before the mission start is 75% of the fight and quite enjoyable. I do have one criticism - like other tactics games, once you figure out the general flow (use counter-elements, line up melee units to chain back-attack combos, stack stat boosts), the battles start to become a bit repetitive. Every game tries to mix this up, and this game does so by introducing a layered buff called 'Apex' that prevents critical hits and defense debuffs (since inflicting -def on enemies is the best way to kill the 1000+ hp/mb bosses), with the buff layers being stripped on hit. Unfortunately, the presence of that apex buff means that the best characters in the game are the two specifically designed to counter it (one having an anti-Apex weapon, the other a melee character with a multi-hit combo). The final boss and post-game bosses are extremely difficult without those characters, but quite easy with them, which is a sign of party imbalance. Again, however, many, many tactics games share this flaw, so it's hard to ding this one in specific.A great forty hour sink. Make sure to set battle speed to 2x in the menu before you start the game, and keep an eye out for that -defense on hit scroll, which is crucial to many of the encounters.

_childDocuments_.review: The story so far has been light-hearted and nice, the characters feel believable. The combat and team-building is great and keeps me coming back every day for more. While the gameplay seems to be simplistic at first, the choices you can make before combat even starts and of course during combat make this game really enjoyable. Even though there are no different classes for your main characters, you unlock different equipment for them later on, basically changing the way they handle. For example, a ranged caster might become a melee or a healer a damage dealer. Then there is the summoning system, a kind of monster collection game, which enables you to refine your team even further. While there are some monsters that are simply stronger, I feel like most of them have some use-case, depending on the encounter. Monsters do have a certain summoning cost, so you can not bring all of your strongest monsters from the start, but maybe only one of them and some weaker ones on the side.On that note, the "rock-paper-scissor" like element system is also nice, because it kinda "forces" you to try out new teams, spells or elements for your characters to be as efficient as possible. You do not "have to" rebuild your team, however you might be a bit slower.The spell system is also quite unique. In essence, only one character is the real spellcaster, but you can cast those spells on the turn of every team member - one spell per round. There is no "mana" to cast spells, but the stronger they become, the longer their cooldown. You can equip up to three spells, which vary from healing, single target or even map-wide damage, teleporting and so on. There is a very handy spell which even lets you pick-up items from anywhere on the map. This eases the collection of some materials, summoning cards, equipment or spells by a lot at a very little cost.A little bit into the game you also unlock ultimate abilties, which you can either use to gain very strong buffs (e.g. a party-wide attack boost until the end of the battle) or to inflict massive damage on enemies. And your characters can gain ultimate charges quickly, and you can cast them multiple times during combat. But beware, as enemy leaders also have their own unique ultimate abiliities. Those tend to one-shot your team if you are not careful - positioning is key.I'm not too sure about some of the negative reviews. Many people appear to be confused about the gameplay, but for me it has been very clear from the beginning. Sometimes you might not know what a certain buff or debuff does until you encounter it, but otherwise there is no hidden information at all. All stats and abilities are displayed as symbols and/or text and are short, but descriptive.Enemy leaders getting revived by their allies happens, but has not been a real problem for me so far. You tend to kill the smaller enemies first anyway, as they are less bulky. In fact, the game even rewards you for keeping the bosses alive (by subduing them). Them being "damage sponges" is also not entirely correct. You just have to use the correct elements against them, which is part of the strategic element of this game after all.Enemies outnumbering you also hasn't been a problem at all. You do not need to pull each enemy individually if you just use the correct team. However, I do recommend getting a tank that can guard your characters. Otherwise, some encounters tend to one-shot your team quickly.While I haven't finished the game yet, I can highly recommend this to every Tactics fan.
_childDocuments_.name: Fae Tactics

_childDocuments_.review: StoryIt is a wholesome story, the ending ties everything together nicely, unexpectedly but definitely in a very fulfilling way. The dialogues and character reactions have an innocence in them while not coming off as silly, much like ffta. There are also some sad and gruesome events that flesh out the world, balance it and give it a more realistic approach.9/10Gameplay-Your character moves and attacks, can also buff themselves or another friendly unit instead of attacking and some attacks inflict debuffs dependent on element. Can also react to enemy attacks or evade them. Some special attack modifiers like high ground.-"Apex" negates crits from the opposing element the unit is weak on (until its apex charges run out), bosses have them and certain scrolls you cn equip give you similar benefits.-You can use some magic with the form of talismans that only the protagonist can cast and needs to be alive to do that too which consist of buffing, damaging, debuffing, healing and some utility like teleport for example. All the talismans, start with a time counter on them, the stronger they are the longer it takes to be ready for use. Only 1 spell per turn no matter how many cooldowns available you have.-Aside the basic party of 3 heroes you can also have an extra up to 3 monsters which you get sometimes as rewards from that specific slain enemy for a max total party of 6.There is strategy involved for those who like to think their turns, not a great deal but you will feel accomplished enough planning out some of your rounds.A lot of the combat however is dependent on countering the enemies element by chosing/customizing your own units accordingly much like pokemon types, so a bit of scouting and reading enemies before the fight starts will go a long way.The fights in general are repetitive but i found them fun enough regardless and the story engaging enough to not wane my interest and desire to finish the game.7.5/10Party Management -Your heroes start with a basic weapon and as the story unfolds certain missions reward you with another weapon for that specific hero, you dont chose who to equip it on, its predetermined on who it goes on. Not much changes with how you play the game with your new weapon however the biggest one is that the new weapon might have a new element in it meaning your hero can now spec and counter other enemy element types offering you flexibility in how you build your team vs the various challenges. There is earth, water, fire, wind, ice, electricity, arcane and martial-In the party management you can also chose your talismans and equip your heroes with scrolls which are some extra passive buffs to play around with.-When you level you can attribute points in 3 categories which r roughly attack, defense or reaction with breakpoints boosts for every 5 points and a big final boost if you max a stat.-Between every fight mission you can play a mini memory game matching all cards before the timer runs off that also gives you minor buffs.-Finally you can also upgrade your bike and various other mechanical parts by picking up materials from slain enemies or on the map for story progression, passive power boosts and other goodies.Overall is neat and involved but id have liked to have seen actual gear management, points for love and effort put into it!7.5/10

_childDocuments_.review: Very ambitious tactical rpg.Fae Tactics is one of the many western Strategy RPGs (SRPGs) which are now available on Steam. While most of these games clearly orient themselves on a Japanese predecessor (Fell Seal: Arbiters Mark and Dark Crystal Tactics are very similar to Final Fantasy Tactics, Dark Deity is very similar to Fire Emblem, Himeko Sutori is very similar to Ogre Battle, etc. etc.) Fae Tactics definitely does its own thing. This games mechanic are wild, from common mechanics like back attack and elevation advantage, to uncommon mechanics like elemental crits and combo attacks, to downright absurd stuff like wait skills and the barrier system.Overall this is great for veterans of the genre. 15 hours in and I am still learning new mechanics, just today I exactly understood how Apex functions for example. This weird and bountifull chest of crazy design ideas is also coupled with a steep difficulty, which while never unfair for someone with experience, has lead to a few game overs here and there.This excellent, deep and exotic combat experience is combined with great art, good characters, decent music and a story that leaves me scratching my head most of the time. The world and the plots its inhabitants follow are just a little too crazy to keep my immersion, and when I am hunting magical earmuffs or helping magical chickens hatch the dialogue is amusing, but the stories will not stick with me long.This is a very clear recommendation for any fan of the genre, as the wealth of new ideas makes this by far the most ambitious SRPG on steam. If I had to name one game this is closest to I would say Disgaea, as positioning and movement matter a lot aswell and it has the same weird charm, but it is not about making broken uber units like in Disgaea. While I do not think that the game was too successfull, as the steep difficulty scared a few players and journalists off, I certainly hope it was successfull enough to lead to a second entry. While the obscurity and challenge may make this one rough to get into, it is also very rewarding once you grasp all the mechanics and obliterate even the strongest encounters.
_childDocuments_.name: Fae Tactics

_childDocuments_.review: Right from the start, this game gives off a good impression that it seems to maintain as far as I've played. The combat system is easy to pick up but offers a great breadth of options and decent amount of depth. There's also a solid amount of control over your build/party makeup. Bonus XP rewards for finishing battles quickly and taking advantage of elemental weaknesses (along with collectible items on the field) keeps the pacing where it should be and prevents even the early battles from feeling like timewasters. Information is presented very well both inside and outside combat, with full info about units and their abilities (which are extremely varied) available via mouseover.
_childDocuments_.name: Fae Tactics

_childDocuments_.review: When I first started the game, I was unimpressed because you could only attack and move and I thought that was how it was going to continue to be. I was very wrong, it just slowly unlocks new systems for you, and after a short time I realized how much depth and customization there is. In addition to your party, you get to pick your summoned monsters, trait points (that you can redistribute whenever you want), spells, passive abilities, and gear (more passive effects). You also unlock a camp to play a matching mini game to give you a food buff before fights.On top of that, the story is non-linear and you can pick which rumors or points of interest you want to investigate and you get new party members as you go.  The artstyle is also great and I love the monster designs.Overall, more than worth even full price.

The story isn't anything to write home about, but I don't think that hampers the experience in any way.10/10. Would defeat God with a sniper rifle again.
