_childDocuments_.review: It takes a long time for all the systems to open up to you so the gameplay can seem kinda shallow initially, but by the end it comes together into one of the most fun systems I've played.  Unlike most SRPGs, all enemies and their information (element, skills, movement, attack etc) is visible to you before the battle starts, and you're able to plan around it.  So, the planning phase is very well thought out and unique, making crafting strats/choosing chars and skills engaging.Acquiring skills/spells/characters is mostly organic, but can be frustrating due to RNG.  Defeated enemies have a chance to drop a scroll (equippable passive), food (restores HP/barrier) or talisman (spell or summon card ).  I was able to unlock most of the scrolls and spells playing normally but had to grind a bit for the summons.1/2 HUGE problems imo is the amount of missables.  A few secret characters, some OP equipment, skills, summons cool.  But I didn't fulfill a special (IIRC also unspecified) condition in ONE battle and was locked out of 60%+ of the Gem system.  That's a bit harsh imo.Ngl, this is the main reason I even looked at the game. The sprites and artwork are top notch.  Spell/skill effects are incredibly stylish, with big bold damage numbers and loud, crisp sound effects.  When you hit a combo crit chain or nuke the field with an Ultra attack, it feels stupid powerful.  This game doesn't really look like an indie.The maps are just as bright and detailed as the sprites, and come with their own hazards that, for the most part, affect the enemy just as much as you.  The exception being cannons, which can be very obnoxious.Menus and icons are also detailed and easy to distinguish.  2/2 HUGE problems, however, is the inconsistency with explanations.  I'm a veteran SRPG player and was way too far into this not-so-easy game before I understood where to find all of the information.  Supplementary help/tooltip screens would've gone a long way.  The one help screen that does exist is very informative, so it's odd that there aren't more.It starts slow but turns out pretty good tbh.  But also tbh, the writing and dialog is not that good and took me out a lot.  Despite that, by the end I found myself impressed by the lore, journey and conclusion.  Was also a LOT longer than expected too, like holy s***.  It really is crazy that this is an indie.  I dare say the core story has the potential to be as grand as FFT; and like FFT, I one day hope for a Fae Tactics: War of the Pio-Pio with QoL changes and a new script.So yea, this game ain't a shoe-in for Hall of Fame SRPG but I wouldn't be mad at all if someone put it on the ballot.
_childDocuments_.name: Fae Tactics

_childDocuments_.review: Truly a masterpiece. The art style is amazing, the story is creative and unique (which is a rarity for rpgs these days), the soundtrack slaps and the combat system is simple to understand but hard to master. There's also a bunch of hard to find secrets which reminded me of how I played games in my childhood with no idea of what to do and whenever something happened it was a marvel. I've completed 2 and will probably play it again soon.
_childDocuments_.name: Fae Tactics

_childDocuments_.review: Though comparing games is not always productive, I came into Fae Tactics having Fellseal: Arbiter's Mark fresh on my mind. Initially I found the story, the setting, the tactics in the former to pale in comparison to the latter... until a few hours in and I found that I had been stealthily served an excellent tutorial and was diving headlong into a deeply engaging story to the point where I now look at Fellseal with new criticism and appreciation.The gameplay of Fae Tactics is so smooth and deceptively simple starting out but grows into a rich tactical experience by the midpoint and finishes before the game feels unwelcome. The fact you can't make an irreversible mistake in your characters' builds means no need to re-roll (like in Fellseal) also lets this game be a perfect intro into the tactics RPG genre while still providing stimulation for a veteran.The story takes an interesting approach of being very, very small at first, just a girl, her broken motorbike, her dog, and a little bird. Seems like a Disney channel Y-7 tv show premise, but slowly, gently, the world's lore and story turns into one of atrocities, cosmic terror, moral ambiguity and bittersweet resolutions. I felt Fellseal laid  the 10 out of 10 foundation for how a tactics story is told, but Fae Tactics, starting very small and so was able to continually up the stakes until the very end, whereas Fellseal was a journey of peaks and valleys, albeit had the benefit of always making one feel you were at the end of the mystery, only to find you had yet another layer of the onion to undo.In my head, I don't think I will ever be able to divorce these two games, but one always makes me think of the other in how they differ and yet both serve as masterful examples of the genre. I can only conclude with how different they made me feel.Fellseal made me feel like I had read a good book and was eager to read a possible sequel. Fae Tactics made me feel like I had dinner with my five closest friends in our tiny Pacific Northwest town, just before we all started heading off to college, marriage, and careers, the final meal that all six of us would be in the same room to share.
_childDocuments_.name: Fae Tactics

_childDocuments_.review: IF you liked Final Fantasy Tactics? I think you'd like this. While it is certainly not a clone ,with it's own takes on many things (The spell system, the option to wait, assist, or attack getting different effects)... My only complaint is the fact that assist gives XP even if the assist action does nothing, while waiting does not, even if the wait action does self or area buff.
_childDocuments_.name: Fae Tactics

_childDocuments_.review: The core mechanics are solid, and the rock-scissors-paper elements provide enough breadth and depth to be considered tactically challenging. The art style is good, and the story isn't too bad. The characters are relatively engaging and well developed. I just don't have the kind of time these days to play a slow paced game. The specific gripe I have is that the game rewards careful planning, movement and slowly killing all enemies and leaving the boss enemies last. It further enforces this by not retrieving dropped items at end of battle, so you have go out of your way to pick up items. But then they have a ridiculous mechanic where enemies can cast magic barrier every turn until you get these mega tanks with 200+ shield. I lost interest in this game, after a really long battle (3 sisters) and accidentally killing one. The game is punishing mainly because it's so slow. Overall though, if you like Final Fantasy Tactics or Orge Tactics, Fae Tactics is a good little sister to those games.
_childDocuments_.name: Fae Tactics

_childDocuments_.review: This game is AMAZING.I was completely taken by surprise with it. I was expecting a mediocre-to-good tactics game, which lovers of the genre may know already, rarely produces exceptional games these days (exceptions such as Banner Saga).Though Fae Tactics is not as good as Banner Saga, it is a great game in its own right. It's got its own "twist" with the fae summons, and is the first game in DECADES to correctly capture the Final Fantasy Tactics Advance "vibe" - which is somethign everyone tries to do and fail miserably.This game absolutely gets it right. Allow yourself to play it for a couple hours and you will be pleasantly surprised as well.This game needs an expansion or sequel. It's great and it standout among its peers.There are quite a few little problems that keep it from being a superb, exceptional game, but this is 100% worth your money even without a discount.
_childDocuments_.name: Fae Tactics

_childDocuments_.review: A spiritual successor to the Final Fantasy Tactics series, Fae Tactics does a wonderful job recapturing the spirit of the original games, while adding plenty of fun and original features to keep things feeling fresh. Many very powerful stories are told during the course of the game with lots of very unique and interesting characters. A must buy if you are a fan of tactics RPG games!
_childDocuments_.name: Fae Tactics

_childDocuments_.review: Nice turn base game with unique tactic depend on your combination.Combination of scroll, summon and weapon resulted in different play style in each match.I love this game but I didn't play new game+.So if you aren't player who may play finished game again, I recommend to search about hidden character and weapon before you play this game. If you missed it you might unable to unlock those character or weapon in this round.
_childDocuments_.name: Fae Tactics

_childDocuments_.review: I don't know if anyone will see this but Fae Tactics is 100% worth it. You love cute games? You love tactics games? You love collecting things? You love great feedback and responsivity? You love being able to cater your party and equipment to most battles you face because you can't brute force your way through things? You love feeling clever for taking down strong opponents?This is your game.  I've played for 19 hours and I'm already enjoying it more, overall, than the 100 hours I put into Fallout 4 and the 50 or so hours I put into Fallout New Vegas.
_childDocuments_.name: Fae Tactics

_childDocuments_.review: I have wanted a game similar to Final Fantasy Tactics for a very long time and this title definitely scratches that itch. It doesn't have a complex job system like FFT, but it makes up for that in other little ways to create diversity of strategy. Still making my way through, but it is challenging and fun. Definitely recommend.
_childDocuments_.name: Fae Tactics

_childDocuments_.review: An extremely fun tactics game with simplified mechanics that give you excellent control of building your team without needing to balance skills/classes/builds for each character. It can be a little annoying at the start when you have very few teammates/summons to build your team with in order to accommodate for the terrain and to counter the enemy team, but that is going to be common for most tactics games.Every part of this game distills your options into clear cut and very impactful choices, meaning if something goes wrong with how you approach a battle, you will know exactly why and what you need to improve on in the future. Implementing specific elemental types onto the units (akin to Pokemon) is absolutely genius in my opinion, because these type advantages not only affect what team you are going to use, but how you allocate your teammates trait points into their “offense”, “defense”, and “utility” traits, the formation and movement of your team, and what talismans you bring. Talismans are spells that you can use one of every round to damage/debuff/buff/heal etc, which you will pick to round out any potential weaknesses your team may have. Each teammate and summon have a few large differences that make each one have their own niche to fill out. Even later into the game, I still found myself using weaker summons from the start to balance out my team.The only real gripe I have about the game are the boss fights in order to get gems, which are another way to greatly customize the way your team plays. The first few are fine, but the rest feel like they were simply designed to be long and annoying, but not particularly difficult. The game itself also feels a bit short, which doesn’t really give you enough time to fully explore the late game experience, but new game+ does help with that.The story is thoroughly enjoyable, but there isn’t really anything that especially stands out about it. The setting is really well done and there great story moments, character interactions, and fun references throughout that liven up the experience and draw you in when some of the more impactful moments hit.If you like tactics games or you are looking for a fun turn based strategy game, I would recommend giving Fae Tactics a try. As a person who really likes the planning and battling parts of tactics games, but not exactly the heavy micromanaging of individual units, this game was right up my alley. I sincerely hope to see a sequel and I look forward to the future projects of everyone involved in the development of this Fae Tactics.
_childDocuments_.name: Fae Tactics

_childDocuments_.review: Not a terrible game, But it could use some work with displaying information.The game is largely designed around your mouse/cursor, However it doesn't take into account the mouse buttons. You want to check an enemy's stats? Hover over them. Want to check their attack range? Hover over them. There's no way to actually keep this information on screen, And if you accidentally mouse over something else it will override the text box.Specifically for managing their attack ranges, I wish instead of having to hold right click while hovering a unit, Right click would simply be a toggle and you could leave multiple enemies ranges visible. It's much easier than jumping back between multiple units to see who's exposed.You also don't seem to be able to pan the camera at the edge of the screen if there's a text box occupying that spot, Which is a minor nuisance.
_childDocuments_.name: Fae Tactics

_childDocuments_.review: This is the tactics game I didn't even know I was missing. The characters all have interesting stories and the main story is pretty good. While there are some challenging parts no fight is impossible as long as you have patience and prepare carefully. Usually the right party, equipment, summons, or spells  can make a difficult fight a lot easier. If you are looking for a tactics game to play give this one a chance.
_childDocuments_.name: Fae Tactics

_childDocuments_.review: I have a positive impression of this game, but I had some issues with it that are worth mentioning.The visuals are great and it's pretty clear that it was considered a core part of the game development. No character look generic and there are a ton of them if you consider the enemies and possible summons.The plot is not great, but not bad. The main characters have a lot of personality, but they are used in developments that are kind of predictable and will act in overly good ways for little reason.My main problem with this game is it's combat mechanics and how cryptic some of them are. Some games suffer from information dumps and boring tutorials. This game have none of it. There are very few in game tutorials and they, alone, will not lead you to the level of understandment you need to finish it.Some bosses can only be beaten when very specific strategies are applied and, sometimes, they are not clear from the get go. If you try to advance the game blindly you are very likely to lose a lot and have to farm to defeat some harder enemies. Very often, the battle is decided right after it starts, because you can't change any part of the party compositions and attributes and you have little to no room to compensate for that with your decisions during the battle, meaning that you will often have to restart them and sometimes farm scrolls to be able to beat it.Some bosses also have unique mechanics that are never explained and you will have to try different things to beat them, which is bad, because you will have to restart the battle and change your composition after you realize your mistakes.The battle system is not actually bad, but it's unforgiving and requires repetition which is something that I really dislike. Any repetition should be optional and you should be able to make decisions on the run without having to replay half hour of the game. This is the first rpg where I feel forced to play this way in a long time.So, I think the game is worth it? Yes, I finished it. But it leans a little on the hardcore side and you must be ready for that.Sorry for the bad english. I'm not a native speaker.
_childDocuments_.name: Fae Tactics

_childDocuments_.review: My opinion: Great game. Lots of units with different magical abilities and creatures. It may be the most magical of any tactics rpg. good music, good art. The story was nice for the most part. Some nice touches. There is a cool thing besides combat too. Plenty of content, more than i expected (sometimes i leave the game on, so hours are higher though). Only minor complaints. Facts about the game: The game adds depth and teaches you over the first several matches. It gets a lot better after that. They also add a couple things later.  You start with 5 or 6 units and get a lot more over time, giving you more ways to play. You can use up to 6 at a time.  You can almost always choose which to use except the main character who is locked in.There is an element system like pokemon. The main character can change elements.Playing on hard and have not had to grind so far (though i have a few extra battles for items). However, if you do certain things in battles you get bonus xp, which i usually do. There are optional battles outside of the story that you can play infinitely.  Some have new maps, orientations or enemies. There is a level system with a few categories of stat points, which you can redistribute at any time.Autosave + Manual Complaints - Some combinations of things are op.  This is nice sometimes but can be disappointing when it's obvious. However they are only available on certain maps. Some minor things are not stated. For example, a couple of items don't seem to stack with a certain mechanic because they would be too strong (  )  .  This is good but i wish they would tell me before I try it. Another example is the boss "Mot", who seems to be unable to take more than 1 damage under certain conditions even though he should take damage based on attack/defense. It seems you're forced to fight Mot the specific way they want you to. However, it's just one boss.When one of your 3 leaders' health goes to 0, they can be revived if they don't get hit ~5 more times. This is generally op imo. However, you can count that as a loss if you want.Bugs:  A few minor If you press the gear icon and go to audio your sfx volume is increased. A few times the text didn't render properly in character stats.If you do play the game know:It is possible to miss certain party members.If you are in the middle of a series of battles, to quit the game and not lose progress, press "exit game".  "Return to map" will start you over before that series of battles.There is a 2x speed mode.
_childDocuments_.name: Fae Tactics

_childDocuments_.review: An absolute gem of an RPG in the vein of SRPG titles such as FF Tactics and Tactics Ogre. The menu-less, fast-paced combat, delightfully colorful cast of characters and robust campaign makes for a wonderful, full SRPG experience. It's writing lacks polish, but otherwise is almost completely bug-free and runs very well. The enemy AI works well, with a few understandable and inoffensive quirks.  Playing on Hard difficulty gives a nice, balanced challenge. There's good strategic variety in the maps and all menus and systems work quickly and efficiently. Load times are fast.  The game has crafting, creature collecting and a loot system, but it integrates very well into the combat and rarely turns into a joyless grind. Out of all the maps I played, I had to use grindy "Free Battle" mechanics maybe 4-5 times, which amounted to 1-2% of the whole experience. I didn't collect everything I saw nor stressed about it, yet managed to fill up most collectible categories to almost 90%. The most delightful thing about this game was the simple yet strategic combat that emphasized correct strategies and party setups instead of making certain characters overpowered for everything.My only real critiques are the following:- The name and tutorial of this game made it feel like a generic cash-grab game, and made me almost give up out of expecting a mediocre experience. The game takes a while to introduce all of it's fantastic features, and seems like a way more simple, unpolished game in the beginning.- Some timed missions require the player to gather a certain number of loot items. These items are mentioned in a cut-scene when the mission starts, but are not visible on the HUD. Small gripe, but given that one such mission unlocks one of the most powerful units in the game, I wanted to point this out.5/5 experience. Chef's kiss.
_childDocuments_.name: Fae Tactics

_childDocuments_.review: I LOVED this game. I won't go into too much detail, because others already have.But let me just say that the cleverness, originality and elegance of this game's design makes me embarrassed of the various ideas I've had, over the years, of what could be done with tactics RPGs.The game isn't perfect, there are a few rough edges here and there. The difficulty curve can be inconsistent, mostly in the early game, when you don't have many options of who/what to bring into encounters and you may not have fully grasped the meta-game, yet. But overall, this was probably the game that has impressed and engaged me the most, in the past few years.(Also, if my playtime seems low, it's because Steam doesn't seem to log offline play. But I got a good 30-40 hours)
_childDocuments_.name: Fae Tactics

_childDocuments_.review: I just beat the game and I'm crying so hard T-T This was one of the best RPGs I've ever played, one of the best stories I've ever played! And maybe the single best *ending* in any game I've played. What a modern masterpiece; games haven't had heart like this since I was a child! The ending is so great, I hope to god there's a Fae Tactics 2!! This series DESERVES it!
_childDocuments_.name: Fae Tactics

_childDocuments_.review: Enjoyable, cutesy strategy game with fine pixel art and strong Nintendo vibes that give it a certain kind of charm and innocence. The game is not addictive as I tend to play it for about an hour every time but every lost battle invites to give it another go with a slightly different approach. An important difference with other tactics games (Disgaea and Final Fantasy Tactics) is that this game has much less controls to be bothered with, for increased playability. A lot of things trigger automatically, so while you need to be aware of them for full advantage, there are no endless menu's to wade through. Furthermore, the game keeps adding more interesting things to discover, such as various summons with different elemental strengths and weaknesses. And I have yet to unlock another party member! You can also first have a look at the board to see strengths and weaknesses of your foes so you can come prepared with the right spells and summons.
_childDocuments_.name: Fae Tactics

_childDocuments_.review: Let me preface this by saying, I'm not not normally one to play tactical strategy games. I've played Advance Wars, and Wargroove, but that's the extent of things. This game has similar elements (IE, one unit/element is better off fighting what's weak to it), but it has no map control or capture mechanics.This game is absolutely AMAZING at easing new players into the mechanics. Easily one of the best games I've ever played in that aspect. There's no "tutorial", but it introduces mechanics one by one, so you don't get overwhelmed. You can press space bar at any time to find out what element is weak to what. It's fantastic.The characters, and artwork, are great. The interactions between said characters, are incredibly amusing. I've actually grown attached to the characters in my party, which is something I can't really say about a lot of other games. It also helps that there's a fair few characters that appeal to the furry trash side of me, but it doesn't detract from the game at all.That being said. It does have a slight issue. As others have said, difficulty in this game WILL ramp up, and there's no way to make it easier (as far as I know). You -will- be changing out your team members, summons, and equipment between fights, sometimes, one after another. Some points can very much feel like a slog, you're going to lose bonuses and efficiency, but there's almost always a way to mitigate things by changing out something.If you don't mind switching your gear and summons between fights, or the difficulty ramp-up after the first area, I definitely recommend this game!
_childDocuments_.name: Fae Tactics

_childDocuments_.review: All told, I think this game is a fun pick up if you got it like me on sale. If you really waned a FFT/FFTA or Tactics Ogre fix this game can definitely hit the spot. But, there is a but here, if the biggest things you loved about those games was strictly the combat you'll have a not so satisfying experience.Let's just knock out the good real quick, the sprites and world look great. Peony is a simple girl as far as main characters go but she's generally hard to dislike. Nice, upbeat, helpful and she can take care of herself just fine. No ones motivations are what you'd called extensive but mostly everyone is likable if not tolerable and you won't mind the stint through the story being told.There are a fairly decent amount of summons to collect, new weapons for each character to use (up to 3).  Scrolls to buff what stats or aspects of the game you like, spells to pick to your liking followed by a secret character or two. It's a neat package with aspects to explore and work with if you're the experimenting type.Now, for the big negative and it honestly is that there isn't much of the way of actual tactics in this game. If you saw reviews saying this game is hard or stupidly easy its because there essentially is a right way to play this game. The elemental RPS and the Bird's Eye bonus in this game are so absurdly strong there really are only two solutions to the hordes of enemies you have to fight. Stack a team with scrolls and weapons of the dominant element to crush everything or have a unit run/leap to the high ground and nuke everything beneath them.  For reference an end game enemy had 2000 health at the level cap of 60. Bird's Eye bonus made the attack deal 3250 damage and it couldn't be evaded.In other tactics games you could build teams and handle things the way you want to for a situation after thinking about it. Here there is a winning formula that very aggressively says what units to bring and what you slot in and out to handle the situation. Depending on who you are that's fine but it feels noticeable in a bad way that the only choices one can make are ones to win or just suffer because you are trying to use a team/summon composition that you personally like. Other notes the game does have some crashing, nothing big the game auto saves almost everywhere so you'll never lose much of anything. They mostly occurred from menuing too fast after starting a free battle so like 5-6 crashes over my play time, nothing significant lost but worth mentioning.All told though I really did like this game and had more than my share of fun with my play through. I know the negative stands out but it is what you'll be engaging with the most. Sometimes an enemy will have the high ground, or an ultra, etc, and you'll get laid out but that's par for the course. If you can get past that though it is a fun tactics game even if you can put some big quotes around "tactics."
_childDocuments_.name: Fae Tactics

_childDocuments_.review: I just finished my first playthrough.  I consider myself a TRPG guru--one of my favorite genre.   Conclusion: I loved this game.  If you're on the fence and happen to read this, don't hesitate any further.  I thought it was appropriately challenging; not too difficult, and almost all battle restarts were because I didn't like suffering the loss of a summon for the end of battle bonus, and I made it a point never to use free battles.  The story was decent/good, the gameplay fantastic, and I already find myself wishing this game was longer.  The only con I can think of was the collector in me found myself frequently restarting the game if I didn't get any luck bonus in the campfire events.If any devs happen to read this, know this one person really loved your game!
_childDocuments_.name: Fae Tactics

_childDocuments_.review: Fae Tactics is a neat indie tactics joint! It took a while (at least for me) to take off, but once I got a few hours in I really started to enjoy it. (It's a good game to load in and do like, 1-2 maps real quick on a lunch break or smth). The UI is a little sketchy and I'm not *wild* about how the skill point system works, but the spells/different units are fun to play with and the maps are pretty! 8/10 would recommend if you like grid based tactics stuff.Also note: would recommend playing in windowed mode on a lower resolution, it'll make everything look much nicer :)
_childDocuments_.name: Fae Tactics

_childDocuments_.review: Clearly passionately crafted by a small dev team, this game has a tight focus in its world and design that makes it feel cohesive.The thing that sets this game apart from similar "FFTA-Looking" games is actually the limitations it imposes on you. The choice to limit each character by having no "battle action menu" means there can be greater exploration of the actions each character has, and let's face it, 80% of the time you have each character in a traditional tactics game use the same ability every turn anyway.If you just want more FFT and nothing else, this game does not have the complex character growth that FFT-inspired Job Systems have. However, you can still customise the main characters between battles (changing actions and elements, reassigning skill points, etc), and you have a good roster of support summons to bring into battles, which means functionally you still have a lot of choice.For me this is a 9/10 or 10/10, and the fact that it came out of a two-person design team (plus composer) is incredible. The campfire minigame is a bit out of place to me, and due to it needing you to make fast clicks all over a grid in a short time frame, it kills the perfect accessibility that most tactics games have, which is a pity.
_childDocuments_.name: Fae Tactics

_childDocuments_.review: If you enjoyed Final Fantasy Tactics Advance, but thought you spent too much of the battles scrolling through tiny hard-to-read menus: Pick this up. It's got all of the squad-based tactical depth, but with less RNG dodge-fests and a contextual action system that removes in-battle menus entirely. The characters are quickly endearing and don't wear out their welcome, the world is an engaging bundle of fantasy post-apocalypse, and the art is absolutely charming pixel-work that holds up at high-ish resolution (though I haven't tried a 4K setup or anything).There are a fair few small spelling and grammar errors, but they really don't stop the flow of the conversations sections. Having a wonderful time with this one.
_childDocuments_.name: Fae Tactics

_childDocuments_.review: At the time of this review I'm about 40 hours into Fae Tactics and but have yet to complete the main plot line. Its an Indie game with a surprising amount of meat on its bones and by-and-large the quality has remained consistent throughout. I quite liked some of the story beats, some were silly, some were a little predictable, some were heart-wrenching, some just put a smile on my face. The most important point though about the story bits is that almost all of them are paired with fights that live up to their implications and impact on the characters.The AI is surprisingly competent. Sure, like most other tactics games you've definitely got a leg-up by being able to survey the battlefield and build a team around it but the game can still throw some curve balls your way. This is especially true in the case of some boss battles, stages in environments that impose modifiers (increased chances of being inflicted by x, reduced movement for characters that don't fly, etc.) and (something I am personally very guilty of) taking sup-optimal plays in order to collect, well, collectables. Its the kind of stuff that you can't stop unless you are paying attention and see it one or two turns in advance. Although at times you'll probably still give an audible "what!? That's how that worked????" as a freaking bat bounces through your team then suddenly decides to do 180 and boomerangs everyone critting along the way.The art is beautiful. depending on the resolution and size of you monitor the character portraits can get a little fuzy but the sprites and animations are all quality stuff.Lastly, I feel I should mention I'm a little biased on this one. The producers of FT: Endless Fluff is a development team that I've been following for a while after their release of Valdis Story: Abyssal City. They are a team of two with soul and I really quite like them so take this all with a bit of salt on the side.All in all: a good game, 8/10 would die to bats again.
_childDocuments_.name: Fae Tactics

_childDocuments_.review: Put over 100 hours into this game and I don't regret it. Ended up doing a normal playthrough and a NG+ playthrough. The combat of the game can be broken down into a few sections:The game makes a distinct difference between a leader and non-leader unit. Leaders are units that contribute to the story of the game, have access to different types of equipment (which you unlock with side quests and/or using the character a lot), and an ultimate ability bar. Leaders also have 3 different types of stats you can invest into, which revolve around more damage, more survivability, or more utility. These stats also have an additional effect for every 5 points you put into them (up to 20 per stat), and maxing a stat also give you an additional effect related to that stat.The main character of the game, Peony, is always required in combat (which is, imo, a bit of a letdown for replay-ability). The reason for this is that she is required to summon the  that help you out in combat.Fae are additional units that can assist you in combat. Fae are summoned by Peony at the start of a fight, and can be viewed as Pokémon that are kept in Yu-gi-oh! cards. Fae have their own summoning cost, which takes up a part of your summoning capacity (capacity can be upgraded). To acquire Fae you beat them in combat, which gives a chance of them dropping their card. Picking up this card and finishing the fight lets you indefinitely summon them from the next fight onwards if you wish to do so.Fae are generally used to complement your leaders, as they (apart from the most expensive Fae) are not strong enough on their own to take on many enemies.The game has 7 "elements": Arcane, Lightning, Ice, Water, Earth, Wind, and Fire. There is an easy-to-access in-game guide as to which element hits harder/weaker against other elements. Each element also represents a type of buff you can give to an ally (a wind unit that targets an ally for a buff will give that ally additional movement, for example). Every in-game day, an element will be buffed (on Sundays, Arcane gets buffed, for example). Usually you won't have to care too much about this, but if at any point a Fire boss is giving you a hard time, you might want to do some non-story fights until you reach water day and try again. Some leader gear changes their element, too. Peony starts out as an Arcane unit, but can change element while in arcane mode by equipping an elemental .While defeating enemies, or reaching treasure chests during combat, you might find scrolls. Scrolls are items that can be equipped by leaders, which either modifies them in some way. You have scrolls that increase attack, protect you from super effect hits X times, or modify your character in some different way (like +1 movement, or bonus damage vs buffed enemies). The main issue with scrolls is that some of them can make a hard boss a cakewalk, or make average leaders amazing, raising the question whether they should all be available from the start (I got some of the last scrolls once I was halfway through NG+).While Peony isn't downed in combat, she may use of up to 3 spells. Spells are cards that have their own effect/radius/cooldown. The variety of spells allows you to enable certain playstyles, or cover up your team's weaknesses. Just like with scrolls, however, spells have to be unlocked in a variety of ways, meaning the bigger variety of playstyles usually open up in NG+. Peony can also be upgraded to -1 the cooldown of her spells that are still on cooldown whenever she gets a killing blow on an enemy, making higher cooldown spells more viable if you invest in Peony as a DPS.Some boss fights in the game have a boss guarded by pylons that buff the boss every turn. To weaken the boss you have to destroy these pylons, but hitting them triggers a "Flux" effect. Flux causes the pylon to randomly teleport somewhere else on the map if the hit doesn't kill it. If a boss is already giving you a hard time 'cause you can't gear yourself up to fight it in an ideal scenario (not having the right equipment/Fae/spells), having one or more of your characters chase down the pylons while the boss is beating down on your team can be pretty frustrating. And to add insult to injury, the boss often can summon additional pylons every x turns.Once you are perfectly geared up bosses can become kinda stale if you min-max for it. Min-maxing entails using 1 certain character that completely trivializes most bosses once its fully decked out, and putting a tank next to it to prevent it from dying, even the final boss is not safe from this tactic. The character in question can:- Deal damage just by starting their turn - Revive itself at the beginning of every round- Passively heal its tank if its close enough to the unit, which the tank should be anyway- Drop enemy Res once you got its story related weapon (Res protects against debuffs, making it possible to debuff bosses that usually are debuff immune)- Drop enemy Apex (Apex protects against super effective hits X times)- Drop enemy defense if you give it a -def on hit scroll.- Chain a melee hit when its not their turn, despite being a ranged character (Chain hits are in any other case melee exclusive). This triggers all the above "drop" effects again.Chaining these drop effects ~5 times/turn makes bosses have no res/apex, and negative defense. Want to make your boss fights harder by not using this character? You can, but this character is forced on you in the final boss battle, though it makes sense story-wise. Even bosses with intimidatingly large health/shield bars go down in less than 10 turns if you use this strategy.In the end I still recommend this game a lot. The aspects of the game I don't like are small enough that they don't ruin my experience with the game by much. The fact that I wanted to do another playthrough  after finishing it should add to how much I enjoyed the game. I would say NG+ is a lot more fun than the initial playthrough. While your leaders are once again unlocked via story progression, all the other things you unlocked (Fae/Spells/Equipment), are instantly available again, letting your second playthrough be a bit more creative. NG+ also makes it so your leaders usually have all their stat trees maxed out, making it more viable to play without a tank in a lot of scenarios.

_childDocuments_.review: I was skeptical before buying this game, but it turned out to be one of the most enjoyable tactics games I've played in years. The mechanics are complex enough to be interesting while not overwhelming. There are a variety of party members (including 3 hidden ones) each of whom has three distinct play styles (depending on your choice of weapon). Battles are very manageable in size - typically, you will command up to 6 units against perhaps a dozen enemies - and are quick enough to fuel a 'one more battle' feeling. There are a variety of mission types, including wave defense and escape missions (whose AI I never struggled with).Contrary to other reviews, I did not experience any need to grind whatsoever. Enemies scale to your level, and lower level party members appear to receive more experience to help them catch up. Boss fights can be challenging (I think my most difficult one took 4 or 5 tries), but it is very quick and easy to restart a fight. I did not find boss fights to be a slog.My biggest surprise with this game is how it kept adding more content right up until the end. I was two thirds through the game when it basically doubled the amount of craftable gear, and on top of that added a whole new type of equipment slot. Fae Tactics managed to perfectly string me along, adding new mechanics and content just when it may otherwise have gone stale.My only real disappointment aside from some minor quality of life issues was the story, which was only slightly above average. The game borrows from several common tropes, most egregiously with a "God" worshipping super religious and xenophobic empire bent on genocide. Despite that, I was impressed with the game's endings (yes, plural) - each character has multiple epilogues to unlock, as do certain side stories.My playthrough (unlocking about 85% of the available content) took 40 hours, and there is apparently a new game plus that I haven't explored. Exceptional value for money. Bug-free, with amazing music by Sam English. I wholeheartedly recommend this game to fans of the tactics genre. Very well done, Endlessfluff Games.

_childDocuments_.review: It's going to be a hesitant thumbs-up, with a few reservations, from me. I'm a big fan of the Tactical RPG genre, and it's pretty rare to see one that does its own thing - and does it well - without blatantly aping Final Fantasy Tactics and/or Disgaea. The characters are interesting and likable, the story is interesting and nuanced, and I really enjoyed the way you have to go off the beaten path and do side-content in order to unlock new weapons for your crew - new weapons that radically change their tactical role, rather than just being an arbitrary attack-boost.There's much more good that can be said about it - the idea of combining a trio of powerful 'characters' with 1-3 more expendable summons is interesting and well-implemented, the curse/enchant system is a novel take on your classic buff/status ailment setup that actually makes ailments worthwhile, and the story presents many challenging strategic scenarios for you to cut your teeth on, rather than just being 'kill everything on the map' every time.The big drawback that makes me unable to recommend it without reservation is how little it respects your time. Not only are all cutscenes and character interactions unskippable, you also can't fast-forward through the enemy moves... which may not SOUND so bad, but in the endgame, you're up against dozens of foes, most of whom will have passives, auras, wait-skills, and other miscellany that will make the enemy turn take ABSOLUTELY BLEEDING AGES. I can think of many ways that this could have been expedited, with a dedicated 'fast-forward' button - as can be found in, ironically, Disgaea - being the simplest and most straightforward. Perhaps doing your own thing without taking hints from the established juggernauts isn't ALWAYS a good thing?Time, time, ask me for anything but time... but, hey, if you DO have the time and patience to not get frustrated with how long a single turn can wind up taking, then it's a really good, wonderfully original game!

_childDocuments_.review: Posting this recommendation after 72 hours, my first playthrough-- though the game is not quite 70 hours long, which I will address later.I would heartily recommend this game to fans of games like Final Fantasy Tactics, or anyone who likes highly tactical, turn-based, grid-based RPGs. Unfortunately, my recommendation comes with some caveats:The game design, worldbuilding, visual and audio design are phenomenal,  an absolutely stunning homage to the best of PSX-era sprite graphics and music. The graphical presentation is colorful and expressive and fluid and it really draws you into the game's setting. Special shout-out to the soundtrack music by Sam English (according to the game's credits) which combines the sort of "standard fantasy" musical sound with an intriguing Western vibe.Top notch.What keeps this game from being an A+, 10/10 experience are many, frequent, glaring quality control issues-- it does not feel like a finished product. The in-game dialog is in desperate need of a couple of proofreading passes and the game crashed on me several times, including once that forced me to delete my save and start over-- except, for some reason, my new save file had *some* of the non-story advancements I'd acquired on my "deleted" save file.Call it a testament to just how good everything else about this game is that I persisted through my first playthrough-- and will now be starting my second, to see how much changes based on gameplay decisions.

The characters themselves are just as colorful as the scenery; their dynamic seems to be evolving over time as well and interactions change depending on who I bring to where. The soundtrack is full of jams too! There's a built-in crafting system for long-term buffs and a camping mini-game for temporary buffs between story events as well. The biggest draw is the combat mechanics. The options between Attacking, using your Wait skill, or Assisting in a single turn brings a lot of utility to all characters, something that I find  other tactics-esque games can be lacking in. Altogether, it's a fun game that I've already put 24 hours into within a week of purchase. The combat is addictive and I constantly find myself saying, "Just one more battle...". I highly recommend this to others.

_childDocuments_.review: Summary: If I could give this a neutral review, I would. Overall, the game is wonderful and functional, so I believe more people will enjoy it over not enjoy it. I was disappointed, but this game was still definitely worth the money for me. I played only on Hard difficulty. Analisys:Pros: (These are just good, no point in explaining)- Story: Cute and nice. It's not the best thing ever, but it's good enough to care about.- World: Fantastic and very well made. - Difficulty: Actually difficult. You need to understand what you want to do, plan and execute tactics in combat.- Gameplay and controls are okay. I would like things to move faster, but it was still serviceable. - Artstyle is very pretty in my opinion. Cons: (These are not good, and I explain why)- Since the game operates like FF Tactics, I had an expectation of being able to customize characters however I want to. In hard difficulty, this is not possible: The game's design around having to build the majority/entirety of the team for every single encounter forces the player to divert from whatever they imagined their characters or builds would be doing. - Some (allied) units(Fae) are unusable in Hard mode. Many of the units you can bring with you will simply result in a lost combat 80% of the time, simply because they cost too much and can't carry as much as other units. Simply put, if a unit can't attack and subsequently survive to the next round, it's literally worse than a unit that just follows the rest of the team and supports. Since every map has a LOT of enemies on it, no unit can stray from the main group. At all. Nothing can tank 6 hits between turns without other units healing it. Note: units that are bad in a player's hand are not bad in the enemy team because enemies are not limited by number. Something that costs as much as 4 units for you is something that will appear on the enemy side with 4 units supporting it. This is fine for difficulty's sake, but it just makes these units useless for the player.- Some decisions in the game are just bizarre. I didn't even understand that some of these were decisions. One example is a character tells your MC to come alone. I just figured that the MC will automatically go alone if I press the button, but no. Instead, when I arrived, it brought the full team and the NPC got mad at me. This strange mistake cost me in something that would not re-appear for the rest of the run. Overall, it's an enjoyable game. However, the imbalance of some units, combined with the difficulty, the counter-element mechanics in the game, and the ability to re-speciallize your leaders leads to being unable to customize your team the way you fantasize about, and takes away from the RPG feeling of the game leaving just a high-level tactical game behind it. Even without being an RPG it's still fun to play, but this is the realization that took me away from the game - I wanted to customize my leaders in certain ways, but it turns out that you MUST customize 90% of your party every fight in a way tailored to the fight or you will be flat-out unable to win.

_childDocuments_.review: This is actually really good. I remember reading a few reviews saying the battle would go forever with enemies shielding themselves, but honestly, the fights are very doable if you play your hand right on elemental weaknesses (always handy holding LB any time, thanks to game!).The core of the gameplay revolves around: 1) Elemental weaknesses (big deal)2) Pokemon (no, seriously!) to get more variety for countering elemental weaknesses. 3) Global damage effect cards both you and the leaders in the enemy team can use after a few turns of cooldown. 4) Passive and Offensive skills change depending on your element. What makes the game interesting to me is the collectible aspect. You start with your 3 heroes which gives you some variety from the get-go of the game possibilities. The dog can guard nearby allies and passively attack an enemy in a chain, provided he is beside the enemy. The girl can from the start "ghost" an ally to infiltrate heavily guarded enemies. The bird can swim and gain a bonus while doing so. Only certain units can swim or fly, and you can even later throw enemies in the water for the instant kill (or getting insta killed too!). From here the game adds more: Characters can equip scrolls for bonus modifiers. The girl elemental changes with some scrolls, granting her the associated strengths and weaknesses. You also have a chance to obtain the monster card when you killed it, which means you can now use it. Monsters come with different elements too and getting a new element open more possibilities. Elite monsters may drop their cards instead, also opening more global effect card options. Both global effect cards and monsters have a capacity you can increase over time too (but I won't say more to not spoil). The battles can get tricky even on normal and the game rewards you for not letting any unit die and even subdue all enemy elites without killing them. While the amount of detail may seem like a lot, the game does a good job introducing things slowly to you, and the loading screen offers tips as reminders too. At the end of the day, at the start of every battle, I found myself navigating the screen looking for the enemy weaknesses, and changing my hand both of Fae (your "pokemons") and spell cards (as some have elemental affinity), as that alone would dictate getting nuked with criticals, or nuking the enemy with critical, but not to the point it would make it a breeze.Totally recommend the game. It starts a bit slow for a veteran in games like this, but give it an hour, fight your first real boss, get a few Fae, and give the game a chance. You may be surprised. 9/10 - Would get knocked out on the water again by a witch. Just wish there was a bit more to the outer world.

_childDocuments_.review: It's really fun, and I love to see any games attempting to tackle the genre FFT sits in. This game does well with what it has, offering new ideas in the genre that I really like, but it's very limited by its scope. _childDocuments_.review: Fae Tactics is a neat little Tactical RPG that does its own thing, which is generally for the best.  There is quite a bit of content, especially for an indie game and there is an actual story as well, which is sadly something too many indie devs don't spend enough time fleshing out in general.  While not the most groundbreaking plot in the existence of gaming, I found the story engaging enough all the way to the end that I actually wanted to know what was going on.  The game has some charm to it, and even some humor sprinkled here and there to keep things entertaining.The systems in place are rather simple, but they work.  Instead of giving the player characters that have a gargantuan list of skills and abilities to learn, Fae Tactics keep it to a minimum.  Whenever you enter battle, your characters have one attack skill, one assist skill, and one passive skill that triggers on a turn that you wait without taking any action.  Your party leaders also have Ultra attacks and assist skills.  Furthermore, your party leaders also unlock more weapons as the story progresses, changing their role on the team.  Water weapons turn the unit into a healer type, for example, meaning there are quite a few possibilities for different party configurations.  Finally, each of your party leaders can also equip a scroll, that will usually buff statistics or give different advantages, or even change the usefulness of some abilities.On top of your party leaders, you also can get summons to take part into battle.  You collect those by getting their card after you defeat them into battle, making it also a bit of a monster collector of sorts.  Summons get no equipment or scrolls, meaning you can't change their role as you would with a party leader.  The strength of the summons you can carry in battle depend on how advanced your bike is.  You don't really ride the bike per say, but upgrading the bike is necessary to complete the game, and reaching all the areas of the game.  Most battles are pretty straight forward, with some more difficult ones along the way (usually boss battles).  The game is not really hard per say, especially if you have played other tactical RPGs before, but because the game gives the player a lot of leeway about the order the player tackles the content down, some areas/battles/bosses might seem extremely hard due to not having specific summons or party members unlocked yet.  As a result, the game gives the impression that it has uneven difficulty spikes, which is fine because save for one particular event, you can pretty much do any of the quest lines in any order you want, so if a boss gives you too much problems, you can usually just revisit the battle later.All in all, it is a pretty solid title.  The only net negative I have to mention is that sadly, Fae Tactics utilizes the overused and utterly unfun "Save the NPC" battles at times with an NPC with the IQ of a swiss cheese.  Think Rafa in FFT, or Arycelle or Haborym in Tactics Ogre.  Some battles also need for you to wait on an NPC to go stand on a tile.  In one particular instance, the NPC would just not go in that direction at all, which definitely can be frustrating.  Thankfully, Fae Tactics has a "Retry" option that allows you to reset the battle (without having to go through the dialogue again).Otherwise, very fun game and totally worth the price tag, which at the moment of this review, is 19.99$.  A solid 8/10 for me, definitely worth a playthrough if you are a fan of the genre.

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoyed my time with this game. It does bring back some nostalgia with regards to Final Fantasy Tactics, a game that I truely loved.In this game  you play various tactical battles with your party of up to 6 characters against various groups in different compositions. There are 2 kinds of team members: story characters (which can have equipment and story quests, and also specced with perk-points as they level up) and summons. For both groups the members can level up as you use them more in battles (or get less XP passively when benched) and you can field up to 3 of them. Each character belongs to a particular element, each with favorable and unfavorable matchups against other elements, and each character typically has different mobility options, (triggered) passives, attacks and support abilities. Playing around with them, finding nice synergies and optimal team composition for a given oponent composition I found enjoying.I would describe combat as okay. After some time, combat felt biased towards min-maxing element matches, verticality and dealing large amounts of damage yourself and the oponent where nuance seems to start falling to the background. This was the point in the game that I started no longer enjoying it, which was after roughly 23 hours of gameplay.The amount of customization you have available is sizeable. Team composition (determining synergies between member like their support abilities or attack/movement patterns) plays a big role as mentioned earlier, but also the items/perk customization makes for some nice exploratory gameplay. And then there is the ability to bring 3 spells into combat, each with their own effects and cooldowns.The parts that I did not enjoy as much, was the story telling, menu navigation and the controls. I found the narrative not interesting and there wasn't really a way for me to skip them. So certain sections I just had to 'grind' through the layers of dialog boxes until I got to the part of the game that I at least enjoyed. And if you lose are particular battle: tough, do that dialog grind over.Controls and menu navigation can be described as clunky. The usaged of the mouse in the game feels... off. Somehow the feedback just doesn't feel right to me.Oh, and lastly there is the 'cooking' mini-game, which is some needless distraction that gives you some random free buff by playing a kind of memory game with a time/turn-limit. This could have been turned in perhaps a more interesting custimization option instead.All in all, I do think I got my money's worth out of this game, even though I got 'burned out' on it after some significant time playing it. So yeah, get's a thumbs up from me! :)

_childDocuments_.review: Ever since Final Fantasy Tactics, I have had an itch for Tactics genre games. _childDocuments_.review: Very cool game with great art, story and music HOWEVER you have to do really special things, like saving a random NPC in one mission, upgrade certain objects before a certain time, not kill certain monsters, play a certain amount of time with X character, and all other type of secret objectives to either get characters that you can DEFINITELY miss or weapons that you can also miss...all this culminating in the fact that if you didn't do EVERYTHING right you can't have the perfect ending :S. _childDocuments_.review: It's hard to say if this game is good or not. It's fairly simple, which is neither good or bad. There's some major problems with proofreading, though. Mama (a word you'll be seeing a *lot*) is sometimes capitalized and sometimes it isn't, regardless of what grammar would say. If there's a use for the reflex stat, I don't recall it ever being mentioned. The victory conditions don't always tell you the truth and sometimes one person holds both sides of the conversation. Despite that, the game does have its moments, though having two different harvesting minigames is probably one too many. An extremely qualified yes, I would say.

_childDocuments_.review: A joy of a game. If you're a fan of tactic games this is one that manages to have clear inspirations taken from other games through the years but maintains its own strong identity. Very solid story, does exactly what it wants to do, and doesn't overstay its welcome. Run through story mode, twice if you want to do it on both difficulties, and you'll have a grand time. Leave 100% runs for if you just really like free battling.Pros:Cons:

_childDocuments_.review: Excellent and simple, Fae Tactics was a nice return to isometric tactial RPGs a la Final Fantasy Tactics (99% sure that's what this is based off of, anyway).General combat mechanics takes an interesting approach to what I would expect from most strategy games, as rather than having many characters that have different distributions of stats and skills based off of classes or weapon loadouts, Fae Tactics has its roles for playable units and enemies very consolidated. For example, all Water units have forms of healing and all Fire units have skills that let other units deal more damage.With this, gameplay does not see as much customization as one would have in Final Fantasy Tactics, where mixing and matching classes would allow for a ridiculous number of possibilities, including many gamebreaking ones. That said, Fae Tactics is very well balanced due to this and the only ridiculous unit one may obtain is only near the end of the game.In terms of story and dialogue, the dialogue sometimes feels slow due to the camera usually needing to pan over a character before they speak if it's on a battle arena. The overall story feels very loose throughout the majority of the game, only showing hints of any plotlines tying together maybe 60% of the way through the game. Overall, though, it's serviceable and I felt as though it did have decently well-thought plotlines.Despite the game mostly being about following various storylines with what felt like little leeway into sidequests, there is good enough freedom to do grinding and even do optional sidequests. I actually missed a couple of equipment pieces due to killing certain enemies or not bringing a character in a related quest. Take that however you will, but I enjoyed how unknown the game is and the lack of guides or anything.Overall, Fae Tactics was a fun experience. I didn't 100% and haven't done the New Game+, as I am not sure when I'll end up getting to it due to moving on to other games, but it was a great romp, getting to flex my brain matter in fights. But not flexing *too* hard--the normal mode was certainly easier than speed chess--but a fun ~40 hours regardless.
_childDocuments_.name: Fae Tactics

_childDocuments_.review: You liked Final Fantasy Tactics (1, advance, a2) ?You will LOVE this game !It innovates is some aspect that make the turns go quicker without lessening the possibilities.This game is hard, even on normal, and will make you learn the simple and advanced concepts of the game as you discover new things. So play on normal first.When you finish it and experienced its great story, go look at Fellseal Arbiters Mark for a more FFT-like TTRPG with a more modern approach.The swiftness and low menuing in Fae Tactics will make you understand the greatness of its simplicity yet immensly rich gameplay
_childDocuments_.name: Fae Tactics

_childDocuments_.review: This game is reminiscent of Final Fantasy Tactics.  Overall I would recommend it, though there are also some game design elements that could use further work.Pros:-Simple interface when using a mouse and keyboard (haven't tried with controller)-Slow progression that allows for easy learning of game dynamics-Fun graphics and sprites-Cool and innovative combat mechanics that are captivating-A dog companion!Cons:-There can be a strong sense of randomness to the games where a single misstep can flip the entire balance of power on the board - particularly if by RNG the computer makes several smart moves in a row.  Difficulty seems to be primarily built around "give the computer lots of guys - then the AI will derp itself to a reasonable level of difficulty".  While this can lead to a feeling that "you haven't won until you have won", it can also lead to going through the motions again following a loss-The elements feature feels a bit too much like rock/paper/scissors.  The right elemental combination can wipe out a map easily, while the incorrect one makes a map impossible-Story feels a bit all over the place.  The world is cross-over between sorta steam punk, sorta pure fantasy.  I enjoyed the framework for the world, but the characters and progression of the story didn't stick the landing for me
_childDocuments_.name: Fae Tactics

_childDocuments_.review: There are a TON of "Tactics" style games out there and this one is a Gem.The tightness of the mechanics takes some getting used to. - This isn't like the other tactics RPGs where you can unga-bunga to winSimple and effective.I agree with some other comments that the story isn't something to write home about - but if we're being honest with ourselves, its still better than 8/10 of the games in the same genre. At least the world and visuals are *interesting* and *different*.Art is gorgeous, everyone can see that. EXCEPT Peony's portrait leaves a lot to be desired. I wish she didn't have her mouth open like that for the entire game. We're in a city being oppressed by a totalitarian techno-religious state and she has the "OOOOO" expression from Speed racer every time she speaks....All that being said, 9/10 I recommend this game to all my friends

_childDocuments_.review: 7/10Take Final Fantasy Tactics advance(FFTA), strip away all job progression, remove reaction/support/actions skills mastery, and add in a sprinkle of Pokemon, we get Fae Tactics. It scratches the itch left by Final Fantasy Tactics, but without the "build your own character" that some player of FFT might like.I like the way they manage to streamline the combat system so much that we have a truly menuless combat.Making skills that seemed like a no brainer skill to use while there are no enemies in attack range (the 'Take Aim' skill in FFTA's Archer) be a "wait" skill is just brilliant. Having support skill tied to the element also means that we don't need to purposefully build a support oriented character, as with the right element the damage dealer can also be a support.Because all obtainable characters (excluding summons) are named, they will most likely go through a series of character arc. Almost every new weapon that they obtain ties in to their character story arc, which really make the weapon feels special to the character.The music (other than the menu screen theme song) felt very in tuned with the environment of the game, It is very reminiscent of GBA era music. There is the familiar "hype up for battle" track, the "♥♥♥♥'s about to go down" track, and my favourite: A certain boxing fighter's  theme. I love that when I hear the music in loading screen going into battles I can grasp what kind of fight I'm going into. And inversely, when the music pauses and there is only total silent in the loading screen, I'll know that this fight is going to be intense AF.The main character, Peony, is not as good a character in battle and in story. Battle wise, she can deal damage via changing elements to deal "super effective" damage, but is outclass by other attacker, and there are summons that can tank better than her. The worst part is that, despite being mediocre in almost everything, she is required to participate in every combat. As by design she is the only one who can summon creatures and cast spells. Story wise, she is the typical kind hearted shounen anime protag that wants to help everybody that she can because "helping is good", which makes her fall flat at times and there doesn't seem to be a stake involve for her story arc.  By designing a menuless combat, this game sacrificed the options in combat that allowed on the fly change of tactics. For example in FFTA, an Archer can learn a bunch of shots that can inflict various status ailment, which allow one to disarm(disable), immobilize, blind, or charm enemies, which might mean adverting the crisis of losing the backline. This game only have spells which can kinda equate, hence players are forced to strategize for the fight before hand, and hope that the 3 spells they took into combat can act as a backup plan, or forcing a strategy to work.The scrolls which is the only part that felt like "building" a character felt imbalanced. Some scrolls are so op with certain characters that it should just be always equipped with that character , while some scrolls are just there to gather dust in the game data. It felt like the scrolls can play a much bigger role, like giving certain special abilities to the user, allowing chaining attacks, lower enemy resistance to status ailment on hit, allow changing of movement types, allow changing the defense element typing from the offense element typing, the list goes on. It felt like there is just so much more potential to unlock from this but as of current, it feels underwhelming.Play this game for the gameplay, the story is....adequate. If you like SRPGs, give this game a try and you might like it. It falls short on certain aspect and there are still some bugs lingering in the game, but with devs still actively updating this game I hope that the bugs will be gone for good.
_childDocuments_.name: Fae Tactics

_childDocuments_.review: Simplest thing I can say about this game is "it scratches the itch left behind by Final Fantasy Tactics:Advance, that I honestly haven't been able to find many other games with this particular style in a very long time. It's more focused on individual units than games like Fire Emblem or Wargrove that try to cover a whole battlefield, and personally, that specific difference is my jam.Gameplay is solid, though each individual turn is generally a little on the simpler side with each unit usually only having 2-3 actions available, but it plays well and there is a decent amount of strategy. One thing I really like is the ability to 'aid' allies instead of just passing your turn, most characters can do at least something during their turn so it feels less wasteful. The game gives you a decent amount of information at any moment, so you can make moderately informed decisions about opponents actions, once you learn what each unit does. While the story isn't anything crazy, it is interesting, with characters that are more than just 1 note personalities and some interesting questions that left me curious where the game was going.I genuinely do recommend the game, the sprites are visually distinct and easy to identify, there's generally a decent variety of options to change up your strategy in combat, and it's not easy, however there are a handful of things that do get very frustrating. The following is a list of general nitpicks that I found annoyed me/ I would like to see changed, but even with these, I have been enjoying the game so far and recommend any fan of the "smaller battle / single unit tactics" genre give it a shot1. One of my biggest gripes is that I don't believe the game allows you enough detailedinformation to make good decisions in advance. This is mostly the apparent with several bosses with certain special attacks. You get to see certain things when examining the boss before a fight, but 20 turns in when you learn the boss has a "everyone near me dies" attack and you brought lots of melee units to deal with his minions.. that doesn't feel fair when you're forced to reset from information you didn't have access to.2. This game has a MAJOR focus on a "rock/paper/scissors" aka a type advantage system, however it seems.. rather extreme. Example: enemy boss is surrounded by fire minions, so bring a water creature to deal with them. Except the boss is electric, so the moment your water creature gets in range, the boss simply walks forward, and one shots not only the water creature, but the 3 people behind him as well. This often leads to spending several turns baiting the minions far away from the boss so he hopefully won't join in the fight, instead of any more interesting strategy 2b. This is demonstrated even more extremely when a boss has almost 1000 health, and one character with an advantageous element may do 600 damage in one attack... meanwhile everyone else will maybe do 30-100 damage at most. This ends up with several boss fights just being "get this one person in range and hope you don't miss so she can 1shot him" instead of being more strategically in depth, such as trying to set up combos between units. It also severely limits the units you can bring, because if you don't bring "water for fire boss" then you're left to plinking away at his massive health bar while he 1 shots units from accross the arena, except many of his minions are super effective against water units. I understand this is where strategy of 'defending your units' comes in, but it often feels rather cheap when an enemy minion will suicide charge into your whole team to murder one of yours (permanently) only for the boss to resummon him a few turns later3. To kind of focus the point a little bit, enemy bosses seem to be a bit overtuned, while enemy minions seem to be undertuned, quite often it's possible for one character to kill an enemy minion in a single hit, even when not doing 'super effective' damage, and yet enemy bosses are able to soak up 10-20 hits from anything that isn't 'super effective' AND kill multiple units every turn (even when doing 'not very effective' damage) This is compounded even more as, the more time you take to kill minions, the longer a boss will just sit there and constantly buff themselves, causing a very frustrating loop of "rush in and aggro the boss as fast as possible... so he starts 1shotting units, but doesn't sit there buffing himself" or "take 10 turns to kill all the minions so nothing can interfere with you fighting the boss, but he has now buffed himself so much it will take another 10 turns to kill him, hope you can kill him before he murders all your units"4. The game has a modest crafting system, when you beat enemies, they might drop a crafting component, this is fine, as it gives you alternate targets on the field, but I really wish that there was some way to "pick up item next to you" quite often I find myself killing a target, who drops an item 1 space over, then wasting that unit's next turn taking just one step to pick up the thing that enemy dropped. This often leads to fights feeling quite drawn out as my units take very small steps, killing a target, then looting, or I'm leaving the last unit in a fight alive with 1-2 health left while i spend multiple turns running units around the field to pick things up. This gets extra frustrating, because the game rewards you for beating fights quickly, yet wants you to waste extra turns picking things up5. the 'ultra' attack animations start to feel like they drag on if a fight has been going on for a while, I would appreciate a way to speed them up.5b. as well, when one unit "gives shield to everyone nearby" it would be nice if the camera didn't take 2 seconds to pan to each individual person (who is already on screen)6. I appreciate how the game has certain challenges "beat the battle in few turns" and "don't finish off enemy bosses" to get bonus rewards/exp. but this feels a bit like a broken "win more" loop. But if you are in a position where your units are strong enough to kill multiple bosses at once, in only a few hits, then you probably are strong enough you don't need that extra exp. Especially given how i feel bosses are 'overtuned' as mentioned before7. This may be a very minor nitpick, but it's left me confused for quite a while. In this world, a witch is defined as "a human who can use magic" and our main character is a human, who can use magic, yet she constantly insists "I am not a witch" and several hours into the plot, still has not explained how she is different, or why it matters
