_childDocuments_.review: This is an excellent tactics game. It has a compelling story and characters with art that's always enjoyable to look at (though just a tiny bit more graphical polish in the UI elements would have gone a long way). More than anything, the combat system is great. It's challenging, so it forces you to engage with it instead of just blazing ahead mindlessly, and it's very rewarding when it all comes together. If you like tactics RPGs, add this one to your list.
_childDocuments_.name: Fae Tactics

_childDocuments_.review: This game brings me back to my nostalgic days of playing Final Fantasy Tactics on my Gameboy Flip thingy.I absolutely love it, if you are a fan of Turn-Based Strategy this game certainly scratches that itch and does it in a fun way. I enjoy the difficulty as well, since nowadays I find that it's a bit easy to play these types of games. I would like to see one improvement and that is a tweak to the AI, I wish they would all attack me at once, I think the game thinks I can't handle it. But I think I can. Anyway, Would be fun to have a difficulty meter for us to decide :) Thanks for making this wonderful game.
_childDocuments_.name: Fae Tactics

_childDocuments_.review: Strategy elements are interesting and varied enough, the story is some fluffy fairytale for when you just want to relax with silly BS nonsense. Unfortunately the game is too console-ish. You can only save from the map, not in-battle. And there are series of 3-5 very intensive battles that you have to go through because you lose all progress when exiting. Oh, and babysitting dumb NPC "allies" is huge pain in the A, I thought the game industry has grown out of this nonsense.
_childDocuments_.name: Fae Tactics

_childDocuments_.review: This is probably the best Tactical RPG I've played since Final Fantasy Tactics. I've played a lot of these. Everything from Vandal Hearts, Tactics: Ogre, Fell Seal, to Children of Zodiarcs. The gameplay is refreshing. It does something traditional, and new. Instead of having tons of tedious menus, you can use just your mouse and a single hand to do all actions. NO MENUS! Everything from attacks, movement, ultimate moves, enchantments, and spells. All without any menus!The story is interesting. Most stories get too bogged down by trying to be complicated and boring, but this one is light and refreshing. A girl looking for her mom who helps people and makes friends along the way.You collect units you defeat in battle and summon them to help you. It's that Pokemon sort of Aesthetic, or like in FF:T when you charm someone to your team.I only have a single complaint. Your characters can equip 1 of 42 scrolls. Instead of showing a spreadsheet of the scrolls, you have to cycle through all 42, one at a time.That's it. That is my only complaint. You have to cycle through a single item.Update after completing the game:It's an amazing game. My favorite Tactical RPG to date. It even beats out Final Fantasy Tactics. The gameplay, mechanics, and story are just so good.I beat it in 46 hours and I only did 2 hours of grinding. It's a very long game and you will get your money's worth.
_childDocuments_.name: Fae Tactics

_childDocuments_.review: My favorite game this year. It's a spiritual successor to my favorite childhood game, Final Fantasy Tactics Advance. The combat is fun and I appreciate just the right level of complexity between the stat system, weapons, and characters. The story is written in a way that quickly makes you care about the characters, and the music is 10/10. The pixel art is wonderful and the Pokemon-esque Fae collection grew on me (had to get those 6 secret Fae!). If there is anything I can do to support the developers and pray for DLC, a sequel, or another tactics game like this -- I'm dying to help.
_childDocuments_.name: Fae Tactics

_childDocuments_.review: -Beautiful pixel art backed up by an appropriate soundtrack-Deep tactical combat on the back of positioning, distance, height difference, basic and support abilities, ultra abilities that get charged as the fight goes on, global spells you can bring along and an additional elements system (ie. water counters fire but is weak against air)-Battle screen as clean as can be, no disturbing details, while at the same time every detail you could need is available via hover-Team setup, character customization and spell pool all adjustable on the fly pre-combat saving you all the downtime of wandering between menus -Various battle arenas and enemy setups keep the onslaught on fights interesting-Between fights you can take a break playing a cooking minigame for temporary buffs, further tweaking your setup or upgrading your inventory for permanent stat boosts or other advantages (ie. increased xp or loot gain etc.)-Nothing major after almost 10 hours of gameplay-A few suggestions: hotkeys for every action you can take for comfort; once in a blue moon it could come in handy if you could rotate the board; alternative portraits could spice up the conversations and last but not least making it easier to figure out where to go to follow a specific story line I think it's pretty obvious  whether you're a rookie or a vet tactics player. Just a tip for your journey: if a fight appears to be unfair or unmanageable, instead of brute forcing it, try a different team composition or stat setup.
_childDocuments_.name: Fae Tactics

_childDocuments_.review: Very cute little game. If you like Final Fantasy Tactics or Disgaea, have a look at this one. If you're interested in getting into these types of games, this is probably a good one to start on as things have been streamlined a lot; each turn a character can move, and then attack an enemy, assist an ally or wait, buffing themselves. Its nice to have something this simple to chill out with, but so far I feel it lacks the depth that other games in this genre have. So if you're a veteran, and want complexity and control, this might be /too/ streamlined for you. (eg you can't save ultimate moves, you have to use them as soon as you have them) I'm enjoying it so far though I do prefer Disgaea so far for its depth, as I've played a fair few games like this.
_childDocuments_.name: Fae Tactics

_childDocuments_.review: Would recommend this to anyone who is into tile turn based strategy games or who want to feel what they're like. The game itself can be rather harsh during battles, so if you lose on turn 20(example), you'll have to restart the entire fight. I'd also recommend reading/paying attention to the lore on the tip screen or what the characters are saying during interaction as it'll serve for the character's plot. Overall really good game for those who wish to improve their thinking, get a good laugh, enjoy TB(tile-turn based) games and want to look at a game with interesting lore(personally.)
_childDocuments_.name: Fae Tactics

_childDocuments_.review: pretty good overall, however my one complaint is that the game has a tendency to throw you into a chain of multiple fights without any warning one after another, thankfully the game saves between these fights and you can still swap out items and party members freely, but if you want to back out and go to a new area for a bit, say if a difficult mission is frustrating you or you just want a change of scenery, you'll have to restart the entire chain, it's really not that big a deal though
_childDocuments_.name: Fae Tactics

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who loves tactics games in general, and has been disappointed by quite a few of the more recent ones to come out from various game devs, Fae Tactics hits that perfect feel of what a tactics game needs. Challenging without being impossible. Diverse but not overwhelming cast of playable characters. Absolutely AMAZING music by Sam English. Unique mechanics. A mostly well written story with just a couple iffy lines here and there.Honestly, fell in love with this game's characters and style, and it's most likely my game of the year.

_childDocuments_.review: This is what happens when you want to make Final Fantasy Tactics, but never, ever want the player to have to look at a menu screen during combat. Turns out you don't really need that endless list of abilities where you only ever use three. You can cut everyone down to three abilities and let the player figure out which ones to use where. Play it because you already played Fell Seal, and you want to try something a little different this time.

_childDocuments_.review: Review em portugues no link: English Review: I met Fae Tactics when looking for games in the style of Pokémon. Games where I could train creatures and use them to get into fight against others. In the video in question, Fae Tactics was present. I really liked what I saw, but I still didn't have a fixed idea of buying it. So in June,the temporary Steam Demo was released and that's where I tried it for the first time. Those who already know the blog know about the experience since I already made a post about his demo here. Anyway ,release date arrived and I was able to purchase the game.he story starts from a simple point: Peony, our protagonist, is a human who manages to manipulate Mana (basically magic) and went in search of her Mama, as she calls her mother. Accompanied by Chico, the dog and Payachin, a bird of the Pio-pio breed, they set off in search. As Peony can’t Not help anyone in trouble, she continually deviates from her journey,at the same time not so much. All of this is just the beginning of something bigger. The game has several stories from the regions, some more and others less tied to the main story.After a few small tutorials, the world gradually expands, starting with the Doro region, most characterized by its deserts. Each battle involving history unfolds bringing new characters, new locations and a new depth to the world.Battles take place in turns and move in squares. The correct position to defeat enemies without giving them a chance to react, or prepare it’s one of the most influential mechanics in the game. It is so important to know where to place your team since if you don’t pay attention, they can be instantaneously killed or be harmed by other elements on the map.The team is limited to up to 6 members, one of which must be Peony. By her side, two more units categorized as leaders, which are usually the condition for victory and losses in battles. Defeat enemy leaders and win. Of course, it's not that simple and that's where the magic of the game comes in: Peony summons copies of the creatures known as Fae, but her powers are limited by her summoning ability (which can be increased throughout the game). These creatures are the second major component of the game's versatility.The third component is spells, which vary between support and damage. Each has a number of turns to charge and recharge and only three types can be used in a battle. It is always good to pay attention to the enemies of the level and take units and spells  that benefit you in some way against them.You will definitely have to exchange spells, Fae and Leaders,maybe even often. This is quite interesting, as it will force you to experiment with units that you might not normally have, until you are surprised by their usefulness(or not). While some Fae are outclassed by others,Leaders have all their own strengths and you won’t feel like some are worse than others, it becomes more of a situational necessity.The difficulty of the game is well leveled. While smaller battles are relatively easy, boss battles are much more difficult, since some of them always have a catch. Ultimately, these little surprises made everything more dynamic, making rethinking, positioning and strategies a necessity to face challenges.The soundtrack of this game is wonderful. I can go days without even playing and at the same time have fresh themes in my mind. Sam English did a lot of work, managing to achieve happy, mysterious and tense themes. The soundtrack  follows all the moments perfectly.The main story unfolds little by little, and obviously Peony will be related to the events. Still, I was surprised by the number of tragic events that occur in the story, one of the characters I love the most suffering the most. All "leader" characters have a past to deal with  and each with their own personality, fights for it.The game has casual updates, partly bug fixes, however the developers hope to add more content to the game, something they apparently did with their previous games (Valdis Story and Legend of Fae).The game has high replayability too, especially for those looking to complete everything, including all good endings.Fae Tactics was the first game of the year that I was excited about and that met my expectations. I loved the characters and the world, Peony and her friends will be kept in my memory for a while.As for the game, I plan to revisit in a harder  difficulty and who knows maybe I’ll get all the good endings. Very recommended for those who enjoy RPGs and tactical games.
_childDocuments_.name: Fae Tactics

_childDocuments_.review: A worthy love letter to Tactical RPGs and Monster Tamer games!The battle system is intuitive and not overly complicated, while still giving enough depth to truly strategize your position. Are you above or below an enemy? Do you have multiple units adjacent to your target? Which direction are you attacking from? Are there stage hazards? Everything matters in your decision making!Fae Tactic's soundtrack is atmospheric and absolutely enjoyable. It helps underline the fantastical themes of the games without ever being boring or repetitive. Truly hoping for a vinyl release at some point *fingers crossed*The character and monster design is also stunning. Lots of attention to detail in beautiful and high quality pixel art and the monster variation is amazing. When it comes to Monster Tamer games there's often dull designs or ones you not feel as much as others (which is totally normal and a preference thing), but for this title it happened multiple times where I have been like "I can NOT let that one slip away". Overall if you are a fan of either genre I feel like you can get enough out of the game for you to have some good fun, but if you enjoy both of these genres you are straight up missing out on not giving it a chance!
_childDocuments_.name: Fae Tactics

_childDocuments_.review: What a marvelous game! I've been craving for another EndlessFluff game for years and this was an incredible reward.With such a simple mecanic of choosing to attack, assist and waiting and not a list of different moves for each character/class, the game can be seen as too simple and repetitive, but it's certainly not the case.The game gives you plenty of choices to explore different tatics and rewards you by trying different approchs with a great sensation of "I did it!". Some battles seem impossible to do without the right setup, but once you get the hang of the game and what are your available resources, you can experiment more dynamic playstyle than spamming ranged attacks while getting out of range from the boss.There are a lot of secrets, so don't feel bad if you miss some stuff on your first playthrough. Keep exploring so you can find different weapons, characters, summons and spells.Finally, storywise, it's not necessary for you to play the previous games from the studio, but you get a nice plus from knowing some references. The game narrative is simple but you understand the feelings of each character and starts to relate to then, wanting to know more.Definitely a buy at full price! Hours of fun and more rewarding than many AAA games that I played recently.

_childDocuments_.review: Much like Valdys Story, this game is completely and utterly amazing!When you take into consideration this game was made by 2 people everything goes from awesome to unbelievable!Th story is awesome, the characters are fun and quirky, it has excellent female characters, the art is amazing, the music and sounds are incredible! I could keep singing high praises for this game forever, honestly.Valdys Story quickly became my favorite metroidvania after the 2D Metroids, but Fae Tactics is hands down my favorite Tactics like game by a long shot!Even though i love FFTA and FFTA2 to death this game takes the cake easily, the way they rethinked tactics combat mechanics and team building into something completely and insanely fluid is award worthy! Ive had so much fun having to reconstruct my teams to beat the harder stages it was unreal!Honestly, if you like Tactics games, do yourself a favor and buy this game, you will not be let down.And if you play and reach Dagon and go "F-this game its too hard!!" just remember that you have to rebuild your team and choose different spells, think outside the box and you will start to understand the beauty of this games mechanics!

_childDocuments_.review: For those who loved final fantasy tactics and tactics ogre, it's no surprise this game is fun. The game is rough at some edges, but it's a great game and i wish more like it existed. The story is charming and not too dense, the gameplay is on point, art and animation are cutesy and lovingly done, even though i'm not in love with the art style it works. At the core this is a spiritual succesor to those games and it plays great.  Each character can only move and then either attack, help an ally or wait. sometimes that wait triggers a skill too, so it's really fast and easy to play.The whole game is designed around encounters, so the time spent in pure story is not too long, the story moves mainly through encounters, and the pacing is great, that's what reminds me most of FFTactics Advance. Theres not too many "cutscenes" or pure dialog encounters, and when they appear they are snappy and interesting. Writing is fine, and the unique mechanics are very interesting. The way you start summoning the enemies to fight with you, it's like pokemon meets FFT, in short, the progression is relevant and fun, and you get many ways to tune your strategy.Much like FFTA, the game is not too easy. I mean, it isn't really "hard", it's just challenging enough that you can't just stomp your way into the encounters with mere levels, you need to pay attention to enemy type, and have a general plan, the fact that you ocassionally lose or retry an encounter is quite fun, because games like xcom are spotty in balance, those can be either too easy or to punishing depending on your settings. Now, not all is well. The font is objectively ugly. and the way it's just inserted on top of pixel art elements is just... not great. It's quite dissonant. And that is what i dislike about the game, the UX design is not the best. There are elements that are not clear and never explained, the scaling seems odd and the fonts just make it look like a visual novel. The "eat" minigame it's just a nuissance to me, but that's personal preference. Finally, what i miss. Jobs. Thats what i loved the most, tinkering with jobs, leveling my characters and making those stories in my head. I really wish some form of job progression existed. Equipment and weapons. I really love tinkering with the detailed stuff for each character and class, and in Fae Tactics this has been streamlined, along with magic and special skills.All said, i wholeheartedly recommend it and i hope Endlessfluff does more games like it.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is not Tactics Ogre. It does not have complex, interelated stat boosts/class stats/relationship whatevers. Fae Tactics is delightfully simple with each character having an average of 3.4 different actions they can take on any given turn. Another cool part of Fae Tactics is that it encourages customizability. You can completely reorganize the stats of any leader unit from the before fight screen and there are all different kinds of summon units that can fit any kind of playstyle. The game is also cute, for lack of a better word. Most of the characters have charm to them and each line they say is more likely to be enjoyable than not so. Summarized: Good game, fun.

_childDocuments_.review: I've been waiting for Fae Tactics since I first saw a preview of the artwork, and I've finally got hold of it and have to say I wasn't disappointed at all. I never got to play the original Final Fantasy Tactics games to compare but it's generally being said that FT is a spiritual successor to those games, and tonally from what I've seen I think that's accurate, although this game's writing is a little weaker than what you'd expect from a AAA studio - whatever. The game looks AMAZING, in a slow-burning, subtle way with a fair breadth of character and location designs that get switched up a lot and shown at different times of day, which is a lovely touch.  Crucially though, the gameplay does live up to the design, for me at least. Level design is solid, with a strong emphasis on building your team for the specific battle you're going into. The different units are fun to collect and strategically meaningful, and there's a lot of room for putting together interesting synergies.

_childDocuments_.review: Fae Tactics is an excellent turn-based tactics RPG, and well worth the twenty bucks I paid for it.Players follow Peony, a young witch, as she travels through a world changed by the fusion of the magic and non-magic realms, in search of her mother. The story is relatively standard fare: as you travel, things get complicated. You pick up companions along the way, level up, and become capable of more diverse tactics. The game limits you, with a few exceptions, to three main characters on the field at once and up to three summoned monster characters, earned by defeating creatures in fights. Each character is assigned an element with strengths and weaknesses, encouraging players to rotate characters in and out. I found it satisfying to have to consider both my offensive and defensive choices before battles. Players can also select three spells for Peony to cast in battle, which was especially helpful to shore up weaknesses or overcome unique tactical needs. Because of this mechanic, Peony is required in your party, and tactical choices often need to take into account protecting her, because if she is knocked unconscious, you lose the ability to use those spells. Each character gets a chance to shine in sidequests that unlock further equipment options, and a trait system allows you to customize your characters before each fight.A story event in this game is often more than one fight; events can contain up to four battles in a row, which can be fun but exhausting as well. The game does perform an autosave before combat, though, so it's easy to take a break if you're tired or frustrated with a battle. On the flip side, because combat can take so long, defeats still sometimes feel punishing, even when you can start that stage of the event over right away. In practice, once I stopped trying to rush into combat and gained more diversity in tactics, I lost much less.The focus on different tactical choices is where Fae Tactics really shines. Some maps have environmental effects that can help or harm your characters. There are fights that are defensive in nature, where characters need only survive several rounds. I had fights where the best strategy was to keep the party close together and maximize combo attacks and teamwork, where other fights required characters to spread out to handle multiple threats at once. Occasionally, this leads to frustrations (escorting an uncontrollable NPC to a particular point on the map was rough), but unlike similar games like Final Fantasy Tactics or Fell Arbiter, once I beat a fight, I had a strong sense that my tactics, not my levels or sheer number of abilities, were what got me through.In between fights, Fae Tactics uses an item/crafting system and a cooking minigame to further enhance your party. There's nothing particularly exciting there, for the most part, but it does give the player a chance to wind down for a minute or two between battles. The crafting system does tie in to unlocking more areas, which lead to new story events in the game, as well as the ability to summon stronger monsters, so it does motivate the player to collect items during fights.There are enough secrets and sidequests that I didn't manage to do everything in Fae Tactics on my first playthrough, but it apparently has a new game+ option that I look forward to trying out. My first playthrough took about 60 hours, so if you're looking to fill some time, this is an excellent game for it. It seems like, right now, not a lot of people are playing this game, but I hope that this changes, because it definitely satisfies that tactical RPG itch.

_childDocuments_.review: I was in love with the art and new mechanics, but I can't fully enjoy or recommend it right now.My first discontent was with the lack of items and customization - with the only differentiation being the addition of percentages for some statuses as the units level up, which gives no sense of reward. The monsters that you can summon have no possible customization and are extremely fragile having a very limited utility. The initial position is not determined by the player (HUGE FAIL to a tactical game). There is no currency, shops, consumables and gear besides a piece for which there are only 3 options for each main character - really breaking the rpg vibe. There is an extreme lack of information on relevant and impactful content such as the influence of the zodiac, what are the ultra (especial moves) that bosses can do, which and how events "may change over time" and daily bonuses and modifications leading to a feeling of uncertainty averse to the tactical planning that the game requires.It would be great if there was an in game codex where you could check a guide and tips about the features, mechanics and all important factors that can lead to irreparable mistakes. I’m asking for the minimum information on what can influence the run, they don't need to be detailed if the devs want to intentionally leaves things to be discovered, but please provide the basic so that the player can know what to consider when planning his saga (especially for min-max players).There is also a lot of content that can be lost due to random and unknown factors. Weapons that can only be dropped at limited times in history, suicidal NPC that influence the saga, spells that can only be taken on a single map and bosses that need to be defeated in a specfic way (being extra hard as defeating then without killing the leaders) to reward you with a quest. In addition to enemies stepping on top of your items or talismans (and so deleting then) that can only be acquired by luck from enemies that appear very few times.It's okay for an item or achievement to be missable, but there are so MANY OF THEM. You really can’t just enjoy the run because there are a lot of factors (which the game doesn’t even clarify) that can result in the loss of very important content forcing you to restart the same fight countless times in several situations.
_childDocuments_.name: Fae Tactics

_childDocuments_.review: This game is so charming and fun! The characters are written so well. The battles have a learning curve, but they are not overly difficult, just enough to challenge you and make you think. I have deeply enjoyed this game and I definitely recommend it to anyone that likes fantasy and/or tactics games!

_childDocuments_.review: Phew, I'm done!This was an exciting game, I started it for the idea of having a tactics game with an amazing pixel art style but I stayed for the amazing cast and surprising complexity - far beyond what the demo even showed. There are so many battles here I was flawed on until I swapped in the perfect team, and the cast of characters and summons are so diverse (especially when you realise you can unlock additional equipment and spells to further customise your party).Really pleased, time well spent. I played through on normal and found most of it managable, bar a few of the boss fights. Luckily there is only one point where you get "locked out" of training in other levels and its all well signposted.
_childDocuments_.name: Fae Tactics

_childDocuments_.review: On the whole, this is a really fun tactics style game. The characters are cute, the world and lore is interesting, and its definitely challenging. It's definitely worth picking up and playing if you enjoy SRPGs.However, with that said, the game isn't perfect. There's some clunkiness with swapping accessories and changing party members (I didn't even realize I could change party members for the first few missions that I had the ability to do so), but its manageable. The bigger issues I have are with how the game represents mission difficulty and the inability to skip cutscenes/pre-fight dialogue. It's not clear how hard a given fight will be by looking at it on the menu, and so I found myself going into missions under-leveled. This led to me dying over and over and deciding to go back later. Normally, this wouldn't be a big deal, but going back later also forced me to watch the pre-fight dialogue multiple times. A "skip dialogue" option would be great.Overall though, the game is charming enough for those things to not really matter and I genuinely recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: Fae Tactics

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty nifty tactics RPG. I really liked the approach to menuless combat, there is sufficient tactical complexity choosing  which action to do each turn. I also found the strategic layer of choosing to respec your build, summons and spells for battles hit the right combination between simple and meaningful.  The pixel art is generally nice to look at with a good variety in units. The music also goes well with the game and the writing gives a good flavour. I had two major pain points. I majorly disliked the computer controlled allies in missions, felt that the AI would make unnecessary trouble and that could mean you unknowingly miss some secrets. I also felt like I had trouble understanding all the mechanics until I read more deeply online. The information is probably there somewhere in the game but there could be a better way to expose it. A few more convenience I would have liked are ways to skip battle animations and save during multi-stage battles. Ultimately once I found the time and figured out how to approach the game I had a blast with the all my tactical battles.
_childDocuments_.name: Fae Tactics

_childDocuments_.review: Soft yes. The art style is nice, and what music there is fits well enough. The biggest issue is with the leader combat. If any leader runs out of health they enter a down/prone state and can be revived by any allied unit. This can be fun when it's your units but when you spend an entire turn to down an enemy leader only to have some random minion revive it and give it a free turn where it casts the ultimate it gets for being beaten up and then 1 shots your entire team it turns your sure win into a loss seemingly based entirely on luck. It's probably the worst thing about the game.

_childDocuments_.name: Fae Tactics

_childDocuments_.review: I love this game. I highly recommend it. It has been itching that Final Fantasy Tactics itch I have been aching to scratch for some time. My original issues with the game have been fixed and they seem to be updating the game pretty regularly since its release which is good on the developers. Some of the complaints in the reviews have been fixed so please keep that in mind as you read other older reviews. I am 70 hours in as of this writing and I still have not finished the story. The combat is simple but elegant. The story takes a bit to take off at first but honestly its worth it. I personally did story battles every time they were available but in retrospect I believe taking the time to do a few free battles in between may have rounded out my spell/passive selection. I want to keep this as spoiler-free as possible, story wise. You play as a girl named Peony who has magic which is unheard of in humans, so everyone calls her a witch. You can use 3 leader-type units (including her) which can be revived when killed, and up to 3 Fae, which are Peony's familiars and both can be swapped out at will between battles to suit the current battlefields needs. On release, the Fae would die instantly when their HP hit zero, but the developers have recently introduced the ability for your Fae to revive once each with a passive called Guts. Originally they were very fragile but Guts has alleviated that issue, I feel. Each unit has an element, and each element allows you to buff another unit with whats called an "assisting" ability. Preventing critical hits, enhancing damage, avoiding ranged attacks, stealth, all manipulate your characters in different ways. Conversely, enemies can inflict you with curses, which are debuffs. Poison, Blindness, Frozen, etc. Curses can overwrite Assisting abilities and vice versa. When you kill an enemy it has a chance to drop a scroll, which you can think of as your leader-type units equipment. This buffs you or your whole team in various ways, too many to count. They will more commonly will drop pieces of material which can be used to upgrade your overall passives such as permanent defense for your whole team or more Fae summoning cost capacity. Lastly there is magic in this game but it is moreso just from Peony. You can equip 3 spells for a fight and it will take a certain number of turns to prime before you can use it. This includes things like buffing units, healing, cursing enemies, map-wide aoes, etc. Magic is acquired via chests on the map and rarely some other sources.What I have enjoyed the most about Fae tactics are the bosses. Overall they've all felt pretty unique and it becomes a challenge to use the right units to overcome the enemies strengths and weaknesses. There are also alternate stories depending on your choices in battle. Choosing to not execute an enemy leader can lead to some great things! I think any more than that would violate my spoiler-free goals so I will leave it there.I do hope you'll give Fae Tactics a try. Sure, there are more complex tactical RPG's out there but Fae Tactics is pretty amazing to me. Thank you for reading! <3
_childDocuments_.name: Fae Tactics

_childDocuments_.review: A charming tactics game, scratches that itch pretty well.My personal tactics game was Tactics Ogre from the PS1, and this isn't the same breed. While I am slightly disappointed by Fae Tactics ability to customize your squad being honestly pretty limited, that seems part of the design. Your summoned monsters represent half your squad, and they are basically Tactics pokemon. They will never be exceptional, they will never be your design, they simply are what they are at every level and how you play is more about which ones you bring to the fight.That's a downside for me, but to be clear the game is designed well around this feature. There are many interesting little fae pokemon to collect, and getting new ones from battle is always satisfying. A strong majority of them do feel unique, though you will find your favorites before long.The art is pretty and the sound track is delightfully nostalgic for me. This is a story driven game and it's engaging. Protagonist Peony is a nearly self aware character. She isn't very bright, is way too powerful, and her unflinching trust of exposition and NPC's is played for heroism and laughs. Her behavior basically demands being the protagonist in some adventure, and she doesn't much care which one she gets into.
_childDocuments_.name: Fae Tactics

_childDocuments_.review: I really do like this game. It has fantastic artwork, and some really clever ideas when approaching the tactics style game play. I will say, I have reached one point where I have four different battles I can participate in, and ALL of them have trounced me. No contest, destroyed outright. I feel like there may be some balance issues, I do understand a lot of the negative reviews because of them. It is demoralizing to just get crushed on every available path. I do alter my teams frequently. I do adjust summons and spells. I target specific characters down, and I feel like I'm doing what I should be doing, its just not enough in some battles. I do think that the passive abilities of some boss-type characters is a little absurd, and chain attacks are extremely broken when used by the enemy, with next to no affect when used by your own characters.I think I get both sides of the argument currently going on, and frankly if I had made the mistake of selecting Hard mode from the start, I would be absolutely furious with the game. I'm going to keep going and trying, because when you do get it right it's rewarding. I do wish there was a bit more ramp, and that the game didn't scale the way it currently does.
_childDocuments_.name: Fae Tactics

_childDocuments_.review: This game is simply amazing, a fun, light hearted and interesting tatical RPG. It has creative and unique mechanics, customization is simple yet highly impactful. It allows you to respec your team for each fight, so I found myself constantly experimenting with stats to get through different challanges.The game is fairly difficult, with some brutal fights, but never once it felt I won or lost undeservedly due to RNG or cheesy mechanics, I was allways able to find a strategy that gave me the upperhand and was consistent, and due to you being able to respec your main rooster every fight you are forced to reinvent your team composition constantly to get trhough certain bosses, allways keeping you on your toes and giving every character a chance to shine (playing on hardest difficulty).The devs are still active, listening to the community and delivering changes and fixes we asked for.Makes for a fun 60h+ game with amazing story, lovely characters, interesting mechanics, secrets to discover and much more.I had a realy fun time with my first playthrough, and can't wait to start my NG+.
_childDocuments_.name: Fae Tactics

_childDocuments_.review: Unique TRPG where 'tactics' actually matter. This means everything from planning the fight to executing it. The game lets you choose 3 main characters from a unique roster, each of which has their own quirks and later on weapons that can drastically change their gameplay; 3 spells from a large array of support, damage, and utility cards you can find while playing; and a large cast of summonable monsters that have their own strengths. Add to that the ability to respec your characters, and often readjust your roster and monsters between fights, and you have an open canvas to work with.This game is not easy. You really need to play to your party's strengths, and that means taking advantage of Pokemon-like elements as well as different movement types, attack range, and enemy abilities and buffs. You need to be flexible - a rigid thinker who wants to run through the game with a particular comp is going to fail.It's incredible what was accomplished with the game's engine - there is a lot of depth here and it's keeping me on my toes. The sprites are great and have a lot of personality, and overall I am enjoying the music.Boss fights are difficult, and there are some fights that have annoying mechanics, but for the most part I feel like this game has an appropriate difficulty curve that provides a challenge just like the RPGs of decades past. Definitely a breath of fresh air!
_childDocuments_.name: Fae Tactics

_childDocuments_.review: Edit : This game is phenomenal ! The more you play, the more it will surprise you with great game design decisions. It is really something else. You have a lot of choices to make all the time, and each can and will impact the outcome of the fight. Yet every character has maximum 4 options. Easy to learn, hard to master, and damn you have a few tool but each is a thousand doors of options. I love Valdys Story and I love Fae Tactics, this dev is doing some really unique job and I can't understand where the recognition is for such a good work. Below is the first impression I had, before edit :This game is both simple and damn smart.The UI is clean, you get all the informations you need when you search for them without menues in the actions.Also, the game solves a lot of problems with classical tactical games of this breed. Example : How do you tank in a game like this ? You make it so if a character can takes the hits of an ennemy, for any allies within X tiles. Bam, positioning matters to tanks and other roles with just one basic competence. Also, you start the game with already a lot of tools at your disposal. No need to wait hours before making actuals plans.Valdys Story was already a great metroidvania, and EndlessfluffGames did it again, they took a genra I love and made it their own way, and it's an awesome way.
_childDocuments_.name: Fae Tactics

_childDocuments_.review: I'm on the fence about continuing to recommend the game after my last review, but I will continue to recommend it only for true TBS-RPG fans who are willing to walk in to this game with an open mind. Here are some observations:Honestly I have had some fun with it but I do not think I will be finishing this game due to its lack of polish and my repeated frustrations with progression choices. I did get a good ~15 hours out of it but I will have to keep looking for a game that scratches that FFT itch.
_childDocuments_.name: Fae Tactics

_childDocuments_.review: This game is amazing. I have been waiting for it for some time now and it has not disappointed me one bit. I loved FF tactics growing up and this does such a great job of taking that style gameplay and streamlining it and adding new style to the genre. You don't live in menus for each character, you just play. Some might think that get's rid of the depth but there is still so much here while in battle. If you like tactics games I simply can't recommend this more! it's beautiful, good story, great gameplay all wrapped up in this little indie title that is currently my GoTY.
_childDocuments_.name: Fae Tactics

_childDocuments_.review: Fae Tactics is a fun tactical RPG. It's all about the fights which you enter through a menu so there's no walking around in this game. The story seems to be in the background but that hardly matters.For me, it was a bit frustrating at first because while the first couple of fights are supposed to explain how fighting works, the game omits crucial information about its mechanics. For example, there is no diagonal attacking, not even ranged. Moreover, if you moved somewhere with the intent to attack only to find out you can't reach your enemy after all, clicking RMB undoes your movement. This is so helpful to know but the game doesn't tell you. Why?Anyways, after figuring out all the mechanics, this is an enjoyable and cute game with good music.
_childDocuments_.name: Fae Tactics

_childDocuments_.review: Solid tactics gameplay, easy controls, and mostly great art. It definitely seems like this game is unpolished though. The UI is messy, animations look weird, and some things just feel very placeholder. There's also little to no tutorial and a lot of the mechanics are just thrown at you, and it can be hard to know what's going on. I'd say this game is actually a touch too complex, but if you're up for the challenge of figuring it out, there's some really great gameplay to be had.
_childDocuments_.name: Fae Tactics

_childDocuments_.review: Huge fun of the devs - creators of Valdis StoryThe game is very good but it is in need of QoL improvements, keybinds, key shortcuts, key words explained in team building menu, hazard terrain has no discription, different font etc.I really like it and anyone who enjoys turnbased tactics games we'll love it. I'm not a huge fan of world scaling to your level, but it kind of works here and makes it so you cannot simply grind easy missions in preparations for boss fight - it also makes most fights challenging also.Huge fan, can't wait for other games from EndlessFluff
_childDocuments_.name: Fae Tactics

_childDocuments_.review: this is just a premature review from my first look of the game (about 5 hours). the game is pretty good and fun, better than i was expecting, i was looking for something similar to final fantasy tactics, or tactics ogre. i'd say this is pretty close and satisfied my wants well. the combat is simple yet engaging (as much as a turn based can get). and the sprite animations are satisfying to see when pulling off cool combos in battle. music is nice enough that it doesn't get annoying and the story (from what i've read about it since i am only 5 hours in) is nothing too fancy and was not really the reason i found myself drawn into playing, but decent nonetheless. the only gripe i have with the game from my game time is as far as i can tell, the is no way to turn the board. i have had a couple times where an enemy is either the enemy is behind my units, or on the other side of some high ground and i had no idea they were there until they moved in for an attack or something. other than that, i would say it's worth the price. 7.5/10
_childDocuments_.name: Fae Tactics

_childDocuments_.review: I'll surely have to update this review later, as I'm less far into Fae Tacitcs than my steam hours would suggest, but GREAT FIRST IMPRESSION so far.As more critical reviews have noted, there are missing QoL features (it lacks tooltip support during planning phases, it lacks an encyclopedia of buffs/debuffs/etc), and there are surely some bugs to fix, but the game is being quickly patched. Regardless of the minor issues I've faced which you can find either minor or major, I have had a blast so far. I would warn that Hard Mode is not tuned for first playthroughs, judging by other people's frustrated responses to starting with it on.I'm sold on the mechanical premise of the game, which aims to make individual units' turns easy to process quickly. Basically: You can Attack, Assist (target an ally to do something beneficial) or Wait (target yourself to do something beneficial). Each unit has potentially many passives (such as the ability to permanently shred Defense, or deal bonus damage to flying targets), which tend to be worth enough conscious consideration to scratch the depth itch. I'm not disappointed by the presence of many other carefully considered mechanics... it is the Valdis Story developer making a game inspired by FFT, after all. Just don't expect character customization like FFT's; the focus is ALL on mechanically interesting combat, and gradual expansion of your access to things as a whole.It's really pretty, with cute characters, including monsters you are very well expected to utilize. Great music and sfx. The story is decent as far as I've played, but don't expect the story to wow you like that of Final Fantasy Tactics. In fact, it'd be healthy to not compare it too harshly to FFT (or your nostalgic perception of FFT), but I don't have to tell you not to expect perfection from a $20 indie game, do I?We'll see where it goes as the game progresses, but again, great first impression, and I'm happy to support EndlessFluff after Valdis Story~ <3
_childDocuments_.name: Fae Tactics

_childDocuments_.review: This game is hard. I guess it will turn a lot of people off. But you must try it, it's not something unbeatable. You have to strategies more good. But the gameplay is SO much fun, really challenging and depth too.I have a little bit complaint, but it's just a minor issue. This is a good game. Recommended.

Only small complaints are hero/companion new skills/selection,or ANY equipment please(not including those passive stats from scrolls)!!! _childDocuments_.review: Pretty awesome old school SRPG, I was hesitant at first with alot of the mechanic's and overall style but 3 hour's in and I am very much enjoying this title already. _childDocuments_.name: Fae Tactics

_childDocuments_.review: I have been anticipating Fae Tactic's release for a while now and starting the first few minutes of the game has me excited. I have to say that the pixel art, animation, character motion and emotes are so perfect. From what I've seen so far, visually, this game surpasses FFT in style. Whoever did the art for this game should be extremely proud. Amazing!Updated review after my showstopper issues have been resolved: great tactical game! Love the complex enough strategy achieved while remaining simplified (no nested skill submenus). The writing for the story elements of the game is on point. I enjoy how the story starts with trying to find mom instead of the search for the power core to stop the world from being destroyed by some arch evil. So much more personal and interesting storytelling.The title screen suggests that not being able to set the resolution will be a big, blurry, dealbreaker, however in-game the resolution and scaling look perfect. Seems kind of weird that the title screen doesn't start the player off with the correct impression of the game.If I could give one critical suggestion it would be to improve the way the game reads during fights. What icon means what, whether an effect is temporary (like impacts the next attack) or is permanent, or is a reactive skill does not read off the screen very easily. Basic UX concepts need to be refined like grouping of icons, or badging them or the colors  etc. I don't think I'm stupid but when I move my cursor over a unit I just don't get a feel for what that unit does.After seeing several Kickstarters promising to deliver a spiritual successor to FFT and missing the mark by a mile, it is great to finally see something that might be worthy of that title.
_childDocuments_.name: Fae Tactics

_childDocuments_.review: I truly am a sucker for a FFT spiritual successor. having just completed the tutorial levels I have truly come to enjoy all the little details that truly made FFT a hit in my book. some examples would be the option to set direction the character faces at the end of a turn, another feature I like is the turn order. Fae tactics has beautiful yet very chess like levels that are both nostalgic but refreshing. One small complaint I have is the choice to do less menu's during combat. I truly enjoy menu based combat even now with all the current technology its fun to sit down to a classic FF. I found it easy to enjoy the starting characters and the bond between the starting characters. Will update as I progress in game.
_childDocuments_.name: Fae Tactics

_childDocuments_.review: Initial impressions are extremely positive.The graphics are gorgeously animated and colorful.The soundtrack reminds me alot of Wild Arms XF. Its got very much a wildwest feel to it which fits with the story.Check it out here: Gameplay is where its at though. You can customize your party with skillpoints, different accessorys, various action cards and summons(mercenaries). While cconsidering elemental advantages elevation, terrain, and unit types. I really dig how they made it work without menues and through contextual commands alone. There are stil many tactical elements and actions to consider but it flows much better since you don't have to interrupt the battle to scroll though a menu.

name: Moving Out
detailed_description: Moving Out is a ridiculous physics-based moving simulator that brings new meaning to 'couch co-op'! Are you ready for an exciting career in furniture? As a newly certified Furniture Arrangement & Relocation Technician, you’ll take on moving jobs all across the busy town of Packmore. Smooth Moves may not be the biggest moving company, but there’s no task too dangerous or strange for this busy team of go-getters. Grow your business to brave new heights, recruit colourful customizable characters, and save your town from furniture peril! Co-op! Enjoy the story mode solo as an independent contractor or team up with some friends. Up to four players can cozy up on the couch to argue over the best way to move a couch. Test your skills AND your friendship! Physics! Are pesky doors and windows standing in your furniture’s way? Just blast through them with physics! Lift, toss and smash your way to the fastest times! Action! Learn the ropes in a series of increasingly precarious and fantastical moving jobs. How a bed gets from point A to point B is never a straight line, so throw out the training manual and get creative! Adventure! Every moving company starts small, but as your reputation ranks up, so do your destinations. Move through sleepy suburbs, frenzied farms, haunted houses, virtual reality and lands beyond! Characters! Recruit a unique cast of colorful characters, each packed with a passion for manual labor! Assist Mode! Are you a rookie? No problem! Adjust the game’s difficulty so anyone can play! Don’t wait! Grab your friends and become a certified moving master in Moving Out!

_childDocuments_.review: I first became aware of Moving Out (MO) from watching people on YouTube, and seeing them practically demolish a house while loading up a moving van looked like silly fun. When my friend visited, we gave the game a try, and enjoyed similar antics. Like other games centered around wacky coop, it winds up being more difficult than the visuals suggest, which can make it frustrating. However, after giving it enough time, it also becomes somewhat addictive, with various objectives to strive for. You, and up to three friends, will have a checklist of items to load into a moving truck, some of which will need to be worked on together due to its weight. Most of the time, these include expected objects, such as furniture, boxes, and household items. However, as you progress, more atypical objects will be introduced, such as canisters filled with green goo. Additionally, the layout and themes become more advanced, as you go from houses and a mansion, to an abandoned, flame-spewing factory. Each of the 30 story stages have medals to earn by loading everything onto the truck fast enough, and completing three unique objectives per stage. These range from taking specific paths when loading items, to not breaking any windows.If you're playing by yourself, the game makes accommodations, by reducing the number of items you have to move, and in some situations changing what they are. Also, if moving something like a bed, you can simply do it by yourself, when if others are present, you'll need help. Having played the game in both circumstances, I found that although it was easier to complete objectives on my own, the gameplay wasn't as much fun. The chaos that came from playing with someone else gave it more interest, whereas on my own, it was much more methodical, like finishing a set of tasks. The controls can be a bit touchy, but I found them functional most of the time. It's possible to play using either a controller or keyboard, and I liked how the controller handled. If with a second person, you can swing a larger item to build momentum and throw it, which is necessary in some situations. One downside is how there isn't a direct way to rotate your character or items you're holding. Instead, it's indirectly controlled by moving your character. Another problem is that sometimes, furniture would get stuck in ways that didn't always make sense. For instance, I'd be pulling a bed through a door frame, making good progress, but it'd get stuck suddenly. To get it free, I'd have to drop this end, go to the other side, adjust it, and then I could pull it through.To my surprise, there is a story in MO. It's set sometime in the 1970's or 80's, based on the VHS tapes and Atari consoles. As workers for the moving company Smooth Moves, finishing jobs and earning more business, they stumble into shady business going around in the town of Packmore. Will they put an end to it, or unwittingly aid and abet in nefarious, furniture-related dealings? There's definitely a cheesy sense of humor to the story and dialogue between characters, but it's all harmless silliness that should keep a smile on your face.The game's style somewhat has a corny training video vibe to it, but only in certain areas, such as the start screen. Otherwise, the 3D visuals are smooth, clean, and crisp, with vibrant colors to them. I enjoy the cartoonish look to the aesthetic, which helps with the house-wrecking action. This is also shown when your character gets destroyed, as they go up in a puff of smoke, and respawn in a large cardboard box that falls from the sky.The songs in the game are lively, with strong percussion elements to them. They carry a lot of energy, and resonate with the 80's dynamic well. At least, when I go out of my way to listen to them. Otherwise, they tend to blend into the background, and aren't incredibly memorable. There's not much variety to what actions you take in the game, which does limit the sound effects. However, they're all suitable and fitting. For instance, when windows are broken, or you and a friend toss a couch across a body of water.🌟 As you earn medals for completing objectives and clearing stages fast enough, you unlock optional stages to play. They're almost like mini-games, and change up what you focus on in story mode, helping to diversify the gameplay. 🌟 The developers stuck around with the game for a while after it was released, providing regular updates.❌ The heave-ho function can be annoying to coordinate. Each person has to be on opposite ends of the same item, push the button, and when one person lets go, the item is thrown. It makes sense, but it still can be awkward to work with.❌ Some of the stage objectives aren't at all clear, such as on stage Guava Run. The third objective simply says Ahh Push It... and the requirements are rather specific and atypical. I had to look up a guide to figure it out.🔍 I'd suggest turning on Assist Mode from the beginning, primarily to increase the time requirements on earning gold and platinum medals. It doesn't make the game “easier,” as everything else is the same, but it simplifies trying to 100% it. Plus, there's no penalties for doing so. 🔍 It can help to consider how you'd approach moving items in real-life. For example, pushing items typically isn't very effective, and sometimes you have to drop an object and pick it up in a different spot in order to move it.🔍 It's helpful to move larger items into the truck first. Otherwise, you might have to reorganize and move items in the truck, just to get something else to fit inside. At times, I was frustrated by the game, but overall I'd say that I had a good time with MO. It's certainly one you'd want to play with friends, as it's much more enjoyable that way, even if you won't be as likely to earn all the medals. If you're so inclined, you can always replay it on your own. It has a light-hearted tone that makes returning to it easy, which is why I was working on earning all the achievements. However, some of them seem to be broken, as I should have all of them, or very close to it by now, yet am still missing five. Regardless, I recommend MO as a local coop game to play with your friends, but if you want to complete it, wait for further patches before making an attempt.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is for you if:-You enjoy couch coop games and have others to play it with.-You want a less complex game where less skilled players can just join in and have fun.-You want a game that offers fun in short bursts (Suitable for party games).This game is not for you if:-You are looking for a game with complex mechanics.-You are getting it for the Single Player.-You are looking for Online Multiplayer.-Your only alternative to couch coop is Steam Remote Play.Overall experience:-In a nutshell, the goal in the game is to move out items from a location to your truck as FAST AS YOU CAN.Pros:+Lighthearted and can be hilarious while doing the simplest of chores due to the physics and vibrant locations.+Cutesy themed which will appeal to all ages. Characters offer a good amount of customization.+Stages are decently made with new ways to tackle challenges.+Mechanics and physics are polished enough to get the job done.+Versatile Multiplayer control customization etc. 2 Gamepad & 2 Keyboard is possible. Cons:-Can get repetitive as the mechanics are very basic.-Lacks depth.-No Online Multiplayer.While I would prefer a more in-depth game, this does appeal to less-hardcore gamers and my group had a blast playing it in short burst.

_childDocuments_.review: The negative reviews left so far are almost exclusively about the fact that the game is local coop only, a fact that is clearly advertised on the store page. Not sure why so many people would by a game that is listed as local coop and then complain that it doesn't have online gameplay. Obviously not. Anyways, I played the first ~5 levels and they were pretty fun so far. Excited to see what the rest of the game has to offer. Games like these, such as Overcooked, always start off in a way that seems normal and then they ramp up until it's too much to keep up with. No game-breaking bugs and the character customization is an adorable feature that is a noticable improvement from Overcooked.
_childDocuments_.name: Moving Out

_childDocuments_.review: I like this game, but I feel Moving Out has a difficulty crisis.If you just go ahead and gun through the levels with no care for gold/platinum, then there won't be much challenge to deliver. It basically only becomes a matter of time before you beat the game, 30 short levels and all. You'll probably not think much of what you just played if you do this.However, actually trying to get gold/platinum in every level...oh my lord.The game suddenly becomes a frustrating gauntlet of trial and error, and not because its you're some casual gamer (although, perhaps maybe I have a skill issue), but because the physics and collision get in the way. Beds getting stuck, items not registering as "in the truck" because one tiny pixel is off, and ghosts. The game suddenly asks so much of you that making ONE tiny mistake is basically a dead run that you have to reset.At least there's assist mode, which helps makes the game more manageable...and also makes the gold- heck, platinum ranks so horribly easy. It's both a band aid solution and an overcooked solution. That said, I at least had fun when I stopped trying to go for gold. Which was causing me to have negative opinions on this game because I was attempting something that was optional that I didn't like. To add more positive vibes, the soundtrack is pretty great, I like the character design- PUT SOME RESPECT ON MY MAN DIALS THE TV BOY, HES MY MAN. The levels themselves were at least creative with their mechanics, credit were credit is due. Some cute 80's/90's media references here and there (someone in the team REALLY loved Atari.), and I imagine multiplayer being the true way to play this game and really enjoy it...because I kinda went through the whole game alone...heh.At the very least, Moving Out gets a recommendation from me. It's a fun diversion if you play through the game semi casually, but somewhat a struggle for those wanting to go beyond that. There's a good time in here, you just have to unpack it with presumably a friend.For the TL;DR people (which is probably most of you), Moving Out is a good game, but its probably better if you have a friend or 3 more.
_childDocuments_.name: Moving Out

_childDocuments_.review: This game is currently in the Humble Bundle for February 2021.  If you are interested in the game and it's before March 2nd, 2021, consider picking up the game as part of the current monthly bundle.After an playing an hour to review for the Humble Choice February 2021 Bundle: So take Overcooked 2 from two months ago, add in stricter time limits, more intensity and you have Moving out,  Oh yeah, you’re moving someone else’s stuff instead of making food for customers. Moving Out’s premise is simple, take all the tagged items, put them on your truck and that’s it.  It’s a simple concept but it can get complicated fast.  Space is usually at a premium for your truck, there are several large objects that you need more than one person to carry, and the time limits are pretty tight.  I teamed up with my daughter, Daylyn, on this one and as completionists, we were trying to get gold and spent about 40 minutes trying to beat the first level.  This is not an easy game.  But don’t worry, there are Assist modes that I applaud, reminding me of Celeste, though a bit simpler.  The assist modes mean everyone should be able to tackle the rather challenging game. I played for fifteen minutes in single-player mode also… It’s not awful, but this is a game intended for two or more players, as important mechanics are missing in singleplayer. Play this if you thought Overcooked 2 was too easy or didn’t end in enough shouting matches.  Also, play this if you want to play a good co-op game, but be prepared for a really solid challenge and a serious need for teamwork, because you will need it. If you enjoyed this review or want to know what I think of other games in the bundle, check out the full review on or subscribe to my youtube channel:

_childDocuments_.review: Moving Out is a couch-coop physics-based action game for up to four players. It's best compared to Overcooked but instead of cooking you and your friends need to carry heavy objects into a moving truck. Moving out is pretty simple. You move around, have a button to grab, and one to throw objects. Some objects need to be carried by at least two people (a big bed for example) while most others can be carried by yourself. Some of them are heavy but can be carried alone. One feature is to throw objects. Even heavy objects that need to be carried by two people can be thrown. This gameplay feature allows you to play around with your surroundings and find new ways to beat your high score. There are 30 different levels in total. You unlock a new one after every 'Move'. For every mission, you get a medal (bronze, silver, gold, and platinum). Aside from that, there are three bonus objectives for each level (breaking all windows, breaking no windows, etc.). It is fun for completists but nothing more. Stages are different enough thanks to the weather (snow), animals (turtle, chicken, etc.), and how the environment is arranged. This ensures a tactical layer to this action-packed fun little game. Moving Out is a fun couch co-op game and thanks to steams Remote Play feature even playable online. It's on sale often enough and you'll have a fun few hours with it. It's rather short if you're not looking to get every stage to platinum and get every bonus objective. Is it better than overcooked? Definitely not. But someday you and your soulmate or friend will have enough of it. Then it's time to get this gem on sale!Is it fun alone? Not so much to be honest. Most of the fun comes from playing with somebody you know!Get it on sale if you have friends to play with!

_childDocuments_.review: This game has great potential, but the execution needs improvement.The core idea is mindless fun: enjoying the spectacle of your team trying to efficiently move items from a house into a van amidst chaotic, uncoordinated panic. The hilarious moments of failing to coordinate, such as struggling to move a large couch or misjudging a throw and causing havoc, should be the core enjoyable experience.However, the introduction of difficult challenges and time constraints detracts from this fun. To achieve anything beyond "level completed," you need to play flawlessly, as any mistake costs you the gold medal. Challenges that discourage the mindless fun and require a serious, meticulous approach create an internal conflict in the game's intended experience.The game should embrace its mindless chaotic comedy. Like having higher currency rewards based on how much is moved within the set time would allow players to relax and enjoy the chaos. Let players use this currency between levels for costumes and upgrades or something. This would motivate coordinated efforts without punishing the entire team for embracing the intended chaotic madness.Overall, this game presents itself as a chill, whimsical party game, but it is actually an unforgiving and difficult test of precision and patience. Don't play this is you have any tendencies of being a completionist.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't have a lot of playtime on this game yet but fully believe it deserves a thumbs up.  It's true, this game is couch co-op only but that's exactly how I play my games anyway.  My wife and I play Overcooked all the time and were curious how this would compare.So far, we view it as more laid back than Overcooked but not in a bad way!  With Overcooked, you're constantly looking to make sure you're cooking the right food and serving it all in the correct order.  While the challenge and strategy of Overcooked is fun, it can also be tiring.  We found that with this game so far, we can sort of do our own thing and call for help when moving larger objects.  We found ourselves laughing a lot as we try and maneuver the corner couch out the front door.  Pivot...PIVOT!  It's been refreshing for us to dive into this game and take a break from trying to get 4 stars on everything in Overcooked.   The bonus objectives in this game are unique and fun and introduce a new element to the level rather than just, "do it all the same but faster".  The controls feel really good like Overcooked. _childDocuments_.review: Moving Out is a charming, lovingly crafted couch co-op game. I've seen a lot of people comparing it to Overcooked, but I can say with certainty, I enjoy Moving Out a lot more, and don't need to drink or run the risk of losing my voice playing it unlike Overcooked.Moving Out consists of levels where you have to move furniture, many requiring 2 people to efficiently move, while trying to go fast enough to get gold medals. In my experience, it takes 3 tries tops to get gold medals, as once you have a strategy in place, you can get gold with ~20 seconds to spare. This makes it a lot less high stakes and stressful like Overcooked, and honestly a lot more fun to play. You'll constanatly find yourself in hilarious situations with the janky physics. Forgot to unplug that device you threw? Well now it sling-shotted out the window, around a corner, and into another room. There's even higher difficulty "challege" stages through the arcade. The first one being, you have to carry a couch through a suspended maze. Definitely a challenge, but for some reason we couldn't stop deliriously laughing, on what in another game, would frustrate us. Go to fast and someone falls off, just hanging on to the edge of the couch over the abyss. "My time has come" we'd say, as we let go and fall into nothing.TL;DR Great, hilarious game, made with a lot of love. Definitely play through parsec, as we literally had no issues with latency etc. playing from west coast to the south of the US.

_childDocuments_.review: By the Makers of Overcooked, with just as much Charm and Chaos to annoy your friends with. In this Game you play a bunch of "professional" Mover Personal which forgot that while clearing out Buildings, it might be important that the Objects shouldn't be broken when delivered. But do you care? No. Your Job is to get in, and get stuff out as fast as possible.Either do it on your own, or bring some friends to beat Levels in the quickest or even most creative manner possible, while following a cute little Story of saving Packmore from missplaced Furniture and a Thief.Make your way through clearing out Houses, Barns and Mansions, to even Office Buildings, Factories and Spacestations. Break Doors and TVs. Throw around fragile Objects. Slap Ghosts. Throw Couches through Windows, Move disobidient Chickens. It's up to you how you get your Job done, aslong as it's done fast.And the best part? No matter how good you are at the game, i guarantee you this Game will offer something of joy for you. If it's the vibrant Colours, the playful Design or the "Mover Helpers" Menu which lets you adjust Difficulty while not hindering your Progress.It's a game for everybody, and it's even better with Friends.(This Game only features Couch Co-op, so you'll have to use Remote Play, and that's pretty much it's only flaw.)

_childDocuments_.review: Moving out is a great two player, up to 4 player, game.  It is one that will test your relationships with your playing partners, but one that will also result in a lot of laughter as well.  You are tasked with moving furniture out of homes, apartments, businesses, and more.  You have a certain time in order to get a gold medal, silver medal or bronze.  Once you beat the level once, you are given 3 objectives that you can do in each level.  Sometimes you need to not get hit by a car, or not touch the snow.  Some are simple, but some are a bit more complex.  There are a few hidden objects to find for collector's sake, but also for achievement's sake as well.The original game offers you 30 levels, and the DLC offers you 13 levels.  All are fun, and different scenery to play with.  The original is more like what you would expect to see in a real community while the DLC is more tropical club med style of scenery, though the levels still vary.  Different obstacles arise as you progress through the game.  Ghosts suddenly appear in certain levels who grab you and scare you.  Rakes can be stepped on that lift up and smack you in the face making you dizzy and stunned for a moment.  All of it is meant to waste more of your time.There is a back story to the entire thing, and while it's completely forgettable as the main gameplay is where the focus is and should be, the main storyline, if you read it, is pretty darn funny.  The movers are idiots, but so is the boss, and the devs weren't shy about making fun of the characters you play.The graphics are good, nothing too fancy, but work real well the atmosphere of the game.  It is very cartoony and colorful with bright colors, nothing dark and nothing realistic at all.  The animations are all good, including when you smack your partner, which you can do.  The controls are where it gets a bit sticky.  It's easy to maneuver your character by yourself, but once you have more than one person dragging a couch or a larger item, it is not as intuitive as you'd think to control things while two people are in control.  This requires you to communicate, yell, laugh, and do anything you can to make your partner understand how to coordinate moving the furniture.You'll move everything from couches, to refrigerators, to boxes.  At times you'll be asked to move farm animals, and it keeps going from there, the list of items you need to move is fairly endless and fun.  The game offers a lot of replayability mainly through the objectives but also with the number of achievements that you can unlock.  All of them are fun, but a few are a bit more tedious and I wish the devs had provided better guidance to let you know which mailboxes you had already slapped or which toilets you had already sa on (there's the humor I spoke of).I highly recommend playing this if you have a fun player #2 you can play with or if you have more players that wish to get down on this amazing couch co-op.
_childDocuments_.name: Moving Out

_childDocuments_.review: I stumbled upon this game out of the blue, and it didn't take me long to realise that this game had an interesting and unique concept.Upon first playing this game, and throughout, it was an utter blast of hilarity to say the least! _childDocuments_.review: There is literally no reason why a game released in 2020 doesn't have online co-op. Full stop.We are in the middle of a global pandemic and this seems incredibly ineffective in dealing with that fact. Remote play is borderline unplayable at worst and works but is awful and frustrating at best. Overcooked 1 has a similar issues and is similarly not really  that much fun to play. Why is it that Overcooked 2 works for co-op online but not these two games? Regardless, I feel like this experience has soured my desire in playing games made by SMG studio. I got this in a sale pack, so I do not feel the need for a refund but I strong encourage people not to buy this game until online co-op is patched in.The fact that I am writing this 1/11/2021 means that this is highly unlikely to get the fix it needs. _childDocuments_.review: Moving on from the morose lines my face is drawing, then,  From its cartoon explosion aesthetic, the inventive levels, the emphasis on physics-based wanton destruction, the narrative that takes an absurd turn, the boppy music, the fun prodding at our reality with a late-capitalist boss and perfect, unflinching workers, being able to play a toaster that shoots toast constantly - what pandemic, I ask you?Don't let this be an overlooked Overcooked, then. A publisher in common has never made more sense for any two (three) games. Both are fun, arcade abstractions of repetitive work where you have to find organisation in chaos to succeed.  Mine repeatedly berated me in a roundabout way, referring to me by my in-game character, 'the egg.' He had a hail mary approach whenever timing was critical, constantly tried to solo two player items, and a bad instinct for how to get large items round corners other than shouting 'pivot!' every time. He was perfect! There aren't (with a few exceptions) separate jobs to allocate. Just move the objects together efficiently. That's it. The same escalation of creative level design still occurs. Normal houses and kitchens give way to absurd gauntlets wherein barriers of fire and brimstone and acid and dubstep make moving from A to B just that little bit harder once you have the advantage of being mind melded on your side. It's less frustrating here than in the Overcooked games, though. Moving from A to B is always the focus, so placing more barriers feels a more natural evolution than in Overcooked where finding a team dynamic and taking on different roles feels like it's being detracted from. It can be a buggy, inelegant solution and people just don't have (online) friends like they used to. I live with my girlfriend and that's my life. My one seamlessly made Swedish friend on Hunt Showdown unfriended me in a heartbreaking turn of events that deserves TV dramatisation. I much preferred GTFO's approach of Discord-facilitated matchmaking, but if you can put in the work, perhaps resorting to the forums, it's not the worst thing in the world. If you have friends, it's a whole different story. You need only have one copy between four, what I can only imagine as perfect teeth, always-smiling *ahem* people. Not a bad value proposition for the absolute winners out there. Winning again as they do! Exploring its gameplay limits through added complexities of gaps, conveyor belts, ghosts, fans, turntables, flames and crushers, and satisfyingly capping it off with one final hair-pullingly tricky gauntlet. A sigh of a relief. A hearty handshake in recognition of your now forever augmented friendship and you separate into the night (whilst still remaining indoors if you're in lockdown) whistling a happy tune. What's on Netflix?
