_childDocuments_.review: A unique turn-based dungeon crawler with a pleasantly uncanny vibe. Shares a surprising amount of DNA with classical roguelikes, despite its streamlined and abstract sense of movement and space. Much like in Nethack, you're looking to minimize losses and take meaningful risks while building a powerful enough cocktail of gear effects to carry you through the sadistic later stages. The prevalence of floating bombs and other enemies with unique behaviors forces you to keep moving and refining your strategy... and occasionally to accept your death at the hands of a sadistic RNG. What's life without a little pain?
_childDocuments_.name: Ring of Pain

_childDocuments_.review: Ring of Pain is a lot of fun, and since I've started playing the game, the devs have added extra content twice. There was a lunar new year update that added a different game mode/win condition, with different items. And then recently there was another update which added even more items, rooms, and difficulty levels. Really appreciate the level of support and dedication from the devs.As for the game itself, it takes a bit of time to understand what works and what doesn't, but it's so entertaining and satisfying when you do get that perfect run. It's a fun little game, with a cute but creepy artstyle, and with easy to learn but hard to master mechanics. I really enjoy RoP a lot, and find myself just leaving it open in the background while I do other things, and then coming back to it to continue my run when I'm free.My only two issues with the game are:1. there is no save feature, which I assume is a conscious decision, but it does make it a bit hard sometimes when you know that you only have a limited amount of time to play, so it is a bit pointless.2. this was only confusing when I first started playing, but-  your health bar is coloured green. health potions are pink. and so when I would get poisoned, I would look at the health bar and think I was continuously poisoned because I would only notice the health bar was green when I did fight the poison guys. Now I just realise it's always green, but it may be better for new players if the health bar is pink like the health potions? Just a suggestion. Regardless great game, lots of fun. love the RPG similarities in picking up armor/gear/items with stats, instead of having a full "hand" of active cards to play. a cute twist on a "deckbuilder".

_childDocuments_.review: I had a good time playing the game for a dozen hours, then I uninstalled, and probably won't come back. Here is why : So, I installed the game. The gameplay feedback loop is perfect ! The mechanics are easy to learn. The game is easy to play. Maybe a bit too easy ? I think I was able to finish the game on my fifth try. Then I tried the other ending. And voilà.Yes, there are higher difficulty modes, and alternate starters.Except... I am not invested enough to grind those. See, I have 200+ hours on Slay the Spires, so I have to compare the two games. I beat Slay the Spires on Ascension 20 with all characters. It was hard. I had to learn a lot. But it was very rewarding. I wanted to see all encounters, try all combos, understand the boss patterns, best the mobs even against the odds.Ring of Pain is different, in that it lacks everything that kept me engaged in StS :- enemies are really simple, not much to understand there- there are barely any scenarized encounters (I counted less than 10)- there isn't much decision making aside of what gear to take or destroy -- and once you are geared, you can go through ten levels without using a single neuron- it is always 100% correct to spend your souls on the biggest chest you can find, which removes yet another layer of decision that existed in StS- the lore is almost non-existent, and the way it's delivered didn't feel good or engaging to meAll in all, I bought the game on sales for 6€, and I think that's a fair price. It simply doesn't have the content and depth that warrant a higher price.But I want to encourage the developpers. The game is nice. It has great qualities. For me, the one thing it lacks the most is writing, and interactions. Writing is what makes us like a game. With barely anything to say, Ring of Pain leave a bland impression, despite the intriging art direction. Whereas interaction is where the real depth of gameplay lies. I have found myself looking for the Miracle room every run, because this was the most interactive thing that exists in the game. For a game that sells itself on decision making, it's too light, sorry.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: this is a brainy puzzle game that is easy to learn and though to master. If this sounds interesting it might be your cup of tea.Atmosferic, brainy and deceptively simple yet deep. The game is a about making well defined choices with clear and predictable consequences. Many reviews complain about the game being too difficult, too random or too luck-dependent. Lately I find myself winning 80% of runs, so I think they might have been too hasty to judge. Other say that the game is too simple or shallow. Being simple is not a bad thing, and I don't think it is shallow. There are dozens of items with more being added with every update. There are very interesting item interactions, and multiple mechanics that are simple to understand yet difficult to master. Finally, the developer really cares about the game and keeps releasing content updates and implemented user request in spite of the game not raking in much money. So even if this does not end up being your cup of tea, don't feel too bad about spending a few bucks on this, as you are supporting a promising indie developer.

_childDocuments_.review: Ring of Pain is built in a mechanically tight way that requires very careful stat placement and equipment selection.But it wants to extend your playtime so it uses excessively high randomness in stats and equipment coupled with the best items being behind achievement unlocks in order to prevent you from capitalizing on a good build or mechanic mastery until you have invested enough time in it.It lacks the hard choices in trade-offs of Slay the Spire or Monster Train and instead you primarily just get whatever the seed gives you.The main Pro is that it's simplistic enough it can be played very quickly and the RNG is so high that you don't feel much responsibility for losing a game or two.I also enjoyed the theme, though it is not conveyed well in-game. I enjoyed playing it for the first few hours, until I learned more about it, then I went and killed the harder final boss out of obligation and realized it really doesn't have a lot more to show me.

_childDocuments_.review: Tl;DR I really like positionals and strategy 10/10 As time of review i have played 3.8 hours (finally decided to buy it after playing on another acc):The good: -Good sountrack/Atmosphere                 -Gameplay/Tactical thinking                 -Artwork & Design (grim and dark, sweet)                 -292 Unique cards (for now)                 -There are even harder modes ( for that extra itch of pain)                 -Positionals in Arena (this gameplay feature is so addicting)The bad: -little RNGRoP simply explained is a roquelike deck builder but with a cool gameplay twist:Once you enter the arena a ring of  cards (monsters, items, exits,...) is formed and 2 front cards are placed to you: This is eventually a smaller interactive ring of pain. _childDocuments_.review: Ring of Pain is only contending with Star Renegades for Top Indie Game of 2020 to me.  And it's a complete sleep-hit, I didn't see it coming at all. You look at two cards at a time.  You can interact with either, or attempt to pass them.  The cards are arranged in a circle, so you don't lose an opportunity if you pass a card, but you can't see exactly what is on the next card unless you have a specific item or have seen it before.  There are tons of conditions that can make the choice to do that impactful.  If passing a monster, you may get attacked if you roll poorly on 'sneaking.'  That's damage you don't get to answer.  You could also walk in distance of a monster that has range on its attack, tipping your health below a safe threshold to turn back.  You could also get in range of a potion that saves your life from an oncoming threat. There are tons of types of threats, and they are all in plain view when faced with them.  Some monsters have thorns for a few turns in a row, others move around the circle in a specific direction and attack if they pass you.  Some steal your currency.  Others consume any other enemy and assume all the stats their own.  You have to make the decision to fight  carefully.  There are many conditions in which it's just a bad idea to even try to get loot from the level because you will almost certainly die. Without spoiling the concept of bosses here, as it plays into the story, they are very different and compelling.  Your choices have a dramatic impact on if you can beat the final fight or not.  I was genuinely thrilled and chilled by the presentation of one of the bosses.

_childDocuments_.review: This game, at its core, is very poorly balanced. From the absolutely punishing RNG to the downright unfair matchups you have to contend with as things get progressively harder. What is both insulting and infuriating to the point of frustration, is that it almost feels as if most build paths are either unreliable or too difficult to find synergies with. The fact a run can end after playing strategically, and making decisions in good faith in order to keep going, there are legitimate "run enders" that will chew you up and spit you back out without any remorse or hesitance. So why do I recommend it still? This game speaks to the inner masochist in me, that at its core, finds delight in very punishing, and challenging games. Obviously, if you've played something like Slay the Spire, as many fans of card builders have, this offers a similar experience of praying for RNG and throwing yourself into a wall for hours on end, only to get no further than when you first started. It's both a bitterness and desire to travel further than you did before to chase that rush of trying to figure out the best way to get further. This game captures atmosphere very well, with the unsettling characters and designs, this is executed VERY well when it comes to both pacing and setting a mood. Not knowing if your next step will be your last is always tempting to chase, as I have very much ended runs in less than 10 seconds, while also ending runs right before I get to the end, equally frustrated regardless of the outcome. At the writing of this review, I already have 122 runs I've died on with just over 7.5 hours spend subjecting myself to CBT. I can appreciate just how badly this game keeps sucking me back in, but it definitely needs more viable options when it comes to item builds, as currently unless you are extremely lucky, and get every possible stat boosting item and card, you get punished for just moving left or right eventually, as chip damage is both annoying and lacks any sort of charm, as the stat checks for stealth are hit or miss at best. Overall, I can completely respect anyone who is a fan of punishing games for the sake of challenge, but I would also argue, there is a lot of artificial difficulty in this game also, as some enemies are not meant to be killed obviously, but it's almost to the point of excessive obnoxiousness when getting far enough gives the enemies incredibly high damage and defense, meaning dodging becomes your main source of progression, it becomes tedious and overall poor game design. All of that being said, I would still urge anyone seeking a challenge to play this. It's designed to be a slow burn in progressing anyways I would wager, as rushing head first into a run usually results in just enough carelessness to end a run in one to two poor choices, which ALSO is incredibly annoying. I can only hope as time goes on, I figure out a way to bring things full circle in the Ring of Pain 6/10 Spoons

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a refreshing and innovative title in a saturated genre. It is absolutely worth your time if you enjoy a brutal challenge and deceptively complex card games.With stats and gear familiar to any RPG veteran, Ring of Pain's twist is that the dungeon is comprised entirely of cards. Make no mistake, this game is a , not roguelite. There is no carryover between runs outside of the items you unlock by completing various challenges.Another way I would phrase my recommendation of this title is, surprisingly, by relating it to certain board games. If you enjoy Mage Knight, Gloomhaven, or One Deck Dungeon, there's a good chance you'll enjoy this.While it receives many comparisons with Slay the Spire, be warned: this is not a similar game. Ring of Pain is almost like a tabletop card game that the designers decided would be easier to implement in a virtual space. As such, it feels wonderfully simple and self-contained while still providing incredible variation, strategic depth, and replayability. In my 22 hours with the game I have yet to play two similar runs.Ring of Pain plays like a dungeon crawler presented as a literal ring of cards. The player always sees two cards in front of them, and has four essential actions available: interact (or attack) left, pass left, interact (or attack) right, pass right. The entire game will be played using only these actions, with exceptions like a couple of unique rooms and the occasional spell items. You will navigate through increasingly difficult levels of the dungeon, fighting off enemies and fleeing overwhelming threats, while assembling an arsenal capable of taking you to the next level.In this way, Ring of Pain is wonderfully simple and easy to learn. It spoon feeds the player very little information about the game, taking a similar approach to games like Dark Souls. It will teach you by repeatedly, brutally, destroying you.The challenge is this: using these four actions, can you put together an assortment of gear that will allow you to defeat the threats presented? Nearly every item in the game offers a benefit and a detriment simultaneously. The player is expected to minimize the downsides of their gear while maximizing the boons provided.The last thing I'll offer is that the atmosphere in Ring of Pain is quite the achievement. It manages to create an ambience of forboding and creepiness. The creature design is unsettling and the sounds are unnerving. If you enjoy a setting that tells a story, you'll enjoy the Ring.This gets a definite recommend from me. It's a huge bonus that the developer support has been outstanding. Free updates are ongoing. You can join the game's discord and talk to the devs there, participate in competitions to design custom cards, and submit feedback straight to the dev team. This is the gold standard for developers supporting their game's community.

_childDocuments_.review: I did enjoy the game and am a fan of these types of rouge like card games that require you to think. I'm at twenty nine hours and came to the decision that for 20 bucks the game is pretty much worth the price; however, I do have major issues with the game after playing it through. The first is that at the start of the game you are guaranteed to lose your first 15 or so attempts, some of it may due to not knowing the game, but it is mostly because the best items are locked behind achievements that basically ensure you win the game. To be honest this kind of made me upset because instead of the game making you feel good for overcoming obstacles by understanding the game and thinking it basically comes down to picking up the legendary item that lets you wipe the entire floor in a few seconds. Because of this when you unlock a lot of the gear at end game meaning 12 hours you basically become a god that cannot be destroyed even on hard difficulty the game is a bit too easy given the gear you unlock. The second issue that I have with it is that there is not build diversity to this game at all, unlike slay the spire where you have multiple decks and builds for each character this game only relies on basic combat damage to really clear the mobs. The poison and freeze mechanics are fun; however, do not have nearly as good items compaired to raw damage output so you will drop them immediately upon seeing a better item. I still recommend the game, but would like to see more build diversity added to it and a better challenge mode, since hard is still not difficult enough. Also I do not like the daily dungeons since they are honestly very boring. Once you have played it once it is over, since they are not randomly generated related to enemy types, spawns, and the loot drops and rolls. It would be better if the dailies were random dungeons with ridiculous buffs to certain gear or the monsters.All in all I'd give it a 7/10 good but has some issues.Edit: Since the following updates the game has addressed my issues previously stated and am happy to give it a 9/10 score.
_childDocuments_.name: Ring of Pain

_childDocuments_.review: Its generally an ok game but lacking when looking at some details in terms of its design and polishing.In my experience most actions you perform end up being a choice between one death or another as the game only offers you two choices on what to do most of the time.This comes because you can only proceed left or right with a maximum of three possible actions you can perform in the entire game.That means especially in later stages, you either were dead to begin with or end up making a total gamble with chances vastly agains you and then its hardly your fault you lost.Thats already the case from the very first round and where you can basically just restart it.I describe that first "Ring" as an example.So the first ring features 4hp "rats" and 6hp "rats".The lower ones deal you two damage, the higher ones 3. You have 12.Now, if the arrangement of the first ring is, that you have an explosive monster to your left plus 2-3 rats following, you can simply forget that side because you will die in an instant.Its either a 100% death chance when fighting or  a 80% chance of losing the attempt of skipping a card. At least three times in a row, which means you get the same damage as if you just attacked.Leaves the right side.Theres a chance that one side features items that buff you, which you need or otherwise you will take too much damage during the first ring.But if odds are against you, the the other side features the remaining rats and the exit plus the loot cards appearing exactly at the back of the "dungeon" ring.That means, going right or left with combat kills you 100%, as you need three attacks to a rat with 6hp (you deal two damage) which in return deals 3 damage to you.You can kill one, but not more and if you decide to fight, you also cant bypass the next one by sneaking.You also cant sneak by them all, because a failed attempt deals 2-3 free damage to you, which has a high chance to happen as your success rate to sneak is too low from the beginning.That means you lost without playing.Its a gamble in these situations, not playing.And even if you ended up passing through and survive, you end up too weak.Im not talking about having the option to get out for free undamaged and im also not talking about the fact that you possibly could prepare for such situations later, because you cant.Im talking about the game screwing you with randomness and dooming your run because of its design, not your "skill" (decisions).On top come major issues with the information the game gives you.Even if you considered making a choice between only two options as a good idea, your choices often are made uninformed and the game makes it hard for you to properly asses what will happen if you go that route.It claims the opposite, ofcourse, in its tutorial by saying and i quote:"The expected damage you will receive by performing this action is shown at your healthbar".And theoretically it does. When you hover over an action, like attacking a creature, the healthbar shows how much life you would lose.However, its inconsistent and the math doesnt add up.For example:A creature you attack gets to attack back, your defense is high enough to block the damage but it has 2 "breakthrough" damage (a mechanic actually never explained in the game) that will go through your defense and deal damage to your life.I have several items equipped adding enough defense.I see i would gain 2 breakthrough damage from the monster, but decide to go that way and attack anyway.I end up losing nothing, for no obvious reason.No effect prevented the breakthrough damage, but the healthbar gave me the information that i would lose 2 health.Yet i didnt.I also made two screenshots where the math doesnt add up and the result contradicts all rules the game gives.It also has a problem with proper item descriptions to the effects they have or they just outright dont work.An item that pushes back a monster card when hit worked in one run. In a later run i found it again but its effect didnt trigger.This causes a lot of confusion on me as a player, as when i have to trial and error through the game using item effects to find out what they do, it should at least be consistent with what they do.Another issue are effects that are unclear on what they cause.One item states it increases "Souldamage" by 2. Nowhere in the game is explained what the heck "Souldamage" even is.Theres no tooltip on it, no expanded explanation. I still dont know after over 7 hours playtime.Another item claims that it gains plus 2 defense when i equipped another ice item, no item states whether its an ice item.And when i thought i had one, the effect didnt trigger.All in all, the game doesnt offer a lot of choice and the choice it offers isnt an educated one, due to a lack of proper information flow, lacking mechanics explanation, missing tooltips on effects and outright wrong calculations or contradictions to previously established rules.I have only one rule when it comes to games:Their ruleset has to stay consistent and true no matter what happens and no matter who uses them.As long as it stays that way, intended or not, i cant recommend it.Especially since it has a quite high asking price for what it offers.With the above considered, its gameplay design does NOT offer enough depth anywhere near other popular card games.- Two modes: Standard Mode (with the option to enable tutorial) and Daily Dungeon- 180 item cards- Many different monsters with their own effects and abilities, strengths or weaknesses (sadly with lacking information on what some of those effects actually are)- Nice music- A cool story twist with rhymes (that after several runs become dull due to a lack of dialogue options and thus repeated interactions.)- Nice artwork- Some sort of "i want to try again" feeling plus lots of interesting item synergies- You are not playing any cards but only equip items- Limited choice in terms of your decisions and limited choice in terms of your outcome as there are only three action types: Moving one step, attacking/interacting, using a spell you have equipped.- No additional modes i know of.- Once you unlocked the cards, you are basically done with your meta progression and can only try to beat the games randomness.- Not enough content to keep me motivated to play much longer. Enemies become samey after some time, story is barely existant, items while interesting come so random that its a total gamble on what combination you will find. Thus you cant create a strategy but rather optimize what you are dealt.- Information is not on point, contradicting or missing. Theres also no monster glossary.The game can be fun for a bit and its not bad, but its lacking.Considering the asked price it sits quite far beyond what its worth especially considering that its gameplay is much simpler than other, cheaper, card games.I say, get it on a sale only. If you are totally on gambling with chances and dicerolling with the odds against you, go for it.If you expect creating your own build and experimenting with it, forget about it.Its rather a game for 20 minutes inbetween something you need your head for.

_childDocuments_.review: Ring of Pain does a few things differently from other Rogue-like Deck Builders - but not in a good way, to be as fun or engaging as its competition. It's a mediocre title that as the developer put it:  This unfortunately is to the detriment of player engagement, fun, and the feeling that any given run is building to an outcome of the player's choosing. Instead the outcome becomes more a result of the player's moment to moment reactions to the randomness thrown in their way by the game. Where most deck builders use randomness to force players to commit to an overall strategy for completion - Ring of Pain abandons that in favor or randomness for its own sake. In this way Ring of Pain doesn't really have a brain on its shoulders and should be thought of as a kind of Rogue-like Dungeon platformer (that relies on cards) rather than a more  deck-building title in the vein of Monster Train or Slay the Spire. And like many platformers - once you've gone through the game's gauntlet and beat it once or twice - replaying it doesn't add much.If you haven't played Slay the Spire or Monster Train - skip Ring of Pain. If you have and you're looking for something in the genre - take note - this game is a shallow and less rewarding experience.While Ring of Pain does have some unique and interesting qualities - it needs far more iteration and interrogation into how to craft a fun and rewarding journey for the player that operates in more than 1-dimension.

_childDocuments_.review: - my personal opinion - I really want to like this game, but I feel like it falls a little bit short on some aspects.It's randomly generated, but it feels a lot more limited when compared to other games. Most items do not change the experience at all but just give plain stats. Only the rarer items that are available near the end of a run have some kind of strong effect like freezing enemies when your HP is below 25% health or damaging both enemies in front of you whenever you attack, but even that feels quite lackluster.The combination of a relatively heavy RNG system and the feeling that items are just a random dice roll of stats and not even something visual or interactable just kinda makes it feel like you've understood the game within a couple of hours of playing.The style is incredibly cool, however it feels surface level as 99% of the dialogue is two lines of cryptic haiku BS.  If you love games like Slay The Spire you'll probably like this too. It's a very cool game in its core.

_childDocuments_.review: Lovely little game, this is. You kill stuff, grab a pile of equipment to deck out your unknown protagonist, and hope you achieve your min-maxing event horizon before the enemies overwhelm you. There is a very nicely balanced element of strategy involved in how you move around the ring of cards, depending on the placement of the enemies. Initially this game can feel like it's giving you "impossible" RNG with an unkillable combo of enemies at certain levels, but as you understand the mechanics of each enemy and the benefits of your items, I promise this will ease off. And when you get that first unkillable build, it feels good.I do have a fairly standard criticism associated with these sorts of roguelites, in that you will very often die when you encounter a new enemy, simply because the game does not give you particularly detailed information about what the creature does or how it behaves. You have to find out by walking up to it, examining it, nodding sagely, then dying to 16 poison damage.Another small issue is regarding the damage projection. When you mouse over an enemy in preparation to fight it, the game will give you a visual preview of how much health the enemy will lose, how much health you will lose, along with any other forecast effects. The vast majority of the time. On occasions the damage projection system has lied to me, resulting in a tragic, avoidable death. I must stress that these occasions are very rare, and shouldn't sour your experience much.Overall, a solid purchase in my book.

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of those games where the shortcomings of Steam’s up or down rating system really become clear. I did end up giving Ring of Pain a “thumbs up” due to the game’s unique art style, the fast paced nature of its runs compared to other roguelike card battlers e.g. Slay the Spire and Monster Train, and the fact that I found myself coming back to it almost despite myself.That being said, this is not a game without its flaws. I found Ring of Pain’s mechanics to be shallow compared to those of other card battlers and it suffers from an almost complete lack of story. At times it felt like Ring of Pain was a demo for another game rather than a full experience in and of itself. $20 isn’t a terrible asking price but I recommend waiting until you can get it on sale for $15 or less. My biggest gripe with this game has already been raised by several other reviewers: the excessive RNG. All card battlers contain an element of RNG, that’s part of the experience, but I can’t think of any other game where RNG plays as large a role as it does in Ring of Pain. RNG will determine your starting stats, enemy placement, the enemies you’ll face, and which items you are (or aren’t) offered. In fact, Ring of Pain is the only card battler I can think of where RNG plays MORE of a role in the outcome of a run than player skill.I’ll leave you with this: if you’re looking for a roguelike card battler, buy Griftlands first, it’s a far superior game and retails at the same price.

_childDocuments_.review: I generally like games that have a degree of chance, provided they have ways to mitigate bad luck through strategy. What happens in those first few rings is almost entirely down to luck, and runs end far too frequently before you've had a chance to make an interesting choice. It's presented brilliantly and there's some great ideas here; certainly pick it up if it's cheap. If there were a bit more strategy involved it'd be a recommend, but as it is I don't think it does quite enough.

_childDocuments_.review: Initial Review [8 hours playtime total]: My first impressions of the game are that it isn't exactly a fulfilling experience. I never felt like I made better decisions on the runs where I won; I just got lucky with gear and the game wins itself. On the runs where I died, 99% of the time I died to slime enemies that explode & deal lots of damage... You generally can avoid them, but sometimes you will get very unlucky due to their positioning which leaves you unable to avoid lethal damage (as you progress through the game, the slime that explodes deals more and more damage) and die from something mostly out of your control. The difficulty does not seem consistent or well thought out either as there are several other issues like this that will leave you frustrated and the only way to really conquer any of these hurdles is to get lucky enough for how the enemy layout of a given room doesn't spawn in a way that completely ***** you over or get some of the few very broken items that completely makes the rest of your run a (near) breeze.Also, I'm not really sure why this game is tagged as a card game. There is nothing that feels like a card game about it besides the fact that the items you pick up & the enemies you face are all on card plates. Another popular series that has "cards" is the total war series where your units are placed on card plates, but you don't see that being called a card game... Your "character" is a faceless avatar that you buff throughout a run with the "cards" (items) you acquire. There is no turns or strategy of how you play your cards, though there can be synergy between them - but that doesn't make it a card game.  The base game mechanic is that you attack first if your speed is higher or second if slower. The strategy is simply getting lucky with the items you find and how you move around the room (every room is a circle of enemies, items, & stat upgrades - with the occasional teleport type card or room scramble card). But I've already stated in my first paragraph that sometimes your movement about the room doesn't matter. You are sometimes ****** the moment you entered a given room.Edit 1 [22 hours playtime total]: The game gets even more reliant on RNG at the harder difficulties & you seem to need a complete god run to even have a chance to win (you NEED at least a few of the best items and/or synergies). The developer seems to like picking out certain reviews that mention the complete RNG nature and all they seem to say is that it's totally fine and within your control. This could not be further from the truth. I have played numerous roguelikes/roguelites and this one is one of the worst offenders I can think of that has too many elements out of your control.Edit 2 [42 hours playtime total]: You might think I seem ridiculous putting so many hours into this game and still leaving a negative review, but please let me elaborate that most of these hours are spent playing this game while watching a stream or movie, which this game is actually decent for. But if you are looking for a Monster Train or Slay the Spire type game in terms of depth just look elsewhere. I try to be fair to most games I play barring completely broken and unplayable games, but after beating this game all the way through hard difficulty choosing light & medium difficulty choosing dark, it has become painfully clear this game has the depth of a puddle. Everything in this game just comes off like a complete gamble which in my opinion is a complete no-no for a well designed roguelike. There needs to always be a manageable level of control for the player that helps them successfully complete a run or you might as well be playing slot machines. Just look at a real  roguelike card game like Slay The Spire where some of the best players can consistently streak on the hardest difficulty. That's because the game provides at least a bare minimum of info & tools for how to go about building your deck. In other roguelike games like Isaac it's fine to use RNG as more of a crutch due to mechanical ability being able to carry you through an entire run (there is no item playthroughs beating the entire game free for you to watch on youtube). But this game doesn't have that. It's all tied to RNG.

While you can certainly lose a run via bad decisions, you can't be sure you'll win with good ones.Once the spell is broken, this game becomes a fairly mindless click-fest.  You can finish runs in 20 minutes or less (much less when the slot machine decides you'll be getting nothing but garbage loot), and while the experience is still pretty fun, it's just not super fulfilling.If you want a quick, luck heavy, simplified dungeon crawling experience with loot, this is for you.  If you want thinking, strategic play, high skill ceilings, and fulfilling victories, maybe this is not ideal.

_childDocuments_.review: There are a number of roguelikes that try to imitate the most successful ones out there, but Ring of Pain is the real deal.  If you're interested in being challenged to make calculated strategic choices, Ring of Pain delivers nicely.  The titular 'ring' stage layout offers a unique twist on combat and the strategy has been highly calibrated.  The game does, however, share some weaknesses with StS and virtually all games in the genre.  It offers only hints at a plot; if a strong story is important to you then you'll have to look elsewhere.  It also struggles to create a challenging final scenario despite offering two separate endgame paths; in my experience if you get off the ground early on you'll cruise through the ending without too much trouble.  You're still required to pay attention and play well, but you'll usually scale to be more than strong enough for the finale.  Overall, Ring of Pain offers a variety of ways to play through many unique, well-balanced synergistic builds.  For its innovative strategic concepts, well-polished basics and careful balancing, it deserves recognition as one of the leading games in the turn-based roguelike genre.

_childDocuments_.review: I really wish there was a third option for recommending things, like a "maybe", but y'know.Now... in the day I've had this game, I have developed a love-hate relationship with it.I love it because it's actually quite addicting, the gimmick of it is pretty neat, it can be fun when it wants to be, and the artstyle is beautiful.I hate it for one of the reasons above. It can be fun /when it wants to be/.I haven't won a run yet. Never have I had a death in this game that felt like it was my fault, except the one time I misclicked and accidentally smacked Owl without meaning to. Every death has felt like it was because the game gave me nothing good, or I simply had streak of terrible RNG. And the ending sequences can ♥♥♥♥ you over real fast, even if you have a perfect run. I think the ending sequences are my biggest gripe with the game, because they do feel incredibly unfun.But, of course, I can't get too mad, because, well, that's all this game is. RNG. Whether you get a good run is up to the roll of the dice, and obviously it can't be that bad if I keep coming back to it.If you really think it looks good, go ahead and get it, but just keep this in mind: This game is very bipolar. When you're winning, it's great! When you're losing, augh. Depending on the run, you get everything you could ever need, an okay setup, or nothing good at all. In some runs, one single bad roll ruins you, while in others, you can ♥♥♥♥ up 500 times and somehow still be on track for a win. It's really weird.The RNG of the game can make it feel aggressively unfun at times, so. Yeah.If you don't mind having your every run dictated by incredibly bipolar RNG, then go ahead and get it, it's pretty neat, and I do actually like it, despite my gripes. If rampant RNG is something that pisses you off, though, then this DEFINITELY isn't the game for you.

_childDocuments_.review: Needs a larger pool of loot to draw from, but more content is promised and the developer is giving active feedback - focused on Discord, but present on Steam forums as well.Balance feels great already. From a simple system of attack/loot, move/stealth, use spell/scroll, there's a lot of resource management to be had. Ring of Pain delivers a moderately deep experience, yet the controls are simple and runs short. There are a lot of complaints about excessive RNG/enemy power creep, and I don't understand them. An experienced player is likely to clear the default difficulty on a majority of their runs, and at the time of this review I have cleared all difficulties at least once each.Do note that a significant chunk of the item pool is behind achievement unlocks, a pet peeve of mine. However, most of them will be unlocked with natural play, and those that aren't can be done relatively quickly if you know they exist. Examples of the latter include over-using a shrine to lower your max HP to 1, or not doing certain actions before Floor 6 that you'd normally do like consuming heal potions or killing enemies.Still, the core experience is great, so I can overlook the mild progression elements with the item pool. Recommended.

_childDocuments_.review: A lovable mix of trippy, edgy and straight up weird. Ring of pain is a nice take on the card based dungeon crawler, where it's not about deck building but more about solving a puzzle based the options you are presented, while trying to improve your character with items and stats. Unforgiving and yet addicting The game really lives up to the pain part of its name. Don't expect to get through it without struggle. Even in runs when i felt strong, the game quickly reminded me, that one mistake or just bad luck can end your pathetic existance.Combine all of that with the good balance of artwork, music and whatever sounds those creatures you encounter make and you got yourself a great game to sink many hours into, even when you still have no clue what the hell this place is.And hail the Onion Suit!

_childDocuments_.review: PROSRing of pain has incredible visuals and sound design. The game's atmosphere will drag you in and allow you to visit a truly unique universe, full of creepy birds and creatures. The gameplay is intuitive and fun. It's simple, yet as you explore the game, you realize that the decisions are more complex than you may have expected at first.CONSWhile the gameplay is surprisingly complex for a game of this style (where you rarely have more than a few options at a time), after playing for a while it does get very repetitive. The difficulty of the game is less the about the decisions that you make, and more about the item lottery. Sure, it's easy to make mistakes, but even by playing very well, you will still often find yourself dying simply because you didn't get the right items.CONCLUSIONWhile I do recommend the game, I do so with a warning that it probably won't last you as long as you would expect from a rogue-like game.

_childDocuments_.review: It's hard to describe Ring of Pain accurately without just asking someone to watch some gameplay of it. I found this card-based roguelike to be a great snappy game to quickly drop into. Even if a run would usually only last around 30 minutes, I would struggle to resist the temptation of 'just one more run'. Most of the gameplay here is a mix of making calculated decisions and inventory management. Which sounds terribly boring but Ring of Pain has been wonderfully ballanced and the variety from run to run can be huge!Score: 8.5 / 10Pros:-The game's art style is unique.-The UI will give you a detailed representation of what would happen for every choice you make. Very few things are a surprise in Ring of Pain.-Build variation is huge and the achievements do a great job of pushing you to try new and challenging builds.-The best items in this game really are very powerful and can do all kinds of wild things to empower you.-Great game for the Steamdeck and other handhelds.Cons:-While the UI does usually do a good job of telling what will happen next, it sometimes can't keep up with some of the crazier builds in the game. These instances can lead to some disappointing deaths.-One or two of the hardest achievements in the game might be a little over-tuned.

_childDocuments_.review: This game caught me by surprise.I got it in a bundle or something. I am NOT a big fan of card games. I expected to try it out for a few minutes, delete it and move on.But something about it caught me.It's not really a card game at all, as in you picking cards from a hand and playing them. It's more like a very simple dungeon crawler. You can go left, or right. You can also attack the enemy or interact with the object on the left or right. The entire dungeon circles around on a big wheel, so if you go in one direction long enough you come back where you started. The goal is to level up as much as possible and move on.There is enough meat on these bones to keep me engaged for 100+ hours. It's the perfect podcast game. Play some audio and give the game another spin, see how far you can get this time.The downsides are card-like visuals (personal taste) and dour presentation in general. I've completed the game several times and still have no freaking idea what's it even about. I am getting literally nothing from the story.I'd still strongly recommend this one if you're into zen podcast pacifier roguelikes.

_childDocuments_.review: A refreshing roguelike that lays it all out there -- every mechanic is intuitive, and every turn your decision is made with full view of enemy intentions. But it still completely punishes you and kills you in 50 different ways. In a way, it's kind of a perfect game, because it's a simple idea really but it explores every nook and cranny of that idea, and has a surprising number of hidden chambers to explore.Each round is also exactly the right length, enough to make an accidental death move your cursor toward "one more round" plenty of times. And the metaprogression is really just achievements = gear, which is exciting to unlock but not necessarily OP. Most of the later gear is for really weirdo builds that are hard to pull off, which is a fun endgame imho.TL;DR nice balance, creepy owl, fun loop, well worth it! B+

_childDocuments_.review: Ring of Pain is a surprisingly addictive card game that will keep you hooked for hours on end. You'll find yourself drawn into the mysterious dungeon, eager to uncover its secrets and defeat its fierce monsters. The gameplay is challenging, but not so difficult that it becomes frustrating. While the graphics may not be on the same level as Cybertronian technology, they are surprisingly atmospheric and add to the game's overall mood. The creatures may not be as ferocious as Decepticon beasts, but they still manage to be menacing in their own right. The gameplay is where Ring of Pain truly shines. The card system is easy to learn, but there is enough depth and strategy to keep even the most experienced players engaged. Each turn brings new challenges and opportunities, and the sense of progression as you venture deeper into the dungeon is incredibly satisfying. Overall, Ring of Pain is a game that I can recommend to those who seek a challenging and addictive gameplay experience. While it may not be on the same level as true battle, it is still a worthy pastime for those puny humans who lack the ability to join the Decepticon ranks. I suppose I'll give credit where credit is due, Ring of Pain is more addictive than a dose of energon.

_childDocuments_.review: Not sure what anyone sees in this game. Isn't actually a card builder so IDK why it is labeled as such. You pick an item you equip but theres no deck or strategy or really turns. All you do is just attack creatures then they attack you. The game is basically a coin flip simulator as its almost all random and RNG with a player having little agency. Sometimes you get good items, sometimes the entire floor is poorly designed exploding enemies that you cant attack but sneaking past you only have 25% chance, or poison enemies that do the same or guys with range attacks that can auto hit you from across the circle while you cant do anything. You'll have a good deck going then just instant die due to bad luck with nothing you can do about it instead of card games where you can make mistakes or build a deck and synergies, in this you just add stats to your character then hit attack. Pretty mindless and monotonous and boring, as you dont feel you progress or learn how to play better since theres not much to it and its all just random without you doing much. So you never feel like you could have done something differently or crafted a different deck or anything at all, you just feel unfulfilled. All you unlock from repeated plays is a few new items to maybe find but there was no real incentive. Was expecting a fun intricate involved game like a Roguebook or Monster train but its just like pulling a slot machine, when you lose you don't know why you were playing in the first place. Feels like the worst part of roguelikes without any of the benefits. But like slot machines im sure its addictive for some people as runs are over in 10 minutes. 5/10.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is excellent. Both the art and the mechanics are simple but masterfully executed. The ring of cards idea is very well fleshed out and I really appreciate the implementation of stealth mechanics. There are so many items, spells, monsters, and dungeon types. For as relatively simple as the core mechanics are, I'm very impressed with how much variety the developers were able to pack into this game. My biggest complaint would be that RNG can still throw the game but I feel that most of the time it is very balanced and how you build your stats as you progress will normally be the main factor that determines how far you get. Its very easy to make a dumb mistake and lose everything but with enough practice (and a little luck) the game becomes very manageable. Additionally I wanted to mention how much charm this game has. The developers clearly had a sense of humor and I appreciate the addition of what I believe to be a few "hidden" references to other games. I've also greatly enjoyed collecting achievements for this game because most of them are actually fun and challenging instead of seeming like an afterthought(like achievements in some games I've played). Overall, I would highly recommend this game to anyone who is a fan of deck-builders and/or rougelikes(-lites). The game can be played in short bursts or hours at a time and it is very accessible as a result. Good game, something I would recommend to people who liked Slay the Spire.

With its stunning artwork and engaging narrative, Ring of Pain is a must-play for anyone looking for an immersive gaming experience.

_childDocuments_.review: Ring of PAAAAAIN is a rogue card game.  Put it down after 4.5 hours of playing and will probably pick it up again later.  Used a mouse to play.  Difficulty is easy (to figure out) and frustrating (to beat).  This is on the shallow end of the card game pool out there.  There's more random chance, less strategy and you don't play cards so much as collect cards that will help you get further later.  Each card is either a monster you have to fight, a door, or a treasure that either enhances your skills or gives you armor.  The more doors you go through, the further you complete the ring until you get toasted, poisoned, or gutted to death by bad luck or monsters that are way more powerful than you are.  The more new cards you uncover, the more opportunity you get to claw out a deeper ring for yourself.It's actually a pretty enjoyable game is you play just to experience the dungeon crawling venture.  But the same enemies do get old.  There's a sense of progression that wears thin with repeated deaths.  The biggest downside was a monster encourages you to kill puppies.  :( There is no joy in killing puppies. But if you openly choose Not to kill puppies, the game is playable and entertaining for a few playthoughs.

_childDocuments_.review: I love this game. It's very addictive. At the start, there is a steep learning curve. Don't let the simplistic graphics fool you, there is definitely some RNG involved, but as you "git gud" how you deal with that is mostly strategy. You also pick up new cards during failed runs to help you with the next.  Learn from your mistakes and try again. The game doesn't hold your hand in that you have to figure out things for yourself. And sometimes it can feel punishing, but if you like roguelike card games, then you're used to that.  The first time you meet an enemy, you might choose the wrong direction (left or right) and die. There are a lot of different items that you can pick up, some single use. You have to be strategic in how and when you use those items. If you don't, you die. I love that. _childDocuments_.review: In case someone shrugs off the review as a newbie whining about the genre: I love card and strategy games. Some of my favorites of similar genre are STS, Trials of Fire, Griftlands, Monster train, Nowhere prophet... This review is as constructive and blunt as it can get.While it's definitely not everyone's cup of tea, it's unique enough to stand out. They went for a "depressed creepy" art approach which gives you kinda of Binding of Isaac vibes. A bit "12 year old" at times but it is at very least refreshing and polished. Some monster visuals could be a bit more detailed, but generally pickups and tiles are well made. Clean, simple, efficient. Just what you want out of a simplified game like this, nobody wants extra clutter.Here's where it gets ugly. To be blunt... it's shallow as f**k. It feels like a flash game in a fancy suit.You will be deciding whether to trade blows, dodge mobs while risking getting hit, calculate where the self exploding mobs will land in order to not get blown to bits and damage other mobs instead, while generally simply balancing HP taken vs HP healed. That's pretty much it. However, to get to a point where your feel your moves start to matter more and there is considerable tactical planning in advance instead of running away from mobs way stronger than you, you need the all mighty god with you. The god of...RNG is a vital part of rogue-lites and card games. However, when RNG becomes the majority of your game and the rest of it is shallow, even the avid fans of the genre will have to look cross-eyed in order not to see this is as a slot machine. To get any sort of meaningful progress, you will have to get lucky with the combination of loot, mob placement and mob types. Only then, you will feel like your moves slowly become to matter more and you are in control of the pace to some degree. And yes, we are talking about the type of RNG where you can do everything "correct" to your best abilities, yet get consecutively boned. And not boned like a DnD dice roll where you fail to do enough damage. At least you had a choice there but failed the throw. Here, the dices are the whole map/mob/item layout and your effect on them is minimal. On the plus side, newcomers to the genre may look at the game as a gambling simulator, so if that appeals to you, go ahead and buy it.Don't expect any deep mechanics here or your skill being something that really matters. Not a single time through all losses or victories have i felt like i have played better or worse, misplayed a move or done something brilliantly. It all came down to the god of RNG, so if you would like to play , i highly recommend it to you. If they will add more depth to the game, this review is subject to change, but at this point of a full release, it's a bitter disappointment.

_childDocuments_.review: (TL;DR: A fresh dungeon crawler, with a few caveats for a player's taste in roguelikes. The devs have improved the game's balancing quite a bit since release!)First of all, this game is a real gem. The cartoonish whimsy and unsettling horror blend really well together, and the core gameplay design feels great.My initial review was negative, due to how RNG governed early game success far more than player skill. But it was a close call, given how much I liked most of what Ring of Pain does. Now the devs have made some subtle yet critical changes to the early game, which give runs a more solid base to start making early tactical decisions off of.I had also mentioned that 2 hours (my playtime on first reviewing it) might have been too little time to really get how the game works; that was true! Now with 20+ hours of gameplay, having gotten all endings multiple times and having tried out many kinds of builds, this review should be much more representative of the full game.Let's start with some basic praise:The artwork, music, sound design, premise, tone, interface design, input feedback, and (most of) the rhyming dialogues are all fantastic, and are what drew me in initially. Daily Dungeons have also been unexpectedly good puzzle-solving experiences.The elements of player skill in Ring of Pain are also really engaging! Such as:- Luring mobile enemies into better positions- Holding on to spells for the perfect life-saving moment- Realizing when a spell should be cast immediately instead of waiting- Learning when a monster should be fought for souls, and when it should be avoided- Learning when you can linger on a floor and when you need to haul ass to an exit- Unlocking unknown rooms to give your future self better navigation info on future runs- Choosing which rooms you can handle with your current build, and when to take a safer path- Rationing souls between low-level gear offerings and saving up for big chests or niche spells- Finding low-risk opportunities to potentially tank a bunch of Curse before healing and exiting- Recognizing synergies and capitalizing on them with your play style and future gear choices- Staying aware of how enemies further back are moving and learning how to close in on them- Recognizing when your favorite piece of gear is actually less good than the weirder low-level alternative you just found-Recognizing when the legendary mega-item you just found is actually not as good as your current blue item for this specific run's synergies... and the list goes on. There's solid depth here, and it's great. It's not as deep as some other games of its ilk, but I wouldn't say it's shallow, either.So what have the devs improved since launch? For me these 3 changes stand out:#1: The random aspects of the early game, namely how many items and potions you find on the first few floors, are now far less variable; you always find enough stuff to have a decent chance of putting together a workable starting kit. Item offerings are still the randomized dual choices, but that brings us to ...#2: Re-rolling item offerings is now cheaper, and for common items the first re-roll is now free! This provides far more flexibility to the start, which in turn allows you to start making real decisions on floor 1. It also means that you'll have a more dependable package of souls leaving the first few floors, which snowballs into giving you more choices on future floors.#3: When Owl offers you a free item, now it's almost always something that would occupy an empty slot. This might seem trivial, but before this change I was turning down Owl's scavenged gift 9 times out of 10 due to already having something better. It's just a feel-good change that winds up having a disproportionately positive effect on my runs.There were other balancing tweaks and a few enemy nerfs, but these three are what I think did the most. I also commend the devs for fielding such a diverse set of criticism from players and responding with such simple yet effective changes!Finally, how does the game feel to play after a lot of experience with it + balance changes?> Post balance changes, I've almost always felt like my deaths are due to poor decisions that I could have anticipated and avoided beforehand, not due to just having an unwinnable starting kit. The biggest improvement I've felt in my own skill as a player has been learning to make hard choices that feel iffy short-term, but improve survival chances long-term; I've also gotten better at realizing when taking a seemingly simple action will lead to my inevitable demise. You can lose a run with a few simple misplays, and that feels perfect for Ring of Pain.> I still feel iffy about the % chances that are littered all over this game's design, and how those percentages are mostly geared towards randomizing your ability to block, mitigate, and recover from damage. But part of why I dislike this might be due to how open the game is with these percentages, whereas in something like Slay the Spire similar random elements would be obscured by the numberless RNG of card order in your deck and enemy intents on future turns. So despite my personal dislike of rolling dice to see if an action succeeds, having the odds be totally transparent can make up for it, as can having few random elements elsewhere. Speaking of which:> In Ring of Pain, enemy behavior is entirely predictable, meaning you can plan around them and make tactical decisions several turns in advance. So long as you have some method of mitigating or avoiding explosive enemies, you've got options. Every monster that can move is revealed as soon as you enter a floor, while static hazards remain hidden until you get close. This gives a lot of value to items that reveal all cards on a floor, while still giving runs without those items the agency to plan around Drifters and Scroungers and the like. (Truly huge monsters can also be spotted due to their slightly larger card sizes!) All this serves to reduce randomness and increase player agency.> The five stats each play their role, but their importance fluctuates as you go deeper:   - Early game, Damage and Speed can be very strong choices to focus on; getting to the point where you can insta-kill early enemies saves you more health and earns you more souls than Defense or Clarity upgrades would have. BUT:   - Having too little Clarity can still result in having too few souls to open mimic chests later on!   - The speed, damage, and/or defense of certain enemies jumps dramatically as you push deeper, and a damage/speed combo won't pull you through unless you've got something else to fall back on. Playing a one-trick pony is a death sentence, as is relying on stats alone; you need some special abilities from items and spells to pull you out of deadly situations.   - You also need to be able to deal damage indirectly to get through certain mid-game enemies. Poison, splash damage, light damage, and manipulation of explosive enemies are all ways of getting around foes with unbeatable defense or speed, and will keep you alive long enough to start outclassing them with raw stats. Having indirect damage early on can also partially mitigate having a low Damage stat.   - Late game, your stats tend to start going nuts, which can radically shift the balance of your build. 50+ Clarity means you no longer get cursed, tons of Defense can make your Parry % climb to 100, etc. Having ludicrous Speed seems pointless on the base difficulty mode.> Honestly, my biggest current issue with the game is this: the two legendary jar items are absurdly OP, especially Light Concoction. Soul Hourglass at least requires some good synergies to really go crazy, but either of them makes Clarity the most important end-game stat, and Light Concoction pretty much invalidates whatever other item synergies you had going on. Compared to other legendary items, these two probably need to be toned down. Just a little bit.

_childDocuments_.review: Fun roguelike, and definitely a unique take on dungeon crawling, if you want to call it that.  Just don't come in expecting to win most of the time.  While that's true for many roguelikes, Ring of Pain is HEAVY on RNG.  And unlike many other roguelikes, you can usually take something away from a loss - learning something new, adapting your strategy for next run, "oh well at least I tried it this way instead", etc. - with Ring of Pain while runs are usually fun, most of the time when you lose it's just because the RNGJesus wasn't in your favor.  And I'm talking sometimes you'll lose a run in under a minute on the first level simply due to RNG (runs are typically under 30 minutes anyway once you understand the game).If you enjoy roguelikes and don't mind the frustration factor of losing hard sometimes, you'll probably like this game.  It's fun for a while, but you don't feel like you're in control or able to dictate a run most of the time by decisions you make, so much as with the cards you're dealt.  In it's current state it's good, but maybe a bit shallow on content or overall fun factor to get at full price.  Maybe wait for a 20% or more off sale.  Solid game though that could definitely get better in the future with some updates.

_childDocuments_.review: There is a growing sub-genre of deckbuilders where enemies are cards themselves rather than standalone battles, and the strategy comes down to navigating between cards in two dimensions (e.g. Krumit's Tale and Pyrene) or even one dimension (e.g. Ring of Pain). Although it sounds promising, the extra complexity from navigation does not compensate simplistic fights.Ring of Pain is supposed to shift the focus on choosing between items and spells and on moving left or right, but these decisions play a negligeble role in the outcome of a run. As in simpler games like Monster Train, I succeed if I get an overpowered item early on (e.g. boosting max health from potions) and fail otherwise. Without overpowered items, it's a matter of time until I die from a single hit (e.g. from an exploding enemy).The fresh mechanics (e.g. stealth, passing + pushing) remain gimmicky because there are barely any enemies against whom to use these mechanics. For instance, an enemy can either move to you to explode or remain stationary, so there is no need to calculate several steps ahead and account for complex interactions.Worst of all, there are simply too many levels, too many enemies and too many items, reducing the value of those things. If a player wants to succeed in reasonable time, he must act before thinking and pray for the best.

_childDocuments_.review: If you appreciate the genre of deck building board and video games, but find yourself growing tired of 'ideal builds' or the management/constant shuffling of said genre, this game is for you. If you appreciate inventory management and making choices on what to keep or toss, look no further.The best way I can describe this lovely game is a randomly generated dungeon filled with a choose-your-own-adventure elements tossed in here and there. The 'dungeon' is a series of pre-determined but randomly assigned rooms that you will be attempting to survive. There is no 'deck' for your character, just equipment slots for you to manage as you obtain gear. The gear provides you stats and mini-bonuses that CAN all stack/interact with one another to allow fun, unique opportunities that occur frequently enough to make you feel really cool, but not often enough that they become standard in a run and therefore predictable and boring.While all of the titled 'rooms' are pre-determined with bad guy types and relative strengths, their positions are randomized and there are enough monsters and things that move and switch assignments enough to make each run feel like a small, unique puzzle to resolve each time you go through. While your primary ability to obtain things will be by defeating opponents, you are not required to do so and without spoiling anything there are ways to obtain the 'soul' currency without murdering everything in sight. The 'sneak' feature is simple and provides just enough strategic incentive to make me actively try it many times during a run, either for positioning or just plain surviving.The randomness of the dungeon design and loot tables does lead to a degree of 'luck' in terms of gear/loot that you find during your run, but that's basically the definition of every roguelite style game in existence. If you don't enjoy knowing that in said room you'll find X items or what not, you should know enough about this genre game already to not be reading this review or considering buying this game in the first place. All in all, this game is very well made, has entertained me for over 60 hours thus far, has multiple difficulties to continue the challenge/enjoyment, has fun achievements to strive for, and is a game I can potentially complete in 20 minutes to an hour, depending on what I'm trying to achieve and a degree of luck/skill. I only wish there was plans to add more to the game and there may be, but I'm not one that follows a lot of game news or updates, I just enjoy being pleasantly surprised when new stuff comes.

_childDocuments_.review: Quick Description:-Ring of Pain is dungeon crawling deckbuilder w/ a sinister aesthetic and tone.  This game is a mix of Darkest Dungeon, Slay the Spire, and a big splash of creativity.  The learning curve is slightly steeper than the average game, but oh boy is this game fun and addicting!What's Good:-I think that the greatest strength of ROP is how different and unique every runs feels.  Over the course of a run you will pick up so much gear, which can lead to really dynamic synergies.  As I became more comfortable w/ the game, I started adjusting to the items that I found.  I would change my entire approach if I found a couple of items that perfectly compliment each other.  -Meta progression is king in roguelights!  I really love the way meta progression works in ROP.  You will unlock something new almost every run.  There are tons of really cool cards to unlock that really shake up the runs.  You can also unlock new options for starting gear, as well as harder modes.  I'm about 12 hrs in and I still have plenty more to unlock.-Deckbuilders aren't typically known for their impressive visuals (Gordian Quest and Monster Train may have something to say about that).  ROP looks so cool visually.  I love the way enemies all appear in a circle which is something I've never seen before in a game.  I'm also a huge fan of the dark and brutal tone that is mixed w/ just enough light to balance it out.-The skill ceiling is quite high b/c of the complexity of dungeons.  You may enter a room w/ 20+ monsters and a dozen forms of gear, upgrades, or treasure.  Every decision is crucial, and a single mistake can destroy an otherwise perfect run.  This is a game you could sink a ton of hrs into.-Although it's a bit overwhelming b/c of the sheer volume of gear you will gain, it is extremely easy to play the game mechanically.  You can do everything from your mouse and this game is extremely responsive.  This sounds like a weird thing to be happy about, but b/c you may make 30 decisions in a single room, actions need to respond fast to your choices.  This game nails this aspect of the genre.Could Use Some Changes:-This game is a bit more complex than the average game in this genre.  You have quite a bit of gear and every single item can synergize w/ everything else in your inventory.  If you are less experienced w/ this genre, you may find it a bit intimidating early on.  I promise that it's worth the investment and things start to click quickly.-This game can be quite volatile, especially late game.  It's really easy to accidentally blow yourself up if you have the right upgrades.  You have to really be careful b/c it's easy to start a chain reaction that causes half the room to die and spew splash damage everywhere.  I've had a few of my runs end this way, and it's heartbreaking.Consensus:-Solid Game (Tier 3 and makes up 35% of my reviews).  I really like this game and I plan to continue playing this for some time.  I love how this game nudges you to try out new and creative playstyles.  Adjusting to what gear you find is by far the most important and fun part of this experience imo.  I'm really excited to try out Hard Mode, which I just unlocked recently.  If you love deckbuilders or dungeon crawlers, then this is a must own!

_childDocuments_.review: Extremely good game; took me 107 hours to get all the achievements, but when new content releases I'll definitely be back.Ring of Pain is a card-game roguelike focused around gathering stat boosts and items to utilize interactions between different cards to propel you throughout the run. There's plenty of gameplay shown, but a rundown:- Attack increases the damage done on a attack.- Defense reduces the amount of damage taken, as well as adding a chance to parry piercing damage if your defense negates non-piercing damage.- Speed determines who attacks first, and increases dodge/sneak chance.- Clarity increases health from potions, crit chance, and souls from kills.Every item takes up its respective slot, and then gives stats and/or a passive. Scrolls and spellbooks are active items, and do not take up your turn when used.A turn passes when any of the following occurs:- You move past an item.- You sneak past an enemy.- You attack an enemy.- You pick up an item. With that in mind, certain enemies can be standard enemies with no special characteristics, meaning they remain in the location they are in, and only have an effect when you try to sneak past or attack it. Other enemies are special: -Ranged enemies will deal damage after a turn ends, if you are in their range.-Other enemies will move towards you every turn, then once in front of you, will attack after the turn ends (assuming they are still in front of you.)-Other enemies will move towards you every turn, then once in front of you, prepare to detonate, dealing damage to you and the cards next to it. Killing these cards will cause them to detonate, also, meaning if you position between two explosive cards and one detonates, you can get slapped pretty bad.There are special rooms that involve either special enemies, altars, NPC's, and have special things inside, which usually are worth it long-term, assuming you survive them.All around, the way turns progress and the way decisions affect the dungeon (and each run, by extension) is extremely interactive, and your items and how the rings are generated provide a lot of unique experiences. A lot of incredibly strong enemies have specific weaknesses that can be exploited, and using how the ring is generated against itself feels incredibly rewarding. One of my favorite games of all time.

Dying will be a plenty but perhaps there's a light at the end of this tunnel.If you enjoy Slay the Spire but dislike building decks, then this is for you. It's simpler but still requires a great deal of wits, especially when you really get into knock-back mechanic and chaining explosive enemies.My only complaint about the game is the equipment choices doesn't feel too impactful early except for "get good stats". Some equipment are borderline terrible to the point that it is better to toss it. It feels as if the dev added a free reroll just to reduce the chances of obtaining them. I'm looking at you, Blood Ritual.

_childDocuments_.review: Picked this up from the Humble Bundle thinking it looked alright and proceeded to sink hours into it. Ring of Pain is one of the few games on here that is uniquely its own thing. Sure, the genres of it aren't anything new but the way the game mechanically functions is. In short, you start a run and either interact with a card or skip over it and either of these count as a turn. This allows enemies to move or attack or do some other action depending on the type of enemy they are. As the player you are attacking, getting an item or sneaking past a card. Whilst simple on the surface the game nails the feeling of building a run in something like Isaac where you're hedging your resources and life to get through each floor and building up as you go. I will say the game starts out quite rough and at first I was on the fence with it as the game has a rather steep learning curve along with a tonne of items locked behind achievements. Once you play more, learn and unlock more items, the game gets much easier overall. It's definitely something worth sticking with past the few painful first hours as you need to learn what enemies do, how your stats function and how the games mechanics work. One of the key elements at play in the game is learning the stats of enemies and how to utilise your stats and synergies as well as gambling your currency gained from killing enemies to reroll items to best fit what you're going for. All in all if you want to win you're going to need to figure out what items come from where and what works with what as there are differing rarity boxes and spells that can be gained as you progress or as you take more challenging rooms. Aesthetically it's solid, it has its own style and perspective. The game has an eerie and macabre aesthetic and soundtrack to boot which all fit well. All of the sfx and vfx elevate the game to something more as the crunchy hit sounds and effects all lean in to making the game more engaging. All in all it's a solid game and well worth the time and money invested once you get to grips with it.

_childDocuments_.review: This game doesn't offer a lot in the way of strategic agency.  Your decisions don't feel very consequential here.  More than anything, this feels like a stat-check or inventory-check game, which is fueled by whatever the RNG gods hands you.Do you get awarded an anti-poison item earlier?  Cool, slimes are trivial to you now.  Oh you dont have that item?  Well I guess you have to spend your entire run fleeing from them until you find the anti-poison item.  Oh you didnt find enough stealth items to escape them safely?  I guess you are going to get punched in the back every time you try to run away from them.Did you get awarded an anti-explosion item?  Nice, now the bomb enemies cant threaten you anymore. Oh you don't have anti-explosion shield?  Well half your health bar will get blasted every time you pop them then.It's not really engaging to put hope in getting a relevant dice roll, rather than trying to think my way out of certain situations.I think RNG definitely has a place in roguelikes.  Trial By Fire is an extremely punishing roguelike game that can sometimes mess you up with randomness, but you at least have the means to set yourself up to try and absorb a really bad situation when it turns up.  Or at the very least, remember how you died and adjust your strat moving forward - with Ring of Pain it was like, "well i guess my inventory will decide if I can fight or if I have to run"There's no real deckbuilding to this game, and there's no real strategy to enemy encounters.  There isn't any real navigation choice either.  This is more of a linear dungeon crawler where your choices are dictated by an inventory slot machine.  Once I kinda saw the game loop for what it was, it got extremely boring really fast.If you are super into this theme or the art style or the music (all of which are pretty cool), this might be a decent pickup for $5 or something, but considering how much strategic depth and polish you can get from a $20 title like Monster Train or Roguebook, I can't really recommend getting Ring of Pain at that price point.

_childDocuments_.review: Game is lacking in real options/decisions. Most games will play out exactly the same way despite quite a lot of items to choose from. It seems like the developers intended for people to take the optional rooms to try power themselves up, but even fully completing every room and taking every challenge room, it's still a toss of the dice if you'll be lucky enough to get the right items and stats to make it past the mid game.There's no real depth at all which is a shame because the art/levels/music and mechanics are otherwise amazing. If I had to simplify what it feels like, it's basically slay the spire, but you can only use 'strike'.What this game needs is a few core items that might dictate the build path you decide to go and an increase number of choices to choose from instead of just 'heres 1 item, take it or don't'.
