_childDocuments_.review: This game reminds me a lot of if Reigns were a dungeon crawler...but that being said, this game is a unique one, so no comparison is going to be completely accurate.Essentially, I'd call this game a fast-paced roguelike dungeon-crawler with some card game elements. The "card" elements take the form of the dungeon; each dungeon level is made up of several cards, with some being hostile, some being friendly, and some being neutral. You have two cards in front of you at any given time and can rotate through the "deck" or interact with the cards. Sometimes interactions will be forced when you try to rotate through the deck (usually monsters attacking you if you fail a stealth check). So the goal is to make it to the exit of each floor while killing as much as you can for souls, the game's currency (without losing out on too much health; health stays between floors after all), as well as picking up treasure along the way. As it turns out, early game RNG was addressed in the latest update and I can safely say skill is the predominant factor in success now! Like any game with roguelike elements, RNG will definitely work with/against you, but a single instance (or even a few instances) of RNG shouldn't be a run ender, or else the run was liable to fail anyways.But either way, a simple description of the game is going to be a bit confusing and doesn't do it justice; try the demo! The demo should be enough for you to tell if you're going to like the game or not. Notably, the main game is a more updated version with unlockables and also doesn't cut you off like the demo does; the demo cuts you off roughly around 1/3 of the way into a run, and runs get more interesting the later they go...And a quick tip since I struggled with this; run away or pass by exploders if you can! They deal pathetic melee damage so failing a stealth check basically doesn't matter, and the ones that chase you and try to self destruct won't follow you on the explosion turn, so you can flee to safety.

_childDocuments_.review: RING OF PAIN is a brand new roguelike, card crawler game released on October 15th, published by Humble Games and developed by Simon Boxer and Twice Different, available on Steam and Nintendo Switch.Ring of Pain is not your regular deck-builder video game - a genre that has received a ton of love from indie gems such as Slay the Spire, One Step from Eden, and Monster Train. Ring Of Pain doesn’t have you building your deck - instead it centers around your stats and different loot that changes different variables in the game (such as attack, defense, speed / initiative, and more). These stats will allow you to either mow down enemies or sneakily bypass them in hopes of avoiding damage (or worse). Ring of Pain’s aesthetic is generally spooky. Which is perfect for the time of year we’re in and the time of year it was released. With incredibly detailed, monstrous, and disturbing creatures - this is where the “card” functionality comes into play. Each “dungeon” is set up in a ring, in which you can move left or right. Enemies, potions, books, scrolls, and more populate the Ring of Pain as cards - and it’s your job to make it to an exit alive and bear the brunt of what comes next. For killing enemies, you’ll receive souls. You spend these souls on upgrades, potions, or utilize them in other ways that might be a little spoiler-y. Just know that there is a wide swath of dungeon types, including stores, shrines, and more - even speaking with The Owl (the face of the game) and the opposite of The Owl - something I’m not going to spoil here. Aside from the main ‘campaign’, there is a daily dungeon mode - which provides specific modifiers to a run and a leaderboard to rank you against your friends and the world. After completing a handful of runs, you’ll also unlock The Collection - where you can go and check out items you’ve unlocked and read the pros and cons of each item - definitely to help you learn synergies and avoid certain items). Ring of Pain is, largely, a game of chance and risk vs reward. While it feels insurmountable and brutal sometimes, you’re never frustrated that the game was unfair in how a run unfolds - you ALWAYS know just exactly you screwed up. Runs can last mere seconds to 30+ minutes and has an incredibly quick transition back into a new run - which is great because, at least in the beginning, you’ll be learning the functions of the game and be dying quite a bit - all along unlocking new items along the way. Ring of Pain already has a lot of love from the roguelike community and is poised to become my next “just one more run” experience - Simon and his team have created something beautiful (and a little haunting) - and the future is set up for easy content drops if they so choose.

_childDocuments_.review: Ring of Pain is a game that artistically holds itself up high above many other games of it's kind- and even similar. Mechanically it has some polishing to do but the foundations of the game are both promising and friendly to people who take their time to read and understand the system.That being said it would be unfair if I said this game entirely rewards you for your time learning the system. You will face RNG roadblocks you simply can't get away from and will prematurely end a run that you probably should've succeeded in.Items are interesting, have meaningful interactions and can the sound design of the game are very satisfying. Aesthetically you won't find many if any like it, presenting itself in a shattered stained nightmare of dull colors highlighted by vibrant ones. What the game mechanically lacks is carried by atmosphere and will inevitably catch up to that.Even with the frustrating RNG there's a lot of satisfaction and strange item combinations to experiment with. You just need a little bit of patience and some time to sit with it to appreciate what the development team aimed for. I don't really play card games that much but this one has me hooked.Also the OST is unparalleled for the mood it strikes up. This really helps you sit down with it for a long time. Play the game, tell the dev team what you think. They tend to respond, listen and follow up.

_childDocuments_.review: Design: 8.8/10+ Fresh concept of delivering the dungeon in a RING form moving only left and right rather than the standard linear line form. However they are basically the same but still presents a fresh feeling due to the RING format.+ Extremely simple to grasp but hard to master. Having only a few stats, Ring of Pain can be easily understood. With RNG of course a factor, it is actually possible to only become better after dying a few times.- RNG dungeon rooms but "fixed" content in rooms. Despite having different path and encounter of dungeon rooms, the rooms itself are not really RNG with the monsters being similar with only slight changes to the positions and chest, potitions and eq spawn rates. Note: This might change with difficulty? I haven't test that out yet.- Terminologies not explained. Not able to utilised some mechanics well only after personally testing the water which would most probably end up in death as players are not able to utilise it the first time seeing new terms such as freeze. Even veteran players falters at this.- Personally, I find the content slightly short, however since its really polished, I think the pricing is fine. With this discount, its really a grab I find. :)Art & Effects: 9/10+ Art is extremely consistent and polished. + Effects synergise with the art and does not affect the music. Simple, clean and good+ Great choice of colour scheme makes the game dark and spooky.UI & UX: 9.8/10+ Great choice on fonts, really makes the game easy to read,  yet not breaking the dark and spooky ambience. Well done in fitting this contrasting design.+ Intuitive. Great job making this game a one click feedback game. With the customization of equipments with sets and effects, this lets player really feel they are in control of at least themself when the dungeon is already spooky and mysterious. Of course we would want to protect and survive. This control design was a great, exemplary choice.Music & Ambience: 8.5/10+ Music is wonderful, it does make the game mysterious and spooky.+ The ambience is well-crafted, good use of colour scheme on art and with the music, remarkable.Story: 8/10+ Still a mystery to me even though dying countless times and finishing the ring once. - As there is no saving of the story choices, if a players was to take a long duration to play this game, they might forget what this story is actually is. The gist is simple to grasp but not the details as there is not much linear choices which is great but at the same time, players are required to piece the puzzle, which fits the mystery but again, does not work well for players who would play this over a long duration.TLDR: SummaryOverall, Ring of Pain brings in an extremely fresh concept of the "Ring" dungeon, only to move left or right. If think in liner form, its actually just a line but displayed in a Ring format. However that itself is unique and fresh. Anyone into, dungeon, rougelite and abit of mystery would dig this. That said, I find the content rather short and can only be completed at least after a few attempts of death as players grasp to understand the monsters, terminologies and path which are randomised in the position and encounter rate. Design: 8.8/10Art & Effects: 9/10UI & UX: 9.8/10Music & Ambience: 8.5/10Story: 8/10Overall Rating: 8.82/10

_childDocuments_.review: Very well designed and very addictive. I love this game so much that I buy a few copies more for my friends to try, and they love it.  And if you are a board game enthusiast like me, you will definitely love it. This is feel like one.  Every stage is a puzzle of its own. You really have to know the nature of each creature to be able to deal with it effectively or use it for your own terms. Each run you feel like you grow with it, with the build you chose. And at each end, you would feel the urge to press the Play Again button right away. You would want to try it again, and again, and again, and again. See if you could make any difference this time around. Too bad, luck plays a significant role here! No matter how good of the game you are, if you have a bad luck, you will lose. Well, to be more elaborate, you will need certain items to help you go through the run, depending on the build you like. But if you cannot find any of them in the late game, you are screwed. Some level is random in a way that makes you die or have no way out. But you will learn to mitigate the chance of that happening again by having a certain kind of items, skills, or planning to have enough health for the given room. But if you play it long enough, you will know whether this run is good or not, just around stage 5 on. So you can just restart and redo it again. From my experience, there is no use of dragging yourself further much if you are struggle too much on current one or two level. You won't make it far for sure.  But if you are relatively new to the game, bringing yourself through as far as possible is the way you learn how each of them works, so you can prepare yourself for it. All in all, I would say, this is going to be one of my favorite games of all time. LOVE IT. LOVE IT.

_childDocuments_.review: I really want to like this game, but as it stand now there's way too many glaring issues that when put together makes it impossible to recommend it to anyone. Shame, I really like the overall design of it.1. The random element is the unfun kind. Yes, roguelike is supposed to be random, but that means when there's down there's also up. This is not the case here. It's just down, down, and down. Start a run, if you spawn next to enemies instead of chests and upgrades you'll probably die. If you not, and you get garbage items that didn't immediately improve combat potency, you'll probably die. Repeat the same conundrum over and over, constantly fighting uphill, the enemies scaling to a ridiculous extent where they'll have lopsided stats that if you fail to properly match, guess it, you'll probably die. Different run will start varying around a third to halfway through when you finally start getting good drops that'll alter your choices of build and further drops, but the gameplay loop before that point is the exact same chore with minor variations where most of your attempt will fail unless you get good streak of luck.2. Problematic death system. You'll die a lot. That's fine, perfectly normal and to be expected. However, you gain nothing from those deaths. Meta unlock is based on achievements, a decent chunk of the cards locked behind some tedious conditions that you'll need to fulfil mid-run. A tall order when you're too busy trying to survive, bringing only frustration to the table especially if the cause of death is one of the instances the game decides to ♥♥♥♥ you over.3. When combined together, it made an unflattering combination. You just die, over and over, not making any progress, hoping that your luck stacks up enough that you'll maybe get a glimpse of the good part. It's a disrespect of the players' time, demanding so much effort to be put in while being so miserly with the reward. It's not worth the hassle.If you just want to get a feel of it, only completing each path once in normal mode you'll probably have an enjoyable experience. It's a fresh take, got nice atmosphere, and actually allow you to get into the meat of the game. But if you aim to fully complete it, dont bother.

_childDocuments_.review: Alright, I'll do my best to keep this review neat and concise. I will preface by saying that I tried the closed beta of this game.Ring of Pain is a Dungeon Crawler Card Game where the player chooses to go left or right and attack monsters. You have stats and manage item slots with items found across dungeons, progressing deeper and deeper into this "ring" until you reach the end. You have Attack and Defense, Speed to determine whether you or the monster attacks first, and Clarity, which manages how much healing you get from potions, Curse chances, and additional Souls (currency) is acquired per monster kill. Item slots are individualized, meaning if you find a weapon, it goes in the weapon slot and if you find a new weapon, you have to make a choice of either chucking your old one for the new one or keeping the old one.Positives: The game's presentation is really strong and there is a puzzle element to the game, trying to balance your stats to have an even enough spread to handle the amount of monsters the game throws at you. Positioning is actually very important in the game, attempting to maneuver the ring so you can have health potions a click away or a bomb enemy to explode into another monster is always satisfying to watch. The game is surprisingly vibrant and unsettling which adds to the ambiance the story is attempting to set, of an unwilling individual going down a cycle amidst the warring factions of light and darkness. It's not as clear cut as light and dark, and the story has room for interpretation but you're mostly sticking around for the gameplay, which is tight...Negatives: ... Is what I would say if the game wasn't so RNG reliant in the early game. Runs are often decided for you within the first 3 to 4 floors depending on what item drops you get and what stat boosts you acquire. Did you get a bad start with just one item spawning in the base floor? Tough marbles, you've gotta push on. It also feels pretty bad to get items and then be offered free ones by the Owl, only to have the free offered item be something that would consume your other item since it takes up that space.Conclusion: I've played 33 hours of this game and although I've butted with the game mechanics on a number of occasions, that damn Owl has me in its talons and has me there for good. I'd recommend this game to those that like dungeon crawlers where you're focused on stat building and monster slaying, as well as puzzle people trying to tactically decide whether to eat explosive damage for just a few more souls to open a chest is the last decision you make when jumping down to a floor with no potions. The developers have been vocal in saying they plan to support the game with content updates in future and they've received enough feedback from the closed beta that they have a list they can act upon. I give this game a positive vote of confidence.And so, with flourish, I'm here to say;This game is worth a look and play.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall Score: 8.5/10On a list of free game codes I was given, this game didn't really stand out. The name sounds painfully generic, or indicative of genres I generally don't bother with. Still, I looked it up anyway, and immediately identified it as a "Card Battler". I said to myself "oh, why not"; Card Battlers tend to always have something at least a little interesting in order to stand out amongst their kin, and I figured hey, it's free, no reason not to.I was not prepared for how much I ended up enjoying it.It's remarkably easy to pick up on the game concept right away, given how simplistic it is in practice. The depth comes from the strategies that develop organically (though rather uncontrollably) as you gain equipment and raise your stats, and those strategies become more varied and effective the longer your run goes and the more runs you do. Equippable Items are the backbone of the gameplay, and can have wildly varying effects on your stats and various aspects of the gameplay in general. The more runs you do and the more you do in each run, the more items you unlock for potentially being dealt to you on subsequent runs, and the more potential builds and strategies you can acquire.There are a few cons to the gameplay, most of which are rooted in the eternal pitting of wills against the RNG. The game pretty much hinges its entire "conflict identity" on RNG, which is fairly common for Roguelikes and Roguelites, and especially Card Battlers, and it's easy to understand why most people aren't fond of that approach to game design. Yet for Ring of Pain, many of the flaws are reduced to mere annoyances by the virtue of a single consideration: The game is designed to have each run take a very short amount of time, and the more familiar you get with the game, the quicker it becomes as the routine of the more foundational strategies sets in.Generally, the only runs that last longer than around 5 minutes and 7 or 8 main floors are the ones where you're doing fairly well. The momentum builds spectacularly when you manage to lock into a working build. I have no way of accurately confirming this, but I strongly suspect that obtaining a given item weighs the item generation tables towards other items that synergize with them. This can lead to gratifying snowball effects, especially if you land good synergies early-on. Even if you don't land any great synergies, with over 350 different items available, you'll at least never lack for interesting twists and turns on each run.The only unmitigated flaw in the game is the fact that there seems to be no indication of how to unlock each item. Each unlock has requirements that must be met to add the item to your collection, some of which are esoteric or highly unlikely to happen organically. I suppose such a design strategy is meant to encourage replayability, but it's still a bit galling.At time of writing, I only have 8.7 hours in the game, but that playtime contains at least 25 runs and over 200 item unlocks. I've reached the point where if I make it past Floor 4 it means I already have a decent build going, which means more consistent momentum more often. I imagine there will be a point where the novelties wear off, but at this rate I can't imagine it'll be before the 20-hour mark.As someone who usually gets bored pretty quick of short-term games with only so much variation in the main gameplay loop, I found this game to be surprisingly easy to snack on, and the speed of each run really drives that. Twenty bucks is a decent price as far as I'm concerned, but given it's published by Humble Games, that means it's practically guaranteed to go on sale several times a year. Whenever it does, I'd seriously recommend picking it up and giving it a try.\o<o/

_childDocuments_.review: Pain isn't just the name—it's a core mechanical theme. You'll pop explosive enemies to take down others, equip loot that lowers a stat into the negatives, and agonize over increasingly complex either-or decisions. Playing the game will make you feel like a scrappy survivor!What I enjoy most is how the game handles equipment progression. While you can find potent combos, the staggered availability of more powerful items in the late game discourages you from marrying early-game synergies. I often choose equipment on a room-by-room basis to outspeed or mitigate damage from specific enemy types.If you've grown tired of card-based roguelikes, give this one a try! It's totally unique. Got it as a gift from a friend, and it's stuck in my craw. You know, in a good way. But you'll have to be into unlocking cards through achievements to extend the life of the game; there aren't many difficulties yet, and no larger ascension system. But it seems like more will be added.EDIT: The game has plenty of run variations now thanks to its expanded selection of starting items and difficulties. This one'll last you a while.Also: opt into the beta! There's more stuff!

_childDocuments_.review: Played the hell out of the demo, and am more than pleasantly surprised with the full release content. While this game relies a lot on strategy, you have to make what you can of the "cards" you are dealt (literally). RNG is either your friend or your complete enemy, and the complete randomized nature of the game makes it enjoyable to play over and over. That on top of the interesting creatures, stunning art, and incredibly atmospheric sound design make for an amazing game!

_childDocuments_.review: What a (pleasant) surprise ! Didn't know what to expect when I got this game, I just saw one of my favourite streamers playing it and enjoying it, it looked really cool, so I thought I should give it a go.The atmosphere and graphics are so original (and amazing) and work very well to immerse you in this creepy world. Definitely one of the main point for me in this game.The gameplay itself is really interesting as well, it looks like a card game but isn't. It's a dungeon crawler / roguelike based on "circle" movement, and it leads to very unusual but rewarding decisions ! The progression over the length of a run with items/stats is also great, and leads to a different strategy every time you play.The devs have even more planned for the future, let's see where this goes ! But it's definitely worth picking up already, this is a really good game in its current state.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: Buy if you are a Roguelike lover and are looking for a mid-length experience. Otherwise, be wary of difficulty but expect great atmosphere and and neat mechanics.I got this game off of humble choice and like it, but with some caveats.- The difficulty can be brutal, later enemies will end your run if you haven't learned how to deal with them.- Certain builds rely heavily on RNG getting the right set up (particularly low item runs).- The lore provides an great gameplay atmosphere but is ultimately too vague to draw any real conclusions.- There's plenty to do but I wouldn't give it the same longevity as an Isaac or Slay the Spire.On the other hand- The game really nails the risk/reward choices.- There's an amazing satisfaction in learning to navigate each room type and enemy.- It's really fun to get your build to coalesce and hit that late-game power trip.- The controls and sound effects are great and killing several enemies in a row is super satisfying- The ring of cards is a really cool mechanic and is explored well without being overwhelming.

_childDocuments_.review: There is a lot of reliance on luck which determines whether you stand a chance making it to the end or not.And yet, I can only recommend it.Addicting game. The art style is fantastic, the game mechanics are pretty unique and very fun, and oh holy #### is that owl creepy.
_childDocuments_.name: Ring of Pain

_childDocuments_.review: Really good atmosphere in this game. Developers are responsive and are still planning to add a lot to the game. There is no deck, you just have items and a pile of stats. The game is more about the decisions you make navigating the ring. _childDocuments_.review: This game is insane. It is such a unique type of card rougelike and the art work it is fun. It is hard. Before you get into this game know that it had rng that sometimes you can't squeeze through. Like for example, Like you almost lost a hard level and you go to another just to be squeezed in between giant man with big penor and S N A K E. Either one gets you killed regardless of trying to pass or you hope to god you have an item or pass sneakily (assuming they aren't enemies that hit you just for being on the screen.)It reminds me of the binding of isaac in a way. The binding of isaac when you have weak items through out the run then you will feel like a pile of garbage while everything just feels too good. But on the other hand, when you get the right items you steam roll. This is kinda the same way but you get more items that do less throughout the run  (if the makes sense). For example, if you get brimstone and some damage you are pretty much set. However, similarly to isaac again, most of the time I die out of sheer stupidity. Like playing a curse item while i'm poisoned. It reduces my health to 2 and the poison kills me. Or I fight an enemy that obviously does enough damage to kill me but I don't pay attention.(BTW sometimes it's better to just run. _childDocuments_.review: If you are looking in to getting this game and are not familiar with the type of game: Ring of pain is IMO closest related to turn-based dungeon crawlers. The art style as well as the atmosphere would definitely carry this game had the game been any less fun. Min-maxing and risk taking is the name of the game here. _childDocuments_.review: Honestly a very intriguing game with a lovely artstyle and vibe. But there are bigger issues in terms of the gameplay and rng elements in the game. I think there are some elements and aspects of the game that are way less important compared to others. For example i found most of my runs would usually end at 10-20 rooms max just because my defense was low. The game is way too stat prioritized around defense for you to have any good runs in my own experience because this is the only stat in the game that puts you ahead early without too many consequences and also by seeing alot of gameplay prior to me playing. When a shulker appears early and your defense stat is low you can almost never find anything to play around since he follows up on you very quick and in some ways there can be up to 2-3 meaning he will be there and youre forced to exit because your other stats just dont compare to him. Or when a creature can corner you that is meant to kill you and if you arent lucky enough to find an exit, youre dead and theres usually 2 of him that blocks your path before the exit. These things seems way too inavoidable and you feel like its a restart if you start in a room with creatures that have those stats, when you haven't been able to build a strong enough stat like defense to either skip them or try kill them in the first place. You would think speed and attack would be important but there are some explosive affixes that just immedietly deals 20 flat damage early on too, you can avoid them more easily but its like they want you to skip them and if you have no good options to do, so you also feel an immense amount of rng being placed at you. The last thing is clarity, a stat that can improve your curse resistance which is you rolling a dice whetever youre gonna lose all your health or get a good amount of healing back. This stat is almost in no case good to pick because even if you have 80% to succeed on getting your heal back, the one time you dont youve taken a too big risk and simple has 1 health. I have nothing against this game,personally i would love to come back to it another day if the stats are being revamped. But for now theres a too big gap between the needed and important stats that determine if you will make it far or the ones that depend on your luck.EDIT: Devs really doing good work. 2 patches with balancing in 3 days and roadmap announced soon just a week after release. Can i recommend this game now? Yes. A very good community so far with good devs that listens to feedback and pinpoints the most wanted/needed patches. Great start great potential

_childDocuments_.review: Ring of Pain is one of the most unusual and most fun Roguelikes I've ever played. When I first started with the game, I was turned off from the mechanics and didn't play the game for a very long time.It was much later when I gave the game a second chance. The reason why I didn't like the game first was because the game lacks a lot of convenient information for the player.You, as player, must find out how all the different mechanics work together. While there is a tutorial in the game, it only explains the basic gameplay mechanics and leaves you clueless about anything else. Because of that lack of information, the player will experience a lot of frustrating moments when he starts playing."How could I know that this would happen?!"Generally, the first 50 runs or so the player will probably only try to understand how the mechanics work, what enemies do, what items do and so on. There are so many hidden mechanics in the game, that you will be surprised a lot.But that's where the fun starts. Once you reach a certain point of knowledge, the game starts to "click", you see patterns you haven't noticed before and start performing better, eventually reaching your first victory. Now you want more.But let's go over the mechanics first. Ring of Pain features a very unique approach to the dungeon crawler formular, dungeon rooms are presented as a ring of cards, that you can rotate left and right. You alwys face two cards in front of you and clicking on them lets you interact with their mechanics. Potions heal you on the spot, corpses give you a free item of a specific rarity and monsters, well, monsters fight you.But Ring of Pain features a different approach on those moments. The dungeon reacts to you instead of you to the dungeon. You always make your move first and everything in the dungeon reacts to that. The dynamic of action, reaction is the core gameplay loop. A fight only happens if you start it, which means clicking on a monster. A monster will attack you back (or attack first depending on who has the higher speed) and if neither of you dies, you can decide again to initiate an attack. Monsters (unless their effect says so) won't attack you on their own unless you provoke them.You can simply bypass monsters by walking left or right from them, but this will provoke a single attack. You can either block or dodge the attack depending on your stats or just tank it with your health. Or, if you have a high stealth stat, you also can bypass the monster unnoticed.It is up to the player to decide how he approaches each room, what monster to take first or if he just wants to leave the room. You could go through the dungeon, not killing anything and just taking loot on the way.There are some more active monsters which will seek you out but those will still only act after the player did something. Those monsters are usually serious threats because they break the usual mechanic of the game, and they are meant to be dealt with first. I really like this dynamic because the player must assess threats accordingly before he can check rooms for valuables. In many rooms there is also a so-called "scrounger", a scavenging fiend who drops loot if killed fast enough. However, he will slowly make his way to the room exit and escape if you take too much time dealing with other stuff.The player has a large inventory, but each slot in his inventory is for a specific item type. For example, you can have only one helmet item and have to discard your last helmet if you find a new one, but you also have slots for shoes, gloves, weapons among other stuff. Items generally give you positive or negative stats and many of them also have secondary special effects. Some items might have high stats but no special ability, some have negative stats but a very powerful skill. Understanding what items work well on you is important for beating the game. Many items seem useless at first glance, but their true power appears in combination with other items. Synergies are very strong in this game and a lot of items are designed in a way that they interact with each other. A simple example would be that Infected Necklace which gives you amazing stats but with the insane drawback that you get 10 poison stacks when equipping it. Poison damage is very difficult to migrate because it deals its damage each turn until either the stacks run out, you leave a dungeon room or find a potion. But if you use the item with Time Rift, which negates poison damage as long as you don't fight any monster, you can easily dodge the damage until you get out of the room. The game is full of situations like this, and it always feels rewarding when you find a great combo. On that note, let's address the elephant in the room: The game is brutally hard. Monsters always hit hard, no matter how good you progress through your run, you always feel outmatched, and a lot of your potential is locked behind RNG. The game has a ton of different items and since many of them are intended to work only good with other items, you might cripple yourself by picking up one item, believing you would find a fitting match later. One thing the game will teach you is that you need to min-max to win. There is no other way, the entire game is built around the fact that you have to sacrifice stats and power in one direction to maximize build. This is reflected in many mechanics of the game. There player can find stat tablets which present him one of three stats to choose from, to increase the stat by one. In some cases, however you get 4 stat points for your selection, but you will lose one point in ALL other stats. This will force the player early to make decisions in what direction he wants to build and gives the player a raging clue about the true nature of the game. Items work in a similar way. Like I said before, there are many items with drawbacks and while some items can turn these drawbacks into positives, the general idea is that you play around the drawbacks and accept them because the other stats, the item gives you, help your build. A build that tries to max out every stat evenly will fail. All my wins so far were runs where I crippled at least one of my stats very hard but reached an insanely high number on one or two other stats. Therefore, I want to point out how loot works in this game. There are two main ways to get items, one is corpses, the other mimics. Corpses give you one free item, but you cannot decide what you get, you can only decide if you take it or not. Mimics on the other hand are living chests that "sell" you their items for souls, the currency of the game. Each mimic has a cost which is tied to the rarity of the items it contains. You always see the rarity of the mimic but not what it holds. Not before paying, that is. The two items it presents are totally random, but the player might reroll the items by paying more souls. While this does not entirely solve the RNG issue, it reduces it by giving the player a way to skip unfavorable items until he gets something he wants. Let's also address the visuals of the game. The game features a very dark and surreal aesthetic and I love it. Every monster and every item has a detailed, hand-drawn artwork to boot and everything looks dark and grim and otherworldly to you. The eerie soundtrack matches the visuals of the game and while playing the game you will feel like you are in some nightmarish world which tries to crush you in every possible way. Overall, I would suggest this game to people who like hard and challenging games and don't mind strong RNG elements. The game takes a lot of time to get into and even more time to master but it is a rewarding experience because once you understand how all the mechanics, items and monsters fit together, you can weave through the dungeon and create powerhouse builds. That feeling of creating an absolute broken build is always fantastic and all the hardships you had to endure until that point were worth it.

_childDocuments_.review: Finally got 100% achievements and completion and it took me around 100 hours!Thoughts on the game:- Fun and challenging with a heavy dose of RNG on top!- Rarest achievement/challenge, , was one of the easier ones to do, whereas the challenge that I did last and struggled most with was  because it required 99% luck for the stars to align and 1% skill. Still fun and felt accomplishing when I got it!- Artwork is so good in my opinion!- Story/Lore (yeah it has that too believe it or not) is vague enough to leave room for interpretation which is always nice, especially if you are into that.- Worth the price since I got at least 100 hours of fun and entertainment out of it (with more to come for sure!)So if you like card games and a bit of a creepy factor on top of that, with fun and challenging achievements to boot, then do yourself a favour and grab this! 10/10 - one of my favourite singleplayer battle card games out there for sure!

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a clear example of a dev team that instead of just jumping on the next sub-genre bandwagon, they clearly spent time studying and reinventing what makes it great in the first place. Ring of Pain could have easily been just another rip-off of Slay the Spire, but the game tells its own dark and cryptic story with some very unique mechanics. Late game challenges end up funneling the player towards some specific powerful combos, so I would really like to see more content added in future updates. Art style is unique and menacingly beautiful. Story is just cryptic enough to make you want to dive back in and see more endings. All-in-all, it is totally worth your time and money.

_childDocuments_.review: Excellent dungeon crawler, challenging but fair, and very fun to 100%. It has the right type of RNG : you don't know what equipment or bonuses you'll get, but you'll know the immediate consequences of your actions since the hits always land and you can see the exact damage inflicted. The smallest mistake and you die though, it may then be pretty painful... especially at the beginning.  But you'll know better next run and in the end, beating the game is more about knowing what to do than what loot you get. Many achievements make you play differently and unlock new items, keeping the game fresh for a  long time.

_childDocuments_.name: Ring of Pain

_childDocuments_.review: Ring of Pain is a solid roguelite experience with elements of deck building. A more strategic and thoughtful title in a genre that's usually fast paced and hectic. Despite this, it feels exciting and engaging, never slow.Ring of Pain's strongest quality is the interactions between different effects. Getting hit by explosive enemies because your polearm attacks enemies as you approach? Try the coin that freezes enemies when they are reduced below 25% hp. Synergies are more than just "increase x by x if you also have x" They are based around emergent properties that arise from many different effects occurring at once. Real strategy and buildcrafting are possible, allowing the game to stay fun after multiple runs.Sound design and artstyle are unique and enjoyable. The creepy atmosphere of the game adds a lot to the experience. And it is quite creepy. The characters, ambient sounds, cryptic rhyme, and unsettling story are all excellent.Overall solid purchase, sale or not. But this is Steam, where the entire catalog gets massive discounts multiple times a year, so you might as well get it on sale. (also has an active discord community get in here and support candle)
_childDocuments_.name: Ring of Pain

_childDocuments_.review: It ain't a deckbuilder, and it ain't a dungeon crawler...it's something new, entirely! In a few years, we'll have more games of this type, but for now Ring of Pain is pioneering new ideas in gameplay, and they've hit upon an incredibly solid idea.The best way I can describe it is as a card drafting game, but the cards actively work against you. The gameplay is incredibly addictive (JUST ONE MORE RUN), and there is a surprising amount of depth in the choices you end up making. Strong recommend!

I'm glad this was one of the  humble choice games or else i might not have given it another chance.

_childDocuments_.review: I am honestly very surprised how much I enjoyed playing this game. I didn’t expect it to be this much fun at all.Ring of Pain is a roguelike card game with lots of RNG elements. The game itself is easy to play. The controls are minimalistic. You basically just click through the cards. It is nevertheless extremely hard to master. You must choose wisely and pick the right items if you want to succeed. Should you attack a monster, or should you try to sneak by? Augment your health, or your damage? Take short-cuts or loot the whole level? These are some examples of the decisions you need to take. Some items will help you out by giving you special abilities (f.e. freezing rings).Once you die, you lost everything. Every session starts under the same conditions. You don’t keep any items and you aren’t stronger or weaker than before. You will then find new, or the same items. It is random.The atmosphere is dark and “spooky”. It is well done.To sum it up, an unexpectedly fun game.
_childDocuments_.name: Ring of Pain

_childDocuments_.review: Um... yeah. Play this game.This is maybe a strange observation but Ring of Pain kinda feels like a Halloween themed April fools joke and that isn't the criticism it sounds like. It just very much has the vibe of an experimental indie game like Inscryption that lacks the polish of something like Slay the Spire or Monster Train.It isn't exactly buggy but the balance feels a bit off. There are maybe two builds that actually worked for me and a ♥♥♥♥ million items that just clog the game up. 80% of the time your best bet is just to take the freezing crown and then ignore most if not all of the pick ups. A combination of freeze and high speed is, to put it mildly, completely ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ game breaking.That being said, I've spent 20 hours to date playing, so clearly it's doing something right. It feels like in 6 or so years, an amazing 10/10 game is going to come out and people will look back through the early work of the devs who made it and will find Ring of Pain was the first game they made.Very much worth your time, but I wouldn't end a friendship with someone if they said they didn't like it.
_childDocuments_.name: Ring of Pain

_childDocuments_.review: First off, I would like to commend the creators of this game for its enticing art style. The environment is a amazing blend of vivid, wild colours with detailed shading. As for gameplay, the mechanics are easy to understand and the itemization is diverse. This game will challenge your decision making to the nth degree as I have face palmed many times making a move I regretted. If you like dungeon crawlers and turn-based strategy (with cards) I definitely recommend picking this up.
_childDocuments_.name: Ring of Pain

_childDocuments_.review: After playing I still got a strong feeling that this game is not finished. Something important is missing in gameplay. It is good and it is deffinitly recommended to try and play, but not perfect. This game starts with the feeling of mystery, but gameplay is pretty simple. We collect stats, try to survive and then beat the end. Instead of journey feeling, it is a feeling that game have two parts and first part is preparation for second one. _childDocuments_.review: Ring of Pain is yet another indie title that apparently wasn't play-tested to completion. The randomness and difficulty that this game has has basically two settings: one, you get a good start on your first level and you can make it a few more levels if you pray for good items, and two, you die almost instantly on the first level because the developer didn't balance or play test their own game. There is no in-between. "But it's a rougelike! It gets easier the more you play it!" If you think that makes a game good, please stay away from game development. There is something objectively flawed with the rougelike genre and it bugs the hell out of me that people are too naive to see it. It teaches people that their game is difficult from the start. Very simple concept. This means, most people who approach it and fail a run over something stupid are just going to drop the game right then and there! This is why I believe you don't see any high budget titles that have even attempted the genre. Anyways, if you like rougelikes, be my guest and have fun getting angry, but if you actually like having fun, save your money for something better, which honestly shouldn't be hard considering how bad this one is.
_childDocuments_.name: Ring of Pain

_childDocuments_.review: The variety of equipment in this game is the selling point for me. Each piece of equipment you pick up feels like it has an impact on playstyle and allows for some interesting combinations. There are numerous effects like "freeze on attack with 4 or less items equipped" or "10% stealth for each empty inventory slot" so taking every item you come across isn't always the best option. Things like "explosions heal, potions have no effect" or "gain 10 speed, combat order is reversed" make for some fun builds as well. Once you unlock the second difficulty you are able to pick your own starting item, allowing some combinations to come together a bit easier.Also, this does an excellent job at feeling fast-paced for something that is basically a rotating circle of cards. Enemy variety isn't gigantic, but each one feels significantly different. Some explode, others chase you, some have ranged attacks, some consume other creatures and gain their strength if you don't kill them quick enough, and others escape with treasure if you don't stop them in a certain amount of turns, etc.

_childDocuments_.review: After playing this on steam, and then buying it again on switch (where my hour count is MUCH higher), I can safely say this is the most a game has hooked me since Hades. The layers of complexity gradually reveal themselves the deeper into the twisted world you dive. Does RNG sometimes end a run unfairly? yes. Does RNG sometimes work in your favor? Also yes.  This has become my pick up and play game at night. Just do a round before bed and see what happens.  It plays so fast, and thanks to the large amount of inventory slots, games can feel very different from one run to the next while mechanically your decisions are still simple and streamlined. Do not go in expecting a deck builder a-la Slay the Spire. This is something else entirely. While the look of the game is card based, I would hesitate to call it a card game and more of a spacial puzzle that is continually trying to kill you in different ways.  I have seen 1 ending thus far and am excited to continue banging my head against this thing until I have all items unlocked.For Fans of: Card Crawl - Miracle Merchant - Card Thief - pick up and put down quick game sessionsNot for fans of: meticulously balanced items, fairness, winning all the time.

_childDocuments_.review: Ring of Pain has a beautiful presentation and a superficially interesting spin on deckbuilding roguelikes but ultimately fails to deliver an experience with predictable, meaningful decisions and the replayability that follows. Ring of Pain subverts normal card game formula by dealing a group of cards in a ring for each encounter. The player is faced with two cards in this ring on each turn. They can elect to attack either card or rotate the ring left or right. This requires a "stealth" roll if attempting to rotate past a hostile creature. Whether or not a stealth is successful is determined by RNG based on character states. The player collects items that fill 13 items slots as they progress. The player can also collect a reusable spell with a cooldown and a single use spell that is consumed on use. Most items are picked from a choice between two. Players have some ability to choose a route to move through encounters and can potentially control the level of risk and reward they face. Despite any turn being only a choice of 4 actions (attack/interact with either card or move either direction), Ring of Pain has some unexpectedly complex scenarios by virtue of the range of cards that appear in the ring. These can include stat ups, health potions, item drops and portals that allow movement. Also included are monsters which can have a range of effects including ranged attacks, movement and (very commonly) on-death explosions. Ring of Pain is aggressively balanced and is clearly not intended for players to have a high win-rate. You will spend most of your game time on a knife's edge where a single bad combat with a creature will kill you. At the time of writing this review, I have played 7 hours of this game and in that time have seen most of the items and all of the rooms and bosses. A significant proportion of my time has been spent butting my head against the game's difficulty and RNG. Unfortunately, not in a satisfying way. Game difficulty is not a problem in and of itself- most of my favourite games are difficult roguelikes. My dissatisfaction with Ring of Pain comes from the combination of limited decisions, high difficulty and too much randomness in the core mechanics. The sneak mechanic is a pure diceroll that will often dictate whether or not a run succeeds. There are also VERY common "curse items" that will give a stat boost or health potion on a diceroll where they may also cost a large amount of your health. These instances of randomness are coupled with randomness more agreeable to roguelikes in the form of random items and layouts. In comments one of the devs made on the subreddit for this game, they suggested that  players should be taking more risks early in order to become more powerful. I think this attitude towards balance is emblematic of what this game is getting wrong. Taking early risk for reward forces you to play more aggressively, which means engaging with mechanics that are just coinflips - cursed items and card manipulation through sneaking.  For example, completing early challenge rooms relies on the following layers of randomness:1) Getting a challenge room layout in the random cards in a ring2) Having had enough useful items drop that you aren't behind the power curve of the basic creatures in the challenge room and don't die to basic attacks3) Having positive dicerolls on stealth attempts 4) Having positive dicerolls on curse itemsThe latter two are simply not engaging for a player and will frequently create situations where your run will instantly end. There is a very good reason why randomness is usually all but completely absent from aggressively balanced card games (for example, both MTG and Slay the Spire have very limited instances of randomness). This is because randomness means that the impact of player choice and knowledge on an outcome is less important.  A veteran player has proportionally less ability to effect the outcome of the game, which lessens the value of time they have spent mastering it and increases the importance of just trying over and over to get good rolls. Build to build balance is also an issue, with builds that damage on movement (the spear item) being completely out of step with the power level of the other items. If you look at videos where people have completed the game, most of them will have the spear item.I enjoyed around the first 5 hours I spent on this game but do not see myself coming back to it. I feel that I stopped learning to leverage game mechanics more effectively at around the 5 hour mark and since then have just been playing a slot machine to get enough successful random events in a row to get a good run. If you are looking for a roguelike experience with a long, rewarding learning curve, I do not recommend this game at full price.

_childDocuments_.review: The thing is... I would've played this if it were a typical Dungeon Crawler... The cutsey/creepy switch of atmosphere is really good.Ring of Pain puts you in the shoes of some unknown creature, that wakes up in the dungeon. Overseen by an odd looking "owl" thing, you are tasked to go to the light below... descending depths until you reach the very end. There are overall only two endings, one wholly dependent on whether you meet the Entity. At first the game sounds very cute, but a few depths in you'll realize that this is not a dream, but a nightmare. The messages are very cryptic, the characters are very creepy and the monsters you meet in your journey are increasingly brutal. You can also find equipment cards along the way, that will make your life a bit easier on the long run! Depending on what build you're going for, card rolls can either play in your favour or against you! You can reroll most cards but if you're not careful, you'd be stuck with equipment or spells you do not want. There is also syngergy sometimes between equipment, and following which paths you opt for, you can find shrines that either boost or debuff you, sometimes in the worst ways possible.Other than that, when the storyline falls completely flat (there isn't one, mostly), you're left with a Hand of Fate clone that's, in my opinion, a  Dungeon Crawler. I had fun playing it through Medium mode, but not Hard, as at some point it got quite unfair.
_childDocuments_.name: Ring of Pain

_childDocuments_.review: While I've played this game maybe to the point where it gets a bit repetitive and I've nearly dried it out, I think this game is one of the best deckbuilders I've played by a long shot. While it is a little reliant on RNG at times, it has systems that are unique and well designed, and feels incredibly polished and refined. There are many builds you can go with that can be super creative and fun, and making the right decisions for your build is crucial to winning in this game. It also has a really interesting "horror" feel to it that makes it all the more intriguing.☺☺☺☺
_childDocuments_.name: Ring of Pain

_childDocuments_.review: Ring of Pain is a(nother) roguelike card game with beautiful art and some unique ideas. Compared to other roguelike card games, Ring of Pain has more randomness to it than most. In a typical roguelike card game, it is mostly the player's ability to adapt to the (random) card selection they are given throughout the run that decides whether they succeed or not. In Ring of Pain, almost every move you make (every breath you take) is up to chance. Hence, the gameplay is heavily dependent on luck and the best strategy may not be enough to remedy this.While Ring of Pain is charming and unique, I recommend going for a more skill-based roguelike card game.
_childDocuments_.name: Ring of Pain

_childDocuments_.review: I am a 45 yo father, probably one of the oldest people playing this game. I am a single father to my Son, who is 14 now. My son got this game for Christmas in 2021 from his uncle, so we installed it on his computer and he started playing. By the end of the week he had 24 hours on this game. This was horrible for me, as it was already hard for me to find ways to spend time with my son, as he is always out with his friends or just watching YouTube. So i decided to make a Steam account and get this game to see if I could maybe play alongside him. I loaded into the game, picked my character and world and started playing but I was stuck on what you where supposed to do. I asked my Son for help and he hosted a game for me to join. I loved it as it was the best time I had spent with my Son since my wife had died. This game has ever since brought me and my son closer again and now we actually spend time together outside the house together as well. This game reminded me that there's fun to be had in everything, and it has brought both me and my Son many happy memories.

_childDocuments_.review: The title doesn't lie. You are in a ring, and it's filled with pain.A stat-focused card rouge-lite with some evil big bird warden watching over you as you slay dreadful abominations and equip dishcloth rags as armor. It's fairly unique gameplay as you literally go around a ring of enemies to kill and items to grab as you delve deeper into the dungeon.A full run can last as long as half an hour (expect to die a lot before then) and the total number of equips + difficulty levels give sufficient variety (can always afford to add more). The gameplay might get samey after a while but at that point, it's probably time to quit. Anyway, I believe the devs are still pushing updates for the game, so that's a plus.The sound design is great as well. It's always satisfying to smack enemies and chug potions, despite being mere clicks. There's a daily dungeon run too (with fixed layout) but the settings seem unfair and I usually end up dying on the first few levels. This might just be a 'me' problem though.Overall, Ring of Pain is not a pain to play. Yea.
_childDocuments_.name: Ring of Pain

_childDocuments_.review: There's a decent game here but it's way overpriced. Ring of Pain boils down the "Card Battler" format to its simplest elements, turning 45 min-1 hr games into an average of 10 min games. However, it still holds firmly onto the bad tenets of the genre: strong RNG and quick deaths. Initially I found myself hooked on the rapid fire format but once I realized I had only gotten the Bad Ending, I didn't feel much motivation to continue on through the insane difficulty of finishing the Good Ending. This honestly feels like a mobile version of Slay the Spire and belongs at a $2 Play Store price with paid expansions or card packs. The devs are definitely passionate about their product but it still needs some work (a save on quit is currently in beta, for example). This is a cautious recommendation (only if its on sale) for fans of the genre in the hopes that the developers continue to improve it. For now, I really don't feel like continuing to play it because it feels way too similar to other Card Battlers outside of the creepy atmosphere.

_childDocuments_.review: What a fun and epic little indie game! :)I like turn based games and card based games too, so this was rigtht up my alley.At first, it looks very daunting and you might die super fast and feel like the game is too much but dont despair, it takes a while to learn the enemies attacks, how the mechanics work and item synergies and in a day or two you will start winning and you wont be able to stop exploring the game to unlock new items and your desire to discover new item combos will grow and grow.The art, sfx and music are very good and it brings out this mystery of who you are, what they are, where the ♥♥♥♥ are we? what's that? WHY is this happening?! haha.. fguring it all out its all part of the fun.A game run usually takes under an hour so, dying and restarting over and over again doesnt feel like a waste of time since what you do counts for achievement counters, learning the game, finding new paths and geting better at the game, you dont feel like wasted time which is greatThe goal of the game is learning what you need before the final boss battle and getting those resources to survive it. There are two ending routes, dark and light and each has its own mechanics which you will need to learn to beat each one. The boss battles are EPIC, they did such great work with the music and mechanics.Achievements are numerous and challenging, you will spend around 50+ hours to get to 100%.No missable achievements, hunting all of them was very fun.Ring of Pain gets 4 friendly smiling owl out of 5 Zalgo-Inspired dark whispering voices.

_childDocuments_.review: The art is fantastic, and most of the game play is just great. However, here are a fair bit of sudden deaths that feel like ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ that either you can do nothing about, in a not fun way, or that a creature has a new move you've never seen before that isn't telegraphed well enough, so you die by surprise. The death by surprise reeeeeally sucks. The game is addicting until that happens and I quit, then I come back, rinse and repeat. Otherwise the other 60% of deaths are either just a bad run or my fault for not planning the room well enough, and that's where it feels just awesome. If those 40% of not-fun deaths went away, I would be raving about this game to everyone I know.

On one hand the presentation is absolutely flawless, the game feel like a mystery and beckon you to dive in head first to find the answer. _childDocuments_.review: I understand the different strategy this game tries to incentivize, but it really devolves to choosing the path of least resistance to all of the stat boosts and items (and ignoring the more powerful enemies on the other path). That's the best part of the game and surprisingly works well. However, even then the decision isn't difficult and there's not really any strategy to speak of. Obtaining the boosts you need and items with powerful-enough effects is not only completely luck-based but is the main determinant in whether you win or not, so most of the game relies on luck. Even after I got the hang of the game, I could recognize whether I messed up or it was impossible to win, and while I messed up more when I first started playing, toward the end I wasn't making significant mistakes anymore and found the latter (impossible to win) to be true in the majority of cases, which confirmed the hunch I was getting from the beginning but desperately wanted to give this game the benefit of the doubt.If you enter a Question Mark room and encounter something you're not equipped to handle, then you're just dead. If you don't get items that synergize well together, then you're just dead. In most runs, you'll basically have to decide which stat to forsake, except most of the stats you can't forsake without having very specific items equipped that you can only obtain randomly. And this is all without considering how this game has four % chance stats (parry, crit, dodge, and stealth). I surprisingly find Darkest Dungeon 2 to handle luck better, a game that doesn't know how to properly handle luck either but I still enjoy playing.This is impressive for a first project, but you can definitely tell this is someone's first project.

_childDocuments_.review: I have many hours in this on xbox gamepass for PC, so ignore the current hours played, it's so good I bought it on steam as I no longer subscribe to that service.It's a roguelike card game game with a lot of replay value and longevity, it takes a lot of runs to unlock all the cards, infact I never unlocked them all on xbox gamepass and I played it a lot.I won't say what happens when you complete a run, just to say that there's more options.  Not that you'll be finishing it much, the RNG can be cruel sometimes, but I like that.  And the more cards you unlock the more random things get.Some people moan about RNG in games like this, they seem to want to finish it every time, but I like RNG stuff like this, just when you think it's going great, up pops the RNG with 2 nasty 20 exploding enemies. It's hard to build an item list with synergy because of the RNG, it's possible but not something you can really except to do..If you like card roguelike games then you like this and you'll get many many hours out of it.One of my favourite games this year.
_childDocuments_.name: Ring of Pain

_childDocuments_.review: Wow, this game is amazing. A lot of roguelikes have tried the "odd gameplay loop, simple mechanics" route but I feel very few have achieved it to the level of success of Ring of Pain. There are 6 actions at any given moment, move left, move right, interact left, interact right, spell, and scroll. But I really can not say there's ever a moment playing this game where it feels linear and that is due to the INCREDIBLE item design. Runs play incredibly differently every time and there are so many ways to build a run. And for the completionist like myself this game has some of the best achievement design I have ever seen. I love how much intentionality there was in every achievement and being able to plan a run to complete multiple achievements at once is incredibly gratifying. I just completed 100% and am really excited to go back in and beat every candle on every difficulty just for fun.If you're a strategy roguelike fan, this game is, without a doubt, one of the greats.

_childDocuments_.review: Entertaining, but I can't quite recommend it. This is where the "RNG of Pain" joke goes. Maybe I just don't get the early game, but it does not quite work for me. There are too many little ways where the early half-ish of the game is a bunch of little rolls of the dice, and you die if a few in a row go badly. You can escape some of them, but escape too many and guarantee failure because you are not building up for the late game. Not quite enough choices, and what choices there are are usually of the form "pick one of two" with a possible option of "reset the two" first. Was this made for mobile first, where "swipe left or right" as the basic game interface makes more sense?That said, it is fairly entertaining. If you don't mind rolling the dice for a few runs to find a decent starting point or combo, this is what board gamers would call a "beer and pretzels" game. It is not something you can put a lot of intellectual weight or strategy into, but it can be interesting to see how the dice fall this time and entertaining when you get your overpowered combo rolling, and then you're reminding yourself to watch for the scenarios that can still kill you.Net recommendation: about one step down from "good but not great," without great confidence in that assessment? It has some fun atmosphere and mechanics, but I don't know who I'd recommend the game to.

Luck is involved in getting the right item combinations, but players have a lot of weight on how that luck plays out. One wrong move can mean death, no matter how good your build. I've finally finished Hard difficulty for the first time. It took...*checks steam* nearly 50 hours of playing.
_childDocuments_.name: Ring of Pain

_childDocuments_.review: I didn't like the game at first. I actually refunded it. It stayed on my mind for a few months and I had to try again. Oh boy was I right to give it a second chance. It is NOT a card game. It's a game about stats, growing stronger and making decisions. The game has a randomness variable, but you have the control most of the time. Definitely one of my favourite roguelikes. Strongly recommended.
_childDocuments_.name: Ring of Pain

_childDocuments_.review: It's fun, but falsely advertised. The game isn't a roguelite: there is no permanent progression, just the ability to expand your card pool by completing runs. Because this game is so RNG-dependent, the cards you unlock are about as likely to hurtful as helpful in your runs. If you want Slay the Spire At Home, it is a pretty good game; but if you want a roguelite deckbuilder, it doesn't exist here. It also unfortunately took me more than two hours to figure out that permanent progression would not be forthcoming, so I couldn't get a refund. The game will be good if you go into it understanding that it is a roguelike, not a roguelite, but I'm disappointed.

_childDocuments_.review: Another difficult rogue-lite strategy card battler in the vein of Slay the Spire or Monster train, but with enough a twist to keep things fresh. I didn't like it as much as the previously mentioned games at first for some reason, but after a few tries it got its hooks into me good just like them. Instead of gathering and playing cards in your hand like in most of these, you instead gather stats and classic RPG equipment in predefined slots (shield, armor, gem, spellbook, scroll...). In front of you in each "room", you have circle of cards. Click on one of the two cards right in front of you to activate the card - if it is a treasure pick it up, a monster you attack it. There is no randomness, you see exactly how much damage you give and receive. Special monster attacks, positive and negative item abilities, and moving explosive monsters makes movement, attacking and selecting the right equipment almost like a chess game. Recommended for fans of puzzle games, and very difficult rogue-lites.
_childDocuments_.name: Ring of Pain

_childDocuments_.review: Cute little game. It's technically a "card game" (and technically correct is the best kind of correct), but in essence, it's actually a dungeon crawler. It's incredibly simplistic in gameplay - a ring of cards spawns, and you're supposed to move along it until you get to the exit to the next level. You can go either left or right, interacting with the closest cards next to you, or try to pass them by - but careful, if the card is a monster, it may still attack you if you fail to sneak past!Other than monsters (that get increasingly more complex and deadly as the dungeons go on), you'll also run into mimics, who, for once, are friendly and will let you loot them without attacking. Some of the more fancy ones may wanna demand you pay up first, but they won't want to gnaw on your delicious adventurer flanks. There will also be free-standing equipment cards, spell cards, stat boost cards, health potion cards, maybe-health-maybe-curse potion cards, shuffle-the-cards cards, and dungeon exit cards - some of which lead to special side areas with a specific design theme in mind; e.g., "Volatile" will always be full of exploding monsters, and "Patience" will always kill you if you dally.From then on it's all about managing the stats and making your decisions where to go next - you can always see the full ring and what kind of cards are coming up, but, excepting the two closest cards, not necessarily all the details about them will be revealed until you get closer. RNG? Yeah, there's RNG, and sometimes it will murderize you brutally, but thankfully, that's mostly going to happen in the first few areas, if you got deeper in (10+ levels), chances are, you're only going to die if you mess up yourself - and believe you me, there are  many chances to mess up...)The gameplay being as simple and fast as it is, it doesn't get too frustrating as you get repeatedly mauled and mangled, but as you unlock more items to use, you'll be eventually able to pull of some mean combos, turn the tables on the monsters.Having a lot of fun with this one!

_childDocuments_.review: I wish steam offered a Middle review. this game 100% deserves lots of credit. The art, sound design, aesthetics and soundtrack are ON POINT. ON. POINT. This game is AWESOME in everything aesthetics. Equally, many of the game's systems are GREAT. It feels like the mechanics of the game are a perfect mix of simple to understand but strategic and interesting.Now, I LOVE Roguelikes and Roguelites and Rogue-whatevers, mainly, I like the feeling of getting better at them over the course of many, many, runs. Slowly chipping away and getting closer and closer to victory. Not every run gets further than the last, obviously, sometimes you make mistakes early or whatever.In the time I've played. Out of the 7 Runs I've played: My first run was by FAR my best, and I didn't know anything, and I made it all the way to floor 15, I was pretty much just clicking stuff that looked cool, battling monsters and waiting for the game to kill me. Each run afterwards I paid MUCH more attention to the game's mechanics and thought about each action as much as I could, only to have my furthest floor in these runs be floor 8.You probably, can learn the proper strategies for this game and make it through most of the time, but it just seems like getting a few broken items lets you braindead SMASH autoclicker through the game. If I had the items and luck I had in that first run now, I would've beaten the game. I guarantee it. _childDocuments_.review: I am 32 years old.My ex-wife and I have a daughter together, and we adopted our son together. Both are now 4 years old.When we were going through our separation, I felt lost and unhappy. I was self-destructive. One day, I was so angry with everything spiraling out of control that I punched a concrete wall in a moment of overwhelming emotion. This resulted in breaking my fifth metacarpal in my right hand—the hand I worked with, played games with, and used to carry my children to bed—the hand I desperately needed to ensure I could continue providing.Upon learning the severity of the self-inflicted damage, I became almost suicidal. Keep in mind that just a few months before this, I was the happiest man, with no history of depression or anxiety. I had never experienced anger outbursts, nor was I the type to break down and cry, but I was in a tough situation that truly prevented me from seeing the light on the other side.With nothing better to do, I looked for a game I could play WITH ONE HAND while recovering. Somehow, I stumbled upon this game and read some of the comments. I decided it was worth a try... I must admit I didn't beat the game, nor did I play as much as some of you. In fact, I may have played this game for only a day or two. That being said, after doing so, I had a new joy and hope for life. I managed to leave behind the pain and suffering that had been thrust upon me. I could experience the joy and happiness of other people. I relaxed for 5 ♥♥♥♥ minutes listening to this music, long enough to realize that I would be okay.After realizing this, I turned off the game and went back to work. My hand hurt a lot, but I was motivated. I stopped feeling so sorry for myself and became the father I needed to be at that moment, not the weak boy I was behaving like.Today, I am close friends with the mother of my children. We don't fight, argue, or say hurtful things to each other. We are parents and friends.Now I have 3 children. My third child is, wait, ALSO 4 YEARS OLD. _childDocuments_.review: In rougelites, especially turn-based ones like this without any execution challenge, the primary interest has to come from the gameplay possibilities of the random elements, particularly the upgrade system. Slay the Spire became a gold standard for a reason; it's endlessly complex despite just moving from room to room because of the endless levels of interplay and synergy between the cards and relics you can find. Infinite complexity deriving from finite mechanics.So the fact that gameplay in Ring of Pain boils down to clicking on the card you want to trade attack and defense numbers with, and occasionally do a single use ability, shouldn't preclude this game's combat being interesting. There are multiple enemy properties, attack types, and other things to interact with. But the problem becomes that none of these effects interact with eachother in interesting ways. The only real decision you can make at any time is to click on the least threatening card at the moment, and occasionally run away. The real problem is that actual game-changing properties are usually tied to limited-use items, and can't ever become part of your playstyle. It's a numbers game and not much else.

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of the most unique games I've played in a long time. Basically a card based dungeon crawler, the twist is how the dungeons are presented. Every new dungeon is presented in a circular ring of cards, with the front two facing you. If any enemy is in front of you, you can choose to attack it or try to sneak past it. Some enemies explode in your face, causing unblockable damage, other enemies poison you or try to attack you from a distance. Sometimes the best thing you can do is just make a run for the exit or face certain death. Be aware this is a roguelike so death means death!What's fascinating about this game is just how customisable your build is. You have a total of 15 different areas you can equip items on to, from charms to necklaces to face masks as well as the regular arms and legs etc. With 291 unlockable items to potentially equip, your playthrough can be very different depending on how you choose to build your character. I've gotten really far into the game as a stealthy rogue who snuck past all the strong enemies and only picked off the weak ones. I've also gotten really far as a tank who can absorb most hits and freezes enemies on most attacks. Although I've not managed to beat the game (after 23 attempts!) it seems that both types of build are viable options to win the game.The sense of adventure and discovery is amazing for the first several hours. There are many unique scenario dungeons to come across. There are also a huge amount of interesting achievements to strive for.Finally, the sound and art design for this game is amazing. As you delve deeper into the dungeon you feel an increasing sense of foreboding. Some of the creatures look truly grotesque and make really horrible sounds. It gives the game a terrific atmosphere.Overall, although my play time is only 7 hours, I feel like I've already gotten lots out of this game. I've died 23 times and am keen to keep pushing on to hopefully make it to the end!
_childDocuments_.name: Ring of Pain

_childDocuments_.review: Art is great. First few hours are mysterious, confusing in a good way. Does lots of good set up for story and world. Main characters are interesting, and roguelike format makes for a nice initial drip-feed of information and context. High difficulty works out because you don't really expect to get anywhere, just see the sights. After a while, you'll probably get to the major inflection point for the plot, which is where things start to unravel. At this point, all the mysteries being built up look like they're about to get answered. Except, you're not actually likely to see what happens, because the big revelation is gated by an exponential spike in difficulty, not reasonably doable the first time you get to it, and not likely to be for a long while.Once you reach that inflection point for the first time, the feeling that the end is in sight sets in, atmosphere of mystery dissipates. However, grinding does not significantly reduce difficulty (only widens pool of loot), and many hours of subsequent play are necessary to unlock full range of items, roll for particular builds, etc. Nothing new happens on any gameplay or story fronts during this time, runs get extremely predictable, so you get very bored very quickly. Other spikes in difficulty preceding that point mean that if you got that far at all, you've probably "solved" the game and figured out your preferred builds, so that long grind doesn't even really feel like a time to experiment or discover.I'm giving this the thumbs down based on the miserable grind that sets in after you reach that key plot point for the first time. This might be less of a problem if you personally have enough control over your own brain to be satisfied with not actually reaching the end, unlocking all items, etc. If you're able to shut down your completionist brain and leave mysteries to be mysteries, then I would actually recommend the game on the strength of those first few hours.
