_childDocuments_.review: Steam REALLY needs a "mixed feelings" rating. The game is fun and I enjoy the story, but there is so much difficulty it's making the game feel more rng based than I think it should. The game makes a point of letting you know the consequences of your decisions so that you can plan what you wish to do. This is great, except when it gives you no options or no good options. Times when your only choice is to "Just Die". Times when whether you go left or right the outcome will be exactly the same. If particularly unlucky this can come as early as the second floor.The hidden time limit per floor before you are auto-killed feels like a particularly arbitrary punishment for playing the game well.Edit: After playing for a few more hours I can no longer recommend this game. I'm not willing to give up on it but I regret paying $20 for it now. So not worth it. The game is, if anything, even more rng dependant than I thought now that I understand the game a bit more. As the developer commented enemy stats are constant, which means if you don't RANDOMLY get one of the very few viable loot combos you Just Lose. Period.Additionally, it seems the developer misunderstood part of my review when they replied so I will explain further. Despite what they said there IS some kind of intentional hidden turn limit per floor before the game gives you ONE turn of warning to exit the level immediately or automatically ends your run regardless of current hp. It's a pretty generous limit so I guarantee you will never encounter this unless you are using the pike that allows you to auto attack when passing a card (it's a rare yellow grade loot item). When I'm WINNING a run by using strategy, an opportunity which is usually denied the player in this game due to consistent poor luck with loot, I don't want to feel like the game is punishing me for playing the game properly.There are over a hundred loot items, loot is chosen randomly, and most don't combo well or at all. A pro tip is to take note of the reshuffle button at the top of the screen when you get a choice between two pieces of loot. You most likely WILL need to use it in order to get something useful for your current build. Don't choose items just based on stats. You need to make some sort of build based on gear effects that is supported by your stats. Stats alone are not enough. Consider saving up 140 souls or whatever it is to buy yellow tier items from mimics if you can survive all the way to floor 8 or whenever they show up. Some of that loot might be game changing if the game allows you to use it properly after obtaining it.

_childDocuments_.review: Ring of Pain is a hard one to rate.The RNG feels sketchy and I have yet to complete a ring (I have played for just over four hours at this point and it feels like the RNG is stacked). That said, it has a wonderful aesthetic and is very appealing visually. The sound is very well done and and it's obvious the developers put a lot into this game. It wouldn't take huge changes to make this a great title and I'm sure there are a lot of masochists who already think it is, but I think RNG should be just a tiny bit kinder than what has been implemented here.The other thing I'll say is that I didn't refund it due to the amazing strengths it does have. I'm just going to keep playing it occasionally, hoping for the minor tweak that will make this slightly more friendly, and in the meantime, I'll just pretend it's like solitaire but with a few of the cards missing from the deck - still fun, but never expecting a win. There is something strangely addictive about the game - normally I would have quit and never looked back after this much defeat. That I have "wasted" four hours on this is telling. I originally did not recommend this but the owl got to me. #%&#@$ owl.

_childDocuments_.review: Ring of Pain is an extremely stylized roguelite deckbuilder similar to Slay the Spire with a very interesting gameplay mechanic of having all the cards in the deck in a circle.So in Ring of Pain you are placed in front of a circle of cards that contain enemies, treasures, potions, weapons, armor, spells and more. And your goal is to get to the exit. The enemies that will sometimes block your path you have two options for. Firstly you can fight them and trade blows until you or them, hopefully them, dies, or you can try to skip past them. You can also find a ton of different items in the game to equip to increase your stats like damage, armor, health, crit chance, speed, and more along with having cool unique effects.And when you get to the exit you go to the next level in what makes up this ring of levels. Sometimes you will have random events like fountains or shops or sometimes you will meet this creepy bird that is supposedly guiding you or this weird darkness that is somehow helping you.And you keep doing this and getting further and further and if you win there are a couple more difficulty levels to attempt to beat.There is also a daily challenge mode that has different random modifiers that has leaderboards and in terms of progression you can unlock new items to find in future runs.There are a ton of achievements, like in Binding of Isaac, and a lot of them will actually unlock a new item so you can try to unlock them all and get all the items while trying to beat the game.And so the gameplay in itself is very fun, the runs don’t last too long and it makes you want to keep playing over and over. And also the game is pretty brutal. There are some runs I just die in the first like minute because of some mistake I made that tragically kills me.And it definitely matches the overall creepy theme and vibes the game gives off. All the card art is very stylized in this scratchy type of way but it's not overly dark which is nice. And it has a very horror-like soundtrack that has those stereotypical horror stings if you know what I mean.So the game is definitely fun and I really enjoy the unique mechanic of having the entire deck in a ring. It seemed like a gimmick at first but once I started playing and noticing how the cards even interacted with themselves depending on their placement it really impressed me because it gives the game more strategic depth.I don’t think the game is the next binding of Isaac with thousands of hours of gameplay in it but I don’t think it needs to be. It is a very satisfying roguelite deck builder that brings a lot of new things to the table in between the gameplay and the presentation. So if you are a fan of of deck building roguelites like Slay the Spire or Monster Train I would highly, highly recommend this game.

_childDocuments_.review: Ring of Pain is one of the more interesting games i've played. You navigate each level's 'ring' of items and cards, interacting with the front two at any given time. But the others are not necessarily absent otherwise. Position, navigation, and enemies doing the same creates a lot of mechanical opportunities. The items of the game are numerous, and affect the above paradigm in many ways. Enough so, that it makes other games feel restrained by the lack of having a space to navigate as a component of play itself. (Versus an overworld where 'navigation' is closer to traversal without a consideration beyond time spent.)This reignites a lot of the exploration and strategy that Slay the Spire invoked, but with a lot more consideration of itemization and navigation. All wrapped into a delightfully thick inky and playfully distressing box.

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely recommend this, even at full price. As all roguelike games, RNG is there though.Every choice, every action, every turn has impact, and the UI leaves nothing to guesswork, the (albeit simple, with the knowledge you as the player get) calculations done based on your actions appear to be seamless in producing the correct end result.Absolutely a recommend, I had not realised over 3 hours had passed when I could pull myself out of it to write this. I had it recommended as a "deck builder", but it's not. So don't trust steam recommendation in that regard.The sound track is amazing as well, generally I play any game without music, bar a few exceptions, and this has a sound track that hits the atmosphere right on the spot.If you are a fan of rogue likes, you should give this a try. _childDocuments_.review: Ring of Pain is brilliant.It scratches a similar itch for me as Fidel Dungeon Rescue does, in the sense that it takes the familiar format of a dungeon crawler, but executes it in an original way. The result has a strategy-focused, puzzle-esque feel to it, all while retaining a very fast game pace that makes it excellent for quickly hopping into the game when you want to take a break.Combine this with one of the most unique visual aesthetics I've seen in indie games (and that says a lot, because creativity abounds endlessly in this scene) that's creepy and colorful at once, and you have an absolute banger of a game that's also continually being updated by the developers, for whom this clearly is a passion project with a lot of love put into it.I'll admit that the writing or lore is kinda passing me by. It feels cryptic to the point where I'm not sure I'd get it even if I looked up some elaborate explanation on a wiki or on YouTube. But! It's still interesting, because what little dialogue you'll find scattered about is written in an intriguing way. And hey, the main focus of the game are the mechanics. And as I've mentioned before, those are brilliant.Go buy Ring of Pain.

_childDocuments_.review: Ring of pain is a roguelite, card based dungeon crawler. Instead of having a deck of cards the dungeon itself is represented by cards. Monsters, treasures, potions, exits, items are all represented by the cards. You walk in a circle through the room encountering the objects. When you do leave the room through an exit door you find yourself in the master ring. There are special rooms for wishing, events, rewards and other themed rooms that you may encounter.Features    A large amount of items and item sets to use and combine.    Normal mode with unlocks and achievements    Hard mode     Daily dungeon mode with leaderboards tracking your first/best try both globally and with all your steam friends.     Twitch Integration I can recommend this game especially for those who played Slay the Spire or Monster Train or similar games. The game gets more addicting the more items you unlock and you discover the synergies of special items for a newstrategy in the next run.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: this game is for sadomasochists who believe the universe is ruled by chaos and misery. Needs a massive rework of the gear and enemy layering to build towards actual progression. All the pieces are here for a masterpiece that sets itself apart from a lot of the rest of the genre (StS, Monster Train, etc.).I'm not entirely sure what changed between the demo and this game but they honestly felt like two totally different games. In the demo there was a tremendous amount of synergy to be derived from the various equipment that one could equip. In the full game, every incremental piece of gear felt like deficits created an effect of me spinning my wheels. With one build I'd end up with -2 poison damage while sitting at 20 defense. This allowed me to block and parry for a while, but in the end I was unable to kill anything after a few rooms. In another build I'd end up amassing enough attack points but I'd end up dying to a guy throwing darts like 5 other guys behind him, killing me before I could even move. And then there are other rooms where there are two invincible enemies that move ever closer to killing you...leaving the only option to have a spell that generates a door in front of you to leave. No spell, no dice.How to improve: total rng will not allow for fun in this game...especially with the current unbalanced set of gear and problematic layering of enemies. In other words, the progression system needs a pretty massive rework. Each piece of gear doesn't feel like a "yes!", as much as a "well, I guess." Every time I took a spell there was no process of probability to go through to determine whether I should use this. It just ended up being "well ok I guess I should just use this now?"You have all the pieces sir. Its just a matter of assembling them in a way that builds progression.Also you should upgrade the UI for unlocking new cards. I missed it my first 5 runs or so.

_childDocuments_.review: Ring of Pain is a little slow to start; the first 3-4 hours were a bit of a slog, as I had absolutely no idea what I was doing. I couldn't really see any synergies and was just bumbling around at random, dying in all sorts of embarrassing ways, getting achievements for doing so, and unlocking items. And only after I've unlocked a bunch of them the game really clicked for me - and then it was just a matter of time before I could confidently construct a build that'd get me past the final boss. Oh, and real quick: this is not a deckbuilder, even if it has the aesthetic of one. To misquote a friend of mine, "It's as much of a deckbuilder as Baldur's Gate is. That is, if you think of your equipment as cards, then sure."The game's basic systems are rather self-explanatory. Attack, defense, speed; they work the way you'd expect. If you click on an enemy card, it initiates a combat round, with attack order determined by speed. It's instant, and you always get HP predictions on hover, so planning ahead is easy. It lulls you into thinking that this game is a simple affair; but while I wouldn't call Ring of Pain "deep", it definitely isn't simple, either.Take the spinning cards, for instance. You can only directly interact with the two cards that are in front of you. You can move past them if you don't want to deal with them at the moment; the enemies won't let you do that though, not without taking a free shot at you - unless you  past. Yes, this game has stealth. Oh, that enemy is moving when I do? Are they running towards me or from me? Luckily, the game gives you that info, but that's another thing to pay attention to. And then there's the whole thing where you need to avoid explosive enemies and the chain reactions they can cause...But the real depth, the real "meat" of the game lies in its multitude of secondary stats and the way they interact with both each other and the primary ones. I won't write too much about that, as discovering this stuff is where the fun is, but let me give you an example. There's an item which gives you -1 attack, but instead causes you to deal 1 soul damage to a random enemy while attacking. Okay, a bit weird, but whatever. But then you find another item - which increases soul damage by 3. And suddenly you find yourself killing lots of enemies around the ring without even encountering them. That's the kind of thing you need to do to win - and it gives you quite a rush when you manage to pull it off.With all that said, Ring of Pain sadly ends up being a rather mediocre game. As in, it's okay, but just okay; but there's nothing to really ignite that flame in your soul, nothing to really grab you by the metaphorical balls. The lore promises to be interesting, but I found it too ambiguous. The rhyming dialogue is pretty good, but without a solid game to back it up, it just ends up fading into the background. The aesthetic and enemy design are definitely appealing, but... I don't know, there's something that irks me about it. It's very... "zoomer gothic"? Take it or leave it.My biggest complaint, however, is this slow wind-up I mentioned before. The way I see it - and it's entirely possible I'm wrong - it's not feasible to win unless you've unlocked a bunch of stuff, which you can use to construct a winning build. This, sadly, is the natural conclusion to the meta progression design which so many roguelikes have these days; and to me, it just feels like padding. As if the game told me: "You can't win until you just mess around for a few hours." There are games that are far more deserving of your time. But if you're looking for a quick if a little shallow roguelike, then this might be it. I did beat it in the end; and while there certainly was some fun at the end of this journey, the majority of it was just a mediocre slog. Take that for what you will.

_childDocuments_.review: A hidden gem waiting to be found. Similar to other roguelite card games like Slay the Spire and Inscryption, it has the right balance that captivates you and lets your learn the mechanics at a good pace. The game is called Ring of Pain because the rooms, or dungeons, are shaped like a ring. Each room is a node in the overarching map, which is also ring shaped. Numbered rooms are the "core" rooms, with special doors leading to extra rooms (once you've visited one, it will be marked at the top of the door, so prioritise scouting these first). There is a fixed 15 rooms to reach the final boss, which will then win you the game. You unlock more gear as you play, which is the death mechanic of this game.Dungeons========At the front are two cards, which you can choose to interact with or navigate to one side. Using your spellbook will cost a turn, as will interacting with the cards in front of you, and moving. You can use a scroll at any time, which doesn't eat up a turn.Equipment=========You have a fixed starting item, which cannot be changed inside a run, but beating either end boss will let you change that at the start of a run. I recommend fighting the Owl boss first (right candle) as it's easier, and will help you get more familiar with mechanics. You can equip an item into a gear slot and replace it if you get a new one, but cannot discard without using the wishing well or special scroll. Some items have charges, which acts differently depending on the type of gear. Most jar slot items have depleting charges, some of which activate when exiting a dungeon, or when gaining a stat upgrade. Once depleted, the jar is useless. You can get a scroll to add +3 charges to jars. The spellbook is an active item that when used requires kills to recharge the item. The rest of the gear acts similarly, but trigger passively. e.g. freeze every 6 attacks.Game Style==========It's possible to play with different synergies to beat the game, but for the default (normal) difficulty I found focusing on attack, then speed (roughly 1:1 or 5:3 ratio), with some HP and clarity (2:1 ratio) is a reliable method for beating the game. About 30 attack, 30 speed, 20 HP and 10 clarify should be enough to win. You can also play around with poison builds, reflect builds etc.---{ Rating }---9 / 10---{ PC Requirements }---☑ Potato☐ Decent☐ Fast☐ Rich boi☐ Ask NASA if they have a spare computer---{ Audience }---☐ Beginner☐ Casual Gamer☑ Normal Gamer☐ Expert---{ Graphics }---☐ You forget what reality is☐ Beautiful☑ Good☐ Decent☐ Bad---{ Audio }---☐ Eargasm☑ Great☐ Good☐ Okay☐ Bad---{ Gameplay }---☑ Great☑ Fun☑ Challenging☐ Generic☐ Frustrating---{ Difficulty }---☐ Just press 'W'☐ Easy☑ Easy to learn / Hard to master☐ Difficult☐ Dark Souls---{ Grind }---☐ Nothing to grind☐ Only if you care about leaderboards☐ Isn't necessary to progress☑ Normal☐ Too much grind---{ Story }---☐ No Story☑ Bad / Generic☐ Some lore☐ Good☐ Fantastic---{ Game Time }---☐ Really short (0 - 3 hours)☐ Short (4 - 8 hours)☐ Few hours (10 - 20 hours) [if you focus on the main story]☑ Many hours (20 - 40)☐ Long (40 - 60 hours) [if you complete everything]☐ Very Long (61 - 100 hours)☐ Extremely Long (101+ hours)---{ Replayability }---☐ It's a one-time experience☐ Only for achievements☑ If you wait a few months / years☐ Definitely☑ Infinitely replayable---{ Bugs }---☑ Never heard of☐ Minor bugs☐ Can get annoying☐ Lots of bugs☐ Bugs destroy the game---{ Price }---☑ Full price☐ Wait for Sale☐ If u have some spare money left☐ You could also just burn your money

_childDocuments_.review: It's a sharp, well put-together roguelike. Navigating the ring is more of a puzzle than a test of skill - the game's turn-based and mostly deterministic, so progress mostly comes as you learn the enemies and how they interact with each other. There are a lot of ways to die in this game, especially when you're still figuring things out, but runs are quick enough that the deaths don't get in the way of the fun of learning the system. The art side is equally sharp. The rhyming tidbits are vague and cryptic by design, but they work well to set a mood along with the surreal graphics. I'm still not sure if it's a metaphor about emotional healing or just an edgy haunted dream world, but it's dripping with style either way. I don't know how much staying power it has past the 7.5 hours I played, but I had a really good time exploring the starting difficulty either way.
_childDocuments_.name: Ring of Pain

_childDocuments_.review: So this is a good game, just in general. There's plenty of things to like about it and most other comments have made good points.The soundtrack, the gameplay, and what minor story there is are all great parts of this game. It's a game that even on normal most runs I still die on. It's a very good example of a roguelike game, though it's not really a "card" game beyond objects being portrayed by cards. There's no deck or drawing which IMHO are key parts of card games.Now I want to talk about hard mode. Look I'm a sucker for difficulty, Dark Souls is a series I love every game from and there isn't an ounce of material in those games I haven't seen. However, this game suffers from "non-interactable" difficulty. There are hard mode runs that you can't win, just like games a solitaire where there is no combination of moves to win, I fully believe that is true here.When it comes to build variety I feel like there's really only two style of successful builds I've had so far, both with a fairly similar playstyle. Both focus on aoe either with items that hit all around them or through end game items that trigger of healing.  That's it, I've never got a poison, soul damage, thorns, frozen, just hit things, knockback, or even crit into endgame. Though of those I think crit has the best chance if I keep doing runs.The final small problem I have is that the early levels 1-7 are just not really enjoyable levels, comparatively  to late game levels as your builds aren't going anywhere. Though this is just a minor note.However, that's it for my issues, everything else about this game is fantastic, while it's not really Slay the Spire levels of quality yet, I could see this game surpassing Slay the Spire with more updates!
_childDocuments_.name: Ring of Pain

_childDocuments_.review: I've only been playing for a few hours and I am already in love. I highly recommend this game to people who enjoy Slay the Spire or Darkest Dungeon as it gives off vibes of both of those. Its difficult, its strange and genuinely unsettling at times (in a good way), and visually pleasing. I hope this game continues to expand as I can't get enough of it and would love to have ever-growing creepy content.
_childDocuments_.name: Ring of Pain

_childDocuments_.review: If your a fan of Slay The Spire, One Deck Dungeon, Inscription, or any other card based game Ring of Pain is worth a play.I've fallen in love with the cuddly, creepy atmosphere where you loop around each floor interacting with mimic chests, inner demons, and cute frogs and dogs. Every run has a ton of variety from the items to the rooms. No one style of play is best. Trying to break the game with OP equipment combinations or even starting with a useless spoon for the added challenge.I'm personally happiest with how much content is in this beautiful game and the updates that keep adding more. I can tell how much love was put into it.
_childDocuments_.name: Ring of Pain

_childDocuments_.review: Ring of Pain has very strong art direction. Art, music, writing and gameplay all tie into a cohesive vision of the dark and twisted world.The play of making meaningful risk/reward decisions with each turn is very engaging and exciting.Variety of drops, encounters and rooms on each run makes me think about my decisions differently, and keep me excited for the next one.I'm loving it, and I'm looking forward to playing more.
_childDocuments_.name: Ring of Pain

_childDocuments_.review: Ring of Pain is a roguelike / card game / dungeon crawler mashup. Levels are generated randomly from decks of cards, and arranged in a format (like a ring) which lets you observe the level and strategise. As you interact with cards the dungeon dynamically adjusts based on what you're doing. Ring of Pain blends elements of modern roguelike/roguelite dungeon crawlers (Binding of Isaac, Enter the Gungeon etc) with a turn-based card game, set in a world distorted by your mind. A cryptic world of fear and delusion.

name: Amnesia: Rebirth
detailed_description: You can’t let out a breath. The creature is only inches away. Its sole purpose - to feed off your terror. And so you crouch in the dark, trying to stop the fear rising, trying to silence what lies within you. “I know you. I know what you're capable of.” In Amnesia: Rebirth, you are Tasi Trianon, waking up deep in the desert of Algeria. Days have passed. Where have you been? What did you do? Where are the others? Retrace your journey, pull together the fragments of your shattered past; it is your only chance to survive the pitiless horror that threatens to devour you. “Do not allow yourself anger, do not allow yourself to fear.” Time is against you. Step into Tasi’s shoes and guide her through her personal terror and pain. While you struggle to make your way through a desolate landscape, you must also struggle with your own hopes, fears, and bitter regrets. And still you must continue, step by step, knowing that if you fail you will lose everything. First-person narrative horror experience Explore environments and uncover their histories. Overcome puzzles that stand in your way. Carefully manage your limited resources, both physical and mental. Encounter horrific creatures and use your wits and understanding of the world to escape them. Also available in Adventure Mode for those who want the story and adventure without the horror.

_childDocuments_.review: I'll get straight to the point:Is it scarier than Amnesia: The Dark Descent? No.Is the game revolutionary? Also no.Is the game solid enough for a fun horror experience?  Yes, for the most part.Amnesia: Rebirth is better AND worse than The Dark Descent and SOMA in many ways. The variety of environments, sound design, resources management and puzzle design are great and definitely hold Rebirth a strong case in those aspects, along with some pretty tense monster encounters.However, Frictional chose very weird and perhaps half-baked design decisions which affected the pacing and the narrative of the game for the worse. The game itself feels a bit rushed and rough around the edges, especially in the narrative aspects, making it hard to care for most of the characters. The game struggles with what it wants to tell you at first.Even so, the game gets really good in its second half, focusing on an otherworldly plot that ties in to the original game from 2010. I'm certain that fans of the original game will find this one enjoyable, although not without disappointment. 6/10.
_childDocuments_.name: Amnesia: Rebirth

_childDocuments_.review: I've been a fan of Frictional Games since 2011 when I first played Amnesia: The Dark Descent. I've since played their Penumbra trilogy, SOMA, and was pretty active in the modding community at the peak of ATDD custom stories. SOMA currently sits in one of my top 5 favorite games of all time and it set a pretty high bar for Frictional Games in my eyes. The story, the pacing, the enemies, all so digestible and emotionally deep!Rebirth however, feels short and convoluted. My main complaints are: On the positive, the music is nostalgic, the sound design and voice acting is amazing as usual, and the presentation is top-notch. The Traveler's Pendant was REALLY cool yet horribly underutilized. But really the negatives far outweigh the positives for me. I apologize for the wall of text but I have a lot of trust and appreciation with the folks at Frictional Games for being such an inspiration to me and to see this game fall flat like this was honestly quite a shock. I think they're at their strongest when they work with sci-fi and despite my complaints here, I look forward to seeing what they do next.
_childDocuments_.name: Amnesia: Rebirth

_childDocuments_.review: Well, I'm putting a negative on this one, the game is not bad, but as a huge fan of Frictional Games' works since the Penumbra series this time I'd like to ring the "careful not to stray" bell in the hope that they will notice it.I didn't have a great time with Amnesia: Rebirth, not a terrible time thankfully, but still, not the best of times, and I'd like to express why, as I replayed The Dark Descent and SOMA very recently before.First I'd like to talk about the positives, the environments are absolutely stunning, if there is something to keep in the game without any doubts, it's the art direction. Despite a very limited technical aspect by today standards, the environments are incredible, texturing is wonderful with heavy use of clever parallax mapping, and while the texture resolution in general can feel limited, it is one the best examples of texture resolution doesn't matter for a game to look great. The use of dynamic lighting is generous too and makes the environments pop and feel alive (or dead but in a striking way if you prefer haha).Sadly, as far as I'm concerned, I think it is where the positives ends, the story is interesting, but takes a while to pick up, and most importantly, is horribly told. You are bombarded with flashbacks and an incredible amount of notes to read, and 80% of those notes are not interesting at all and feels like padding and time consuming for nothing honestly. Amnesia TDD did a much better job at this because it was a game about immersion and gameplay/atmosphere first and story second, so there was just the right amount of lore to keep you interested, and cleverly paced to not overwhelm you.One can argue that SOMA kind of suffers from the same issue, but SOMA somehow feels more mature in that direction, and I feel that the story is much better presented, and overall much more interesting, but that may just be me being a huge Cyberpunk themes nerd.But that's not the main reason of the negative review, the main reason is the gameplay. In 10 years, there has been literally no evolution, and in fact regressions, on the Penumbra/Amnesia formula. The game feels way too easy, scripted, and convoluted. The stealth mechanics and general gameplay systems feel way too simple and outdated, and again, I've replayed TDD and SOMA recently and they are just way more interesting, even SOMA with the absence of inventory screen and mental health asks more things from the player (remember Theta labs?). Also what's with the level design? The "hub" feel is almost completely gone and the game is almost 100% linear now?TDD was a game about immersion and horror, SOMA was a game about story telling and existential horror, but Rebirth? It feels like the game doesn't know what it is trying to be, and has very serious pacing problems. The ending has some cool moments but it's too little too late, and also too short.With each game, while Frictional Games' creations still feel interesting to play in a way or an other, it seems that they are slowly fading away from what made them special in the first place. And I'm not necessary talking about "making scary games", but about making games that aims to challenge the player's emotions, in all the good ways the medium is capable of, and not only in the form of interactive linear dramas (thankfully we're not there yet, but we're getting dangerously close).Be ambitious! not only on the creation itself, but on what it expects from the player! Crazy puzzles! Challenging but readable sections! Challenging level design! All tied with a competent story that keeps us engaged and a focus on immersion, it doesn't need to be the best story ever made!
_childDocuments_.name: Amnesia: Rebirth

_childDocuments_.review: Amnesia: Rebirth is a direct sequel to The Dark Descent. Unlike A Machine for Pigs, it has stronger ties to the original game, although you won't be in the same setting, or playing as the original protagonist.Instead, you play as Tasi, a plane crash survivor that sets out to look for her missing crewmembers, in the deserts of Algeria. If you know the story of the Dark Descent, you'll know why that's quite exciting. I will refrain from talking about the more interesting aspects of the narrative in this game, because there are a lot of really cool things at play here that are best discovered if you play the game blind.Rebirth is similar to TDD in a lot of ways, however very different at the same time. Like the developers' previous game, SOMA, Rebirth is filled with a lot more narration by your character. She will voice her thoughts, and comment on notes after you have read them. All with fantastic voice acting. Because of this, I found that there wasn't a constant feel of existential dread like in TDD, but that tradeoff comes with a very intriguing story. There are some beautiful environments, intriguing concepts, and an overarching story that kept me on the edge of my seat. TDD had a great story too, but it did manage to scare me just a smidge more.That's not to downplay Rebirth's horror sections. In between comforting areas filled with warm sunlight, you will be hunted, and chased by creepy monsters. The designers did a great job at constantly playing with your expectations of when they will appear, and tricking you into undesirable positions. And the sound design helps bring it all to life in a terrifying way.There's an additional option to lie down on the ground, which makes you even more hidden. It makes for some really creepy moments, when you can just see the monster's legs walking on the other side of a desk you're behind.Like in TDD, you have a lantern that can be filled with oil, as well as a match that can be lit for a smaller radius of lighting. While the match burns, you can light a few other environmental lamps, which removes the need to use 100 tinderboxes per room, if you're clever with your match usage.The game does a great job at rewarding you for thoroughly investigating rooms. Items are hidden in very interesting spots, covered in other junk, and it helps make the place feel real, like it was lived in.Puzzles are still a thing in this game, and I found them to be overall very clever. They're not too hard, and not too easy. You have to think outside the box just enough to have you scratch your head for a bit, only to get a satisfying feeling of accomplishment after you figure it out.The only slight downfall of the game is from a technical point of view. Sometimes the graphics look a bit dated, and there are limited FPS and Audio options. But those are very miniscule complaints.Overall, I think it's a great sequel, with just the right amount of familiarity, while at the same time bringing loads of really cool concepts to the game. There are tons of great surprises that I didn't want to showcase, so if you like the idea of a horror game that's heavy on narrative, with some superb voice acting and setpieces, I highly recommend playing Rebirth.
_childDocuments_.name: Amnesia: Rebirth

_childDocuments_.review: The Amnesia series returns once more with this third instalment and has had many fans, including myself eager to see the improvements from the past game, and the cult hit Amnesia: The Dark Descent (ATDD). Unfortunately, Amnesia: Rebirth misses its mark and has many shortcomings, but still manages to be a decent narrative experience overall. Many of its 'flaws' will be seen differently by each individual as they're quite subjective in nature. Whilst I recommend this game as a whole, there are many aspects to it that are awry.+ Excellent, poignant voice acting.+ Variety of settings whilst maintaining its focus on dark gloomy environments.+ ATDD nostalgia, with the memory tubes, door icons, sanity sounds, matches etc.+ 3 varying endings with differing moral choices towards the games conclusion.+ Thoughtful puzzles.+ Exploration to find light sources/memories- Very convoluted, disjointed, and difficult story to follow with multiple characters and jumbled memories.- Lack of character development. - Pregnancy mechanics, checking your baby bump to increase sanity becomes tiresome very quickly, especially with the protagonist’s comments.- Lack of enemies. Many areas are totally safe and remove any tension previously created.- Constant, forced immersion ruining cut-scenes	- Can only hold 10 packets of matches at one time.The protagonist, Tasi Trianon finds herself in the heart of the Algerian desert after a plane crash. Stranded and alone, with fragmented and scant memories, she ventures off into the unknown, impelled to move forward and search for her missing husband. During her trek, Tasi realises that she doesn't only have her own life and survival to consider, but also that of her unborn baby. Driven by her maternal instincts and strong will, she ventures deeper into the darkness, compelled to escape and find normality once more. This becomes the core of the game, in a quite mature and maternal approach to the survival horror genre, however, this may understandably, not appeal to everyone.Understandably, most players, including myself, are going to compare this to ATDD and whilst gameplay is somewhat similar, I wouldn't say that it is an improvement on its predecessor. The harrowing atmosphere which we know so well from ATDD I found to be completely lacking. I played for hours without bumping paths with a single enemy and once I did, the constant baby coddling and reoccurring cutscenes were sure to remove any feelings of dread previously created. All enemies (there are just 2 types) can only be found in the last 2-3 hours of the game. Gratefully, Frictional Games have kept their sanity mechanism which can be increased through light, but also uniquely through touching your pregnant stomach. At first, I thought this was interesting and realistic in that it would give a sense of comfort, however, at least for me, this became trite very quickly. A monster could be just around the corner, staring right at me and I can touch my stomach and speak to it with the same repeated baby-talk 'shh little one, it will be ok' and the enemy doesn't hear me and my sanity is suddenly improved.I actually question Rebirth as a survival horror game, as these elements are so few and far between, I found it to be mostly a narrative Sci-Fi-horror mix. Those looking to relive the fright and jumps of ATDD should look elsewhere. Although I consider myself a veteran horror player, I did not find this game scary in the slightest and it should not be played with only this in mind. The game is dark and gritty, but has more of a focus on a Sci-Fi, SOMA-like atmosphere as opposed to fear inducing elements.Furthermore, Rebirth is extremely forgiving in its gameplay. I believe I only died once when I was lost, but if players do die, you are respawned closer to the exit and sometimes the enemies even despawn. With already so little enemy interactions, the areas that do require stealth/hiding are thrilling. To make this even easier seems counterproductive if the aim of the game is to have a survival horror tag but remove the survival aspects. There are multiple NPC's scattered throughout the journey, some can even be spoken with. For any ATDD fans, we know that this is a strange concept. I found that it removed the fear and loneliness that was once curated so expertly before, creating yet another safe environment. We are introduced to an array of characters within minutes of starting the game, most of which I forgot shortly after.  Followed by an ever-increasing convoluted story and lack of character depth, I found myself not really caring about her baby or any of the other people. Tasi's memories are scattered, but she remembers the people she was travelling with, her husband, who she was etc. Completely opposite to ATDD where everything was unknown until the end. It is also not clear how she got amnesia although players can make assumptions. The cut-scenes are forced throughout the game, triggered by progress but becomes more of a nuisance in their recurrence, especially in the beginning areas which are just memories of Tasi's happy family life - boring. On a positive note, I liked the inclusion of moral choices relating to her baby as well as the 3 different ending paths. With each ending contrasting one another, this encourages replays, combined with the motivation of Steam achievements. I don't remember once playing an Amnesia title and stopping to think how stunning the environment looks, but that's exactly what happens with Rebirth. Instead of sticking to the gloomy, caliginous paths, Frictional Games decides to switch things up with including both indoor and outdoor areas, sunsets, ruins, water features and more.  That being said, the gritty areas are still just as dark as in their previous titles and the need for illumination is ever prevalent which is fantastic.The voice acting is very well done, as expected. The decreasing sanity sounds are just as I remember in ATDD, however the monsters are not and I didn't notice any outstanding factors in the sound design as a whole, which is disappointing. Yet, I understand that the developers are taking on a new approach, trying to find a happy medium between SOMA and the original Amnesia, between Sci-Fi and horror and this must be a daunting task. Combined with the new addition of a female, pregnant protagonist which is not commonplace at all in many games, so I praise their bravery to try something new. Without a focus on the horror factor/monsters, I can understand why the sound design wasn't as memorable as the series used to be, but I hope this can be improved upon in future games.I experienced no issues or glitches and the game played smoothly.Amnesia: Rebirth is daring in its approach, deviating so fiercely from its immensely popular predecessor and whilst it is severely lacking in survival horror elements, it does manage to find its footing within its narrative story-telling and Sci-Fi focus. Despite its convoluted story and odd pregnancy mechanics, it is clear that Frictional Games are trying to merge the success of SOMA and ATDD into Rebirth but narrowly misses the intended mark and ends up being a decent game which I enjoyed, but is immeasurable to their aforementioned titles.
_childDocuments_.name: Amnesia: Rebirth

_childDocuments_.review: I loved the dark atmosphere, simple puzzles and exploration. The story and dialogue are well done and thoughtful. I played in Adventure Mode, which lets you play at your own pace without any monsters attacking you. This made the game more accessible to me as a disabled person, since I can't think quickly enough for the regular scary mode. They also did a great job keeping me on track with hints. I never got lost or stuck on a puzzle for too long. It was engaging all the way through and gave me a sense of accomplishment.

_childDocuments_.review: If I could apply the Suffering From Success meme to any game developer, it would be Frictional.You might read that and think I'm referring to some kind of loss of the Frictional magic in this game compared to their previous releases, but you'd be wrong.I'm referring to the player reception of this game. Frictional's two most recent titles before  were lauded as genre-defining masterpieces that would set a new standard for survival horror in the following years. Two, their playerbase decided, is a repeating pattern- and as anyone who has watched a hype-train pull into the station knows: passionate fans plus sky-high expectations rarely bode well. Regardless of how good  is, it will never be good enough for some, because it's neither the game they convinced themselves they were going get, nor is it the game they got . Comparison is, after all, the enemy of contentment. Let's dissect this a little further: a good chunk of negative reviews for this game are from players who measure  not by how it fares as a stand-alone horror game, but by how closely it replicates . Shockingly, the devs did not decide to create the same game they made a decade ago. I'd even argue that if the devs were the type to endlessly retread old ground,  (and ) would never have been made at all. The former was also released at a time when we were all a decade younger and, for the novelty of it all, less experienced with this brand of run-and-hide horror game. These players have, sadly, been cheated out of a great horror experience by their own nostalgia. Another chunk seem to be from folks who are all too aware that  and  were game-changers, and are disappointed that  does not attempt to reinvent the wheel. These players have been cheated out of a great horror experience by their own expectation that a Frictional game must always bring something revolutionary to the table. One more (thankfully smaller) chunk of players seem to be, for one reason or another, disgruntled that the player character is a pregnant woman who dares to speak. There's already even a mod to "shut her up". Make of that what you will.I am not trying to claim the game is flawless by pointing these things out. What I am trying to point out though, is that much of the negative reception here (critics seem to unanimously rate it between 8-9.5/10) is the result of fans judging it against their personal expectations, rather than judging it as a game. So, how does the game fare as a stand-alone horror experience, then?Pretty excellently, but let me make this clear: if shotgun-toting, zombie-killing carnage is what you look for in a survival horror game, then this is not for you. If you need combat or constant action to keep your attention, this is not for you. If you're the type to take your time, soak up the atmosphere, to seek out and read the torn notes scattered around for any clue as to how you got into this situation, to peak around shadowy corners in fear of what may lie ahead? This is for you. If you can immerse yourself in what the protagonist is feeling in the moment; if you can see yourself feeling terrified for Tasi as she cowers behind a crumbling pillar, cradling her stomach as horrifying images flash across your vision amid the shuffling horror that is smelling you out in the darkness? This is for you.The atmosphere seems to bear down on you from all sides as though alive and hellbent on turning you into a claustrophobe. The tension can become so thick and oppressive that Tasi's fear seems to bleed through the screen and into your body (in a good way, you're here to be scared, after all). Emotional terror weighed heavily on my heart, too. It's hard to not feel anxious and protective as you listen to Tasi cooing shakily to her unborn child, trying to claw back the last vestiges of her own sanity. At times, you might feel your spine tingle as you crawl across the floor, knowing, but being unable to see, that whatever stalks the shadows is tailing close behind. You might even feel like you need to take a breather from the game now and then.I won't give much else away, as this game is best enjoyed blind. If you want to experience fear and vulnerability as you step into the protagonist's shoes, if you want atmospheric, story-driven horror, a dash of mystery, or just a bloody good sequel that fleshes out some of the otherworldly aspects of  (provided you can take off your nostalgia goggles first), this is for you. I advise above all else, to play it for yourself and make your own verdict. For me, it's clearly a solid addition to the Frictional library, and one of the greatest immersive horror experiences out there.9/10

_childDocuments_.review: ok i have to say, i went into rebirth reading all of these disappointed reviews and whatnot, expecting the game to be pretty lackluster and not very horror driven. and then i played the game. what the hell is everyone thinking? it might just be nostalgia blindness for the original and they actually don't like it for the reasons they liked it, idk. But i played these games back to back and I can tell you right now there are moments in rebirth that scare me more than in the dark descent. Not to mention the storytelling - its such an enthralling and emotional rollercoaster that kept me engaged from start to finish, really right in there with tasi every moment wanting her to make it out alive due to not only her being herself, but also a spoiler reason i won't say. There are game mechanics that tie in with the narrative in a way i never thought could work but did, and it was so innovative and fun to see that.maybe most people are just looking for "scare me now, other stuff later". but frictional was never really about that, and it frustrates me to see people putting this game down because there's more focus on the narrative and they think it dillutes the horror. if you're looking for a horror game thats just solely for simple scares, then go for outlast or something like that. but if you're looking for a game that keeps you immersed and brings you into a world of their own making, then finally taking that opportunity to instill fear and tension into your every move, then amnesia is your thing. this game is completely worth the money and more, especially from this indie dev team. its well executed, very thoroughly thought out, and there are many tense moments keeping you on edge. No, the flashing images popping up on screen are not trying to scare you, the images have significance and the way it jumps out enhances that significance to the plot. if you know frictional, then you know this fact.And whoever says this is not an amnesia game, you must have amnesia about TDD.

_childDocuments_.review: A severe disappointment, even more so given this game's ancestry. Spoilers. tries to portray itself as the next entry in what should be a renowned horror series given how infamous  has become over the last decade. But unfortunately, the game gets bogged down in trying to craft an emotional narrative that doesn't really land and sacrifices a lot of the horror and game play that made the first entry so memorable.The game play of  itself starts out with the implication that you'll be re-creating the same flow as . Light is scarce, there's a sanity system, monsters lurking around you need to hide from. But it's only after playing for a couple of hours that these elements barely factor into what you do, especially with the creatures. Actual dangerous encounters and scary moments are incredibly far and few between, instead trading this off for scripted chase sequences, an abundance of darkness that is more frustrating to navigate than frightening and the incredibly weak jumpscare attempts when your fear is too high. Any moments of tension are also frequently ruined by Tasi not shutting up whenever  happens to her. While she is voice acted well, her need to fill in any dead space with mutterings and comments to no one break immersion because it's a reminder that the game is happening to  and not to you. The monster encounters are extremely easy because of this as well, with Tasi giving you outright warnings you're about to be spotted or you shouldn't do a particular action because she says you shouldn't. Even if they do, there's no sense of threat from the prospect of dying or letting fear go too high anyway. Either of these things happen, you're forced into watching a 'scary' barrage of images that don't make sense before the equivalent of a QTE comes up to get you back playing. Sometimes, this even puts you  the section that caused the non-Game Over, meaning that the game essentially completes the section for you if you mess up.Which leads to the plot. The story of  feels incomplete, for lack of a better term. Much like , the details that explain more thoroughly what's going on are relegated to discoverable notes and fragments, most of which don't tell you a lot on their own unless you want to expand and confuse the mythos surrounding the Orbs. This is especially apparent in tablets in the alternate world, where you're thrown all these different terminologies of how that world operates and who these people are but without any background information to understand what they mean. While some of the call backs to the original game were welcome, both in note and event form, they don't feel like they add much to the story  game is trying to tell and are more like little jabs of "remember this?". Even worse, with how often the game forces you into scripted sequences you can't get away from, the notes are easily missable unless you waste a bunch of time trying to check everywhere to get them. Though I understood the general flow of events, the finer details were missing and I was given no encouragement to backtrack and find more because of how bland the game play was for most of the game.The side plot regarding Tasi's past also feels half-baked. You're given painfully obvious clues about Alys' fate hours before you're told what happened, and this isn't helped by the over-the-top dream sequences which hammer the point home with the subtlety of... well, a hammer. These don't add much to Tasi as a character except to explain why she has this sudden obsession with keeping Amari alive despite the baby's presence being a direct rip-off of  (growing unnaturally fast and is hinted to be cursed or whatever the case may be up until the end of the game). Daniel and Oswald from the first two games felt more well realised and believable because they did horrible things out of selfishness and tried to atone for them later. Tasi feels like the modern trend of generating forced sympathy for a character because horrible things happened  them instead. I get that the attempt was to make a more human and relateable story compared to the original game, more akin to SOMA, but SOMA was able to tell such a story incredibly well  breaking the immersion of being in PATHOS-II. If this was an attempt to try and recapture that magic, they failed.I can at least say the presentation of the game is probably its strongest asset, especially when it comes to the art design of the alternate world you frequently travel to and the more elaborate desert areas of temples and villages. The sound design is also very well realised, especially in regards to the machinery and the creatures. But presentation alone doesn't get you very far on its own, which is where the game falls flat.If you're looking for a weird mixture of science fiction and personal drama in a game that doesn't challenge you very much, then maybe  will appeal to you. But if you were like me and were expecting a strong survival horror experience where the story was a means to disturb and enhance the level of horror that Frictional is capable of, then you're going to walk away sorely disappointed.

_childDocuments_.review: A followup to the 2010 classic horror game , Rebirth simultaneously managed to impress and disappoint, terrify and bore me. The atmosphere, lore and world building is top notch. It was fantastic to see how the in-game Universe had been expanded without giving away too much of the mystery.Set in the 1930s on an expedition to the then French Algeria, Tasi, our protagonist awakens onboard a crashed aeroplane unable to recollect the events that lead to her being there. Seemingly alone, disorientated and with no sign of her crew including that of her husband she sets out across the hot desert sands following the debris in an attempt to piece together what happened and find rescue.The core gameplay hasn’t deviated much from Frictionals’ previous games. Sneaking past threats, solving environmental puzzles, scavenging items, and managing fuel to illuminate the darkness to prevent insanity. The game is very generous with how much the protagonist can withstand. There are a couple of mechanics that I don’t remember from previous games, the first being literally running away and then lying prone until you’re left alone and the second is talking to yourself to calm down after being involved in stressful events. I found there was far less reliance on utilising distractions in your strategy to manoeuvre across levels, in fact I don’t remember even doing it once in an attempt to outwit the creatures, likewise no need to keep doors shut. Enemies are tough and fast but there is a heavy reliance on scripted and linear sequenced events rather than actual encounters which became very noticeable in subsequent playthroughs. One key moment that stuck out as an annoyance was I came across a trap and thought ‘I will throw something at it to set it off’, in doing so the script that took over had my character panic like she had walked into it rather than an active choice made on her part to avoid it. The correct choice is to jump over the tripwire, not an impossibility as you jump like a heptathlete on the moon but still felt illogical at the time. Other than that, having autonomy taken away for unskippable dialogue to play out was dull - nothing quite like being forced to stare at a ladder you’re not allowed to use just because the protagonist won’t shut up and can’t multitask. hahaThe main story is very slow, taking its time to reveal snippets about what is actually going on and where you are. This isn’t a bad thing, the pacing felt natural but made it difficult (especially in the beginning) to understand why I should continue and why I should care about the characters involved. There were payoffs for my patience and persistence but I can’t say I liked any of the endings. I also wish there was more opportunity during the game to explore morality options whether seen or unseen. There’s only one significant choice to make outside of the endings and as far as I can tell it doesn’t make a difference to the rest of the game. The environments are fantastic, some of the most ambitious I have seen from this developer. Detailed and varied, new places feel like new places - they’ve come a long way from what I remember being a series of dilapidated stone hallways in ‘The Dark Descent’. The play with fear in both dark and light areas is brilliant - from the exposure and vulnerability in the bright expansive desert where you’re forced to seek shade to the cramped and claustrophobic tunnels that make you hope a light is just around the corner. Combined with the phenomenal sound design this makes for some truly petrifying moments. ‘Adventure Mode’ was introduced several months after the initial launch of the game and provides a lighter story focused experience. Key changes are: some creature encounters are almost entirely removed, those that remain don’t attack unless provoked; darkness no longer affects the protagonist and areas are more brightly lit; also no jumpscares. The trade-off being the addition of a few very simple puzzles (see: drag item). This mode is ideal for achievement collectors to pick up any missed achievements (aside from two which can only be gained in the original mode). A small testament to how good the atmosphere can be, I still felt unsettled knowing nothing could hurt me in this mode after having already beat the Original mode.I like this game, it’s a lot better than the travesty some had led me to believe it is but it's definitely not groundbreaking and it didn’t have the same impact as The Dark Descent did. I think it does deserve a chance, and if you’re willing to take it I recommend allowing yourself to become immersed with headphones and zero distractions.
_childDocuments_.name: Amnesia: Rebirth

_childDocuments_.review: This is a tough game to review, partly because it's very story driven and I don't want to go into spoiler territory, and partly because of the quality of the games that preceded it. That last point won't mean much to horror newbies, so I have to view it two ways: both as a fresh experience, and from the point of view of a perhaps more jaded perspective.This is going to be relatively straightforward. For those who aren't over exposed to the horror genre, and are up for another bout of hide and seek, alternated with run like ♥♥♥♥, this is a great game. Dripping in atmosphere, with some genuinely unsettling sound effects and music, this is the work of masters when it comes to ♥♥♥♥ your pants ambience.  If you're looking to be scared then you're in the right place.For those who aren't new to the genre.......*sighs* well, this is going to depend on what you hoped for. Have Frictional Games improved from SOMA? Have they transcended the, IMO,  pinnacle of storytelling in the genre of spooky, first person, stealthy horror games? Have they made revolutionary steps in the gameplay? Have they reasserted themselves as the top dogs after several strong contenders for the crown in recent (ish) years? (Outlast, Apsulov, Maid Of Sker etc) In short.....are you hoping this will rock your world?Because you could be ever, ever (ever!) so slightly disappointed if you'd hoped for a new wave of mechanics or approach to  what is now well worn schtick for the developers. What is here is done at a very polished level, and they haven't slacked off as such, since it's expertly crafted. But it's also nothing new, beyond them doubling down on the narrative and greatly refining the environmental physics puzzles. More of the same but better, albeit depending on your stance as to whether more is better. Don't like the monster avoiding gameplay? great - it's at least 2+ hours into the game before you even encounter one. So for a very long time it feels like the worlds most nerve wracking walking simulator, and can get a bit boring until it lets loose.When it lets loose it goes hard addressing the fact it's done ♥♥♥♥ all but smoke and mirrors up to this point, and if you wanted monster encounters then you've got 'em big time. All that build up to make it all the more terrifying when you actually encounter something? It's either dull as ♥♥♥♥ or necessary legwork to give the monsters a deserved sense of menace. The latter half of the game with it's noticeably relentless pacing of stealth and chase encounters? It's either a long overdue compensation to finally sink your teeth into something with intense action, or an inconvenience as you face yet another frustrating by-the-numbers sequence with only one viable way to play it..... i.e slowlyPersonally I'm in it for the frights and for the pant-♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥  gameplay, and so it was a bit of a barrier finding it's largely just the story up front with a few shocks for quite a long time. Though when the ♥♥♥♥ did finally hit the fan they've lost none of their touch at making pulse pounding tension, it's just that they're repeating familiar things by now, if you've played all of their games like I have.  Story-wise it's engaging, and really well told with great writing and voice-acting. I don't think that it was overall as fulfilling as SOMA' but there's no doubt they've stepped up a level with their ambition and creativity. The end result just didn't hit me as hard as SOMA, despite having some memorable moments where the morality of your actions comes into question.It's enjoyable, but doesn't quite work when you see it all at the end. Decent enough science fiction horror to be sure, yet this is the follow up to an absolute cracker and will not stay in the memory like that game does.As a game it has enough substance to keep my interest, albeit feeling like a walking simulator for a good few hours to begin with. The puzzles are nice to solve, the scares work, and it's fairly terrifying once they stop teasing you and actually have some enemy. You can easily see they've got better in most departments, unless you wanted them trying something new. Because this is revolution, rather than evolution, it is the refinement that comes from this being their third iteration and the increase in their confidence and abilities. In a nutshell:  despite how polished and involving it is, it's still gameplay you've done many times before.I recommend it, as despite a few misgivings which hopefully I've detailed well enough for you here (albeit vaguely regarding the plot, so as to avoid spoilers) to decide if you want to jump in, I did enjoy my time with it. Probably a boring as ♥♥♥♥ to read review, but I wanted to discuss it without giving anything away, as the story is still worth having its mysteries preserved. It just lacks a little when compared to the emotional and philosophical gut-punches its predecessor slammed you with. If you gave yourself over to their previous games, then this should equally grab you. If, however, you have horror genre fatigue then this won't rejuvenate your interest.If you found this review to be helpful then why not check out my curator page here:

_childDocuments_.review: Amnesia: Rebirth is a first-person science-fantasy survival-horror adventure game developed by Frictional Games for the HPL Engine 3.5. Set nearly a century after the events of Amnesia: The Dark Descent, player-character Tasi Trianon is pitted in a fight for survival against the gruesome aftermath of forgotten choices with interdimensional ramifications in a sun-scorched, howling Algerian desert.When I wrote my review of SOMA, Frictional's previous release, I mused on how the company strove (and continues to strive) for a gameplay-oriented harmony of profound themes and emotions with a mechanical basis for thoughtful, conscious player-interaction. To my interpretation, there is a theoretical perfect balance wherein all combined features of the design coalesce into a single experience which impresses upon the player something narratively and experientially intense and affecting, and this is the primary end-point which Frictional has aspired to, through the use of iteratively experimental and ambitious implementations of game-design across its titles. The goal is to create something the landscape of gaming hasn't truly seen, arguably, but this journey that started with Penumbra has, in my opinion, been somewhat misrepresented. I'll get right to the point: Frictional Games is not a revolutionary or groundbreaking studio. It doesn't seek to, with every initial release, create something unrecognizably new or astonishing, and it never really has.Apart from its very first title, Penumbra: Overture, every game it's released has been deeply married to (and informed by) the flaws and successes of the prior title, inasmuch as it relates to this goal of "ludonarrative harmony" (so to speak). I would argue each title has had its own unique inspirations and ideas that were fresh and innovative, but Frictional doesn't operate with a goal towards innovation per se, rather iteration. It uses each title to iterate upon the last with a single endpoint in mind, changing as it becomes clear it is necessary to change. This isn't to say it's stuck in the past; its eyes are very much focused on the future. But the big, groundbreaking, innovative game which Frictional aspires to create is one which it is willing to share its work on: the prototypes and attempts it crafts along the way. This is what Amnesia: The Dark Descent was, and it's what SOMA was as well.I suspect people get off calling Amnesia: The Dark Descent groundbreaking because they hadn't played the Penumbra duology which came before it, or perhaps the lone inspiration that guided that game's design was encompassing enough -- affecting and impactful enough -- to so thoroughly impress its players in a way no game, including Penumbra, ever had before. I would say this is the same story behind how SOMA got received, as despite its stripping down of Amnesia's gameplay to a near "back to basics" degree, close to exactly what Amnesia: A Machine For Pigs tried two years previously, it too was regarded as something forward-looking and progressive for the medium with its heavier story-focus, even to the detriment of its monster-encounters and basic gameplay.Amnesia: Rebirth, too, has an ace up its sleeves, one I can't spoil here. Suffice it to say it's created a unification of Amnesia's core gameplay and SOMA's presentation with a number of thematic and mechanical ideas so out there I assumed they, too, would be globally represented as key features of yet another "groundbreaking" and "innovative" horror title, from what is, at this point, one of the most highly regarded practitioners in the genre's medium. One such feature is something akin to a dedicated "empathy" button, whose narrative and emotional contextualization shifts as the game calls for. It's a fantastic way to systemically break the tension, and creates a player-initiated flow of suspense and relief facilitated by the oppressively clockwork sanity mechanics. The puzzles are more involved, requiring deeper, more meticulous analysis of the events and environments being presented to you. The monster encounters, too, are made weightier and more challenging. They aren't any harder than SOMA's encounters, but the ambiguity and the tighter level design cooperate with their improved senses to make encounters that feel robust and affectingly "fail-able". I know this, because I failed during the tutorial encounter a portion into the game. I observed in my SOMA review that no section of that game quite matched the level of terror evoked by the prison level of Amnesia. In this game, certain portions surpassed it.They've incorporated a sense of blockbuster swagger inherited from its previous title SOMA, a sense of sheer storytelling confidence and pacing which is difficult to achieve but easy to grasp, and the horror, too, has these qualities. There is a playful, devilish glee with which the game wears you down, at first thrilling and nostalgic, and slowly reaching a zenith of suspense and weight which feels impenetrable. Yet the story pushes you forward, building sympathy and stakes, motivational, emotional involvement. This, itself, was achieved in SOMA to a glowing degree, but the integration into gameplay afforded by Rebirth's innovations is unlike anything found there. The story of Rebirth asked me deeply unsettling questions. The gameplay of Rebirth forced ME to ask similar questions to myself. But these questions were player-authored. I was placed into a role which was deeply immersive, not because of its similarities to my own life, but in spite of how different it was, and because of how cleverly presented and implemented the new mechanics were.Despite the mindboggling work --  the gorgeous detailing and intimate storytelling -- these novel mechanical adjustments and inspired design-oriented alterations made to both the Amnesia and SOMA formulas -- the spell seems to be breaking for many of Frictional's fans, and it's worrying. People seem to expect something as unexpected and unfamiliar as Amnesia: The Dark Descent was, back in 2010. But not only is that an unrealistic standard, it's not how Frictional Games operates, nor is it how it operated back then. Amnesia: Rebirth should, and I think someday will, be judged purely on both its own merits as a work of art and in how it pushed the bar forward for Frictional's aspirations. In terms of how it lives up to The Dark Descent's legacy: not even that game lived up to it, to those discerning players in 2010 who could recognize it for the iteration -- rather than innovation -- that it was. Amnesia: Rebirth is a terrifying and beautiful adventure across multiple worlds, 8-10 hours of landscapes and ideas larger in scope than anything yet attempted by the company, put forward in service of something deeply personal and profound, a gripping tale that will transport most players into a shockingly unique protagonist, rendered by the player's hand and by thousands of hours of meticulous, inspired developer effort. This isn't Frictional's magnum opus, but neither were any of its previous titles. Amnesia: Rebirth is, like all of those, another bold, large step in the right direction, worthy of being remembered.

_childDocuments_.review: This game deserves so much more love. It's really good. All the negative reviews have to be from people who loved The Dark Descent and wanted basically the same exact thing. This is not the same, but in no way is it a worse game because of that. It's different which is exactly what this series needed.This may not be as horrifying, but it is still scary with good intense moments that keep you on edge. The story is great, and ties in with The Dark Descent in ways that are extremely satisfying. The engine is a good upgrade from the previous two games. With that, the gameplay is close to the same as previous games, but more enjoyable with the new engine and great graphics.Audio and dialogue is *chefs kiss*. The dialogue of the character you play as is really well written and voiced and doesn't break immersion like some other horror games I've played. It feels genuine and adds a lot to the game.The darkness and lack of matches coupled with the extremely fast draining lantern can be a little rough at times, but that has to be my only complaint and it is in no way game breaking. There are game modes and mods that can easily fix that if it's too annoying for you. And they brought back custom stories..Come on guys. Seriously don't listen to the negative reviews. While The Dark Descent is a classic and great game, this one might honestly be my new favorite. And I have over 150 hours in the original Amnesia, so that's saying something. Buy it
