_childDocuments_.review: I've been a supporter of Frictional Games ever since Penumbra: Black Plague, where they proved that blending together Point & Click Adventure, Survival Horror, and First Person Narrative games made for a very compelling game. I really enjoyed Amnesia: The Dark Descent and Justine from both a narrative and gameplay perspective, and even the outsourced A Machine for Pigs contained a strong story to compensate for its weaker gameplay. SOMA was the peak of Frictional's development trajectory, as a science-fiction horror narrative that combined a sublimely executed story full of existential dread with gameplay mechanics that had been streamlined and refined into creating an experience that still holds up to this day. I had the hope that SOMA marked the period of Frictional perfecting their game development philosophy, and that it would inform the trajectory of their future titles. Learning that they had responded to criticism about SOMA's ludonarrative confusion by coming up with two different follow-up projects, one focusing more on science-fiction/philosophical themes and the other refining the horror gameplay (presumably this), I was curious to see if this game would show any signs of improvement over the rough patches of the earlier Amnesia titles.Unfortunately, I would have to say this game is just a Regression. I find it very hard to believe that this project had been worked on for over a year, let alone since 2015, and the disappointment of this game makes me worried about the quality of the other upcoming project. Perhaps this was a rushed side-job with the brand of Amnesia slapped on to keep Frictional afloat while they prioritize their true passion project, but I find it very baffling that the game that ostensibly wanted a "stronger horror focus" would instead be even more bogged-down with intrusive narrative elements, made all the worse by comparatively inferior writing/pacing and gameplay. If anything I felt more like I was playing a Tomb Raider spinoff by way of BioShock Infinite's bombastic (yet intellectually deficient) storytelling.That is not to say I hate this game. I do find the moments set in the real world, such as the abandoned fortress and the cistern, to be beautifully rendered and a nostalgic reminder of the skill that still remains at Frictional; but they remain all too rare, bogged down with comparatively uninspired visits to an alternate dimension that feels more like a Stargate fanfic than anything Lovecraftian as SOMA or even the previous Amnesia had accomplished. The gameplay mechanics also feel like a disappointing regression from even Penumbra, with a ludicrously reduced carrying capacity, monster encounters that ironically punish you by removing the monster once you are bound to be caught by the extra-frustrating gimmick of the monster now grabbing and immobilizing you instead of simply hitting you like in previous games, a 'death mechanic' that is ultimately more tedious than frightening (compounded by darkness now outright killing Tasi instead of lowering her sanity), and even fewer horror sequences than A Machine for Pigs (although there remain a few encounters that I do genuinely like.) There is nothing that matches the adrenaline rush of Amnesia 1's water monster, however, a comparison made all the more grating due to Rebirth including a sequence clearly invoking that memory. The game also bafflingly includes a dimension-crossing artifact that is extremely underused (and treated with an odd lack of wonder by the characters), feeling like another undercooked idea.Perhaps my biggest gripe actually has to do with the baffling decision to replace textual reminders/objectives with vague wordless sketches; this led to me being stuck on puzzles for far too long, as the sketch only told me what I was looking at rather than hinted at what I needed to do. What was wrong with dropping hints in text or even having the main character verbally provide hints if the player was stuck? It feels like a pretentious show-off of a developer's sketching ability, rather than something useful for players.The absence of the writer who worked on both Amnesia 1 and SOMA is greatly felt here, with a narrative that is over-stuffed with underdeveloped characters who seem to serve mostly as slasher-film fodder, a pacing that is both comically padded (the floor gives way under Tasi and sends her away from her objective least FIVE times) yet criminally rushed, an extremely predictable and paper-thin main plot and a clumsily-told past narrative, and a lead character whose great tragedy is not being nearly as developed as prior Frictional protagonists. Even Justine feels like a more fleshed-out character. There is a mechanic where Tasi gets to monologue to herself, something that could've provided great opportunities for character development but sadly disintegrate into repetitive variations of her telling her baby that she's scared. The Metroid: Other M comparisons I've seen people compare this game to may be a little unfair, as Tasi was not previously established to be a 'badass', but the game repeatedly hammers into us from the opening sequence the same generic points about her and her backstory; yet we know very little of her compared to the in-depth backstory that Amnesia 1's loading screens gave about Daniel, and Simon's tragic past was concisely told to us in a 10-minute opening sequence whereas Tasi's single trauma is drawn out agonizingly slow across the entire game to the point it overshadows anything else about her characterization. I feel like this game is a rough draft full of underdeveloped ideas that, with much more playtesting and development time, could have actually been great. I really wanted to dig the premise of playing a pregnant woman in a horrific situation, and I appreciated the idea of subverting expectations by going for an experience more focused on the archaeological and science-fiction elements hinted at in the prior Amnesia titles. But I really feel as if with this title, Frictional is losing their touch by creating a game that seems to have learned nothing from SOMA or even Amnesia's success as games and instead is trying to tell a story that, tragically, its writer does not seem properly equipped for.I do really hope that Frictional uses the reception of this game to help steer the track of their future project(s) away from Rebirth's failures and back onto what made SOMA work so well. It does hurt me to have to give this game a 'thumbs down' as I do not consider it bad, so much as a big disappointment that I would've gladly accepted waiting longer for.Play at your own risk.

_childDocuments_.review: And so, my journey through the more relevant entries in Frictional's catalogue is coming to an end—and what a journey it has been! I’ve braved the horrifying halls of Brennenburg Castle, pondered oblivion amidst the waves in , and snoozed through the soporific occurrences of , all in preparation for my descent into the Bunker. But, before I could put it all behind me, Frictional were waiting at the end with a second entry into the series that put them on the map all those years ago: . Something was off, though. Would you believe me if I told you that this is the poorest user-reviewed game on Metacritic that the company has developed? Looking at Steam’s user reviews doesn’t produce a more hopeful result, and the consensus is rather murky even among my friends who have dared to review the game. The positive reviews can’t recommend it without a bit of apprehension. The negative ones do the opposite without hesitation. So, what's the secret behind  divisive reception? Is it that much worse than what came before? I don't think so. Rather,  is quite late to the party, trying something new with a formula that was all out of tricks, at a time when everyone was waiting for an encore.The original  was released in 2010 to strong reviews and an even stronger footprint in the industry. Horror games didn’t want to be  and  anymore as neither of those two were themselves at the time. Instead, games wanted to be , and so many of them tried to. So, many. Oh my god, that’s a lot of horror games! still follows this design philosophy. That is, instead of carefully managing ammo while navigating labyrinthine environments, you manage your sanity and light, with a larger focus on story and puzzles along the way. From the very start, you can tell it’s a game made by Frictional. Just like in the last , our adventure starts in Algeria, though a century later and without a getaway to Prussia any time soon. Even with the setting changing from cold medieval dungeons to deserts underneath the scorching African sun,  has that “WTF is that?” art direction that Frictional have established themselves as the kings of by this point, weaving together creative enemy design and breathtaking architecture that slowly takes over the more mundane locations you’ll find at adventure's start. Landing herself into supernatural-force-infested waters is Tasi Trianon, an engineering technician whose expedition plane crashes over the Algerian desert. Time passes, Tasi wakes up, and things are stranger than they ought to be. She sets off to find the rest of her crew, and so begins a new kind of dark descent for the modern age.But, before we continue, here’s a fun little challenge: outside of , how many games have followed the “” formula and did so successfully—if success isn’t exclusively measured by how much money or YouTube Let’s Plays were made? How many of them are critical darlings today? I can’t think of any that fit the bill, and even  came across as woefully out of touch in 2017, right before  “revived” survival horror. It seems to me that the formula, outside very few examples that did its own thing with it, has no staying power. It’s like everyone misunderstood the assignment; if you’re stripping away all mechanical potential to disempower the player and not coming up with a different key design to elevate your game, what exactly are you doing?And I know that’s hard; it’s why combat is the most common way of doing away with your obstacles in gaming. Building mechanical depth through it is a lot more straightforward than coming up with all these other systems that could potentially prove cumbersome. However, when a game does succeed, it’s frequently a high point in the medium. That is why, in the era of “psychological horror”, a game like  can come across as “an underrated gem” in retrospect. It dared to give back the player a little bit of power while still not removing the more popular choice to run away.I think Frictional realised this early. I think that’s why  was so mechanically barren even when compared to . Merely disempowering the player wasn’t enough on its own; besides, players already knew how to deal with it. They needed something new and found it in marrying environmental storytelling to the horror of the game’s setting, making its mechanics truly psychological, not creating fear from startling the player or having them perform an unwieldy task while tensions are high, but from the way the player thought about what was happening around them. Even the public wisened up to this, in a way— featuring player death and seaweed automatons chasing you around in primitive psychological horror fashion netted it its harshest criticism.To that end,  doesn't try to merely take further the design that made  stand out so much, nor be a pure return to  more mechanically oriented frights. Instead, it's an attempt to create a mechanically solid survival horror experience, with tighter pacing and  philosophical edge. For example, there’s no health to keep track of this time around—it’s all in the sanity—and while your lantern again has oil to burn off of and matches that serve to create a new light source, much like the original’s tinderboxes, it’s a lot more limited and pushed towards increased interactivity. Unlike tinderboxes, matches aren’t a prompt that shows up next to an unlit brazier, but a limited tool you have to manually carry and align with anything flammable before they rapidly burn out. As for what was to be  holdover, the team again went with a more mature story that seamlessly makes its points through game mechanics, yet an established series praised for its puzzle design proved to be a much less hospitable environment where leaning fully into this design philosophy was never going to fly. is so full of excellent puzzles that they not only get in the way of its storytelling, but the horror as well. They’re probably the best designed, most immersive puzzles Frictional has ever created, in every facet—visuals, mechanics, worldbuilding—and they effectively help this game stand out from what is the slothful mould of a psychological horror game of the 2010s, but it's almost as if they have no place here. Actually, a lot of the game's elements get in front of each other. An unbroken narrative such as  can't work as well when it's split up by elaborate puzzles. Horror sections can't be as expansive and punishing as they were in  when they stand to break the immersion and pacing.  comes across as an immature experience, pieced together out of the studio's best ideas that suffocate everything else that's also included.Contrary to its name, that’s what  is—the tolling bell at the end of an era. A title interested in exploring the uncharted aspects of its predecessors to their limits, more so than reliving the glory days. In its stride, it somewhat ignored the highlights of those titles, resulting in a less cohesive game, taken too far off course for all those who expected another bold new step in the same direction. In the end, it is a fitting bookend to the era and, after putting it off for so long, the reason Henri finally bought a gun.

_childDocuments_.review: If Amnesia Rebirth were the only Amnesia game to exist then it would be a fine game but that's all. Not great but just fine. Having read many of the criticisms of the game it's my opinion that some are solid and others didn't reflect the experience fairly.______________________________________________________________ The current top review for this game claims to have up to 600 hours logged on Amnesia: Rebirth, given my playtime that would be equivalent to roughly 73 playthroughs. Unless you're a speedrunner that makes no sense whatsoever, the real source of their play time is mentioned being custom games and content creation. There is little if any review of the main game and their experience is not the way most people will play the game let alone the expected way to play the game. But yeah I have 600 unlogged hours on shower with your dad simulator so I'm pretty much an expert.Anyways this isn't a review of a review so lets try and give a comprehensive review of the core aspects of the game with only 8.2 hours logged.This is one of the most important things for a horror game to nail and luckily for Amnesia Rebirth's it ends up being it's strongest aspect. One of the coolest features is how it takes place in the same world as it's forebear The Dark Descent. Unplanned sequels often have a very hard time incorporating the established lore without retconning things or being overly "fan servicey". Rebirth manages to do this without any issue and it was really refreshing and even nostalgic to expand the lore of its universe. Similarily refreshing is the non traditional desert egyptian horror setting. Where some people may find issue is it's primary method of delivering exposition. This is going to be through loading screens and notes that are found in the world. These have a lot of detail put into them and are were worth my time to read however that may not fit some peoples preference.Brief synopsis - a pregnant wife and her husband crash land in the desert. You playing as the wife (Tasi) wake up in the plane crash to realize that everybody has left you so you begin your journey to find your husband and piece together your memory. This is fairly intriguing although the plot has a significant problem with regards to the Amnesia motif - much of what you end up remembering is more interesting than what happens in the current plot. This could be acceptable in some cases but really the majority of events that the player experiences are really of no consequence and end up feeling contrived. This is demonstrated by multiple plot points of "and then the ground gave out and Tasi ends up further behind than she was before". Sure events like this can be alright in moderation, but here they don't advance the plot and just hold it hostage to buffer out the playthrough. This is just incredibly on the nose later in the game with the  This experience just ends up being tedious like a game of snakes and no ladders.Another significant problem is  Another problem I had with the story is that it is essentially a .Lastly, the multiple endings were all pretty good but unfortunately I can't help but feel underwhelmed because of the lackluster player controlled journey.Rebirth's gameplay isn't much different from Dark Descent or Soma and ends up being a sort of in between. A surprising aspect of Rebirth is the level design. It's actually quite good. Many areas loop back together or have locked doors that get used and generally speaking the areas felt realistic to inhabit and navigate. The set pieces were well crafted and fun to look at. Unfortunately though, there are a few "walking simulator" parts that felt very boring and even like they wasted a good set piece -  The puzzles weren't really exceptional and they were pretty much bog-standard for the franchise so far so it's hard to complain about that.There was also an attempt for a resource management aspect with regards to the light and dark but it fell incredibly flat. There's so many matches and oil cannisters in the game that it undermines the whole aspect of it. There's so many that it's to the point that you will invariably end up wondering "why the hell are these matches and oil cans in here of ALL PLACES". A dilemma the gameplay has is its reliance on Tasi to react to what is happening. It's problematic because you're playing as a character with their own established traits which throws a wrench into immersion. This problem is compounded on because for most the game it is just Tasi. Because of this she is forced to react to most of what is happening which ends up being a large burden for one character to bear (SOMA did a great job side stepping this issue with Catherine). The end result is that Tasi will often react to things in an expected manner, but just as often in other similar cases not react at all. While it is okay if Tasi's reactions don't align with the players, it's the inconsistency in application that hurt my immersion in believing Tasi is an actual character experiencing this world.While this is a gameplay aspect,  it's arguably the defining aspect of any Amnesia game so it warrants it's own section. Horror is undoubtedly a complicated genre/reaction so some people's reactions may differ from my own. For reference I will say that I've found all the Amnesia games tend to be scary for the first half but to then become more action oriented in the latter half (SOMA was an exception and managed to be keep it's horror thrill to the very end). Rebirth doesn't buck this trend and in my experience the horror was similarly front loaded. I didn't really find the final "monster" to be all that scary either but it's conceivable that somebody else might. So really I can't say that Rebirth did a bad job, I just can't say it managed to be exceptional. And funnily enough that ends up being my overall sentiment to the game. Amnesia Rebirth was a game with solid ideas and an underwhelming execution. A lot of this let down does come in comparison to Dark Descent and SOMA but even then it ends up being a serviceable game. I think for its ~$30 price tag it's not really that worth it but for around half that it's fairly priced. Finally if Frictional can take the good parts of Rebirth and polish it up then I'm confident future Amnesia games have potential.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR/Conclusion at the bottom! Will keep Story-spoilers blacked out!I'm a longtime Frictional Games fan. I've played all their games that came after Penumbra: Overture. Loved every one of them, especially SOMA. I was very hyped for this game, hearing that it takes place in Algeria where Daniel found the orb made me really hyped for it. Sadly, it fell short.--------------------------------------The areas in the game goes back and forth, but they can be divided up in to the desert, caves/nests, otherworld and underground. First half of the game takes mostly place in the desert and caves/nests. This is where the game shines. The Fort which is a simple building with three floors in the desert is superb. This is where you first meet a harvester. In the cutscenes they talk about the place being infested by Ghuls which I liked at first but when meeting the monster it looks just like the harvesters you meet later in the game. This place however captures the same feeling you got in ATDD and sometimes SOMA. The soundplay was very good and the tension was kept at a high all the time. Second half of the game mostly takes place in the otherworld or the underground which is a weird "mix" between caves and the otherworld. This is where the game falls in its gameplay-quality. Throughout the game the otherworld was a safe place, when you got there you could relax and dive in to the deep lore that they've set up. Towards the end the otherworld becomes a hide and seek playground with searchers everywhere. All the areas in the game looks amazing though. They've really upped their game on the looks and it allows for a great immersion into the world of Amnesia.--------------------------------------The story can be divided into two sections which overlap towards the end. The "family story" and the "curse story". -------------------------------------- This is not explained in any way throughout the whole game.   --------------------------------------Minor cons:-------------------------------------- non-gripping story with old gameplay mechanics and lackluster enemies. Compare it to SOMA which changed into a more story-heavy game but still upped their gameplay mechanics. Rebirth just feels like a shallow attempt to make the "next amnesia". Could've been really good, the lore is there but it's not fully used.

_childDocuments_.review: This game oh man.... where to start. Let's start with saying i 'barely recommend this' and i now understand why so many reviews were so conflicted. Some Pro & Con listing is in order now: Pro:- Strong middle game and actually a pretty decent end game despite what some say. Got to take what is offered even though this is not something that will be remembered. - Good protagonist design- Once the vitae business from earlier Amnesia games is introduced then the game really begins. It is like hitting a button. The ride really starts to pick up from there. - Some really sick stuff with the protagonist 'condition'. Note this game is really NSFW as people passing by might be going a little 'wtf are you doing' with some of the stuff going in the screen pretty disturbing POV stuff. So i guess the old rule 'play this alone in a dark room' still stands. More so now than usual as the horror parts are brought up close.  Con: - By far the most atrocious early game of just about anything i have played lately. Who's idea was it to attempt to shoehorn into the player visuals and audio 'explaining' the background of the protagonists? Way way too much way too early. It fails completely to make the player care at that early stage. Only much much later is there some kind of meaning to it all. I see many have quit the game at 2-3 hours and given a negative. I was so close myself too i just wanted to quit.  Considering the way the protagonist was designed a much lesser approach or even a Gordon Freeman type of non-speaking protagonist would have had a bigger impact and shortened the plain bad early game.  - Walking sim early game. By the time you are suddenly forced to do puzzles it is really hard. Physics engine in the elevator puzzle is atrocious and it took way too much time to solve it considering how dead simple it was. As for the cannon puzzle it was fine but the player is just not in the 'mood' to solve it as the game has been a walking sim this far and as a result the two first puzzles in the game are the hardest. Not because of actual difficulty but because physics engine or player just not understanding that bringing a big object near a another key object will suddenly make the object 'snap' into place. Later on puzzles that are much harder are solved easily as now the player is 'in the mood' as directed by the game. It is hard to explain what i am trying to say here so i guess i'll just conclude here that 'early game has very little in common with mid to late game'. it is like two different games. And this thing cannot be just ignored. This difference is probably why so many are conflicted with the game. 5.5/10 Recommended but only barely. Get it on sales but not worth full price.

_childDocuments_.review: I must say, it pains me to not recommend this game. I pre-ordered (I very rarely do) and I want to love it so bad, but Amnesia: Rebirth makes it very difficult to. It all comes down to not living up to the expectations I put on a game with the same title as the Amnesia: The Dark Descent that I love. I'll try to break down what works and what doesn't. Let me just say that I love the introduction, all the way from waking up to the plane up until the "water-level". It is mostly well-presented, you're in a beautiful desert setting, you're all alone and you have no idea what to expect. The only direction you have is the doctor trying to contact you on the radio, in vein, and traces of the other survivors that you follow. The flashbacks keep you interested and the sketchbook is charming, at first. Finally, the village is brilliant. The setting I appreciated the most, but was utilized the least. The first encounter with a monster and how drawn out it was really brought back the feelings from the first game. It was done masterfully.Replacing tinderboxes with matches was a brilliant decision. They run out faster if you move around, but you can effectively light 3-5 light sources with every match. Navigating through the cave systems with a matchbox before getting the lantern felt great. So much tension created there.They might be far from AAA standards, but for me the art style did a lot. Again, mostly the desert setting got me, I'm not a fan of the "other" setting, at all.Something The Dark Descent did extremely well was providing a story outside of what your character was experiencing without interrupting the game. Rebirth did the exact opposite. You get constantly interrupted on your journey, be it through a flashback that requires your sketchbook to take up the entire screen and pause the game, or suddenly being teleported to a dream. It can be extremely frustrating and at the very least it pulls you straight out of the immersion the game has built up. Sometimes the game slows you down with a voice over and sound effects and TDD players will be used to, why Frictional didn't decide to do that every time I cannot understand.So, whenever you are in the dark you get the "black worms" creeping onto the screen. I had no issue with that in itself, only how fast your sanity drops. You  play in the darkness because of how fast it drops, especially so if there's a monster nearby! So, what happens when your sanity drops too far? It's as cheap as images flashing onto the screen with a loud sound effect, and if it drops even further you'll literally get a seizure and you have to spam WASD and move the mouse around to be able to do anything again. So, if a monster appears you  find a place close by, plant your face on the ground and wait for it to disappear or walk far enough from you so you can sneak past it. Looking at the monster for a while will give you a seizure, so you'll have to rely on sound. This could be fine if the seizures and flashing images weren't a thing, but unfortunately they are. I managed to get killed from having a seizure when sneaking away from a monster. Wasn't very dark and I wasn't even looking at it, but of course that's not enough to prevent your character from standing up and panicing and then get caught.But wait! There's a way to counter it! .So many bad decisions here. Starting with the non-spoilers, she talks way too much. All the time actually, doesn't matter if she needs to hide or whatever, she'll have a remark whatever you do. Usually it's  or . It's painful how passionate the game is about pulling you out of any immersion you get.  Her voice acting is flowless as well, which is something I could look past if she wasn't talking all. the. time. I grew to dislike her quite a lot, even more so as the story progressed. So, instead of having a less talkative character like Daniel, you get a very talkative character that you straight up dislike.After the getting through the water-level, it's just dull isn't it? I guessed the entirety of the plot a few hours in, which left me frustrated as Tasi was doing stupid things I wouldn't have done if I had a choice (you don't have a choice). The setting necessary for the story is intriguing for the first 15 minutes you spend in it, then it just becomes a question of why they chose it. It's so distant from anything you can relate to that it effectively removes any fear factor. Think if aliens made the pyramids. That's where it's at. It's sci-fi fantasy, and too much of it. Combined with all the other elements all the fright is removed. There's  to relate to, so there's nothing to fear. That takes us to the main problem and why I cannot recommend the game.You get so disconnected to the story and environment that you end up being frustrated/annoyed most of the time. The game before the water-level and the game after it is like night and day. Night is scary, day is not. The game is constantly working against itself, trying to reel you in and the forcing you out again with the blink of an eye. Lack of direction? Wanting too much? I don't know what ultimately made the game into the schizophrenic mess it is, but it really doesn't matter, I'm disappointed to the point of heartbreak. Maybe I could recommend this for the upcoming custom stories, but we'll see if that has any success.

_childDocuments_.review: It's hard to start with this game. Over all, Rebirth is a solid experience. My first playthrough ended in two sessions, an eight hour journey spanning over with a dear friend. There's a lot to say about this game. I'm going to try and keep this spoiler-free, so even if you haven't beat the game, you can read it. I'll start with the positives first.This game has really, really good atmosphere and sound design. You will constantly look at beautiful scenery, even if you're in the desert, in a cave, etc. It's so fun to walk around and be immersed in the world. The sound design continues to amaze me, a trait from SOMA.The world building is fantastic, and you can really take your time reading notes, letters, interacting with the enviroment with physics, and stuff like that. Most things reacts to the way you expect it to...The gameplay is more of a refinement of the originals, which is not to say they're bad. They're nice. They made the tinderbox mechanic... make more sense. In the original, it was not a surprise to end the game with 30-40s matches (not counting hard mode). The amulet is a nice addition. The health seems to be your sanity this time. They pumped the darkness big time, and they made the darkness... somewhat of a threat by reducing your health more often while you're in the dark.  However I must admit, I don't think the game punishes you that much for failing segments. I barely died in my entire playthrough and I think that part of what made tensions high in dark descent is if you die, the enemy may change its location and such. Still, the tension is high. Also, the puzzles are neat - they aren't impossible, but some can be hard to figure out.For any lore lovers, there is a lot of notes in the game you can collect and read.Now onto some of my negatives...The voice acting is quite nice, but... I must say I am disappointed in the main character's frequency of talking. One of the best reasons why I liked the original Penumbra, or the dark descent is that your character never talked during gameplay section. Your thoughts are your own. Penumbra handled it the best, in my opinion, the only talking was during the intros. The rest is by text as Philip examines thing. Daniel went a step further, only in flashbacks and notes. Soma started this trend of talking, and had the protag talking through at some segments, usually at scenes where there's another 'thing' near-by, but he was still mostly quiet in the entire game.But this game? Oh boy, get used to it fast - Tasi will talk about a lot of things. At first I was okay with it, but hours in, but later on I just wanted her to shut up. It's hard to immerse in a horror game when your protag has those kinds of moments where they just yammer on things. It's not that bad, but it's a pet peeve of mine.The story. The story is... well. I'll leave your own judgement for that, but just know that I'm not very happy with it. My biggest complaint is I feel like, in a horror game, the priority should be about player immersion. Something about being trapped and wanting to get out. Something about an extreme loneliness (which, rebirth has, it just doesn't feel like it because Tasi talks a lot). Many, many many many people will not be able to relate to Tasi or this game's story. For the most part, you won't feel as if you're Tasi - you are merely observing her, guiding her to her goals. This is different from Penumbra and the dark descent where it was easier to relate to the character. Still, it's written well. I just wish the game wasn't so focused on narration... There's also some loose points in the story where some stuff isn't explained.This game is too forgiving. I'm not a god gamer by any means, but I screwed up multiple times this playthrough and I was mostly let off the hook. I haven't died 'once', apart from me falling in some place. It's not very tense if your enemies just keep giving you chances. While I appreciate the modern approach to horror games which is to never put the player in a dying spot in the first place, I think you should stick to old-school for this where if you screw up, you get punished by setting back, and perhaps the enemy spawns somewhere else to keep it interesting.Over all, it's not a bad game and it's a very good experience. However, witnessing the ending can feel very lukewarm. But it's important to look at a game as a whole, and as a whole this product is not bad. If you're on the fence, get it on a sale. If you have been a fan of the old amenisa and just want more like it, then get this. If you never liked them, then don't bother -- there's nothing new here for you.

_childDocuments_.review: Okay, maybe I am being mean now. But what happens if you lock highly talented graphics and level artists in a room together with poor game designers?  I tell you. Amnesia: Rebirth happens. It's such a shame. Really, the game looks great. The graphics, the levels, the environments, it's all top notch.  Sound design is pretty decent too. But the gameplay, o my, where to start. Rebirth is not very scary. It's mostly annoying. Right from the start you are being overwhelmed with flashbacks. You walk ten meters - flashback. And another ten meters - flashback. Some of those are actually interesting, at least in the beginning, as they tell you small chunks of the story. But few interesting flashbacks would have been better than uncountable boring ones. And most flashbacks ARE boring. This gets especially bad towards the end where you just want the game to end... And I wanted to end the game at some point. Because everything just became too annoying. Like: that stupid BABY. It's annoying enough to hear a frying eggs sound whenever you spent more than 3 seconds in the dark. But as soon as you got a big belly, you need to calm that stupid Baby every few seconds and stop the gameplay to listen to boring "shhhhh all will be good little one, don't be scared, Momma's here"... Zzzzz ZZzzzz..... oh sorry, back to more annoyance. Enemy encounters. They are so much fun. You can not hide under tables or inside cupboards no more so you have to sneak around enemies that can just teleport through the rooms. Sneaking around will make you even slower than your normal snail speed walking so yay, what fun. And once the enemy grabbed you, you are supposed to wildly slam some keys to get free. Great. I guess they did that because the developers don't really know how to move and animate NPCs. So they just need to tractor-beam you to force you into a *cough* fight. If you get defeated, you don't die but you get respawned at a different point in the room. But only after a super boring takes-forever-death-sequence. Also annoying. So all in all: Amnesia: Rebirth is an ANNOYING game. Which drives me nuts because the game looks so damn good! I finished the game mostly because I wanted to see where the setting - not the story! - would take me. But do I recommend this game? No, sorry. I was glad when the game was over. I prolly didn't get the best ending but do I care? No.

_childDocuments_.review: Highly underrated. Really good game and really good horror game. Though I do think it isn't as good as amnesia the dark descent. Most people seem to have gone into this game expecting it to be almost exactly the same as the original. It is much more like a mixture of SOMA and the dark descent. I do not understand why so many people have a problem with playing as Tasi, and a lot of people refuse to try to get immersed in the game. Playing as a pregnant woman is really unique idea for a horror game and feel like they do it well. With the main reason Tasi is still going is because of the baby. Though the changes to the sanity mechanic is definitely a step back. I am tired of seeing reviews that are insanely long summarizing the story and saying everything about the game is bad. Like some people were saying that the match system was bad and you got to much matches, like have you ever played amnesia the dark descent? I ended amnesia the dark descent with 50 kindling. This game is certified good. If you think you will like it, but are worried about the reviews I recommend trying it.

_childDocuments_.review: If metaphors where games, Frictional Games new entry in the  series, titled  wouldn't necessarily be a masterwork from the studio, instead it's just smart fun that is enjoyable to play. With just the right amount of scares to ensure your teeth remain on edge and with a clever story that is never heavy-handed considering the subject matter around bereavement, mental health issues and the lengths one will go for self preservation through biological means, especially when that biological basis of human behaviour is truly tested. It does occasionally get a bit silly at times when you have to continuously press a button to bond with your unborn child in order to reduce your sanity and keep your character from completely flipping out given the nerve jangling shredder the plot puts the main character, Tasi Trianon, through.Frictional isn't exactly interested here in pushing the mould they help define forward and in many ways  plays out a like a curio its protagonists seek, making the game feel oddly dated for a 2020 release especially given how Capcom has recently found the path back to their horror roots with  and the  remake.  employs the same gameplay loop as the previous two adventures, where you are mostly pushed through linear levels avoiding things that go bump in the night all the while solving puzzles (some of which are simple, some a little more complex). Nothing in the puzzle department is overtly difficult though and with a little trial and error most should be able to solve them.It's clear, especially from the first entry in the series, that Frictional Games is heavily inspired by H.P. Lovecraft's works and  is no different. I did find the story this time around to be more cohesive than that of , although personally I prefer the dark and depraved story of  over the cosmic-styled horror of the Frictional entries. I find the second entry's story way more disturbing because it speaks more to the dark corners of a human's heart. can be a bit plodding at the start and I can see many a gamer getting quite listless during the first few hours of the game, because much like  those first few hours are spent on the setup, dressing the stage for what is to come. Where the game really comes to life is in the dark, claustrophobic tunnels Tasi soon finds herself exploring. From here on the game builds tension with minimal fuss but displaying little imagination which was slightly disappointing; and while the game can be diabolically clever at times, it stays within the narrow limits of its own cleverness so that it doesn't appear too pretentious.  Recommended for gamer's who enjoy a slower, although no less scary, horror adventure that addresses some thought provoking issues around grief, motherhood, mental illness and the lengths one mother will go to protect her unborn child even despite the titles shortcomings.

_childDocuments_.review: The negative reviews for this game are insanely nit-picky. No, this is not Dark Descent 2.0However, the monsters are still scary, the environment is still memorable, and I would argue that the story telling is stronger in Rebirth. Most of the negative reviews weigh far too much on comparisons to Dark Descent, and I don't think it does this game justice. And I won't be surprised if I see the same reviews for The Bunker once that comes out. Essentially, any deviation from TDD's original gameplay is a "no no" for these people.

_childDocuments_.review: So I beat this in one sitting, and for the asking price I think this was a good purchase; took me a little over 10 hours to beat it.Good:+ Atmosphere is great; this game captures the heat of deserts, and dark caves, and caverns very well. Those topped off with great audio design really gets you immersed in the horror this game has to offer.+ Story is unpredictable, and very interesting to watch unfold. + Genuinely scary at times; now it is scary... at first. The further you get into the game the less frightening it becomes, which almost made me put this as a negative, however I find that this just happens with all horror games once you understand what you're avoiding, or what is hunting you, so I won't put it as a negative. Plus others may not have this kind of issue with the game, as I believe myself to be rather numb to horror in 99% of situations.+ Has a very unique gameplay mechanic that plays a big role in the story: I can't particularly say what this is without getting into spoilers, however it is somewhat similar to a game that we got last year, and that's all I will say.+ Great soundtrackBad: - As a sequel, save for a few elements (about two) from the first game making a return, as well as some collectible letters with references this game could have easily been completely stand-alone from the Amnesia series. Now I'm putting this as a bad thing, because I, as a fan of the original, was disappointed by the lack of connection to the original in A Machine for Pigs, and was hoping this would provide more of a connection, and while it does, its still not enough for my liking. That being said I know this was likely done purposefully, to keep players new to the series from having to play through the original, so I don't put this here as a terrible bad thing, just a bit disappointing.- The light sources; my god, from the second you begin this game it becomes apparent that matches and lamp oil are going to be difficult to come by, which be fine... if these two light sources lasted a decent amount of time, but they don't a match lasts about 10 seconds, and the lamp, when full, runs out of oil in 5 minutes. The trouble doesn't stop there though; without light you build up "fear" and once its built up too much you suffer a blackout that can set your progress back. Lanterns and fires lit in the environment will reduce your fear, but the second you leave the light source you fear level immediately boosts right back to being on the verge of a mental breakdown. It got to be extremely irritating in the later half of the game.- Story is unpredictable... to a point. As I said above, this game has an unpredictable story, but the further into you get you start to notice things that will make it rather easy to guess what is going to happen later, before they want you to, and whatever things you can't guess, in most regards, are due to the fact that its so vague, and not told, that by the time you beat it there's still questions that you never had answered, in fact, this game only creates more questions you might've had after beating the original. - I felt the monster designs were pretty one note, and seemed uninspired when compared to the first game; there's only two types, with the first monster type you encounter having different appearances in certain situations. The second one is just plain irritating at times.- Protagonist talks too much, and I'm the kind of person that doesn't usually care about this. Considering the nature of the story and what happens in it, I suppose it makes sense why she is talking so often, however I can't imagine why Frictional Games wouldn't have realized people would've disliked this.Conclusion:I know my negatives seem to make this look like I wouldn't be recommending it, but I am recommending it. It's very clear and obvious how much work went into this game, and the lore runs very deep in it. It's not a masterpiece, it's not amazing, it's great, even with its flaws. I just don't know why, but the whole time I was playing the last quarter of the game, I couldn't shake this feeling that this game felt like an Amnesia game, if it were made by Red Barrels, who are behind the Outlast series. Just reminded me a lot of Outlast 2 I suppose.

_childDocuments_.review: I tried my best to immerse myself (playing alone, pitch black room, headphones) but the game is just simply not scary at all and not immersive. It feels like a weird desert drama with sci-fi.The main problems are the constant cutscenes, flashbacks and the MC always talking to herself "oh my baby oh my husband yada yada" Which ends up getting cringey and annoying. There's also a game mechanic of having to rub your belly and talk to it which again just ends up being annoying and breaks immersion. I felt tension and dread maybe for 10% of the game in a few of the earlier sections, other than that the game is a bore.Regarding enemy encounters they're few and far between and feel overly scripted (monster jumps out for a quick scare then disappears instantly or scripted chase sequence). I can't remember ever being faced with a proper patrolling enemy once so most of the game is essentially walking around doing puzzles without a care in the world because nothing ever happens. You need to find a balance, Outlast for example goes perhaps too hard with frequent enemy encounters so it loses its impact but in this game they're so rare you end up waiting for something to happen.The desert setting although aesthetically pretty at times gets kinda bland (constant tunnels, caves , sand and rocks) and was not to my taste.The fear mechanic is also just annoying, if you enter darkness for just 10 seconds or so you start getting spammed with fnaf style jumpscares.The story is okay.It feels like frictional games has almost exclusively thought only about narrative and story. While completely forgetting what makes for immersive gameplay that creates an atmosphere of dread and tension.The game is not completely awful, I can tell it's fairly well-made so i would rate it 4-5/10 but that's a great disappointment to SOMA and TDD which were both incredible, this feels like a big downgrade in almost every regard.If you want an emotional relationship drama game with hints of horror you might like this. If you're looking for terror and tension this won't be the game for you.

_childDocuments_.review: Amnesia: The Dark Descent undeniably changed the horror genre forever. From the way that players interacted with doors, to the presentation of its insanity mechanic, every element within the title was fresh. It all lent to the high dosage of fear that the game provided at its launch; struggling to swing open a heavy door while being chased only to barely graze it and close it once more right in your own face, cowering in a corner and being afraid to peak at what monstrous enemy is breathing their wet breath in the next hallway, and uncertainty of where the plot would even land you in the end. In the years since its release, the Amnesia series has spawned countless knockoffs, none of which have truly captured the sheer terror that the original was able to traumatize players with. The franchise eventually lost its way with A Machine for Pigs, which was a simple walking simulator that had almost an on-rails, carnival of frights demeanor to its gameplay. Now, with the aptly titled Amnesia: Rebirth, one question begs to be answered: is this the true return to form for Frictional Games' horror monolith?The year is 1937, your name is Tasi, and you're on a plane destined for Algeria. Accompanied by many other expeditioners and your husband, Salim, you're setting off to uncover ancient ruins that lay in caves beneath the sands. The plane ends up abruptly crashing, and the amount of time that you've been knocked out is unknown. Your expedition crew is gone, and you're left to pick up their trail to find them and figure out what's going on and how much time has passed. Along the way to the first cave, you soon stumble across a compass, a Traveler's Amulet; an alien device that can let you see portals between Earth and dead alien civilizations. It doesn't take long for things to start getting weird, especially when you feel a kick in your belly... and a heartbeat... of all the things that you've forgotten, how could you forget that you were pregnant?First and foremost, we need to stop right here and give some love to the fact that this is a high-profile horror game that isn't set in a creepy mansion, spooky asylum, or whatever other cliche and nauseatingly overdone setting you want to throw in here. Wandering the vast and endless desert, sticking to the shade so you don't get broiled alive under the unrepressed sun, and feeling hopelessly lost and alone is a very unique concept for this genre. As is crawling through crumbling ruins that seem to house timeworn artefacts from both the Egyptian and Mayan cultures. The setting shifts between the desert and an ancient, sinister alien civilization, whose evil has been disturbed by the expeditioners. Tasi is able to see portals into the advanced city with a compass she found near the plane's crash site, and with it she finds herself hopping through the fabric of space and time itself.All of the usual Amnesia mechanics are back this time, but time manipulation is new territory for Frictional Games and it's not exactly an unwelcomed incorporation. It's a little out of place at first, until the story starts to unfold. The new mechanics lend to fairly complex puzzles as well, given that the extraterrestrial city is full of unfamiliar symbols, strange objects that open doors in different ways, and portals that can be created. Once you get used to the almost H.R. Giger design of this alien world, you'll find yourself back in the barren desert. There are an abundance of puzzles to solve in Amnesia: Rebirth, and many of them do require complex problem solving skills in order to overcome. None of these enigmas feel out of place, and they all tie in one way or another to appropriate story-driven progression. In other words they all have a purpose, they do not exist just because they can, unlike in a lot of other horror games that've come about in the last few years.Both the alien world and desert with its ruins look good, but the Amnesia engine (HPL) is showing its age; as are the developer's assets. The textures are... old. Visually, this title looks like it could've been released at any point in the last four years. There's also a distinct lack of atmospheric details as well. There's no dust, no fog, no particles in the alien world. The lighting is also quite bland in comparison to most modern releases. If you play games for their visual prowess, this is not going to be one that your eyeballs will thank you for. Though what is forgotten visually is somewhat made up for audibly, as there is an amazing musical score that encompasses the entire 9-12 hours of playtime that you'll get out of the campaign.There is one huge problem with Amnesia: Rebirth, however, and that's the fact that enemies despawn. You could, and should, play the game normally; cowering in corners to avoid terrifying deformed humanoid creatures bent on your destruction. But you could also just run straight into them and die, and respawn. If you do, they're almost always nowhere to be found, and if they are around they're placed very, very far away. If this was intentional on the part of Frictional Games, perhaps it would be best to make it an option or to have more than one difficulty. If you decide to cheese it through, you're removing a lot of the scare factors and simply cheating your own self out of a good time.It's unfortunate that so many fans and reviewers alike are holding Amnesia: Rebirth to the bar that its grandfather set ten years ago, instead of regarding it as its own entity. Too often do we look back at games through nostalgic lenses, only to revisit them and be disappointed. That's not to say that The Dark Descent cannot still hold its own today, but it's certainly not as frightening upon a revisit. Humbly, I do declare that Amnesia: Rebirth is a true return to form for the franchise as a whole, after Frictional Games lost their way with the walking simulator nature, boring puzzles, and cliche story of A Machine for Pigs. Many frights await in this release, with most of them being spontaneous and unforeseeable.The Horror Network  |  Click for Gore

_childDocuments_.review: Amnesia: Rebirth is a completely logical evolution of Frictional Games's style. Some people are disliking the game for a variety of reasons, some of which are totally fair; others are totally ridiculous (all the nonsensical rambling against the supposedly SJW devs and "politically correct") but some were "fault" of Frictional themselves for using the Amnesia title. Because even if personally I find that Rebirth carries some of the quintessential elements that characterized The Dark Descent (and is as such perfectly justified in carrying that name), Amnesia is a title that carries a number of potent expectations and not all of them are fulfilled.Is Rebirth as scary as Dark Descent? No, not at all, so if the scares are the only (or the most important) thing you seek in this game, stay away. As far as actual scares and tension go, Rebirth is way more similar to SOMA, in that you've got some extremely tense set pieces and a small handful of parts that I found truly terrifying, but you'll be mostly taking in the atmosphere and solving puzzles. The important thing is that this game has a thick, immersive atmosphere. Frictional absolutely do not disappoint in this regard. There are a number of environments and situations and the game always kept me engaged.Much like SOMA, the focus here is on the story and narrative. And it's a very intriguing story indeed, with very familiar Amnesia concepts and ties to the lore, later devolving into sci-fi territory. Initially, there are some fantastic Lovecraft suggestions (and I'm not talking about "tentacle monsters", but more about desert ruins and lost cities) but then they kind of dissolve into the sci-fi style, which isn't my preference but I can respect it nonetheless. The central plotline revolves around the difficulties of motherhood (no, despite what nonsensical hater reviews say, checking on the baby is NOT a mandatory mechanic, it is OPTIONAL) and the importance of family, and yeah, the main character talks often. If this is a deal breaker well, don't buy this game. I personally found the story engaging and with very good voice acting for the most part. It's not on SOMA level, but SOMA is one of the greatest narrative masterpieces in gaming for me so I didn't expect it to surpass it.Mechanically, the game is still very simple, but I really love the resource management in this one. Because you can only carry a limited amount of matches and lamp oil, you have to be very deliberate in balancing staying in the dark and illuminate your surroundings to avoid accumulating too much fear. It's tense because the resources are limited, but it's absolutely doable if you're not spamming matches and lamp randomly. Moreover, strategic use of the matches (and careful movements while you have one lit) can allow you to light multiple torches, thus keeping areas well lit as a "fear safe" area that won't drain any more resources from you. It gives the game way more gameplay engagement than simply walking around and solving puzzles. I loved its implementation without a doubt. The only big con I found in the game is a very annoying maze section that's kinda trial and error and while not being terribly long definitely outstays its welcome.The engine definitely shows its age, but it's still good looking with some great lighting. The sound design is also pretty spot on, as I expected from Frictional. Overall, Rebirth is another great game from Frictional. I don't like it as much as SOMA and it won't be as iconic as The Dark Descent for obvious reasons but I'm really happy to have purchased it and played it. The amount of negative reviews may be discouraging but you should really check it out if the things I mentioned earlier aren't deal breakers and you like a good narrative experience with some actual engaging mechanics and a horror atmosphere.Original polemic "review" below.---------------------------------I don't like to make a review for a game I've not finished, especially if I've played so little of it. But I REALLY wanted to counterbalance at least ONE of the negative reviews Amnesia: Rebirth is getting, most of which are completely ludicrous (though there are fair and completely understandable negative reviews from people that... I don't know... played a decent chunk of the bloody game).Yes, using the Amnesia name bears certain implications. Key elements of the previous game ARE indeed present here, just... not the emphasis on scares. The game is RIDICULOUSLY immersive and delightfully lovecraftian (and it pains me to have to remind it, but Lovecraft is not all about the "tentacle monsters" as the mainstream likes to think he bloody is).Not liking the different take on Amnesia by Frictional is one thing. Playing it for a while and refunding it because it's not for you is perfectly fine. Not giving it even a FRAGMENT of a fair chance and writing a half hassed review because "OmG noT sCArY" is pretty damn dumb.Will update this into a proper, less polemic review once I've finished the game.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm going to compare this to Amnesia: Dark Descent because it's my gold standard for horror. Mechanically Rebirth is leagues ahead, everything is easier to control (although panic-closing a door is still a pain), graphically it's (obviously) far superior. Story-wise, I actually enjoy Rebirth more; the story is more interesting and better told (both directly and indirectly). The puzzles are about equal in cleverness, but it seems like the Rebirth puzzles are more often "safe". It's not always the case but I remember feeling panicked trying to solve a puzzle far more often in Dark Descent. All this leads up to the fact that I feel the horror aspect was better done in Dark Descent which is really the point of the game. Rebirth surpasses it in a lot of other ways, but that's the important one for me... but it's still really good: 8/10.Also the no-monster mode is a great idea for people that just want a creepy puzzle game without the fear of dying. It's not for me, but I appreciate it's a great idea.
_childDocuments_.name: Amnesia: Rebirth

_childDocuments_.review: (NO MAJOR SPOILERS)Was very excited to see this game getting announced and very excited to play it once it had finally came out, but sadly Rebirth was a disappointment for me.  The game has a few bright spots with the cool sci-fi aesthetic and decent characters, but it doesn't feel like an Amnesia game at all.  I felt like I was suppose to be emotionally connected with the protagonist and while I did find her story very interesting toward the end, it overall fell flat at the start for me so anything that happened afterward was stuff I didn't care about.  The story is a pretty big drag and the game trolls you at least 3 separate times making you think you were about to be done, but then something goes completely wrong which just made me hate the game more.The worst part about this game is the puzzles in my opinion.  They aren't fun to do and don't require any brainpower to actually complete.  There is literally one puzzle where you're just suppose to trial and error the entire thing without any hints which is horrible game design and shouldn't even be considered a puzzle at that point.  Don't get me wrong, some of the puzzles are somewhat decent and actually nice to do at certain points in the game, but I don't blame people if they look up guides for some of these puzzles because most of them are poorly designed, have really vague clues that barely help you actually finish them, and don't feel rewarding to go through.One of the main parts of the Amnesia games that I loved was being terrified while hiding and running from the monsters.  In this game, there are barely any parts where I was hiding from something, let alone felt at least in danger.  The chase parts where you're running away from monsters didn't make me panic or scared at all and instead just left me wondering when I was going to be finished with this game.  There was literally a bug in the game that I encountered where the monster just spawned and stood in one spot and didn't attack which made me completely lose any sense of fear for the rest of playing that I once had.  (One of the many bugs I encountered in the game)Overall, this game is super mediocre and for an Amnesia game, this is pretty bad and I think this is the worst one in the entire series.  There are only slight references to The Dark Descent in the story which is the only part that ever made it feel close to an Amnesia game (the references were at least cool).  If you are a fan of the Amnesia series then I don't think it's that bad of a decision to buy this game, but I would prepare yourself to be let down.  I hope if another game is added in the series that Frictional Games will learn from their mistakes and realize what went wrong in the development for this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Amnesia: Rebirth

_childDocuments_.review: I'll be honest, this game was good but not in the sense of "another good Amnesia game." I don't know if it's the fact that this game strayed so far from the original Amnesia style/story type or if it was because of all the hand holding, but I don't think I would play this game again. It held up to the traditional puzzle solving style similar to the previous Amnesia games, but something about this just lacked what the previous games each had. I feel that if this game was released without the "Amnesia" title attached to it, it would have been excellent and I would have enjoyed it more. But with the title attached and part of the series, I feel it was a huge let down. There were many areas of the game in which I would have to relaunch it simply because of bugs that caused me to become trapped and rendered the game unplayable as well as certain puzzles that essentially handed you the answer after 1 failed attempt. (Notably the area in which you enter a sort of labyrinth and must find the exit, all the while avoid an enemy who is hunting you) I would say if you have never played another Amnesia game and this is your first encounter with the franchise, by all means start with this one. It's gorgeous in terms of graphics and the soundtrack/ambiance in this one is far superior in comparison with its predecessors, but if you have played the previous games and are teetering on this one... Save your money,

_childDocuments_.review: Another fantastic game from FrictionalGames.Thought provoking, at times quite intense, and genuinely scary. It is a little buggy but not game breaking in anyway. There were three floating objects in one particular room, also one object in another room wasn't linked to the chain it was dangling on correctly- it appeared disconnected if you get me. There was one moment where the monster totally froze on me and I had to reload to correct it. The story was very good. Immerse yourself in the game for a fun experience. Best played with headphones. Throughout the game, I kept thinking of what was happening and designing all sorts of synopsis of the game. Very thought provoking in this sense. If you enjoy horror, suspenseful games, I highly recommend this. If you have played previous FrictionalGames, then, Rebirth has strong SOMA vibes. To give you an idea.

_childDocuments_.review: As a long time fan of Frictional Games, I can not in good conscience recommend this game.Let me preface this by saying that I do not discredit the several talented designers, artists, animators, programmers, voice actors, etc. who have worked on this game or were involved with its production, nor do I necessarily blame them for its shortcomings or faults. Many of these people were clearly passionate about the game they were creating, and many were involved in the development of previous titles (particularly SOMA). The fault here lies with poor decision making on the part of project leads and the heads of the company.I have “played” this game for several hundred hours in total, many of which are not recorded on Steam. I have worked with and played through a version of the main game for over half a year, and am the author or am a contributor for several mods (notably Quiet Protagonist, as well as the work-in-progress mod Amnesia Classic). I have dedicated a considerable amount of time this past year into improving and refining several aspects of Amnesia Rebirth in order to make it into something that I and others could enjoy, but without changing the game completely there is nothing that can be done that isn't effectively a band-aid solution to more serious issues in its design and design philosophy.What I have been left with from that experience is an intimate knowledge of a deeply flawed game and engine, which exists as the product of a company which is now completely different than the Frictional Games that made Penumbra, Amnesia, and SOMA. It is a game full of wasted potential and rushed level design, shoddy and nonsensical programming, broken features, cut content, and poor creative direction. Is it the worst game I have played? No. Is it even necessarily a bad game? Also no. It is, however, a symptom of the internal turmoil which has occurred within Frictional Games over these past few years, and is a testament to the complexity of game development and of the gaming industry as whole.I wanted to write a full, comprehensive review for Rebirth and go into its issues further – what exactly it did wrong and what it did right, what was interesting about it and what was trite, how it struggled as a narrative and as a game and how it failed to make me care about its world or characters. How the company outright lied to its fanbase about the nature of the game in prerelease blog postings and intentionally cherry picked the “best” segments of the game to showcase in it’s marketing campaign. How said marketing campaign was almost nonexistent, had very little to do with the actual game, and very heavily tried to depend on the support of streamers, content creators, and let’s players in an effort to replicate the success of the original Amnesia: The Dark Descent. And yet, after so much time spent with this game one way or another, any enthusiasm I had for such an undertaking has long since faded, and all I'm left with is a deep feeling of disappointment.All I will say is: If you are the long time Frictional Games fan such as myself, you will be disappointed. It’s something that’s still probably worth playing at least once for the experience alone, but overall Amnesia: Rebirth is something that is nowhere near the quality of their past titles, and is not associated with the original creative talent that was responsible for spawning and/or supporting an undeniably influential era of horror and storytelling.

_childDocuments_.review: It's an excellent example of a good horror game. I really enjoyed the storyline! During the whole process,step by step, grain by grain, you get your memories together and ultimately the picture is crystal clear. There's also a great feature that I like about the game. Once you feel relief and it seems that you're almost safe,the game delivers you deeper and deeper,making you much more anxious. I definitely adore Frictional Games' stories. So this story isn't an exception.

_childDocuments_.review: Definitely an improvement from "A Machine for Pigs". It was not as tense as "The Dark Descent", but this could be because I am used to the Frictional Games formula. Story-wise, it was definitely a downgrade from "SOMA", I still have a very vague idea of what happened, whereas "SOMA" made me question the nature of human consciousness 🤷🏻‍♀️Gameplay-wise, I think the amulet was underutilized for puzzles, I was really expecting at least a more interesting level design, akin to Dishonored 2's Aramis Stilton's mansion.  Also, the oil lamp was utterly useless, which made it more annoying to use than helpful. I preferred staying in the dark, than trying to rely on a lamp that burned through a full tank within a minute. The lamp is technically supposed to have a capacity of 500ml which IRL would take a few hours to run out, it could at least last 10 minutes in game...I'd say matches were also way too commonly found and in really improbable places to boot  However, considering the lamp is pretty much dead weight, I am glad matches are everywhere.Still, "Rebirth" is a return to Amnesia's roots and it was an enjoyable experience with some good scares throughout. I hope the "Bunker" adds stuff like adaptive AI and more intricate puzzles to solve, to improve upon that formula.
_childDocuments_.name: Amnesia: Rebirth

_childDocuments_.review: A real disappointment compared to anything Frictionnal Games has done so far. We've all wanted a sequel to The Dark Descent, which was an especially amazing game with a good amount of horror and story. Instead, we got what Rebirth is, and it's not very pretty. While I have completed the game almost a year ago (time sure flies), I still remember to this day everything that I liked, and disliked about this game.First, I want to point out that this game is not about horror. It has nothing to do with the first game at all. The maps are more linear and also way less spooky. Only a few parts of the games were actually scary (The fort, especially, with a ghoul stalking you, reminded me a lot about what made the Dark Descent so awesome). That place was super scary because it was dark and there was weird noises everywhere. I was literally too scared to continue playing. But then I did. And boy, did I miss that place. The rest of the game was dragging itself with a nonsensical story and no more horror, or at least not too much. You get a few more or less scary place with some scripted chase with the ghoul and the shadow (The fleshy thing you encounter in The Dark Descent), and a few puzzles that require just a few neurons to complete. What a mess, where is my horror-focused game? Even SOMA (That I loved), that was even more of a walking simulator, did it's job much better than Rebirth did, because it was genuinely scary, and the story gave me a lot of thought.Second, the story is average at best. The developers tried to make me care about some important characters but because they were not developed at all I just wouldn't give an f. Like the death of Tasi's husband, Salim. You discover soon enough that he is dead, and what? I did not even know the guy, why should I care? The character that I control is much more affected than I am. But let's talk about that. Tasi keeps whining about anything. She keeps talking and talking and talking. Like could you please shut it for a moment, I am trying to get immersed in a story, stop trying to force me to feel like the devs intended me to. Seriously, she just won't shut up for the whole game, and it only gets worse when she discovers that she is pregnant.... The game starts becoming a "touch your belly to restore your sanity" simulator because she keeps reminding you of the "little one", name you will hear maybe 20-30 times throughout your playthrough. Also, Tasi is dumb in general. Her decisions killed everyone, but I guess I'm not gonna spoil, if you still wanna see for yourself. The game also make use of flashbacks to tell you the story. Well, a sh$tload of flashbacks. You will get a ridiculous amount of them, to the point it breaks the pacing completely, while also trying to, once again, make you care about the characters. You will also sometimes be in the otherworld, The Dark Descent Alexandre's home, to accomplish a few puzzles. It is nice to be able to visit the place, but that was also terribly done. Overall, the story is a huge mess and tries to convey things to the player and utterly fails at it.Finally, the gameplay elements. Do you remember about the tinderboxes and the lantern in The Dark Descent? Well scrap all of those things and give a nerfed to the ground lantern and matches that give very low light for no more than 8 seconds each. Yep, you heard right. Those matches will be your primary source of light because you can store up to 10 (ten!) of them in your inventory and they can help you light things up. I think it is ridiculous to limit the amount of matches you can own because they are already pretty bad by themselves, so 10 matches don't help you for very long. luckily you should find enough to be able to survive, but still, it's not like they take a lot of space. Also forget about the lantern. This thing eats oil like there is no tomorrow. A full lantern doesn't last more than a minute or 2. I am not even joking. You can keep 3 of each oil bottle with you (small, medium and large), and these are not common and most of the time, hidden in the levels. Since you can't use the lantern much you will end up using the matches more often, and not be able to see anything 10cm ahead of you, until you run out of them because yeah, they get consumed faster if you move... And the sanity system will jumpscare you to tell you it's getting low, because doing it like The Dark Descent wasn't spooky enough. Not to mention that, if you ever "die" or lose your sanity fully, you will just get teleported further in the level for the most part, probably to make the game more "accessible" and more casual. Yeah, no, thank you.So yeah overall, I do not recommend this game, especially if you wanted a sequel to the excellent The Dark Descent. This game is a pure disaster on many levels and doesn't deserve any of your attention. The story contradicts the lore from The Dark Descent and a Machine for a Pig, while also trying to make you feel things for characters you have never known anything about, and the gameplay is a exactly what you should not do. You could say this is a salty review, and it is, because I am severely disappointed by the overall experience.Frictionnal Games themselves responded to the mixed response on their game that you can read here : "We’re seeing a lot of mixed reactions when it comes to these types of consequences. For some people the mechanics we opted for worked out great. They felt a true sense of something big being at stake. For others, however, the whole narrative implication seems to have slipped past them completely."According to them, it is basically my fault for not understanding the game. I will definitely remember that.

_childDocuments_.review: Most of the way through right now and all I have to say is JEEZUS. As someone who liked the story of SOMA a ton, and who wasn't too scared when Amnesia first came out, this game actually has intensity. _childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like this game because Frictional Games makes some of the best horror-games I've played, but I feel they didn't follow the design-philosophy from their past games. Some of the largest gripes I have with the game:Most of the mechanics designed to convey fear are awful, the 'fear' QTE's disrupt the gameplay, the same with the mechanics regarding the baby. They feel like artificial barriers that take me out of the actual game, that you need to deal with them before you are able to progress.A lot of revelations that should've had their emotional punch just don't carry their weight because the legwork that should make us care about the other characters is non-existing. There's a huge dissonance between what Tasi feels and what we feel when these revelations happen. And then there's certain cutscenes that are clearly designed to make us feel sad about Tasi's past, they are so artificially inserted that they really miss their intended punch and feel like cheap grabs to get to our feelings.The timeline of a lot of events don't make sense, this was always a good part in the previous games, the environment and notes always give you a good idea what went on, but that's missing in this game. How did the protagonist end up in the plane again at the start of the game. Frictional wanted their mystery to be unfolded from Tasi's eyes as how she backtracked what she and her team did after the crash but the legwork to give it their logical conclusion isn't there, it doesn't make sense at all how she got there again. There's similar issues like that scattered through the game.World events (monsters getting a scripted attack etc) don't make sense after the initial attack (enemies drop their chase etc). Characters that you need to chase are blatantly waiting for you to get close enough before they progress. This takes away all immersion and scream that they are sacrificing logic and solid worldbuilding to get their cheap dialogue in. The main story had a lot of potential, and again, it misses the legwork to carry the emotional impact. I will look forward to Frictional Games next game because I know that they are capable of making some of the best horrorgames with engaging stories. But this game isn't one of them.

_childDocuments_.review:
You can't let out a breath. The creature is only inches away. Its sole purpose - to feed off your terror. And so you crouch in the dark, trying to stop the fear rising, trying to silence what lies within you. "I know you. I know what you're capable of." In Amnesia: Rebirth, you are Tasi Trianon, waking up deep in the desert of Algeria. Days have passed. Where have you been? What did you do? Where are the others? Retrace your journey, pull together the fragments of your shattered past; it is your only chance to survive the pitiless horror that threatens to devour you.

"Do not allow yourself anger, do not allow yourself to fear."

Time is against you. Step into Tasi's shoes and guide her through her personal terror and pain. While you struggle to make your way through a desolate landscape, you must also struggle with your own hopes, fears, and bitter regrets. And still you must continue, step by step, knowing that if you fail you will lose everything.

* First-person narrative horror experience
* Explore environments and uncover their histories.
* Overcome puzzles that stand in your way.
* Carefully manage your limited resources, both physical and mental.
* Encounter horrific creatures and use your wits and understanding of the world to escape them.
